methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** The best stock-picking book (the 20 stocks whose own rise, after removing the market's move, was strongest over the past year) only steps aside when SPY drops below its 200-day average, and it checks that once a month. The bet was that its worst fall was the fast 1998 crash, which a gate checked every week, and made quicker with a shorter average or a "SPY is 8% off its high" trip, would have dodged.

**How it was set up.** The same monthly 20-stock list as the parent. Every week the book asks whether the market is healthy. If not, it goes to cash. If yes, it buys this month's list back, even in the middle of the month. Three versions:
- the plain 200-day test, just checked weekly instead of monthly (the control);
- SPY must be above both its 200-day and its 100-day average;
- the 200-day test plus an exit whenever SPY is more than 8% below its highest close of the last six months.

(Assumption, written down before the run: a 50-day version and a "6% off the three-month high" version were dropped before anything ran, because the lab's built-in safety test uses a made-up market in which those gates are always off at the one date it checks, so it could not prove they were coded correctly.)

**Result (practice period 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 116 trials in the lab).** Rejected. All three beat SPY on return but fell further than the 20% limit, and none comes near the luck bar.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Return per unit of fall | Luck score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 200-day, checked weekly | +692% | +11.0% | 25.2% | 1.56 | 2,116 | 0.44 | 0.69 |
| 200-day and 100-day, weekly | +702% | +11.1% | 29.8% | 1.68 | 2,209 | 0.37 | 0.79 |
| 200-day plus 8%-off-high trip, weekly | +681% | +10.9% | 22.3% | 1.56 | 2,173 | 0.49 | 0.69 |
| *Same book, gate checked monthly (M0020-W-NOSTOP)* | *+1,565%* | *+15.3%* | *19.3%* | *2.11* | *1,620* | *0.79* | *0.91* |
| *Monthly parent (M0007-N20-RAW)* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.77* | *0.91* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest drop from a peak to a later low (the limit is 20%). "Gains vs losses" is money made on winning trades divided by money lost on losing ones (the floor is 1.3). The luck score (DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of 116 lucky tries. The bar is 0.90, and these sit at 0.69-0.79, far below it.

**Failed conditions.** Worst fall over the 20% limit by 5.2, 9.8 and 2.3 points. Luck score under 0.90 by 0.21, 0.11 and 0.21. Return, gains vs losses and trade count all passed.

**Where the falls happened.** I replayed the recorded control and 8%-trip versions next to their monthly twin (same settings, nothing new recorded) to see the dates:
- Monthly twin's worst falls: May-Jul 2006 (19.3%), Jul-Sep 1998 (18.7%), Apr-May 2010 (17.9%), Jul-Aug 2011 (17.0%).
- Weekly 200-day: Apr-Sep 2010 (25.2%), then a slow 22.4% slide from May 2006 to Jul 2009. 1998 no longer shows up in the top five.
- Worst years: weekly 200-day lost 6.9% in 2015. Year by year it gave back the most where SPY hovered near its average: 2000 (-1% vs +23% for the monthly twin), 2007 (0% vs +7%), 2009 (+11% vs +33%), 2010 (-3% vs +7%).

**Why.** Two things, both named in the expected failure before the run:
1. *1998 was never the binding fall.* The weekly gate did its job there: 1998 went from +16% to +21%, and that crash dropped out of the top five falls. But the monthly twin's worst fall is May-Jul 2006, when momentum stocks dropped while SPY stayed above its averages (as M0009's notes already found for the older momentum book). No SPY gate can see that, so the best this approach could ever do was 19.3%.
2. *Checking the gate every week whipsaws.* When SPY moves sideways around its 200-day line (2000, 2007, mid-2010, 2015), a weekly check sells after each dip below the line and buys back after each rise above it, a little higher each time. This book holds the most volatile stocks, so each round trip loses more than SPY would. That turned a 6-week dip in 2010 into a 5-month 25% slide, and cost about 4 points a year. Checked monthly, the same rule mostly ignores those crossings. The faster 100-day leg made it worse (29.8%) because it crosses even more often. The 8% trip helped a little (22.3%), because a real 8% fall is rarer than a line crossing, but it rides on top of the same weekly 200-day whipsaw.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis failed: the worst fall rose instead of falling to 13-16%, and return per unit of fall halved instead of rising. Both parts of the expected failure happened: whipsaw cost about 4 points a year (worse than the "several points" guessed), and the binding fall is a momentum-only crash (2006, not the guessed 2000) that a market gate cannot see.

**Compared with near misses.** The lab's best books control this fall with a brake on the book's own swings (M0011, M0022: 12-14% worst fall), not with a market switch. Nothing here comes close.

**My opinion:** Faster market gates are a dead end for this book, and I would not spend another trial on SPY-based exit rules, with or without hysteresis bands. The market switch is already at its useful speed when checked monthly. The two worst falls left (2006 and mid-2010) are momentum-specific, and the brake has to read momentum itself, not the market. Next I would test a gate on the momentum factor: step aside when the gap between this month's top-ranked and bottom-ranked stocks has collapsed over the last few weeks, which is the signature of a momentum unwind. The book's own volatility brake (the M0022 line) remains the strongest lead in the lab.
methods.verdict: Checking the market switch every week, and making it faster, dodged the 1998 crash but whipsawed in sideways markets: +10.9-11.1% a year vs SPY's 7.9%, but worst falls of 22-30% vs 19.3% for the same book checked monthly. Its real worst fall (2006) is a momentum-only crash no market switch can see.

methods.name: Momentum braked by the basket's own drawdown, not its volatility
methods.hypothesis: M0002's worst falls (Mar-Aug 2006, Aug 1998, Apr-Jun 2010, Apr-Sep 2011) happened with SPY above its 200-day average and the book's 3-month vol near its median, so the vol gate was shut while the loss was made. A brake on the held basket's own distance below its 126-day peak (full size above -d, linear down to a floor by -2d), checked weekly on the monthly basket, fires within a week of a reversal. It should cut max DD below M0002-REL-85's 18.4%, toward 15%, at a smaller CAGR cost than vol scaling because it de-risks only during the fall itself; HELD-D8-MW should land at max DD <= 15% with CAGR above SPY TR's +7.9%.
methods.expectedFailure: Whipsaw. Momentum unwinds are sharp V-shapes (2009, 2001): the brake sells near the bottom and the book misses the rebound until the basket makes a new high, so CAGR drops 2-4 points while max DD only falls to 16-17%, because the first -d of every fall is taken at full size and the 2006 unwind was a series of -8% steps. The 'targets' control should do nothing (fresh momentum picks sit near their highs), and the monthly-only variant should react too late to matter.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

## What we tried

The parent idea (M0002) braked the momentum strategy when its own day-to-day swings got unusually large. It beat the market but its worst fall stayed at 17.5-21.8%, over the 15% limit, because the big losses came in calm-looking markets. This method brakes on **the loss itself**: when the stocks we hold have fallen more than 8% from their best level of the last six months, we start selling down, reaching 25% invested by a 16% fall (one variant goes all the way to cash). The stock picks are the same top-20 momentum basket (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND) chosen once a month. Five variants re-check the brake weekly or daily on that monthly basket; one checks it only at the monthly re-pick.

## Results (1996 → Oct 2015, SPY with dividends: +7.9% a year)

| Variant | Yearly return | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unbraked parent basket (F4) | +16.2% | 22.2% | 2.27 | 1154 |
| Brake at -8%, checked monthly | +15.6% | 22.3% | 2.28 | 1155 |
| Brake at -8%, checked daily | +10.3% | 23.9% | 1.69 | 1449 |
| Brake at -8%, checked weekly (main bet) | +10.4% | 29.7% | 1.59 | 1387 |
| Brake at -6%, weekly | +9.5% | 27.7% | 1.58 | 1393 |
| Brake to cash, weekly | +9.9% | 32.9% | 1.58 | 1399 |
| Control: brake measured on new picks, weekly | +10.8% | 32.4% | 1.61 | 1387 |

All six beat SPY on return, and all six fail the 15% worst-fall limit, by 7 to 18 points. The best (monthly check, +15.6% a year) is essentially the unbraked basket: its DSR (the chance the edge is real after the lab's 100 tries) is 0.87, below the 0.95 bar. The worst year of the monthly variant is 2015 (-2.0%); the weekly main bet's worst year is 2011 (-8.9%).

## Why it failed

**The hypothesis failed, and backwards.** Checking more often made the worst fall *bigger*: 22% unbraked, 24% daily, 30% weekly. Two things happened.

1. **Whipsaw, worse than expected.** Momentum falls come as sharp V's (spring 2000, Aug 1998, May 2010, Aug 2011). The brake only engages after an 8% loss, so the first 8% of every fall is taken in full. It then sells near the bottom, and it only buys back once the basket has recovered half its fall. Spring 2000 shows it plainly: the weekly variant went from 3.57 to 2.74 (-23%) while the unbraked basket, holding through, was at a new high by August. Each V locks in a loss, and a string of them adds up to a deeper fall than just sitting still. Selling after a loss and buying after a gain is a cost in exactly the markets momentum lives in.
2. **The weekly check also re-checks the market's 200-day trend filter.** On a weekly re-scale the picker runs again, so if SPY dips under its 200-day average for a week the whole book is sold, and it is not bought back until the next monthly re-pick. That adds more sell-low/miss-the-rebound trips (late 2007, mid 2009 here). The control proves this matters: measuring the *new* picks (which by construction sit near their highs, so the brake should almost never fire) did just as badly as measuring the held book (32% vs 30%). So most of the damage in the weekly variants comes from the faster re-check machinery, not from the brake alone. I cannot separate the two from these trials; that is the next idea.

**The monthly check did nothing useful.** At a month start the held basket has usually either already rebounded or not yet fallen 8%: the 2006 unwind that sets the worst fall was a slow grind of small monthly losses (6.69 → 5.73 from March to August, about -14% month-end to month-end), which the brake never caught at a monthly check.

**Expected failure:** half right. Whipsaw happened and cost 5-6 points a year, more than the 2-4 I guessed, and the monthly variant did react too late. But I expected the worst fall to come down to 16-17%; instead it went up.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

M0002-REL-85 (12.6% a year, 18.4% worst fall) is clearly better than every variant here. M0007-N20-RAW (15.0%, 19.6%) remains the best return-per-fall in the lab. A drawdown brake on a single 20-stock basket is the wrong tool.

## My opinion:

Drop the "brake on losses" direction for the momentum book. A stop-loss on a momentum portfolio is a bet that falls keep going, and on this data they mostly snap back, so it pays the round trip every time. The one useful thing this run surfaced is a confound in the lab's own machinery: a weekly re-scale also re-runs the trend filter, so every "check risk weekly" result so far (here and M0004) mixes two effects. The next trial should be the plain monthly basket with a weekly re-scale and *no* brake, to price that machinery by itself; only then can any faster risk check be judged fairly. For actually reaching the 15% limit, I'd put effort into what we hold (residual momentum, more names) rather than when we hold it.
methods.verdict: Braking when our stocks fall 8% made things worse, not safer: checked weekly the worst fall grew from 22% to 30% and return dropped to about 10% a year, because momentum falls snap back and the brake sells near the bottom; checked monthly it barely fired.

methods.name: The de-levering dial set to land exactly on the 15% drawdown limit
methods.hypothesis: M0001 and M0002 together trace a near-straight line from (DD 11.0%, CAGR 6.1%) to (DD 22.2%, CAGR 16.2%), with max DD per unit of average exposure flat at ~35 across all nine trials. The line crosses DD = 15% at CAGR 9-10%, above SPY TR's 7.9%. One setting between M0002-MED-TV12 (DD 17.5%, exposure 0.50) and M0001-TV12 (DD 12.9%, exposure 0.37) -- relative mode at ref_mult ~0.70, or absolute mode at a 10% target with the gate at 0.85x median -- should be the lab's first trial to pass max DD, beats SPY, PF and trade count together. It will still fail DSR (~0.85 vs 0.95), so this is worth exactly one run as a recorded frontier point, not a tuning campaign.

methods.name: 52-week-high momentum: rank on nearness to the yearly high, not past return
methods.sourceRef: George & Hwang (2004), The 52-week high and momentum investing, J. Finance 59(5), doi:10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x; Momentum crashes and the 52-week high, FAJ 2023
methods.hypothesis: Every momentum book in the lab ranks on 12-1 total or residual return, and its binding drawdowns (Mar-Aug 2006, Aug 1998, spring 2010/2011) are crowd unwinds of last year's big risers while SPY stays above its 200-day average. Nearness to the 52-week high captures most of momentum's return without its reversal, and momentum crashes concentrate in winners far below their highs. Ranking the top-20 by close / 252-day max close (ties by 12-1 return), with F4's screen, monthly rebalance and SPY 200-day gate, holds steadier names less exposed to speculative unwinds: max DD below F4's 22.2% at comparable CAGR, and the 50/50 blend with raw residual momentum below M0007-N20-RAW's 19.6%. Kill the direction if no variant gets max DD below 19.6%.
methods.expectedFailure: Nearness to the high is a low-volatility, late-cycle tilt: the names at their highs in a calm bull market are the same crowded quality/defensive leaders that sold off together in May 2006 and 2011, so the drawdown barely moves (19-22%) while CAGR drops 2-4 points because the pure nearness rank skips the strongest early-trend rebounders. Ties at nearness 1.0 in strong markets make the pure rank collapse into plain 12-1 momentum, so N20 looks like F4.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

## What we tried

Every momentum strategy in the lab picks the stocks that rose most over the past year. This one
picks the stocks trading **closest to their own highest price of the past year** (George & Hwang,
2004). The idea: a stock sitting at its high after a steady climb is a calmer holding than one
that doubled off a crash low, and the crowd unwinds that hurt momentum hit the second kind.
Everything else is the same as the lab's reference momentum book (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND): same
stock screen, rebalance once a month, equal weights, and all cash whenever SPY is below its
200-day average.

Four versions, fixed before the run:

| Version | What it holds | Yearly return (CAGR) | Worst fall | Gains vs losses (PF) | Trades | DSR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N20 | 20 stocks nearest their high | +8.0% | 18.0% | 1.53 | 2,670 | 0.61 |
| N30 | 30 stocks nearest their high | +8.3% | 17.3% | 1.61 | 3,604 | 0.74 |
| N20-BLEND | 20 stocks, half "near the high", half residual momentum | +9.7% | 16.8% | 1.54 | 2,162 | 0.70 |
| N30-BLEND | 30 stocks, same blend | +9.0% | **15.6%** | 1.64 | 2,863 | 0.72 |

SPY with dividends reinvested: **+7.9% a year** over the same 1996-2015 window.
For comparison, the lab's best so far, residual momentum (M0007-N20-RAW): +15.0% a year, worst fall 19.6%.

## Against the go-live rules

- **Beat SPY:** all four did, but the two pure versions only barely (+8.0% and +8.3% against +7.9%,
  about the same as just holding the index).
- **Worst fall at most 15%:** all four failed. The closest, N30-BLEND, lost 15.6% at its worst:
  0.6 points over the line. That is the nearest any method in the lab has come while also beating SPY
  on a fully stock-picking book, but over is over.
- **Gains vs losses at least 1.3 and 100+ trades:** all passed easily.
- **DSR at least 0.95:** all failed (0.61-0.74). DSR is the chance the result is real skill rather
  than luck, after allowing for the 94 strategies the lab has now tried. At 0.7 it is roughly a
  coin flip weighted slightly toward real; not good enough.

## When it hurt

On the month-end equity curve, every version's worst stretch is the same: the end of June to the
end of August 1998 (the Russian default / LTCM shock), while SPY was still above its 200-day
average, so the safety switch never fired. The worst calendar year for all four is 2015 (-6% for
the pure versions, -10% to -11% for the blends).

## Why

**The drawdown did shrink, as hoped.** Stocks near their highs are, by construction, ones that have
not fallen recently and are not the bounce-back rockets of a speculative rally. Every version came
in under residual momentum's 19.6% and well under the reference book's 22.2%.

**But the return went with it, far more than expected.** Looking year by year, the pure "near the
high" book made +14% in 1999 and -2% in 2000, where residual momentum made +56% and +21%; and
+16%/+33%/+5% in 2012-2014 against +33%/+47%/+18%. In strong, broad bull markets dozens of stocks
sit at or within a hair of their high, so the ranking becomes a near-random draw among quiet
large companies at their high rather than a pick of the strongest movers. The pick ends up close
to "an equal-weighted slice of the index that steps aside in bear markets", which is what its
+8% a year looks like. Blending in residual momentum brought back some of the bite (+9.7%) and
kept most of the safety.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- Hypothesis: "worst fall below 22.2% at comparable return". **Half held.** The worst fall dropped
  (15.6-18.0%), but the return was not comparable: 5-8 points a year lower than the parents.
- Expected failure: "the worst fall barely moves while return drops 2-4 points". **Wrong on the
  fall, too optimistic on the return.** The fall did move; the return dropped twice as much as feared.
- The kill rule ("kill if no version gets under 19.6%") was **not** triggered: all four did.

## My opinion:

"Nearness to the high" is a good **brake** and a bad **engine**. As the thing that picks stocks it
is too blunt: in good markets too many names tie at the top and the book loses the strong movers
that make momentum worth holding. But it clearly removes the stocks that cause the falls. So the
next step is to use it as a **filter, not a ranking**: keep residual momentum (the lab's best
engine) doing the picking, but only among stocks within, say, 10-20% of their yearly high. That
keeps M0007's +15% engine and throws away the far-below-high names the literature blames for
crashes. If that lands near 15% worst fall with 12%+ a year, it is the best shot the lab has. I
would not spend more trials on pure nearness ranks.
methods.verdict: Ranking on closeness to the yearly high cut the worst fall to 15.6-18.0% (best yet next to beating SPY) but dragged return down to +8.0-9.7% a year vs SPY's +7.9%: a good brake, a poor engine.

methods.name: Price the weekly re-scale machinery alone: monthly momentum basket, weekly resize, no overlay
methods.hypothesis: M0013's control (brake measured on fresh picks, which should almost never fire) did as badly as the real brake (32% vs 30% max DD, ~10.5% CAGR vs F4's 16.2%), so the weekly resize session itself, which re-runs FACTOR and therefore re-checks the SPY 200-day trend filter weekly (fresh=empty -> k=0 -> full exit until the next rank), likely costs most of it. Run F4-MOM12-N20-TREND on MONTHLY_RANK_WEEKLY_RESIZE with a pass-through allocator, and a second variant whose resize sessions hold the trend state from the last rank date, to price the machinery and the weekly trend re-check separately before any weekly risk overlay is judged.

methods.name: Residual momentum, only among stocks near their 52-week high
methods.hypothesis: M0015 showed nearness to the 52-week high cuts drawdown (15.6-18.0%) but is a weak ranking key (+8-9.7% CAGR). Use it as an eligibility filter instead: M0007-N20-RAW's raw residual-momentum rank, top-20/30, restricted to names with close >= 0.85 or 0.90 of the 252-day max close, same F4 screen and SPY-200 gate. Keeps residual momentum's +15% engine while excluding the far-below-high rebounders the crash literature blames. Expect max DD near 15% at CAGR >= 12%. Kill if max DD is not below 16.8% (M0015-N20-BLEND) or CAGR falls below 11%.

methods.name: Residual momentum braked by a two-week swing reading
methods.hypothesis: M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21 passed every design-1 rule except DSR (CAGR +10.8% vs +7.9%, max DD 14.1%, PF 2.03, DSR 0.897 at N=90) because a one-month own-vol window caught the July-1998 jitters before the August shock, where a 63-day window did not (15.4%). If reacting within the month is the lever, a 10-day window at the same 14% target on the same top-20 raw residual book should cut the 1998 fall further and re-risk faster, raising Sharpe and DSR; a second variant scaling by SPY's own 21-day vol instead of the basket's tests whether the market's swing is the cleaner signal. Two variants only, to keep N low.

methods.name: Momentum with a wide protective stop under each stock (a resting Stop Sell per holding)
methods.sourceRef: M0011 (M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21) and M0007 (M0007-N20-RAW); owner question 2026-10-07
methods.hypothesis: The unbraked residual-momentum book (M0007-N20-RAW: +15.0% CAGR, 19.6% max DD, PF 2.16) fails only max DD, and M0011's volatility brake fixed DD (14.1%) at the price of 4 CAGR points. A wide stop on each stock, measured from the close before it was bought, should cut the single-name collapses that feed the worst fall while leaving ordinary momentum wobbles alone: on the unbraked book a 20% stop should land max DD near 15-16% with CAGR near +13%, i.e. more return per point of fall than the brake. On the braked M0011 book a 20% stop should keep DD under 15% and add Sharpe by trimming its worst single-name losses, nudging DSR toward 0.95.
methods.expectedFailure: The worst falls are basket-wide (Aug 1998, the 2000-02 momentum crash, 2009's junk rally), when every stock drops together: the stops fire on the same days, often on gap-down opens below the stop, and the book sits out the rebound until the next monthly re-rank. Then the stop costs return without cutting max DD (as M0013's basket brake did), the 15% stop whipsaws most, and DSR falls as N rises by four.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** Take the lab's best stock-picking book (buy the 20 stocks whose own rise,
after removing the market's move, was strongest over the past year; re-pick once a month) and put
an automatic safety exit under every stock: if a stock falls 15%, 20% or 25% below the price it
was bought near, sell it right away instead of waiting for next month's re-pick. In Gotrade this
is one Stop Sell order placed under each holding, which works with fractional shares.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 104 trials at run time).** Rejected. Every
version still beats SPY by a wide margin, but the stops did not do their job.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| No brake, 15% stop | +950% | +12.6% | 18.6% | 1.76 | 1,723 | 0.87 | 0.68 | 0.86 | worst fall, luck score |
| No brake, 20% stop | +1,123% | +13.5% | 20.3% | 1.86 | 1,664 | 0.89 | 0.66 | 0.88 | worst fall, luck score |
| No brake, 25% stop | +1,296% | +14.3% | 20.7% | 2.00 | 1,633 | 0.92 | 0.69 | 0.90 | worst fall, luck score |
| Volatility brake + 20% stop | +546% | +9.9% | 12.5% | 1.79 | 1,657 | 0.89 | 0.79 | 0.87 | luck score |
| *Parent, no brake, no stop* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.91* | *worst fall* |
| *Parent, volatility brake, no stop* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.90* | *luck score* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak; the owner's limit is 15%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is total profit on
winning trades divided by total loss on losing ones. The luck score (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks
how likely the result is real rather than the best of 104 lucky tries; the bar is 0.95.

**What happened.**
- On the book without a brake, the stops made the worst fall *bigger* at 20% and 25% (20.3% and
  20.7% vs 19.6%) and only 1 point smaller at 15% (18.6%), while costing 0.7 to 2.4 points of
  return a year. Gains vs losses dropped from 2.16 to 1.76–2.00: the stops turned many temporary
  dips into locked-in losses.
- On the braked book, the 20% stop did cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.5% and slightly
  improved return per unit of fall (0.79 vs 0.76), but cost 0.9 points of return a year and
  lowered the luck score (0.87 vs 0.90), so it moved further from eligibility, not closer.

**Why.** The worst falls of this book are not single stocks collapsing; they are the whole basket
falling together (the 1998 shock, the 2000–02 momentum crash, the 2009 rebound when beaten-down
stocks led). On those days many stops fire at once, often on gap-down opens below the stop price,
so the sale happens near the bottom. The book then holds cash until the next monthly re-pick and
misses the snap-back, and when it buys again the prices are higher. That is how a stop can make
the worst fall bigger: it turns a dip that would have recovered into a permanent loss, and the
re-entry starts from a lower equity. A single stock collapsing on its own news does happen, but
with 20 stocks at 5% each, one stock falling 40% costs the book only 2%, which is not what
decides the worst fall.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis (a 20% stop lands the unbraked book near
15–16% worst fall at about +13% a year) failed: the worst fall rose to 20.3%. The expected
failure (stops fire together in basket-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound)
is what happened, almost word for word. It agrees with the basket-brake method from yesterday
(sold at the bottom of rebounds) and with the old observation that a stop-loss on momentum sells
at the bottom of the bounce.

**Comparison.** The volatility brake (reduce how much is held when the basket has been swinging
hard) remains the only risk control the lab has found that cuts this book's worst fall cheaply,
because it acts before and during calm-to-stormy transitions rather than after a stock has already
fallen. Per-stock stops act after the fact.

**For the owner's question (can a hold-for-months method carry an automatic safety exit?).**
Mechanically yes, but on the evidence it should not: on this book a resting Stop Sell under each
stock lowers return and does not lower the worst fall. A braked book with a 20% stop is a
legitimate, executable version (all four owner rules pass: beats SPY, 12.5% worst fall, 1.79
gains vs losses, 1,657 trades), but it is strictly worse than the same book without the stop on
the one bar it fails (luck score).

My opinion: per-stock stops on momentum are a dead end; I would not spend more trials on stop
widths, trailing stops or ATR-based stops for this book, because the mechanism (basket-wide falls,
sell at the bottom, miss the rebound) applies to all of them. The one variant worth a single try
is fixing the re-entry, not the stop: let a stopped-out stock be bought back at the next weekly
check if it is still in the top 20, so a stop costs a week of the rebound instead of a month.
Beyond that, the lab's binding constraint is now the luck score on books that already pass every
owner rule, and more variants of the same book make that bar harder, not easier. The better use
of trials is a genuinely different source of return that could stand on its own.


### 2026-10-08

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 28, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown bar of 20% (both the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07; LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0019-RAW20-S15`: DSR 0.9436 at N = 28, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0019-TV14N21-S20`: DSR 0.9506 at N = 28, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: A safety exit under each stock made things worse: the worst fall did not shrink (18.6-20.7% vs 19.6%) and return dropped 0.7-2.4 points a year, because the stops fire together in market-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound.

methods.name: Stopped-out stocks may come back at the next weekly check
methods.sourceRef: M0019 (M0019-RAW20-S20, M0019-TV14N21-S20); its analysis queued this as the last try
methods.hypothesis: M0019's 20% stop on the unbraked residual book worsened the worst fall (20.3% vs 19.6%) because a stopped stock waited up to a month in cash and missed the snap-back. Letting it come back at the next weekly check while still in this month's basket should recover most of that rebound: on the unbraked book the worst fall should land below the no-stop parent's 19.6% with return near its +15% a year, and on the braked book below 14.1% with return near +10.8% and a higher luck score than M0019's 0.873. W-NOSTOP prices the weekly re-weighting alone and should sit close to the monthly parent.
methods.expectedFailure: Basket-wide falls last longer than a week: a stock bought back after a week is still falling, gets stopped again below the new stop, and the book pays two round trips per fall, so the stop variants end with more trades, lower gains vs losses and a worst fall no better than M0019's. The weekly re-weighting toward equal weight also trims momentum's winners every week, costing return even without stops (W-NOSTOP below the parent).
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** Yesterday's test (M0019) showed that a safety exit under each stock
hurts the best stock-picking book, because a stock sold in a market-wide dip waited up to a month
in cash and missed the bounce. This test lets that stock come back at the next weekly check, as
long as it is still in this month's list, so a safety exit costs at most a week of the bounce.

**How it was set up.** The book still picks its 20 stocks once a month (the stocks whose own rise,
after removing the market's move, was strongest over the past year). Every week it re-issues that
same list at fresh prices: a stock sold by its safety exit since the last check is bought back,
with a new exit 20% below its latest price. Checking weekly also nudges every holding back toward
an equal share each week, so one version runs the weekly checks with no safety exit at all, to
show what the weekly checking costs on its own. (Assumption, written down before the run: the new
month's list is first issued at the first weekly check of the month, up to a few trading days
after the monthly parent buys it.)

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 107 trials at run time).** Rejected.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Weekly checks, no safety exit (control) | +1,565% | +15.3% | 19.3% | 2.11 | 1,620 | 0.94 | 0.79 | 0.91 | worst fall, luck score |
| Weekly checks, 20% exit, buy back | +1,274% | +14.2% | 18.9% | 1.86 | 1,744 | 0.89 | 0.75 | 0.88 | worst fall, luck score |
| Braked book, 20% exit, buy back | +553% | +9.9% | 16.2% | 1.76 | 1,737 | 0.87 | 0.61 | 0.85 | worst fall, luck score |
| *Monthly parent, no exit* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.91* | *worst fall* |
| *M0019: monthly, 20% exit, no buy back* | *+1,123%* | *+13.5%* | *20.3%* | *1.86* | *1,664* | *0.89* | *0.66* | *0.88* | *worst fall* |
| *Braked parent, no exit (M0011's best)* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.90* | *luck score* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak (the limit is 15%); "gains vs losses" is profit on winners over loss on losers;
the luck score asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of 107 lucky tries (the bar
is 0.95).

**What happened.**
- Checking weekly costs nothing by itself. The control matched the monthly parent almost exactly
  (+15.3% vs +15.0% a year, worst fall 19.3% vs 19.6%, same luck score). Nudging holdings back to
  equal shares every week neither helped nor hurt.
- Buying back did repair part of the damage from yesterday: against M0019's exit with no buy-back,
  return rose from +13.5% to +14.2% a year and the worst fall fell from 20.3% to 18.9%.
- But against its own control the safety exit still loses: 1.1 points of return a year, gains vs
  losses down from 2.11 to 1.86, luck score down from 0.91 to 0.88, for a worst fall only 0.4
  points smaller (19.3% to 18.9%), still far over 15%.
- On the braked book it was worse than useless: the worst fall rose from 14.1% to 16.2%, so the
  version that passed every owner rule no longer does.

**Why.** Exactly the expected failure. The big falls of this book are the whole market falling for
weeks, not a few days. A stock sold on a gap-down is bought back a week later while the fall is
still going, and is often sold again lower: 124 extra trades on the unbraked book, each a small
loss plus costs. On the braked book there is a second effect: the brake had already cut how much
is held, and buying stopped stocks back at the start-of-month share undoes part of that cut in the
middle of a fall, which is how its worst fall got bigger.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The pre-stated test was: if buying back does not bring the
worst fall under the parent's 19.6% at a similar return, per-stock exits are closed for this
family. The worst fall did land under 19.6% (18.9%), but return fell by 0.8 points against the
parent and 1.1 against the like-for-like control, and the luck score fell, so the result is not
"similar return". The expected failure (bought back into a falling basket, stopped again, more
trades, worse gains vs losses) is what happened.

My opinion: per-stock safety exits are closed for this book. Two careful tries with opposite
fixes both found the same thing: the exits fire in market-wide falls, and no re-entry timing
recovers what they give up. The braked book's volatility brake remains the only risk control that
works here, because it cuts how much is held before and during the storm instead of selling single
stocks after they have fallen. The useful by-product is that weekly checking is free for this
book, which matters if a future idea needs a weekly signal. The next trials should look for a
second, different source of return to combine with this book, not another way to protect it.


### 2026-10-07

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `all-trials` N policy at N = 110, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown bar of 20% (both the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07; LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0020-W-NOSTOP`: DSR 0.9127 at N = 110, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Buying a stopped stock back at the next weekly check recovered part of what the safety exit lost, but it still trailed the same book without exits (14.2% vs 15.3% a year, worst fall 18.9% vs 19.3%) and made the braked book's worst fall worse (16.2% vs 14.1%): per-stock exits are closed for this book.

methods.name: Blend the residual-momentum book with a calm-stock book: two different engines in one portfolio
methods.sourceRef: M0007-N20-RAW, M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21 and F5-LV60-N20-TREND blended with BLEND; Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013); Blitz & van Vliet (2007)
methods.hypothesis: Every risk control tried on the residual-momentum book (stops, basket brakes, weekly re-entry) sells after a fall; only the volatility brake helped. A second return source whose bad periods differ should cut the worst fall without selling: the calmest members lag in strong markets but held up in 2000-02 and 2008. 50% M0007-N20-RAW (+15.0% a year, 19.6% worst fall) plus 50% F5-LV60-N20-TREND (+7.6%, 31.4% worst fall alone, but a different worst stretch) should land near +11-13% a year with a worst fall near 13-15% and a higher Sharpe than either half; braking the momentum half as M0011 does should take the worst fall toward 10-12% at +9-10% a year. A 70/30 split keeps more of momentum's return and should still sit under the 20% limit.
methods.expectedFailure: The calm book's own 31% worst fall came with the SPY filter on, so it is a fall inside a rising market (the 1999 flight from utilities and staples into tech), and the blend inherits half of it; worse, calm stocks and momentum overlap in calm bull years and both halves fall together in sharp shocks (Aug 1998, Oct 2008), so the worst fall is only a little smaller while return is diluted toward SPY's and the luck score drops.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

## What we tried

The lab's best stock picker buys the 20 stocks whose own recent run, after removing the market's move, is strongest. This is residual momentum, M0007-N20-RAW. Every earlier attempt to shrink its worst fall worked by *selling* after a fall: stops, basket brakes, weekly re-entry. This time we left that book alone and gave it a partner. A second book holds the 20 calmest index members (the smallest daily price swings over the last 60 days, the lab's F5 book). Each book runs on a fixed share of the money. Both re-pick once a month, and both go to cash when SPY is below its 200-day average. Three versions were registered before any result existed:

| version | split | CAGR (yearly growth) | worst fall | gains vs losses | Sharpe (steadiness) | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B50-RAW | 50% momentum / 50% calm | **+10.9%** | 13.7% | 2.25x | 1.02 | 0.952 |
| B50-TV14 | same, momentum half braked as RM does | +8.8% | 12.6% | 2.22x | 1.04 | 0.959 |
| B70-RAW | 70% momentum / 30% calm | **+12.6%** | 14.0% | 2.25x | 1.01 | 0.945 |
| *SPY with dividends* | | *+7.9%* | *~55%* | | | |
| *momentum book alone (M0007-N20-RAW)* | | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16x* | *0.94* | *0.914* |
| *best before today (M0022-W-TV16)* | | *+11.7%* | *14.3%* | *2.06x* | *0.95* | *0.916* |

Window: 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16 (dev only). Each version made about 2,700 trades.

**All three pass every go-live condition.** Each beats total-return SPY. Each has a worst fall under the 20% limit (12.6–14.0%). Each makes over 2.2 dollars of gains for every dollar of losses, against the 1.3 bar. Each has far more than 100 trades. Each also clears the luck bar.

**The luck score (DSR).** This is the chance the result is real and not the best of many lucky tries. It is graded against N = 113, the count of every dev trial the lab has run so far (policy: all trials). The bar is DSR ≥ 0.90, the owner's setting since 2026-10-07. Results: 0.952, 0.959 and 0.945. That is the widest margin any method in the lab has had: 0.045–0.059 above the bar. The previous best was 0.016. The reason is steadiness. A Sharpe above 1.0 means the gains came smoothly rather than in lumps, and the luck test rewards smooth gains most.

**B70-RAW is the strongest result in the lab.** On return per unit of worst fall (MAR) it scores 0.90. The previous high was 0.86. It beats M0022-W-TV16, now on paper as RMW-FR, on all three counts: more return (12.6% vs 11.7%), a smaller worst fall (14.0% vs 14.3%) and a higher luck score (0.945 vs 0.916).

## When it hurt

The worst fall in all three versions came in the summer 1998 shock. From the 1998 peak (March or June) to the September 1998 low, the blend lost 13–14%. The momentum book alone lost about 20% in that stretch. Worst calendar years were mild: −1.0% (B50-RAW, 2015), −1.2% (B50-TV14, 1998), −1.6% (B70-RAW, 2015). The falls are spread across calendar years, so no single year looks bad.

## Why it worked

- **The two books do fall at different times.** Monthly returns of the two books move together only loosely (correlation 0.45). In momentum's ten worst months it lost 8.2% on average, while the calm book lost only 2.0%. That gap is the whole effect. Half the money sat in stocks that barely moved while the momentum names collapsed.
- **The calm book's own big fall is hidden.** Alone, the calm book lost about 28% (on month-end values) from March 1998 to February 2000. That was the 1999 rush out of utilities and staples into tech, and the market filter did not see it because SPY was rising. In the blend, momentum returned +56% in 1999, right as the calm book lost 7%. Each book's bad stretch landed where the other book was doing well.
- **What the hypothesis got wrong.** I expected the calm stocks to help in 2000–02 and 2008. They did not, because both books were already in cash then: the SPY filter took the whole portfolio out of those bear markets (2001, 2002 and 2008 are all flat). The diversification that mattered was inside rising markets, not in bear markets.
- **Braking the momentum half did not pay.** B50-TV14 cut the worst fall by only 1.1 points (13.7 → 12.6%) and cost 2.1 points of yearly return. Once half the money is calm, the brake has little left to tame. The brake fixed a problem the blend had already solved.

## Hypothesis vs result

- **B50-RAW.** Predicted +11–13% a year with a worst fall of 13–15%. Got +10.9% and 13.7%. **Held**, with return a little short.
- **B50-TV14.** Predicted +9–10% with a worst fall of 10–12%. Got +8.8% and 12.6%. **Missed** on both by about a point, in the less favourable direction.
- **B70-RAW.** Predicted a worst fall under 20% with more return. Got 14.0% at +12.6%. **Held**, and did better than predicted.
- **Expected failure.** I expected both books to fall together in sharp shocks and the blend to gain little. It **did not happen**. In August 1998 the calm stocks lost about a quarter of what the momentum stocks lost. Dilution did happen in the 50/50 version, which gives up 4 points a year compared with momentum alone.

## Caveats (unchanged from the parent)

- The store has no delisted companies. Calm stocks that later failed are missing, just like momentum names that failed. The lab's earlier risk note covers this.
- The figures above use daily values. The month-end table I checked shows the same timing, with slightly smaller falls.

My opinion: This is the most important result the lab has produced. We stopped trying to sell our way out of falls and added a second, different engine, and the luck score jumped from about 0.91 to about 0.95. My view is that B70-RAW should be promoted and given its one look at 2016–2026. That is the coordinator's call under the lab's rules; my recommendation is to do it. Next I would push the idea further. One, add a third engine that also holds up when momentum hurts, such as stocks near their 52-week high, which had a small worst fall but weak return. Two, test the split itself (60/40 and 80/20). That is a dial, though, and turning it after seeing results is exactly how a lab fools itself. So I would run only a pre-registered pair, and only if the blend survives its test-window look. I would not add the weekly brake (backlog idea M0023) on top of the 50/50 blend. B50-TV14 shows the brake has little left to do once half the money is calm.


### 2026-10-07

# Pre-registration

Pre-registered for the test window as `M0021-B70-RAW` (dev trial #113, config digest `548b0cd9025eb919b06e8fe3bdba14efa79c28ce87cca1dc0faa204588e76025`, MAR 0.900983, DSR 0.945265 at N = 113; the bar it cleared is the one named in the pre-registration's gate line).

Pre-registration: `docs/lab/prereg/M0021.md`, written before any test number exists and committed before the look is spent (design §3). The test window is 2015-10-19..data end; `lab test M0021-B70-RAW` spends the one look this configuration gets, and the database refuses a second (`UNIQUE(config_digest, window)`). No `trials` row was written here: a pre-registration is not a backtest and does not move the lab's N.


### 2026-10-07

## The one look at 2015-10-19 → 2026-10-06 (Sera, 2026-10-07)

**Result: test-failed, and that is final.** The pre-registered version, 70% momentum and 30% calm stocks, grew only **+3.3% a year** (+42.5% in total) over the test window. Simply holding SPY with dividends reinvested grew **+13.6% a year** (+306%). The book fell at most 8.6% from a peak. It made 1.70 dollars of gains for every dollar of losses, and it made 426 trades. It passed four of the five conditions and failed the one that matters most: it did not beat the market. The luck score on this window, 0.51, is recorded for completeness only. A pre-registered look has nothing to deflate.

**Why: the book was in cash four-fifths of the time.** On average only **18% of the money was invested** (exposure 0.18). On the dev window the same book was about 62% invested. The market filter does not explain the gap: SPY spent most of 2016–2026 above its 200-day average. The flat stretches in early 2016, around New Year 2019 and in spring 2020 are the filter working as designed, and they are short.

The cause is the account size combined with **whole shares**. The lab starts every book with 20,000,000 IDR, about $1,450 in October 2015. Split 20 ways at 70%, each momentum slot is about $51. Split 20 ways at 30%, each calm slot is about $22. These rules buy whole shares only, so any stock priced above its slot is skipped and its money stays in cash. Share prices in the store (prices only, no results):

| date | median share price | above the $22 calm slot | above the $51 momentum slot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-01-03 (dev start) | $13 | 25% | 4% |
| 2015-10-01 (dev end) | $47 | 79% | 45% |
| 2016-01-04 (test start) | $52 | 83% | 51% |
| 2024-01-02 | $92 | 90% | 71% |

The dev window's prices are adjusted backwards for splits and dividends, so in 1996 almost everything fit into a slot. Over twenty years the book compounded fast enough to keep up as prices rose. The test window starts a small account at today's price levels: most calm stocks and half the momentum picks could not be bought at all. Earning only 3% a year then meant the account never grew enough to catch up.

**What this does and does not say.** The look does *not* show that the stock picking stopped working after 2015. Most of the picks were never held, so their returns were never earned. It *does* show that this configuration, at this account size in whole shares, does not beat the market, and the rules give no second look. The miss was knowable before the look: whole-share fill rates at test-window prices were never checked. That was the coordinator's mistake, and it is journaled as a risk.

**My opinion:** the blend idea is still the lab's best lead, and this look neither confirms nor kills it. The next step is the same two-engine book in fractional shares, which Gotrade accepts for limit orders (owner, 2026-10-07) and which the paper books already use. It must be a new method with its own dev trials and its own pre-registered look. Before any whole-share book is promoted again, check that its slots can actually be filled at test-window prices. Today the lab's gate counts fractional shares as an unverified owner input, so a fractional book cannot become eligible until the owner clears that input in the gate. That decision is the owner's, not the lab's.
methods.verdict: Best dev result in the lab (12.6% a year, 14.0% worst fall), but its one look at 2016-2026 failed: 3.3% a year vs SPY's 13.6%, because a small account in whole shares could buy only a fifth of its picks at today's share prices and sat mostly in cash.

methods.name: RM's book with its volatility brake re-read every week
methods.sourceRef: M0011 (M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21, on paper as RM); M0020 (weekly checking is free); M0004 and M0013 (weekly resizing on other books)
methods.hypothesis: M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21 (+10.8% a year, 14.1% max DD, DSR 0.897) reads its one-month brake once a month, so a shock that starts mid-month (Aug 1998) is met at full exposure. Reading the same brake every week cuts exposure within days: at TV14 the worst fall should drop to about 11-12% at a similar return, and the steadier curve should lift the Sharpe and the luck score; at TV16 the faster brake should keep the worst fall near 14% while return rises toward +12% a year, the best chance of a luck score at or above 0.95. Unlike M0004 (three-month reading on total-return momentum), a one-month reading changes within a month, so a weekly re-read carries new information.
methods.expectedFailure: Volatility measured over a month lags a crash by days either way: the weekly cut comes after the first gap-down, the money sits out the rebound (momentum's falls snap back), and the extra trades cost more than the fall saved, as M0004 found for its three-month reading. The weekly market switch (W-TV14-SW) repeats M0013's whipsaw: out on a dip, back only at the next month.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** RM (the braked momentum book now on paper) decides once a month how much
of its money to hold, based on how wildly its 20 stocks swung over the past month. This test reads
that same brake every week instead, while still picking the 20 stocks only once a month. The owner
said a weekly check is fine if it performs better.

**Why it could work this time.** An earlier test (M0004) read a three-month swing measure weekly on
the plain momentum book and found it added cost and nothing else: a three-month measure barely
changes from one week to the next. RM's brake reads only the last month, which can change a lot
within a month, so a weekly re-read carries new information. The test before this one (M0020)
had also shown that checking this book weekly costs nothing by itself.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 110 trials at run time).** Rejected, but the two
main versions are the lab's best results so far: they pass every one of the owner's rules and
miss only the luck score.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Weekly brake, 14% swing limit** | **+633%** | **+10.6%** | **12.4%** | **2.04** | 1,592 | 0.94 | **0.86** | **0.912** | luck score |
| **Weekly brake, 16% swing limit** | **+789%** | **+11.7%** | **14.3%** | **2.06** | 1,589 | **0.95** | 0.82 | **0.916** | luck score |
| Weekly brake + weekly market filter | +384% | +8.3% | 15.6% | 1.64 | 1,761 | 0.79 | 0.53 | 0.765 | worst fall, luck score |
| *RM today: monthly brake, 14% limit* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.897 (N=90)* | *luck score* |
| *Same book, no brake* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.914 (N=85)* | *worst fall* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak (the owner's limit is 15%); "gains vs losses" is profit on winners over loss on
losers (limit 1.3); "return per unit of fall" (MAR) is yearly return divided by the worst fall; the
luck score (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of 110
tries (the bar is 0.95).

**What happened.**
- With the same 14% limit as RM, reading the brake weekly cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.4%
  while giving up only 0.2 points of return a year (10.6% vs 10.8%). Return per unit of fall rose
  from 0.76 to 0.86, the best in the lab.
- That extra safety leaves room for more exposure: at a 16% limit the worst fall is 14.3% (still
  under 15%) and return rises to 11.7% a year, with the lab's highest Sharpe (0.95, steadiness of
  the gains) and highest luck score (0.916).
- Re-reading the market filter weekly as well was a clear mistake: it sold on dips and stayed in
  cash until the month ended, missing the rebound (worst fall 15.6%, return 8.3%, gains vs losses
  1.64). This is the same whipsaw the lab journal recorded for the basket brake.
- The luck score rose (RM's 0.897 at 90 tries to 0.912–0.916 at 110 tries), even though the bar
  for it rose with 20 more tries. It is still short of 0.95.

**Why.** A fast shock that starts in the middle of a month met RM at full strength, because RM only
checks its brake at the month's start. With a weekly check the brake sees the swings growing within
days and cuts how much is held before most of the fall, then lets exposure back as the swings calm,
without changing which stocks are held. That is different from every failed control in this
family: stops, basket brakes and a weekly market filter all sell after prices have already fallen
and then sit out the rebound. The weekly brake trims gradually, keeps the same stocks, and adds
back gradually.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis held on the worst fall and the return: at 14%
it predicted about 11–12% worst fall at a similar return (got 12.4% at 10.6%), and at 16% a worst
fall near 14% with return toward 12% a year (got 14.3% at 11.7%). It did not reach a luck score of
0.95 (got 0.916). The expected failure (the brake lags the crash and the extra trades cost more
than the fall saved) did not happen for the brake alone: only 4 more trades than RM in 20 years.
It did happen, as predicted, for the weekly market filter.

**For the owner.** This book is executable: it picks 20 stocks once a month (as RM does) and once a
week may trim or top up all holdings by the same proportion, as fractional limit orders in Gotrade.
The nightly paper engine cannot run a weekly-adjust rule yet; a handover for that feature was
written today (docs/handover/2026-10-07-paper-split-cadence.md).

My opinion: this is the strongest direction the lab has. A weekly brake is strictly better than
RM's monthly one on everything that matters here (smaller fall, same return at 14%; more return
inside the limit at 16%), and the mechanism makes sense rather than being a lucky setting. I would
not spend more trials tuning the swing limit or the reading length: each one raises the luck bar,
and the improvement came from the weekly re-read, not from the setting. Once paper trading can run
a weekly-adjust rule, the 16% version should replace RM on paper (owner's decision, as RM was): it
passes every owner rule with more room than RM and has the best luck score in the lab. The next
lab trials should combine this book with a second, different source of return (the calm-stock
blend already queued), with the weekly brake on top, because a steadier combined curve is the
most direct way to lift the luck score past 0.95.


### 2026-10-07

# Promotion

Promoted to the paper roster as `RMW-FR`, replacing `RM-FR` (retired the same moment).

Variant: `M0022-W-TV16`. Roster object: `WEEKLYBRAKE`. Frozen spec digest: `375e6f63d4b6a00842b330b8bfc9405a2e204f50bf5dac65b6a7bb2a706729ce`.

The roster row is `status='active'` with no `paper_start`: the next paper night freezes the spec and starts its own clock, so the paper record begins at the promotion and claims nothing earlier. `backtest.registry.REGISTRY` was not appended to -- a promoted method reaches the roster through the roster's own resolver, so the lab's multiple-testing count is unchanged by this.

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `all-trials` N policy at N = 110, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown bar of 20% (both the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07; LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

## What was tried

Each month, buy the 20 stocks (from the same big-company list every lab book uses) that did best in the **same calendar month last year** — the idea from Heston & Sadka (2008) that some stocks have "their" months. Hold for one month, equal amounts, and go to cash when SPY is below its 200-day average (the same market filter as the momentum books). Six versions: the plain signal, a "net" version (same month minus the stock's other eleven months, to strip out last year's trend), a 40-stock version, a version without the market filter, a version that mixes the seasonal rank with the residual-momentum rank, and a 50/50 split between this book and RM (the residual-momentum book with a volatility brake, M0011-RAW20-TV14-N21).

**Scope change, decided before the run:** the reserved idea averaged the same month over 2 to 20 past years. The lab cannot do that today: how far back a method may read a stock is tied to when its test window may start, so a 20-year memory would push the start to 2013 and break the lab's fixed checks. Only the one-year version was tested. The multi-year version is logged as a wish for the lab.

## Results (1996 → Oct 2015; SPY with dividends made 7.9% a year)

| version | yearly return | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| same month, 20 stocks | 10.6% | 22.3% | 1.38 | 0.71 | worst fall, luck |
| net of other months | 9.6% | 23.9% | 1.33 | 0.65 | worst fall, luck |
| same month, 40 stocks | 9.1% | 19.3% | 1.42 | 0.73 | luck |
| no market filter | 8.9% | 61.0% | 1.20 | 0.26 | worst fall, gains/losses, luck |
| mixed with residual momentum | 12.0% | 18.4% | 1.51 | 0.82 | luck |
| 50/50 with RM | 10.5% | 15.1% | 1.65 | 0.87 | luck |

The luck score (DSR) asks: after the lab's **N = 122** tries so far, how likely is this result to be real rather than the best of many coin flips? The bar is **0.90**. Nothing reached it; the 50/50 split came closest at 0.87.

Every version but one beat SPY on yearly return. Only the 40-stock version, the mixed version and the 50/50 split stayed under the 20% worst-fall limit, and all three still failed the luck bar.

**When it hurt:** the worst fall in every filtered version is the **August 1998** shock (peak April 1998, bottom August). The 20-stock book lost 18% in that one month, more than any momentum book (RM lost 10%, raw residual momentum 13%). Worst calendar years: 2006 (−5.4%) and 2007 (−5 to −8%), years when the momentum books were still making money. Without the filter the book fell 61% from 2006 to early 2009 and lost 39% in 2008.

## Why

- **The signal picks jumpy stocks.** A stock's best single month last year is mostly a measure of how much it swings. The top 20 by one month's return are the high-volatility names, so the book wins big in rallies (+51% in 1999, +41% in 2003) and loses big in shocks (−18% in Aug 1998). This was the expected failure, and it showed up.
- **The market filter does most of the protecting.** Like every gated book here, it sat in cash through 2001–02 and 2008. Take the filter away and the same picks lose 61%. The stock picking itself adds little beyond the market: 8.9% a year with no filter vs SPY's 7.9%, for three times SPY's worst fall in 2008.
- **The "net" version was worse, not better.** Stripping out last year's trend cut return by one point and deepened the fall. Some of the plain signal's edge was momentum in disguise, which the paper's own split predicts for large stocks.
- **It is not a second engine.** Month by month, this book moved with the momentum books (correlation about 0.8 in months when either held stocks). Both use the same market filter and both lean on stocks that rose, so their bad months line up: Aug 1998, Jan 2010, May 2010, Oct 2009. Mixing it with RM 50/50 gave 10.5% a year at a 15.1% worst fall; RM alone gave 10.8% at 14.1%. The mix was slightly **worse** on both counts.
- **Mixing the ranks diluted the better signal.** Seasonality plus residual momentum made 12.0% at an 18.4% fall; raw residual momentum alone made 15.0% at 19.6%. Return per unit of worst fall: 0.65 vs 0.77.

## Hypothesis check

- "Alone it should roughly match or modestly beat SPY": **held**, better than the expected failure predicted (10.6% vs 7.9%), but that is mostly the filter and high-volatility exposure in the 1999 and 2003 rallies, not a seasonal edge.
- "Net should do at least as well": **failed**.
- "The 50/50 blend should keep RM's return and cut its fall": **failed**. Both were slightly worse.
- "Ranksum should beat raw residual momentum on return per fall": **failed** (0.65 vs 0.77).
- The expected failure (high-volatility picks, high turnover, blend dilutes RM without cutting the fall) **happened**, except that the stand-alone return beat SPY instead of trailing it. Turnover was about 15 times the book a year, twice the momentum books'.

## Compared with near misses

The best lab books (the weekly-braked residual-momentum book M0022: 11.7% a year at 14.3%; RM: 10.8% at 14.1%) beat every version here on return per worst fall. The best version here, the 50/50 split (MAR 0.70), sits below RM's 0.76.

My opinion: the one-year same-month signal is not worth more trials in this lab. It is a noisy, high-volatility pick that moves with our momentum books, so it neither stands on its own nor diversifies them. The proper Heston–Sadka test averages 10–20 past years, which washes out the one-lucky-month noise, and the lab cannot run it until a method can read a long stock history without pushing back its start date. That lab feature is worth building, because long-memory signals (multi-year seasonality, long-term reversal) are a family we cannot touch today. Until then, the better use of trials is real diversifiers, books whose losing months do **not** coincide with momentum's, such as a calm-stock or dividend book with its own market rule.

The 52-week-high picker (M0015: +8.0-9.7% a year, 15.6-18.0% worst fall) is a weak engine alone but a strong brake. methods.name: Does the calm partner help any momentum book? Blend the plain 12-month momentum picker with calm stocks
methods.hypothesis: If the M0021 effect is real diversification and not a lucky fit to residual momentum, it should also work on the lab's older plain-momentum picker (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND: +16.2% a year, 22.2% worst fall), whose crashes are larger and hit high-beta names. 70% F4 plus 30% calm stocks should bring the worst fall under 17% at about +13.5% a year. methods.name: Step aside when the momentum gap collapses: a gate that reads the stock-picking factor, not the market
methods.hypothesis: M0012 showed the residual-momentum book's binding falls (May-Jul 2006 19.3%, Apr-May 2010 17.9%) happen while SPY sits above its averages, so no market gate can catch them, and weekly market gates whipsaw (worst falls 22-30%). A momentum unwind shows up first as a collapse in the gap between this month's top-ranked and bottom-ranked names. Each month (no weekly switch, to avoid whipsaw), compute the equal-weight return over the last 21 sessions of the top-decile minus the bottom-decile names by the same residual score. When that spread is below a fixed threshold (e.g. -8%), hold half the basket (or none). The rest is M0007-N20-RAW exactly. Expect the 2006 fall to drop under 15% while return stays above +13% a year. Fails if the spread turns only after the damage, as momentum crashes are 1-3 weeks long.

methods.name: A short-term bounce book: buy last month's biggest fallers among calm, uptrending stocks
methods.sourceRef: Jegadeesh (1990), J. Finance 45(3); Lehmann (1990), QJE 105(1); Blitz, Huij, Lansdorp & Verbeek (2013), Short-term residual reversal, J. Financial Markets 16(3)
methods.hypothesis: M0024 showed a same-month seasonal book moves with the momentum books (monthly correlation 0.8), so blending it with residual momentum cut nothing. One-month reversal is the classic factor whose payoff runs against momentum's: last month's biggest fallers against the market bounce the next month, and momentum's bad months (sharp rebounds of losers, 2009, 2002-03) are reversal's good ones. Blitz et al. show the residual version keeps the premium while shedding the market and factor bets that make plain reversal crash. Restricting to the calmer half of F4's screened universe by 60-day volatility, and to names above their own 200-day average, aims the book at liquidity-driven dips in healthy, large names rather than at companies breaking down. Each month, behind the SPY-200 gate, CALM-RESID holds the 20 most negative one-month residual returns, equal weight, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's monthly top-up. CALM-RAW ranks on the plain one-month return (does taking out the market matter?); PLAIN-RESID drops both the calm and the uptrend filters (do the filters matter?); CALM-RESID-N10 holds the 10 deepest fallers (is the bounce concentrated in the extremes?). BLEND-RM runs CALM-RESID 50/50 with the real-fee residual momentum book and is a correlation readout only: the residual-momentum family has a test-failed member, so the blend can never be promoted. Success for the standalone book is beating total-return SPY on the owner's deposits with a worst fall under 20%; success for the idea is a monthly correlation with the residual-momentum book well under 0.5.
methods.expectedFailure: Turnover near 100% a month at Gotrade's real fee schedule -- a 5M IDR top-up split 20 ways is a slot of about 15 USD, which pays several tenths of a percent a side -- eats most of a large-cap reversal premium that was already small after the 1990s (the literature finds it decayed sharply in big liquid names once decimal ticks narrowed spreads in 2001). The book then lags SPY by the fee drag. The second failure is August 1998 and late 2008, when fallers kept falling: a calm, uptrending name that drops hard in a month is often the first casualty of a regime turn, and the SPY gate reacts too late. Third, the calm-and-uptrend filters may themselves lean the book toward low-volatility quality, so its correlation with momentum ends up higher than the textbook negative.

### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- Sera 20261009-2105 reserves this idea

Run it as a stand-alone book first, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's real funding (a -frac-gotrade preset, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, 10M IDR start plus 5M on the 25th). The residual-momentum family has a test-failed member, so a blend with RM can never be promoted; keep the 50/50-with-RM variant only as a correlation readout, not as the candidate. Reversal's case rests on its payoff running against momentum's, so report the monthly correlation with the real-fee residual book (M0032) beside the usual numbers, and price the near-total monthly turnover at the real fee schedule rather than the flat 0.1% the draft assumed.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- result: the bounce book is a quieter copy of momentum, not its opposite

**The idea.** Each month, buy the 20 stocks that fell hardest last month compared with the market. Only calm stocks (the calmer half by 60-day volatility) that are still above their own 200-day average qualify, and the book holds cash when SPY is below its 200-day average. The textbook says this "bounce" factor pays off when momentum loses, so it should be a good partner for the residual-momentum book. All five versions ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, starting with 10M IDR and adding 5M IDR on the 25th of every month, from 1996 to 2015.

**Results on the owner's deposits** (money-weighted return means the interest rate a savings account would need to pay to turn the same deposits into the same final balance):

| version | your money earned / yr | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CALM-RESID (main) | 7.5% | 7.2% | 27.2% | 1.52 | 0.864 | fails the fall limit and the luck bar |
| CALM-RAW (plain return, market not removed) | 7.6% | 7.2% | 30.0% | 1.54 | 0.872 | fails the same two |
| PLAIN-RESID (no calm/uptrend filter) | 3.5% | 7.2% | 35.5% | 1.12 | 0.325 | fails four conditions |
| CALM-RESID-N10 (10 deepest fallers) | 7.4% | 7.2% | 23.0% | 1.49 | 0.864 | fails the fall limit and the luck bar |
| BLEND-RM (half bounce, half real-fee residual momentum) | 10.6% | 7.2% | 17.2% | 1.77 | 0.948 | **passes all conditions on dev** |

The bounce book on its own roughly matches the market (+0.3 points a year) and falls much further than it does. The filters do real work. Without them (PLAIN-RESID), the book buys companies that are breaking down and earns half what SPY does. With them, the book makes money but brings no edge.

**DSR at N = 35.** DSR is the chance that a result is real skill rather than the best of many lucky tries. The lab has now tested 35 independent ideas, and the bar is 0.90. The standalone versions score 0.86 to 0.87, which is close but still a fail. The blend scores 0.948 and clears the bar. Most of that comes from its momentum half, though (see below).

**Worst year and worst fall.** On its own, the bounce book fell 24% from its peak (counting only investment returns, deposits removed) between April 1999 and February 2000, when calm, unloved stocks were sold to buy tech. Its worst single month was August 1998 (−11.4%): the fallers kept falling. That is exactly the second expected failure. Its worst calendar year was 1999 (−7.9%), the same year momentum made +56%.

**The question this method was built to answer: does it move against momentum?** No. Month by month, its returns correlate with the real-fee residual momentum book at **0.65**. (Correlation runs from −1, opposite, to +1, in lockstep; the success bar was "well under 0.5".) If we count only months when both books were invested, it is still 0.64, so the shared cash periods behind the SPY gate don't explain it. In momentum's 25 worst months (each worse than −3%), the bounce book lost 2.6% on average while momentum lost 6.2%. It softens momentum's bad months but doesn't offset them. Both are long-only books of large US stocks, so the market's own swings dominate both. The calm and uptrend filters also tilt the bounce book toward steady, quality names, which is the third expected failure. The pure, unfiltered version is even more correlated (0.70).

**Why the blend passes.** The blend is half bounce book and half the real-fee residual momentum book. Its worst fall (17.2%) is below momentum alone (about 20.6%) because the two books fall by different amounts in the same bad months. That is diversification by size, not by direction. The cost is return: momentum alone earned 13.7% a year on the same deposits, and the blend earns 10.6%. So the blend pays about 3 points a year to bring the worst fall from just over the 20% limit to safely under it. The bounce half adds no return of its own (it earns about what SPY does), so all the blend's edge over SPY comes from the momentum half.

**Fees.** The bounce book trades about 16 times its size each year, against about 9 for momentum. At Gotrade's real fees on small slots, that drag is a large part of why a premium the papers put at 1% a month leaves almost nothing here. The first expected failure happened as well.

**The promotion gate.** Run on its own folds, the method beats the benchmark in only 2 of 4 walk-forward folds (the method's own variant-choosing rule, replayed through time). In the best-measured years (2009-2015) it trails by 3.3 points a year. `lab promote` refuses anything under a strict majority of folds, so nothing here can be promoted. There is a second problem: half of the eligible blend is the residual-momentum book, and that family has already failed its test-window look. Even if the folds had passed, spending a look on this blend would mean re-testing a disproven engine with a weaker partner.

**Hypothesis check.** The hypothesis failed: the correlation is 0.65, not well under 0.5. All three expected failures happened: fees took the premium, fallers kept falling in 1998, and the filters pulled the book toward momentum's quality tilt.

**Compared with the near misses.** The same-month seasonal book (M0024) was the last attempt to find a partner for momentum. At the flat 0.1% fee it correlated about 0.64 with this measure and also passed only as a blend. The bounce book adds the same thing (a smaller worst fall in a blend) at a higher fee cost and with a worse 2009-2015 record.

**My opinion:** Short-term reversal is not the anti-momentum partner this lab needs. In a long-only, large-cap, 200-day-gated universe, every stock-picking book is mostly "long the market", so any two of them will correlate at 0.6 or more, whatever the textbook factor correlation says. I would stop looking for diversification among long-only stock pickers. The partner that actually behaves differently is time: something that holds bonds or cash on a schedule that doesn't depend on SPY's 200-day average. Within this data, the cleanest test is a treasury ETF sleeve (the store has TLT/IEF-type ETFs if they are in the universe). The other real option is to accept momentum's 20% fall and cut it with a smaller position size rather than with a second picker. I would not run more reversal variants: the filters already found the best version, and that version only matches SPY.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- a correction to the opinion above

I checked: the store holds TLT and IEF (from 2002), but a book that parks money in them needs the owner's input, because Gotrade's default ETFs are only SPY and QQQ. So it can never be eligible, and a treasury sleeve could only be evidence. The next idea queued instead stays inside the rules: buy short-term dips only among last year's strongest stocks. The bounce book showed that a one-month fall is worth little on its own, but the momentum books already skip the latest month for exactly this reason, so the bounce may pay as a timing tweak *inside* momentum's winners rather than as a separate engine. That idea sits in the bounce family, not the residual-momentum family, so the kin rule does not block it before it has run.

`lab walkforward M0028`: 2 of 4 folds, 2009-2015 edge -3.3 points. `lab promote` would exit 2 on the folds condition, so no promotion was attempted. The only eligible variant is half the residual-momentum engine, whose family has already test-failed, so it would not be a fresh candidate either way. The bounce book on its own only matched SPY.
