lost between 22.2% and 22.8% from a peak, and the limit is 20%. So the method is rejected. Worse,
all five fell further than the book they were built on, which lost 20.6%. Whichever way the twenty
names were chosen, the fall was the same.

That is not a mystery once you look at when the falls happened. The drizzle book's worst fall ran
from 7 July to 22 August 2011 — six weeks, the debt-ceiling fight and the euro scare. The combined
book's and the residual drizzle book's worst falls both ran from 17 July to 31 August 1998 — six
weeks, Russia defaulting and the LTCM hedge fund blowing up. These are market-wide crashes that
arrive in weeks. The 200-day average that this book uses to step aside takes months to turn, so it
was still fully invested when they hit, and when the whole market drops 15% in six weeks it does
not matter one bit whether your twenty names got their gains smoothly or in jumps. **Choosing better
names cannot fix a fall caused by owning stocks at all.** Only owning less — a brake on position
size — can.

**The mirror died on the residual ranking, and that is the most useful thing here.** On the plain
one-year ranking, drizzle beat jumps by 2.3 points. On the residual ranking, drizzle earned 11.90%
and jumps earned 11.99% — identical, and if anything the wrong way round. Gains-to-losses 1.85
against 1.83. Nothing. The signal that was worth 2.3 points a year on one pool was worth zero on
the other.

My first guess was that the residual ranking already prefers smooth names, leaving nothing to sort.
I measured it rather than assuming it, on 76 quarterly dates across the window, and **that guess was
wrong.** Average smoothness of the forty names picked by plain gain: +0.065. Of the forty picked by
the residual ranking: +0.052 — *less* smooth, not more. And the spread of smoothness inside the
residual pool was slightly *wider* (0.053 against 0.049), so there was, if anything, more to sort
on, not less. The two pools only share about 18 of their 40 names, so they really are different
books.

What I think is actually going on: **I measured the wrong return stream.** The residual ranking
scores a stock on its move after the market's own move is taken out. But I counted up days and down
days on the stock's *total* daily return — market move included. For a stock chosen because its
market-adjusted drift was steady, the up-and-down pattern of its raw price is mostly the market's
pattern, not the stock's, so the count says nothing about the thing the ranking cared about. The
matched pair separated by 2.3 points; the mismatched pair separated by zero. That is a clean reading
and it points directly at the next experiment: count the up and down days of the *residual* returns,
the same stream the residual ranking is built on. I have queued it.

The honest alternative is duller: the effect simply is not there for residual winners. I cannot rule
it out from this run. But the measurement above rules out the "nothing left to sort" story, and
"measure the path of the same thing you ranked on" is a cheap and specific test that settles it
either way.

**How likely is this to be real rather than luck?** The lab scores that with a number called DSR,
which discounts a result by how many different ideas have been tried — because if you try enough
things, something will look good by accident. The lab counts 31 distinct methods now, and your bar
since 7 October is 0.90. The drizzle book scores 0.923, the combined book 0.924, both residual
versions 0.937 and 0.943. All clear the bar. The jumps book scores 0.799 and does not — which is
itself the right answer, since it is the version that is supposed to be bad. Note the irony worth
keeping in mind: the *highest* luck score in this batch, 0.943, belongs to the jumps-on-residual
book, a configuration I registered in advance as meaningless. That score measures steadiness, not
whether an idea makes sense.

**Worst year, and how much of the time it was invested.** The drizzle book's worst calendar year was
2011, down 4.2%. The combined book's was 2006, down just 1.0%. All five were invested about 69.5% of
the time — identical to the book they came from, which is expected, since the market trend gate was
untouched.

**Did the hypothesis hold?** Half of it, and I said in advance which half I expected. I wrote that
smoothness would show up "first in the gains-to-losses ratio and the worst fall rather than in the
return." It showed up strongly in gains-to-losses (2.09 against 1.72) and in the return (2.3 points
a year, more than I expected). It showed up in the worst fall **not at all** — and I had written that
"a smaller worst fall at the same return is the result that would matter most here." That is the
result I wanted and did not get.

**Did the expected failure happen?** Partly, and in a way that is worth recording precisely.

* I feared the mirror would fail to separate — that this universe of 539 big, heavily watched names
  would have had the effect arbitraged out of it, since the paper's effect is strongest in small,
  ignored stocks. **That did not happen on the plain ranking.** It is alive and worth 2.3 points a
  year even among the most watched companies in America. That genuinely surprised me.
* I feared halving the pool would cost more momentum than the smoothness was worth. **Not against
  the control it was registered against** — the drizzle book beat the jumps book clearly. But I have
  to be straight about a gap: the lab has never run the plain twenty-name one-year-gain book at real
  fees on your real deposits, so I cannot tell you whether the drizzle book beats *that*. The only
  clean comparison this run supports is drizzle against jumps, and that one it wins.
* I feared the residual side would be redundant. **It was worse than redundant — it was empty**, and
  measuring it told me why I had probably built it wrong.

**Compared with your current best book.** All five of these lose to it: 12.1% at a 22.8% fall against
13.7% at a 20.6% fall. Both were measured the same way, at the same real fees, on the same deposits,
in the same run, so that comparison is apples to apples with nothing hidden. The smoothness idea, as
built here, does not improve on what you already have.

**My opinion:** this direction is worth more trials, but not the ones I just ran. The finding that
matters is narrow and solid — among last year's winners, the ones that got there quietly keep going
and the ones that got there in jumps give it back, worth 2.3 points a year and a quarter less churn,
even in large liquid stocks. The finding that does not matter is everything I built on top of it:
swapping the ranking underneath broke it, and nothing about choosing names was ever going to touch a
22% fall caused by a six-week market crash. Do not spend a test-window look on any of these five.
They fail the fall limit on the development window, and four looks have already been spent on books
that failed on the real window for reasons the development window could not see.

Two things next, and I have queued both. First and more interesting: measure smoothness on the
*same* return stream you ranked on — count the up and down days of the market-adjusted move, not the
raw price — inside the residual book. That is a one-line change to a measure that already works, and
this run is good evidence that the mismatch is why the residual version died. If it works it adds
quality to the book you already trade, and the lower churn pays for itself in fees. Second and
duller: the combined book has the best gains-to-losses ratio of any real-fee book in this lab, 2.17,
and the lowest churn, so it is the cheapest book to run a position-size brake on. Your residual book
showed what that brake costs — the lab measured it this week — and it is expensive, roughly a point
and a half of yearly return for every point of fall removed near the limit. Buying 2.8 points of fall
at that rate would cost about four points of return and land near 8%, barely above the market. So I
expect that second one to fail, and I am queuing it anyway, because "expensive" measured once is
worth more than "expensive" assumed forever. The first idea is the one I would spend the next run on.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0036-RM-CONT`: DSR 0.9057 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0036-RM-DISC`: DSR 0.9133 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Among last year's winners, the ones that climbed quietly beat the ones that jumped by 2.3 points a year (12.1% vs 9.8% on your deposits, 572k vs 436k ended) with a quarter less churn — but every version still fell 22%, over the 20% limit, because a six-week market crash does not care which names you picked.

methods.name: Blend total and residual momentum instead of choosing between them
methods.sourceRef: insight 58's third recommendation; M0007/M0032 (residual) against F4-MOM12 (total)
methods.hypothesis: Insight 58's third recommendation, held back from the 2026-10-09 batch only because the batch had four slots and this was the fifth idea. The lab has treated total momentum and residual momentum as rivals: F4-MOM12-N20-TREND earns +16.2% a year on dev with a 22.2% worst fall, M0007-N20-RAW earns +15.0% with 19.6%, and stripping the market's move out of the ranking was filed as a virtue. Insight 58 complicates that: refusing high-beta names is exactly how a beta-stripped book makes itself a standing bet against a narrow, mega-cap-led market, which is the regime that has run almost unbroken since late 2023. A rank-average of the two scores, or a weight sweep from pure total to pure residual, would say what the lab has never asked: whether the two signals are substitutes or complements, and where on that line the worst fall is smallest per point of return. Run at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares on the monthly-hold-frac-gotrade preset, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th, so the answer is directly comparable with M0032.

methods.name: Regime gate on the yield curve, not on price: stand down for two years after it inverts
methods.hypothesis: The inverted yield curve as a recession signal was published by Estrella & Hardouvelis (1991) and Estrella & Mishkin (1996) and has been on the NY Fed's site monthly since the late 1990s, so it was public through the whole dev window: any edge is not from being early to it, but from the fact that a bond-market signal cannot be traded away by stock traders. Sharpened from the idea row: no credit-spread series exists in the store, so this tests the term-spread half alone, on 10-year minus 13-week bill (the NY Fed's 10y-3m) and, as a second reading, 10-year minus 5-year. Every lab book uses a SPY 200-day trend gate, which reads the price it protects and whipsaws in corrections that never become bear markets. The curve inverts 6-18 months before a recession and has usually re-steepened by the time stocks fall, so the gate is a WATCH: open from the first inverted day until 730 calendar days after the last one (two years: the literature's lead plus the bear market; an assumption, not fitted). WATCH variants sit in cash while it is open (macro only, no price). 2KEY variants sit in cash only while the watch is open AND SPY closes at or below its 200-day average: the trend gate armed only after the curve has warned. Claim: the trend gate's false alarms (1998, 2010, 2011, 2015) came with a steep curve and its real saves (2000-2002, 2007-2009) came after an inversion, so 2KEY keeps the saves and drops the whipsaws. Hosts as M0039 (not momentum: every momentum book moves with one that already lost its test look): (1) SPY, decided every session; (2) M0076-X-M's big-dividend-raise book (20 slots at 5%, rest in SPY) with its own SPY-200 switch removed, re-picked monthly, re-scaled weekly. All variants fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits. Variants: SPY-WATCH, SPY-2KEY, DIV-OPEN (control, no gate), DIV-WATCH, DIV-2KEY, DIV-2KEY-5Y (2KEY on 10y-5y). Controls on record: M0039-SPY-200 (SPY 200-day switch, same daily rules) and M0039-DIV (the book behind its SPY-200 switch, same weekly rules). Assumed: cash earns nothing; a spread reading needs both yields dated the same day; before 1993-11-02 the watch is closed. Success: the 2KEY gate beats the plain 200-day switch on the same host in funded return without a deeper worst fall, its 2009-2015 cost is under a point a year against the ungated host, and a DIV variant beats total-return SPY within the 25% worst-fall limit.
methods.expectedFailure: Two inversions in twenty years is two data points: the dev window holds only 2000 and 2006-07 on 10y-3m, so whatever the result, the luck check sees a gate that fired twice and the evidence is thin by construction. WATCH sells SPY in August 2000 and September 2006 and misses the last 15-20% of the 2006-07 rally and the first months of the 2009 rebound (the watch stays open until May 2009), so SPY-WATCH may save 2008 and still lose on return; it trades a handful of times, so it fails the 100-trade bar regardless. 2KEY outside a watch is buy-and-hold, so it keeps the 1998 fall (about 19% on SPY) and the 2011 fall; inside a watch it is the 200-day switch, which whipsawed in 2000-2002 and 2008. So 2KEY may equal the 200-day switch through both bears and beat it only by the fees and lost days of 2010-2015 whipsaws: a real but small gain, perhaps a point a year in 2009-2015 and nothing before. 10y-5y inverts in late 1994, mid-1998 and 2000 but barely in 2006, so the 5Y watch is open during 1998 (helping) and closed through 2008 (no protection at all), likely worse than 10y-3m. The dividend book's own worst fall (about 22-25%) came in 1998-2002; without its own switch DIV-OPEN may fall 35-50% in 2008, and if the watch fails to cut it in time DIV-WATCH and DIV-2KEY inherit that. No variant is likely to clear the 0.90 luck bar.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

Unblocked: the missing data arrived. Only the yield-curve half arrived. The 13-week Treasury bill and the 5-, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields, in percent, now load from the research store's market series (the store calls them T13W, T5Y, T10Y and T30Y). The longer yields start on 2 November 1993 and the bill on 29 January 1993. The 10-year minus 13-week spread exists on 4,966 of the 4,984 trading days the dev window holds index members (99.6%). The 18 missing days are bond-market holidays, where the last published yield carries over, so the spread covers the whole dev window: 19.8 of 19.8 years. Two differences from the idea as written. First, the spread is 10-year minus 13-week bill, not 10-year minus 2-year: no 2-year series was available. Second, the credit-spread half (corporate BAA yield minus the 10-year) and the inflation-protected yield are still unavailable, because the paid data plan has no corporate or inflation-protected bond yields. So only the yield-curve gate is testable, and a test must say it tests that half alone.

It was blocked on: FRED daily series in the research store: T10Y2Y (term spread), BAA10Y (credit spread), DGS10, DFII10. Free API, no key needed; needs a research_store loader and a manifest file beside fx.csv.


### 2026-10-16

## What was tried

When the 10-year Treasury yield drops below the 3-month bill yield, the yield curve has "inverted". Bond traders are betting that rates will fall, which usually means they expect a recession. Two papers from the 1990s (Estrella and Hardouvelis 1991, Estrella and Mishkin 1996) showed that this signal has led every US recession since the 1960s, and the New York Fed has published it every month since the late 1990s. So the idea was never a secret. The bet here is a different one: stock traders cannot trade a bond-market signal away.

The original idea asked for the yield curve **and** the gap between corporate and Treasury bond yields (a credit spread). The store holds no corporate yields, so this tested the curve alone. It read the curve two ways: the 10-year minus the 13-week bill (the New York Fed's version), and the 10-year minus the 5-year.

The curve gives its warning a long time ahead. A recession usually starts 6 to 18 months after an inversion, and by the time stocks fall the curve has often turned normal again. "Sit in cash while the curve is inverted" would therefore sell early and buy back just before the damage. The gate is built as a **watch** instead. It opens on the first inverted day and stays open for two years after the last one. The two-year length was set beforehand from the literature's lead time plus the length of a bear market; it was not fitted to results. Two ways to use the watch:

- **WATCH**: sit in cash for as long as the watch is open. Price plays no part.
- **2KEY**: sit in cash only while the watch is open **and** SPY is at or below its 200-day average. This is the trend switch every book in the lab already uses, switched on only after the curve has warned.

On the 13-week reading, the dev window holds just two inversions: August 2000 to January 2001, and August 2006 to May 2007. So the watch was open from August 2000 to January 2003, and again from August 2006 to May 2009.

Hosts were the same as the fear-index gate (M0039), so the two gates compare like for like. No momentum books were used, because every momentum book now moves with one that has already failed its test look.
- **SPY** itself, checked every trading day.
- **The big-dividend-raise book** from M0076-X-M: up to 20 companies that just raised their dividend by 25% or more, with the rest in SPY. Its own 200-day switch was **removed**, so the curve gate replaces the trend switch instead of sitting on top of it. The book is re-picked monthly and re-checked weekly.

Every variant traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly deposits. Cash earned no interest.

## Result

| variant | your money, per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall (recorded) | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY-WATCH | +10.9% | +7.9% | 18.9% | failed: only 2 trades (100 needed) |
| SPY-2KEY | +10.9% | +7.7% | 23.1% | failed: only 23 trades |
| DIV-OPEN (control, no gate) | +9.3% | +7.2% | 57.6% | failed: fall over the 50% screen, luck |
| DIV-WATCH | +12.6% | +7.2% | 25.7% | **passed the dev screen** |
| DIV-2KEY | +12.5% | +7.2% | 25.7% | **passed the dev screen** |
| DIV-2KEY-5Y | +12.3% | +7.2% | 29.5% | **passed the dev screen** |

The controls already on record ran on the same rules:

- SPY behind its 200-day switch (M0039-SPY-200): +5.3% a year.
- The dividend book behind its own 200-day switch (M0039-DIV): +6.0% a year.

The curve gate beat the trend switch on both hosts, by about 5 to 6 points a year.

**The luck check (DSR).** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab now judges at N = 106: one look per distinct method, read off the lab's status. The bar is 0.90. DIV-WATCH scored 0.964, DIV-2KEY 0.955, DIV-2KEY-5Y 0.903 and SPY-WATCH 0.961. Read the scores with care, though. They measure how smooth the curve is. They cannot measure that the gate made only two decisions in twenty years (see below).

**The worst fall.** The recorded 25.7% is measured with the deposits still inside. That passes the lab's dev screen (50%) but sits just over the 25% bar for real money in design §1. With the deposits taken out, month-end values give a worst fall of 22.3% for DIV-WATCH, in the summer of 2011. The fall came from the dividend book itself in a scare the curve never warned about. It was not a crash the gate missed.

## Where the gains came from, era by era

Growth per year, with the deposits taken out so a fall shows its real depth. The numbers come from each trial's recorded month-end curve. SPY's column is total-return SPY from the store's prices.

| era | SPY | SPY-WATCH | SPY-2KEY | SPY-200 | DIV-OPEN | DIV (200-day) | DIV-WATCH | DIV-2KEY | DIV-2KEY-5Y |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +6.9% | +13.6% | +11.7% | +3.8% | +8.1% | +9.8% | +14.8% | +14.6% | +8.6% |
| 2003-2008 | +1.3% | +7.2% | +8.2% | +4.3% | +3.9% | +6.2% | +11.0% | +11.7% | +9.5% |
| 2009-2015 | +14.9% | +12.8% | +13.5% | +7.8% | +18.1% | +7.0% | +15.3% | +14.8% | +19.1% |
| 2000-2002 | -12.6% | -0.2% | -3.8% | -10.9% | -12.7% | -5.9% | +0.2% | -0.2% | -8.2% |
| 2007-2009 | -5.1% | +3.6% | +3.9% | +3.9% | -6.6% | +1.4% | +3.3% | +1.5% | +10.2% |
| 2009 alone | +25.2% | +11.2% | +15.7% | +15.7% | +29.3% | +7.0% | +10.2% | +7.0% | +37.2% |

What this shows:

- **Both bear markets were dodged almost whole.** The watch opened in August 2000 and September 2006, months before each fall began. DIV-WATCH came through 2000-2002 flat, where SPY lost 12.6% a year. It came through 2007-2009 up 3.3% a year, where SPY lost 5.1%.
- **The trend switch's real cost was its false alarms in good years.** In 2009-2015 the dividend book behind the 200-day switch made +7.0% a year. The same book with no switch made +18.1%. The switch sold in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 scares and bought back after each rebound. During those years the curve was steep and the watch was closed, so DIV-WATCH stayed invested and made +15.3%. This is the hypothesis's main claim, and it held.
- **The watch cost the start of 2009.** The 2006-07 inversion ended in May 2007, so the watch stayed open until May 2009. It missed the rebound from the March low, and DIV-WATCH made +10.2% in 2009 where the open book made +29.3%. That is most of the 2.8 points a year DIV-WATCH gave up to its ungated host in 2009-2015. It is the expected failure, and it happened as written.
- **2KEY was no better than WATCH.** Inside a watch it is the trend switch, which whipsawed through 2000-2002, and outside a watch both are simply invested. So DIV-2KEY and DIV-WATCH ended almost the same. The hypothesis expected 2KEY to win by the whipsaws it avoids, and it did not.
- **The 10-year minus 5-year reading was a different and luckier gate.** It inverted in 1998 and 2000 but hardly in 2006. Its watch closed in time to catch the 2009 rebound (+37.2%) but left 2000-2002 half unprotected (-8.2% a year). Its fine 2009-2015 number comes from being out of the market at the right moment by accident, not from reading the cycle better.

## Is it real? The honest problems

1. **Two decisions in twenty years.** The 13-week gate made exactly two calls, and both were right. A coin also comes up heads twice in a row one time in four. The luck check scores the smoothness of the curve those two calls produced. It cannot see that the calls themselves are a sample of two.
2. **The two-year length was chosen knowing roughly where the bear markets ended.** It was set before the run, and the reason was written down (the literature's lead plus a bear market's length). But the writer knew that 2002 and 2009 were the bottoms. A one-year watch would have bought back into the middle of both falls. This is hindsight in the design, even with no result in hand.
3. **The walk-forward folds split 2 to 2.** In the lab's four three-year folds, the variant each fold would have picked won 2003-2005 and 2006-2008. It lost 2009-2011, where DIV-2KEY made +26% against SPY's +61% because it missed the 2009 rebound. It tied 2012-2014, at +65.8% against +65.9%. DIV-WATCH on its own won 3 of the 4. The hard gate needs a majority of folds won by the method's own picks, so `lab promote` refuses M0038, and that refusal is correct. A method whose best variant changes from fold to fold is a selection, not a rule.
4. **The host is a dividend-raise book, and its own edge is fading.** DIV-OPEN had no gate at all, yet still beat SPY by 3 points a year in 2009-2015. Part of what DIV-WATCH earned is that book's edge, not the gate's. The gate's own contribution is the difference against DIV-OPEN: about +6.7 points a year over 1996-2002, +7.1 over 2003-2008 and -2.8 over 2009-2015.
5. **What the curve has done since 2015 is public knowledge, and it is a warning.** The 10-year minus 3-month curve inverted briefly in 2019, then again from late 2022 into late 2024, the longest inversion on record. No bear market followed the second one. This is general bond-market history, not anything read from the lab's test window. A two-year watch would have sat in cash through much of the 2023-2025 rally. That is exactly the false alarm the dev window, with its two clean events, could never show.

## The check with dead companies added back

The dev store has no prices for most companies that later went bankrupt or were bought out. The lab keeps a second store with most of them restored, so each variant was re-run on it. The SPY variants hold only SPY, so nothing changed. The dividend-book variants lost about a point a year:

| variant | your money, per year: dev store, then with dead companies | worst fall | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead over SPY a year (your money) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DIV-OPEN | +9.3% -> +7.9% | 57.6% -> 59.2% | 0.554 -> 0.469 | +2.5% -> +1.1% |
| DIV-WATCH | +12.6% -> +11.4% | 25.7% -> 27.0% | 0.964 -> 0.933 | -1.1% -> -2.1% |
| DIV-2KEY | +12.5% -> +11.5% | 25.7% -> 27.0% | 0.955 -> 0.925 | -1.6% -> -2.7% |
| DIV-2KEY-5Y | +12.3% -> +11.6% | 29.5% -> 29.6% | 0.903 -> 0.889 | +2.7% -> +1.4% |

Every gated dividend variant still beats SPY by about 4 points a year with the dead companies included. That point a year is the dividend book's picks being flattered by the missing failures. The gate itself does not depend on stock prices, so it is not affected.

The last column uses the lab's own measure: money-weighted, deposits included. On that measure DIV-WATCH **trailed** SPY by 1.1 points a year in 2009-2015, and by 2.1 points with dead companies included. The era table above strips the deposits out and shows +15.3% against +14.9% instead. The gap between the two is the deposits: the money that arrived in early 2009 sat in cash through the rebound. Either way, the gated book roughly matched SPY in the best-covered years and did not beat it. The whole lead was earned in 2000-2008, by being out of the market during two bear markets.

So the buy signal for survivorship-free data does not fire. Walk-forward and the 2009-2015 era both point the same way.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Partly. The core claim held on dev: the curve gate kept the trend switch's two big saves and dropped its 2010-2015 whipsaws, beating the trend switch by 5 to 6 points a year on both hosts. The 2KEY refinement added nothing. The expected failures showed up as written: the late return in 2009, the 100-trade bar failed on SPY, the 10y-5y reading behaving worse in 2000-2002, and the two-data-point problem. The one surprise was size. The dev result is far better than expected, and with two events, a result that good should make us more suspicious, not less.

My opinion: this is the most interesting risk control the lab has found, and the least proven. Its record rests on two calls, and anyone who has read about 2022-2024 knows the third call was wrong. I would not spend a test look on it as it stands, and the hard gate will not let me anyway. The direction is worth one or two more trials, aimed at its two weak points. First, close the watch early once SPY has climbed back above its 200-day average after the watch has been open a year, so it stops missing the rebound off the bottom. Second, put the watch on a plain market-shaped host instead of the dividend book, so the gate's own effect is measured without another edge on top. If the early-exit version still dodges 2000-2002 and 2008 and wins a majority of folds, it is the first gate here worth a counted look.


### 2026-10-16

Sera, 2026-10-16: not promoted. The hard gate refuses this method: when the best version is re-picked inside each walk-forward stretch it wins 2 of 4, short of the strict majority the gate requires (the dividend-book watch version alone wins 3 of 4, but the gate judges the pick, and the pick changed). Its kin is clean, so the refusal is on the folds alone. No buy signal: besides the folds, its 2009-2015 lead on the money-weighted measure is negative (about -1.1% a year, -2.1% on the survivorship-check store). The switch made only two calls in twenty years, so its fine dev record rests on two events.
methods.verdict: Passed the dev screen but refused for a test look: it sat out both bear markets after the yield curve warned, yet those were its only two calls in twenty years, and it only matched SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: Risk gate on the VIX term structure, which turns days before a 200-day average
methods.hypothesis: The VIX term structure as a stress signal has been public since VIX futures listed (2004) and widely traded by volatility funds since about 2012, so the dev window (to 2015) sees it before most of the crowd. The 200-day trend gate reacts only after the market has fallen a long way; the one-month fear index rising above the three-month one marks the start of a shock, so a gate on it should step aside sooner. Hosts, chosen so no momentum book is involved (every momentum book moves with a book that already lost its test look): (1) SPY itself, decided every session, cash when the gate is off, fractional at Gotrade's real fees; (2) M0076-X-M's big-dividend-raise book (20 slots, rest in SPY, behind its SPY-200 switch), re-picked monthly and re-scaled weekly so the gate can cut it between re-picks. Variants: SPY-TS (off while VIX/VIX3M >= 1.00), SPY-SPIKE (off while VIX >= 1.20x its own 63-session mean: a proxy for inversion that covers the whole window, mid-1998 included), SPY-200 (control: the SPY 200-day switch on the same daily rules), DIV (control: the host on the weekly-resize rules, no VIX gate), DIV-TS and DIV-SPIKE (the host behind each gate). VIX3M starts 2006-07-17; before it the TS gate is on, so TS variants equal their controls trade for trade until mid-2006 and the paired difference is the gate over 2006-2015, which includes 2008, the May 2010 flash crash and August 2011. Assumed: cash earns nothing (no T-bill credit), a series value older than 7 days is no reading (gate on), the gate reads the fear index's close on day d and trades at the next open. Success: the gated host beats its control on funded return with a shallower worst fall over 2006-2015, and a gated variant beats total-return SPY within the 20% worst fall with a positive 2009-2015 edge.
methods.expectedFailure: Inversions are frequent, brief and mostly harmless (August 2007, May 2010, August 2011, October 2014, August 2015 all reversed within weeks), so the gate sells after the first drop and buys back after the rebound, paying Gotrade's fees both ways and missing the recovery days that follow fear spikes. Over 2006-2015 SPY's worst fall (2008) would be cut, but the 2009-2015 years, a long rally punctuated by short scares, should cost the gated SPY a point or more a year against plain SPY. SPY-TS before mid-2006 is SPY less fees, so over the full window it cannot beat SPY by much even if the gate works; its worst fall from 1996-2003 (the 2000-2002 bear, about 47%) is untouched, so SPY-TS fails the 20% limit regardless. SPY-SPIKE covers that bear market, but 2001-2002 was a slow grind with few spikes, so it likely still falls well over 20%. On the dividend host the weekly cut re-enters only at the next monthly re-pick, so every false alarm costs up to a month out of the market; the host's 21.9% worst fall came in the 1998-2002 fast falls, which the TS gate cannot see, so DIV-TS likely keeps that fall and only DIV-SPIKE can address it. Cash earning nothing understates the gate slightly in 2006-2008.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

Unblocked: the missing data arrived. The fear index and its three-month version now load from the research store's market series (the store calls them VIX and VIX3M; the three-month series was named VXV until November 2007, and the store uses the newer name wherever both exist). The three-month series starts on 17 July 2006, so this gate can be tested on 2,331 of the 4,984 trading days the dev window holds index members: 46.8%, about 9.3 of 19.8 years, mid-2006 to October 2015. That span includes the 2008 crash, the May 2010 flash crash and the August 2011 downgrade. It does not include the mid-1998 fall this idea was written for, nor 2000-2002. The two names of the three-month series agree on 1,987 of the 1,996 days they overlap and differ by at most 1.05 points (15 October 2014). A fair test compares the gate with the same book over the same 2006-2015 span, not over the whole window.

It was blocked on: CBOE VIX and VIX3M daily closes in the research store. Free; VIX3M history starts 2002-09, so the gate is only testable on the back half of the dev window.


### 2026-10-11

Sera 20261011-1815 reserves this. Host choice: gate SPY itself (SPY vs cash at the T-bill rate, fractional at Gotrade's real fees), with the big-dividend-raise book as a second host, not a momentum book. Every momentum book now moves with a book that has already lost its test look (residual correlation 0.92-0.97), so a gated momentum book could never be promoted whatever its numbers. Paired control: the same host ungated and with the SPY-200 switch, over the same mid-2006 to October 2015 span the VIX3M series covers.


### 2026-10-11

## What was tried

The fear index (VIX) measures how much protection traders are paying for over the next month. A sister index (VIX3M) measures the same over three months. Normally the one-month reading sits below the three-month one. When a shock hits, the one-month reading jumps above it; traders call this the curve "inverting". The idea was that an inversion marks the *start* of a fall, while the 200-day average only reacts once the market is already well down. So a book that steps into cash on an inversion should fall less.

The three-month series only starts in July 2006, so the term-structure gate could only act from mid-2006 to October 2015. Before that it stays on, and the gated book matches its host trade for trade. A second gate covers the whole window: step out when the fear index is 20% or more above its own three-month average (a "fear spike"), which roughly tracks an inversion.

Two hosts, neither of them momentum books (every momentum book now moves with one that already failed its test look):

- **SPY itself**, checked every trading day, in cash while the gate is off. Controls: SPY (the benchmark) and SPY behind its 200-day average on the same daily rules (SPY-200).
- **The big-dividend-raise book** (the M0076-X-M book: up to 20 companies that just raised their dividend 25% or more, the rest in SPY, behind its own SPY-200 switch). It is re-picked monthly and re-checked weekly, so the gate can cut it between re-picks. Control: the same book on the same weekly rules with no fear gate (DIV).

All six run in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly deposits. Assumed before the run and written in the method: cash earns no interest, a fear reading more than 7 days old counts as no reading (gate on), and the gate reads day d's close and trades at the next open.

## Result

Every variant lost to SPY on the owner's deposits, and **every gate lost to its own ungated control**.

| variant | your money, per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY-TS (term-structure gate) | +5.0% | +7.9% | 47.5% | beats SPY, fall, trades, luck |
| SPY-SPIKE (fear-spike gate) | +3.3% | +7.9% | 63.6% | beats SPY, fall, gains vs losses, luck |
| SPY-200 (control) | +5.3% | +7.7% | 34.6% | beats SPY, fall, trades, luck |
| DIV (control, no gate) | +6.0% | +7.2% | 25.1% | beats SPY, fall, luck |
| DIV-TS | +3.4% | +7.2% | 23.5% | beats SPY, fall, gains vs losses, luck |
| DIV-SPIKE | +3.8% | +7.2% | 20.4% | beats SPY, fall, luck |

The luck check (DSR: how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries) was 0.17-0.70 against the 0.90 bar, at N = 62 (one look per distinct method in the lab). None came close.

## Where the gate lost: the paired comparison by era

Growth per year with the deposits taken back out, so a fall reads as deep as it really was:

| era | SPY | SPY-TS | SPY-SPIKE | SPY-200 | DIV | DIV-TS | DIV-SPIKE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996 to mid-2006 | +8.5% | +8.4% | +2.6% | +4.6% | +10.4% | +10.4% | +9.6% |
| mid-2006 to 2008 | -11.5% | -11.0% | -13.4% | +2.2% | +1.5% | -0.8% | +2.2% |
| 2009-2015 | +16.7% | +10.2% | +11.6% | +7.9% | +7.1% | +3.0% | +2.9% |

- **In 2008 the term-structure gate barely helped.** SPY-TS fell 45% from May 2007 to March 2009, against SPY's 51%. The curve stayed normal through the slow first year of the bear market (late 2007 to August 2008, when SPY was already down about 20%). It only inverted after Lehman, by which time the 200-day average had long since turned. So the premise was wrong: in the one big crash the window holds, the inversion came *later* than the trend signal, not earlier.
- **In 2009-2015 it cost 6.5 points a year.** The fear curve inverted in May 2010, August 2011, late 2014 and August 2015. Each time the gate sold after the first drop and bought back after the rebound. The days just after a fear spike are some of the market's best, and the gate sat them out. This is the expected failure, but much bigger than the "point or more" written down.
- **The fear-spike gate was worse everywhere.** Over 1996-2006 it turned SPY's +8.5% a year into +2.6%: it sold into every scare of 1997-2003 and missed every rebound, and still fell 60% from 2000 to 2009.
- **On the dividend book both gates took return and gave back almost no safety.** DIV-SPIKE's worst fall (19.4%) only just squeaks under the 20% limit, and it got there by earning 4 points a year less than its control in 2009-2015.

## A second finding: the weekly frame itself is expensive

The DIV control is the same dividend book as M0076-X-M, only re-checked weekly instead of monthly. That change alone took it from +11.8% a year to +7.7% (deposits removed, 1996-2015), from +13.6% to +7.1% in 2009-2015, and deepened its worst fall from 16.6% to 23.3%. The reason is how the engine handles a weekly cut: when the SPY-200 switch turns off mid-month the whole book goes to cash, and it can only come back at the next monthly re-pick. Each false alarm costs up to a month out of the market. So a weekly cut with monthly re-entry is a bad frame for any book, independent of the gate. This agrees with what the weekly-repick variants of M0076 showed (+5-6% vs +10-11%).

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The term structure did not turn days before the 200-day average in 2008; it turned weeks after it. And in the short scares it did catch, stepping out cost more than it saved, because rebounds come fast after fear peaks. The expected failure happened, and worse than expected. The written-down guess that DIV-TS could not fix the dividend book's 1998-2002 fall was right in a different way: with the weekly frame the host's worst fall moved to 2011-2012 (23.3%), and the term-structure gate cut it only to 20.3%, still over the limit.

The fear-index curve is published and has been traded by volatility funds since about 2012; even a dev win would likely have faded. It did not get that far.

**My opinion:** using the fear curve to step *out* is dead, on both hosts and both readings, and I would not spend another variation on exits. What the run did show is that the biggest returns sit right after the fear peaks. That points the other way: the fear curve may be useful as a *re-entry* signal. The 200-day switch's known cost is coming back late after a crash (2009, 2011 recoveries). A book that leaves on the 200-day average but returns as soon as the fear curve is back to normal (one-month below three-month) might keep the switch's protection and cut its late-return cost. That is one clean test, and I have queued it. Separately, the weekly-cut/monthly-return frame should be avoided for every book; the monthly frame wins by 4 points a year here.
methods.verdict: Rejected: stepping out when the fear index's curve inverts cost SPY 6.5 points a year in 2009-2015 and saved little in 2008, where the curve turned after the 200-day average did

methods.name: Avoid the crowded side of momentum using short interest
methods.sourceRef: FINRA consolidated short interest, published twice monthly, free
methods.hypothesis: Momentum crashes are partly a short-squeeze and crowding phenomenon, and this lab has eleven flavours of momentum and no measure of how crowded any of its picks are. Rank on residual momentum as M0007 does, then drop or underweight the names in the top decile of short interest as a share of float. Expected failure: in a long-only book the crowded names are often simply the best momentum names, so the filter cuts the winners and the return falls more than the drawdown does; or the twice-monthly publication lag makes the measure stale exactly when it would matter.
methods.blockedOn: FINRA consolidated short interest, twice monthly per symbol, plus shares float to make it a ratio. Free download; needs a loader and a point-in-time join on the settlement date, never the publication date.

methods.name: The real-fee residual book behind the fast crash gate, aimed at the summer-of-1998 shock
methods.hypothesis: M0033 proved by elimination that a trailing-volatility brake cannot defend this book: five strengths from TV22 down to TV14 were tested on the real-fee fractional funded configuration, and the worst fall sat at 19.9-20.0% across the three that kept the return, because the binding episode is Jul-Aug 1998 -- fast, and arriving after a calm stretch, so a 21-day volatility estimate reads scale 1.0 on the way in and clamps only during the rebound (skew worsens monotonically from -0.32 unbraked to -0.59 at TV18, the fingerprint of taking none of the fall and some of the recovery). The fall is therefore a timing problem, not a sizing problem, and the lab already owns a tool shaped for it: M0012's fast crash gate, which reads the market's own sudden move over days rather than the basket's trailing jumpiness over a month. This method puts M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT behind that gate instead of under the volatility brake -- same ranking, same screen, same SPY-200 trend gate, same fractional shares at Gotrade's measured fees on the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, so the only change from M0032 is the crash gate. I expect it to cut the 20.65% fall to the mid-to-high teens while giving up far less than the brake did, because it acts on the days that actually made the fall rather than taxing every month to pay for days it never catches: the brake charged 1.8 points of yearly return per point of fall removed at the light end, where M0032's unbraked book has the lab's best return per unit of fall at 0.66 and every braked version is worse. The bar to clear is the parent's: beat a deposit-matched SPY's 7.2% a year by a wide margin, keep gains-to-losses near 2.0, and land the worst fall with real room under 20% rather than the three ten-thousandths of a point M0033 cleared it by. 2-4 variants spanning the gate's trigger threshold and its re-entry delay, all fixed before the run.

methods.name: Cut exposure on the account's own fall, not on a forecast of it: the real-fee residual book under a drawdown brake
methods.hypothesis: The companion to M0041, and the opposite philosophy. M0033 showed that forecasting trouble from last month's jumpiness fails on this book because its worst fall (Jul-Aug 1998) begins in calm weather: the brake is off on the way in and on during the rebound, so it worsens the downside lopsidedness from -0.32 to -0.59 while leaving the fall at 19.9%. A drawdown brake makes no forecast at all. It reads the account's own equity against its running peak and cuts exposure once the loss passes a threshold, restoring it as the account recovers -- it responds to the loss rather than predicting it, which is the right shape for a shock nobody can see coming. M0013 already built this machinery for the total-return momentum book (basket_drawdown_brake) and it is the lab's untested answer to exactly this failure mode; the backlog has carried it as M0009 since before the real-fee era. This method applies it to M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT: same ranking, same screen, same trend gate, fractional shares at Gotrade's measured fees on the monthly top-up, so the only change from the parent is the brake. The honest worry, written before the run: a drawdown brake sells after the fall has started and buys back after the recovery has started, which is the textbook way to lock in a loss -- M0019 already showed that protective stops on this family 'fire together in market-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound', costing 0.7-2.4 points a year while barely moving the worst fall. So the variants must span the trigger depth (a shallow trigger acts early and whipsaws, a deep one acts too late to help) and the re-entry rule, 3-5 of them fixed in advance. I expect this to beat the volatility brake on the same book -- a lower fall per point of return given up than the brake's 1.8 at the light end -- but I would not be surprised if it, too, cannot beat simply running unbraked, which still holds the lab's best return per unit of fall at 0.66. Either answer settles whether this book's drawdown can be managed at all, or whether it has to be accepted and the method judged on its return.

methods.name: Residual information discreteness: count the up and down days of the residual, not the price
methods.hypothesis: M0036 found the frog-in-the-pan effect alive in this universe on the TOTAL-momentum pool (CONT 12.08% a year money-weighted vs DISC 9.78%, PF 2.09 vs 1.72, turnover 6.42 vs 8.44, 572k vs 436k ended on 149,338 USD paid in) and completely dead on the RESIDUAL pool (RM-CONT 11.90% vs RM-DISC 11.99%, PF 1.85 vs 1.83 -- no separation at all). The obvious explanation, that the residual pool is already continuous so there is nothing left to sort, was MEASURED on 76 quarterly dates 1997-2015 and is false: mean continuity of the top-40 by residual momentum was +0.0516 against +0.0645 for the top-40 by total momentum, with a slightly WIDER within-pool spread (0.0530 vs 0.0490), and the two pools share only 17.7 of 40 names. The remaining explanation is a measurement mismatch: M0036 counted up and down days on each stock's TOTAL daily return while the residual pool is ranked on the market-model RESIDUAL. For a name chosen because its residual drift was steady, the sign pattern of its raw price is dominated by the market's sign pattern, so the count carries no information about the stream the ranking cared about. This method computes information discreteness on the residual daily returns themselves -- sign(cumulative residual) x (share of negative residual days minus share of positive residual days) over the same 12-1 window, from the residuals residual_scores already forms -- and sorts the top-40 residual-momentum pool by it. Frame unchanged from M0032 and M0036: F4's screen, SPY-200 trend gate, top-20, monthly, equal weights, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th. Variants: residual-continuous, its registered residual-discrete mirror, and a blended residual-momentum-plus-residual-continuity rank. The mirror is mandatory -- it is the only thing that made M0036's total-momentum result mean anything. I expect the separation to come back at roughly the size it had on the total pool (2 points a year, a quarter less churn) and I expect the worst fall to stay near 20-22% and the method to be rejected on the fall exactly as M0036 was: this buys quality per trade, not safety. If the separation does come back it is a cheap quality gain on the book the owner already trades, and the lower turnover pays for itself at Gotrade's real fees. If it does not come back, the honest conclusion is that the attention effect is absent for residual winners, which closes the family.

methods.name: A brake on the quietest book: the drizzle blend under an own-volatility target
methods.sourceRef: M0036-BLEND (Da, Gurun & Warachka 2014) + M0001's own-volatility overlay (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015) at M0033's targets, on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade
methods.hypothesis: M0036-BLEND has the best gains-to-losses ratio of any real-fee book in the lab (2.17) and the lowest turnover (6.42 against 8.4-9.5 for every other real-fee book), earning 11.95% a year money-weighted against 7.19% for deposit-matched SPY, and it fails one condition only: a 22.28% worst fall against the 20% limit, taken between 17 July and 31 August 1998. Low turnover matters here because a position-size brake works by trading exposure up and down, and at Gotrade's real fees the cheapest book to brake is the one that already trades least. This method puts M0001's own-volatility target over M0036-BLEND's picks, at the same targets M0033 measured on the residual book, and nothing else changes. M0033 priced this exact brake on a sibling: on M0032 it took the fall from 20.65% to 19.98% at a 22% target (costing 1.2 points of annual money-weighted return), to 19.94% at 18% (2.1 points) and to 16.39% at 14% (3.9 points). I therefore EXPECT THIS TO FAIL, and I am registering it so the expectation is measured rather than assumed: buying 2.3 points of fall at roughly a point and a half of return per point of fall would cost about three points and land near 9% a year, still above the deposit-matched market but well below the 13.68% of the book the owner already has, and the luck score would likely drop below the 0.90 bar as the daily Sharpe falls. The one way it surprises me is if the drizzle book's falls are concentrated in weeks where the BOOK itself was visibly jumpy beforehand -- 1998 and 2011 were both preceded by rising volatility, unlike the calm pre-fall markets that defeated M0002 -- in which case the brake catches more of the fall per point of return than it did on the residual book. Variants: own-vol targets of 22%, 18% and 14% on a 21-session reading, plus one no-brake control re-stating BLEND under the same allocator so the comparison is within-run; the control should reproduce M0036-BLEND's numbers exactly.
methods.expectedFailure: The 1998 fall arrived faster than a one-month volatility reading can follow, so the light 22% target sits at full exposure through it and buys almost nothing, the 18% target buys about a point of fall and stays above 20%, and only the 14% target clears the limit -- at a cost of three to four points of yearly return and a luck score under 0.90. A second way it fails: a calm, continuous-momentum basket has low own volatility most of the time, so the brake binds rarely and then all at once, and the monthly resize trades it places at the bottom of a fall lock in losses that the unbraked book would have recovered; the braked variants then lose return without a matching fall cut.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The drizzle blend (M0036-BLEND) picks 20 stocks whose past year's rise came in many small steady days, not a few big jumps. It earned your money 11.95% a year against 7.19% for the same deposits put into SPY, and it failed one rule only: its worst fall was 22.28%, over the 20% limit. That fall happened in the summer of 1998.

This method kept those exact picks and added a brake. Each month it measures how jumpy the 20-stock basket was over the last 21 trading days. If the basket was jumpier than a target, it buys less and holds the rest in cash. There were three targets (22%, 18% and 14% yearly volatility), plus a control with no brake. Everything ran at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares, with 5,000,000 IDR added on the 25th of each month.

## Results (dev window 1996 to 2015, money-weighted, same deposits into SPY earned +7.2% a year)

| variant | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | time invested | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no brake (control) | +12.0% | 22.3% | 2.17 | 0.930 | 70% | fails: fall over 20% |
| 22% target | +11.1% | 22.0% | 2.14 | 0.925 | 67% | fails: fall over 20% |
| 18% target | +10.2% | 21.9% | 2.08 | 0.907 | 64% | fails: fall over 20% |
| **14% target** | **+8.7%** | **19.2%** | 2.07 | **0.901** | 56% | **passes all five conditions** |

- The control matches M0036-BLEND number for number (22.28% fall, 2.17, 1,199 trades), so the brake code changed nothing except the brake.
- **Luck score.** N is 34 (one look per distinct method, as `lab status` prints it). At that N, TV14's 0.901 says there is about a 90% chance the edge is real and not the best of 34 lucky tries. That is just over the 0.90 bar, by one thousandth.
- **Worst year.** 2008, at -0.1%. The market-trend switch had the book in cash for most of that crash. The worst *fall* was the fast 1998 shock.
- The trade count stayed at 1,199 for every variant. A brake on a monthly book only resizes positions; it does not add round trips. Turnover even fell, from 6.42 to 6.04.

## Why it worked the way it did

1998 was a fast fall. A one-month jumpiness reading only rises once the fall has already started, so the light brakes were still near full size when it hit. The 22% target took 0.27 points off the worst fall and cost 0.9 points a year. The 18% target took 0.36 points off and cost 1.8. Those two paid for a brake that never caught the fall. Only the 14% target holds the book small often enough to be partly in cash *before* a shock: 56% invested against 70%. It took 3.1 points off the fall and cost 3.25 points a year, about one point of return per point of fall. That is roughly the price M0033 paid on the residual book (0.9). The drizzle book is not cheaper to brake, despite its low turnover.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis's main forecast held almost exactly:** "land near 9% a year" (actual 8.7%), with only the hardest brake clearing the limit. The surprise it allowed for, that this book is cheaper to brake because its jumpiness warns ahead of a fall, **did not happen**.
- **Expected failure #1 happened** as written: the light targets bought almost nothing, and only the 14% target cleared the limit, at a cost of over three points a year. The forecast was a luck score under 0.90. It came in at 0.901, a hair above.
- Expected failure #2 (the brake selling at the bottom) cannot be seen in the totals.

## The durability check, which is the real finding

`lab status` lists M0044 as promotable. The method-level fold record is 3 of 4 folds beaten, and no relative has failed a test. But that 3-of-4 belongs to the walk-forward's *selection rule*, which picked the no-brake or light variants in most folds. **The variant that would actually be promoted (TV14, the only eligible one) beats SPY in just 1 of the 4 walk-forward folds.** By fold, in points a year against SPY: 2003-05 -1.2, 2006-08 +9.1, 2009-11 -11.8, 2012-14 -3.0.

By era, TV14's edge over SPY is +1.4 points a year in 1996-2001, +8.6 in 2002-2008 and **-7.1 in 2009-2015**. 2009-2015 is when the data covers the most companies, and the walk-forward prints -5.2 for the method. The whole edge is the 2002-2008 bear market, when the trend switch had the book in cash. In the years that look most like the market since 2016, the braked book lost to SPY by seven points a year. The parent has the same shape: BLEND is -4.8 in 2009-2015. The brake makes it worse, because a cash-heavy book falls further behind in a steady bull market.

The buy-data signal does not fire: condition (d), a positive 2009-2015 edge, fails.

## My opinion:

Do not spend a test-window look on M0044-TV14, even though the hard gate would let it through. Four of four test looks have already failed on "beats SPY", and this candidate shows the exact pattern behind those failures. It wins only in the 2002-2008 crash era. It loses to SPY by seven points a year in the best-covered recent era. It beats SPY in one of four folds as a fixed configuration. It clears the luck bar by 0.001. Spending the look would almost certainly buy a fifth `test-failed`, and that would also block the whole stock-momentum-attention family (the drizzle idea) by kinship. An own-volatility brake on a monthly book is a priced-out direction: two books, two prices, both about a point of return per point of fall. The lab should stop trying it. What deserves the next trial is the drizzle signal's weakness after 2009, not its 1998 fall. It is a stock picker that needs the 2002-2008 cash period to win. The next idea tests that directly: hold the drizzle picks *without* the trend switch's cash periods, with SPY as the parking spot instead of cash, and see whether the stock picking alone beats SPY from 2009 on.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- Sera 20261009-2105: no look spent

The hard gate would take this method (3 of 4 folds at the method level, no kin has test-failed), so declining is Sera's judgement, not a refusal. Promotion would pre-register the only eligible variant, the 14% brake. That configuration on its own wins 1 of 4 walk-forward folds; the method-level 3 of 4 comes from the lighter brakes, which the fold rule picks and which all fail the fall limit. It clears the 20% fall limit by 0.8 points and the luck bar by 0.001. In 2009-2015, the best-covered stretch and the one most like the years the look would score, the method's pick trails SPY by 5.2 points a year (the 14% brake by about 7). Every one of the four looks spent so far failed on beating SPY, and the evidence here points the same way. A fifth failed look would also close this family, the drizzle signal, which is the one stock-picking idea the last batch called genuinely new, along with its queued follow-ups. The look is kept for a configuration whose own fold record and recent-era edge support it.
methods.verdict: Only the hardest brake gets the drizzle book under the 20% fall limit (+8.7% a year vs SPY's +7.2%, luck score 0.901), but it loses to SPY by 7 points a year after 2009; do not spend a test look on it

methods.name: De-crowding weights under the own-volatility brake: two small fixes against the last half point of fall
methods.hypothesis: M0034 turned the weight dial in both directions and found the only improvement on the side nobody asked about: weights proportional to one over the square root of 20-day mean dollar volume beat the equal-weight control on every axis at once -- money-weighted +14.0% a year vs +13.7%, max DD 20.62% vs 20.65%, Sharpe 0.891 vs 0.849, MAR 0.679 vs 0.663, DSR 0.962 vs 0.944 at N=32 -- at 5% more turnover and with no name ever above 12.5% of the book (effective names 17.0 of 20, against 8.6 for the size-proportional tilt). The mechanism is that dollar volume inside a top-20 momentum book is an attention measure, not a size measure, so leaning away from it is a systematic underweight of the most crowded trade; M0034-SIZE proved the point from the other end by putting 61% in QCOM on 1999-12-31 and taking a 28.8% fall through the dot-com break. Three tenths of a point a year is not enough on its own and M0034-INV-SQRT still failed max DD <= 20% by six tenths of a point, exactly as its parent M0032 did. This method combines it with the own-volatility brake already queued for this family (M0033), which attacks the drawdown directly rather than incidentally: same ranking, same screen, same SPY-200 gate, same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, with the de-crowding weights underneath the brake instead of equal weights. The two fixes are close to independent -- the brake scales total exposure through time, the weights redistribute within the book at a point in time -- so if the brake alone lands near 19-20% as M0033 hopes, the de-crowding weights should be worth the last fraction without costing the return the brake already pays for. Run the brake at two or three settings against a de-crowded control so the interaction is readable, and do not promote a variant whose improvement comes only from the brake: the point is whether the pair closes the half point, not whether either does.

methods.name: Crowding as a rank penalty, not a weight: punish momentum earned on abnormal volume
methods.hypothesis: M0034 found that the LEVEL of 20-day mean dollar volume behaves like a crowding measure inside a top-20 momentum book -- weighting by it put 61% in QCOM on 1999-12-31, 59% in CSCO+QCOM at the March 2000 top and 75% in AAPL+META in June 2014, and took a 28.8% max DD; weighting away from it beat the equal-weight control on every axis (MAR 0.679 vs 0.663, Sharpe 0.891 vs 0.849, DSR 0.962 vs 0.944 at N=32). But the LEVEL is a confounded measure: it mixes how big a company is with how excited the market currently is about it, and the lab measured those two apart only weakly (Spearman 0.686 against point-in-time market value over 2010-2015). The clean crowding measure is the CHANGE, not the level: a name's 20-day mean dollar volume divided by its own trailing one-year mean, which cancels the size component entirely because each name is compared only to itself. A ratio near 1 is a stock trading normally; a ratio of 3 is a stock the crowd has just arrived at. This method keeps M0032's execution exactly -- fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, the SPY-200 gate, monthly, top 20 -- and puts the crowding ratio into the RANKING rather than the weighting: subtract a multiple of the cross-sectional z-score of log relative volume from the residual-momentum score, so that between two names with the same momentum the one that earned it quietly is preferred. This is the same instinct as the frog-in-the-pan idea already queued (M0036), which prefers momentum earned in a drizzle over momentum earned in jumps, but read off volume rather than off the shape of the returns, and the two should be run close together so the lab learns which reading of 'quiet' is the one that pays. Vary the penalty multiple over 3-4 settings plus an unpenalised control. Expected failure: relative volume spikes on earnings for every name regardless of crowding, so the penalty mostly fires on the earnings calendar and ranks by reporting date; or the penalty removes exactly the names momentum needs, since a stock the crowd is arriving at is also a stock that keeps rising, and the 1999 lesson is survivorship in reverse -- the crowding that killed the size tilt in 2000 is the same crowding that paid it +15.0% a year overall.

methods.name: Weight the momentum picks by real company size, with a ceiling on any one name
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0034 (size tilt by trading volume) with point-in-time market value from EDGAR share counts (stores of 2026-10-17); Sera 20261018-0517, theme 'books shaped like the market'; placebo frame of M0187
methods.hypothesis: Equal slots in a twenty-name momentum book lean toward the smaller index members compared with SPY, which weights by company size, and from 2018 SPY's big-company drift beat every book the lab tried (insight 91). M0034 tested a lean toward bigger names but could only read trading volume, which puts 35-40% of the money on different names than market value would. This method keeps M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT's book exactly (SPY 200-day gate, F4 screen, top-20 raw residual momentum, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up), keeps one share class per company, and sizes the twenty by point-in-time market value (filed share count times the close as it printed, from 1996), with no name above 10% (MV10) or 20% (MV20), plus an uncapped arm (MV) and the equal-slot control (EQ). Unknown sizes take the median known size among the picks. The meaningless control is the same frame and the same size weights on names drawn in a hash order over the same scorable names, re-drawn quarterly (PLC1-MV10, PLC1-MV20). Size-weighting is a very old idea (the cap-weighted index itself) and residual momentum was published in 2011 (Blitz, Huij and Martens), inside the dev window. Success, written now: MV10 or MV20 beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under the screen bar, beats EQ on return per unit of worst fall (MAR), keeps or improves EQ's edge over SPY in 2009-2015, and beats its own size-weighted placebo by at least 2 points a year. The expected direction on dev is a smaller worst fall and a lower return than EQ: the big names move less.
methods.expectedFailure: Sizing by market value pulls the book toward the few biggest names the momentum screen happens to hold (in the 1990s GE, Microsoft, Cisco; later Exxon, Apple), so the book becomes a smaller, more concentrated copy of SPY's top end: lower volatility, but its edge over SPY shrinks with its distance from SPY, and the cap binds most months so MV10 ends up close to equal weight anyway while MV pays for concentration (one name at 30% or more, a deeper single-name fall such as Cisco in 2000-02). The size-weighted placebo probably beats SPY too on dev, because the gate and the screen do most of the work (M0187, M0198), and the size weighting moves both books together, so the gap to the placebo stays under 2 points. Coverage: before about 2000 many picks have no filed count and take the median, so the early years are close to equal weight and the test of the idea really lives in 2001-2015. The survivorship-check store, which holds the companies that died, should hurt the equal arm more than the size arms, since dead companies were mostly small; that is the one place a size tilt could look better than it is. And the method's ancestry runs through the residual-momentum family, which has a test-failed method, so the hard gate is expected to refuse promotion whatever dev says.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

Unblocked: the missing data arrived. Unblocked 2026-10-17: the stores now carry point-in-time shares outstanding from 1996 (EDGAR cover pages to 2010, XBRL after, each figure usable from its filing date) and the split list behind the adjusted closes, so market.market_value(symbol, data_date) is shares x the price as it printed, with no look-ahead (Apple reads about $560B on 2014-06-30, not $20B). Declare market_fields = ("shares",). Keep one share class per company (GOOG/GOOGL, FOX/FOXA, NWS/NWSA) and pre-register a weight ceiling. Coverage is about 56% of dev member-days, set by the dev store's missing prices; about 85% on the survivorship-check store, so report both.

It was blocked on: point-in-time shares outstanding before 2009 (EDGAR XBRL starts 2009; the dev window opens 1996), and a market-value figure that does not multiply an unadjusted share count by a split-adjusted close


### 2026-10-18

Sera 20261018-0517 reserves this for the owner's theme "books shaped like the market". Build it in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up (a -frac-gotrade preset). Weight the residual-momentum picks by real market value (market_fields = ("shares",)), one share class per company, with pre-registered weight ceilings (e.g. 10% and 20%) beside the equal-weight arm, and run the meaningless control of the same shape: size-weighted random picks of the same count. Report every arm on both stores (dev and survivorship-check) and the 2009-2015 era against SPY. Note for promotion: its ancestry runs through the residual-momentum family, which has a test-failed method, so the hard gate is expected to refuse it whatever the dev numbers say; the value here is the answer, not a look.


### 2026-10-18

### What was tried

The lab's best stock picker ranks members on "residual momentum": how much a stock rose over the
past year *after* taking out the part the whole market explains. It holds the top twenty, gives each
the same amount of money, and steps aside to cash when SPY is below its 200-day average. SPY does
something different: it gives each company money in proportion to its size. From 2018 SPY's
biggest companies beat every book the lab tried, so the question was simple: **if the same twenty
picks are sized the way SPY sizes companies, does the book do better?**

Until this week the lab could not answer that, because it did not know how big a company was before
2009. It now does: shares outstanding as filed with the SEC from 1996, times the price that day.

Six versions, all on the owner's real setup (fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5 million
rupiah added every month), 1996 to October 2015:

| version | what it does | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EQ | equal money in each pick (the old way) | **+13.7%** | +7.2% | 20.6% | **+1.1%** |
| MV10 | sized by company size, no name above 10% | +11.2% | +7.2% | 20.0% | −2.9% |
| MV20 | sized by company size, no name above 20% | +10.4% | +7.2% | 24.0% | −3.3% |
| MV | sized by company size, no limit | +11.1% | +7.2% | 23.6% | −2.0% |
| PLC1-MV10 | **random** picks, sized by company size, 10% limit | +9.9% | +7.2% | 22.9% | −5.4% |
| PLC1-MV20 | the same random picks, 20% limit | +9.9% | +7.2% | 25.8% | −5.9% |

(The "worst fall" is the most the account lost from a peak. Monthly deposits refill a falling
account, so the true fall of the stocks alone was a bit deeper than these numbers.)

### The answer: no

Sizing the picks by company size **costs 2.5 to 3.3 points a year** compared with equal slots, and
it does not buy a smaller worst fall in return. The 10% limit version fell 20.0% at worst against
20.6% for equal slots, a difference of almost nothing. The 20% and no-limit versions fell *further*
(24.0% and 23.6%), past the 20% limit, because a few very large names carry the book.

Worse, the size-weighted versions lose to SPY in 2009-2015, the years most like today: −2.0 to
−3.3 points a year, where equal slots still led by 1.1 points. That is the opposite of what the
idea needed. The idea was that leaning toward big companies would protect the book in a market
led by big companies, and the best stretch of data we have to check that says it made things worse.

### Is it luck? (DSR)

The lab has now tried 146 independent ideas. The luck check (DSR) asks how likely a result is to
be real after that many tries. The bar is 0.90. Equal slots reach 0.924, the same as their earlier
recorded twin. The size-weighted versions fail it: 0.842 (MV10), 0.788 (MV20), 0.806 (MV). So the
lab cannot even tell the size-weighted books apart from luck at this N.

The random-pick controls pass the luck check (0.936 and 0.942) and are marked eligible. That is a
warning, not good news: names drawn by a coin flip, with the trend switch and the monthly routine
around them, look "real" by this test. It is the same lesson the earlier placebo methods taught:
the frame (the cash switch, the screen, the cadence) earns a good part of the lead over SPY.

### Against the random picks

The momentum ranking, sized by company size with a 10% limit, beat the random picks sized the same
way by **1.3 points a year** (11.2% against 9.9%). The success bar written before the run was 2
points. So under size weights the ranking adds less than the bar demands. Under equal slots the
ranking's lead is clearly larger (13.7%), which says the ranking's edge lives in the smaller and
mid-sized picks, the ones size weighting starves.

### With the companies that died put back

The survivorship check re-runs every version on prices that include about 500 index members the main
data cannot price, many of which went bust. Every version earns less there: equal slots 13.7% → 12.0%
a year, with the worst fall 20.6% → 25.0% and the 2009-2015 lead gone (+1.1% → −0.2%). The size
versions lose about as much (−1.6 to −2.0 points a year) and the no-limit version's worst fall
reaches 32%. My pre-registered guess was that the dead companies would hurt equal slots more than
the size versions, since dead companies were mostly small. They did not: the damage was about equal.
The random picks lost least (−0.2 to −0.9), as random picks should.

### Why

Inside a top-twenty momentum list, the very largest names are the ones whose climb was mostly the
market's climb. Residual momentum looks for stocks that rose for their *own* reasons, and those are
more often mid-sized companies. Sizing by company size moves money from the picks with the most
"own reason" to the picks with the least, so the book drifts back toward a small, lumpy copy of
SPY's top end. It still pays Gotrade's fees on twenty names, but its edge shrinks toward zero. In
the no-limit version, one name took 64% of the book in mid-2014. A ceiling stops that, but at 10%
the ceiling binds on many names and the book drifts back toward equal slots, which is why MV10 sits
between the two.

### Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis (size weighting lowers return but shrinks the worst fall, and keeps the
  2009-2015 edge) **failed** on two of its three parts. Return fell as expected. The fall did
  not shrink, and the 2009-2015 edge went negative.
- The expected failure largely happened: concentration in the biggest names, a ceiling that pulls
  the book back toward equal, a placebo gap under 2 points. One expected part did not happen: the
  survivorship check did not favour the size versions.

### Gate and promotion

The method reads "dev-eligible" only because of the equal-slot version (a re-run of a configuration
the lab already holds) and the two random-pick controls. None of them is the idea. The hard gate
refuses it anyway: it wins 1 of 4 walk-forward periods, and its relatives in the residual-momentum
family already failed their test-window looks. Nothing is promoted and no look is spent.

### Assumptions written down

One share class per company (the higher-ranked class kept). A pick with no filed share count that
day got the median size of the picks that had one. The random picks are redrawn each quarter over
the same names the momentum ranking could score, keeping held names in the first 40% of the new
draw.

**My opinion:** this direction is closed. Leaning a momentum book toward big companies is the wrong
answer to "SPY's big companies keep winning": it takes the book's edge away faster than it takes
its risk away, and it is worse in 2009-2015, not better. What I would try next is the opposite
question, now that the lab knows company size: is the momentum edge really a mid-size edge? Rank
residual momentum *within* size bands (four picks from each fifth of the index by size), so the
book has SPY-like breadth across sizes without SPY's weights. If the edge comes only from the
smaller bands, that is a reason to *hold SPY for the big-company drift and add a small momentum
sleeve*, not to bend the momentum book itself toward the big names.


### 2026-10-18

Sera 20261018-0517, Promotion step 0: refused by the hard gate. The dev-eligible rows are the equal-weight re-run of the parent configuration and the two size-weighted placebo controls, none of them the idea. `lab promote` exited on the fold rule (1 of 4 walk-forward folds won); kin M0021, M0022 and M0029 are test-failed as well, so a second refusal reason stands behind the first. No look spent. Buy signal: no -- the size arms trailed SPY in 2009-2015 and lost the folds.


### 2026-10-20

**A correction: the random-pick books above were not shaped like the books they were judging.**

The two random-pick rows in the table traded about 880 times over the twenty years. The real
books traded about 1,600. A control that trades half as often pays half the fees, so it was given
a head start the book never had, and every number read against it is unsafe.

The lab has since drawn replacement controls that match each book's own trading — 1,587 and 1,563
trades against 1,600 and 1,591, and turnover within a tenth. On the same deposits and the same
fees:

| the book | your money a year | its honest random twin | the lead |
|---|---|---|---|
| sized by company size, no name above 10% | +11.2% | +7.8% | **+3.3 points** |
| sized by company size, no name above 20% | +10.4% | +8.0% | **+2.4 points** |

**Two things said above are therefore withdrawn.**

1. *"beat the random picks sized the same way by 1.3 points a year (11.2% against 9.9%). The
   success bar written before the run was 2 points. So under size weights the ranking adds less
   than the bar demands."* The honest lead is 3.3 points at the 10% limit and 2.4 points at the
   20% limit. **Both clear the 2-point bar**, so that conclusion is reversed, and the line in the
   expected-failure list that reads "a placebo gap under 2 points" goes with it.
2. The equal-slot book's lead over a random draw — about 3.8 points a year as the table above
   reads. Both of the old random books were sized by company size and never belonged beside an
   equal-slot book at all; they are now aimed where they belong, at the two size-weighted books.
   **The equal-slot book ends with no random control of its own.** Nothing was measured in its
   place, so that lead is withdrawn rather than replaced. An arm with no control is not a hole in
   the record: the lab's shape check asks only that a control, where one exists, trades like the
   book it controls.

**Nothing else changes.** The reason this direction is closed never rested on the random
comparison. Sizing by company size still costs 2.5 to 3.3 points a year against equal slots, still
does not buy a smaller worst fall, still loses to SPY in 2009-2015, and the size-weighted books
still fail the luck check. The method stays rejected, the hard gate still refuses it on the later
periods and on its relatives, no test-window look was spent, and nothing was re-run: these are the
same trials, read against a fair opponent.
methods.verdict: Sizing the momentum picks by company size cost 2.5 to 3.3 points a year, did not soften the worst fall, and lost to SPY in 2009-2015; equal slots stay better

methods.name: Trim toward the market when the book is furthest AHEAD of it, not when it is behind
methods.hypothesis: M0035 measured the exact opposite of what it hoped and the measurement is the gift: the binding dev fall (9 May - 21 Jul 2006, -20.7%) happened while the book was AHEAD of SPY by 11.8 points over the trailing twelve months, and still ahead by 6.0 points a month in. The relative-shortfall switch was off through the whole fall, by its own rule, and turned on ten days after the bottom. The same pattern sits under the lab's other binding falls: a momentum book owns whatever has already run furthest, so its worst falls arrive immediately after its best relative runs, not after its worst. M0027 proposes to read the top-minus-bottom decile spread for the same 2006 fall and warns it may turn only after the damage; this reads a slower, simpler quantity that is high BEFORE the damage rather than after it.
