Keep M0032 verbatim -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 trend gate, monthly, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th -- and reuse M0035's shadow-book machinery unchanged, only inverting the comparison: when the book's trailing twelve-month return is AHEAD of SPY's by more than a threshold, trim the stock book to a fraction of the account and hold the rest in SPY, releasing as the lead narrows. Variants sweep the threshold (ahead by 10, 15 and 20 points) and the trim (hold three quarters, hold half), against the same unbraked control. This is the only go-live condition the whole residual-momentum family still fails: M0032 and all six M0035 variants miss max DD <= 20% by about six tenths of a point and nothing else. If trimming after a big relative run takes 20.6% below 20% while costing less than the roughly one point a year it would have to cost to still beat a deposit-matched SPY by five points, the family finally has a dev-eligible member at real fees. Expected failure: the lead is a near-permanent state for a book that beat SPY by seven points a year on dev, so an ahead-by-10 trigger is on most of the time and simply becomes a permanent half-SPY core wearing a disguise -- in which case M0030's always-on core is the honest version of it and this adds nothing but a dial. The second failure is that trimming a winner is the classic way to cap the upside without capping the fall, since the 2006 drop took three months from a peak the trim would have been on for, but at only a quarter to a half of the book the fall is reduced by a quarter to a half of six tenths of a point -- not enough.

methods.name: The market-core-plus-momentum book at Gotrade's real fees: the twin its promotion needs
methods.hypothesis: M0035 and its two siblings agree that the lab's 20% worst-fall wall only moves when the book holds less ALL the time rather than less sometimes: five different pickers spanned six tenths of a point of fall (M0036), six conditional relative-shortfall settings moved it not at all (M0035, every variant at 20.6%), and the only thing that reached a 16.4% fall was a permanent own-volatility cut that gave up about two points of yearly return (M0033-TV14-N21). M0030-C50T is the lab's other permanent holder-of-less: half SPY, half the residual-momentum book, 12.7% a year on dev at an 18.6% worst fall, under the limit, and it is dev-eligible today. But it ran on monthly-hold-frac at the old flat 0.1% a trade, so its numbers cannot be compared with the real-fee ones and, under the promotion rule in force since M0031, it cannot be promoted as it stands: a method from M0030 or earlier needs lab costs run on it first, and then its best variant re-registered as a one-variant variation on the -gotrade preset and re-run on dev before a test-window look may be spent. This idea is that twin. One variant, M0030-C50T's configuration verbatim -- BLEND of the timed SPY core at 50% with RESIDMOM on M0011's RAW20 params at 50% -- on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's monthly top-up, so the look is spent on the configuration paper would actually trade. The hypothesis is that it survives: the blend turns over about the same 1,615 times as M0032, roughly 80 trades a year, which is slow enough that a fee schedule with a ten-cent floor cannot eat the margin, and M0032 already showed this exact fee change costing a point and a half a year while leaving every condition it cleared still cleared. Expected failure: the SPY core halves the stock book's slot sizes, so each stock order is a -35 slice where the ten-cent floor is half a percent a side rather than a quarter, and the fee drag lands well above M0032's 15.6% of gross trade profit -- pushing the money-weighted return under the deposit-matched SPY even though the lump-sum version beat it, which is the one way a core-plus-satellite book can fail a funded comparison that its unfunded parent passed.

methods.name: Momentum earned overnight only: rank on the gaps between yesterday's close and today's open
methods.sourceRef: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), A tug of war: overnight versus intraday expected returns, Journal of Financial Economics 134(1), 192-213, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.03.011
methods.hypothesis: Lou, Polk and Skouras find that essentially all of momentum's abnormal return is earned overnight (close to next open), while the intraday part (open to close) of the same stocks runs the other way, because individuals push prices overnight and institutions trade against the characteristic during the day; the split is strongest in large, high-price stocks, which is F4's universe. The lab has ranked on twelve-month total and residual return eleven ways and never separated WHEN the return was earned. Each month, among F4's screened members, rank on the sum of the last twelve months' (skip the latest month) overnight log returns and hold the top 20 equal weight behind the SPY 200-day gate, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding. Variants: ON (overnight rank), ID (intraday rank, the control the paper says should lose), TOT (plain 12-1 total momentum in the same run, the yardstick), TUG (overnight rank minus intraday rank, the paper's tug-of-war spread as a long-only pick) and TOT-ON (the 40 best total-momentum names, then the 20 of them whose gain came most overnight). Success: ON or TOT-ON beats TOT on return per unit of worst fall and ID is the worst of the set. Assumption: the store's prices are split-adjusted, not dividend-adjusted, and an allocator cannot see dividends, so the ex-dividend gap stays inside the overnight leg; this tilts ON slightly away from high-yield names and is not corrected.
methods.expectedFailure: Daily open prices before about 2001 are noisy (fractional ticks, opens recorded equal to the prior close on thin days) and split adjustment can leave rounding in the open, so the overnight sum carries measurement noise the close-to-close sum does not. Overnight returns are small and the twelve-month sum is dominated by a handful of earnings-announcement gaps, so ON may simply be an earnings-surprise momentum book with the same 20%-plus fall in 1998 and 2008 as every other momentum book. Worse, ranking on the overnight leg alone rewards names with large gap risk -- high-volatility, high-news stocks -- so ON's worst fall may be larger than TOT's, not smaller. The intraday control may not lose either: in a large-cap universe the intraday leg is the institutional leg and may carry the low-volatility tilt that has helped every blend in this lab.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

A stock's daily move has two parts. The **overnight** part is the jump from yesterday's close to today's open. The **daytime** part is the move from the open to the close. A 2019 study (Lou, Polk and Skouras) found that nearly all of momentum's extra return comes overnight. The daytime part of the same stocks tends to go the other way. This method tests that on our stocks. Each month it ranks the stocks by the last year's overnight jumps only, skipping the latest month, and holds the top 20.

Everything else stays the same as the lab's standard momentum book: the same 539 large stocks and liquidity screen, all cash when SPY is below its 200-day average, 20 names in equal amounts, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and your funding plan (10M IDR to start, then 5M IDR on the 25th of each month). The five versions:

- **ON**: the 20 stocks with the biggest overnight gains.
- **ID**: the 20 stocks with the biggest daytime gains. This is the control. The study says it should do worst.
- **TOT**: plain 12-month momentum, run in the same test as the yardstick.
- **TUG**: overnight rank minus daytime rank, the study's "tug of war" spread, buying only.
- **TOT-ON**: the 40 best plain-momentum stocks, then the 20 of them whose gain came most overnight.

## Results (dev window 1996 → Oct 2015, your deposits)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ON | **16.9%** | 7.2% | 30.5% | 2.83 | 0.973 |
| TOT-ON | **15.1%** | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 |
| TOT (yardstick) | 13.8% | 7.2% | 23.3% | 2.05 | 0.940 |
| TUG | 12.0% | 7.2% | 35.8% | 1.98 | 0.890 |
| ID (control) | 8.1% | 7.2% | 27.7% | 1.67 | 0.720 |

ON and TOT-ON are the two highest returns on your deposits the lab has recorded at real fees. The next best is the size-tilted residual book at 15.0%, which fell 28.8% at its worst. The real-fee residual book (the lab's reference) earned 13.7% with a 20.6% worst fall.

**Every version fails the same rule: the worst fall must be no more than 20%.** TOT-ON misses by 2.8 points and ON by 10.5 points. Every other rule passes for ON, TOT-ON and TOT: they beat SPY, gains outweigh losses by far more than 1.3×, and they make over 100 trades.

**Luck test.** The DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at N = 36, the lab's count of independent tries, against the bar of 0.90. ON (0.973), TOT-ON (0.956) and TOT (0.940) clear it. TUG (0.890) and ID (0.720) do not.

## When it hurt

- **ON**'s worst fall ran from spring 2011 to spring 2012: the August 2011 debt-ceiling selloff, then a weak May 2012. The overnight ranking had loaded up on names that gap on news, and those fell hardest when the market fell. Its worst calendar year is 2011 (−6.9%).
- **TOT-ON**'s worst fall is the summer of 1998, the Russia/LTCM shock, when every momentum book in this lab falls. The SPY 200-day gate turns off only after the damage. Its worst calendar year is only 2015 (−1.8%).
- **TOT**'s worst fall was in mid-2006.
- 2001–2003 and 2008–mid-2009 are flat on every curve: the trend gate held cash. On average about 70% of the money was invested.

## Why

The study's split shows up clearly here. Ranking on the overnight part alone beat ranking on the whole return by 3.1 points a year. Ranking on the daytime part alone barely beat SPY (8.1% vs 7.2%). So the daytime half of momentum carries almost none of its reward in this universe either. The control lost, as the study predicts. That is the strongest evidence that the effect is real and not a fluke of the window.

The cost is in the falls. Overnight jumps cluster in stocks that make news: earnings surprises, upgrades, deals. A book full of those stocks moves together when the market panics, so ON's worst fall is the biggest of the safe-looking versions. TOT-ON keeps the plain-momentum filter first. That holds onto the steadier winners and uses the overnight measure only to choose among them. It keeps most of the return gain (+1.3 points over TOT), and its worst fall is a little smaller than TOT's (22.8% vs 23.3%). Its gains-vs-losses ratio is much better (2.41 vs 2.05).

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: held.** ON and TOT-ON both beat TOT on return per unit of worst fall (MAR, return divided by worst fall: TOT-ON 0.66 vs TOT 0.59). ID was the worst of the set.
- **Expected failure: partly happened.** I predicted ON would carry the same 20%-plus falls as every momentum book, possibly larger because it favours stocks that gap. That is exactly what happened to ON (30.5%), and TUG was worse still (35.8%). The worry about noisy pre-2001 opens did not show up as a weak result: ON's edge holds across the window.
- **Assumption kept:** dividends are not visible to the ranking, so the price drop on each ex-dividend morning counts as an overnight loss. That tilts ON a little away from high-dividend stocks. A version with dividends added back may score differently.

## Other checks (report only; no trial recorded)

- **Walk-forward:** 3 of 4 out-of-sample folds beaten, with a +1.1% edge in 2009–2015, the years when the store's coverage is best. The walk-forward shows "not dev-eligible" only because nothing in this method cleared the 20% fall limit.
- **Narrow vs broad markets:** ON pays in both (+6.9% / +11.7% vs SPY). TOT-ON's edge is mostly in narrow months (+16.0% vs +3.4%).
- No version is dev-eligible, so nothing was promoted and no test-window look was spent.

## My opinion:

This is the most interesting new signal the lab has found in a while, and it is worth more trials. The control lost as the study predicts, the overnight versions top the lab's funded returns, and the edge survives into 2009–2015. TOT-ON is the version to build on. It failed only the fall limit, by under 3 points, and the fall is the familiar summer-1998 shock, not something new. Next I would put TOT-ON's selection under the lab's existing tools that shrink falls without changing the picks: an own-volatility brake read weekly (which cut the residual book's fall from 14.1% to 12.4%), or a wider 30-name book. I would also try the overnight split on the residual ranking, the lab's best ranking key. One caution: the overnight family is new, so no test-window failure counts against it yet. That makes it one of the few lines that could still reach a counted look.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0050-ON`: DSR 0.9513 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0050-TOT-ON`: DSR 0.9239 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Momentum earned overnight is the real thing: picking last year's winners by their overnight jumps earned your money 15.1-16.9% a year vs 7.2% in SPY, the lab's best funded results, while the daytime-only control barely beat SPY - but every version still fell more than 20% at its worst (22.8% at best, in the 1998 shock).

methods.name: Buy the stocks about to pay their dividend: the dividend-month premium
methods.sourceRef: Hartzmark & Solomon (2013), The dividend month premium, J. Financial Economics 109(3), 640-660, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.02.015
methods.hypothesis: Hartzmark and Solomon (working paper 2011, published 2013) find stocks earn about 0.4-0.5 points a month more in months they are predicted to pay a dividend -- they paid one in the same calendar month a year earlier, or three months earlier -- with returns rising into the ex-date, consistent with price pressure from investors who want dividends. It is predicted from the dividend history alone, which the research store holds and the market now carries point in time. This is a calendar mechanism the lab has never tried: it reads neither past return nor volatility rank as its signal, so its picks should be largely unrelated to the momentum books that failed their looks. Each month, among F4's screened members, hold the stocks predicted to go ex-dividend in the coming month, equal weight, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade. Variants: ALL-T (every predicted payer, behind the SPY 200-day gate), ALL (every predicted payer, always invested), Y20-T (the 20 highest trailing yields among them, gated), LV20-T (the 20 calmest among them, gated) and OFF20-T (the control: the 20 highest-yield payers NOT predicted to pay this month, gated), so Y20-T minus OFF20-T isolates the month effect from the yield effect. Success: a predicted-payer variant beats SPY TR on dev within the 20% drawdown limit, beats its off-month control, and keeps a positive edge in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The paper's sample ends in 2011 and its working paper circulated from 2011, so the dev window covers the pre-publication years only; any edge here is the kind that fades once traded. A quarter to a third of large caps pay in any month, so ALL is close to an equal-weight dividend-payer index (100+ names): it tilts to smaller, value-ish members and bets against SPY's big-company drift, and near-total monthly turnover pays Gotrade's $0.10 minimum on every order, which on a 10M IDR start is several percent a year by itself. Not modelled and against the method: the book engine credits 100% of each dividend in cash, but the owner's account loses the US withholding tax on every dividend (30%, or 15% under the Indonesia treaty with a W-8BEN). A book that rotates into each month's payers collects roughly three times SPY's dividend yield, so the unmodelled tax drag is about 1-2 points a year larger than on SPY; the analysis will estimate it from the dividends the run credited. In 2008 payers fell with the market, so the ungated ALL book should fall well over 20%, and even gated, 1998-2002 value-versus-growth swings may leave it behind SPY for years. The off-month control may do as well as Y20-T, which would mean the yield tilt, not the calendar, carries any result.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The idea comes from Hartzmark and Solomon (circulated 2011, published 2013). Stocks tend to rise in the months they are expected to pay a dividend, because investors who want the dividend buy ahead of the payment date. "Expected to pay" is read from history: the stock paid in the same calendar month a year ago, or three months ago. The paper found about half a point a month extra on US stocks from 1927 to 2011.

This needed new plumbing first. The research store always held every cash dividend, but the strategies could never see the payment calendar. The market now carries the calendar, and a strategy only sees dividends whose ex-date is on or before the day it decides (commit bff39a4, with tests showing no future date leaks in). The lab's run command also had to stop treating "reads more than prices" as "reads company accounts" (commit 6a22a01).

Each month, among index members with a $5+ price and enough daily trading, the book holds the stocks predicted to pay next month, in equal fractional slots, at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's funding plan (10M IDR, then 5M IDR every month). Five versions:

| version | what it holds | your money a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALL-T | every predicted payer (about 100), cash when SPY is below its 200-day average | +6.5% | +7.2% | 29% | 0.68 |
| ALL | every predicted payer, always invested | +5.2% | +7.2% | 58% | 0.33 |
| Y20-T | the 20 highest-yield predicted payers, with the SPY gate | +6.8% | +7.2% | 38% | 0.71 |
| LV20-T | the 20 calmest predicted payers, with the gate | +5.3% | +7.2% | 37% | 0.70 |
| OFF20-T (control) | the 20 highest-yield payers NOT due to pay next month, with the gate | **+8.3%** | +7.2% | 33% | 0.80 |

## Result

**Rejected.** None of the four dividend-month books beat SPY. Every version broke the 20% worst-fall limit, the ungated one badly (58%, in 2008). None reached the luck bar. The DSR (deflated Sharpe ratio) is how likely a result is real rather than the best of many lucky tries. The bar is 0.90, and the lab now counts N = 45 independent methods. The best was 0.80, and that was the control.

The control matters most. OFF20-T holds the same kind of high-yield stocks but avoids the month they pay. It beat every "about to pay" book and beat SPY by about one point a year. That is the **opposite** of the paper's claim. On these stocks, in these years, holding a stock into its payment month did not pay.

It also failed the durability checks:

- **Walk-forward:** won 1 of 4 test folds. A fold is a stretch of years the method was scored on after being chosen without seeing them.
- **2009-2015:** −3.2 points a year against SPY. That stretch is the best-covered data and the most like today.

The real-fee runs below start with no deposits, so read them for their shape, not their level:

| years | ALL-T | Y20-T | LV20-T | OFF20-T | SPY (with dividends) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +4.5% | +4.2% | +5.8% | +4.9% | +6.6% |
| 2003-2008 | +2.3% | +6.6% | +4.9% | +4.6% | +1.7% |
| 2009-2015 | +1.9% | +7.9% | +4.9% | +12.5% | +14.5% |

Every book was ahead of SPY in 2003-2008, the long run for value and dividend stocks. Every one fell far behind after 2009. That is the lab's familiar pattern: an edge earned before 2009 and gone in the years most like today.

The worst falls happened at the March 2000 peak of the tech bubble, not in 2008. Dividend payers (utilities, banks, staples) fell while the market kept rising. The SPY 200-day gate never switched to cash, because SPY itself was still above its average.

## Why

1. **Fees from turning the whole book over.** Next month's payers are mostly not this month's, so the book sells nearly everything every month. ALL made 16,000 trades in twenty years. Gotrade's minimum fee is about $0.13 per order (the $0.10 minimum plus regulatory fee and VAT). With 100 names in a small account, that is 3-8% of the slot each time. With no deposits, fees took about 8% of ALL-T's money a year and 14% of ALL's. The 20-name books paid about 5%. The control paid 3.4%, because a stock that won't pay next month is often still in the book the month after.
2. **The premium itself looks small or missing here.** Comparing Y20-T with the control, and allowing for the extra fees, the dividend month added something only in 2003-2008. By 2009-2015 the control was 4-5 points a year ahead. The paper was circulated in 2011. Like other published effects in this lab, it does not survive into the years after publication.
3. **A bet against big companies.** Equal-weight dividend payers tilt to smaller and value-type members. From 2009, SPY's big-company growth drift left them behind, which is insight 91 again.

## Dividend tax: not modelled, and it makes this worse

The backtest credits each dividend in full. The owner's account loses the US withholding tax on every dividend: 30%, or 15% with the treaty form. Without deposits, Y20-T collected dividends worth about 7% of the account a year, ALL about 5.4%, and SPY about 2%. At 30% withholding, Y20-T loses about 2.1 points a year, against about 0.6 for SPY. That would take its +6.8% to roughly +5.3%, well behind SPY's roughly +6.6% after tax. The control collected almost nothing (0.2% a year), because it holds stocks only in months they don't pay. So it would lose almost no tax.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis failed.** The dividend month did not earn a premium net of what it costs to chase. Its own control beat it.
- **The expected failures all happened.** The ALL book behaved like a dividend-payer index. Turnover fees ate it. The ungated book fell 58% in 2008. The control matched or beat the dividend-month picks, so whatever this family has comes from the yield tilt, not the calendar. One surprise: the gated books' worst fall came in 2000, not 2008.

## Compared with others

The best version, OFF20-T, is a high-yield book that skips payment months. It lands near the lab's other rejected value-type books: beats SPY on average, then breaks the fall limit and lags after 2009. It is nowhere near the residual-momentum near misses on worst fall (12-14%). It is not a momentum book, so the momentum family's failures don't count against it as kin. But it fails on its own record.

## My opinion

The dividend-month premium is dead for this owner: it pays to chase ex-dates only before fees, before tax and before 2009, and none of those hold for him. Don't run more variations of "buy before the dividend". What this run did teach is the reverse and is worth one cheap follow-up: at a 15-30% withholding rate, a long-only Indonesian account should avoid ex-dates rather than seek them. The off-month control is that idea by accident: it beat SPY by a point a year with almost no dividend tax. I would test it once on purpose, as a tax-aware overlay on the lab's best calm-stock or momentum books (skip a name in the month it goes ex, replace it with the next one), not as a stand-alone high-yield book, which still falls 33% and lags after 2009. More valuable than any single method: the lab should model the withholding tax in the cash ledger, because every high-dividend result it has recorded overstates the owner's money.
methods.verdict: Rejected: buying stocks just before their dividend lost to SPY after fees and fell 29-58%; its own control, which skips the dividend month, did better

methods.name: Hold the stock book only over the turn of the month, SPY the rest of the time
methods.sourceRef: Lakonishok & Smidt (1988), Are seasonal anomalies real? A ninety-year perspective, Rev. Financial Studies 1(4); McConnell & Xu (2008), Equity returns at the turn of the month, Financial Analysts Journal 64(2)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1988 and again in 2008, so the dev window (1996-2015) straddles the second publication. McConnell and Xu find that across 1926-2005 essentially all of the US equity premium arrived in the four sessions from the last trading day of a month through the third of the next. If the flows behind it persist, extra market exposure held only then earns the premium at several times its usual daily rate. Held as a tilt, never as cash: SPY all month, and over five sessions (bought at the open of the second-last session, sold at the open of the fourth) a slice of 25%, 50% or 100% moves into the 20 highest 60-day-beta names among F4's screened index members, equal weight, fractional, at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's funding; a fourth variant swaps the whole book into QQQ instead (two large orders, not forty small ones), and a fifth moves the 50% slice over a mid-month window of the same length (sessions 9-13) as the control that separates the calendar from plain beta and fees. Success: a TOM variant beats SPY TR with a worst fall under 20% and beats its mid-month control by a clear margin.
methods.expectedFailure: The fees eat it. Every month the slice makes a round trip into the tilt and back, and so does the SPY it replaces: at Gotrade's schedule (0.2% trading fee, a minimum of $0.10, regulatory fee and 11% VAT on top) that is about 1.2% of the slice a month, some 14% of it a year, while a 1.5-beta basket over five sessions adds perhaps 0.3-0.5% a month even if the effect is intact. So every variant lags SPY, the 100% switch most of all, and the mid-month control lags by about the same amount, which would say the calendar adds little after costs. The effect has also faded since 2008, so 2009-2015 shows the least.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

An old finding, published in 1988 and again in 2008: in US stocks, most of the market's yearly gain
arrives in a handful of days around the turn of each month. These are the last trading day of a
month and the first three of the next, when salaries and pension money get invested. If that still
holds, extra market exposure held only on those days should earn more than the same exposure held
at any other time.

The test held SPY all month. Over five trading days around each month's turn, it moved part of the
money into the 20 index stocks that move most with the market ("high-beta" stocks, which tend to
rise about 1.5 times as much as the market on a good day), and then moved it back. There were five
versions:

- **T25 / T50 / T100**: move 25%, 50% or all of the money into the high-beta stocks for those five days.
- **Q100**: move all of it from SPY into QQQ (the Nasdaq-100 fund) for those days. That is only two orders each way, instead of forty small ones.
- **MID50**: the control. It moves the same 50% for five days in the middle of the month (trading days 9-13). If the turn of the month is special, T50 should clearly beat it.

Every version used fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and the owner's monthly deposits, over
1996-2015.

## Result: every version lost to SPY, and the more it traded, the worse it did

| version | your money, per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T25 | +5.0% | +7.2% | 58.8% | 1.02 |
| T50 | +2.8% | +7.2% | 66.5% | 1.02 |
| T100 | −1.5% | +7.2% | 79.0% | 0.96 |
| Q100 (1999-2015) | −2.3% | +7.5% | 82.7% | 0.89 |
| MID50 (control) | +1.8% | +7.2% | 67.8% | 1.04 |

All five failed four of the go-live conditions: beat SPY, worst fall at most 20%, gains at least 1.3
times losses, and the luck bar. The worst fall is measured on the book without its deposits. SPY
itself fell about 55% in 2008, and this book holds SPY nearly all the time, plus a fee leak, so its
falls are deeper still. The worst year was 2008 for every version (−30% to −47%).

**Luck score (DSR).** This asks how likely the result is real rather than luck, after the lab's N = 44
independent tries (read from `lab status`, policy "methods"). The bar is 0.90. The best version
scored 0.25, so it is nowhere near.

## Why

**1. Fees.** Each month the slice makes a full round trip, out of SPY into the tilt and back again.
At Gotrade's schedule (a 0.2% trading fee with a $0.10 minimum, a regulatory fee, and 11% VAT on
top), that costs about 1.2% of the slice every month, or roughly 14% of it a year. The results line
up with that almost exactly:

- T25 lagged SPY by about 2 points a year.
- T50 lagged by about 4.5 points.
- T100 lagged by about 9 points.
- Q100 lagged by about 10 points, even though it placed only 392 orders. A fee charged as a
  percentage costs the same whether the money moves in two orders or forty.

**2. The turn of the month was not special in 1996-2015.** I checked SPY's own daily returns,
before any fees. This check is outside the lab and is not a trial:

| era | turn-of-month days | mid-month days (9-13) | all other days |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +0.086% a day | +0.113% a day | −0.041% a day |
| 2003-2008 | +0.062% | +0.030% | −0.031% |
| 2009-2015 | +0.081% | +0.086% | +0.020% |

The turn-of-month days did beat the "all other days" group in every era. But the mid-month window
did about as well in two of the three eras. So in this window the paper's "all the premium arrives
at the turn" is not visible. The daily noise is about 1.2%, so with roughly 300 days per cell the
differences between the two windows are within luck.

On the lab's own runs, T50 beat its mid-month control by 1.0 point a year (+2.8% vs +1.8%). That is
a small difference, and both lose badly to SPY.

At the best case of about 0.08% a day over four days, the market earns about 0.3% around each
turn. A slice with 1.5 times the market's moves adds about 0.15% of the slice a month, against the
1.2% the round trip costs. Even a much stronger effect could not pay for the trading.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. **The expected failure happened as written.** The fees ate it, the full switch was the worst,
and the mid-month control lagged by almost the same amount. The prediction that the effect "faded
after 2008" is not quite what happened: in this data it was never clearly special in 1996-2015 to
begin with.

## Compared with near misses

None. Nothing in this family came close. For comparison, the lab's best real-fee books (monthly
momentum books that trade once a month and keep most names month to month) pay a fraction of this
turnover.

## My opinion

This direction is dead for this owner. Any calendar trick that needs a round trip every month has
to earn more than about 1.2% of the money moved per trip at Gotrade's fees. No published calendar
effect in large US stocks is that big, and the one tested here was not even distinguishable from an
ordinary mid-month week in 1996-2015. Do not spend more method ids on turn-of-month, holiday or
day-of-week timing.

The one useful idea left is to use the calendar for free. A strategy that already has to trade once
a month could schedule that trade to land around the month's turn, rather than paying extra for
it. Even that would be a small tweak, not an edge. I would point the next runs at ideas whose
trading is no more frequent than monthly.
methods.verdict: Rejected: moving money into high-beta stocks around each month's turn lost to SPY in every version (from +5.0% a year down to -2.3%, vs SPY's +7.2%); the monthly round trip costs more in fees than the turn of the month ever earned, and in 1996-2015 those days were no better than a mid-month week

methods.name: Overnight-picked winners under a weekly volatility brake: the 1998 fall is the only thing left to fix
methods.sourceRef: M0050-TOT-ON (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019) + M0022's weekly own-volatility brake (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade, funded monthly
methods.hypothesis: M0050-TOT-ON (the 40 best 12-1 momentum names, then the 20 whose gain came most overnight) earned 15.1% a year on the owner's deposits at real fees against 7.2% for deposit-matched SPY, DSR 0.956 at N=36, gains-to-losses 2.41, and failed one condition only: a 22.8% worst fall in the summer-1998 shock. That shock started inside a month, which is exactly the case a weekly re-read of the basket's own volatility was built for: on the residual book the weekly brake cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.4% at the same target. Keep TOT-ON's selection exactly, choose the basket monthly, and every week scale it by min(1, target / its own one-month volatility), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding. Variants: targets of 14%, 16% and 18% a year on the 20-name book; a 30-name book (pool 60) at 16%, which should be steadier and so brake less; and the overnight sort run inside the residual-momentum pool (M0007-N20-RAW's ranking, the real-fee residual book's) at 16%. I expect TOTON20-TV18 to be the best trade-off: the overnight book runs hotter than the residual book (it carries news-gap stocks), so an 18% target binds in shocks without clamping calm years, and should land near an 18-19% fall while keeping about 13.5-14% a year funded. Success: at least one version under the 20% fall limit with a funded return above the real-fee residual book's 13.7%. The residual-pool version should have the shallowest fall, because residual ranking strips out market beta before the overnight sort adds news exposure back.
methods.expectedFailure: Every brake in this lab has cost about one point of yearly return per point of fall it saved (insight on M0044). Buying 2.8 points of fall at that rate leaves about 12% a year, under the residual book's 13.7%, so the success bar fails even if the fall bar passes. Worse, weekly resizing at Gotrade's real fees places many small orders on a 20-30 name book funded 5M IDR a month: each resize pays the 0.10 USD floor on slices worth tens of dollars, which can eat the overnight edge's 1.3-point lead over plain momentum. The 1998 fall was fast (mid-July to end of August): a one-month volatility reading may still be low at the first weekly check after the drop starts, so the light 18% target buys little. The 30-name version may dilute the overnight sort into plain momentum and lose the edge. The residual pool may conflict with the overnight sort: residual winners are the steady, low-gap names, so the overnight leg among them may be mostly dividend noise.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

M0050's best version (TOT-ON) picks the 40 strongest stocks of the past year, then keeps the 20 whose gain came mostly **overnight** (the jump from one day's close to the next day's open). On your deposits it earned 15.1% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits in SPY. It failed one rule only: it fell 22.8% at its worst, in the summer-1998 shock. The limit is 20%.

This method keeps exactly the same picks and adds the lab's **weekly volatility brake**. The basket is still chosen once a month. Every week, the brake checks how much the 20 stocks together swung over the last month. If they swung more than a set target, it sells part of every holding and parks the money in cash. Everything runs in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, with your funding plan (10M IDR to start, then 5M IDR a month).

Five versions, all fixed before any result:
- **TOTON20-TV14 / TV16 / TV18**: the 20-name book with the brake set to 14%, 16% and 18% a year.
- **TOTON30-TV16**: 30 names chosen from the 60 strongest, at 16%.
- **RESON20-TV16**: the overnight sort run inside the residual-momentum pool (the lab's real-fee reference book's ranking), at 16%.

## Results (dev window 1996 → Oct 2015, your deposits, real fees)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no brake (M0050-TOT-ON, parent) | 15.1% | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 | failed fall |
| TOTON20-TV18 | 11.1% | 7.2% | 21.0% | 2.13 | 0.931 | failed fall |
| TOTON20-TV16 | 10.5% | 7.2% | 18.8% | 2.16 | 0.931 | passes |
| TOTON30-TV16 | 10.6% | 7.2% | 19.0% | 2.27 | **0.949** | passes |
| RESON20-TV16 | 10.2% | 7.2% | 17.5% | 1.83 | 0.934 | passes |
| TOTON20-TV14 | 9.3% | 7.2% | 16.3% | 2.12 | 0.917 | passes |

Four of five versions pass every go-live rule on the dev window, so the method is marked dev-eligible. They all beat SPY, all fell less than 20%, gains outweighed losses by far more than the 1.3× required, and all traded more than 100 times.

**The luck test.** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at N = 37, the lab's count of independent methods, against the bar of 0.90. All five clear it. The 30-name version clears it best (0.949).

**But the success bar I set failed, badly.** I asked for a version under the 20% fall limit that still earned more than the 13.7% a year of the real-fee residual-momentum book (M0032). The best passing version earned 10.6%. It even trails the residual book's own braked twin (M0033-TV22, 12.5% a year with a 20.0% fall).

**Worst years.** Every version's worst calendar year is 2011, and a mild one: −2.8% to −5.4%.

## The price of the brake

The brake took 4.0 points off the worst fall (22.8% → 18.8% at 16%). It cost 4.6 points of yearly return (15.1% → 10.5%). That is worse than the roughly one point of return per point of fall that every other brake in this lab has cost. The 18% target bought only 1.8 points of fall and still cost 4.0 points of return.

**Why so expensive here?** The overnight book picks stocks that jump on news: earnings surprises, upgrades, deals. Those stocks are jumpy all the time, not just in crashes. So a volatility brake reads this book as "too risky" in ordinary months too, and keeps it partly in cash while it is quietly making money. The brake cannot tell good jumpiness (news gaps that keep going up) from bad jumpiness (a market panic). On the calmer residual book, the brake only clamps in real shocks, which is why it was cheap there.

The fee worry did not come true in the way I feared. The trade count stayed at 1,100 for every 20-name version, exactly the parent's count. The cost came from sitting in cash, not from fees.

## Durability checks (report only, nothing recorded)

- **Walk-forward folds: 2 of 4.** The lab re-ran the choice four times, each time picking a version using only the years before, then scoring it on years it had never seen. It beat SPY in only two of the four. The lab's hard gate needs a clear majority, so `lab promote` would refuse this method.
- **2009–2015, the years with the most complete data: −3.8% a year against SPY.** The edge lives in the earlier years. That is the pattern that warned of the four methods that later failed out of sample.
- **Market breadth:** pays in both narrow and broad markets, except the hardest brake (TV14), which pays only when a few big names carry the index. As the lab has learned, this test rarely separates good from bad methods.

So no buy signal: it misses (c) the folds and (d) the 2009–2015 edge.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: failed.** I expected TV18 to land near an 18–19% fall at 13.5–14% a year. It landed at a 21.0% fall and 11.1%. I expected the residual-pool version to have the shallowest fall at the same target. It did (17.5%), but with the weakest gains vs losses (1.83).
- **Expected failure: happened, and worse than written.** I wrote that the brake would cost about a point per point of fall and leave about 12% a year. It cost more than that and left 10.5%.
- The 30-name version did not dilute the edge. It was the best of the five on gains vs losses and on luck.

My opinion: Volatility-braking the overnight book is a dead end. The brake is the wrong tool for a book whose whole edge is in jumpy stocks. It sells exactly the jumpiness that pays. And the fold record (2 of 4, losing to SPY in 2009–2015) says even the unbraked edge may be fading as the data gets more complete. I would not spend another trial on brake targets here. If this family gets another try, the fix for the 1998 fall has to come from what is picked, not from how much is held: for example, drop the stocks whose overnight gain came from one or two huge gaps (likely one-off earnings jumps), and keep those that drifted up overnight steadily. That keeps the book's character and should make it calmer without paying to sit in cash. Before that, though, the lab should check how the unbraked overnight book did in 2009–2015. If it also lost to SPY there, drop the family.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- Sera 20261009-2105: the hard gate refuses

`lab walkforward M0053`: 2 of 4 folds, 2009-2015 edge -3.8 points. `lab promote` would exit 2 on the folds condition, so no promotion was attempted. The brake bought the 20% limit at about four points of yearly return and lost the unbraked parent's fold record (3 of 4) and its positive recent-era edge (+1.1): the brake removed the part of the book that worked.


### 2026-10-12

# Amendment: the weekly brake off, and the market switch off

Three new versions, written down and committed before they ran, recorded under this book's own
name. No new book was created, so the luck hurdle stayed at 74.

**With the brake off, this book earns substantially more and falls further than the owner allows.**
On the total-momentum pool, your money would have earned 14.9% a year against 7.2% for the same
deposits in the market, up from 10.5% with the brake on — and the worst fall went from 18.8% to
22.8%. On the residual pool the same trade: 14.4% a year against 10.2% braked, with the worst fall
going from 17.5% to 22.4%. Both make more in gains than in losses than their braked versions do
(2.37x and 2.02x), both keep their luck scores above the 0.90 bar, and both fail on the worst-fall
condition alone.

The prediction was written down before the run and it held to the decimal: 22.8% and 22.4% were
predicted, 22.79% and 22.41% were measured. These numbers are directly comparable to this book's
five earlier versions — same money, same monthly top-up, same real Gotrade fees — so the trade is a
clean one to state. The brake buys about four points of worst fall and costs about four and a half
points a year of return. That is a price the owner can look at and judge, which is what recording
it was for.

**Taking the 200-day market switch off instead was simply bad.** Return fell to 8.7% a year, barely
ahead of the market's 7.2%, and the worst fall more than doubled to 37.1%. Its luck score collapsed
to 0.689. So on this book the brake and the switch are not two versions of the same idea: the brake
is selling something that pays, and the switch is buying something worth having.

The walk-forward reading is the better news and the one not to over-read: this book wins 3 of 4
folds, is stable across them, and keeps a small positive edge after 2009 (+0.5%). That is the
strongest durability reading of the two books measured today. It still promotes nothing — every
version that earns the return breaks the risk limit, and no intermediate brake setting was tried,
because picking one after seeing these numbers is tuning to a result.
methods.verdict: Taking the weekly brake off lifts your money from about 10.4% a year to about 14.7%, and lifts the worst fall from roughly 18% to roughly 22.6% — past your 20% limit, so neither unbraked version is eligible. Taking the 200-day market switch off instead is worse on both counts at once: 8.7% a year and a 37% fall. The brake is the price of staying inside your risk limit; the switch is not a drag on this book at all.

methods.name: Drizzle picks without the cash periods: park in SPY instead of cash when the trend switch is off
methods.sourceRef: M0044 / M0036-BLEND (Da, Gurun & Warachka 2014), with the SPY-200 switch's cash replaced by SPY or removed, on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade
methods.hypothesis: The drizzle blend (M0036-BLEND: twenty stocks ranked on 12-1 momentum rank plus continuity rank) and its braked twin M0044 earn their whole edge over SPY in 2002-2008, when the SPY-200 trend switch held them in cash through the crash, and trail SPY by 4.8 (BLEND) to 7.1 (M0044-TV14) points a year in 2009-2015, the best-covered era of the data. That says the stock picking itself may add nothing and the switch's cash is doing the work. This method separates the two. ALWAYS-IN removes the switch and holds the same twenty picks every month; it measures the picking alone. PARK-SPY keeps the switch but holds SPY instead of cash while it is off, so the book is always in the market and the picks only ever replace SPY; HALF-PARK holds half SPY, half cash while the switch is off. Same screen, monthly, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, 5,000,000 IDR added on the 25th. Expected: in 2009-2015 the switch was on almost all the time, so all three variants should look like BLEND there and still trail SPY by roughly 4-5 points a year; if ALWAYS-IN trails SPY over 2009-2015, the drizzle signal adds nothing in this universe in the modern era and the family should be closed. Over the whole dev window ALWAYS-IN and PARK-SPY should take the full 2000-2002 and 2008 falls (SPY fell about 55%), so their worst fall breaks the 20% limit by a wide margin, while HALF-PARK lands between. None of the three is expected to be eligible; the method is registered as the diagnostic the family's next decision rests on.
methods.expectedFailure: The way this fails to be informative: the switch was not idle in 2009-2015 (it was off for parts of 2010, 2011 and 2015), so ALWAYS-IN's 2009-2015 gap differs from BLEND's for switch reasons, not picking reasons; the within-run comparison PARK-SPY vs ALWAYS-IN then carries the answer. The way it fails as a strategy: worst fall 40% or more for ALWAYS-IN and PARK-SPY in 2008, at most a point a year of return over SPY in exchange, and a luck score far below 0.90. A surprise would be ALWAYS-IN beating SPY in 2009-2015, which would mean the switch's whipsaws, not the picking, cost BLEND its modern-era return.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The drizzle blend picks 20 stocks whose past year's rise came in many small, steady days rather than a few big jumps. It has a "trend switch": when SPY is below its 200-day average, the whole book sits in cash. Its edge over SPY came almost entirely from 2002-2008, when that switch kept it in cash through the crash. In 2009-2015 it trailed SPY by about 5 points a year.

So the question was: **is the stock picking worth anything, or is it all the switch?** Three versions, same picks, same monthly trading, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5,000,000 IDR added on the 25th:

- **ALWAYS-IN**: no switch. Hold the 20 picks every month, no matter what. This is the picking alone.
- **PARK-SPY**: keep the switch, but while it is off hold SPY instead of cash.
- **HALF-PARK**: while the switch is off, hold half SPY, half cash.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015; the same deposits into SPY earned +7.2% a year)

| version | your money a year | worst fall | worst year | gains vs losses | luck score | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent: drizzle blend (cash when off) | +12.0% | 22.3% | - | 2.17 | 0.930 | fails: fall just over 20% |
| ALWAYS-IN | +8.2% | 59.9% | 2008, -43.5% | 1.48 | 0.605 | fails badly |
| PARK-SPY | +9.7% | 53.8% | 2008, -37.0% | 1.71 | 0.688 | fails badly |
| HALF-PARK | +11.0% | 32.3% | 2008, -20.1% | 1.93 | 0.866 | fails: fall and luck score |

Rejected on every version. The worst falls are two to three times the 20% limit. The luck score (DSR: how likely the result is real rather than the best of many lucky tries) is judged at N = 38 independent methods against the 0.90 bar. All three miss it, ALWAYS-IN by a mile. Time invested was 97% for ALWAYS-IN and PARK-SPY, 83% for HALF-PARK, so these numbers measure the method, not idle cash.

## The real finding: the picking edge, era by era

Edge = yearly growth minus SPY's, over the same months (sliced from the recorded curves, nothing re-run):

| era | SPY | parent (cash when off) | ALWAYS-IN (picks only) | PARK-SPY | HALF-PARK |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2001 | +11.9% | +9.8 | **+8.8** | +9.5 | +9.8 |
| 2002-2008 | -1.4% | +10.5 | **+1.2** | +1.5 | +6.1 |
| 2009-2015 | +16.7% | -4.9 | **-2.3** | +0.7 | -2.0 |

Read the ALWAYS-IN column: that is what the picking alone is worth. It is +8.8 points a year in the late 1990s, +1.2 in 2002-2008, and **-2.3 in 2009-2015**. The edge shrinks steadily, and it shrinks exactly as the data covers more of the index (48% of index members priced in 1996, 74% by 2014). That is the pattern you would expect if part of the early edge is the data's missing dead companies, or simply a strategy that worked in the dot-com era and stopped.

The switch, on the other hand, was worth about 9 points a year in 2002-2008 (parent +10.5 vs picks alone +1.2). In 2009-2015 it cost about 2.6 points (parent -4.9 vs picks alone -2.3), because it sat in cash during the spring 2009 rebound.

PARK-SPY is the only version that did not lose to SPY in 2009-2015 (+0.7). The reason is specific: in early 2009 the switch was off, so it held SPY through the rebound, while ALWAYS-IN held last year's winners, which is the classic "momentum crash" (last year's winners lag hard when a beaten-down market bounces). That +0.7 is the switch steering away from the picks at the right moment, not the picks themselves.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis's core question got a clear answer: **ALWAYS-IN trails SPY in 2009-2015**, so by the rule I wrote before running, the drizzle signal adds nothing in this universe in the modern era, and the family's picking should be treated as closed.
- I expected all three to look like the parent in 2009-2015 (about -4 to -5). Wrong: the switch was off more in early 2009 than I allowed for, so the versions spread out (-2.3 to +0.7). That is the "fails to be informative" case I registered, and as planned the PARK-SPY vs ALWAYS-IN comparison carried the answer.
- Expected worst falls of 40% or more for ALWAYS-IN and PARK-SPY: happened (59.9%, 53.8%). Luck score far below 0.90: happened.

## Walk-forward

The method wins 3 of 4 walk-forward folds by its own selection rule (which picks HALF-PARK, the best on paper), with a -1.9 point edge in 2009-2015. It is not dev-eligible, so nothing is promotable. No buy signal.

## Assumptions

No in-run control: the parent configuration is already recorded at the same real fees (M0036-BLEND), so re-running it would add nothing. HALF-PARK was added beside the two reserved variants as a middle point; it does not change N (one method, one look).

**My opinion:** stop spending trials on the drizzle picks. The lab now has the same answer three ways: the picking edge was large in the 1990s and is gone after 2009, and every win this family showed was the trend switch keeping it in cash through 2008. The one thing worth carrying forward is not the drizzle signal but the shape PARK-SPY revealed: hold the market, not last year's winners, in the months right after a bear market, since that is when momentum books lose most. I would test that as a general rule on the lab's best picker, not on this one, and I expect it to fix a few points of 2009, not the 2008 fall; the fall still needs cash.
methods.verdict: The drizzle picks alone lose to SPY by 2.3 points a year after 2009, and every version falls 32-60% at its worst; the family's edge was the cash switch, not the picking

methods.name: Buy the dip inside the winners: last year's strongest stocks, entered after a bad month
methods.hypothesis: The bounce book showed a one-month fall is worth little as a stand-alone signal (about SPY's return, a 27% worst fall), but the classic 12-1 momentum skips the latest month precisely because recent losers bounce. Among the top 60 names by plain 12-1 total momentum (not residual, so the family is not the test-failed residual one), hold the 20 with the worst last-month return relative to the market, equal weight, SPY-200 gate, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the monthly top-up. Controls: the 20 with the best last month (the mirror), and plain top-20 momentum. Success means beating the plain momentum control on the worst fall at similar return, and winning a majority of walk-forward folds. Expected failure: the pullback pushes the book down into weaker momentum names and the 2009 junk rally still hits it, the same way it hit the parent.

methods.name: Steady overnight drift, not one big gap: overnight winners without the single-jump stocks
methods.sourceRef: M0050-TOT-ON (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.03.011) with the steady-path idea of Da, Gurun & Warachka (2014) moved onto the overnight leg
methods.hypothesis: M0050-TOT-ON earned 15.1% a year on the owner's deposits at real fees with a 22.8% worst fall (summer 1998) and kept its edge out of sample in walk-forward (3 of 4 folds, positive in 2009-2015); M0053 showed a volatility brake fixes the fall only by giving up 4.6 points of return and the fold record. Fix the fall through selection instead. Among the 40 best 12-1 momentum names (60 for a 30-name book), rank on the past year's overnight log-return sum after removing each name's 3 (TRIM3) or 5 (TRIM5) largest overnight values, or on the share of positive overnight sessions (POS), so the book holds names that drift up overnight steadily rather than ones carried by one or two earnings jumps; jump-driven names are news-sensitive and gap down together in a shock. Unbraked, monthly, equal weight, SPY 200-day gate, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, owner's funding. Variants: TRIM3-N20, TRIM5-N20, POS-N20, TRIM3-N30, POS-N30. Success: a version with worst fall under 20% and funded return above 13.7% (the real-fee residual book), and a majority of walk-forward folds beaten.
methods.expectedFailure: The 1998 fall that sank M0050-TOT-ON was a market-wide momentum crash, not a cluster of earnings-gap reversals, so a steadier overnight path may pick nearly the same names and fall nearly as far; the pool of 40 already fixes most of the book (20 of 40), so the sort has limited room to change anything. Trimming the big gaps may also remove exactly the earnings-news drift that carries the overnight edge, so return may drop toward plain momentum's 13.8% without the fall improving. POS is the most exposed: before about 2001 many opens equal the prior close, so the share of positive nights partly measures how often a stock's open was recorded, i.e. data noise, and may tilt to the most liquid names. Thirty names should cut the fall by spreading the book but dilute return.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The parent method (M0050-TOT-ON) buys last year's 40 strongest stocks, then keeps the 20 whose gain came mostly **overnight** (the jump from one day's close to the next day's open). It earned 15.1% a year on your deposits at real fees, but its worst fall was 22.8%, over the 20% limit. A volatility brake (M0053) fixed the fall but cut the return to about 10.5% a year.

This method tried to fix the fall by choosing **different stocks** instead of braking. The idea: some stocks earn their overnight gain from one or two huge jumps (usually earnings news). Those news-driven stocks might all drop together in a shock. So prefer stocks that rise a little, night after night. Three ways to measure "steady":

- **TRIM3 / TRIM5**: add up the past year's overnight moves, but leave out each stock's 3 (or 5) biggest up-nights.
- **POS**: the share of nights the stock rose overnight.

Each was run with 20 names (picked from the 40 strongest) and 30 names (from the 60 strongest). Everything else is the parent's: same stocks, all cash when SPY is under its 200-day average, monthly, equal amounts, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, your funding plan (10M IDR, then 5M IDR a month).

## Results (dev window 1996 → Oct 2015, your deposits)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent TOT-ON (M0050) | 15.1% | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 |
| TRIM3-N20 | 15.0% | 7.2% | 23.2% | 2.34 | 0.963 |
| TRIM5-N20 | 14.8% | 7.2% | 22.9% | 2.35 | 0.960 |
| POS-N20 | 13.9% | 7.2% | 25.6% | 2.26 | 0.940 |
| TRIM3-N30 | 13.5% | 7.2% | 23.7% | 2.36 | 0.958 |
| POS-N30 | 13.1% | 7.2% | 24.6% | 2.34 | 0.949 |

**All five fail one rule: the worst fall must be at most 20%.** The best miss is TRIM5 by 2.9 points. Every other rule passes: all beat SPY by about double, gains outweigh losses more than 2 to 1, and all make over 1,000 trades.

**Luck test.** The DSR says how likely a result is real rather than the lucky best of many tries. It was judged at N = 39 (the lab's count of independent methods tried) against the bar of 0.90. All five clear it (0.940-0.963). The return is real; the fall is the problem.

**Walk-forward.** Picking the variant using only past data, then scoring it on later years, the method beat SPY in 3 of 4 folds and was still slightly ahead (+0.2% a year) in 2009-2015, the years where the data is most complete. That is the same durability the parent showed. It would pass the promotion gate's fold rule if it passed the fall rule; it does not.

## When it hurt

Every version took its worst fall in the same place as the parent: the summer of 1998 (the Russia default and LTCM shock), August 1998 especially. On month-end values alone each lost about 14.5-16% in that one month; the full fall, measured day by day, is the 23-26% above. Worst calendar years are mild (2011 or 2015, -2% to -4%), because the SPY trend switch puts the book in cash for most of 2001-2003 and 2008-2009. On average 69-70% of the money was invested, the same as the parent.

## Why

The fall was not caused by which kind of overnight winner the book held. In August 1998 the whole momentum pool fell together: strong stocks of every kind were sold at once. Choosing 20 of the 40 strongest by a steadier measure still leaves the book holding 20 of those same 40 strong stocks, and the 40 dropped as a group. The steady sort moved the fall by a few tenths of a point either way.

Trimming the big nights cost almost nothing (15.0% vs 15.1%), which says the overnight edge is not mostly in a few earnings jumps. It is spread across many ordinary nights. That is a useful fact about the edge, even though it did not help the fall.

POS (counting up-nights) was worst on both counts: lower return and a deeper fall. A likely reason, as feared before the run: before about 2001 many recorded opens equal the previous close, so "share of up-nights" partly measures data quality, not behaviour.

Going to 30 names did not reduce the fall, and it cut return by 1.5 points. Spreading the book across more momentum stocks does not help when all momentum stocks fall together.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (a steadier overnight path fixes the fall) **did not hold**. The expected failure happened almost word for word: "the 1998 fall was a market-wide momentum crash, not a cluster of earnings-gap reversals, so a steadier overnight path may pick nearly the same names and fall nearly as far." The part of the expected failure that did not happen: trimming did not hurt return.

## Compared with near misses

- Parent M0050-TOT-ON: 15.1%, 22.8% fall. TRIM3 is a statistical twin of it.
- M0053 (the same book with a weekly volatility brake): 10.5-10.6%, 18.8-19.0% fall, eligible but lost to SPY in 2009-2015.
- The real-fee residual book (M0032, the lab's reference): 13.7%, 20.6% fall.

## My opinion:

Stock selection inside the momentum pool is a dead end for this fall. Three different ways to choose 20 of the 40 all land within a point of 23%, because the crash was in the pool, not in the choice. More sorting variants would only spend luck budget. The overnight edge itself is solid (it survives trimming, three of four folds, positive in 2009-2015), so the next try should change **what the book is exposed to when momentum crashes**, not which momentum stocks it holds. Two candidates: hold the overnight winners that move least with the market (low beta), since the 1998 and 2011 drops hit high-beta names hardest, or pair the overnight book with something that rose in August 1998 (long Treasuries are not tradable here, but low-volatility stocks are). I queued the low-beta version; it is the cheaper experiment and keeps the return engine intact.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0056-TRIM3-N20`: DSR 0.9322 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0056-TRIM5-N20`: DSR 0.9276 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0056-TRIM3-N30`: DSR 0.9245 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0056-POS-N30`: DSR 0.9095 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Picking steadier overnight winners changed almost nothing: 13.1-15.0% a year on your money vs 7.2% in SPY, but the worst fall stayed 22.9-25.6% (limit 20%), because in the 1998 shock all momentum stocks fell together

methods.name: Short-term momentum: last month's winners among the most heavily traded stocks keep going
methods.sourceRef: Medhat & Schmeling (2022), Short-term Momentum, Review of Financial Studies 35(3)
methods.hypothesis: Medhat and Schmeling find that last month's return reverses among low-turnover stocks but continues among high-turnover stocks: the reversal everyone knows hides a continuation in the stocks the market is actively trading on news. The store has no share counts before 2009, so turnover is proxied by abnormal volume: the stock's mean daily share volume over the last 21 sessions divided by its own mean over the 252 before (volume in the store is split-adjusted). Inside F4's liquidity and membership screen, behind the SPY-200 trend gate (an assumption carried over from the family the lab already runs, so the result is comparable with M0028), among names above their own 200-day average, HIGH-N20 takes the top fifth by abnormal volume and holds the 20 with the highest one-month return, equal weight, monthly, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). HIGH-N30 holds 30. LOW-N20 is the control: the same ranking in the bottom fifth by abnormal volume, which the paper says should reverse and lose. ALL-N20 skips the volume sort (plain one-month winners) to show whether the volume conditioning adds anything. Success: HIGH beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under 20%, LOW is clearly worse than HIGH, ALL sits between them, and the edge survives a majority of walk-forward folds at real fees.
methods.expectedFailure: This is a near-100%-a-month churn book, so Gotrade's fees on 15-35 USD slots take several tenths of a percent each side and may eat a premium the paper measured in all-CRSP stocks, mostly small ones. Large caps may show little continuation: the paper's effect is strongest in the top turnover decile of the whole market, and a fifth of ~300 uptrending index names is a blunter cut. Abnormal volume is a weaker proxy than turnover: a volume spike after a crash is also a high-volume month, so the high bucket may buy one-month winners that are only bouncing. The shocks of 1998, 2000-02 and 2008 hit last month's hot stocks hardest, so the worst fall may pass 20%. If the control is no worse than HIGH, the paper's split did not carry over to this universe.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What we tested

A 2022 paper (Medhat & Schmeling) says last month's winners **keep winning** when the stock is
being traded heavily, and **give back** their gains when it is traded thinly. We had no share
counts before 2009, so "traded heavily" meant: the stock's volume over the last month compared
with its own normal volume over the year before. Each month, among index stocks in an uptrend
(and only while SPY is above its 200-day average), we bought the 20 biggest one-month winners
from the busiest fifth (HIGH-N20), the same with 30 names (HIGH-N30), the same from the
quietest fifth (LOW-N20, the control the paper says should lose), and from all of them with no
volume sort (ALL-N20). Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5M IDR added every month.

## Result: the opposite of the paper

| variant | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HIGH-N20 (busiest fifth) | +6.5% | +7.2% | 22.0% | 1.32 | 0.67 |
| HIGH-N30 | +6.6% | +7.2% | 19.0% | 1.38 | 0.70 |
| LOW-N20 (quietest fifth, the control) | **+8.2%** | +7.2% | 18.7% | 1.40 | 0.85 |
| ALL-N20 (no volume sort) | +6.9% | +7.2% | 23.0% | 1.31 | 0.54 |

- **HIGH-N20** lost to SPY by 0.7 points a year and fell 22% at its worst, over the 20% limit.
- **HIGH-N30** lost to SPY by 0.6 points a year; its worst fall (19%) was inside the limit.
- **LOW-N20**, the "should lose" control, beat SPY by a point a year with a worst fall of 18.7%.
  It failed only the luck test: DSR 0.85 against the bar of 0.90. DSR asks how likely the
  result is real rather than the best of many lucky tries; the lab judged it at N = 40 (one
  look per distinct method, as `lab status` counts them).
- **ALL-N20** sits between, as expected, and lost to SPY.
- The worst calendar year was 2015 for every variant (HIGH-N20 −11%, LOW-N20 −4.8%, ALL −17.6%).
  The SPY trend switch kept the books mostly in cash through 2008, so the crash year is not where
  the damage came from; the damage came from choppy markets where last month's hot stock turned.

The ordering is the paper's exactly upside down: quiet winners > all winners > busy winners.

## Walk-forward and durability

`lab walkforward M0057`: the variant the lab's own rule would have picked (stable across folds)
beat SPY in **1 of 4** folds, and its edge in 2009-2015, the years where our data covers the most
index members, was **−8.6%**. So even the LOW control's dev win lives in the early, thin-data
years and is gone by the recent era. Not eligible, and the hard gate would refuse it anyway on
folds.

## Why

The paper's effect is measured across all US stocks, most of them small, where heavy trading
means news is still being priced in. Among large index names, a volume surge after a big month
mostly means the crowd has already arrived: the move is late, hot money is in, and it tends to
fade. This is the older Lee & Swaminathan (2000) finding: **low-volume winners keep winning,
high-volume winners mean-revert**, because volume marks where a stock sits in its popularity
cycle. It also fits the lab's "frog in the pan" work (the drizzle picker, M0036/M0044): gains
that arrive quietly are under-noticed and keep going; gains that arrive loudly are already
priced. Our proxy (abnormal volume, not turnover) also catches post-crash panic volume, which is
the failure the pre-registration named.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- Hypothesis: **rejected.** HIGH lost to SPY and LOW beat HIGH, not the reverse.
- Expected failure: partly happened. Fees did not kill it outright (all variants within about a
  point of SPY), the 20% fall limit was breached by HIGH-N20 and ALL-N20 as feared, and "if the
  control is no worse than HIGH, the split did not carry over" is exactly what happened, with a
  sign flip.

## Compared with near relatives

- The bounce book (M0028, buy last month's biggest fallers) also failed the fold majority (2 of 4).
  One-month signals in large caps, either direction, have not held up across eras here.
- The 12-month residual-momentum books still sit far ahead on dev (MAR 0.77-0.86 vs 0.29-0.44
  here), at the cost of a family already disproven out of sample.

**My opinion:** the "busy stocks keep going" direction is dead for large caps and I would not
spend another trial on it. The interesting thing is the flip: quiet winners beat busy winners,
which agrees with two older lines of evidence (Lee & Swaminathan; frog in the pan). But the
quiet-winner edge here is one month long, earned in the 1990s, and negative in 2009-2015, so I
would not chase it as a one-month book either. What I would try next is using volume as a
**filter on the 12-month momentum book**, not as its own signal: skip the 12-month winners whose
volume has surged, keep the quiet ones. That tests the same lesson on a signal with a longer,
better-documented life. It must stand on plain 12-month momentum, not the residual version: the residual family has already failed out of sample and the hard gate would refuse anything descended from it. The queued crowding-penalty idea (M0046) tests a softer form of this on the residual book; the new idea is the plain-momentum, hard-filter version.
methods.verdict: Rejected: busy-stock winners lost to SPY (+6.5% vs +7.2% a year); the quiet-stock control did better (+8.2%) but failed the luck test and lost in recent years

methods.name: The illiquidity premium among large companies: hold the S&P names that trade thinnest for their size
methods.sourceRef: Amihud (2002), Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects, Journal of Financial Markets 5(1), 31-56, doi:10.1016/S1386-4181(01)00024-6
methods.hypothesis: Amihud shows that stocks whose prices move most per dollar traded (the average of absolute daily return divided by dollar volume) earn a premium for being harder to trade. Inside the point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 every name is easy for a 20M IDR account to trade, so the owner collects a premium for a cost it never pays. Each month, among members priced at $5 or more (F4's screen with its 20M-dollar volume floor removed, because that floor cuts exactly the thin tail), rank on Amihud illiquidity over the past 252 bars and hold the most illiquid names equal weight, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade. Ranking is cross-sectional each month, so the decades-long rise in market-wide volume does not matter. Variants: ILL20-T and ILL30-T (20 / 30 most illiquid behind the SPY 200-day gate), ILL20 and ILL30 (no gate), and LIQ20-T (the 20 most liquid behind the gate: the control, which should trail). Success: an ILL variant beats SPY TR on dev within the drawdown limit, the control does worse, and the edge survives the walk-forward folds and the 2009-2015 high-coverage era.
methods.expectedFailure: Among large caps, illiquidity is mostly smallness: the most illiquid S&P names are the smallest members, so this is a small-cap tilt, and the store's survivorship gap flatters small caps most (the small members that died are the ones missing). The edge may sit in 2000-2006, the great small-and-value run, and vanish by 2009-2015. Small, thin members fell hard in 2008 and in the 2002 bottom, so without the trend gate the worst fall should break 20%, and even with it 1998 and 2008 may push it over. Thin names also cost more in real spreads than Gotrade's fee schedule charges, which the backtest does not see.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

Amihud's illiquidity measure asks: how far does a stock's price move for each dollar traded? Stocks that move a lot per dollar are "thin", and the 2002 paper found thin stocks pay extra for that. Every month this method took the S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members priced at $5 or more, measured each one's thinness over the past year, and held the 20 (or 30) thinnest in equal slots, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly 5M IDR top-up. Two versions sat in cash whenever SPY was under its 200-day average; two were always invested. A control held the 20 *most* heavily traded names.

Assumption made without asking: the usual F4 floor of $20M traded a day was removed, because that floor throws out exactly the thin names being tested, and every index member is easy to trade for a $1,250 account.

## Result vs SPY (dev window, 1996 to 2015)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | luck check (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 thinnest, trend switch (ILL20-T) | +12.7% | +7.2% | 26.4% | 0.965 | worst fall over 20% |
| 30 thinnest, trend switch (ILL30-T) | +12.5% | +7.2% | 25.8% | 0.968 | worst fall over 20% |
| 20 thinnest, always in (ILL20) | +12.1% | +7.2% | 67.5% | 0.748 | worst fall, luck |
| 30 thinnest, always in (ILL30) | +12.9% | +7.2% | 64.4% | 0.785 | worst fall, luck |
| 20 most traded, trend switch (control) | +8.1% | +7.2% | 17.6% | 0.883 | luck |

The thin books earned about 5 points a year more than SPY on the same deposits. The best of them still lost 26% from a peak at its worst, over the 20% limit, so all five are rejected. Without the trend switch the thin books lost two-thirds of their value in 2008 (worst year −48%).

DSR is the lab's "is this real or luck" score after counting every idea tried. The bar is 0.90, and N is 41 independent methods (read off lab status). The gated thin books clear it easily (0.965, 0.968); the ungated ones do not.

## The part that decides it: when the edge was earned

- **Walk-forward folds** (train on the past, score on unseen years): the method beat SPY in **1 of 4** folds. The hard gate needs a majority. This would be refused even if the drawdown were fixed.
- **2009-2015, the years the data is most complete:** the edge was **−6.9% a year**. The whole twenty-year lead was earned before 2009.
- **Narrow vs broad markets:** the thin books win +15.7% a year vs SPY in months when the average stock beats the index ("broad"), and lose −8.6% a year in months a few big names carry it ("narrow"). The control is the exact mirror: +11.2% narrow, −5.5% broad.

## Why

Among index members, "thin for its size" mostly means "small". The illiquid book is an equal-weight small-and-mid-cap bet inside the index. That bet paid hugely from 2000 to 2006, when small and value stocks ran while the big tech names collapsed, and stopped paying once large names took over after 2009. On top of that, the store is missing many index members that later died, and those are disproportionately the small, thin ones, so the early-year result is flattered too. The 26% worst fall is small stocks falling together in a crash faster than the 200-day switch can react.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis held in its narrow form: thin names did beat thick names (+12.7% vs +8.1% a year), and the control trailed. But the expected failure happened almost word for word: it is a small-cap tilt, its edge lives before 2009 and is negative in 2009-2015, and the worst fall broke 20% even with the trend switch.

## Compared with near misses

The best gated thin book (MAR 0.48, return per unit of worst fall) is far below the residual-momentum and blend books (MAR 0.77-0.90 at the flat fee). Its DSR is higher than most of them, which says the 1996-2015 average is not luck, but it is the average of one long regime, not a repeatable edge. Interesting side note: the most-traded control (+8.1%, worst fall 17.6%, profit factor 5.2) is the calmest book in this run, and it pays in narrow markets, which is the market the test window has had.

My opinion: the illiquidity premium inside the S&P is a dead end for Seer. It is a small-cap bet in disguise, and the lab already knows the test window (2016-2026) was a big-company market, where this book would lose; the folds and the 2009-2015 number say the same thing on data we are allowed to look at. I would not spend more trials making it calmer. The useful lesson runs the other way: the heavily traded control paid in narrow markets with a small fall, so the next try should be a "big, busy names" book that pairs liquidity with a return signal, built to win the narrow regime that cost every roster strategy its test look.
