methods.name: Overnight winners that move least with the market: low-beta stocks inside the overnight momentum book
methods.sourceRef: M0056 / M0050-TOT-ON (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.03.011) with a market-beta screen on the momentum pool, after Frazzini & Pedersen (2014), Betting against beta
methods.hypothesis: M0056 showed that re-sorting the 40 strongest momentum names by a steadier overnight path leaves the 23% summer-1998 fall untouched (22.9-25.6% across five versions) while keeping 13-15% a year, because the whole pool falls together in a momentum crash. Change the crash exposure instead: among the 40 best 12-1 momentum names, drop the 10 (DROP10) or 20 (DROP20) with the highest 126-session daily beta to SPY and keep the 20 with the largest overnight sum; or rank the 40 on overnight sum divided by beta floored at 0.3 (RATIO); or drop the 10 highest-beta names on a 252-session beta (DROP10-B252, the estimate-length check); or start from the 60 best and drop the 30 highest-beta (P60-DROP30). High-beta momentum names carried the 1998 and 2011 drops; low-beta winners should keep the overnight drift (which M0056 showed is broad, not jump-driven) with a smaller fall. Unbraked, monthly, equal weight, SPY 200-day gate, 20 names, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, owner's funding. Published 2019 (the overnight split) and 2014 (betting against beta): the dev window ends 2015 and predates the overnight paper's crowd. Success: a version with worst fall under 20%, funded return above 13.7% (the real-fee residual book), a positive edge on SPY in 2009-2015 and a majority of walk-forward folds kept.
methods.expectedFailure: The 1998 shock was a momentum crash in which the strong stocks fell together whatever their beta: a 126-session beta measured in a calm first half of 1998 may not rank the names that later fell hardest, so the fall may barely move, as it did for M0056. A low-beta cut also leans the book toward defensive, slower names, which costs return in the 2003-2007 and 2009-2015 rallies, exactly the years SPY's big-company drift is hardest to beat; DROP20 and P60-DROP30 are most exposed to that. RATIO can be dominated by the beta floor and pick only utilities-like names. Even if one version clears the fall, it is still a 12-month momentum book: the hard gate's behaviour rule may read it as kin of the test-failed momentum books (residual correlation 0.85 or more), so a dev pass may not be promotable. And the overnight edge is a published anomaly that inverted from 2018 for M0050, so a good dev result is likely to fade out of sample.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What was tried

The parent books buy last year's 40 strongest stocks, then keep the 20 whose gain came mostly **overnight** (from one day's close to the next day's open). They earn about 15% a year on your deposits, but their worst fall is about 23%, over the 20% limit. All of them took that fall in the summer 1998 shock. The last try (M0056) chose the 20 by a steadier overnight path and changed nothing, because the whole pool of strong stocks fell together.

This method instead cuts out the strong stocks that **move most with the market**. That is "beta": a beta of 1.5 means a stock tends to move 1.5% when SPY moves 1%. The idea was that high-beta winners take the biggest hits in a shock, so leaving them out should soften the fall and keep the overnight gain. Five versions:

- **DROP10**: of the 40 strongest, drop the 10 with the highest beta (measured over the last six months), then keep the 20 best overnight earners.
- **DROP20**: keep only the 20 lowest-beta of the 40. The overnight sort no longer has any say.
- **RATIO**: rank the 40 on overnight gain divided by beta, so a calm stock with a good overnight record ranks first.
- **DROP10-B252**: DROP10 with beta measured over a year instead of six months.
- **P60-DROP30**: start from the 60 strongest, drop the 30 highest-beta, then keep the 20 best overnight earners.

Everything else is the parent's: all cash when SPY is under its 200-day average, monthly, equal amounts, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and your funding plan (10M IDR, then 5M IDR a month).

## Results (dev window 1996 to Oct 2015, your deposits)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent M0050-TOT-ON | 15.1% | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 (old N) | fall |
| M0056-TRIM3-N20 | 15.0% | 7.2% | 23.2% | 2.34 | 0.963 (old N) | fall |
| DROP10 | 12.4% | 7.2% | 20.5% | 2.02 | 0.910 | fall (by 0.5 pt) |
| DROP20 | 10.6% | 7.2% | **19.8%** | 2.05 | 0.867 | luck test |
| RATIO | **15.3%** | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.40 | 0.949 | fall |
| DROP10-B252 | 11.6% | 7.2% | 20.9% | 2.06 | 0.882 | fall, luck test |
| P60-DROP30 | 10.1% | 7.2% | 25.1% | 1.94 | 0.835 | fall, luck test |

All five are rejected. Every version beats SPY on your deposits, and gains outweigh losses about 2 to 1. Only DROP20 gets under the 20% fall limit (19.8%), and it then fails the luck test.

**Luck test.** The DSR estimates how likely a result is real rather than the lucky best of many tries. The lab judged it at N = 69, its current count of independent methods tried, against the bar of 0.90. DROP10 (0.910) and RATIO (0.949) clear it. DROP20 (0.867) does not, because it earns too little for its swings to stand out from luck after 69 tries.

**Walk-forward.** Each fold chooses the version using only earlier years, then scores it on later years it has not seen. The method beat SPY in 3 of 4 folds. But in 2009-2015, the years with the most complete data and the ones most like today, it trailed SPY by 2.7% a year. M0056 was still +0.2% ahead there. The low-beta cut gave away the most edge in exactly the years that count most.

## When it hurt

Every version's worst month was again August 1998 (Russia's default and the LTCM hedge fund collapse). On month-end values the 1998 drop shrank only a little: 14.9% for the parent, 14.0% for DROP10, 11.8% for DROP20 and 12.6% for P60-DROP30. The August 2011 drop shrank more (parent 8.1%, DROP10 6.2%, P60-DROP30 4.5%). P60-DROP30's full day-by-day worst fall (25.1%) is deeper than its 1998 month-end drop, so it took a separate deep fall elsewhere, probably in the choppy 1999-2000 years (its worst calendar year is 1999). The book was about 70% invested on average, the same as the parent, so these falls are not a cash effect. Worst calendar years are mild (-0.1% to -2.2%) because the SPY switch keeps the book in cash for most of 2001-2003 and 2008-2009.

## Why

Beta did point at part of the crash risk: every cut softened August 2011 and, a little, August 1998. But the cut works like a dimmer, not a switch. Removing high-beta names also removes the names that carry the gains in a rally, so return falls about as fast as the fall shrinks: 15.1% to 12.4% to 10.6% while the fall goes 22.8% to 20.5% to 19.8%. Return per unit of fall (MAR) got worse, not better: 0.65 for the parent against 0.60 and 0.53. In August 1998 the momentum pool fell together whatever each stock's beta had been in the calm months before. A six-month beta measured in a quiet market says little about who falls in a crash, as feared before the run.

RATIO is the odd one out. Dividing by beta mostly re-ordered the same names. It ended a statistical twin of the parent (15.3% a year, 22.8% fall), so this score does not lean on low beta much.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (low-beta winners keep the overnight gain with a smaller fall) **did not hold**: the fall got smaller only where the return got smaller too. The expected failure happened in both parts written before the run. The 1998 fall "may barely move", and it moved 1-3 points. The low-beta lean "costs return in the 2003-2007 and 2009-2015 rallies", and the 2009-2015 edge went from +0.2% to -2.7% a year. The kin question never came up, because nothing was eligible.

## Compared with near misses

- M0053 (the same book with a weekly volatility brake) fixed the fall at 18.8-19.0% for about 10.5% a year. DROP20 lands at almost the same place (19.8%, 10.6%) by a different road. Two unrelated brakes buying the same trade suggests this is the price of the fall in this book, not a quirk of one method.
- The real-fee residual book (M0032): 13.7% a year, 20.6% fall. DROP10 is a little worse on both.

## My opinion:

Stop filtering stocks inside this momentum pool. Steadiness (M0056), beta (this method) and a volatility brake (M0053) all land on the same line: each point of fall removed costs about a point of return a year, and the 2009-2015 edge goes first. The overnight momentum book's 23% fall is a property of holding strong stocks in a momentum crash. No way of choosing among strong stocks removes it. If this family gets another try, it should add something that rose in August 1998 rather than subtract from the pool: hold the overnight book half in SPY, so the fall is roughly halved while SPY's big-company drift is matched in the years it is hardest to beat. I queued that as the next idea. I would not spend more ids on beta, volatility or path filters here.

methods.name: Ride the earnings-day jump: buy big caps after a high-volume up gap, hold two months
methods.sourceRef: Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam (2008), Earnings announcements are full of surprises, SSRN 909563; Mohrschladt & Baars (MAX reverses unless tied to an announcement); Garfinkel & Sokobin (2006), JAR

The store has no earnings dates, but an announcement in a big company leaves a footprint in daily bars: an opening gap on volume at least 3 times the stock's 60-day median. Brandt et al. show the three-day return around the announcement predicts a drift for about 60 trading days, and Mohrschladt and Baars find a big jump tied to news keeps going. So: inside F4's liquidity and membership screen, a stock qualifies when, in the last 60 sessions, it had a day with volume >= 3x its median, an up gap at the open, and a three-day return (day before to day after) at least 4 points above SPY's over the same days. The volume proxy also catches non-earnings news (takeover bids, index adds) whose jumps revert or freeze. If QUIET does as well as N20-TREND, the edge is plain short-term momentum, not news.

### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The research data has no earnings dates. But when a big company reports, its daily bars usually show it: the stock opens with a jump (a "gap") and trades three or more times its normal volume. Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara and Venkatachalam (2008) found that the three-day move around an earnings report tends to keep going in the same direction for about 60 trading days. So this book buys stocks whose latest "news day" was a strong up gap: volume at least 3 times the 60-day median, an opening gap up, and a three-day return at least 4 points better than SPY's over the same days. It holds up to 20 of them at 5% each, keeps each one while its news day is under 60 sessions old, and puts any unused slots into SPY. While SPY is below its 200-day average, the book holds cash. Trades are in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees.

Five fixed variants, all registered before any result: N20-TREND (re-picked weekly), N20-ALWAYS (weekly, never steps out to cash), N30-TREND (weekly, 30 slots), QUIET-N20-TREND (control: the same jumps on *ordinary* volume, so probably no news) and M-N20-TREND (the N20-TREND signal, re-picked monthly).

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, on the owner's monthly deposits)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M-N20-TREND (monthly) | **+11.6%** | +7.2% | 25.2% | 1.93 | **0.918** |
| N20-ALWAYS (weekly, no switch) | +9.2% | +7.2% | 72.7% | 1.39 | 0.558 |
| N20-TREND (weekly) | +5.0% | +7.2% | 35.4% | 1.27 | 0.394 |
| N30-TREND (weekly) | +4.1% | +7.2% | 32.6% | 1.23 | 0.392 |
| QUIET control (weekly) | +2.9% | +7.2% | 32.2% | 1.15 | 0.235 |

The method is **rejected**. The monthly variant comes very close. It beats total-return SPY by 4.4 points a year on the same deposits. Its gains are almost twice its losses (1.93, against a bar of 1.3). It clears the luck bar: a DSR of 0.918 against the 0.90 bar, with the lab's N at 42 (one look per method). In plain words, after 42 different ideas have been tried, there is roughly a 92% chance its edge is more than luck. The only condition it fails is the worst fall: **25.2% on the funded account, against a 20% limit**. Taking the deposits out (they refill a falling account), the fall was 23.6%, from April to September 1998, when the summer crash hit before the monthly SPY-200 check could move the book to cash. The weekly variants fail several conditions at once.

## By era (no deposits, the book's own yearly return vs SPY)

| era | M-N20-TREND | N20-ALWAYS (weekly) | N20-TREND (weekly) | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +11.1% | +13.4% | +3.0% | +6.2% |
| 2003-2008 | +6.3% | -3.1% | +1.8% | +2.3% |
| **2009-2015** | **+17.7%** | **+20.1%** | +9.9% | +14.8% |

The 2009-2015 result matters most. Those are the best-covered years in the data and the ones most like today, and every edge in the last batch was earned before 2009.
