methods.name: Buy the laggard of a pair that usually moves together: the long side of pairs trading
methods.sourceRef: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst (2006), Pairs trading: performance of a relative-value arbitrage rule, Rev. Financial Studies 19(3), doi:10.1093/rfs/hhj020; Do & Faff (2010), Does simple pairs trading still work?, FAJ 66(4)
methods.hypothesis: Gatev et al. (published 2006, working paper from 1999) match each stock with the partner whose normalised price path tracked it most closely over a 12-month formation window, trade the 20 closest pairs for the next six months, and open a pair when its gap passes two formation standard deviations, earning about 11% a year 1962-2002 before costs; Do and Faff find the profit fell after 2002 but held up in turbulent years such as 2008-2009. Gotrade is long only, so this book holds only the cheap leg: every week, among F4's screened point-in-time members, pairs are formed on the 252 sessions before the current half-year, and the laggard of each open pair is held at 5% of the book until the gap closes, the gap reaches 4 sigmas (stop), or 40 sessions pass, at most 20 legs, the rest of the money in SPY, everything in cash while SPY is under its 200-day average. The signal is relative reversal, the opposite of momentum, so its moves should be unlike the failed momentum books. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on a weekly book rule (weekly-hold-frac-gotrade, no promotion preset yet). Variants: P20 (Gatev's 20 pairs); P50 (50 pairs, more legs open, more of the book in stocks); P50-CASH (P50 with the rest in cash: the legs alone, does the laggard beat what SPY would have done with that money?); P50-K15 (opens at 1.5 sigmas: more, smaller bets); P50-NOGATE (no trend gate: what the gate is worth). Success: a SPY-parked variant beats total-return SPY on the owner's deposits with a worst fall under 20%, and P50-CASH shows the legs earn more than SPY per dollar invested. Judge 2009-2015 first.
methods.expectedFailure: The long leg alone carries the market and little of the spread: most of Gatev's profit came from the short leg falling, and the laggard is often lagging for a reason (bad news), so the cheap legs roughly match SPY and the book becomes SPY minus fees. With only a handful of pairs open at a time the book is mostly SPY anyway, so any edge is diluted to near nothing. The store holds no delisted names, so laggards that went on to die are missing and the result is flattered (run survivorship_coverage). Gotrade's per-order fees on 5% legs held a few weeks, plus the weekly SPY resize, eat what is left. The trend gate will keep the worst fall near 20% but whipsaw in 2010-2012 and 2015 and cost the 2009-2015 era. A published 2006 rule that Do and Faff already saw fading after 2002 is likely to look weakest in the best-covered, most recent years.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

Pairs trading, as Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst described it in 2006. Find two stocks whose prices moved together closely for a year. When they drift apart, bet that they come back together. The paper buys the cheaper one and sells short the dearer one. Gotrade can't sell short, so this book only buys the cheaper one (the "laggard"). Each laggard got 5% of the account and was held until the pair came back together, the gap grew to four times its normal size (a stop), or 40 trading days passed. The rest of the money sat in SPY. Everything went to cash while SPY was below its 200-day average. The book was checked weekly, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly 5M IDR top-ups.

Five versions: P20 (the paper's 20 closest pairs), P50 (50 pairs, so more legs open), P50-CASH (the same with the spare money in cash instead of SPY: this tests the laggards on their own), P50-K15 (opens a bet at a smaller gap) and P50-NOGATE (no 200-day switch).

Assumption made without asking: there is no weekly real-fee preset yet, so the book ran on a weekly rule set at Gotrade's real fees built for this method. If a version had won, promotion would have needed that preset added first.

## Result: a clear loss on every version

Money-weighted yearly return on the owner's deposits, compared with putting the same deposits into SPY with dividends reinvested (+7.2% a year, 1996 to 2015):

| version | yearly return | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P20 | +2.9% | 27.1% | 1.45 | 0.39 |
| P50 | +2.5% | 27.3% | 1.19 | 0.35 |
| P50-CASH | +1.2% | 22.3% | 1.12 | 0.23 |
| P50-K15 | +2.0% | 31.7% | 1.13 | 0.24 |
| P50-NOGATE | +5.8% | 55.4% | 1.36 | 0.48 |

Every version failed "beats SPY" and "worst fall at most 20%". Four of the five also failed "gains at least 1.3 times losses". None came near the luck bar: DSR (the chance the result is real and not luck after the lab's N = 43 independent tries) had to be at least 0.90, and the best version reached 0.48. Since even the face value loses, the luck test hardly matters.

The worst year was 2007 for the 50-pair books (−11.9% for P50): laggards in summer and autumn 2007 kept lagging. The version without the switch fell 55% in 2008, the same as the market. The 200-day switch kept the gated books out of 2008 but still let them fall 27% from a peak, mostly in whipsaws.

**2009-2015, the first filter:** the walk-forward check scored the method −2.8% a year against SPY in that era, and it lost all four of its test folds. The market-breadth report says it "pays in neither": it lost to SPY both in months when a few big names carried the index and in months when most stocks rose.

## Why it failed

1. **The laggards earned less than the money parked beside them.** P50-CASH is the cleanest test. It holds only the laggards and keeps the rest in cash. It made +1.2% a year. Adding the laggards to a book that is otherwise SPY (P50) made the result worse than SPY alone. So, in this data, buying the cheap leg of a pair earns less than the market. In Gatev's trades, the profit came mostly from the gap closing, and the gap often closed because the dearer stock fell back, not because the cheap one rose. With no short side, the book keeps the half of the trade that loses: a stock that lagged a close partner for a reason (bad news) often keeps lagging.
2. **The fees and the switching cost more.** Each week the book bought or sold small legs and resized SPY. Each small order at Gotrade's fee schedule costs several tenths of a percent. The 200-day switch moves the whole account in and out of the market every time SPY crosses its average. That is the gap between P50-NOGATE (+5.8%) and P50 (+2.5%), and it is not a pairs effect.
3. **More pairs or earlier entries did not help.** Fifty pairs instead of 20 lowered the gains-vs-losses ratio from 1.45 to 1.19. Opening at a smaller gap (1.5 instead of 2) lowered it again to 1.13 and deepened the worst fall to 32%. Weaker gaps are mostly noise.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the long leg alone carries the market and little of the gap, and the fees and the switch ate what was left. The bias from missing delisted stocks would have flattered this book, since laggards that went on to die are absent. It lost anyway, so that bias does not change the verdict.

## Compared with near misses

The closest books in the lab (the momentum and calm-stock books, MAR 0.7-0.9) beat SPY on dev by 3 to 7 points a year. This book trails SPY by 4 to 6 points with the switch on. It is the opposite signal to momentum (it buys relative losers), and it lost about as much as momentum books gained. That fits what the short-term-bounce book (M0028) found: buying recent relative losers among big US companies has not paid at real fees.

**My opinion:** this direction is dead for a long-only account, and more pair variants are not worth spending tries on. Pairs trading earns its money from the gap closing, and without the short side that is half a trade, the losing half. The one useful thing it showed is that the 200-day switch on a mostly-SPY book costs about three points a year in whipsaws (P50 against P50-NOGATE). That deserves its own test: a plain SPY book with and without the switch at real fees, so the lab knows what the switch itself costs before giving it credit or blame in any other book. Next, I'd queue the opposite of this result: buy the leader of a broken pair (relative strength within close pairs). If pairs only close because the leader falls, the leader is the stock to avoid, not the one to buy, and the test would show whether "lag versus a close partner" carries information at all.
methods.verdict: Rejected: buying only the cheap side of a pair lost to SPY by 4-6 points a year (+2.9% vs +7.2% on the deposits) and fell 27%; the laggards alone barely beat cash

methods.name: Time the monthly rebalance to the month's turn: the same momentum book, traded on the second-last session instead of the first
methods.hypothesis: M0052 showed that buying the turn of the month as an extra trade costs about 1.2% of the money moved per month at Gotrade's fees, far more than the effect earns. A book that already rebalances monthly pays that trip anyway, so moving its rebalance from the first session of the month to the second-last one costs nothing extra. Fresh money (the 25th-of-month deposit and the new picks) would then be invested before the month-end inflow days rather than after them. Test: the real-fee fractional plain-momentum or residual-momentum book with only the rebalance day moved. Expected: a difference within noise (under half a point a year), because on SPY in 1996-2015 the turn-of-month days were no better than a mid-month week. Its value is to settle whether rebalance timing matters at all for the lab's monthly books. Warning: it is kin of the failed momentum books by behaviour, so it can never be promoted; it is evidence only.

methods.name: The monthly earnings-day book under the weekly volatility brake: aimed at the summer-1998 fall
methods.sourceRef: M0063-M-N20-TREND (Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam 2008, SSRN 909563) + M0022's weekly own-volatility brake (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade, funded monthly
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008, so the dev window can only show the edge from before and just after it was widely known; 2009-2015 is judged first. M0063-M-N20-TREND beat SPY by 4.4 points a year on dev with gains 1.93x its losses, a luck score of 0.918 and +17.7% vs +14.8% a year in 2009-2015, and failed only the worst fall: 25.2% funded (23.6% without deposits, April-September 1998), before the monthly SPY-200 check could react. Keep the monthly news-day pick exactly (volume >= 3x the 60-day median, an up gap, a 3-day jump >= 4 points over SPY, 20 slots of 5%, the rest in SPY, SPY-200 switch read monthly) and every week scale the whole basket by min(1, target / its own 21-session volatility), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding. Variants: M-TV14, M-TV16, M-TV18 (brake targets 14/16/18% a year); M-ALWAYS-TV16 (no SPY-200 switch at all, the brake alone as crash protection: the weekly no-switch book beat SPY by 5 points a year in 2009-2015, so the switch may cost more than it saves); and W-MTREND (picks re-made weekly as M0063-N20-TREND, but the SPY-200 switch read only on the month's anchor date, unbraked, on M0063's assumed weekly-hold-frac-gotrade preset), which tests whether M0063's weekly book failed because of switch whipsaw rather than its picks. I expect M-TV16 to be the best trade-off: the basket is 5% slots plus an SPY park, so its own volatility should sit near 16-18% in calm years and the brake bites mainly in shocks. Success: at least one variant under the 20% fall limit that still beats total-return SPY with DSR >= 0.90 and beats SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: Every brake in this lab has cost about one point of yearly return per point of fall it saved, and this book's lead was earned partly in the 2009 rebound (+50% that year), when trailing volatility is still high and the brake holds the book partly in cash. That could push the luck score under 0.90 even if the fall passes. The 1998 fall was fast (mid-July to end of August): a one-month volatility reading may still be low at the first weekly check after the drop starts. Weekly resizing at Gotrade's real fees places many small orders on 5% slots of a small account. M-ALWAYS-TV16 may take too much of SPY's 2008 fall before the brake catches up. W-MTREND may still whipsaw within a month's picks and pay five times the turnover. And this is a published 2008 anomaly, so a strong dev result may have faded in 2016-2026.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

The parent, M0063's monthly "news-day" book, buys big stocks right after a day that looks like an earnings report: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal trading volume, and a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's. It holds up to 20 of them at 5% each and keeps the rest in SPY. It steps out to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average, but only checks that once a month. It beat SPY by 4.4 points a year on dev and passed the luck bar. It failed one thing: a worst fall of 25.2% (23.6% without the monthly deposits), from April to September 1998.

This method kept that book exactly and added a **weekly volatility brake**. Every week it measures how jumpy the whole basket has been over the last month (21 sessions). When that is above a target, it shrinks every holding by the same amount and keeps the difference in cash. The brake pulled several momentum books under the fall limit before. Five variants were registered before any result:

- **M-TV14 / M-TV16 / M-TV18**: the monthly book braked to a target of 14%, 16% or 18% yearly volatility.
- **M-ALWAYS-TV16**: no SPY-200 switch at all. The brake alone guards against crashes.
- **W-MTREND**: no brake. The picks are re-made every week, as in M0063's weekly book, but the SPY-200 switch is read only once a month. This tests whether the weekly book failed because the switch flipped back and forth too often.

All trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall (funded) | worst fall (no deposits) | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent M0063-M-N20-TREND | +11.6% | +7.2% | 25.2% | 23.6% | 1.93 | 0.918 |
| M-TV14 | +7.8% | +7.2% | 21.6% | 20.2% | 1.75 | 0.769 |
| M-TV16 | +8.9% | +7.2% | 23.3% | 22.1% | 1.82 | 0.818 |
| M-TV18 | +9.5% | +7.2% | 24.4% | 23.1% | 1.83 | 0.832 |
| M-ALWAYS-TV16 | +8.3% | +7.2% | 41.9% | 36.9% | 1.58 | 0.604 |
| W-MTREND | **+10.9%** | +7.2% | 27.3% | 26.2% | 1.76 | 0.869 |

**Rejected.** Every variant beat SPY on the same deposits, and every one failed two conditions: the worst fall (limit 20%) and the luck bar. The luck score (DSR) is the chance the result is more than luck after accounting for how many ideas the lab has tried. Here N was 47 at the time of the run (one look per method), and the bar is 0.90. The best score was 0.869, from W-MTREND. The braked versions scored 0.77-0.83, well below the parent's 0.918.

## By era (no deposits, yearly return)

| era | parent | M-TV14 | M-TV16 | M-TV18 | ALWAYS-TV16 | W-MTREND | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +11.1% | +6.5% | +7.5% | +8.0% | +4.2% | +10.6% | +6.2% |
| 2003-2008 | +6.3% | +5.1% | +5.5% | +6.3% | +4.2% | +5.6% | +2.3% |
| **2009-2015** | **+17.7%** | +11.6% | +13.4% | +14.0% | +15.7% | **+16.7%** | +14.8% |

In 2009-2015, the best-covered years and the most like today, **all three braked monthly books lose to SPY**. The parent beat it by 3 points a year. The brake turned a lead into a deficit. The walk-forward check (the lab's out-of-sample re-check) agrees: the variants it would have picked beat SPY in 3 of 4 folds, but by -0.2% a year in 2009-2015.

## Why

- **The brake hardly touched the 1998 fall.** The fall ran from April to August 1998. The early months were a slow slide in calm markets, so the one-month volatility reading stayed low and the brake did not engage. By the time volatility spiked in August, most of the loss was already taken. The hardest brake (14%) cut the fall from 23.6% to 20.2%, still above the limit. That is about 3 points of fall bought with almost 4 points a year of return.
- **The brake took the 2009 rebound.** The parent earned +49.9% in 2009. The braked books earned +21% to +27%. After 2008, trailing volatility stayed high for months, so the brake kept the book partly in cash for the best stretch the strategy ever had. This was the expected failure, and it happened in full.
- **The SPY-200 switch earns its keep here.** Without it (M-ALWAYS-TV16), the book fell 37% from 2000 to 2002 and lost 16% in 2008. The brake reacted too late in both.
- **The monthly switch check fixed the weekly book.** M0063's weekly book earned +5.0% a year on the owner's money. W-MTREND has the same weekly picks with the switch read monthly, and it earned +10.9%. In 2009-2015 that is +16.7% against +9.9%, and gains vs losses went from 1.27 to 1.76. So the weekly book's failure was the switch flipping back and forth, not its picks. But it still fell 26% in summer 1998, and its luck score of 0.869 misses the 0.90 bar.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. I expected M-TV16 to land under 20% with most of the return kept. It fell 22% and kept less than half of the lead over SPY. The expected failure came true in both forms: the rebound was lost and the 1998 slide was too slow for a one-month reading. The side question (was the weekly book killed by switch whipsaw?) has a clear yes.

## Compared with near misses

This repeats what M0033 found for the residual-momentum book: a trailing-volatility brake cannot defend against a fall that starts calm. M0041 (queued, not yet run) already argued the 1998 fall is a timing problem, not a sizing problem. This method is the second piece of evidence for that, on a book that does not move like momentum.

## My opinion:

The volatility brake is the wrong tool for this book, and I would not try another strength of it. The picks are still the best non-momentum lead in the lab. The parent and W-MTREND both beat SPY in 2009-2015, and the volume filter is doing real work. The 1998 fall needs a gate that reacts to the market's own sudden drop within days, and then waits until a monthly check before buying back in. That way it cannot flip back and forth the way the weekly SPY-200 check did. I would try the monthly book and W-MTREND behind that kind of fast crash exit with slow re-entry next. If that cannot get the 1998 fall under 20% without losing the 2009 rebound, this family's honest result is "a good idea that can't meet a 20% fall limit", and we should move on.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the volatility brake barely dented the 1998 fall (20-23%, limit 20%) and gave up the 2009 rebound, so it lost to SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: Dodge the dividend on purpose: calm dividend payers, each benched in the month it goes ex
methods.hypothesis: M0051's off-month control (the 20 highest-yield payers not due to pay next month) beat every dividend-month book and SPY by about a point a year, with almost no dividend tax, because it never holds a stock on its ex-date. For a long-only Indonesian account losing 15-30% of every dividend, avoiding ex-dates is worth something; chasing them is not. But that control fell 33% at its worst, mostly at the 2000 bubble peak, and lagged SPY in 2009-2015. Test the avoidance on purpose: among payers with a trailing yield, keep the 30 calmest by 60-day volatility, excluding any predicted to go ex next month (read point in time from the market's dividend calendar), behind the SPY 200-day gate, monthly, fractional, Gotrade fees; variants at 20 and 30 names and a yield-ranked twin. Run it only after the lab models dividend withholding (feature-wish insight 101) if that lands first, so the tax saving is measured, not assumed. Expected failure: the calm, high-yield tilt still falls with value stocks in 2000 and lags big-company growth after 2009, so it beats SPY on average but breaks the 20% limit.

methods.name: The leader of a broken pair, held a month: does running ahead of a close partner predict anything?
methods.hypothesis: M0064 found that the laggard of a broken pair earns less than the market at Gotrade's real fees, because pairs mostly close by the leader falling back. Test the other side to learn whether lag versus a close partner carries information at all: each month (not weekly, to cut fees and the switch's whipsaw), among F4's screened members, form Gatev pairs on the prior 252 sessions and hold the stock that has run 2 or more formation sigmas ahead of its partner, equal weight, rest in SPY, monthly 200-day gate, fractional shares on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade. Expected failure: the leader is simply a short-term winner, so the book moves with the failed momentum books and is refused as their kin by behaviour (check the residual correlation before spending variants); or, if pairs really close by the leader falling, it loses outright, which would confirm M0064's reading and close the family.

methods.name: Buy the long-term losers: big index members that fell furthest over the past three to five years, skipping the last year
methods.sourceRef: De Bondt & Thaler (1985), Does the Stock Market Overreact?, Journal of Finance 40(3), 793-805; see also https://faculty.georgetown.edu/qw50/LTR.pdf
methods.hypothesis: Published 1985, so the dev window 1996-2015 is already after the crowd knew it. Investors overreact over several years, so the index members that lost most over months -60..-13 (skipping the latest 12 months, to keep clear of momentum) rebound over the next one to three years. Each month, among point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members priced at $5 or more with over 20M dollars traded a day (F4's screen, which keeps the book to big names), rank on that formation return and hold the 20 lowest equal weight, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade; slots the screen cannot fill (names need five years of bars, so before about 1998 few qualify) hold SPY. Variants: L60-N20 (60-month formation, 20 names), L36-N20 (36-month formation), L60-N30 (30 names), L60-N20-T (the SPY 200-day switch: cash while SPY is below its average), and W60-N20 (the 20 long-term WINNERS: the control, which should trail the losers). The reserved idea's quarterly re-pick is not run: the lab has no quarterly real-fee preset, and a five-year signal barely moves month to month. Success: a losers variant beats SPY TR on dev with the worst fall at or under 20%, the winners control does worse, and the edge holds in 2009-2015. Its monthly result should NOT move with the failed momentum books -- it is close to their opposite.
methods.expectedFailure: The published evidence says long-term reversal lives in small and equal-weighted stocks and does not survive risk adjustment after about 2003; among big index members the losers are mostly the riskiest, most beaten-down companies, so the book may be nothing but extra market risk: deep falls in 2001-2002 and 2008 (a worst fall well over 20% without the switch), and a strong 2003 and 2009 rebound that makes the average look better than the ride. The store has no delisted names, so the losers that went on to die are missing and the ones that survived are exactly the rebounders: survivorship flatters this method more than almost any other, most of all in the low-coverage late 1990s. Expect L60-N20 to trail SPY in 2009-2015 once the 2009 bounce is past, and the switch variant to cut the fall but also the rebound the idea lives on.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What we tried

Each month the book held the 20 big index companies whose shares had fallen the most over the past five years, leaving out the most recent year. The idea comes from De Bondt and Thaler (1985): investors overreact to years of bad news, so the worst long-term losers tend to bounce back. Empty slots held SPY. The book ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's 5 million rupiah topped up every month. Five versions ran:

- five-year losers, 20 names (L60-N20)
- three-year losers (L36-N20)
- 30 names (L60-N30)
- the SPY 200-day switch, sitting in cash while SPY is below its 200-day average (L60-N20-T)
- the five-year **winners**, as a control (W60-N20)

## Result: rejected

Every version earned more than SPY. Every version also broke the 20% limit on the worst fall, most of them by a wide margin.

| version | your money earned a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| five-year losers, 20 names | +9.0% | +7.2% | 71% | 0.56 |
| three-year losers | +9.8% | +7.2% | 72% | 0.57 |
| 30 names | +7.4% | +7.2% | 71% | 0.48 |
| losers + 200-day switch | +9.8% | +7.2% | 34% | 0.81 |
| winners (control) | +7.3% | +7.2% | 74% | 0.36 |

- **Worst fall.** Without the switch, the book lost about seven tenths of its value from peak to bottom, measured with the deposits taken out. SPY's own worst fall over these years was about 51%. Even with the switch the book fell 34% (24.5% with the deposits removed), well over the 20% limit. Its worst calendar year was 2008, down 47% (SPY was down 35%). With the switch on, the worst year became 2011, down 18%.
- **Luck score (DSR).** This is how likely the result is real rather than a lucky draw after all the methods the lab has tried. Here N = 48 looks, and the bar is 0.90. The best version scored 0.81, so it fails this test too. The others score 0.36 to 0.57, which is close to a coin flip.
- **Gains vs losses.** The money made on winning trades was 1.5 to 1.85 times the money lost on losing ones. That passes.

## Where the edge came from

Here is each version against SPY in points a year, with deposits removed:

| years | SPY | 5-yr losers | 3-yr losers | losers + switch | winners |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-1999 | +25.7% | −2.6 | −4.2 | −8.6 | +0.7 |
| 2000-2002 | −13.4% | **+24.3** | +26.2 | +18.8 | −6.1 |
| 2003-2007 | +13.4% | −3.4 | −2.3 | −5.3 | +9.4 |
| 2008 | −35.1% | −11.2 | −10.4 | +35.1 (in cash) | −24.8 |
| 2009 | +41.7% | **+43.6** | +33.4 | +3.0 | +27.7 |
| 2010-2015 | +14.1% | −0.5 | +2.3 | −4.4 | +1.6 |

The whole twenty-year edge comes from two episodes:

1. **2000-2002.** When the tech bubble burst, the five-year losers were the old-economy companies nobody had wanted in the late 1990s. They held up while tech collapsed.
2. **2009.** After the crash, the most beaten-down companies jumped the hardest off the bottom, the "junk rally".

In every ordinary stretch the losers trailed SPY: by 2.6 points a year in the late 1990s, 3.4 in 2003-2007 and 11 in 2008. In 2010-2015 they roughly tied. The 2009-2015 era as a whole reads +5.0 points a year, but that is the single year 2009. Strip it out and 2010-2015 is −0.5 for the main version.

The breadth report says the same thing from a different angle. Every version "pays only in broad" markets: about 20 points a year behind SPY in months when a few big names carried the index, and about 23 points ahead when the average stock did well. This is a bet against the market's big-company drift. From 2018 that drift has been the strongest force in the market (insight 91).

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Partly, and in the wrong way.** The losers did beat the winners control over the whole window (+2.8 vs +0.4 points a year, five-year books), which is what the paper predicts. But the gap came from crashes and rebounds, not from a steady rebound of overreacted stocks. In 2003-2007 the winners beat the losers by about 13 points a year.

**The expected failure happened almost word for word.** The falls in 2001-2002 and 2008 went far past 20%. A strong 2009 rebound makes the average look better than the ride. The switch cut the fall but also cut the rebound: in 2009 it gained only 3 points over SPY instead of 44.

Survivorship flatters this method more than most others. The store has no companies that later died. Among long-term losers, the ones that went bankrupt (in 2001-2002 and 2008-2009 especially) are exactly the ones missing, and the ones left are the survivors that bounced. So even the +2.8 points a year is likely an overstatement.

## Compared with the lab's near misses

The momentum books that came closest to eligible (the residual-momentum family) fell 12-20% at their worst. This book falls three to five times further for a similar or smaller average edge. It is close to the opposite of momentum, so it would diversify a momentum book on paper. But on its own it carries far too much risk for what it pays.

**My opinion:** Long-term reversal among big companies is not worth more trials as a stand-alone book. It is a crash-and-rebound bet wearing a "value" coat. Its edge is two episodes, both of which survivorship flatters, and it loses in the calm years that make up most of the time. The one direction I would still try is using it as a small partner to a momentum book. Momentum crashed in exactly the rebound months (2009) where this book shone, so a 70/30 blend might cut the momentum book's worst months without giving much up. But momentum's kin has already failed its test, so that blend would be refused by the gate. I would not spend an id on it either. A better use of the next id is the open question this result points to again: judge every equal-weighted book against the equal-weight S&P as well as SPY, because this book's whole story is "average stock vs big stock".
methods.verdict: Rejected: beat SPY only through the 2000-02 crash and the 2009 rebound, trailed it in calm years, and fell about 70% at its worst (34% even with the trend switch)

methods.name: Follow a dividend raise: buy big companies right after they raise or start their dividend, hold for months
methods.sourceRef: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Price Reactions to Dividend Initiations and Omissions, JF 50(2); https://www.nber.org/papers/w4778; Boehme & Sorescu (2002), JF 57(2)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-1995 (NBER w4778, then the Journal of Finance), so most of the dev window (1996-2015) is after the crowd could know it; it survives only if the signal is slow enough that nobody arbitraged it. A dividend raise is a manager's costly signal of confidence, and Michaely, Thaler and Womack report the price keeps drifting up for months after an initiation (about +7.5% over 12 months). The store holds every member's cash dividends by ex-date, so the event is visible point in time on the ex-date. A member's latest payment is a raise when it is 10% or more above the median of its up-to-four previous payments in the prior 400 days (and no more than double, which drops one-off specials), or an initiation when nothing went ex in the 400 days before and the stock has price history from before that. Inside F4's liquidity and membership screen, hold up to 20 such names at 5% each while the event is younger than the hold (held names keep their slot; then the newest ex-dates), park the rest in SPY, re-picked monthly, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade. It ranks on a corporate decision, not past returns, so its picks should move apart from the failed momentum books. Variants: R10-H6-T (raise >= 10%, hold 182 days, behind the SPY-200 switch), R10-H12-T (hold 365 days), R25-H6-T (raise >= 25%), R10-H6 (no switch: the picking alone, always invested) and FLAT-H6-T (control: payers whose latest dividend was unchanged within 1%, same hold and switch), so R10-H6-T minus FLAT-H6-T isolates the raise from merely being a steady payer. Success: a raise variant beats total-return SPY on dev within the 20% worst fall, beats FLAT-H6-T, and keeps a positive edge over SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The drift was reported mainly for equal-weighted small stocks, and Boehme and Sorescu (2002) found it largely disappears once measured carefully; among big index members it may be gone. The ex-date lags the announcement by two to six weeks, so part of any drift is already in the price before the book can see it. Many big payers raise every year by 10% or more, so the raise set may be large and close to an equal-weight 'dividend grower' index: value-ish, lower-volatility names that trailed SPY's big-company growth in 1997-2000 and from 2009, so the book may lag SPY in exactly the 2009-2015 years that matter. Behind the SPY-200 switch the 1998 and 2011 fast falls still land before the switch turns, so the worst fall may sit near the 20% limit; the ungated R10-H6 should take most of SPY's 2008 fall (well over 20%). Not modelled and against the method: the book is credited 100% of every dividend while the owner loses 15-30% to US withholding tax, though at about SPY's yield this costs no more than holding SPY does. If FLAT-H6-T does as well as the raise books, the raise carries no information.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

When a company raises its dividend, its managers are betting their own cash that profits will hold up. Michaely, Thaler and Womack (1995) found that after a company starts paying a dividend, its price keeps drifting up for months. This book looks for the same signal in big US companies. The research data has every member's dividends by **ex-date** (the day a buyer stops getting the next payment). It has no announcement dates, so the book only sees a raise on its ex-date, usually two to six weeks after it was announced.

A payment counts as a **raise** when it is at least 10% (or 25%) above the median of the company's previous four payments, and no more than double (so one-off special dividends don't count). A **first payment** counts too, when nothing was paid in the 400 days before. The book holds up to 20 such companies at 5% each while the raise is younger than six months (or twelve), and puts the rest in SPY. It re-picks once a month and steps into cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It trades fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits.

Five variants were fixed before any result:

- **R10-H6-T**: raises of 10% or more, held six months
- **R10-H12-T**: the same, held twelve months
- **R25-H6-T**: only raises of 25% or more
- **R10-H6**: no step into cash
- **FLAT-H6-T**: the control, payers whose dividend did *not* change

Assumed and written down before the run: the ex-date stands in for the announcement date. A quarterly payer's raise usually qualifies again on its next payment, because the median of the last four payments trails behind, so in practice a raise is held for about a quarter longer than the stated hold.

## Results against total-return SPY (1996 – Oct 2015, dev window)

On the owner's deposits, SPY with dividends reinvested earned **+7.2% a year**.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R10-H6-T | +8.1% | 29.2% | 2.33 | 0.81 | worst fall, luck |
| R10-H12-T | +8.2% | 29.2% | 2.39 | 0.82 | worst fall, luck |
| **R25-H6-T** | **+10.9%** | **21.9%** | **2.81** | **0.946** | **worst fall only** |
| R10-H6 (no cash switch) | +8.1% | 55.5% | 1.89 | 0.59 | worst fall, luck |
| FLAT-H6-T (control) | +9.5% | 27.2% | 2.81 | 0.88 | worst fall, luck |

The **worst fall** is the biggest drop from a peak, and the limit is 20%. **Gains vs losses** (the profit factor) is total winning trades over total losing trades, and must be at least 1.3. The **luck check** (DSR, the deflated Sharpe ratio) is how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab now counts N = 49 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90.

The big-raise book R25-H6-T came close. It beat SPY by 3.7 points a year, passed the luck check at 0.946 against the 0.90 bar, and had a healthy 2.81 gains-vs-losses ratio. It failed on one condition: its worst fall was 21.9%, against the 20% limit. Measured month-end to month-end with the deposits taken out, its deepest fall was 16.6%, from April 2011 to May 2012 (the US debt-downgrade summer), so the 21.9% is a deeper drop inside the months. Its worst calendar year was 2011, at −7.7%.

## By era: where the edge came from

The edge over SPY in points a year, measured with the deposits removed:

| era | SPY | R10-H6-T | R25-H6-T | FLAT (control) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2001 | +11.9% | −1.5 | +1.9 | −3.2 |
| 2002-2008 | −1.4% | +6.9 | +10.1 | +10.0 |
| 2009-2015 | +16.7% | −5.5 | **−3.1** | −5.0 |

That table holds three lessons:

1. **2002-2008 is the cash switch, not the dividend.** Every book that stepped out to cash while SPY was below its 200-day average missed most of the 2001-2002 and 2008 falls. The control gets the same +10 points as the big-raise book. Every trend-switched book in this lab shows that pattern.
2. **2009-2015, the era most like today, loses to SPY.** Every variant lagged, the best one (R25) by 3.1 points a year. Walk-forward agrees: the variant the lab's own rule would have picked won only 2 of 4 folds, with a 2009-2015 edge of −4.9%. The hard gate wants a majority of folds, so this method could not be promoted even if its worst fall had been under 20%.
3. **A big raise does carry information, but only relative to other payers.** R25 beat the control in every era: by about 5 points a year in 1996-2001, 0.1 in 2002-2008 and 1.9 in 2009-2015. The 10% raise books did *not* beat the control overall (+8.1% vs +9.5%), because a 10% raise is too common among big payers to mean much: 200 to 490 such raises happen a year.

The breadth report agrees. The 10% books and the control earn only in "broad" months (when the average stock beats the index). R25 earns in narrow and broad months alike, which is the one encouraging sign.

## Why

Dividend payers held in equal slots form a value-leaning, steady, mid-to-large-company book. That is exactly the shape that lost to SPY's big-growth-company drift after 2009 (insight 91). Picking the companies with the biggest raises improves on that base by a couple of points a year, but not enough to overcome it. The ex-date lag also hands the first weeks of any drift to people who read the announcement.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis:** partly held. A big raise beat steady payers in every era. But no raise variant beat SPY within the 20% worst fall, and none kept an edge in 2009-2015.
- **Expected failure:** it happened largely as written. The 10% raise set was close to a "dividend grower" index and lagged SPY from 2009. The 1998 fall hit the switched books before the switch turned (the 10% books fell 20% in 1998-2000 with deposits removed). The ungated book took SPY's 2008 fall (55%). And the flat control did as well as the 10% raise books.

## Comparison with near misses

The nearest kin in spirit is the earnings-day jump book (M0063), another corporate-event book with SPY filling the empty slots. Its monthly version earned +11.6% a year and fell 25%, and it *beat* SPY in 2009-2015 by 1.4 points. R25 is slightly safer (21.9% worst fall) but loses the era that matters. The dividend-month book (M0051) lost to SPY outright, so dividend timing remains a weak family.

**My opinion:** The dividend-raise idea as a standalone book is not worth more variants. Its only real win, the 2002-2008 cash switch, is not its own, and it lags SPY after 2009 like every equal-weighted payer book. The one piece worth keeping is that a *big* raise (25%+) beats steady payers by about 2 points a year in every era. That is a ranking signal, not a book. I would try it once as a tilt inside a book shaped like SPY: big raisers among the 100 most-traded members, with half the money in SPY as a core, so the size bet stops fighting the market. If that still lags SPY in 2009-2015, this family should close.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0070-R25-H6-T`: DSR 0.9274 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Close miss: big dividend raisers beat SPY by 3.7 points a year and passed the luck check, but fell 21.9% (limit 20%) and lost to SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: The high-volume premium: buy big stocks after a week of unusually heavy trading that did NOT come with a big price move
methods.sourceRef: Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin (2001), The High-Volume Return Premium, Journal of Finance 56(3), 877-919; https://rodneywhitecenter.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/9901.pdf
methods.hypothesis: Published 2001 (working paper 1999), so most of the dev window is after the crowd could trade it; 2009-2015 is judged first. Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin find that a stock whose trading volume is unusually high against its own last 50 days earns more over the next month, whatever its return in the burst: the burst makes it visible to more investors, which raises demand. The earnings-day book found an edge in heavy volume WITH an up jump; this tests whether volume alone carries it. Each month, inside F4's liquidity and membership screen, score every member by its mean volume over the last week (or last day) divided by the median of the 49 sessions before it, keep the top tenth, drop names whose return over the same window was more than 5 points (3 points for the one-day window) away from SPY's, and hold the 20 most extreme bursts at 5% each for a month, the rest in SPY. The ranking is on volume and a near-zero move, not on past returns, so it should not move like the failed momentum books. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's monthly deposits. Variants: WEEK-T (week window, behind the SPY-200 switch: all cash while SPY is below its 200-day average), DAY-T (last day only, GKM's own window), WEEK-ALWAYS (no switch: the picking alone), WEEK-ANYMOVE-T (no move cap: high volume whatever the price did) and LOW-WEEK-T (control: the LOWEST-volume tenth with the same cap, which GKM say trails). Success: WEEK-T beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under 20%, beats SPY in 2009-2015, and LOW is clearly worse.
methods.expectedFailure: The premium is small, well under a point a month, and smaller in big stocks; the book turns over almost completely every month, and at Gotrade's real fees on 5% slots the round trip may eat most of it. A heavy-volume week with no price move is often a quarterly index rebalance, an options expiry or a block trade, not new attention, which would dilute the signal. The SPY-200 switch carries the crash years as it did for every trend-switched book, so summer 1998 may again push the worst fall past 20%, and WEEK-ALWAYS should take most of SPY's 2008 fall. If the no-cap version wins clearly and the capped one doesn't, the edge was the jump, i.e. the earnings-day book again. Equal weight among index members leans small next to SPY, and SPY's big-company drift beat every such book after 2018.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin (2001) found that a stock trading on unusually heavy volume, compared with its own last 50 days, tends to rise over the next month whatever its price did during the burst. Their explanation: heavy trading makes a stock noticed, and being noticed brings new buyers. The earnings-day book (M0063) already found an edge in heavy volume that came *with* a big up jump. This method asks whether the volume alone carries that edge.

Each month, among index members that pass the usual liquidity screen, every stock is scored by its average volume over the last week (or the last day), divided by its median volume over the 49 sessions before that. The top tenth is kept. Stocks whose price moved more than 5 points away from SPY's over the same week (3 points for the one-day window) are dropped, so this is not the earnings-jump book again. The 20 biggest bursts are held at 5% each for a month, and any empty slots go into SPY. While SPY is below its 200-day average, the book holds cash. Trades are in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly deposits.

Five variants, all fixed before any result: WEEK-T (the main one), DAY-T (the paper's own one-day window), WEEK-ALWAYS (never steps out to cash), WEEK-ANYMOVE-T (no cap on the price move) and LOW-WEEK-T (control: the *quietest* tenth, which the paper says should trail).

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LOW-WEEK-T (quiet control) | **+7.8%** | +7.2% | 27.1% | 1.35 | 0.754 |
| WEEK-T (main) | +7.3% | +7.2% | 19.3% | 1.41 | 0.783 |
| WEEK-ALWAYS | +7.3% | +7.2% | 54.7% | 1.28 | 0.497 |
| WEEK-ANYMOVE-T | +6.8% | +7.2% | 22.6% | 1.34 | 0.595 |
| DAY-T | +4.9% | +7.2% | 22.5% | 1.24 | 0.542 |

The method is **rejected**. The main variant ties SPY: +7.3% a year against +7.2%, a tenth of a point. Its worst fall, 19.3%, is just inside the 20% limit, and its gains are 1.41 times its losses (bar 1.3). It fails the luck test. The DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than luck, given how many ideas the lab has tried. It is 0.783, against a bar of 0.90, with the lab's N at 46 (one look per distinct method). A tenth of a point over SPY is exactly what luck looks like.

The deeper failure is the control. **The quietest stocks did better than the busiest ones** (+7.8% against +7.3%). That is the opposite of what the paper predicts. The one-day window, the paper's own design, did worst of all: 2.3 points a year behind SPY.

## By era and by kind of market

- **Walk-forward** (the lab picks a variant using only the years before each test slice, then scores it on years it has not seen): it beat SPY in **1 of 4** slices. In 2009-2015, the best-covered years and the ones most like today, its edge was **+0.4% a year**, close to nothing.
- **Narrow vs broad markets.** In "narrow" months a few giant companies carry the index; in "broad" months the average stock does well. The main variant earned +0.2% over SPY in narrow months and +0.6% in broad ones, which is to say nothing in either. The variants with more stock exposure (no cash switch, no move cap, the quiet control) all *lost* to SPY in narrow months (by 2.6 to 6.8 points a year) and won in broad ones. That is the equal-weight shape of the book: a small-company tilt, not a volume edge.
- **Worst fall without the deposits.** WEEK-ALWAYS lost 31% in 2008 alone and 55% from its peak, about SPY's fall. Holding 20 index stocks does not protect against a crash. The main variant's 19.3% fall happened while the cash switch was doing its usual work.

## Why

- **In big, heavily watched companies, there is no attention left to win.** The paper's effect is strongest in small, little-followed stocks. An S&P 500 member is already watched by every analyst and fund, so a busy week does not make it any better known. What an unusual week of volume *without* a price move usually is, in a big company, is mechanical: a quarterly index rebalance, options expiry, a large fund moving a block of shares. None of those bring new buyers.
- **The jump was the edge, not the volume.** The earnings-day book, built on heavy volume *with* an up jump, earned +11.6% a year against SPY's +7.2% in its monthly form. Take the jump away and the edge is gone. Removing the move cap (ANYMOVE) did not help either, because with a symmetric cap removed the book catches down-jumps as well as up-jumps. The direction of the news matters, and volume alone does not say which way it went.
- **Turnover at real fees.** The book replaces almost every name every month (2,400 trades over twenty years). At Gotrade's fee on a 5% slot of a small account, that is several tenths of a point a year handed over. On an edge this thin, that decides the result.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis did not hold: high volume did not beat low volume, and the main variant did not beat SPY in a way that counts. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the premium was too small in big stocks to survive monthly turnover at real fees, and a heavy week with no move is mostly mechanical trading, not new attention. The cash switch kept the main variant just under the 20% fall limit, better than I feared.

## Compared with near relatives

- **The earnings-day book (M0063), monthly form:** +11.6% a year, worst fall 25.2%. This method's best: +7.3%, worst fall 19.3%. The four-point difference is what the up jump was worth.
- **The busy-stock short-term winners (M0057):** that one also found the *quiet* control beating the busy picks (+8.2% against +6.5%). Two independent tests now say the same thing: among big index stocks, heavy trading on its own predicts nothing good, and slightly bad.

My opinion: this direction is finished. Volume on its own is not an edge in big US stocks after fees. Two methods now show quiet stocks beating busy ones, and the one-day window the paper used was the worst variant here. What *did* work is volume as a sign that news arrived, combined with which way the price went. That is the earnings-day book, and its open problem is its 1998 fall, not its signal. I would not spend another id on volume-visibility. I would spend it on that book: a version that only takes a jump when it lands well above a stock's normal daily range, so routine big days are left out.
methods.verdict: Rejected: heavy trading without a price move tied SPY (+7.3% vs +7.2% a year) and failed the luck test; the quietest stocks did better than the busiest, so volume alone is not the edge

methods.name: Earnings-day jumps measured against the stock's own normal swing: only take a news day that is large for that stock
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0063-M-N20-TREND (Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam 2008, SSRN 909563), the jump standardised as in standardised unexpected earnings (Foster, Olsen & Shevlin 1984; Bernard & Thomas 1989)
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008 (the earnings-day drift) and 1984-1989 (standardised surprises), so the dev window can only show the edge from before and just after it was widely known; 2009-2015 is judged first. M0063-M-N20-TREND beat SPY by 4.4 points a year on dev with gains 1.93x its losses and a luck score of 0.918, and failed only the worst fall: 25.2% funded, April-September 1998. M0071 showed volume alone carries no edge, so the jump is the signal. A fixed 4-point jump treats a calm utility and a volatile chip stock alike; dividing the three-day market-adjusted jump by the stock's own daily volatility over the 60 sessions before the news day (z = jump / sd) keeps the genuinely surprising news days and drops routine big days of jumpy stocks, which should be the names that fell hardest in summer 1998. Same frame as M0063-M-N20-TREND exactly (volume >= 3x the 60-day median, up gap, 60-session hold, 20 slots of 5%, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, re-picked monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Variants: Z2 (raw jump >= 4 points AND z >= 2, ranked by z), Z3 (raw >= 4 AND z >= 3, ranked by z), Z2-RAWRANK (the Z2 filter, ranked by the raw jump as the parent did: separates the filter from the ranking), Z3-NOFLOOR (z >= 3 alone, no raw floor, ranked by z: admits calm stocks whose 2-3 point jump is a real shock for them). The raw-jump control is the parent's own recorded trial M0063-M-N20-TREND: same preset, same fees, same funding, so it is compared directly and not re-run (its configuration has already run on dev). I expect Z2 to be best. Success: a variant with a worst fall under 20% that still beats total-return SPY with DSR >= 0.90 and beats SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The 1998 fall was market-wide (SPY fell about 19% July-August) and the monthly SPY-200 switch was late; with 20 slots and the rest in SPY the book's fall is mostly the market's, so better picks may not shrink it below 20%. Standardising tilts the book toward calm, low-volatility names (utilities, staples), which lag in strong rebounds like 2009 and the 1999 tech run, so the excess over SPY may shrink and the luck score fall under 0.90. Z3 may leave many slots empty and drift toward plain SPY. A z-score on a 60-day sd is noisy: a stock calm for two months then hit by news reads as a huge surprise even when the move was ordinary for it over a year. And this is a published anomaly, so a strong dev result may have faded in 2016-2026.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What was tried

The parent book (M0063's monthly "news-day" book) buys big stocks right after a day that looks like an earnings report: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal trading volume, and a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's. It holds up to 20 of them at 5% each, keeps the rest in SPY, and goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average (checked monthly). It beat SPY by 4.4 points a year and passed the luck bar, but its worst fall was 25.2% (limit 20%), in summer 1998.

The idea here: a 4-point jump is a shock for a calm utility but an ordinary week for a jumpy chip stock. So measure each jump against the stock's own normal daily swing over the 60 days before the news (the "z-score": jump divided by the stock's typical daily move), and keep only the news days that were big *for that stock*. The hope was that this drops the jumpy names that fell hardest in 1998.

Four fixed variants, registered before any result, all on the parent's exact frame (monthly, 20 slots, SPY in empty slots, SPY-200 switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5M IDR monthly deposits):

- **Z2**: the parent's 4-point rule *and* at least 2 of the stock's own daily swings, ranked by that z-score.
- **Z3**: the same with at least 3 swings.
- **Z2-RAWRANK**: the Z2 filter, but ranked by the raw jump as the parent did. This separates "which news days are kept" from "which ones get the slots".
- **Z3-NOFLOOR**: at least 3 swings, no 4-point floor, so calm stocks with a 2-3 point jump can enter.

The raw-jump control is the parent's own recorded trial (same preset, fees and deposits), not a re-run.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, on the owner's monthly deposits)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall (funded) | worst fall (no deposits) | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent M0063-M-N20-TREND | +11.6% | +7.2% | 25.2% | 23.6% | 1.93 | 0.918 |
| **Z2-RAWRANK** | **+12.3%** | +7.2% | 23.8% | 22.4% | 1.98 | **0.914** |
| Z2 | +10.7% | +7.2% | 23.3% | 21.7% | 2.05 | 0.884 |
| Z3 | +10.4% | +7.2% | 23.1% | 22.0% | 1.95 | 0.883 |
| Z3-NOFLOOR | +10.2% | +7.2% | 23.0% | 21.7% | 1.94 | 0.882 |

**Rejected.** Every variant beats total-return SPY on the same deposits, and every one has gains about twice its losses (bar 1.3). Every one fails the worst-fall limit: 23-24% on the funded account, 21.7-22.4% with the deposits taken out (deposits refill a falling account, so the no-deposit figure is the honest one). All four falls are the same fall as the parent's: March to September 1998.

The luck score: the lab's N is 59 (one look per distinct method). Only Z2-RAWRANK clears the 0.90 bar (0.914): after 59 ideas, about a 91% chance its edge is more than luck. The three z-ranked variants fall just under (0.88).

## By era (no deposits, the book's own yearly return)

| era | parent | Z2-RAWRANK | Z2 | Z3 | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +11.0% | +12.1% | +9.4% | +10.3% | +6.7% |
| 2003-2008 | +6.3% | +6.9% | +7.7% | +6.1% | +2.3% |
| **2009-2015** | +17.8% | **+18.6%** | +15.3% | +15.5% | +14.9% |

In the best-covered, most modern years (2009-2015), Z2-RAWRANK beat SPY by almost 4 points a year, a little more than the parent. The z-ranked books barely beat SPY there (+0.4 to +0.6 points). The walk-forward check (the lab picks a variant knowing only the past, then scores it on years it never saw) had the method beating SPY in 3 of 4 folds, but with a **-1.1%** edge in 2009-2015, because the folds kept picking a z-ranked variant.

## Why

- **The filter helped the fall a little, not enough.** Dropping the routine big days of jumpy stocks cut the 1998 fall by 1.2-1.9 points (23.6% to 21.7-22.4%, no deposits). That is the right direction and confirms part of the idea: some of the 1998 damage was jumpy names. But most of the fall was timing. In 1998 SPY ended up +28% while every one of these books lost 3-6%: the book fell with the market in July-August, then the monthly SPY-200 check moved it to cash near the bottom and it missed much of the rebound. Better picks cannot fix a switch that sells late and buys back late.
- **Ranking by the z-score costs money.** Same filter, two rankings: ranked by the raw jump it earned +12.3% a year, ranked by z it earned +10.7%. Ranking by z prefers the calmest stocks with the biggest *relative* jumps, which are the slow movers. They lagged in the strong years: 2009 (+40% vs +55% for raw ranking), 1999, 2013. This is exactly the expected failure ("standardising tilts the book toward calm names that lag in rebounds").
- **The biggest raw jumps among the genuinely surprising days are the best picks.** Z2-RAWRANK is the parent with the routine jumpy-stock days removed, and it beat the parent on return, 2009-2015 and the fall, while the luck score held above the bar. So the z-score is useful as a *filter* and harmful as a *ranking*.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (standardising keeps the real surprises and shrinks the 1998 fall below 20%) held only halfway: the picks got slightly better and the fall slightly smaller, but no variant got under 20%. The expected failure happened on both counts: the 1998 fall was mostly the switch's timing, and the z-ranking tilted the book to slow names that lagged in rebounds. Z3 did not drift to plain SPY: it still averaged about 70% invested in picks-plus-park, the same as the parent.

## Comparison with near misses

The parent and its earlier fix, the weekly volatility brake (M0066), were measured at the same real fees, so they compare directly. The brake got its best variant to 21.6% but lost the luck bar and the 2009-2015 lead. This filter gets to 22.4% while keeping both. Neither crosses 20%. Two attacks on the picks and the basket's size have now moved the 1998 fall by about 2 points each. The remaining 2 points sit in the safety switch.

My opinion: this family is still the most interesting non-momentum direction in the lab. It ranks on news, moves differently from the failed momentum books, beats SPY in 2009-2015 and clears the luck bar. But I will stop changing the picks. The picks are now good enough. The fall is the monthly SPY-200 switch selling into the 1998 crash and buying back late. The next try should keep Z2-RAWRANK's picks exactly and change only the safety switch: a fast exit (SPY closing below its 50-day average, or VIX jumping above its 3-month VIX) checked weekly, with re-entry still on the monthly date so it cannot whipsaw the way the weekly book did. That is the existing backlog idea M0075 ("fast crash exit with slow, monthly re-entry"), and it should be run on these filtered picks.


### 2026-10-11

## Correction after reading 1998 month by month

The "Why" above says most of the 1998 fall was the switch's timing. The monthly numbers (no deposits) say it was about half and half:

| 1998 | SPY | parent | Z2-RAWRANK |
|---|---|---|---|
| May | -2.0% | -7.3% | -6.2% |
| July | -1.4% | -2.5% | -2.8% |
| August | -14.1% | -18.6% | -18.2% |
| September | +6.4% | 0% (cash) | 0% (cash) |
| October | +8.1% | 0% (cash) | 0% (cash) |

From April to August SPY lost about 12%. The book lost about 22%, and it was fully invested the whole time (the switch did nothing until the end of August). So about 10 points of the fall came from the picks themselves. In May they fell three times as hard as SPY, and in the August crash they fell harder too. 1998 was a narrow market: a few giant companies carried the index while most stocks fell. An equal-weight book of 20 news-day names, many of them mid-sized index members, lost against the giants. Then the switch moved the book to cash right at the August bottom and missed the +15% in September and October. That missed rebound is why 1998 ended at -3.5% against SPY's +28%, but it does not add to the worst fall.

So there are two different fixes, and the plan in "My opinion" changes. A fast exit could only have saved part of August (the month the switch slept through). The other half needs picks that don't lag when the giants lead. I now think the better next try is to stop equal-weighting the news-day names and size them toward the biggest companies, so the book is closer to SPY's own shape in a narrow year. The fast-exit idea (M0075) stays queued as the second attack.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0072-Z2-RAWRANK`: DSR 0.9109 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Close miss: measuring each news-day jump against the stock's normal swing improved the picks (+12.3% a year vs SPY's +7.2%, luck bar passed) but the 1998 fall still reached 22-24% (limit 20%)

methods.name: Turnaround losers: big companies that fell hardest over five years but have risen over the past year
methods.sourceRef: Variation of M0069 (De Bondt & Thaler 1985, Journal of Finance 40(3)); the value-plus-momentum confirmation from Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013), Value and Momentum Everywhere, Journal of Finance 68(3)
methods.hypothesis: Long-term reversal was published in 1985 and value-plus-momentum in 2013, so the dev window 1996-2015 sits after the first and before the second became crowded. M0069 showed that buying five-year losers pays only through crashes and rebounds, and that most of its 70% fall came from buying companies still falling (2001-2002, 2008). Require the second half of a turnaround before buying. Each month, among point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members on F4's $5 / 20M-dollar screen, take the bottom fifth by the months -60..-13 return and hold 20 of them equal weight, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, empty slots in SPY. Variants: R12-N20 (the 20 with the best last-12-month return), UP-N20 (only names up over the last 12 months and above their own 200-day average, most beaten first; few qualify in a bear market, so it drifts into SPY), R12-L36 (the 36-month formation), R12-N20-T (R12-N20 in cash while SPY is under its 200-day average) and KNIFE-N20 (the control: the 20 with the WORST last 12 months, still falling, which should do worst). Success: a turnaround variant beats SPY TR on dev with a worst fall at or under 20%, beats KNIFE-N20 and M0069's L60-N20, and keeps an edge in 2009-2015 beyond the single year 2009.
methods.expectedFailure: The 12-month filter turns the book into momentum among cheap names, so its month-to-month result may move with the failed momentum books (the gate's behaviour kin) and it inherits momentum's crash: in spring 2009 the turnaround names were the defensive ones, and the junk rally that made M0069's average came off a bottom with negative trailing returns, so that rebound is lost. In 2001-2002 many old-economy losers were already rising, so the filter keeps that episode; in 2008 the losers that had risen in 2007 fell with everything else, so the worst fall is still likely well over 20% without the switch. Equal weight among beaten names bets against SPY's big-company drift, so 2010-2015 likely trails SPY. Survivorship still flatters losers that lived. UP-N20 may simply hold SPY much of the time and tie it.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What we tried

The parent method (M0069) bought the big index companies that had fallen most over five years. It beat SPY, but only through two episodes: the 2000-2002 tech crash and the 2009 rebound. Along the way it fell about 70% from a peak, mostly because it kept buying companies that were still falling.

This method added one condition: buy a long-term loser only once it has started to recover. Each month it took the bottom fifth of big index companies by their return over the past five years (leaving out the latest year), then picked 20 of them using the last 12 months. It ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's 5 million rupiah added each month. Empty slots held SPY. Five versions ran:

- **R12-N20:** the 20 losers with the best last year
- **UP-N20:** only losers that are up on the year *and* above their own 200-day average, most beaten first
- **R12-L36:** the same as R12-N20, but with a three-year look-back instead of five
- **R12-N20-T:** R12-N20 plus the SPY 200-day switch. The book sits in cash while SPY is below its 200-day average.
- **KNIFE-N20:** the control. It buys the 20 losers with the *worst* last year, the ones still falling.

## Result: rejected

| version | your money earned a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| best last year (R12-N20) | +5.5% | +7.2% | 57% | 1.27 | 0.42 |
| confirmed turn (UP-N20) | +9.5% | +7.2% | 54% | 1.69 | 0.62 |
| three-year version (R12-L36) | +8.0% | +7.2% | 56% | 1.42 | 0.51 |
| best last year + switch (R12-N20-T) | +8.1% | +7.2% | 27% | 1.70 | 0.74 |
| still falling (control) | +7.3% | +7.2% | 80% | 1.57 | 0.36 |

- **The worst fall decides it.** The limit is 20%. Every version broke it. Even the switch version lost 27.5% from a peak on the daily account. Measured only at month-ends, with the deposits taken out, it fell 17%, so the daily fall is the one that counts against the limit. The others lost more than half their value at some point.
- **Luck score (DSR).** This is how likely the result is real rather than a lucky draw after everything the lab has tried. It was scored at N = 68 looks (one per distinct method) against the bar of 0.90. The best version reached 0.74, so it fails. The others score 0.36 to 0.62, close to a coin flip.
- **R12-N20 failed outright.** It trailed SPY (+5.5% vs +7.2%), and its gains were only 1.27 times its losses, under the 1.3 bar.

## Year by year: points a year ahead of or behind SPY (deposits removed)

| years | SPY | parent: 5-yr losers | best last year | confirmed turn | three-year | + switch | still falling |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-1999 | +25.9% | −2.8 | −4.6 | −7.3 | −3.2 | −9.1 | −8.8 |
| 2000-2002 | −14.4% | +22.9 | +22.4 | +20.7 | +17.4 | +20.2 | **+25.9** |
| 2003-2007 | +12.5% | −2.8 | −1.7 | +2.0 | +0.1 | −3.5 | −3.6 |
| 2008 | −36.5% | −10.3 | **+0.2** | +1.2 | −0.4 | +36.3 (cash) | −17.3 |
| 2009 | +26.3% | +20.1 | **−20.8** | −10.7 | −8.2 | −1.1 | **+36.1** |
| 2010-2015 | +13.1% | +0.8 | −5.1 | +1.2 | −1.5 | −6.2 | −1.6 |
| 2009-2015 | +14.9% | +3.2 | −7.3 | −0.5 | −2.5 | −5.5 | +2.9 |

## Why

The filter did what it was meant to do in 2008. Losers that had been rising fell about as much as SPY, not 10 to 17 points more like the parent and the control. But the same filter threw away the year that paid. In 2009 the companies that bounced hardest were the ones that had fallen hardest in the past year, which is exactly what the filter excludes. The "still falling" control won 2009 by 36 points, and the turnaround book lost it by 21. Over a full cycle the two effects roughly cancel. What is left is a book that still falls more than half in a crash and trails SPY in the years since 2009, the years that look most like today.

The 2000-2002 edge is the same in every version, the control included. That episode was old-economy companies holding up while tech collapsed, so it was never about which losers you picked. Without it, no version beats SPY.

The breadth report agrees. Every version "pays only in broad" markets, the months when the average stock beat the index. The best balance, from the switch version, is −1.8 points a year in narrow months and +4.4 in broad ones. A book of beaten-down companies is a bet against SPY's big-company drift, and that drift has been the strongest force in the market since 2018.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**No.** The idea was to keep the rebounds and skip the falling knives. The book skipped the knives in 2008, but the rebound it kept was only 2000-2002, which needed no filter. It lost the 2009 rebound. None of the turnaround versions beat the parent's 2009-2015 lead of +3.2 points a year. The best of them, the confirmed-turn version, was −0.5 points, about a tie with SPY.

**The expected failure happened as written.** The pre-registration said the 2009 bounce would be lost because it came off a bottom with negative trailing returns. It said 2008 would still push the worst fall over 20% without the switch, and that 2010-2015 would likely trail SPY. All three came true. The one part that read better than expected: the confirmed-turn version did not just sit in SPY. It earned +9.5% a year, the best of the five, but it fell 54% on the way.

Survivorship still flatters this whole family. The store has no companies that later died, and those are concentrated among long-term losers.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished as a stand-alone book. Two methods and ten versions now say the same thing: among big US companies, the long-term-loser effect is one episode (2000-2002) plus one junk rally (2009). Any filter that removes the danger also removes the junk rally. No version clears a 20% worst fall without a market switch, and the switch costs the rebound. I would not spend another variation on picking which losers to buy. The one question left worth a single trial is whether this family helps as a small partner next to SPY. It made its money in exactly the years SPY lost (2000-2002), so a 20% slice beside a mostly-SPY book could lower the worst fall without dragging the average much. Even that is a long shot, because since 2009 the slice would mostly have trailed.
methods.verdict: Rejected: waiting for beaten-down big companies to turn up skipped the 2008 knife but lost the 2009 rebound; no version beat SPY since 2009 and all fell over 27% at their worst

methods.name: Big dividend raisers as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: the 100 most-traded members, half the money in SPY
methods.hypothesis: M0070 showed a 25%+ dividend raise beats steady payers by about 2 points a year in every era, but an equal-slot payer book loses to SPY's big-company drift after 2009 (-3.1 points a year for the big-raise book). Keep the signal and remove the size bet: only members in the top 100 by 60-day dollar volume, raises of 25%+ or first payments held six months, up to 10 names at 5% each, with at least 50% always in SPY, re-picked monthly at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares. Variants: with and without the SPY-200 cash switch, and the 50%-SPY core with steady payers as the control. Success means beating SPY in 2009-2015 with a worst fall under 20%.
