Success for the data: D beats X by half a point a year or more on funded CAGR at equal or lower worst fall, and holds up in 2009-2015. A pre-run data count (no returns): at mid-2000/2005/2012 about 205-280 qualifying members had all 8 payments dated; the lead spread's 10th percentile is 1.3-2.3 days and median 8-10 days, the ex-gap spread's 10th percentile 0.5 days, with 10-17 exact ties at 0 (ties go to held names, then the symbol). Assumed: a special dividend inside the window counts as a payment and can read as a cut after it (it disqualifies, which is the conservative side); split-adjusted amounts are comparable across a split.
methods.expectedFailure: Regularity mostly marks big, steady, low-volatility payers (utilities, staples, REITs, old industrials): the filter may just re-create the calm-stock book under a new name, and lag SPY in 2009-2015 when growth led. D and X may pick largely the same companies, so the paired difference may be noise. The 20-name book is concentrated in a few sectors, so its worst fall may track utilities/financials (2008 banks were regular payers until they cut). A book of index members equal-weighted leans small next to SPY, the shape every strategy has lost on since 2018. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

Four earlier methods in this batch (M0076, M0077, M0078, M0081) asked whether the dividend **announcement dates** the owner paid for let the lab act earlier. They did not: a few tenths of a point a year either way. This method asked a different question: is the announcement date useful as a **quality filter** instead of a clock?

The idea: a board that announces each dividend the same number of days before it goes ex, every time, and never cuts it, is a company that plans its cash. Among big index companies (S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members, $5+ price, $20M+ a day traded) with at least 8 dividends in the last 3 years and no cut among the last 8, it held the ones whose announcement-to-ex gap varied least (the "D" versions). The rest of the money sat in SPY, and everything went to cash while SPY was below its 200-day average. Monthly, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's monthly top-ups.

The fair comparison was built in: each "D" version had an "X" twin that ranked on how evenly spaced the **ex-dates** were, using no announcement data at all. D minus X is what the paid-for dates add as a filter. A fifth version (D-EARLY) took the steady boards that announce furthest ahead.

## Results (1996-2015, real fees, owner's deposits)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | DSR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-N20: 20 steadiest announcers | +7.7% | +7.2% | 29.7% | 0.80 |
| X-N20: 20 steadiest ex-date spacing | +8.1% | +7.2% | 35.6% | 0.83 |
| D-N40: 40 steadiest announcers | +8.9% | +7.2% | 23.1% | 0.91 |
| X-N40: 40 steadiest ex-date spacing | +9.1% | +7.2% | 27.0% | 0.93 |
| D-EARLY-N20: steady and earliest | +8.0% | +7.2% | 24.2% | 0.82 |

All five are **rejected**. Every one beat SPY over twenty years, by half a point to two points a year, but every one fell more than the 20% limit at its worst (23% to 36%). DSR is the chance the result is real rather than luck after the lab's N = 54 distinct methods; the bar is 0.90. The two 40-name versions cleared it (0.91 and 0.93), the 20-name ones did not.

## Did the announcement dates help as a filter?

**No.** D minus X, per year on the owner's deposits: **-0.4 points** at 20 names and **-0.2 points** at 40. The D versions fell a little less at their worst (29.7% vs 35.6%; 23.1% vs 27.0%), but earned slightly less. Not the half-point win the hypothesis asked for.

The striking part: **the two arms held almost entirely different companies.** At seven dates checked between 1998 and 2015, the 20-name D and X books shared only 0 to 4 stocks. Yet their returns came out within half a point of each other in every era. So the regularity score itself, whichever way it is measured, is picking noise inside a pool. What drives the result is the pool: big companies that have paid 8+ steady, uncut dividends in three years, behind the 200-day switch.

## Where the result came from (book without the deposits, versus SPY)

| era | D-N20 | X-N20 | D-N40 | X-N40 | D-EARLY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2001 | -2.9 | -4.6 | -2.1 | -2.5 | -3.1 |
| 2002-2008 | +7.2 | +10.5 | +9.2 | +9.1 | +8.0 |
| 2009-2015 | -6.4 | -7.5 | -5.6 | -5.0 | -6.3 |

(points a year ahead of or behind SPY with dividends)

- **The whole edge is 2002-2008**, and most of that is the 200-day switch stepping out of the 2008 crash, which every switched book in this lab gets.
- **In 2009-2015, the years most like today, every version lagged SPY by 5 to 7.5 points a year.** That alone rules the direction out (lesson of insight 89/91/93).
- **The worst fall came in 1998-2000, not 2008.** From early 1998 to February 2000 the steady payers drifted down while SPY rose in the dot-com run: the 20-name D book lost about 26% from its peak (book alone, monthly). Steady dividend payers are "old economy" companies, and in a growth-led market they fall behind and even fall outright. The switch does not help there, because SPY was above its 200-day line the whole time.
- Walk-forward (4 folds, 2003-2014): the lab's own choice beat SPY in **1 of 4** folds, and the 2009-2015 edge it reads is -4.9 points. Breadth: every version pays only in "broad" months (when the average stock beats the index) and loses 2-5 points a year in narrow ones, when a few giants carry SPY.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: D did not beat X by half a point, and nothing held up in 2009-2015. The expected failure mostly happened: the book lagged SPY in 2009-2015 when growth led, and D and X differed by noise. One part was wrong: the books were **not** mostly utilities and staples. They were banks, oil majors and industrials (PNC, State Street, Fifth Third, Exxon, Chevron, Emerson, Eaton, 3M, IBM, UPS). That is "old big value", which is exactly why 1998-2000 and 2009-2015 hurt.

## Compared with the near misses

The big-raise book M0070-R25-H6-T (same screen, switch and fees) did +1.9 / +10.1 / -3.1 points a year across the three eras and fell 16.6% at worst. This method did -2.1 / +9.2 / -5.6 at its best (D-N40). A raise is news; a steady schedule is not. M0081's first-dividend book did -0.6 / +9.2 / -7.6. Three dividend books in a row share the same shape: the 2008 switch carries them, and 2009-2015 sinks them.

**My opinion:** This direction is finished, and so, I think, is the paid-for announcement data as a stock picker. Five methods now say the dates add nothing, as a clock or as a filter. The more useful lesson is the pool effect: two books with almost no stocks in common gave the same result, so a ranking inside "steady big dividend payers" is cosmetic, and any dividend-based book here is really a bet on old-economy value against SPY's growth giants. That bet lost in 1998-2000 and 2009-2015 and, by everything the owner's money runs showed, since 2018 too. I would not spend another id on dividend schedules. If the lab tries dividends again, it should be as a small tilt inside a market-shaped book (weighted like SPY, not equally), so the experiment measures the dividend signal and not the value-versus-growth bet.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0082-X-N40`: DSR 0.9053 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Steady dividend schedules: picked almost entirely different stocks from the ex-date control yet earned the same; every version fell 23-36% at worst and lagged SPY by 5-7 points a year in 2009-2015

methods.name: Raises the market cheered: big dividend raises whose stock beat SPY over the two days after the announcement
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0076 (M0070-R25-H6-T's book); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); reaction-direction filter after M0063; declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-1995 (dividend-change drift) and the announcement-reaction literature is older still, so most of the dev window is after the crowd knew both. M0076 showed that seeing a big raise on its declaration day instead of its ex-date adds nothing to the timing (0.3-1.1 points a year worse in all three pairs): the one-day reaction is gone before the next open and the slow drift is caught either way. What the declaration date really carries is the market's reaction to the news. Keep M0070's monthly big-raise book (latest dividend >= 25% over the median of up to four prior payments in 400 days and at most double, or a first payment; up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, held names first then the newest event, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) but admit a raise only when its total return beat SPY's over the two sessions starting the event date (close before to close of the next session, dividends in the window added back since closes are not dividend-adjusted; the event waits until that window has closed). Variants, all monthly: A-UP announced and cheered (the idea); X-UP the paired ex-date control, the same filter over the two sessions starting the ex-date, all the old data allowed; A-DN / X-DN the reaction-negative controls; A-UP-D / X-UP-D the up pair counting only dividends that carry a declaration date, so the undated ~13% (whose announced reaction is really an ex-date reaction) cannot blur it. Unfiltered controls already exist: M0076-A-M (+10.3% a year funded) and M0076-X-M (+10.9%). The quantity of interest is A-UP minus X-UP on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, 2009-2015 and walk-forward folds, and UP minus DN in each arm. Success for the data: A-UP beats X-UP by a point a year or more and beats A-DN, with the dated pair agreeing in sign.
methods.expectedFailure: The filter roughly halves the set of live raises, so fewer of the 20 slots fill and more of the book sits in SPY; the edge then shrinks toward SPY's whether the filter selects or not. The two-day excess return of a big company is mostly noise (market moves, unrelated news) rather than a verdict on the dividend, so A-UP and A-DN may differ by little; and short-term reversal (M0028) would make a hot two-day start a small negative. The ex-date control may score the same as the announced arm because the drift is slow and either window samples similar noise. M0070's weaknesses carry over: worst fall near the 20% limit (21-22% in fast falls before the SPY-200 switch turns), and lagging SPY in 2009-2015 when big-company growth led. A widely published anomaly from the 1990s: even a real dev edge is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## The question

Sera's question for this batch: **does the dividend announcement data help?** M0076 already showed that seeing a big dividend raise on its announcement day, about three weeks before it goes ex, adds nothing to *timing*. This method asks the other thing the announcement date can tell us: **how did the market react?**

The book is M0070's big-raise book, unchanged. It holds up to 20 big index companies whose latest dividend was at least 25% above their usual payment (or a first payment), each at 5% for six months, keeps the rest in SPY, re-picks monthly, and goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees.

The new rule: a raise only gets in if the stock **beat SPY over the two trading days starting the event day** (from the close the day before to the close of the next day, with any dividend paid in that window added back, because the stored prices are not adjusted for dividends).

## The pairs (all fixed before any result)

- **A** = event day is the announcement day; **X** = event day is the ex-date (all the old data, no announcement dates needed).
- **UP** = only raises the market cheered; **DN** = only raises it shrugged off (the control).
- **-D** = only dividends that carry an announcement date, in both arms, so the 13% without one cannot blur the pair.
- The unfiltered controls already exist: M0076-A-M and M0076-X-M.

## Results (owner's deposits, real fees, 1996-2015; SPY on the same deposits +7.2% a year)

| variant | your money per year | worst fall (with deposits / book alone, monthly) | DSR | 2009-2015 (book alone) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-UP | +9.8% | 19.9% / 15.8% | 0.873 | +12.6% |
| X-UP | +10.6% | 21.1% / 16.0% | 0.918 | +12.5% |
| A-DN | +8.8% | 21.0% / 15.1% | 0.860 | +9.9% |
| X-DN | +8.8% | 25.5% / 18.5% | 0.829 | +11.1% |
| A-UP-D | +9.8% | 21.3% / 15.4% | 0.871 | +12.7% |
| **X-UP-D** | **+10.8%** | **19.9%** / 15.6% | **0.922** | +12.9% |
| *M0076-A-M (no filter)* | +10.3% | 21.3% / 16.1% | 0.932 | +12.4% |
| *M0076-X-M (no filter)* | +10.9% | 21.9% / 16.6% | 0.946 | +13.4% |

SPY alone earned +14.8% a year in 2009-2015. Every variant lagged it there, by 2 to 5 points.

## Announcement minus ex-date (the value of the data)

Paired monthly differences, deposits taken out:

- **UP pair:** announced earned 0.8 points a year less on the deposits (+9.8% vs +10.6%). Monthly, it trailed by 0.047% (t = −0.95), and was ahead in only 7 of 20 years. 2009-2015 was a tie (+12.6% vs +12.5%). The worst fall was a little smaller (19.9% vs 21.1%). DSR was lower (0.873 vs 0.918).
- **Dated-only UP pair:** announced earned 1.0 point a year less (+9.8% vs +10.8%). Monthly: −0.054% (t = −1.09), ahead in 8 of 20 years. 2009-2015 +12.7% vs +12.9%. Worst fall 21.3% vs 19.9%. DSR 0.871 vs 0.922.
- **DN pair:** a dead tie (+8.8% vs +8.8%; t = +0.35).
- **Walk-forward:** the lab's own pick won 2 of 4 folds and changed between folds. It lagged SPY by 3.4 points a year in 2009-2015. Not a majority.

**All three pairs say the same as M0076: the announcement date does not help.** Measuring the market's reaction from the announcement day is no better than measuring it from the ex-date, and slightly worse in both UP pairs. The coverage gap was not hiding anything: the dated-only pair agrees in sign and size.

## Does the reaction filter itself help?

The filter keeps the cheered raises and drops the shrugged-off ones:

- UP beat DN in both arms: by 1.0 point a year on announcement (t = +0.71), and by 1.8 points on ex-date (t = +1.54). Both are suggestive at best, not real evidence.
- **But no UP version beat the unfiltered book.** A-UP earned +9.8% vs +10.3% unfiltered; X-UP earned +10.6% vs +10.9%. The shrugged-off raises *still* earn the drift (+8.8%, well above SPY's +7.2%). Dropping them leaves slots empty for SPY to fill, and SPY earns less than the raises it replaced. So the filter sorts raises slightly, but it costs more than it sorts.
- Exposure was 70% in every variant, same as the unfiltered book. The empty slots go to SPY, so the "invested" share doesn't move; what moves is how much of the book is raises versus SPY.

## The eligible one, read honestly

X-UP-D (the ex-date, dated-only *control*) cleared the dev gate:
- beat SPY: +10.8% vs +7.2% a year on deposits
- worst fall 19.9%, under the 20% limit by 0.1 point
- gains vs losses (profit factor) 3.05
- DSR 0.922 at N = 56 methods, over the 0.90 bar. That means a result this good is fairly unlikely to be pure luck after 56 tries.

This is a hair-thin pass. Its own twin with the undated dividends included (X-UP) fell 21.1%, and the unfiltered parent fell 21.9%. So the 0.1 point margin depends on which 13% of events happen to be counted, not on the idea.

It also fails what matters for promotion. It lagged SPY in 2009-2015 (+12.9% vs +14.8%). And the walk-forward is 2 of 4, so `lab promote` will refuse it (hard gate F). It is the control arm, not the idea. **No buy signal:** (c) the folds and (d) a positive 2009-2015 edge both fail.

## Why

A big company's two-day move against SPY is mostly unrelated news and market noise. The dividend raise is one of many things the price is reacting to. The slow drift after a big raise is what this family earns. It shows up in cheered and shrugged-off raises alike, so a filter that halves the set mostly swaps raise drift for SPY. Measuring the reaction three weeks earlier, on the announcement day, sees no better signal, because the announcement-day move is just as noisy.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: A-UP did not beat X-UP by a point (it lost by 0.8), and the dated pair agrees. A-UP did beat A-DN by a point, but neither one beat the book without a filter. The expected failure happened almost word for word. The filter thinned the raises, the edge shrank toward SPY's, the worst fall stayed around 20-21%, and the book lagged SPY in 2009-2015.

## My opinion:

The dividend announcement dates have now been tested three ways (timing in M0076, first-ever dividends in M0081, the market's reaction here). They added nothing each time. I would stop spending ids on *when* or *how* this book learns of a raise. The raise drift is real on dev, but it is slow and the ex-date catches it fine. This family's real problem is structural: it lags SPY in 2009-2015 and it fails the folds, because 20 equal 5% slots in big-dividend-raisers lean against SPY's big-company growth. The next try worth an id should attack that directly. Weight the raise slots by company size (dollar volume as the stand-in), or cut the slots and let SPY carry more, and judge it first on 2009-2015. If it still lags SPY there, the family is done.


### 2026-10-10

### Sera 20261010-1742: promotion refused by the hard gate

M0083's only dev-eligible variant is X-UP-D: the ex-date timed, dated-only control, which uses no announcement timing at all. `lab promote` would refuse it on the fold condition, so I did not run it. It wins 2 of 4 walk-forward folds (the pick changed between folds), and the gate wants a strict majority. Its kin are clean (nothing in stock-dividend-change-drift or its ancestry has test-failed). Its edge over SPY in 2009-2015, the highest-coverage era, is -3.4 points a year. That means no buy signal, and no test-window look is spent.
methods.verdict: Dev-eligible only by a hair, on the ex-date control (X-UP-D, 19.9% worst fall): measuring the market's reaction from the announcement day earned 0.8-1.0 pt a year LESS than from the ex-date, and no reaction filter beat the unfiltered book; folds 2 of 4, lags SPY 2009-2015

methods.name: Price the safety switch on its own: SPY behind its 200-day average, read weekly, monthly, with a band or not at all
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0078 (its JOINT-EX arm was almost a pure SPY-behind-the-switch book); Faber (2007), A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation; Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992), Simple technical trading rules, JF 47(5)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1992 (the banded moving-average rule) and 2007 (Faber's 10-month average), on top of decades of trend-following lore, so the dev window sees every version of this switch long after the crowd knew it and the plain switch is expected to lag SPY in 2009-2015. The point is to PRICE the frame, not to find an edge. Half the lab's books sit behind the same switch -- all cash while SPY closes under its 200-day average -- and every post-mortem since M0063 has blamed the switch rather than the picks, always by inference from a book that also held stocks. M0078's JOINT-EX arm held SPY behind a WEEKLY switch almost all the time and earned +3.9% a year on the owner's deposits against +7.2% for the same deposits in SPY, which puts the weekly switch at about 3 points a year at Gotrade's real fees; M0063 showed the same book at +5.0% weekly against +11.6% monthly; M0101 found that on a MONTHLY dividend book a 3% band deepened the worst fall from 18.7% to 20.4% and widened the 2009-2015 lag from -2.6 to -3.1 points. All three readings are confounded by the stocks those books held. This method removes them: hold ONLY SPY at full weight behind the switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, and vary nothing but the reading. Variants cross the rank cadence with the reading rule: ALWAYS (no switch, monthly -- buy SPY and hold, the yardstick through the identical fee, deposit and rounding path); WEEKLY and MONTHLY (the strict close > SMA200 gate, F4's trend_on unchanged, read at each cadence); BAND3-W and BAND3-M (M0101's band_on unchanged at 3%, off below 0.97 of the average and back on above 1.03, read at each cadence); FABER-M (M0101's faber_on unchanged, month-end close above its 10-month mean). Every variant shares one 253-bar lookback, so all six are scored on the same sessions and each paired difference is the switch alone. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: a 100%-SPY book cannot beat SPY except by sidestepping 2000-2002 and 2008 for more than whipsaw costs, so no variant is expected to pass the go-live bars, and none should be promoted. The hypothesis under test is that MONTHLY beats WEEKLY by 2 or more points a year on the owner's deposits with a similar worst fall. If it does, every weekly event book in the lab (M0063, M0066, M0072, M0078, M0092) lost to its frame rather than to its signal, and should be re-framed on the monthly switch before any of them is abandoned. The second question is whether the 3% band is worth anything once no stock-picking can mask it, at either cadence.
methods.expectedFailure: The switch's whole value is the 2000-2002 and 2008 falls it sits out, and both land in the first two thirds of the dev window, so MONTHLY may look fine over 1996-2015 and still lose to SPY from 2009 -- which is exactly what M0096 and M0101 found on a book. Every variant then reads 'the switch costs money in the era most like today and earned its keep only in two crashes', and the lab learns a price without learning a frame to use. ALWAYS and the switched variants will not differ by much in worst fall if the 2008 exit comes late: SPY had already fallen well over 20% before its 200-day average was crossed convincingly in the 1998 and 2011 fast drops, so the switched variants may breach the 20% bar just as ALWAYS does (SPY's own 1996-2015 worst fall is about 55%). The cadence difference may also be smaller than the 3 points inferred from M0078: that book paid weekly fees on 20 stock slots as well as on the switch, so a SPY-only weekly book trades far less and the frame may price out nearer 1 point, which would mean the weekly event books lost to their signals after all. Trade counts will be tiny (a few dozen switch flips over 20 years), so profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless here and no variant will clear the luck bar; the funded return and the era split are the only readable numbers. Not modelled: interest on the cash held while the switch is off, which flatters SPY and penalises every switched variant -- in the 1996-2007 part of the window US cash paid 3-5% a year, so the true cost of sitting out is lower than measured and the gap this method reports is an upper bound on the switch's cost.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

## The question

Half the strategies in this lab carry the same safety rule. It says: **when the S&P 500 tracker
(SPY) closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything and sit in
cash; when it closes back above, buy again.** Every post-mortem since the news-day book has
ended by blaming that rule rather than the stocks the book picked. But every one of those tests
mixed the two together, so the blame was always a guess.

This test takes the stocks away. Each version here **holds nothing but SPY**, at full weight,
and the only thing that changes is how the safety rule is read. Whatever comes out is the price
of the frame itself, and every future strategy can read it off before spending an idea on it.

Six versions, fixed before any result:

- **ALWAYS** — no safety rule at all. Buy SPY, hold it, add each month's deposit. The yardstick.
- **WEEKLY** — the plain rule, checked once a week. This is the frame the news-day books used.
- **MONTHLY** — the same plain rule, checked once a month. The frame the dividend books used.
- **BAND3-W** — a gentler rule checked weekly: leave only when SPY is **3% below** its average,
  and come back only when it is **3% above**. The dead zone is meant to stop it flip-flopping.
- **BAND3-M** — the same gentler rule, checked monthly.
- **FABER-M** — a famous published version (Faber, 2007): month-end price above its 10-month
  average.

All six trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, start with 10 million rupiah and take
5 million more on the 25th of every month — 260 deposits over 1994 to 2015, about $162,000 of
real money put in. Returns below are measured in dollars, so the rupiah's long slide adds
nothing to any of these numbers.

## What happened

SPY itself, with dividends, on the same deposits: **+7.7% a year.**

| version | your money per year | worst fall | times in and out | gains vs losses | luck check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS (no rule) | +7.7% | **55.0%** | 0 | — | 0.51 |
| WEEKLY | **+4.4%** | 33.1% | 40 | 2.3 | 0.47 |
| MONTHLY | **+9.1%** | **18.9%** | 11 | very high | 0.88 |
| BAND3-W | +7.8% | 18.9% | 10 | very high | 0.82 |
| BAND3-M | +8.7% | 20.7% | 9 | very high | 0.87 |
| FABER-M | +8.5% | 18.9% | 13 | very high | 0.84 |

**Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a high point; the owner's limit is 20%. **Gains vs
losses** (profit factor) is useless here — these books make about one trade a year, and a book
that only ever sells after a long rise shows an enormous ratio that means nothing. **Luck check**
(DSR) asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of many tries; the lab counted
**N = 73** independent tries when this ran (one per strategy that has ever been tested, the
"methods" rule in force since 8 October), and the owner's bar is **0.90**.

**No version passes.** The method is rejected. The closest, MONTHLY, beats SPY by 1.4 points a
year with a worst fall of 18.9% — inside the 20% limit — but it fails on two conditions: it makes
only 11 trades where the lab requires 100, and its luck score of 0.884 is just under 0.90. Both
failures say the same thing: **eleven decisions in twenty-two years is not evidence, however good
the eleven look.**

## The first answer: the weekly check costs 4.7 points a year

That is the headline. Same rule, same market, same fees — read once a week instead of once a
month and the owner's money grows at +4.4% a year instead of +9.1%.

And it is **not** the trading fees. I re-ran all six with the fees switched off entirely:

| version | with Gotrade's fees | with no fees at all | what the fees cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS | +7.67% | +7.70% | 0.03 points a year |
| WEEKLY | +4.35% | +5.31% | **0.95** |
| MONTHLY | +9.13% | +9.39% | 0.26 |
| BAND3-W | +7.78% | +8.04% | 0.26 |
| BAND3-M | +8.73% | +8.97% | 0.24 |
| FABER-M | +8.48% | +8.79% | 0.31 |

Fees explain **0.7 of the 4.7 points**. The other **4.0 points is simply buying and selling at
worse prices.**

The clincher is stronger than that. The weekly and the monthly version use the **identical
rule**, and that rule says the same thing on the same days: read on every one of the 5,469
trading days in the window, it says "stay out" on 1,562 of them, 28.6%, for both. The two
versions differ in one thing only — how often the book is allowed to listen. And they ended up
spending **almost exactly the same time invested**: 70.2% for the weekly one, 71.1% for the
monthly, 71.6 to 71.9% for the other three. Being out of the market is not what separates them.
What separates them is how often they changed their mind inside that same time: the weekly
version turned the whole book over **four times as much** as the monthly one, for nothing.

This is what a whipsaw costs, measured. Checking more often does not get you out faster in a real
crash — a real crash lasts months, so a monthly check catches it too. It only gets you out faster
in a dip that was about to end, which means selling near the bottom and buying back higher.

## The second answer: every one of these rules is wrong for today

Here is each version's own growth, with the deposits stripped out so a top-up is never counted as
a gain, split by era:

| version | 1994-2015 | 1994-2002 | 2003-2008 | **2009-2015** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS (= SPY) | 8.8% | 8.8% | 2.7% | **16.6%** |
| WEEKLY | 5.6% | 6.9% | 4.0% | **5.5%** |
| MONTHLY | 9.6% | 9.9% | 8.2% | **10.7%** |
| BAND3-W | 8.5% | 9.4% | 6.8% | **9.1%** |
| BAND3-M | 9.5% | 10.6% | 7.5% | **10.1%** |
| FABER-M | 9.0% | 9.2% | 8.2% | **9.8%** |

**In 2009-2015 — the stretch of years most like the one the owner is actually investing in —
every safety rule lost to simply holding SPY, by between 6 and 11 points a year.** The best of
them, the monthly one, gave up 5.9 points a year in that era. That is the lab's first filter, and
all six fail it.

The whole twenty-two-year advantage comes from three calendar years, and nowhere else:

| year | hold SPY | MONTHLY rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1998 | **+29.9%** | +10.1% |
| 2001 | −16.8% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2002 | −22.4% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2003 | **+34.6%** | +24.3% |
| 2008 | −34.9% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2009 | **+41.6%** | +23.6% |
| 2010 | **+21.1%** | +11.7% |
| 2015 | **+4.9%** | −3.5% |

Sitting out 2001, 2002 and 2008 is worth a great deal. Paying for it costs 18 points in 2009
alone, because the rule was still in cash while the market turned, and another 19 points across
1998, 2003, 2010 and 2015. Over the full window the three crash years win by a nose: +9.6% a year
against +8.8% for holding. Over the last seven years of the window they lose badly.

The market-shape check agrees. The monthly rule earns **+5.6% a year over SPY in months when a
few big companies carry the index** and **−1.1% in months when the typical company keeps up**.
That is the signature of insurance, not of an edge: it pays out in a panic and bleeds the rest of
the time.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Yes, and by more than predicted.** I wrote beforehand that monthly would beat weekly by 2 or
more points a year with a similar worst fall. It beat it by 4.7 points, and its worst fall was
*gentler* (18.9% against 33.1%) rather than similar — reading less often made the book both
richer and safer, which I did not expect. I also wrote that the gap might shrink to about 1 point
once the stock slots were removed, because the weekly event books paid weekly fees on twenty
stock positions as well as on the switch. That guess was wrong: the gap is nearly as wide on a
one-position book as it was on a twenty-position one (the news-day book read +5.0% weekly against
+11.6% monthly, a 6.6-point gap, on the same 200-day rule).

**The expected failure also happened, word for word.** I wrote that the rule's whole value is the
crashes it sits out, that both big ones land early in the window, and that every version might
look fine over the full window and still lose from 2009. All six do exactly that.

The second question — whether the 3% dead zone is worth anything on its own — came out
**half yes**. At the weekly cadence the band is worth **+3.4 points a year** (+4.4% to +7.8%): it
cuts the flip-flopping from a turnover of 3.4 to 0.9, almost exactly the monthly figure. At the
monthly cadence it is worth **−0.4 points** (+9.1% to +8.7%) and it pushes the worst fall from
18.9% to 20.7%, over the limit. So the band is a **repair for reading too often**, not an
improvement in its own right. Waiting a month does the same job for free and slightly better,
which is the same thing the dividend book found when the band was tried on top of it.

Faber's published version lands between the two monthly versions and adds nothing. Its reading is
a month-end price against a 10-month average, which is a slightly slower version of the same
idea, and it behaves like one.

## Compared with the books this frame was borrowed from

- The news-day book on the **weekly** rule earned +5.0% a year; on the **monthly** rule, +11.6%.
  The gap, 6.6 points, is larger than the 4.7 measured here on SPY alone, so on that book some of
  the loss really was the weekly re-picking of stocks — but most of it was the frame.
- The earnings-and-dividend pair book's control arm, which was almost pure SPY behind the weekly
  rule, earned +3.9% against +7.2% for SPY. That was read at the time as "the weekly switch costs
  about 3 points a year". This run says the honest figure is **4.7 points**, and names where it
  goes: 0.7 to fees and 4.0 to worse prices.
- The calm-dividend book found a 3% band deepened its worst fall and widened its 2009-2015 lag.
  The same thing happens here with no stocks in the way, so that was the band, not the dividends.

One caution on comparing numbers across the lab: this method needs only a year of run-up where a
stock book needs more, so it was scored from **1994-01-28**, about two years earlier than most
lab methods. Its SPY yardstick is therefore +7.7% a year, not the +7.2% quoted elsewhere. Every
comparison **inside** this method is exact — all six versions ran on identical sessions — but a
figure here and a figure from another method are not measured on the same years.

## Two things this measurement does not include

1. **Interest on the cash.** While a safety rule is off, the book holds dollars earning nothing.
   In reality US Treasury bills paid real interest for most of this window. Every switched version
   sat in cash about 29% of the time, so the versions above are understated by roughly the
   average bill rate times that share. I could not put a number on it: the lab's store format
   allows a file of market-wide series, including Treasury yields, but the store these runs used
   does not contain one, and the only other route — parking the idle money in a Treasury-bill
   fund — cannot be tested either, because the fund the lab knows about has no prices before
   May 2007 and the years with real interest rates are all before that. So the figures above are
   an **upper bound on the rule's cost**: it looks worse here than it was, by something of the
   order of one point a year across 1994 to 2007.
2. **Taxes.** Not modelled anywhere in the lab.

Neither changes the conclusion about 2009-2015, where short-term interest rates were near zero.

## What the out-of-sample checks said

On the four later stretches the method was never tuned on, it beat the market in **1 of 4** —
a majority is required and it is nowhere near. In the best-covered era it was level, because the
fold picker chose the no-rule version there, which is the same thing as SPY. No buy signal; there
is no case for paying for better price history on the back of this.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished as a search for an edge, and it should never again be
treated as a free safety feature bolted onto a stock picker. Two things follow and I would act on
both. First, every book in this lab that reads the safety rule **weekly** has been handicapped by
about 4.7 points a year for reasons that have nothing to do with its own idea — the news-day
book, the earnings-jump books and the pair book were all judged while carrying that handicap, and
their verdicts are not safe. Any of them worth a second look should be re-run on the monthly
reading first, and the lab should stop writing new weekly-cadence books altogether; there is now
a measured price for doing so and it is far larger than any event edge found here. Second, the
rule's only real product is crash insurance, and the premium is 6 points a year in the era that
matters. I would not buy that premium. But the single largest piece of it is recoverable: the
rule lost 18 points in 2009 alone by staying in cash through the turn, because the same slow
average that got it out in 2008 kept it out until mid-2009. A rule that **leaves slowly and
returns quickly** — out on the 200-day average, back in on something that reacts in weeks rather
than months — would keep the 2008 and 2002 exits and give back far less of 2009 and 2003. That is
the one variation of this family I would spend an id on, and I have queued it. If it also loses in
2009-2015, the safety rule is dead in every form and the lab should delete it from every book and
accept the 55% fall as the price of owning the market.


### 2026-10-12

## The question

Half the strategies in this lab carry the same safety rule. It says: **when the S&P 500 tracker
(SPY) closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything and sit in
cash; when it closes back above, buy again.** Every post-mortem since the news-day book has
ended by blaming that rule rather than the stocks the book picked. But every one of those tests
mixed the two together, so the blame was always a guess.

This test takes the stocks away. Each version here **holds nothing but SPY**, at full weight,
and the only thing that changes is how the safety rule is read. Whatever comes out is the price
of the frame itself, and every future strategy can read it off before spending an idea on it.

Six versions, fixed before any result:

- **ALWAYS** — no safety rule at all. Buy SPY, hold it, add each month's deposit. The yardstick.
- **WEEKLY** — the plain rule, checked once a week. This is the frame the news-day books used.
- **MONTHLY** — the same plain rule, checked once a month. The frame the dividend books used.
- **BAND3-W** — a gentler rule checked weekly: leave only when SPY is **3% below** its average,
  and come back only when it is **3% above**. The dead zone is meant to stop it flip-flopping.
- **BAND3-M** — the same gentler rule, checked monthly.
- **FABER-M** — a famous published version (Faber, 2007): month-end price above its 10-month
  average.

All six trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, start with 10 million rupiah and take
5 million more on the 25th of every month — 260 deposits over 1994 to 2015, about $162,000 of
real money put in. Returns below are measured in dollars, so the rupiah's long slide adds
nothing to any of these numbers.

## What happened

SPY itself, with dividends, on the same deposits: **+7.7% a year.**

| version | your money per year | worst fall | times in and out | gains vs losses | luck check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS (no rule) | +7.7% | **55.0%** | 0 | — | 0.51 |
| WEEKLY | **+4.4%** | 33.1% | 40 | 2.3 | 0.47 |
| MONTHLY | **+9.1%** | **18.9%** | 11 | very high | 0.88 |
| BAND3-W | +7.8% | 18.9% | 10 | very high | 0.82 |
| BAND3-M | +8.7% | 20.7% | 9 | very high | 0.87 |
| FABER-M | +8.5% | 18.9% | 13 | very high | 0.84 |

**Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a high point; the owner's limit is 20%. **Gains vs
losses** (profit factor) is useless here — these books make about one trade a year, and a book
that only ever sells after a long rise shows an enormous ratio that means nothing. **Luck check**
(DSR) asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of many tries; the lab counted
**N = 73** independent tries when this ran (one per strategy that has ever been tested, the
"methods" rule in force since 8 October), and the owner's bar is **0.90**.

**No version passes.** The method is rejected. The closest, MONTHLY, beats SPY by 1.4 points a
year with a worst fall of 18.9% — inside the 20% limit — but it fails on two conditions: it makes
only 11 trades where the lab requires 100, and its luck score of 0.884 is just under 0.90. Both
failures say the same thing: **eleven decisions in twenty-two years is not evidence, however good
the eleven look.**

## The first answer: the weekly check costs 4.7 points a year

That is the headline. Same rule, same market, same fees — read once a week instead of once a
month and the owner's money grows at +4.4% a year instead of +9.1%.

And it is **not** the trading fees. I re-ran all six with the fees switched off entirely:

| version | with Gotrade's fees | with no fees at all | what the fees cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS | +7.67% | +7.70% | 0.03 points a year |
| WEEKLY | +4.35% | +5.31% | **0.95** |
| MONTHLY | +9.13% | +9.39% | 0.26 |
| BAND3-W | +7.78% | +8.04% | 0.26 |
| BAND3-M | +8.73% | +8.97% | 0.24 |
| FABER-M | +8.48% | +8.79% | 0.31 |

Fees explain **0.7 of the 4.7 points**. The other **4.0 points is simply buying and selling at
worse prices.**

The clincher is stronger than that. The weekly and the monthly version use the **identical
rule**, and that rule says the same thing on the same days: read on every one of the 5,469
trading days in the window, it says "stay out" on 1,562 of them, 28.6%, for both. The two
versions differ in one thing only — how often the book is allowed to listen. And they ended up
spending **almost exactly the same time invested**: 70.2% for the weekly one, 71.1% for the
monthly, 71.6 to 71.9% for the other three. Being out of the market is not what separates them.
What separates them is how often they changed their mind inside that same time: the weekly
version turned the whole book over **four times as much** as the monthly one, for nothing.

This is what a whipsaw costs, measured. Checking more often does not get you out faster in a real
crash — a real crash lasts months, so a monthly check catches it too. It only gets you out faster
in a dip that was about to end, which means selling near the bottom and buying back higher.

## The second answer: every one of these rules is wrong for today

Here is each version's own growth, with the deposits stripped out so a top-up is never counted as
a gain, split by era:

| version | 1994-2015 | 1994-2002 | 2003-2008 | **2009-2015** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALWAYS (= SPY) | 8.8% | 8.8% | 2.7% | **16.6%** |
| WEEKLY | 5.6% | 6.9% | 4.0% | **5.5%** |
| MONTHLY | 9.6% | 9.9% | 8.2% | **10.7%** |
| BAND3-W | 8.5% | 9.4% | 6.8% | **9.1%** |
| BAND3-M | 9.5% | 10.6% | 7.5% | **10.1%** |
| FABER-M | 9.0% | 9.2% | 8.2% | **9.8%** |

**In 2009-2015 — the stretch of years most like the one the owner is actually investing in —
every safety rule lost to simply holding SPY, by between 6 and 11 points a year.** The best of
them, the monthly one, gave up 5.9 points a year in that era. That is the lab's first filter, and
all six fail it.

The whole twenty-two-year advantage comes from three calendar years, and nowhere else:

| year | hold SPY | MONTHLY rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1998 | **+29.9%** | +10.1% |
| 2001 | −16.8% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2002 | −22.4% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2003 | **+34.6%** | +24.3% |
| 2008 | −34.9% | **0.0%** (in cash all year) |
| 2009 | **+41.6%** | +23.6% |
| 2010 | **+21.1%** | +11.7% |
| 2015 | **+4.9%** | −3.5% |

Sitting out 2001, 2002 and 2008 is worth a great deal. Paying for it costs 18 points in 2009
alone, because the rule was still in cash while the market turned, and another 19 points across
1998, 2003, 2010 and 2015. Over the full window the three crash years win by a nose: +9.6% a year
against +8.8% for holding. Over the last seven years of the window they lose badly.

The market-shape check agrees. The monthly rule earns **+5.6% a year over SPY in months when a
few big companies carry the index** and **−1.1% in months when the typical company keeps up**.
That is the signature of insurance, not of an edge: it pays out in a panic and bleeds the rest of
the time.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Yes, and by more than predicted.** I wrote beforehand that monthly would beat weekly by 2 or
more points a year with a similar worst fall. It beat it by 4.7 points, and its worst fall was
*gentler* (18.9% against 33.1%) rather than similar — reading less often made the book both
richer and safer, which I did not expect. I also wrote that the gap might shrink to about 1 point
once the stock slots were removed, because the weekly event books paid weekly fees on twenty
stock positions as well as on the switch. That guess was wrong: the gap is nearly as wide on a
one-position book as it was on a twenty-position one (the news-day book read +5.0% weekly against
+11.6% monthly, a 6.6-point gap, on the same 200-day rule).

**The expected failure also happened, word for word.** I wrote that the rule's whole value is the
crashes it sits out, that both big ones land early in the window, and that every version might
look fine over the full window and still lose from 2009. All six do exactly that.

The second question — whether the 3% dead zone is worth anything on its own — came out
**half yes**. At the weekly cadence the band is worth **+3.4 points a year** (+4.4% to +7.8%): it
cuts the flip-flopping from a turnover of 3.4 to 0.9, almost exactly the monthly figure. At the
monthly cadence it is worth **−0.4 points** (+9.1% to +8.7%) and it pushes the worst fall from
18.9% to 20.7%, over the limit. So the band is a **repair for reading too often**, not an
improvement in its own right. Waiting a month does the same job for free and slightly better,
which is the same thing the dividend book found when the band was tried on top of it.

Faber's published version lands between the two monthly versions and adds nothing. Its reading is
a month-end price against a 10-month average, which is a slightly slower version of the same
idea, and it behaves like one.

## An important limit: 4.7 points is the cost of the *frame*, not a number to subtract from every book

It would be easy to read the headline as "every weekly strategy in this lab was handicapped by
4.7 points a year". **That is not what this measures, and the lab already contains the evidence
against it.**

The late-declaration dividend book ran both cadences on identical settings at real fees — the
only other clean pair in the lab. Its three monthly arms earned +11.1%, +10.9% and +10.4% a year;
its three weekly arms, the same books read weekly, earned +10.1%, +10.3% and +9.9%. The cadence
was worth **0.5 to 1.0 points a year**, not 4.7. What it *was* worth a lot of is safety: the
weekly arms fell 25.5 to 26.0% from a peak where the monthly arms fell 21.3 to 22.0%, about
4 points deeper.

So the frame's cost is not a constant that transfers. It scales with how much of the money the
frame is actually holding when it flips:

| book | what it holds behind the rule | weekly-minus-monthly, money per year |
|---|---|---|
| this one | nothing but SPY — the rule is the whole book | **−4.7 points** |
| the earnings-and-dividend pair's control arm | about 90% SPY, a name or two of stock | about −3.3 points |
| the late-declaration dividend book | twenty calm dividend payers | **−0.5 to −1.0 points** |

The reason is plain once it is laid out. A whipsaw costs whatever it sells low and buys back
high. When the book is all SPY, a whipsaw sells and rebuys all of it. When the book is twenty
calm dividend payers that it was going to re-pick anyway, the forced sale overlaps with trading
it would have done regardless, and calm stocks move less than the index does in the dips that
trigger a whipsaw in the first place.

The news-day book's weekly arm (+5.0% a year) against its monthly arm (+11.6%) looks like a
6.6-point frame cost, but that pair is not clean: the weekly arm also re-picked twenty stock
slots every week, 1,930 trades against 1,214, so most of that gap is weekly stock churn and not
the safety rule at all.

**What does transfer** is the direction and the drawdown. In every pair in the lab, reading the
rule more often made the book poorer *and* made its worst fall deeper. Nothing has ever been
improved by reading it weekly.
- The calm-dividend book found a 3% band deepened its worst fall and widened its 2009-2015 lag.
  The same thing happens here with no stocks in the way, so that was the band, not the dividends.

One caution on comparing numbers across the lab: this method needs only a year of run-up where a
stock book needs more, so it was scored from **1994-01-28**, about two years earlier than most
lab methods. Its SPY yardstick is therefore +7.7% a year, not the +7.2% quoted elsewhere. Every
comparison **inside** this method is exact — all six versions ran on identical sessions — but a
figure here and a figure from another method are not measured on the same years.

## Two things this measurement does not include

1. **Interest on the cash.** While a safety rule is off, the book holds dollars earning nothing.
   In reality US Treasury bills paid real interest for most of this window. Every switched version
   sat in cash about 29% of the time, so the versions above are understated by roughly the
   average bill rate times that share. I could not put a number on it: the lab's store format
   allows a file of market-wide series, including Treasury yields, but the store these runs used
   does not contain one, and the only other route — parking the idle money in a Treasury-bill
   fund — cannot be tested either, because the fund the lab knows about has no prices before
   May 2007 and the years with real interest rates are all before that. So the figures above are
   an **upper bound on the rule's cost**: it looks worse here than it was, by something of the
   order of one point a year across 1994 to 2007.
2. **Taxes.** Not modelled anywhere in the lab.

Neither changes the conclusion about 2009-2015, where short-term interest rates were near zero.

## What the out-of-sample checks said

On the four later stretches the method was never tuned on, it beat the market in **1 of 4** —
a majority is required and it is nowhere near. In the best-covered era it was level, because the
fold picker chose the no-rule version there, which is the same thing as SPY. No buy signal; there
is no case for paying for better price history on the back of this.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished as a search for an edge, and the useful output is a
price list, not a strategy. Three things follow and I would act on all three.

First, **stop writing new strategies that check the safety rule weekly.** The frame is never
improved by reading it more often — in every paired test the lab has, the weekly reading was
poorer and fell further — and on a book that is mostly parked in the market behind the rule it
costs up to 4.7 points a year. Monthly should be the default, and a weekly reading should have to
argue for itself.

Second, **do not go back and re-run the shelved weekly books on the monthly reading as a batch.**
I was about to recommend that and the lab's own evidence says it would be a waste. The one clean
paired test on a real stock book put the cadence at well under a point a year of return, so the
weekly event books lost to their own signals, not to their frame, and re-framing will not rescue
them. The exception is any book that sat mostly in the market behind the rule rather than in its
own picks — those were measuring the frame more than their idea, and the earnings-and-dividend
pair book is the clear case.

Third, and the only thing here worth a new idea: **the rule's one real product is crash
insurance, and the premium is about six points a year in the years that look most like today.**
I would not buy that at the price. But the single biggest piece of the premium is recoverable.
The rule lost 18 points in 2009 alone by sitting in cash through the turn, because the same slow
200-day average that correctly got it out in 2008 kept it out until well into the recovery; 2003
cost another 10 points the same way. A rule that is **slow to leave and quick to return** — out on
the monthly 200-day check, back in on something that reacts in weeks — would keep the 2002 and
2008 exits while giving back far less of 2003 and 2009. That is the one variation of this family
worth an id, and I have queued it. It is a clean test, because the exit is held fixed and only
the return trigger moves, so whatever it earns is attributable. If it too loses in 2009-2015,
the safety rule is dead in every form, and the lab should drop it from every book and accept
that owning the market means accepting a 55% fall.
methods.verdict: The safety switch priced alone: reading it weekly instead of monthly costs 4.7 points a year (only 0.7 of it fees), and every version of it lost 6 to 11 points a year to simply holding SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: A late dividend declaration as a warning: step out of a stock whose board has not declared on its usual schedule
methods.sourceRef: Kalay & Loewenstein (1985), JFE 14(3), late announcements carry bad news; Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2), post-omission drift; batch finding M0076-M0081; declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Kalay and Loewenstein (1985) report that dividend announcements made later than the usual schedule carry worse news; published 1985, so the whole dev window is after it. Only declaration dates can show a board is late before the ex-date was due. A stock is a regular payer after an event when 8+ events fall in the prior 1095 days; its usual spacing is the median gap between its last 8 events (at least 20 days); under decl timing its last 8 events must all carry a declaration date; it turns late on the 10th NYSE session after last event + spacing with no new event known, and stays late until the next event is known or 182 days pass. The overlay removes late names from the host's universe and holdings. Host: M0076-X-M (= M0070-R25-H6-T, big dividend raises seen on the ex-date, up to 20 F4-screened members at 5%, rest in SPY, SPY-200 switch, monthly), the strongest dividend book, which holds stocks for six months after a raise and so meets their next declarations. Fractional at Gotrade's real fees. Six variants, a 2x3 grid: timing off (HOST, must reproduce M0076-X-M) / decl (events on the declaration day, the ex-date where undated) / ex (paired control: events on the ex-date, the data the store had before the EODHD pull), each on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade (-M) and on weekly rules with the host still choosing monthly and only the warning read weekly (-W, weekly-hold-frac-gotrade, dev only; no weekly SPY switch: M0076/M0078 showed it costs 3-5 points a year). The value of the data is DECL minus EX; the value of the warning is EX minus HOST; weekly minus monthly is the value of acting fast. Assumed: the late-event diagnostic (count of late spells and the 3- and 6-month return after them vs SPY, decl vs ex) is run as a report after the trials, not before. Counted before registering (counts only, no returns): about 170 late spells a year under decl vs about 30 under ex, among some 400 payers, so declaration schedules are far noisier than ex-date schedules. The store drops dividends whose ex-date is after 2015-10-16, so declarations made in the last weeks of the window are missing and decl reads a few false late spells in Sep-Oct 2015 (both arms, decl more). Success: DECL-M beats HOST-M and EX-M on funded CAGR or worst fall by half a point or more, same sign on the weekly pair.
methods.expectedFailure: Lateness is rare among big regular payers and mostly clerical: a board meeting moved, a holiday, a switch of quarter-end, a missing row in the data. The host only holds a name for six months after a raise, by when its board has just shown confidence, so few of its holdings ever go late; the overlay may change under 2% of trades like M0077's cut alarm. The ex-date schedule flags the same boards only a week or two later, so DECL minus EX is likely under half a point. The weekly arms pay Gotrade fees on weekly resizes of 5% slots and the SPY park, which may cost more than any warning saves. The host's own weaknesses carry over: worst fall 21.9%, over the 20% limit, and lagging SPY in 2009-2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

The batch question: **is the dividend announcement data we bought worth anything?** Earlier runs found it useless as an earlier *buy* signal. This run asked whether it works as a *sell* warning.

Most big companies announce their dividend on a steady rhythm, about every three months. An old paper (Kalay and Loewenstein, 1985) found that when a board announces *later than usual*, the news tends to be bad. Only the announcement dates can tell us a board is late before the payment itself was due. So the rule was:

- A **regular payer** has made 8 or more announcements in the last three years (all with a known announcement date).
- Its **usual spacing** is the middle value of the gaps between its last 8 announcements.
- If 10 trading days pass beyond that spacing with no new announcement, the stock is **late**: the book sells it and will not buy it until the board announces again (at most six months).

The warning was laid over the lab's best dividend book: it buys big companies that just raised their dividend by 25% or more, holds up to 20 of them for six months at 5% each, keeps the rest in SPY, and steps into cash when SPY is below its 200-day average. Everything ran at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares, from 1996 to 2015.

Six versions, a 2-by-3 grid:

- **HOST**: no warning. It reproduced its earlier recorded result to the decimal (10.9% a year on your deposits), so the setup is sound.
- **DECL**: lateness measured on the **announcement** schedule (the new data).
- **EX**: the same rule on the **ex-dividend date** schedule (what the store knew before the data was bought). This is the fair comparison.
- Each once checked **monthly** (-M), and once checked **weekly** (-W: the book still picks monthly, only the warning is read every week).

## Results (your money a year, deposits included; SPY earned 7.2% on the same deposits)

| | HOST | DECL | EX | DECL − EX | EX − HOST |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly, a year | 10.91% | 10.45% | 11.06% | **−0.61 pts** | +0.16 |
| Monthly, worst fall | 21.9% | 21.3% | 22.0% | 0.7 better | ~0 |
| Monthly, trades | 540 | 583 | 543 | | |
| Weekly, a year | 10.26% | 9.93% | 10.08% | **−0.15 pts** | −0.18 |
| Weekly, worst fall | 25.7% | 26.0% | 25.5% | | |

- Every version beat SPY by about 3 points a year, but **all of that is the host book's own edge** (the earlier big-raise book). The warning added nothing.
- Every version **failed the 20% worst-fall limit** (21.3% to 26.0%). The monthly announcement version came closest at 21.3%, still over the line.
- The weekly clock cost the host 0.6 points a year and made its worst fall 4 points deeper (25.7%), even with no warning at all. Weekly re-weighting of 20 small slots plus the SPY share pays more fees and, it seems, sells at worse moments.
- Walk-forward: the lab's own way of picking a version won only 2 of 4 test folds (a fold trains on earlier years and scores later years it has not seen), and the picked version trailed SPY by 2.7 points a year in 2009-2015 (the book without deposits), the era most like today.
- **Luck check (DSR):** how likely the result is real rather than luck after all the methods the lab has tried. Judged at N = 57 against the bar of 0.90, the versions read 0.905 to 0.932. That clears the bar, but it measures the host book; the warning itself only moved it down.

## Did the signal exist at all?

Before looking at fees I checked the warning on its own, across every stock in the store from 1997 to 2014:

| | late spells | stock vs SPY, next 3 months | next 6 months |
|---|---|---|---|
| Late on the announcement schedule | 3,280 | +1.25% | +2.62% |
| Late on the ex-date schedule | 647 | +1.76% | +4.37% |
| Every regular payer, any quarter (baseline) | 20,317 | +1.20% | +2.20% |

**A late stock did no worse than any other regular payer.** If anything it did a little better. (All numbers are flattered by the store's missing dead companies, but that hits the late and the baseline rows alike.)

## Why

- **Announcement schedules are noisy.** Under the same rule, about 170 stocks a year were "late" on their announcement schedule against about 30 on their ex-date schedule. Boards move meetings around, tie the dividend to earnings dates that drift, and skip a regular slot for a holiday. The payment calendar itself (the ex-date) stays steady. So most "late announcements" are not news at all.
- **The book sold good stocks for nothing.** DECL-M made 43 extra trades (8% more), selling names that had just raised their dividend, only to see the board announce a few days later as usual. Those were fee-paying exits from stocks that kept drifting up.
- **Real trouble is rare in this book.** A company that raised its dividend 25% in the last six months is very unlikely to skip the next one. The ex-date warning fired on only 3 trades; it barely touched the book (+0.16 pts, inside noise).

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (a late announcement warns of bad news, and acting on it helps) **did not hold**: the late stocks did not underperform at all. The expected failure happened mostly as written: the ex-date warning changed under 1% of trades, and the weekly arms paid more than they saved. One part was wrong: the announcement warning did *not* fire rarely. It fired often, and that is why it hurt.

## Compared with the batch

Same story as the raise-on-announcement test (0.3-1.1 points a year worse) and the cut alarm (under 0.1 point either way): the announcement dates have now been tried as an earlier buy, an earlier cut alarm, an earnings filter, a discipline ranking and a lateness warning. None earned half a point a year.

**My opinion:** stop spending method ids on the announcement dates as a timing signal. Five tries say the market prices a dividend announcement on the day it lands, and the steady part of dividend behaviour lives in the ex-date calendar the store already had. The host book itself is still interesting (3+ points a year over SPY on your deposits), but its two real problems are its worst fall just over 20% and its weak 2009-2015. The next useful try attacks those directly: the same big-raise book with a smaller share in each name and a larger SPY core, aiming the worst fall under 20% while keeping most of the edge. That is already queued as the market-shaped dividend tilt idea, and I would run it next.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0085-HOST-M`: DSR 0.9274 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0085-DECL-M`: DSR 0.9150 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0085-EX-M`: DSR 0.9306 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0085-HOST-W`: DSR 0.9156 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0085-DECL-W`: DSR 0.9033 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0085-EX-W`: DSR 0.9095 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Rejected: stepping out of stocks whose board announced its dividend late cost 0.6 points a year vs the same rule on ex-dates; late announcers did no worse than other payers

methods.name: A free head start for the momentum book: prefer picks whose dividend is still ahead of them
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0079 (announcement-to-ex window); Hartzmark & Solomon (2013), The dividend month premium, JFE 109(3); Kalay & Loewenstein (1985), JFE 14(3); host F4-MOM12-N20-TREND; declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1985 (announcement-to-ex drift) and 2013 (dividend month premium), so both were public for all or most of the dev window. M0079 showed a daily announcement-to-ex book cannot pay Gotrade's fees; its ex-date control fell hardest because it held stocks right after they went ex. So keep an existing monthly book's fee bill and use the calendar only to re-order its ranking. Host: the plain 12-month momentum book (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND: F4's members and liquidity screen, top 20 by 12-1 momentum at 5% each, cash while SPY is at or below its 200-day average, checked monthly, never weekly -- the weekly switch cost 3-5 points a year in M0076/M0078), monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees. Tilt: score = momentum percentile + 0.05 when a dividend goes ex after the next session and within 35 days of it, - 0.05 when one went ex in the last 10 sessions (about 20 places in a 400-name ranking). Variants: HOST (no tilt; reproduces the host exactly, checked against FACTOR's own targets before the run); TILT-ANN (the ahead half from declared dividends, known for certain); TILT-EX (the paired control: the ahead half guessed from past ex-dates, last ex plus the median gap -- all the lab had before); TILT-ANN-D / TILT-EX-D (the same pair counting only dividends that carry a declaration date, so coverage cannot blur it). methods.expectedFailure: A tilt of 20 places swaps perhaps 3-6 of 20 names a month, and a dividend's run-up is a fraction of a percent, so ANN minus EX is likely well under a point a year and |t| < 1: the ex-date guess already gets most quarterly payers' next date right within a week or two, so the arms pick mostly the same names. Momentum winners are often non-payers or low payers, so the tilt bites on fewer names than in a calm-stock book. M0076, M0078, M0079 and M0083 all found the declaration date added nothing or a little negative, and M0079 found announcement timing slightly negative in 2009-2015, so the most likely answer is no. The host's own weaknesses carry over: the plain momentum book fell about 22% at its worst (over the 20% limit) and lagged SPY in 2009-2015 when big-company growth led; a tilt toward payers moves it toward value-ish names, which hurts in 1998-2000 and from 2009. Withholding tax on the dividends the tilt collects is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## The question

The owner asked for a definite yes or no: **do the dividend announcement dates we bought make a method we already have any better?** This is the batch's last slot, so it asks the question as cleanly as the lab can.

**The host** is the plain 12-month momentum book (the lab's F4-MOM12-N20-TREND). Every month it buys the 20 big index companies that rose most over the past year (skipping the last month), 5% each. It goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average, checked once a month. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up.

Before anything else I checked the host was reproduced exactly. My "no tilt" version and the lab's original momentum allocator gave identical results on every one of 4,984 trading days, with the same 1,162 trades. So every difference below comes from the tilt, not from a rebuilt host.

**The tilt** costs no extra trading days. It only reshuffles the monthly ranking:
- a stock gets a **push up** (about 20 places in a ranking of ~400) when a dividend is expected to go ex within the next five weeks, so the book holds it into the payment;
- a stock gets a **push down** when it went ex in the last 10 trading days, so the book avoids the slump right after the payment.

The push down only uses ex-dates that have already happened, so it is the same in both arms. The arms differ only in how they know a dividend is coming:
- **TILT-ANN** knows from the board's announcement. That is certain, but it only works for dividends that carry an announcement date.
- **TILT-EX** (the paired control) *guesses* the next ex-date from past ones: the last ex-date plus the usual gap between payments. That is all the lab had before the announcement data.
- **-D** versions count only dividends that carry an announcement date, in both arms, so the 13% without one cannot blur the pair.

## Results, 1996-2015

SPY on the same deposits earned +7.2% a year.

| variant | your money per year (with deposits) | book alone per year | worst fall: with deposits / book alone (monthly) | gains vs losses | DSR | 2009-2015, book alone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HOST | +13.8% | +15.5% | 23.3% / 18.8% | 2.05 | 0.903 | +14.4% |
| TILT-ANN | +13.1% | +14.6% | 23.6% / 18.7% | 1.91 | 0.869 | +14.4% |
| TILT-EX | +13.8% | +15.3% | 23.2% / 17.1% | 1.98 | 0.902 | +14.8% |
| TILT-ANN-D | +13.4% | +14.9% | 23.6% / 18.7% | 1.95 | 0.882 | +14.8% |
| TILT-EX-D | +13.8% | +15.3% | 23.2% / 17.1% | 1.98 | 0.901 | +14.9% |

"Book alone" takes the monthly deposits out. Deposits refill a falling account, so the with-deposit numbers flatter the book. The lab's daily worst-fall measure (the 23% column) is the one the gate reads.

Every variant failed the same gate: **worst fall 23.2-23.6%, over the 20% limit.** This is the host's own fall. It comes from the 1998 and 2011 crashes, which arrive before a monthly SPY-200 check can react. TILT-ANN and TILT-ANN-D also failed the luck bar: DSR 0.869 and 0.882, under 0.90. DSR is the chance the result is real rather than luck, given the lab has now tried N = 58 distinct methods.

## Announcement minus ex-date: the answer

These are paired differences on the de-funded monthly returns, 237 months.

| | ANN minus EX | dated-only ANN-D minus EX-D |
|---|---|---|
| your money per year (with deposits) | **−0.7 points** (+13.1% vs +13.8%) | **−0.4 points** (+13.4% vs +13.8%) |
| book alone per year | −0.7 points (+14.6% vs +15.3%) | −0.4 points (+14.9% vs +15.3%) |
| mean monthly difference | −0.058% | −0.034% |
| **t-stat** | **−1.53** | **−0.98** |
| months the announcement arm was ahead | 36% | 37% |
| years it was ahead | 9 of 20 | 8 of 20 |
| worst fall, with deposits | 23.6% vs 23.2% (worse) | 23.6% vs 23.2% (worse) |
| worst fall, book alone | 18.7% vs 17.1% (worse) | 18.7% vs 17.1% (worse) |
| DSR | 0.869 vs 0.902 | 0.882 vs 0.901 |
| 2009-2015 | −0.4 points (t = −0.46) | −0.1 points (t = −0.03) |
| walk-forward folds (2003-05, 2006-08, 2009-11, 2012-14) | −1.1, −0.6, +0.3, −1.5: **ahead in 1 of 4** | −1.0, −0.4, +0.3, −0.5: **ahead in 1 of 4** |

**The answer is no.** The pre-registered "definite yes" needed the announcement arm to win by a point a year with t ≥ 2. It lost by 0.4-0.7 points instead. The t-stats point the wrong way, though neither is big enough to count as real evidence of harm. The dated-only pair agrees in sign, so the coverage gap is not hiding a win. 2009-2015 is a tie. The announcement arm was behind on every measure: money, worst fall, DSR, folds.

That makes **five methods in a row** with the same answer: M0076, M0078, M0079, M0083 and now M0086. Seeing a dividend on its announcement day rather than guessing it from the calendar adds nothing to a book this lab can trade. If anything it costs a little.

## Does the tilt itself help the host?

No:
- Against the untilted host, TILT-EX lost 0.2 points a year (t = −0.52) and TILT-ANN lost 0.9 points (t = −1.81).
- In 2009-2015 both tilts were a hair *ahead* of the host (+0.4 points, t ≈ +0.4). In 1996-2008 both were behind. That pattern is noise around zero.
- The ex-date version made the book-alone worst fall smaller (17.1% vs 18.8%). But the gate's daily worst fall barely moved (23.2% vs 23.3%), so it cannot rescue the host from its 20% failure.

## Why

- **The guess is already good.** Most big companies pay every quarter on a steady schedule. "Last ex-date plus the usual gap" lands within days of the real date, so the announcement tells a monthly book almost nothing new. The arms held different stocks in 74% of months, but those differences were small swaps around the edges.
- **What the announcement adds is the wrong half.** The extra names TILT-ANN gets are boards that declare early or pay irregularly. The announcement-day jump has already happened before the next open (M0076 found the same). Hartzmark and Solomon's dividend-month premium is tied to the *predicted* dividend month, the one investors can see coming without news. That is exactly what TILT-EX already uses.
- **A 20-place nudge on a momentum ranking trades momentum for dividend timing.** Every name pushed in replaces a stronger winner. A dividend's run-up is a fraction of a percent. Momentum's spread between the 15th and 35th name is worth more over a month, so the tilt mildly hurts whichever way it is timed.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: the announcement arm did not beat the ex-date arm in either pair.

The expected failure happened almost as written. The difference was under a point a year. The guess already got most payers right. The answer matched M0076/M0078/M0079/M0083. The host still fell more than 20%. One part was wrong: I expected |t| < 1, but the full pair reached t = −1.53. The announcement arm was a little *worse*, not merely equal.

Walk-forward: the lab's own pick (the ex-date arm or the host) beat SPY in 3 of 4 folds. But it lagged SPY by 1.9 points a year in 2009-2015 on the walk-forward's measure, and it is not dev-eligible. No buy signal.

## My opinion:

The dividend announcement data is settled for this lab: **it does not improve any method we have tried it on.** Five paired tests, two kinds of host (dividend-event books and a plain momentum book), weekly, monthly and daily clocks. The best it ever did was tie the ex-date control. The free calendar guess already carries everything a monthly book can use. I would stop spending method ids on "announcement date versus ex-date" questions. The EODHD key is better spent on what the lab cannot guess: delisted companies' prices, to check that the momentum and dividend edges are not survivorship artefacts. The host itself still beats SPY by about six points a year on dev but fails the 20% fall limit, and lags SPY in 2009-2015. Its fall comes from fast crashes before a monthly check can react. The next useful work is on that fall, not on the dividend calendar.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 98, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0086-HOST`: DSR 0.9053 at N = 98, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0086-TILT-EX`: DSR 0.9045 at N = 98, against DSR >= 0.90.
- `M0086-TILT-EX-D`: DSR 0.9036 at N = 98, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: Definite no: timing the dividend tilt from announcement dates earned 0.7 pt a year LESS than guessing from past ex-dates (t = -1.53; dated-only pair -0.4, t = -0.98), tied in 2009-2015, behind in 3 of 4 folds; host fails the 20% fall limit (23%)

methods.hypothesis: Every version of the big-raise book (M0070, M0076, M0083) beat SPY on dev funded but lagged it by 2-5 points a year in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 walk-forward folds: 20 equal 5% slots lean toward the smaller index members while SPY's big-company drift led (insight 91). Keep M0070-R25-H6-T's event, hold and SPY-200 switch on the ex-date (announcement timing is settled: M0076, M0083), but weight live raises by their 63-day median dollar volume (the store has no market cap), capped at 10% each, total raise sleeve capped at 50%, rest SPY; plus a 10-slot equal-weight control. methods.name: Calm big raisers: the big-dividend-raise book keeping only the steadier half of the raisers, to pull its worst fall under 20%
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0070 (R25-H6-T, re-run as M0076-X-M); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); low-volatility anomaly: Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006), JF 61(1); Baker, Bradley & Wurgler (2011), FAJ 67(1)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1995 (dividend-change drift) and 2006 (low volatility), so most of the dev window is after the crowd knew the drift and half of it before the calm-stock idea was widely traded. M0070's big-raise book (latest dividend >= 25% over the median of up to four prior payments in 400 days and at most double, or a first payment, seen on its ex-date; up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, held names first then the newest event, rest in SPY, monthly, behind the SPY-200 switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) beats SPY by about 3.7 points a year on the deposits (+10.9% vs +7.2%) and fails only on its worst fall (21.9%), with a weak 2009-2015. The raisers that swing most are the ones that dragged the 1998-2002 falls; a raiser that is also calm should keep the drift and lose less. On each monthly re-pick, measure every live raiser's daily swing (population stdev of its last 126 close-to-close returns) and keep only those at or below a median, held names included; the freed 5% slots go to SPY. It ranks on dividend raises, filtered by swing, so the family stays dividend-change-drift.
