Halving the live raisers leaves more of the book in SPY, so the result may simply converge on SPY: a smaller fall and a smaller edge, and the fall that is left is SPY's own fall before the 200-day switch turns (the switch, not the picks, sets the floor). Monthly re-checking held names against a moving median adds turnover at Gotrade's fees on 5% slots. The 1998-2002 falls may have come from the SPY part of the book rather than the jumpy raisers. A widely published anomaly from the 1990s: even a real dev edge is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## The question

The **big-raise book** buys up to 20 big index companies whose latest dividend is at least 25% above their usual payment. It holds each for six months at 5% of the money, keeps the rest in SPY, re-picks monthly and steps into cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It beat SPY on the owner's deposits (+10.9% a year vs +7.2%) and failed only one condition: its **worst fall** (biggest drop from a peak) was 21.9%, over the 20% limit.

The idea here: drop the raisers that swing around a lot day to day, and keep only the calmer half. Calm stocks usually fall less. The freed 5% slots go into SPY.

The "swing" is how much a stock's price moved per day over the last 126 trading days (about six months), the standard deviation of its daily returns. Held stocks are re-checked every month too, so a holding that turns jumpy is sold.

## Variants, fixed before any result

- **X-M**: the book unchanged, as a check that the setup reproduces the old result.
- **C-LIVE** (the idea): keep raisers at or below the median swing of that month's raisers.
- **J-LIVE** (control): keep only the *jumpier* half. If it does as well as C-LIVE, the swing does not matter.
- **C-ALL**: keep raisers calmer than the median big-company member, a fixed market-wide bar.
- **C-LIVE-63**: the calm half, measured on a faster three-month swing.

All trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on 20M IDR plus 5M IDR every month.

## Results (dev years 1996-2015, the owner's deposits)

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| X-M (unchanged) | +10.9% | 21.9% | 2.81 | 0.930 | −3.0 pts | fails worst fall |
| **C-LIVE** | +10.1% | **19.5%** | 3.48 | 0.929 | −3.6 pts | passes |
| J-LIVE (jumpy) | +9.2% | 26.9% | 2.25 | 0.814 | −5.9 pts | fails worst fall, luck |
| C-ALL | +10.0% | 18.8% | 4.06 | 0.921 | −3.9 pts | passes |
| **C-LIVE-63** | **+10.6%** | **18.7%** | 3.52 | **0.945** | −2.6 pts | passes |

X-M reproduced the old book exactly (540 trades, 21.9%), so the comparison is fair.

**Gains vs losses** (profit factor) is the total of winning trades over the total of losing trades; the floor is 1.3. **DSR** is the luck check: how likely the result is real and not the best of many tries. The lab counted N = 62 independent tries when this was judged, and the bar is 0.90. C-LIVE-63's 0.945 means roughly a 94% chance that its edge over SPY is not luck, *on these years*.

Three variants pass every condition on the dev years. **But none can be promoted.** The hard gate also checks the method on four later stretches it never trained on ("walk-forward folds"). It beat SPY in only **2 of the 4**, and the gate wants a majority. The weak stretch is the same one as always: **2009-2015**, the years most like today, where every variant lagged SPY by 2.6 to 5.9 points a year.

## Did the filter work? Yes, at what it was built for

- **Calm vs jumpy is a real difference.** The calm half fell at most 19.5%, the jumpy half 26.9%. The calm half also earned more (+10.1% vs +9.2%) and passed the luck check, where the jumpy half did not. The swing does matter.
- **Worst year improved a lot.** 2011 went from −7.7% (unchanged book) to −2.9% (C-LIVE).
- **The faster swing was best.** C-LIVE-63 kept nearly all the return (+10.6% vs +10.9%) and cut the worst fall to 18.7%. A three-month swing sees a stock getting jumpy sooner.

## What did not change: 2009-2015

The expected failure happened as written. The calm raisers are mostly utilities, food, household goods and old industrials. After 2009 the market was led by big growth companies, and a book of steady dividend raisers simply rose more slowly. Filtering for calm made that gap a little *wider* for the median cut (−3.0 to −3.6 points a year) and slightly narrower only with the fast swing (−2.6).

## The check with the missing companies

The lab's price history is missing many companies that later died. Re-run with most of them put back:
- C-LIVE-63's worst fall goes from 18.7% to **20.0%**, right on the limit, and C-LIVE's from 19.5% to **21.8%**, over it.
- The lead over SPY barely moves (C-LIVE-63 +3.4% a year either way), but 2009-2015 gets worse (−2.6 to −3.2 points).
- The fold record stays at 2 of 4.

So the drawdown margin is thin: some of the calm-half safety came from not seeing companies that collapsed.

## Comparison with the family

The parent big-raise book (M0070-R25-H6-T, same fees) earned +10.9% with a 21.9% worst fall. Seeing the raise on its announcement day (M0076) added nothing. Keeping only raises the market cheered (M0083) passed on dev but also won only 2 of 4 folds. This calm filter is the best version of the family on worst fall and on the luck check, and it hits the same wall in the same years.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: held on the dev average.** The calm half kept most of the drift and fell less; the jumpy control was clearly worse.
- **Expected failure: also happened.** The calm half lagged in 2009-2015, and the fall that is left sits right at the limit once dead companies are put back.

This is a widely published idea (dividend drift 1995, low volatility 2006). Even its dev edge, earned mostly before 2009, is likely to fade.

**My opinion:** This filter does what it promises. It turns a book that fell too far into one that passes on average, and the jumpy-half control proves the swing is doing the work. But the family's real problem was never the drawdown, it is 2009-2015, and no filter on *which raisers* to hold has fixed that in four tries. I would stop adding filters to the big-raise book. The one honest test left is to use the calm big raisers as a small tilt beside a large SPY core (for example 70% SPY, 30% calm raisers). That lowers the bet against big growth companies directly, instead of hoping a better choice of dividend stocks will out-run them. If that still loses 2009-2015, close the family.


### 2026-10-11

Sera 20261011-1815, promotion step 0b: `lab promote M0088` refused (exit 2) on the walk-forward condition. The book beat SPY in 2 of 4 folds, stable, with a 2009-2015 edge of -2.6 points a year. Its kin is clean (no test-failed method in its family or ancestry), so the folds alone stopped it. No look was spent. Buy signal: no. It fails the fold majority, and it trails SPY in the highest-coverage era 2009-2015. On the survivorship-check history the worst fall goes from 18.7% to 20.0%.
methods.verdict: Close miss: keeping only the calmer half of the big dividend raisers cut the worst fall from 22% to 19% and passed every check on average (+10.6% a year vs SPY's +7.2%), but it still lost to SPY in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 later test stretches

methods.name: Two half-books a fortnight apart: the 12-month momentum book split into two tranches that re-pick on alternate halves of the month
methods.hypothesis: M0086 reproduced the plain 12-month momentum book exactly at real fees: it beats SPY by about six points a year on dev but falls 23% at its worst, over the 20% limit, because the 1998 and 2011 crashes land between monthly checks of the SPY-200 switch, and a weekly switch costs 3-5 points a year (M0076/M0078). Splitting the money into two half-books that each re-pick monthly but two weeks apart (tranching, Hoffstein's rebalance-timing luck, 2019-2020) halves the chance that the whole book misses a switch, at no extra trades per name. Variants: one book (the host), two tranches, four weekly tranches; all fractional at Gotrade fees, 20 names per tranche. Expected failure: tranching cuts timing luck but not the size of a fast crash; worst fall may only move from 23% to 21%, and the book still lags SPY in 2009-2015.

methods.name: Dividend signal as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: big uncut payers weighted by how much they trade, not equally
methods.hypothesis: M0082 showed any ranking inside steady big dividend payers gives the same result: the equal-weighted payer pool is a value-versus-growth bet that lost 1998-2000 and 2009-2015. Isolate the dividend signal from that bet: hold the 60 most-traded members (dollar volume as the size proxy), weighted by dollar volume like SPY, and only tilt: members with 8+ uncut dividends in 3 years get 1.5x weight, non-payers 0.75x, renormalised; monthly, fractional, Gotrade fees, SPY-200 switch on a monthly clock. Control twin: same book with no tilt. Success: the tilt beats its no-tilt twin in 2009-2015 and does not lag SPY there by more than 1 point a year. Expected failure: the no-tilt twin itself lags SPY (top-60 by dollar volume is not cap weight), and the tilt adds or removes a few tenths either way.

methods.name: Skip the lottery tickets: hold the big index members whose biggest one-day jump last month was smallest
methods.sourceRef: Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw (2011), Maxing out: stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns, JFE 99(2), 427-446, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2010.08.014
methods.hypothesis: Investors overpay for stocks that recently had a lottery-like single-day spike, so the stocks whose largest daily return over the past month (MAX) is highest go on to underperform and the lowest-MAX stocks outperform (BCW 2011, published 2011 with a 2009 working paper: a decile spread above 1% a month on 1962-2005, robust to size, momentum, reversal and skewness). Book: each month, among F4-screened point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members ($5 price, 20M-dollar daily volume), rank on the average of the 5 largest daily returns over the last 21 sessions (MAX5, the less noisy variant) and hold the 20 lowest at 5% each, behind the SPY 200-day switch, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Variants: LO5-N20-T (the book), LO1-N20-T (BCW's single-day MAX), LO5-N40-T (40 names), LO5-N20 (no switch, always invested), and HI5-N20-T, the paired control holding the 20 highest-MAX names, which must trail: the effect has to show as a spread, not only as low beta. It ranks on a lottery measure, not on past trend, so it should not move with the failed momentum books. Success: a LO variant beats SPY TR on dev within the 20% drawdown limit, the control trails it clearly, and the edge holds in 2009-2015 and in a majority of walk-forward folds.
methods.expectedFailure: In large caps MAX is mostly low volatility in disguise: the lowest-MAX names are the calm utilities, staples and drug makers, so the book is a low-beta book. Behind a trend switch it should have a shallow worst fall, but low-vol large caps lagged the 2009-2015 growth run and the late-1990s tech run, so the likeliest failure is trailing SPY TR on CAGR: a smoother ride that earns less. A published anomaly fades, and BCW was circulating from 2009, so whatever edge shows is likely front-loaded before 2009. The control may not trail by much in 1996-2000, when lottery stocks were the winners.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What we tried

A well-known finding from 2011 (Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw, "Maxing out") is that people overpay for "lottery ticket" stocks: shares that just had one huge up day. The paper found that those stocks do worse over the next month and the calmest ones do better. We tested this on big US companies. Each month we ranked the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 members by their biggest daily jumps over the past month. We held the 20 with the smallest jumps, in equal amounts. We moved to cash when SPY was below its 200-day average. Trades were in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees. One version did the opposite and held the 20 *biggest* jumpers. That was the check: if the idea is right, it should do worse.

## Result: a tie with SPY at best, and the "lottery" side won

On the owner's monthly deposits from 1996 to 2015:

| Version | Your money per year | Same deposits in SPY | Worst fall (without deposits) | Gains vs losses | Luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 calmest, average of 5 biggest days (the main book) | +7.1% | +7.2% | 30% | 1.56 | 0.897 |
| 20 calmest, single biggest day | +6.0% | +7.2% | 35% | 1.43 | 0.748 |
| 40 calmest, average of 5 biggest days | +7.0% | +7.2% | 32% | 1.60 | 0.850 |
| 20 calmest, never steps aside | +6.4% | +7.2% | 45% | 1.32 | 0.571 |
| **20 biggest jumpers (the check)** | **+8.1%** | +7.2% | 34% | 1.28 | 0.481 |

- **Beat SPY:** failed. The main book came within 0.1 point a year of SPY but still lost. Every calm version lost.
- **Worst fall under 20%:** failed everywhere. The main book fell 30% at its worst, counted without the deposits. On the funded account the deepest monthly drop was only 11%, in the summer of 1998. That is the deposits refilling a falling account, so the funded number makes the fall look gentler than it was.
- **Gains vs losses (profit factor) of at least 1.3:** passed by every calm version. The check failed it at 1.28.
- **DSR at least 0.90:** the main book reached 0.897, just under. DSR asks how likely the result is real rather than luck, after allowing for the 61 independent ideas the lab has tried (N = 61). It is the only version close to the bar.
- **Worst year:** 1999, down 6% while tech stocks soared.
- **Walk-forward (training on the past, then scoring on unseen years):** the lab's own way of picking a version beat SPY in only 1 of 4 test slices. In 2009-2015, the years with the best data, it trailed SPY by 4.1% a year.

## Why it failed

1. **The effect pointed the wrong way here.** The paper says the calm stocks should beat the jumpers. In our check the jumpers earned about 1 point a year *more*. They also had a weaker gains-vs-losses ratio and a worse luck score, which is what a riskier book looks like. Among big companies, a stock with big up days is mostly just a jumpy stock, and jumpy stocks earned more over these 20 years. The "overpaying for lottery tickets" effect is strongest in small, little-traded stocks. Those are outside our list of big index members.
2. **"Small biggest jump" turned out to mean "low volatility."** The calm book filled up with utilities, food and drug makers. It fell behind in the 1999 tech rally and again in 2009-2015. That is exactly the failure we wrote down before the run.
3. **The cash switch could not save the worst fall.** Calm stocks still fell hard in quick crashes like August 1998, before SPY dropped below its 200-day average. The version that never stepped aside fell 45% in 2008.
4. **Missing data probably helped the jumpers.** The store has no prices for companies that later died, and lottery-type stocks are the most likely to have died. So the jumpers' edge may be partly made up by the data, while the calm side's loss is real.

## Hypothesis vs what happened

The hypothesis failed. Calm stocks did not beat jumpy stocks among big US companies. The expected failure (a low-volatility book that trails SPY on a rising market) happened almost word for word. The worst fall was also larger than we expected.

## Compared with near misses

The closest methods in the lab are momentum blends. They beat SPY by several points a year on dev and then failed on the later years. This book does not even beat SPY on dev. It does have one useful property: it ranks on how calm a stock was last month, not on its trend, so it probably moves differently from the failed momentum books. That is worth something only as an ingredient in a mix, not on its own.

My opinion: drop "skip the lottery tickets" as a stand-alone book. Among big companies it is just a low-volatility tilt, and low volatility has not beaten SPY on this list. Two things are worth trying next. The first is to use it as a filter inside a book that already has a return edge: drop the 20% biggest jumpers from a momentum or dividend-raise book. The second is a cleaner version of the paper's claim. The paper says to avoid jumpers whose spikes came from news-less swings, so rank on the biggest jump measured against the stock's own normal swing, which separates a real lottery spike from ordinary jumpiness. I would try the filter first, because the check showed the jumpers were not losers here, and a filter that removes winners would show up quickly.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the calm stocks tied SPY at best and fell 30% at their worst, and the 'lottery' stocks they skipped actually did better

methods.name: News-day picks sized toward the giants: the filtered earnings-day book weighted by trading value instead of equal slots
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam 2008, SSRN 909563, with M0072's own-swing filter); trading value as the size stand-in because the store has no shares outstanding before 2009
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008 (the earnings-day drift), so the dev window can only show the edge from before and just after it was widely known; 2009-2015 is judged first. M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (news days kept only when the jump is at least 4 points and at least 2 of the stock's own daily swings, ranked by the raw jump) earned +12.3% a year vs SPY's +7.2% on the owner's deposits, cleared the luck bar (0.914 at N=59) and beat SPY by almost 4 points a year in 2009-2015, but fell 22.4% (no deposits) in 1998. Month by month, about 10 of those points were the picks lagging SPY from April to August 1998 while fully invested: a narrow, giant-led market in which 20 equal 5% slots of mostly mid-sized members sank. Keep Z2-RAWRANK's event, filter, ranking, held-first rule, 60-session hold, SPY park, monthly SPY-200 switch and real-fee fractional preset (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) exactly; change only the slot sizes. Size is read as trading value, the median close x volume over the 60 sessions ending on the data date (a point-in-time stand-in for company size; the store has no shares outstanding before 2009; a median so the news day's own volume spike does not rank the name). The picks share the same money the 20-slot book gives them (n picks get n x 5%), each capped at 10%, the rest SPY. Variants: DV-CAP10 (in proportion to trading value), SQRT-CAP10 (to its square root, a half-way lean), TOP100-EW (screened members narrowed first to the 100 most-traded, then Z2-RAWRANK's picks at equal 5%: is the edge alive inside the giants alone?). The equal-weight control is the parent's own recorded trial M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (same preset, fees and deposits), not re-run. I expect SQRT-CAP10 to be best. Success: worst fall under 20% with the excess over SPY and a luck score >= 0.90 kept, and positive against SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The news-day drift is strongest in smaller, less-followed names (the 2008 paper and the earnings-drift literature before it), so leaning toward giants may give back much of the edge and the luck score may drop under 0.90; TOP100-EW may hold few picks and drift toward plain SPY. The August 1998 crash hit everything and the monthly SPY-200 switch sold late and bought back late, so the switch may still owe about half the fall and no variant reach 20%. A 10% cap on two or three giants makes the book less diversified, so one bad earnings reaction in a big slot costs more than it did in a 5% slot. Trading value is a rough proxy: busy mid-caps after news and heavily traded tech names in 1999-2000 read as 'big', which may tilt the book into the bubble. Back-adjusted closes understate older trading value for high-yield payers a little. And this is a published anomaly, so a strong dev result may have faded in 2016-2026.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What was tried

The parent, the filtered news-day book (M0072-Z2-RAWRANK), buys big index members right after a day that looks like an earnings report: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal volume, a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's, and that gain at least twice the stock's normal daily swing. It holds up to 20 such names at 5% each for about three months, keeps the rest in SPY, and goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average (checked monthly). It beat SPY clearly and passed the luck bar. Its one failure was the worst fall: 22.4% with the deposits taken out, March to September 1998 (limit 20%).

The idea here: in spring and summer 1998 a few giant companies carried the market while most mid-sized stocks fell. If the book had leaned toward the big names, the way SPY itself does, it might have lagged less. So the picks were kept exactly the same and only the money per pick changed.

The store has no share counts before 2009, so "big" was measured by **trading value**: the typical (median) dollar amount traded per day over the last 60 sessions. A median, so the news day's own burst of trading does not make a stock look bigger.

Three fixed variants, written down before any result, all at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares on the owner's 5M IDR monthly deposits:

- **DV-CAP10**: the picks share the same money the 20-slot book gives them, split by trading value, no pick above 10%.
- **SQRT-CAP10**: the same, split by the square root of trading value, a half-way lean.
- **TOP100-EW**: only the 100 most-traded screened members may be picked, at equal 5% slots.

The equal-slot control is the parent's own recorded trial, at the same fees and deposits.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall (funded) | worst fall (no deposits) | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent, equal 5% slots | +12.3% | +7.2% | 23.8% | 22.4% | 1.98 | 0.914 |
| DV-CAP10 | +12.1% | +7.2% | 25.6% | 24.5% | 2.03 | 0.886 |
| **SQRT-CAP10** | **+12.4%** | +7.2% | 24.6% | 23.5% | 2.05 | **0.911** |
| TOP100-EW | +8.2% | +7.2% | 24.5% | 21.6% | 1.94 | 0.777 |

**Rejected.** All three beat total-return SPY on the same deposits, and all have gains about twice their losses (bar 1.3). All three fail the worst-fall limit of 20%. Leaning toward the big names made the fall **worse**, not better: 23.5-24.5% without deposits against the parent's 22.4%. The fall is the same one every time, March to August 1998.

The luck score: N was 64 when this ran (one look per distinct method in the lab), and the bar is 0.90. SQRT-CAP10 clears it at 0.911: after 64 ideas, about a 91% chance its edge is more than luck. DV-CAP10 (0.886) and TOP100-EW (0.777) do not.

## By era (no deposits, the book's own yearly return)

| era | parent | DV-CAP10 | SQRT-CAP10 | TOP100-EW | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +12.2% | +13.6% | +13.9% | +11.6% | +6.7% |
| 2003-2008 | +6.9% | +6.2% | +6.6% | +7.0% | +2.3% |
| **2009-2015** | +18.5% | +17.7% | +18.0% | **+9.4%** | +14.9% |

In the modern, best-covered years (2009-2015) the size-weighted books still beat SPY by about 3 points a year, a little less than the parent. The book restricted to the 100 most-traded names **lost to SPY by 5.5 points a year** there: in 2009 it made +20% when SPY made about +26% and the parent made +55%. The walk-forward check (pick a variant knowing only the past, score it on years it never saw) beat SPY in 3 of 4 folds with a +1.7% edge in 2009-2015.

Year by year, the weighted books gained most in 1999 (+22-25% against the parent's +14%) and lost most in 2007 (-4% to -7% against +1%). That is the bubble tilt the expected failure warned about: the most heavily traded names in 1999 were the hot tech stocks.

## Why

- **The 1998 lag was not about small slots.** The weighted books lost more from April to August 1998 (-23.5% to -24.5%) than the equal-slot book (-22.3%). The busiest news-day names that spring were not the steady giants that carried SPY. They were the heavily traded, fast-moving names, and they fell hard when the market cracked. Trading value picks out "busy", not "big and safe".
- **The edge lives in the less-crowded names.** Taking away everything outside the 100 most-traded members kept the fall smallest (21.6%) but took most of the edge with it, and in 2009-2015 the book lost to SPY. This matches the published finding that the drift after earnings news is strongest where fewer people are watching. It also confirms the lab's broader lesson: this book's edge is partly a bet against SPY's big-company shape.
- **The fall is still the safety switch.** Every variant, whatever its sizes, has the same peak (March 1998) and the same trough (August 1998). The monthly SPY-200 check sold late into the August crash. Sizing cannot reach that.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: leaning toward the giants did not shrink the 1998 fall, it deepened it. The expected failure happened on three counts: the edge thinned toward the giants (TOP100-EW lost the luck bar and 2009-2015), the switch still owned the fall, and trading value tilted the book into the 1999 bubble. The one surprise was that the square-root lean kept the parent's return and luck score almost exactly, so sizing is close to neutral for return and harmful for the fall.

## Comparison with near misses

The parent and its relatives were all measured at the same real fees, so they compare directly. The weekly volatility brake (M0066) got to 21.6% but lost the luck bar; the own-swing filter (M0072) got to 22.4% and kept it; this sizing change went back up to 23.5-24.5%. Three attacks on the picks and sizes have now failed to get under 20%. The one untried lever is the switch itself.

My opinion: stop changing the picks and their sizes in this family. This run settles that the 1998 fall is not a picking problem: different sizes, a different universe, a different filter, and the fall moves by a point or two around the same March-to-August window. The next try should keep the parent's picks and equal slots exactly and attack only the switch: a fast weekly exit when SPY closes below its 50-day average or the fear index jumps above its three-month version, with re-entry only on the monthly date. That is the queued idea "fast crash exit with slow, monthly re-entry" (M0075), and it should run on the filtered picks rather than the original ones. I would not spend more ids on giant-tilting this book; the edge is in the names SPY under-weights, and that has to be accepted or the family dropped.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0092-SQRT-CAP10`: DSR 0.9043 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1530)

## The buy signal fired, and the look is held

`lab walkforward` reads M0092 as clearing all four buy-signal conditions: dev-eligible at the bars in force (DSR 0.911 at N = 106, against 0.90), kin clean, 3 of 4 walk-forward folds won, and a positive 2009-2015 edge (+1.7 pts a year). It is the first method in the lab to fire the signal. `lab promote` would take it.

Promotion step 0 passes: the variant runs in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade).

Step 0b, the durability reports:

| check | dev store | survivorship-check store |
|---|---|---|
| your money a year (SPY +7.2%) | +12.4% | +11.3% |
| worst fall (funded) | 24.6% | 27.5% |
| gains vs losses | 2.05 | 1.94 |
| luck score at recorded N=64 | 0.911 | 0.814 |
| 2009-2015 lead over SPY | +1.7 | +1.0 |
| walk-forward folds | 3 of 4 | 2 of 4, pick changed |

Regime: +0.1 pts a month over SPY in narrow markets, +8.9 in broad ones. The whole edge lives in broad markets, and the test window (2015-2026) is the narrowest market in the record.

## Decision: no look this batch

The check store is the free half of what the buy signal says to buy, and it already answers part of the question: with most of the vanished companies put back, the book loses its fold majority, its luck score falls well under the bar, and its worst fall crosses the 25% real-money limit. Had that store been the dev store, the hard gate would have refused it. The check store is a cross-check and not a gate (EODHD_SURVIVORSHIP_MARKET_PLAN D1), so this is a judgment, not a rule: a look is spent once and a failed one closes the whole news-day family through the kin rule, which would also close the two queued repairs aimed at this book's 1998 fall (M0075, M0098). The family gets its repairs first; the look waits for a variant that holds its folds on both stores. Status stays dev-eligible.
methods.verdict: Rejected: weighting the news-day picks toward the most-traded giants made the 1998 fall worse (23.5-24.5% vs 22.4%, limit 20%) and the giants-only book lost to SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: A true lottery spike, not just a jumpy stock: rank big members on their biggest recent day measured against their own normal swing
methods.sourceRef: Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw (2011), Maxing out: stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns, JFE 99(2), 427-446, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2010.08.014; variation of M0091
methods.hypothesis: M0091 showed that raw MAX among big index members is a volatility measure: the lowest-MAX book was a low-volatility book that tied SPY and fell 30%, and the highest-MAX control beat it. BCW (2011, working paper 2009) argue the overpricing comes from the spike itself, not from volatility. Scale MAX5 over the last 21 sessions by the stdev of the 60 daily returns before that window, so the rank asks how extreme the biggest days were for this stock, not how jumpy the stock is. Book: the 20 lowest scaled-MAX F4-screened point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members ($5 price, 20M-dollar volume) at 5% each, behind the SPY 200-day switch, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Variants: LO5-S60-N20-T (the book), LO1-S60-N20-T (single biggest day, scaled), LO5-S60-N40-T (40 names), LO5-S120-N20-T (a 120-day yardstick), and HI5-S60-N20-T, the paired control holding the 20 highest scaled spikes, which must trail. Success: a LO variant beats SPY TR on dev within the 20% drawdown limit, the control trails it clearly, the edge is positive in 2009-2015 and holds in a majority of walk-forward folds.
methods.expectedFailure: Once volatility is taken out, MAX among liquid large caps carries little information: the low book becomes a near-random, index-like equal-weight book of members whose last month was unremarkable for them, and it trails SPY's big-company drift (equal weighting tilts small inside the S&P). The high side is partly the names that just had an earnings jump or news shock, and the lab has seen post-earnings drift pay in this universe, so the control may beat the book again -- the spike as good news, not as a lottery ticket. A published anomaly fades, and BCW circulated from 2009, so whatever edge shows is likely front-loaded before 2009. The trend switch cannot catch fast crashes like August 1998, so the worst fall is likely above 20% as in the parent.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What we tried

The parent method skipped "lottery ticket" stocks: shares with huge up days in the last month. Among big companies, that turned out to mean "skip the jumpy stocks". The book filled with calm utilities and food makers and only tied SPY. This time each stock's biggest days are measured **against its own normal swing**. A 4% day is huge for a soup company and ordinary for a chip maker. Each month we averaged a stock's five biggest daily gains over the last 21 trading days. We divided that by how much the stock usually moved a day over the 60 trading days before that. Then we held the 20 S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 members with the *least* unusual recent spikes, in equal amounts. Like the parent, the book moved to cash when SPY was below its 200-day average. It traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees. The check version held the 20 with the *most* unusual spikes, which should do worse if the idea is right.

## Result: a clear win on the twenty-year average, and the check lost badly

On the owner's monthly deposits from 1996 to 2015 (SPY with the same deposits earned +7.2% a year):

| Version | Your money per year | Worst fall (without deposits) | Gains vs losses | Luck check (DSR) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 least unusual, 5 biggest days, 60-day yardstick (the main book) | **+10.7%** | 24.1% | 1.51 | **0.921** | passes the dev screen |
| same, single biggest day | +8.9% | 24.7% | 1.43 | 0.809 | luck check failed |
| same, 40 names | +8.7% | 22.9% | 1.44 | 0.852 | luck check failed |
| same, 120-day yardstick | +9.5% | 26.4% | 1.44 | 0.846 | luck check failed |
| **20 most unusual spikes (the check)** | **+4.8%** | 21.6% | 1.23 | 0.327 | lost to SPY |

- **Beat SPY:** yes, all four "calm" versions did. The main book beat it by 3.5 points a year.
- **Worst fall:** 24.1% for the main book, measured without deposits. That is inside the lab's 25% screen and the 25% real-money limit. It came in the 2011 sell-off, the book's worst year (−10.2%).
- **Gains vs losses (profit factor):** 1.51, above the 1.3 minimum.
- **DSR at least 0.90:** 0.921 for the main book. DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than luck, after allowing for the 109 independent ideas the lab had tried when this ran (N = 109). It cleared the 0.90 bar, but only just. The other versions did not.
- **The check trailed clearly.** The most-unusual-spike book earned 6 points a year less than the main book and 2.4 points less than SPY. The parent showed no such gap: there the "lottery" side *won*. Scaling by each stock's own swing turned a volatility ranking into a real spread.

## Where it falls apart: the walk-forward and the recent years

- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4.** Each slice trains on the past and scores on years it has not seen. The book won 2006-2008 (+21% while SPY lost 25%, mostly the cash switch) and 2012-2014 (+82% vs +66%). It lost 2003-2005 (+39% vs +52%) and 2009-2011 (+44% vs +61%). A majority is needed. Two of four is a coin flip, so the lab's hard gate will refuse to promote it.
- **2009-2015, the best-covered years, trailed SPY by 2.5% a year.** This is the lab's first filter, and it failed it.
- **Narrow and broad markets.** The book earned +7.4% a year more than SPY in months when most stocks rose together. It lost 2.3% a year in months when a few giants carried the index. Its whole edge comes from the broad months, the shape that has been scarce since 2018.
- **With dead companies added back** (the check store): the main book still beat SPY, +9.5% vs +7.2% a year, with the same 24% worst fall. But its 2009-2015 gap widened from −2.5% to −5.7% a year, and its gains-vs-losses fell from 1.51 to 1.41. The 120-day version's lead shrank to almost nothing. Part of the twenty-year edge came from the companies the main store is missing.

## Why it worked where it did

A stock's biggest days were small next to its usual swing for one of two reasons. Either it had no news, or it used to be jumpy and has calmed down. So unlike the parent, this book is not a low-volatility book. It holds ordinary and even formerly lively stocks, as long as nothing dramatic just happened. The check book holds stocks that just had a shock far outside their normal range. Shocks are often good news (earnings beats, takeover talk). Those stocks gave the gain back on average, which is the overpricing the 2011 paper describes. The spread is real on dev. But the book is still an equal-weight basket of index members, which quietly favours the smaller ones. So it wins when the whole market rises together and loses when the giants lead. That pattern explains why 2009-2011 and the narrow months hurt.

## Hypothesis vs what happened

The hypothesis largely held on the twenty-year average. Removing volatility turned a dud into a spread: the calm book beat SPY within the drawdown limit, and the check trailed clearly. It failed its own stricter conditions: a positive 2009-2015 edge and a majority of walk-forward slices. The expected failure was "an index-like book that trails SPY's big-company drift". That did not happen on the average, but it did happen in exactly the years and market shape we feared. The worst fall stayed under 25%, better than the 30% we expected from the parent.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

The parent's best calm book earned +7.1% a year, fell 30% and had a DSR of 0.897. Its check *beat* it. This book earns +10.7%, falls 24.1%, has a DSR of 0.921, and its check loses by 6 points. Both ran at Gotrade's real fees, so the comparison is fair. Against the lab's near misses, a MAR of 0.45 (yearly growth divided by worst fall) is mid-table. It shares their weakness: years before 2009 carry the twenty-year win.

## My opinion:

This is the best result the lottery family has produced, and the spread is real. The check lost by 6 points a year, and that is the evidence the parent lacked. But it is not a candidate for money. It loses the walk-forward slices, trails SPY in 2009-2015 (more so once dead companies are counted), and makes all its money when the broad market rises together. That is the exact pattern behind every test-window failure so far. The gate will refuse it, and it should. The direction is still worth one more trial, aimed at the equal-weight problem rather than the signal. Use the spread on the big-company side only: rank only the 150 most-traded members by scaled spike (the store has no company sizes, so daily trading value stands in for size), so the book is not betting against SPY's big-company drift. If that version still beats SPY in 2009-2015, the idea has something. If it does not, the spike signal is just an equal-weight small-company tilt in disguise and the family should be closed.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1530)

Not promoted: dev-eligible, but `lab promote` would refuse on the folds (2 of 4; kin clean). The picks trail SPY in 2009-2015 (-2.5 pts, -5.7 on the survivorship-check store), so no buy signal.
methods.verdict: Beat SPY over twenty years (+10.7% a year vs +7.2%) and the spiky stocks it skipped lost badly, but it trailed SPY in 2009-2015 and lost half its test slices

methods.name: Leave on the 200-day average, come back when fear calms: the dividend-raise book re-entering as soon as the fear index's curve is normal again
methods.hypothesis: M0039 showed that stepping out on an inverted fear curve misses the fast rebounds after fear peaks (gated SPY lost 6.5 points a year in 2009-2015), and that the 200-day switch's main cost is coming back late. Keep the big-dividend-raise book's monthly SPY-200 exit, but on any weekly check while the book is out, re-enter (SPY first, the raisers at the next re-pick) once VIX is back below VIX3M for 5 sessions, instead of waiting for SPY to climb back over its 200-day average. Needs an engine path that lets a weekly check re-enter a cut basket (today a resize session can only cut; re-entry waits for the monthly re-pick) -- or encode the re-entry inside a monthly-ranked SPY-only host first. Controls: the host on its monthly frame (M0076-X-M) and the same host with the plain SPY-200 re-entry. Testable only mid-2006 to 2015 (VIX3M start). Published: VIX term-structure as a contrarian signal, Simon & Campasano 2014; expect fading. Expected failure: the curve normalises in bear-market rallies (spring 2008, mid-2002 has no VIX3M) and walks the book back into the second leg of a fall.

methods.name: Calm big raisers as a small tilt beside a large SPY core: 70% SPY, 30% in the calm half of the big dividend raisers

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## The question

The **calm big-raise book** (from M0088) buys big index companies that just raised their dividend by at least 25%, keeps only the calmer half of them, and parks the rest of the money in SPY. A safety switch moves everything to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It passed every check on the dev years but beat SPY in only 2 of 4 later test stretches, because it lagged SPY by about 2.7 points a year in 2009-2015.

The idea here was to hold a big fixed slice of SPY (the "core") and run the calm raisers only in what is left. The core owns the giant companies that led 2009-2015, so it should shrink that lag.

## Variants, fixed before any result

- **T70** (the idea): 70% SPY core, 30% calm raisers (slots of 1.5% instead of 5%). The 200-day switch moves the whole account to cash.
- **T50**: the same with a 50% core.
- **T85**: the same with an 85% core.
- **S70**: 70% SPY core held all the time; the switch only empties the raisers' part. This shows what the switch is buying.

All trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on 20M IDR plus 5M IDR a month.

## Results (dev years 1996-2015, the owner's deposits)

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**. The parent (all raisers, no core) made +10.6%.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T70 | +9.2% | 18.8% | 8.10 | 0.892 | −5.1 pts | fails luck check |
| **T50** | **+9.6%** | 18.8% | 5.49 | **0.912** (0.907 at N=66) | −4.4 pts | passes on average |
| T85 | +8.9% | 18.9% | 14.69 | 0.873 | −5.6 pts | fails luck check |
| S70 | +8.3% | **42.9%** | 2.73 | 0.636 | −0.8 pts | fails worst fall, luck |
| parent (M0088-C-LIVE-63) | +10.6% | 18.7% | 3.52 | 0.945 | −2.7 pts | passed on average |

The "2009-2015 vs SPY" column is the book's yearly growth minus SPY's in those years, with the deposits taken out.

**Gains vs losses** (profit factor) is winning trades over losing trades; the floor is 1.3. The very high numbers here are a side effect of the big SPY holding: it is rarely sold at a loss. **DSR** is the luck check: how likely the edge is real after all the tries the lab has made. The lab counts N = 66 independent tries now (65 when this ran), and the bar is 0.90. T50's 0.907 just clears it. T70 and T85 do not.

T50 passed every condition on the dev average, so the lab marked the method **dev-eligible**. **It cannot be promoted.** The hard gate checks the method on four later stretches it was never tuned on, and it beat SPY in only **2 of 4**. The gate needs a majority. The 2009-2015 lag got **worse**, not better: −4.4 to −5.6 points a year against the parent's −2.7.

The worst fall (about 19%) came in the summer-1998 shock, before the 200-day switch had turned. S70, which keeps the core in SPY through every fall, lost 34% from October 2007 to February 2009 on its monthly balance and 43% at the worst day. That is well over the 20% limit, as expected.

## Why: the switch, not the raisers, is the 2009-2015 problem

Split by era (deposits removed, edge over SPY in points a year):

| era | T85 (mostly timed SPY) | T50 | parent (all raisers) | S70 (core always held) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2001 | −0.3 | +0.2 | +0.9 | +0.2 |
| 2002-2008 | +8.5 | +8.7 | +9.0 | +2.8 |
| 2009-2015 | −5.6 | −4.4 | −2.7 | −0.8 |

Read across the rows. The more of the book that sits in **SPY behind the 200-day switch**, the worse 2009-2015 gets. T85 is almost pure "SPY with a 200-day switch", and it lagged SPY by 5.6 points a year there. The switch sold in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and bought back higher each time. Each **raiser** added in place of switched SPY *narrowed* that gap. The parent, with the most raisers, had the smallest gap among the switched books. So in 2009-2015 the calm raisers beat SPY-behind-the-switch. The thing losing to SPY was the switch.

The other half of the story is 2002-2008. The switched books earned +8.5 to +9 points a year over SPY there, nearly all of it from sitting in cash through 2008. S70, without the switch on its core, kept only +2.8. So the switch is both where this family's edge comes from (it dodged 2008) and why it fails in the recent years (it whipsawed in 2010-2015). A twenty-year average hides that trade.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The core was meant to cut the 2009-2015 lag, and it widened it. The expected failure happened, though for a different reason than I wrote. I expected the core to "dilute the edge toward SPY" and leave the folds where they were. The folds did stay at 2 of 4, and T70 and T85 fell under the luck bar as predicted. But the core did not converge on SPY. It converged on *SPY behind a 200-day switch*, which is a worse thing to hold in 2009-2015 than the raisers. S70 broke the 20% limit in 2008, as predicted (43% against my guess of about 38%).

The anomaly behind the raisers (1995) and the calm-stock filter (2006) are both widely published, so a real dev edge would still be likely to fade after 2015.

## My opinion:

Stop adding SPY to this book. That direction is closed: more switched SPY makes the recent years worse, and SPY with no switch breaks the worst-fall limit. The useful finding is that the calm raisers did *not* lose to the switched market in 2009-2015. The switch did. The next trial should keep the parent's 100% raisers book and change only how the switch reads the market. Use a switch that whipsaws less: leave only when SPY is clearly below its 200-day average (say 3% under) and return only when it is clearly back above. If the 2009-2015 gap shrinks while 2008 is still dodged, the folds may finally move. If a banded switch also lags, the family's edge is the 2008 exit and nothing else, and it should be retired.


### 2026-10-11

### 2026-10-11 (Sera sera-20261011-1838, promotion check)

Promotion considered and refused by the hard gate. M0096-T50 is dev-eligible (DSR 0.907 at N=66, worst fall 18.8%, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, so the fit check needs no twin), but the walk-forward record is 2 of 4 folds, for the picks and for T50 alone, and its 2009-2015 edge is negative (about -4.4 points a year, worse than M0088's -2.7). Kin is clean; the refusal is on the folds condition only. No buy signal: it fails both the folds and the positive-2009-2015 conditions. No look spent; the batch moved on.
methods.verdict: Rejected direction: putting half or more of the calm dividend-raiser book into SPY passed on average (+9.6% a year vs SPY's +7.2%) but lagged SPY even more in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 later stretches; the safety switch, not the raisers, causes the recent lag

methods.name: Own the typical stock only when it is keeping up: equal-weight index members when they lead SPY, SPY when the giants lead
methods.sourceRef: Hussman, Jan 2025 (cap- vs equal-weight persistence); Blitz (2025), Implications of Increased Index Concentration for Active Investors; RSP/SPY relative-strength rotation lore
methods.hypothesis: Sera's 20261011-1815 synthesis: every equal-slot book in the lab loses ground whenever a few giant companies lead the market and wins when the typical member keeps up, so time the bet itself instead of the picks. Equal- vs cap-weight relative strength is old lore (RSP listed 2003); the concentration papers are 2024-2025, after the dev window, so dev sees the idea before any crowd traded it, but also before the 2016-2024 giant-led era it is meant for. Book: each month read the lead -- the equal-weight trailing total return of the 100 most-traded point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members (60-day median dollar volume) minus SPY's over the same bars. Lead above zero: hold the basket, equal weights; else 100% SPY. Monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade), funded on the owner's monthly top-up. The basket is an evenly spaced 20-name sample of the 100 by dollar-volume rank (5% slots), because the simulator only tops up a held name that is 1% of equity below target, so a 100-slot book would leave the monthly deposits in cash; T100-L6 holds all 100 to measure that drag. Variants: S20-L6 (the book), S20-L3 and S20-L12 (3 and 12 months), S20-L6-B1 (a one-point dead zone against whipsaw), S20-ALWAYS (control: the basket every month, no switch), T100-L6. SPY always is the benchmark itself. Success: a switch variant beats SPY TR with a worst fall under 20%, beats the always-basket control, is positive in 2009-2015, and wins a majority of walk-forward folds.
methods.expectedFailure: Relative strength between equal and cap weight is weakly persistent at monthly horizons, so the switch whipsaws: it moves into SPY after the basket has already lagged and back after it has already caught up, paying Gotrade's fees on 20 names each way for nothing. On dev (1996-2015) the equal-weight basket beat SPY in most years after 2000, so the switch may just track the always-basket control with extra cost and a few badly timed SPY months. Neither side of the switch has any crash protection: SPY fell about 55% in 2007-2009 and the basket will have fallen as much or more, so every variant very likely fails the 20% worst-fall limit; the idea can at best show a return edge that a later method would put behind a risk switch. The reading set is today's members, a small survivorship lean toward the basket.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

**What this tested.** Every equal-slot book in the lab falls behind SPY whenever a few giant
companies carry the market. So instead of picking better stocks, this method tried to time the
bet itself. Each month it compared two things over the last few months: how the average big
company did (the 100 most-traded index members, each counted equally) and how SPY did. If the
average company was ahead, it held an equal-weight basket of those companies. If the giants were
ahead, it held SPY. Monthly, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5 million rupiah added on
the 25th of every month, 1996 to 2015.

The basket was normally a 20-name sample of the 100: every fifth name by trading size, so the
sample ran from the giants down to the hundredth name. I chose 20 because the simulator only
tops up a holding once it is 1% of the account below target, and in a 100-name book each name
is only 1%, so I expected new deposits to sit idle. One variant held all 100 to measure that.

**Result: rejected on every count that matters.**

| version | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 names, 6-month reading (the book) | +3.5% | +7.2% | 63% | 1.12 | 0.20 |
| 20 names, 3-month reading | +4.6% | +7.2% | 61% | 1.19 | 0.20 |
| 20 names, 12-month reading | +3.5% | +7.2% | 60% | 1.12 | 0.16 |
| 20 names, 6 months, 1-point dead zone | +3.2% | +7.2% | 63% | 1.11 | 0.17 |
| 20 names, never switch (control) | +3.2% | +7.2% | 63% | 1.08 | 0.15 |
| all 100 names, 6-month reading | +7.4% | +7.2% | 56% | 2.39 | 0.42 |

- **Beats SPY:** only the 100-name version, and only by 0.2 of a point a year: a tie.
- **Worst fall:** 56-64% for every version, all in 2008 (worst calendar year −38% to −45%).
  The limit is 20%. Neither side of the switch protects against a crash, as expected.
- **Gains vs losses (profit factor, needs 1.3):** the 20-name versions sit at 1.1-1.2.
- **Luck check:** with 66 methods tried, the best version's chance of being a real edge rather
  than luck (DSR) is 0.42 against a bar of 0.90. None comes close.
- **Later stretches (walk-forward):** the lab's own way of picking a version won 1 of 4 later
  periods, and lost to SPY by 1.0 point a year over 2009-2015, the years most like today.

**Did the switch itself do anything?** A little, not enough. Against the never-switch control
(+3.2% a year), the 6-month switch added 0.3 of a point and the 3-month switch 1.4 points. The
lab's breadth report shows where: in "narrow" months, when SPY beat its own average member, the
control lost 9.9 points a year to SPY and the 3-month switch only 5.9. So the reading does catch
some of the giant-led stretches, but late and only partly. In "broad" months the switch gave a
little back (+1.2 → −0.2 for the 3-month version), because it was sometimes sitting in SPY when
the average company came back. The one-point dead zone, meant to stop flip-flopping, made it
worse (+3.2%): it held each side longer after the turn, which is the expensive part.

**Why the 20-name sample did so badly.** It traded 3,000-3,500 times against 1,621 for the
100-name book holding five times as many names. Taking "every fifth name by trading size" means
the sample changes whenever ranks shift a little: a company sliding from 15th to 16th leaves the
sample and its neighbour comes in. Every month the book sold and bought names for no reason the
idea cared about, paying Gotrade's minimum fee on small slots each time. That was my design
mistake, not the market's. The 100-name version had none of that churn. It also stayed 86%
invested (the 20-name ones 96%): less idle cash than I feared, because every switch to SPY and
back re-buys every slot at full size and puts the idle deposits back to work.

**Hypothesis and expected failure.** The hypothesis did not hold: the switch did not turn the
equal-weight basket into a winner. The expected failure happened as written. The switch mostly
tracked the always-basket control, the dead zone did not fix the timing, and there was no crash
protection, so every version failed the 20% worst-fall limit by a wide margin. The reading set is
today's index members, which leans slightly toward the basket (companies join after they rise).
That makes the basket look slightly better than it really was, so the true result is a little worse.

**Compared with the lab.** The best near misses (the momentum and blend books) beat SPY by 3-8
points a year on dev with worst falls of 12-20%. This method's best version tied SPY with a 56%
fall. It is not near anything.

My opinion: as a book of its own, this direction is finished. Holding the average big company
instead of SPY earned nothing on 1996-2015 once Gotrade's fees were paid. A timing switch on top
can only add what it catches, about one point a year at best here, and it has no answer to a
crash. What is worth keeping is the reading itself: a lead that turns negative when the giants
take over did catch part of the narrow stretches. The next try uses it as a brake on a book that
already has an edge and is not tied to the failed momentum books: the calm big-dividend-raise
book, moved into SPY whenever the average big company is behind SPY over three months. If the
reading cannot even lift that book's 2009-2015 years, which is where that book fails, the idea
is dead in every form.
methods.verdict: Rejected: switching between the average big company and SPY on who led the last few months tied SPY at best (+7.4% a year vs +7.2%), fell 56-64% in 2008, and won 1 of 4 later stretches

methods.hypothesis: M0088 (the calmer half of the big dividend raisers) passed every check on average but lost to SPY in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 later stretches. methods.sourceRef: variation of M0088 (C-LIVE-63 unchanged); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006), JF 61(1); Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992), JF 47(5) banded moving-average rule; Faber (2007), 10-month average
methods.hypothesis: Published 1995 (dividend-change drift), 2006 (low volatility), 1992 and 2007 (banded and 10-month trend switches). M0096 showed the calm big-raise book's 2009-2015 lag belongs to the SPY-200 switch: more switched SPY widened the gap (-5.6 points a year at an 85% core vs -2.7 for M0088-C-LIVE-63), while the switch's 2008 exit earned about +9 points a year in 2002-2008. Keep M0088-C-LIVE-63 unchanged (big dividend raisers seen on the ex-date, calm half of the live raisers on a 63-session swing, up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, rest in SPY, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) and replace only the switch. A wider band (BAND-5) trades fewer whipsaws for a deeper fall. Faber's monthly reading is the most published switch of all and may simply match the control. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## The question

The **calm big-raise book** buys big index companies whose latest dividend is at least 25% above their usual payment. It keeps only the calmer half of them and holds each one at 5% of the money for up to six months, with the rest in SPY. It re-picks monthly. When SPY is below its 200-day average it moves everything into cash. That is its **safety switch**.

The last trial found that the switch, not the stocks, is why this book lagged SPY in 2009-2015. The switch sold in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and bought back higher each time. It also earned the book's 2002-2008 edge by sitting out 2008.

This trial kept the book exactly as it was and changed only how the switch reads the market. The aim was a switch that whipsaws less: one that needs a clear break to leave and a clear recovery to come back.

## Variants, fixed before any result

- **CTRL**: the old switch, unchanged. This checks that the setup reproduces the parent.
- **BAND-3** (the idea): leave when SPY closes 3% under its 200-day average. Come back only when it closes 3% over.
- **BAND-5**: the same with a 5% band.
- **FABER**: a famous published switch (Faber, 2007). SPY's month-end price above its 10-month average.

All variants trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on 20M IDR plus 5M IDR every month.

## Results (dev years 1996-2015, the owner's deposits)

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CTRL (old switch) | +10.6% | 18.7% | 3.52 | 0.945 | −2.6 pts | passes |
| BAND-3 | +10.4% | **20.4%** | 3.47 | 0.938 | −3.1 pts | fails worst fall |
| BAND-5 | +10.1% | **20.4%** | 3.41 | 0.927 | −5.0 pts | fails worst fall |
| FABER | +10.0% | 18.7% | 3.16 | 0.914 | −3.5 pts | passes |

CTRL reproduced the parent exactly: 528 trades, an 18.7% worst fall and the same total return. So the comparison is fair.

**Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a peak, and the limit is 20%. **Gains vs losses** (profit factor) is winning trades over losing trades, with a floor of 1.3. **DSR** is the luck check: how likely the edge is real and not the best of many tries. The lab now counts N = 70 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90. Every variant clears it.

Two variants (CTRL and FABER) pass every condition on the dev average, so the lab marked the method **dev-eligible**. **It cannot be promoted.** On the four later stretches it was never tuned on (walk-forward folds), it beat SPY in only **2 of 4**, and the hard gate needs a majority. The variant it would pick also changed from fold to fold.

## Why the gentler switch did not help

I listed when each switch went to cash, read at each month's end:

| switch | 2009-2015 exits | months in cash, 2009-2015 |
|---|---|---|
| old switch | May 2010, Aug 2011, Aug 2015 | 16 |
| 3% band | May 2010, Aug 2011, Aug 2015 | 17 |
| 5% band | Jun 2010, Aug 2011, Aug 2015 | 17 |
| Faber | May 2010, Aug 2010, Aug 2011, Aug 2015 | 15 |

**Every switch left in the same three corrections.** The 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips were real falls of 10-19%. They were not small wobbles around the line. Each one went through a 3% band, and through a 5% band too. So a band removes no whipsaw in the years that matter. All it does is come back later, a month after each recovery had started. That is why the 2009-2015 gap got *wider* as the band got wider: −2.6, then −3.1, then −5.0 points a year.

The bands did remove small false exits in 1999 and 2005, as designed. They also left the market and came back later around 1998 and 2007, which pushed the worst fall from 18.7% to 20.4%, over the limit. Faber's monthly reading kept the worst fall at 18.7%, but it flipped twice in summer 2010 and lagged more in 2009-2015 than the old switch did.

The lesson is plain. **The 2009-2015 lag is not switch noise.** A trend switch is a bet that a fall below the 200-day average will keep falling. In 2010-2015, every such fall was a V that recovered within months. No way of reading the same line fixes that. Every switch sat out 15-17 of those 82 months, and SPY rose through most of them.

## The check with the missing companies

The lab's price history is missing many companies that later died. With most of them put back, the edge over SPY barely moves (about +3.3 to +3.4% a year for CTRL and BAND-3). But 2009-2015 gets about 0.6 points a year worse on every variant. CTRL's worst fall rises to 20.0%, right on the limit. The folds stay at 2 of 4.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The banded switch was supposed to shrink the 2009-2015 gap to under 1 point a year. It widened it. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the band exits later, the worst fall crosses 20%, and the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips crossed the band anyway. Faber's switch roughly matched the control, also as expected.

These trend switches (1992, 2007) and the dividend drift (1995) are all widely published, so even the dev edge is likely to fade after 2015.

## My opinion:

Stop tuning the 200-day switch. Three ways of reading it all left in the same three dips, so the line itself is the problem, not how it is read. This family's record is now clear. Its whole edge is the 2008 exit, and the same exit costs it 2.6 points a year or more in calm, V-shaped years like 2009-2015, which look like today. The one switch idea still worth a single trial changes the *return*, not the exit: leave on the 200-day average as now, but come back as soon as SPY closes back above its 50-day average. That way the book misses the start of a crash but not the start of a recovery. If that cannot get 2009-2015 within 1 point of SPY, retire the dividend-raise family's switched books and keep the raisers only as evidence.


### 2026-10-11

Sera 20261011-1912: promotion not attempted because the hard gate refuses it (lab status): M0101-CTRL wins 2 of 4 walk-forward folds, the pick changes across folds, kin clean. The eligible variant is the unchanged control, which reproduces M0088-C-LIVE-63 exactly, so no new configuration cleared dev; both banded switches and the Faber switch did worse in 2009-2015. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-11

## What was tried

The idea is the "Dividend Aristocrats" one. Hold big companies that have raised their dividend every year for many years. Here "raised" means the typical (median) payment in a calendar year was higher than the year before. The streak is read only from dividends already paid by the decision date. The book holds up to 40 such companies in equal slots, longest streaks first, and puts the rest of the money in SPY. It re-picks monthly, buys fractional shares and pays Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up. The main versions had **no safety switch**. One control used the usual rule of going to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average.

Five versions, recorded as trials #332-#336: 5-, 7- and 10-year streaks with 40 names, a 5-year streak with 25 names, and the switched 5-year control.

## Result vs SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | your money a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5-yr streak, 40 names | +7.7% | +7.2% | **59.4%** | 1.42 | 0.51 |
| 7-yr streak, 40 names | +7.1% | +7.2% | **59.1%** | 1.32 | 0.44 |
| 10-yr streak, 40 names | +6.9% | +7.2% | **59.0%** | 1.41 | 0.38 |
| 5-yr streak, 25 names | +7.5% | +7.2% | **58.7%** | 1.85 | 0.48 |
| control: 5-yr + SPY 200-day switch | +8.7% | +7.2% | 21.4% | 7.44 | 0.88 |

Every version failed. The four no-switch books fell almost 60% from their peak, three times the 20% limit and worse than SPY's own fall in 2007-09. Two of them did not even beat SPY. The switched control came closest. It earned 1.5 points a year more than SPY and lost at most 21.4%, but that is still over the 20% bar (and "close" is not a pass). Its luck score was 0.878, under the 0.90 bar.

**Luck test (DSR).** After counting every distinct method the lab has tried (N = 70 on the day of the run), the luck score asks how likely the result is real rather than a lucky draw. It has to reach 0.90. The no-switch books scored 0.38 to 0.51, which is close to a coin flip. The switched control reached 0.878.

**Walk-forward folds.** These score the method on years it did not choose from. It beat SPY in 2 of 4, short of the majority the gate wants. In 2009-2015, the years most like today, it trailed SPY by **3.9 points a year**. Breadth reading: the 5-year book earned its small edge only in "broad" months, when the average stock beat the index, and lost 2.3 points a year in "narrow" months led by a few giants. That is the same shape that has beaten every book in this lab.

## Worst year and when the fall hit

The worst calendar year was 2008, at -31.5% with deposits refilling the account. The 59% fall is the book with deposits taken out, and it ran from 2007 into March 2009. On the deposits alone the fall looks much gentler than it really was.

## Why: the mechanism

The long-streak list in mid-2008 is the reason. When the five-year screen is ranked by streak, almost everything ties at the longest streak the store can see (14 years). So in practice the ranking falls to "most traded". In June 2008 that put Wells Fargo, US Bancorp, Truist, State Street, Regions, KeyCorp, Fifth Third, Lincoln National, **Freddie Mac**, GE, Vornado and Kimco in the book. Banks, insurers and property trusts had some of the longest dividend-raise records in America right up to the crisis. They were also the companies that collapsed and cut.

The screen made it worse by reading whole calendar years. A bank that cut in mid-2008 still showed an unbroken streak until January 2009, so the book held it through the whole collapse. The published "Aristocrats fell only 22% in 2008" comes from an index that removes cutters and weights its members differently. A plain "raised every year" screen on our members does not reproduce it.

Longer streaks did not help. The 7- and 10-year books held the same banks, because those had raised for 14 years too, and they had less of the 1999-2003 edge.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed. Without a switch, long dividend growers did **not** fall much less in 2008; here they fell more than SPY.

The expected failure came true in two parts. The book lagged in 2009-2015 (-3.9 points a year), and the worst fall broke 20% without a switch. It broke it far worse than written down (59%, not "may pass 20%"), because the 2008 list was led by financials and the yearly screen sold cutters only in January.

## Comparison with near misses

M0096 (calm big raisers beside a SPY core) was the reason to drop the switch. It suggested the switch, not the dividend stocks, lost to SPY in 2009-2015. This run says the opposite for a streak book. With the switch on it earned +8.7% a year against SPY's +7.2% and fell at most 21%. With the switch off it earned +7.7% and fell 59%. On these companies, the switch is what kept the fall survivable.

The switched control's 21.4% fall and 0.878 luck score sit close to the calm-raiser family's near misses, and its fold record is no better. All of these were measured at Gotrade's real fees, so they compare directly.

The survivorship check (re-running on the store that includes dead companies) was not run. That check matters before a promotion, and nothing here is promotable. It would make the result worse, not better: a company that cut and then died is missing from the dev store.

## My opinion

A plain "raised every year" screen is not worth more variants. It is dividend-raise-drift with a slower trigger, and its 2008 crash came from what the streak rewards: steady payers who had never had a bad year until they did, mostly banks. The one thing worth one more trial is the **cut exit**. Drop a company the day a lower payment goes ex, not the next January, and keep the switched streak book otherwise as is. If that cannot pull the switched version under 20% and lift its 2009-2015 record, this family should be closed. I would not spend more ids on streak length or book size. They barely moved anything.

methods.name: The overnight winners as a minority partner: half the money in SPY, half in the overnight momentum book
methods.hypothesis: Three in-pool fixes for the overnight momentum book's 23% summer-1998 fall (a volatility brake, a steady-path sort, a low-beta cut) all traded one point of fall for one point of return and lost the 2009-2015 edge first. Stop filtering the pool; dilute it instead. Hold a fixed SPY core (50% and 70%) and run M0050-TOT-ON unbraked in the rest, on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding, with the SPY-200 switch on the sleeve only (the core stays invested) or on the whole book. A half-SPY book should roughly halve the momentum-crash fall while matching SPY's big-company drift in 2009-2015, the years every momentum book lost. Expected failure: M0030 (a SPY core with a residual-momentum satellite) won only 2 of 4 folds because the core dilutes the edge as much as the fall; the overnight sleeve's behaviour may read as kin of the test-failed momentum books under the gate's correlation rule (the core lowers the residual correlation only if it is measured after removing SPY, which it is, so likely not); and the overnight anomaly was published in 2019 and inverted from 2018.

methods.name: Beaten-down companies as a small crash cushion beside SPY: 80% SPY, 20% the five-year losers, rebalanced monthly
methods.sourceRef: Variation of M0073 and M0069 (De Bondt & Thaler 1985, Does the Stock Market Overreact?, Journal of Finance 40(3)); the core-satellite frame of M0030
methods.hypothesis: Long-term reversal was published in 1985, so the dev window is already after the crowd knew it. The five-year losers (M0069) and the turnaround losers (M0073) earned all their lead over SPY in 2000-2002 and 2009, and fell over half in 2008 as stand-alone books. As a fixed slice beside an always-held SPY core, their 2000-2002 lead (about +20 points a year while SPY fell) should lift the core in a tech-style crash, while the core keeps SPY's big-company drift. Each month the book holds 80% SPY and 20% a losers slice, resized back to those shares, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, on the owner's deposits. Variants: C80-UP (20% M0073-UP-N20: losers that have turned up, the best stand-alone version), C80-L60 (20% M0069-L60-N20: the plain 20 biggest five-year losers), C70-UP (30% of the confirmed-turn slice: the dose check), and C80-W60 (the control: 20% the five-year WINNERS, the same shape on the other side of the sort). Success: a losers variant beats SPY TR on dev, beats the winners control, leads SPY in 2000-2002, and the dose check moves the same way as the slice.
methods.expectedFailure: SPY alone fell about 55% from its 2007 peak, and an 80% SPY core with an unbraked 20% slice of beaten-down companies cannot fall much less than that: every variant should break the 20% worst-fall limit by a wide margin, so none can be eligible and the trial is worth running only for what it says about the slice. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

## What we tried

Two earlier methods bought big index companies that had fallen hardest over five years. One bought them plainly. The other waited until they had started rising again. On their own, both beat SPY only through two episodes, the 2000-2002 tech crash and the 2009 rebound, and both lost more than half their value in 2008.

This method asked whether they work better as a small side-dish than as a meal. Each month it held **80% SPY** and **20% a slice of beaten-down companies**, and brought both back to those shares each month. Every version traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's real deposits: 10 million rupiah to start, then 5 million on the 25th of each month. Four versions ran:

- **C80-UP:** 80% SPY, 20% losers that have turned up (the best of the earlier stand-alone books)
- **C80-L60:** 80% SPY, 20% the plain 20 biggest five-year losers
- **C70-UP:** 70% SPY, 30% the turned-up losers (does more of the slice do more?)
- **C80-W60, the control:** 80% SPY, 20% the five-year *winners*, the same shape from the other end of the list

## Result: rejected

| version | your money earned a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | worst year | gains vs losses | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 80/20 turned-up losers | +7.6% | +7.2% | 55% | 2008, −36% | 1.83 | 0.47 |
| 80/20 plain losers | +7.5% | +7.2% | 57% | 2008, −38% | 1.64 | 0.47 |
| 70/30 turned-up losers | +7.9% | +7.2% | 54% | 2008, −36% | 1.82 | 0.50 |
| 80/20 winners (control) | +7.6% | +7.2% | 57% | 2008, −40% | 1.77 | 0.44 |

- **Worst fall.** Every version lost 54-57% from a peak, which is SPY's own 2007-2009 fall. That breaks the lab's looser screen of 50%, and it is nowhere near the 25% the owner's real-money bar allows. A 20% slice cannot cushion an 80% SPY position. The 2008 numbers make this concrete: SPY lost about 37% that year, and the best blend lost 36%.
- **Luck score (DSR).** This is how likely the result is real rather than a lucky draw after all the lab's tries. It was judged at N = 105 looks (one per distinct method) against the bar of 0.90. Every version scored 0.44-0.50, close to a coin flip. A lead of 0.3-0.7 points a year over twenty years is too small to tell apart from luck.
- **Out-of-sample folds.** The 70/30 version won 2 of 4 three-year stretches (2003-2005 and 2012-2014) and lost 2006-2008 and 2009-2011. That is no better than chance.

## The control decides it

The whole idea was that *beaten-down* companies are the cushion. The control holds the opposite companies, the five-year winners, and it earned the same: +7.6% a year, the same as the turned-up losers and more than the plain losers. In 2009-2015, the years most like today, the winners slice did *best* (+0.8 points a year ahead of SPY, against +0.1 for the turned-up losers). The losers slice earned its keep in exactly one place: 2008, when it lost 4 points less than the winners slice. Over twenty years, that small cushion is all it gave.

So the 0.3-0.7 point lead is not about losers. Any 20-name equal-weight slice next to SPY, rebalanced monthly, picks up a few tenths of a point from equal weighting and rebalancing. The market-shape check agrees. Every version made its lead in "broad" months, when the average stock beat the index, and gave it back in "narrow" months, when a few giants carried SPY. That is the signature of an equal-weight tilt, not of a stock-picking edge.

## Checking against dead companies

The lab's price store lacks about half of the index companies that later died. A second store adds most of them back. On that store, every version earned slightly less (0.1 to 0.4 points a year). The plain-losers version went from 0.3 points ahead of SPY to 0.1 behind, and its 2009-2015 lead fell from +0.6 to −0.5. That is what you would expect when the missing companies are exactly the losers that kept losing. The turned-up version barely moved, because waiting for the turn already screens those companies out.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: did not hold.** The losers slice did not beat the winners control, and the extra slice in the 70/30 version added only +0.3 points a year, inside the noise. The tech-crash help does show up in the first fold (2003-2005 won by 5 points), but a 20% slice dilutes it to almost nothing.
- **Expected failure: half right.** The worst fall broke the limit by a wide margin, as predicted. The prediction that the blends would trail SPY after 2009 was wrong: they roughly tied it (between −0.5 and +0.8 points a year on either store). An 80% SPY core simply makes every blend look like SPY.

## Comparison with the parents

On their own, the turned-up losers earned +9.5% a year at a 54% worst fall, and the plain losers did about the same as SPY at a 70% worst fall. Mixing either with 80% SPY gave up most of that return and kept almost all of the fall. That is the worst of both: SPY's crash depth with SPY's return, plus fees.

My opinion: This direction is finished. A slice of stocks beside SPY cannot cushion SPY, because in a real crash every stock falls together. The losers slice here behaved no differently from the winners slice, so "beaten-down" carries no information worth paying for. If the lab wants a crash partner for an SPY core, the partner has to be something that rises or at least holds while stocks fall, such as short-term Treasuries or cash raised by a rule. Or the beaten-down slice should be bought only *after* a crash has already happened, when the rebound evidence lives (2003, 2009). I have queued that second idea, because it uses only data and order types the lab already has. I would not spend another id on a fixed-share stock slice beside SPY.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a fifth of beaten-down companies beside SPY fell as far as SPY (55%) and earned no more than a slice of last-decade winners did

methods.name: Calm big raisers with a fast way back in: leave when SPY falls under its 200-day average, return as soon as it closes back above its 50-day average
methods.hypothesis: M0101 showed every reading of the SPY-200 switch (strict, 3% and 5% bands, Faber's month-end 10-month average) exited the same 2010, 2011 and 2015 corrections; the bands only re-entered later and widened the 2009-2015 gap (-2.6, -3.1, -5.0 points a year). methods.name: Calm big raisers that leave one at a time: each holding sold when it falls under its own 200-day average, instead of selling the whole book when the market does
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0088 (C-LIVE-63); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006), JF 61(1); Faber (2007), JWM 9(4) for the 200-day frame
methods.hypothesis: Three batches agree that the market-wide SPY-200 switch, not the dividend raisers, is what loses to SPY after 2009: it sold the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips whole and bought back higher, and M0101 showed that no gentler, banded or slower reading of the same switch fixes it, because those dips were real falls that bounced before any market-wide rule could get back in. The switch is also what earned the family its 2002-2008 edge by sitting out 2008, so it cannot simply be deleted. This tests a different machine for the same job.
