Keep M0088-C-LIVE-63's calm big-raiser book exactly as it is (big raise seen on its ex-date, up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, held names first then the newest event, calm half of the live raisers on a 63-session swing, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees), delete the SPY-200 gate entirely, park the slack in cash rather than SPY, and refuse to hold any individual raiser whose close is at or below the mean of its own last 200 closes. Exposure then falls gradually as names drop out one by one rather than all at once, and rebuilds name by name as each stock recovers, so a six-week dip that most holdings ride through costs a fraction of the book rather than all of it, while a 2008 in which almost every name breaks down still empties the book. Variants: HOST, the paired control, is M0088-C-LIVE-63 unchanged and must reproduce its numbers (+10.6% a year, 18.7% worst fall) at the same fees in the same run; NONE is the naked book with no gate of any kind and cash for the empty slots, the yardstick the per-stock exit is measured against; STOCK200 adds the per-stock exit with the freed 5% slots in cash, which is the idea; STOCK200-SPREAD hands the freed weight to the surviving names instead, holding total exposure at what the unfiltered book would have held so that only the choice of names changes — the pair separates de-risking from name selection; BOTH runs the per-stock exit behind the old SPY-200 switch, to see whether the two are substitutes or complements. It still ranks on dividend raises, so the family stays dividend-change-drift. Success: STOCK200 beats SPY total return on deposit-matched money over the dev window with a worst fall under 20%, and — the thing that matters — a smaller 2009-2015 gap to SPY than M0088's -2.6 points a year, with a majority of the walk-forward folds won.
methods.expectedFailure: A per-stock trend exit is slower than the market switch in a fast crash and is paid for in whipsaw on every individual name, so it may give back more in trading costs and late exits than the market switch cost in whipsaw; on 5% slots at Gotrade's real fees a $28 order pays about 0.47%, and twenty names churning in and out of their own averages is several times the host's turnover. 2008 may still breach 20% because calm dividend raisers break down together and the per-stock rule only sells after each one is already well down. The calm raisers are mostly utilities, staples and old industrials, which lagged big-company growth after 2009, so removing the market switch may fix the dip whipsaw and still leave the 2009-2015 gap, which would mean the picks, not the gate, are the problem and the family should close. STOCK200-SPREAD may simply be a more concentrated version of NONE and fall further. Dividend drift was published in 1995 and low volatility in 2006, so even a real dev edge earned mostly before 2009 is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

## The question

The **calm big-raiser book** buys up to 20 big companies that have just raised their dividend by at
least a quarter, holds each for six months at 5% of the money, keeps only the calmer half of them,
and re-picks every month. In its best form (M0088-C-LIVE-63) it earned **+10.6% a year** on the
owner's deposits against SPY's **+7.2%**, fell at most 18.7%, and passed every go-live condition.
It has still never been promoted, because it loses to SPY in 2009-2015 — the years most like today
— and wins only 2 of the 4 later stretches the gate checks.

Three batches have now blamed the same thing: the **market-wide safety switch**. The book steps
entirely into cash whenever SPY closes below its 200-day average, and that switch sold the 2010,
2011 and 2015 dips whole and bought back higher. M0101 showed that softening the switch — a 3% or
5% band, a slower Faber reading — does not help, because those dips were real falls that bounced
before any market-wide rule could get back in.

So this run swaps the machine instead of tuning it. **Delete the market switch. Instead, refuse to
hold any individual stock trading below its own 200-day average.** The book then empties gradually,
one name at a time, as each holding breaks down, and refills name by name as each recovers. A
six-week dip that most holdings ride through should cost a slice of the book rather than all of it;
a 2008 in which nearly everything breaks down should still empty it.

## The five versions, fixed before any result

| | market switch | each stock's own 200-day | spare money |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HOST** | yes | no | parked in SPY |
| **NONE** | no | no | cash |
| **STOCK200** | no | **yes** | cash |
| **STOCK200-SPREAD** | no | **yes** | handed to the surviving stocks |
| **BOTH** | yes | **yes** | cash |

HOST is the paired control: it is M0088-C-LIVE-63 unchanged, so we can check the setup reproduces
the old result before trusting anything else. It did, exactly — +10.6% a year, 18.7% worst fall,
528 trades. The comparison below is therefore fair.

SPREAD exists to split the trend exit in two. Dropping a stock does two different things: it takes
money off the table, and it avoids a weak name. STOCK200 does both. SPREAD hands the freed money to
the stocks that survived, so the book holds exactly as much as it would have anyway and **only the
choice of names changes**. If SPREAD is no better than NONE, then picking by a stock's own trend is
worth nothing and the whole benefit is simply holding less.

All five trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on 20M rupiah plus 5M every month.

## Results, dev years 1996-2015

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**.

| version | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check | how much was invested | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HOST (the old book) | **+10.6%** | 18.7% | 3.52 | 0.946 | 70% | passes everything |
| NONE (no safety at all) | +6.8% | 26.3% | 2.46 | 0.716 | 42% | **loses to SPY** |
| STOCK200 (the idea) | +5.9% | **13.1%** | 2.44 | 0.857 | 32% | **loses to SPY** |
| STOCK200-SPREAD | +6.5% | 26.1% | 2.06 | 0.676 | 42% | **loses to SPY** |
| BOTH | +5.7% | **13.1%** | 2.71 | 0.898 | 28% | **loses to SPY** |

**Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a peak, measured on the book without its monthly deposits —
top-ups refill a falling account and make a fall read gentler than it was. **Gains vs losses**
(profit factor) is the total of winning trades divided by the total of losing trades; the floor is
1.3, and every version clears it. The **luck check** (DSR) is the chance the result is real rather
than the best of many tries: the lab deflated these at **N = 71** independent looks (it counts one
look per method, not per version, floored at a measured participation ratio) and the bar is
**0.90**, the owner's setting since 2026-10-07. Only HOST clears it.

## The thing this run actually found

**Every version that removes the parked SPY loses to SPY.** Not narrowly, and not only after 2009.
Here is each version's yearly lead over SPY, deposits stripped out, era by era:

| version | 1996-2002 | 2003-2008 | 2008 alone | 2009-2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HOST | **+4.6** | **+6.3** | **+34.8** | −2.6 |
| NONE | −4.4 | +1.1 | +20.5 | −5.7 |
| STOCK200 | −4.7 | +1.5 | +29.5 | −8.0 |
| STOCK200-SPREAD | −4.7 | +2.2 | +22.0 | −6.7 |
| BOTH | −4.3 | +1.6 | +34.8 | −8.8 |

Read the first column. HOST beats SPY by 4.6 points a year in 1996-2002. Strip out the parked SPY
and the same dividend picks, in the same years, **lose by about 4.5 points a year** — whether the
market switch is on (BOTH, −4.3) or off (NONE, −4.4). The switch is worth almost nothing in that
era on its own. The parked SPY is worth about nine points a year.

That is the finding, and it is bigger than the question this run set out to answer. **The calm
big-raiser book never beat the market. The SPY sitting inside it did.** The dividend raisers only
fill about 42% of the book's twenty slots, so more than half the money is idle. HOST puts roughly
28 points of that idle money into SPY and then times that SPY with the 200-day switch, which is why
it lost nothing at all in 2008 while SPY lost 34.8%. What looked like a dividend strategy with a
safety switch is really **a timed SPY holding with a dividend satellite bolted on that subtracts
value** — the satellite trails SPY in every era measured here.

M0096 said half of this a batch ago: putting *more* money into SPY (50-85%) still passed on average
but widened the 2009-2015 gap. This run says the rest of it, from the other direction.

## Did the per-stock exit work?

**As a brake, yes — better than the market switch.** It is the best risk control the family has had:

- The worst fall halves, **26.3% to 13.1%**, the lowest of any book in this family.
- 2008 goes from **−14.3% to −5.3%**, where SPY lost 34.8%.
- Worst year improves from −16.7% to −7.4%; risk-adjusted return (MAR) rises from 0.26 to 0.45 and
  Sharpe from 0.66 to 0.78.
- It costs about **0.9 points a year** of return, and it was not meaningfully slower than the market
  switch in the crash — the switch's 2008 was flat, the per-stock exit's was −5.3%, a 5-point gap,
  not the disaster the expected failure warned about.

**And it makes the market switch redundant.** BOTH against STOCK200 is the clean test: adding the
old market-wide switch on top of the per-stock exit leaves the worst fall *identical* (13.1% both),
costs 0.2 points a year overall and 0.8 points in 2009-2015. They are substitutes, not complements,
and the market switch is the one with no job left.

**As a stock picker, no — it is worth exactly nothing.** SPREAD holds the same amount of money as
NONE (42% invested either way) and differs only in which names it holds. It earns +6.5% against
NONE's +6.8%, falls 26.1% against 26.3%, and its gains-to-losses ratio is *worse* (2.06 vs 2.46).
Dropping a stock because it trades under its own average does not pick better stocks. All of the
benefit is simply holding less money during falls.

## 2009-2015: the gap got wider, not narrower

The whole point was to shrink the 2009-2015 lag. It grew. HOST lags by 2.6 points a year; STOCK200
lags by 8.0. The mechanism is exactly the one the switch suffered from, only now paid twenty times
over: individual stocks dip below their own averages constantly in a rising market, so the book
keeps selling and buying back higher, and it sat only 32% invested through the best stretch for
stocks in the window. Trading the breakdowns was not the problem; **being out of the market was**.

The regime report agrees and adds nothing new: HOST "pays in both" narrow and broad markets, the
other four pay in neither, and the persistence line is flat (6 of 202 windows positive).

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis is disproved, and in an instructive way.** The per-stock exit did empty the book
  gradually and did refill it name by name, exactly as described. It just did not help, because the
  premise was wrong: the market switch was never what stood between this family and SPY. Without
  the parked SPY the picks lose in every era, switch or no switch.
- **The expected failure half happened.** The whipsaw cost was real but modest (0.9 points a year),
  and 2008 did *not* breach 20% — the per-stock exit handled the crash better than predicted, at
  −5.3%. What did happen is the third warning, written out before the run: *"removing the market
  switch may fix the dip whipsaw and still leave the 2009-2015 gap, which would mean the picks, not
  the gate, are the problem and the family should close."* That is what the numbers say.
- SPREAD "may simply be a more concentrated version of NONE" — correct, almost to the decimal.

## Can it be promoted?

No, and no test-window look was spent or is worth spending. The method reads dev-eligible only
because of HOST, which is a deliberate copy of M0088-C-LIVE-63. `lab walkforward M0107` refuses it
on the same ground M0088 was refused: **2 of 4 folds won, the pick is unstable, and the 2009-2015
edge is −2.6%**. No buy signal: survivorship-free price history is still not worth paying for here.

## Comparison with the family

The whole family, same real fees: the plain big-raise book +10.9% a year with a 21.9% worst fall;
seeing the raise on its announcement day (M0076) added nothing; keeping only raises the market
cheered (M0083) passed on dev and won 2 of 4 folds; the calm filter (M0088) cut the fall to 18.7%
and won 2 of 4 folds; a gentler switch (M0101) made things worse; a bigger SPY core (M0096) passed
on average and widened the 2009-2015 gap. Six methods, thirty-five variants, one wall. This run is
the first to take the SPY out of the book and look at the dividend picks on their own, and the
answer is that they were never the engine.

**My opinion:** Close this family. Six methods have now tried to fix the same book by changing
which raisers to hold, when to see the raise, how much SPY to carry and how to time the exit, and
every one of them lands at 2 of 4 folds with a negative 2009-2015 edge. This run explains why: the
dividend raisers have no edge over SPY on their own in any era of the dev window, so every passing
result in the family was the parked SPY and its 200-day timing wearing a dividend costume. No
further filter on *which* raisers to buy can repair that, and I would spend no more method ids on
it.

Two things here are worth carrying out of the family, though, and both are about the machinery
rather than the dividends:

1. **The per-stock trend exit is the family's best brake and it retires the market-wide switch.**
   Half the drawdown, a tenth of 2008's loss, 0.9 points a year in cost, and the market switch adds
   nothing once it is in place. That is a general-purpose risk control, and it has never been tried
   on a book that actually has an edge. I would put it on the residual-momentum book (M0007/M0022),
   which beats SPY by 3 to 7 points a year on dev and fails or nearly fails on its worst fall
   (19.6% for M0007-N20-RAW, 23.5% once dead companies are put back). That is the open question I
   queued, and it is the one I would run next.
2. **A book that cannot fill its own slots should be measured for what it really is.** This one
   sat 42% invested and quietly earned its keep from the other 58%. Any method that parks its
   spare money in SPY needs its picks measured without the park before anyone believes the picks.
methods.verdict: Rejected direction, and it explains the whole family: take the parked SPY out of the calm big-raiser book and the dividend picks lose to SPY in every era, so the family's edge was always the SPY inside it; the per-stock exit halved the worst fall to 13% and made the market-wide switch redundant, but could not make losing picks win

methods.name: The stocks that fall least: hold the big names whose own worst twelve-month fall was mildest
methods.sourceRef: Maximum Drawdown, Recovery, and Momentum, Journal of Risk and Financial Management 14(11) 542 (2021), doi:10.3390/jrfm14110542; Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang (2006), Journal of Finance 61(1), 259-299 for the low-risk anomaly beside it
methods.hypothesis: Every method in this lab that beats SPY on average dies on the 20% worst-fall rule, and the only answer tried so far is a market-wide timing switch, which three batches have shown loses more after 2009 than it saves. This tries the other answer: pick stocks that do not fall much in the first place. Each month, among F4-screened point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members ($5 price, 20M-dollar daily volume), measure every name's own worst peak-to-trough fall over the past 252 closes and hold the 20 mildest at 5% each, equal weighted, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade), with no market switch of any kind. A stock's own past drawdown is not its volatility and not its beta: it reads the shape of the loss rather than its average size, so it penalises a name that fell 40% once and recovered while sparing one that merely jiggles, and the published work finds it ranks the cross-section better than either. The lab has tested calm (volatility) and low-swing-with-the-market (beta) filters inside other books and found both cut the return about as much as they cut the fall; the open question is whether ranking on the fall itself breaks that one-for-one trade. Variants: DD20 and DD40 (the 20 or 40 mildest), DD20-L18 (an eighteen-month drawdown window instead of one year, so a book picked in 2009 still remembers 2008 -- the longest window the method contract fixture can prove), WORST20 (the 20 deepest, the paired control that must trail), and EW40-DV (the 40 most-traded eligible members, equal weighted) as the yardstick that says how much of any result is just equal weighting rather than the drawdown rank -- it is also the equal-weight big-company yardstick insight 91 asked for. Turnover should be low, so fees should not decide this one. Success: a DD variant beats SPY TR on deposit-matched money with a worst fall under 20%, clears a majority of the walk-forward folds, beats the EW40-DV yardstick, and the control trails it clearly.
methods.expectedFailure: The mildest-fall names before 2008 were financials and utilities, exactly the group that then fell hardest, so the signal may be a trap in precisely the crash it is meant to survive: a book picked in mid-2007 on 2006-2007 drawdowns would have been full of banks. A long-only equity book with no timing rule has nowhere to hide in 2008, so the 20% bar may be out of reach whatever it holds. The likeliest quieter failure is that the drawdown rank collapses onto low volatility in large caps, in which case this is the calm-stock book again: a shallower fall bought with a lower return, trailing SPY on CAGR through the 2009-2015 growth run, and no better than EW40-DV. The paper is from 2021, well after the dev window ends, so the dev window at least sees the signal before any crowd traded this particular form of it; but the low-risk anomaly it sits beside has been traded since 2006 and has faded.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# The stocks that fall least — what happened

## The idea in one line

Every strategy this lab has found that beats the market on average has died on the same rule:
at some point it lost more than 20% from its peak, and the owner's bar is 20%. The only fix
tried so far is a switch that steps out of the market when the market turns down, and three
batches have now shown that switch costs more after 2009 than it saves. So this run tried the
other fix: stop trying to time anything, and simply buy the stocks that do not fall much.

Each month it looked at every big, heavily traded company in the index, measured how far that
company's own share price had fallen from its own high at the worst point of the past year, and
bought the twenty that had fallen least. Equal money in each, re-picked monthly, always
invested, no market switch of any kind, at the real fees Gotrade charges.

## The result

Measured on the owner's real saving plan — Rp 5,000,000 on the 25th of every month from January
1996, 237 deposits in all — against the same deposits put into the market itself:

| What it held | Your money earned | The market earned | Worst fall | Gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The 20 that fell least | **+8.3% a year** | +7.2% a year | **42.5%** | 2.05 |
| The 40 that fell least | +8.3% a year | +7.2% a year | 44.0% | 2.04 |
| The 20 that fell least, measured over 18 months | +7.6% a year | +7.2% a year | 42.0% | 2.23 |
| The 20 that fell **most** (the control) | +6.2% a year | +7.2% a year | 79.1% | 1.66 |
| The 40 most-traded names, equal money in each | +5.8% a year | +7.2% a year | 62.2% | 1.25 |

"Gains vs losses" is the profit factor: how many dollars of winning trades came for each dollar
of losing trades. Above 1.3 is the lab's bar, and the first three clear it comfortably.

**The good news: the ranking is real.** The twenty mildest fallers earned 2.1 points a year more
than the twenty hardest fallers, and 2.5 points more than simply spreading the same money evenly
across the forty most-traded big names. That last comparison matters most, because it was put in
on purpose to catch a cheat: if the whole result had come from holding twenty equal slices
instead of a market-shaped portfolio, the plain equal-money book would have done just as well.
It did not. Something in the ranking was genuinely picking better companies.

**The bad news, and it is fatal: the book still fell 42.5%.** The entire point of this idea was
to build something that does not fall more than 20%. It fell more than twice that. It did fall
less than the controls — 42.5% against 62% for the plain equal-money book and 79% for the
hardest fallers — so the signal does reduce the damage. It just does not come close to reducing
it enough. In 2008 the book lost 29.4% in the year.

The lab also judges how likely a result is to be real rather than luck, after allowing for how
many different things have been tried. That score came out at 0.72 for the best version, against
a bar of 0.90, counting 72 looks — one for each distinct method the lab has ever run, which is
the owner's rule for what counts as an independent try. So even setting the fall aside, this is
not yet distinguishable from a lucky draw.

## Why it failed

The measure and the problem are not the same kind of thing.

A company's own worst fall over the past year is mostly a statement about that company. The
owner's 20% rule is about the whole account, and the account's worst fall is driven by the
moments when *every* company falls at once. In 2008 there was nowhere in the index to stand. The
ranking faithfully found the twenty companies that had been steadiest through 2006 and 2007 —
and those were banks, insurers and utilities, which then fell hardest of all. This was written
down as the expected failure before the run, and it is exactly what happened.

So the signal works in calm times, where it separates good companies from bad ones, and stops
working in exactly the moment it was hired for. The 18-month version was built to test whether
the measure needed a crash in its memory; it had the steadiest ride of the three and the best
gains-to-losses ratio, but earned less and still fell 42%. Remembering an older crash did not
help predict the next one.

There is a second, quieter problem. The lab re-ran this across four separate stretches of
history, each time choosing the version using only what was known at the time and then scoring it
on years it had never seen. It won 2 of those 4. And over 2009 to 2015 — the years with the best
data and the ones most like today — it earned **2.3 points a year less** than the market. That
matches what three earlier batches found: the long-run advantage was earned before 2009 and has
not been there since.

## Against the lab's near misses

The best drawdown control this lab has ever managed is the calm-company blend, which kept its
worst fall near 14%. That one ranks on how much a share price jiggles day to day, not on how far
it has fallen. This run is the direct test of whether the fall itself is the better measure, and
the answer is no: ranking on the fall gave a 42% fall where ranking on the jiggle gave 14%. A
return comparison between the two is not available here, because that older method was measured
when the lab still assumed a flat 0.1% trading cost, and this one pays Gotrade's real fees;
comparing them on money would let the fee assumption decide the answer instead of the idea. The
shape comparison stands on its own.

All the figures above are in dollars, not rupiah, so none of them are flattered by the rupiah's
fall.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Half of it. The claim that a company's own past fall ranks the cross-section better than nothing
held: the mild beat the deep by 2.1 points and beat plain equal weighting by 2.5. The claim that
this would break the one-for-one trade between return and risk — that it would give a smaller
fall without giving up return — failed outright. The fall was not smaller in any useful sense.
Both halves of the expected failure happened: the pre-crash steady names were financials, and a
fully invested share portfolio had nowhere to hide in 2008.

## My opinion

This direction is finished, and I would not spend another method id on ranking stocks by their
own past fall. Two things kill it, and they are independent. First, it does not do the one job it
was hired for: a 42.5% fall against a 20% bar is not a near miss, it is the wrong kind of answer.
Second, even the part that did work — the genuine 2.1 to 2.5 point advantage over the controls —
is a pre-2009 effect, worth 2.3 points a year *less* than the market in the recent years that
matter most. A variation that tunes the window, the book size or the weighting would be polishing
an edge that is already gone.

The more useful thing this run proved is a negative that applies to the whole lab: the owner's
20% rule is not a stock-picking problem and cannot be solved by choosing better companies. Every
version here, including the deliberately terrible control, fell between 42% and 79%, and the
40-point spread between them in return produced only a 20-point spread in the fall. Choosing
companies moves the return a lot and the fall a little. The fall is set by how much of the money
is in shares at all when the market breaks, which is an exposure question, not a selection one.

So what I would try next is the mechanical fix to the exact thing that broke. A company's own
worst fall mixes two things that should be separated: how much it fell because the whole market
fell, and how much it fell on its own account. In 2008 the first term swamped the second, which
is why the ranking turned to noise precisely when it was needed. The clean version measures only
the second: for each company, how much of the market's *down* days it actually participated in,
over the past year — its downside participation. A company that gives back only half of the
market's bad days is making a different claim from one that merely had a quiet year, and that
claim is about crashes specifically. I have queued that as the next idea. I expect it to earn
less than the market, because books of shock-absorbing companies usually do, and I would rather
learn that cleanly than tune this one further.
methods.verdict: The ranking picked better companies, but the book still fell 42% against a 20% limit: a company's own past fall says nothing about the day every company falls at once.

methods.name: A brake on the account's own fall: trim in proportion to how far the book is below its own high, priced on a plain equal-weight book
methods.sourceRef: Black & Perold (1992), Theory of constant proportion portfolio insurance, JEDC 16(3-4), 403-426; Grossman & Zhou (1993), Optimal investment strategies for controlling drawdowns, Mathematical Finance 3(3), 241-276 -- both reduced here to a proportional dial
methods.hypothesis: The lab has exactly one drawdown machine in service, the market-wide SPY-200 switch, and it is binary: it sells everything on a line crossing and buys everything back on another, which is why it loses in dips that bounce before it can return. A proportional brake has no line to cross. Read the book's own equity curve and hold a fraction of full exposure that falls as the book falls below its own running high -- full exposure at the high, a straight line down to a floor by the time the book is down a set amount, the rest in cash -- so a 4% dip costs a small, quickly restored slice of the book instead of all of it, while a 2008 that keeps grinding lower keeps cutting until little is left. Price it on a deliberately neutral base, an equal-weight book of the 50 most-traded index members with no stock picking at all, so the measurement is of the brake and nothing else, and so the result transfers to every clean book in the lab rather than to one family. The brake reads a gross shadow index of that same book rebuilt from bars, never the funded account, for two reasons: a brake that reads its own braked account is a ratchet that never re-enters, and a deposit-fed account's high is lifted by every top-up, which would make the brake bite for a reason that has nothing to do with the market. Variants: TAPER-20-W and TAPER-30-W (full exposure at the high, all cash by a 20% or 30% book drawdown, read weekly), TAPER-20-M (the same 20% taper read monthly, to price the clock separately from the shape), TAPER-20-W-F50 (the same taper stopping at half exposure rather than cash), and two controls with the brake off, EW-ALL on the monthly clock and EW-ALL-W on the weekly one, so the braked runs are read against a yardstick that pays the same trading costs. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits, the -frac-gotrade presets, which matters here because the brake trades on every move and a 20M IDR book pays a minimum fee per order. Two things were calibrated on the dev window before the variants were fixed, on the unbraked book's exposure and falls alone and never on a braked return: the book holds 50 names rather than 30, because the 30 most-traded names in March 2000 were the dot-coms and that book fell 70% where SPY fell 56%, which is not a neutral base; and the running high is the last year's rather than the last three years', because a three-year high holds the 2000 top against the book all through the 2003-2007 recovery and would lose the best-covered years by construction. Success is a measurement first: state plainly what the brake costs per year over 2009-2015 and what it saves in 2000-2002 and 2008, against the same book unbraked. Eligibility would need a braked book to beat SPY TR on deposit-matched money with a worst fall under 20% and a majority of folds. Assumption recorded before the run: the reserved idea asked for a brake read DAILY, and the book engine cannot do that at a monthly rank cadence -- the two promotable fractional real-fee presets resize monthly and weekly and there is no daily-resize preset -- so weekly is the fastest clock here and a feature wish is journalled for the preset.
methods.expectedFailure: A drawdown brake sells after the fall has already happened and buys back after the recovery has already happened, which is the whipsaw the market switch suffers, only paid continuously instead of occasionally; it may well cost more than it saves. The most likely shape of the result is that the braked books land 1-3 points a year below the controls with a worst fall that is better by less than that, because a V-shaped fall -- 1998, 2010, 2011, and the second half of 2008's rebound -- trims on the way down and is still trimmed on the way up. The weekly clock should make this worse, not better: it reacts sooner and so is wrong sooner, and at 50 slots on a 20M IDR book every re-scale pays Gotrade's fee on fifty $29 orders, about half a point a side, which is why the weekly control exists at all. The second way it fails is quieter: an equal-weight book of the most-traded index members is a bet against SPY's big-company shape even before the brake, and every lab book of that shape lost to a deposit-matched SPY after 2018, so the base itself may trail SPY TR on dev and make the brake's cost academic. The third way is that the shadow index and the real book drift apart -- the shadow is membership-free and gross -- so the brake fires on a drawdown the account did not have; the analysis checks the two against each other rather than assuming they agree.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# M0109 — a brake on the book's own fall

## What was tried

A plain book with no stock picking in it at all: the 50 index members that trade the most money,
held in equal slices, re-chosen once a month. Then one machine on top of it — a **brake**. Every
time the book is checked, we ask how far it sits below its own highest point of the last year. At
the high, the money is fully invested. The further below, the more is moved to cash, in a straight
line, until at a 20% (or 30%) fall the book is entirely in cash. Nothing is sold on a crossing
line; the amount held simply slides up and down with the fall.

Six versions ran. Two are controls with the brake switched off, one on each trading clock, so that
every number below is the brake's own doing and not the cost of trading. All six buy fractional
shares and pay Gotrade's real fees on the owner's real plan: Rp 5,000,000 on the 25th of each
month, 237 deposits between January 1996 and October 2015.

## What happened

Money-weighted return — what the owner's actual deposits would have earned:

| version | the brake | your money earned | worst fall | gains vs losses | 2008 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY, same deposits | — | **+7.2% a year** | — | — | — |
| EW-ALL-W | off (weekly clock) | +7.0% a year | 54.6% | 1.37 | −38.0% |
| EW-ALL | off (monthly clock) | +6.5% a year | 57.2% | 1.31 | −40.3% |
| TAPER-30-W | all cash by a 30% fall | +6.1% a year | 23.9% | 1.56 | −20.3% |
| TAPER-20-M | all cash by a 20% fall, monthly | +5.6% a year | **19.3%** | 1.63 | −14.2% |
| TAPER-20-W-F50 | down to half by a 20% fall | +5.5% a year | 37.4% | 1.33 | −25.7% |
| TAPER-20-W | all cash by a 20% fall, weekly | +5.3% a year | **17.8%** | 1.60 | −12.3% |

**Every version lost to SPY**, so every version is rejected. Two of them — the two 20% tapers —
are the first books in this lab to come through a full twenty years with a worst fall under the
owner's 20% limit, but they bought that by giving up return, and the rule is beat SPY *and* stay
under 20%, not one or the other.

"Gains vs losses" is the profit factor: money made on winning trades divided by money lost on
losing ones. Every braked version is around 1.6, comfortably over the 1.3 the rules ask for. The
unbraked controls sit at 1.31–1.37, barely over.

**Could this be luck?** The lab scores that with a number called DSR — roughly, how likely it is
that a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The owner's bar is 0.90. The best of
these six scores **0.670**, judged against **74** independent looks, which is what the lab's
counting rule resolves to today (one look per distinct method, with a floor for how alike those
methods are). So no: even setting the SPY comparison aside, these results are not strong enough to
rule out luck.

**The worst fall, and when.** Every version's worst stretch began at the same place: the end of
October 2007. The unbraked book bottomed out in February 2009, 50% down. The 20% taper bottomed
out 17% down — but not until **June 2010**, sixteen months after the unbraked book had already hit
its floor and started climbing. That single fact is the whole story of this method, and it is
explained below.

These falls are measured on the book with the deposits taken out. That matters: monthly top-ups
keep refilling a falling account, so a fall always reads gentler than it was if you leave them in.

## What the brake cost and what it saved

This is what the method was built to measure, and it measured it cleanly. Return a year, deposits
removed, by stretch of history:

| stretch | book, no brake | book, 20% taper | brake's effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1996–1999 | +24.4% | +16.8% | **−7.6 points a year** |
| 2000–2002 | −12.5% | −1.1% | **+11.4 points a year** |
| 2003–2007 | +13.1% | +8.6% | −4.5 points a year |
| 2008–2009 | −4.5% | −0.1% | +4.4 points a year |
| 2009–2015 | +16.3% | +6.3% | **−10.0 points a year** |
| whole window | +7.8% | +6.5% | −1.3 points a year |

And the falls over the same stretches: 2000–2002, 45.9% without the brake and 12.9% with it;
2008–2009, 45.9% without and 6.5% with.

Read the bottom row first. **Over twenty years the brake cost 1.3 points a year and cut the worst
fall from 50% to 17%.** Thirty-three points of protection for one and a third points of return is,
on its face, the best risk trade this lab has ever measured. The gentler 30% taper is better still
on that ratio: 0.6 points a year for a fall of 24% instead of 50%.

Now read the rest, because it is the reason this is rejected anyway. The brake's saving is
concentrated entirely in two crashes, and its cost is concentrated entirely in the recoveries and
bull runs between them — **including ten points a year across 2009–2015**, which is the stretch
the lab treats as the first filter, because it is the best-covered in the data and the most like
today. A machine that pays in 2000 and 2008 and bleeds in 2010–2015 is being asked to predict
which of those the next decade looks like. Nobody can.

## Why

A fall-based brake is always late in both directions, and the data put numbers on both halves.

**Late getting out** costs little. By the time the book is 10% down the damage is done, so the
brake does not avoid the first half of a crash. What it does avoid is the second half, and in a
grinding bear — 2000 to 2002, 2007 to 2009 — the second half is most of it. That is why the saving
is so large in exactly those two windows and nowhere else.

**Late getting back in** costs a great deal, and it costs it every time the market dips and
bounces. The brake only restores money as the book climbs back toward its own high of the last
year, which takes months. The 20% taper's worst fall ending in **June 2010** is this exact
mechanism caught in the act: the market bottomed in March 2009 and ran hard for a year, and the
braked book spent that year gradually buying back in at steadily higher prices. It was never down
much — but it was down for a very long time.

2009–2015 was full of dips that bounced: 2010, 2011, the summer of 2015. The unbraked book fell at
most 15% in that whole stretch, which is to say the brake was triggered repeatedly by corrections
that did not need protecting against, and each time it sold low and bought back higher. Ten points
a year is the bill for that.

The half-brake version answers a related question and answers it badly. Stopping the taper at half
exposure instead of cash cost almost as much return (−5.9 points a year in 2009–2015) while
keeping a 37% fall. The trimming happens on the same days either way, so you pay nearly the full
price for a fraction of the protection. If you are going to brake, brake properly.

The clock barely mattered. Reading the brake weekly instead of monthly cost 0.4 points a year and
bought 1.7 points of fall — close to a wash, and the extra trading was small (1,441 trades against
1,349) because exposure is moved in steps of 5% and small wobbles move nothing.

## Did the idea hold, and did it fail the way I said it would

The hypothesis said a proportional brake would avoid the whipsaw a yes/no switch suffers. **Half
right.** It genuinely is gentler — a 4% dip costs a small slice rather than everything — and the
protection it delivers is real and large. But "gentler whipsaw, paid continuously" turned out to
cost about what the violent kind costs, because it is paid on every dip rather than on a few.

Three failures were written down before the run. Two happened:

1. **The brake costs more than it saves in the quiet years.** Predicted 1–3 points a year below
   the controls; actual 1.3 over the full window, so this was called almost exactly. What I did
   not predict was how lopsided it is by era.
2. **The base itself would trail SPY.** It did: the plain most-traded book earned 7.0% a year on
   the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, and 7.8% against 8.9% with the deposits taken out.
   Equal slices of 50 big names is a bet against the market's own big-company shape, and it lost
   that bet — mildly, but it lost it. So the brake was bolted onto something that was already
   behind, which makes its cost academic.

The third did **not** happen, and this is the method's most useful finding. The brake reads a
rebuilt stand-in for the book — priced from prices alone, with no fees, no deposits and no
membership records — rather than the real account, and I expected the two to drift apart and the
brake to fire on falls the account never had. They did not drift. Month to month the stand-in and
the real book move together at a correlation of **0.979**, they earn the identical 7.83% a year
over twenty years, their readings of how far down the book is differ by **1.2 points on average**,
and of the roughly fifty months where either said the book was more than 10% down, they agreed on
forty-eight. The stand-in is a faithful proxy.

## Against the rest of the lab

The lab's only working drawdown machine until now was the market-wide 200-day switch: sell
everything when SPY closes below its 200-day average, buy everything back when it closes above.
This brake protects far better — a 17% worst fall over twenty years, where no trend-switched book
in the lab has come in under 19% — and it does so without ever making an all-or-nothing call.

But it is not competitive on return, and it was never going to be: it is a risk machine, not a
picker. The books closest to passing the lab's rules earn 10–15% a year by choosing stocks well;
this one earns 5–7% by choosing stocks not at all and then standing partly aside. Its best MAR —
return divided by worst fall — is 0.30, against 0.90 for the best blend in the lab. That is the
correct comparison to draw: **the brake fixed the risk and could not create the return**.

No comparison with an older method's recorded numbers is made here, because every variant in this
method paid Gotrade's real fees and the older trials assumed a flat 0.1%; the two are not
comparable without re-running the old one at real fees.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth more trials, and I would spend them on one specific fix rather than on
more tapers.**

The measurement is the asset here, not the method. We now know the exchange rate on this lab's own
data: a proportional fall-brake buys roughly 26 points of worst fall for 0.6 points of return a
year, or 33 points for 1.3. Nothing else in the lab trades that favourably. We also know exactly
where the bill is paid — in dips that bounce — and that is a fixable problem, not an inherent one.

The fix is a **dead zone**. The brake currently starts trimming the moment the book is a fraction
below its high, which means every routine 10% correction triggers it. But the unbraked book's
worst fall across all of 2009–2015 was only 15%. A brake that does nothing at all until the book
is 15% down, and only then tapers to cash by 35%, would have been close to dormant through the
entire 2009–2015 stretch — the ten-point bill largely erased — while still engaging hard in 2000
and 2008, where falls reached 46%. That is the single highest-value variation I can see from this
result and I have queued it.

The second thing worth trying is making the brake **asymmetric**: slow to sell, fast to buy back.
The June 2010 bottom shows that almost all of the recovery cost comes from re-entering on the same
slow dial that governs the exit. Restoring exposure on a short recovery signal instead of waiting
for the year-high to heal attacks the same ten points from the other side. Queued as well.

What I would *not* do is try more taper widths or more clocks on this base. Those dials are now
measured and they behave predictably; the base itself trails SPY, so no setting of them will
produce a winner here. When one of the fixes above works, the brake should be re-priced on a book
that already beats SPY — at which point it stops being a measurement and becomes a candidate.

One honest caveat on all of the above. Two choices in this method — holding 50 names rather than
30, and reading the high over one year rather than three — were made by looking at the dev window
before the variants were fixed. Both were made on the unbraked book's exposure and falls alone,
never on a braked return, and both were made to stop the experiment being degenerate rather than
to find a winner: the 30 most-traded names in March 2000 were the dot-coms and fell 70%, and a
three-year high holds the 2000 peak against the book all through the 2003–2007 recovery. They are
still two choices informed by the answer sheet, and the DSR above does not know about them.
methods.verdict: Cut the worst fall from 50% to 17% for about 1.3 points a year, but gave up 10 points a year in 2009-2015, and the plain book underneath already trailed SPY.

methods.name: Companies that sit out the market's bad days: rank on how much of the market's falls a stock actually joined in
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0108 (own worst twelve-month fall), splitting its signal into a market half and an own-account half; Ang, Chen and Xing (2006), 'Downside Risk', Review of Financial Studies 19(4), 1191-1239 is the published form of the market half
methods.hypothesis: M0108 ranked big index members on their own worst twelve-month fall and the book still fell 42.5%, because that measure mixes two things: how much a stock fell because the whole market fell, and how much it fell on its own account. In 2008 the first term swamped the second, so the rank turned to noise in exactly the moment it was hired for, and the steadiest names through 2006-07 were banks and utilities. This separates the two terms and ranks on each alone. For each F4-screened member, over the past 252 sessions take only the sessions on which SPY closed down, and measure the stock's downside participation: the sum of its returns on those days divided by the sum of SPY's returns on those days. Hold the 20 lowest at 5% each, equal weighted, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, no market switch -- the point is to find out whether shelter can be bought by selection alone, and a switch would confound it. Variants: DP20 and DP40; DP20-UP, which ranks on upside participation minus downside participation, because a stock that simply does nothing in both directions is cash with extra fees; HI20, the paired control holding the 20 highest downside participants, which must fall harder; and IDIO20, which holds the 20 whose *market-model residual* fell least -- M0108's other half, isolated, so the verdict can attribute any result to one term or the other. Success: a DP variant beats SPY TR on deposit-matched money, the control falls visibly harder, AND -- the condition M0108 failed -- the worst fall is materially under the 42% that ranking on the raw fall produced. Even a book that trails SPY but genuinely halves the crash would be the first evidence in this lab that shelter is purchasable by selection.
methods.expectedFailure: Downside participation is close to beta measured on half the sample, and low-beta books trail badly through growth runs, so the likeliest outcome is 2 to 3 points a year below SPY through 2009-2015 with a fall still well over the 25% real-money bar. The published form dates from 2006 and the low-risk anomaly beside it has been crowded since, so even a clean dev-window edge should be expected to fade out of sample. If the fall does not improve on M0108's 42.5% on either half of the split -- neither the market term nor the idiosyncratic one -- that is the decisive evidence that the drawdown bar cannot be reached by stock selection at all, which is worth knowing and should close the whole line rather than spawn another variation of it.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# Can you buy shelter by picking stocks? Now we know the price of it.

## What this run asked

The method before this one bought the twenty big companies whose own share price had fallen
least over the past year. The book still fell 42.5% from its peak, against the owner's 25%
real-money limit. The reason is that "how far did this company fall" adds together two very
different things: the part of the fall that happened because *the whole market* fell, and the
part that was the company's own doing. In 2008 the first part was so large it drowned the
second, so the ranking stopped meaning anything in exactly the month it was hired for.

This run split those two apart and ranked on each one on its own.

* **How much of the market's bad days did this company join in?** Take only the sessions where
  the market closed down over the past year, add up what the stock did on those days, and divide
  by what the market did on the same days. A reading of 0.6 means "when the market fell, this
  name gave back about three fifths of it". Hold the twenty lowest. (Two sizes: twenty names and
  forty.)
* **The reverse**, as a control: hold the twenty that joined in *most*. If the measure is real,
  this book has to fall much harder. If it doesn't, the whole thing is noise.
* **The asymmetry**: most of the market's good days, least of its bad ones. A stock that simply
  does nothing in either direction is cash with extra fees, and the plain shelter ranking cannot
  tell the two apart.
* **The company's own fall, with the market's part stripped out** — the other half of the
  previous method's measure, isolated, so the verdict can say which half (if either) was useful.

Everything is twenty or forty equal slots, re-picked monthly, bought in fractional shares at the
real fees Gotrade charges, always fully invested, with no market-timing switch of any kind. The
point was to find out what stock *selection* alone can do about a crash; a switch would have
muddied the answer.

## The result

On the owner's real saving plan — Rp 5,000,000 on the 25th of every month from January 1996,
237 deposits — against the same deposits put into the market itself. The "worst fall" column is
measured with the deposits taken out, so a monthly top-up refilling a falling account cannot make
any of these look gentler than they were. **The market itself fell 55.2% over this window.**

| What it held | Your money earned | Worst fall | 2008 | Gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The 40 that joined in least of the falls | **+8.1% a year** | **39.9%** | −25.6% | 2.12 |
| The 20 whose own-account path fell least | +7.6% a year | 41.4% | −22.7% | 1.64 |
| The 20 that joined in least of the falls | +7.0% a year | 43.3% | −29.6% | 1.76 |
| The 20 most asymmetric (most ups, fewest downs) | +10.3% a year | **74.0%** | −57.6% | 1.50 |
| The 20 that joined in **most** (the control) | +4.0% a year | **90.6%** | −55.0% | 1.40 |
| The same deposits in the market | +7.2% a year | 55.2% | −36.8% | — |

Three of the five beat the market's +7.2%. None of them passed. All five were rejected.

## The one thing that genuinely worked

The ranking is **not** noise. Line the five books up by how much of the market's falls they were
built to join in, and their worst falls come out in exactly that order: 39.9%, 41.4%, 43.3%,
74.0%, 90.6%. The control — the book deliberately filled with the most market-exposed names —
fell more than twice as far as the sheltered one and earned barely half as much. A measure that
sorts a crash that cleanly, across twenty years, is reading something real.

So the honest finding is not "it didn't work". It is: **selection buys shelter, and here is
exactly how much.** The market fell 55.2%. The best shelter twenty years of hindsight could pick
out of the index fell 39.9%. That is 15 points of the 30 points needed to reach the owner's 25%
limit — about half the distance, and the half that is cheap. The rest is not there to be bought
by choosing names.

Splitting the previous method's measure in two changed almost nothing. Its mixed version fell
42.5%. The market half alone falls 43.3%, the company's own half alone falls 41.4%, and the
wider forty-name version 39.9%. Every one of those lands in the same narrow band. Whatever
stops a long-only book of big American companies from falling less than about 40% in 2008, it
is not something a better ranking can get around: on the day everything falls, everything falls.

## What the shelter costs, and when it is charged

Look at the last seven years of the window, 2009 to 2015 — the best-covered years in the data
and the ones most like today. The market earned +15.0% a year. The sheltered books earned 3 to
6 points a year *less* than that. The two books built out of the most market-exposed names
earned 5 to 8 points a year *more*.

The mechanism is plain once you see it. The companies that fall hardest in the crash are the
same companies that lead the way back out of it. Buying shelter means standing aside for the
recovery, and in this window the recovery was worth far more than the crash cost. Over the full
twenty years the trade looks roughly even — which is how a sheltered book can still show +8.1%
a year against the market's +7.2% — but that evenness is an average over two opposite eras, and
the owner's money lives entirely in the second one.

This is the same pattern the lab has now found several times: a strategy's twenty-year edge was
earned before 2009, and after 2009 it lags.

## The one surprise

The asymmetry book — most of the market's up days, fewest of its down days — earned **+10.3% a
year, 3.1 points clear of the market**, and in 2009-2015 it beat the market by 7.7 points a year,
the best figure in this run by a wide margin. Then it fell 74%.

That is not a shelter signal at all; it is a return signal wearing a shelter signal's clothes.
Dividing a stock's good days by its bad days mostly measures how much it outruns the market
*after* allowing for how much it swings with it — which is a quality worth owning, bought with a
lot of swing. It is the only thing in this run that looks like the start of something, and it is
worth a run of its own behind the market-trend switch that the lab has measured as helping every
one of twenty-two variants it has been tried on.

## Is this luck?

The lab's luck score asks how likely a result is to be real rather than a lucky draw, given how
many distinct strategies have now been tried. The lab is at 84 methods, and the bar the owner set
is 0.90. The best of these five scores **0.655**. The others run from 0.17 to 0.57. Not close —
and that is before the fold test below, which these fail outright.

## The checks that confirm it

**Split the window into four separate stretches and score each one.** The method won **0 of 4**.
Not one stretch. A strategy that wins its twenty-year average and loses every piece of it is a
selection, not an edge.

**Re-run it on fuller price history.** The lab's main price history is missing roughly four in
ten of the companies that actually sat in the index — overwhelmingly the ones that went bankrupt
or were bought, which is a flattering hole. Re-run against the fuller set, all five books earn
less: the best one drops from +8.1% to +7.4% a year, which leaves it just 0.2 points ahead of the
market instead of 0.9, and its worst fall deepens from 39.9% to 42.3%. The thin win was mostly
the missing dead companies. The control's fall deepens to 97.0% and its return goes negative.

## Did the hypothesis hold? Did the expected failure happen?

The hypothesis failed on the condition it set itself. It asked for a sheltered book that beat the
market *and* fell materially less than the previous method's 42.5%. The forty-name version beat
the market by 0.9 points a year and fell 39.9% — 2.6 points better, where 15 points were needed.
That is not material; it is the same answer with a wider book.

The expected failure, written before the run, said the likeliest outcome was "2 to 3 points a
year below the market through 2009-2015 with a fall still well over the 25% bar". The real
figures are 3.0 to 5.8 points a year below, with falls of 39.9% to 43.3%. It happened, slightly
worse than predicted. The control working as designed was also predicted, and did.

The pre-registration named a sixth version that was dropped before the run: the same twenty
names weighted by how heavily each trades, rather than equally. Another method measured exactly
that an hour earlier, across three different parent strategies, and found it costs about a point
of return a year every time. Re-measuring a settled number would have wasted the slot, so it went
to the own-account-fall version instead, which is what made the attribution above possible.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and I would close it rather than vary it. Two methods have now asked
whether a long-only book of big American companies can be kept under the owner's fall limit by
choosing better names, and the answer has come back the same way twice, from four different
angles: the best shelter available in the whole index is a 40% fall. Selection takes you from
55% to 40% and stops. The remaining 15 points are not a ranking problem; they are the simple fact
that in a real crash the correlation between every large company goes to one, and a book that is
always fully invested has nowhere to stand. The only tools that can close that last gap are the
ones that reduce how much is invested — a market switch, a cash sleeve, or a brake on the book's
own fall — and those are separate lines the lab already has open.

I would also stop treating low-risk selection as free. This run put a number on it: every point
of shelter was paid for with 3 to 6 points a year of lost recovery in the one era that most
resembles today. Any future method that reaches for a calm, low-swing or low-fall screen should
be made to show it is *not* buying that trade again.

What I would actually run next is the asymmetry book, which arrived in this run as a side effect
and is the only genuinely new thing in it: it beat the market by 3.1 points a year over twenty
years and by 7.7 points a year in 2009-2015, which is the opposite of everything else in this
lab's record, and its single defect — a 74% fall — is precisely the defect the market-trend
switch is measured to fix. I have queued it, together with a smaller idea that uses this run's
one durable finding properly: the market-participation measure is a good *exclusion screen*, not
a good ranking, so the thing to do with it is drop the most exposed quarter of an existing
book and see whether the fall moves without the return moving.
methods.verdict: Picking shelter works and is not enough: the market fell 55%, the best-sheltered book 40%, the most-exposed 91% — and every point of shelter cost 3 to 6 points a year of lost recovery after 2009.

methods.name: The lab's best book, weighted the way the market weights: does equal slots cost it the point and a half M0108 measured?
methods.hypothesis: M0108's EW40-DV yardstick was put in to separate a drawdown rank from plain equal weighting, and it answered a different and bigger question by accident: equal money across the 40 most-traded big index members earned 5.8% a year on the owner's deposits where SPY TR earned 7.2%, and fell 62% from its peak. So equal weighting the big names cost about 1.4 points a year and roughly doubled the crash damage over 1996-2015. Every stock-picking book in this lab uses equal slots, which means every one of them carries that handicap and has to earn it back before it is level with doing nothing. This measures the handicap where it matters, on a book that actually wins rather than on a neutral slice. Take the residual-momentum book at real fees (M0032's configuration, the realistic twin of the lab's long-standing near miss) and change one thing only: distribute the money across the chosen names in proportion to each name's 20-day average dollar volume instead of equally, so the book is shaped more like the market and less like a bet on the smaller members. Variants: DV-WEIGHT (dollar-volume proportional), DV-CAPPED (the same, with no single name above 15% so one giant cannot become the book), SQRT-DV (proportional to the square root of dollar volume, a half-step between equal and market-shaped, which is the usual compromise), and EQ (the unchanged equal-weight book re-run in the same batch, so the comparison is like for like at identical fees rather than against a recorded trial). Success: a weighted variant beats the equal-weight twin on deposit-matched money, and the whole set says plainly how large the equal-weighting handicap is inside a winning book. Expected failure: dollar volume is not market value, it is trading activity, and the most heavily traded names are often the most contested rather than the largest, so the weighting may tilt toward volatile giants and deepen the fall instead of shallowing it. The near-miss books also earn part of their edge from the smaller index members (insight 91), in which case market-shaping them will trade return away for a steadier ride and land in the same one-for-one trap every risk filter in this lab has fallen into.

methods.name: The residual-momentum book braked one stock at a time: each holding sold under its own 200-day average, with no market-wide switch
methods.hypothesis: M0107 found that a per-stock trend exit is a strictly better brake than the market-wide SPY-200 switch: on the calm big-raiser book it cut the worst fall from 26.3% to 13.1%, held 2008 to -5.3% where SPY lost 34.8%, cost about 0.9 points a year, and once it was in place the old market switch added nothing at all (identical 13.1% worst fall with both rules running, -0.2 points a year for the extra switch). It is therefore a substitute for the switch, not a complement. M0107 also proved, with a paired same-exposure arm, that the exit adds nothing as a stock picker - all of its value is holding less money during falls. But M0107 could not show the brake's worth, because the book it braked had no edge: strip the parked SPY out of the big-raiser book and the picks lose to SPY in every era. This idea puts the brake on a book that does have an edge. The residual-momentum books are the lab's closest misses and they fail, or nearly fail, on exactly the thing the brake fixes: M0007-N20-RAW earns +15.0% a year against SPY's +7.9% with a 19.6% worst fall that becomes 23.5% once dead companies are put back, and M0020-W-NOSTOP +15.3% at 19.3%. Take M0022-W-TV14's or M0007-N20-RAW's configuration verbatim, delete the SPY-200 switch, and refuse to hold any individual name trading at or below the mean of its own last 200 closes, the freed slot weight going to cash. Variants should include the host unchanged as a paired control, the per-stock exit alone, both brakes together, and at least one faster average (100 sessions) because a 200-day average on a momentum name is slow relative to a monthly re-pick. Everything fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits. Success: the worst fall falls under 15% while the lead over SPY stays above 3 points a year, the 2009-2015 edge stays positive, and a majority of the walk-forward folds are won - which would be the first method in the lab to clear the buy signal. Expected failure: momentum names are jumpy by construction and cross their own 200-day average far more often than dividend raisers do, so the whipsaw bill at Gotrade's real fees on 5% slots could be several times the 0.9 points M0107 paid; and the exit may simply sell the winners that make momentum work, cutting the return by more than it cuts the fall, which is the failure M0059 already found when it dropped the stocks that swing most with the market.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

### 2026-10-12 — Sera 20261012-0832, coordinator decision: do not run this as written

The brake is the right idea on the wrong host. M0112 is filed under family
`stock-residual-momentum` with parent M0022, and M0022 reads test-failed, so the hard gate's kin
walk refuses it on two separate grounds at once — same family, and an ancestor through
`parent_id` — before any number it produces is looked at. A residual-momentum book would also
almost certainly trip the behaviour test (D14): M0007-N20-RAW already moves with M0022's tested
variant at 0.98 residual correlation, and a braked version of the same picks will move with it
too. So this is not the lab's best live shot at the buy signal; it is the one shot that cannot
clear it however well it scores, and running it would spend a slot to learn a number nobody is
allowed to act on.

What survives is the question underneath it, and M0107 sharpened it. The per-stock 200-day exit
is the best drawdown machine the lab has found: it took the calm raiser book from a 26.3% worst
fall to 13.1%, turned 2008 from −14.3% into −5.3%, cost about 0.9 points a year, and made the
market-wide switch redundant rather than complementary (BOTH leaves the worst fall identical at
13.1% and costs a further 0.2 points a year — substitutes, not complements).

It needs a host with a real picking edge. The trouble is that the only books in this lab with a
demonstrated picking edge are the momentum and residual-momentum families, and every one of them
is kin-blocked; while the kin-clean books that looked like they had an edge turn out, after
M0107, to have been earning it from parked SPY rather than from their picks. Finding a clean book
whose *picks* beat SPY is now the lab's binding problem, and it is a bigger one than the drawdown
rule the brake solves. The next method to carry this brake must be a book with no test-failed kin
whose picks, held naked — no parked SPY, no gate — already beat SPY on their own. The honest
first step is to find one, not to bolt the brake onto a book the gate has already closed.

methods.name: Slow to leave, quick to return: keep the 200-day exit and vary only how fast the safety rule buys back
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0084 (the safety switch priced on its own, SPY only)
methods.hypothesis: The moving-average switch is old -- published 1992 (the banded rule) and 2007 (Faber's 10-month version) -- so nothing here is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies to it; what is new is which HALF of it is being paid for. M0084 priced the switch alone and found its whole 22-year advantage is sitting out 2001, 2002 and 2008, paid for everywhere else: it lost 18 points in 2009 alone and 10 points in 2003, both times because the same slow 200-day average that correctly got it out kept it out through the recovery, and in 2009-2015 every reading of it lost 6 to 11 points a year to simply holding SPY. The exit is the good half; the return is the expensive half. So hold the exit fixed -- at the monthly check, SPY's close under its 200-day average goes to cash, f_factor.trend_on unchanged -- and move ONLY the trigger that buys back. Frame: SPY only at full weight, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, the same 253-bar lookback as M0084, so every variant is scored on the same sessions and the paired difference against M0084-MONTHLY (+9.1% a year funded, 18.9% worst fall, 11 trades, de-funded +10.7% in 2009-2015 against SPY's +16.6%) is the buy-back trigger alone. The asymmetry is expressed through the held set: the exit rule is applied only while SPY is held, the entry rule only while it is not. Six buy-backs, all read from SPY's own closes with no new data: SMA200 (the control, which must reproduce M0084-MONTHLY's 11 trades and 18.9% fall under this allocator id, or the machinery is wrong); SMA50 and SMA20 (back in above the 50-day or 20-day average while still under the 200-day one); UP63 (back in when the 63-session return is positive); HIGH20 (back in at a 20-session high); and SMA50-W, the asymmetric CADENCE -- the 50-day trigger read WEEKLY while the exit is gated to one check a month, the one place where reading more often might pay, since M0084 showed weekly reading is destructive only when it also causes selling. SUCCESS: a variant that keeps the 2001, 2002 and 2008 exits, keeps the worst fall inside the bars in force, and closes at least half of M0084-MONTHLY's 5.9-point 2009-2015 gap to SPY. Eligibility is not expected -- a 100%-SPY book cannot beat SPY except by sidestepping crashes for more than whipsaw costs, and the trade counts will be far under 100 -- so the paired differences are the result. Note the window starts 1994-01-28 here, not the usual 1996-01-03, so compare only with M0084's numbers. Note also that the drawdown bars moved on 2026-10-14: the dev screen is 50% and the real-money bar 25%, where the idea row was written against the old 20%.
methods.expectedFailure: The obvious way this fails is whipsaw, and it is designed in: an entry that fires above the 50-day or 20-day average, or at a 20-session high, can fire while SPY is still well under its 200-day average -- which is precisely a bear-market bounce. The book then buys back into 2001, 2002 or 2008, the next monthly check sees it still under the 200-day line and sells again, and the variant pays the fall it was supposed to sit out plus the fees. SMA20 and HIGH20 are the most exposed; UP63 is the most protected, because a positive 63-session return is hard to produce inside a crash, and it may therefore buy back barely sooner than the control and recover nothing. The likeliest overall outcome is that the fast triggers trade the 2009 recovery gap for a deeper 2008 fall -- better in the era most like today, worse exactly where the switch earns its keep -- which would mean the switch's two halves cannot be separated and the lab should stop trying. Trade counts stay tiny (tens over 22 years), so profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless here and no variant will clear the luck bar at N=82; the funded return, the worst fall and the 2009-2015 era split are the only readable numbers. SMA50-W carries one extra risk the others do not: its monthly exit check is an approximation -- the weekly check whose data date lands in the last seven calendar days of its month -- so a holiday-shifted month can give it two exit checks or none, and its flip count should be read against the control's before anything else about it is believed. Not modelled anywhere: interest on the cash held while the switch is off, which flatters SPY and penalises every switched variant, so every gap reported here is an upper bound on the switch's cost.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

## The question

Half the strategies in this lab carry the same safety rule: **when the S&P 500 tracker (SPY)
closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything and sit in cash;
when it closes back above, buy again.**

Last week's test of that rule on its own (the "price the safety switch" run) found something
uncomfortable. The rule's entire twenty-two-year advantage is the three falls it sits out —
2001, 2002 and 2008. It pays for them everywhere else, and it pays most heavily right after a
crash: in 2009 it made 21.5% while simply holding SPY made far more, because **the same slow
average that correctly got it out kept it out through the recovery**. Over 2009–2015 — the
stretch of history most like today — every reading of it lost between 6 and 11 points a year to
just holding SPY.

So the rule has two halves. The **exit** is the good half. The **way back in** is the expensive
half. This test freezes the exit and changes nothing but the trigger that buys back.

Everything else is held identical to the earlier test on purpose: hold **nothing but SPY**, at
full weight, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, starting with 10 million rupiah and
adding 5 million on the 25th of every month — 260 deposits, about $162,000 of real money put in
between 1994 and 2015. The exit is byte-for-byte the same rule in all six versions. Returns are
measured in dollars, so the rupiah's long slide adds nothing to any number here.

Six ways back in, all fixed before any result was seen, all read from SPY's own price history:

- **SMA200** — the control. The buy-back is the same test as the exit, so this *is* the old
  symmetric rule. It had to reproduce the earlier run exactly, or the machinery would be wrong.
- **SMA50** — back in when SPY closes above its 50-day average, while still below the 200-day one.
- **SMA20** — the same, but the 20-day average. The fastest trigger.
- **UP63** — back in when SPY's return over the last quarter (63 trading days) turns positive.
- **HIGH20** — back in when SPY closes at its highest in 20 sessions.
- **SMA50-W** — the 50-day trigger checked **weekly** while the exit stays once a month. The one
  place where looking more often might pay, since the earlier test showed frequent checking is
  destructive only when it also causes *selling*.

**The control reproduced the earlier run exactly** — same 11 in-and-outs, same 18.9% worst fall,
same total return to the last decimal. The machinery is sound, so every difference below is the
buy-back trigger and nothing else.

## What happened

SPY itself, dividends included, on the same deposits: **+7.7% a year.**

| way back in | your money per year | worst fall | times in and out | 2009–2015 a year | behind SPY then |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMA200 (the control) | +9.1% | 18.9% | 11 | +10.7% | −5.9 pts |
| **UP63 (last quarter positive)** | **+9.7%** | **20.7%** | 18 | **+12.6%** | **−4.0 pts** |
| SMA50 | +8.1% | 25.3% | 24 | +11.8% | −4.8 pts |
| SMA20 | +7.9% | 29.6% | 30 | +11.8% | −4.8 pts |
| SMA50-W (weekly checking) | +7.9% | 35.6% | 43 | +12.4% | −4.2 pts |
| HIGH20 | +6.4% | 27.1% | 12 | +6.8% | −9.8 pts |

("Worst fall" is the deepest drop from a previous high. The 2009–2015 column has the monthly
deposits stripped out first, so a top-up is never mistaken for a gain; SPY made +16.6% a year
over that stretch on the same basis.)

**One version beat the control on both counts that matter.** UP63 — buy back when SPY's last
quarter is up — earned **+9.7% a year on the owner's deposits against the control's +9.1% and
SPY's +7.7%**, and in 2009–2015 it made +12.6% a year where the control made +10.7%. Its worst
fall in that modern stretch was 10.1%, slightly *shallower* than the control's 10.4%, so the
extra return was not bought with extra risk.

## Why — the mechanism, year by year

This is the table that explains everything. Each number is that calendar year's return with the
deposits removed.

| year | SMA200 | SMA50 | SMA20 | **UP63** | HIGH20 | SMA50-W |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2001 | 0.0% | −8.8% | −15.2% | **−2.8%** | +0.4% | −6.0% |
| 2002 | 0.0% | +1.6% | +9.3% | **+5.0%** | 0.0% | −5.8% |
| 2003 | +22.0% | +22.1% | +22.0% | **+17.8%** | +15.1% | +13.3% |
| 2008 | −0.0% | −10.7% | −9.1% | **+0.5%** | −0.0% | −1.1% |
| 2009 | +21.5% | +19.7% | +19.7% | **+29.3%** | +19.7% | +18.4% |
| 2010 | +6.7% | +1.2% | +1.2% | **+6.8%** | −2.7% | +5.8% |

Read 2008 and 2009 together and the whole result is there.

**The price-level triggers bought their 2009 improvement with the crashes.** SMA50 and SMA20 say
"come back when the price is above a short average". In a crash the price bounces above short
averages constantly — that is what a bear-market rally *is*. So they bought back into the middle
of 2008 and lost 10.7% and 9.1% in a year the control sat out for nothing, and into 2001 for
−8.8% and −15.2%. Their worst falls went from 18.9% to 25.3% and 29.6%. They did improve
2009–2015 by about a point a year, and they paid for it several times over.

**The quarter-return trigger did not.** Asking for a *positive three-month return* is a different
question from asking whether the price is above a line. Inside a real crash the last quarter is
almost never up, so UP63 stayed out: it lost nothing in 2008 (+0.5%) and almost nothing in 2001
(−2.8%). But once a bottom is actually behind you, a quarter turns positive long before a
200-day average does — which is why UP63 made **+29.3% in 2009 against the control's +21.5%**,
nearly eight points of pure recovery the control slept through. It gave some back in 2003
(+17.8% against +22.0%), and some in the 1990s, but its wins land late in the window where the
account is large and its losses land early where it is small — so on the owner's actual deposits
the gap is wider (+0.6 points a year) than on the raw curve (+0.2 points).

**HIGH20 is the experiment running the other way, and it is the most useful number here.** A
20-session high is *harder* to reach after a long fall than a 200-day average crossing, so
HIGH20 is not a faster trigger at all — it is a **slower** one. It cost 2.7 points a year against
the control, fell 27.1% at worst, and in 2009–2015 made 6.8% a year against SPY's 16.6% — nearly
ten points behind. Slowing the way back in is strictly worse. That brackets the finding from
both sides: the lag is real and it is expensive.

**Checking weekly failed badly.** SMA50-W traded 43 times — four times the control — and fell
35.6% at worst, the deepest of all six. Looking more often only gave the price-level trigger more
chances to fire inside a bear rally, and a once-a-month exit could not undo them fast enough. The
earlier run's lesson ("frequent checking hurts when it causes selling") does not flip just
because the frequent part is buying.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Partly, and it falls short of its own bar.** It was written in advance that a success meant a
version that (a) keeps the 2001, 2002 and 2008 exits, (b) keeps the worst fall inside the bars in
force, and (c) closes **at least half** of the control's 5.9-point gap to SPY in 2009–2015.

UP63 clears (a) and (b): it sat out 2008 completely, sat out most of 2001, and fell 20.7% at
worst, inside today's 25% real-money limit and well inside the 50% development screen. It **fails
(c)**: it closed 1.9 points of the 5.9-point gap — a third, not a half — and is still 4 points a
year behind simply holding SPY in the years most like today.

The expected failure was written down too, and it happened exactly as predicted: whipsaw. SMA20
and SMA50-W were named in advance as the most exposed, and they were. UP63 was named as the most
protected, and it was. What was *not* predicted is that the protection would come free — the
pre-written guess was that UP63 would be so cautious it recovered nothing, and instead it
recovered the most.

## The honest limits

**No version here can ever be approved for money, and none was ever going to be.** A book holding
only SPY trades a handful of times a decade: the best version made 18 in-and-outs in 22 years
against the 100 closed trades the owner's rules require, so every version failed on trade count
alone, and the method is recorded as rejected. That was stated before the run. **This is a
measurement of a frame that other strategies sit behind, not a candidate.**

**The luck test.** UP63 scored 0.874 on the deflated Sharpe — the lab's measure of how likely a
result is real rather than a lucky draw after many tries — against a bar of 0.90, judged at
N=83, meaning 83 distinct methods have been looked at in this lab. It misses, as does the
control at 0.877. With 18 trades that test is in any case reading a very thin record.

**It loses the out-of-sample folds.** Scored on four rolling windows rather than one long
average, this method won 1 of 4. A result that wins its twenty-year average and loses the folds
is a selection, not an edge — and the one fold it won was 2006–2008, which is precisely the
crash the exit is good at. That is consistent with everything above and it is a warning.

**Every version pays only in narrow markets.** Split by whether the index beat the average of its
own members, all six earn their keep in narrow months and *lose* in broad ones (UP63: +5.5% narrow,
−0.6% broad). This frame is a bet on the market's shape as much as on timing.

**The survivorship cross-check is a clean no-op here**, as it should be: this book never holds an
individual company, so re-running it on the history that includes dead companies changes nothing,
to the decimal. That is a useful confirmation that the cross-check does what it claims.

**Not modelled:** interest on the cash held while the rule is out of the market. In the 1990s and
2000s US cash paid 3–5% a year, so every gap reported here is an upper bound on what sitting out
really cost.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth more trials, and I would spend the next one immediately — but not on a
SPY-only book.**

The finding is real and it is narrow: *the way back in matters, the trigger has to be a
