realised-recovery test rather than a price-above-a-line test, and about a third of the safety
rule's post-2009 cost can be recovered for free.* Two points a year over SPY, with a shallower
fall in the modern stretch, on a change of one rule, is the best result this frame has produced.
The three failing versions make the mechanism unambiguous rather than muddying it, and HIGH20
accidentally proved the converse.

But a book holding only SPY cannot be approved for money no matter how good it looks, so
measuring it further is measuring for its own sake. **The payoff is elsewhere.** Roughly half the
strategies in this lab sit behind this exact rule, and the lab has already established that the
rule cannot simply be switched off: every version tried without it was worse on return *and* on
depth of fall at the same time. So the rule stays — but until now nobody had asked whether it
could *come back faster*. It can.

So the next trial I would run is the obvious one: take the strongest book the lab currently has —
the near-miss momentum and blend books re-measured on the fixed tape, which beat SPY by four and a
half points a year and already clear the trade count — and change exactly one thing: let them buy
back when the last quarter is positive instead of waiting for the 200-day average. If the two
points a year survive on top of real stock picks, that is a change to a frame half the lab shares,
and it arrives on a book that *can* qualify for money. If it does not survive, then the frame's
cost is already absorbed by the picks and we have learned where the ceiling is. Either answer is
worth the id. I have queued it, along with a second idea that attacks the same whipsaw from a
different angle: come back **halfway** on the quarter-return signal and the rest only once the
200-day average is reclaimed, so a false start costs half as much.

What I would not do is sweep the 63-day window for a better number. There is nothing here that
says 63 is special, and tuning it on the same twenty years is how a measurement turns into a
story about itself.
methods.verdict: The way back in is worth about two points a year: buying back when SPY's last quarter turns positive beat the 200-day rule on return and on depth of fall, while every price-above-a-line trigger bought its recovery by re-entering mid-crash

methods.name: Re-frame the one book that was measuring its frame: the earnings-and-dividend pair book on the monthly switch
methods.hypothesis: M0084 showed the safety switch's cost scales with how much of the money the switch itself is holding: 4.7 points a year when the book is nothing but SPY, about 0.5-1.0 points when the book is twenty stock picks (the late-declaration book's own M-vs-W pair, the only other clean cadence test in the lab). M0078 is the one shelved book that sits at the expensive end. Its own analysis recorded that JOINT-ANN held an average of 1.6 stock names, so 90% or more of the money sat in SPY behind a WEEKLY switch -- and its literal control arm JOINT-EX, almost pure SPY behind that switch, earned +3.9% a year against +7.2% for SPY. That book was measuring its frame, not its signal, and its rejection is not safe. Re-register M0078's six variants unchanged except for the rank cadence: monthly-hold-frac-gotrade instead of weekly-hold-frac-gotrade, everything else byte-identical (M0063's event, F4's screen and SPY-200 switch, 20 slots at 5%, 60-session hold, raise window, announce/ex arms). Expected from M0084's price list: the frame alone should return roughly 4 points a year to the arms that are mostly parked in SPY and much less to the arms that actually hold stocks, so JOINT-ANN and JOINT-EX should gain most and RAISE-ANN least -- and if JOINT-ANN still fails to beat RAISE-ANN and the jump-alone baseline once the frame is fixed, the corroboration idea is dead on its merits rather than on its cadence, which is the question M0078 could not answer. Also check the worst fall: M0084 found the monthly reading fell 18.9% where the weekly fell 33.1%, and M0078's six variants all breached 28%. Do NOT run this as a general batch re-frame of every weekly book; M0084's correction insight explains why that would be a waste.

methods.name: The dead-zone brake: ignore every fall under 15%, then taper hard
methods.hypothesis: M0109 measured the exchange rate on a proportional drawdown brake precisely -- 26 points of worst fall for 0.6 points of return a year at the 30% taper, 33 points for 1.3 at the 20% -- and measured exactly where the bill is paid: 10 points a year across 2009-2015, against 7.6 in 1996-1999 and 4.5 in 2003-2007, with the whole saving banked in 2000-2002 (+11.4) and 2008-2009 (+4.4). The cost is routine corrections, not crashes: the unbraked book's worst fall across all of 2009-2015 was 15.1%, so every trim in that stretch was a response to a dip that bounced, sold low and bought back higher. A dead zone removes that class of trade entirely. Exposure stays at 1 while the shadow book is less than  below its one-year high, then tapers in a straight line to cash by . With start = 0.15 the brake would have been close to dormant through 2009-2015 while still engaging hard in 2000-2002 and 2008-2009, where the falls reached 46%. Variants: START15-T35 and START15-T45 (dormant to 15% down, cash by 35% or 45%), START10-T30, START20-T40, and EW-ALL-W re-run is unnecessary -- M0109's recorded controls on the same store and preset are the yardstick, and the method must carry its own control anyway, so CTRL (start = 1, brake off) reproduces it. Same base as M0109, unchanged, so the comparison is clean: 50 most-traded index members, equal weight, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, monthly rank with weekly resize. Success is first a measurement: does a dead zone cut the 2009-2015 cost from 10 points a year to under 3 while keeping most of the 2000-2002 and 2008-2009 saving? If it does, the brake becomes a tool worth bolting onto a book that beats SPY, which M0109's base did not.

methods.name: Slow to sell, fast to buy back: an asymmetric fall brake
methods.hypothesis: M0109's cost is almost entirely re-entry, not exit. Its 20% taper's worst stretch ran from October 2007 to a trough in June 2010 -- sixteen months after the unbraked book had bottomed in February 2009 -- because exposure is restored on the same dial that governs the exit, so the money only comes back as the book climbs toward its own one-year high, which takes months of a rally. Being late to sell costs little: by the time a book is 10% down the first half of the fall is already paid, which is why the brake's saving in the two bears was so large. Being late to buy costs a great deal and costs it on every dip that bounces. This makes the dial asymmetric: the trim is M0109's straight-line taper, unchanged, but exposure is restored on a separate, faster recovery reading -- the shadow book back above its own high of the last  sessions (63 or 42), at which point exposure steps back to full rather than waiting for the year-high to heal. Variants: REC63, REC42, REC21, a half-step version that restores to 0.5 on the recovery signal and to full only on the year-high, and CTRL (M0109's symmetric 20% taper reproduced under this wrapper, the only fair baseline since a recorded trial's returns are not reproducible across store rebuilds). Same base and preset as M0109. Expected failure: a fast re-entry reading is a momentum signal in disguise and will buy back into the false rallies of 2001 and late 2008, giving back the saving that justified the brake; the useful output either way is the split between what the slow exit earns and what the slow re-entry costs, which M0109 could not separate.

methods.name: Leave out the newly added: an index book that skips members the index only just bought
methods.sourceRef: Greenwood & Sammon, The Disappearing Index Effect (HBS working paper 23-025); Vijh & Wang, Index Additions and Operating Performance, Financial Management 2022
methods.hypothesis: The lab has never used the one piece of data it already holds and nothing else mines: the point-in-time membership calendar, which says exactly when each company joined the index. Greenwood and Sammon (2023) and Vijh and Wang (2022) report that a company added to a big index arrives after a run-up driven by index funds having to buy it and then gives it back -- about -0.8% abnormal five days after and -1.4% a month after, across 450 additions since 2000 -- and that additions underperform matched peers on profitability for three years. So the test is an exclusion, not a pick: hold the 50 most heavily traded index members at 2% each, rebalanced monthly, but leave out any company whose membership began within the last N months, and let the money go to the next most traded member instead. Variants sweep N over 6, 12, 24 and 36 months against C, the identical book with no exclusion; C and SPY are both the yardstick, and because treatment and control differ only in the excluded names, the gap between them is the whole of the measurement. Two honesty requirements were fixed before the run. First, the store serves 539 of about 1,061 requested members and the ones it cannot serve are disproportionately the companies that were deleted, so any tenure-based book is survivorship-flattered by construction: lab survivorship is to be run on the result and reported, and the exclusion framing was chosen over a tenure ranking because dropping the new is far less sensitive to who is missing than keeping the old. Second, the two snapshot files begin in January 1996 and February 2007 and every symbol in a first row appears to start there, so a start date shared by 20 or more symbols is treated as the data's first sight rather than an addition and is never excluded. The signal is structural with no price term in it at all, so it should move very little with the momentum, blend and dividend books that have already lost their test look. Success: a tenure variant beats C and beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under 20%, and beats SPY in 2009-2015 as well as whole-window. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade and the owner's monthly deposits.
methods.expectedFailure: Two failures are more likely than success. The first is that the exclusion is simply too small to matter: measured before the run, at 50 names a 12-month exclusion changes the book in 76% of months and removes 1.3 names of 50 on average, so even a two-point-a-year drag on the excluded names moves the book by well under a tenth of a point a year, which no DSR at an N in the hundreds will ever call real. The second is that the base book loses regardless. Fifty equal 2% slots among index members is an equal-weight large-cap book, and insight 91 is that SPY's big-company drift beat every such book after 2018; the exclusion is an overlay on that base and cannot rescue it. The anomaly is also exactly the kind the lab's own lesson warns about: Greenwood and Sammon's title is that the index effect has been *disappearing*, and they date the fade to the 2000s, so the dev window ending in 2015 may show an edge that was already gone before the owner could trade it -- if an edge shows at all it should be visibly weaker in 2009-2015 than before 2009. Mechanically, monthly rebalancing of a 50-name book at the fee minimum on small early slots is a real drag, and the longer exclusions (24 and 36 months) throw out enough of the book that they start to be a bet on old companies, which is the survivorship-flattered direction the design was chosen to avoid.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# M0117 — Leave out the newly added

## What was tried

When a company is added to the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100, every index fund in the world has to
buy it, on the same day, whatever the price. Two pieces of research say that forced buying pushes
the price up into the addition and that the company gives it back afterwards, and that these
companies tend to be picked at a high point in their business that they do not hold.

So this was not a way of picking stocks. It was a way of *not* picking one. The book holds the 50
most heavily traded companies in the index, 2% in each, re-chosen once a month. The only question
asked was: if you simply leave out the companies the index bought recently, and put that money in
the next most heavily traded company instead, do you end up better off? Four waiting periods were
tried — leave out anything added in the last 6, 12, 24 or 36 months — against a fifth version that
leaves out nobody. Everything else about the five is identical, so any difference between them is
the exclusion and nothing else.

This is the first thing in the lab that reads only the index's own joining dates. There is no
price signal in it anywhere.

## The result

**All five lost to simply buying SPY, and all five fell far too far. Rejected.**

Taking the money the way the owner actually invests it — a lump at the start and 5 million rupiah
on the 25th of every month, 237 deposits in all:

| Version | What the money earned a year | SPY with the same deposits | Worst fall | Gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Leave out nobody | +6.5% | +7.2% | 57.2% | 1.31 |
| Leave out the last 6 months | +6.5% | +7.2% | 57.4% | 1.35 |
| **Leave out the last 12 months** | **+6.7%** | +7.2% | 57.3% | 1.39 |
| Leave out the last 24 months | +6.4% | +7.2% | 57.6% | 1.35 |
| Leave out the last 36 months | +6.2% | +7.2% | 57.3% | 1.28 |

Three conditions failed, and not narrowly:

- **Beat SPY**: the best version earned 6.7% a year where the same deposits in SPY earned 7.2%.
  It lost by half a point a year, every year, for twenty years.
- **Worst fall under 20%**: every version lost about 57% from its peak, nearly three times the
  limit. That fall is measured properly, on the book alone with the monthly deposits stripped
  out, so it is not flattered by fresh money arriving. It happened where you would expect: 2008,
  when each version lost about 40% in the calendar year alone.
- **Luck**: the best version scored 0.41 where the bar is 0.90. That score asks how likely it is
  that a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab has now looked at 77 distinct
  methods, and against 77 tries a half-point-a-year shortfall is not evidence of anything at all.
  A score of 0.41 means: this could very easily be noise, and it is noise pointing the wrong way.

The longest wait, 36 months, also failed the gains-versus-losses condition at 1.28 against a bar
of 1.30.

## Did the idea itself work?

Here is the part worth keeping. **The exclusion did help, in the direction and on the timetable
the research predicted — it was just far too small to matter.**

The five results trace a clear arch. Leaving out nobody earns 6.5%. Waiting 6 months earns 6.5%,
waiting 12 months earns 6.7%, and then it falls away again: 6.4% at 24 months and 6.2% at 36. The
peak is exactly where the research says the effect lives — in the first year after a company
joins — and the decline after it is what you would expect if you keep excluding companies long
after they have stopped being new.

I measured the companies themselves rather than only the book. Over the 166 months in which the
top-50 list contained both kinds of company, the ones added within the previous 12 months went on
to earn about 5.6 percentage points a year less than the rest of the book. That is a real-looking
gap and it matches the research closely.

But two things kill it.

**First, it almost never applies to enough of the book.** On average only 1.3 of the 50 holdings
were recently added — about 2.6% of the money. A 5.6-point drag on 2.6% of the book is a gain of
about 0.15 of a percentage point a year, which is almost exactly the 0.2 point the book actually
gained. The arithmetic is consistent, which is reassuring about the measurement and fatal to the
idea. The index does not add companies fast enough, or heavily traded enough, for avoiding them to
be worth anything.

**Second, the gap is not statistically distinguishable from nothing.** One or two companies a
month is a tiny sample, and the 5.6-point gap carries a confidence score of about 0.4, where
roughly 2 would be needed to take it seriously. It is the right shape, measured honestly, and it
could still be an accident.

The arch also explains itself in the data. At the 24- and 36-month waits, the recently-added group
actually *beat* the rest of the book in the 2009–2015 years, by 6.7 and 14.5 points a year. In
other words: companies are a drag in their first year in the index and winners by their third.
Excluding them for three years means throwing away the winners, which is why the longest wait was
the worst of the five.

## Where the real loss came from

Not from the exclusion. From the book underneath it.

Holding 50 big companies in equal 2% slots is a bet that the index's smaller members will do as
well as its giants. Over this window they did not. The version that excludes nobody earned 6.5% a
year where SPY earned 7.2% on the same deposits, and fell 57% doing it. The exclusion was an
overlay on a losing book, and 0.2 of a point cannot rescue a book that is half a point behind.

This is the lab's insight 91 showing up again, and importantly it shows up *inside* the dev
window this time. The lab already knew that equal-weight books lost to SPY's big-company drift
after 2018. This says they were losing to it in 1996–2015 as well, once the money is counted the
way the owner actually deposits it. The twenty-year headline returns look close — the book made
slightly less in total than SPY — but the money-weighted number is worse than the headline,
because the deposits keep arriving and the book's weakest stretch is its later years.

## Was the expected failure right?

Mostly, and the one thing I got wrong is interesting.

I wrote before the run that the exclusion would be too small to matter and that the base book
would lose regardless. Both happened, and the "too small to matter" prediction was right almost to
the decimal.

I also wrote that the effect should be *weaker* in 2009–2015 than before 2009, because the
research that found it is titled "The Disappearing Index Effect" and dates the fade to the 2000s.
That was wrong in sign. The 12-month gap was 3.5 points a year before 2009 and 9.7 points a year
in 2009–2015 — larger in the recent years, not smaller. I will not make much of it, because
neither number is statistically solid and the recent sample is only 56 months. But it is the
opposite of what the published fade story predicts, and it is worth remembering the next time the
lab discounts an anomaly for being old.

## The honesty checks

The pre-registration promised two things.

The first was handled before the run and worked: the two membership files begin in January 1996
and February 2007, and every company listed in a first row looks like it joined on that day. Left
unhandled, the book would have been empty for its first three years and would have thrown out half
the Nasdaq-100 in February 2007. Treating a joining date shared by 20 or more companies as "the
records start here" rather than "the index bought these" removes both artefacts cleanly — the
busiest genuine addition day in the whole store has 9 companies, so there is no grey area.

The second could not be done, and I am flagging it rather than quietly dropping it. I promised to
re-run this on the survivorship-check store, which adds prices for the companies that died and
were deleted. **That store does not exist on this machine and the EODHD price cache it is built
from is not here either**, so there is nothing to build it from without a paid download. This
matters more for this method than for most: the store prices 539 of about 1,061 companies that
were ever members, and the ones it cannot price are disproportionately the ones that were thrown
out of the index. A method whose whole subject is how long companies stay in the index is the most
exposed thing the lab could run on a store with that hole in it. The result is a rejection either
way — adding the dead companies back has only ever made results worse, never better — so the
verdict is safe. But if anyone ever revisits this direction, the check store has to come first.

## What else the free reports said

The walk-forward test splits the window into four stretches and asks whether the method would have
beaten SPY in each. It won 1 of 4, and was not stable across them. Its edge in 2009–2015 — the
best-covered years and the ones most like today — was +0.1%, which is to say nothing at all. No
buy signal; survivorship-free price history is not worth paying for on the strength of this.

Every version here was run at Gotrade's real fees from the start, so there is no old-fees
comparison to make and none of these numbers are flattered by the lab's retired 0.1% assumption.

## My opinion

**This direction is finished as a way of beating SPY, and I would not spend another method id on
the exclusion itself.** The effect is real-shaped, correctly timed, and about forty times too
small to pay for the book it has to sit on. The index adds one or two heavily traded companies a
quarter; you cannot build a return out of avoiding them.

But the run produced one thing worth more than the method: a clean, deliberately boring control.
The 50-most-traded equal-weight book earned 6.5% a year against SPY's 7.2% and fell 57%, measured
on the owner's real deposits at real fees, over twenty years. The lab has never had that number
written down. Every stock-picking book it has built is, underneath the signal, some version of
this book — and this book loses to SPY before any signal is added. That reframes the whole search:
a picking rule does not need to be good, it needs to be good enough to overcome a roughly
half-point-a-year structural handicap and a 57% fall. Several of the near misses are only winning
by about that much.

So what I would try next is the opposite end of the same question. Insight 91 says the lab keeps
betting against the market's shape by equal-weighting. The obvious, cheap, never-run test is to
stop fighting it: take the same 50 members and weight them by how heavily they trade instead of
equally, which tilts toward the giants the way SPY does without needing market-cap data the lab
does not have and cannot trust (the lab's market-cap figure is known to be broken). If that single
change closes most of the half-point gap and cuts the 57% fall, then the lab's real problem has
never been its signals — it has been its weighting — and every near miss deserves re-running that
way. If it does not close the gap, that is equally worth knowing, and it costs one method id to
find out. That is the idea I am queuing.
methods.verdict: Rejected: leaving out the index's newest members helped by 0.2 of a point a year, exactly as the arithmetic predicted and far too little — the equal-weight book underneath it lost to SPY by half a point a year and fell 57%.

methods.name: Pick stocks only when stocks are worth picking: the spread between index members as the exposure clock
methods.sourceRef: Gorman, Sapra & Weigand, The Cross-Sectional Dispersion of Stock Returns, Alpha and the Information Ratio (SSRN 1444868, 2010); Stock-selection timing, J. Banking & Finance (2021)
methods.hypothesis: Every safety rule this lab has priced reads the market's own level -- SPY against its 200-day average -- and M0084 measured that rule to death: essentially one 2008 trade that four books share, 6 to 11 points a year of cost after 2009, and another 4.7 points for reading it weekly instead of monthly. This prices a different clock, one that reads the cross-section. Published 2010 and 2021, so the dev window sees the 2010 finding only part pre-crowd and should be expected to fade; the 2021 restatement is entirely after the dev window. Each month: take the 100 most-traded point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members (60-day median dollar volume), measure the cross-sectional standard deviation of their trailing one-month total returns, and compare today's reading with the median of the last 252 such readings. At or above it the members are moving apart, so there is something for a picker to pick: hold the basket -- 50 equal 2% slots, an evenly spaced sample of the 100 by dollar-volume rank. Below it they move together and nothing is worth picking: hold 100% SPY. Monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade), funded on the owner's monthly top-up. Variants: D21-M252 (the book); D63-M252 (a three-month spread, slower and less noisy); D21-M126 (the same spread against a six-month normal, so the threshold adapts twice as fast and the clock may flip more often); D21-M252-Q70 (the basket only in the widest 30% of readings); D21-M252-INV (the identical clock read the other way, because a clock tested in one direction only is half a test); ALWAYS (control: the basket every month, no clock). All six share one 315-bar lookback, so every paired difference is the clock and not the calendar. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: both sides of this clock are fully invested in equities, so none of the six can sidestep 2008 and none is expected to clear the 20% worst-fall bar or to be promoted. The question under test is whether any clocked arm beats the ALWAYS control by a point a year or more on the owner's deposits with no worse fall, and -- separately, because every gate in this lab earns its whole reputation in one autumn -- whether it is still ahead of the control over 2009-2015 alone.
methods.expectedFailure: Cross-sectional dispersion is not a neutral statistic: it spikes in crises. The widest spreads in 1996-2015 are 2000-2002 and 2008, exactly when an equal-weight basket of members is punished hardest relative to SPY, so the plain reading (wide spread -> basket) may well buy the basket into both falls and look worse than the control on return AND on worst fall at once. If that happens the INV arm will look good for the same mechanical reason and will be a crisis-avoidance rule wearing a dispersion costume, not evidence that the paper's finding transfers -- the paper's claim is about the spread between good and bad PICKED portfolios, and an unpicked equal-weight basket may simply have no exposure to it. Dispersion is also strongly autocorrelated and slow, so against its own trailing median the clock will sit on one side for years at a time, give only a handful of flips over twenty years, and have far too few switch decisions for its result to be anything but a story about 2000 and 2008 -- M0084's exact failure. The Q70 arm will be in SPY most of the time and will converge on buy-and-hold SPY minus fees. Both sides are fully invested, so every variant almost certainly fails the 20% worst-fall bar (SPY itself fell about 55% over 1996-2015) and probably the luck bar too; the funded return, the gap to the control, and the 2009-2015 split are the only readable numbers. The historical cross-section is computed over today's member list, which leans the threshold slightly toward SPY. Not modelled: interest on cash, of which there is none here -- the book is always in SPY or in stocks, so unlike M0084 this method is not flattered by an unpaid cash yield.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

## The question

Almost every safety rule this lab has tested reads the same thing: the price of the market
itself. Is SPY above or below its average price of the last 200 days? We priced that rule on its
own recently and it was a disappointment — essentially one good trade in 2008, and a cost of 6 to
11 points a year in every stretch since.

So this test asks whether a completely different kind of clock works better. Not the market's
**level**, but the **spread between the companies inside it**.

The thought is an appealing one, and there are published papers behind it. Some months the big
companies all move together — everything up two percent, everything down two percent. Other
months they scatter: one up fifteen, one down twelve. The claim is that scattering months are
when picking stocks is worth doing, and together-months are when it is not, and that you can see
which kind of month you are in *before* it happens by looking at how spread out the last month's
returns already were.

So: **when the companies move apart, own a basket of them. When they move together, just own the
market.**

I priced the clock on its own, with no stock-picking formula anywhere in it, the same way we
priced the 200-day rule on its own. That is deliberate. If you bolt a new clock onto a
stock-picker and the result is bad, you never learn which half was bad.

Six versions, all fixed in writing before any result:

- **D21-M252** — the main one. Measure how spread out the last month's returns were across the
  100 most-traded big companies. Compare that to the typical reading of the last year. Above
  typical: hold a 50-name equal-slice basket of those companies. Below: hold SPY.
- **D63-M252** — the same, but measuring three months of returns instead of one.
- **D21-M126** — the same, but "typical" means the last six months instead of the last year.
- **D21-M252-Q70** — a stricter bar: own the basket only in the most scattered 30% of readings.
- **D21-M252-INV** — **the identical clock read backwards**: own the basket when the companies
  move *together*. A clock tested in one direction only is half a test.
- **ALWAYS** — the control. Hold the 50-name basket every single month and never look at the
  clock at all. This is the number everything else has to beat.

All six were given the same amount of history to warm up, so every one is scored on exactly the
same days and every difference between them is the clock, not the calendar.

## What happened

Money-weighted return means: what the owner's actual deposits would have earned — 10,000,000 IDR
to start and 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of every month, 237 deposits. That is the honest number,
because a book that is fed every month looks better than it was if you only read its total.

| Version | Your money earned | vs. the no-clock control | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ALWAYS** (no clock) | **+6.0% a year** | — | 59.0% | 1.25 | 5,888 |
| D63-M252 | +5.4% | **−0.6** | 59.2% | 1.27 | 4,013 |
| D21-M252-Q70 | +5.2% | **−0.8** | 58.8% | 1.33 | 2,887 |
| D21-M252-INV (backwards) | +4.9% | **−1.1** | 57.9% | 1.27 | 4,463 |
| D21-M126 | +4.6% | **−1.4** | 58.7% | 1.22 | 4,073 |
| D21-M252 (the main one) | +4.4% | **−1.6** | 58.7% | 1.20 | 4,157 |
| *the same deposits in SPY* | *+7.2%* | — | — | — | — |

Read the middle column, because it is the whole experiment. **Every single version that consults
the clock earned less than the version that ignores it.** Not one of the six beat SPY either —
the best was the control at +6.0% against SPY's +7.2%.

"Worst fall" is how much the book lost from its highest point to its lowest. Every version fell
about 58-59%, against the rule's limit of 20%. That was expected and written down beforehand:
both sides of this clock are fully invested in shares, so nothing here could sit out 2008. This
method was never a candidate to trade; it was built to produce a number.

**On luck.** Deflated Sharpe ratio is the lab's answer to "could this be a fluke?" It takes the
result, then charges it for how many different ideas we have already tried — because if you try
enough things, something will look good by accident. These versions scored between 0.197 and
0.335. The bar is 0.90, and the N they were charged against is **76** — that is how many
genuinely independent looks the lab reckons it has taken (one per distinct method, then reduced
because many of our methods move together and so do not count as separate tries; there are 382
trial rows behind those 76). A score of 0.2 to 0.3 means: nowhere close. Nothing here is a real
edge even before the luck charge, so the luck charge is not what killed it.

**Worst year.** 2008 for every version, down 38-41%. The drop came in the autumn of 2008 and did
not recover until 2009.

**No rupiah figures here**, deliberately. From 2018 the falling rupiah added Rp 86-155 million to
every version of an earlier method and made a losing book look acceptable. This test runs
1996-2015 and is reported in percent for exactly that reason.

## Why it failed — three findings, and the third is the useful one

**1. It is not the trading costs.** This is the first thing to rule out, and it rules out
cleanly. The control traded **the most** of anything here — 5,888 trades, more than any clocked
version — and still won. Switching to SPY means holding one thing instead of fifty, so every
clocked version traded *less* and paid *less* in fees, and still finished behind. The clock lost
money by being wrong, not by being expensive.

**2. The direction was not the problem.** This is the finding I most wanted and least expected to
get so cleanly. If the paper's idea were right but I had the sign upside down, then reading the
clock backwards would have *made money*. It did not: the backwards version cost 1.1 points a
year, right alongside the forwards version's 1.6. **Both directions lose.** You cannot explain
that with a sign error. The only explanation left is that the spread between companies carries no
useful information about this particular choice at all — and when a signal is pure noise, acting
on it in *either* direction costs you the trading, which is exactly the pattern in the table.

**3. It did not even help in 2008, which is where a clock is supposed to earn its living.** The
200-day rule, for all its faults, at least got out of the 2008 crash. This one did not. In 2008
the control fell 40.9%; the main clocked version fell 40.5%. Four tenths of one percent. The
reason is mechanical and, in hindsight, obvious: **the spread between companies is already wide
when a crash starts.** Scattering is what a crisis looks like. So the rule "companies are moving
apart, therefore own the basket of companies" held the book in shares all the way down. The
signal I hoped would say "now is the time to pick" was in fact saying "a crisis is underway" —
and then pointing the book straight into it.

And in the stretch most like today, 2009-2015, it was worse again, not better: the control lagged
SPY by 1.6 points a year, the main clocked version by 3.6.

**Did the hypothesis hold?** No, in every part. I asked whether any clocked version could beat the
no-clock control by a point a year with no worse fall. None beat it at all. I asked separately
whether any stayed ahead over 2009-2015 alone. None did.

**Did the expected failure happen?** Yes, and almost exactly as written. I wrote beforehand that
the spread spikes in crises, that this would point the book into 2000-2002 and 2008, and that the
backwards version would then look good "for the same mechanical reason". It is worth being honest
that the last part is the one thing I got wrong, and the way I got it wrong is informative: the
backwards version did fall slightly less (57.9% against 59.0%) and did lose slightly less in 2008
— but it still lost money overall, which is stronger evidence against the signal than what I
predicted. I expected to end up unable to tell "no information" apart from "wrong sign". The
result settled it.

**One thing this does not prove.** The papers are about the gap between a *good* basket of picked
stocks and a *bad* one. My basket is not picked — it is 50 companies sliced equally out of the
hundred most-traded, which is a different way of weighting the index, not a stock-picking
formula. So the honest statement is: **the spread between companies does not time the choice
between an equal-slice basket and the market.** It is not proof that it cannot time a real
stock-picker. I chose not to test that, on purpose: every picker this lab has that is good enough
to be worth clocking belongs to a family where four methods have already failed out of sample,
which means the result could never be promoted and the measurement would be spent on a book the
gate would refuse anyway.

## The thing I did not go looking for

The control is the most interesting number in this run, and it is about something else entirely.

A 50-name equal-slice basket of the 100 most-traded big companies earned **+6.0% a year** on the
owner's deposits over twenty years at real fees. The breadth-switch method ran the *same universe
with the same fees and the same monthly cadence* but held **20** names instead of 50, with no
clock, and earned **+3.2%**.

Same hundred companies. Same costs. Same months. **Nearly three points a year of difference from
nothing but how finely the universe was sliced.** That is larger than any clock this lab has
priced, including the 200-day rule.

And I do not think it is really about concentration, because the trade counts point somewhere
else. Holding 20 of 100 took 3,479 trades; holding 50 of 100 took 5,888. More names, more
trading. The reason is that both books *sample* their universe — they take every second name, or
every fifth — and the ranking that decides the sample reshuffles every month. Names fall in and
out of the sample constantly, and every one of those is a round trip paid for with nothing gained.
A book that simply held all 100 would never sample at all, and would only trade when a company
genuinely left the top hundred.

I want to be careful here, because the obvious comparison is not available: the breadth method's
100-name version *did* have a clock on it, so it is not a clean control and I will not quote it as
one. That is precisely why this needs its own run rather than another paragraph of inference — and
it is the next idea below.

## My opinion

**Stop here on dispersion as a switch. It is dead, and it died cleanly.** I would not spend
another method id on timing anything with the spread between companies, and I say that with more
confidence than a single failed result usually earns, because of the backwards version. One
losing test tells you an idea did not work. A test where the idea *and its exact opposite* both
lose tells you the signal is empty, and empty signals do not come back to life with a different
lookback or a different threshold. Four of the six versions here were already parameter sweeps,
and they landed in a band 1.2 points wide with the no-clock control sitting above all of them.
There is no tuning left to do.

I would also draw a wider conclusion, because this is now the second clock priced on its own and
the second to come back worthless. Both the 200-day rule and this one looked compelling in
writing and cost money in practice. The lab has spent a lot of ideas on *when to be invested*, and
every honest measurement of that question has come back negative. I would stop opening new
timing families for a while.

What I would do instead is chase the accident in the control. The strongest number in this run has
nothing to do with the clock: slicing the same hundred companies 20 ways versus 50 ways moved the
owner's return by nearly three points a year, and the trade counts suggest the culprit is the
monthly reshuffling of *which* names get held, not how many. If that is right it is a cheap and
general fix — it would apply to every book in this lab, not just this one, and it costs nothing to
own more of your universe instead of resampling it each month. That is where the next method id
should go, and the queued idea below separates the two causes properly: hold all 100, hold 50
sampled across the range, and hold the top 50 outright, on one universe with one cadence, so that
"how many names" and "how much resampling" stop being the same number.

I would rate that follow-up as the most promising thing this run produced, and the dispersion
clock as a closed question.
methods.verdict: Rejected: timing the book on how far apart the big companies are moving cost 0.6 to 1.6 points a year against simply not timing it — and reading the clock backwards cost money too, so the signal is empty rather than inverted

methods.name: Where the monthly top-up goes: buy the laggard instead of topping everything up evenly
methods.hypothesis: Every method this lab has run differs in which stocks it picks. None has ever varied where the owner's new money goes, and that is the one free lever left: the monthly top-up is being deposited anyway, so steering it costs no extra round trip and almost no fee. Five deployment rules run on one fixed book with no stock picking in it -- the 20 most-traded index members, M0109's screen -- so that the deployment rule is the only thing that varies and the picker cannot be the thing that fails. A holding's weight is set to its one-month drift raised to a signed power: EQ puts every name back on an equal slot, which buys the laggards and sells the leaders; PRORATA reproduces the drift, so nothing is traded and the deposit spreads across the book in proportion to what is already there; LEAD overshoots upward so the deposit buys last month's winners; LAG overshoots downward so it buys last month's losers harder than equal; and HOLD turns the resize machinery off altogether, so nothing is ever trimmed or topped up and the deposit waits in cash for the next rotation. The reason this might matter is mechanical rather than predictive: buying the laggard rebalances without ever selling, so it avoids the sell-side fee and holds the book at its weights through a fall, where a pro-rata top-up quietly lets the winners run. Success is a measurement, not a candidate: the host book has no edge and M0109 already measured its 50-name version at 7.0% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, so no arm here is expected to be eligible. What is wanted is the spread between the arms, stated in money-weighted return against deposit-matched SPY and never in CAGR, with the fees each rule paid reported separately from what it earned, and the worst fall of each reported too, since buying the laggard should bend the fall and buying the leader should worsen it. Two things were measured on the dev window before the variants were fixed, on the book's drift statistics alone and never on a return. First, the book engine only trades when a holding's gap from its target exceeds 1% of equity, so at 50 equal slots the gap clears that band in 0.1% of name-months and at 20 slots in 4.2%; the lab's own record agrees, since M0109's monthly and weekly 50-name controls made the identical 1,338 trades. At the sizes this lab normally runs, every rule in this file is the same rule -- which is itself the finding -- and the host therefore holds 20 names, the largest book on which the lever fires at all. Second, the month's deposit is about a third of the account in month one, 7% at one year and 0.4% at twenty, so per holding it clears that 1% band only for the first three months or so: after that the deposit can fund a new entry but can never top up an existing holding. Steering the deposit is therefore a young-account lever, worth most in the first two or three years, which is exactly where the owner is now and exactly what a twenty-year average understates, so the analysis reads the eras and not the average. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's real monthly top-up throughout, because a deposit rule measured at a flat 0.1% on whole shares is measuring nothing.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely result is that the five arms land within a few tenths of a point a year of each other and the whole lever is worth less than the fees it costs to pull, because the 1% resize band swallows it: even at 20 names only about 4% of name-months ever trade, which is roughly three quarters of one holding a month. If that happens the honest answer is that deposit steering is not a lever at this lab's book sizes at all, and the next question is whether the band should scale with the slot rather than with the account. The second way this fails is the host. Twenty of the most-traded names in March 2000 were the dot-coms, and M0109 measured the 30-name version of this book falling 70% against SPY's 56%; a 20-name version will fall further still, so every arm breaks the 20% drawdown bar and the 2000-2002 crash may dominate the spread between the arms instead of the deployment rule doing it. The analysis therefore has to read the arms era by era and say plainly if one crash is carrying the answer. The third way is subtler and would invert the finding: buying the laggard every month inside a fixed universe is a short-term reversal bet wearing a bookkeeping costume, and the lab has found short-term reversal to be weak in big liquid names, so LAG may simply lose to LEAD for a reason that has nothing to do with deposits. If LEAD beats LAG, the mechanical story is dead and the right reading is that letting winners run inside a liquid large-cap book pays, which is the same lesson insight 91 drew about SPY's big-company drift. The fourth is that HOLD wins on fees by trading least and the lab mistakes cheapness for an edge; the fee column is reported separately for exactly that reason.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# M0119 — where the monthly top-up goes

## What I was asking

Every strategy this lab has tried so far differs in **which** stocks it buys. None has ever
varied **where your new money goes**. You pay in 5 million rupiah on the 25th of every month.
That money has to be spent on something, and nobody has ever checked whether it matters which
holding it is spent on.

There is a sensible-sounding argument that it should matter, and it is about plumbing rather
than about predicting anything. Suppose you hold twenty stocks in equal slices. A month later
some have risen and some have fallen, so the slices are no longer equal. You can put the month's
new money into the ones that have fallen behind — which puts the book back to equal slices
*without ever selling anything*. That saves you the selling fee, and it keeps the book balanced
through a bad patch instead of quietly letting a few winners take over. It sounds like a free
lever: the money is going in anyway, so steering it costs nothing extra.

I tested five ways of spending the deposit, on one fixed shopping list so that the list itself
could not be what succeeded or failed:

| | what the deposit does |
|---|---|
| **Buy the laggards hardest** | pushes money past equal, into whatever fell most last month |
| **Back to equal slices** | tops the fallers up until every holding is the same size again |
| **Leave it alone** | spreads the money across the book in proportion to what is already there |
| **Buy the leaders** | pushes money into whatever rose most last month |
| **Spend nothing** | never touches an existing holding; the money waits in cash for a new name |

The shopping list is the same in all five: the twenty most heavily traded big American companies,
in equal slices, refreshed monthly. Nothing is ranked on performance. It is a deliberately dull
book, borrowed from the drawdown-brake study, so that the only thing that varies is the deposit
rule.

## What happened

Your money, after fees, against the same deposits put into the market (SPY):

| the deposit goes to | your money a year | vs the market | worst fall | gains vs losses | invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the laggards, hardest | **+5.1%** | −2.1% | 76% | 1.09 | 97% |
| back to equal slices | **+5.5%** | −1.7% | 75% | 1.15 | 96% |
| left alone | **+6.2%** | −1.0% | 73% | 1.22 | 97% |
| the leaders | **+6.2%** | −1.0% | 73% | 1.24 | 97% |
| nowhere (cash) | **+4.7%** | −2.5% | 69% | 1.09 | **77%** |

The market earned +7.2% a year on the same deposits. **Every version lost**, which was expected
and is not the point — this book has no stock picking in it and was never going to win.

The point is the order, and it is perfectly clean. **The harder you push the deposit toward
whatever has just fallen, the worse you do — and not on one measure, on every measure at once.**
Going from "buy the leaders" down to "buy the laggards hardest" costs 1.1 percentage points a
year, deepens the worst fall by three points, and turns 1.24 of gains per unit of loss into 1.09.
There is no trade-off here where you buy safety with return. The laggard rule is simply worse at
both.

The sensible-sounding argument was wrong, and it was wrong in the direction I wrote down before
the run as the way this would most likely embarrass itself.

## Why — and this is the whole mechanism

Look at 2008 on its own. That column separates the five versions more than anything else does:

| the deposit goes to | 2008, vs the market |
|---|---|
| the laggards, hardest | **−9.3%** |
| back to equal slices | −6.7% |
| left alone | −4.4% |
| the leaders | −3.3% |
| nowhere (cash) | **+4.7%** |

In a crash, "the holding that has fallen furthest below its slice" is not a bargain waiting to
bounce. It is the company that is in the most trouble. A rule that automatically sends every
month's new money to whatever is falling fastest is a rule that **feeds the fire** — it is
catching a falling knife, once a month, with fresh money, for as long as the crash lasts. That is
where the extra three points of fall come from, and that is why the laggard rule loses on safety
as well as on return.

The mirror test confirms it rather than leaving it to chance. I ran the opposite rule — push the
money toward last month's *winners* — purely to check the effect had a direction and was not just
an artefact of one version trading less than another. It did have a direction, and the winners
side is the good side.

## The bigger finding, which is not about steering at all

Look at the last row. "Spend nothing" is the worst version of the five, by a clear margin, and
the reason is in the last column: **it was only 77% invested**, where every other version was
96–97%.

That is the deposit sitting in cash waiting for something to buy. Over twenty years it cost
**1.5 percentage points a year** against simply spreading the money across what you already own.
It bought exactly one thing in return — a softer 2008, because cash does not fall — and it paid
for that cushion in every single other year, including a 2.8-point-a-year shortfall in 2009–2015,
the stretch that most resembles today.

So the ranking of what actually matters is:

1. **Getting the deposit invested at all: worth about 1.5 points a year.**
2. Where you steer it once invested: worth about 0.7 points a year, and the intuitive direction
   is the wrong one.

The first number is twice the second, and unlike the second it requires no judgement and carries
no risk of being backwards. **Spend the deposit promptly and spread it across what you already
hold.** That is the practical finding.

## Could this just be cheaper trading?

No, and the data rules it out cleanly. If the differences were about fees, the version that trades
least would win. "Spend nothing" never trims or tops up a single holding — it is by construction
the cheapest of the five — and it came last by a wide margin. The version that does the most
re-sizing came first. Fees cannot be the explanation when the cheapest arm loses and the busiest
arm wins. (All five made the same 727 completed trades, because the shopping list was identical;
they differed only in the top-ups and trims in between.)

One thing I could not do: the reports do not break out the fee bill as a separate column, so I can
show that fees are not driving the answer but cannot say precisely what each rule paid. I have
asked for that column.

## A caution I wrote down beforehand, and which turned out to matter less than feared

Before running this I warned that the book itself is extreme: the twenty most heavily traded
American companies in March 2000 were the dot-coms, so this book was always going to fall
catastrophically in 2000–2002, and I worried that one crash would decide the whole comparison.

It did not. Across 1996–2002 the five versions land within a point of each other and are not even
in order. The clean ordering comes from 2003–2008 and from 2008 itself. So the finding rests on
the 2008 crash and the years around it rather than on the dot-com bust — one crash, still, which
is a genuine limitation, but a different and better-covered one than I feared.

I should also be plain that the 69–76% falls in that table are a property of this deliberately
narrow book, not of the deposit rules. Your limit is 20%. Nothing here is a candidate for your
money and nothing here was built to be.

## The honest reinterpretation

Here is the part I do not want to oversell. Weighting toward "what rose last month" and weighting
toward "what fell last month" is, underneath the deposit framing, a mild bet on short-term
momentum. I flagged this before the run as the way the result could be real and still not mean
what it appears to mean, and that is exactly what happened.

So the fair statement is two separate findings, not one:

- **About deposits (mechanical, trustworthy):** deploying the deposit promptly is worth about 1.5
  points a year. This is plumbing and I believe it transfers to any book.
- **About steering (predictive, weaker):** inside a fixed list of big liquid companies, sizing
  toward recent winners beat sizing toward recent losers by about 1.1 points a year. This is a
  real measured effect with a clean sign, but it is a market bet, not plumbing, and it belongs to
  the same family of questions as the lab's short-term reversal work. It may fade.

## Was it luck?

No — but that question barely arises here, because nothing won. The luck test asks how likely a
result is to be real rather than a fluke, after accounting for how many different strategies this
lab has now tried. Your bar is 0.90 and the lab has now looked at 78 distinct methods. The five
versions score 0.14 to 0.27, far under the bar. That is the correct answer for five versions of a
book that lost to the market by 1 to 2.5 points a year: there is nothing here that needs a luck
test to reject.

What the luck test does *not* cover, and should not be read as covering, is the comparison
*between* the five. That comparison is clean for a different reason: the five share one shopping
list, one set of trades, one window and one fee schedule, so the only difference between them is
the deposit rule. That is a controlled comparison, which is worth more here than a significance
number.

None of these figures contain any currency effect. The deposits are converted at one fixed
exchange rate for every version, so the rupiah's ups and downs cancel out entirely and what you
see is the strategy.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did it fail the way I said it would

**The hypothesis was wrong, and cleanly so.** I wrote that buying the laggard should help because
it rebalances without selling and holds the book together through a fall. It did the opposite on
both counts: it earned less *and* fell further, because in a fall the laggard is the sick company.

Of the four failures I wrote down before the run, two happened and two did not:

1. *"The five arms will land within a few tenths of a point and the lever will be worth less than
   its fees."* **Did not happen.** The spread is 1.5 points a year, which is large.
2. *"The dot-com crash will dominate the comparison."* **Did not happen** — 1996–2002 is flat and
   unordered across the five.
3. *"Buying the laggard is short-term reversal in disguise; if the leader rule wins, the
   mechanical story is dead."* **Happened exactly.** The leader rule won. I have reported this as
   the reinterpretation above rather than quietly keeping the deposit framing.
4. *"The do-nothing arm will win on cheapness and we will mistake that for an edge."* **Did not
   happen** — it lost by the most, which is what killed the fee explanation.

## Comparison with the parent

The host book is the 50-name version from M0109, shrunk to 20 names so the deposit rule could
move any money at all. Both paid the same real Gotrade fees, so the numbers are directly
comparable with no adjustment. M0109's plain 50-name book earned +7.0% a year on your deposits
and fell 57%. Shrinking it to 20 names cost 0.8 to 2.3 points a year depending on the deposit rule
and deepened the fall to 69–76%. **Concentration into the twenty busiest names was expensive and
dangerous** — which is worth recording on its own, because "hold fewer, bigger names" is an
intuition that keeps coming up and this is a clean measurement of what it costs.

## What I established before running, which changed the design

Two measurements, made on the book's drift statistics alone and never on a return, and both
written into the pre-registration before any variant was fixed.

First, **the simulator will not trade a small difference.** It only trims or tops up a holding
when the gap from its target exceeds 1% of the whole account. With 50 equal slices that needs a
50% relative move, so it essentially never fires: the gap clears the band in 0.1% of
holding-months. The lab's own record confirms it — M0109's monthly and weekly 50-name versions
made the *identical* 1,338 trades, because at 50 names there was nothing for the re-sizing
machinery to do. At 20 names it fires 4.2% of the time. **At the book sizes this lab normally
runs, all five of these rules are the same rule.** That is why the book here holds 20 names.

Second, **the deposit is a young-account lever.** Your 5 million a month is about a third of the
account in month one, 7% after a year, 1.5% after five years and 0.4% after twenty. Spread over
twenty holdings that clears the 1% band only for about the first three months. After that the
deposit can fund a brand-new holding but can never top up an existing one. So this whole question
matters most in an account's first two or three years — **which is exactly where you are now**,
and exactly what a twenty-year average flattens into invisibility.

## My opinion

**This direction is finished as a search for an edge, and it has produced one instruction worth
keeping.**

The instruction is: get the deposit invested, promptly, across what you already hold. It is worth
about 1.5 points a year, it needs no forecast, and it is the largest free number this lab has
found that does not depend on picking the right stocks. I would apply it to whatever strategy
eventually wins, and I would stop treating undeployed cash as harmless.

I would **not** spend more method ids on steering the deposit. The measurement is done, the sign
is clean, and the honest reading is that what I measured was mild short-term momentum in position
sizing rather than a deposit effect. If the lab wants to pursue "size toward recent winners", that
is a stock-picking question and should be registered as one, on a book that can actually win,
rather than smuggled in as plumbing.

There is one thing here I do think deserves a method id, and I have queued it. The 1% trading
band is specified as a share of the **account**, not of a **slot**. That single choice means every
book this lab runs at 20 names or more is, in practice, never rebalanced at all — the trims and
top-ups that the strategy files appear to specify simply never execute. Nobody decided that; it
fell out of a constant. Before the lab draws any more conclusions about rebalancing, somebody
should price the alternative — a band measured against the slot, so that a 50-name book rebalances
on the same relative drift a 12-name book does. That is not a trading idea, it is a question about
whether this lab's simulator has been quietly testing what it thinks it has been testing, and I
would want the answer before trusting any future result that depends on re-sizing.

One caveat on everything above. The ordering of the five rests on 2003–2008 and on 2008 in
particular, which is one crash. It is a better-covered and more modern crash than the dot-com
bust, and the ordering is consistent across return, fall and gains-to-losses rather than showing
up on one measure alone, which is why I believe it. But it is still one crash, and a deposit rule
that looks good because of how it behaved in 2008 is a deposit rule that has been tested once.
methods.verdict: Rejected, and the intuition was backwards: sending each month's top-up to whatever had fallen furthest earned 1.1 points a year less than sending it to whatever had risen, and fell three points further at the same time, because in a crash the laggard is the sick company. The finding worth keeping is simpler and bigger: the version that left the deposit in cash was only 77% invested and lost 1.5 points a year for it, so getting the money invested promptly matters twice as much as where you steer it.

methods.name: A safety rule that cannot be fitted: step aside by the calendar, not by the chart
methods.sourceRef: Bouman & Jacobsen (2002), The Halloween Indicator, 'Sell in May and Go Away': Another Puzzle, American Economic Review 92(5); the lab's own M0084 measurement of the SPY 200-day switch
methods.hypothesis: Published 2002 and heavily publicised since, so the dev window's second half already sees a crowd that knows it, and a fade after 2009 is the base case rather than a surprise. THE POINT IS TO PRICE THE FRAME, NOT TO FIND AN EDGE, exactly as M0084 did for the 200-day switch: a 100%-SPY book cannot beat SPY except by sitting out falls for less than the rallies it also sits out, so no SPY-layer variant is expected to clear the go-live bars and none should be promoted. M0084 measured the switch alone and found the monthly reading worth +1.4 points a year on the owner's deposits (+9.1% against +7.7% for buy-and-hold SPY) at an 18.9% worst fall against SPY's 55%, the weekly reading worth -3.3 points, and every reading 6 to 11 points a year behind plain SPY in 2009-2015. The question here is whether a clock that never reads a price buys the same insurance more cheaply. It has three properties nothing else in the lab has: it cannot be overfitted to the price series because it never reads it (no window, no band, no cadence to tune, and both stretches were named in print before the dev window opened); it flips twice a year, so Gotrade's real fees barely touch it where the weekly switch paid 0.7 points a year in fees alone; and it was out through September and October 2008 by construction rather than by reacting. Six variants, a 2x3 grid of two underlying books by three clock settings, every paired difference the clock alone. SPY-ALWAYS and EW20-ALWAYS are the no-clock controls through the identical fee, deposit and rounding path; HALLOWEEN holds November through April (Bouman & Jacobsen's window); SEPOCT holds every month except September and October. The underlying EW20 book is the 20 index members with the largest 20-day dollar volume, equal weight, monthly, with the lab's standard screen and its 200-day trend gate switched OFF -- a market-shaped book that ranks on size of trading rather than on anything that forecasts return, so it has no fitted signal for the clock to interact with and no kin among the lab's four out-of-sample failures, all of which rank on past return. Every variant shares the 253-bar lookback M0084 ran on, so all six and all six of M0084's are scored on the same sessions and the same deposits. The hypothesis under test, stated as a number: the HALLOWEEN clock on SPY gives up no more than 2 points a year of funded return against SPY-ALWAYS while cutting the worst fall by at least 20 points, which would make it cheaper insurance than the monthly 200-day switch bought for a +1.4 point gain at a 36-point drawdown cut. The second question is whether the narrow SEPOCT clock keeps more of the return for most of the protection, since it is out for two months a year rather than six. The third is whether the clock is worth more on an equal-weight book of big names than on SPY, since the seasonal effect is documented as larger in the average stock than in the cap-weighted index. WHAT WILL BE REPORTED WHETHER IT FLATTERS THE CLOCK OR NOT: the clock's contribution in 2008 separately from its contribution in 2009-2015, and the count of distinct May-October stretches the whole twenty-year result actually rests on -- if the answer is two autumns, the analysis will say so in those words, because that is the 200-day switch's disease wearing a different coat.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely outcome is that the twenty-year result rests on two or three summers -- 1998, 2002 and 2008 -- and that stripping them leaves the clock costing money, which is exactly what M0084 found for the switch and what insights 89, 91 and 93 found for every twenty-year edge in the lab. In 2009-2015 almost every May-October stretch was positive (2010, 2011 and 2015 are the exceptions and only 2011 badly so), so the clock should lag plain SPY by 2 to 5 points a year in the era most like today, and the lab will have learned a price without learning a frame to use. The 2008 dodge is also likely to be far less clean than it looks: the Halloween clock holds November through April, so it was fully invested through November 2008 (-7%) and January-February 2009 (-8% and -11%), and may well breach the 20% drawdown bar on that leg alone despite sitting out September and October. Trade counts on the SPY layer will be tiny -- two flips a year, about 40 over the window -- so profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless there and the >= 100 trades condition fails by construction; the funded return, the worst fall and the era split are the only readable numbers on that layer. The EW20 layer has the opposite problem: 20 slots re-picked monthly with no trend gate of any kind, so EW20-ALWAYS should fall 50% or more in 2008 (M0024's ungated book fell 61%) and both clocked versions should breach 20% too, because neither clock is out in the autumn of 2008 AND the winter that followed. Ranking big members by dollar volume may also simply reproduce SPY with extra fees and a small-company tilt, in which case the EW20 column adds nothing the SPY column did not already say. Not modelled, and it cuts in the clock's favour: interest on the cash held while the clock is off. The Halloween clock is out for half of every year and US cash paid 3-5% a year over most of 1994-2007, so the un-modelled interest is worth roughly 1.5 to 2.5 points a year to it, and every return reported for a clocked variant is therefore a lower bound. Finally, the whole exercise may be unanswerable at this sample size: twenty-one summers is twenty-one observations, the standard error on a seasonal mean that thin is several points a year, and no honest reading of it can separate a real calendar effect from a run of luck. If that is what the numbers say, the analysis will say it and the method will be rejected.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

## The question

Half the strategies in this lab carry the same safety rule: **when the S&P 500 tracker (SPY)
closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything and sit in cash.**
Yesterday's test of that rule on its own found it worth +1.4 points a year on the owner's
deposits, and that it cut the worst fall from 55% to 19%.

But that rule reads the price chart, and anything that reads the price chart can be tuned until
it looks good on the years you already have. So this test asks a different question:

> **Is there a safety rule that cannot be tuned at all, and is it any good?**

A calendar is such a rule. "Sell in May and go away, come back on Halloween" is older than any
of us, and it was written up properly in a well-known 2002 economics paper. It has three
properties nothing else in this lab has:

- **It cannot be fitted to the price**, because it never looks at the price. There is no window
  length, no threshold, no reading cadence to choose. Both versions tested here were named in
  print before this test window even opens.
- **It trades twice a year**, so Gotrade's fees barely touch it. The weekly version of the
  200-day rule paid 0.7 points a year in fees alone.
- **It was out of the market through September and October 2008 automatically**, a month before
  the 200-day rule reacted — because it was never going to be in, not because it saw anything.

## What was tested

Six versions: two underlying books crossed with three calendar settings, so that every
difference you read is the calendar and nothing else.

The two books:

- **SPY** — hold the S&P 500 tracker at full weight. The calendar measured bare, with no stock
  picking in the way.
- **EW20** — hold the 20 index members that trade the most dollars a day, equal amounts,
  re-picked monthly. A market-shaped book with **no stock-picking rule of its own** (it ranks on
  how much a name trades, not on anything that forecasts return) and **no 200-day filter**, so
  the calendar is the only timing rule in it.

The three calendar settings:

- **ALWAYS** — no calendar. The control.
- **HALLOWEEN** — hold from 1 November through 30 April, cash the other six months.
- **SEPOCT** — hold every month except September and October, the two the folklore blames.

All six trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, start with 10 million rupiah and take
5 million more on the 25th of every month. The returns below are **measured in dollars**, so the
rupiah's long slide adds nothing to any of these numbers. All six share the same 253-day run-up
as the 200-day-rule test, so the two tests are scored on the same days and the same deposits and
can be read side by side without any adjustment.

## What happened

**The bare market.** SPY with dividends, on the owner's deposits: **+7.7% a year.**

| version | your money per year | worst fall | times in and out | gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no calendar (control) | **+7.7%** | 55.0% | 0 | — |
| Halloween (Nov–Apr) | **+6.3%** | 36.2% | 22 | 5.85 |
| out in Sep–Oct only | **+5.7%** | 42.1% | 22 | 3.48 |

**The 20 most-traded names, equal amounts** (1996 → 2015; the same deposits into SPY made +7.2%):

| version | your money per year | worst fall | trades | gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no calendar (control) | **+5.7%** | 74.4% | 727 | 1.15 |
| Halloween (Nov–Apr) | **+3.6%** | 60.9% | 699 | 1.55 |
| out in Sep–Oct only | **+4.2%** | 64.6% | 949 | 1.42 |

Every one of the six failed the go-live conditions, and all six failed on **beating SPY** and on
the **20% worst-fall limit**. Nothing here was close.

**The luck check.** The lab deflates every result by how many times it has looked. That count
(**N = 75** — one look per distinct method in the lab, floored at how independent the methods'
actual results are) sets the bar at **0.90**. The best of these six scored **0.56** and the worst
**0.21**. None of them is remotely distinguishable from luck, which is the honest reading when a
twenty-year result rests on 22 summers.

## The number this test existed to produce

Here is the whole thing in one line, against the 200-day rule measured yesterday on the identical
days, deposits and fees:

| safety rule | return vs no rule | worst fall vs no rule |
|---|---|---|
| 200-day average, read monthly | **+1.4 points a year** | **55% → 19%** |
| Halloween calendar | **−1.4 points a year** | **55% → 36%** |
| out in Sep–Oct only | **−2.0 points a year** | **55% → 42%** |

**The rule that can be fitted beats the rule that cannot, on return and on safety at the same
time.** That is not a close call and it is not the answer I expected to be able to state so
cleanly. The calendar costs you money *and* leaves you with twice the fall.

## How thin is the calendar's case? Two summers and one autumn

I promised before the run to say how many separate stretches of calendar the twenty-year result
actually rests on. Here is every May-to-October stretch in the window, with dividends:

- 22 summers. **8 were losses, 14 were gains.** Compounded, the whole set of summers made
  **+28.9%** while the winters made **+342.4%**. That gap is the entire Halloween story.
- Remove the **three worst summers — 2008 (−30.7%), 2002 (−18.3%) and 2001 (−16.2%)** — and the
  remaining 19 summers compound to **+171.2%**, an average of **+5.6%** each. There is nothing
  left to step aside from.

So the answer is: **three summers out of twenty-two carry all of it, and they are the dot-com
bust and the financial crisis.** That is the same disease as the 200-day rule, wearing a
different coat — except the 200-day rule at least got paid for catching them.

The September–October version is thinner still: 5 losses in 22 autumns, and **one of them
(2008, −23.9%) is larger than the other four put together.**

## Then and now

Split the window where the lab always splits it:

- **1994–2008**: the average summer made **+0.7%**, and 5 of 15 were losses. Stepping aside cost
  almost nothing, and in 2008 it was worth a fortune — the calendar turned a −36.6% year into a
  −10.8% year, about **26 points saved in that one year.**
- **2009–2015**, the best-covered years and the ones most like today: the average summer made
  **+4.4%**, and **September and October were positive in all seven of those years**, averaging
  +4.8%. The lab's own walk-forward check puts this method **5.3 points a year behind SPY** over
  that stretch, and it won only **1 of its 4 folds**.

So: a 26-point insurance payout in 2008, bought with a premium of 1.4 to 2.0 points a year for
twenty-two years, which is roughly 31 to 44 points of forgone compounding. Even on the dev
window's own numbers, the policy cost more than it paid.

## Why

- **Nearly all of the market's gains do land in winter, and that is not useful.** The winters
  compounded +342% against the summers' +29%, which looks damning until you notice the summers
  were still *positive*. A rule that sits out something with a positive average has to be paid
  for in dodged disasters, and there were only three.
- **The 2008 dodge is much less clean than it sounds.** The calendar was out through September
  and October 2008 and then walked straight back in on 1 November — into November 2008 (−7%),
  January 2009 (−8%) and February 2009 (−11%). Its worst fall runs from April 2007 to
  **9 March 2009**, the exact same bottom as simply holding SPY. It did not avoid the crisis; it
  took a 36% version of it instead of a 55% version.
- **Equal-weighting the biggest names is itself a losing bet, before any calendar.** The 20
  most-traded index members in equal amounts made **+5.7% a year against SPY's +7.2%**, with a
  **74% worst fall**. That is a finding in its own right and it points the same way as the
  owner's money runs did: betting against the market's cap-weighted shape costs about a point
  and a half a year and roughly 20 extra points of fall. The calendar made that book worse still.
- **The calendar is worth *less* on a stock book, not more.** The textbook claim is that the
  seasonal effect is larger in the average stock than in the index. Here it was the opposite:
  the Halloween clock cost 1.4 points on SPY and **2.1 points** on the equal-weight book, and
  left it with a 61% fall. Whatever seasonality is in the average big stock, it is smaller than
  the cost of being out of it.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Half of it, and the half that matters failed.** I pre-registered this test: *the Halloween
clock gives up no more than 2 points a year while cutting the worst fall by at least 20 points.*
It gave up 1.4 points — inside the limit — but cut the fall by only **18.8 points**, just short.
And the comparison that actually decides it was never in doubt once both numbers were on the
table: the 200-day rule cut 36 points *and* made money.

**The expected failure happened, almost word for word.** I wrote beforehand that the result would
rest on 1998, 2002 and 2008 (it rests on 2001, 2002 and 2008); that the 2009–2015 lag would be 2
to 5 points (it is 5.3); that the clock would hold straight through November 2008 and
January–February 2009 and breach the 20% limit on that leg alone (it did, ending at the same
9 March 2009 bottom); and that the ungated 20-name book would fall more than 50% in 2008 (it fell
74% peak to trough and 44.5% in the calendar year).

**One thing cuts in the calendar's favour and is not modelled:** interest on the cash it holds
while it is out. The Halloween version is out half of every year, and US cash paid 3–5% a year
over most of 1994–2007, so roughly 1.5 to 2.5 points a year of real income is missing from its
column. That is enough to close the 1.4-point gap to the control and then some. It is **not**
enough to change the verdict, because the 200-day rule holds cash too and would collect the same
interest while beating the calendar by a further 2.8 points and 17 points of fall. The ranking is
unaffected; only the absolute level is understated.

## My opinion:

**This direction is finished, and I would not spend another method id on a calendar rule.** The
test did its job: it closed a question that would otherwise have kept coming back every time
someone argued that the 200-day rule is overfitted. The answer is that the un-fittable
alternative is comprehensively worse — worse return and worse safety, at the same time, on the
same days and the same deposits — and the reason is not subtle. Summers are positive on average.
A rule that sits out something positive must be paid for in avoided disasters, and twenty-two
years contain three of those, all in the first two-thirds of the window.

The genuinely useful result here is the one I did not go looking for: **equal-weighting the 20
most-traded index members lost to SPY by 1.5 points a year with a 74% worst fall.** That is the
cleanest measurement this lab has of the thing the owner's money runs kept hinting at — that
SPY's concentration in its biggest companies is not a weakness to diversify away but the opponent
you have to beat. It is also a free yardstick for every future book: any strategy that holds
twenty-odd big names equally starts 1.5 points a year behind SPY before its stock-picking rule
does anything at all, and must earn that back before it has earned anything. I have queued that
as the next idea — the same measurement against the published equal-weight S&P, extended to 30,
40 and 50 names, so we learn whether the penalty is equal-weighting itself or just holding too
few names.

What I would **not** do next is try a third calendar (turn-of-month, January, pre-holiday).
M0052 already tested the turn of the month and it sits at the bottom of the family table. The
lesson generalises: in a twenty-year window, any rule that acts on a handful of calendar
occasions has a handful of observations behind it, and the lab's own luck bar will refuse it long
before the owner's money is at risk. The 200-day rule survives this test as the lab's safety rule,
not because it is elegant, but because it is the only one that has been measured against a real
alternative and won.
methods.verdict: The calendar rule that cannot be fitted lost to the 200-day rule that can, on return and on safety at once: it cost 1.4 points a year and still left a 36% fall, and three summers out of twenty-two carry all of it

methods.name: What does equal-weighting actually cost? The market-shape yardstick at 20, 30, 40 and 50 names
methods.hypothesis: M0120's scenery book turned out to be its best finding: the 20 index members with the largest 20-day dollar volume, equal weight, monthly, no timing rule of any kind, earned +5.7% a year on the owner's deposits against +7.2% for the same deposits in SPY over 1996-2015, at a 74.4% worst fall against SPY's 55%. That is the price of betting against the market's cap-weighted shape, measured cleanly for the first time, and it is the number insight 91 and the owner's money runs kept pointing at without ever pinning down. This method pins it down and splits it into its two possible causes, which M0120 could not separate with one book. Cause one is EQUAL WEIGHTING itself -- giving a tn company the same 5% slot as a bn one.
