Cause two is CONCENTRATION -- holding only 20 names, so the book is a thin, high-variance sample of the market rather than the market. Six variants on MONTHLY_HOLD_FRAC_GOTRADE, all reusing M0120's screen (f_factor.factor_rows, trend=None, no gate, rank on 20-day dollar volume descending) so the picks are identical in kind and only the shape changes: EW20, EW30, EW40, EW50 (equal weight, widening the book; if concentration is the cause the gap to SPY should close steadily as the count rises), and DV20, DV50 (the same names weighted in PROPORTION to their 20-day dollar volume rather than equally, which is the closest thing the store can build to a cap-weighted book; if equal weighting is the cause these two should land much nearer SPY at the same name counts). Read the pair EW20 vs DV20 and the ladder EW20->EW50 together: they decompose the 1.5-point penalty into a weighting part and a breadth part. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY -- none of these picks stocks, so none should beat SPY and none should be promoted. What the lab gets is a starting handicap it can subtract from every future book before crediting its picking rule, and an answer to the open question from the owner's money runs: whether a 20-40 name equal-weight book is betting against the market's shape (and how much that costs) or merely holding a noisy sample of it. Report the handicap separately for 1996-2008 and 2009-2015, because the whole lab has learned that a twenty-year average hides the era that matters.

methods.name: Does the market-shape handicap explain the lab's whole 0-for-5 record? Three near-eligible books re-sized by trading value against their own equal-weight twins
methods.sourceRef: parents M0088-C-LIVE-63, M0082-X-N40 and M0076-X-M, each run twice; insight 58 (the roster's common shortfall to deposit-matched SPY), insight 91 (equal weighting as a bet against the market's shape), M0117-C (the shape priced alone: 6.5% a year against SPY's 7.2%, a 57% fall), M0092 (the same swap on one event-drift parent, which failed)
methods.hypothesis: Every book in this lab holds equal slots and SPY does not, and M0117-C priced that choice alone at roughly half a point a year before any signal is added. If the handicap is roughly constant it is most of the roster's shortfall, and 146 methods have been blaming their picking rules for a loss the portfolio's SHAPE was always going to deliver. This method tests it directly instead of by inference. Three near-eligible parents with no test-failed kin -- the calm big-raiser book M0088-C-LIVE-63, the declaration-discipline book M0082-X-N40 and the announcement-timed raise book M0076-X-M -- each run twice in this one batch on the owner's real deposits at Gotrade's real fees, monthly, in fractional shares. Both arms pass through the same wrapper and differ in one field: the picks are spread equally, or in proportion to their 60-session median trading value capped at 10% of the account. The parent chooses the same names in the same order either way, and each parent's SPY park keeps its weight untouched, so the invested fraction matches and the paired difference is the weighting scheme and nothing else. The hypothesis: each trading-value twin beats its own equal-weight control by roughly 1 to 1.5 points a year with a materially shallower worst fall, in which case equal weighting is a free handicap every book here has been paying and the fix is a sizing change rather than a new signal. Prior evidence points the other way and is stated before the run: M0092 made this exact swap on the filtered news-day book and the trading-value arm deepened the 1998 fall (23.5-24.5% against 22.4%) while still losing to SPY after 2009. That was one parent; this is three, paired. Trading value is a proxy for size and not market value -- the lab's own market-cap figure is broken (unadjusted share count times split-adjusted close) -- and no verdict from this method may claim a cap-weighted book was built.
methods.expectedFailure: What would make this method's answer wrong rather than merely negative. (1) Trading value is not market value. A book re-sized by it leans toward heavily traded names, which correlates with size but also with turmoil in the name; a twin that wins may be paid for the second thing. The verdict must say 'trading value', never 'cap-weighted'. (2) Concentration is the mechanism and the risk at once. M0092's twin deepened its worst fall, and the 10% cap is the only thing standing between a volume tilt and a one-stock bet -- the lab has seen 61% in a single name when that cap was absent. If a twin wins on return and loses on worst fall, the honest reading is that the handicap and the risk have different causes, not that the shape theory is confirmed. (3) The parents all park in SPY, and the park is untouched here by construction; a parent that is mostly parked has little for the weighting to act on, so a null result on M0088 specifically may mean 'not much was re-weighted' rather than 'weighting does not help'. The share of account in picks versus park must be reported beside each pair. (4) Three parents from two families is not the lab. A win here licenses re-running the near misses this way; it does not license a claim about every book on the books. (5) The dev window contains dot-com and 2008, both of which punish concentration, while the era the lab is judged on was carried by a few giant names. A twin that loses on dev may still be the right shape for the test window, and this method cannot see that -- so a negative result closes the dev-window question only, and must be written that way. (6) If every twin lands within 0.2 points a year of its control, the weighting scheme is empty at this cap and the finding is that the handicap M0117-C measured does not transfer to books that pick.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

The market-shape theory is dead for the dev window, and it died the same way on all three books.

Each pair differed in one field. Weighting the picks by how heavily they trade, instead of
equally, cost return every single time: the calm big-raiser book fell from 10.6% a year to 10.2%,
the declaration book from 9.1% to 7.9%, and the announcement-timed raise book from 10.9% to 10.1%.
Three for three against, averaging about 0.8 of a point a year, where the hypothesis predicted a
GAIN of 1 to 1.5 points. It also cost the luck score in all three (0.942 to 0.924, 0.905 to 0.836,
0.927 to 0.892), which pushed two of the three twins out of eligibility on their own.

So the half-point handicap measured on a book with no picking rule does not transfer to books that
pick. Equal weighting is not a free handicap these books have been paying, and the lab's 146
methods were not losing a fight they never knew they were in. Whatever is wrong with the roster,
this is not it -- which was the question, and the answer is no.

What the swap IS good for, and this is worth keeping. It cut the worst fall in two of the three,
and in one of them substantially: the declaration book's worst fall went from 27.0% to 21.2%, and
the announcement book's from 21.9% to 20.5%. That is the mirror image of what M0092 found on the
news-day book, where the same swap made the fall deeper. Weighting toward heavily traded names is
therefore a drawdown tool that charges about a point a year for the service, and whether it helps
or hurts the fall depends on the book -- it is not a free lunch in either direction.

Stated plainly because it bounds the finding: this closes the question for the dev window only.
That window contains the dot-com crash and 2008, and both punish concentration; the years the lab
is actually judged on were carried by a handful of very large companies. A tilt toward the biggest
names losing over 1996-2015 does not mean it would lose over 2016-2026, and nothing here can see
that. What it does mean is that the shape theory cannot explain the roster's record, because the
roster's record was earned on this window.

Trading value is a stand-in for company size, not company size itself -- the lab's own market-cap
figure is known to be broken -- so nothing here says a cap-weighted book was tested. Prior evidence
pointed this way already: M0092 ran the same swap on one event-drift book and it failed there too.
Three more parents, paired in one batch, now say the same thing.
methods.verdict: Rejected direction, and it closes the question: weighting the picks by how heavily they trade cost return on all three books (-0.4, -1.2 and -0.8 points a year) where a gain of 1 to 1.5 was predicted, and cost the luck score on all three. Equal weighting is not the free handicap the lab's 0-for-5 record was blamed on. It does cut the worst fall on two of the three (27.0% to 21.2% on the declaration book), so it is a drawdown tool that charges about a point a year, not a shape fix. Dev window only -- those years punish concentration and the years we are judged on did not.

methods.name: Hold your shortlist, do not resample it: separating how many names a book owns from how often it swaps them
methods.sourceRef: M0118 (ALWAYS arm) and M0097 (S20-ALWAYS arm): the same basket at two slot counts
methods.hypothesis: M0118's no-clock control is the finding, and it is about construction, not timing. Two methods have now held an equal-weight basket carved from the same shortlist -- the 100 most-traded point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members by 60-day median dollar volume -- at Gotrade's real fees, monthly, fractional, on the owner's top-up, over the same 1996-2015 window: M0097-S20-ALWAYS held 20 and earned +3.2% a year on the deposits; M0118-ALWAYS held 50 and earned +6.0%. Nearly three points a year from slot count alone, larger than any clock the lab has priced including M0084's 200-day switch. But the trade counts say it is probably NOT concentration: 20 slots took 3479 trades and 50 took 5888, because both SAMPLE the shortlist (every k-th name by dollar-volume rank) and that ranking reshuffles monthly, so names churn in and out for no reason connected to any signal. M0097's all-100 arm took only 1621 trades -- but it was CLOCKED, so it is not a control and must not be quoted as one; that missing control is why this needs its own run. Design: one shortlist, one cadence, one fee model, no clock anywhere, and vary only construction, so slot count and resampling stop being the same number. Arms: TOP50 and TOP20 take the top half and top fifth of the shortlist outright, selling a name only when it leaves that band; SAMPLE50 and SAMPLE20 take every second and every fifth name, reproducing the M0118 and M0097 constructions under one shared lookback so the 20-vs-50 comparison is within one method rather than across two; ALL100 holds the whole shortlist at 1% each, the no-churn limit of the ladder. The sixth arm is not a construction at all: the book engine tops a held name up only once it is off by 1% of the WHOLE ACCOUNT, and in a 100-name book each slot is 1% of the account, so a monthly deposit can never reach a held name and money is deployed only by turnover -- which would make the least-churning arm also the slowest to invest and the ladder unreadable. ALL100-TB is the same all-100 book on the target-basis band (20% of the holding's own target), so the ALL100 / ALL100-TB pair prices that cash drag directly. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: every arm is fully invested in equities with no safety rule of any kind, so all six carry 2008 in full and none is expected to clear the real-money 25% worst-fall bar; the dev screen is 50% and a 100-name book of the biggest members may sit near it, so screening through is possible but is not the point. The readable numbers are the funded return, the trade count, the money-in-picks share and the 2009-2015 split. The hypothesis under test: at equal slot count the no-sampling arm beats the sampling arm, and the gap is roughly the churn the trade counts predict. If TOP50 beats SAMPLE50 by a point a year or more, every sampled book in the lab is paying a construction tax that has nothing to do with its signal, and the fix is free.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely outcome is that the slot-count ladder is real but is a cash story, not a concentration story: ALL100 under the equity band deploys the owner's deposits only through turnover, and with the least turnover of any arm it may sit on a large and growing cash pile, so it could post the best money-in-picks-adjusted return and the worst funded return at once, or the reverse. If ALL100 and ALL100-TB differ by more than a point a year, nothing in the ladder can be read as slot count until the band is controlled, and the honest verdict is that the M0097-vs-M0118 gap was never measured. The second likely failure is that TOP and SAMPLE barely differ: an evenly spaced sample of a dollar-volume ranking is not a random sample, it is a stratified one, and its churn may be small enough that the fee difference is tenths of a point rather than the point-a-year the trade counts suggest -- the extra trades of a sampled book are mostly tiny boundary swaps whose fee is a few cents on a $28 order. Third, TOP20 is twenty mega-caps and is close to a cap-weighted index with the weights thrown away, so it may beat SAMPLE20 for a reason that has nothing to do with churn: it simply owns the companies that led, which is the market-shape effect M0122 just priced and found costly to chase. Fourth, all six are fully invested through 2000-2002 and 2008 and will fall 50-60%, so beats-SPY-TR and the worst-fall screen are the conditions that decide eligibility and the luck bar will be far out of reach at N in the eighties. Not modelled: interest on idle cash, which matters most to exactly the arm (ALL100) whose cash pile this method is trying to measure, so the cash drag reported here is an upper bound on the real one.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

## What this tested

Two earlier experiments held the same kind of basket: take the 100 most heavily traded big
American companies, own a slice of them equally, rebalance once a month, pay Gotrade's real fees,
add 5 million rupiah on the 25th of every month, 1996 to 2015. One of them held 20 of the 100 and
earned **+3.2% a year** on the money paid in. The other held 50 and earned **+6.0%**. Nearly three
points a year, apparently from nothing but owning more names.

That looked like one of the biggest effects this lab had ever measured — bigger than any
market-timing rule it has priced. It was worth checking, because both of those baskets chose
their names the same slightly odd way: they sorted the 100 companies by how much money changes
hands in them, then took **every second name**, or **every fifth name**, down that list. The
sorting is redone every month. So a company that drifts from fifth place to sixth gets sold, and
whoever is now fifth gets bought — for no reason at all. The two experiments were therefore
changing *two* things at once, how many names they owned and how much pointless swapping they
did, and could not tell them apart.

So this method ran six versions of the same basket. No market timing anywhere, one shortlist, one
monthly rhythm, one fee schedule. Only the shape changed:

- **ALL100** — own all 100, 1% each.
- **TOP50 / TOP20** — own the busiest 50, or the busiest 20, outright. A name is sold only when it
  genuinely drops out of that group.
- **SAMPLE50 / SAMPLE20** — every second name, every fifth name: the two older constructions,
  rebuilt here so the comparison happens inside one experiment.
- **ALL100-TB** — the same all-100 basket, with one setting changed that turned out to matter more
  than everything else on this list put together. More on that below.

## The results

| version | names owned | your money, a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | share of the account actually invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ALL100-TB** | 100 | **+8.6%** | +7.2% | 59% | 1.30 | 859 | 96% |
| TOP20 | 20 | +7.3% | +7.2% | 69% | 1.47 | 294 | 96% |
| TOP50 | 50 | +6.5% | +7.2% | 57% | 1.25 | 529 | 87% |
| SAMPLE50 | 50 | +6.0% | +7.2% | 59% | 1.25 | 5,888 | 96% |
| ALL100 | 100 | +5.5% | +7.2% | 38% | 1.38 | 859 | **51%** |
| SAMPLE20 | 20 | +2.5% | +7.2% | 60% | 1.05 | 3,481 | 96% |

"Your money, a year" is the money-weighted return — what the deposits actually earned, which is
the only honest way to score a book that is fed 5 million rupiah a month. "Worst fall" is how far
the account dropped from a previous high, measured without the deposits, because monthly top-ups
refill a falling account and make a fall look gentler than it was. "Gains vs losses" (profit
factor) is total winnings divided by total losses; the go-live bar is 1.3. The rightmost column is
new and is the whole story.

**None of the six is eligible.** Every one of them is fully invested in shares with no safety rule
of any kind, so all six rode 2000-2002 and 2008 down in full. The worst falls run from 38% to 69%,
against a dev screen of 50% and a real-money limit of 25%. That was pre-registered as the expected
outcome: this was a measurement, not a candidate.

## Finding 1: half of a 100-name account was never invested at all

Look at the two all-100 rows. **Same picks. Same dates. The same 859 trades.** The only difference
is a single setting that decides when the simulator tops a holding back up: the normal setting
tops up a holding once it has drifted 1% **of the whole account** away from where it should be.

In a 100-name basket each holding *is* 1% of the account. So a monthly deposit can never move any
holding far enough to qualify — arithmetically it never can, at any account size. New money
therefore reached the basket only when a company dropped off the shortlist and was replaced, and
in a basket that barely changes, that is almost never.

The result: **ALL100 kept only 51% of the account invested.** Half the owner's deposits sat in
cash for twenty years. Switch to the other setting, where a holding is topped up once it is 20%
away from its *own* intended size, and the same basket is 96% invested — and earns **3.1 points a
year more**, +8.6% against +5.5%.

This also explains why ALL100 has the gentlest fall on the whole list, 38% against 59%. That was
never risk management. It was an accidental cash pile.

And the effect is not confined to 100-name books. TOP50 was 87% invested; TOP20 was 96%. **The
share of the account that gets invested is set by how much a book trades, not by anything its
designer chose.** A book that trades little quietly becomes part cash. Every result this lab has
recorded was measured on the 1%-of-the-whole-account setting.

## Finding 2: the three-point "more names is better" effect was not about the number of names

Once the cash is controlled, the original claim inverts. At roughly 96% invested throughout:
all 100 names earned +8.6%, 20 busiest names earned +7.3%, 50 sampled names +6.0%, 20 sampled
names +2.5%. Owning more was *better*, not worse, and the earlier 20-versus-50 gap was never a
slot-count effect. It was the sampling.

## Finding 3: sampling a ranking is enormously expensive, and the cost is not mainly fees

Here is the swapping, as a share of the basket replaced each month:

| version | basket replaced per month |
|---|---|
| ALL100 | 4% |
| TOP50 | 4% |
| TOP20 | 6% |
| SAMPLE50 | **50%** |
| SAMPLE20 | **73%** |

Taking every fifth name off a list that is re-sorted monthly means rebuilding nearly
three-quarters of the portfolio every month. Nothing about that is a decision; it is entirely an
artefact of where the sampling boundaries happen to fall.

At 50 names the damage is about what the fees predict. TOP50 earned +6.5% against SAMPLE50's
+6.0%, and TOP50 did it while 8 points *less* invested — so like for like, not sampling was worth
roughly a point a year, and this lab's own measurement of monthly trading costs (about 1.6% a year
to replace a whole book every month) accounts for most of it.

At 20 names the damage is four times larger than fees can explain. TOP20 and SAMPLE20 were both
96% invested, both held 20 names, both drew from the same shortlist, both paid the same fee
schedule — and TOP20 earned **+7.3% against +2.5%, a gap of 4.8 points a year**. Fees explain
perhaps 1.1 of that. The rest is *which* companies: TOP20 owns the twenty giants, SAMPLE20 owns a
spread running down to the hundredth name, and over this window the giants won. SAMPLE20's gains
barely exceeded its losses at all (1.05, where 1.0 is break-even), which is what a portfolio looks
like when most of its activity is noise.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**Half.** Not sampling beat sampling at both name counts, as predicted — the direction was right
every time. But the claim that the gap would be "roughly the churn the trade counts predict" holds
only at 50 names. At 20 names the gap is four times too big for fees, and the honest explanation is
that the two baskets simply own different companies.

**The expected failure happened, and bigger than written.** The pre-registration said that if the
two all-100 versions differed by more than a point a year, nothing in the ladder could be read as a
slot-count effect until the cash was controlled. They differ by 3.1 points. So by the standard set
before the run: the earlier three-point gap between the 20-name and 50-name baskets was never a
measurement of how many names to own, and should not be cited as one again.

## How it compares with its parents

SAMPLE50 is the same configuration the 50-name basket ran before, and it reproduced it exactly:
+22,545.4% total, 59.0% worst fall, 5,888 trades, to the digit. SAMPLE20 is very nearly the
20-name basket's configuration and came within 0.7 of a point (+2.5% against +3.2%); the small
difference is that this method demands a slightly different history length of each company before
it will rank it, so a handful of names differ at the edges. The bridge works: the numbers below
are comparable with both parents, same fees, same window, same deposits.

## The luck check

The best version scored **0.50 on the DSR**, against a bar of **0.90**. DSR asks how likely a
result is to be real rather than a lucky draw, after accounting for how many different ideas the
lab has tried — 85 distinct methods at the time of this run. Half is nowhere near. That is the
expected reading for a basket with no stock-picking idea in it at all: it beat SPY by 1.4 points a
year, which is not a wide enough margin to survive being discounted for 85 attempts. Neither the
bar nor the counting rule is mine to move.

## Where the money was made and lost

On the lab's normal price history — and the next section takes this away again — the all-100
basket with the money properly invested beat SPY in every era measured: +1.6% a year
over 1996-2002, +1.7% over 2003-2008, **+1.5% over 2009-2015** — the best-covered and most
present-day stretch, and the one this lab treats as the first filter. It won 3 of the lab's 4
walk-forward folds, losing only the one containing 2008, where it fell 4 points a year harder than
SPY. Its worst calendar year was 2008, down 40.8%.

The sampled 20-name basket is the mirror image: behind SPY by 4.7 points a year before 2002 and by
**7.5 points a year over 2009-2015**. It is the single worst construction in this experiment and it
is, unfortunately, close to what an earlier method in this lab was actually measuring.

## Finding 4: the dead companies erase all of it

The lab keeps a second price history for exactly this check. The one these six ran on prices 539
companies — the ones still around to be priced. The check history prices 989, including the
companies that went bankrupt or were taken over and vanished. Re-running all six on it, at the same
capital and the same deposits, is free: it records nothing and spends no test look.

| version | your money a year, normal history | ...with the dead companies priced | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| ALL100-TB | +8.6% | **+6.4%** | 59% → 62% |
| TOP20 | +7.3% | +6.0% | 69% → **81%** |
| TOP50 | +6.5% | +5.3% | 57% → 69% |
| SAMPLE50 | +6.0% | +3.3% | 59% → 70% |
| ALL100 | +5.5% | +4.8% | 38% → 45% |
| SAMPLE20 | +2.5% | +2.7% | 60% → 72% |

SPY earns +7.2% on both. **Not one of the six beats it once the companies that died are in the
data.** The best version's 1.4-point lead over SPY turns into a 0.8-point *lag*; its
gains-vs-losses reading drops from 1.30 to 1.02, which is break-even; and its advantage in the
modern 2009-2015 stretch shrinks from +1.5 points a year to +0.4. Five of the six earn less, and
every single one falls further — by 3 to 12 points, with the 20-giants version falling 81%.

That is as clean a verdict as this lab gets. The apparent edge in equal-weighting the busiest
index members was not an edge. It was the absence of the companies that failed. The whole family —
this method and the two baskets before it — has nothing in it.

## What killed the best version

ALL100-TB beat SPY on both ways of counting, won 3 of the 4 walk-forward folds, and was positive
in the modern era — on the normal history. It fails three ways. It fell **59%** at its worst,
against a 50% dev screen and the owner's 25% real-money limit: not close, and not fixable by
tuning. Its gains-vs-losses reading was **1.2975** against a bar of 1.30, missed by three
thousandths. And the survivorship check above removes the reason to care about either, because
with the dead companies priced it does not beat SPY at all.

**My opinion:** five of the six backtests here are now worthless, and so is the family they belong
to. Equal-weighting a basket of the busiest big American companies does not beat SPY; it only looks
like it does because the lab's main price history cannot price the companies that went under, and
this construction is maximally exposed to that gap — it owns everything on the shortlist, so every
missing failure is a missing loss. I would not spend another method id on any version of this
basket, with or without a timing rule on top, and the two earlier baskets' results should be read
the same way from now on.

The run was still worth its id, because of the thing it found by accident. A single simulator
setting — one nobody chose deliberately, that has been the same in every trial this lab has ever
recorded — was holding **half of a 100-name account in cash** and about an eighth of a 50-name
account. It is the rule that decides when a holding gets topped up, and it measures the shortfall
against 1% of the *whole account*, which a 1% holding can never reach. Switching it to measure
against the holding's own size was worth **3.1 points a year** on the normal history and **1.6
points** on the check history — the only finding in this run that survives the survivorship test,
and larger than most stock-picking edges this lab has measured. It also means every recorded result
here was run on a book that was partly a cash position, with the cash share set by how much the
book happened to trade rather than by anything its author chose: that flatters the worst falls of
slow-trading books and drags their returns, in no consistent direction across methods.

So the next method id should go to the near misses, re-run on the setting that actually invests the
money. M0021-B70-RAW already clears every go-live condition and fails only the luck bar; it holds 70
names and trades about 11 a month, so it is near-certainly under-invested in exactly this way, and
a book that is more invested earns more, which raises its MAR and its luck score together. That is a
cheap, direct attempt at the one wall this lab keeps hitting, and it is where I would go next.
methods.verdict: Rejected, and it takes two older methods with it: the basket's apparent edge was the missing dead companies, and the three-point 'more names is better' gap was never slot count — but half of a 100-name account was silently sitting in cash, and fixing that was worth 3.1 points a year

methods.name: Run every new on-off rule backwards in the same batch, as a standing variant slot
methods.hypothesis: Not a trading idea: a cheap change to how the lab spends its six variant slots, raised because M0118 is the first method whose inverted arm paid for itself. M0118 priced a dispersion clock and lost 1.6 pts/yr to its own no-clock control; the INV arm -- the identical clock read the other way -- lost 1.1. Both directions losing is what separates 'this signal is empty' from 'this signal is pointing the wrong way', and only the second is fixable by flipping. Without the INV arm the honest verdict would have had to stay open and the lab would have owed the direction a follow-up method id; with it, dispersion-as-a-switch is closed in one run. M0084 did not have one and its verdict rests on inference; M0097 did not have one either. The cost is one of six slots in a batch that already spends three or four on parameter sweeps that land within a point of each other, which is the worst value per slot the lab buys. Proposal: for any method whose core is a binary exposure rule (hold A when the reading is above a threshold, hold B otherwise), the pre-registration carries a mandatory inverted twin and a mandatory no-rule control, and the sweep gets what is left. This is a convention to argue for in docs/plans/2026-10-04-method-lab-design.md rather than code -- but if it is worth enforcing, the natural place is a check in lab/hardgate.py or the lab runner that warns when a switch-shaped method registers neither an inverted arm nor a control. Judge it by re-reading the three switch methods the lab has: how many of their verdicts would have been stronger or cheaper with the pair, and how many sweep arms would have had to go to pay for it.

methods.name: Stop fighting the market's shape: the same fifty members, weighted by how heavily they trade instead of equally
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0117-C (the signal-free fifty-name control); insight 91; M0034 for the trading-value weighting and the per-name ceiling; M0122 for the same swap on picked books
methods.hypothesis: M0117 produced the control the lab never had: the fifty most heavily traded index members in equal 2% slots, on the owner's real deposits at Gotrade's real fees, earned 6.5% a year against SPY's 7.2% and fell 57%, over 1996-2015. That is a half-point-a-year structural handicap paid before any signal is added, and insight 91 says the cause is equal weighting betting against the market's shape. This tests the fix directly and changes exactly one thing: keep M0117-C's universe, screen, monthly cadence, rules preset (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade: fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees) and funding, and weight each holding by its 20-day mean dollar volume instead of 1/50. Dollar volume stands in for size because the lab's market-cap figure is broken and EDGAR share counts start in 2009, while trading value is sound from 1993 and needs no new data. Variants: EQ, M0117-C's equal weight re-run under this allocator as the matched control; DV, raw trading-value weight; DV-C10 and DV-C05, the same with no name above 10% or 5%; SQRT, square-root weight as a half-way house. M0122 already showed this swap costs return on books that carry a signal; this asks it on the book with none, which is what says whether the lab's yardstick is biased. M0123-TOP20 (the twenty most traded, equal) earned 7.3% against TOP50's 6.5%, a hint that leaning toward the biggest names helps the plain book. Success: a weighted version closes most of the half-point gap to SPY AND cuts the 57% fall materially, and does so in 2009-2015 too. Weighting by size is not a published anomaly; it is how SPY itself is built, so there is no edge here to fade -- the best outcome is matching SPY, not beating it.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely result is that no version beats SPY and none fixes the fall. Fifty large companies weighted by size is a rough copy of SPY with fifty names instead of five hundred, so at best it tracks SPY minus Gotrade's fees on monthly resizing, and minus the fee minimum's bite on the many small slots early on. The 57% fall is 2000-2002 and 2008, which SPY itself fell 55% through; weighting cannot remove a market fall, only reshuffle it, so the worst-fall condition probably stays failed on every variant and the luck score stays far under 0.90. The interesting failure is closing the return gap while keeping the fall, which would say the handicap and the risk have different causes. The uncapped DV version may concentrate in one or two giants (M0034's SIZE put up to 61% in one stock) and fall harder than equal in 2000-2002, when the most traded names were the tech leaders. Survivorship cuts against this test too: the dev store is missing many of the small dead members, so the equal-weight control is flattered and the gap it shows is understated.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

# M0125: the same fifty companies, sized by how heavily they trade

## What was tried

The lab's plainest book holds the 50 most heavily traded companies in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100,
2% in each, and re-chooses them once a month. It has no stock-picking signal at all. Over 1996-2015,
on the owner's real deposits (10 million rupiah at the start, then 5 million on the 25th of every
month) and paying Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares, it earned 6.5% a year. The same deposits
in SPY earned 7.2%. One explanation is that giving every company the same 2% bets against how the
market is built. In SPY the giants carry far more weight than the small members.

This method changed one thing only: how big each of the fifty slots is. Everything else was kept
exactly as before: the same fifty names, the same monthly cadence, fractional shares, Gotrade's real
fees and the same deposits. The size of each slot was set by the company's average daily trading
value (shares traded times price, averaged over 20 days), which the lab can measure from 1993. The
lab's own market-value figure is known to be wrong, so trading value stood in for size.

Five versions:

- **Equal**: 2% each, the old book, re-run as the matched control.
- **By trading value**: each company sized in proportion to how much it trades.
- **By trading value, at most 10%** in any one company, the rest spread over the others.
- **By trading value, at most 5%** in any one company.
- **Half-way**: sized by the square root of trading value, which leans the same way but less.

## The result

**All five lost to SPY, and the four sized versions fell much further than the equal one.
Rejected.**

| Version | Earned a year | SPY, same deposits | Worst fall | Gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal (control) | +6.5% | +7.2% | 57.2% | 1.31 |
| By trading value | +6.3% | +7.2% | 72.9% | 0.99 |
| **At most 10% each** | **+6.9%** | +7.2% | 72.4% | 0.99 |
| At most 5% each | +6.4% | +7.2% | 68.9% | 1.02 |
| Half-way | +6.6% | +7.2% | 64.0% | 1.14 |

The equal version reproduced the old book to the decimal (6.5%, a 57.2% fall), so the comparison
is clean: every difference in the table is the sizing and nothing else.

What failed:

- **Beat SPY**: no version did. The best, capped at 10%, closed most of the gap but still trailed by
  0.3 of a point a year.
- **Worst fall**: the lab's screen allows a 50% fall (the real-money bar is 25%). The equal book
  already broke it at 57%. Sizing by trading value made it worse, to 64-73%. That fall is measured
  on the book alone, with the monthly deposits taken out so fresh money does not hide it. The worst
  year was 2008 every time: −40% for equal, −47% for the full lean.
- **Gains vs losses**: the closed trades' total gains divided by total losses must be at least 1.3.
  Every sized version came in at 0.99-1.14.
- **Luck**: the luck score (DSR) asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of
  many tries. The bar is 0.90, and the lab now counts 104 distinct tries. The best score here was
  0.38. A result this close to SPY is indistinguishable from luck.
- **Walk-forward**: the method won only 1 of 4 later three-year stretches against SPY.

## Why: trading value measures the crowd, not size

At the start the expected failure was a book that leaned into a few giants. It did that, but not
on the giants. Trading value is size *times how hot the stock is*, and the hot part dominates at
the worst moments. On 31 December 1999 the full-lean book had 13% in Qualcomm, 12% in Microsoft,
8% in Cisco, 6% in Intel and 5% in Oracle: almost half the money in five technology stocks, right
before they lost most of their value. General Electric and Exxon were both far bigger companies than
Qualcomm then, but they traded less, so the book gave them 4% and less. At the end of 2007 the book's banks (Citigroup, Goldman Sachs) were
among its largest holdings because everyone was trading them, and 2008 followed. Google even
counted twice, once for each of its two share classes.

The capped versions did not fix this. A 10% ceiling binds on only one or two names. The other top
names were already under it, so in early 2000 the capped book still held 46% in the same six
technology stocks. The 5% cap did spread the money more, but it also lost most of the return.

The month-by-month split says the same thing. In months when a few big names carried the index,
the full-lean book beat SPY by 11 points a year (annualised). In months when the rest of the
market did better, it lost 7. Equal weighting sat between the two at +0.7 and −1.4. Sizing by
trading value made the book a stronger bet on the crowd's favourites, in both directions.

## The two things worth keeping

**First, the shape handicap is real in the years that matter most.** From 2009 to 2015, the years
most like today, equal weighting trailed SPY by 0.4 of a point a year. Every sized version beat
SPY there: +1.9 points for the 10% cap, +0.7 for the full lean, +0.5 for the 5% cap and the half-way
version.

**Second, the check on the history that includes the companies that died agrees, and it says
something sharper.** The lab's usual price history is missing about half of the index's past
members, mostly the ones that failed. Re-running the five versions on a history that includes most
of them:

| Version | Usual history | With the dead companies | Worst fall, with them |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equal | +6.5% | +4.2% | 72.1% |
| By trading value | +6.3% | +5.2% | 81.1% |
| At most 10% each | +6.9% | +5.6% | 80.6% |
| At most 5% each | +6.4% | +5.0% | 80.4% |
| Half-way | +6.6% | +4.8% | 76.8% |

With the dead companies put back, equal weighting loses 3 points a year to SPY, not 0.7. The usual
history flattered it badly, because the companies that collapsed were often the smaller members an
equal book over-owns. The sized versions lose less of their return (1.1-1.8 points, against 2.3
for equal). So the handicap from equal weighting is bigger than the lab thought, and leaning
toward bigger companies does recover some of it. But every version falls more than 76% on that
history. That rules out any of them as a book to own.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Half of it. The return gap closed: the 10%-capped version recovered 0.4 of the 0.7 point on the
usual history, and more on the fuller one. But the fall got far worse, not better. This is the
"interesting failure" written down before the run: the handicap and the risk have different causes.
The handicap comes from under-owning the companies that grow. The fall comes from owning whatever
the crowd is chasing when it turns. Trading value fixes the first by doing more of the second.

The expected failure partly happened: the book did concentrate and did fall harder in 2000-2002
and 2008. What was not expected is *where* it concentrated: on the most traded names, not the
biggest.

## Compared with the near misses

The lab's earlier trading-value sizing on books that already picked stocks (the momentum book and
three event-driven books) also cost return and changed the fall. This run says why that happened,
and why it should not be read as "equal weighting is fine". Trading value is the wrong stand-in for
size. It loads up on manias, and that was the cost those books paid, not size itself.

**My opinion:** Stop using trading value as a size measure. It is the cause of both this failure
and the earlier ones. The shape question is still open and still matters: on the fuller history,
equal weighting costs 3 points a year before any signal is added. Every near miss that beats SPY
by a point or two may simply be paying that handicap better than the control. The next trial should
size the fifty by a measure of size that does not swing with excitement: trading value averaged
over a full year instead of 20 days, with the two Google share classes counted once. If that
still cannot track SPY within a few tenths of a point with a fall no worse than SPY's own 55%, the
lab should stop building index-member books for owners who can just buy SPY, and treat SPY itself
as the base that any signal must add to.
methods.verdict: Rejected: sizing the fifty by how heavily they trade bought back part of the shortfall to SPY but loaded up on whatever the crowd was chasing — half the money in five tech stocks at the end of 1999 — and deepened the worst fall from 57% to as much as 73%.

methods.name: Re-weight the closest near miss: the calm-stock blend sized by trading volume rather than equal slots
methods.hypothesis: Conditional on the volume-weighting idea showing that equal weighting costs about half a point a year and a chunk of the drawdown, the lab's near misses need re-reading. M0021-B70-RAW is the closest thing the lab has to a pass (MAR 0.90, +12.6% against SPY's +7.9%, 14.0% worst fall, DSR 0.945 at the bars in force) and it is an equal-weight book. If equal weighting is a half-point-a-year handicap, then M0021's edge is understated by that much and its real picking edge is larger than recorded; if instead its edge IS the small-company tilt that equal weighting produces, then weighting by trading volume should erase most of it. Those two readings predict opposite results from the same single change, which is why this is worth one id: keep M0021-B70-RAW's picks, params, cadence, rules preset and funding exactly, and change only the slot sizing to dollar-volume weight with the same cap ladder the parent idea settles on. Success: the weighted twin keeps or improves the parent's margin over SPY while reducing its worst fall, which would make it the strongest promotion candidate in the lab. Failure, and the more informative outcome, is the margin collapsing, which would say the lab's best result to date is a size bet wearing a stock-picking costume and would explain why four of four test-window looks have failed against a cap-weighted SPY.

methods.name: Rebalance on the slot, not on the account: pricing the trading threshold that never fires
methods.sourceRef: M0119 (the deposit-deployment method, whose closing paragraph queued this one) for the question; M0109 for the neutral 50-name base book and its 1338-identical-trades evidence; M0139 for the nearest prior art, which measured the two bases on a high-churn gated book and found almost nothing; insight 479 for the 1.25 points a year the weighting arrangement was worth on identical names and identical trades
methods.hypothesis: The book engine trims or tops up a holding only once its gap from target is worth at least a band, and under the equity basis -- the basis of every recorded trial in this lab before 2026-10-12 -- that band is 1% of the WHOLE account and does not scale with the slot. At fifty equal slots it is half a holding, and the gap clears it in 0.1% of holding-months (0.8% at 30 names, 4.2% at 20, 16.2% at 12); M0109's monthly and weekly 50-name controls made the identical 1338 trades. So every book this lab runs at 20 names or more is in practice never rebalanced, whatever its method file says. This method prices the alternative on a book whose picks do no stock picking at all: M0109's unbraked base, the 50 most-traded index members at equal weight, with ONE allocator and ONE params object across every arm, so all five are handed byte-identical targets on byte-identical dates and the ONLY difference between them is how far a holding may drift before it is traded back. The ladder is the control at 1% of the account (half a slot, the status quo) and four treatments at 33%, 20%, 10% and 0% of the holding's own target, 0% being a full rebalance to 1/50 on every month start -- the textbook monthly rebalance, and the only arm that unambiguously is one. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fee schedule, the owner's funding plan, against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days. PREDICTIONS, written now. (1) Trade count rises monotonically as the band tightens, from near the book's forced minimum at the control to roughly fifty orders per month start at 0%. (2) RETURN IS NOT MONOTONE. Gotrade charges a minimum per order and a rebalancing trade is a slot's DRIFT, not a slot: at a $29 slot a 10% drift is a $2.90 order paying about 4.5% to trade, so the fee bill explodes as the band tightens while the rebalancing benefit does not. Expect the ladder to rise from the control to some middle rung and then collapse, with the 0% arm the worst arm in the lab by a wide margin. Where it turns is the deliverable. (3) Worst fall improves slightly and monotonically with tightening, because never trimming lets a winner grow into a concentration the book never agreed to; largest around 2000-2002, when the most-traded list was the dot-coms. (4) The 2009-2015 column decides whether any of this transfers; a band effect that lives only in 1996-2002 is a reading of a bubble. (5) No arm is expected to be a candidate and none is being pursued as one: the base is M0109's, which trailed SPY, and an equal-weight book of the most-traded members is a bet against SPY's big-company shape before any band is applied. ASSUMPTIONS RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN: the band's size needed a new rule-set lever (TradeRules.resize_band, a post-pins no-op lever that moves no recorded digest), and the three new rungs are one-off rule sets rather than presets, which makes them unpromotable by construction -- accepted, with a feature wish journalled. Success here is a measurement, not a candidate: state what genuine monthly rebalancing costs in fees and pays in return and in worst fall, on a book whose picks do not change, so the number transfers to every book in the lab.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest disappointment is that the ladder is swamped by its own fee bill and says nothing about rebalancing at all. Gotrade's minimum is charged per order and a drift trade is tiny, so if even the 33% rung pays more in fees than it recovers in return, the honest reading is that this is a measurement of a 20,000,000 IDR account's order economics rather than of rebalancing, and the verdict must say so and must quote the turnover and the fee bill beside the return so the two can be told apart. The second way it fails is that the band turns out not to bind even at 33%, because the dollar-volume ranking already replaces enough of the book each month that holdings never get the chance to drift -- which is precisely what happened to M0139 on a high-churn book -- in which case the control and the first two treatments record near-identical trade counts and the finding is that this base was not slow enough either. The third is survivorship: the dev store prices no delisted names and this book holds fifty of the shortlist, so the names that drifted furthest down are disproportionately the ones missing; a rebalancing rule buys the fallers, so if the dead companies are absent the trimming-and-topping-up arms are flattered, and the widest-moving arm must be survivorship-checked and the result quoted beside the dev column. The fourth is that the effect is real but lives entirely in 2000-2002, where the most-traded list was the dot-coms and the equal-weight book fell 58%: a rule that only helps in one bubble has been tested once. The fifth is that the deposits soften every arm's worst fall alike, so none of these falls may be lined up against an unfunded trial's.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-20

# M0127 — the trading threshold that never fires, and what it was quietly costing

## This is a ruler, not a strategy

Nothing here is a candidate and nothing is being proposed for your money. The book used below
holds the fifty most-traded big American companies in equal amounts and does no stock picking at
all. It fell 57% at its worst, which is more than twice the 25% you allow. It exists only so that
one thing can be measured cleanly: **a rule inside the simulator that nobody chose on purpose, and
that has been shaping every wide book this lab has ever run.**

## The rule, and why it was broken

When a holding drifts away from the size it is supposed to be, the simulator only trades it back
if the gap is big enough to be worth a trade. Fair enough. The problem is what "big enough" was
measured against: **one per cent of the whole account**, rather than one per cent of the holding.

That number does not shrink as a book gets wider. Hold twelve names and each is about 8% of the
account, so a 1% gap is an eighth of the holding — a sensible trigger. Hold fifty names and each
is 2% of the account, so a 1% gap is **half the holding**. The name has to roughly halve or double
before anything happens. In practice nothing ever happens.

There is a one-line way to say this, and it is worth remembering:

> **A book of N equal names has been running on a trigger of N per cent of a holding.**
> Twenty names, 20%. Fifty names, 50%. A hundred names, 100% — it can never fire.

So the twenty-name book you actually hold has been fine all along. Everything wider than that has
been running a rule its own method file did not describe.

## What was run

Five versions of the identical book. Same fifty names, same dates, same equal shares, same
fractional trading, same real Gotrade fees, same 10 million rupiah start and 5 million a month.
The **only** difference between them is how far a holding may drift before it is traded back:

| version | trigger |
|---|---|
| E1 | 1% of the whole account — the old rule, and half a holding here |
| T33 | a third of the holding |
| T20 | a fifth of the holding — the rule the lab switched to on 12 October |
| T10 | a tenth of the holding |
| T00 | nothing at all — every holding is put back to exactly its share every month |

All five were run in one sweep on one copy of the price data, so none of the differences below is
an artefact of the data being rebuilt in between.

## The result

| version | money left idle | money moved a year | your money a year | worst fall | 2009–2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **E1 (old rule)** | **11.4%** | 2.86x | **+6.46%** | **57.2%** | **−0.4%** |
| T33 | 6.6% | 2.91x | +6.56% | 58.8% | −0.1% |
| **T20 (current rule)** | **3.8%** | 3.00x | **+6.92%** | **59.2%** | **+0.5%** |
| T10 | 2.2% | 3.13x | +6.86% | 59.7% | +0.5% |
| **T00 (full rebalance)** | **1.4%** | 3.38x | **+6.95%** | **59.5%** | **+0.5%** |
| SPY, same deposits | — | — | +7.19% | — | — |

**Every version lost to simply buying SPY with the same money.** That is the base book's fault, not
the trigger's, and it is why all five are rejected.

## What genuine monthly rebalancing costs, and what it pays

This is the number the method exists to produce, so here it is plainly. Going from the old rule to
a full monthly rebalance, on a book whose picks are identical:

**It pays:**

* **+0.49 points a year** of your own money's return (+6.46% → +6.95%).
* **+0.9 points a year over 2009–2015**, and it flips the sign: that stretch went from losing to
  SPY by 0.4 points a year to beating it by 0.5. Those are the best-covered and most modern years
  in the window, which is the stretch that matters most.

**It costs:**

* **+0.11 points a year in fees.** The whole fee bill over twenty years went from $15,490 to
  $19,933 on $148,088 of deposits — $4,443 more. This was measured, not estimated: every version
  was run a second time with the fees switched off, so the gap between the two runs *is* the fee
  bill.
* **2.4 points of deeper worst fall** (57.2% → 59.5%). Only about 0.2 of that is the fees; the
  rest is real, and the reason is simple — rebalancing buys whatever has fallen, so in a market
  that keeps grinding lower it keeps buying on the way down. The worst year, 2008, went from
  −40.3% to −42.5%, and the only stretch where the old rule won was 2003–2008.
* **+18% more money moved each year** (2.86 turns to 3.38).

**And almost all of it arrives on the first step.** Going from the old rule to the current
one-fifth rule captures +0.46 of the +0.49 points. Tightening further to a tenth, or to a full
rebalance, adds three hundredths of a point for a third more trading. **The lab's switch on 12
October was the right call, and there is nothing left to win by tightening it further.**

## Why it pays — and it is not what we assumed

The honest mechanism is **cash, not rebalancing**. Under the old rule the account sat **11.4% in
cash it never chose to hold**: your monthly deposit could buy a brand-new holding but could never
top up one you already owned, because the top-up never cleared the trigger. The fixed rule puts
that money to work, and idle cash falls to 3.8%.

The evidence that this, and not the trimming itself, is the engine:

* idle cash falls by **ten points** across the ladder while the amount of trading rises by only
  **18%**;
* the gain stops exactly where the idle cash stops falling;
* the one step that buys a lot of extra trading for very little extra invested money — a tenth to
  a full rebalance — adds essentially nothing.

**What this does NOT settle**, and I want to be exact rather than flattering: this run cannot
split the gain between "the money got invested" and "trimming winners to feed losers is worth
something by itself". The two move together here. A separate journal entry recently priced the
second effect at about 1.25 points a year on identical names; **that number is not confirmed or
denied by anything above**, and I am not claiming a share of this 0.49 for it in either direction.
Splitting the two needs a book held at a fixed amount of cash on both sides, which is queued.

## With the failed companies put back

The dev data holds no companies that went bust, so every result above is flattered. The same five
versions were re-run on the check data, which puts most of the dead companies back.

The base book is wrecked by it, as expected: +6.9% a year becomes +4.7%, and the worst fall goes
from 59% to 73%. **But the trigger's own margin survives, and grows.** Over 2009–2015 the gap
between the old rule and the fixed one is **+0.9 points a year on the clean data and +1.3 points
on the honest data.** This is unusual — nearly everything in this lab shrinks when the dead
companies come back. It makes sense here, because the trigger's job is to get the deposit
invested, and that works whatever the names turn out to be.

## Did the predictions hold?

Three of five were written down before the run and three of them were **wrong**, which is worth
more than if they had been right.

1. **"Trading will rise step by step."** Half right, and I had the wrong meter. The trade counter
   did not move at all — all five recorded the same 1,338 trades — because that counter counts
   buying and selling a name, not the small top-ups and trims a trigger controls. Money moved
   *did* rise step by step. **A book whose only difference is its trigger will always look
   identical on trade count. Read money moved, and read idle cash.**
2. **"Fees will explode and the full rebalance will be the worst version in the lab."** Wrong, and
   badly. The extra fee bill was eleven hundredths of a point a year, not several points. My
   arithmetic assumed a $29 holding paying the broker's minimum on every little top-up — true in
   1996, meaningless by 2010, because the account had grown. **The minimum-fee problem is a
   small-young-account problem, and a twenty-year window spends most of its life not being one.**
   It still bites you *today*, which is the part worth carrying forward.
3. **"The worst fall will improve."** Wrong, and backwards. It got 2.4 points deeper, for a
   mechanical reason I should have seen: rebalancing buys the fallers.
4. **"2009–2015 decides whether this transfers."** Held, and it answered yes — that is where the
   effect is largest.
5. **"No version will be a candidate."** Held. All five rejected.

The expected failure I wrote — "the trigger will not bind even at a third, as happened on the
earlier high-churn book" — **did not happen**: it bound at every rung. Choosing a slow book was
the right call, and is the reason this run says something the earlier one could not.

## The luck test

The lab judges whether a result is real or a fluke with a score that gets harsher the more ideas
have been tried. The bar is 0.90 and the count is now 168 separate methods. These five score
**0.41 to 0.44** — far below. That is expected and not a disappointment: the book loses to SPY, so
there is nothing for the luck test to confirm. It also lost three of its four walk-forward
periods. **None of that touches the measurement**, which is a difference between two versions of
one book, not a claim that the book works.

## My opinion

**The direction is finished, and it produced a number I would act on.**

The finding is that a rule nobody chose was leaving about a tenth of a wide account sitting in
cash, and fixing it is worth roughly half a point a year — more like a point a year in the modern
era, and more still once the failed companies are put back. It costs about a tenth of a point in
fees and two and a half points of deeper worst fall. That trade is worth taking, and the lab has
already taken it.

Three concrete things follow.

**First, the twenty-name book you hold was never affected.** Twenty names on the old rule *is* the
new rule, exactly, by arithmetic — and the lab has confirmed it to the last decimal place. No
roster decision needs revisiting.

**Second, every comparison this lab has ever drawn between a wide book and a narrow one is
suspect, and not by a little.** The wide one was sitting in more cash, and nobody was told. Any
conclusion of the form "holding more names earns less" taken before 12 October was measuring the
trigger at least in part. I would not re-run them all, but I would refuse to quote any of them
without saying so.

**Third, do not tighten past a fifth of a holding.** Everything below that is more trading for no
return and a slightly worse fall. If a preset is ever added for this, a fifth is the right number
and the other rungs should not exist.

What I would do next, and have queued: separate the two halves of this gain. Everything above is
consistent with "the money got invested" being the whole story and the trimming being worth
nothing — but it is also consistent with the trimming being worth something and the cash less. The
clean way to find out is to hold the amount of invested money fixed on both sides and vary only
the trigger. Until that is run, nobody should quote a share.

One caveat on all of it. The deepening of the worst fall rests on 2003–2008, which is one crash,
and the 2.4 points is small enough that another crash could easily move it. The cash finding does
not depend on any crash at all, and is the part I would rely on.
methods.verdict: A trigger nobody chose was leaving a tenth of a wide book sitting in cash; fixing it is worth about half a point a year, nearly a point in the modern era, for a tenth of a point in fees and a two-point deeper fall — and the rule the lab already switched to captures almost all of it.

methods.sourceRef: M0030-SAT100, M0007-N20-RAW, M0021-B70-RAW, M0020-W-NOSTOP; controls from M0120-EW20-ALWAYS; docs/plans/HANDOVER_20261012-measure-then-learn.md section 2 item 4; insight 211
methods.hypothesis: A re-measurement, not a discovery. Every near miss here was measured on a tape that paid nothing on idle cash and resized a holding only when it drifted by 1% of the whole account. Both are fixed now as explicit levers: the band is 20% of the holding's own target, and idle cash earns the 13-week T-bill yield read the session before. All six variants run in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fee schedule, funded on the owner's plan (the opening book plus 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of every month) against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days, and every comparison below is that money-weighted pair. THE BAND ARITHMETIC, stated before the run: a 20-name equal-weight slot is 5% of the account and 20% of 5% is exactly 1%, the old band. So for RAW20-CASH, RAW20, W-NOSTOP-CASH and both controls the band fix changes nothing by construction, and RAW20 is expected to reproduce M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT -- the same picks at Gotrade's fees on the old band: money-weighted 13.7% a year against 7.2% for deposit-matched SPY, a 20.6% worst fall, gains 1.98 times losses, 1,607 trades -- to within what a different starting capital can move. A material gap there is a finding about the simulator before it is anything about the method. The band bites only on the blend, whose momentum slots are 3.5% of the account (band 0.7%) and calm slots 1.5% (band 0.3%): B70-CASH should trade visibly more often per name than any 20-name book here and pay for it in small-trim fees. THE CASH YIELD is where the tape moves. The gated books sit out roughly 30% of the months (M0030-SAT100 was 69% invested), and those months earn 3-5% a year before 2008 and almost nothing after it. Expected: RAW20-CASH leads RAW20 by 0.5 to 1.5 points a year of money-weighted return, almost all of it before 2008, with a worst fall within half a point of RAW20's. EW20-CASH, invested about 96% of the time, gains under 0.3 points and stays about 1.5 points a year behind deposit-matched SPY with a worst fall near 74% (M0120-EW20-ALWAYS: 5.7% against 7.2%). EW20-GATED-CASH should land near the gated most-liquid book the lab already measured (M0058-LIQ20-T: 8.1% against 7.2%, a 17.6% worst fall) plus its share of the cash interest. PICKING OR SHAPE, and the rule this method will be read by, fixed now: on this one tape, a near miss's PICKING is its money-weighted lead over deposit-matched SPY minus the gated control's lead; the GATE is the gated control's lead minus the ungated control's; the SHAPE is the ungated control's lead (negative means holding equal amounts cost money against the market). The picks are credited with an edge only if a twin beats the gated control by more than 1 point a year; otherwise the honest reading is that the near miss won on the gate and the shape. Expected: RAW20-CASH beats the gated control by 4 to 6 points a year, so the residual-momentum near misses were winning on their picks and not on their shape; the shape costs about 1.5 points a year; the gate is worth 2 to 3 points a year over the whole window, almost all of it in 2001-2002 and 2008. W-NOSTOP-CASH lands within half a point of RAW20-CASH, because with the band unchanged at 20 names the weekly re-issue still has almost nothing to do -- so insight 211's point that weekly against monthly measured nothing should hold for 20-name books even on the fixed tape. B70-CASH lands between RAW20-CASH and the gated control, its calm sleeve diluting the picks. WHAT THIS METHOD CANNOT DO is be promoted. Its line runs through M0029 and M0021, both test-failed, so the hard gate refuses it on kin whatever it scores; and every cash-yield variant carries the owner input cash-yield (Gotrade paying interest on idle dollars is not verified), which keeps it ineligible. Only RAW20 can be eligible, and it is expected to miss the 20% drawdown bar by about the 0.6 points M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT did. It is a measurement, registered as a method so that it is held to this prediction; it adds one idea to the lab's count.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest disappointment is that this confirms rather than changes anything: for five of the six variants the band fix is arithmetically a no-op and the cash yield is worth about a point, so the near misses land where they were, a fraction of a point either side of the 20% drawdown bar, and the method's real contribution is the control pair. Specific failures written now. (1) The picking edge may live in 1996-2002, where the dev store prices the fewest of the companies that later died: the survivorship check of 2026-10-10 took 1 to 1.4 points a year off the momentum books and pushed M0007-N20-RAW's worst fall from 19.6% to 23.5%. The picking reading must be quoted beside the check's, and if a twin's lead over the gated control falls under 1 point a year on the survivorship-check store, the answer becomes 'not clearly picking'. (2) The gated control holds the 20 most-traded members, which are the biggest companies; the near misses pick from the whole liquid pool. Part of what this method calls picking may be a tilt toward smaller members, and this method cannot separate the two. (3) The cash lever is new. If RAW20-CASH beats RAW20 by more than 2 points a year, that is a reason to audit the accrual before it is a result. (4) If W-NOSTOP-CASH differs from RAW20-CASH by more than a point, the cause is the weekly re-issue of the monthly basket at fresh prices, not the band, and must be reported that way. (5) Deposits soften every worst fall here alike; none of them may be lined up against an unfunded parent's. (6) The picking edge may be a pre-2009 edge only: if the twins trail the gated control over 2009-2015 the verdict says so first, because that is the era most like today.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# M0128 — the near misses on the fixed tape, beside plain equal-weight books

## What changed on the tape

Two things the old measuring tape got wrong are now fixed. First, money sitting in cash now earns
interest at the 13-week US Treasury bill rate (read the day before, so nothing peeks ahead).
Second, the rule for "is this holding far enough off its target to be worth a trade" is now
measured against the holding's own target (20% of it) instead of against the whole account (1%
of it). For a twenty-stock book where every name gets an equal 5% slot, 20% of 5% is exactly the
old 1%, so the second fix changes nothing there. It only bites on books with smaller slots: here,
the 70/30 blend, whose slots are 3.5% and 1.5% of the account.

## The headline table

All six variants start 1996-01-03 and end 2015-10-16, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees.
Each starts with 10,000,000 IDR and adds 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of every month (237 deposits,
about 148,000 USD in all). "The same deposits in SPY" puts the identical money into the S&P 500
fund on the identical days, so the two numbers in each row are a fair pair. "Lead" is the first
minus the second, in points a year.

| variant | what your money earned (a year) | the same deposits in SPY | lead | worst fall (deposits soften this) | gains against losses | trades | share of the time invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAW20-CASH (the momentum top 20, cash earns interest) | 14.2% | 7.2% | +7.0 | 20.6% | 1.98 | 1,607 | 69% |
| RAW20 (the same, no interest) | 13.7% | 7.2% | +6.5 | 20.6% | 1.98 | 1,607 | 69% |
| B70-CASH (70% momentum, 30% calm stocks) | 12.2% | 7.2% | +5.0 | 18.2% | 2.03 | 2,786 | 69% |
| W-NOSTOP-CASH (the momentum basket re-issued weekly) | 13.7% | 7.2% | +6.5 | 21.9% | 1.92 | 1,628 | 70% |
| EW20-CASH (control: 20 most-traded names, equal amounts, always in) | 5.7% | 7.2% | −1.5 | 74.1% | 1.15 | 727 | 96% |
| EW20-GATED-CASH (control: the same 20, out of the market below SPY's 200-day average) | 9.7% | 7.2% | +2.5 | 21.5% | 2.65 | 708 | 69% |

History rows, on the old tape, for comparison:

| earlier measurement | what your money earned | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT (the momentum top 20, real fees, old band) | 13.7% | 7.2% | 20.6% | funded, same plan |
| M0120-EW20-ALWAYS (the plain 20, real fees, old band) | 5.7% | 7.2% | 74.4% | funded, same plan |
| M0021-B70-RAW at real fees (lab costs, today) | 10.9% CAGR | 7.9% CAGR | 14.1% | *unfunded*: a single lump sum, not comparable column-for-column |
| M0020-W-NOSTOP at real fees (lab costs, today) | 13.4% CAGR | 7.9% CAGR | 19.4% | *unfunded* |

## Picking, gate, shape

On one tape, with one set of deposits and one fee schedule:

- **Picking** (a near miss's lead minus the gated control's lead): the momentum top 20 adds
  +4.6 points a year, the weekly version +4.1, the blend +2.5.
- **The market switch** (the gated control's lead minus the ungated control's): +3.9 points a year.
- **The shape** (the ungated control's lead): −1.5 points a year. Holding equal amounts of the
  twenty biggest names, always invested, cost money against simply holding the market.

The bar fixed before the run was: credit the picks only if a twin beats the gated control by more
than 1 point a year. All three twins clear it. On the survivorship-check store (the dead companies
added back), the leads become: momentum top 20 +5.4, weekly +5.2, blend +4.1, gated control +1.9,
ungated control −3.0. Picking is then +3.5 (momentum), +3.3 (weekly), +2.2 (blend); the switch
+4.9; the shape −3.0. **Picking is credited on both stores.**

## What the cash was worth, and what the band was worth

Interest on idle cash added +0.54 points a year to the momentum book (14.2% against 13.7%), at the
bottom of the predicted 0.5 to 1.5, with no change to the worst fall. The always-invested control
gained +0.06. The band change was worth exactly nothing for the momentum top 20: RAW20 reproduces
the old real-fee measurement to the fourth decimal (13.68% both, the same 1,607 trades). The blend
is where it bites: 2,786 trades against the old 2,700 at real fees, a little more small trimming.

## Weekly against monthly

The weekly re-issue trails the monthly book by 0.5 points a year of lead, with 21 more trades and
a deeper worst fall (21.9% against 20.6%). Right at the edge of the predicted "within half a
point". Weekly against monthly still measures almost nothing for a twenty-stock book.

## Luck after N tries

N is now 79 (it was 78 before this method); test-window looks stay at 4. The luck-adjusted score
(DSR, which asks "could this be the best of 79 coin flips?") is 0.936 for the momentum top 20 with
cash, 0.914 without, 0.955 for the blend, 0.931 weekly, 0.846 for the gated control and 0.251 for
the ungated one. Caveat: in a funded run each deposit day looks like a big up day, which flatters
the daily numbers this score is built from.

## Worst year and when the worst fall came

The worst calendar year for the momentum books was 2015 (−4.1%), for the weekly one 2011
(−3.8%), for the gated control 2011 (−8.0%) and for the ungated control 2008 (−44.5%). The worst
fall of every gated book came in the summer of 1998. The ungated control's came from late 2007 to
early 2009. Deposits make every fall here look shallower than it would on a single lump sum.

## The survivorship check

With the companies that later died added back, every variant earns less (all six). 2009–2015 first,
because it is the era most like today: the momentum top 20's lead over SPY goes from +1.1 to +0.0
points a year, the weekly one from +0.9 to −1.0, the blend from −1.2 to −1.7. The gated control's
was −6.0, then −6.5. Whole window: the momentum top 20 earns 12.6% instead of 14.2%, with a worst
fall of 25.0% instead of 20.6%. The blend's worst fall rises from 18.2% to 19.6%, still inside the
limit, but it carries the cash owner input and is test-failed kin, so it cannot go anywhere.

## Hypothesis held? Expected failure happened?

- Band a no-op for 20-name books: **held** exactly (+0.0000).
- Cash +0.5 to +1.5 points: **held**, at the low end (+0.54).
- Picking +4 to +6 for the momentum top 20: **held** (+4.6 dev, +3.5 survivorship).
- Shape about −1.5: **held** (−1.5 dev; −3.0 survivorship).
- Switch +2 to +3: **beaten** (+3.9 dev, +4.9 survivorship). The switch is worth more than
  predicted, all of it before 2009.
- Weekly within 0.5 of monthly: **held at the edge** (−0.51).
- Blend between the momentum book and the gated control: **held** (+5.0, between +7.0 and +2.5).
- Gated control near the gated most-liquid book plus interest: **missed upward** (9.7% against
  8.1%).
- Failure 1 (picking under 1 point on the survivorship store): did not happen.
- Failure 2 (picking partly a tilt toward smaller names): cannot be ruled out by this method.
- Failure 3 (cash > 2 points, audit the lever): did not happen.
- Failure 4 (weekly differs by > 1 point): did not happen.
- Failure 5: honoured; the parents' unfunded rows are kept apart.
- Failure 6 (picking a pre-2009 edge only): **partly happened.** Over 2009–2015 the twins still
  beat the gated control by about 7 points a year (+1.1 against −6.0), but only because the switch
  hurt the plain book badly in that era. Against SPY itself the momentum lead after 2009 is +1.1
  on the dev store and zero once the dead companies are added back.

## Why

Momentum picks names that have already been rising; behind a market switch that steps aside in a
falling market, that keeps the book out of the 2001–2002 and 2008 collapses and in the strongest
names on the way back up. Equal amounts in the twenty biggest names is a worse version of the
market itself (no tilt to winners, more weight on the laggards), so it trails SPY. The switch alone
rescues most of that, through the two crashes. After 2009 the market rarely fell below its 200-day
average for long, so the switch only cost re-entry fees and missed rebounds (2010, 2011, 2015),
which is why the gated control trails SPY by 6 points a year there.

## My opinion:

The question is answered: the momentum near misses were winning on their picks, by about three
and a half to four and a half points a year over a plain switched book, and the equal-weight shape
was a cost, not the source. The fixed tape changed almost nothing for them, which is itself useful:
the old numbers were honest for twenty-stock books. But the picking edge is a 1996–2008 edge. After
2009 it is about one point a year against SPY on the dev store and nothing with the dead companies
added back, and the worst fall still lands past the limit. I would not search further among
twenty-stock momentum variants; the next useful test is where the new band actually matters, a
fifty-stock momentum book on the fixed tape, which spreads the bets and should soften the worst
fall. That is queued as the next idea.


### 2026-10-14

# Re-evaluation

Re-evaluated under the `methods` N policy at N = 81, against `DSR >= 0.90` and a max drawdown screen of 50% (the luck bar is the owner's risk appetite, set 2026-10-07, LAB_LUCK_GATE_PLAN.md Decisions D1 and D6; the drawdown screen was split off the owner's real-money bar on 2026-10-14, design §18).

Every condition was re-read against the bars in force today: the four threshold conditions from this method's own recorded columns, and the luck test from the same deflated Sharpe at the same N. No recorded column changed: `trials` is append-only, and every `dsr`, `eligible`, `failed` and `n_trials_at_run` this method recorded still reads exactly as it did -- including the `DSR >= 0.95` and `max DD <= 15%` labels that rejected it, which name the bars of their own day.

The variant this unblocks:

- `M0128-RAW20`: DSR 0.9122 at N = 81, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.
methods.verdict: On the fixed tape the momentum near misses beat a plain twenty-stock book behind the same market switch by about four and a half points a year: they were winning on their picks, not their shape. Most of that edge was earned before 2009.

methods.sourceRef: M0128 note and insight, 2026-10-12
methods.hypothesis: The momentum picks earned their lead in a twenty-stock book, but its worst fall still lands past the limit and the new target-relative rebalancing band does nothing at twenty names. Spread the same residual-momentum ranking over fifty names, behind the same market switch, on the fixed tape (band on the holding's target, cash earns the T-bill), beside a gated plain fifty-stock control: the wider book should soften the worst fall at a small cost in lead, and it is the first book where the fixed band actually changes the trades.

methods.name: A learned stock ranker: gradient-boosted trees combine the lab's own signals, refitted once a year
methods.sourceRef: Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020), Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning, Review of Financial Studies 33(5); handover 2026-10-12 (measure then learn), Step 1 item 5
methods.hypothesis: Every method in this lab ranks on one hand-chosen signal, and the closest near misses all lean on the same one, residual momentum. Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) found that regression trees combining many such signals rank US stocks better than any linear combination. This method asks whether a small part of that survives where this lab has to live: large-cap index members, long only, monthly, Gotrade's real fees, fractional shares, the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits, and a resize band measured against each holding's own target. THE MODEL: scikit-learn's histogram gradient-boosted trees, refitted once a year at the last session of each year on every month-end sample since January 1996 whose next-21-session return rank was already known by then (an expanding window, nothing read after the decision date). Seven features the lab already computes, each rank-normalised per date: 12-1 momentum, 60-day volatility, 20-day dollar volume, M0007-N20-RAW's residual momentum, distance from the 52-week high, M0070's dividend-raise event and the trailing dividend yield; the PF20 variant adds the four SEC EDGAR factors (value, quality, profitability, earnings surprise). The book holds the top N predictions at equal weight. The first refit with enough history (35 labelled month-ends) is 1998-12-31; until then every variant, the control included, holds SPY, so 1996-1998 is the same in all six and every paired difference below is the model alone. SIX VARIANTS, THE ONLY SETTINGS EVER TRIED: no hyperparameter was tuned on the dev window off the books, and none will be; a change after a result is a new method. The base tree is Strategy B's pre-registered setting (learning rate 0.05, 300 trees, 15 leaves, at least 200 samples per leaf, L2 1.0), fixed on 2026-10-03 for a different book and never searched; the regularised tree (100 trees, 7 leaves, 1,000 per leaf, L2 10) is the one fixed alternative. The seed is 0 and is inert at this sample size. P20 and P50 hold the top 20 and top 50; P50-REG is the regularised tree at 50; P20-GATE is P20 behind the lab's standing SPY 200-day switch; PF20 is P20 with the fundamentals; DV20 is the CONTROL, the same 20-name equal-weight book on the same screen, window and SPY-before-the-model rule, picked by 20-day dollar volume, which forecasts nothing. The control is deliberately not a momentum book: the hard gate reads every variant's behaviour, and one momentum variant moving with the four test-failed momentum books would bar every tree variant from promotion. The comparison with momentum is made in the analysis against the lab's recorded real-fee momentum books instead. FUNDAMENTALS: the store's EDGAR panel can rank 20 names on only 31.5% of the dev window (none of 1996-2008, 5 of 12 months of 2009, all of 2010-2015), so the run is recorded under --allow-coverage 0.31, knowingly; before 2009 the four columns are empty and PF20 should pick what P20 picks, so PF20 minus P20 measures the fundamentals in 2010-2015 only.
