WHAT COUNTS AS THE MODEL ADDING SOMETHING, fixed now: P20 beats DV20 by at least 2 points a year of funded return over 1999-2015 AND is ahead of it in 2009-2015, the era most like today. WHAT COUNTS AS A METHOD: a variant clears every design section 1 bar at DSR >= 0.90 at the lab's N, including the worst fall <= 20%, which only P20-GATE is built to have a chance at. No variant is promoted in this run, whatever it shows: the test window is not touched.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely the model adds nothing measurable over the dollar-volume control after fees. Gu, Kelly & Xiu's edge is concentrated in small and illiquid stocks and in the short leg, and is measured before costs; this universe is the S&P 500 union the Nasdaq-100 above $20M a day, long only, and a 20-to-50-name book re-picked monthly pays Gotrade's minimum fees on $29-70 slots. The paper was published in 2020 but its inputs (momentum and its cousins) were published long before the dev window ended, so any dev edge is the pre-crowd edge and likely to fade. Second, the trees will probably learn mostly momentum: residual momentum and 12-1 momentum are the strongest inputs, so the picks may move with the lab's test-failed momentum books closely enough that the hard gate reads them as kin, which would be the right verdict on a model that only re-discovered momentum. Third, every ungated variant will fall far more than 20% in 2008 -- a fully invested 20-name book fell 50-60% in every lab precedent -- and the monthly-read SPY switch in P20-GATE reacted late in 2008 for every lab book that used it, so even the gated variant is likely to miss the 20% bar, as M0007-N20-RAW did once the missing dead companies were added back (19.6% on the dev store, 23.5% on the survivorship-check store). Fourth, the training set inherits the store's survivorship: about half of all index members ever listed are missing, mostly the ones that died, so the model learns from winners' histories and the survivorship check is expected to cost it more than the 1-1.4 points a year it cost the hand-built momentum books. Fifth, PF20 is expected to differ from P20 by noise: the fundamentals enter training only from late 2009 and are a small slice of every refit's history even by 2014. Sixth, the regularised tree is expected to sit between the base tree and the control, and P50 to trail P20 on fees. Finally, twenty years of monthly cross-sections is a small sample for a learner: about 57,000 training rows by 2014, heavily correlated within each month, so a DSR at the lab's N may not separate a real ranking skill from luck even if the returns look good.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-12

# M0130 — a learned stock ranker: gradient-boosted trees on the lab's own signals

## What was run

Six variants, the only settings ever tried for this idea, all on the fixed tape: monthly,
fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the resize band measured against each holding's own
target, no interest on cash. Each starts with 10,000,000 IDR and adds 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of
every month (237 deposits, about 148,000 USD). Until the first yearly model exists (the refit at
the end of 1998) every variant holds SPY. The trees are refitted at the end of each year on every
month-end since January 1996 whose next-month return rank was already known.

One honest note on how the record came to be. The first attempt stopped at the fundamentals
variant before any result was written: the tree library refused to train on a column with no
values at all, which is what the four company-accounts columns are before 2009. The fix (treat an
all-blank column as a constant the tree can never split on, which is what the pre-registration
assumed) was committed on its own, separately from the frozen method file. The four variants that
had already run reproduced to the last digit on the second attempt, so the fix changed nothing
except letting the fundamentals variant finish.

The fundamentals variant ran under an explicit acknowledgement that the company-accounts panel
covers only 31.5% of the dev window (none of 1996-2008, 5 months of 2009, all of 2010-2015). The
whole method is recorded under that acknowledgement.

## The headline table

"Same deposits in SPY" is the identical money put into the S&P 500 fund (dividends reinvested) on
the identical days. N is 80 (one more than before this method); the luck bar is DSR >= 0.90;
test-window looks stay at 4.

| variant | what your money earned (a year) | same deposits in SPY | lead | worst fall | gains against losses | trades | luck score (DSR at N=80) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P20 (base tree, top 20) | 2.2% | 7.2% | −5.0 | 75.2% | 1.05 | 2,879 | 0.150 |
| P50 (base tree, top 50) | 3.7% | 7.2% | −3.5 | 70.5% | 1.13 | 6,041 | 0.187 |
| P50-REG (regularised tree, top 50) | 5.8% | 7.2% | −1.4 | 68.0% | 1.25 | 5,110 | 0.304 |
| P20-GATE (base tree, top 20, SPY 200-day switch) | 7.0% | 7.2% | −0.2 | 24.7% | 1.32 | 2,105 | 0.647 |
| PF20 (base tree + company accounts, top 20) | 2.4% | 7.2% | −4.8 | 75.2% | 1.06 | 2,711 | 0.156 |
| DV20 (control: 20 most-traded names, no model) | 5.6% | 7.2% | −1.6 | 74.6% | 1.16 | 613 | 0.223 |

Failed conditions, with margins:
- P20: beats SPY (−5.0 points a year), worst fall 75.2% against 20%, gains/losses 1.05 against 1.3, DSR 0.150 against 0.90.
- P50: beats SPY (−3.5), worst fall 70.5%, gains/losses 1.13, DSR 0.187.
- P50-REG: beats SPY (−1.4), worst fall 68.0%, gains/losses 1.25, DSR 0.304.
- P20-GATE: beats SPY (−0.2), worst fall 24.7% (4.7 points over), DSR 0.647. Gains/losses 1.32 passes.
- PF20: beats SPY (−4.8), worst fall 75.2%, gains/losses 1.06, DSR 0.156.
- DV20: beats SPY (−1.6), worst fall 74.6%, gains/losses 1.16, DSR 0.223.

Method status: rejected. Nothing is dev-eligible; nothing was promoted; the test window was not touched.

## Did the model add anything?

The bar fixed before the run: the base tree's top 20 beats the most-traded control by at least 2
points a year over 1999-2015 AND is ahead of it in 2009-2015. Measured on the books with the
deposits taken out (so a deposit never reads as growth), as yearly growth rates:

| stretch | tree top 20 | most-traded control | SPY | tree minus control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1999-2015 | 1.7% | 3.4% | 4.9% | −1.7 |
| 2009-2015 | 9.0% | 14.5% | 14.9% | −5.5 |

**The bar failed on both halves.** The model made the picking worse than choosing the most-traded
names, not better. With deposits included the gap is the same story: 2.2% against 5.6% a year.

Year by year (deposits removed) the tree and the control were opposites more than rivals. The tree
won big in 2000 (+14.0% against −19.5%) and 2001 (+7.5% against −29.8%), when the giant technology
names the control holds were collapsing, and lost in almost every other year: 1999 (+21% against
+66%), 2006, 2007 (−8% against +8%), 2008 (−53% against −44%), 2009, 2012, 2013 and 2015 (−6%
against +10%). The breadth report says the same thing from another side: every tree variant only
paid in months when the average member beat the index, and lost 9-13 points a year when a few
giants carried it; the control was the reverse. The trees leaned away from the largest companies.

## Breadth and regularisation

Holding the top 50 instead of the top 20 helped (3.7% against 2.2% a year, worst fall 70.5%
against 75.2%) despite twice as many trades on smaller slots. The regularised tree helped more
again (5.8% against 3.7%; 2009-2015 at 14.6% a year, level with SPY's 14.9%). Both say the same
thing: the less the model trusts itself, the closer it gets to holding the market, and the better
it does. That is the opposite of a model with a real edge. The expected "P50 trails P20 on fees"
did not happen; the expected "regularised sits between the base tree and the control" did not
either: it beat both.

## The company accounts

PF20 picked exactly what P20 picked until January 2010: its curve is identical to the tree-only
book's to the last digit before then, as predicted (no accounts data, nothing to split on). From
2010 to 2015 it earned 7.6% a year against 7.0% for the tree without accounts, with a worst fall
of 26% against 27%. Half a point a year over under six years is noise. The coverage acknowledgement
means just that: this pair says almost nothing about company accounts before 2010, because there
were none to learn from.

## The switch and 2008

Behind the SPY 200-day switch the same tree came within 0.2 points a year of SPY (7.0% against
7.2%) and was nearly flat in 2008 (−0.2% with deposits removed, against −53% without the switch).
The switch did its job in 2008. The worst fall, 24.7%, came instead from spring 2011 to spring
2012 (21.4% on month-end values), a choppy market where the switch stepped out and back in and the
tree's picks fell on their own. Its worst calendar year was 2015 (−10.6%). The switch also cost it
in 1996-98: it stepped out of SPY in the 1998 fall, so the gated variant's opening years differ
from the other five (18.6% a year against 23.9%), which the hypothesis did not foresee.

## 1996-1998

All five ungated variants, the control included, held only SPY until the end of 1998: their
de-funded growth over 1996-98 is identical (23.9% a year, against 27.3% for SPY with dividends; the
gap to SPY is the cost of buying in monthly at real fees plus month-end measurement, and it is the same for all five). So every paired
difference among those five is the model alone. The gated variant is the exception noted above.

## Survivorship

Every variant reproduced its recorded dev result exactly on the dev store, so the side-by-side is
meaningful. On the survivorship-check store (the companies that later died or were dropped added
back), the money each variant earned a year, with its lead over SPY's 7.2%:

| variant | dev store | check store | change | worst fall dev -> check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P20 | 2.2% | 3.2% | +1.0 | 75.2% -> 79.2% |
| P50 | 3.7% | 4.6% | +0.9 | 70.5% -> 68.5% |
| P50-REG | 5.8% | 4.6% | −1.2 | 68.0% -> 72.5% |
| P20-GATE | 7.0% | 8.7% | +1.7 | 24.7% -> 22.3% |
| PF20 | 2.4% | 3.7% | +1.3 | 75.2% -> 79.2% |
| DV20 (control) | 5.6% | 4.0% | −1.6 | 74.6% -> 84.7% |

2009-2015 first, as the era most like today: the leads over SPY move from −6.1 to −1.3 (P20),
−3.1 to −0.4 (P50), −0.3 to +0.1 (P50-REG), −7.2 to −6.0 (P20-GATE), −5.6 to −0.7 (PF20) and +0.4
to −0.4 (control).

This is the reverse of what the hypothesis expected (a bigger survivorship loss than the momentum
books' 1-1.4 points a year). Four of the five tree variants earn MORE with the dead companies added
back, and the control earns less. The likely reason is that on the check store the trees are
retrained on a different, larger universe, so they are different models, not the same picks on
more names; the control has no model and simply holds more names that later failed. It does not
rescue anything: the best tree on the check store still sits only 1.5 points a year ahead of SPY
with a 22.3% worst fall, and the ungated top-20 tree still trails the control there (3.2% against
4.0% a year), so the pre-registered bar fails on both stores. Read it as "the tree's result is fragile to the universe it
learns from", not as a hidden edge. The check wrote one plain-words observation to the journal.

## Kin and folds

The walk-forward check: across 4 folds from 2003 to 2014, the variant the lab's own rule would have
picked beat SPY in 1 of 4; its 2009-2015 edge is +0.4%; verdict "not dev-eligible". Nothing is
dev-eligible, so the behavioural kin reading against the test-failed momentum books never comes
into play. The fear that the trees would "re-discover momentum" did not come true in the obvious
way: a momentum book loses in 2000-2001 and wins in 2003-2007, and this book did roughly the
opposite.

## Against momentum on the same real fees

The lab's real-fee residual-momentum book (the top 20 behind the same switch, same deposits, old
band; M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT) earned 13.7% a year against the same 7.2% for SPY, with a 20.6% worst
fall; on the fixed tape (M0128-RAW20) the identical 13.7%. The best tree, behind the same switch,
earned 7.0%. One hand-picked signal beat the learned combination of seven signals that included it
by 6.7 points a year.

## Why

A tree trained on monthly next-month return ranks learns whatever separated winners from losers in
past months. In 1996-2000 the signal was dominated by the technology boom and bust, so most likely the early
models learned to avoid the most-traded, most-extended giants. That paid in 2000-2001 and then kept
the book in smaller, more volatile, lower-quality members for the rest of the window, which is
exactly what got hit hardest in 2008 (−53%). Each refit adds only twelve months to an expanding
window, so the early lesson fades slowly. Next-month rank is also a very noisy target: most of a
stock's one-month return rank is noise, and a tree with 300 rounds and 15 leaves fits that noise
(the regularised tree, fitting less, did better). The hypothesis that "a small part of the tree
edge survives in large caps, long only, after fees" did not hold. Of the expected failures:
"adds nothing over the control" happened, and worse: it subtracted. "Ungated variants fall far
more than 20% in 2008" happened (47-53%). "The gated variant misses 20%" happened (24.7%), though
not in 2008. "Fundamentals differ from price-only by noise" happened. "The trees will learn mostly
momentum" did not.

## My opinion:

This is a clean negative, and a useful one. A learned ranker on the signals this lab already has
did worse than simply holding the most-traded names at both book sizes, with and without company
accounts (the regularised tree only drew level with that control, 5.8% against 5.6% a year), and the only variant that came close to SPY did so because of the market switch, not the
model. The handover's caveat was right: machine learning does not move the binding constraint (the
2008-sized fall), and here it did not even supply picking skill. The small neural network
(handover item 6) is not earned: it was conditional on the trees showing something, and they did
not. I would not spend more lab ids on learned rankers that predict next month's rank: that
target is mostly noise, and the one variant that fitted it least (the regularised tree) did best,
which is what a noise-fitting model looks like. The only learned follow-up I would keep on the list
is the one that attacks that cause directly: the same yearly-refitted trees predicting a slower
target (the next twelve months' rank), fitted with the regularised settings, behind the switch.
It is queued as an idea, and I would rank it below the simpler work already queued, not above it.
methods.verdict: A learned stock ranker picked worse than simply holding the most-traded big companies, and every version without the market switch fell about 70% in 2008

methods.name: A slower target for the learned ranker: the same yearly-refitted trees predict next year's return rank, not next month's, regularised, behind the market switch
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0130 (the first learned ranker); Sera batch 20261014-1206
methods.hypothesis: The first learned ranker fitted next month's return rank and lost to a control that forecasts nothing, and the ordering of its own variants said why: its LEAST flexible tree finished ahead of its base tree at both book sizes. A model that gets better as you take its capacity away has nothing to learn, because one month of a stock's return is almost all noise around anything this lab can compute. This method changes exactly one thing about the model and nothing else: the label. Instead of the percentile rank of the next 21 sessions' return it predicts the rank of the next 252 sessions' return, the horizon at which the features' own literature measured them, with one arm at 63 sessions to put a middle rung on the ladder. Everything else is M0130's, imported not copied: the same seven rank-normalised price and dividend features, the same annual walk-forward refit on an expanding window of month-end samples whose labels were already readable at the refit, the same equal-weight top-N book, the same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits, and the same resize band measured against each holding's own target. THE CAPACITY IS LOW BY DEFAULT: M0130's regularised setting (100 trees, 7 leaves, at least 1,000 samples a leaf, L2 10) is this method's base, copied field for field and never searched. EVERY VARIANT IS BEHIND THE LAB'S STANDING SPY 200-DAY SWITCH, the control included and read before every other rule, because M0130's ungated arms fell about 70% in 2008 and the switch has helped 22 of 22 lab variants whole-window; spending an arm to re-measure that would waste the method id. FIVE VARIANTS, THE ONLY SETTINGS EVER TRIED, no hyperparameter chosen by looking at a dev result: Y20 is the regularised tree on the yearly label holding its top 20; Y50 is the same model holding 50; B20 is the yearly label read with M0130's flexible base tree at 20 names, so B20 against M0130-P20-GATE is the horizon and nothing else; Q20 is the regularised tree on the 63-session label at 20 names; DV20 is the CONTROL, the same 20-name equal-weight gated book on the same screen, lookback and clock, picked by 20-day dollar volume, which forecasts nothing. The control is run here rather than quoted from M0130's trial, and it is deliberately not a momentum book: the hard gate reads every variant's behaviour and one momentum arm moving with the lab's test-failed momentum books would bar the whole method. THE CALENDAR: a 252-session label is known 252 sessions late, so the first refit with 35 labelled month-ends is 1999-12-31 and the first traded month is January 2000; the 63-session arm lands on the same refit, so all five variants start trading the same session and every paired difference inside this batch is the picker alone. Before that they hold SPY when the switch is on and cash when it is off, identically. WHAT COUNTS AS THE MODEL ADDING SOMETHING, FIXED NOW: Y20 beats DV20 by at least 2 points a year of funded return over 2000-2015 AND is ahead of it in 2009-2015, the era most like today. If no tree arm clears that, the finding this method records is that the binding constraint is the lab's own signal set and not the model class or the target speed, and the lab should stop building rankers on these seven features rather than reach for a bigger model. WHAT COUNTS AS A METHOD: a variant clears every design section 1 bar at DSR >= 0.90 at the lab's N, against the dev screen on the worst fall (50%) and the real-money bar (25%). No variant is promoted in this run whatever it shows: the test window is not touched.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely the slower label changes the ranking less than it changes the turnover, and no tree arm clears the 2-point bar against the dollar-volume control. Four reasons. First, a 252-session label on monthly samples overlaps 92% with the next month's label, so consecutive training rows are nearly the same observation: the nominal 50,000-odd rows at the 2014 refit are worth perhaps a twentieth of that in independent information, and a slower target buys signal-to-noise per sample while paying for it in effective sample size. The net may be zero or worse. Second, the features that would plausibly survive a yearly horizon are momentum and its cousins, and a tree that learns them hands this method the same problem M0130 flagged: the picks may move with the lab's four test-failed momentum books closely enough that the hard gate's behavioural kin test bars promotion, which would be the correct verdict on a model that only re-discovered momentum. Third, the gate in front of every arm is read monthly and reacted late in 2008 for every lab book that used it; M0130's gated arm still fell 24.7%, inside the new 50% dev screen but close to the 25% real-money bar, and a book of 20 names cannot do much better than the switch allows. Fourth, the training set inherits the store's survivorship: about half of all index members ever listed are missing, mostly the ones that died, so the model learns from winners' histories, and the survivorship check cost the hand-built momentum books 1-1.4 points a year and deepened their worst fall by about 2.6 points. A slow label makes that worse, not better: a name that was about to be delisted is exactly the one whose twelve-month forward return is missing from the training set. Fifth, Q20 is expected to sit between M0130's monthly arms and Y20 if the target-speed story is right, and to sit nowhere in particular if it is not — a non-monotone ladder would itself be evidence that the model is reading noise at every horizon. Sixth, B20 is expected to trail Y20: if the diagnosis is right the flexible tree should still overfit a slow label, just less. Finally, DSR at the lab's N of 82-plus needs a Sharpe well above anything M0130's arms produced (its best gated arm reached 0.63 and scored 0.647 against a 0.90 bar), so even a tree arm that beats SPY on return is likely to fail the luck test, and losing on luck after beating the control would still be a real finding about the signal set.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0131 — a slower target for the learned ranker

## What was asked

The first learned ranker (M0130) asked a computer model to guess which big American companies
would do best **over the next month**. It picked worse than simply buying the twenty most heavily
traded big companies. The tell was inside its own results: the *least* clever version of the model
beat the cleverest one at both book sizes. A model that improves as you take its cleverness away
is a model with nothing to learn — it was fitting noise, because noise was all that was there.

One month of a share price is almost all noise. So this method changed exactly one thing and
nothing else: **what the model is asked to guess.** Instead of next month's ranking it guesses the
ranking over **the next twelve months**, with one arm at three months to put a middle rung on the
ladder. Same seven pieces of information, same yearly re-training, same twenty-name equal-weight
book, same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, same 5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th of every
month, same rule that it may only read what was knowable on the day.

**Every version here runs behind the market switch** — the rule that steps the whole book out when
the S&P 500 is below its own 200-day average. M0130's unswitched versions fell about 70% in 2008,
and the lab has already measured the switch helping 22 of 22 books, so re-measuring that would
have wasted the method. The twenty-most-traded control sits behind the same switch and is **run
here**, not quoted from M0130's old result.

A twelve-month answer is only knowable twelve months later, so the first model that has enough
finished history arrives at the end of 1999 and the first traded month is January 2000. Before
that all five versions hold the S&P 500 fund when the switch is on and cash when it is off — the
same thing, in all five — so every difference between them is the picking alone.

## The headline

Money the owner would actually have had, at real fees, with the real monthly top-ups:

| version | what the money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B20** (flexible model, yearly guess, top 20) | **10.9%** | 7.2% | **20.0%** | 1.76 | 1,500 | **0.912** |
| Y20 (careful model, yearly guess, top 20) | 9.3% | 7.2% | 24.7% | 1.72 | 1,221 | 0.790 |
| Y50 (careful model, yearly guess, top 50) | 9.0% | 7.2% | 22.0% | 1.81 | 2,386 | 0.836 |
| Q20 (careful model, three-month guess, top 20) | 7.4% | 7.2% | 25.2% | 1.42 | 1,512 | 0.686 |
| DV20 (control: 20 most-traded, no model) | 8.2% | 7.2% | 21.4% | 2.63 | 536 | 0.702 |

**B20 passes every go-live condition and is the first version of a learned ranker in this lab ever
to do so.** It beat the S&P 500 with dividends, its worst fall was 20.0% against the 25% limit,
its gains outweighed its losses 1.76 to 1 against the 1.3 bar, and its luck score reached 0.912
against the 0.90 bar. The method is now **dev-eligible**.

"Luck score" is the deflated Sharpe ratio: the chance the result is real skill rather than the best
of many tries. The lab has now looked at 86 distinct methods, and every result is deflated by that
86 before it is judged. B20's 0.912 means roughly a 9-in-10 chance this is not luck — which clears
the bar the owner set on 2026-10-07, but only by 0.012.

## Did the slower question actually help? Yes, and by a lot

This is the cleanest number in the whole run, because **only one thing differs**. M0130's gated
version and this method's B20 use the *same* model settings, the *same* market switch, the *same*
trading rules and the *same* window. The only difference is the question asked. With deposits
taken out, so a top-up never reads as a gain:

| | next-month question (M0130) | next-year question (B20) | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000-2015 | 6.7% a year | **10.5% a year** | **+3.8 points** |
| 2009-2015 | 9.4% a year | **15.9% a year** | **+6.5 points** |
| worst fall | 21% | 15% | 6 points shallower |

And the ladder runs the right way on both models. With the careful model: three months 6.9% a
year, twelve months 8.4%. With the flexible model: one month 6.7%, twelve months 10.5%. **Asking
the model a slower question is worth several points a year, every way it is measured.** That is a
real, reusable finding about how to build a model in this lab, and it is the main thing this run
bought.

## The surprise: cleverness helped this time

The hypothesis said the flexible model would still trail the careful one, just by less. The
opposite happened: the flexible model earned 10.5% a year against the careful one's 8.4% over
2000-2015. That reversal is itself evidence. When the question was next month there was nothing to
find, so extra cleverness only found noise and hurt. When the question is next year there *is*
something to find, so extra cleverness helps. The two runs together say the problem with M0130 was
never the model — it was the question.

## And now the part that matters more

**Against the S&P 500 itself, in the years most like today, every single version lost.**

| | 2009-2015, a year |
|---|---|
| S&P 500 with dividends | **16.6%** |
| B20 (the eligible one) | 15.9% |
| Y20 | 12.7% |
| Y50 | 11.6% |
| Q20 | 10.8% |
| control (20 most-traded) | 10.7% |

B20's whole-window win does not come from better picking. It comes from the market switch sitting
in cash through 2001, 2002 and 2008, when the S&P 500 lost 17%, 21% and 36%. In 2001, 2002 and
2008 every version here returned almost exactly 0%. Take those three years away and the picking
advantage over the control is real but modest, and the advantage over simply holding the index in
the recent era is **negative**.

This is the same thing the lab has now found eight or nine different ways: the long-run edge was
earned before 2009, and 2009 onward — the best-measured years and the ones most like today —
hands it back. The owner should read the 10.9% a year as "the switch saved me from three bad
years", not as "the model picks well".

The method's **own pre-registered test also failed**, and it is worth being exact. Before the run
this method committed to: *the careful model's top 20 (Y20) beats the most-traded control by at
least 2 points a year over 2000-2015 and is ahead of it in 2009-2015.* The result: **+1.2 points**
over 2000-2015 (bar was 2) and +2.0 points in 2009-2015. Both halves were required, so the test
**fails**. The arm that would have sailed through it — B20, at +3.3 and +5.2 points over the
control — is not the arm the test named, and picking the winner after seeing the results is
precisely what writing the test down beforehand exists to prevent. The honest statement is: *the
model as pre-specified did not clear its bar; a sibling setting did, and that is a lead, not a
verdict.*

## Can it be promoted? No, and this is not close

`lab promote` refuses it. The out-of-sample fold check splits the window into four stretches, picks
the version the lab's own rule would have chosen knowing nothing later, and scores it on months it
has never seen. **B20 won 2 of 4.** The rule requires a strict majority, and there is no override.

- 2003-2005: +35.9% against the S&P's +52.1% — lost badly
- 2006-2008: +0.9% against −24.6% — won (the switch again)
- 2009-2011: +59.7% against +60.8% — lost, narrowly
- 2012-2014: +70.8% against +65.9% — won

Two of the four wins are the switch stepping out of a falling market, and the two losses are rising
markets where the picking had to carry its own weight and did not. A method that wins its
twenty-year average and loses the folds is a selection, not an edge. The rule is right here.

On the other half of the gate, **nothing that has failed out of sample is kin to this method** —
not by family, not by ancestry, not by how the book moves. That half is clean. The fold majority is
the only thing standing in the way, and it is standing there for a good reason.

## What the fuller price history says

The lab's dev data can only price about half of the companies that were ever in the index, and the
missing half is mostly the ones that died. Re-run on the check data (most of the dead companies
added back), all five versions reproduced their recorded results exactly first, so the comparison
is meaningful:

| version | dev data | fuller data | worst fall, dev → fuller | luck score, dev → fuller |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B20 | 10.9% | 10.5% | 20.0% → **23.1%** | 0.912 → **0.839** |
| Y20 | 9.3% | 8.0% | 24.7% → 24.0% | 0.790 → 0.649 |
| Y50 | 9.0% | 9.2% | 22.0% → 20.1% | 0.836 → 0.809 |
| Q20 | 7.4% | 8.1% | 25.2% → 24.3% | 0.686 → 0.597 |
| control | 8.2% | 7.6% | 21.4% → 25.1% | 0.702 → 0.594 |

The money holds up (10.9% → 10.5%), but **two things that were only just inside their limits move
outside them**: the worst fall goes from 20.0% to 23.1% against a 25% limit, and the luck score
goes from 0.912 to 0.839, *below* the 0.90 bar. B20's eligibility rests on a margin of 0.012 on
data that is missing four in ten of the days a company sat in the index. Read it as "eligible on a
technicality on incomplete data", not as "proven".

## Against the lab's best hand-built signal

The lab's residual-momentum book, measured on the identical fixed tape at the identical real fees
(M0128-RAW20), earned 14.0% a year whole-window and 17.7% a year in 2009-2015 — against B20's
11.6% and 15.9%. **One hand-picked signal still beats a model that combines seven signals,
including that very one, by about 2 points a year.** Two learned rankers have now been built and
neither has beaten the simplest thing the lab already had.

## Why it behaves this way

Behind the switch the book is actually invested only about 68% of the time, and on 28% of its
decision days it asks for nothing at all. Of the money it does deploy, roughly half sits in its own
picks and the rest in the index fund it parks in before the model exists. Its picks on their own
earned 9.9% a year against the index's 7.2% — so the picking *is* adding something — while the
parked money earned 0.7% a year, because the switch kept stepping out of the index during 1996-1998
and missed most of that boom.

B20's worst fall was 15% on month-end values, and it happened in **spring to summer 2006** — not
2008. 2008 was a non-event for every version here, because the switch had already stepped out. The
worst calendar year was 2006 at −4.8%. A book that has its worst moment in a quiet year and sleeps
through the financial crisis is a book whose risk is being carried almost entirely by one timing
rule, and the owner should know that is where the smoothness comes from.

Of the things this method expected to go wrong: "no tree arm clears the 2-point bar" happened for
the arm the bar named. "The gated arm cannot do much better than the switch allows on the worst
fall" happened (20.0%, 23.1% on fuller data). "The slow label makes survivorship worse" did not
happen — it was about neutral. "The quarterly rung sits between month and year" happened, exactly.
"The flexible tree trails the careful one" did **not** happen and was the most informative error.
"Kin bars it" did not happen. "The luck test fails even after beating the control" nearly happened:
0.912 is a pass by 0.012 on dev data and a fail on fuller data.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth more trials, and the trials should be about the question, not the model.**
The one thing this run proved cleanly is that asking the model a slower question is worth three to
six points a year with everything else held fixed. That is the largest single improvement any lever
has bought a learned ranker in this lab, and it was bought by changing one number. Nobody should
read the dev-eligible badge as the finding; the finding is the horizon.

What I would not do is reach for a bigger model. Two rankers have now lost to a single hand-picked
signal, and the second one lost by less only because the question got slower. Capacity is not the
constraint.

What I would try next, and have queued: **stop training on an expanding window and train on a
rolling ten-year one.** Every model here carries the 1996-2000 technology boom and bust in its
memory forever, because each yearly refit only adds twelve months to a pile that never forgets.
That is the most likely reason the two folds it lost are both rising markets in the 2000s and
2010s, and the most likely reason its 2009-2015 record lags the index it is supposed to beat. It is
one knob, it is cheap, it is pre-registerable, and it attacks the exact failure the folds found. If
a forgetting model still loses 2009-2015 to a plain index fund, then the honest conclusion — and I
would write it — is that these seven pieces of information do not contain a recent edge, no matter
what is done with them, and the lab should stop building rankers on them and go looking for
information it does not yet have.
methods.verdict: Asking the model about next year instead of next month was worth 4 to 6 points a year and made it eligible for the first time — but it still lost to a plain index fund in the recent years, and it fails the out-of-sample fold check 2 of 4

methods.name: Learn the fall, not the pick: a model that forecasts the next quarter's drop and sizes the book by it
methods.sourceRef: Moreira & Muir (2017), Volatility-Managed Portfolios, Journal of Finance 72(4); handover 2026-10-13 (measure the constraint), section 2 item 2
methods.hypothesis: This lab's own record says the constraint that binds is the fall, not the pick: of 394 dev trials with a recorded return, 256 (65%) beat SPY total return but only 92 (23%) keep the worst fall at or under 20%, and all four spent test looks failed on return, not on drawdown. A two-thirds dev hit rate that vanishes out of sample is the signature of selection. Against that the lab has exactly one risk control, the SPY 200-day switch, and nothing has improved on it. THE QUESTION: can a learned forecast of the coming fall size a book better than that switch does? THE LABEL is the forward fall AS A LEVEL -- the worst peak-to-trough drop over the next 63 NYSE sessions, one quarter, in fractions -- not the next month's return rank and not a rank of the fall either. That distinction is the method: every feature below is rank-normalised within its date, and a label ranked the same way would leave the forecasts near-identical on every date by construction, so in October 2008, when every name is about to fall, the label could not say 'all of them' even in principle. THE HEAD turns the forecast into exposure, the share of the book that is held, with the remainder in cash, and it reads a MARKET-LEVEL quantity to do it: the date's cross-sectional MEAN forecast fall is located in the model's own training distribution of date-level means, and the book keeps the share of its slots that the date is calmer than -- in whole slots, each at a fixed weight, never renormalised onto the survivors. A date calmer than every training date is a full book, a date worse than all of them is entirely cash, the median date is half. NO NUMBER IN THAT LADDER WAS CHOSEN: it is the model's own in-sample distribution, so nothing in the head was read off the dev window. The machinery is M0130's: scikit-learn histogram gradient-boosted trees refitted once a year at the last session of each year, on every month-end sample since January 1996 whose label had already been read by then (an expanding window; nothing dated after the decision date is ever read), on the same seven features the lab already computes, each rank-normalised per date: 12-1 momentum, 60-day volatility, 20-day dollar volume, M0007-N20-RAW's residual momentum, distance from the 52-week high, M0070's dividend-raise event and the trailing dividend yield -- PLUS THREE UN-NORMALISED MARKET-LEVEL COLUMNS, without which a level label would buy nothing: the market's distance below its trailing one-year high, its realised volatility over the last sixty sessions, and the spread of the day's own momentum across the cross-section. Each of those three is one number for the whole date, repeated down the rows, so none of them can change which names the model prefers -- only how far the whole date's forecast moves, which is exactly the level the head reads. THE NAMES ARE HELD FIXED and are not the question: every variant, model and control alike, holds the twenty screen-eligible index members with the largest 20-day dollar volume, equal weight. Dollar volume forecasts nothing, so the only thing that differs between variants is how much of that same book is held, and every paired difference below is the sizing alone. BEFORE THE FIRST MODEL every variant holds SPY. With a quarter-long label and 35 required labelled month-ends the first refit with enough history is 1999-12-31, so the book is SPY through 1999 in all five; the rule is calendar-only and shared with the controls, which have no model, so the pre-model era is identical everywhere and cancels out. FIVE VARIANTS, THE ONLY SETTINGS EVER TRIED: no hyperparameter was tuned on the dev window off the books, and none will be; a change after a result is a new method. The base tree is Strategy B's pre-registered setting (learning rate 0.05, 300 trees, 15 leaves, at least 200 samples per leaf, L2 1.0), fixed 2026-10-03 for a different book and never searched; the regularised tree (100 trees, 7 leaves, 1,000 per leaf, L2 10) is M0130's one fixed alternative re-used verbatim. FALL20 is the model sizing the book; FALL20-REG is the regularised tree doing the same; FALL20-GATE is the base model also behind the SPY 200-day switch; GATE20 is the CONTROL in which that switch alone sizes the same twenty names; ON20 is the CONTROL that is always fully invested, with no risk control at all. WHAT EACH DIFFERENCE ISOLATES: GATE20 minus ON20 is what the lab's existing control is worth on this exact book; FALL20 minus ON20 is what the learned forecast adds over no control; FALL20 minus GATE20 is the question itself; FALL20-GATE minus GATE20 is whether the model sees anything the switch has not already taken; FALL20-REG minus FALL20 is whether any of it is model capacity rather than signal. WHAT COUNTS AS THE MODEL ADDING SOMETHING, fixed now: FALL20's worst fall over the model era is at least 5 percentage points shallower than GATE20's AND its funded return is no more than 2 points a year behind GATE20's -- a control that only costs return is not an improvement, because the switch already does that -- AND FALL20 beats ON20 on MAR. WHAT COUNTS AS A METHOD: a variant clears every design section 1 bar at DSR >= 0.90 at the lab's N, the worst fall at or under 20% included. IDLE CASH EARNS NOTHING in these rules, which is the version the owner can actually trade; it biases every exposure-reducing variant downward, and the FALL20-minus-GATE20 comparison absorbs nearly all of that because GATE20 sits in cash too. NO VARIANT IS PROMOTED in this run whatever it shows: the test window is not touched.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely the model's exposure ladder turns out to be a slow volatility target wearing a new name. Realised volatility is the most persistent of the seven features and is already one of them, and a forward-fall label over a quarter is largely a volatility label, so the forecast will probably track trailing volatility closely enough that the book cuts exposure when volatility is already high -- which is after the fall has begun, not before it. The lab has priced volatility targets before and they did not clear the 20% bar, and two of the three market-level columns -- the market's own realised volatility, and its distance below its one-year high -- are precisely the inputs a slow volatility target would use, so the head has every opportunity to rediscover one. Second, the level may be too coarse to be worth reading: the exposure ladder is driven by a single number a date, the cross-sectional mean forecast, located in a training distribution of at most a couple of hundred date-level means, so the ladder's resolution is one slot per few percentiles and the book may end up moving between full and nearly full on almost every date. If the realised exposure turns out to sit in a narrow band -- say between eighteen and twenty of the twenty slots on nine dates in ten -- then FALL20 will be nearly indistinguishable from ON20 whatever the forecast said, and the honest verdict is that the question was asked too quietly to hear the answer. (The flat-exposure failure this method was originally at risk of -- a label ranked within each date, which cannot encode a market-wide fall at all -- was removed before pre-registration: the label is a level and the feature matrix carries un-normalised market columns. That the exposure moves at all, and falls in 2008, was measured on the dev window before this file was committed. What was NOT measured, and is the open risk, is whether it moves ENOUGH and in the right years.) Third, the SPY 200-day switch is a very hard thing to beat on this window for a reason that is not skill: it caught 2008, the one year that dominates every whole-window drawdown number, and the lab has already measured that nearly all of the switch's whole-window value is that single year and that it has been a drag since 2009. So GATE20 is likely to win the whole window on the strength of 2008 and lose 2009-2015, and a model that is better than it after 2009 may still look worse over the full record. Fourth, the fall is broader than one crash: of the 302 dev trials that breached 20%, the worst year is 2008 for 103 of them but 2011 for 51 and 2015 for 50, so a forecast that only learns the shape of 2008 will not keep the fall under 20% and no variant here will clear design section 1. Fifth, cutting exposure costs return in a window SPY roughly quadrupled over, and with idle cash earning nothing every reduction is a pure drag on the return side of every bar; the monthly decision cadence also means the book cannot step aside faster than once a month, which was late in 2008 for every lab book that used the switch. Sixth, the training set inherits the store's survivorship -- about half of the index members ever listed are missing, mostly the ones that died -- and a fall model trained on survivors' histories has systematically seen fewer catastrophic falls than really happened, which should make it optimistic exactly where it matters most. Seventh, twenty years of monthly cross-sections is a small and heavily correlated sample for a learner, and a quarter-long label makes neighbouring month-ends overlap by two thirds, so the effective sample is roughly a third of the row count and the DSR at the lab's N may not separate a real sizing skill from luck even if the returns look good. Finally, the regularised arm is expected to sit between the base model and the controls, and if it does not -- if the regularised tree is clearly better -- that is evidence the base tree was overfitting the label and the right reading is that neither setting found anything.

methods.name: Lean into the swing, then step out of it: the most-asymmetric companies behind the market-trend switch
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0110 (the up/down participation spread, ungated), putting the lab's 200-day market switch in front of it; the buy-back of the fifth arm is M0113-UP63
methods.hypothesis: M0110-DP20-UP was a side effect of a shelter run and was the only thing in it that looked like an edge: ranking F4-screened members on upside participation minus downside participation (both measured over the past 252 sessions, the stock's summed return on SPY's up days over SPY's own, less the same on SPY's down days) and holding the 20 highest earned +10.3% a year against SPY TR's +7.2% on deposit-matched money, and beat SPY by 7.7 points a year over 2009-2015 -- the best post-2009 figure recorded in this lab, and the opposite sign to every other dev-window edge, all of which were earned before 2009. Its one defect is a 74.0% worst fall, with 2008 at -57.6%. That defect is exactly the one the SPY 200-day trend gate is measured to fix: it helped 22 of 22 variants whole-window, and the gate-off arms were worse on return AND drawdown at once. This re-runs the same ranking with the gate on. Variants: the plain gated book at 20 and 40 names; an ungated 40-name arm as the paired control that must fall harder; one arm that ranks on the same spread but requires upside participation above 1.0 outright, to separate 'outruns the market both ways' from 'simply swings more'; and one that keeps the 200-day exit but buys back on M0113's measured-better trigger, a positive last quarter. Success: a gated variant keeps most of the +3.1 point whole-window lead and most of the +7.7 point 2009-2015 lead while bringing the fall under 50% on the dev screen and ideally near 25%.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the gate and this ranking want opposite things. The lab's own measurement of the 200-day switch is that it earns its whole twenty-year advantage in 2001, 2002 and 2008 and pays for it everywhere else, and over 2009-2015 every reading of it lost 6 to 11 points a year to simply holding SPY (M0084, M0113). This method's entire claim is a +7.7 point lead over 2009-2015. The most-asymmetric names are the ones that give the most back in a fall and run hardest in the recovery, so the gate will sell them after the fall has happened and buy them back after the bounce has happened -- it should cut the 74% fall and cut the post-2009 lead with it, and the honest outcome is a book that passes the drawdown screen and no longer beats SPY where it matters. The second failure is identity: the spread rank may simply be high-beta momentum under a new name, in which case it will read as behavioural kin of the test-failed momentum books once it has a gated curve, and the hard gate will bar promotion however good the numbers look. That correlation is to be measured and reported early, not hoped away. The third is survivorship: M0110's asymmetry arm lost 2.0 points a year on the fuller price history, more than any other arm except the control, so part of the edge is companies the dev store cannot price. Publication risk is low -- the up/down capture ratio is an old practitioner measure and the asymmetry direction is not the crowded one -- but a high-beta book dressed as a factor is exactly what fades first when the market's shape favours the largest companies, which is what beat every strategy this lab tried after 2018.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# The best book this lab has ever measured, and the two reasons it still cannot be bought

## What this run asked

Yesterday's method tried to buy shelter by picking companies that sit out the market's bad
days. It worked a little and cost a lot. But one arm of it pointed the other way, and that arm
is why this run exists.

That arm ranked companies on an **asymmetry**: over the past year, how much of the market's good
days did this company join in, minus how much of its bad days. A reading of 1.4 against 0.9 means
"when the market rose this name rose about 40% more, and when it fell it gave back only about
nine tenths of the fall". Hold the twenty most asymmetric. On the owner's real saving plan that
earned 10.3% a year against 7.2% for the same money put into the market, **and it beat the market
by 7.7 points a year over 2009 to 2015** — which matters far more than it sounds. Of the eighty-odd
methods this lab has judged, about a quarter beat the market across twenty years and then lost to
it after 2009, and every other advantage the lab holds was earned *before* 2009. This one was the
only one pointing the right way in time, and 2009-2015 is the stretch most like today.

Its single flaw was the size of the fall: **74% from peak to trough, with 2008 down 57.6%** —
against a 50% screen on this window and the owner's 25% limit for real money. That flaw is the one
the lab has already measured a cure for. Putting the book behind the market's own trend — out
whenever the market closes below its 200-day average, in otherwise — helped 22 of 22 versions
tested across this lab, and every switch-off version was worse on return *and* on the fall at the
same time.

So this run put the switch in front of the same ranking, and kept a switch-off twin so the
switch's whole contribution stays measured rather than assumed. Five books, all forty or twenty
equal slots, re-picked monthly, bought in fractional shares at the real fees Gotrade charges, on
the owner's real deposits of Rp 5,000,000 on the 25th of every month since January 1996.

## The result

The "worst fall" column takes the deposits out first, so a monthly top-up refilling a falling
account cannot make any of these read gentler than it was. **The market itself fell 55.2% over
this window and earned 7.2% a year on the same deposits.**

| Book | Your money earned | Worst fall | Worst year | Gains vs losses | 2009-2015 vs market |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 names, switch on, back in on a positive quarter | **+16.7% a year** | 22.7% | 2011, −1.9% | 2.39 | **+4.5 pts a year** |
| 20 names, switch on | +15.6% | 22.7% | 2011, −2.5% | 2.40 | +2.1 |
| 20 names, switch on, only names that outrun on the way up | +15.5% | 24.5% | 2011, −1.1% | 2.33 | +1.1 |
| 40 names, switch on | +13.5% | **21.6%** | 2008, −0.3% | **2.63** | +0.4 |
| 40 names, **switch off** (the control) | +9.6% | **69.1%** | 2008, −51.4% | 1.59 | +5.3 |
| The same deposits in the market | +7.2% | 55.2% | 2008, −36.8% | — | — |
| *Last year's same ranking, 20 names, switch off* | *+10.3%* | *74.0%* | *2008, −57.6%* | *1.50* | *+7.7* |

**Four of the five passed every condition the lab screens on.** The best of them is the strongest
book this lab has recorded: 16.7% a year against the market's 7.2%, a worst fall of 22.7% where
the market fell 55.2%, 2.39 dollars of gains for every dollar of losses, 1,256 trades, and a worst
calendar year of −1.9% in 2011. It won 4 of the 4 period-by-period checks on its own, and the
method as a whole won 3 of 4.

## Was it luck?

The lab's luck score asks how likely a result this good is to be real rather than the best of many
tries. It is deflated by every distinct method the lab has ever run — 87 of them at the moment this
ran — and the owner's bar since 2026-10-07 is 0.90. The best book scores **0.926**, and the other
three passing books score 0.920 to 0.922. All four clear the bar. Neither the bar nor the way the
count is taken is mine to move, and neither moved.

## Why it worked

The switch is worth **6.0 points a year and 51 points of fall** on the identical twenty-name
ranking: 10.3% a year at a 74% fall without it, 15.6% a year at a 22.7% fall with it. That is a
bigger gain than the switch has produced anywhere else in this lab, and the reason is specific to
what this ranking buys. The most asymmetric companies are, by construction, the ones that move
hardest in both directions. They are the best names to own in a rising market and the worst to own
in a falling one, so the single cheapest thing you can do for them is not be holding them when the
market is falling. The switch-off control makes the same point from the other side: it fell 69.1%
and gave back more than half its 2008.

The second finding is smaller and cleaner. Everything about the two best books is identical except
how they come back after the switch has sold: one waits for the price to climb back over its
200-day average, the other comes back as soon as the market's **last three months have actually
made money**. The second earned 1.1 points a year more at *exactly the same* worst fall, 22.7% for
both. On the market alone, the same swap was worth only 0.6 points and cost 1.8 points of fall.
It is worth more here, and the reason follows from the first finding: this book's recovery is
bigger than the market's, so every month spent out of the recovery costs more.

The third finding is a negative one worth recording. Filtering to names that genuinely outrun the
market on its up days — not just names that fall less on its bad days — changed nothing: 15.5% a
year against 15.6%, and a slightly *deeper* fall. The asymmetry ranking was already doing that job.
The filter was a guard against a failure that does not occur.

## What the hypothesis got right, and what it got wrong

The hypothesis asked for a switched-on book that kept most of the whole-window lead and most of the
2009-2015 lead while bringing the fall under 50% and ideally near 25%. It got **more** than the
whole-window lead it asked for (8.4 to 9.5 points a year against the parent's 3.1) and a fall of
22.7%, better than the target. It did **not** keep the 2009-2015 lead: 7.7 points became 4.5 at
best and 0.4 at worst.

That is the first of the three failures written down before the run, and it happened as described.
The switch earns its keep in 2001, 2002 and 2008 and pays for it the rest of the time; the
switch-off control still holds the biggest recent lead of any book here, +5.3 points. So the honest
statement is: **the switch bought a 51-point reduction in the fall and paid for it with about
three to seven points a year of the recent-years lead.** On every measure the lab actually
screens on, that trade is overwhelmingly worth making. The recent-years lead stayed positive,
which is the condition that separates this method from almost everything else the lab holds.

The second written failure also happened, and it is the one that stops the method. The third did
not happen, and inverted into something more interesting.

## The two reasons it still cannot be bought

**One: it is the same book as something that has already failed out of sample.** The lab's
promotion rule refuses any method that moves like a book that has already spent its one look at
the years after 2015 and lost. Strip the market's share out of this book's monthly returns and what
is left moves with the tested overnight-momentum book at **0.91**, against a bar of 0.85. A new
name does not make it a new book. The rule exits without writing anything, there is no override,
and looking for one is exactly the mechanism that produced the lab's 0-for-5 record. This was
written down as the likely failure before the run, and it is the one that landed.

**Two: on a fuller price history, three of the four passing books fall past the owner's real-money
limit.** The lab's usual price history is missing roughly half the companies that ever sat in the
index, overwhelmingly the ones that went bankrupt or were bought. Re-running every version with
those companies added back:

| Book | Earned, usual → fuller | Worst fall, usual → fuller |
|---|---|---|
| 20 names, positive-quarter re-entry | +16.7% → **+17.5%** | 22.7% → **29.4%** |
| 20 names, switch on | +15.6% → +16.4% | 22.7% → **29.4%** |
| 20 names, up-filter | +15.5% → +16.7% | 24.5% → **29.3%** |
| **40 names, switch on** | +13.5% → **+14.8%** | 21.6% → **23.2%** |
| 40 names, switch off | +9.6% → +9.9% | 69.1% → 70.9% |

**Every single version earns more with the dead companies added back.** That has not happened to
any method in this lab before; the usual direction is a loss of about half a point a year, and the
parent of this method lost 2.0. So the third written failure — that the edge was partly an artefact
of missing companies — is not merely absent, it runs backwards. This ranking was finding real
companies that really ran, and some of them later died, and holding them on the way up and being
sold out of them by the switch was profitable.

But the falls deepen, and they deepen where it counts. The twenty-name books go from a comfortable
22.7% to **29.4%**, past the owner's 25% line, and the lab's promotion rule now refuses on exactly
that number. **The forty-name book is the only one that stays under: 23.2%.** It is also the one
whose recent-years lead is weakest, +0.4 points on the usual history and +1.9 on the fuller one.

## The buy signal: three of four

The lab holds a standing rule about when survivorship-free price history becomes worth paying for.
It fires on four conditions together. This method clears **(a)** the screen, **(c)** a majority of
the period-by-period checks, and **(d)** a positive lead in the best-covered recent years — but
fails **(b)**, because it moves like a book that already failed. The signal does not fire, and the
lab's own check says so in those words. Three of four is the closest anything has come.

## A number that changes how width should be read

Twenty names to forty moved the worst fall by **1.1 points** on the usual price history, and by
**6.2 points** on the fuller one. A separate method measured today found that going from twenty
names to seventy moved the fall by less than a point and cost 2.8 points a year — and concluded
that width buys no safety behind a switch. On the usual history that is exactly what this run
shows too. On the fuller history it is wrong by a factor of six. Width's protection is invisible
in the lab's default price history because the companies it protects you from are the ones that
history is missing. Any width decision taken on the usual history alone has been reading the
wrong number.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth more trials than anything else currently in the lab, and the next trial
is obvious and cheap.**

What has actually been established here is not one book but a mechanism, measured three ways: the
asymmetry ranking finds companies that genuinely outrun the market, the switch converts their
violence from a liability into an advantage worth six points a year, and coming back on a positive
quarter instead of a price cross is worth another point for free. Those are three independent
measurements pointing the same way, two of which replicate findings from elsewhere in the lab on a
book that is unlike the ones they were measured on. And the fuller price history makes the returns
*better*, which no method here has ever done.

The method is blocked, and correctly so, by a behavioural tie to a book that already failed out of
sample. But that tie is reported for the twenty-name version, and the lab reports only the single
strongest tie per failed book — so **the forty-name version's own behaviour has never been
measured.** That matters, because the forty-name version is the only configuration in this run
that stays under the owner's real-money fall limit on the fuller price history, and it is a
materially different book: twice the names, half the concentration, a different fall profile, and
a worst year of −0.3% in 2008 against the market's −36.8%.

So the next method is the forty-name gated book, registered alone, so its own tie is measured
rather than inherited from its wider family. If it reads at or above 0.85 as well, then this whole
direction genuinely is the lab's one momentum book wearing another costume, the honest conclusion
is that the asymmetry ranking is high-participation momentum, and the line should close with that
stated plainly. If it reads below, the lab has a book that passes the screen, passes the periods,
holds a positive recent-years lead, and survives the dead companies — which would be the first
time all four have been true at once, and the moment to buy real price history.

What I would **not** do is chase the recent-years lead by weakening the switch. The switch-off
control holds the biggest recent lead in this run and falls 69%. That trade has now been offered
three times in this lab and refused three times, and the reason is the same every time: the owner
cannot hold a book through a 69% fall, so a lead he cannot survive to collect is not a lead.
methods.verdict: The switch turned the lab's most violent edge into its best book — 16.7% a year against the market's 7.2% at a 22.7% fall — and it still cannot be bought: it moves like a book that already failed out of sample, and only the 40-name version stays under the owner's fall limit once the dead companies are added back.

methods.name: Market participation as an exclusion, not a ranking: drop the most exposed quarter of a book that already works
methods.hypothesis: M0110 proved that downside participation (the stock's summed return on SPY's down days over the past 252 sessions, divided by SPY's own summed return on those days) orders a crash cleanly: five books built along that ranking fell 39.9%, 41.4%, 43.3%, 74.0% and 90.6% in exactly the order the ranking predicted. What it also proved is that using it as the book's ranking key is a bad trade, because the 20 lowest participants are a low-beta book that lost 3 to 6 points a year to SPY over 2009-2015. The obvious remaining use is as a screen rather than a ranker: keep an existing engine's ranking, and simply refuse to hold the most market-exposed quarter of the eligible universe. That costs the book only its most exposed names rather than replacing its whole selection, so it should give up far less return than ranking on participation did. Apply it to an engine whose kin is clean so a result is promotable -- M0072's z-scored event book and M0092's volume-capped jump book are the only two the hard gate currently calls promotable -- rather than to a momentum engine, which would read as behavioural kin of the test-failed books whatever it is called. Variants: each of the two engines unchanged as the control, each with the top-quartile participants excluded, and one with the top half excluded to price the dose. Success: the fall drops by at least 5 points with less than 1 point a year of return given up, measured against the control in the same run, and the 2009-2015 lead does not go backwards -- if it does, this is the low-beta trade again in a smaller dose and should be dropped. Expected failure: the excluded names are the engine's best performers, because the same exposure that deepens the fall is what earns the return, in which case the screen costs about what ranking on it cost and the whole participation measure is closed for good.

methods.name: Put the quarter-return buy-back under a real stock book: the near misses, three months sooner
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0128 (the near misses on the fixed tape); frame and trigger from M0113-UP63
methods.hypothesis: The 200-day switch is old (the banded rule 1992, Faber's monthly version 2007), so nothing here is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies; what is new is which HALF of it is paid for. M0113 held the exit fixed and moved only the buy-back on a SPY-only book: a positive 63-session return (UP63) returned +32.14% a year funded against the symmetric control's +31.68% and a deposit-matched SPY's +30.57%, while every price-LEVEL trigger lost -- above the 50-day average +30.86% at a 25.25% fall, above the 20-day average +30.76% at 29.58%, both from buying bear rallies -- and re-entering LATER, at a 20-session high, was worst of all (+29.56%, a 27.07% fall, the one arm that lost to SPY). Faster beats slower and realised return beats price level, bracketed on both sides. The mechanism: inside a real crash a positive three-month return is nearly impossible, but after a genuine bottom a quarter turns positive long before a 200-day average does. M0113 could not be a candidate -- 11 to 43 trades in 22 years against a 100-trade condition -- so it measured a frame. This method spends that frame on M0128's two strongest fixed-tape books, which trade 1,607 and 2,786 times and sit behind the identical switch. EXACTLY ONE THING CHANGES: the inner books' own 200-day gate (FactorParams.trend) is stripped to None and the identical gate is re-applied from outside, asymmetrically through `held` -- exit rule while in, entry rule while out. Applied symmetrically an outer gate IS the stateless inner gate, so M0135-RAW20-SMA200 is M0128-RAW20 re-expressed and MUST reproduce its row (+37.64% against +32.40%, a 20.65% worst fall, gains 1.98 times losses, 1,607 trades, 69.4% invested, DSR 0.9142). If it does not, the machinery is wrong and none of the other five numbers is readable; that check comes before every other claim in the analysis. ALL SIX RUN ON ONE PRESET, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband -- the fixed tape, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fee schedule, the owner's monthly deposits, and NO T-bill credit on idle cash -- so the arms are mutually comparable and every one of them can be eligible, which the cash-yield owner input would have prevented. Idle cash earning nothing flatters whichever arm is out least, i.e. the faster buy-backs; the size of that thumb, stated now: on SPY the swap moved time-in-market 71.1% to 73.4%, and 1996-2015 T-bills paid about 2.5% a year, so the bias on the paired difference is roughly 2.5% x 2.3% = under 0.1 points a year, and any gap smaller than that is noise for this reason alone. PREDICTIONS, written before the run. (1) UP63 raises time-in-market by 2 to 4 points on both books, mostly in 2003 and 2009. (2) It adds 0.5 to 2 points a year of funded return over its own paired control on each book -- less than it added on SPY alone in relative terms, because a book that is out of the market less often than a pure switch has less re-entry lag to recover, and because M0128's picks already earn 3.5 to 4.5 points a year over a plain switched equal-weight book and may absorb what the frame costs. (3) The worst fall DEEPENS by 1 to 3 points, more than the 1.8 points it deepened on SPY, because what gets bought back into a bear rally here is twenty individual momentum names rather than the index, and individual names fall further. On RAW20 that starts at 20.65% and is already past the owner's 25% real-money bar's comfort; on B70 it starts at 18.23% and has room. Both stay inside the 50% dev screen either way, so drawdown will not be what rejects this. (4) The gain must be visible in 2009-2015, the best-covered era and the one most like today, or it is a pre-2009 artefact and the verdict says so first -- this is the condition the idea is really being judged on, because M0128's own picking edge collapsed to about a point a year after 2009. (5) UP126 lands between the control and UP63 and UP21 overshoots into bear rallies, which would make 63 a point on a monotone ramp rather than a peak; if instead UP21 wins, the finding is simply 'sooner is better' and the quarter is arbitrary, and that is a different and weaker claim. SUCCESS: a variant that keeps its worst fall inside 25%, keeps over 100 trades, and adds at least a point a year over its OWN paired control with the gain present after 2009. WHAT THIS CANNOT DO is be promoted, and that is known now rather than discovered later: the line runs through M0128 to M0030, the blend's ingredients are M0021's (test-failed) and M0029 is its fixed-fee twin (test-failed), and behavioural kin will match these curves to M0022's. The hard gate refuses on kin whatever this scores. It is registered as a method because it is a real measurement that must be held to these predictions, and it adds one look to the lab's N.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest outcome is that the two points a year do not survive contact with real picks. M0128's books are already 3.5 to 4.5 points a year better than a plain switched equal-weight book, and they are invested 69% of the time rather than a pure switch's 71%; a book with less re-entry lag has less to recover, so the frame's gain can shrink to nothing or to under the 0.1-point noise floor the cash-interest bias sets. If the paired differences land inside a tenth of a point, the honest verdict is that the buy-back finding is a property of holding the index and does not transfer, which would be a real result about a frame roughly half the lab shares. The second risk is the one the SPY run already showed in miniature and which should be LARGER here: a faster buy-back puts twenty individual momentum names, not the index, back into a bear rally. Individual names fall further than the index, so the 1.8 points of extra worst fall UP63 cost on SPY could be 3 to 5 points here, and on RAW20 that starts from 20.65%. A variant that buys a point of return with four points of fall has not improved anything the owner cares about, and the verdict must read the pair together rather than quote the return alone. Third, and the way this method could fool itself: the gain may be one event. UP63's whole SPY advantage plausibly lives in 2009, where the slow average kept the control out through the recovery. One good year inside twenty, on a method whose kin already fail out of sample, is not an edge; it is a single draw. The analysis must report the year-by-year difference and the 2009-2015 split before the whole-window average, and M0113's own fold record is the warning -- it won 1 of 4 walk-forward folds and the fold it won was the 2006-2008 crash, which is the stretch the exit is already good at rather than evidence about the entry. Fourth, the machinery. If RAW20-SMA200 does not reproduce M0128-RAW20 to within what nothing should move, the gate-stripping or the `bool(held)` reading of 'in or out' is wrong, and the correct response is to report the method as unreadable rather than to explain the gap away. The specific way `bool(held)` can part from the truth is an 'on' session where the inner book targets nothing, which would hand the next check to the entry rule; the control's trade count against M0128-RAW20's 1,607 is what detects it. Fifth, deposits soften every worst fall here alike and the rupiah's fall is not in these dev-window numbers at all, so none of these may be lined up against an unfunded parent's. Sixth, the DSR. RAW20's control sits at 0.9142 against a 0.90 bar at N = 86 and rising; N has grown since M0128 ran, so a variant can lose eligibility here purely because the lab has looked more times, and that must be reported as the lab's cost rather than the method's failure.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# Buying back three months sooner, under a book that actually picks stocks

## The question

Most of this lab's best books share one safety rule. When the S&P 500 tracker SPY closes below
its own average price of the last 200 trading days, the book sells everything and sits in cash.
When it closes back above that average, the book buys again.

Yesterday's work (M0113) took that rule apart on a book holding nothing but SPY, and found the
two halves are not equally good. The selling half earns its keep: it sat out 2001, 2002 and 2008.
The buying-back half is slow and expensive — a 200-day average takes months to turn after a
market bottom, so the book watches the recovery from the sidelines. Replacing only the buy-back,
with "come back when SPY's last three months have actually made money", beat the original. Coming
back on a price crossing instead was worse, and coming back even later was worse still.

But that test could not become a real candidate. A book that only holds SPY trades about a dozen
times in twenty-two years, and this lab requires at least a hundred closed trades before it will
believe anything. It measured a *frame*, not a strategy.

This method puts that frame under two books that do trade enough: the twenty-stock momentum book
and the seventy-thirty blend of momentum and calm stocks, both of which sit behind that exact
safety rule today. Exactly one thing was changed — the buy-back — and each book was run twice,
once unchanged and once with the new buy-back, in the same batch, on the same days, with the same
deposits and the same fees, so the difference is the buy-back and nothing else.

## First, proof the measurement is honest

Before anything else: the unchanged twenty-stock arm had to come out identical to the same book
measured two days ago, or the rewiring would have changed something silently and no number here
would mean anything. It did, to every digit the lab records — the same 20.65% worst fall, the
same 1.98 ratio of gains to losses, the same 1,607 trades, the same 69.4% of the time invested.
The lab's independent behaviour check agrees: the unchanged blend arm moves with the already-
tested blend at a correlation of 1.00, which is to say it *is* that book. The machinery is clean,
so the rest can be read.

## What happened

All figures below are money-weighted: what your actual money earned, counting that you add
5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th of every month, measured against putting those identical deposits
into SPY on the identical days. SPY earned +7.2% a year that way. "Worst fall" is the deepest
drop from a peak. "Gains vs losses" is total winnings divided by total losses — above 1.0 means
the winners outweigh the losers.

| Book | Buy-back rule | A year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20-stock momentum | 200-day average (unchanged) | +13.7% | 20.65% | 1.98 | 1,607 | 69.4% |
| 20-stock momentum | **positive last quarter** | **+14.7%** | **20.67%** | 1.98 | 1,731 | 71.7% |
| 70/30 blend | 200-day average (unchanged) | +11.7% | 18.25% | 2.03 | 2,786 | 69.3% |
| 70/30 blend | **positive last quarter** | **+12.4%** | **19.12%** | 2.02 | 3,035 | 71.6% |
| 70/30 blend | positive last half-year | +10.9% | 19.12% | 1.90 | 2,898 | 70.2% |
| 70/30 blend | positive last month | +11.4% | 23.64% | 1.78 | 3,320 | 75.6% |

**The frame transferred.** Buying back on a positive quarter added **one point a year** to the
twenty-stock book and **0.66 of a point** to the blend, over each book's own unchanged twin. Both
are far above the 0.1-point measurement noise this method wrote down before the run as its own
floor.

**And it was nearly free.** The thing I predicted would go wrong did not. I wrote beforehand that
buying back sooner would put twenty individual stocks, not the index, into a false recovery, and
that the worst fall would therefore deepen by one to three points. On the twenty-stock book the
worst fall moved by **two hundredths of a point** — 20.65% to 20.67%. On the blend it deepened by
0.87 of a point. The books also stayed out of the market almost exactly as much as before: time
invested rose by 2.3 points on both, the same 2.3 points it rose on SPY alone. The faster
buy-back is not simply "be in the market more"; it is "be in the market at better moments".

**Three months is a real sweet spot, not an arbitrary number.** This is the part I did not
expect. One month was much worse than doing nothing at all: it bought false recoveries, deepened
the worst fall by 5.4 points to 23.64%, and dropped gains-vs-losses from 2.03 to 1.78. Six months
was *also* worse than doing nothing, by 0.8 of a point a year. So the quarter is a peak with a
worse answer on each side of it, which is much stronger evidence than a number sitting on a slope
would have been. The reason is readable: one month is short enough to turn positive inside a
crash, and six months is nearly as slow as the 200-day average it was meant to replace.

**The luck score went up, not down.** The lab deflates every result by how many times it has
looked for one — 90 looks now. The score it produces runs 0 to 1 and the owner's bar is 0.90,
meaning a result must look at least 90% likely to be real rather than a lucky draw. The faster
buy-back *raised* that score on both books, from 0.914 to 0.928 and from 0.935 to 0.941. The
extra point a year was not bought with extra wobble.

## Where the gain actually came from

This is where the method has to be honest about itself. I traced the gap between each pair month
by month. It did not accumulate steadily. On the twenty-stock book the two paths are identical
for years at a time, and essentially the whole difference opens in four months:

- **November–December 2002: +13%.** The big one. The unchanged book sold out in mid-2001 and sat
  in cash until April 2003 — you can see it in the data, earning nothing but the deposits for
  twenty-two straight months. The new rule noticed that the three months after the October 2002
  market low had actually made money, bought back in November, caught the sharp recovery, and was
  back out in January before it reversed. One re-entry.
- **May 2008: +4.3%**, and **May–June 2009: +2.2%** — the same mechanism at the 2008–09 bottom.
- **January–February 2012: +1.9%.**

Against those, it gave back 4.1% in November 1998 and 1.8% in June 2005 buying recoveries that
did not hold.

So the whole edge is a handful of crisis re-entries. That is not a criticism of the mechanism —
it is exactly what the mechanism is *for*, and a rule that only matters after crashes can only
pay after crashes. But it does mean the evidence rests on perhaps four events in twenty years,
and four events is a small number to build on.

## The test that mattered most

Before running this I wrote down which condition would decide it: the gain had to show up in
2009–2015, the stretch the lab's price history covers best and the one most like today. An edge
that only exists before 2009 is usually an artefact of missing data rather than a real effect.

It passed, on both books and in both directions:

| Book | Lead over SPY, 2009–2015, per year | With the missing companies added back |
|---|---|---|
| 20-stock, unchanged | +1.1% | −0.2% |
| 20-stock, **positive quarter** | **+1.7%** | **+0.9%** |
| Blend, unchanged | −1.2% | −1.9% |
| Blend, **positive quarter** | **−0.5%** | **−1.0%** |

The faster buy-back improved the modern era by 0.6 to 0.7 of a point a year on both books, and by
*more* — 0.9 to 1.1 points — once the companies that went bankrupt or were bought out are put
back into the price history. That is the right direction: the improvement is not an artefact of
the lab's data being too clean.

Note what this table also says, quietly: the blend still **loses** to SPY after 2009 even with the
better buy-back. The buy-back fixes a frame; it does not fix a book.

## Where it fails

**On fuller price history the twenty-stock book falls 25.05%.** The lab normally prices only
companies that still exist, which flatters anything that held stocks through a crash. Re-run with
the dead companies restored, both twenty-stock arms fall 25.05% — exactly at your 25% real-money
limit, and the identical figure that already refuses an older cousin of this book. The blend is
the sturdy one: it falls 20.78% on the same fuller history, comfortably inside the limit.

**The books are disproven relatives.** The lab refuses to promote a method whose close kin have
already failed a real out-of-sample test, and there is no override. This method's unchanged blend
arm moves with a book that already failed at a correlation of **1.00**, and with two others at
0.99 and 0.92. They are the same books wearing a new name. I wrote this refusal into the
pre-registration before the run rather than discovering it afterwards, and it happened exactly as
written. So: four of six arms cleared every numerical condition, the method is marked
