dev-eligible, it has the best risk-adjusted score in its family, it won three of four
walk-forward folds (and the single best arm won three of four on its own) — **and it cannot be
promoted, because of what it was built on, not because of how it scored.**

For the same reason there is no buy signal on survivorship-free data. Of the four conditions that
would justify paying for it, this method clears being dev-eligible, clears the folds, and clears
having a positive modern-era edge; it fails the kin condition. Three of four is not the signal.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Mostly yes, and the two places I was wrong both matter.

- *Right:* the frame transferred, at 0.98 and 0.66 points a year against a predicted 0.5 to 2.
- *Right:* time invested rose 2.3 points, inside the predicted 2 to 4.
- *Right:* the gain shows after 2009, which was the condition I said would decide it.
- *Right:* promotion is refused on kin, predicted before the run.
- **Wrong, and better than expected:** I predicted the worst fall would deepen by 1 to 3 points.
  It deepened by 0.02 on the twenty-stock book. The bear-rally risk, which was the main reason to
  doubt this would transfer, did not materialise at three months — though it emphatically did at
  one month, which is the same risk showing up exactly where theory says it should.
- **Wrong, and more interesting:** I predicted six months would land between the unchanged rule
  and three months. It landed *below* the unchanged rule. Three months is a peak, not a point on
  a ramp. That is better evidence than I expected to get, and it is the finding I would keep.
- *The stated failure that did happen:* the gain is a handful of events, not a steady drip.

## My opinion:

This direction is worth more trials, and I would spend them on the frame rather than on these
books. What was learned here is portable and the books it was learned on are dead. Buying back
when the last quarter has actually made money, instead of when a price crosses a slow average, is
worth roughly half a point to a point a year, costs almost nothing in extra fall at three months,
raises the luck score rather than lowering it, survives the removal of the data's survivorship
flattery, and improves rather than decays in the modern era. It reproduced on two different books
and at a cleanly bracketed setting. That is about as much corroboration as a free measurement can
give.

What it cannot do is rescue a momentum book. Both books here are, by the lab's own behaviour
test, the same books that already lost their one out-of-sample look — one of them at a
correlation of 1.00. Running better machinery on a disproven engine produces a better disproven
engine. I would stop testing this frame on residual-momentum books entirely.

Two things I would do next, in order.

First, and this is what I have queued: **ask whether realised return beats a price crossing on
the selling side too.** Every experiment so far has frozen the exit at the 200-day average and
moved only the entry, because yesterday's result said the exit was the good half. But "the exit
is good" and "the exit is optimally expressed" are different claims, and the second one has never
been tested. If a positive quarter is a better reason to buy than a price crossing, a negative
quarter may be a better reason to sell — earlier in 2008, and without the false alarms a price
line generates in choppy markets. That is the one untried cell in this grid, it costs nothing new
to build because both pieces already exist, and it would be measured on a book with clean
relatives so the answer can actually go somewhere.

Second, if that works, carry the whole switch to a family with no failed kin. The lab has
dev-eligible methods today whose relatives are clean but which lose their walk-forward folds. A
frame worth most of a point a year, concentrated precisely in the recovery years where those
methods lose, is a plausible way to flip one — and unlike everything in this method's family, a
win there could actually reach a real test.
methods.verdict: Dev-eligible and promotion refused: buying back when the last quarter has actually made money beat the 200-day price crossing on both books, by one point a year and 0.66 of a point, for two hundredths of a point of extra fall — but the books themselves are the ones that already failed their real test.

methods.name: Come back halfway first: a staged re-entry that makes a false start cost half as much
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0113 (the 200-day exit held fixed, only the buy-back moved)
methods.hypothesis: M0113 showed the buy-back half of the shared 200-day safety switch is where the money goes, and that the two failure modes sit on opposite sides of one knob. Buy back too slowly (the symmetric 200-day control, or a 20-session high) and the recovery is slept through: the control lost 5.9 points a year to SPY over 2009-2015 and the 20-session high lost 9.8. Buy back too eagerly on a price-above-a-line test (the 50-day or 20-day average) and the money is back inside the crash: 2008 went from flat to -10.7%, 2001 to -15.2%, and the worst fall from 18.9% to 25-36%. M0113-UP63 found a trigger that avoids both by asking a harder question (a positive 63-session return), but it still closed only about a third of the 2009-2015 gap, so the knob is not yet where it should be. This method attacks the same whipsaw from a different direction: instead of a better ON/OFF trigger, make the position SIZE the thing that moves. The exit is unchanged -- a fresh break below the 200-day average goes all the way to cash -- and re-entry comes in steps: a part position when the early trigger fires, the rest only once SPY has reclaimed its 200-day average. A false start then costs half (or a third) of what it cost the 50-day trigger, while a genuine bottom is participated in from months earlier, which is exactly the asymmetry M0113's year-by-year table asks for. The switch's two halves are nothing new -- the banded moving-average rule is 1992 and Faber's ten-month version 2007 -- so no fade argument applies; what is new is paying for the buy-back in instalments rather than all at once. Frame: SPY only, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, the same 253-bar lookback as M0084 and M0113, so all three are scored on exactly the same sessions and every difference is the staging alone. Six variants: the two paired controls SMA200 (which must reproduce M0084-MONTHLY's 11 trades and 0.483 MAR) and UP63 (which must reproduce M0113-UP63's 18 trades and 0.469 MAR); HALF-UP63 and HALF-SMA50 (half in on the quarter-return and on the 50-day cross respectively, full in above the 200-day); THIRDS-UP63 (a third on the quarter-return, two thirds above the 50-day average, the rest above the 200-day, so the ramp has three steps); and HALF-UP63-HOLD (the same as HALF-UP63 but the half position is NOT sold if the early trigger reverses, only on a fresh 200-day break, which tests whether the re-selling or the re-buying is what costs). SUCCESS: a staged variant that beats M0113-UP63's funded return AND closes at least half of the control's 5.9-point 2009-2015 gap, without pushing the worst fall past 25%. Eligibility is not expected -- a 100%-SPY book cannot clear the 100-trade bar and the trade counts will be in the tens -- so the paired differences are the result, and profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless here. Note the window starts 1994-01-28, not the usual 1996-01-03, so compare only with M0084's and M0113's numbers.
methods.expectedFailure: The obvious failure is that half a position earns half the recovery, so the staged versions land exactly halfway between the control and UP63 on every number and teach nothing a weighted average of the two would not have told us -- in which case the answer is that the trigger, not the sizing, is the lever, and this family should be closed. The second risk is that holding a part position through a continued fall is the worst of both worlds: exposed to the crash and under-exposed to the recovery, which would show up as a deeper fall than UP63 with no more return. May 2008 is the specific date to look at: SPY's 63-session return turned positive that spring while it was still under its 200-day average and more than a month past its break, so every staged variant is expected to be holding a part position going into the autumn of 2008, and HALF-UP63-HOLD to still be holding it at the bottom. The third risk is mechanical and is why the two controls exist: the book engine tells an allocator only whether SPY is held, never how much, so the ladder's rung is recovered from price with a 32-session freshness test rather than from the book's state. If that recovery is wrong, the exit is no longer M0084's and the paired differences are unreadable -- SMA200 and UP63 reproducing their parents to the decimal is the check, and if either misses, nothing else here should be believed. Fourth, the ladder trades more than the binary switch by construction (a trim and an add where the switch had one flip), and at Gotrade's real fees on a 20M IDR book those part-sized orders pay the worst of the fee schedule, so some of the gap will be eaten before it is earned. Not modelled anywhere: interest on the cash held while the switch is off or half off, which flatters SPY and penalises every switched variant, so every gap reported here is an upper bound on the switch's cost.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# M0136 — Come back halfway first

**The question.** Seer's safety rule sells everything when the market falls below its 200-day
average. That rule is the reason half the strategies here survived 2001, 2002 and 2008 — and it is
also expensive, because the same slow average that got us out keeps us out through the recovery.
The previous method, M0113, asked *when* to buy back and found a good answer. This one asks a
different question: instead of a better moment to buy back, what if we **bought back in
instalments** — half the money on an early signal, the other half only once the market has truly
reclaimed its 200-day average? A false start would then cost half as much, while a real bottom is
caught months earlier.

Six versions were run, all holding nothing but SPY, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees,
on the owner's real monthly top-ups, over 1994 to October 2015 — the same sessions as the two
earlier methods, so every number below is a like-for-like comparison.

## The headline

Nothing here qualifies for money, and nothing was expected to. A book that holds only SPY trades
about once a year, so it can never reach the 100 closed trades the rules require, and the luck
score (DSR — how likely a result is real rather than a fluke after this many tries) lands at
0.89 against a bar of 0.90, judged at N=152 distinct methods. Both of those were written down
before the run. **This method is a measurement of a frame, not a candidate.** Its job was to
answer one question, and it answered it clearly.

Money-weighted return — what the owner's own deposits would actually have earned:

| version | the money earned | vs same deposits in SPY | worst fall | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the plain 200-day rule (control) | **+9.1% a year** | +7.7% | 18.9% | 11 |
| buy back all at once on a positive quarter (M0113's best) | **+9.7%** | +7.7% | 20.7% | 18 |
| half on the quarter, rest above the 200-day | +9.2% | +7.7% | 18.9% | 15 |
| half on the 50-day cross, rest above the 200-day | +8.7% | +7.7% | 18.9% | 19 |
| thirds (quarter, 50-day, 200-day) | +8.5% | +7.7% | 19.1% | 19 |
| half on the quarter, and keep the half | **+9.3%** | +7.7% | 18.9% | 13 |

**Every version beat SPY on the owner's deposits, and none of them beat buying back all at once.**
The best staged version earned +9.3% a year where the existing all-at-once rule earned +9.7%. The
pre-registered success test was "beat +9.7% **and** close at least half of the control's post-2009
gap to SPY". It failed both halves. Staging is not an improvement on a good buy-back signal.

Two checks confirm the numbers can be trusted: the two control versions were deliberately built to
re-run the earlier methods under this new code, and they reproduced them to the decimal — the
plain rule gave 11 trades and an 18.9% fall exactly like its parent, the all-at-once rule 18
trades and a 20.7% fall exactly like its parent. The machinery is sound, so the differences below
are the staging and nothing else.

## But staging did something, and it is worth knowing

Strip the deposits out (monthly top-ups refill a falling account and make every fall look gentler
than it was) and look at the two most revealing years — the ones where buying back too eagerly
cost real money.

| | 2001 | 2008 | whole window | 2009–2015 | worst fall | when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| buy back on the 50-day cross, **all at once** | −8.8% | **−10.7%** | +8.7%/yr | +10.3%/yr | **23.6%** | Feb 2009 |
| the same signal, **half at a time** | −5.5% | **−5.4%** | +9.1%/yr | +11.1%/yr | **15.3%** | Sep 1998 |

That is the mechanism working exactly as designed, and it is a big effect. The 50-day cross is the
*eager* signal: it fires on bear-market bounces, so the money is back inside the crash. Halving the
first step halved the 2008 damage almost to the decimal (−10.7% became −5.4%), cut 2001's damage by
more than a third, added 0.4 points a year of return, and — the striking part — **took the worst
fall from 23.6% down to 15.3%, and moved it off the 2008 crash entirely.** For the halved version
the deepest hole in twenty-two years is no longer a crash at all; it is the choppy autumn of 1998.

Now the same comparison on the *good* signal:

| | 2001 | 2008 | whole window | 2009–2015 | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| buy back on a positive quarter, **all at once** | −2.8% | +0.5% | +9.9%/yr | **+12.4%/yr** | 15.3% |
| the same signal, **half at a time** | −1.8% | +0.2% | +9.6%/yr | +11.0%/yr | 15.3% |

Nothing left to save. The positive-quarter signal almost never fires inside a crash, so it had no
false start to insure against — and the insurance premium (half the recovery) was paid anyway.

**So the finding is this: position sizing is a repair for a bad buy-back signal, not an improvement
on a good one.** It bought the eager signal an 8-point-shallower worst fall and a better return at
the same time, which is rare in this lab. It bought the careful signal nothing, and charged it 0.3
points a year. And a repaired bad signal (+9.1%) still loses to a good signal used at full size
(+9.7%), so there is no route to a better rule through this door.

The three-step version is the clearest warning. Adding a middle rung at the 50-day average put
*two thirds* of the money back into the market in mid-2008 — it lost 7.1% that year where the
two-step version lost nothing, and its worst fall is the only one that still lands on the February
2009 bottom (17.6%). More steps is not more caution; a middle rung built on an eager signal is just
the eager signal with extra words.

## An honest caveat that turned into the next idea

To keep the exit identical to the earlier methods, the code uses a rule I chose and wrote down
before the run: a drop below the 200-day average that happens within about a month and a half of
the market being *above* that line counts as a fresh break and goes all the way to cash, with no
instalment allowed. Without it, a fall out of a full position would quietly become a trim to a half
position, and the exit would no longer be the one M0113 and M0084 measured.

That guard is doing more damage than the halving is. Look at 2011 and 2012: the market dipped
below its 200-day average in August 2011 and recovered before the year was out — a short break. The
all-at-once version got back in and earned −0.4% and +13.6% in those two years. The staged version
was still inside its blackout, never took the half step, and earned −2.1% and +9.8% — which is
*exactly* what the plain 200-day control earned, to the decimal. It behaved as if the staging did
not exist. Those two years alone account for about 5.5 points of the roughly 10 points the staged
version gives up over 2009–2015; the actual halving accounts for about 4 (all of it in 2009).

In plain terms: **the staged rule was switched off for most of the modern era by a safety guard,
and still beat SPY on the owner's deposits.** The guard is too long. One check's blackout, rather
than a month and a half, would let the instalment rule act on ordinary dips too, and that version
has not been measured.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did the expected failure happen?

The hypothesis said a false start would cost half as much. It does — precisely half, on the signal
that actually produces false starts. The hypothesis also said this would be enough to beat the
all-at-once rule. It is not, and that part is wrong.

The expected failure was written as "the staged versions land halfway between the control and the
all-at-once version on every number and teach nothing". That is half-right and in an interesting
way: on **return** they landed between the two, but on **depth of fall** they did not split the
difference — they took the *better* of the two outright, keeping the control's shallow 18.9% fall
while picking up part of the recovery. The second expected failure, that holding a part position
through a continuing fall would be the worst of both worlds, also happened, but only to the
three-step version, and on exactly the date named in advance (mid-2008).

The sticky version — where the half position is kept instead of being re-sold when the early signal
reverses — answers a sub-question cleanly: it saved two round trips and ended 0.1 points a year
ahead, losing in 2001's chop and winning it back in 2003. **Re-selling and re-buying cost about the
same; neither is the villain.**

Two checks were deliberately skipped, and the reason is recorded here rather than assumed: the
survivorship cross-check adds back the index companies that died, and this book never holds an
index company — only SPY — so it cannot move a single number. The promotion durability checks were
also skipped because nothing here is eligible for promotion.

## My opinion

**This specific direction is finished, and I would close it. One narrow follow-up is worth an id,
and it is not about sizing at all.**

The question "should the buy-back be paid in instalments?" now has an answer, and it is no — not on
SPY, and not with a good signal. Instalments are insurance, and the lab has already found the
signal that does not need insuring. Running more rungs, more weights or more trigger pairs on a
SPY-only book would be measuring for its own sake, and a SPY-only book can never qualify for the
owner's money anyway.

What I would spend the next id on is the blackout, because the measurement above accidentally
proved it is the binding constraint, not the sizing: the staged rule spent 2011 through 2015
behaving like the plain 200-day control because a safety guard I wrote switched it off, and it
*still* beat SPY. Shorten the guard to a single check and the instalment rule finally gets to act
on ordinary dips rather than only on generational bottoms. That is a one-line change with a
measurable, pre-registered prediction attached, and if it does not recover those five points then
the sizing question is closed for good rather than closed on a technicality.

The second thing I would do — and the one with real money behind it — is take the finding to where
it pays. Halving the first step turned the eager signal's worst fall from 23.6% into 15.3% while
*raising* its return. SPY's own falls are shallow compared with a stock book's, so an 8-point
improvement on SPY hints at something larger on a book that actually picks stocks. The near-miss
momentum books fail the real-money bar on depth of fall, not on return. A staged re-entry sitting
underneath one of those is the first idea I have seen that attacks that specific failure without
costing return, and that is the experiment worth running.

What I would not do is sweep the step sizes. There is nothing in this data that says a half is
better than a 40% or a 60%, and tuning that on the same twenty-two years is how a measurement turns
into a story about itself.
methods.verdict: Buying back in instalments halves the damage a hasty signal does, but the lab's careful signal had no damage to halve — so staging repairs a bad rule and costs a good one 0.3 points a year.

methods.name: A forgetting ranker: the yearly-horizon trees retrained on a rolling ten-year window instead of an ever-growing one
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0131 (the slow-target learned ranker); Sera batch 20261014-1242
methods.hypothesis: M0131 showed that asking the trees about the next twelve months instead of the next month is worth 3.8 points a year over 2000-2015 and 6.5 points over 2009-2015, with the model, the gate, the tape and the window all held fixed; and that with a slow label the flexible tree beats the regularised one, reversing M0130. What it did not fix is where the money comes from: every arm lost to SPY in 2009-2015 (best 15.9% against 16.6%), the whole-window win is the SPY 200-day switch sitting in cash through 2001, 2002 and 2008, and the walk-forward record is 2 of 4 folds with BOTH losses in rising markets (2003-05 +35.9% against SPY's +52.1%; 2009-11 +59.7% against +60.8%), which is what refuses promotion. THE SUSPECT IS MEMORY. Every refit so far adds twelve months to an expanding window that starts in January 1996 and never forgets, so the 1996-2000 technology boom and bust is still a large share of the 2012 model's training set and the tilt M0130 diagnosed -- away from the largest, most-extended names -- never decays. A tilt learned in 1999-2002 is exactly the tilt that loses to a rising large-cap market, which is exactly where M0131's two folds failed. This method keeps M0131-B20 exactly -- the flexible tree, the 252-session label, the top 20, the SPY 200-day switch, the fixed tape at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits -- and changes one field: the training window becomes the most recent N calendar years of labelled month-ends rather than everything since 1996. NO NEW MACHINERY: train_start already exists, already enters the model key and the config digest, and already drives training_dates; a rolling window is that field moved with the refit anchor, and no file that has run is edited. THE WINDOW IS CLIPPED AT 1996-01-31, so a rolling arm is IDENTICAL to the expanding arm until the roll bites: the 5-year arm first differs at the 2001 refit (the 2002 book year), the 10-year arm at the 2006 refit (the 2007 book year). Seven of sixteen traded years are the same book in the 10-year arm by construction. That is the dev window's length, not a flaw, and it has a useful consequence that is written down here before any result: THE 5-YEAR ARM IS THE INSTRUMENT FOR THE 2003-05 FOLD AND THE 10-YEAR ARM FOR THE 2009-11 FOLD, the two folds M0131 lost. The readiness rule is read on the floor date in every arm, so all five variants start trading the same session, January 2000, and every paired difference in this batch is the training window alone; a 5-year window always holds at least 47 labelled month-ends against the 35 a model needs, so no arm ever sits in cash for want of training rows. FIVE VARIANTS, THE ONLY SETTINGS EVER TRIED, none chosen by looking at a dev result: R10 is the ten-year rolling window on M0131-B20's tree; R5 is the five-year window on the same tree; EXP is the unchanged expanding window, which is B20's economics under this method's allocator and therefore BOTH the in-batch control and a correctness check -- if EXP does not reproduce B20's recorded numbers the wrapper has a bug and the batch is void; R10REG is the ten-year window read with M0131's regularised tree, the secondary question of whether forgetting (40% fewer training rows) restores the capacity ordering M0131 reversed; DV20 is the CONTROL, M0131's gated 20-name dollar-volume book re-run here so the what-does-the-model-add comparison never crosses a trial boundary. Every arm is gated: M0130's ungated arms fell about 70% in 2008 and the switch has helped 22 of 22 lab variants whole-window. WHAT COUNTS AS AN IMPROVEMENT, FIXED IN ADVANCE AND NOT NEGOTIABLE AFTERWARDS: a rolling arm beats the expanding arm over 2009-2015 de-funded AND wins at least 3 of its 4 walk-forward folds. The arm that clears it must be one the bar named; an arm that clears it by accident is not the result. If neither rolling arm clears it, the honest reading this method records is that the lab's seven signals contain no recent edge however the model is trained, and the lab should stop building rankers on them and go looking for information it does not have. WHAT COUNTS AS A METHOD: a variant clears every design section 1 bar at DSR >= 0.90 at the lab's N, against the dev screen on the worst fall (50%) and the real-money bar (25%). No variant is promoted in this run whatever it shows: the test window is not touched.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely forgetting costs more in sample size than it buys in relevance, and no rolling arm clears the pre-registered bar. Six reasons, written before the run. First, the arithmetic: a ten-year window at the 2014 refit holds roughly 108 labelled month-ends against the expanding window's 216, so about half the rows, and a 252-session label on monthly samples already overlaps 92% between neighbours, so the EFFECTIVE sample is perhaps a twentieth of the nominal one either way. Halving an already tiny effective sample is the most likely way to make a noisy model noisier; the five-year arm halves it again. Second, M0131's own evidence points the other way on capacity: with a slow label the FLEXIBLE tree won, which says the model was data-limited, not regime-confused, and a data-limited model is hurt by forgetting. Third, the roll barely reaches the 2003-05 fold in the ten-year arm at all (it is identical to the expanding arm until the 2007 book year), so even a real regime effect can only show in one of the two folds the method is aiming at, and 3 of 4 folds may be arithmetically out of reach for R10. Fourth, the result is still a gate result underneath: M0131's exposure was 68% and its picks alone earned 9.9% a year, so a training-window change can only move the 32% of the time the book is actually invested, and it cannot touch the cash years 2001, 2002 and 2008 that produced the whole-window win. Fifth, survivorship: the check store already deepened B20's worst fall from 20.0% to 23.1% and dropped its DSR to 0.839, under the 0.90 bar, so eligibility here rests on a margin measured on data missing four in ten index-member days -- and a rolling window makes it worse, because a short window weights the recent, better-covered years less than an expanding one weights them in aggregate. Sixth, the DSR at N = 86 and rising needs a Sharpe above anything either ranker has produced, so even an arm that beats the expanding control on return is likely to fail the luck test. The most informative failure would be R5 beating R10 while both lose to EXP: that would say the window matters and the direction is the opposite of the one this method guessed, which is still a finding. The least informative would be all three within noise of each other, which would close the ranker direction on this signal set.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0137 — a forgetting ranker

## What was asked

The lab's learned stock picker (M0131) trains a computer model once a year on **everything it has
ever seen**, starting in January 1996. By 2012 that model is still carrying the 1996-2000
technology boom and bust as a large slice of its lessons. M0131 cleared the lab's bars for the
first time but was refused promotion because it lost two of its four out-of-sample checks — and
**both losses were rising markets**. That is exactly what a picker with a stale grudge against the
biggest, most-extended companies would look like.

So this method changed one thing and nothing else: **how far back the model is allowed to
remember.** Instead of everything since 1996, the yearly re-training looks at only the most recent
ten years — and, in a second version, only five. Everything else is M0131's best version held
fixed: the same model, the same question ("which of these will do best over the next twelve
months"), the same twenty names, the same rule that steps the whole book out when the S&P 500 is
below its own 200-day average, the same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, the same
5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th of every month.

**The bar was written down before the run and is not negotiable afterwards:** a forgetting version
had to beat the remembering version over 2009-2015 **and** win at least three of its four
out-of-sample checks.

## The answer: it failed, and it failed in a straight line

Money the owner would actually have had, at real fees, with the real monthly top-ups:

| version | how much it remembers | what the money earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **remembering** (control) | everything since 1996 | **+10.9%** | 20.0% | 1.76 | **0.912** |
| forgets past 10 years | about half as much | +10.0% | **18.4%** | 1.64 | 0.882 |
| forgets past 5 years | about a quarter as much | +9.1% | 19.3% | 1.53 | 0.848 |
| forgets past 10 years, simpler model | about half as much | +9.3% | 23.7% | 1.68 | 0.797 |
| no model at all (control) | — | +8.2% | 21.4% | 2.63 | 0.702 |

The same deposits put into an S&P 500 fund earned **+7.2% a year**.

Read the first three rows top to bottom. **Every single measure gets worse the more the model
forgets** — what the money earned, how reliably gains beat losses, the steadiness of the ride, and
the luck score. Five different measures, three rungs, and all five agree on the same order. That is
not noise. It is a dose-response curve, and it points the opposite way to the idea being tested.

The era the whole idea was built around says the same thing, even more plainly. Here is how each
version did against the S&P 500 in **2009-2015** — the recent, best-covered years, the ones most
like today, and the years a forgetful model was supposed to be *better* at:

| version | lead over the index a year, 2009-2015 |
|---|---|
| remembering | **−0.7%** |
| forgets past 10 years | −2.0% |
| forgets past 5 years | −4.4% |

Forgetting the distant past made the model **worse at the recent past**. The stale-memory story is
dead, and it is dead in the one place it had to be alive.

The out-of-sample checks went the same way: **1 of 4**, against M0131's 2 of 4. Forgetting lost a
check that remembering had won.

## Why — the mechanism, not just the numbers

Three pieces of evidence point at one cause, and it is not the one the method guessed.

**One: the model is starved, not confused.** The ten-year window gives the 2014 re-training about
108 months of lessons against 216; the five-year window gives 48. Halving the lessons cost 0.9
points a year, halving them again cost another 0.9. The model behaves exactly like something that
has too little to learn from — give it more, it does better; take some away, it does worse, by an
amount that tracks how much you took.

**Two: the simpler model lost too.** The fourth version asked the opposite question — if the model
has less to learn from, should it be made less clever to compensate? It earned less (+9.3% against
+10.0%) and fell further (23.7% against 18.4%). So at a shorter memory the *cleverer* model still
wins, exactly as it does at full memory. Everything says "needs more information". Nothing says
"needs less flexibility" or "is confused by old lessons".

**Three: the old years were never the problem in the first place.** By construction the ten-year
version is the *same book* as the remembering one until 2007, and the five-year version until 2002
— there simply is not enough history before 1996 for the window to bite earlier. The three versions
therefore have **identical** 1996-2002 results, which is a useful check that the machinery did what
it said. Where they differ is 2003 onwards, and that is where forgetting loses ground. The 1999
lessons the method suspected of poisoning the 2012 model turn out to be lessons worth keeping.

## The honest counterpoint

Forgetting is not worthless. The ten-year version had the **shallowest fall of the whole batch**,
18.4% against the remembering version's 20.0%. Measured as return-per-unit-of-fall the two are a
dead heat (0.54 against 0.55). So forgetting buys a calmer ride at close to a fair price in return.
That is a real, if small, finding — but it is not what this method asked, and the bar it set was
about picking skill in the recent era, which forgetting made worse. The arm that happens to look
good on a measure the bar did not name is not the result, and it will not be dressed up as one.

## Where this leaves the whole direction

Strip out the safety switch and the picture is stark. These books sit in their own picks only
**68% of the time**; on 28% of decision days they hold nothing at all. The picking alone earned
+9.9% a year for the remembering version against the index's +7.2% — but in 2009-2015 the picking
alone **lost** to the index, by 0.7 points. The twenty-year win is largely the switch sitting in
cash through 2001, 2002 and 2008, where it gained 34.8 points over the index in 2008 alone. Three
learned rankers now, and not one of them has out-picked a plain index fund in the recent years.

The model does clearly beat a book that forecasts nothing: the twenty-most-traded control earned
+8.2% against the remembering version's +10.9%, and trailed by 5.9 points in 2009-2015 against
0.7. So the model *is* learning something real. It is just not learning enough, from these seven
pieces of information, to beat the index in the years that matter — and the lab's best
**hand-built** single signal still earns about 14.0% a year on this identical tape and fees, well
ahead of all of it.

## The check that made it worse: forgetting is fragile

The lab's dev price history is missing about half the companies that were ever in the index,
mostly the ones that died. There is a second, fuller history kept for exactly this check, and
re-running every version on it is free — no new trial, no spent look. Here is what adding the dead
companies back did:

| version | earned a year, clean history | earned a year, fuller history | damage |
|---|---|---|---|
| remembering | +10.9% | +10.5% | **−0.4 points** |
| forgets past 10 years | +10.0% | +7.5% | **−2.5 points** |
| forgets past 5 years | +9.1% | +6.4% | **−2.7 points** |
| no model at all | +8.2% | +7.6% | −0.6 points |

And in 2009-2015 the gap against the index widened from −2.0% to **−6.4%** for the ten-year
version and from −4.4% to **−9.2%** for the five-year one, while the remembering version barely
moved, from −0.7% to −0.9%. On the fuller history the five-year version stops beating the index
altogether: −0.8% a year behind it.

**Forgetting is about six times more sensitive to the hole in the data than remembering is**, and
that makes sense once stated. A model that trains on twenty years absorbs a batch of newly added
companies into a long average and barely shifts. A model that trains on five years has its entire
set of lessons reshaped by them. Short memory does not just cost information — it amplifies
whatever is wrong with the information that is left. That is a reason to distrust short training
windows in this lab generally, not only here.

The remembering version's own caveat is unchanged and still matters: its worst fall deepens from
20.0% to 23.1% on the fuller history and its luck score drops from 0.912 to 0.839, under the 0.90
bar. Its eligibility rests on a thin margin measured on data missing four in ten index-member days.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did the expected failure happen?

The hypothesis failed outright, on both halves of its own bar, in the opposite direction. The
expected failure written before the run called it almost exactly: its first reason was that
forgetting would cost more in sample size than it bought in relevance, and its second was that
M0131's evidence already said the model was data-limited rather than regime-confused. Both are now
measured rather than argued. It also named the most informative failure as "the window matters and
the direction is the opposite of the one this method guessed" — which is what happened, with the
refinement that the direction is not merely opposite but smoothly, monotonically opposite.

## On luck

The best version here scores **0.912** on the lab's luck test, where the bar is **0.90**. That
score asks: after 89 separate ideas have been tried, how likely is it that this result is real
skill rather than the best of many coin flips? The 89 is the lab's count of distinct methods tried,
and the 0.90 bar is the owner's own risk setting from 2026-10-07. Neither is mine to move. But the
version that scores 0.912 is the **control** — the one that changes nothing and simply re-measures
M0131's best arm. Both forgetting versions score below the bar: 0.882 and 0.848. So this method is
recorded as eligible only through an arm that adds no new idea, and the out-of-sample record of
1 of 4 refuses promotion regardless.

## The worst stretch, and the rupiah

The worst fall was 18.4% for the ten-year version and 20.0% for the remembering one, both measured
on the book with the monthly deposits stripped out — a top-up refills a falling account and makes a
fall read gentler than it was, so this is the honest version of the number. Both are inside the
owner's 25% real-money limit. The worst calendar year for the forgetting versions was 2015, at
−8.7% and −14.5%; for the remembering version it was 2006, at −4.8%. The returns above are the
money-weighted figures on actual deposits, not a headline percentage, because a funded book's
headline growth rate counts the top-ups as if they were gains.


## The buy signal did not fire

The lab has a standing rule for when buying survivorship-free price history becomes worth the
money: a method must be eligible, have no failed relatives, win a majority of its out-of-sample
checks, and show a *positive* edge in 2009-2015. This method clears none of the last three. The
out-of-sample record is 1 of 4 and the 2009-2015 edge is negative for every version. No purchase
is warranted on this evidence.

## My opinion

**This direction is finished, and I would not spend another method on the training window.** The
result is not a near miss or a noisy wash — it is a clean, monotone dose-response curve pointing
the wrong way on five independent measures at once, confirmed by a free re-run on fuller data that
punishes the forgetting versions six times harder than the control. Three separate facts now say
the same thing: more history helps, a cleverer model helps, and a shorter memory amplifies bad
data. The picker is **starved of information**, not confused by stale information. Every remaining
knob on the model — window length, capacity, target speed — has now been turned, and the thing
that moved the needle was always the one that gave the model more to work with.

So I would stop tuning the learner and change what it is allowed to look at. Two things follow
directly, and I have queued both. **First, and sharper: is it rows, or is it years?** The versions
here differ in both at once — ten years is half the months *and* half the distinct market
conditions. Re-training the same model on a weekly grid of samples instead of a monthly one
roughly quadruples the rows from exactly the same years, with no new information and no new
peeking. If that helps, the model is short of raw examples and the fix is cheap. If it does
nothing, the model is short of *distinct conditions*, and no amount of resampling will ever help —
which would close the question for good. **Second: give it something it has never seen.** The
seven things this picker reads are all per-company price and dividend facts. The store already
holds market-wide daily readings it has never been offered — the fear index and its term structure,
Treasury yields across four maturities, gold — point-in-time and free. The lab's own fall model
already uses market-level readings precisely because a per-company rank cannot express "everything
is about to drop". A ranker that can tell 2007 from 2013 is the first genuinely new information
this direction has been given since it started, and it costs nothing to try.

I would also record, against the day someone is tempted again, that the one thing forgetting did
buy was a calmer ride — the shallowest fall in the batch, 18.4% — at almost exactly a fair price in
lost return. If a future method needs a gentler book rather than a richer one, a rolling window is
a known, measured lever. It is simply not a way to pick better stocks.


### 2026-10-14

## Addendum: the out-of-sample checks convicted forgetting on their own

Reading the fold record more closely sharpens the verdict, and in a way that is worth writing
down because it is independent of everything above.

The lab's out-of-sample check works in four slices. In each slice it trains on what came before,
then picks the version of the method the lab's own rule would have named **knowing nothing about
the future**, and scores only that one on months it has never seen. It is allowed to name a
different version in different slices.

The remembering version, scored alone across all four slices, wins **2 of 4** — exactly matching
M0131's best arm, one more confirmation that the two are the same book. But the method as a whole
scores **1 of 4**. The difference is entirely the selection: in the third and fourth slices the
rule looked at the evidence available at the time and chose the **five-year forgetting version** —
and it lost both, by 6.5 points in 2009-2011 and 2.1 points in 2012-2014.

That is the cleanest possible statement of the problem. The forgetting versions did not merely
score worse on the twenty-year average. They looked *better* at the moment of choosing and were
then worse at the thing that matters. A short memory makes the model more responsive to whatever
just happened, which is exactly what makes it look convincing in a backtest and exactly what makes
it fail next year. Forgetting did not just fail to fix the out-of-sample problem this method was
built to fix — it made it worse, and it did so by being more persuasive.
methods.verdict: Forgetting the distant past made the picker worse, in a straight line — half the memory cost 0.9 points a year, a quarter cost 1.8, and it fell further behind in the recent years it was meant to fix

methods.name: Ask the fall model a yearly question too: the learned fall-sizing head on a 252-session horizon instead of 63
methods.hypothesis: M0131 measured that stretching the ranker's label from 21 sessions to 252 is worth 3.8 points a year over 2000-2015 and 6.5 over 2009-2015 with every other field held fixed, and that the ladder is monotone at 21, 63 and 252 sessions on both tree settings. The learned fall-sizing head (M0132, rejected) was pre-registered on a 63-session horizon on the reasoning that a fall is a path and a month of a path is mostly noise -- the same reasoning M0131 has now shown was right and not carried far enough for the ranker. This method keeps M0132's fall model exactly as pre-registered -- the same raw downside level label (never rank-normalised), the same three un-normalised market-level columns, the same whole-slot sizing ladder read off the model's own in-sample prediction distribution, the same fixed tape at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits -- and changes one field: the fall horizon becomes 252 sessions. Arms to fix now: 252 sessions sized, 252 sessions with the ladder ignored (the ordering-only control), the recorded 63-session arm as the in-batch twin, and the SPY 200-day switch alone as the standing yardstick the sizing head has to beat, because memory says the switch beat M0132's learned brake on return and drawdown at once. WHAT COUNTS AS AN IMPROVEMENT, fixed now: the 252-session sized arm beats the SPY 200-day switch on BOTH funded return and worst fall over 2000-2015 and is not behind it in 2009-2015. The switch has helped 22 of 22 lab variants whole-window; a learned brake that cannot beat one free moving average is not worth carrying.

methods.name: How many names should the book hold, asked on a tape that actually invests the deposits
methods.sourceRef: M0128 (the near misses on the fixed tape) for the preset and the band arithmetic; M0123 (the 1%-of-equity band left a 100-name book 51% invested) for the finding this re-opens; M0007's own N10/N20/N30 sweep for the conclusion under test; trials 129 and 388 for the 20-name rung
methods.hypothesis: A measurement, pre-registered so that it is held to a prediction. The lab's name-count evidence -- M0007's N10/N20/N30 sweep, MAR 0.51/0.64/0.63 at exposure 0.68/0.66/0.63 -- was taken on a tape where the rebalance band is 1% of the WHOLE account rather than a share of the slot. That band does not scale with the slot, so it binds harder the more names a book holds, and the owner's monthly deposit then reaches a wide book almost only through turnover. M0123 priced that at 51% invested against 96% on an ungated 100-name basket, worth 3.1 points a year. So the sweep the twenty-name roster rests on compared a fully invested narrow book against progressively cash-heavier wide ones, and its conclusion is partly a reading of the tape. This method asks the question again with the tape fixed: M0007-N20-RAW's picks verbatim (raw cumulative market-model residual over 12-1 months, equal money, all cash while SPY is under its 200-day average), at 35, 50 and 70 names, each run twice -- once on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, where the band is 20% of the holding's own target, and once on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the old 1%-of-equity basis. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's plan (10,000,000 IDR opening and 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of every month), against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days. No cash yield on any arm, so no arm carries an owner input. THE TWENTY-NAME RUNG IS NOT RE-RUN, and that is an assumption stated before the run. It is already recorded twice -- M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT on the equity basis and M0128-RAW20 on the target basis -- and the two are identical to the last digit (exposure 0.694043390520648 both, 20.6% worst fall, 1,607 trades), because 20% of a 5% slot is exactly 1% of equity. The no-op the arithmetic predicts is therefore already confirmed, lab run would refuse those digests, and the three arms that would have reproduced them go to the equity-basis twins instead, where the confound actually lives. WHAT IS PREDICTED, in numbers, before any result. (1) THE CONFOUND GROWS WITH WIDTH. Equity-basis exposure should fall monotonically with name count while target-basis exposure stays flat near the 0.694 that the gate alone permits: the gap should be roughly nil at 20 names, small at 35 (the band is 35% of a slot), clear at 50 (50% of a slot) and widest at 70 (70% of a slot) -- 2 to 10 points of exposure at 70, less than M0123's 45 because this book turns over about 8.9 times a year against that basket's much slower churn, and turnover is the other way a deposit reaches a holding. (2) THE SWEEP, read on the fixed tape. The honest prior is that concentration still pays something, because a residual-momentum edge genuinely decays down the ranking, but far less than the old sweep said: on the target basis the funded return should fall by less from 20 to 70 names than the equity-basis column does, and the worst fall should improve with width, because 70 equal slots cannot be hurt by one name the way 20 can. 20 names is 13.7% a year funded at a 20.6% worst fall; the 70-name target-basis arm is predicted between 11% and 13.5% a year at a worst fall of 16% to 19%. (3) MAR, which is return over worst fall, is where width could actually win: if the fall improves faster than the return decays, a 35- or 50-name book out-MARs the 20-name one, and the roster's width is wrong. That is the one outcome of this method that would change what the owner holds. (4) DEPOSIT-MATCHED SPY earns 7.2% a year over this window, and every arm here is expected to beat it, as every residual-momentum book in this lab has on dev. PROMOTION IS NOT AVAILABLE and that is accepted up front: this line runs through M0007 and M0128, and M0007 is test-failed, so the hard gate refuses it on kin whatever it scores. The value is the measurement and the roster decision it informs, not a candidate.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest disappointment is that the fixed tape barely moves anything, because this book is not M0123's basket: it turns over about 8.9 times a year and the SPY 200-day gate liquidates it outright in 2001, 2002 and 2008, so deposits already reach it through churn and the band has little left to do. If equity-basis and target-basis exposure differ by under a point at 70 names, the verdict must say plainly that the confound is real but small in THIS family, that M0123's 45-point gap was a property of a slow basket rather than of wide books in general, and that the roster's twenty names were not chosen on a broken measurement after all. Specific failures written now. (1) THE SCREEN, not the band, could short the 70-name arm: it admits 64-97 names in 1996, so that arm is structurally under-filled in its first year by up to six names. Any exposure gap inside 1996 must be charged to the screen, and only gaps outside it to the band. (2) THE GATE DOMINATES THE CASH. Every arm sits near 69% invested because the gate is off for three whole years; a band difference of a point or two is a small share of a large cash position, and must never be reported as though the book were otherwise fully invested. (3) WIDTH COSTS FEES. Gotrade's schedule bites hardest on small orders, and a 70-name book at 20,000,000 IDR opening capital has slots near 18 USD in its early years, where the fee is a far larger share of the order than on a 5% slot. Some of any return decay with width will be fees rather than signal decay, and the trade counts and turnover must be quoted so the two can be told apart. (4) SURVIVORSHIP. The dev store prices no delisted names, and a wider book owns more of the shortlist, so it is more exposed to the missing failures exactly as M0123's all-shortlist basket was -- which lost its whole edge on the check store. The widest arm must be survivorship-checked the same day and the result quoted beside the dev column, and if the width advantage shrinks there the verdict says the width advantage was partly the missing dead companies. (5) THE PRE-2009 TRAP. Every twenty-year edge this lab has found was earned before 2009. If width only helps before 2009 and not over 2009-2015, the roster recommendation must say so first, because those are the years most like today. (6) DEPOSITS SOFTEN EVERY WORST FALL HERE ALIKE; none of these numbers may be lined up against an unfunded parent's, and the 20-name rung quoted from trial 388 is funded on the identical plan, which is the only reason it is comparable at all.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0139 — how many stocks should the book hold, asked on a tape that actually invests the money

## Why this was run again

The list of stocks the paper account holds is twenty names long, and that number came from one
measurement: the same picking rule was run holding ten, twenty and thirty names, and twenty came
out best. Yesterday a different experiment found something that made that measurement suspect.

The simulator tops a holding back up to its target only once it has drifted far enough to be
worth a trade, and "far enough" was measured against **one per cent of the whole account**, not
against the size of the holding. That number does not shrink as the book gets wider. In a
twenty-name book each stock is five per cent of the account, so a one per cent gap is a fifth of
the holding — a reasonable trigger. In a hundred-name book each stock is one per cent, so the
gap can never be reached at all, and the owner's monthly deposit never gets spent on anything he
already owns. The earlier experiment measured a hundred-name basket sitting **51% invested** where
the identical basket on the fixed rule sat **96% invested**, worth 3.1 points a year.

If that applied here, then the old ten/twenty/thirty comparison was not comparing concentration.
It was comparing a fully invested narrow book against progressively more cash-heavy wide ones, and
the roster's twenty names rest on it. So the question was asked again, with the rule fixed.

## What was run

The picks are unchanged from the lab's best-known momentum book: rank the big, liquid American
companies on how far they ran **after taking out the part the whole market explains**, over the
last twelve months skipping the most recent one; hold the best N, equal money in each; sit in cash
entirely whenever the S&P 500 itself is below its 200-day average. Only two things vary:

* **how many names** — 35, 50 or 70;
* **where the top-up trigger is measured** — against the holding's own target (the fixed rule) or
  against one per cent of the whole account (the old rule).

Everything else is identical: fractional shares, Gotrade's real fee schedule, 10,000,000 rupiah to
start and 5,000,000 rupiah added on the 25th of every month, 1996 to October 2015, against an S&P
500 fund fed exactly the same money on exactly the same days.

**The twenty-name rung was not re-run, and that was decided before the run.** It already exists
twice in the lab's record — once on each rule — and the two are identical to the last decimal
place, because a fifth of a five per cent slot *is* one per cent of the account. The arithmetic
said they must be the same and the record confirms it, so the three arms that would have
reproduced a known identity went to the old-rule twins of the wider books instead.

## The headline: how much of the account was actually invested

This is the number the whole run exists to produce, so it comes first. "Share invested" is the
fraction of the account that was in stocks rather than sitting in cash, averaged over the whole
twenty years.

| names | old rule (1% of the account) | fixed rule (a fifth of the holding) | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 69.40% | 69.40% | **0.00 pts** (the same run, twice) |
| 35 | 69.05% | 69.41% | +0.36 pts |
| 50 | 68.71% | 69.43% | +0.72 pts |
| 70 | 67.90% | 69.34% | +1.43 pts |

The leak is real, and it behaves exactly as the arithmetic says it must. Under the old rule the
trigger is 20% of a holding at twenty names, 35% at thirty-five, 50% at fifty and 70% at seventy —
it overshoots the sensible trigger by 0, 15, 30 and 50 percentage points of a holding, and the
cash left behind comes out at 0.00, 0.36, 0.72 and 1.43 points. Near enough a straight line.

**And it is twenty to thirty times smaller than the hundred-name basket's 45-point leak.** That
is the single most useful thing this run found, and it is worth being precise about why. A
deposit reaches a holding two ways: the top-up rule, or ordinary trading. This book trades about
eight times its own value a year and the market switch liquidates it outright in 2001, 2002 and
2008, so its deposits were already being spent whatever the top-up rule said. The basket that
leaked 45 points traded about 4% of itself a month and had no switch, so the top-up rule was the
*only* route in and it was shut.

So the thing that decides whether an old result is confounded is **how fast the book traded**,
not how many names it held. A slow, wide, always-invested book is badly confounded. A fast one,
or one with a market switch, is barely confounded at all.

Two side-effects worth keeping. The old rule also makes the book hold slightly *less* cash the
narrower it is, so every arm sits near 69% invested rather than near 96% — that remaining 31% is
the market switch sitting in cash through 2001, 2002 and 2008, not the top-up rule, and no
reading below should pretend otherwise. And the fixed rule's invested share is flat to within
a tenth of a point across every width, which is exactly what it was supposed to do.

## What the money did

Money-weighted return: what the owner's actual deposits earned, against the same deposits put
into an S&P 500 fund on the same days, which earned **7.2% a year**. All eight rows start with
10,000,000 rupiah and add 5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th of every month — 237 deposits, about
148,000 US dollars in all.

| names | old rule | fixed rule | worst fall (fixed rule) | gains ÷ losses | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | **+13.7%** | **+13.7%** | 20.6% | 1.98 | 1,607 |
| 35 | +12.8% | +13.1% | 19.6% | 2.10 | 2,548 |
| 50 | +11.2% | +11.3% | 20.7% | 1.96 | 3,367 |
| 70 | +10.8% | +10.9% | 19.9% | 2.04 | 4,169 |

Three readings, in order of importance.

**1. The old conclusion survives the fix. Twenty names still wins.** Going from twenty names to
seventy costs 2.8 points a year on the fixed tape and 2.9 points on the old one. The confound was
worth one tenth of a point of that. The roster's twenty names were *not* chosen on a broken
measurement, and nothing here is a reason to change what the paper account holds.

**2. A wider book did not fall less, which is the prediction this run got wrong.** The
pre-registered guess was that seventy equal slots would be harder to hurt than twenty, and that
the worst fall would improve to somewhere between 16% and 19%. It did not: 20.6%, 19.6%, 20.7%,
19.9% — flat, and not in any order. The reason is that the market switch has already taken out
the falls that diversification could help with. What is left are the drops that happen while the
switch says "invested", and those are market-wide: owning seventy momentum stocks instead of
twenty does not protect you from a market that falls on everything at once. **You cannot buy
safety with width in a book that already has a market switch.** You buy it with the switch, or
not at all.

**3. Risk-adjusted, nothing changes either.** Return divided by worst fall: 0.663 at twenty names,
0.666 at thirty-five, 0.547 at fifty, 0.548 at seventy. Thirty-five ties twenty to within three
thousandths — a tie, not a win — and fifty and seventy are clearly worse. The one outcome that
would have changed what the owner holds did not happen.

## The luck bar

The lab now counts **88 distinct methods** tried. Every result has to be discounted for that: the
more rules you try, the more likely the best one is luck. The measure is the deflated Sharpe
ratio — in plain words, the probability that a result this good is real rather than the best of
88 coin flips — and the owner's bar is **0.90**.

All six arms clear it: 0.944 at thirty-five names on the fixed rule, 0.934 on the old rule, and
0.911 to 0.921 for the wider arms. All six also clear every other go-live condition, which is why
the lab marked the method eligible on the development window.

One caution about comparing these to older numbers. **The luck score is computed at the number of
tries on the day the run happened**, and it is a record, not a verdict. The identical twenty-name
book reads 0.939 as trial 129 (when 29 methods had been tried) and 0.914 as trial 388 (when 79
had been). Same book, same returns, different score. So the six numbers above may be compared
with each other — they all ran at 88 — and with nothing older.

## The checks that matter more than the gate

Being eligible on the development window is the weakest thing the lab can say. Three harder reads
were run, all of them free and none of them spending the one remaining look at recent years.

**The companies that went under.** The lab's main price history only holds companies that are
still listed, so every backtest on it quietly skips the firms that failed. The check history adds
most of them back. Re-run there, the picture gets worse at every width and worst at the widest:

| names | fixed rule, main history | fixed rule, check history | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | +13.1% | +12.1% | −0.9 pts |
| 50 | +11.3% | +11.9% | +0.6 pts |
| 70 | +10.9% | +10.9% | −0.0 pts |

Gains-to-losses drops on every single arm, from about 2.0 to about 1.85. The narrow end loses
most, which is the opposite of what was predicted — a wider book owns more of the list, so it was
supposed to be the one more exposed to the missing failures. It is not. The reading is that the
picks at the very top of the ranking were slightly flattered by survivors, and that the width
question itself is largely unaffected: the fall-off from thirty-five to seventy names is 2.2
points on the main history and 1.2 points on the check history. Smaller, still there, still
pointing the same way.

**The years most like today.** This is where the run stops being a width question and becomes a
verdict on the book. Over **2009–2015** — the best-covered stretch of the window and the one most
like the market the owner trades now — here is the lead over the same deposits in an S&P 500 fund:

| names | main history | check history |
|---|---|---|
| 35 | **+0.5%** | **−1.7%** |
| 50 | −1.9% | −2.4% |
| 70 | −2.1% | −3.5% |

**Every number there is negative except one, and that one flips negative the moment the dead
companies are priced.** The lead gets worse the wider the book, consistently, on both histories.
So in the modern era this book did not beat the market at any width, and widening it made the gap
worse rather than better. The twenty-year average of +13.1% a year is almost entirely an edge
earned before 2009, which is the pattern every twenty-year edge in this lab has shown.

**The fold record.** Split the window into four stretches and score each on months it was never
fitted on: 3 of 4 won, on both histories. That passes the lab's fold rule. It is also the only
one of the three checks that says anything encouraging, and the fold it lost — 2009 to 2011,
+41.9% against the market's +60.8% — is the modern one.

## Is the width penalty just trading costs? No — and that was worth measuring

A wider book takes more trades and each one is smaller, and Gotrade charges a minimum of ten
cents an order, so the obvious suspicion is that wide books lose on fees rather than on worse
picks. The pre-registration said so. It is wrong, and the free fee report settles it at every
width:

| names | fees paid | fee drag, as a share of gross trading profit | trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | $90,883 | 14.3% | 1,607 |
| 35 | $74,996 | 13.6% | 2,548 |
| 50 | $62,099 | 14.6% | 3,365 |
| 60 | $57,790 | 14.3% | 3,753 |

The drag is **flat across width** — about one dollar in seven of gross trading profit, wherever
you sit — and the total bill actually *falls* as the book widens, because a wider book turns over
fewer dollars even though it writes more tickets.

The same sweep run at the lab's old pretend fee of 0.1% a trade confirms it from the other side:
the width penalty is there too (15.0%, 14.0%, 12.3%, 11.9% a year at 20/35/50/60 names), and it is
if anything slightly *larger* than at real fees. Both fee worlds pick twenty names as the best.

So the decay from twenty names to seventy is the picking signal genuinely getting weaker as you
go further down the ranking. It is not an artefact of a small account paying order minimums. That
is the honest answer, and it is the one that generalises — if the account were ten times bigger,
twenty names would still beat seventy.

Worth stating plainly for its own sake, though: **real fees cost this book 1.3 points a year**
(15.0% down to 13.7% at twenty names) and eat about 14% of everything it makes gross. That is
the price of trading, not of width.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Four predictions were written down before the run. Scoring them honestly:

1. **"The cash leak grows with the number of names."** *Right in shape, wrong in size.* It grows
   monotonically and almost exactly in proportion to how far the old trigger overshoots a holding
   — but the predicted 2 to 10 points at seventy names came in at **1.43**. The pre-registered
   failure case said that if the gap came in under a point the finding was "real but small in this
   family"; at 1.4 points that is the right reading, barely on the other side of the line.
2. **"The wider book falls less."** *Wrong.* Predicted a 16–19% worst fall at seventy names;
   got 19.9%, and no ordering at all across the four widths.
3. **"Thirty-five or fifty names might win on return-per-unit-of-fall."** *Not supported.*
   Thirty-five tied twenty to three thousandths. Fifty and seventy were clearly worse.
4. **"Every arm beats the same deposits put into the market."** *Right*, all six, over the full
   twenty years — and, as the modern-era table above shows, that is a statement about 1996–2008
   far more than about the market the owner trades now.

The pre-registered expected failure — "the fixed tape barely moves anything, because this book
already trades fast and the market switch already liquidates it" — is **exactly what happened**,
and it is the most useful thing here.

## What this means for the lab's other 440 results

The reason this run mattered was the worry that every name-count comparison in the lab was
confounded. The answer is narrower and more useful than "yes" or "no":

**A pre-2026-10-12 result is confounded in proportion to how slowly its book traded, not to how
many names it held.** The top-up rule and ordinary trading are two routes for a deposit to reach
a holding; the rule only matters when the other route is shut. Concretely:

* a book with a market switch, or one that replaces a large share of its holdings every month —
  which covers the whole momentum family, the near misses and the roster — leaks **1 point or
  less** of invested share, worth about a tenth of a point a year;
* a slow, always-invested, wide basket leaks **tens of points**, which is what happened to the
  hundred-name basket yesterday and is worth multiple points a year.

That turns an audit of hundreds of trials into a one-column check: sort by turnover, look at the
slow end. The fast end can be read as recorded.

## Why this cannot be promoted, and why that was known in advance

The lab refuses to promote a method when a close relative has already failed on the untouched
recent years. This book's relatives — the blend, the volatility-braked version, the
fractional-share twin — have all been tested and all failed. The refusal was written into the
pre-registration before the run, and the method was registered anyway, because the owner mirrors
the paper account with real money and "how many names" is a live decision that deserved a
prediction on the record rather than a free report that nobody is accountable to.

Nothing here was spent on the recent years. The lab has used **4 of its test-window looks** and
still has them all available for a method that earns one. This run added one method to the count
of tries (now 88) and six backtests to the record.

## My opinion

**The roster should keep twenty names, and this question should now be closed.** It was worth
re-asking — the confound was real and nobody knew how big it was in this family — but the answer
is that it was worth a tenth of a point a year here, the old conclusion stands on its own feet,
and three separate measurements (the fixed tape, the old tape, and the pretend-fee control) all
pick twenty. I would not spend another method id on the width of this book.

I would also stop expecting diversification to fix drawdowns in a book that has a market switch.
That is the genuinely new thing here: going from twenty names to seventy — three and a half times
the diversification — changed the worst fall by less than a point in either direction, because the
switch has already removed the falls that spreading out can help with. Any future idea whose pitch
is "hold more names to fall less" should be read against this and will probably not be worth an id.

What I would *not* conclude is that this book is good. Strip the pre-2009 years out and it loses
to the market at every width, and loses by more the wider it gets; price the companies that went
under and the one positive modern number turns negative. That is the same shape as the four
test-window failures already in the record, and it is a warning about the whole residual-momentum
family rather than about width.

So the next trials should go somewhere else entirely, and I have queued two:

1. **The other direction.** Twenty is the narrow end of everything ever measured on the fixed
   tape at real fees; ten and fifteen have only been measured on the old whole-share tape at
   pretend fees, where ten scored worst. Fractional shares and real fees change that arithmetic,
   and the fee report above shows the drag does not punish small books the way it was assumed to.
   If the signal genuinely decays down the ranking — which is this run's finding — then the top
   ten should beat the top twenty, and the limit is how much worse the falls get. That is a real
   question with a real answer and it is the natural continuation of this result.
2. **Width without the switch.** The reason width bought no safety here is that the market switch
   had already done the job. Whether width would help a book with no switch is unmeasured and is
   the cleaner test of the diversification claim: the ungated twenty-name book fell 51%, and if
   seventy names ungated falls meaningfully less, then width *is* a drawdown tool and it was
   simply redundant here. If it falls just as far, the diversification story is dead outright and
   a lot of future ideas can be skipped.

Of the two, the second is the more valuable, because it answers a question that applies to every
book in the lab rather than to one family's parameter.
methods.verdict: Twenty names still wins: the broken top-up rule cost a wide book only 1.4 points of invested money here, not the 45 it cost a slow basket, and holding seventy names instead of twenty gave up 2.8 points a year while making the worst fall no gentler at all.

methods.name: Ask the trading-frequency question again, now that trading is no longer how the money gets invested
methods.sourceRef: M0123: invested share tracked turnover, not design (ALL100 51% at 4% monthly turnover, SAMPLE50 96% at 50%); lab turnover report
methods.hypothesis: M0123 found something that contaminates every cadence comparison this lab has recorded. On the old top-up rule a deposit cannot reach a holding the book already owns, so new money is invested ONLY when the book sells one name and buys another. Invested share therefore tracks turnover rather than design: measured across six arms of one basket on one shortlist, a book replacing 4% of itself a month ran 51% invested, one replacing 50% a month ran 96%, and the gap was worth 3.1 points a year. Every monthly-versus-weekly-versus-daily comparison the lab has made was thus scoring the faster arm on a more fully invested account while charging it more fees, with the two effects pulling opposite ways and neither measured. The lab's own fee arithmetic says re-picking a whole book every session needs 290% a year to break even, weekly 32%, monthly 1.63% -- but those are the fee side alone. On the target-basis band every cadence is roughly fully invested whatever it trades, so the question can finally be asked cleanly: hold the picks fixed and vary only how often they are re-picked. Book: the residual-momentum picks at 20 names, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, no cash yield, target-basis band throughout. Arms: monthly re-pick (the roster's cadence); monthly re-pick with a weekly resize; weekly re-pick; and a quarterly re-pick, which no lab method has priced and which the fee arithmetic says should be the cheapest book this lab has ever run. Success is a measurement: the funded return, the worst fall and the invested share of each, with the fee bill stated separately, so the cadence's cost and its deployment benefit are finally two numbers instead of one. Expected: once deployment is held constant the slower cadences win by close to the fee difference and no more, which would make the weekly-versus-monthly result the lab already recorded an overstatement; and quarterly may beat monthly outright, since monthly re-picking of a momentum book costs 1.63% a year for a signal that barely changes in four weeks. Promotion is refused on kin for this line, which is accepted: the deliverable is a clean price on a lever the roster uses every night.

methods.name: Does width protect a book with no market switch? The ungated residual book at 20 and 70 names
methods.hypothesis: M0139 measured that widening the residual-momentum book from 20 names to 70 changed the worst fall by less than a point in either direction (20.6%, 19.6%, 20.7%, 19.9% at 20/35/50/70, every arm equally invested on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband) while costing 2.8 points a year of funded return. The stated mechanism is that the SPY 200-day gate has ALREADY removed the falls diversification could help with -- it liquidates the book outright in 2001, 2002 and 2008 -- so the remaining falls happen inside gate-on months and are market-wide, where owning 70 momentum names instead of 20 is no protection. That mechanism is an explanation, not a measurement, and it is testable: M0007-N20-NOTREND is the same picks with the gate off and it fell 51.0% at 20 names (trial on monthly-hold at the old flat fee, exposure 0.915). Run the ungated book at 20 and 70 names on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband -- fractional, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's monthly top-up, no cash yield, so the tape matches M0139's exactly and the two methods' numbers are directly comparable. Four arms: N20-NOGATE, N70-NOGATE, and the same two with the gate on at 20 and 70 for a within-method anchor are NOT needed (M0139 and trial 388 already hold them on the identical tape), so spend the arms on widths instead: 20, 35, 50 and 70, all ungated. Success is a measurement with two clean outcomes. If the ungated 70-name book falls MATERIALLY less than the ungated 20-name book -- say 51% down to 40% or below -- then width IS a drawdown tool, it was simply redundant behind the gate, and a whole class of future ideas ('hold more names to fall less') stays alive for ungated designs. If it falls essentially as far, the diversification story is dead outright for momentum books: concentration risk was never what was hurting them, and every such idea can be skipped without a trial. Either answer is worth an id because it applies to every book in the lab, not to one family's parameter. Expected: the fall improves but far less than the extra names suggest -- momentum names are strongly correlated with each other and with the market, so 70 of them are not 70 independent bets; a guess of 51% down to 44-48% at 70 names, which would make width a weak tool rather than a real one. PROMOTION IS NOT AVAILABLE: the line runs through M0007, M0021, M0022 and M0029, all test-failed, so the hard gate refuses it on kin whatever it scores. It is a measurement about the lab's search, registered as a method so it is held to the prediction above.

methods.name: Below twenty: does concentration keep paying at 10 and 15 names on the fixed tape at real fees?
methods.hypothesis: M0139's finding is that the residual-momentum signal genuinely decays down the ranking: funded return falls 13.7% -> 13.1% -> 11.3% -> 10.9% a year from 20 to 35 to 50 to 70 names, and the free fee report shows this is NOT fee drag (the drag is 14.3%, 13.6%, 14.6%, 14.3% of gross trading P&L at 20/35/50/60 -- flat across width -- and the total fee bill FALLS as the book widens because a wide book turns over fewer dollars; the flat-0.1% control decays by 3.1 points over the same widths against gotrade's 2.8, so if anything real fees punish width LESS). If the signal decays monotonically, the top 10 should beat the top 20, and the only question is how much worse the falls get. That direction has never been measured on the current tape. The lab's only narrow evidence is M0007-N10 at MAR 0.512 vs N20 at 0.636 -- but that ran on monthly-hold: WHOLE shares, the flat 0.1% fee, unfunded, and the old 1%-of-equity band. Whole shares alone can invalidate it, because M0021 spent a test look learning that a whole-share book at this account size sits in cash; and M0007-N10's recorded exposure is 0.676, above N20's 0.658, which is the opposite of a cash problem and suggests the N10 penalty there was real drawdown rather than an artefact -- worth knowing for certain rather than assuming. Note the owner's standing instruction (lab/name_count.py docstring, handover 2b CORRECTED): do NOT plan a name-count reduction on fee grounds -- measured at 17,841 IDR/USD a 20-name book pays 0.614% an order by month three against 0.612% for 11 names, two thousandths of a per cent apart. This idea respects that: the fee case is settled and is not the argument. The argument is the merits, and M0139 supplied a reason to expect narrower to win that did not exist before. Run 10, 14 and 20 names... except 20 is already recorded on this exact tape (trial 388, 13.7% funded, 20.6% fall, MAR 0.663), so spend the arms on 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16, all on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's monthly top-up, no cash yield, RESIDMOM with ResidParams(inner=FactorParams(rank='momentum', top=K, trend=('SPY',200)), scaled=False) -- M0007-N20-RAW's params with only top moved, exactly as M0139 did, so all five arms are directly comparable to trial 388 and to M0139's four. Success is a measurement: whether funded return keeps rising as names are removed, and where the worst fall crosses the owner's 25% real-money limit. Expected: return rises to a peak somewhere near 10-14 names and the worst fall deepens steadily, so MAR peaks before the return does; the binding constraint below 20 is the fall, not the fee and not the signal. A plausible shape is 14 names at about 14.5% a year and a 23% fall, 10 names at about 15% and a 26-28% fall -- over the real-money limit, which would make 12-16 the honest answer and 20 only mildly conservative. The risk that would make this a null result: at 8-10 names a single bad pick is 10-12% of the account, so the falls may blow out far faster than the return improves, and the whole range below 20 is simply worse. PROMOTION IS NOT AVAILABLE (kin M0007, M0021, M0022, M0029 are all test-failed), so this is a roster-information run, not a candidate.

methods.name: Sell on a bad quarter, not a crossed line: move the safety switch's exit, on a book whose kin is clean
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0101 (the calm big raisers behind a choice of switch); the asymmetric frame and both triggers are M0113's, mirrored from the entry side to the exit side
methods.hypothesis: The moving-average switch is old -- the banded rule 1992, Faber's monthly version 2007 -- so nothing here is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies; what is new is which HALF of it is being paid for, and this is the half nobody has moved. The lab has now priced the ENTRY half three times and got the same answer each time: on SPY alone (M0113-UP63, +32.14% funded against the symmetric control's +31.68%), on two stock books (M0135, +0.98 and +0.66 points a year for +0.02 and +0.87 points of worst fall, with DSR RISING on both and the paired gain LARGER on the survivorship-check store), and on a third (M0133, +1.1 points a year at an identical worst fall). Buying back when SPY's last 63 sessions have actually returned positive beats buying back on a price cross, and 63 is an INTERIOR PEAK rather than a point on a ramp: 21 sessions was worse than changing nothing and 126 was also worse, which is far stronger evidence than a monotone trend.
