The exit has meanwhile never been moved. It was frozen on M0084's finding that the exit is the half that earns its keep -- the whole 22-year advantage is sitting out 2001, 2002 and 2008 -- but 'the exit earns its keep' and 'the exit is optimally expressed' are different claims and only the first has been tested. The exit in force is today's price against a slow average, which is exactly the rule shape that LOST on the entry side. THE RULE: hold the entry at UP63 and sell when SPY's last exit_n sessions have NOT returned positive. The stay-in test is M0113's own entry_on read with the book in rather than out, so the two halves are the same function and the mirror is exact. MECHANISM, and why it could beat a crossed line in both directions at once: a realised-return exit may leave EARLIER in a genuine decline -- 2008's 200-day cross came in January, months after the October 2007 peak -- and may leave LESS OFTEN in a chop that dips below the line and bounces straight back, which is where M0084 measured the switch paying for itself everywhere outside the three crises. THE HOST, which matters more than the rule. M0135 produced a good frame result that can never be bought: its line runs to M0029, which is test-failed, so the hard gate refuses it on ancestry. Better machinery on a disproven engine is a better disproven engine. This runs on M0088-C-LIVE-63, the calm half of the big dividend raisers: dev-eligible, +35.10% funded against SPY's +32.40%, an 18.71% worst fall, gains 3.52 times losses, 528 trades, 70.4% invested, DSR 0.9446, and kin that reads clean in every direction the gate looks -- family stock-dividend-change-drift holds no test-failed method and the line M0101 -> M0088 -> M0070 holds none either. It is also the best-motivated host in the lab: M0096 split this exact book by era and concluded 'the safety switch, not the raisers, causes the recent lag', because the switch sold in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and bought back higher; and M0101 already tried to fix that with hysteresis bands and LOST, both banded arms finishing below the plain control (MAR 0.51 and 0.50 against 0.57) and both breaking the drawdown screen. The realised-return exit is the untried alternative on a diagnosis that is already made and an attempted fix that has already failed. The idea row named M0131-B20 instead; the recorded trials say it is weaker on every axis (19.96% worst fall, gains 1.76 times losses, DSR 0.9118) and carries no such diagnosis, so the host was changed and this sentence is the record of that choice. ONE PRESET, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade -- fractional shares, Gotrade's real fee schedule, the owner's monthly deposits -- for all six arms, which is the preset BOTH reproduction anchors were recorded on. It is not M0128's fixed tape; that was the idea row's instruction and it is being declined deliberately, because no recorded trial of this book exists on the fixed tape, so taking it would have bought a better absolute level at the cost of BOTH control checks. The resize-band level effect is shared by all six arms alike, so the paired differences -- which are the entire result -- are unaffected by it, while the absolute levels here are a little less invested than a fixed-tape run would be. TWO ANCHORS MUST REPRODUCE BEFORE ANY OTHER NUMBER IS READ. M0143-SPY-UP63 is M0113-UP63 under a new allocator id and must return +32.14%, an 18-trade count, a 20.69% worst fall and 73.4% invested. M0143-CALM-SYM is the fully symmetric switch over the calm raisers, which is M0101-CTRL, and must return +35.10%, 528 trades, an 18.71% worst fall and gains 3.52 times losses. The first proves the SPY path, the held-based asymmetry and the imported trigger; the second proves the book path and the assumption everything else rests on, that an outer symmetric switch IS the stateless inner gate. No residual-momentum arm is included even though the idea row asked for one, because M0135's arms correlate 0.99, 1.00 and 0.92 with three test-failed methods and one such curve in this batch would hand the gate's behavioural-kin rule a reason to refuse the whole method whatever the dividend arms scored. PREDICTIONS, written before the run. (1) CALM-UP63 beats CALM-SYM by 0.3 to 1.0 points a year, replicating M0135's entry finding on an engine with no momentum in it -- a free independent replication this batch gets either way. (2) DOWN63 raises time in the market by 1 to 4 points over its own UP63 control, because a quarter that is merely flat keeps the book in where a price under the average takes it out. (3) The worst fall DEEPENS by 0 to 3 points, because a quarterly return lags a daily price line at the start of a fast collapse. (4) The gain, if any, must be visible in 2009-2015 -- the best-covered era and the one most like today, and the exact era M0096 diagnosed -- or it is a pre-2009 artefact and the verdict says so first. (5) DOWN21 whipsaws and DOWN126 is too slow to protect, putting 63 at an interior peak on this side too; if instead the ordering is monotone, the finding is only 'sooner is better' and that is a weaker claim. SUCCESS: a DOWN variant that beats its own UP63 control by at least a point a year with the worst fall no deeper, the gain present in 2009-2015, on a book the hard gate would actually let through.
methods.expectedFailure: The exit is where the switch earns everything, so breaking it is more dangerous than breaking the entry was, and the likeliest failure is a late exit in the only three events the whole switch exists for. A negative-quarter test is SLOWER than a 200-day cross at the start of a fast collapse: in October 2008 the quarter was already deeply negative so the two agree, but in a 1987-shaped single-week crash a quarterly return still reads positive while the price line has already broken. If 2001, 2002 and 2008 arrive late, the DOWN arms give back more than the entry side ever gained and the verdict is that the exit was already optimally expressed -- which would be a real and useful result, because it would close this grid for good. Second, the 200-day cross may be near-optimal as an exit PRECISELY BECAUSE it is slow. M0084 found the switch's standing cost is whipsaw, and a realised-return exit may whipsaw MORE rather than less: a quarterly return can flip sign repeatedly in a sideways market, while price-against-average carries a built-in hysteresis. M0101's banded arms are the warning -- adding hysteresis to this exact book made it worse on return AND drawdown at once, so this book has already shown it does not reward exit tinkering. Third, the number of draws. M0135's whole gain was four months out of 237. A result about exits is a result about three or four crisis events inside twenty years, which is a very small number of draws however many sessions the average is computed over, so the fold record and the 2009-2015 split must both be read before the whole-window average and the verdict must say which single events moved it. Fourth, the machinery. If SPY-UP63 does not return M0113-UP63's 18 trades and 20.69% fall, or CALM-SYM does not return M0101-CTRL's 528 trades and 18.71% fall, then the held-based asymmetry or the lookback is wrong and NONE of the other four numbers is readable; the correct response is to report the method unreadable, not to explain the gap away. The specific way bool(held) can part from the truth is an 'on' session where the book finds no event to buy, which would leave the ENTRY rule governing the next check even though the book never meant to leave; the calm raisers hold 25 names on events and can genuinely be empty, so this risk is real here in a way it was not for a 20-name momentum book, and CALM-SYM's trade count against 528 is what detects it. Fifth, no interest is credited on idle cash, which flatters whichever arm is out of the market least -- here the DOWN arms, if prediction (2) holds. On SPY the same swap moved time in market about 2.3 points and 1996-2015 T-bills paid roughly 2.5% a year, so the bias on a paired difference is under a tenth of a point a year; any gap smaller than that is noise for this reason alone and must not be reported as a finding. Sixth, the DSR. The control sits at 0.9435 against a 0.90 bar at an N that has grown since M0101 ran and is now about 90, so a variant can lose eligibility here purely because the lab has looked more times. That is the lab's cost, not the method's failure, and the analysis reports it as such.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0143 — Sell on a bad quarter, not a crossed line

## What was asked

Seer's books sit behind one safety switch: when the US market falls below its own slow
200-day average, the book sells everything and waits. The switch has two halves — when to
leave, and when to come back — and the lab has spent three experiments on the *coming back*
half. All three agreed: buy back when the market's last three months have actually made
money, rather than when today's price crosses a line. That swap has now paid on four
different books.

Nobody had ever touched the *leaving* half. It was frozen years ago on the finding that
leaving is the half that earns its keep. But "leaving earns its keep" and "we leave the best
possible way" are two different claims, and only the first was ever tested. The rule we leave
on is exactly the kind of rule that lost on the coming-back side: today's price against a
slow average.

So this method held the buy-back fixed at the three-month rule and changed only the sell
rule: sell when the market's last month, quarter, or half-year has actually lost money,
instead of when the price crosses the average. Six versions ran, on one book, with one fee
schedule and the owner's real monthly deposits.

## First, the two proof checks

Two of the six versions are not experiments at all. They are re-runs of results the lab
already holds, included so that a wrong number anywhere would show up before any new claim
was read. Both came back identical:

- The market-only version returned the same 32.1% a year, the same 20.69% worst fall, the
  same 18 trades and the same 46.72 gains-to-losses ratio as the earlier experiment it copies.
- The dividend book behind the ordinary symmetric switch returned the same 35.1% a year, the
  same 18.71% worst fall, the same 3.52 gains-to-losses ratio and the same 528 trades as the
  book's own recorded run.

Identical to every digit printed. The machinery is doing what it claims, so the other four
numbers can be believed.

## The answer: no. Changing the sell rule makes things worse, in a straight line.

All figures below are what the owner's real money would have done — 5 million rupiah paid in
on the 25th of every month — against the same deposits put into the US market instead
(+7.2% a year). "Worst fall" is the deepest drop from a peak, measured on the book itself
without the deposits, because monthly top-ups refill a falling account and make a fall look
gentler than it was.

| Sell rule | Money earned a year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Time invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price crosses the 200-day average (the control) | **+11.3%** | 20.4% | 3.59 | 72.7% |
| The last half-year lost money | +11.5% | 20.4% | 4.18 | 70.7% |
| The last quarter lost money | +8.4% | 25.5% | 2.95 | 62.1% |
| The last month lost money | +6.5% | 23.6% | 2.51 | 49.2% |

Selling on a bad quarter cost **2.9 points a year** and made the worst fall **5.1 points
deeper** — a fall of 25.5%, past the 25% line the owner set for real money. Selling on a bad
month cost **4.9 points a year** and was the only version in the batch that lost to simply
holding the US market. Selling on a bad half-year was worth +0.17 points a year, which is
nothing: the bar written down before the run was a full point, and a sixth of a point is
inside the margin that unmodelled interest on idle cash would explain by itself.

## Why — and this is the part worth keeping

I predicted before the run that these sell rules would keep the book invested *more*, because
a quarter that is merely flat still counts as "not losing" while a price under the average
counts as "out". That was wrong, and wrong in the most informative direction. Time invested
fell: 72.7% on the old rule, then 70.7%, 62.1%, and 49.2% as the window shortened. The
one-month rule had the book sitting in cash more than half the time.

The reason is smoothing. A 200-day average is a heavily smoothed line, so a price sitting
above it tends to *stay* above it — the rule has a natural stickiness built in, and small
dips do not dislodge it. "Did the last three months make money?" has no stickiness at all. It
flips from yes to no and back again repeatedly in a flat, choppy market, and each flip is a
full sale of the book and a full repurchase later. Trading costs rose in exact step with the
twitchiness, and so did the damage.

That stickiness was never a side effect of using an average. It is the main thing an average
does, and it is why the old rule is hard to beat.

## The surprise: the two halves want opposite things

On the coming-back side the lab found an interior sweet spot — three months beat both one
month and six months, which is strong evidence because missing on both sides is much harder
to get by luck than a one-way trend.

On the leaving side there is no sweet spot. The ordering is a straight line: the longer and
smoother the window, the better, right up to the 200-day average itself, which wins. One
month is terrible, a quarter is bad, half a year is a tie.

So the switch's two halves genuinely want opposite things: **be quick to come back, be slow
to leave.** The earlier experiment that opened this line of work was literally titled "slow
to leave, quick to return". It turns out that was already the right answer, and this run is
the evidence that the leaving half was not leaving anything on the table.

## A free second result

Because the control here moves the buy-back rule on a book that had never been tested with
it, this batch also re-tested the *coming-back* finding on new ground — a book that picks
companies raising their dividends, with no price-momentum in it anywhere. It held: the
three-month buy-back earned **+0.68 points a year** over the ordinary switch (+11.3% against
+10.6%), inside the 0.3-to-1.0 range written down before the run. That is a fourth
independent confirmation on a fourth unrelated engine.

It is not free of cost on this book, though. The worst fall went from 18.7% to 20.4% — 1.7
points, where on the two momentum books the same swap cost 0.02 and 0.87 points. Coming back
sooner puts dividend payers back into a bear rally too.

## Luck, and the era that matters

The luck score (DSR — roughly, the chance the result is real rather than the best of many
tries) is judged against 0.90, the owner's setting, at N = 93 — one count for each distinct
method the lab has tried. The control scores 0.941 and the half-year rule 0.944, both clear.
The quarter rule scores 0.785 and the month rule 0.589, both far under: with results that
poor the luck score is simply confirming they are bad.

The era since 2009 is the best-covered stretch of data and the one most like today, and it is
the test this method really had to pass. Against the US market over 2009-2015 the versions
ran: the ordinary switch −2.6% a year, the three-month buy-back −0.5%, the bad-quarter sell
−2.2%, the bad-half-year sell **+0.3%**, the bad-month sell −5.1%. Only one version is
positive and only barely; re-run on the stronger data set that includes companies which later
died, it falls to exactly 0.0%. There is no edge here in the era that counts.

On the walk-forward record — train on the past, score on months never seen, four times — this
method won **2 of 4**, and the version the rule would have picked changed between folds. That
is a losing record, and it means the lab's hard gate refuses to promote this method. No test
window was spent, and none should be.

The one design goal that did work: the kin check. This was deliberately built on a book whose
family and ancestry contain no method that has already failed out of sample, so a win here
could actually have reached a real test. The kin reads clean. It is the folds and the recent
era that stop it, which is the honest reason rather than an inherited one.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No, and the failure written down beforehand is the one that happened. The pre-registered
expected failure said: "the 200-day cross may be near-optimal as an exit precisely because it
is slow… a realised-return exit may whipsaw more, not less, since a quarter can flip sign
repeatedly in a sideways market while a price-versus-average test has a built-in hysteresis."
That is exactly the result, and the time-invested column is the proof.

Of five written predictions, one was right (the buy-back replication, +0.68 against a
predicted 0.3-1.0). Four were wrong: time invested fell instead of rising, the worst fall
deepened by more than predicted, the gain after 2009 did not appear, and there was no sweet
spot in the middle.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and I think that is worth more than another near-miss. The lab
has now priced both halves of its safety switch, and the answer is settled in opposite
directions: the coming-back half was improvable and has been improved four times on four
different books; the leaving half was already right, and every attempt to make it cleverer
makes it twitchier, costs time in the market, and deepens the fall. I would not spend another
method id on the sell trigger, and I would treat the 200-day average's stickiness as a
feature the lab should protect rather than a crudeness it should refine. This book has now
rejected two separate attempts to improve its exit — hysteresis bands earlier, realised
returns here — which is about as clear as a book can be.

What I would try next is the one thing this run points at that nobody has tested. The damage
here was caused entirely by *how often the rule changes its mind*, not by what it measures.
That suggests the useful lever is not a better sell signal but a cooling-off period: once the
book has sold, require the switch to stay settled for a minimum stretch before it may act
again, so a single choppy month cannot produce a sell-and-rebuy pair. The lab has never
tested a minimum holding time on the switch itself, this run gives a clean measurement of
what each flip costs, and it would apply to every gated book in the lab at once rather than
to one family. I have queued it.
methods.verdict: Rejected direction: the safety switch's sell rule was already right — replacing the 200-day average with a realised-return test made the book twitchier, cut time invested from 73% to 62% and 49%, and cost up to 4.9 points a year; the buy-back half, re-tested here on a dividend book, won again (+0.68 points a year)

methods.name: Market-state columns for the learned ranker: the trees see the fear gauge and the yield curve, not only one company against another
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0137 (the forgetting ranker); Sera batch 20261014-1312
methods.hypothesis: Three levers have been turned on this picker and all three are spent. M0130 turned model capacity and found a model with nothing to learn (its least flexible arm did best, and every arm lost to a control that forecasts nothing). M0131 turned the target horizon and found 3.8 points a year over 2000-2015 and 6.5 over 2009-2015, making B20 the lab's first and only eligible learned ranker. M0137 turned memory and found a monotone dose-response in the WRONG direction: halving the training window cost 0.9 points a year and quartering it cost 1.8, the 2009-2015 lead fell from -0.7% to -2.0% to -4.4%, and the survivorship check punished the short windows about six times harder. Three facts now agree: more history helps, more capacity helps, short memory is fragile. The picker is INFORMATION-STARVED, not regime-confused. And every one of those three levers is a knob on the MODEL. WHAT HAS NEVER MOVED IS WHAT THE MODEL MAY LOOK AT. All seven features are per-company and every one is rank-normalised across the cross-section of its own date, so by construction the picker cannot tell 2008 from 2013: within any date the ranks are uniform whatever the market is doing. The lab's own fall model already fixes this for its own question and its docstring argues the case explicitly -- a per-date rank cannot encode 'every name on this date is about to fall thirty per cent', only a level can -- and it appends three un-normalised market-level columns for exactly that reason. The ranker was never given the same. THE MECHANISM IS AN INTERACTION, NOT A LEVEL SHIFT, and this corrects the idea row this method was reserved under. A per-date constant column cannot change a LINEAR model's ranking, but a TREE that splits on it sends every row of a date down the same branch and then applies DIFFERENT per-company splits on the two sides. So a market-state column selects WHICH PER-COMPANY RULE RANKS THAT DATE. 'When fear is high prefer the names nearest their 52-week high; when it is low prefer residual momentum' is a rule this model can now express and could not express before, and that, not a shift in the level of its predictions, is what this method is testing. THE SOURCE IS FREE AND ALREADY POINT IN TIME: Market.series serves VIX from 1993, the four Treasury yields from 1993, and the rest, read through value_on/upto which cannot see past the decision date; declaring that this method reads them means lab run refuses a store without them, which is the right failure. THE COLUMNS ARE FOUR, AND NOT THE ONES THE IDEA ROW NAMED, for a measured reason written down before the run: the store's three-month fear series begins 2006-07-17 and gold begins 2000-08-30, so a term-structure or gold column would be missing for six of the sixteen traded years and -- worse -- the model refit at the end of 2008, the single most informative regime in the window, would have had about two and a half years of it to learn from. A column absent exactly where the regime story lives tests the store, not the idea. So the fear pair is the VIX level and the VIX against the mean of its own last 252 published rows (M0039's pre-registered whole-window proxy for an inverted curve, chosen by M0039 for this same coverage reason), and the rate pair is the ten-year yield and the ten-year minus the thirteen-week slope. All four cover every training row this method ever sees. A reading older than seven calendar days is NaN, M0039's constant, imported not restated; NaN means not known, never zero, and the trees bin it into its own branch. FIVE VARIANTS, THE ONLY SETTINGS EVER TRIED, none chosen by looking at a dev result: CTRL is the unchanged seven-feature book, which is M0137-EXP, which is M0131-B20, and it is BOTH the in-batch control and a correctness check -- the augmentation returns the base cross-section object itself when the column set is empty, so CTRL must reproduce EXP's recorded numbers bit for bit, and if it does not the wrapper has a bug and the batch is void; FEAR adds the two fear columns; RATE adds the two rate columns; BOTH adds all four; DV20 is the CONTROL, M0131's gated 20-name dollar-volume book re-run here so the what-does-the-model-add comparison never crosses a trial boundary. Every arm is gated at the SPY 200-day switch, the control included and read first, because M0130's ungated arms fell about 70% in 2008 and the switch has helped 22 of 22 lab variants whole-window. THE TENSION THAT CREATES IS NAMED NOW: the gate is itself a market-state reading and it is where the whole-window win has come from so far (M0131's exposure was 68%, its picks alone earned 9.9% a year). A column that merely re-discovers a worse version of the gate on the 68% of days the gate already said 'on' is a null result wearing a new coat, and the analysis will report the picks alone beside the gated book so the two cannot be confused. WHAT COUNTS AS AN IMPROVEMENT, FIXED NOW AND NOT NEGOTIABLE AFTERWARDS: a market-state arm beats the seven-feature control over 2009-2015 de-funded AND wins at least 3 of its 4 walk-forward folds -- the same bar M0137 set and failed, because it is the right bar and failing it honestly is the point. The arm that clears it must be one the bar named; an arm that clears it by accident is not the result. IF NO ARM CLEARS IT, the learned-ranker direction is closed on this signal set: the lab will have changed the model's capacity, its target, its memory and its inputs and found no recent edge in any of them, and it should stop building rankers and go looking for information it does not have. WHAT COUNTS AS A METHOD: a variant clears every design section 1 bar at DSR >= 0.90 at the lab's N, against the dev screen on the worst fall (50%) and the real-money bar (25%). No variant is promoted in this run whatever it shows: the test window is not touched.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely the market-state columns are the thinnest information the model has ever been given, and no arm clears the pre-registered bar. Six reasons, written before the run. FIRST AND STRONGEST, the effective sample size. Every per-company feature has about 57,000 training rows at the 2014 refit. A market-state column is a per-DATE scalar, so however many rows it is broadcast down it carries at most 216 distinct values -- one per training month-end -- and because the label is a 252-session forward return on monthly samples, neighbouring dates overlap 92%. The number of genuinely independent REGIME observations over 1996-2014 is not 216 but something nearer the count of business cycles: two, perhaps three. Asking a 300-iteration tree with 15 leaves to learn a regime interaction from two or three independent regimes is the textbook recipe for memorising 'in 2008, do this' and generalising nothing. The lab's own fall model lives with exactly this limitation and is honest about it. SECOND, the rate levels are non-stationary in a way the fear columns are not. The ten-year yield falls from about 7% in 1996 to about 2% by 2015 and never returns, so a tree whose splits were learned on 1996-2008 rate levels sends EVERY date from 2009 on down the same terminal branch: the RATE arm may be arithmetically incapable of distinguishing anything in the era the bar is scored on, which would be a null result caused by the column's own distribution rather than by the idea. The slope is better behaved and inverted before both of the window's recessions, so if any rate column earns its place it should be that one, and the arm is built so the two can be told apart. THIRD, the gate has already taken the regime signal. The SPY 200-day switch is a market-state reading, it sits in front of every arm, and it produced the whole-window win: M0131 held no pick on 28% of decision days and returned about 0% in 2001, 2002 and 2008. On the 68% of days the switch says 'on' the market is by construction above its own 200-day average, which is most of the low-fear days, so the fear columns may have almost no variation left to read where the book is actually invested. A column that only fires when the book is already in cash cannot change a single trade. FOURTH, interaction needs more data than a main effect, not less. The mechanism this method is built on is 'rank differently in different regimes', which asks the model to fit a separate per-company rule per regime out of a sample that was already too small for one rule -- M0130's whole finding was a model with nothing to learn, and M0131's flexible-tree win says it is data-limited. Splitting a data-limited sample by regime is the direction that makes it worse. FIFTH, survivorship is unchanged and unhelped: the check store already deepened B20's worst fall from 20.0% to 23.1% and dropped its DSR to 0.839, under the 0.90 bar, so any eligibility here still rests on data missing four in ten index-member days, and a regime column cannot restore a dead company. SIXTH, DSR at N = 90 and rising needs a Sharpe above anything any of the three rankers has produced (the best is 0.84), so even an arm that beats the control on return is likely to fail the luck test. THE MOST INFORMATIVE FAILURE would be FEAR clearing the 2009-2015 leg and failing the folds: that would say the regime signal is real in sample and does not survive being chosen, which is M0137's finding about short memory arriving by a second road and would close the direction harder than a flat null. THE LEAST INFORMATIVE would be all four arms within noise of CTRL, which would say the columns were never split on at all -- and that is checkable, because a tree that never splits on a column produces a book identical to CTRL's, trade for trade.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0144 — letting the picker see what kind of day it is

## What was asked

Seer has a stock picker that learns. Once a year it studies two decades of history and works out,
from seven facts about each company, which companies tend to do well over the following year. It
then buys the twenty it likes best.

It has been improved three times, and every improvement was a change to the **machine**: how
complicated it is allowed to be, how far ahead it is asked to look, how much history it is allowed
to remember. The first two helped. The third made it worse in a straight line.

What never changed is **what the machine is allowed to look at**. All seven facts are about one
company compared with other companies on the same day — is this one cheaper, faster, steadier than
that one. And every fact is converted into a league-table position before the machine sees it. The
consequence is strange and easy to miss: **the picker literally cannot tell October 2008 from June
2013.** On any given day it sees only the league table, and a league table looks the same in a
panic as it does in a calm market. Somebody is always top.

So this method gave it four new things to look at, all of them about the market as a whole rather
than about any one company:

* the **fear gauge** — how nervous the options market is, in its usual units;
* **fear against its own recent normal** — today's reading divided by its average over the past
  year, so a reading of 1.5 means "half again as jumpy as lately";
* the **ten-year government lending rate**;
* the **gap between the ten-year rate and the three-month rate** — the "yield curve", which goes
  negative before recessions.

All four come from data Seer already downloads and stores. Nothing was bought. Each is read the
way a person reading a newspaper that morning would read it: only figures published on or before
the day the decision is made, and a figure more than a week stale is treated as unknown rather
than guessed at.

## Why this might work, and why it is a sharper idea than it sounds

A reasonable objection is that a number which is the same for every company on a given day cannot
change which company you prefer. That is true of simple arithmetic models, and it is **false** of
the kind of model Seer uses here, which is a tree of yes/no questions.

A tree can ask "is fear above 30?" at the top. Every company on that day goes down the same side.
But the questions *underneath* the two sides can be different questions. So the model can now
learn a rule it could never express before:

> when the market is frightened, prefer the companies closest to their twelve-month high;
> when it is calm, prefer the ones with the best momentum after stripping out the market.

It does not change how much is held. It changes **which rule picks**. That is the whole idea, and
it is worth stating plainly because it determines what counts as evidence.

## The bar, written before any result

> A market-state version must beat the plain seven-fact version over **2009–2015**, the recent
> years that look most like today, **and** win at least **3 of its 4 out-of-sample checks.**

Both halves. This is the same bar the previous method set itself and failed, and it is kept
deliberately.

## What happened

Four versions were run, plus two controls, all on identical rules: fractional shares, Gotrade's
real fees, the owner's 5,000,000 rupiah monthly deposit, and the standing safety switch that moves
to cash when the market is below its own 200-day average.

| version | what it sees | earned a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | 2009–2015 vs SPY | checks won |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| plain (control) | the seven company facts | +10.9% | +7.2% | 20.0% | −0.7% | 1 of 4 |
| **+ fear** | and the two fear readings | +10.0% | +7.2% | **18.1%** | **−5.2%** | 1 of 4 |
| **+ rates** | and the two rate readings | +10.3% | +7.2% | **28.4%** | **−0.3%** | 1 of 4 |
| **+ both** | and all four | **+11.1%** | +7.2% | 20.6% | −1.7% | 1 of 4 |
| no model at all | buys the most-traded big firms | +8.2% | +7.2% | 21.4% | −5.9% | 1 of 4 |

"Worst fall" is the deepest drop from a previous peak, measured on the picking alone with the
monthly deposits taken out — a steady top-up refills a falling account and makes a bad year look
gentler than it was. The limit for real money is 25%.

**First, the batch is sound.** The plain control reproduced the previous method's result to the
last digit — same return, same worst fall, same 1,500 trades. So nothing here is a wiring bug;
every difference in the table is the new information and nothing else.

**The bar failed, on every single version.** Not one won more than **1 of its 4** out-of-sample
checks. The second half of the bar is not close, it is not arguable, and it fails for all four
arms identically. That settles it regardless of anything else in the table, and it is the finding.

**The recent-years half fails too, for three of the four.** Fear made 2009–2015 dramatically
*worse*: from 0.7 points behind SPY to **5.2 points behind**. Both-together made it worse as well.
Only the rates version nudged it the right way — from 0.7 points behind to 0.3 points behind — and
that is a 0.4-point improvement inside a sub-period where it still loses, bought at the price of
**the worst fall in the batch, 28.4%**, which is past the 25% limit for real money and more than
eight points worse than the control. That is not an improvement anyone should want.

## Why it failed, which is the part worth keeping

**The columns were definitely used.** This matters, because the dullest possible outcome would
have been the model ignoring the new information entirely, which would have taught nothing. It
did not ignore it: the four versions traded differently (1,435 to 1,637 trades against the
control's 1,500), fell differently, and earned differently. The model genuinely learned
regime-dependent rules.

**And it changed only what it was supposed to change.** Every version held its own stock picks for
the same **68%** of the time, asked for the same average of **10.6** names, and sat out the same
**28.3%** of decision days. Those figures are identical to a tenth of a point across all five.
So the new information never once moved the safety switch or the size of the book — it moved only
*which companies were bought*. The mechanism did exactly what was claimed for it, and the result
is therefore a clean verdict on the idea rather than on some side effect.

**The reason it does not help is arithmetic, and it was written down before the run.** Each
company fact has about 57,000 training examples. A market-wide reading has at most **216** —
one per month in the training history — because it is the same number for everyone on a given
day. Worse, because the model is asked about the following *year*, neighbouring months overlap by
about 92%, so consecutive readings are nearly the same observation. The number of genuinely
separate market conditions in 1996–2014 is not 216; it is closer to the number of business cycles,
which is **two, maybe three.** Asking a model to learn "what to do in a panic" from two panics is
asking it to memorise 1998, 2002 and 2008, and that is precisely what it did.

The fear version shows the memorisation beautifully. Every scare in its lessons — 1998, 2001–02,
2008 — was a genuine collapse followed by a violent recovery led by the most beaten-down names. So
it learned: *when fear spikes, buy the wreckage*. Then came 2010, 2011 and 2015, where fear spiked
inside a bull market led by the biggest, steadiest companies and no wreckage-recovery followed. It
applied the crisis playbook to things that were not crises, and lost 4.5 points a year of relative
performance in exactly the years that matter most.

The rates version shows a second, separate failure. The ten-year rate falls from about 7% in 1996
to about 2% by 2015 **and never goes back up**. So every split the model learned about rate levels
was learned in a world that no longer exists, and every date after 2009 falls off the bottom of
its experience into the same bucket. Its worst year is 2011 at −11.7% against the control's worst
year of −4.8% — 2011 being exactly when the curve was flattened deliberately by the central bank
into territory the model had never seen. This was predicted in the method's written-down
expected failure, and it happened.

## The fuller-history check

Seer's main price history is missing most of the companies that went bust, which flatters
everything. Re-running on the fuller history that puts them back costs nothing. Here the picture
is interesting and I will not oversell it:

| version | earned a year, clean history | earned a year, fuller history | worst fall, clean → fuller |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain (control) | +10.9% | +10.5% | 20.0% → **23.1%** |
| + fear | +10.0% | +9.6% | 18.1% → 18.3% |
| + rates | +10.3% | +9.3% | 28.4% → 24.9% |
| **+ both** | +11.1% | **+11.1%** | 20.6% → **18.9%** |
| no model | +8.2% | +7.6% | 21.4% → 25.1% |

The both-together version is the only one in the batch that loses essentially nothing when the
dead companies are restored, and the only one whose worst fall stays under 20% on both versions of
history — the control's crosses 20% and goes to 23.1%. I record that because it is true and
because it is the sort of thing that is easy to lose. I do **not** claim it means anything yet: a
0.2-point edge over the control across twenty years sits well inside the spread of this very batch
(the other two versions came in 0.9 and 0.6 points *below* the control), and the out-of-sample
record, 1 of 4, says plainly that this is not an edge anyone can lean on. One arm landing slightly
above the control out of four tries is what chance looks like.

Note also that the rates version's one success evaporates here: its 2009–2015 figure goes from 0.3
points behind SPY on the thin history to **2.9 points behind** on the fuller one. The single leg
of the bar that anything cleared was an artefact of the missing companies.

## Picking versus the safety switch

The previous methods' wins have mostly come from the safety switch sitting in cash, not from
clever picking, so the two are reported apart here. The control's own stock picks, judged alone,
beat SPY by **2.8 points a year**; the whole book including its cash beat SPY by 3.7 points; and
the money parked while the switch was off *lost* to SPY by 6.5 points a year. So the picking is
real and the switch is real and they are different things.

But because every version in this batch had identical exposure, **this batch contains no switch
effect at all.** Every difference in the table above is pure stock selection. That is the cleanest
version of this test the lab has ever run, and the answer it gives is no.

## The luck test

Seer scores every result for how likely it is to be real rather than a lucky draw, and it deflates
that score by how many distinct ideas the lab has tried — because the more things you try, the more
likely one of them looks good by accident. At this run the lab had tried **92** distinct methods,
and the owner's standing requirement is a score of **0.90 or better**.

| version | luck score | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| plain (control) | 0.912 | passes |
| + both | 0.904 | passes |
| + fear | 0.900 | fails, by a rounding margin |
| + rates | 0.798 | fails clearly |
| no model | 0.702 | fails clearly |

So two versions pass the luck test. That is not the same as being worth money: the luck test asks
whether the twenty-year average is real, and the out-of-sample checks ask whether it keeps working
on years the model has never seen. Here the first says yes and the second says no, 1 of 4, and when
those two disagree the second one is the one that has been right about this lab's history. Neither
the 0.90 bar nor the count of 92 is mine to move; both are printed by the lab and set by the owner.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did the expected failure happen?

The hypothesis did not hold. The expected failure happened, and it happened for the first and
second of the six reasons written down beforehand, in the order they were written: too few
genuinely independent market conditions to learn from, and rate levels that never return.

The third written-down worry — that the safety switch had already taken the regime signal — turns
out **not** to be the explanation, because the switch was untouched in every arm. The sixth — the
luck test — bit as predicted: the fear version came in at 0.900 against a 0.90 bar and failed by a
rounding margin; the rates version at 0.798.

## What this means for the lab's learned picker

Four levers have now been pulled on this picker: how complicated it may be, how far ahead it
looks, how much it remembers, and now what it may look at. **All four are spent.** The capacity
lever said the model had nothing to learn. The horizon lever was the only one that paid. The
memory lever said forgetting makes it worse. And this one says the market-wide context it was
missing is real information that it genuinely uses — and still does not help, because there is not
enough of it to learn from.

The honest conclusion is the one written into this method before it ran: **the learned-picker
direction is closed on this set of signals.** Not because the model is wrong, but because every
remaining knob turns on the same seven company facts and two or three market conditions, and no
amount of cleverness manufactures information that is not there.

**My opinion:** stop building rankers on these seven signals. I am confident about this, and I
would rather say so now than spend four more method ids proving it slowly. The evidence is
consistent across four methods and three different kinds of change, and the out-of-sample record
has been 1 or 2 of 4 every single time — the twenty-year averages keep looking fine and the folds
keep saying it is a selection, not an edge. That pattern does not reward another knob.

Two things I would do instead, in order. **First, and this is the one I would actually spend the
next id on: go and get information the lab does not have.** The seven facts are all price and
dividend arithmetic, which is the one thing every other market participant also has for free. The
lab holds an SEC filings panel it has barely used because it only starts in 2009 — but 2009–2015
is precisely the era every method keeps losing in, so a picker built *only* on that era, judged
only there, trades twenty years of flattering history for seven honest ones. That is a real
trade-off and I think it is the right way round, and it is a different kind of idea from anything
tried so far. **Second**, if anyone insists on one more ranker, the only version worth a look is
both-columns-together with the fear and rate pairs fed in as changes rather than levels — the rate
level's failure here is entirely a non-stationarity problem and it has a known fix. But I would
rate that a tidying-up exercise with a low ceiling, not a search for an edge, and I would not
spend an id on it before the fundamentals idea.

What I would **not** do is promote anything here. The both-together version clears the lab's
eligibility bars and is the best learned picker this lab has produced — and it won 1 of its 4
out-of-sample checks, which is the lab's own definition of a result that will not survive contact
with the future. The gate is right to refuse it, and I would refuse it without the gate.
methods.verdict: Showing the picker the fear gauge and the yield curve changed which stocks it bought and nothing else — and it failed the bar this method set itself, on every arm

methods.name: Rows or years? The same ranker retrained on a weekly sample grid instead of month-ends
methods.hypothesis: M0137 measured a clean monotone penalty for forgetting: 216 labelled month-ends earn 10.9% a year, 108 earn 10.0%, 48 earn 9.1%, with profit factor, Sharpe, DSR and the 2009-2015 lead all ordered the same way. But the three arms differ in TWO things at once, and M0137 could not separate them: a ten-year window has half the ROWS and half the distinct MARKET CONDITIONS. Those two have opposite implications. If the binding constraint is raw examples, the fix is cheap and local. If it is distinct conditions, no amount of resampling will ever help and the direction is closed -- and that is worth knowing before anyone spends another method on the model. This variation separates them with the one lever that adds rows while holding years exactly fixed: sample the training grid weekly instead of monthly. The same 1996-2015 history, the same seven features, the same 252-session forward-return-rank label, the same annual refit anchors, the same expanding window, the same flexible tree, the same top 20 behind the same SPY 200-day switch, the same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Only the set of sample dates changes, from the last NYSE session of each month to every Friday (or the week's last session), which takes the 2014 refit from about 216 rows-per-name to about 940, a factor of 4.3, with not one new year, not one new feature and not one new day of data read. THE HONEST PRIOR, written now: weekly samples overlap far more than monthly ones -- a 252-session label on neighbouring weeks shares 98% of its window against 92% for neighbouring months -- so the EFFECTIVE sample barely grows even as the nominal one quadruples. The most likely outcome is therefore no change, and no change is the informative answer: it would say the model is short of distinct conditions rather than raw rows, which closes the resampling route permanently and sends the lab to new information instead (see the market-state idea queued alongside this one). A clear improvement would say the opposite, that the learner is genuinely example-starved, and would make a denser grid a standing part of every future ranker. NOTE THE COST HONESTLY: month-end sampling is not only a convention, it is the decision calendar -- the book trades monthly -- so a weekly training grid trains on dates the book never trades. That is legitimate (the model learns a cross-sectional ordering, not a trading rule) but it must be said in the analysis, and one arm should keep the monthly grid as the in-batch control so the comparison never crosses a trial boundary. Arms to fix in advance: the monthly grid as control (must reproduce M0137-EXP), the weekly grid, a fortnightly grid as the ladder's middle rung, and the gated dollar-volume control. Same bar as M0137: beat the control over 2009-2015 de-funded AND win at least 3 of 4 walk-forward folds.

methods.name: The wide asymmetry book, alone, so its own behaviour is measured instead of inherited
methods.hypothesis: M0133 was refused promotion on kin, not on numbers: M0133-G20 moves with the test-failed M0002-REL-85 at 0.91 residual correlation, against the 0.85 bar (D14). That reading belongs to the 20-name arm. behavioural_kin reports one twin per FAILED method -- the strongest across a method's variants -- so M0133-G40's own correlation has never been computed, and the whole method inherited the 20-name arm's reading. G40 is also the only M0133 arm that stays under the owner's 25% real-money fall on the survivorship-check store (21.6% dev, 23.2% check, against 29.4% for every 20-name arm), it earns +13.5% a year funded vs SPY TR's +7.2% at PF 2.63 and DSR 0.922 at N=87, its worst year is 2008 at -0.3%, and all five M0133 arms earn MORE on the fuller history -- the first method in this lab to do so. This registers the 40-name gated book alone so its own behaviour is measured. One or two variants only, so nothing else moves: G40's exact configuration (CaptureParams-equivalent spread rank, 40 equal slots, gate on, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade), plus optionally the same book with M0113's positive-quarter buy-back, which was worth +1.1 points a year at an identical worst fall on the 20-name arm. Success: the book stays eligible AND its residual correlation against every test-failed book reads under 0.85, in which case all four buy-signal conditions hold at once for the first time (dev-eligible, kin clean, 3 of 4 folds, +1.9% 2009-2015 edge on the check store) and survivorship-free price history becomes worth buying. Failure, equally valuable: it reads at or above 0.85 too, which says the asymmetry rank IS high-participation momentum however wide the book, and the whole stock-updown-asymmetry line should close with that stated plainly rather than spawn a third variation.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# The forty-name asymmetry book, measured on its own: 0.90, and the line closes

## What this was reserved to settle

Yesterday's best book was the asymmetry picker: rank companies on how much of the market's good
days they join in, minus how much of its bad days, hold the top names, and step out of the market
whenever it closes below its 200-day average. On the owner's real saving plan its five versions
earned 13.5% to 16.7% a year against 7.2% for the same money put into the market, and they were
the first books in this lab that the dead companies made *better* rather than worse.

It was refused promotion on one thing only: it moves too much like a book the lab already tried
out of sample and lost with. The lab's limit is 0.85 on that measure. The reading was 0.91.

But that 0.91 was never measured on the version that matters. The lab's check keeps only the
single closest-moving version per failed book, so the twenty-name version's reading stood in for
the whole method, and the **forty-name** version's own number was never computed. That mattered
because the forty-name version is the only one of the five that stays inside the owner's 25%
fall limit once the dead companies are added back — 23.2%, where every twenty-name version goes
to 29.4%. The one version that could ever be funded was the one version whose number did not
exist.

So: register the forty-name book on its own, force the number to be computed on it, and report
it whatever it says.

## The number

**0.8964.** Above the 0.85 line. The forty-name book is refused on its own reading, not on an
inherited one.

It did not need a new method id to find that out. The check compares recorded month-by-month
results, and the backtest never looks at which method id it is run under — so the forty-name
book registered alone would produce the identical curve it has already produced, and the number
can be read off the curve the lab already holds. It was, and it is 0.8964. Registering a
duplicate of a book the lab has already measured, purely to re-derive a number already in hand,
would have cost the whole lab one more independent try — which is applied backwards to every
result ever recorded here, shaving a little confidence off all of them. That is a real price for
no information, so it was not paid.

For completeness, everything else about this book checks out, measured the same way:

| What | Forty-name book, on its own |
|---|---|
| Earned, on the owner's deposits | **+13.5% a year**, against +7.2% for the same deposits in the market |
| Worst fall, deposits taken out | **21.6%** (23.2% with the dead companies added back) |
| Gains vs losses | 2.63 to 1 |
| Worst year | 2008, **−0.3%**, when the market lost 36.8% |
| Luck score | 0.922, against the 0.90 bar, at 90 tries |
| Period-by-period record | **3 of 4**, on its own results alone |

Four of the five things the lab asks for hold. The fifth does not, and it is the one that stops
everything.

## Why it is refused, and what the refusal is actually seeing

The obvious suspicion was that the test is fooled by the market switch: both books sit in cash
in the same months, so of course they look alike. Three checks say that is wrong.

**One: it is not the cash months.** Throw away every month in which either book was sitting out,
and compare only the 168 months both were actually invested. The reading barely moves — 0.896
becomes 0.877.

**Two: it is not the companies.** Month by month across the whole twenty years, the forty names
this book holds and the forty a plain momentum book holds **share 18.7% of their names on
average** — against 15.3% if the two rankings were unrelated to each other. They are, to a very
good approximation, picking different companies out of the same pool of about 262.

**Three: it is not an artefact of the test.** Twenty-four books of forty names drawn **at random**
from the same pool, behind the same switch, were measured against every real book here. They read
0.48 to 0.78, and not one of the 96 comparisons crossed the 0.85 line — against this very book
they read 0.64 at most 0.70. So the test is not simply labelling anything that steps out of the
market. A book has to genuinely move like another to be caught, and this one does: 0.90 against
the failed book, where a random book of its exact shape reads 0.64.

Put together, those three say something sharper than "it is momentum in disguise". **It holds
different companies and still behaves identically.** The asymmetry ranking is not finding the
same names momentum finds; it is finding different names with the same temperament — the ones
that run hardest when the market runs and give the most back when it turns. Hold forty of those
behind a market switch and you get the momentum book's month-by-month life whoever you actually
bought.

That is exactly the failure this method's own paperwork predicted before it ran. The written
expectation said the spread rank "may simply be high-beta momentum under a new name, in which
case it will read as behavioural kin of the test-failed momentum books once it has a gated curve,
and the hard gate will bar promotion however good the numbers look". It does, and it did.

## The one arm that is behaviourally free, and its price

The switch-off version is clean on this test: 0.57 against the failed book, nowhere near the
line, and a random book reads higher against some real books than it reads against this one. It
is the only version of this idea the lab would be allowed to promote.

It falls **69.1%**, and lost 51.4% in 2008.

So the choice this method offers is between a book that cannot be promoted and a book that
cannot be held. That is not a near miss; it is a closed door, and it closes the whole
stock-updown-asymmetry line as currently built. Both of the method's written outcomes were
"valuable" — this is the second one, and it should be said plainly rather than framed around.

## My opinion

**Stop building books on this ranking behind the market switch, and do not spend a method id
re-asking this question in another costume.** The direction has now been measured four ways —
whole-window return, the recent years, the dead companies, and behaviour — and the first three
are the best this lab has recorded while the fourth is a hard refusal that the evidence above
says is correct rather than a technicality. Another twenty-name or sixty-name or differently
filtered version of the same ranking behind the same switch will land in the same place, because
what is being caught is the temperament of the companies, which the book size does not change.

**What is worth trying is the one combination not yet tested: this ranking kept invested, braked
by something other than the market's trend.** The switch-off arm is behaviourally clean and
earns 9.6% a year; its only defect is the 69% fall. Every brake this lab has tried on *the
market* produces the behaviour that gets a book refused. A brake on the **book's own** falling
equity, or on its own jumpiness, cuts the fall without putting the book in cash in the same
months as every other book here — which is precisely what the kin test is measuring. If such a
version gets the fall under 50% on this window and keeps even half the return, it would be the
first book in this lab that is eligible, survives the dead companies, and is behaviourally free
at the same time. That is the next thing I would spend an id on, and it is queued.

**And the lab needs to be able to read this number without spending an id.** This whole cycle
existed because a method's behaviour reading could not be seen per version until a method was
registered and run. A report-only command that prints any recorded version's reading against
every failed book would have answered it in a second, for nothing, and would have stopped
yesterday's method being refused on a number belonging to a different version of itself. That is
queued as a wish.
methods.verdict: Measured on the right book at last: the forty-name asymmetry picker moves with a book that already failed out of sample at 0.90, above the 0.85 limit — it holds different companies than the momentum books and still behaves exactly like them, so the line closes.

methods.name: Does width protect, or only cost? Ask it on the history that has the failures in it
methods.sourceRef: M0133 for the engine, the 20- and 40-name equity-basis rungs and the 6.2-point check-store gap; M0139 for the flat dev-store width curve this contradicts and for the band-basis arithmetic; M0123 for the equity-basis cash leak; M0110-DP20-UP and M0133-N40 for the ungated 20- and 40-name rungs the sixth arm extends
methods.hypothesis: A measurement, pre-registered so that it is held to numbers rather than to a story. Two methods measured book width on the same morning and disagreed by a factor of six, and the difference between them was the price history, not the method. M0139 swept 20, 35, 50 and 70 names on a tape that invests the deposits and recorded worst falls of 20.6%, 19.6%, 20.7% and 19.9% -- flat and unordered across a 3.5x widening -- and concluded that width buys no safety behind a market switch. M0133 asked 20 against 40 on the survivorship-check store and found 22.7% -> 21.6% on the dev store (1.1 points) against 29.4% -> 23.2% on the check store (6.2 points), which straddles the owner's 25% real-money bar. The mechanism that reconciles them is plain and is the thing under test: width is protection against ONE company failing alone, the dev store prices no delisted name (48% of index members in 1996 rising to 74% in 2014, the missing 522 disproportionately the bankrupt and the bought-out), so a tape with the single-name collapses removed can show only what width costs and never what it saves. If that is right, every slot-count result this lab holds -- the paper roster's twenty names included -- was read off a measurement blind in one direction. WHAT IS RUN. M0133's engine imported verbatim (rank F4-screened members on upside participation minus downside participation over 252 sessions, hold the K highest in equal slots, all cash while SPY is under its 200-day average), at K = 20, 30, 40, 55 and 70, plus one ungated 70-name arm. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's plan (10,000,000 IDR opening, 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th), against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days. The preset is monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, the target basis, because the equity basis leaves a wide book partly in cash and this method measures falls AT WIDTH, which is exactly where that artefact bites; W20 and W40 sit against M0133's recorded equity-basis twins so the basis change is measured, not assumed. Every arm is then re-read on the check store through lab survivorship, which is report-only, records no trial and spends no look. WHAT IS PREDICTED, in numbers, before any result. (1) THE DEV CURVE IS FLAT. The five gated dev-store falls should sit inside 20.5% to 23.5% with no reliable ordering in width, reproducing M0139's finding on a second engine: 20 names near M0133's 22.7%, 70 names no more than 2 points gentler. (2) THE CHECK CURVE FALLS, MONOTONICALLY. The same five arms on the check store should start near 29.4% at 20 names and decline every rung: roughly 26% at 30, 23% at 40 (M0133's recorded figure, which the basis change should move by under a point), 21.5% at 55 and 20.5% at 70. Equivalently, the paired gap between the two curves should shrink from about 6.7 points at 20 names to under 1.5 points at 70, because a wide book has little left for the missing failures to take. (3) THE PRICE OF THAT PROTECTION IS RETURN. Funded return should decay with width as it did in both parents -- M0133 gave up 2.1 points a year from 20 to 40 names, M0139 2.8 points from 20 to 70 -- so the 70-name arm is predicted between 11% and 13.5% a year against the 20-name arm's 15.6% and deposit-matched SPY's 7.2%. Both halves belong in the verdict: protection that costs more than it saves is not a recommendation. (4) THE DECISION NUMBER IS MAR ON THE CHECK STORE. If dev-store MAR picks 20 names while check-store MAR picks 40 or 55, then the lab's entire width record is biased narrow by a knowable amount, and that correction factor -- not this book -- is the deliverable. (5) THE SIXTH ARM SAYS WHETHER THE GATE IS WHY WIDTH LOOKS USELESS. Ungated, the recorded dev falls are 74.0% at 20 names (M0110-DP20-UP) and 69.1% at 40 (M0133-N40), already 4.9 points of width effect where the gated arms show 1.1. Ungated 70 is predicted at 60% to 67% on dev and deeper still on the check store. If width moves an ungated book on dev and not a gated one, then the switch has already removed the falls spreading out can help with, and M0139's conclusion is right about gated books and wrong as a general claim -- which is the open question M0139's own analysis named as the more valuable of its two. PROMOTION IS NOT AVAILABLE: the line runs M0133 -> M0110 and M0133's 20-name arm reads 0.91 behavioural correlation with a test-failed book against a 0.85 line. Accepted before the run.
methods.expectedFailure: The failure that would matter most is the dull one: BOTH CURVES FLAT. If the check-store fall sits within 1.5 points across 20 to 70 names, then M0133's 6.2 points was one pair's idiosyncrasy -- two arms, one comparison, no curve -- M0139's conclusion stands unchanged and unqualified, and the honest verdict says so first and plainly rather than hunting for a width effect in a subgroup. That outcome is worth the id: it would stop the lab spending further ids on slot counts. Specific failures written now. (1) THE CURVE COULD GO THE WRONG WAY. A wider book owns more of the shortlist and therefore more of the companies the dev store cannot price, so the check store could punish width rather than reward it -- which is exactly what happened to M0123's all-shortlist basket, which lost its entire edge there. A rising check-store fall curve would mean width concentrates survivorship exposure instead of diluting single-name risk, and would be a stronger argument for twenty names than any dev-store number. (2) ONE ERA COULD BE DOING ALL THE WORK. If the whole check-store width effect is 2008 and the 2009-2015 falls are identical across widths, then this is a measurement of one crisis and not of width, and the verdict must say which years the gap lives in before it says anything else -- 2009-2015 is the best-covered stretch and the one most like today. (3) REPRODUCTION FIRST. lab survivorship prints a dev re-run beside the recorded trial; if any arm does not reproduce, its side-by-side is meaningless and must be dropped from the curve rather than quoted. The same applies to the W20 and W40 arms against M0133's equity-basis twins: if the basis change moves the dev fall by more than a point, the two methods' numbers are not interchangeable and the curve must be read inside this method alone. (4) FEES AND FILL AT THE WIDE END. Gotrade's schedule bites hardest on small orders and this account ramps from 10,000,000 IDR, so a 70-name book holds slots near 18 USD in its early years; some of the return decay with width will be fees rather than signal decay, and trade counts and turnover must be quoted so the two can be told apart. The 70-name arms are also structurally short by up to six names in 1996, and any exposure gap inside that year belongs to the screen. (5) THE CHECK STORE IS A CROSS-CHECK, NOT TRUTH. It adds most of the members the dev store cannot price, not all of them, and real collapses were kept while data errors were cleaned -- a judgement call. It is not a gate here, lab run and lab test refuse it, and nothing in this method may be reported as though its numbers were the dev store's. (6) DEPOSITS SOFTEN EVERY FALL HERE ALIKE and no figure may be lined up against an unfunded trial. (7) THE UNGATED ARM WILL FAIL THE SCREEN and is expected to: a 60%-plus fall is outside the 50% dev screen, let alone the 25% real-money bar. It is evidence about the mechanism, never a candidate, and must not be reported as a near miss.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0147 — does holding more companies protect you, or only cost you?

## The question, and why it needed asking twice

Yesterday and this morning the lab asked the same question twice and got two different answers.

One experiment held the same picking rule at 20, 35, 50 and 70 companies and measured how far
the account fell from its highest point: 20.6%, 19.6%, 20.7%, 19.9%. Flat, and not even in
order, across a book three and a half times wider. It concluded that spreading wider buys no
safety, and on the price history it read, that is exactly right.

Another experiment asked the narrower version — 20 companies against 40 — on our **check
history**, the fuller copy that adds back most of the companies our usual history cannot price.
There the worst fall went from 29.4% to 23.2%. Six points, where the usual history had shown one.

Six times the answer, from the same question. That is not a detail. The owner's limit for real
money is a 25% fall, so one of those two readings puts a twenty-company book inside the limit and
the other puts it outside.

The reason the two disagree is worth stating in one sentence, because once it is said it is
obvious. **Spreading your money wider is protection against one company collapsing on its own,
and the companies that collapse on their own are precisely the ones our usual price history does
not contain — because they stopped existing.** Our usual history prices about 48% of index
members in 1996 and 74% in 2014; the 522 it cannot price are overwhelmingly the bankrupt and the
bought-out. A history with the collapses removed can show you what spreading wider *costs* and
can never show you what it *saves*.

So this method measured the whole curve, on both histories at once, and wrote down what it
expected before it looked.

## What was run

One picking rule, held at five widths. The rule is the one that scored best in the lab this
week: among big, liquid American companies, measure how much more than the market each one rises
on the market's good days, subtract how much of the market's bad days it joins in, hold the
highest-scoring ones in equal amounts — and sit entirely in cash whenever the S&P 500 is below
its 200-day average. Widths: 20, 30, 40, 55 and 70 companies. A sixth version holds 70 companies
with the cash rule switched off, as a control.

Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's real plan: 10 million rupiah to open and 5
million on the 25th of every month, 237 deposits, against a plain S&P 500 fund fed the identical
money on the identical days. Every version was then re-run on the check history. That re-run is a
report, not a new attempt: it costs none of the lab's one-shot looks at the years after 2015.

One deliberate fix first. The simulator used to top a holding back up only once it had drifted by
1% **of the whole account**, which a wide book can never reach — so a wide book quietly sat in
cash and its fall looked gentler than it was. This method uses the fixed rule, and the check
confirms it worked: **every width here had 70.0% of its money in its own picks, to within a tenth
of a point.** None of the curve below is a cash illusion. The other 30% is the cash rule, which
is out of the market on 28.3% of decision days.

## The result

Worst fall from a peak, the same six books, on the two histories:

| companies held | usual history | check history | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 22.7% | **29.4%** | +6.7 |
| 30 | 21.0% | **26.2%** | +5.3 |
| 40 | 21.5% | 23.1% | +1.6 |
| 55 | 20.2% | 20.4% | +0.2 |
| 70 | 20.6% | 20.3% | −0.3 |
| 70, cash rule off | 63.5% | 66.3% | +2.9 |

Read the left column alone and the earlier conclusion is confirmed: 2.1 points of movement
across a book three and a half times wider, and not even in order. Read the right column and
spreading wider takes **9.1 points** off the worst fall, every single rung, in order, no
exceptions.

And the two columns converge. The penalty the check history applies shrinks from 6.7 points at 20
companies to nothing at 55, because by then the book is wide enough that no single company's
collapse can do much to it. **The gap between our two histories is not a constant. It is a
measurement of how exposed a book is to one company dying, and it closes as the book widens.**

## It is not one book's quirk — the roster's own family does the same thing

The obvious worry is that this is one picking rule behaving oddly. So the same two-history reading
was taken of the momentum book the paper roster actually holds, at the widths already recorded:

| companies held | usual history | check history | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 20.7% | **25.1%** | +4.4 |
| 35 | 19.6% | 20.1% | +0.5 |
| 50 | 20.7% | 20.0% | −0.7 |
| 70 | 19.9% | 19.8% | −0.1 |

Same shape, same size, same collapse of the gap. Flat on the usual history — 0.8 of a point across
the whole range — and 5.3 points of real protection on the fuller one.

**And that twenty-company book is the roster.** On the fuller price history it falls 25.1%, which
is outside the owner's 25% limit for real money. So is the twenty-company version of this
method's own book, at 29.4%.

## Which width you would actually choose, and how the answer flips

The lab's own score for "return per unit of fall" — the money-weighted yearly return divided by
the worst fall — across the five widths:

| companies held | usual history | check history |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 0.69 | 0.56 ← worst |
| 30 | **0.70** ← best | 0.58 |
| 40 | 0.64 | 0.65 |
| 55 | 0.62 | **0.68** ← best |
| 70 | 0.58 | 0.65 |

**On the usual history the best width is 30 companies and the score falls away steadily from
there. On the fuller history the best width is 55, and 20 — the roster's number — is the worst of
the five.** The ranking does not shift. It inverts. That is the finding.

## What it costs

Spreading wider is not free, and the price is real. Money-weighted yearly return falls from
+15.6% at 20 companies to +11.9% at 70, against +7.2% for the same deposits in an index fund. So
going from 20 to 70 gives up 3.7 points a year to take 9.1 points off the worst fall.

That decay is the signal thinning out down the ranking, not fees. Three things say so: the
money actually invested is flat at 70.0% across every width, so it is not cash; the gains-to-losses
ratio stays between 2.40 and 2.64 at every width, so the trades are not getting worse; and the
earlier experiment measured the fee drag directly and found it flat in width, with the total bill
*falling* as the book widens. The trade count does rise, 1,118 to 3,095, but each trade is smaller.

Worth noting separately: on the fuller history **every version earned more, not less** — between
0.6 and 1.3 points a year. That is unusual here, and it is the second time this engine has done
it. Adding the dead companies back makes this book richer because it owns violent companies while
they are running and is in cash when the market turns down, which is when they died.

## The control that explains the mechanism

The sixth version holds 70 companies with the cash rule switched off. With that rule off, the
recorded falls by width on the usual history are 74.0% at 20 companies, 69.1% at 40 and 63.5% at
70 — spreading wider takes **10.5 points** off, visibly, on the very history where it looked
useless behind the cash rule. On the fuller history the same two endpoints read 75.9% and 66.3%,
a 9.6-point gain.

So the mechanism is now measured rather than argued. A book falls for two separate reasons: the
whole market drops, or one of its companies collapses alone. The cash rule removes the first. Our
usual price history removes the second. Behind the cash rule, on the usual history, **both have
been taken away, so width has nothing left to do and reads as pure cost.** Put the dead companies
back and half the job reappears. Take the cash rule away and the other half does.

## Did the predictions hold?

All five, close to the number.

1. Predicted the usual-history curve flat between 20.5% and 23.5% with no reliable ordering. It
   came in at 20.2%–22.7%, non-monotone. **Held.**
2. Predicted the check-history curve to start near 29.4% and decline every rung — roughly 26, 23,
   21.5, 20.5. Measured: 29.4, 26.2, 23.1, 20.4, 20.3. Predicted the gap to shrink from 6.7 points
   to under 1.5. Measured: 6.7 to −0.3. **Held, to within a few tenths at every rung.**
3. Predicted return decay with the 70-company version between 11% and 13.5% a year. It is 11.9%.
   **Held.**
4. Predicted that if the two histories rank the widths differently, that inversion is the
   deliverable. They do. **Held.**
5. Predicted the ungated 70-company version at 60%–67% on the usual history. It is 63.5%. **Held.**

The expected failures mostly did not happen. The curve did not go the wrong way. Every version
reproduced its recorded result exactly before the comparison was made. The change of top-up rule
turned out to be a literal no-op at 20 companies — this method's 20-company version is identical
to the earlier one to the last digit — and worth 0.1 of a point of fall at 40, so the two methods'
numbers are interchangeable after all.

**One expected failure could not be fully discharged, and it must be said plainly.** The check-run
reports how far each book fell but not *when*. So "the whole width effect might be one bad year"
cannot be ruled out from this report. What can be said: the book is in cash through 2001, 2002 and
2008, so its falls are not the famous crises; its worst calendar year at 20 companies is 2011; and
its lead over the index across 2009–2015 — the best-covered, most present-day stretch — moves the
same way the falls do: the wide versions *gain* on the fuller history (the 70-company book from
−1.9% to −0.3%, the 55 from −1.0% to +0.4%, the 40 from +0.7% to +1.9%) while the two narrow ones
slip about a fifth of a point. So the recent years tell the same story as the falls rather than
contradicting it. That is suggestive, not conclusive. A dated fall in the check report would settle it, and
that is queued.

## What it does not change

This book cannot be promoted, and that was accepted before the run. It moves like three books that
already spent their one look at the years after 2015 and lost. The fold check passes, 3 of 4, and
the luck score is 0.92–0.94 against a 0.90 bar at 91 tries — but the identity test refuses it and
there is no way around that, correctly. Three of the four conditions for buying proper price
history are met; the fourth is not, and no buy signal fires.

The fuller history is also a cross-check, not the truth. It adds *most* of the companies our usual
one cannot price, not all; real collapses were kept and data errors cleaned, which is a judgement
call. Nothing above should be read as if it were the usual history's number.

## My opinion

**This is the most important result I have produced, and it is not about this book at all. Every
width and slot-count number this lab holds is wrong in a knowable direction, and I now know the
size of the correction.**

The lab has been settling "how many companies should the book hold" on a price history that is
structurally incapable of showing the benefit. Not noisy — blind. Two families, nine width pairs,
measured today under controlled conditions, agree: at 20 companies the usual history understates
the worst fall by 4.4 to 6.7 points; at 35–40 by 0 to 1.6; at 50 and above by nothing at all. The
lab's existing rule on this reads each variant's measured penalty one at a time and refuses to use
an average, because across 102 variants the penalty ranged from −9 to +14 points. My reading says
much of that spread is one variable — how many names the book holds — and that is testable against
the committed grid. I would test it next, because if it holds, the lab can correct a width
decision without owning the fuller history at all.

**The concrete thing the owner should know: the roster's twenty names are the least safe width
available, not the safest.** The momentum book the roster holds falls 25.1% on the fuller history,
just outside his 25% limit, where the usual history reports a comfortable 20.7%. Widening it to 35
would have taken that fall to 20.1%. On the usual history that costs 0.6 of a point a year; on the
fuller one it costs nothing at all — the 35-company version actually earns 0.1 of a point *more*.
A five-point gentler fall for nothing is not a trade-off, and the usual history cannot see it. I am not recommending a roster change on one morning's work, and I
have not made one — but the evidence the roster's width rests on is now known to be measured
blind, and that should be re-opened deliberately rather than left standing.

**What I would not do is chase this book.** It is refused on identity and should stay refused; the
0-for-5 record is what happens when that rule gets argued around. Its value here was as a clean
instrument for measuring the tape, and it did that job well.

So the two things I have queued are: re-read the committed survivorship grid to see whether the
drawdown penalty is predicted by book width across all 102 variants, which would turn this from
one morning's finding into a rule the lab can apply everywhere; and re-ask the roster's own width
question deliberately on the fuller history, since the number the roster rests on is now known to
be the one measurement that history cannot make.
methods.verdict: Width protects, and our usual price history cannot see it: the same five books fall 22.7% to 20.6% as they widen on the usual history and 29.4% to 20.3% on the one that keeps the companies that died — so the best width flips from 30 names to 55, and the roster's twenty is the least safe of the five, not the safest.

methods.name: A cooling-off period on the safety switch: make it stay settled before it may flip again
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0143 (the calm big raisers behind an asymmetric switch); the switch frame and both triggers are M0113's; the hysteresis that is being bought is M0101's goal bought in the time domain instead of the price domain
methods.hypothesis: M0143 answered the exit question and the answer was no, but it answered a second question nobody asked, and that one has a live lever in it. Every DOWN arm lost in exact proportion to HOW OFTEN IT CHANGED ITS MIND, not to what it measured. Time invested fell monotonically with the window: 72.7% (SMA200 exit), 70.7% (DOWN126), 62.1% (DOWN63), 49.2% (DOWN21), and turnover rose monotonically the other way (5.37, 5.20, 5.65, 6.40).
