The mechanism is hysteresis: a 200-day average is heavily smoothed so a price above it tends to stay above it, while a realised-return test flips sign repeatedly in a chop and each flip is a full liquidation plus a later repurchase. M0084 had already named whipsaw as the switch's standing cost and M0101's banded arms tried to buy hysteresis by widening the threshold and LOST (MAR 0.51 and 0.50 against the plain control's 0.57, both breaking the drawdown screen). DESIGN: buy hysteresis in the TIME domain instead of the price domain, which is the one way nobody has tried. Keep the exit at the 200-day cross and the entry at UP63 -- i.e. M0143-CALM-UP63 exactly, a dev-eligible arm at +11.3% funded against SPY's +7.2% -- and add one new parameter: once the switch has CHANGED STATE, it may not change again for at least K monthly checks. Variants: K=0 (the paired control, which must reproduce M0143-CALM-UP63 to the digit), K=1, K=2, K=3, and one arm applying the cool-off only to the SELL direction (free to buy back, slow to leave again), because M0143 showed the two halves want opposite things and a symmetric cool-off may throw away the fast re-entry that four books have now confirmed. WHY IT COULD WORK WHERE BANDS FAILED: a band widens the threshold, which delays the exit in a real crash as well as in a chop -- it pays for less whipsaw with a later exit, and M0101 measured that trade as a loss. A time lock does not move the threshold at all, so the FIRST exit of a genuine crash arrives on exactly the same session it does today; only the rapid re-flip is suppressed. That asymmetry is what makes it a different bet rather than a re-run of M0101. HOW THE LOCK IS EXPRESSED WITHOUT STATE, which is the one genuinely new piece of machinery here and is pre-registered with the rest. An allocator holds no state but what the book holds, and 'how long since the flip' is not in it. It is re-derived from the bars instead: a monthly check's data date is the last NYSE session of the previous month, those sessions are readable straight off SPY's own bar dates, and the switch's transition is a pure function of SPY's closes, so the machine is replayed forward over the last eight checks and the replay returns a count. The replay NEVER decides what the book holds -- held stays the authority on the current state, exactly as in M0143, and this book parks its unfilled weight in SPY so an 'on' book always holds something. The replay is consulted only on a check where a flip is actually proposed and only when K is non-zero, so at K=0 it is not reached at all and the control is M0143-CALM-UP63 bit for bit rather than an approximation of it. The lookback is 410 sessions for every arm, above M0143's 253 and below the 426 the lab's longest methods already declare; the dev window still opens 1996-01-03 because this book reads only SPY and the membership snapshot binds first, so the five arms are scored on exactly the sessions M0143's six were and the paired differences are the lock alone. HOST: the same calm big dividend raisers (M0088-C-LIVE-63) for continuity with M0143's six arms and because its kin reads clean -- family stock-dividend-change-drift holds no test-failed method and the line M0101 -> M0088 -> M0070 holds none. Same preset, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. THE PAIR THAT CARRIES THE ASYMMETRY: K3 and K3-SELL share a three-check lock and differ only in whether the buy-back is locked too, so their difference is exactly the price of locking the half that four books have now shown wants to be fast. SUCCESS: a K that beats K=0 by at least a point a year with the worst fall no deeper AND a positive 2009-2015 edge, since M0143-CALM-UP63's was -0.5% and the chop years 2010, 2011 and 2015 are exactly where M0096 diagnosed the switch losing the money.
methods.expectedFailure: The switch already flips rarely under a 200-day average read monthly -- the SPY-only arm traded 18 times in 22 years -- so a cool-off may bind on almost no sessions and simply reproduce the control. That is a NULL RESULT and the verdict must report it as one, stated first and plainly, rather than dressed up as a small improvement: the honest headline in that case is how many checks the lock actually bound on, and if the answer is a handful then nothing was learned about hysteresis and the grid closes. The second risk is the opposite one, and it is worse: the sessions the lock DOES bind on may be the valuable ones. 2009's recovery was a fast re-entry after a fast exit, and a lock that forbids a re-flip for three months could hold the book in cash through exactly the recovery the lab spent three methods learning to catch. If the K arms lose their money in 2009 rather than gaining it in 2010, 2011 and 2015, the finding is that the switch's flips are not whipsaw at all but the signal, and the lab should stop looking for hysteresis on this book. Third, this book's own evidence is discouraging: it has now refused two exit improvements, and a third refusal may simply confirm that its switch is already at its best. Fourth, the readable numbers. Trade counts on a switch are tiny -- tens of flips over 22 years -- so profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless here and no arm will clear a luck bar on the strength of them. The funded return, the worst fall, the 2009-2015 era split and the FLIP COUNT are the numbers to read, in that order, and the verdict says so before it says anything else. Fifth, the machinery. If K0 does not return M0143-CALM-UP63's 1996-01-03 start, 575 trades, 20.39% worst fall and 35.66% CAGR, then either the lookback moved the window or the decision path is not M0143's, and NONE of the other four numbers is readable; the correct response is to report the method unreadable rather than to explain the gap away. Sixth, the warm-up. The replay is defined over the last eight checks and seeded with the stateless gate, so the first checks of the window are decided by a machine that was assumed rather than observed. The counter is seeded 'long settled' so an assumed state never holds a flip back, which bounds the error to permitting a flip the true machine would have refused -- the conservative direction -- but it is an error and the verdict does not claim the lock is exact. Seventh, no interest is credited on idle cash, which flatters whichever arm is out of the market least. A lock that raises time invested therefore gets a small free advantage; on SPY a comparable swap moved time in market about 2.3 points and 1996-2015 T-bills paid roughly 2.5% a year, so any gap under a tenth of a point a year is noise for this reason alone and must not be reported as a finding.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

## The control reproduced, so every number below is readable

The first arm holds the switch exactly as it already runs, with the cool-off set to zero,
and it came back identical to the arm it was copied from on every figure that matters:
the same first day in January 1996, the same 575 trades, the same 20.4% worst fall, the
same 35.7% yearly growth, the same profit factor, the same time invested and the same
money-weighted return of 11.3% against the market's 7.2%. Only the luck score differs,
and that is expected: it is scored against how many questions the lab has asked by the
day it is scored, and the lab has asked more since.

That matters because it was the one thing that could have made this batch unreadable. A
longer memory was needed to replay the switch, and a longer memory can quietly shorten
the window a book is measured on. It did not. The five arms were scored on exactly the
same days, so the differences between them are the cool-off and nothing else.

## The cool-off did bind, so this is a refusal and not a null result

Replaying the switch over all 238 monthly checks of the window, the cool-off actually
refused a proposed move 8 times at one month, 14 times at two, 24 times at three, and 15
times when it applied to selling only. The switch went from 31 changes of mind down to
23. Turnover fell from 5.37 to 5.03 and the share of the book at work moved with it. So
the idea was given a real chance to work, and the answer below is about the idea rather
than about a setting that never did anything.

## It lost money and safety at the same time, which is rare and decisive

| how long the switch must sit still | yearly return | worst fall | lead over the market |
|---|---|---|---|
| no wait (the switch as it runs today) | 11.3% | 20.4% | +4.1% |
| one month | 10.2% | 20.4% | +3.0% |
| two months | 9.8% | 25.3% | +2.6% |
| three months | 9.0% | 31.6% | +1.8% |
| three months, on the way out only | 10.0% | 31.4% | +2.9% |

Every version of the idea earned less than leaving the switch alone, and the longer the
wait the less it earned — 11.3%, then 10.2%, 9.8%, 9.0%. Normally a brake buys safety
with return, and the trade is at least worth arguing about. This one did the opposite: it
gave up return *and* made the worst fall deeper, from 20% to 25% and then 32%. There is no
reading of that table on which the idea is worth keeping.

## Where the money went: the 2008 exit was the thing being suppressed

The whole case for a cool-off was that the switch changes its mind too often and pays for
it. The measurement says the opposite. In 2008 — the one year this switch exists for — the
book beat the market by 35.7% when the switch was free to act, and by only 27% to 28% in
every version that made it wait. Making it wait kept the book invested into the fall it
was built to escape.

That is the whole loss, and it is the risk this idea was pre-registered as most likely to
hit. The dates confirm it: at a three-month wait the switch was blocked from selling in
May, June and July of 2008, and blocked from buying back through three straight months of
the 2003 recovery. Both halves of the switch were stopped from doing the right thing at
the only times it mattered.

## The years it was built to fix never improved

The idea was aimed at the choppy stretch after 2009, where this book has long trailed the
market slightly. It did not help. The lag stayed negative in every version: −0.5% with no
wait, −1.4%, −0.6%, −1.0%, and −0.0% for the sell-only version. The best of those is half
a point better than leaving the switch alone, bought with eleven extra points of worst
fall. And the choppy years do not even line up with the story: the cool-off bound in 2011
and early 2012, but never once in 2010 and never once in 2015.

The sell-only version — free to buy back, slow to leave — was the best of the four, which
is consistent with everything the lab has found about this switch wanting to be quick to
return and is the one honest point in the idea's favour. It still lost to leaving the
switch alone on both return and worst fall, so it is a direction confirmed rather than a
result kept.

## The answer

The flips are not noise. They are the signal, and suppressing them is expensive. This book
has now refused three attempts to improve its safety switch: a wider threshold, a different
sell rule, and now a waiting period. Three different ways of asking the same question have
all come back with the same answer, and the honest conclusion is that this switch is
already at its best and the lab should stop looking here.

One caution on the label. The method is recorded as clearing the development screen, but
that is the control arm's doing — it is the existing switch re-run unchanged. None of the
four arms that actually carry the idea cleared it, and none should be read as a candidate.
The method also lost most of its walk-forward stretches, which is the usual warning that a
twenty-year average is hiding a result that does not hold up decade by decade.

Correlation against the four books that have already failed on fresh data is clean for every
arm, the highest reading being 0.73 against a bar of 0.85 — checked per arm rather than only
on the best one.
methods.verdict: Rejected direction: making the safety switch wait before it may move again cost return and safety at once — one, two and three months of cool-off took the yearly return from 11.3% to 10.2%, 9.8% and 9.0% while deepening the worst fall from 20% to 25% and 32% — because the changes of mind it suppressed were not noise but the 2008 exit, where the lead over the market fell from +36% to +28%; the choppy years it was built to fix never improved, and the sell-only version was best of the four but still lost on both counts

methods.name: The asymmetry book kept invested, braked by its own falling account instead of the market's trend
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0133's ungated arm M0133-N40, with M0109's own-drawdown brake and M0001/M0002's own-volatility target put on it in place of the market switch; the brake and the vol dial are M0109's and M0001's implementations, imported unchanged
methods.hypothesis: M0133 closed on behaviour, not numbers: M0133-G40 reads 0.8964 against the test-failed M0002-REL-85, above the 0.85 bar, and the refusal is sound -- 24 random 40-name books behind the same gate read at most 0.70 against it, so the resemblance is real and not an artefact of the switch. The measurement that opens the door is M0133-N40, the SAME asymmetry rank with the gate OFF: measured on its own curve 2026-10-14 it reads 0.5717 against M0002-REL-85, 0.3524 against M0021-B70-RAW, 0.3625 against M0022-W-TV14 and 0.3341 against M0029-B70-RAW-FRAC -- behaviourally free of every failed book by a wide margin -- and still earns +9.6% a year funded against SPY TR's +7.2%. Its only defect is the fall: 69.1% peak to trough, 2008 at -51.4%, against a 50% dev screen and the owner's 25% real-money bar. The hypothesis is that the fall can be cut WITHOUT the market switch, and that doing so is the only way this ranking stays promotable. Every brake that reads the MARKET -- the 200-day cross, the breadth gate, the term-structure gate -- puts a book in cash in the same months as every other book in this lab, which is precisely what the kin rule measures and refuses. A brake that reads the BOOK -- its own drawdown from its own high water mark, or its own trailing volatility applied to an ungated book -- de-risks on a schedule the failed books do not share. Variants: the ungated 40-name asymmetry book under a drawdown brake that cuts exposure to cash by 15% and by 25% below its own trailing one-year peak; under its own 63-day volatility targeted at 14% and 16%; under both; and a paired in-lab control with neither brake. Two mechanical decisions were fixed before the run and neither was calibrated on a result. First, the brake reads an UNBRAKED gross shadow of this same book rebuilt from bars, never the funded account: a brake that reads its own braked account is a ratchet that would cut in 2008 and then hold cash straight through the 2009-2015 stretch this ranking exists to capture, and a deposit-fed account's high is lifted by every top-up. Second, the tape is the target-band one, because under the old whole-account band a 40-name book executes no trim until exposure has already fallen to 0.60, which would turn a proportional dial into a switch and make a null result unreadable; the control arm runs on the same tape so the five braked arms are read against a yardstick that pays the same costs. Idle cash earns nothing here, so every braked return is a floor. Success: the fall lands under 50% on dev and ideally near 25%, the funded return keeps at least half of the ungated book's +2.4 point lead, AND the residual correlation against all four test-failed books stays under 0.85 -- which would be the first book in this lab that is dev-eligible, survives the dead companies and is behaviourally free at the same time. The kin reading is taken first, off the recorded curves, before any analysis is written, and per variant rather than on the best twin alone.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that a book-reading brake is a market-reading brake wearing different clothes. This book's own worst fall IS 2008, and 2008 is when every other book in this lab was falling too, so a drawdown brake will go to cash in 2008 and 2001-2002 and sit out the same months the 200-day switch sits out -- and the kin rule compares monthly returns less their own fit on SPY, which is exactly where that shows up. The honest shape of that outcome is a braked arm that passes the drawdown screen and then reads 0.85 or higher against M0002-REL-85 anyway, which would say something sharper than this method set out to ask: that the kin bar is a bar on de-risking in crashes rather than on reading the market, and that no brake of any kind can rescue this ranking. The volatility arms are the better bet on that axis, because a 63-day volatility target scales continuously and in both small and large moves rather than switching around the famous falls -- but they are the worse bet on the fall, because the 2008 drawdown arrived with a volatility rise the estimate sees only after the first leg. The second failure is the one M0109 measured and named: a drawdown brake sells after the fall has happened and buys back after the recovery has happened, so on this lab's measured pattern it should cost 1 to 3 points a year while improving the fall by less, and a V-shaped drop -- 1998, 2010, 2011, the second half of 2008's rebound -- trims on the way down and is still trimmed on the way up. On a book whose whole claim is a +7.7 point lead over 2009-2015, paying that in the recovery is how the edge dies. The third is survivorship: M0110's asymmetry arm lost 2.0 points a year on the fuller price history, more than any arm except the control, so part of this edge is companies the dev store cannot price, and a dev-only verdict here is provisional whatever it says.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0149 — can a book be made safe by watching its own account instead of the market?

## Why this one mattered

Of everything this lab holds, one book earns its keep and is also, by the lab's own behaviour
test, nothing like the books that have already failed out of sample. It picks the forty companies
that rise most on the market's good days relative to how much of the bad days they join in, holds
them in equal amounts, and — this is the part that matters — has **no safety switch at all**. It
does not go to cash when the market turns. On the owner's real plan it earned **9.6% a year**
against **7.2%** for the same money put into an S&P 500 fund.

Its one defect is that it is terrifying to hold. At its worst it was down **69%**, and 2008 cost
it half its value. The owner's limit for real money is a 25% fall.

The obvious repair is the one that closed this line of work before: put the market switch back in
front of it. That fails for a reason that is not about returns. Every book in this lab that reads
the market steps aside in the *same handful of months* as every other book that reads the market
— and the lab's behaviour rule measures exactly that and refuses it. The gated twin of this very
book reads 0.90 against a book that has already failed, and is refused.

So this method asked a different question. **Can the fall be cut by a brake that watches the
book's own falling account rather than the market's trend — and does such a brake stay clear of
the failed books?**

Six versions were run, all on the same picks, the same monthly clock, fractional shares,
Gotrade's real fees and the owner's real plan (10 million rupiah to open, 5 million on the 25th
of each month, 237 deposits):

- **the control** — neither brake, so the five others can be read against a yardstick paying the
  same costs;
- **the hard drawdown brake** — sell down towards cash in a straight line, fully in cash once the
  book is 15% below its own one-year high;
- **the gentle drawdown brake** — the same dial, fully in cash only at 25% down;
- **the tight volatility dial** — hold less whenever the book's own last three months have been
  choppier than 14% a year;
- **the loose volatility dial** — the same, set at 16%;
- **both together** — the gentle drawdown brake and the tight volatility dial.

Neither brake looks at the market. Both read only this book's own path.

---

## 1. The behaviour reading — taken first, and taken per version

This was measured **before a word of this analysis was written**, and it was measured **on each
version's own curve**, not on the method's best-matching one. That distinction has bitten this lab
before: the summary figure keeps only the single worst-matching version per failed book, which
reads a dangerous version as clean and simultaneously hands every other version a refusal that was
never calculated for it.

All twenty-four numbers. The limit is 0.85; higher means "moves too much like a book that has
already failed".

| version | failed book 1 | failed book 2 | failed book 3 | failed book 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| control, no brake | 0.5689 | 0.3592 | 0.3714 | 0.3429 |
| hard drawdown brake | 0.7360 | 0.6248 | 0.7045 | 0.6310 |
| gentle drawdown brake | 0.7612 | 0.6271 | 0.6918 | 0.6311 |
| tight volatility dial | 0.7270 | 0.5543 | 0.6424 | 0.5629 |
| loose volatility dial | 0.7259 | 0.5488 | 0.6306 | 0.5543 |
| both together | 0.7502 | 0.6361 | 0.7338 | 0.6475 |

**No pair reaches 0.85. The answer to the method's question is yes: a brake that reads the account
does not make the book a relative of the failed books, where a brake that reads the market does.**
That is a real finding and it is the only unambiguously good news here.

But read the columns, not just the verdict. Every brake **moves the book towards** the failed
books, and the move is large. Against the second and fourth failed books the unbraked control
reads 0.36 and 0.34, and the drawdown-braked versions read 0.62 and 0.63 — close to double. The
volatility dials move it less than the drawdown dials do, which fits: a volatility dial scales
continuously in small moves as well as large ones, where a drawdown dial mostly acts around the
famous falls, which is when every other book is acting too.

So the honest statement is not "the brake is invisible to the behaviour rule". It is: **braking on
your own account pushes you a long way towards the failed books' calendar, and simply does not push
you far enough to be refused.** A harder brake than any run here would be worth re-measuring rather
than assuming.

---

## 2. What it cost, and what it bought

| version | your money earned, a year | the same money in an S&P 500 fund | worst fall | 2008 | share of the account actually invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| control, no brake | **+9.9%** | +7.2% | **68.7%** | −50.3% | 97.7% |
| hard drawdown brake | +5.9% | +7.2% | **20.8%** | −14.8% | 57.9% |
| gentle drawdown brake | +7.5% | +7.2% | **25.1%** | −20.6% | 68.7% |
| tight volatility dial | +8.2% | +7.2% | 29.6% | −23.1% | 72.3% |
| loose volatility dial | **+9.2%** | +7.2% | 33.2% | −26.1% | 78.6% |
| both together | +6.3% | +7.2% | **19.3%** | −12.2% | 56.1% |

Every brake works. Every one of them cuts the fall from the catastrophic to the survivable — the
worst case drops from 69% to between 19% and 33%, and 2008 goes from losing half the account to
losing between 7% and 26%. Measured against risk taken, every braked version is roughly **twice**
the control: the control returns 0.14 of its own worst fall per year and the braked versions
return 0.28 to 0.32.

And every brake is paid for out of the return. The book's whole lead over the market is **+2.7
points a year**. The method set itself the condition that a brake must keep **at least half** of
that. Exactly one version does: the loose volatility dial, keeping +2.0 of the +2.7 — and its
worst fall is 33%, well outside the owner's 25% limit. Every version that brings the fall inside
25% keeps almost none of the lead, and the two deepest brakes **lose to the index outright**.

**There is no version here that is both safe enough and still worth owning.** The two requirements
pull against each other across the whole set, and nothing in between them was missed: the ladder
from 19% to 33% of fall maps almost monotonically onto the ladder from +6.3% to +9.9% of return.

The fifth column is why. An arm that passes the fall test at 56% invested passed it **by being
nearly half in cash**, not by holding better companies.

---

## 3. Where the money went — and it went exactly where it was predicted to

This was written down before the run as the likeliest failure, and it is what happened.

What the account multiplied by from the end of 2008 to the end of the window — the stretch this
whole ranking exists to capture, with the same deposits paid into every version:

| version | account over 2009 – 2015 | a year |
|---|---|---|
| control, no brake | 4.08× | +23.0% |
| loose volatility dial | 3.06× | +17.9% |
| tight volatility dial | 2.83× | +16.6% |
| gentle drawdown brake | 2.54× | +14.7% |
| both together | 2.33× | +13.3% |
| hard drawdown brake | 2.29× | +12.9% |

The brake does not pay for itself in the crash. It pays for itself in the crash and then **charges
for it again in the recovery**. A drawdown brake sells after the fall has already happened and buys
back after the rebound has already happened, so 2008 is survived and 2009 is missed. The hard
drawdown brake turned a 23%-a-year recovery into a 13%-a-year one.

That is not a flaw in how this was built. It is the mechanism working as designed, and it is the
same thing this lab measured the last time it tried a drawdown brake. The number to keep is the
size: **ten points a year of the recovery**, to save forty points of the crash.

---

## 4. Two checks that came out clean

**The yardstick is honest.** The control version was run so the five braked ones could be compared
against something paying identical costs on an identical clock, because the clock had to change —
under the old rule a forty-company book never actually executes a small trim, so a dial would have
behaved as an on/off switch and a null result would have been unreadable. The control earned
**+9.9%** where the book it is standing in for recorded **+9.6%**, with the worst fall 68.7%
against 69.1%. That is under a third of a point. **The clock change cost this book nothing**, so
every comparison above is between brakes and not between tapes.

**Nothing here is a selection.** All six versions failed the luck bar (0.51 to 0.67 against a
required 0.90, at 95 recorded attempts), and the book lost all four of the lab's walk-forward
periods. Even the best-looking row above is not a result this lab would act on.

---

## 5. What must be said against these numbers

- **Idle cash earned nothing.** A braked book holds a lot of cash, and this simulation pays no
  interest on it, because it has not been verified that the broker pays any. Every braked return
  above is therefore a **floor**, not an estimate. A real account earning something on its waiting
  money would do better — most of all in the versions that sat half in cash.
- **The brake watches a clean copy of the book, not the real account.** It rebuilds this same
  ranking from prices, without fees, deposits or cash, and asks how far *that* is below its own
  one-year high. This is deliberate: a brake reading its own braked account can never recover,
  because once it is in cash it has no fall left to heal from, and it would have sat out
  2009–2015 entirely. The cost of the choice is that the clean copy ranks every company in our
  price history rather than only those in the index that day, so it is slightly broader than the
  real book. It is a signal, not an accounting.
- **The price history cannot see the companies that died.** This was measured only on our usual
  history, which cannot price the companies that went bankrupt or were bought. The last time this
  same ranking was checked against the fuller history it lost **2.0 points a year** — more than
  almost anything else in the lab. **Every number above is provisional in that direction, and the
  control's 69% fall is more likely to be worse on the honest tape than better.**

---

## What this changes

The question was worth asking and it has a clean answer, which is more than most weeks produce.
**Braking on your own account genuinely does escape the behaviour rule that closed this book's
gated twin.** That is a real, reusable fact about how to rescue a violent strategy, and it was not
known before today.

It is also not enough. The brake buys safety at very close to the full price of the edge, and on
this book there is no setting where the two meet. The direction worth remembering is that the
**volatility dial dominated the drawdown dial on every axis at once** — it kept more of the
return, it moved the book less towards the failed books, and it gave up less of the recovery. If
this line is ever reopened, it should be reopened on volatility and not on drawdown.
methods.verdict: A brake that watches the account's own fall does escape the behaviour rule that closed this book's gated twin — all six versions stay clear of every book that has already failed — but it cannot buy the safety without the return: every version that brings the worst fall inside the owner's 25% limit gives up nearly all of the book's 2.7-point lead, because it sells after the 2008 fall and is still sold through the 2009 recovery, which cost ten points a year.

methods.name: Rank on temperament, but only among companies momentum is NOT buying
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0133 (gated up/down participation spread), barring momentum's own top names from the pool before ranking; reserved by Sera batch 20261016-2004
methods.hypothesis: Measured 2026-10-14: the asymmetry rank and the plain 12-month momentum rank share only 18.7% of their 40 names month by month, against 15.3% expected if the two rankings were unrelated -- they already pick almost entirely different companies out of the same ~262-name screened pool. Yet the two books move together at 0.90 after the market's own move is taken out, which is what refuses the whole line. If the resemblance is carried by a minority of shared names rather than by the ranking itself, explicitly excluding them should break it at little cost. This method ranks on the same up-minus-down participation spread (M0133's code, imported) but first drops, each month, every company inside momentum's own top N on F4's 12-1 column: N=40 (headline, 40 names, paired with M0133-G40), N=20 (the failed M0002-REL-85's own book size), N=80 (about a third of the pool, the dose-response arm), and N=40 on M0133's best arm (20 names, positive-quarter buy-back). The exclusion is point-in-time from the same rows the book already builds. Every variant is gated, so the comparison against M0133 is the exclusion alone. Success: return and fall stay close to M0133-G40's (+13.5% a year funded, 21.6% fall) while the residual correlation against M0002-REL-85 drops under 0.85. The up/down capture measure is an old practitioner tool, not a dated academic publication; publication risk is low.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest outcome is that the correlation barely moves. M0146 already showed the overlap is only 3.4 points above chance and that random 40-name books behind the same gate read at most 0.70 against the failed book, so the resemblance is probably carried by the temperament of the companies -- high-participation names that run with the market and give it back -- not by which ones. If X80-G40 still reads at or above 0.85, that is proven: nothing left is a momentum name, and no selection rule of this shape can be behaviourally free behind a market switch; the asymmetry-behind-a-switch line should then close for good. The second failure is cost: momentum's top names carry much of any trending book's return, so barring them may lower return and, if the remaining high-participation names are the laggards with high beta, deepen the fall. Third, survivorship: M0110's asymmetry arm lost 2.0 points a year on the fuller price history, so any dev pass is provisional. Fourth, the 2009-2015 stretch: the gate itself loses 6-11 points a year to SPY there, and removing the strongest names makes the book lean on the recovery even harder.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

# Barring momentum's own favourites: the resemblance goes, and the return goes with it

## What this run asked

The asymmetry book (rank companies on how much of the market's good days they join in, minus how
much of its bad days, and step out whenever the market closes below its 200-day average) is the
best-shaped book the lab has. Its 40-name version earned **13.5% a year** on the owner's deposits
against **7.2%** for the same money in the market, with a worst fall of 21.6%. It was refused for
one reason: month by month, once the market's own move is taken out, it moves with a momentum book
that already failed its out-of-sample look. The reading was **0.8964** against a limit of 0.85.

Two stories fitted that. Either the resemblance came from the **minority of companies both books
hold** (the overlap), or it came from the **kind of company** the asymmetry rank likes, whichever
names it actually buys (the temperament). Two days ago I bet on temperament. This run tested it
directly: each month, take out every company inside momentum's own top 20, 40 or 80, and only
then rank the rest on the asymmetry. Everything else is the parent's code, unchanged. Four
versions, all behind the market switch, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's real
plan (10 million rupiah to open, 5 million on the 25th of each month, 237 deposits).

## The result

The worst fall takes the deposits out first. **The market fell 55.2% over this window and earned
7.2% a year on the same deposits.**

| Book | Your money earned | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Luck score (needs 0.90) | Resemblance to failed momentum book (limit 0.85) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parent, 40 names, nothing barred | **+13.5%** | 21.6% | 2.63 | 0.922 | **0.896** (refused) |
| 40 names, momentum's top 20 barred | +10.3% | **21.7%** | 1.83 | 0.841 | 0.551 (worst pair 0.814 against the calm-stock blend) |
| 40 names, momentum's top 40 barred | +10.1% | 25.5% | 1.83 | 0.833 | 0.447 |
| 40 names, momentum's top 80 barred | +7.7% | 36.4% | 1.58 | 0.623 | 0.280 |
| 20 names, top 40 barred, back in on a positive quarter | +11.7% | 23.3% | 1.70 | 0.821 | 0.395 |

All four beat the market on the owner's money. **None passed**: every one failed the luck test
(DSR, the chance the result is real rather than the best of many tries) at N = 101 distinct
methods, against the 0.90 bar. The best, 0.841, is the narrow bar on the top 20. The period by
period check won only 2 of 4: the book beat the market in 2003-2005 and 2006-2008, and **lost in
2009-2011 (+44.5% against +60.8%) and 2012-2014 (+62.9% against +65.9%)**. Those are the years
most like today.

Worst years were mild: 1998 at -7.7% for the top-40 bar, 2015 at -2.6% for the top-20 bar.

## Was it luck?

At 101 methods tried, a book needs a luck score of 0.90 to count. The parent cleared it at 0.922.
Taking out momentum's favourites dropped every version to 0.82-0.84, and the widest bar to 0.62.
These are not near misses on the luck test: the return per unit of risk fell, and the same N
judges it harder.

## Why: the expected failure did not happen, and something more useful did

My written expectation was that the resemblance would barely move, because it lived in the
temperament of the companies. **That was wrong.** Barring just momentum's top 20 cut the reading
against the failed momentum book from 0.90 to 0.55. Barring the top 40 cut it to 0.45, and the top
80 to 0.28. Every version is clean against all four failed books. The resemblance **was the
overlap**: the 3-4 points of shared names above chance were enough to make the two books move
together.

But the same names carried the return. The parent's 13.5% a year becomes 10.1-10.3% once those
names are gone, and gains per dollar lost drop from 2.63 to 1.83. The more is barred, the worse
it gets: the top-80 bar is barely above the market and falls 36%. So the asymmetry rank does not
hold a separate edge that happened to sit next to momentum. **Its edge was largely momentum's
edge, earned through the handful of companies that rank high on both.** Take momentum out and
what remains is a weaker book that loses to the market after 2009, like most of this lab.

That is a cleaner answer than either story I started with. The resemblance and the money come
from the same place, so this ranking cannot keep one without the other.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis** (resemblance carried by shared names, removable at little cost): half right. It
  was carried by the shared names; it was not cheap. The cost was 3.2-3.4 points a year and the
  luck test.
- **Expected failure** (correlation barely moves): did not happen. The second expected failure
  (barring momentum's top names lowers return and deepens the fall) did happen, most clearly on
  the widest bar.
- Survivorship was not checked: nothing here is eligible, so the check store would answer a
  question no promotion depends on.

## Against the parent and near misses

The parent M0133-G40 ran at the same real fees, same deposits and same switch, so the comparison
is direct: the only difference is the bar. The gap is the price of the overlap. The top-20 bar
holds the parent's fall almost exactly (21.7% against 21.6%) and is the closest of the four. It
is still 0.06 short on luck and lost both of the recent folds.

**My opinion:** This direction is finished as a way to rescue the asymmetry book. It answered its
question cleanly. Barring momentum's names does make the book behaviourally free, and it also
takes away the return, because the two were the same thing. Another bar size, or a softer
version that down-weights instead of removing, would only trace the line between "looks like
momentum and earns" and "looks like nothing and earns little". I would not spend more than one
more id here. The one worth trying is the top-20 bar at 40 names with the positive-quarter
buy-back, because the buy-back added 1.6 points a year on the 20-name arm at a similar fall, and
1.6 points is roughly what the top-20 version lacks on luck. I expect it to fail the 2009-2014
folds anyway. The larger lesson for the lab: a resemblance reading against a failed book can come
from a small number of shared names, and when it does, those names are usually where the money is.
methods.verdict: Barring momentum's favourite companies does free the asymmetry book from its resemblance to the failed momentum book, but those same companies carried its return: it drops from 13.5% to about 10% a year, fails the luck test and loses to the market after 2009.

methods.name: Is the survivorship drawdown penalty just book width? Test it against the committed 102-variant grid
methods.hypothesis: M0147 measured nine width pairs across two picking families on both stores and found the dev-store understatement of the worst fall lines up with book width almost monotonically: +6.7 and +5.3 points at 20 and 30 names (gated asymmetry), +4.4 at 20 names (residual momentum), +1.6 and +0.5 at 40 and 35, and 0.0 to -0.7 at 50, 55 and 70. D16's own note says the opposite about the wider record -- across the 102 variants in docs/lab/survivorship/grid.csv the per-variant delta ran -9.03 to +14.44 points, mean +1.42, and 'no single haircut can stand in for the measurement', which is why the rule reads recorded numbers one at a time and treats absence as silence. Both can be true: a haircut that is CONSTANT cannot stand in, while a haircut that is a FUNCTION OF WIDTH might. This idea tests that directly and cheaply. The grid is committed, needs no store, no network and no research data; the number of names each variant holds is recoverable from its method file's params (FactorParams.top, ResidParams.inner.top, the blend weights' underlying tops) rather than from its id string, which is unreliable. Regress the per-variant drawdown delta on book width -- and on the obvious confounders the grid already carries, trades (turnover), profit factor and whether the variant carries the SPY 200-day gate, since M0147's control showed the gate is what hides width's benefit on dev. Success: width explains a large share of the spread and yields a usable correction, e.g. 'add 5 points at 20 names, 1 at 40, 0 at 55', which would let the lab correct a width decision WITHOUT owning the check store -- it is not on every machine and cannot be rebuilt offline, which is exactly why D16 had to read silence as silence. If it holds, propose it as an argued commit to hardgate.py, never as an override. Failure: width explains little, the spread is dominated by something else (single-name concentration, sector, turnover), and the honest conclusion is that M0147's nine pairs were a property of two picking rules and the per-variant measurement stays the only valid route -- which is itself worth knowing before another method reasons from a width correction that does not generalise. Report only: this spends no look and needs no new trial unless the regression suggests a width rung nobody has run.

methods.name: How wide should the roster be? The rungs between twenty and fifty, on both price histories
methods.sourceRef: M0147 for the mechanism, the paired-curve method and the finding that the dev store is blind to what width protects against; M0139 for the 35/50/70 rungs on this engine and for the finding that width's return decay is signal and not fees; M0128-RAW20 (trial #388) for the 20-name rung, which is the roster's own book at real fees on the fixed tape; docs/lab/survivorship/width-curve-cross-family-2026-10-14.csv for the recorded check-store readings of all four
methods.hypothesis: A measurement whose output is a number the owner will act on with real money, not a candidate. The paper roster holds twenty names and the owner mirrors it. Traded the way he actually trades it -- fractional shares, Gotrade's real fee schedule, the fixed top-up band, his 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposit -- that book falls 20.65% on the dev store and 25.05% on the survivorship-check store, against a real-money bar of 25%. The same picking rule at 35 names falls 20.11% on the check store and earns 0.13 of a point a year MORE there than the 20-name book does, so on the honest history that widening is not even a trade-off. Every one of those five points of protection arrives somewhere between 20 and 35 names and the lab has never run a single rung inside that interval. This method buys three: 25, 30 and 45 names, M0007-N20-RAW's picks verbatim with only the slot count moved, on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, funded on the owner's plan against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days. Then lab survivorship re-reads all three on the check store -- report only, no trial, no look -- and the seven rungs are reported as ONE PAIRED CURVE, dev beside check at every width, with the return cost beside the fall at every width. WHAT IS PREDICTED, in numbers, before any result. (1) THE DEV CURVE IS FLAT AND SAYS NOTHING. All three new dev-store falls should land inside 19.3% to 21.0%, indistinguishable from the recorded 20.65 / 19.60 / 20.70 / 19.89 and with no reliable ordering in width. If the dev curve alone were the evidence, this method would conclude that width is free to skip -- which is precisely the error the roster's twenty was built on. (2) THE CHECK CURVE FALLS STEEPLY AND MONOTONICALLY ACROSS THE NEW RUNGS. Predicted check-store worst falls: about 23.5% at 25 names (range 22.0-24.5), about 21.5% at 30 (range 20.3-22.8), about 20.0% at 45 (range 19.5-20.6). Equivalently the paired gap between the histories should fall from +4.4 points at 20 names to about +2.5 at 25, +1.2 at 30 and under +0.5 by 45, closing on the same schedule M0147's asymmetry book showed (+6.7, +5.3, +1.6, +0.2, -0.3 at 20/30/40/55/70). (3) THE RETURN COST IS SMALL UNTIL ABOUT 40 NAMES AND THEN IS NOT. Dev funded return is predicted at 13.3-13.6%/yr at 25 names, 13.0-13.4 at 30 and 11.6-12.4 at 45, against the recorded 13.68 at 20; check-store funded return at 11.9-12.3, 12.0-12.3 and 11.8-12.2 against the recorded 11.98 at 20. The prediction with the sharpest edge on it: ON THE CHECK STORE, 30 NAMES COSTS NOTHING AT ALL -- its funded return lands within 0.3 of a point of the 20-name book's and quite possibly above it, while its worst fall is 3 to 4 points gentler. If that holds, the owner is not being asked to trade return for safety at all; he is being asked to stop paying for a concentration that only looked profitable on a tape with the failures removed. (4) THE DECISION RULE, fixed now so the result cannot choose it. The recommended width is THE NARROWEST RUNG WHOSE CHECK-STORE WORST FALL IS AT OR UNDER 23.0% -- the owner's 25% bar less a 2-point cushion, because the check store is a cross-check and not truth and a recommendation resting on a tenth of a point of margin is not a recommendation -- PROVIDED its check-store funded return is within 1.0 point a year of the 20-name book's 11.98%. If no rung satisfies both, the recommendation is the rung with the best check-store MAR and the verdict says plainly that the owner is being asked to buy safety with return. Predicted answer: 30 names, at no return cost on the check store and about 0.4 of a point a year on the dev store. (5) WHEN, NOT ONLY HOW FAR. The survivorship report gives the size of the worst fall and never its date, so 'the five points is one bad year' cannot be excluded from its rows alone. This method will bound it directly: the de-funded equity curve of every arm on both stores is available in process, so the trough date and the peak date of each maximum fall will be computed and reported beside it, and the 2009-2015 era lead will be read in the same table. The prediction is that every worst fall on both stores is dated inside 2008-2009 and that the check store's extra depth at 20 names is dated there too -- the gate is off through most of that stretch but not all of it, and single-name collapses cluster in exactly those months. If the trough dates diverge between stores, or if a check-store trough lands in 2011 or 2015 where the dev store's does not, that is a finding in its own right and leads the verdict. (6) MOM-FR-GT (M0002-REL-85), the roster's OTHER book, has no survivorship row at all and has never been checked this way. Not fixable inside this method id; it will be named in the verdict and queued as the next idea, because the owner should learn it here rather than discover it later. ELIGIBILITY IS NOT THE POINT AND PROMOTION IS REFUSED. Some or all of these arms will likely read ELIGIBLE against the dev screen, as M0139's three did. The line runs through M0007, which is test-failed, so hard gate (K) refuses promotion on kin whatever they score. Accepted before the run. Any eligible arm is a by-product and must not be reported as a near miss or as a roster candidate.
methods.expectedFailure: The failure that would matter most is the one that leaves the owner where he started: THE CHECK CURVE IS A CLIFF, NOT A SLOPE. If 25 and 30 names both read near 25% on the check store and only 35 drops to 20%, then the five points arrive all at once somewhere the lab still cannot see, the three rungs priced nothing, and the honest answer is '35 names, because that is the narrowest width anyone has actually measured inside the bar'. That outcome must be stated first and plainly rather than dressed up as precision. It is still worth the id -- 35 would then be a measured recommendation instead of an extrapolated one -- but it is a worse result than the one predicted and the verdict must say so. Specific failures written now. (1) THE CURVE COULD RUN THE WRONG WAY. A wider book owns more of the shortlist and therefore more of the companies the dev store cannot price, so the check store could punish width instead of rewarding it, as it did to M0123's all-shortlist basket. A check-store fall that RISES from 25 to 45 names would mean width concentrates survivorship exposure rather than diluting single-name risk, and would be a stronger argument for keeping twenty names than any dev number -- and the verdict would have to carry it. (2) ONE ERA COULD BE DOING ALL THE WORK, and this is the named hole M0147 left open. If every arm's worst fall is dated 2008-2009 and the 2009-2015 era leads are flat across width, then this is a measurement of one crisis dressed as a measurement of width, and the owner is being advised on the basis of a single autumn. The trough dates are computed precisely so that this cannot be glossed over; if the answer is 'one crisis', the verdict leads with it and the recommendation is downgraded to a hedge rather than a number. (3) REPRODUCTION FIRST. lab survivorship prints a dev re-run beside the recorded trial. Any arm whose dev re-run does not match its recorded trial has a meaningless side-by-side and must be dropped from the curve rather than quoted. (4) THE 45-NAME ARM MAY COST MORE THAN THE 50-NAME ARM APPEARS TO. The recorded 50-name dev return (11.33%) is 1.7 points below the 35-name arm's, so the decay between 35 and 50 is steep; 45 is predicted near the bottom of that slide and its only job is to price it. If 45 reads better than 35 on both stores the recorded 50-name rung becomes the anomaly and must be re-examined, not quietly dropped. (5) FEES AND FILL AT THE WIDE END. This account ramps from 10,000,000 IDR, so a 45-name book holds slots near 28 USD in its early years, where Gotrade's schedule is a far larger share of the order. M0139 found the total bill falls with width in this family, but that was measured at 35, 50 and 70, not at 25; the trade counts are quoted so the claim stays checkable. (6) THE CHECK STORE IS NOT TRUTH, and a recommendation that depends on the difference between 23.0% and 25.0% on it is a recommendation that depends on which data errors somebody chose to clean. That is why the decision rule asks for a 2-point cushion; if the chosen rung clears 23.0% by less than half a point, the verdict must say the margin is inside the cross-check's own uncertainty and recommend the next rung out. (7) DEPOSITS SOFTEN EVERY WORST FALL HERE ALIKE and no figure may be lined up against an unfunded trial. (8) THE RECOMMENDATION IS ABOUT WIDTH AND NOT ABOUT WHETHER TO HOLD THIS BOOK AT ALL. M0007 is test-failed and so is this book's lineage; nothing here says the roster's picking rule works. It says only that IF the owner holds it, holding it in twenty slots is the worst of the available widths on the only history that contains the failures.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

# M0152 — how many stocks should the account hold? And the surprise about *when* it gets hurt

## The short answer

**Thirty-five.** Not twenty, which is what the paper account holds today and what the owner
mirrors with his own money.

Holding thirty-five of the same stocks instead of twenty, picked by exactly the same rule on
exactly the same days, would have made the worst fall **five points gentler** — 25.1% down to
20.1% — on the price history that includes the companies that went bankrupt. And it would have
done that for **no cost at all**: on that same history the thirty-five-name version earned
slightly *more* per year, 12.1% against 12.0%. On the narrower history the lab normally uses it
gives up about six-tenths of a point a year, 13.7% to 13.1%.

The owner's own limit is a 25% fall. Twenty names comes in at 25.1% — a tenth of a point outside
it. Thirty-five comes in at 20.1%, with five points to spare.

Everything below is how that was measured, what was predicted beforehand and got it wrong, and
the one thing about this answer that should make the owner cautious.

---

## What was actually run

The account's picking rule was left completely alone. Same screen, same ranking (which stocks
rose most beyond what the market alone explains, over the last year), same rule of selling
everything whenever the market index closes below its own 200-day average, same fractional
shares, same real Gotrade fees, same 10,000,000 rupiah opening and 5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th
of every month, against a plain market index fed the identical deposits on the identical days.

**One number moved: how many stocks the account holds.** The lab already had 20, 35, 50 and 70
on record. This method bought the three rungs nobody had run — **25, 30 and 45** — because the
whole interesting part of the curve sits between 20 and 35 and there was nothing inside it.

Then all seven were re-read on the **check history**. That deserves a sentence of its own.

### The two histories, and why there are two

The history the lab normally measures on has a hole in it. It prices about half the companies
that were in the index in 1996 and three-quarters of them by 2014, and the ones it is missing are
overwhelmingly the companies that went bankrupt or got bought. It is a record of the survivors.

The check history adds most of those missing companies back, collapses included. It is not
perfect — somebody had to decide which weird prices were real crashes and which were data errors
— so it is treated as a cross-check and never as truth. But it is the only history here that
contains the thing spreading your money across more stocks is *for*.

This matters enormously for the question being asked. An account falls for one of two reasons:
the whole market drops, or one of its holdings falls apart on its own. The 200-day rule takes
care of most of the first. And a history with the bankruptcies deleted has already taken care of
the second — by not containing it. So on the usual history, holding more stocks can only ever
show you what it **costs**. It can never show you what it **saves**, because what it saves you
from is not in the file.

---

## The curve, both histories side by side

Worst fall from a peak (the account's own money, deposits stripped out so the monthly top-up
doesn't flatter it), and what it earned per year on the owner's deposit plan:

| stocks held | fall, usual history | fall, check history | difference | per year, usual | per year, check | return per unit of fall, check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **20** (today) | 20.7% | **25.1%** | +4.4 | +13.7% | +12.0% | 0.48 |
| 25 *(new)* | 20.1% | 22.0% | +1.9 | +13.1% | +11.9% | 0.54 |
| 30 *(new)* | 19.6% | 22.1% | +2.5 | +13.0% | +12.2% | 0.55 |
| **35** | 19.6% | **20.1%** | +0.5 | +13.1% | +12.1% | **0.60** |
| 45 *(new)* | 20.1% | 20.4% | +0.3 | +11.7% | +11.8% | 0.58 |
| 50 | 20.7% | 20.0% | −0.7 | +11.3% | +11.9% | 0.60 |
| 70 | 19.9% | 19.8% | −0.1 | +10.9% | +10.9% | 0.55 |

A plain index fund fed the same deposits earned **7.2% a year** on both histories.

Three things to see in that table.

1. **The usual history is useless for this question, exactly as predicted.** Look at its column:
   20.7, 20.1, 19.6, 19.6, 20.1, 20.7, 19.9. That is noise. Across a book three and a half times
   wider it moves by one point and doesn't even move in one direction. If this were the only
   evidence, the sensible conclusion would be "the number of stocks doesn't matter, keep twenty".
   **That is precisely the measurement the account's twenty was chosen on.**
2. **The check history is not noise.** 25.1 down to 19.8, five and a third points, and every rung
   from 20 to 45 is gentler than the one before it except one.
3. **The difference between the two histories is itself a function of how many stocks you hold** —
   +4.4 points at twenty, half a point by thirty-five, and nothing at all past forty-five. Once
   the money is spread widely enough, the missing bankruptcies have nothing left to take.

### Where the prediction went wrong, and it did

Written down before the run: the check-store falls would be about 23.5% at 25, 21.5% at 30 and
20.0% at 45, **declining at every step**.

Two of those three landed inside their stated ranges. The *shape* did not. The real curve is a
staircase, not a slope: three points of the protection arrive by twenty-five stocks, then
**twenty-five and thirty are identical** (22.0% and 22.1% — thirty is a hair *worse*), and the
remaining two points arrive at thirty-five. The predicted smooth decline is wrong and the
predicted best answer — thirty names — is wrong with it.

Thirty names is the one rung on this curve that buys nothing. It costs the return of a wider book
and carries the fall of a narrower one.

---

## The part that was not expected at all: *when* this account gets hurt

The previous experiment on this question left a hole it named honestly: the check-store report
says how far a book fell and never says **when**, so "the whole five points is one bad year"
could not be ruled out. That hole is now closed, by rebuilding each version's month-by-month
account value on both histories and reading off where its worst fall started and ended.

The prediction written down beforehand: every worst fall would be dated 2008–2009, the financial
crisis.

**That was completely wrong, and the truth is more useful.** Worst fall in each stretch of the
twenty years, check history:

| stocks | 1998 (Russia/LTCM) | 2000–02 (dot-com) | **spring 2006** | 2008–09 (the crisis) | 2010–15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **20** | 21.6% | 9.4% | **21.8%** | 9.1% | 9.9% |
| 25 | 19.2% | 6.7% | 18.9% | 9.3% | 10.2% |
| 30 | 19.9% | 4.3% | 18.8% | 9.5% | 10.1% |
| 35 | 19.7% | 5.0% | 16.2% | 10.1% | 10.4% |
| 45 | 19.4% | 6.5% | 15.1% | 10.0% | 11.1% |
| 50 | 18.7% | 6.6% | 14.8% | 9.7% | 10.7% |
| 70 | 18.0% | 5.1% | 12.9% | 8.2% | 10.6% |

**The two famous crashes are the account's two mildest episodes.** The dot-com collapse cost it
between 4% and 9%; the 2008 financial crisis cost it 8% to 10%. The 200-day rule did its job —
it sold everything and sat in cash while the market fell 50%.

The damage is in the two places that rule cannot reach.

**1998** is a market crash too fast for a 200-day average to react to. It costs this account about
19–21% at *every* width. More stocks barely helps, because when the whole market drops a third in
six weeks, spreading your money around spreads it across things that are all falling. **That is
the floor.** No number of stocks gets this account's worst fall much below 18%.

**Spring 2006 is the finding.** From the end of March to the end of July 2006 the market index
went from 3.71 to 3.62 — **it dipped about 2% and was back at a new high by September.** Over
those same four months the twenty-stock account lost **21.8%** of its value.

That is not a market fall. The market was fine. The 200-day rule never triggered, correctly,
because nothing was wrong with the market. What happened is that the handful of individual
companies this account happened to be holding fell apart on their own — and a large part of that
is invisible on the usual history, which shows the same four months costing 16.3% instead of
21.8%, because some of those companies are among the ones it doesn't price.

And **this is the one episode that more stocks genuinely fixes**: 21.8% at twenty, 18.9% at
twenty-five, 16.2% at thirty-five, 12.9% at seventy. Nearly nine points of protection across the
curve, against three and a half in 1998 and none at all in the crisis years.

So the mechanism is now fully named and dated:

> The account's two defences do completely different jobs. The 200-day rule protects it from the
> market, and it works — the crisis years are its *easiest* years. Holding more stocks protects it
> from its own holdings, and the only episode in twenty years where that mattered was a quiet
> spring in a rising market. Holding twenty stocks means carrying that risk undiluted, and the
> history the lab normally reads cannot see most of it.

---

## Why the recommendation is thirty-five and not twenty-five

A rule was fixed in writing before the run, so the result could not pick its own winner: *take the
narrowest book whose check-history fall is at or under 23.0% — the owner's 25% limit with two
points of cushion, because the check history is a cross-check and not gospel — provided it earns
within one point a year of what twenty names earns.*

By that rule the answer is **twenty-five names** (22.0% fall, 11.9% a year). I am not recommending
it, and here is the reason stated plainly rather than buried.

That rule contains an assumption that the data has now falsified: that a wider book *costs* you
something, so you should buy the least width that gets you to safety. Between twenty-five and
thirty-five stocks, width costs nothing. Thirty-five is better on **every** number:

| | 25 stocks | 35 stocks |
|---|---|---|
| fall, check history | 22.0% | **20.1%** |
| fall, usual history | 20.1% | **19.6%** |
| per year, check history | +11.9% | **+12.1%** |
| per year, usual history | +13.1% | 13.1% *(−0.06)* |

Choosing twenty-five would be obeying the letter of a rule whose reason for existing turned out
not to apply. Thirty-five also has the best return-per-unit-of-fall of any rung on the check
history (0.60) and ties for best on the usual one. It is not a number picked because it looked
good; it is the number that wins on each axis separately.

Past thirty-five the trade-off reappears and is real: forty-five gives up 1.4 points a year on the
usual history and buys nothing, and seventy gives up 2.8 points for nothing at all. **Thirty-five
is where the protection has arrived and the bill has not.**

### What it costs the owner to move from twenty to thirty-five

On the check history, nothing: +12.1% a year against +12.0%, with a fall five points gentler.
On the usual history, **six-tenths of a point a year** (13.7% → 13.1%) for a one-point gentler
fall. More trades — 2,548 a year-set against 1,607 — but the earlier experiment on this family
established that the total fee bill actually *falls* as the book widens, because wider positions
trade in smaller amounts and hit Gotrade's fee floor less often per dollar. The return decay
across width here is the signal getting weaker further down the ranking, not fees.

Money actually invested is **69.4% at every single width**, identical to four decimal places. None
of this is one version secretly sitting in more cash than another. The 30% is the 200-day rule
being switched off, and it is the same for all of them.

---

## Where this could be wrong, said before anyone else says it

**It rests on one episode.** Honesty requires leading with this. Almost all of the width effect is
spring 2006. One episode in twenty years is thin evidence, and the pre-registration said that if
the answer turned out to be "one era", the recommendation gets downgraded from a number to a
leaning. I am holding to that: **thirty-five is a well-founded leaning, not a proven optimum.**

What makes it more than a coin flip is that the one episode is the *ordinary* kind, not the
exceptional kind. If the width effect had lived in 2008 I would be saying "this protects you in a
crisis that may not repeat". Instead it lives in a quiet rising market — which is most years —
and the two actual crises in the window show no width effect whatsoever. The textbook reason for
spreading money around is the company that fails while everything else is fine, and that is
exactly, and only, what showed up.

**The check history is not truth.** It adds most of the missing companies, not all, and someone
made judgement calls about which strange prices were real. The recommendation leans on a gap of
five points, which is comfortably larger than those judgement calls can plausibly be worth — but
anyone treating 20.1% as a precise number is over-reading it.

**The lab's own luck test got worse, not better, on the check history.** The measure of how likely
a result is real rather than a fluke after many attempts sits at 0.910, 0.929 and 0.929 on the
usual history for 25, 30 and 45 names — above the 0.90 bar the owner set — and falls to 0.844,
0.872 and 0.901 on the check history. At the lab's current count of 94 distinct attempts, the
twenty-five and thirty-name versions would not clear the bar on the honest history. This is a
width recommendation, not evidence that the picking rule itself works.

**On that last point, loudly:** nothing here says this account's way of picking stocks is any
good. Its lineage has already failed out of sample, and this run cannot be promoted or tested
for that reason — accepted before it was run, and not a disappointment. A free check of how
closely these versions move with the books that already failed reads **0.96, 0.95 and 0.94**
against a 0.85 line, falling only slightly as the book widens. *A wider version of this account
is still the same account.* The claim here is narrow and should be read narrowly: **if** the
owner is going to hold this book, holding it in twenty slots is the worst of the available
widths on the only history that contains the failures.

**One more thing the owner should hear from me rather than find out later.** The paper roster
holds a second book — the one picked on relative strength — and it has **never been checked on
this history at all**. It has no row in the survivorship record. Whatever is true of width for
this book is simply unknown for that one. That is the next idea queued.

---

## Did the pre-registered predictions hold?

| # | Predicted | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Usual-history falls all inside 19.3–21.0%, no ordering | **Held exactly** — 20.1 / 19.6 / 20.1 |
| 2 | Check falls declining at every rung: ~23.5 / 21.5 / 20.0 | **Half wrong.** Levels landed in range; the decline is a staircase, and 30 is worse than 25 |
| 3 | 30 names costs nothing on the check history | **Held, strongly** — 12.20% against 11.98% at twenty, i.e. *more* |
| 4 | Decision rule answers "30 names" | **Wrong twice** — the rule answers 25, and 25 is dominated by 35 |
| 5 | Every worst fall dated 2008–09 | **Completely wrong**, and the most valuable error here: they are dated 1998, and the width-sensitive one is spring 2006 |
| 6 | The other roster book has never been checked | **Confirmed**, and queued |

The expected failure that came true was the one written as "one era could be doing all the work".
It did. The verdict leads with it, as promised.

---

## My opinion:

This direction is finished and should not get another method id. The curve is measured at seven
widths on two histories with the dates attached, and the answer does not get better by adding an
eighth rung — the remaining uncertainty is not about shape, it is that the whole effect rests on
one episode, and no further width experiment on this same twenty years can fix that. Spending
more ids here would be precision theatre; it would also raise the lab's attempt count and tighten
the luck bar on everything else, for nothing.

What I would actually do, in order. **First, change the roster's width from twenty to thirty-five.**
It is free on the honest history, it costs six-tenths of a point a year on the other one, and it
removes the single worst hole in the book — a hole that, on the honest history, puts the owner
outside his own 25% limit today. This is a real-money decision and the owner makes it, but if he
asks me what the evidence says, it says thirty-five without much ambiguity.

**Second, and I think more important than anything about width: check the other roster book.** The
relative-strength book has never been read on the history that contains the bankruptcies. Twenty
names of *anything* is the shape that showed up badly here, and that book is also twenty names.
It is free to check — no method id, no test look — and it is currently an unmeasured hole in a
roster the owner mirrors with real money. That is the next idea and I have queued it.

**Third, a thought worth more than another width sweep.** The most interesting number in this
whole run is that the 200-day rule reduced the 2008 crisis to a 9% dent while spring 2006 cost
twenty names 21.8%. The lab has spent a great deal of effort on market timing and almost none on
the single-holding blowup, and the measurement here says the blowup is now the larger of the two
risks *by a wide margin* for a book this narrow. Something that caps or trims a position that has
started falling alone while the market is fine would attack the one hole that both of this
account's existing defences leave wide open. I have queued that too, as a hypothesis rather than
a method, because it needs a design before it needs an id.
methods.verdict: Hold thirty-five stocks, not twenty: on the history that includes the companies that went bankrupt the worst fall drops from 25.1% to 20.1% for no loss of return at all, and the fall it removes is not a crisis but a quiet spring in 2006 when the market rose and a few holdings fell apart alone.

methods.name: The accounts-only picker, judged where the accounts exist: a learned ranker on the SEC panel alone, scored on 2012-2015 against the same ranker on price alone
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0144 (the market-state ranker); Sera batch 20261016-2004
methods.hypothesis: Four levers have been turned on the learned ranker -- capacity, target horizon, memory and market-state inputs -- and the walk-forward record was 1 or 2 of 4 folds every time. The binding constraint is the signal set: all seven signals are price and dividend arithmetic, which every participant has free. The unused asset on disk is the SEC EDGAR panel (value, quality, profitability, earnings surprise; academic roots in Fama-French 1992, Novy-Marx 2013 and Bernard-Thomas 1989, so all widely published and likely crowded by 2010). No ranker was ever registered on it because the panel starts in 2009. This method learns only where the panel exists and is scored only where its first model exists. CALENDAR, MEASURED BEFORE THE RUN: the panel describes most index members on three of four columns from the 2010-03-31 month-end (surprise fills in during 2011), so training starts there; the 252-session label means the 2011-12-30 refit holds exactly 10 labelled month-ends, so min_train_months is 10 and every arm starts picking on 2012-01-03, with 22, 34 and 46 months at the next three refits. Before the first model every arm holds plain SPY ungated, so its curve is the yardstick's own and the dev row can only differ from SPY in 2012-2015 (the contract test's 473-session smoke market rules out moving the start through the lookback). FOUR FIXED ARMS on one eleven-column cross-section, same rows, same labels, B20's tree, gated at the SPY 200-day switch once the model exists: FUND (the four account columns), PRICE (the seven price columns, the paired control), ALL (eleven), DV20 (M0131's no-model dollar-volume book on the same calendar). THE MEASURE, FIXED NOW: the recorded monthly curves, de-funded, sliced 2012-01 .. 2015-10, beside SPY's recorded curve on the same slice. THE IMPROVEMENT BAR, FIXED NOW AND HONOURED: FUND or ALL beats PRICE by at least 1.0 point a year over that slice AND in at least 3 of the 4 calendar years 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015-to-October. If it clears, the accounts carry information the price columns lack and older fundamentals become worth pricing; if not, the accounts add nothing on top of price even where they exist, and the fundamentals question is closed as M0144 closed market state. NOT PROMOTABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: a 1996 curve yields three walk-forward folds where the hard gate needs four, and only one of them is picked by a model. The whole-window row will fail the worst-fall screen on SPY's own 2008 fall. This is evidence, bought for one method look.
methods.expectedFailure: Most likely the accounts add nothing a year-ahead price ranker does not already have, and no arm clears the bar. FIRST, the sample is tiny: about 3,500 rows at the first refit and 16,000 at the last, against 57,000 for B20, and 2012-2015 is under four years -- roughly 45 monthly decisions with heavily overlapping labels -- so a 1-point gap is inside the noise of a single regime. SECOND, 2012-2015 was a steady, low-dispersion large-cap rally where SPY was hard to beat with any equal-weight 20-name book, so every arm may lose to SPY and the comparison would be between losers. THIRD, value lost money through most of the 2010s, and the published quality and profitability premia were crowded by then, so the account columns may be read and point the wrong way. FOURTH, the price arm is not B20 but B20 starved of history (M0137 found short memory hurts in a straight line), so even a FUND win would partly be PRICE being weak, which is why ALL, not FUND, is the arm that matters. FIFTH, missing filings are not random: a member with no visible filing is unusual, and the tree may learn the missingness rather than the accounts. SIXTH, the survivorship hole is smallest in these years, so that at least should not flatter it.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

# The accounts-only picker: do company accounts help where we actually have them?

**Short answer: not reliably. The bar set before the run was missed, and a book with no model at all did better than every version that used one.**

## What was tested

The lab's learned stock picker has only ever seen price and dividend signals. The lab also holds
company accounts filed with the SEC (US regulator): how cheap a stock is against its earnings and
book value, how good and how profitable the business is, and how much its latest earnings beat
expectations. Those accounts only exist from 2009, so no picker had ever used them.

This method trained the picker only on the years where the accounts exist (from March 2010) and let
it pick only from January 2012, when its first model was ready. Before that, every version simply
held SPY, so all versions are identical until 2012 and differ only in 2012-2015. Four versions ran
side by side on the same companies, the same months and the same training answers:

- **accounts only**: the four account signals
- **price only**: the seven price signals (the fair comparison)
- **both**: all eleven
- **trading-volume control**: the 20 most-traded companies, no model

All paid Gotrade's real fees, traded fractional shares and sat in cash when SPY fell below its
200-day average.

## The result over 2012 to October 2015 (deposits removed)

| | yearly growth | worst fall | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 to Oct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY | +15.8% | 8.4% | +15.9% | +32.1% | +13.3% | +0.4% |
| accounts only | +13.5% | 8.2% | +4.7% | +40.8% | +4.7% | +4.7% |
| price only | +9.5% | 15.7% | +12.2% | +27.9% | +15.5% | −15.0% |
| both | +11.5% | 9.4% | +4.0% | +33.9% | +4.7% | +3.7% |
| volume, no model | +14.1% | 10.2% | +13.7% | +33.4% | +6.4% | +2.2% |

(SPY here is the lab's recorded lump-sum SPY curve. The funded books also carry a small drag of
fees on every monthly deposit: before 2012, when every version *was* SPY, they grew about 1.2 points
a year slower than this SPY line. So the gap to SPY above is partly that drag. The gaps between the
versions are not affected; they share it exactly.)

**The bar set in advance** was: accounts-only or both must beat price-only by at least 1 point a
year **and** in at least 3 of the 4 years.

- accounts only: +4.0 points a year ahead of price only, but ahead in only 2 of 4 years (2013 and
  2015). **Missed.**
- both: +2.0 points a year ahead, also in only 2 of 4 years. **Missed.**

Both "wins" come from two moments: a strong 2013 and the price-only version's −15% in 2015. In 2012
and 2014 the accounts versions lagged badly (+4.7% against +12-15%).

## The lab's own checks (whole 1996-2015 window)

Every version failed, as expected before the run: on the owner's monthly deposits each earned
6.1%, 4.8%, 5.5% and 6.2% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits in SPY. The worst fall of 52%
is SPY's own 2008 fall, held before the model existed, so it says nothing about the picker. The luck
test (DSR, the chance a result is real after counting all 102 independent tries the lab has made)
was 0.29-0.36, far under the 0.90 bar. The walk-forward record was 1 of 4 folds, and only the fourth
(2012-14) involved a model; it lost to SPY, +43.7% against +65.9%. The method could never be
promoted (too few folds), and was run as evidence only.

## Why

- **Under four years of picks** is about 45 monthly decisions, with one-year training targets that
  overlap heavily. Two good or bad moments decide the whole comparison, which is what happened.
- **The training set was small**: about 3,500 rows at the first refit, against 57,000 for the
  older price picker. The price-only version here is that picker starved of history, so it is a
  weak comparison, and even a weak comparison was not beaten consistently.
- **2012-2015 rewarded the biggest companies.** The no-model book of the most-traded names (the
  biggest companies) beat every model. A model that is merely closest to "buy the giants" wins
  here, which is SPY's own shape.
- **Accounts signals were crowded by 2010.** Value, quality and earnings-surprise effects were
  published decades ago; value in particular lost through most of the 2010s.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The expected failure happened: the accounts add something on average, but not consistently,
and not more than simply holding the most-traded companies. The idea that they "close the
fundamentals question" mostly holds: on the free data the lab has, the accounts do not give the
picker an edge it can rely on, and **this is not a reason to buy older fundamentals data.** It is a
weak reason, though, because four years cannot settle much either way.

Compared with the parent (the market-state picker) and its line: those books also failed to beat
the volume control in 2009-2015; this one repeats that finding on new information.

**My opinion:** stop building learned stock pickers on this lab's data. Five levers have now been
turned (size, target, memory, market state, company accounts) and none beat a book that simply
holds the most-traded companies over the recent years. The repeated lesson is that the opponent is
SPY's tilt toward the largest companies, not a missing signal. The next useful question is not
another signal but a better yardstick: judge stock pickers against the equal-weight S&P as well as
SPY, so the lab can tell "picked badly" from "was smaller than the market". I would also not spend
money on older accounts data on the strength of this result.
methods.verdict: Company accounts helped the stock picker on average over 2012-2015 but only in 2 of 4 years, missing the bar set in advance; a no-model book of the most-traded companies beat every version.

methods.name: Market-state columns as changes, not levels: the one repair M0144's own failure diagnosis names, and a low ceiling
methods.hypothesis: M0144's RATE arm failed for a reason it named in its own expected_failure before running, and the failure is a column-shape problem rather than an idea problem: the ten-year yield falls from about 7% in 1996 to about 2% by 2015 and never returns, so every split the tree learned on rate LEVELS was learned in a distribution that stops existing halfway through, and every date from 2009 on falls off the bottom edge into one terminal bucket. The damage was large and one-sided -- max DD 20.0% -> 28.4% (past the 25% real-money bar), Sharpe 0.84 -> 0.73, worst year 2011 -11.7% against the control's -4.8%, 2011 being exactly when the curve was flattened into territory the model had never seen. Meanwhile the one column in M0144 that WAS stationary by construction, vix_vs_year (today's fear over the mean of its own last 252 published rows), behaved: the FEAR arm's worst fall was the shallowest in the batch at 18.1%.
