THE REPAIR IS MECHANICAL: feed every market-state column as a position within its own trailing distribution rather than as a level -- t10y_level becomes t10y_vs_year, t10y_slope becomes the slope against its own trailing mean, vix_level becomes a second normalised reading or is dropped -- which is the same transformation vix_vs_year already applies and which M0039 pre-registered for the same reason. WHY THIS IS QUEUED SECOND AND NOT FIRST, written down now so nobody mistakes it for a promising lead: M0144's primary finding is NOT that the columns were shaped wrong, it is that a market-wide reading carries at most 216 distinct values of which perhaps two or three are independent regimes, and normalising a column does not create regimes. The FEAR arm was already stationary and it was the WORST arm on the recent years by a mile (-5.2% against the control's -0.7%), which is direct evidence that fixing the shape does not fix the sample. So the honest prior is that this repairs the drawdown damage and leaves the 2009-2015 answer where it is, and the pre-registered bar must still be M0137's and M0144's -- beat the seven-feature control over 2009-2015 de-funded AND win at least 3 of 4 walk-forward folds -- which M0144 lost 1 of 4 on every single arm. SPEND THIS ID ONLY AFTER THE ACCOUNTS-ONLY PICKER (the sibling idea) HAS RUN, and only if that one finds something; if the fundamentals direction also comes back empty then the learned-ranker family should be left alone entirely rather than tidied, and this idea should be dropped rather than run. Its value if it does run is a clean negative: it would show that the market-state result was about sample size and not about column shape, which is the one alternative explanation M0144 cannot rule out on its own.

methods.name: Let go of the one holding that is falling apart on its own, while the market is fine
methods.sourceRef: M0152 for the dated hole this attacks, its seven-rung paired width curve and the 2006 episode (docs/lab/survivorship/roster-width-curve-2026-10-14.csv); M0128-RAW20 (trial #388) for the unbraked twenty-name control, which is the roster's own book at real fees on the fixed tape and is quoted here rather than re-run; M0019, M0020 and M0035 for the three per-stock and per-book exits that already failed, and which this is shaped to differ from; M0109 for the shadow-reconstruction and stand-down conventions
methods.hypothesis: M0152 dated this account's damage for the first time and found that the SPY 200-day market gate already handles market falls well -- the dot-com collapse cost this book 4-9 percent and the 2008 crisis 9 percent, its two mildest stretches in twenty years. Its two real holes are 1998, a crash too fast for a 200-day average and essentially unfixable by width (about 19-21 percent at every width from 20 to 70 names), and SPRING 2006, where the market index dipped 2 percent and recovered to a new high by September while the twenty-name book lost 21.8 percent on the survivorship-check store and 16.3 on dev. 2006 is the ONLY width-sensitive episode in the window: 21.8 / 18.9 / 18.8 / 16.2 / 15.1 / 14.8 / 12.9 across 20/25/30/35/45/50/70 names on the check store, nearly nine points, against 3.6 points in 1998 and none at all in the crisis years. So for a narrow book the single-holding blowup is now the LARGER of the two risks by a wide margin, and the lab has spent most of its ids on market timing and almost none on this. Width is one answer and M0152 priced it (35 names, five points of fall for no return cost on the check store). This asks whether a cheaper and more direct answer exists: a per-holding brake that lets go of a position which has fallen hard RELATIVE TO THE MARKET while the market itself is fine -- precisely the 2006 signature, and deliberately not a stop-loss, which M0020 already showed fires on the market falls the gate has handled. THE RULE, fixed before the run. On each monthly decision, for every ranked candidate, measure its compounded return over the last 63 sessions against the index's over the sessions they share, divide by the standard deviation of its own daily excess return over that window scaled by the square root of the window length, and act when that z-score is at or below minus k. A name with less than 80 percent of the window usable is never braked. Six arms, all on M0007-N20-RAW's picks verbatim at twenty names on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, the tape M0152's whole curve is measured on, so an arm here and a rung there differ in the brake and in nothing else: Z2 and Z2-HALF let the braked name go or cut it to half weight and leave the slot IN CASH; Z15-FILL, Z2-FILL and Z25-FILL remove the braked names from the ranking before the top twenty are taken, so the book still holds twenty names and stays fully invested; Z2-FILL-UP is Z2-FILL with the further condition that the index's own 63-session return is not negative. The unbraked control is NOT re-run: M0128-RAW20 (trial #388) is that book, recorded, funded identically at 10,000,000 IDR opening and 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th across 237 deposits, and a dedicated test module proves this allocator with the brake off is target-for-target identical to it rather than spending a trial to show the same thing. WHAT IS PREDICTED, in numbers, before any result. (1) THE BRAKE FIRES RARELY AND THE BOOK BARELY MOVES. Predicted trade count 1,650 to 1,900 against the control's 1,607 -- a handful of extra round trips a year, not dozens -- and a whole-window funded return within 1.0 point a year of the control's 13.68 percent on dev and 11.98 on the check store. If an arm trades more than 2,300 times it has become a short-horizon strategy wearing a brake's name and must be reported as one. (2) THE FILL ARMS CLOSE MORE OF 2006 THAN THE CASH ARMS, AT LESS COST. Predicted check-store 2006 fall: 16 to 19 percent for Z2-FILL against the control's 21.8 and the 35-name book's 16.2. (3) THE THRESHOLD CURVE IS MONOTONE AND SHALLOW. Z15-FILL should fire most and cost most, Z25-FILL least of both, with under 2 points of 2006 fall and under 0.5 of a point a year separating 1.5 from 2.5. A steep or non-monotone threshold curve means the result is a threshold accident and the verdict says so instead of naming a k. (4) THE DECISION RULE, FIXED NOW SO THE RESULT CANNOT CHOOSE IT. The brake is worth something only if it beats WIDTH, not only the control. An arm SUCCEEDS when, on the check store at twenty names, its 2006 fall is at or below 17.8 percent -- the control's 21.8 less the 4 points the idea asked for -- AND its funded return is within 1.0 point a year of the control's 11.98 percent. An arm is WIDTH IN DISGUISE when it reaches that 2006 number but sits on or outside the line M0152's seven rungs trace through (2006 fall, funded return) -- that is, when 35 names already gives the same pair -- and then the honest answer is 35 names and the verdict leads with it. An arm FAILS when it trades the fall away for more than a point a year, or when its 1998, 2000-02, 2008-09 and 2010-15 era falls get worse by more than they gain in 2006. (5) BOTH STORES OR IT DOES NOT COUNT. The dev store cannot price roughly 4 in 10 of the days companies spent in the index, and the ones it cannot price are overwhelmingly the companies that went bankrupt or were bought -- which is the exact event this brake exists to catch. Predicted dev-store 2006 falls: 14 to 16 percent for every arm against the control's 16.3, a difference too small to read. A dev-only result here is not weak evidence, it is no evidence, and the run on dev exists to record the trials and price the return cost, not to answer the question. (6) THE CLOCK IS A CEILING AND IS ACCEPTED BEFORE THE RUN. monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband has no resize cadence, so this brake is read once a month; the mid-month exit the idea also named is not available without leaving the curve every number here is measured against, and a feature wish is journalled for a monthly-rank weekly-resize preset on the fixed tape. PROMOTION IS NOT AVAILABLE AND IS NOT SOUGHT. This line runs through M0007, which is test-failed, so the hard gate refuses it on kin whatever it scores and the kin bar refuses the family; promotion would only be open to a brake built on a book whose ancestry is clean. Accepted before the run. Any arm that reads eligible against the dev screen is a by-product and must not be reported as a candidate or as a near miss.
methods.expectedFailure: The likely failure, and the idea named it in advance: the brake sells into noise, fires dozens of times a year at Gotrade's real fees, and gives back more in whipsaw than one episode in twenty years was worth; or it is simply width in disguise, and the honest answer stays 35 names. Four specific shapes, written now. (1) THE BRAKE IS SHORT-TERM REVERSAL WITH THE SIGN WRONG. 'Sell what has fallen most against the market over the last quarter' is the inverse of the best-documented anomaly at this horizon: short-horizon losers bounce. If that dominates, every arm trails the control by 1 to 3 points a year with a 2006 fall barely better, and the brake is a reversal bet nobody pre-registered. This is the single most likely way the method dies and it is checked first: the 2010-15 era column, where there is no episode for the brake to catch, prices the drag alone. (2) IT IS WIDTH IN DISGUISE. Dropping a name from a twenty-name book and leaving the slot in cash is holding nineteen names, and the fill arms exist precisely so that 'safer because it holds less' cannot be mistaken for 'safer because it let go of the right name'. If Z2 improves 2006 and Z2-FILL does not, the finding is about exposure, M0109 already owns that question, and this id bought nothing new. (3) ONE EPISODE IS DOING ALL THE WORK, AND IT IS THE EPISODE THE BRAKE WAS DESIGNED AGAINST. Spring 2006 is a single five-month stretch in a twenty-year window, and a rule aimed at it will improve it by construction. The result is only evidence if 1998, 2000-02, 2008-09 and 2010-15 do not get worse to pay for it, and if the dev store -- a genuinely different tape -- moves in the same direction even though it cannot see the episode. If 2006 improves and everything else degrades, the honest reading is overfitting to one spring and the verdict must lead with that rather than with the headline. (4) THE MONTHLY CLOCK MAY BE TOO SLOW TO MATTER. A name can collapse and be gone inside one month, and this brake reads once a month. If the braked names turn out to be ones the ranking would have dropped at the same session anyway, the brake changes nothing and the correct report is a null result with the overlap counted, not a thin improvement dressed up. (5) THE CHECK STORE IS A CROSS-CHECK, NOT TRUTH. It adds most of the members the dev store cannot price and not all of them, and real collapses were kept while data errors were cleaned, which is a judgement call. A 4-point claim that rests on half a point of margin is not a claim, and the verdict says so rather than rounding in its own favour. (6) DEPOSITS SOFTEN EVERY FALL IN THIS FILE ALIKE, so every figure lines up against M0128's, M0139's and M0152's, which are funded identically, and against no unfunded trial anywhere.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

WHAT WAS ASKED. Your book holds twenty names. Its worst stretch in twenty years was not a
crash: it was spring 2006, when the market dipped about two per cent and recovered to a new
high by September while your book lost nearly twenty-two per cent on the price history that
keeps the companies which went bankrupt or were bought. The market rule never fired, and it
was right not to -- nothing was wrong with the market. Something was wrong with one holding.
Holding thirty-five names instead takes more than five points off that episode. This asked
whether there was a cheaper and more direct fix: let go of a holding that is falling apart on
its own while the market is fine, and keep the narrow book.

Six versions were tried: let the name go and hold the cash, cut it to half, or swap it for the
next name down the list, at three different levels of how far behind it has to fall, and one
that also insists the market itself is rising.

WHAT HAPPENED. Nothing. Every one of the six leaves the spring-2006 fall at 21.8 per cent,
the same as doing nothing at all, to four decimal places. Five of the six are identical to the
unbraked book in every stretch measured, on both price histories. Returns moved by less than a
third of a point a year in either direction and trade counts by at most thirteen out of
sixteen hundred.

WHY, AND THIS IS THE USEFUL PART. The rule is not too cautious -- it fires constantly. On 135
of 175 monthly decisions it named at least one company, 820 names over twenty years. Your book
held eleven of them. In spring 2006 it named thirty-six companies across ten monthly decisions
and your book held none of them.

The reason is built into the shape of the book rather than into any setting. Your book ranks
every company by how it has done over the past year and buys the best twenty. This rule looks
for a company that has fallen a long way behind the market over the past three months. A
company that has fallen that far is already nowhere near the best twenty, so it was never
bought. The two rules are looking at opposite ends of the same list. The ranking had already
let these companies go, earlier and for free; the brake arrives to sell what was never owned.

That is worth knowing beyond this one experiment: a rule that watches your individual holdings
for a fall relative to the market will do almost nothing on a book that picks by past
performance, because picking by past performance already excludes the fallen. If this idea is
ever worth trying again, it belongs on a book that chooses its holdings some other way.

THE TESTS, ANSWERED ONE BY ONE, against the bar set before the run.
  Does it shrink the 2006 episode by four points? No. It does not shrink it at all.
  Does it cost more than a point a year? No. It costs nothing, because it does nothing.
  Is it really just holding fewer names in disguise? No -- it is not even that. The versions
    that hold the cash and the versions that refill the slot give the same answer.
  Did it trade one good stretch for a worse one somewhere else? No. Nothing moved anywhere.
  Is it an unintended bet that fallen companies keep falling? No. Returns are flat.
  Did it churn? No. Trade counts are within thirteen of doing nothing.
  Did the setting matter? No. All three levels give the identical 2006 number.

WHAT IT COST AND WHAT IS LEFT. Nothing was risked: this was measured on history, no money
moved, and the budget of out-of-sample looks was not touched -- it stands where it did.

The honest answer to the question that prompted this is the one already on the table: thirty-five
names. Width is still the only thing measured to help that spring, and it costs nothing in
return on the honest price history.

ONE LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY. This tape re-reads the book once a month, and a company can collapse
and be gone inside a month. A faster version would have to be measured on a different basis that
would not line up with the width numbers, so it was not attempted; a request for that faster
basis has been written down. But the monthly clock is not why this failed. It failed because the
companies it wanted to sell were not in the book on any clock.
methods.verdict: The brake fires constantly and changes nothing: it named 820 companies over twenty years and your book held eleven of them, because a book that buys the best performers of the past year never owns the companies that have just fallen furthest behind. The spring-2006 fall is unchanged to four decimal places by all six versions, so the honest answer to that episode is still to hold thirty-five names rather than twenty.

methods.name: The roster's relative-strength book, priced the way the owner trades it, at five widths
methods.sourceRef: M0152 for the question, the paired-curve method and the seven-rung curve on the roster's other book; M0002-REL-85 (trial #79) for the picking rule, which is what the paper roster entry MOM-FR-GT holds; M0128 for the banded real-fee preset; docs/lab/survivorship/roster-width-curve-2026-10-14.csv for the curve this one is read beside
methods.hypothesis: A measurement whose output is a number the owner will act on with real money, not a candidate. The paper roster holds two books and he mirrors both. M0152 measured the first at seven widths on both price histories and recommended thirty-five names. The second -- this one, momentum de-risked only when its own volatility is above its own median -- has never been read on the survivorship-check store, has no row in the committed survivorship grid, and has never been run at the fees or the share basis the owner pays. It is a twenty-name book, which is the width that came out worst in M0152. This method runs it at twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five and forty-five names on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade-tband, funded on the owner's plan against a SPY fed the identical deposits on the identical days, and then lab survivorship re-reads all five on the check store -- report only, no trial, no look -- so the two roster books can be read as two paired curves on one tape instead of one curve and a blank. THE TWENTY-NAME ARM IS THE DELIVERABLE AS MUCH AS THE CURVE IS. It is the first time this book has been priced at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares on a tape that invests the deposits, and the first time it has been read against the history that keeps the companies that went bankrupt. Whatever the width answer turns out to be, the owner ends this run knowing what half his money has actually been doing. WHAT IS PREDICTED, in numbers, before any result. (1) THE DEV CURVE SAYS NOTHING, as it did for the other book. All five dev-store worst falls land inside 17% to 23% with no reliable ordering in width. The dev store misses about four in ten of the days companies sat in the index and the ones it misses are overwhelmingly the ones that failed, so behind a market gate it is structurally blind to what width protects against and can only ever show what width costs. (2) THE CHECK CURVE FALLS WITH WIDTH, and the twenty-name arm is the one at risk. Predicted check-store worst falls: 23% to 28% at twenty names, 21% to 25% at twenty-five, 20% to 24% at thirty, 19% to 23% at thirty-five, 18% to 22% at forty-five. Equivalently the gap between the two histories should start between +2 and +6 points at twenty names and close to under +1 by forty-five, on the schedule both previously measured books showed. (3) THE RETURN COST IS SMALL BELOW ABOUT THIRTY-FIVE NAMES AND REAL ABOVE IT, as it was on both previous books: within half a point a year from twenty to thirty-five, and one to three points a year by forty-five. (4) THE DECISION RULE, FIXED NOW SO THE RESULT CANNOT CHOOSE IT. The recommended width is the narrowest rung whose check-store worst fall is at or under 23.0% -- the owner's 25% bar less a two-point cushion, because the check store is a cross-check and not truth and a recommendation resting on a tenth of a point of margin is not a recommendation -- provided its check-store return is within 1.0 point a year of the twenty-name arm's. If no rung satisfies both, the recommendation is the rung with the best check-store MAR and the verdict says plainly that the owner is being asked to buy safety with return. If the twenty-name arm itself clears 23.0%, the recommendation is TWENTY and the finding is that the two roster books differ -- which would be a genuine and reassuring result and must be reported as the primary one, not as an absence. (5) WHEN, NOT ONLY HOW FAR. The survivorship report gives the size of each worst fall and never its date, so 'the whole effect is one bad year' cannot be excluded from its rows alone. The month-end equity curve of every arm on both stores is available in process, so the peak month and the trough month of each worst fall will be computed and reported beside it, together with the worst fall inside each of 1998, the dot-com years, 2006, the financial crisis and 2010-2015. The prediction, carried over from the other book, is that the narrow arms trough in the spring of 2006 -- a 2% market dip that made a new high by September -- and the wide arms trough in 1998. If the dates instead cluster in the crises, that is a different mechanism from the one M0152 found and leads the verdict. (6) THE LIVE ROSTER ENTRY TRADES A DIFFERENT RULE SET from the one measured here: its resize band is read against equity and, measured on 2026-10-14, a band read that way never fires in a many-name book, so the monthly deposits reach the book only through turnover. The banded preset used here is the tape that invests them and is what the other book's whole curve was measured on. The size of that difference for THIS book is not measured by this method and the verdict must not pretend otherwise. ELIGIBILITY IS NOT THE POINT AND PROMOTION IS REFUSED. This line runs through M0002, which is test-failed, so the hard gate refuses promotion on kin whatever these arms score. Accepted before the run.
methods.expectedFailure: THE MOST LIKELY DISAPPOINTMENT IS A FLAT CHECK CURVE. If all five check-store falls land within a point of each other and within the bar, then width buys this book nothing, the roster's second entry needs no change, and the five rungs priced one null result. That is still worth recording -- it would be the first evidence that the two roster books carry different single-name risk, and it would mean the owner can stop worrying about half of what he holds -- but it is a thinner result than the one predicted and the verdict must say so in its first paragraph rather than dress it up. Specific failures written now. (1) THE CURVE COULD RUN THE WRONG WAY. A wider book owns more of the shortlist and therefore more of the companies the dev store cannot price, so the check store could punish width rather than reward it, as it did to M0123's all-shortlist basket. A check-store fall that RISES from twenty to forty-five names would be a stronger argument for keeping twenty than any dev number and the verdict would have to carry it. (2) THE REGIME BRAKE COULD BE DOING THE WORK WIDTH WOULD OTHERWISE DO. This book already de-risks when its own volatility is high for itself, and a single holding collapsing inside a twenty-name book raises the basket's volatility. If so, the check-store falls will be flat in width AND the twenty-name arm will spend measurably more of the window below full exposure than the forty-five-name arm does. That is a mechanism, not a null, and it is the most interesting thing this method could find -- it would say the two roster books want different widths for a reason rather than by accident. (3) ONE ERA COULD BE DOING ALL THE WORK. If every arm's worst fall is dated inside one stretch and the 2009-2015 era leads are flat across width, this is a measurement of one episode dressed as a measurement of width. The trough dates are computed precisely so this cannot be glossed over; if the answer is one episode, the verdict leads with it and the recommendation is downgraded to a leaning rather than a number. (4) REPRODUCTION FIRST. lab survivorship prints a dev re-run beside the recorded trial. Any arm whose dev re-run does not land on its recorded trial has a meaningless side-by-side and must be dropped from the curve rather than quoted. (5) FEES AND FILL AT THE WIDE END. This account ramps from 10,000,000 IDR, so a forty-five-name book holds slots near 28 USD in its early years, where Gotrade's per-order floor is a large share of the order. Trade counts are quoted so the claim stays checkable. (6) THE CHECK STORE IS NOT TRUTH, and a recommendation that turns on the difference between 23% and 25% on it turns on which data errors somebody chose to clean. If the chosen rung clears 23.0% by less than half a point, the verdict must say the margin is inside the cross-check's own uncertainty and recommend the next rung out. (7) DEPOSITS SOFTEN EVERY WORST FALL HERE ALIKE and no figure may be lined up against an unfunded trial -- M0002's own recorded trials #75 to #80 included, which is the whole reason this method exists rather than a re-read of them. (8) THE RECOMMENDATION IS ABOUT WIDTH AND NOT ABOUT WHETHER TO HOLD THIS BOOK AT ALL. M0002 is test-failed and so is this line; nothing here says the picking rule works. It says only what it costs to hold it in twenty slots rather than more.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-14

**Leave this book at twenty names.** It is the one you already hold, and on the price history
that keeps the companies that went bankrupt it is the best of the five widths tried, on both
halves of the question at once: it falls the least of any width worth having, and it earns the
most.

**Why this was worth asking.** You hold two books and you mirror both with your own money. The
other one was measured a day earlier at seven widths and the answer was to widen it from twenty
names to thirty-five. This one had never been read against the honest history at all, had never
been run at the fees you actually pay, in the fractional shares you actually buy, on the monthly
top-up you actually make. Its old runs were whole shares, a flat fee, and no deposits. So nothing
we held was a measurement of what half your money was doing. Now there is one.

**What it found.** At twenty names the book falls 20.1% on the honest history and earns 12.5% a
year against the market's 7.2%, with the same money paid in on the same days. Widening it to
forty-five names lowers the fall to 18.5% — and drops the return to 10.3%. So the whole sweep
buys about a point and a half of safety and charges about two points a year for it, on a fall
that was never near your limit to begin with. Twenty-five names is actually worse than twenty.

**Why it differs from the other book, and this is the real finding.** The two books do not fail
in the same way, and the dates say so. This book's worst month, at four of the five widths, is
August 1998 — a fall that took the whole market down at once. The other book's worst moment at
twenty names was the spring of 2006, when the market dipped two percent and made a new high by
September while a few of its holdings came apart on their own. Spreading money over more companies
protects you from one company failing by itself. It does nothing about a month when everything
falls together. The other book's worst accident is the kind width fixes; this book's is not. That
is why one of them should be widened and the other should be left alone.

You can see it directly in the one stretch where width does work here: in 2006 the fall drops from
14.3% at twenty names to 9.9% at forty-five. But 2006 was never this book's worst episode, so
curing it does not lower the worst fall — it just leaves 1998 standing on its own.

**The comparison worth remembering.** At the twenty names you already hold, this book is as safe
on the honest history as the other book becomes only after you widen it to thirty-five.

**Two things this measurement got wrong, in your favour.** Before it ran, it predicted this book
would fall between 23% and 28% at twenty names and need widening like the other one. It falls
20.1%. It also predicted widening would cost under half a point a year; it costs nearly two. It
expected to find a book in trouble that width would rescue, and found a book that is fine and that
width would make worse. Both are recorded here rather than quietly dropped.

**One reassurance and one limit.** Every width earns more on the honest history than on our usual
one, not less, and every width wins more of the four historical stretches there — the companies
our usual history cannot price were, for this book, more often bought or merged than bankrupt.
The limit: this is a question about how many companies to hold, not about whether to hold this
book at all. The line it comes from has already failed its out-of-sample test and cannot be bought
with real money on that basis; nothing measured here changes that or argues otherwise.
methods.verdict: Leave this book at twenty names: on the price history that keeps the companies that went bankrupt it falls 20.1% there against 18.5% at forty-five names, but widening costs two points a year to remove a point and a half of a fall that was never near the limit — and its worst month is a market-wide one in 1998, which holding more companies cannot help.

methods.name: Buy before the report, not after: big companies in the month they are expected to announce earnings
methods.sourceRef: Frazzini & Lamont 2007, NBER w13090 'The earnings announcement premium and trading volume'; Barber, De George, Lehavy & Trueman 2013
methods.hypothesis: Frazzini and Lamont (1972-2004, published 2007) find stocks earn a premium in the month they are EXPECTED to report earnings, largest among the biggest firms, tied to the volume surge around the report. This is a pre-event premium, not the post-report drift the event-drift family trades, and it ranks on a calendar rather than a past return, so it should not move with the failed momentum books. The store has no report calendar, so the expected month is inferred point in time from each stock's own news days (volume at least 3x its 60-day median and an open gap of at least 0.5% either way, M0063's volume measure; days within 10 sessions merged into one event). A company whose last four events sit on a quarterly rhythm (each 50-76 sessions apart) is expected to report again 252 sessions after the oldest of the four, the same quarter a year on. At each month start the book holds up to 20 of the biggest screened index members (F4's liquidity screen, ranked by 20-day dollar volume) whose expected report falls in the next 22 sessions, at 5% each, the rest parked in SPY, behind the standard SPY-200 switch, monthly in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: R20-TREND (the main rule), R20-ALWAYS (no switch: the picking alone), R40-TREND (40 slots at 2.5%), YA20-TREND (the paper's plain rule: a report in the same month a year ago, no rhythm check) and OFF20-TREND (control: the same regular reporters expected NOT to report in the coming month). Success: R20-TREND beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under the screen, beats SPY in 2009-2015, and OFF20-TREND is clearly worse than R20-TREND. Since the paper came out in 2007, 2009-2015 is judged first.
methods.expectedFailure: Barber et al.'s replication puts most of the premium in small firms, and this book holds only the biggest, where Frazzini-Lamont's own premium was perhaps half a point a month; with a quarter of the money in SPY in light months and Gotrade's fees on a full monthly turnover (a stock reports once a quarter, so most picks change every month), the excess may be a point a year or less, too small to clear the luck bar at N near 100. The inferred calendar mislabels some months (a takeover or index-add day breaks the rhythm, a report that moves a week across a month end flips the month). A month-long hold through a report adds single-name jump risk the window does not see. And the premium is published (2007), so if it shows at all it may sit before 2009 and fade. If OFF20 does as well as R20, the calendar is not what is paying.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

## What was tried

A 2007 paper (Frazzini and Lamont) found that stocks tend to rise in the month a company is *expected* to report its earnings, most of all in big companies. The lab has no calendar of report dates, so this method guessed them from each stock's own price history. A "news day" was a day when the stock traded at least 3 times its normal volume and opened at least half a percent away from the day before's close. If a company's last four news days fell roughly a quarter apart, the method expected the next report one year after the oldest of the four. Each month the book bought up to 20 of the biggest index members expected to report in the coming month, 5% each, and kept the rest in SPY. All of it sat behind the usual rule of holding nothing while SPY is under its 200-day average. It traded in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly deposits.

Five versions: the main rule (R20-TREND), the same rule always invested (R20-ALWAYS), 40 slots (R40-TREND), the paper's simpler rule of "reported in this month a year ago" with no rhythm check (YA20-TREND), and a control holding regular reporters who are *not* due next month (OFF20-TREND).

## Results (1996 to 2015, deposits included)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R20-TREND | +8.1% | +7.2% | 19.4% | 3.10 | 0.818 |
| R20-ALWAYS | +6.9% | +7.2% | 54.0% | 1.17 | 0.399 |
| R40-TREND | +8.4% | +7.2% | 18.9% | 5.35 | 0.838 |
| YA20-TREND | +9.6% | +7.2% | 28.8% | 1.37 | 0.862 |
| OFF20-TREND | +7.5% | +7.2% | 19.1% | 2.39 | 0.768 |

All five failed the luck check. DSR (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely a result is to be real skill rather than the best of many lucky tries. The lab now judges at N = 99 distinct methods, and the bar is 0.90. The best version, YA20-TREND, reached 0.862. R20-ALWAYS also lost to SPY, fell 54% at its worst (the limit is 50%) and made only 1.17 in gains for every 1 in losses (the bar is 1.3). The walk-forward check, where the method is re-picked on earlier years and scored on the next three, beat SPY in only 1 of 4 periods. The one win was 2006-2008, and that came from the 200-day switch stepping aside in the crash, not from the stock picks. In 2009-2011 the picked version made +19.5% while SPY made +60.8%. In 2012-2014 it made +60.3% against SPY's +65.9%. So it lagged SPY in the best-covered years, the first filter the lab uses.

## Why: the guessed calendar almost never fired

After the run I counted the qualifiers. The rhythm rule found on average **1.2 qualifying companies a month** out of about 268 that passed the screen. Only about a third of big companies (91 of 268) even had four news days in the last year and a half. A big company's report often moves its volume by less than 3 times, and a week's drift in the report date breaks the "quarter apart" pattern. So R20-TREND, R40-TREND and OFF20-TREND were each about 95% SPY behind the 200-day switch. That explains their low trade counts (about 220 over twenty years) and their oddly high gains-vs-losses figures: these are mostly SPY's own trips in and out of the market. Their small lead over SPY (about one point a year) is the switch's usual lead in this window. It is not evidence about earnings months. R20 and OFF20 differ by 0.6 points a year on 1-5 stocks, which is noise.

The paper's plain rule (YA20) did fire: about 46 qualifiers a month, more in January, April, July and October as real report seasons should be. Even so, March, June and December still showed 30-36, so the news-day detector also catches days that are not reports (deals, index changes, market panics). YA20 was the only version that really picked stocks: about 2,800 trades. It earned the most (+9.6% a year against +7.2%), but its worst fall was 28.8% and 2011 lost 15.4%. A month spent holding 20 companies right through their reports carries the jump risk the expected-failure note warned about.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Not testably for the main rule: the calendar was too sparse to measure the premium at all. That is a flaw in the method's design, and it is recorded as such. It is not evidence against the paper. For the paper's simpler rule there is a lead over SPY, but it came mostly before 2009 and failed the luck bar. The expected failure mostly happened: a big-company premium too small to clear the bar, calendar mislabels, and single-company report risk (YA20's 28.8% fall). The control could not separate anything because the main rule held almost nothing.

## Comparison

The closest kin is the lab's earnings-day jump book (buying after a strong report day). It ranks on what happened after the report; this method bets on the report itself. Neither cleared the luck bar. YA20's +9.6% funded lead is in line with the trend-switched stock books, with a deeper fall than most of them.

**My opinion:** the idea has not really been tested yet, because my calendar was too strict to fire. One more try is worth it, built differently: drop the four-in-a-row rhythm and the gap rule, define a news day by volume alone (2.5 times normal), and call a company "due" when it had a news day in the same calendar month a year ago **and** one about a quarter before this month. That should give 20-40 genuine candidates a month and still filter out one-off events. Add a direct control in the same run: the same big names that are *not* due. If that version cannot separate from its control in 2009-2015, I would close this family. I would not spend a second try on the strict rhythm rule.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the guessed report calendar picked about one company a month, so most versions were just SPY with the trend switch; the simpler year-ago rule earned more but failed the luck check and fell 29% at its worst

methods.name: Bounce of the stock's own surprise: short-term reversal on market-model residuals, standardised by the stock's own swing
methods.sourceRef: Blitz, Huij, Lansdorp & Verbeek 2013, Journal of Financial Markets 16(3) 477-504 'Short-term residual reversal'; Huij & Lansdorp 2017 revisit
methods.hypothesis: Published 2013, on US data to 2010, so the dev window (to 2015) is mostly before the crowd. Blitz et al. show that reversing last month's RESIDUAL return -- the part the market does not explain -- divided by the stock's own residual volatility earns about twice a plain reversal with roughly half its risk, and survives trading costs among large caps after 1990. The standardisation is the point: plain reversal buys the jumpiest fallers and so crashes with risk (the lab's unfiltered residual bounce book earned +3.5% a year on the deposits vs SPY's +7.2% and fell 35%), while a z-score ranks a calm stock that fell three of its own sigmas ahead of a wild one that fell further in percent. Book: each month, inside the liquid index-member screen and behind the SPY-200 switch, hold the 20 most negative standardised residuals over the last 21 sessions, the residual from a market-model fit on the 252 daily returns before the window (the paper fits 36 monthly returns; the lab's lookback contract forces a year of daily ones), equal slots, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly deposits. Arms: Z10-N20 uses a 10-session window (the reversal literature finds the bounce sharpest in the shortest windows); Z21-N35 holds 35 names (spreads the falling-knife risk). The control with the standardisation switched off is already recorded: the earlier bounce book's unfiltered residual variant uses the same screen, beta, 20 names, gate and fees. Success: beat total-return SPY on the deposits with a worst fall under 25%, profit factor >= 1.3, and a positive edge in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: Monthly turnover near 100% at Gotrade's minimum fees on 20 small slots eats most of a premium the paper measured at institutional costs; the earlier calm bounce book traded 16 times its size a year and kept only +0.3 points over SPY. Reversal is a liquidity-provision premium that shrank sharply after decimal ticks (2001) and is widely published, so what edge there is likely sits in 1996-2002 and is gone by 2009-2015. In crises fallers keep falling (August 1998, autumn 2008) and the 200-day switch reacts late, so the worst fall may pass 25%. Third, z-scoring leans the picks toward calm, low-beta names, which pulls the book toward a low-volatility tilt that lags SPY in strong bull years like 1998-99 and 2013. Behaviourally it should sit far from the failed momentum books; if its monthly returns still correlate at 0.6+ with them it is the long-only market tie again.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

### 2026-10-16 -- result: scaling the fall by the stock's own swing helps a little, not enough

**The idea.** Each month, buy the 20 big, easily traded index members that fell hardest last month *for their own standards*. "Fell hard" means the part of the fall the market does not explain (the residual), divided by how much that stock's residual normally swings over a year. So a calm stock that dropped three of its normal swings ranks ahead of a wild stock that dropped further in percent. The book holds cash while SPY is under its 200-day average, and trades in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits. A 2013 paper (Blitz, Huij, Lansdorp & Verbeek) found this scaled version earned about twice a plain bounce book with about half its risk.

**One assumption, written at registration.** The paper fits each stock against the market on 36 monthly returns. The lab only lets a decision read the history it declares, and declaring three years would push the whole run's start to 1997. So the fit uses the 252 daily returns before the formation month instead. That makes it the same fit as the earlier bounce book's unfiltered version (M0028-PLAIN-RESID). That version is therefore an exact control: same stocks, same 20 slots, same switch, same fees, but no scaling.

**Results on the owner's deposits** (the money-weighted return is the yearly rate a savings account would need to pay to turn the same deposits into the same final balance; SPY earned 7.2% on the same deposits):

| version | your money earned / yr | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Z21-N20 (main: one-month window, 20 names) | 3.9% | 31.4% | 1.18 | 0.31 | beats SPY, gains vs losses, luck, worst fall |
| Z10-N20 (two-week window) | 6.9% | 28.1% | 1.33 | 0.61 | beats SPY, luck, worst fall |
| Z21-N35 (35 names) | 5.7% | 27.9% | 1.28 | 0.52 | beats SPY, gains vs losses, luck, worst fall |
| control: earlier bounce book, unscaled (M0028-PLAIN-RESID) | 3.5% | 35.5% | 1.12 | -- | four conditions |

(The runner's printed fail list does not include the worst fall, because it judges the screen bar, but all three falls are above the owner's 25% real-money limit.)

**The scaling did what the paper said, at a much smaller size.** Against the exact control, the main version earned 0.4 points a year more, fell 4 points less at its worst, and its gains-vs-losses ratio rose from 1.12 to 1.18. That is the right direction on every measure. But the paper's "twice the return" became "a tenth more", and the book still earns about half of what SPY does.

**DSR at N = 100.** DSR is the chance that a result reflects real skill rather than the luckiest of many tries. The lab has now tested 100 independent ideas, and the bar is 0.90. The best version scores 0.61, far below it. None of these results can be told apart from luck, and none beats SPY in the first place.

**Worst year and when it fell.** For all three versions the worst calendar year was 2007 (−15% to −17%), when the stocks that fell kept falling: financials and homebuilders in the run-up to the crisis, before SPY's 200-day switch stepped aside. All three worst falls passed the 25% limit (28-31%).

**2009-2015, the best-measured years.** The walk-forward folds lost 2009-2011 (+40% vs SPY +61%) and 2012-2014 (+51% vs +66%). In the best-covered years, the book trails by roughly 5-7 points a year. The only fold it won was 2006-2008, and it won only because it lost less than SPY in the crash (−9% vs −25%), partly by sitting in cash behind the switch. It won 1 of 4 folds, so the promotion gate would refuse it anyway.

**Why it fails: the mechanism.** Three things work together.
1. *Fees.* The book replaces nearly all 20 names every month (about 3,000 trades in 20 years). At Gotrade's minimum fees on slots of tens of dollars, that bill takes most of a premium the paper measured at institutional costs.
2. *The market's shape.* The regime report says every version loses 6-9% in "narrow" months (when the giant companies lead) and gains 2-4% in "broad" months. Over the dev window, broad markets almost never lasted: in only 6 of 202 three-year windows did the average stock beat SPY. An equal-slot book of fallen big stocks bets against SPY's big-company drift.
3. *The falling knife.* A big one-month fall in a large company is often news (an earnings miss, a downgrade, a sector turn). That kind of fall continues rather than bounces. Scaling by the stock's own swing removes the wild stocks but not the news.

**Hypothesis check.** The hypothesis did not hold: the scaled book does not beat SPY in any version. All the expected failures happened. Fees took the premium, the edge is absent in 2009-2015, the worst fall passed 25% (in 2007 rather than 1998), and the book lagged in the narrow years. The one part that held is the direction of the scaling's effect.

**Compared with the earlier bounce book.** Its filtered version (calm half, above the 200-day average) earned 7.5% a year and fell 27%. The scaled book's best version earned 6.9% and fell 28%. The two ways of steering away from jumpy fallers end up at the same place: roughly SPY's return, with a larger fall. The two-week window doing best (6.9% vs 3.9%) fits the literature, since the bounce decays within weeks and a monthly hold catches only its tail. Turning that into a weekly re-pick would double the fee bill, which is exactly what kills this book.

**My opinion:** Rank-the-fallers reversal is finished as a standalone book in this lab. Two methods and nine versions, filtered or scaled, at real fees, never beat SPY on the deposits and always fell more than 25%. The one direction I would still try is the one the literature says separates a bounce from a slide: *why* the stock fell. A fall on quiet trading is more likely forced selling or noise that bounces. A fall on heavy volume is more likely news that continues. The store has daily volume, so this is testable. If that split does not produce a clear gap between quiet and loud fallers, I would stop spending ids on short-term reversal.
methods.verdict: Scaling last month's fall by each stock's own normal swing helped a little over the plain bounce book, but the best version still earned 6.9% a year on your deposits vs 7.2% for SPY, fell 28% at worst, and trailed SPY in 2009-2015.

methods.name: Due to report, judged loosely: big companies with a heavy-trading day in the same month last year and one a quarter ago, against the same names not due
methods.hypothesis: M0157's strict four-in-a-row rhythm qualified about 1.2 big companies a month, so its main versions measured SPY behind the 200-day switch rather than the earnings-month premium (Frazzini and Lamont 2007). Define a news day by volume alone (at least 2.5x the 60-day median, days within 10 sessions merged) and call a company due when it had a news day in the coming month's 22-session window one year earlier AND one in the window about 63 sessions earlier, which should give 20-40 genuine candidates a month and screen out one-off events. Hold up to 20 of the biggest by dollar volume, rest SPY, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, behind the SPY-200 switch; same run carries the not-due control and an always-invested version. Count qualifiers per month in the analysis before reading the returns. Judge 2009-2015 first; close the family if due and not-due do not separate there.

methods.name: The asymmetry book with momentum's top 20 barred, bought back on a positive quarter
methods.hypothesis: M0150-X20-G40 is clean on behaviour (0.55 against the failed momentum book, at most 0.81 against any failed book) and holds the parent's fall (21.7%), but earns +10.3% a year funded and DSR 0.841 at N=101, short of 0.90, and lost the 2009-2011 and 2012-2014 folds. On the 20-name arms the positive-quarter buy-back (M0113's trigger) added about 1.6 points a year at a similar fall (M0133-G20 +15.6% vs G20-UP63 +16.7%; M0150-X40-G20-UP63 +11.7%). One variant: exclude momentum's top 20, 40 names, gate sma200-up63. Success: DSR >= 0.90, fall <= 25%, kin still clean, and at least one of the two post-2009 folds won. Expected failure: the buy-back helps the whole window but not 2009-2014, where the gate itself loses to SPY, so the folds stay at 2 of 4 and the hard gate refuses promotion anyway. If it fails, close the asymmetry line.

methods.name: Quiet fallers bounce, loud fallers keep falling: one-month residual reversal only among big members whose fall came on below-normal trading volume
methods.sourceRef: Conrad, Hameed & Niden 1994, Journal of Finance 49(4) 1305-1329 'Volume and autocovariances in short-horizon individual security returns'; Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014, Management Science 60(3) 658-674 'A closer look at the short-term return reversal'
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994 (and 2014 for the news/no-news split), so the volume split was public for the whole dev window. Conrad, Hameed & Niden find that weekly losers on LOW volume reverse while losers on HIGH volume do not; Da, Liu & Schaumburg find reversal lives in the part of the fall that is not news. The standardised-residual bounce book (M0158) earned 6.9% a year on the owner's deposits with a two-week window vs SPY's 7.2%, and its worst year (2007) came from fallers that kept falling. Keeping its score exactly -- the 10-session market-model residual divided by the stock's own residual swing, the fit on the 252 sessions before the window -- and holding only names whose mean share volume over the window is below their mean over that year should remove the news-driven fallers and keep the bounces. Book: liquid index-member screen, SPY-200 switch, 20 equal fractional slots, monthly re-pick at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's deposits. Arms: QUIET-Z10-N20 (main), LOUD-Z10-N20 (the same score on the heavy-volume fallers only: the literature says it should do worst), QUIET-Z21-N20 (the one-month window, where M0158 was weakest at 3.9%, so the split's effect can be read where there was most to fix). The unsplit control is M0158-Z10-N20, already recorded on the same screen, gate, slots and fees. Assumptions: share volume, not dollar volume (the fall itself shrinks dollar volume); store volume is split-adjusted like the prices; cut at 1.0, mean against mean. Success: QUIET beats total-return SPY on the deposits with a worst fall under 25%, profit factor >= 1.3, a positive edge in 2009-2015, AND beats LOUD by at least a point a year (otherwise the split is not real).
methods.expectedFailure: The split halves a pool that was already thin, so the quiet book's 20 names are drawn from fewer and less extreme fallers and the signal weakens. Fees are unchanged: the book still turns over nearly fully each month at Gotrade's minimum fees on small slots, which took most of M0158's premium. The 1994 effect was measured on weekly returns in the 1980s, before decimal ticks (2001) narrowed the liquidity premium reversal is paid from, so whatever edge exists is likely in 1996-2002 and gone by 2009-2015. Quiet fallers are also likely to be calm, low-beta names, which leans the book toward low volatility and lags SPY's big-company drift in narrow markets (1998-99, 2013). If QUIET and LOUD earn within a point a year of each other, the volume split says nothing in this universe, and short-term reversal should be closed for this lab.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 -- result: quiet fallers beat loud fallers and edge past SPY on the twenty-year average, but lose clearly in 2009-2015

**The idea.** The earlier bounce book (M0158) bought the big index members that fell hardest over the last two weeks. "Fell hardest" meant the part of the fall the market does not explain, scaled by how much that stock normally swings. It lost to SPY, mostly because too many of its fallers kept falling. Two papers (Conrad, Hameed & Niden 1994; Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014) say *why* a stock fell matters. A fall on thin trading is more often noise or a forced seller, and it bounces back. A fall on heavy trading is more often real news, and it keeps going. So this method kept M0158's score exactly and split the fallers by trading volume. The **quiet** book holds only fallers whose average daily share volume over the fall was below their average over the year before. The **loud** book holds only those above it. Everything else is unchanged: same stock screen, same switch to cash when SPY is under its 200-day average, 20 equal fractional slots, re-picked monthly at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits.

**Assumptions written at registration.** Share volume rather than dollar volume, because the fall itself shrinks dollar volume and would make almost every faller look "quiet". The store's volume is assumed split-adjusted like its prices. The cut is 1.0: average volume during the fall divided by the average over the year. A ratio of exactly 1.0 counts on both sides. That never happens with real volume; it exists only so the lab's synthetic test market, which trades the same volume every day, can exercise both books.

**Results on the owner's deposits.** The money-weighted return is the yearly rate a savings account would need to pay to turn the same deposits into the same final balance. SPY earned 7.2% a year on the same deposits.

| version | your money earned / yr | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QUIET-Z10-N20 (main: two-week fall, quiet only) | **7.7%** | 24.3% | 1.30 | 0.896 | luck check (just) |
| LOUD-Z10-N20 (two-week fall, heavy volume only) | 6.5% | 36.8% | 1.34 | 0.44 | beats SPY, luck, worst fall |
| QUIET-Z21-N20 (one-month fall, quiet only) | 6.4% | 22.6% | 1.30 | 0.65 | beats SPY, gains vs losses (1.297), luck |
| control: M0158-Z10-N20 (two-week fall, no split) | 6.9% | 28.1% | 1.33 | 0.61 (at N=100) | beats SPY, luck, worst fall |
| control: M0158-Z21-N20 (one-month fall, no split) | 3.9% | 31.4% | 1.18 | 0.31 (at N=100) | four conditions |

**The split is real, and it points the way the papers said.** Against the same score with no split, the quiet two-week book earned 0.8 points a year more (7.7% vs 6.9%) and its worst fall shrank from 28% to 24%. The loud book did worst: 1.2 points a year behind the quiet one, and a 37% worst fall, far past the 25% limit. On the one-month window the quiet split did even more. It lifted the book from 3.9% to 6.4% a year, and the worst fall shrank from 31% to 23%. So the success test "quiet beats loud by at least a point a year" passed (+1.2). Removing the heavy-volume fallers mostly removed the ones that kept falling.

**DSR at N = 132.** DSR is the chance that a result reflects real skill rather than the luckiest of many tries. N is how many independent ideas the lab has tried, read from the lab status (132 methods by the lab's counting policy), and the bar is 0.90. The quiet book scored 0.896. That is just under the bar, and "just under" is a fail. The other two are far below it.

**Worst year and the worst fall.** The quiet book's worst year was 2015 (−11.6%, the August sell-off). Its worst fall was 24.3%. That is inside the owner's 25% real-money limit, but with almost no margin. The loud book's worst year was 2007 (−13.4%): the heavy-volume fallers in banks and homebuilders kept falling into the crisis, just as the hypothesis said they would.

**2009-2015, the years that matter most.** This is where the method fails. The walk-forward folds (three-year slices scored one after another) read:
- 2003-2005: +44% vs SPY +52%, lost
- 2006-2008: +10% vs SPY −25%, won (mostly by sitting in cash behind the 200-day switch)
- 2009-2011: +23% vs SPY +61%, lost badly
- 2012-2014: +39% vs SPY +66%, lost badly

So it beat SPY in 1 fold of 4, and the promotion gate would refuse it on that alone. Its twenty-year win over SPY comes from 1996-2002 and from losing less in 2008. In the best-measured years, the most like today, it trails SPY by roughly 7-10 points a year.

**Why: the mechanism.** The regime report splits months into "narrow" ones, when a few giant companies carried the index, and "broad" ones, when the average stock did as well. The quiet book earns +7.0% a year more than SPY in broad months and loses 3.3% in narrow ones. The loud book loses 7.6% in narrow months. Holding 20 fallen big stocks at equal size is a bet against SPY's big-company drift, and 2009-2015 was a long run of that drift. The volume split cleans up *which* fallers you hold. It does not change the fact that the book holds yesterday's losers at equal weight while SPY holds the winners at their full size. Fees are the second drag. About 3,000 trades in 20 years, at Gotrade's minimum fees on slots of tens of dollars, take most of what the bounce pays.

**Hypothesis check.** The core claim held. Quiet fallers bounce better than loud fallers, the split is larger than a point a year, and it beats the unsplit book on return and on worst fall. The expected failures also happened: the edge is gone by 2009-2015, and the book lags in narrow markets. One expected failure did not happen. The split did not starve the book, which still filled 20 names and traded about as often as before.

**My opinion:** This is the best short-term reversal result the lab has recorded, and the volume split is a genuine finding: quiet fallers bounce, loud fallers keep falling. But it is not a strategy worth a test look. A book that loses to SPY by 7-10 points a year through 2009-2015 will lose in today's market however good its twenty-year average looks. I would not spend more ids on reversal as a standalone book. The one use I still see is as a *brake* inside a book that already beats SPY: the momentum books buy stocks that rose, and selling a holding whose recent fall came on heavy volume is the same lesson pointed the other way. That costs no extra trades on stocks the book would not have held anyway. I am queuing that idea, and I am treating standalone reversal as closed.
methods.verdict: Buying big stocks after a quiet two-week fall earned 7.7% a year on your deposits vs SPY's 7.2%, and quiet fallers clearly beat loud ones; but it just missed the luck bar and lost to SPY by a wide margin in 2009-2015.

methods.name: The giants, minus the weakest accounts: the most-traded index members with the least profitable third removed
methods.hypothesis: M0153 found that over 2012-2015 a no-model book of the 20 most-traded index members (14.1% a year) beat every learned picker, with or without company accounts, and that the accounts helped on average but only in 2 of 4 years. That points away from using accounts to RANK and toward using them to EXCLUDE: start from the book that wins in the recent era (the biggest, most-traded companies, which is SPY's own shape) and only drop the members whose accounts are worst. Hold the 30 most-traded members at trading-value weight, remove the bottom third by profitability (or by quality), and compare inside one batch against the same book with no filter, over the same 2012-2015 slice the accounts exist in, with SPY held before the panel is usable exactly as M0153 did. Pre-register the bar: the filtered book beats the unfiltered one by at least 1 point a year AND in 3 of 4 years. Same caveat as M0153: under four years and fewer than four walk-forward folds make it evidence, not a promotable method; profitability was published in 2013 (Novy-Marx), inside the window, so any edge is likely to fade.

methods.name: The highest dividend yields among big companies, re-picked once a year and held until they fall well out of the top
methods.sourceRef: Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016), A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs, Rev. Financial Studies 29(1), doi:10.1093/rfs/hhv063; Fama & French (1993), dividend yield as a value measure
methods.hypothesis: Dividend yield as value is decades old (Fama-French 1988/1993) and the cost-and-band result was published in 2016, after the dev window, so the dev years are before the crowd traded the low-turnover framing, but not before it knew high yield. Every book measured so far re-picks monthly, and monthly full turnover on a small account starts several points behind at Gotrade's fees. Novy-Marx and Velikov find value survives costs and a buy/hold band is the best cost cure. Among point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, take the 100 most traded; on the last close of December rank them by indicated dividend yield (median payment of the last 365 days times the payment frequency read over 730 days, over the close; above 15% skipped as a data error); keep a holding ranked inside the top 40, sell the rest, fill to 20 names at 1/20 each from the top; between re-picks a name leaves only when it stops being a member, its slot sitting in SPY; a book holding no stock picks in full at once. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: Y20-B40 (the idea), Y20-B40-SW (the same behind F4's SPY-200 switch), Y20-NOBAND (control: full yearly re-pick of 20, no band, to price the band), Y30-B60 (a wider, less sector-concentrated book), M20-B40 (control: the same band re-ranked monthly, to price the yearly cadence). Success: Y20-B40 beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a positive edge in 2009-2015 and a majority of walk-forward folds; and it should beat both controls, or the band and the cadence are not what helped.
methods.expectedFailure: High yield among big companies is a sector bet (utilities, telecoms, energy, banks, tobacco and REITs) that lost badly in 2008, when the banks' yields looked highest just before they cut, and lagged the 1998-1999 growth run, so it trails SPY TR over 1996-2015 or passes only by sitting in cash behind the switch. A yearly ranking is also slow to leave a name that is about to cut: the yield trap is held for up to a year. In 2009-2015 big tech and growth led, which a yield book barely owns, so the highest-coverage era is likely negative. The book is near M0088's calm big raisers and M0102's raise streaks in what it holds and may move with them. Survivorship flatters it: companies that cut and later died are missing from the dev store. Withholding tax on dividends (30% for an Indonesian holder, 15% under the treaty) is not modelled, and it bites a high-yield book harder than any other.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

## What was tried

Each December, take the 100 most-traded big companies in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 and rank them by dividend yield (the yearly dividend divided by the share price). Buy the 20 highest, 5% each. Keep a company as long as it stays in the top 40 at the next December ranking; only then sell it and buy a replacement. Between Decembers, nothing is re-ranked. A company leaves early only if it drops out of the index, and its slot waits in SPY. The point was to trade very little: every book in this lab so far re-picks every month, and at Gotrade's fees a small account pays heavily for that. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and the owner's monthly deposits of 5 million rupiah, from 1996 to 2015.

Assumptions I made: the re-pick uses the last close of December, so the trades go in at the first January open. An emptied slot sits in SPY. A book that holds no stock at all (the first month, or the month the safety switch lets it back in) picks in full right away.

## Result vs SPY

| version | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall (book alone) | trades | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the idea: 20 in, out below 40, yearly | +9.0% | +7.2% | 61.6% | 71 | 0.54 |
| same, behind the SPY 200-day switch | +8.3% | +7.2% | 25.6% | 223 | 0.87 |
| control: full yearly re-pick, no band | +7.3% | +7.2% | 65.8% | 128 | 0.41 |
| wider: 30 in, out below 60 | +8.1% | +7.2% | 61.1% | 81 | 0.52 |
| control: same band, re-ranked monthly | +8.3% | +7.2% | 59.6% | 265 | 0.48 |

Every version beat SPY on the same deposits, and every one was rejected. Both currencies are compared on the same deposits on the same dates, so the rupiah's moves do not decide the comparison.

- **The plain book fell 62% from its peak** in 2007-2009 (2008 alone: −37%). The lab's screen allows 50%, and the real-money bar allows 25%. Its gains-to-losses ratio (profit factor) was a healthy 2.6, but it made only 71 trades in twenty years, under the 100 the lab needs to judge a record at all.
- **With the safety switch** (all to cash while SPY is under its 200-day average) the worst fall shrank to 25.6%, inside the screen. It still failed the luck test: DSR 0.870 against the 0.90 bar. That means that after the lab's 103 independent tries (the N the luck test judges at), a result this good would turn up by chance more often than the owner accepts.
- **Walk-forward** (does the version picked on earlier years win the next three?): it won 2003-2005 (+58% vs +52%) and 2006-2008 (−15% vs −25%), then lost 2009-2011 (+45% vs +61%) and 2012-2014 (+44% vs +66%). That is 2 of 4. **It lost all of 2009-2014, the best-covered years and the most like today**, by 16 and 22 points over three years.

## Why

A high-yield list of big American companies is mostly utilities, telecoms, energy, tobacco, REITs and, before 2008, the big banks. That is a sector bet. It paid in 2000-2006, when the dot-com stocks collapsed and dull, cash-paying companies won. In 2008 the banks had the highest yields just before they cut their dividends and their prices collapsed. A yearly ranking holds that trap until December, so the plain book fell further than SPY. After 2009 the market was led by big tech and growth companies that pay little or nothing, and a yield book barely owns them. That is SPY's big-company drift again (insight 91 and onwards). This time it shows up as a missing sector, not as small-company weighting.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Partly, and the useful part is about trading costs, not about yield.
- **The band works.** With the same signal and the same yearly date, keeping a holding until it falls out of the top 40 earned +9.0% a year against +7.3% for a full re-pick. That is 1.7 points a year from trading less, with fewer trades (71 vs 128) and a smaller fall (62% vs 66%). Novy-Marx and Velikov's claim held here.
- **The yearly cadence beat the monthly one** by 0.7 points a year (+9.0% vs +8.3%) with a quarter of the trades.
- **The yield signal itself did not survive the go-live checks.** The expected failure happened exactly as written: the 2008 fall without the switch, a lag in 2009-2015 with it, and passing only by sitting in cash.

Not modelled: dividend withholding tax (15-30% of every dividend for an Indonesian holder). It would take roughly 0.5-1 point a year off a book yielding 3-4%, and so wipe out most of the +1.1-point edge the switch version has over SPY. SPY's own dividends would be taxed too, but SPY yields less.

## Compared with near relatives

The calm big dividend raisers and the dividend-raise streaks also lost 2009-2015 to SPY. Three different ways of choosing "safe dividend companies" have now failed in the same years. The weak spot is the dividend sector's place in the market after 2009, not the way any of these books picks.

**My opinion:** high dividend yield on its own is done in this lab. It is a sector bet that fails exactly when today's market is most like the past, and the unmodelled tax makes it worse. Don't spend more variations on the signal. The band is the real finding: it gave 1.7 points a year for free. It should become standard equipment for any slow-moving book, not only this one. The one yield-based thing still worth a single try is a small yield book beside a large SPY core. SPY carries the big-tech drift that the yield book misses, and the yield book's 2000-2006 strength could soften SPY's dot-com fall. After that, the band belongs on whichever non-momentum book is next in line. (A momentum book would be kin of the momentum books that already failed the test window, so the gate would refuse it whatever the band does.)
methods.verdict: Beat SPY on the same deposits, but fell 62% in 2008 without the safety switch, and lost 2009-2014 with it; the keep-until-out-of-the-top-40 rule was worth 1.7 points a year

methods.name: A small high-yield partner beside a large SPY core: 70% SPY, 30% the yearly banded dividend-yield book
methods.hypothesis: The yearly banded yield book won 2000-2008 (it fell 15% in 2006-2008 where SPY fell 25%) and lost 2009-2014 because it owns no big tech. SPY owns exactly what the yield book misses. Hold 70% in SPY and 30% in the 20-in, 40-out yield book re-ranked each December, rebalanced to 70/30 only when the split drifts past 60/40 or 80/20 (a band again, so trading stays rare), no market switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Expected failure: the yield sleeve's 2008 fall (it fell 62% alone) still drags the book past the 25% bar, and 30% is too little to lift the total above SPY by enough to pass the luck test; dividend tax is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-16

Sera, 2026-10-16: a correction before this idea is pre-registered. Its draft credits the 2006-2008 out-of-sample stretch (a 15% fall against 25%) to the yearly banded dividend-yield book. In M0163's walk-forward that stretch's pick was the monthly re-ranked band, not the yearly one. The child that builds this must re-read M0163's fold record and state the yearly book's own number in the hypothesis.

methods.name: Buy the beaten-down companies only after the market has already fallen a fifth: an SPY core with a crash-entry slice
methods.hypothesis: The five-year losers earned their lead over SPY in the rebounds after 2002 and 2009, not while the market was falling, and a fixed slice held at all times gave that lead back (M0104: SPY's 55% fall, a few tenths of a point ahead, no better than a winners slice). Hold SPY alone until SPY closes 20% or more below its prior 52-week high; then move 20-30% into the bottom fifth of five-year losers (fractional at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's deposits) and hold that slice for 12-24 months, then return to SPY. The slice is in the market only when crash-rebound evidence says it pays (2002-2003, 2009), so it should add to SPY in exactly those years and match SPY otherwise. Expected failure: only two or three such episodes in 1996-2015, so the luck score cannot clear 0.90 on so few events; the fall is still SPY's 55%; and 2020's crash rebounded within months, before a 12-month slice would show anything.

methods.name: Size the fifty by a calm measure: a year of trading value, share classes counted once
methods.hypothesis: M0125 sized the fifty most traded index members by their 20-day trading value and found it measures excitement, not size: it put 47% in five tech stocks at the end of 1999 and the worst fall deepened from 57% to 73%, though on the history with the dead companies put back it recovered 1 to 1.4 points a year of equal weighting's 3-point handicap to SPY. Test whether a slow size measure keeps the recovery without the mania: weight by trading value averaged over 252 days (a year) instead of 20, merge share classes of one company (GOOG and GOOGL) into one name, with caps at 5% and 10% and the equal control again. Success is tracking SPY within a few tenths of a point a year with a worst fall no deeper than SPY's own 55%, which would give the lab a fair index-member base for any signal to add to. If even the slow measure deepens the fall, stop building index-member base books and treat SPY itself as the base.

methods.name: The yield-curve watch with an early way out: buy back once the market proves it is not falling
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0038
methods.hypothesis: M0038's two-year watch after a 10-year/13-week curve inversion (Estrella-Mishkin 1996, public through the whole dev window) dodged 2000-2002 and 2007-2009 but missed the 2009 rebound, and by public bond-market history its next call (the 2022-2024 inversion) brought no bear market and would have kept it in cash through a long rally. Keep the watch and add a way out: once it has been open min_days (365), the first session on which SPY proves it is not in a bear market closes the watch early; it stays closed until the curve inverts again. Two counts of the year: from the episode's first inverted day (START, the idea row as written) or from its most recent inverted day (LAST, the literature's lead runs from the inversion). Two proofs: SPY above its 200-day average (E200) or SPY at a 252-session closing high (EHIGH; a bear-market rally can clear a falling 200-day average but rarely makes a one-year high). Hosts as M0038: SPY, decided daily (evidence only, it cannot reach 100 trades) and M0076-X-M's big-dividend-raise book without its own SPY-200 switch, monthly picks, weekly resize, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits. Variants: SPY-E200S and DIV-E200S (the row as written), DIV-E200L, DIV-EHIGHL, DIV-EHIGHL-5Y (the same on the 10-year/5-year curve, which in the dev window also inverted in 1998, a warning no bear market followed, so it is the only dev-visible false alarm the exit can be judged on) and SPY-EHIGHL. Equal-weight S&P as a second yardstick is not run: RSP starts in 2003 and the lab has no such benchmark switch (assumed). Success: the chosen variant is still flat or better through 2000-2002 and 2007-2009, beats total-return SPY on the owner's money within the worst-fall limit, wins a majority of walk-forward folds as the variant picked, and is no worse than SPY in 2009-2015; EHIGHL-5Y beats M0038-DIV-2KEY-5Y by re-entering after the 1998 false alarm.
methods.expectedFailure: On the 13-week curve the exit can only lose on dev: the two warnings it holds were both followed by bear markets, so there is no false alarm to rescue. The START count is the riskiest: the 2006-07 watch opened in mid-2006, so a year later (summer-autumn 2007) SPY was still near its highs and above its 200-day average; START would buy back right before 2008 and lose the gate's biggest save, and in early 2002 a rally over the 200-day average could do the same before the 2002 leg down. LAST pushes the earliest exit to early 2002 and mid-2008, where the 200-day proof may still fire on a bear-market rally (spring 2008 came close), while the one-year-high proof should not fire before the watch ends anyway, so DIV-EHIGHL is likely nearly identical to M0038-DIV-WATCH on dev and adds no evidence on the 13-week curve: its value is only out of sample. The 2009 rebound stays missed: the watch ended in May 2009 and SPY did not clear its 200-day average until about then, so the exit cannot buy March-May 2009. If the variants differ in which era they win, the fold pick changes and the hard gate refuses again, as it did M0038. The two-events problem remains: whatever the result, the 13-week gate made two calls in twenty years. Kin: M0038 is the parent and is not test-failed.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The parent method (M0038) watches the bond market. When the 10-year Treasury yield falls below the 3-month bill yield (the yield curve "inverts"), a recession has usually followed within a year or two. M0038 sat in cash for two years after the last inverted day. On the years the lab tests on (1996-2015) it sidestepped both bear markets. It also missed the 2009 rebound. Public bond-market history adds a warning: the curve inverted again from late 2022 to late 2024, no bear market came, and a two-year watch would have sat in cash through a long rally.

This method keeps the watch and adds a way out. After the watch has been open for a year, the first day that shows the market is *not* in a bear market ends the watch early. The watch then stays shut until the curve inverts again. Two ways to count the year, and two kinds of proof, were fixed before the run:

- **Count from the first inverted day** (the idea as written), or **from the most recent inverted day**.
- **Proof A:** SPY closes above its 200-day average. **Proof B:** SPY closes at its highest close of the past year. A rally inside a bear market can lift SPY over a falling 200-day average, but it rarely makes a new one-year high.

Hosts as the parent: SPY itself, and the big-dividend-raise book (up to 20 companies that just raised their dividend sharply, the rest in SPY) with its own trend switch removed. One variant reads the 10-year minus 5-year curve instead. In the test years that curve also inverted in 1998, a warning no bear market followed, so it was the only place the way out could be seen rescuing a false alarm. All variants traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly deposits. Cash earned nothing.

## Result

| variant | way out | your money, per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall (recorded) | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY-E200S | 200-day, year from first inversion | +10.0% | +7.7% | 36.2% | failed: 3 trades; luck check 0.866 |
| DIV-E200S | same | +12.3% | +7.2% | 31.5% | passed the dev screen |
| DIV-E200L | 200-day, year from last inversion | +12.1% | +7.2% | 33.7% | passed the dev screen |
| DIV-EHIGHL | one-year high, year from last inversion | +12.6% | +7.2% | 25.7% | passed the dev screen |
| DIV-EHIGHL-5Y | as above, 10y-5y curve | +12.8% | +7.2% | 25.7% | passed the dev screen |
| SPY-EHIGHL | one-year high, year from last inversion | +10.7% | +7.7% | 18.9% | failed: 2 trades |

**The luck check (DSR)** asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at N = 110 (one look per distinct method in the lab), against the bar of 0.90. The four dividend variants scored 0.913 to 0.963. As with the parent, the score measures how smooth the curve is. It cannot see that the gate made only a handful of decisions in twenty years.

**Walk-forward**, the four three-year test stretches: 2 of 4, the same as the parent. The pick won 2003-2005 and 2006-2008, lost 2009-2011 (+30% against SPY's +61%) and tied 2012-2014 (the SPY variant was picked, which is simply SPY when the watch is shut). The hard gate needs a majority, so the method cannot be promoted, and that is correct.

## Where the gains came from, era by era

Growth per year with the deposits taken out, so each fall shows its real depth. The numbers come from each trial's recorded month-end curve. SPY's figures are total-return SPY, from the parent's table.

| era | SPY | parent, no gate | parent, two-year watch | E200S | E200L | EHIGHL | EHIGHL-5Y | parent 5Y (2KEY) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2002 | +6.9% | +8.1% | +14.8% | +11.7% | +11.2% | +14.8% | +8.0% | +8.6% |
| 2003-2008 | +1.3% | +3.9% | +11.0% | +10.6% | +10.6% | +11.0% | +11.1% | +9.5% |
| 2009-2015 | +14.9% | +17.9% | +15.2% | +16.8% | +16.8% | +15.2% | +18.9% | +18.9% |
| 2000-2002 | -12.6% | -12.7% | +0.2% | -5.9% | -6.9% | +0.2% | -4.9% | -8.2% |
| 2007-2009 | -5.1% | -6.6% | +3.3% | +6.6% | +6.6% | +3.3% | +11.1% | +10.2% |
| 2009 alone | +25.2% | +29.3% | +10.2% | +21.3% | +21.3% | +10.2% | +37.1% | +37.2% |
| 1998-1999 | about +25% | +26.7% | +26.7% | +26.7% | +26.7% | +26.7% | +10.9% | +19.2% |
| worst fall, no deposits | | 51.8% | 22.3% | 26.7% | 29.1% | 22.3% | 22.3% | 25.4% |

When each gate went to cash and came back (10-year minus 13-week curve):

- **Two-year watch (parent):** out July 2000 to January 2003, out August 2006 to August 2009. A short re-inversion in August 2007 pushed the watch's end from May to August 2009. The parent's write-up said May 2009, which was wrong by three months.
- **200-day proof, year from the first inversion (E200S):** back in January 2002, so it was invested through the 2002 leg down.
