It also bought back on 1 August 2007, right before 2008, and was saved after one week only because the curve inverted again on 7 August 2007. That was luck, not design. It came back in June 2009.
- **200-day proof, year from the last inversion (E200L):** back in March 2002, again before the 2002 leg down; back in June 2009.
- **One-year-high proof (EHIGHL):** never fired before the watch ended on its own. It is the parent's two-year watch, day for day: same trades, same 48,562.7% total.

## What this shows

1. **The 200-day way out costs in one bear and pays in the other.** It bought back in early 2002 on a bear-market rally and lost about 6-7 points a year over 2000-2002 against the plain watch. It bought back in June 2009, two months before the watch ended, and won those points back in 2009. Net over twenty years it is slightly worse than no way out (+12.1-12.3% against +12.6%), and its worst fall is deeper (27-29% against 22%).
2. **The one-year-high way out is safe on these years because it never fires.** That was predicted. Its whole value lies outside the dev window. The 2022-2024 case is exactly what it was built for, and the dev window cannot test it.
3. **The one place a false alarm could be rescued, it came too late.** The 10y-5y curve inverted from May to August 1998. A year counted from August 1998 ran out in August 1999, and SPY made its first one-year high after that in November 1999. So the gate still sat out most of the 1998-1999 rally: +10.9% a year against about +25% for SPY. A one-year wait is too long to make a false alarm cheap. But the 2002 experience shows a shorter wait would buy back inside real bear markets. Both risks cannot be cut at once with price alone.
4. **EHIGHL-5Y "won" for the wrong reason.** It beats the parent's 5Y version (+12.8% against +12.3%, worst fall 25.7% against 29.5%), but almost all of that came in 2007-2009: the 10y-5y curve barely inverted in 2006, so its watch ended in January 2009 and caught the March rebound. That is a lucky timing accident of a weak signal, as in the parent.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No, on the part the dev window can judge. Success needed the picked variant to win a majority of folds and stay level with SPY in 2009-2015. It won 2 of 4. On the lab's money-weighted measure, the picks trailed SPY by 2.4 points a year in 2009-2015. The 1998 false alarm was not rescued in time. The expected failures happened as written: the 2002 re-entry, the one-year-high variant matching the parent exactly, and the pick changing between folds. One prediction was wrong: the 200-day way out *did* buy part of the 2009 rebound, because the parent's watch actually ran until August 2009, not May.

## The check with dead companies added back

The dev store has no prices for most companies that later went bankrupt or were bought out. The lab keeps a second store with most of them restored, and every variant was re-run on it. The SPY variants hold only SPY, so nothing changed. The dividend variants lost 1.1 to 1.3 points a year (EHIGHL +12.6% -> +11.4%, EHIGHL-5Y +12.8% -> +11.7%). The worst fall moved by about a point either way (EHIGHL 25.7% -> 27.0%). The luck scores fell to 0.86-0.93, and both 200-day variants dropped below the 0.90 bar (0.864 and 0.855). Their small 2009-2015 lead on the money-weighted measure (+0.6% a year) turned into a small deficit (-0.6%). Only EHIGHL-5Y keeps a positive 2009-2015 lead (+1.4% a year), and that comes from the 2009 timing accident described above. The gate reads no stock prices, so this loss belongs to the dividend book's picks, not to the gate.

**Buy signal:** does not fire. It needs a majority of folds, and the folds are 2 of 4.

My opinion: this direction is close to its end on the data the lab has. The question that matters, whether a way out stops the curve gate from wasting a false alarm like 2022-2024, has no answer in 1996-2015: the 13-week curve made two calls there and both were right. Every new variant just re-sorts the same two events, and the folds keep splitting 2 to 2 because 2009-2011 always punishes a gate that was in cash for the 2009 rebound. I would not spend more ids re-timing the exit. The useful next step is a different question: does the curve warning help as a *dial* rather than a switch, for example holding half the book in cash while the watch is open instead of all of it? That gives up part of the bear-market save in exchange for half the rebound, and it should make the fold record depend less on getting a handful of dates exactly right.

### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The **calm big raisers** book buys up to 20 big index companies that just raised their dividend by a quarter or more, but only the calmer half (the ones whose daily price swing over the last three months is at or below the middle of the group). Each name gets 5% of the money. A name is held while its raise is under six months old. The rest of the money sits in SPY, and everything steps into cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It re-picks once a month, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, on 20 million rupiah plus 5 million every month.

Each month it also re-checks every name it already holds. A holding that has become a little jumpier than the middle of the group is sold, even though its dividend raise is still fresh. The idea here was that this is waste: a name sitting right at the middle line gets sold and bought back on noise, paying Gotrade's fee on a small 5% slot each time. A sibling test on a dividend-yield book (M0163) found that a "keep it until it falls well out" rule was worth 1.7 points a year.

So the bar to **buy** stayed exactly the same, and only the bar to **keep** a holding was widened.

Assumption I made: the idea row talked about "top 20 in, out below top 30 or 40". This book has no ranking, only the swing cut and the six-month raise clock, so I expressed the band as a swing percentile instead.

## Versions, fixed before any result

- **CTRL**: held names judged at the middle line, like new ones. This is the parent book (M0088-C-LIVE-63) and had to reproduce it.
- **K65 / K75 / K90**: a holding stays while it is calmer than 65%, 75% or 90% of the live raisers.
- **HOLD**: no re-check at all once bought. A name leaves only when its raise is six months old, it leaves the index, or the safety switch empties the book.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | trades | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CTRL (parent) | +10.6% | 18.7% | 528 | 3.52 | 0.945 |
| K65 | +10.5% | 18.6% | 488 | 3.21 | 0.939 |
| K75 | +10.6% | 19.1% | 471 | 3.21 | 0.943 |
| K90 | +10.5% | 18.9% | 462 | 3.11 | 0.942 |
| HOLD | +10.6% | 20.5% | 454 | 3.09 | 0.950 |

CTRL reproduced the parent exactly (528 trades, 18.7% worst fall, +35.1% a year counting deposits as gains), so the comparison is fair.

**This is a null result.** The band did what it was built to do mechanically: trades fell by up to 14% (528 to 454). But the money did not move at all: every version earned +10.5% to +10.6% a year. The differences are a tenth of a point, which is noise.

- **Against SPY:** all five beat SPY by about 3.4 points a year on the deposits and pass every check on these years. The **worst fall** (the biggest drop from a peak) stays under the 20% limit for K65, K75 and K90. HOLD reaches 20.5%: over the 20% go-live limit, though inside the lab's looser 25% screen.
- **Gains vs losses** (profit factor: winning trades in total over losing trades in total; the floor is 1.3) fell from 3.52 to 3.09 as the band widened. The extra trades the band saved were the parent's good exits: a raiser that turns jumpy is more often a raiser about to fall.
- **Luck check (DSR):** judged at N = 107 independent tries in the lab, against a bar of 0.90. All five clear it (0.939 to 0.950). That says the book's edge over SPY on these years is unlikely to be luck. It says nothing new about the band, which added no edge.
- **Walk-forward folds** (four later stretches the method never trained on): **2 of 4**, unchanged. It lost 2003-2005 (+40.8% against SPY's +52.1%) and 2009-2011 (+25.9% against +60.8%), and won 2006-2008 and 2012-2014. The hard gate needs a majority, so this cannot be promoted.
- **2009-2015**, the best-covered years and the most like today: **−2.6 points a year behind SPY**, exactly the parent's gap.

## Why

The fee saving was real but small. 74 fewer trades over twenty years, each paying about half a percent on a 5% slot, comes to a few hundredths of a point a year on the whole account. Meanwhile the exits the band suppressed were not noise. Gains vs losses dropped steadily as the band widened, and HOLD's worst fall grew by nearly two points. When a calm raiser's swing jumps above the middle, that is usually the start of trouble, and selling it was paying for itself. Fewer fees plus worse exits came out even.

The 2009-2015 lag comes from somewhere else entirely. An earlier test (M0096) traced it to the safety switch selling in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and buying back higher. No rule about which raisers to keep can touch that.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: no band version beat the control by half a point. The expected failure happened almost word for word. The band bound on some names, the wider bands slid the worst fall back toward the unfiltered book (HOLD 20.5%), and the fold record stayed at 2 of 4. Unlike the yield book (M0163), this book's monthly re-check was not churn. It was a working exit.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

The parent (M0088-C-LIVE-63) is the control and all numbers here are at the same real Gotrade fees, so no `lab costs` adjustment is needed. Every attempt so far to move this book's fold record has failed. Gentler switch bands (M0101), a quarterly-return exit (M0143), a cooling-off period on the switch (M0148), and now a band on the picks all left it at 2 of 4 with the same 2009-2015 gap.

**My opinion:** this direction is done. Six methods have now tuned the calm big raisers from every side (the switch's entry, its exit, its timing, its core and now its exits on the picks), and none moved the 2009-2015 gap or the folds. The book's edge is a pre-2009 edge, and the parts that could fix it are not in the picks. I would stop varying this book. If the raise signal gets another try, it should be on a different shape of portfolio: the raisers only among the very largest companies, so the book stops betting against SPY's big-company drift, which is what the lab's money runs say beat everything from 2018.

methods.name: Slow-to-react big companies: rank index members by how late their price catches up with the market
methods.sourceRef: Hou & Moskowitz (2005), Market Frictions, Price Delay, and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns, Rev. Financial Studies 18(3), doi:10.1093/rfs/hhi023
methods.hypothesis: Hou and Moskowitz (published 2005, so the dev window is half before and half after the paper) show that stocks whose weekly returns answer to market news with a lag earn a premium that absorbs much of the size and liquidity effects: investors neglect them. Among point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, on the last close of December regress each member's last 52 weekly returns (every fifth SPY session) on SPY's same-week return, and on that plus SPY's four previous weeks; delay = 1 - R2(same week only) / R2(with lags). Hold the 20 most delayed at 1/20 each, keep a holding while it ranks inside the top 40 at the next December, a name leaving early only when it stops being a member (its slot in SPY); a book with no stock picks in full at once. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: D20 (the idea, no switch), D20-SW (behind F4's SPY-200 switch), D40-SW (a 40-name rung, kept inside the top 80), L20-SW (control: the 20 least delayed, same band and switch), D20-BIG-SW (the most delayed within the 200 most traded only, to check the effect is not just small index members). Success: D20-SW beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a positive 2009-2015 edge and a majority of walk-forward folds, and L20-SW clearly trails it.
methods.expectedFailure: Among liquid giants a 52-week delay estimate is mostly noise: the R2 ratio of a stock that barely tracks the market jumps around year to year, so the book is a random draw of low-correlation names. Where it is not noise, the most delayed index members are the smaller, thinner, less followed ones (and low-beta defensives), so the book quietly favours small companies and loses to SPY's big-company drift after 2009 (insight 91), and the dev store prices exactly those members worst, so survivorship flatters it (check lab survivorship). The published effect is a small-cap, pre-2000 effect, and it should fade after 2005. The BIG variant should then show nothing.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

Some companies' share prices react to market news at once; others take a week or a month to catch up. Hou and Moskowitz (2005) found that the slow reactors earn more, because fewer investors watch them. Each December I took every big company in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 that passes the lab's usual size screen and measured, over the past year of weekly returns, how much of its price movement followed *last* month's market moves rather than this week's ("price delay": 0 means it reacts at once, near 1 means it mostly reacts late). The book holds the 20 slowest reactors, 5% each, keeps a company while it stays in the slowest 40 at the next December, and puts any empty slot in SPY. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5 million rupiah a month, 1996-2015.

Assumptions I made: a "week" is five trading sessions counted back from the ranking day, so holidays need no special rule. A company with too little history for a full year of weeks plus four weeks of lags is not ranked.

## Result vs SPY (same deposits, same dates)

| version | your money a year | SPY | worst fall | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the idea: slowest 20, no safety switch | +10.9% | +7.2% | 64.0% | 0.64 |
| slowest 20, behind the SPY 200-day switch | +12.6% | +7.2% | 32.9% | 0.97 |
| slowest 40, behind the switch | +10.9% | +7.2% | 26.2% | 0.96 |
| control: the 20 *fastest* reactors, switch | +10.8% | +7.2% | 23.3% | 0.93 |
| slowest 20 among the 200 most traded only, switch | +10.9% | +7.2% | 32.9% | 0.93 |

Four of five versions passed the lab's dev screen. None passes the real-money bar: every version but the control fell more than 25% from a peak, and the control is not the idea.

- The luck test (DSR) asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab has made 108 independent tries; the bar is 0.90. The switch version scored 0.97, so on its twenty-year average it is not luck.
- **Walk-forward** (pick the best version on the years before, score it on the next three years it never saw) won only 2 of 4 periods: it lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011, won 2006-2008 and 2012-2014. And the version the rule picked each time was the **control**, the fastest reactors, because it had the smallest falls. The lab's hard gate needs a majority, so it will refuse to promote this method.
- **2009-2015**, the best-covered years and the most like today: the switch version led SPY by only 0.6 points a year, and on the survivorship-check prices (which add back companies that later died) it trailed by 1.8. The slowest-40 rung trailed by 2.0. The control trailed by 4.1.
- The fall: the plain book lost 64% in 2007-2009 (2008 alone: −44%), worse than SPY. With the switch the worst fall was 33%, still above 25%.

## Why

The ranking did something: with the same switch, the slowest 20 earned 1.8 points a year more than the fastest 20. But most of every version's lead over SPY comes from the frame the lab has used many times before: equal slots, the 200-day switch that sits in cash through 2001-2002 and 2008, and few trades. The control, which ranks the exact opposite way, still beat SPY by 3.6 points a year.

The slow reactors are the quieter companies the market moves past: smaller index members, dull defensives, companies whose price moves for their own reasons. The narrow-vs-broad check shows it: every slow-reactor version earns its lead in "broad" months, when the average company beats the index, and loses in "narrow" months, when a few giants carry SPY. That is the same headwind (insight 91) that has beaten every equal-weighted book from 2018. Restricting to the 200 most traded companies kept a lead over SPY on dev but lost 1.1 points a year and much of its luck score (0.93 → 0.83) on the survivorship-check prices.

One surprise: without the switch the slowest-20 book led SPY by 7.3 points a year in 2009-2015 (5.6 on the check prices). The switch cost it most of that, by stepping out in the 2010 and 2011 scares and missing the rebounds. The unswitched book falls too far to hold, but the slow reactors themselves did not lose 2009-2015; the brake did.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Partly. The slow reactors beat the fast reactors, as the paper says. But the success test also wanted a majority of walk-forward folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge behind the switch, and both failed. The expected failure was half right. The delay measure was not pure noise: the ranking added 1.8 points a year. The book did lean against SPY's big-company drift. Survivorship cost the big-company version a point a year and the main version only 0.3, smaller than feared.

Compared with the near misses: the slowest 20 behind the switch (+5.4 a year over SPY, 33% fall) sits beside the momentum books (M0007-N20-RAW about +7 on the same deposits) with a deeper fall and a weaker fold record. It is not a better candidate.

**My opinion:** the delay ranking is a real but small tilt, and the on/off switch is the wrong brake for it. The idea is worth exactly one more try: the slowest reactors without the 200-day switch, held down by a gentler dial (scale the book toward SPY as its own volatility rises) so that it keeps the 2009-2015 rebounds the switch threw away. If that cannot get the 2008 fall under 25% while keeping a positive 2009-2015 lead, drop the family. I would not spend a test look on any version here.

### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The parent method (the slowest-to-react companies) picked, each December, the 20 index members whose share price follows the market's moves a week or a month late. Without a brake it fell 64% in 2008. Behind the usual safety switch (all cash while SPY sits under its 200-day average) the fall was 33%, but the switch threw away most of its 2009-2015 lead by stepping out in the 2010 and 2011 scares.

This run kept the same picks, the same yearly re-pick and the same "keep it while it stays in the slowest 40" rule, and swapped the on-off switch for a gentle dial. Each month the book measures how hard its own holdings have been swinging over the last 60 trading days. If they swing more than the target (12% a year), every position shrinks in proportion and the rest waits in cash. Six versions: the idea (12% target), a looser 16% target, a quicker 20-day reading, a version that parks the trimmed money in SPY instead of cash, a 40-company version, and a control that holds the 20 *fastest* reactors under the same dial. All in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5 million rupiah a month, 1996-2015.

Assumptions I made: the dial is read once a month, on the same monthly schedule as the parent, so the brake is the only thing that changed. In the cash versions the SPY slots that fill empty places are shrunk along with the stocks.

## Result vs SPY (same deposits, same dates)

| version | your money a year | SPY | worst fall | 2009-2015 lead | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the idea: 12% dial, rest in cash | +10.0% | +7.2% | 32.1% | −0.1 | 0.84 |
| looser 16% dial | +10.9% | +7.2% | 39.1% | +2.5 | 0.84 |
| 12% dial read on 20 days | +10.1% | +7.2% | 31.0% | +0.4 | 0.86 |
| 12% dial, trimmed money in SPY | +10.9% | +7.2% | 57.2% | +5.9 | 0.71 |
| 40 companies, 12% dial | +8.8% | +7.2% | 36.4% | −2.8 | 0.85 |
| control: 20 fastest reactors, 12% dial | +7.1% | +7.2% | 26.5% | −6.1 | 0.74 |

For comparison, the parent behind the 200-day switch: +12.6% a year, 32.9% worst fall, 2009-2015 lead +0.6, luck test 0.97.

Every version was rejected. None passes the luck test. Every slow-reactor version fell more than 25% from a peak, the real-money limit. The control did not even beat SPY.

- **Luck test (DSR):** how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab has made 113 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90. The best version scored 0.86. The dial costs return in calm years and cuts the fall only a little, so the result is less convincing than the parent's.
- **Walk-forward** (pick the best version on the years before, then score it on three years it never saw): it won 1 of 4 periods. Three times the rule picked the fast-reactor control, because it had the smallest fall, and the control trailed SPY each time (2009-2011: +21.7% vs SPY +60.8%). The lab's hard gate needs a majority.
- **The fall:** the 12% dial lost 32% from a peak, about the same as the parent's switch (33%). Its worst year, 2008, was −25.5%. Reading the dial on 20 days instead of 60 helped a little (31%). Parking the trimmed money in SPY brought SPY's own 2008 crash back in: a 57% fall, as expected.
- **2009-2015**, the best-covered years and the most like today: the dial version led SPY by −0.1 points a year, no better than the switch (+0.6). On the survivorship-check prices, which add back companies that later died, it trailed by 2.2 points. Only the SPY-parking version kept a real lead (+5.9, +3.8 on the check prices), and it falls too far.
- **Survivorship check:** with the dead companies added back, the falls of the cash versions got *smaller* (32% to 26%) and the twenty-year lead held up (+2.8 to +3.0), but the 2009-2015 lead got worse by about 2 points in every version. The fold record read 3 of 4 on those prices. The picks changed, so that number moves with the data and is not a gate.

## Why

The dial did what dials do. It reacts to swings that have already happened. In 2008 the slow reactors were calm until September, so the book went into the fall almost fully invested. Once it was cut back, it then stayed out through the violent rebound in spring 2009. That is the same timing problem as the switch, only spread more thinly. The expected failure ("the dial reacts too late and the book still falls more than 25%") happened almost word for word.

A 12% target is also below what this book normally swings, so in quiet years it held only part of the money in stocks. That cost about 2.6 points a year against the switch version, without buying a smaller fall.

The market-breadth check says the same thing as for the parent. Every slow-reactor version earns its lead in "broad" months, when the average company beats the index (+7 to +11 points a year). It loses 7 points a year in "narrow" months, when a few giants carry SPY. The slow reactors are the smaller, quieter index members. The book is a bet against SPY's big-company drift, and no brake changes that.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The success test wanted a fall of 25% or less with a positive 2009-2015 lead. The cash versions got the first nearly, but only on the check prices, and lost the second. The SPY version kept the second and lost the first. Slow reactors still beat fast reactors under the same brake (+10.0% vs +7.1% a year), so the ranking itself still does something. But the method as a whole is weaker than the parent: lower return, no smaller fall, and a lower luck score.

**My opinion:** drop the price-delay family. Two methods and eleven versions have now shown the same shape: a real but small tilt toward quiet, smaller companies, which pays in broad markets and loses when giants lead. Neither an on-off switch nor a volatility dial gets it under a 25% fall without giving up its 2009-2015 lead. The parent's own advice was to drop the family if this try failed, and I agree. What this run did teach is general: a brake that reads only past swings, checked monthly, does not protect a book that is calm right up to the crash. The next useful experiment is a brake that reads a forward-looking signal, such as the fear index (VIX) jumping above its three-month version. Tried on a book the lab already trusts, it would show whether *any* brake can cut a 2008-style fall without whipsawing through 2010-2011.


### 2026-10-17

**Correction to "My opinion" above:** a fear-index brake (the one-month VIX above the three-month one) was already tried in this lab on the dividend-raise book and rejected (M0039), and its re-entry variation is queued (M0094). So it is not the next step from here. The idea queued from this run is different. The slow-reactor tilt fails because it is a bet on small companies leading, so pair it with a half that wins when the giants lead (the biggest, most traded members, weighted by size of trading). Each half then pays in the months the other loses, and the breadth check can show whether the pair "pays in both".
methods.verdict: A volatility dial instead of the on-off switch fell just as far (31-39%) and kept no 2009-2015 lead; the slow-reactor tilt only pays when small companies lead

methods.name: The spike filter on the busiest names only: rank the 150 most-traded members on their biggest recent days against their own normal swing
methods.sourceRef: Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw (2011), Maxing out: stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns, JFE 99(2), 427-446 (working paper 2009); variation of M0093
methods.hypothesis: M0093 found a real spread: members whose biggest recent days were unusual for them trailed the quiet ones by about 6 points a year on dev, but the equal-weight quiet book earned its lead only in broad months, trailed SPY by 2.5% a year in 2009-2015 (5.7% with dead companies added back) and won 2 of 4 folds. That is the equal-weight small-company tilt fighting SPY's big-company drift, not the signal failing. Restrict the pool to the 150 F4-screened members with the highest 20-day trading value (the store has no market caps; trading value stands in for size) and hold the 20 lowest scaled-MAX5 of those (MAX5 over 21 sessions over the stdev of the 60 returns before), at 5% each, behind the SPY 200-day switch, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Variants: LO5-P150-N20-T (the book), LO5-P100-N20-T (a tighter, bigger-company pool), LO5-P150-N30-T (30 names, closer to the pool's shape), and HI5-P150-N20-T, the paired control holding the 20 highest scaled spikes of the same pool, which must trail. BCW circulated from 2009, so the dev window sees mostly the pre-crowd years. Success needs a LO variant to beat SPY TR on dev within the drawdown limit, the control to trail it, a positive 2009-2015 edge and a walk-forward fold majority.
methods.expectedFailure: Among the busiest names the spike carries less mispricing -- they are the best-arbitraged stocks, and the MAX effect is documented as strongest in small, illiquid names -- so the spread versus the control shrinks toward zero. The most-traded pool tilts to the crowd's favourites of the day (1999-2000 tech, 2007-2008 banks and energy), which deepened the worst fall when the lab weighted by trading value before, so the fall may exceed 25%. And 20 equal-weighted names out of 150 still tilt small inside that pool, so the 2009-2015 gap may narrow without turning positive. A published anomaly fades: whatever edge shows is likely front-loaded before 2009.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What we tried

The parent method skipped stocks whose biggest days last month were unusual *for them*. It ranked each stock's five biggest daily gains over 21 trading days, divided by how much it usually moved a day before that. The 20 calmest members beat SPY over twenty years, and the 20 spikiest trailed by about 6 points a year. But the calm book only won when most stocks rose together. It trailed SPY by 2.5% a year in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 walk-forward slices. Our guess was that the cause was size. An equal-weight basket of index members leans toward the smaller ones, and SPY leans toward the giants.

So this time we used the same ranking, but only among the **150 most-traded members**. The store has no company sizes, so daily trading value stood in for size. Everything else stayed the same: the SPY 200-day cash switch, monthly trades, equal amounts, fractional shares and Gotrade's real fees. The check version held the 20 *spikiest* of the same 150.

## Result: worse on every count

On the owner's monthly deposits, 1996-2015, SPY with the same deposits earned +7.2% a year.

| Version | Your money per year | Worst fall (without deposits) | Gains vs losses | Luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 calmest of the 150 busiest (the main book) | +7.9% | 27.0% | 1.38 | 0.767 | −5.7% a year |
| 20 calmest of the 100 busiest | +7.1% | 25.2% | 1.36 | 0.730 | −7.7% a year |
| 30 calmest of the 150 busiest | +7.5% | 24.8% | 1.38 | 0.760 | −6.7% a year |
| 20 spikiest of the 150 busiest (the check) | +5.3% | 19.7% | 1.27 | 0.336 | −8.0% a year |
| *Parent: 20 calmest of all members* | *+10.7%* | *24.1%* | *1.51* | *0.921* | *−2.5% a year* |

- **Beat SPY:** only barely. The main book was 0.7 points a year ahead, and the 100-name pool fell just behind.
- **Worst fall:** 27.0% for the main book. That is over the 25% screen. The 30-name version stayed just inside it, at 24.8%.
- **Luck check:** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than luck, after the lab's 111 tries so far (N = 111). No version came near the 0.90 bar. The best scored 0.767.
- **Walk-forward: 1 of 4 slices.** The book won only 2006-2008, and that was the cash switch dodging the crash (+3.6% while SPY lost 25%). It lost 2003-2005, 2009-2011 and 2012-2014 by 16 to 26 points per slice.
- **2009-2015 got worse, not better:** −5.7% a year, against the parent's −2.5%.
- **With dead companies added back** (the survivorship-check store), every version earned 1 to 2.4 points a year less. The main book fell behind SPY (−1.7% a year), and its 2009-2015 gap widened to −9%.

## Why

The size story was wrong. Among the busiest names the calm book lagged SPY *more* in 2009-2015, so the parent's lag was not mainly a small-company tilt. Two things happened.

1. **The spread shrank.** The calm book now beats the spiky book by 2.6 points a year, down from 6. The most-traded stocks are the most closely watched, so an unusual jump there is less often a mispricing that later reverses. That is what the 2011 paper found too: the effect is strongest in small, thinly traded stocks. We gave up the part of the pool where the signal lives.
2. **Both sides lost to SPY in 2009-2015,** the calm book by 5.7 points and the spiky book by 8. So no choice inside the pool helped there. Equal weights across 20 big names still trail SPY's few giants in those years. The 200-day switch also costs on quick dips that recover (2010, 2011, 2015). Market shape explains the "broad months only" pattern (+3.9% a year in broad months, −2.8% in narrow ones), and narrowing the pool did not remove it.

## Hypothesis vs what happened

The hypothesis failed. It said the busy pool would close the 2009-2015 gap, and the gap doubled. The expected failure happened almost word for word. The spread shrank among the best-watched names, the worst fall went past 25%, and the 2009-2015 gap stayed negative.

## Compared with the parent

Both ran at Gotrade's real fees, so the comparison is fair. The parent was better on every line: +10.7% vs +7.9% a year, a 24.1% vs 27.0% worst fall, a 0.921 vs 0.767 luck check, and 2 vs 1 walk-forward slices.

## My opinion:

Stop shrinking the pool. The spike signal pays, as far as it pays at all, in the smaller and less-watched index members. Moving to the big names gives up the signal without fixing the 2009-2015 problem. That problem looks like equal weighting plus the cash switch, not the stock choice. The one test left for this family is to keep SPY's own shape and use the signal only to *leave out* names. Hold the busiest members weighted by trading value, close to how SPY weights them, minus the 20 with the most unusual spikes. If that version beats SPY in 2009-2015, the signal adds something on top of the market. If it doesn't, close the lottery family.
methods.verdict: Ranking only the busiest names made it worse: barely ahead of SPY over twenty years, 5.7% a year behind it in 2009-2015, lost 3 of 4 test slices

methods.name: The yield-curve warning as a dial, not a switch: hold half the book in cash while the watch is open
methods.hypothesis: M0038 and M0167 showed the curve watch is all or nothing: two right calls in 1996-2015, but every timing variant re-sorts the same two events and the walk-forward folds split 2 to 2, because 2009-2011 always punishes a gate that was fully in cash for the 2009 rebound. Hold the big-dividend-raise book (its own trend switch removed) at 50% (and a 33% rung) while the 10-year/13-week watch is open, instead of 0%. It gives up part of the bear-market save in exchange for part of the rebound, so the fold record should depend less on getting a handful of dates exactly right. Fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits; the fully-open book and the full switch (M0038-DIV-WATCH) are the controls on record. Success: a majority of folds won by the variant picked, a positive 2009-2015 lead on the money-weighted measure, a worst fall within the limit. Expected failure: half exposure through 2000-2002 and 2008 lets the dividend book's 50% falls through at half size, about 25%, while the 2009 gain is only half recovered, so it trails both controls.

methods.name: Companies that move least with the rest of the market: low correlation, not low volatility (betting against correlation)
methods.sourceRef: Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen & Pedersen (2020), Betting against correlation: Testing theories of the low-risk effect, JFE 135(3), doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.07.003
methods.hypothesis: AFGP (circulated 2017, published 2020, so the whole dev window predates the paper, though betting against beta, its parent, was public from 2010) split the low-risk effect into volatility and correlation: within volatility buckets, stocks with low correlation to the market earn more, which they read as leverage-constrained investors overpaying for high-correlation names. Han et al. argue much of it is a size effect, so among S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members it should be weaker; this is a direct test on big companies. On the last close of each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, compute each one's correlation with SPY from 3 years of overlapping 3-day log returns and its 1-year daily volatility; rank by correlation inside each volatility tercile (rank fraction, 0 = lowest), hold the 20 with the lowest fraction at 1/20 each (so about a third from each tercile: not a low-volatility book), keep a holding while its fraction stays under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: C20 (the idea, no switch), C20-SW (behind F4's SPY-200 switch), C40-SW (a 40-name rung), H20-SW (control: the 20 highest-correlation, same band and switch), P20-SW (plain lowest correlation across everyone, no tercile split, to show what the split adds). Success: C20-SW beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge, and H20-SW trails it clearly.
methods.expectedFailure: Among big companies low correlation is mostly utilities, staples, gold miners and odd one-offs, even inside a volatility tercile, so the book is a defensive sector bet that ties SPY in bad years and trails it badly in the 2009-2015 rise, like the lab's earlier calm-stock books; the high-correlation control (tech and financials) wins the 1990s and 2009-2015 and loses 2000-2002 and 2008, so the pair's gap is a sector cycle, not a premium. Low correlation also tends to mean thin, less followed members, so the book leans small and loses to SPY's big-company drift, and survivorship may flatter it.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

Big companies whose prices move *least* with the market as a whole. Every quarter the book measured how closely each S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 member moved with SPY over the last three years (using overlapping three-day returns, the paper's method). It also measured how jumpy each stock was over the last year. It sorted the stocks into three groups by jumpiness. Inside each group it picked the ones that moved least with the market. Picking from each group stops the book from simply becoming a "calm stocks" book. It held 20 of them (40 in one version) in equal slots. A holding was sold only once it was no longer among the least market-tied 40% of its group. Trades were in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly top-up. The idea comes from Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen and Pedersen (2020, "betting against correlation").

Five versions were registered before any result existed:
- **C20**: 20 names, always invested.
- **C20-SW**: 20 names, out to cash while SPY is under its 200-day average.
- **C40-SW**: 40 names, with the same switch.
- **H20-SW**: the opposite, as a control: the 20 names most tied to the market.
- **P20-SW**: plain lowest correlation, with no split by jumpiness.

## Result against SPY (with dividends), 1996 to October 2015

All figures use the same deposits put into SPY, which earned +7.2% a year.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C20 (no switch) | +13.6% | 42.1% | 9.1 | 0.895 | fails the luck bar |
| C20-SW | +13.3% | 29.8% | 8.0 | 0.982 | eligible on the dev screen |
| **C40-SW** | **+12.0%** | **24.3%** | 7.6 | 0.980 | eligible, and under the 25% real-money fall limit |
| H20-SW (control) | +8.5% | 25.5% | 5.4 | 0.803 | fails |
| P20-SW (no split) | +12.1% | 34.8% | 7.1 | 0.967 | eligible on the dev screen |

- **Luck check.** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than luck after the lab's tries. The lab counts N = 114 independent tries and the bar is 0.90. C40-SW scores 0.98, so luck is an unlikely explanation for the twenty-year average.
- **Worst fall.** Measured on the book without deposits and month by month: C20-SW fell 27% at its worst and C40-SW 22%. SPY fell 50% in the same years.

## Where the edge came from (book without deposits, each year)

- **1997-1999: it lost badly.** In 1998 SPY made +28% and C20-SW lost 12%, because the switch sold it out in the autumn dip. The low-correlation names (oil, gold miners, drug makers, food) sat out the tech bubble.
- **2000: it won hugely.** C20-SW made +25% while SPY fell 10%. Over 1996-2002 as a whole it about tied SPY (6.2% a year vs 6.7%).
- **2003-2008: it won clearly.** It made 11.2% a year against SPY's 2.3%, helped by the switch in 2008.
- **2009-2015: it was still ahead on the lab's normal prices.** It made 19.2% a year against SPY's 14.9%. The expected failure, trailing badly in the 2009-2015 rise, **did not happen** on these prices.
- **The control lost there.** The most market-tied names made 8.9% a year in 2009-2015, against SPY's 14.9%. So the pair split the way the paper predicts.
- **The split by jumpiness helped.** The plain low-correlation book (P20-SW) earned less (15.8% a year in 2009-2015) and fell further (35% vs 30%). Taking names from all three jumpiness groups was worth having.

## Why it is not promotable

**1. The walk-forward folds.** The lab re-plays history four times. Each time it picks the version that looked best up to a cut-off date, then scores that pick on the next three years. In all four replays the version that looked best was **the control** (H20-SW). The 1996-2002 stretch favoured it: banks and GE rode the bubble, and the switch kept it out of 2001-2002. The control then lost 3 of the 4 scored stretches, so the method's record reads 1 of 4. On its own, C40-SW would have won 3 of 4 (it lost only 2009-2011, narrowly). The hard gate reads the method's picks and wants a majority, so `lab promote` refuses it. Putting the control inside the same method cost this method its fold record. That is a design mistake in how I registered it, not a fact about the market.

**2. The dead-companies check.** The survivorship-check store adds prices for index members the normal store cannot price, many of them companies that later collapsed. On that store every version earns less:
- C20-SW's lead over SPY drops from +6.1 to +3.1 points a year. Its 2009-2015 lead flips from +2.8 to **−2.7** points a year.
- C40-SW holds up better: its lead goes from +4.8 to +4.0 points a year, and its luck check stays at 0.98. But its 2009-2015 lead also turns slightly negative, from +0.5 to **−1.3** points a year.

Some of the edge in the best-covered years came from the companies the normal store is missing. The expected failure said survivorship "may flatter it", and it did.

**3. Narrow versus broad markets.** Every low-correlation version earns its edge in months when the average stock beats the index (C40-SW: +7.3% a year in those months). It trails when a few giants carry the index (−2.5%). That is the shape of the market since 2018, which is a warning about the test window.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

- **On the normal prices, yes.** Low correlation, held to within each jumpiness group, beat SPY and beat its own control by a wide margin, in big companies too. The paper's claim survives being moved to large caps.
- **The expected failure half-happened.** The defensive tilt cost it the late-1990s bubble, but it did not lose 2009-2015 on the normal prices. It did lose 2009-2015 once the dead companies were added back.
- **The buy signal did not fire.** That needs a majority of folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge in the method's picks. The picks (the control) read −0.6% a year there.

**My opinion:** This is one of the more honest-looking results the lab has had in a while. The control behaves like a control, the luck check is strong, and the 40-name version stays under the real-money fall limit. It deserves one clean re-run, built without the mistakes:
- **No control inside the method.** H20-SW is already on record here.
- **Only the 200 most-traded members.** That is where the survivorship check bites least, because big liquid names rarely vanish from the data.
- **A 30-name rung** next to the 40-name one.

If that version still wins most folds and keeps a positive 2009-2015 edge on the check store, it is a real candidate for a look. If its 2009-2015 lead stays negative on the check store, the edge was mostly 2000-2008 and the missing dead companies, and this direction should stop there. I would not spend more than one more method on it.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1607)

Not promoted: dev-eligible, but `lab promote` would refuse on the folds (1 of 4: in all four training windows the fold rule picked the high-correlation control H20-SW over the low-correlation books; kin clean). C40-SW alone wins 3 of 4, but the gate reads the selection as well as the variant, and the selection is the honest reading: before each test stretch, the evidence favoured the opposite of the hypothesis. On the survivorship-check store the 2009-2015 lead turns negative (+0.5 -> -1.3 pts a year). No buy signal.
methods.verdict: Stocks that move least with the market beat SPY 1996-2015 (+12% a year vs +7%, worst fall 24%), but the hard gate refuses it: the fold test kept picking the built-in control, and the edge shrinks once dead companies are added back

methods.name: Keep SPY's shape, drop the lottery tickets: the busiest members weighted by trading value, minus the 20 most unusual spikes
methods.hypothesis: M0093 and M0172 showed the scaled-spike spread is real (the 20 most unusual spikes trail the calm names by 2.6-6 points a year) but every equal-weight book of chosen names trailed SPY by 2.5-8% a year in 2009-2015, on both the full pool and the 150 busiest. The lag is the equal weighting and the stock choice fighting SPY's shape, not the spike signal. Hold the 150 most-traded F4-screened members weighted by 20-day trading value (a stand-in for SPY's cap weights), excluding the 20 with the highest scaled MAX5 (21-session MAX5 over the stdev of the 60 prior returns), monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, with and without the SPY 200-day switch; control: the same weighted pool with nothing excluded. Success: beats both SPY TR and the no-exclusion control, including in 2009-2015. Expected failure: excluding 20 of 150 at their trading-value weights moves the book a few tenths of a point a year, inside the fee drag; trading-value weighting overweights the crowd's favourites (1999-2000 tech), deepening the worst fall.

methods.name: A breadth-hedged pair: the slowest reactors beside the biggest companies, so one half pays when small names lead and the other when giants lead
methods.sourceRef: M0169 (Hou & Moskowitz 2005, price delay, RFS 18(3)) and M0171; insight 91 (equal slots bet against SPY's big-company drift); M0122 (trading value as the lab's size proxy)
methods.hypothesis: Every slow-reactor version (M0169, M0171) earned +7 to +11 points a year in broad months, when the average member beats the index, and lost about 7 a year in narrow months, when a few giants carry SPY; that breadth bet, not the brake, is what kept it from a positive 2009-2015 lead. Pair M0169-D20-SW verbatim (the 20 slowest reactors, December re-pick, keep band 40, behind the SPY 200-day switch) with a big half: the 20 screened members with the largest 20-day dollar volume, sized by it and capped at 10% of the half, re-picked monthly behind the same switch, so one half pays in narrow months and the other in broad ones. Price delay was published in 2005, mid dev window; the big half is no published anomaly, only the market's own shape. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, monthly. Variants: P50 (half and half, the idea), P30 (30% slow, 70% big), P50-EQ (half and half, big half in equal slots, to see whether the size-weighting matters), BIG (control: the big half alone). Success: P50 beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, reads 'pays in both' on the breadth check, a positive 2009-2015 lead and a majority of walk-forward folds, and beats BIG.
methods.expectedFailure: The big half is close to SPY itself, and behind the same switch it is close to the lab's plain SPY-switch book, which already trails SPY by whipsawing in 2010-2011; so the blend is that switch book plus half the slow-reactor tilt, and inherits half its narrow-month losses without a full share of its broad-month gains. The 2008 fall stays near the parent's 33% in the slow half and the big half adds its own, so the blend falls 25-30%. Trading value leans to whatever is in turmoil (the busiest names in 2000 and 2008 were the ones crashing), so the dollar-volume half may fall harder than SPY in exactly the crashes the switch is late for. The slow half's dead-company flattery (dev store) is halved, not removed.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The slowest-to-react companies (the parent idea, M0169) earned a lot in months when the average company beat the index, and lost about 7 points a year in months when a few giants carried SPY. The guess was that this "small names vs giants" bet, not the stock picking, is what kept the book from leading SPY in 2009-2015.

So this run paired it with its opposite. Half the money goes to the parent's best version unchanged: the 20 slowest reactors, re-picked each December, behind the usual safety switch (all cash while SPY is under its 200-day average). The other half goes to the 20 most traded index members. Each one is sized by how much money changes hands in it (a stand-in for company size, not true market value), capped at 10% of that half, re-picked monthly and kept behind the same switch. In theory one half pays when small names lead and the other when giants lead.

Four versions: half and half (the idea), 30% slow / 70% big, half and half with the big half in equal slots, and the big half alone as a control. All of them trade in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5 million rupiah a month, 1996-2015.

Assumptions I made: the slow half is the parent's D20-SW configuration exactly. The big half uses the lab's usual $5 / $20M liquidity screen and its 20-day average trading value. Each half keeps its own share of the account through the lab's standard blend, re-balanced monthly.

## Result vs SPY (same deposits, same dates)

| version | your money a year | SPY | worst fall | 2009-2015 lead | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| half and half (the idea) | +10.5% | +7.2% | 20.1% | −4.0 | 0.896 |
| 30 slow / 70 big | +10.4% | +7.2% | 20.9% | −4.4 | 0.885 |
| half and half, big half equal slots | +9.8% | +7.2% | 20.8% | −4.7 | 0.876 |
| control: big half alone | +10.3% | +7.2% | 26.5% | −4.6 | 0.850 |
| parent: slow half alone (M0169-D20-SW) | +12.6% | +7.2% | 32.9% | +0.6 | 0.972 |

Every version beat SPY over twenty years and kept its worst fall well inside the lab's screen. The pair cut the parent's 33% worst fall to 20%, and its worst calendar year was 2011 at −6.3%. All of them failed the luck test. The best one scored 0.896 against the 0.90 bar, judged at N = 115 (one look per distinct method in the lab). That means after 115 ideas tried, a lead this size could too easily be luck. It is a near miss, but "nearly 0.90" is not 0.90.

On the walk-forward folds (four three-year stretches, each judged by a version picked using only the years before it), it won 2 of 4. It won 2006-2008 (+23% while SPY lost 25%) and 2012-2014, and lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011 badly (+21% vs SPY +61%). Two of four is not a majority, so the hard gate would refuse it anyway.

On the survivorship-check prices (dead companies added back), every version earned about 0.2 points a year less, the luck score fell to 0.87, and the 2009-2015 lead stayed at −4.0. The missing dead companies flatter this book a little, not much.

## What the breadth check said

The hedge overshot. The parent "paid only in broad months"; this pair now "pays only in narrow months" (+11.9% a year vs SPY in giant-led months, −1.9% in broad ones). The big half alone reads +20.0 narrow and −5.5 broad. It is a much stronger giants bet than the slow half is a small-names bet, so a 50/50 money split is nowhere near a 50/50 risk split.

## Why: the mechanism

The 2009-2015 problem was never the breadth bet. The control proves it: the big half alone, a book that does well whenever giants lead, still trailed SPY by 4.6 points a year in 2009-2015. Two things did that. The same 200-day switch stepped out in the 2010 and 2011 scares and missed the rebounds. And 2009-2013 was mostly a broad recovery, which a big-name book loses. The pair therefore inherited the switch's whipsaw cost in both halves and lost the slow half's broad-month gains in one of them. The result was −4.0 in the era that matters most, worse than the parent's +0.6.

The twenty-year lead (about +3 a year for every version, the control included) is mostly the switch sitting in cash through 2001-2002 and 2008. That is why the control, a book with no stock-picking idea at all, beats SPY by as much as the pair does. Sizing by trading value helped a little (+0.7 a year over equal slots) and did not deepen the fall here. That is unlike M0092, where it did.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed. The pair did read differently on the breadth check, but in the wrong direction, and its 2009-2015 lead fell instead of turning positive. The expected failure half happened. The big half did behave like a switched SPY and inherited the whipsaw. But the feared 25-30% fall did not happen: the two halves cut each other's 2008 and 1998 falls, and the worst fall was 20%.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

Against M0169-D20-SW (also measured at real fees on the same deposits) the pair gave up 2.1 points a year to cut the worst fall from 33% to 20%. M0171's volatility dial tried to buy the same fall-cut and failed (31-39%). This pair is the first slow-reactor version with a fall near 20%. But it bought that by diluting the idea with a book that needs no idea, which is why the control matches it.

**My opinion:** this direction is done. Pairing a stock-picking tilt with its opposite only dilutes the tilt; it does not repair the 2009-2015 era, because what loses there is the 200-day switch, and both halves carried it. The useful finding is the control: a plain switched big-name book earns the same twenty-year lead as everything built on top of it, so the lab's switched books are largely measuring the switch. Next I would keep the slow reactors behind their switch but pair them with plain SPY with no switch, so the core half never whipsaws. That isolates whether any of the slow-reactor edge survives 2009-2015 once the second half costs nothing there. If it does not, the slow-reactor family should be closed.
methods.verdict: Pairing the slowest reactors with the biggest companies cut the worst fall to 20% but lost 4 points a year to SPY in 2009-2015, and its luck score fell just short (0.896 vs 0.90)

DD12 may trip too late in August 1998 (SPY was 12% down only near the end of the month) to save much. Each exit and re-entry pays Gotrade's charges on 20 small slots. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

This is the filtered news-day book again. It buys big index members right after a day that looks like an earnings report, leans a little toward the busier names, keeps the rest in SPY, and goes to cash at the start of a month when SPY is below its 200-day average. Last try (M0075) added a crash exit: leave when SPY is 8% under its six-month high, and stay out until the next month's check. That saved 1998 but sold low and bought back high in 2000 and 2007.

This time the exit stays the same, but the way back is a price, not a calendar. The book comes back at the next weekly check once SPY has recovered to within a few percent of its high and is above its 200-day average. The gap between "leave" and "come back" stops one noisy day from flipping the book in and out. Everything ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5M IDR monthly deposits, on the weekly-resize preset (monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade).

Four variants, fixed before any result:

- **SQRT-DD8-R4**: leave at 8% under the high, come back within 4%.
- **SQRT-DD8-R2**: the same, come back only within 2%.
- **SQRT-DD12-R4**: leave only at 12% under the high, come back within 4%.
- **EQ-DD8-R4**: the DD8-R4 rule on equal 5% slots (M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's picks), the second host.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, the owner's deposits)

| variant | your money a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall (funded) | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SQRT-DD8-R4 | +10.6% | +7.2% | 25.3% | 1.98 | 0.860 | -0.2 pts |
| SQRT-DD8-R2 | +9.7% | +7.2% | 25.3% | 1.92 | 0.785 | -0.2 pts |
| **SQRT-DD12-R4** | **+11.9%** | +7.2% | **23.4%** | 2.04 | **0.908** | **+0.8 pts** |
| EQ-DD8-R4 | +10.4% | +7.2% | 24.1% | 1.87 | 0.865 | +0.2 pts |
| M0075 SQRT-DD8 (parent, monthly lockout) | +10.6% | +7.2% | 32.8% | 1.88 | 0.862 (N=112) | +1.3 pts |
| M0075 SQRT-NONE (no exit, control) | +12.0% | +7.2% | 25.1% | 2.00 | 0.895 (N=112) | +1.2 pts |

**SQRT-DD12-R4 is dev-eligible.** It beat SPY by 4.7 points a year on the same deposits. Its worst fall was 23.4%, under the 25% limit. Gains were twice the losses (the bar is 1.3). Its luck score of 0.908 clears the 0.90 bar at N=117. N is the number of distinct methods the lab has tried, and the luck score (DSR) is the chance the result is real rather than the best of 117 lucky tries. The other three variants all beat SPY but missed the luck bar.

**But it lost the walk-forward folds: 2 of 4.** The walk-forward test asks whether the lab's own rule, trained on earlier years, would have picked a winner for the next three years. It lost in 2003-2005 (+43% vs SPY +52%) and in 2009-2011 (+53% vs +61%), and won in 2006-2008 (-2% vs -25%) and 2012-2014 (+71% vs +66%). The hard gate needs a majority, so `lab promote` will refuse this method. There is no buy signal: the folds fail, and its 2009-2015 lead is only +0.8 points a year.

## The book alone, without deposits

| | DD8-R4 | DD8-R2 | DD12-R4 | control (M0075 NONE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1998 | +10% | +10% | 0% | -3% |
| 2000 | -7% | -5% | +28% | +28% |
| 2007 | -9% | -9% | -5% | -5% |
| worst fall | 25.6%, Jul 2007-Jul 2009 | 25.6%, same | 23.6%, Oct 2007-Jul 2009 | 25.8%, Mar-Nov 1998 |
| times it went to cash | 18 | 16 | 9 | 9 |
| 1996-2002 / 2003-08 / 2009-15 a year | +8.8 / +5.3 / +16.1 | +7.4 / +3.8 / +15.3 | +13.8 / +6.0 / +16.3 | +13.3 / +6.0 / +16.8 |

(The cash count includes the monthly 200-day switch's own exits.)

## Why

**The price re-entry fixed the parent's worst damage.** The deep 33% fall from 2007-2009 is gone. With DD8 the worst fall is now 25.6%, because the book came back within weeks of each 2007 drop instead of sitting out a whole month. The hypothesis held on that point.

**But DD8 still whipsaws in 2000.** In 2000 SPY fell 8-10% and bounced back to within 4% several times (February, April, May, October). Each round sold after the drop and bought back after most of the bounce. That turned the control's +28% year into -7%. This is the expected failure: a price re-entry narrows the whipsaw but does not remove it, because "back within 4%" happens only after most of the recovery. Waiting for 2% (R2) made each round trip dearer, not cheaper.

**DD12 works mostly by rarely firing.** It trips only on deep falls (end of August 1998, January 2008, plus a few the monthly switch would also have caught). It keeps the control's 2000 and 2007 years untouched, earns three points more in 1998 (0% vs -3%), and trims the worst fall by about 2 points. It left late in 1998, on 31 August, when SPY was already 12% down, as the expected failure foresaw. So DD12-R4 is really the control with a small insurance policy. Its luck score clears 0.90 mainly because it is the control's 0.895 plus a slightly smoother curve, not because of a new edge.

**The folds expose the same thing as before.** The book's lead lives in crashes (2006-2008) and in 2012-2014. It lags in steady bull runs (2003-2005, 2009-2011), when 20 mid-sized picks trail SPY's giants. The narrow-versus-broad split says the same: it pays only in broad markets (+8.8% vs SPY), and loses a little when a few giants lead.

**Survivorship check.** I re-ran it on the store that adds the dead companies. DD12-R4 drops to +11.1% a year (from +11.9%), its worst fall grows to 27.4% (over the limit), its luck score drops to 0.819, and it still wins 2 of 4 folds. Part of the edge was the missing dead companies, as with the rest of this family.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis was half right. A price re-entry did repair M0075's 2007 damage (33% to 25.6%). But I expected DD8-R4 to be best, and it was not: it still whipsawed through 2000. The deeper exit won, and only because it stays out of the way. Expected failures that happened: re-entry after the bounce (2000), a late DD12 exit in 1998, R2 doing worse, and the fold record. Unexpected: one variant just cleared the luck bar.

## Comparison

Against the no-exit control (M0075-SQRT-NONE): +11.9% vs +12.0% a year, worst fall 23.4% vs 25.1%, luck score 0.908 vs 0.895. Against the parent's DD8 lockout: +1.3 points a year and 9 points less worst fall. Against M0092-SQRT-CAP10 on the monthly preset: +11.9% vs +12.4% a year. Some of that gap is the weekly machinery, as M0075 measured.

**My opinion:** The crash-switch direction on this book is exhausted. Three tries (M0066, M0075, M0177) say the same thing. A switch read off SPY either fires often and whipsaws (DD5, SMA100, DD8 with either re-entry) or fires rarely and does almost nothing (DD12). The book's real weakness is not crashes. It lags SPY's giants in steady bull markets, which is why it loses half its folds and why the survivorship store pushes the fall past the limit. I would stop adding exits to the news-day book. The one test worth a slot is the book as a minority partner beside a large SPY core: that attacks the bull-market lag directly, where every switch has failed. I would not spend a test-window look on DD12-R4 even if the gate allowed it, and the gate does not.

The 2009-2015 lead (+0.8) is positive, but without a fold majority there is no buy signal.

methods.sourceRef: variation of M0174 (Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen & Pedersen 2020, JFE 135(3))
methods.hypothesis: M0174's 40-name low-correlation book (correlation with SPY from 3 years of overlapping 3-day returns, ranked inside 1-year volatility terciles, quarterly, 40% keep band, behind the SPY 200-day switch) beat SPY on dev (+12.0% a year funded vs +7.2%, worst fall 24%, DSR 0.98) but its 2009-2015 lead turned from +0.5 to -1.3 points a year on the survivorship-check store, and the fold selection preferred its high-correlation control. The paper was circulated 2017, published 2020, so the dev window predates it, though betting against beta was public from 2010. Restrict the choice to the 200 screened members with the highest 20-day dollar volume on each re-pick date, where dead companies missing from the store should matter least and the book sits closer to SPY's big-company shape. Variants (all behind the switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits): L30-SW and L40-SW (the idea at 30 and 40 names) and H40-SW (control: the 40 highest-correlation names in the same pool, same band; kept on Sera's instruction so the fold selection can still pick against the idea). M0174-C40-SW is reported beside it. Success: L40-SW or L30-SW beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25% and PF >= 1.3, the method's picks win a majority of walk-forward folds, H40-SW trails clearly, and the 2009-2015 lead is positive on both the dev and the survivorship-check store.
methods.expectedFailure: The busiest members are the market-tied ones (banks, tech, big industrials), so inside this pool the least-correlated names are mostly big utilities, staples, drug makers and oil, a defensive sector book that trails the 2009-2015 rise and loses the fold selection to the control again, exactly as M0174 did. Narrowing the pool also shrinks the spread between low and high correlation, so whatever premium M0174 showed partly came from the thinner members this pool drops, and the edge falls toward zero. If the 2009-2015 lead stays negative on the check store, the direction stops.

### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1607)

Sera caution, written before this idea runs: M0174 lost its fold majority because the fold rule kept preferring its high-correlation control. Re-running the winning low-correlation book with the control removed, after seeing that, would win the folds by construction and is the gate-dodging the hard gate exists to close. If this runs, it must keep a paired control in the variant set (the high-correlation book, or SPY-shaped equal weight) so the fold selection can still pick against it, and its analysis must report M0174-C40-SW beside it. A narrower pool (top 200 most traded) is a fair new question; dropping the control is not.


### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The same "companies that move least with the market" book as M0174, but allowed to choose only among the **200 most heavily traded** index members on each quarterly re-pick date. Big, busy companies rarely vanish from the lab's price data, so if M0174's edge came partly from missing dead companies, it should shrink less here. Everything else is M0174 unchanged: correlation with SPY from three years of overlapping three-day returns, ranked inside three groups of jumpiness, a 40% keep band, the SPY 200-day switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up.

Three versions were registered before any result:
- **L30-SW**: 30 names.
- **L40-SW**: 40 names.
- **H40-SW**: the control, the 40 names in the same pool that move *most* with the market.

The idea row said "no built-in control". Sera overruled that before the run, and I agreed: M0174 lost its fold record because the fold rule kept picking its control, and dropping the control after seeing that would win the folds by construction. So the control stayed in.

## Result against SPY (with dividends), 1996 to October 2015

Same deposits put into SPY earned +7.2% a year.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L30-SW | +10.6% | 24.2% | 4.2 | 0.947 | −2.6 pts |
| **L40-SW** | **+11.2%** | **24.3%** | 4.7 | 0.966 | −2.1 pts |
| H40-SW (control) | +9.0% | 21.5% | 4.3 | 0.858 | −6.5 pts |
| M0174-C40-SW (parent, all members) | +12.0% | 24.3% | 7.6 | 0.980 | +0.5 pts |

- **Luck check.** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than luck after the lab's tries. The lab now counts N = 118 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90. Both low-correlation versions clear it (0.95 and 0.97). The control does not (0.86).
- **Worst fall.** Both low-correlation versions lost at most about 24% from a peak, under the 25% real-money limit. SPY lost about 55% in the same years.
- So both L versions are **dev-eligible** on the twenty-year average.

## Why it is still not promotable

**1. The folds, again 1 of 4.** The lab re-plays history four times: it picks the version that looked best up to a cut-off date, then scores it on the next three years. In all four replays the version that looked best was again **the control** (H40-SW). It lost 2003-2005, won 2006-2008 (the switch kept it out of the crash), and lost 2009-2011 and 2012-2014. The hard gate wants a majority, so `lab promote` would refuse it. This time the control was there on purpose, and it still got picked: before every test stretch, the evidence favoured the market-tied names, not the idea.

**2. The best-covered years are negative, even on the lab's normal prices.** In 2009-2015, the years most like today, L40-SW trailed SPY by 2.1 points a year and L30-SW by 2.6. The parent, choosing from all members, was slightly ahead there (+0.5). So the parent's small 2009-2015 lead came from the less-traded members this pool drops.

**3. The dead-companies check now passes, which is the honest part.** On the survivorship-check store (which adds most of the members the normal store cannot price, failed companies included):
- L40-SW earns slightly *more* (+11.7% a year vs +11.2%), its worst fall is 23.0%, and its luck check rises to 0.97.
- L30-SW also earns more (+11.8%), but its worst fall deepens to 31%.
- The control's whole lead disappears (+9.0% → +7.1%, the same as SPY).

So narrowing to the busiest names did what it was meant to do: the edge no longer leans on missing companies. But the 2009-2015 lead stays negative on that store too (L40-SW −2.2 points a year).

**4. Narrow versus broad markets.** Both low-correlation versions earn their edge in months when the average stock beats the index (+5 to +6 points a year) and trail when a few giants carry it (−0.9 to −2.5). The 36-month persistence reading was positive in only 6 of 202 windows on dev; since 2018 it has been positive most of the time. That is a headwind for this book in exactly the years the test window covers.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

- **Partly.** Low correlation still beats high correlation among the busiest companies (+11.2% vs +9.0% a year), and the result is no longer flattered by missing dead companies.
- **The success test failed.** It needed a majority of folds and a positive 2009-2015 lead on both stores. It got 1 of 4 folds and a negative 2009-2015 lead on both.
- **The expected failure happened as written.** The pool's least-correlated names are the defensive sectors; the book trailed the 2009-2015 rise and lost the fold selection to the control again. The pre-registered stop condition ("if the 2009-2015 lead stays negative on the check store, the direction stops") is met.
- **No buy signal**: folds 1 of 4, 2009-2015 edge −2.1%.

**My opinion:** Stop this direction. Two methods now say the same thing: low correlation among big US companies paid from 1998 to 2008, mostly by sitting in defensive sectors through the dot-com bust and then being switched out of 2008, and it did not pay from 2009 on. Narrowing to the busiest names cleaned up the dead-company worry, which makes me more confident the twenty-year average is real, but it is real for the wrong years. The fold rule picking the control four times out of four in two separate methods is the market telling us the opposite tilt looked better before every test stretch. I would not spend another id on correlation as a stock-picking signal. The useful leftover is the market-wide version: how tightly stocks move together, read as a signal about the market itself, not about which stock to own.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1625)

Not promoted: dev-eligible, but `lab promote` would refuse on the folds (1 of 4; with the control kept as Sera asked, the selection picked the high-correlation book H40-SW in all four training windows, as it did for M0174; kin clean). 2009-2015 lead -2.1 pts (dev) and -2.2 (survivorship-check store). No buy signal. Correlation as a stock picker is closed by its own stop condition.

methods.name: Companies that crash with the market: own the stocks investors shun for falling hardest when the market falls hardest (coskewness)
methods.sourceRef: Harvey & Siddique (2000), Conditional Skewness in Asset Pricing Tests, JF 55(3); revisited in Critical Finance Review 2023
methods.hypothesis: Harvey and Siddique (published 2000, so most of the dev window is after publication and the 2023 revisit says the premium survived) find about 3.6% a year for systematic skewness: investors pay up for stocks that do well in market extremes, so the stocks with the most negative coskewness, the ones that fall hardest when the market swings hardest, earn more. On the last close of each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, compute each one's standardized coskewness with SPY from 156 non-overlapping weekly log returns (3 years; the CAPM residual against the squared demeaned market return, HS eq. 11; raw returns, a constant T-bill rate falls into the demeaning); hold the 20 most negative at 1/20 each, keep a holding while its rank fraction stays under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: N20 (the idea, no switch), N20-SW (behind F4's SPY-200 switch), N40-SW (a 40-name rung), P20-SW (control: the 20 most positive, same band and switch), G20-SW (scored by the raw regression coefficient on the squared market return, beta controlled, as the idea row worded it; it scales with the stock's own volatility). Success: N20-SW or N20 beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge, and P20-SW trails it clearly.
methods.expectedFailure: Negative-coskewness names are the high-beta, crash-prone ones (financials, cyclicals, tech in 2000), so the book falls hardest in 2008 and 2000-2002 and its worst fall breaks 25% without the switch; the lab's record on crash repair says the switch will not save it either, selling low and buying back high. Weekly coskewness over three years is a noisy estimate dominated by one or two crash weeks, so the ranking mostly re-sorts by the last crash's losers and the gap to the control is a sector cycle, not a premium. The published premium lives in small stocks and fades after 2000; among index members and in 2009-2015 it may be gone, and the equal-weight book loses to SPY's big-company drift.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

Harvey and Siddique (2000) found that investors dislike stocks that fall hardest when the market swings hardest, so those stocks are priced lower and earn more, by about 3.6% a year in their data. The measure is called **coskewness**: how a stock moves in the weeks when the market makes its biggest moves. A very negative number means the stock tends to fall in those weeks.

Each quarter the book measured every large S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 member over its last three years of weekly returns and held the 20 most negative (or 40 in one rung), equal weight. A holding stayed until it dropped out of the most negative 40%. Empty slots sat in SPY. Everything traded in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly top-up, over 1996 to 2015. The control held the 20 *most positive* names.

Assumptions written down before the run: weekly returns rather than monthly (156 data points instead of 36); plain returns rather than returns above the Treasury-bill rate, since a steady bill rate drops out when the returns are centred; the standardized measure from the paper as the main score, with the paper's raw regression slope as one variant.

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | earned a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 names, no switch | +10.1% | +7.2% | **51.7%** | 2.20 | 0.50 | +0.3% a year |
| 20 names, 200-day switch | +10.8% | +7.2% | 32.0% | 2.97 | 0.87 | −4.0% |
| **40 names, switch** | +10.5% | +7.2% | 22.6% | 2.74 | **0.91** | **−5.6%** |
| control: 20 most positive, switch | +9.2% | +7.2% | 23.2% | 2.67 | 0.85 | −3.6% |
| raw-slope score, switch | +11.3% | +7.2% | 30.9% | 2.26 | 0.81 | −6.2% |

"Worst fall" is the biggest drop from a peak with the deposits taken out. The lab's limit is 25%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is the money made on winning trades divided by the money lost on losing ones; the bar is 1.3. The luck test (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely the result is to be real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at **N = 116** (one look per method in the lab), against the owner's bar of **0.90**.

The 40-name book with the switch cleared every dev condition: it beat SPY by 3.3 points a year, its worst fall was 22.6%, and its luck score was 0.91, only just over 0.90. So the lab marks the method **dev-eligible**. Every other version failed the luck test, and the no-switch book also failed on its 52% fall in 2008.

## Why it will not reach a test look

- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4 folds.** Before each three-year test stretch, the lab's own rule looked back and picked the variant that had done best so far. Every time that was the *control* (the most positive names), never the idea. The control lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011 and won 2006-2008 and 2012-2014. The hard gate needs a majority of at least four folds, so `lab promote` would refuse it. This is the same pattern as the low-correlation book run earlier today: before every test stretch, the opposite of the idea looked better.
- **2009-2015, the years most like today:** the eligible 40-name book trailed SPY by 5.6% a year. All of its twenty-year lead was earned before 2009.
- **Breadth:** the 20-name books paid only in months when the average stock beat the index (+4 to +11% a year in those months) and lost in months when a few giants carried it. That is a bet against SPY's big-company drift.

## The dead-company check

On the survivorship-check store (the same years with most of the dead companies added back), the negative-coskewness books did *slightly better*: the 40-name book earned +10.9% instead of +10.5%, and its 2009-2015 gap shrank from −5.6% to −3.7%. The control and the raw-slope version did worse. So the missing dead companies did not create the edge. But the 40-name book's luck score fell to 0.88 on that store, under the bar, and its folds stayed at 2 of 4.

## Mechanism

The stocks that fall hardest in the market's big weeks are mostly high-beta cyclicals, financials and tech (stocks that swing more than the market). Over 1996-2015 that group had two big runs: the late-1990s boom and the 2003-2007 recovery. That is where the lead came from. Without the switch the book fell 52% in 2008, as expected. The switch cut the fall but cost the 2010-2011 rebound (it sold low and bought back high), and from 2009 the book trailed SPY. The control earned less overall, so a gap exists. But the walk-forward shows the gap was a regime: whichever side had just been winning kept winning for a while, then lost. It does not look like a steady premium.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis held only in its weak form: the most negative names beat the most positive by about 1.3-1.6 points a year over twenty years. It did not hold where it matters, which is a majority of folds and a positive edge in 2009-2015. The expected failure happened almost word for word. The book fell hardest in 2008 (52% with no switch), the switch did not rescue the recent years, and the edge lived before 2009. One part of the expected failure was wrong: the dead-company check did not shrink the edge.

## Compared with near misses

The 40-name book's dev numbers look like the lab's best momentum books (+3.3 points a year, a 22.6% worst fall). It shares their weakness: a lead built in the 1990s and 2003-2007 that disappears after 2009. It is not momentum (it ranks on crash behaviour), but the behaviour-based kin check would likely place it near the high-beta books.

**My opinion:** this direction is not worth a promotion, and it should not be tuned. A gate that rejects the method on folds is right: the control was the better pick before every test stretch, and the 2009-2015 years say no. The one interesting result is the no-switch 20-name book. It is the only version that did not trail SPY in 2009-2015 (+0.3% a year, and +3.7% on the dead-company store). Its 52% fall is the problem, and the lab's record shows that market-timing switches give back the recent years. So the next step is not a better switch. It is a smaller position: the negative-coskewness picks as a minority sleeve beside a SPY core, with no switch. That is one variation; if it trails SPY in 2009-2015, close the family.
