### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera, owner-directed coskewness batch)

Slate note: keep the positive-coskewness book in the sleeve as a paired control variant (Sera rule since M0178), and report M0179-N20 and M0179-N40-SW beside the results. Design from the dev window only. The owner's 2018-2026 calculate-assets run of M0179 (N20 ended well ahead of SPY) is known, so no sleeve size or variant may be chosen because it did well after 2015. This method is the direct answer to the owner's question: can the no-switch upside be kept with a fall inside 25%?


### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

The owner's question: can the coskewness book keep its no-switch upside while falling less than 25%? The earlier version (M0179) held the 20 stocks that fall hardest in the market's biggest weeks. With no market switch it beat SPY, but it fell 52% in 2008. This method keeps most of the money in SPY (the "core") and puts only the rest into those stocks (the "sleeve"). There is no switch. Everything else is M0179's book unchanged: three years of weekly returns, a re-pick every quarter, a holding kept while it stays in the most negative 40%, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, and the owner's monthly top-up, over 1996 to 2015.

Every variant was chosen from dev-window reasoning only. The owner's 2018-2026 run of M0179 was known and played no part in the choice.

| version | what it holds |
|---|---|
| 70/30, 20 names (the idea) | 70% SPY, 30% in the 20 most negative names (1.5% each) |
| 60/40, 20 names | 60% SPY, 40% in the same 20 names (2% each) |
| 70/30, 40 names | 70% SPY, 30% spread over 40 names (0.75% each) |
| control, 70/30 | 70% SPY, 30% in the 20 most *positive* names |
| 70/30 with switch | the idea, but the whole book goes to cash while SPY is under its 200-day average |
| control with switch | the control, same switch |

**Assumption written down before the run:** a SPY core held through 2008 falls about as far as SPY does, near 55%. So no version without a switch can meet 25%. The unswitched versions answer "does the sleeve add anything to SPY?". The switched pair answers "what does getting under 25% cost?".

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | earned a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 70/30, 20 names | +7.9% | +7.2% | **52.6%** | 2.19 | 0.45 | +0.0% a year | 0.99 |
| 60/40, 20 names | +8.3% | +7.2% | **52.0%** | 2.26 | 0.47 | +0.3% | 0.99 |
| 70/30, 40 names | +8.0% | +7.2% | **53.9%** | 2.24 | 0.47 | +0.3% | 0.97 |
| control, 70/30 | +6.5% | +7.2% | **58.4%** | 1.69 | 0.39 | −0.6% | 0.96 |
| 70/30 with switch | +9.4% | +7.2% | 18.4% | 7.36 | **0.889** | **−5.2%** | 0.44 |
| control with switch | +8.8% | +7.2% | 19.0% | 6.32 | 0.867 | −5.3% | 0.44 |
| *M0179, 20 names, no switch* | +10.1% | +7.2% | 51.7% | 2.20 | 0.50 | +0.3% | 1.02 |
| *M0179, 40 names, switch* | +10.5% | +7.2% | 22.6% | 2.74 | 0.91 | −5.6% | 0.41 |

How to read the columns:

- **Earned a year** is the owner's money-weighted return on the deposits.
- **Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a peak, with the deposits taken out. The lab's screen is 50% and the real-money bar is 25%.
- **Gains vs losses** (profit factor) is money made on winning trades divided by money lost on losing ones.
- **The luck test** (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at **N = 119** (one look per method in the lab) against the owner's bar of **0.90**.
- **Beta to SPY** comes from the monthly returns with the deposits taken out. 1.0 means the book moves one-for-one with SPY.

No version passed. The three unswitched sleeves failed on the fall (52-54%, over even the loose 50% screen) and on luck (0.45-0.47). The switched idea came closest: it beat SPY by 2.2 points a year with an 18.4% worst fall. It still missed the luck bar, at 0.889 against 0.90.

## Why it fails

- **The core does exactly what a core does.** With 70% in SPY the book is SPY. Its beta is 0.99, its monthly returns track SPY's at 0.99 correlation, and in 2008 it lost 35% where SPY lost 37%. The sleeve kept roughly a third of M0179's lead: +0.7 points a year against M0179's +2.9. That matches the 30% share almost exactly. The 2009-2015 edge kept the same share too: M0179's +0.3 points became +0.0 to +0.3. Nothing here is a new effect. It is M0179 diluted.
- **The fall cannot get small without timing.** The fall comes from the core, not the sleeve: the control sleeve fell *further* (58%). A 25% bar on an always-invested stock book needs either a switch or bonds. The lab's record says switches give back the recent years, and they did here. With the switch the book trailed SPY by 5.2 points a year in 2009-2015, as M0179's switched book did.
- **The control was nearly as good wherever it mattered.** With the switch on, the negative and positive sleeves ended 0.6 points a year apart. The walk-forward check (each three-year test stretch scored with the variant that looked best on the years before it) picked the *positive* control three times out of four. It won 1 of 4 folds, and the hard gate needs a majority of at least four, so `lab promote` would refuse it even if the luck test passed. Without the switch the negative sleeve did beat the control by 1.4 points a year, but on SPY-sized swings that difference does not reach significance.

## The dead-company check

On the survivorship-check store (the same years with most of the dead companies added back), the unswitched 20-name sleeves did slightly better: the 60/40 book went from +1.1 to +1.6 points a year over SPY, and its 2009-2015 lead from +0.3 to +1.6. That repeats M0179's finding: the missing dead companies did not create this edge. But every luck score fell a little (0.889 to 0.884 for the switched book), the falls barely moved, and the switched book still won 1 of 4 folds.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed. The 70/30 book beat SPY on the deposits and beat its control, but its 2009-2015 edge was zero, it won 1 of 4 folds, and its luck score was 0.45. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the edge diluted in proportion to the sleeve, the fall landed near SPY's and broke the 50% screen, the luck score collapsed, the switched pair met the fall bar but trailed SPY after 2009, and the folds picked the control. My guess of "+0.1 points a year in 2009-2015" was close, at +0.0.

**My opinion:** close coskewness as a stock picker. Over two methods and eleven variants the signal never showed an edge that survives both the luck test and the 2009-2015 years. Whatever it earns is the high-beta boom of the late 1990s and 2003-2007, and a SPY core only shrinks that, it does not clean it. This method answers the owner's question plainly: the no-switch upside cannot be kept with a fall inside 25%, because the fall comes from owning stocks through 2008, not from which stocks. Getting the fall under 25% needs a switch, and the switch costs the recent years. Every M0179 and M0180 variant has a beta between 0.4 and 1.0 and none above 1.1. So the no-switch book's post-2015 run is market exposure plus a small tilt, not a reason to reopen this direction. If anything is left to try here, it is not a sleeve size. It is whether the per-name signal survives when the book weights by company size instead of equally, so that it stops betting against SPY's big-company drift. I queued that as one last idea, and if it trails SPY in 2009-2015 the family is done.


### 2026-10-17

Correction to the last paragraph above: a sibling in this batch had already tried coskewness with the picks sized toward the bigger companies, and it was rejected. So the size-weighted coskewness book was not queued again. The next idea queued from this result is outside the coskewness family: pick the members that beat SPY after their market risk is taken out, keeping the book's risk close to SPY's, so a lead cannot come from riskier stocks in a boom.

methods.name: How tightly stocks move together, as a signal about the market: hold SPY, and read average stock-to-stock correlation as the market's own risk gauge
methods.sourceRef: Pollet & Wilson (2010), Average correlation and stock market returns, Journal of Financial Economics 96(3), 364-380; builds on M0174/M0178, which used correlation to pick stocks rather than to read the market
methods.hypothesis: Pollet & Wilson (2010) split market variance into average variance times average correlation and find that only the correlation half forecasts the market, with a POSITIVE sign: when big stocks move together, the market is risky and the risk is paid for. Trading-room lore says the opposite, that a correlation spike means get out. This lab's two correlation methods (M0174, M0178) showed correlation fails as a stock picker after 2009; this asks whether it reads the market instead, and registers BOTH signs so the answer cannot be a choice made after the fact. The book holds SPY alone, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. The reading is the average pairwise correlation of daily returns among the 100 busiest point-in-time index members with full history, compared against its own last 31 readings over 300 sessions (a band of its own recent history, because average correlation drifts up across the window as index funds grow). Variants, all fixed now: HI-OFF (cash when correlation is top-20% AND SPY is under its 200-day average); HI-OFF-W126 (the same on a six-month correlation window); HI-HALF (half in SPY instead of all cash); HI-ALONE (cash on the correlation reading alone, no trend condition -- the pure anti-paper bet); LO-OFF (the PAPER's sign: cash when correlation is bottom-20% and SPY is under its 200-day average); SPY200 (control: the lab's SPY 200-day switch alone, same window). HI-OFF and LO-OFF are each in cash on a complementary subset of SPY200's cash months, so together they say whether correlation sorts those months at all. SUCCESS: one sign beats SPY200 on funded return AND on 2009-2015 AND its mirror loses, so the correlation reading and not merely 'be in cash less often' did the work. The trade count will be a few dozen, far under the 100-trade floor, so NO variant can be eligible and none is meant to be: the paired differences are the whole result, and that is assumed and accepted before the run.
methods.expectedFailure: The lab has priced four market clocks already -- the SPY 200-day switch (M0084), the typical-stock breadth filter (M0205), the cross-sectional dispersion clock (M0118) and the breadth regime switch (M0097) -- and every one of them cost money once the window reached 2009-2015, because sitting out the 2009 recovery costs more than dodging 2008 saves. The most likely result here is the same: HI-OFF trims a few of the plain switch's exits, which helps a little in 2010-2011 and hurts in 2008, and lands within noise of SPY200 either way. The second most likely result is the one that kills the idea cleanly: HI-OFF and LO-OFF both land near SPY200, which would mean correlation does not sort the switch's cash months at all and the reading is empty -- M0118's verdict, where the idea and its exact opposite both lost. HI-ALONE should be the worst variant, because a correlation band with no trend behind it will sit out strong, tightly-correlated bull runs (1997-1999, 2013) as readily as crashes. Survivorship leans the panel calm at every bottom (the names that fell together hardest are the ones missing from the store), so every high-correlation trigger fires later and weaker than it would on honest data. Profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless on a few dozen trades and no variant should clear the luck bar. Cash earns nothing in the simulator, so every switched variant's measured cost is an upper bound.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# How tightly stocks move together, as a signal about the market

## What was tried

Hold SPY and nothing else. Once a month, measure how closely the 100 busiest big American
companies have been moving together — the average correlation between every pair of them over the
last three months (or six, in one version). Compare today's reading with the same reading taken 30
times over the previous fourteen months. If today sits in the top fifth of that range, the market
is "tight": everything is moving as one. If it sits in the bottom fifth, it is "loose".

There are two opposite stories about what a tight market means, and this run registered both
before seeing any result, so the answer could not be chosen afterwards.

- **The trading-room story.** Everything moving together means everything is being sold together.
  Get out.
- **The academic story.** Pollet and Wilson (2010) found the opposite: a tight market is a risky
  market, and risk is what investors are paid to take, so tight markets have been followed by
  *better* returns, not worse.

Six versions ran, all on the owner's real plan — Rp 10 million to start, Rp 5 million deposited on
the 25th of every month, 237 deposits, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees — from January 1996
to October 2015.

## The result

Money-weighted return, which is what the owner's deposits actually earned. Deposit-matched SPY
earned **+7.2% a year** over the same window.

| version | what it does | a year | worst fall | in the market | round trips |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **the plain switch** (control) | cash whenever SPY is under its 200-day average | **+8.6%** | **18.9%** | 71% | 9 |
| six-month tightness | cash when tight **and** SPY under its average | +8.8% | 29.1% | 84% | 8 |
| the paper's sign | cash when **loose** and SPY under its average | +7.9% | 51.0% | 96% | 3 |
| three-month tightness | cash when tight **and** SPY under its average | +7.5% | 41.4% | 86% | 9 |
| half step | half in SPY on the same tight signal | +7.4% | 46.5% | 93% | 0 |
| tightness alone | cash when tight, ignoring the trend | **+5.7%** | 42.6% | 74% | 21 |

Every version fails the go-live rules, and that was expected and written down before the run: a
book that holds one thing and is asked once a month makes eight to twenty-one round trips in
twenty years, against the rule's floor of 100. Five of the six also fall further than the owner's
20% limit allows. Only the plain switch, at 18.9%, stays inside it.

**The headline is the control.** The plain 200-day switch — no correlation reading at all — won on
return, won on the worst fall by a wide margin, and did it while sitting in cash more often than
any tightness version except the one with no trend behind it. The whole point of this method was
to improve on that switch by picking which of its cash months were the ones worth sitting out.
It did not. Both ways of picking made the fall far deeper and neither made more money that mattered.

### Why: a correlation spike arrives after the crash, not before it

The switch turned off in January 2008 and stayed off. The tightness reading did not reach its top
fifth until **September 2008** — after Lehman, eight months and most of the way down. The same
pattern holds in the previous bear: the switch was off from late 2000, the tightness reading only
came on in April 2001. So the versions that wait for both signals sit through the first half of
every crash. That is the entire explanation for the 41% and 29% falls against the control's 19%:
they were in the market for the part of 2008 the control missed.

Stocks move together *because* they are falling together. By the time you can measure it, you have
already paid for it.

### The number that is genuinely interesting

Set the trading rule aside and just ask what SPY did in the month after each reading. All 237
months, split by the trend and by tightness:

| | loose (bottom fifth) | middle | tight (top fifth) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SPY above its 200-day average** | +0.33% a month (61 months) | +1.10% (80) | **+2.44% (29)** |
| **SPY below its 200-day average** | −2.83% (6) | −0.19% (31) | −0.54% (30) |

Read the top row. Inside a rising market, the tight months were followed by about **+34% a year**
and the loose months by about **+4% a year** — a thirty-point gap, in a clean order, over 170
months. That is Pollet and Wilson's sign, and it is large. The bottom row is where this method
lived, and there the reading does almost nothing: tight months and middling months were both
roughly flat-to-down, and the one eye-catching cell, the −2.83%, is six months whose average is
set by two of them (October 2000, −7.5%, and August 2008, −9.9%). Six months is not a finding.

So the signal is real, it has the academic sign, and it is in the half of the market this method
never looked at. The version that bet against the paper — out of the market whenever things were
tight, trend ignored — was the worst of the six at +5.7% a year, 1.5 points behind simply holding
SPY. That is the same message from the other side.

### What the dead companies did to it

The lab's survivorship-check store adds back most of the companies the normal store cannot price,
including the ones that went bust. Re-running every version there (a report, not a new result):

- The **six-month version — the only one that beat the control** — gave the win back. Its lead
  over SPY fell from +1.7% to +0.8% a year and its worst fall went from 29.1% to **41.9%**, 13
  points deeper. Its apparent edge was partly the missing bankruptcies.
- The three-month version went slightly the other way, +0.4% to +0.8% a year, fall 41.4% to 37.1%.
- The plain switch is identical on both stores, because it reads only SPY and never looks at
  individual companies.

That is the honest answer to "was the one good number real": no.

### The years that matter most

2009-2015 is the best-covered stretch of data and the most like today. Every version lagged SPY
there: the plain switch by 5.9 points a year, the six-month version by 3.9, the three-month by
3.0, the tightness-alone version by 3.6. Only the paper's-sign version was level, and only because
it was barely ever out of the market (96% invested, three round trips in twenty years). This is
the fifth market clock the lab has priced and the fifth to lose money in those years.

### Luck

The lab now judges results against 158 separate method attempts, and asks for a 90% chance the
result is real rather than luck (the owner's setting since 7 October 2026 — in the lab's shorthand,
DSR, the share of the time a result this good would *not* have come from chance given how many
things have been tried). The best version here scores 0.79 and the control 0.87; neither clears
the bar. With eight to twenty-one round trips in twenty years, these scores are close to
meaningless anyway, which was also said before the run.

### The half-step version made no round trips

It went to half weight and back, so no position was ever fully closed — hence zero round trips and
no gains-to-losses figure. It did act: it was 93% invested against the three-month version's 86%.
It is a reminder that this book's "trade count" is not a measure of how busy it was.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**No.** The hypothesis asked for one sign to beat the plain switch on return *and* in 2009-2015,
while its mirror lost. Neither sign beat the switch in 2009-2015, neither beat it on the worst
fall, and the one that beat it on return did so only on the store that is missing the dead
companies.

**The expected failure was mostly right, and one part was wrong.** Right: the tightness-alone
version was the worst of the six, exactly as written; the correlation reading does not sort the
switch's cash months, which was named as the outcome that kills the idea cleanly; no version
cleared the trade floor or the luck bar. Wrong: the prediction was that missing bankruptcies would
make the tight signal fire *later and weaker*, hurting it. In fact adding the dead companies
helped the three-month version slightly and destroyed the six-month one. The honest tape did not
move the reading in one direction; it moved whichever version had been lucky.

## Compared with its relatives

- **The plain 200-day switch** measured on its own (from 1994) earned +9.1% a year with an 18.9%
  worst fall. The control here reproduced that 18.9% exactly on this slightly shorter window, so
  the setup is sound and this is the same object the lab has measured before.
- **The typical-stock breadth filter** asked almost this question with a different thermometer and
  reached the same answer: the control beat it everywhere.
- **The spread-between-companies clock** found that the idea and its exact opposite both lost, and
  called the signal empty. Here both signs land below the control on the same three-month
  reading — the tight version 1.1 points a year behind it, the loose version 0.7 behind — and the
  only version that got above it did so on a six-month window and then lost it to the dead
  companies. The same shape of answer.
- **The two correlation stock-pickers**, this method's parents, used the same measurement to
  choose *which stocks to own* and failed after 2009. The measurement has now failed as a picker
  and as a timer. It has not failed as a description of when the market pays.

## My opinion:

**Stop timing the market with correlation. The direction is closed, and it closed for a reason
worth remembering: a correlation spike is a symptom of a fall, not a warning of one.** Eight
months late into 2008 is not a tuning problem; no threshold, window or hysteresis fixes a signal
that only exists once the damage is done. I would not spend another method id on stepping *out* of
the market on this reading, in any form.

But I would spend one on the table above, and I would spend it soon. The thirty-point-a-year gap
between tight and loose months *inside a rising market* is the largest clean conditional spread I
have seen in this lab's market-wide data, it has the sign a published paper predicts rather than
the sign a trader would guess, and it sits in the 170 months this method ignored. It also points
the opposite way from everything the lab has built: every brake here fires in a falling market,
and this one would fire in a rising one — step down when the rising market goes *quiet and
scattered*, not when it goes loud. That is a genuinely new shape of rule.

Two warnings I would attach to it before anyone gets excited. First, I found that table by looking
at data I had already run, so it is a selected finding and has to be re-registered with its own
controls — including the mirror again, which is the only reason this run is interpretable at all.
Second, the loose-and-rising months are not evenly spread: they cluster in the late 1990s and the
mid-2000s, and a rule built on them may turn out to be a rule about two specific stretches. The
registered version must show its fold record and its 2009-2015 number before anyone believes it.

The second thing I would try, cheaper and more useful to the books the lab already owns: the
stock-picking books all sit behind this same 200-day switch and all die in 2009-2015. If the quiet,
scattered months inside an uptrend are also the months those books lose, then this reading is not a
market timer at all — it is a measurement of when stock-picking works, which is a different and
more valuable thing. That costs one method id to find out.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a correlation spike arrives after the crash, not before it — it only reached its top fifth in September 2008, eight months after the plain 200-day switch had already stepped aside, and the plain switch beat every version here on return and on the worst fall.

methods.name: Is coskewness just a riskier book? Rank by coskewness only among stocks that swing about as much as the market
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0179 (Harvey & Siddique 2000, JF 55(3)); owner-directed coskewness batch 2026-10-17
methods.hypothesis: Harvey and Siddique (published 2000) price coskewness net of beta, but M0179's ranked book of the most negative-coskewness members may still be a disguised high-beta bet: it beat SPY over 1996-2015 on average and fell 52% in 2008 without the switch. Each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, measure beta to SPY and standardized coskewness (HS eq. 11) from the same 156 weekly log returns M0179 uses (beta from that three-year weekly window, not a 60-month monthly one, so both measures share the same weeks: an assumption). methods.expectedFailure: Once beta is matched the spread between the negative and positive books collapses, because M0179's gap was a high-beta tilt riding the late-1990s and 2003-2007 runs; then the coskewness family is closed as a stock picker. The beta-matched books still hold 20-40 equal-weighted members, so they keep the equal-weight lean against SPY's big-company drift and trail SPY in 2009-2015 regardless. A published anomaly (2000) is likely to have faded inside the dev window already, and three-year weekly coskewness is noisy, dominated by one or two crash weeks.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

The earlier coskewness picker (the parent method) bought the stocks that fall hardest in the weeks when the market makes its biggest moves. It beat SPY over 1996-2015 on average but fell 52% in 2008 without the market switch. One explanation: those stocks are simply riskier, swinging more than the market (high **beta**: a beta of 1.0 moves with the market, 1.5 moves half again as much). If so, the "edge" was just extra risk in a rising market.

This method holds beta fixed and asks whether the coskewness ranking still picks better stocks. Each quarter, among the large S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members, it measured every stock's beta and coskewness over the same three years of weekly returns. Then:

- **Tercile versions (T):** split the stocks into three equal groups by beta (low, middle, high), rank by coskewness inside each group, and take about a third of the book from each. The book's beta then sits near the average member's whatever coskewness does.
- **Band version (B20):** rank only the stocks whose beta is between 0.8 and 1.2.
- **Paired controls (TP):** the same beta groups, but the *most positive* coskewness first: the opposite of the idea.

Equal weight, a holding kept while it stays in the best 40% of its group, empty slots in SPY, quarterly re-picks, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly 5 million IDR top-up, 1996 to 2015.

Assumption written down before the run: beta came from the same three-year weekly window as coskewness, not a 60-month monthly window, so both numbers describe the same weeks.

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | earned a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | book's beta to SPY | 2009-2015 vs SPY* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T20: beta-matched, 20 names, no switch | +10.0% | +7.2% | **56.7%** | 2.14 | 0.50 | 0.99 | +1.3% a year |
| T20-SW: same, with 200-day switch | +10.0% | +7.2% | 35.0% | 2.69 | 0.77 | 0.42 | −3.8% |
| **T40-SW: 40 names, switch** | +11.0% | +7.2% | 22.8% | 2.95 | **0.91** | 0.42 | −3.3% |
| B20: beta 0.8-1.2 only, no switch | +10.5% | +7.2% | 44.0% | 2.24 | 0.67 | 0.91 | −1.0% |
| TP20: control, no switch | +7.4% | +7.2% | **66.4%** | 1.98 | 0.52 | 0.93 | +1.2% |
| TP20-SW: control, switch | +8.9% | +7.2% | 26.9% | 2.78 | 0.85 | 0.42 | −2.5% |
| *beside it:* parent, 20 names, no switch | +10.1% | +7.2% | 51.7% | 2.20 | 0.50 | 1.02 | +1.1% |
| *beside it:* parent, 40 names, switch | +10.5% | +7.2% | 22.6% | 2.74 | 0.91 | 0.41 | −4.0% |

*Beta and the 2009-2015 column are measured on monthly returns with the deposits taken out, against SPY. "Worst fall" is the biggest drop from a peak with the deposits taken out; the lab's screen is 50% and the real-money limit is 25%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is money made on winning trades divided by money lost on losing ones; the bar is 1.3. The luck test (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at **N = 121** (one look per method in the lab, as `lab status` printed at the run), against the owner's bar of **0.90**.

The 40-name beta-matched book with the switch cleared every dev condition: it beat SPY by 3.8 points a year with a 22.8% worst fall and a luck score of 0.914. So the lab marks the method **dev-eligible**. Every other version failed the luck test, and both no-switch tercile books broke the 50% fall screen in 2008.

## Why it will not reach a test look

- **Walk-forward: 0 of 4 folds.** Before each three-year test stretch the lab's rule picked the variant that had looked best so far, and every pick lost to SPY: the *control* in 2003-2005 (+31% vs +52%) and 2006-2008 (−44% vs −25%), the eligible 40-name book in 2009-2011 (+36% vs +61%) and 2012-2014 (+63% vs +66%). `lab promote` refuses anything under a majority of four. This is worse than the parent's 2 of 4.
- **2009-2015, the years most like today:** the lab's era read puts the picks 4.8% a year behind SPY.

## The question the method was built to answer

**Was the parent's edge a high-beta tilt? No, and the answer is more damaging than yes would have been.**

- The parent's no-switch book had a beta of **1.02** to SPY. It was never a high-beta book; its 52% fall in 2008 came from owning 20 ordinary-beta cyclicals and financials equally, not from extra beta. Matching beta changed almost nothing: the beta-matched book earned the same +10.0% a year (parent +10.1%) and fell slightly further (56.7%).
- The thing that matters is the gap between the idea and its paired control. Month by month, with deposits taken out, the beta-matched book beat its control by **+0.04% a year** without the switch and *trailed* it by **1.1% a year** with the switch. Neither is distinguishable from zero (t-statistics of 0.02 and −0.55). The parent's switched book against its control: −0.13% a year. In plain words: picking the most negative coskewness and picking the most positive gave the same month-by-month returns.
- Then why does the table show +10.0% against +7.4% for the no-switch pair? The control swings harder (worst fall 66% against 57%) and was hit at the worst moment for the deposits: it lost 45% in 2008, when the account was largest. The money-weighted figure rewards whichever book happened to fall less when the balance was big. That is a timing accident of the deposits, not a stock-picking edge.

So what made every version beat SPY over twenty years? The shape, not the signal: 20-40 screened members held equally, which beats SPY in decades when the average stock beats the giants (the late 1990s after 2000, and 2003-2007) and loses when a few giants carry the index (2009-2015). The lab has measured this shape before; any ranking in this frame inherits it.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: with beta held fixed the negative-coskewness book did not separate from its control, so there is no coskewness premium to harvest among index members in 1996-2015. The expected failure happened almost entirely: the spread collapsed, the books kept the equal-weight lean and trailed SPY from 2009, and the walk-forward picked the control in two folds. One part was wrong in the direction it assumed: the parent was not a high-beta book (beta 1.02), so the spread was never a beta tilt. It was just not there to begin with.

## My opinion

The coskewness family is closed as a stock picker. Two methods, eleven variants and two paired controls say the same thing: the idea and its opposite earn the same month by month, and the twenty-year lead over SPY belongs to the equal-weight shape, which has lost to SPY since 2009. I would not try a minority sleeve or another switch on it: a sleeve of a signal that does not separate from its opposite is a sleeve of the equal-weight shape. What this run does teach is a method problem. Three batches in a row (low correlation, coskewness, this) had a control that looked as good as the idea, so the lab needs a standing placebo: the same frame filled by a fixed, meaningless order. That would show how much of any book's lead over SPY the frame alone delivers before a signal claims it. That is the next idea I queued.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1707, promotion step 0b)

Dev-eligible on M0184-T40-SW, refused by the hard gate: 0 of 4 walk-forward folds (pick changed between the positive-coskewness control and the switched 40-name book), 2009-2015 edge -4.8% a year. No test look spent. The beta-matched book and its positive-coskewness control earned the same month by month (+0.04% a year, t 0.02 without the switch; -1.10% a year, t -0.55 with it). The parent was never a high-beta book: M0179-N20's beta to SPY is 1.02, the switched books about 0.42.

Otherwise M0179's frame: F4's $5 / $20M screen, re-pick each quarter's last close, keep a holding under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Success: turnover falls against M0179, the dev edge over SPY TR holds with worst fall <= 25% (for the switched book), S beats its paired control, the walk-forward selection picks a negative-coskewness variant in a majority of folds and wins them, and the 2009-2015 edge is positive.
methods.expectedFailure: The control's lead before each fold was real: crash-prone stocks pay only in a few episodes (the late 1990s boom, the 2003-2007 recovery) and smoothing cannot create persistence the premium does not have, so the folds stay split. A five-year window leaves the book in SPY until about 1998 (the store starts in 1993), cutting the 1990s years where M0179 earned part of its lead, so the twenty-year edge shrinks. A smoother rank sorts more steadily into high-beta cyclicals, so the no-switch books still fall near 50% in 2008 and the switched one trails SPY in 2009-2015 as M0179's did. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

M0179 picked stocks by **coskewness**: how a stock moves in the weeks when the market makes its biggest moves. The idea was to own the most negative ones, the stocks that fall hardest in those weeks, because investors shun them and so they should earn more. M0179 beat SPY on its twenty-year average. Its walk-forward tests went the other way: before every test stretch the lab's own rule preferred the *opposite* book (the most positive names).

This method asked whether that was measurement noise. A score built from three years of weekly returns is pushed around by one or two crash weeks. So the signal was smoothed in two ways, first separately and then together:

- a **five-year window** (260 weekly returns instead of 156);
- each stock's rank **averaged over its last four quarterly scorings**, so one bad quarter cannot flip it.

Everything else is M0179's frame: the same big-member screen, a re-pick each quarter, a holding kept while it stays in the most negative 40%, empty slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, 1996-2015. Each main version has a **paired control** that holds the most *positive* names with the same smoothing.

Assumptions written down before the run: at the averaged dates the book ranks today's screened stocks; and a five-year window needs prices back to 1991, which the store does not have (it starts in 1993), so until about 1998 the book mostly sat in SPY.

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | earned a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | beta to SPY | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S20: both smoothers, 20 names, no switch | +7.6% | +7.2% | **63.9%** | 3.52 | 0.36 | +1.5% | 1.12 | 118 |
| **S40-SW: both, 40 names, 200-day switch** | **+10.9%** | +7.2% | 27.0% | 4.45 | **0.95** | **−5.0%** | 0.46 | 478 |
| W20: five-year window only | +9.5% | +7.2% | 53.7% | 2.16 | 0.48 | +2.0% | 1.00 | 420 |
| A20: four-quarter average only | +8.6% | +7.2% | 56.8% | 2.17 | 0.43 | −0.5% | 1.07 | 195 |
| C20: control for S20 (most positive) | +7.4% | +7.2% | 68.5% | 2.24 | 0.41 | +3.1% | 0.93 | 112 |
| C40-SW: control for S40-SW | +8.1% | +7.2% | 23.9% | 3.80 | 0.79 | −4.1% | 0.42 | 488 |
| *M0179-N20 (parent, no switch)* | *+10.1%* | *+7.2%* | *51.7%* | *2.20* | *0.50* | *+0.3%* | *1.02* | *506* |
| *M0179-N40-SW (parent, eligible)* | *+10.5%* | *+7.2%* | *22.6%* | *2.74* | *0.91* | *−5.6%* | *0.41* | *1107* |

How to read the table:
- **Worst fall** is the biggest drop from a peak, with the deposits taken out.
- **Gains vs losses** (profit factor) is the money made on winning trades divided by the money lost on losing ones.
- The **luck test** (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at **N = 122** (one look per method in the lab) against the owner's bar of **0.90**.
- **Beta** is how much the book moved for each 1% move in SPY, from monthly returns over 1996-2015. Beta was measured from the recorded curves for this report; the lab does not record it.

The parents' beta was measured the same way. The 2009-2015 figures come from the lab's era split.

The 40-name book with the switch passed every dev condition: +3.7 points a year over SPY, gains 4.45 times its losses, luck score 0.95. So the lab marks the method **dev-eligible**. Two things stand against it:

- **Its worst fall was 27.0%.** That passes the lab's looser dev screen, but it is above the 25% limit for real money (design §1). The parent's 40-name book fell only 22.6%.
- **The walk-forward folds: 1 of 4.** `lab promote` would refuse it.

## The walk-forward, and what changed from M0179

In the walk-forward, the lab's own rule looks back before each three-year test stretch, picks the variant that had done best so far, and scores it on the stretch it has never seen. For M0179 that pick was the control every time. Here the smoothing did change the pick: from 2006 on, it was the idea's own 40-name book in all three later folds. So the steadier signal did make the negative side look better *in advance*. But it then lost two of those three stretches:

- 2003-2005: the 20-name control, +49.6% vs SPY +52.1%. Lost.
- 2006-2008: the 40-name book, +14.9% vs SPY −24.6%. Won, mostly because the switch moved it to cash in the crash.
- 2009-2011: the 40-name book, +32.9% vs SPY +60.8%. Lost badly: the switch missed the rebound.
- 2012-2014: the 40-name book, +65.4% vs SPY +65.9%. Lost by a hair.

So the folds got worse (1 of 4 against M0179's 2 of 4). The one fold it won came from the market switch, not from the stocks it picked.

## The dead-company check

The survivorship-check store is the same years with most of the dead companies added back. On it, the 40-name book earned +10.0% instead of +10.9%. Its luck score fell to 0.88, under the bar, and its folds fell to **0 of 4**. The 20-name control lost 2.2 points a year there. Its +3.1% lead in 2009-2015 turned into −0.3%, so part of the control's good recent years came from the missing failures. The five-year-window-only book held up best: +8.4% a year, still +1.8% over SPY in 2009-2015. But it fell 56% from its peak in 2008.

## Mechanism

The smoothing worked as intended on the signal itself. Turnover fell hard: 118 trades for S20 against 506 for M0179-N20, and 478 for S40-SW against 1107. The 40-name book also beat its paired control by 2.8 points a year, a wider gap than M0179's 1.3-1.6.

But a steadier signal sorts more steadily into the same kind of stock. The 20-name book's beta rose to 1.12, against 1.02 for the parent. That means it holds more of the high-swing cyclicals, financials and tech names. With no switch it fell 64% from 2007 to 2009, worse than the parent's 52%. With the switch it is half in cash in weak markets (beta about 0.46). That protected it in 2000-2002 and 2008, and cost it the 2009-2011 rebound.

The market-breadth split agrees. A **narrow** month is one where a few big companies carried SPY and the average member lagged; a **broad** month is the opposite. Every no-switch book, the controls included, lost 7-12 points a year to SPY in narrow months and won 8-11 in broad ones. The 20-name idea and its control scored almost the same: +7.6% against +7.4% a year. Without the switch, there is no coskewness spread left once the signal is smoothed. What remains is an equal-weight bet that the average stock beats the giants.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis held in two parts.** Turnover fell, and the walk-forward rule now picked a negative-coskewness variant in 3 of 4 folds.
- **It failed in the parts that matter.** Those picks lost 2 of the 3 folds. The 2009-2015 edge of the eligible book is −5.0% a year. The switched book's worst fall (27%) is over the 25% limit. And the 20-name idea did not beat its control.
- **The expected failure happened almost word for word.** The no-switch books fell well over 50% in 2008. The switched book trailed SPY in 2009-2015. The folds stayed split.
- **One expected failure was wrong.** The lost 1990s years did not shrink the edge of the switched book. Its average went up a little, because the switch spared it the 2000-2002 crash, which counts for more in a twenty-year average than the late-1990s boom it missed.

**My opinion:** smoothing turned out to be the right test, and the answer is no. The steadier signal made the idea look better before each test stretch and then lost those stretches. That is the clearest sign yet that coskewness among big US index members is a high-beta, regime-bound tilt, not a premium that persists. Two lab methods now agree, both on dev and with the dead companies added back. The 40-name book's dev numbers are flattering only because the 200-day switch dodged two crashes, and the lab has a long record of switches that give the gains back in the rebound. I would not spend more ids on coskewness as a stock picker. The one open question is whether any spread is left once beta is matched (the sibling method M0184). If that also collapses, close the family. I would not try another smoothing or another switch.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1707, promotion step 0b)

Dev-eligible on M0185-S40-SW (DSR 0.948, worst fall 27.0%: inside the lab's dev screen, over the 25% real-money bar), refused by the hard gate: 1 of 4 walk-forward folds, pick changed. The only fold won was 2006-2008, where the switch dodged the crash; 2009-2011 and 2012-2014 were lost to SPY. On the survivorship-check store folds fall to 0 of 4. No test look spent. Without the switch the smoothed book and its positive-coskewness control are level (+7.6% against +7.4% a year).

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

The parent method (M0179) bought the index members that fall hardest in the market's biggest weeks. The measure for this is called **coskewness**. Its lead over SPY came mostly from before 2009, often from smaller and less-watched members. This method asks whether the same idea works among the companies that actually drive SPY.

Two changes, and nothing else:

- **Only the busiest companies.** Each quarter the book ranked only the 150 (or 200) members with the highest daily trading value. Trading value stands in for company size, because the data has no reliable market values.
- **Bigger companies get bigger slots.** Each pick's weight followed the square root of its trading value, with no name above 10%. One version kept equal slots so the effect of the sizing could be seen.

The score, the three-year window of weekly returns, the quarterly re-pick, the keep band and the rules were all the parent's. Every version traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, 1996 to 2015. The control held the 20 *most positive* names of the same pool, with the same sizing. Nothing was chosen from post-2015 results. The owner's 2018-2026 run of the parent is known, so the pool sizes, book sizes, cap and switch all came from the idea row and the parent's dev record.

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

"Earned a year" is the money-weighted return on the owner's deposits. SPY earned +7.2% on the same deposits. "Worst fall" is the biggest drop from a peak with the deposits taken out; the screen's limit is 25%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is money made on winning trades over money lost on losing ones; the bar is 1.3. **Beta** is how much the book moves when SPY moves 1%: 1.0 moves with the market, 0.5 moves half as much.

| version | earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test | 2009-2015 vs SPY | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 busiest-pool, sqrt-sized, no switch | +10.3% | **57.4%** | 2.52 | 0.43 | **+2.5%** | 1.09 |
| same, 200-day switch | +10.2% | 29.4% | 2.72 | 0.80 | −6.2% | 0.46 |
| 40 names, switch | +9.2% | 23.0% | 2.33 | 0.80 | −6.7% | 0.47 |
| 40 of the 200 busiest, no switch | +9.1% | 52.1% | 2.09 | 0.42 | +0.6% | 1.03 |
| 20 busiest-pool, equal slots, no switch | +11.0% | 51.9% | 2.59 | 0.51 | **+2.6%** | 1.04 |
| control: 20 most positive, sqrt, no switch | +5.2% | 71.1% | 1.47 | 0.35 | −0.9% | 0.92 |
| *parent, 20 names, no switch (M0179-N20)* | *+10.1%* | *51.7%* | *2.20* | *0.50* | *+0.3%* | *1.02* |
| *parent, 40 names, switch (M0179-N40-SW)* | *+10.5%* | *22.6%* | *2.74* | *0.91* | *−5.6%* | *0.41* |

The luck test (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. These trials were judged at **N = 120** (one look per method in the lab) against the owner's bar of **0.90**. No version passed: the best was 0.80. Four of the six also fell more than 50%. The lab marked the method **rejected**.

**Walk-forward: 0 of 4 folds.** Before each three-year stretch, the lab's rule picked the variant that had done best so far. In the first two folds it picked the *control*, which then lost 2003-2005 and fell 47% in 2006-2008. In the last two it picked the 40-name switch book, which badly trailed the 2009-2011 rebound (+23% vs SPY +61%) and roughly matched 2012-2014. The gate needs a majority of at least four folds.

Beta was measured on the monthly returns with deposits removed, over 1996-2015. In 2009-2015 the no-switch books ran at 0.90-0.92 and the switch books at 0.47-0.48, so the switch books' 2009-2015 shortfall is mostly cash and SPY sitting idle during a rising market.

## The dead-company check

On the survivorship-check store, the same years with most of the dead companies added back:

- The **no-switch busiest-pool books lost 2 to 2.5 points a year**, and their worst falls deepened to 67-74%. The 20-name sqrt book's 2009-2015 lead fell from +2.5% to +1.3%, and the equal-slot book's from +2.6% to +1.6%. Part of their edge was the missing companies that collapsed. The busiest names of 2007 included the banks and brokers that died in 2008.
- The switch books barely moved (+0.2 to +0.3 points), because the switch had them out of the market for the 2008 collapse.
- This is the opposite of the parent. There, the dead companies *helped* the negative-coskewness books. Narrowing to the busiest names concentrated the book in exactly the crowded companies that died.

## Mechanism

The idea held more than expected in one way. Inside the busiest pool, the gap between the idea and its control **widened** rather than shrank. The 20 most negative names earned 5 points a year more than the 20 most positive (+3.1% vs −2.0% against SPY). In the parent, over the full screen, the gap was 1.3-1.6 points. So the premium does not live only in the less-watched companies.

But the gap is a crash-time bet. The most negative-coskewness busy names were the high-beta favourites of each era: tech in 2000, and financials and cyclicals in 2007. Without a switch the book carried a beta above 1 and fell 57% in 2008. With the switch it fell 23-29%, but sold low and bought back late, and trailed SPY by more than 6 points a year in 2009-2015. That is the lab's crash-repair record once again.

The square-root sizing did not help. Equal slots earned slightly more (+11.0% vs +10.3%) with the same 2009-2015 edge. Moving money toward the biggest names did not close the shape gap. The shape gap was not what hurt this book; the crash was.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: failed.** No version beat SPY within the 25% fall with a positive 2009-2015 edge. The two versions with a positive 2009-2015 edge fell more than 50%. The two that stayed near the limit trailed SPY by more than 6 points a year from 2009.
- **"Narrowing shrinks the spread": wrong.** The spread to the control grew about threefold.
- **"No-switch falls 45-55%, the switch gives back the rebound": happened.** The no-switch books fell 52-57% (67-74% with dead companies), and the switch cost 2009-2011.
- **"Sqrt sizing narrows the gap but the lead may vanish": partly.** The sizing changed little either way.
- **"Folds stay near 2 of 4": worse.** It won 0 of 4, because the selection kept switching between the control and the switch books.

## Compared with the parent

The no-switch 20-name book is the parent's no-switch book with a better 2009-2015 (+2.5% vs +0.3%), similar twenty-year earnings (+10.3% vs +10.1%) and a deeper fall (57% vs 52%). On the dead-company store the order flips: the parent's 2009-2015 lead rose to +3.7% while this one fell to +1.3%. The switch versions are slightly worse than the parent's on every line.

**My opinion:** the busiest-pool question is answered, and it should not get another tuning. The negative-coskewness premium exists among the big, heavily traded companies, and is larger there than in the full screen. But it is the reward for holding high-beta names through crashes. The switch cannot remove the crash without also removing the reward, and the dead-company check shows the no-switch version leaned on companies that survived by luck. The one untested repair is to strip the crash beta out of the selection itself rather than time it: among the busiest names, take the most negative coskewness only among stocks whose beta to SPY is at or below 1. If the premium is truly about crash risk, it should survive inside the low-beta half. If it vanishes there, it was just beta, and the coskewness family should close.
methods.verdict: Among the busiest companies the crash-prone picks beat their opposites by 5 points a year, but only by holding high-beta stocks through 2008: unprotected they fell 57%, protected they trailed SPY from 2009, and they lost all four walk-forward tests

methods.hypothesis: The last three batches (low correlation, coskewness, beta-matched coskewness) each had a paired control that earned as much as the idea, which says the frame -- F4-screened index members, 20 at equal weight, quarterly re-picks, a 40% keep band, unfilled slots in SPY -- delivers the lead over SPY on its own. Fill exactly that frame (M0179's eligibility and choose path) in the order of a fixed hash of seed, symbol and re-pick month: pure, no run-time randomness, no price information. Three seeds, each with and without the SPY 200-day switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Expected: every seed beats total-return SPY over 1996-2015 by about as much as the coskewness and correlation books (M0179-N20, M0184-T20 and their controls), and trails SPY in 2009-2015. If so the lab gets a standing yardstick: a ranking must beat the placebo's spread of seeds, not SPY alone, and a method whose dev lead sits inside that spread is the frame, not an edge. Not a published anomaly; the frame's lead is the equal-weight, smaller-company lean of 1996-2008 (insight 91). Never to be promoted: it is evidence, and a placebo that clears the gate is a finding about the gate.
methods.expectedFailure: The 'failure' that matters is the placebo landing well below the coskewness and correlation books: then those rankings did carry something and the paired controls were a second, different signal rather than noise. A smaller risk: the seeds spread so widely (a 20-name random book over twenty years) that the yardstick is too wide to reject anything, which would say 20 names is too few to tell signal from luck at all. The placebo turns over more than a sticky real signal (a hash re-drawn each quarter keeps about 40% of holdings), so it pays somewhat more in fees and may trail the frame's real books by that cost alone. Expect a worst fall near 50% without the switch, like M0179-N20.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

# A placebo book: what the frame earns with no idea in it

## What this was

Not a strategy. A control experiment. The last three ideas (the low-correlation book, the
coskewness book, and the coskewness book with beta held fixed) all used the same "frame": take
the index members that pass a basic price and trading screen, hold 20 of them in equal slots,
re-pick every quarter, keep a holding while it stays in the top 40% of the ranking, park any
empty slot in SPY, and (in the switched versions) go to cash when SPY is under its 200-day
average. In each case the "opposite" book, the other end of the same ranking, did about as well
as the idea. That suggests the frame was doing the work, not the ranking.

So this method keeps the frame exactly (same pool, same eligibility rule, same band, same SPY
slots, same switch, same Gotrade fees, same 5M IDR monthly top-up) and fills it in a meaningless
order: a fixed scramble of each stock's ticker and the month. No price information at all.
Three different scrambles (seeds), each with and without the switch.

## Result on the dev window (1996-2015), on the owner's deposits

| book | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| scramble 1, switch | +10.4% | +7.2% | 21.8% | 2.62 | 0.940 |
| scramble 2, switch | +10.3% | +7.2% | 21.1% | 2.40 | 0.904 |
| scramble 3, switch | +11.0% | +7.2% | 19.3% | 2.77 | 0.939 |
| scramble 1, no switch | +11.9% | +7.2% | 52.3% | 2.12 | 0.815 |
| scramble 2, no switch | +8.8% | +7.2% | 61.3% | 1.82 | 0.497 |
| scramble 3, no switch | +11.8% | +7.2% | 55.3% | 2.22 | 0.724 |

For comparison, the real rankings in the same frame:

| book | your money a year | worst fall |
|---|---|---|
| coskewness, 20, switch (M0179-N20-SW) | +10.8% | 32.0% |
| coskewness control, 20, switch (M0179-P20-SW) | +9.2% | 23.2% |
| coskewness, 40, switch (M0179-N40-SW, eligible) | +10.5% | 22.6% |
| beta-matched coskewness, 20, switch (M0184-T20-SW) | +10.0% | 35.0% |
| beta-matched, 40, switch (M0184-T40-SW, eligible) | +11.0% | 22.8% |
| beta-matched control (M0184-TP20-SW) | +8.9% | 26.9% |
| coskewness, 20, no switch (M0179-N20) | +10.1% | 51.7% |
| beta-matched, 20, no switch (M0184-T20) | +10.0% | 56.7% |

**All three switched scrambles passed every dev condition**: they beat total-return SPY, fell at
most 22% (under the 25% screen), made 2.4-2.8 times as much on winning trades as they lost on
losing ones, and cleared the luck test. The luck test (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how
likely a result is real rather than luck after all the tries the lab has made. The lab judges at
N = 123 independent methods against a bar of 0.90. The scrambles scored 0.904-0.940, better than
the coskewness book's 0.866 and its 40-name rung's 0.910.

The unswitched scrambles failed only because their worst fall (52-61%) broke the 50% limit for a
book with no switch. That is the same failure the unswitched coskewness books had (52% and 57%).

The placebo also traded about 60% more than the coskewness books (813-982 trades against about
505), because a fresh scramble each quarter keeps only about 40% of the holdings. So it paid
more in fees and still matched or beat them.

## Is the placebo the same "thing" as the coskewness books?

Yes, by every measure the lab has:

- **Size of the lead.** The scrambles' switched books earn +10.3% to +11.0% a year. Every
  switched coskewness book, idea or control, sits between +8.9% and +11.0%, all inside or just
  below the placebo's range. The coskewness rankings added nothing the scramble did not.
- **Where the lead comes from.** The breadth report splits months into "narrow" (a few big
  names carried the index) and "broad" (the average member beat the index). The unswitched
  scrambles lost 6-11% a year to SPY in narrow months and won 12-16% in broad ones. That is the
  shape of an equal-weight basket of index members. It is not stock picking.
- **2009-2015, the best-covered years.** The switched scrambles trailed SPY by 2.1-4.3% a year,
  like the coskewness books. Oddly, the unswitched scrambles led SPY by 2-6% a year there.
  In those years the switch mostly cost money, selling after dips and buying back higher.
- **Walk-forward.** Picking the best variant on past data and scoring it on the next three
  years beat SPY in 2 of 4 folds (lost 2003-05 and 2009-11, won 2006-08 and 2012-14), the same
  coin-flip record as the coskewness and low-correlation books.
- **Missing dead companies.** Re-run with prices for most of the index members the dev data
  lacks, dead ones included, the scrambles lost 0.4-2.5 points a year in four of six variants
  (scramble 3 switched: +11.0% to +8.9%, worst fall 19.3% to 22.3%, 2009-2015 gap -2.1% to
  -5.2%). That is the usual 1-1.4 point loss the lab measured for its stock-picking books. A
  random book inherits the same survivorship bias, because the bias is in the pool, not in the
  ranking.

One frame book does sit above the placebo: the low-correlation book (M0174-C20-SW, +13.3% a
year), and its own control (+12.1%). But M0174 traded only about 250 times, against 826 for the
placebo. So its edge over the placebo may be lower fees, not a better ranking. The next idea
tests exactly that.

## What this means for the gate

The lab's dev screen (beat SPY, worst fall, gains vs losses, luck test at N) measures a book
against SPY and against zero. It does not measure it against "the same frame with no idea". A
20-name equal-weight basket of screened index members, with SPY as its parking spot and a
200-day switch, beats SPY over 1996-2015 by about 3 points a year. That is the equal-weight
lean of 1996-2008 plus the missing dead companies. It does this with any ordering, so the
screen passes a random book with a luck score of 0.94.

What saves the lab is the hard gate's fold rule. Since the walk-forward wins only 2 of 4
folds, a promotion of this method would be refused. That rule is the only one that sees
through the frame. The DSR does not, because a frame lead is a real, repeatable lead over SPY
on 1996-2015. It just has nothing to do with the ranking, and it does not survive the shift to
big-company markets after 2016.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis held, more strongly than written: every seed beat SPY on the twenty-year
average, by as much as the coskewness and correlation books, and the switched seeds trailed it
in 2009-2015. The expected "failure", a placebo well below the real books, did not happen. The
second risk (seeds so spread out the yardstick is useless) half happened. The switched seeds are
tight (+10.3% to +11.0%). The unswitched seeds spread from +8.8% to +11.9%, so without the
switch a 20-name book cannot be told from luck at all.

## Not for promotion

This method is evidence, written so before the run. It must never be promoted or put on paper,
and the hard gate refuses it on folds in any case. Assumption recorded: as the child session I
leave the promotion decision to the coordinator, and I recommend it not try.

**My opinion:** This is the most useful result the coskewness batch produced. It closes the
coskewness family and the beta-matched variant as stock pickers: they are the frame wearing a
label. Every future method built on this frame should be judged against the placebo's spread
(about +10.3% to +11.0% a year, switched, 20 names), not against SPY's +7.2%. Next, I would run
a "sticky" placebo: a fixed scramble per stock that is not re-drawn each quarter, at 20 and 40
names. That separates the frame's lead from the turnover it pays for, and tells us whether the
low-correlation book's extra two points are a signal or just fewer trades. I would also build
the placebo spread into the lab's reports as a second yardstick beside SPY.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1752, promotion step 0b)

Dev-eligible, and deliberately not a candidate: this is a placebo whose picks follow a fixed, meaningless order. The hard gate refused it anyway (2 of 4 walk-forward folds, not a majority). Its switched books matched or beat the coskewness and low-correlation books and their controls on dev, so the equal-weight quarterly frame with the SPY 200-day switch earns those leads by itself. Any future book in this frame must beat this placebo, not just SPY. No test look spent.
methods.verdict: A random order in the same 20-stock frame did as well as the coskewness books and passed the dev screen: the frame earns the lead, not the ranking. Evidence only, never to be promoted.

methods.name: Steady beaters at market risk: the members with the highest three-year lead over SPY after their beta, beta kept near one
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0180 (the coskewness frame of M0179/M0184, ranked on CAPM alpha instead); Jensen (1968) alpha; De Bondt & Thaler (1985) long-term reversal as the counter-claim
methods.hypothesis: The coskewness books (M0179, M0180, M0184) beat SPY over 1996-2015 from the equal-weight shape, not the signal: the idea and its opposite earned the same month by month. Rank members instead on what is left after market risk. Each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, measure from 156 weekly log returns each member's beta to SPY, its CAPM alpha (mean return less beta times SPY's mean, on raw returns, not over bills: an assumption, small with beta near one) and the alpha's t-statistic. Keep only members with beta between 0.8 and 1.2, so the book carries about SPY's risk and cannot win by being high-beta. Hold the top 20 or 40 at equal weight, keep a holding while its rank fraction stays under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, quarterly, no market switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Variants: A20 (highest alpha, 20 names), A40 (40 names), T20 and T40 (highest alpha t-statistic, the 'steady' reading, where one wild year cannot carry a name), and the paired control L20 (lowest alpha in the same band), kept in the pool so the walk-forward selection can pick against the idea. Alpha persistence in single stocks is a weak published idea (Jensen 1968 measured it in funds; the stock-level form is folklore, with long-term reversal, De Bondt and Thaler 1985, the published counter-claim). Designed from the dev window only. Success: A20 or T20 beats total-return SPY on the deposits with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive 2009-2015 edge, and L20 trails it clearly month by month.
methods.expectedFailure: Long-term reversal: a three-year alpha leader is a three-year winner, and past winners over three to five years tend to give back, so the high-alpha book trails its own low-alpha control, or matches it, as every control in the last three batches did. The book still holds 20-40 equal-weighted members, so it keeps the equal-weight lean against SPY's big-company drift and trails SPY in 2009-2015 whatever the ranking does. No switch means a 2008 fall near SPY's 55%, failing the 25% bar and the 50% dev screen if the band's names fall harder than SPY. Three-year alpha is noisy (its t-statistic rarely exceeds 2), so the T variants mostly re-sort noise. The walk-forward picks the control in some folds and the gate refuses on folds.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

Each quarter the book looked at every index member that passes the usual price and trading screen. It measured three years of weekly returns against SPY's and split each stock's return into two parts:
- the part that just follows the market (its **beta**: 1.0 means it moves one-for-one with SPY)
- what is left over (its **alpha**: how far it ran ahead of what its market risk alone would explain).

It kept only stocks with a beta between 0.8 and 1.2, so the book carries about SPY's risk. It bought the 20 or 40 with the highest alpha, at equal weight, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly deposits. Two variants ranked on the *steadiness* of the alpha instead (its t-statistic: alpha divided by how noisy it is). A paired control held the 20 *lowest*-alpha names.

## A mistake in the build: these books ran behind a market switch

The plan said **no market switch**. The method file left the stock screen's switch at its default, which moves the whole book to cash whenever SPY closes under its 200-day average. So all five variants (the control too) sat in cash through most of 2001-2002 and from early 2008 to mid-2009. You can see it in the record: the account only grows by its deposits in those years, and "worst year 2001 −0.0%" means a flat year in cash, not a lucky one. The recorded trials describe what really ran, because the switch is part of each configuration's fingerprint. But they answer a different question from the one written down. The switch-free book, which the hypothesis asked about, is queued as its own method. I did not edit this one: a method that has run is frozen.

This is not a small detail. The switch is why the worst fall is about 20% instead of the 50-57% the same kind of book took in 2008 without it (the beta-matched coskewness book fell 57%).

## Result vs SPY (dev window, 1996-2015)

| variant | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains ÷ losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A20 (top alpha, 20) | +12.3% | +7.2% | 20.5% | 4.20 | 0.950 |
| A40 (top alpha, 40) | +11.7% | +7.2% | 19.0% | 4.02 | 0.951 |
| T20 (steadiest, 20) | +11.0% | +7.2% | 20.4% | 4.51 | 0.921 |
| T40 (steadiest, 40) | +10.9% | +7.2% | 19.4% | 3.92 | 0.930 |
| L20 (control: lowest alpha) | +9.8% | +7.2% | 28.9% | 2.32 | 0.914 |

Every variant cleared every dev condition: it beat total-return SPY, its worst fall stayed under the lab's screen, and gains ran well ahead of losses. The luck test (DSR, the chance the result is real rather than luck after the lab's 124 tries) cleared the 0.90 bar on all five. **The control cleared it too**, so passing the screen here says more about the frame than the signal.

## Why it will not reach a test look

- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4 folds.** Before each three-year stretch the lab picked the variant that had looked best so far and scored it on years it had not seen. It lost 2003-2005 (+44.7% vs SPY +52.1%), won 2006-2008 (+14.5% vs −24.6%, the switch sitting in cash), lost 2009-2011 (+37.3% vs +60.8%), and won 2012-2014 (+82.7% vs +65.9%). `lab promote` needs a strict majority, so it would refuse: 2 of 4 is a coin flip.
- **2009-2015, the years most like today:** the lab's picks trailed SPY by 2.0% a year. A20 alone trailed by 1.3%.
- **Dead companies:** re-run on the store that adds most of the members the main store cannot price (including companies that died), A20's lead fell from +5.2% to +3.6% a year, its 2009-2015 gap widened to −3.8% a year, and its luck test fell to 0.893, under the bar. The method lost about 1.5 points a year to the missing dead names, at the high end of what stock-picking books lose there.
- No kin has failed a test look, so the kin rule is not what stops it. The folds are.

## Did alpha separate anything? A little in the falls, not in the returns

Month by month, with deposits taken out (my own approximate calculation):
- A20 beat the low-alpha control by about **2.0 points a year**, with a t-statistic of **0.9**. From 2009 it was 1.6 points a year at a t-statistic of 0.5. Neither can be told apart from luck. The steady version (T20) beat the control by only 0.9 points a year (t 0.4).
- Year by year the two traded wins: the control won 1997, 1999, 2003, 2006, 2009 and 2013, often by a lot (2013: +53% against +36%).
- Where they did differ is the falls. The control lost 12.5% in 1998 and 14% in 2007, while A20 made money in both, so the control's worst fall was 26% against A20's 13% (de-funded, my estimate). The lab's market-breadth read says the same thing: the control earned only in broad months, when the average stock beat the giants, and lost 5.3% a year in narrow ones. The high-alpha books earned in both. Low-alpha stocks are the ones that have been losing ground to the market for three years, and they keep doing it when the giants lead.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis was partly right. Ranking on alpha did not lose to its own control, so long-term reversal (past winners giving back) did not appear. But the edge over the control is too small and too noisy to call real. The expected failure happened where it said it would: the 20-40 equal slots still lean against SPY's big-company drift, so every version trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and the walk-forward split 2-2. The predicted 2008 fall near SPY's 55% did not happen, but only because of the switch mistake above, not because of the idea.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

The beta-band coskewness book (M0184-B20: same quarterly frame, same 0.8-1.2 band, no switch) earned about the same over twenty years (my de-funded estimate: +11.5% a year against A20's +12.6%) and fell 44% where A20, behind the switch, fell 20.5%. M0184's switched books with their own control fell 22-31%. So the alpha ranking plus the switch gives a smoother curve than coskewness plus the switch. But the M0184 lesson holds here too: inside this frame, the frame (equal slots of screened members, plus the switch) earns most of the lead, and the ranking adds a point or two at most.

**My opinion:** worth exactly one more trial, and only the clean one: the same alpha ranking with **no** switch, which is what this method was meant to test. If the high-alpha book still beats its control by about 2 points a year without the switch, and falls clearly less in 2008, alpha-within-a-beta-band is a real if modest tilt. The natural home for it would then be a minority sleeve beside a SPY core, not a standalone book, because no 20-name equal-weight book in this lab has beaten SPY in 2009-2015. If the switch-free gap collapses as coskewness's did, close the family. I would not spend another variant on the steadiness reading: it did worse than plain alpha on every measure.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1752, promotion step 0b)

Dev-eligible (A20, DSR 0.950), not promoted: walk-forward 2 of 4 folds, so the hard gate refuses on the folds condition; 2009-2015 edge -2.0% a year, and on the survivorship-check store DSR falls to 0.893.
