methods.name: Stocks that suffer when fear jumps: rank by sensitivity to daily VIX changes and own the least exposed
methods.sourceRef: Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006), The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns, JF 61(1)
methods.hypothesis: Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang (published 2006, so 2006-2015 of the dev window is after publication and the edge may have faded) find that stocks whose returns rise when market volatility jumps earn less, because investors pay for that insurance, so the stocks with the most negative loading on daily fear-index changes earn more (about 1% a month between extreme quintiles in their sample). Unlike coskewness, which the lab twice found to be a high-beta, regime-bound tilt (M0179, M0185), this reads a stock's exposure to fear itself, beyond its market beta. On the last close of each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, regress 252 daily log returns on SPY's daily log return and the daily VIX change in points (one shared fit, so the VIX loading is net of beta); hold the 20 most negative loadings at 1/20 each, keep a holding while its rank fraction stays under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants: N20 (the idea), N40 (a 40-name rung), P20 (control: the 20 most positive loadings, the fear hedges), N20-SW (behind F4's SPY-200 switch), N20-MB (ranked only among members whose market beta is within 0.25 of 1, so the book cannot be a beta tilt). Success: N20 or N20-SW beats total-return SPY with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge, P20 trails it clearly, and N20-MB keeps most of the gap (the edge is not beta).
methods.expectedFailure: The VIX loading is beta in disguise, with an era-dependent sign. Daily VIX changes and SPY's return move together (correlation near -0.7), so the partial loading is collinear with beta. A ranking probe run before this file was committed (rankings only, no returns) showed it: on 2008-06-30 the loading and beta correlate at 0.81 across members, the 20 most negative loadings average beta 0.49 and the 20 most positive 2.34 (homebuilders, Fannie, Freddie, Citi); on 1999-12-31 the correlation is 0.18 and on 2013-12-31 0.35. So N20 is mostly a low-beta book in stressed years and a mixed one in calm years, the control P20 is a leveraged-financials bet, and the gap between them is the low-beta anomaly (already in the lab as calm stocks) plus 2008. Expect N20 to fall less than SPY in 2008 but trail it in the 1995-1999 and 2009-2015 rallies, failing 'beats SPY'; N20-MB, with beta held near 1, loses most of the gap to P20. The published premium lives in small stocks and is post-publication from 2006; among index members it may be gone, and an equal-weight 20-name book loses to SPY's big-company drift.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

A 2006 study (Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang) found that stocks which go *up* when fear jumps act like insurance. Investors overpay for them, so they earn less, and the stocks that get hurt most when fear jumps earn more. "Fear" here is the VIX, the market's own gauge of expected swings. Each quarter the method measured, for every big US company in the index, how much its daily return moved with the daily change in the VIX, after taking out what its normal link to the market (its *beta*) already explains. It then held the 20 stocks hurt most by fear jumps.

Five versions: the 20-stock book (N20), a 40-stock book (N40), a **control** holding the opposite 20 (the fear hedges, P20), the 20-stock book behind the lab's usual "step aside when SPY is below its 200-day average" switch (N20-SW), and a 20-stock book chosen only among stocks that move about as much as the market (beta between 0.75 and 1.25, N20-MB), so it could not just be a bet on jumpy or calm stocks. All in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly top-ups, 1996 to 2015.

## Result against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | your money a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N20 | +9.8% | +7.2% | 67% | 2.26 | 0.41 |
| N40 | +9.6% | +7.2% | 60% | 2.28 | 0.55 |
| P20 (control) | +9.0% | +7.2% | 81% | 2.16 | 0.36 |
| N20-SW | +10.7% | +7.2% | 32% | 2.93 | 0.71 |
| N20-MB | +11.5% | +7.2% | 63% | 1.92 | 0.64 |

Every version beat SPY on the deposits. Without the switch, every one lost 60-81% from a peak (2000-2002 and 2008; N20 lost 50% in 2008 alone), which breaks even the lab's loose 50% screen. N20-SW is the only version inside the drawdown screen. It fails one condition: the **luck test**. The DSR asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab now counts 126 independent tries (N = 126) and asks for 0.90; N20-SW scored 0.71. Rejected.

## Why it is not the fear premium

1. **The control nearly matched it.** If fear exposure were paid, the fear-hedge book should trail clearly. It earned +9.0% against N20's +9.8%, a gap under one point a year. In 2009-2015 the control did *better* (+9.6% a year over SPY against N20's +7.5%). Among big index companies the paper's premium is not there.
2. **It only earns when the average stock beats the index.** Split by month, every version made all its gains in "broad" months, when the typical index member beat SPY, and lost in "narrow" months, when a few giants carried SPY. That is the shape of any equal-weight 20-stock book, not something the fear signal added (the lab's earlier finding on equal-weight books).
3. **Most of the lead was the missing dead companies.** Re-run on the check history that adds back most of the companies that failed or left the index, the no-switch versions' leads mostly vanish: N20 +2.6 → −0.1 points a year, N40 +2.4 → −1.0, P20 +1.8 → −0.9, N20-MB +4.3 → +0.3 (worst fall 63% → 72%). Only the switch version holds (+3.5 → +3.1), and that is the switch avoiding 2008, which the lab has seen many times.
4. **The one survivor fails the first filter.** N20-SW trailed SPY by 2.8 points a year in 2009-2015, the best-covered years and the most like today. The switch sold in the 2010 and 2011 dips and bought back higher. Walk-forward: won 2 of 4 test periods (lost 2006-2008 and 2009-2011), not a majority.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: no clear gap to the control, and none of it after 2009. The pre-registered expected failure was right in its main claim, that the gap between the two books is beta and 2008, not a fear premium. It was wrong in the details:
- I expected N20 to fall *less* than SPY in 2008. It fell 50%, more than SPY. A ranking check run before the trial found N20 holding low-beta names in mid-2008. They were mostly steel, oil-service and mining stocks (STLD, NOV, FCX) whose calm in the oil boom of 2007-08 made them look like low-beta names, and they crashed in late 2008. A one-year window measured a commodity cycle, not the stocks' lasting nature.
- I expected N20 to trail SPY in 2009-2015. On the usual history it led by +7.5%, but that falls to +5.3% with the dead companies added and is matched by the control, so it is the equal-weight rebound, not the signal.
- I expected the beta-matched version to lose most of the gap. On the usual history it was the best version. With the dead companies it lost the most (−4 points a year), so its edge was mostly the missing data.

## Comparison with near relatives

The two coskewness books (crash-with-the-market stocks) told the same story: a stock-risk measure built on the market's swings turns into a beta and a 2008 bet among big companies, with a weak gap to its own control. This method adds that measuring fear directly does not escape that, because the VIX change and the market's own move are nearly the same number on most days (the fit cannot separate them well, so the loading is noisy).

## My opinion

The VIX-loading direction is dead as a stock picker among index members: the control matched it, the premium flips sign after 2009, and the dead-company check takes the lead away. I would not spend another try on a different window length or book size. The one question worth one more try is whether *any* stock selection from this family survives once the equal-weight shape is removed. So the next idea weights the same 20 names by size (dollar volume) and judges them on 2009-2015 first. I expect that to fail too, and if it does, this family should be closed.
methods.verdict: Rejected: beat SPY only through the equal-weight shape and missing dead companies; the opposite (fear-hedge) book did as well, and the one safe version lagged SPY after 2009

methods.name: Stocks whose bad days stood out: buy the members whose recent losses looked worst next to the market, sell the ones whose gains stood out
methods.sourceRef: Cosemans & Frehen (2021), Salience theory and stock prices: Empirical evidence, JFE 140, 460-483
methods.hypothesis: Salience theory (Bordalo, Gennaioli, Shleifer) says investors overweight a stock's returns that stand out most against the market's on the same day. A stock whose biggest stand-out days last month were gains gets overbought and earns less next month; one whose stand-out days were losses gets oversold and earns more. Cosemans and Frehen (2021) build the salience score from the past month's daily returns against the equal-weighted market and find the low-salience (salient-downside) stocks beat the high ones in US stocks 1926-2015, not explained by reversal, lottery demand or news. Published 2021, so the whole dev window is before publication, but their sample covers it, so this is in-sample for the paper. Build: each month, among F4-screened members, the salience-weighted return covariance from the last 21 daily close-to-close returns against the equal-weighted screen average (theta 0.1, delta 0.7, the paper's values); hold the 20 most negative scores, equal 5% slots, monthly, keeping a holding while it ranks inside the top 40 (a band to cut turnover), unfilled slots in SPY, behind the SPY 200-day switch. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly top-up. Arms: S-N40 (40 names, band 80), S-N20-NOSW (no switch). Controls in the same pool: HIGH-N20, the paper's losing end (most positive salience), which should trail the main book clearly; REV-N20, a plain one-month reversal book (lowest 21-day return) on the identical screen, band, slots and switch, so salience can be told apart from reversal. Success: beats SPY TR with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds and a positive 2009-2015 edge, with a clear gap over both controls.
methods.expectedFailure: Salience-downside stocks are mostly last month's losers, so the low-salience book may be short-term reversal under another name: the lab's reversal books (the plain bounce book and the standardised residual bounce book) both trailed SPY on the deposits, the best at 6.9% a year vs 7.2%, fell 28-35% at worst and lagged in 2009-2015. Monthly turnover on 20 small slots at Gotrade's minimum fees eats a one-month effect the paper measured gross of costs; the band helps only if a name stays salient-low for more than a month, which a one-month signal rarely does. The paper's long-short spread lives largely in the short leg (overbought high-salience stocks), which a long-only book cannot trade. In crashes the stocks with stand-out losses keep falling and the 200-day switch reacts late, so the no-switch arm may fall well past 25%. Equal slots in index members lean small against SPY's big-company drift (insight 91), which hurts most in 2013-2015.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 -- result: salience is real and is not plain reversal, but it falls too far and trails SPY in 2009-2015

**The idea.** Each month, look at every big, easily traded index member's last 21 trading days. For each day, measure how much the stock "stood out" from the average member that day (the salience of the day; Cosemans & Frehen 2021, after Bordalo, Gennaioli & Shleifer). Weight the loudest days most. A stock whose loudest days were losses gets a negative score: the paper says investors overreact to those days and the stock is oversold. Buy the 20 (or 40) most negative scores, equal slots, keep a holding while it ranks inside twice the book size, put unfilled slots in SPY, and go to cash while SPY is under its 200-day average. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly deposits.

**One assumption, written at registration.** The paper's "market" is the equal-weighted average of all stocks. The lab used the equal-weighted average of the screened members that day, the cross-section it can price point in time.

**Results on the owner's deposits** (money-weighted: the yearly rate a savings account would need to pay to turn the same deposits into the same final balance; SPY earned 7.2% on the same deposits):

| version | your money earned / yr | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S-N20 (main: 20 names, band 40, switch) | 9.7% | 33.5% | 1.38 | 0.74 | -4.3 pts/yr |
| S-N40 (40 names, band 80, switch) | **10.0%** | 28.6% | 1.52 | **0.87** | -3.1 pts/yr |
| S-N20-NOSW (no switch) | 6.8% | 77.2% | 1.17 | 0.28 | **+4.4 pts/yr** |
| control: HIGH-N20 (the paper's losing end) | 6.1% | 26.1% | 1.24 | 0.48 | -9.0 pts/yr |
| control: REV-N20 (plain one-month reversal) | 4.9% | 35.7% | 1.18 | 0.38 | -9.3 pts/yr |

**What failed.** The lab rejected all five. The best version, S-N40, beat SPY by 2.8 points a year and had a healthy gains-vs-losses ratio of 1.52, but its luck check was 0.87 against the bar of 0.90 at N = 125 (the lab's count of distinct methods tried, floored at the measured participation ratio). In words: after 125 tries, there is roughly a one-in-eight chance a result this good is luck, and the owner's bar is one in ten. Its worst fall, 28.6%, is also over the owner's 25% real-money limit (the lab's screen is looser, so the runner did not list it). And it lost 3.1 points a year to SPY over 2009-2015, the years most like today, which is the lab's first filter.

**The part that is new: salience is not reversal.** The reversal control used the same stocks, band, slots, switch and fees, and only swapped the score for last month's plain return. It earned 4.9% a year to the salience book's 9.7%, fell further, and had a worse gains-vs-losses ratio. The high-salience control, the paper's losing end, earned 6.1%. So the score does sort stocks the way the paper says, and the gap is about 5 points a year over plain reversal. That is the clearest control result the lab has had in the reversal neighbourhood: the earlier bounce books (plain residual and standardised residual) never got above 6.9%.

**Durability.** On the survivorship-check store (the dev prices plus most of the dead companies), every variant earned less: S-N40 fell from 10.0% to 8.8% a year and its 2009-2015 lag widened to 4.3 points; S-N20 fell 1.7 points to 8.0%. That is in line with the other stock-picking books (about 1-1.4 points). The walk-forward record is 2 of 4 folds on dev and 1 of 4 on the check store, so `lab promote` would refuse it anyway. Note that the walk-forward picked the high-salience *control* in its first two folds: putting a control in the pool lets the fold picker choose it.

**Why the switch hurt in 2009-2015 and saved the book in 2008.** The no-switch arm lost 54% in 2008 and 77% from its peak: the stocks whose stand-out days were losses kept losing in the crash. But it led SPY by 4.4 points a year over 2009-2015, because it was fully invested in the beaten-down names when the rebound came, while the switched books sat in cash until SPY got back over its 200-day average in mid-2009 and missed the sharpest months of the bounce. The signal works best exactly when the 200-day switch keeps it out.

**Hypothesis and expected failure.** The hypothesis held on direction: low salience beat high salience by 3.6 points a year and plain reversal by 4.8. It did not hold on the bar. The expected failures that happened: the crash fall (the no-switch arm, 77%), the small-company lean against SPY in 2013-2015 (both switched books lag in 2009-2015), and some fee drag. The one that did not happen: it is not reversal under another name.

**My opinion:** This is the most promising thing the lab has found in the "buy last month's losers" neighbourhood, and it is worth two or three more trials, not a promotion. The problem is not the signal but the frame: equal slots in index members lose to SPY's big-company drift after 2009, and the 200-day switch misses the rebound the signal is best at. I would try the salience score inside a big-company pool (the 100 most traded members), 40 names, with a fast way back in after the switch trips (out under the 200-day average, back as soon as SPY closes over its 50-day average). If that does not lead SPY in 2009-2015, this family is a pre-2009 effect and should be left there.
methods.verdict: Buying stocks whose stand-out days were losses earned 10.0% a year on your deposits vs 7.2% for SPY and clearly beat plain bounce-buying, but it fell 29% at worst, missed the luck bar (0.87 vs 0.90) and trailed SPY in 2009-2015.

methods.name: A sticky placebo: the same frame in a fixed random order that is not re-drawn each quarter, 20 and 40 names
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0187 (the placebo yardstick of the M0174/M0179/M0184 frame); Sera batch 20261017-1808
methods.hypothesis: The quarterly re-drawn placebo (M0187) traded about 60% more than the coskewness books and still matched them; the low-correlation book (M0174-C20-SW, +13.3% a year funded, about 250 trades) sits two points above the placebo's +10.3 to +11.0%. Hash seed and symbol only (no month), so a holding stays while its fixed place keeps it in the 40% band, giving turnover close to a sticky real signal (expected 150-350 trades at 20 names). Seeds 1-3 at 20 names behind the SPY 200-day switch, one 40-name rung behind the switch, and seed 1 at 20 names with trend explicitly None as the no-switch rung; fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up. If the sticky placebo rises to about +12-13% funded, the low-correlation book's lead is low turnover, not correlation, and the frame's yardstick moves up; if it stays near +10.5%, low correlation carries something the frame does not. Each variant's beta to SPY is recorded beside it. Not a published anomaly; the frame's lead is the equal-weight, smaller-company lean of 1996-2008 (insight 91). Never to be promoted: it is evidence.
methods.expectedFailure: A fixed order is a fixed set of about twenty companies held for years, so the three seeds may spread far wider than M0187's (one seed lands on a few big winners, another on a few that languish): the yardstick then becomes too wide to say anything about a two-point gap, and only the 40-name rung reads cleanly. Turnover may also not fall as much as hoped, because index membership changes and the screen still churn the book. Expect every switched seed to trail SPY in 2009-2015 like M0187, and the unswitched rung to fall about 50% in 2008.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

# A sticky placebo: does trading less lift a meaningless book?

## What this was

Not a strategy. A second control experiment. The earlier placebo (M0187) filled the shared
"frame" (index members that pass a basic price and trading screen, 20 in equal slots, re-picked
every quarter, a holding kept while it stays in the top 40%, empty slots parked in SPY, and in
most versions the whole book in cash when SPY is under its 200-day average) in a scrambled order
that was re-drawn every quarter. It matched the real rankings, but it traded a lot (about 800-980
trades), because a fresh scramble keeps only about 40% of the book each quarter.

One frame book sat clearly above that placebo: the low-correlation book (M0174-C20-SW), +13.3% a
year on the owner's deposits with only about 250 trades. The open question was whether its lead
came from its ranking or only from trading less and so paying Gotrade less.

This method keeps the scramble fixed for the whole twenty years: each company gets one place in
the order, forever. A holding leaves only when it drops out of the index, fails the screen, or
new members push it out of the top 40%. That brings the trade count down to the low-correlation
book's level (about 200 trades at 20 names) while still using no price information at all.

Five versions, registered before any result: three scrambles (seeds) at 20 names behind the
switch, one 40-name version behind the switch, and one 20-name version with the switch
explicitly off. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up.

## Result on the dev window (1996 to October 2015), on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends, on the same deposits, earned **+7.2% a year**.

| book | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | luck test (DSR) | beta to SPY | passed the screen? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sticky seed 1, switch | +9.9% | 24.8% | 6.66 | 206 | 0.895 | 0.43 | no (luck test 0.895 < 0.90) |
| sticky seed 2, switch | +11.3% | 20.3% | 8.67 | 213 | 0.963 | 0.46 | yes |
| sticky seed 3, switch | +10.7% | 25.1% | 6.85 | 201 | 0.904 | 0.49 | yes |
| sticky seed 1, 40 names, switch | +9.9% | 19.4% | 7.67 | 427 | 0.924 | 0.42 | yes |
| sticky seed 1, no switch | +8.9% | 52.9% | 0.03 | 15 | 0.622 | 0.94 | no (fall, trades, gains vs losses, luck) |

"Beta to SPY" is how much the book's monthly return moves for each 1% SPY moves, measured on the
book without its deposits. 0.45 means it moved a bit under half as much as the market; the
switch, which sits in cash for long stretches, is most of why it is low.

The placebo it is judged against, and the book that started the question:

| book | your money a year | worst fall | trades | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| re-drawn placebo, switch, three seeds (M0187-H1/H2/H3-SW) | +10.3% to +11.0% | 19-22% | 813-833 | 0.43-0.47 |
| re-drawn placebo, no switch (M0187-H1..H3) | +8.8% to +11.9% | 52-61% | 944-982 | 0.97-1.04 |
| low-correlation book, switch (M0174-C20-SW) | +13.3% | 29.8% | 250 | 0.36 |
| its 40-name rung (M0174-C40-SW) | +12.0% | 24.3% | 555 | 0.37 |
| its "most correlated" control (M0174-H20-SW) | +8.5% | 25.5% | 200 | 0.53 |

## What it says

**Trading less did not lift the placebo.** Cutting trades by three quarters (from about 820 to
about 210) left the switched placebo where it was: +9.9% to +11.3% a year against +10.3% to
+11.0% for the re-drawn one. The 40-name version, which averages away much of the seed luck,
landed at +9.9%. So the hypothesis's first branch, "the low-correlation book's lead is just low
turnover", is not supported. Fees on 600 extra trades over twenty years are worth well under a
point a year here, and the scramble's seed matters more than that (1.4 points between seeds).

**So the low-correlation book still sits about two points above any placebo**, with the lowest
beta of the group (0.36 against 0.42-0.49). Earning more while moving less with the market is
what a real effect would look like. But that book has two strikes already recorded against it:
it won only 1 of 4 walk-forward folds (the fold test kept picking its own control) and its edge
shrank once dead companies were added back. Two points over a 20-name placebo whose seeds spread
1.4 points is suggestive, not proof.

**The yardstick for this frame is now well pinned.** Nine switched placebo books (six re-drawn,
three sticky) plus a 40-name one all land between +9.9% and +11.3% a year, with beta 0.42-0.49
and a worst fall of 19-25%. A ranking in this frame needs to clear about +11.5% before it says
anything beyond the frame.

**Three of four switched sticky placebos passed the lab's dev screen.** They beat SPY, fell at
most 25% (the screen's limit), made 6.7-8.7 times as much on winning trades as on losing ones,
and cleared the luck test (DSR, how likely a result is real rather than luck after all the lab's
tries; judged at N = 127 independent methods against a bar of 0.90). A meaningless book passing
is a finding about the screen, not about this book. It is never to be promoted. The "gains vs
losses" numbers are especially inflated in a sticky book: winners are held for years and only
the names that leave the index (often the fallers) are ever closed, so the few closed trades are
lopsided. The no-switch version shows the extreme: 15 trades in twenty years, gains vs losses
0.03, because nearly every name it ever sold was one the index dropped.

**Where the lead lives.** In 2009-2015, the best-covered years, every switched sticky book trailed
SPY by 1.8-4.3 points a year, like the re-drawn placebo. The unswitched one led SPY by 1.5 points
there, again like the re-drawn placebo's unswitched books: in those years the switch mostly sold
after dips and bought back higher. The breadth split says the switched books earned most of their
lead in "broad" months (when the average index member beat the index), the signature of an
equal-weight basket rather than stock picking.

**Missing dead companies.** Re-run with prices for most of the index members the dev data lacks,
dead ones included, three of five versions earned less: the best one (seed 2) fell from +11.3% to
+9.9% a year, its luck score from 0.963 to 0.896 (below the bar) and its 2009-2015 gap widened
from -1.8 to -3.5 points; the 40-name version fell a point to +8.9%. The other two moved by 0.2
points or less. With the gaps filled, the sticky placebo sits at about +9-11%.

**Walk-forward.** Picking the best version on past data and scoring it on the next three years
beat SPY in 2 of 4 folds (lost 2003-05 and 2009-11, won 2006-08 and 2012-14): the same coin-flip
record as every other book in this frame.

**Worst year and fall.** Behind the switch the worst calendar year was 2015 (-4.4% to -7.0%), and
the deepest fall was 19-25%, measured on the book without its deposits. Without the switch the
book fell 52.9% and lost 34.6% in 2008, as expected.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

The pre-registered test was: if the sticky placebo rises to about +12-13%, the low-correlation
lead was low turnover; if it stays near +10.5%, low correlation carries something. It stayed near
+10.5% (mean of the three 20-name seeds +10.6%). So by the rule written before the result, low
correlation carries something the frame does not. The expected failure (seeds spreading far
wider) half happened: the spread is 1.4 points, a bit wider than the re-drawn placebo's 0.7 but
not so wide that it hides a two-point gap. Turnover did fall as hoped (to about 210 trades).

## My opinion:

The frame question is closed: re-drawn or fixed, the meaningless 20-name book behind the switch
earns about +10-11% a year here, and no amount of fee-trimming changes that. That makes the
low-correlation book the only ranking in this frame that has stood clear of its placebo, and it
deserves one honest follow-up that attacks its known weakness instead of another placebo: test
whether its lead survives on the survivorship-check data against a placebo also run there, and
whether it holds at a matched beta (a placebo book restricted to low-beta names, so the two differ
only in correlation). If low correlation still clears the placebo by two points at matched beta,
it is worth a real variation; if the low-beta placebo closes the gap, the lead was beta and
sector mix and the frame is exhausted. I would not spend more ids on new rankings in this frame
until that is settled.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1808)

A placebo: dev-eligible on three switched variants, and never a promotion candidate, so Sera did not run lab promote on it. Its fold record (2 of 4) would have been refused by the hard gate anyway. Re-drawing the meaningless order less often cut trades from about 820 to about 210 and left the growth in the same band as the reshuffling placebo, so lower trading does not explain the low-correlation book's small lead over the placebo.
methods.verdict: A meaningless book that trades as little as a real one still earned about +10-11% a year: trading less is not what put the low-correlation book two points ahead. Evidence only, never to be promoted.

methods.name: Steady beaters with no switch: the three-year alpha leaders among betas near one, fully invested through every crash
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0188 (the same alpha ranking, run as its hypothesis asked: no SPY 200-day switch); Jensen (1968) alpha; De Bondt & Thaler (1985) long-term reversal as the counter-claim; Sera batch 20261017-1808
methods.hypothesis: The clean test M0188 meant to run. M0188's books accidentally ran behind the SPY 200-day switch (the screen's default trend), so they sat in cash through 2001-2002 and 2008 and could not show whether alpha picks hold up in a crash. Same measures and frame as M0188 (156 weekly returns, CAPM alpha, beta 0.8 to 1.2, quarterly with a 40% keep band, equal weight, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, M0188's own allocator) with the trend set to None explicitly on every variant. Variants: A20, A40, and the low-alpha control L20 (the t-statistic reading is dropped: it trailed plain alpha everywhere in M0188). Yardstick: the placebo book (M0187), the same frame filled in a meaningless order, earned +8.8% to +11.9% a year on the deposits without a switch with worst falls of 52-61%; an alpha book whose result sits inside that spread is the frame, not the ranking. Each variant's beta to SPY is reported. Success: A20 beats SPY TR on the deposits and the top of the placebo spread, its 2008 fall is clearly shallower than L20's, the placebo's and the beta-band coskewness book's (44%), the month-by-month gap over L20 reaches a t-statistic near 2, and a majority of walk-forward folds are won. Not a strongly published anomaly (stock-level alpha persistence is folklore; Jensen 1968 measured funds). Designed from the dev window only.
methods.expectedFailure: Without the switch the 2008 fall sits near 45-55% and fails the 25% bar (the dev screen for a no-switch book is looser, but the go-live bar is not); the 2-point gap over the low-alpha control shrinks or vanishes once crash months count, because three-year winners are not safer in a crash than three-year losers when beta is held near one; the result lands inside the placebo's +8.8% to +11.9% spread; the equal-weight lean keeps 2009-2015 behind SPY; the walk-forward splits. If the gap does hold, the next step is a 30% sleeve beside a SPY core, not a standalone book.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The same book as the steady-beaters method before it (M0188), run the way that method's plan
said and its build did not: **with no market switch**. Each quarter, among index members that
pass the usual price and trading screen, the book measured three years of weekly returns against
SPY's. It kept only stocks that move about one-for-one with the market (beta between 0.8 and 1.2)
and bought the 20 (A20) or 40 (A40) that had run furthest ahead of what that market risk alone
explains (their **alpha**). A paired control (L20) held the 20 *lowest*-alpha names in the same
band. Equal slots, a 40% keep band, empty slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees,
on the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up. The switch was set off explicitly this time (trend = none),
and the book used the earlier method's own code, so nothing else changed.

## Result (dev window, 1996-2015)

| book | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | 2008 | gains ÷ losses | luck test (DSR) | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A20, top alpha | +9.8% | +7.2% | 57.7% | −43.0% | 2.10 | 0.539 | 0.96 |
| A40, top alpha | +10.3% | +7.2% | 54.5% | −38.6% | 2.28 | 0.627 | 0.91 |
| L20, lowest alpha (control) | +8.7% | +7.2% | 70.3% | −40.3% | 2.10 | 0.588 | 1.08 |
| placebo, scramble 1 (M0187-H1) | +11.9% | +7.2% | 52.3% | −31.7% | 2.12 | 0.815 | 1.02 |
| placebo, scramble 2 (M0187-H2) | +8.8% | +7.2% | 61.3% | −31.5% | 1.82 | 0.497 | 1.04 |
| placebo, scramble 3 (M0187-H3) | +11.8% | +7.2% | 55.3% | −38.6% | 2.22 | 0.724 | 0.97 |

"Worst fall" is the deepest drop from a peak on the funded account; the 2008 column is the
calendar year with deposits taken out. Beta is the slope of each book's monthly return on SPY's,
deposits taken out (my own calculation from the recorded curves): 1.0 means it moves one-for-one
with the market. The placebo rows are the meaningless-order book in this same frame, also with no
switch: the yardstick this batch asked every idea to be judged against.

All three variants beat SPY's total return on the deposits, and all three failed two conditions:

- **Worst fall.** 54-70%, past even the looser 50% screen the lab allows a book with no switch,
  and far past the 25% limit for real money.
- **Luck test.** The deflated Sharpe ratio asks how likely the result is real rather than luck
  after all the lab's tries. Judged at N = 129 independent methods against a bar of 0.90, the
  three scored 0.54-0.63: about a coin flip.

## Against the placebo, not just SPY

This is the comparison that matters. The alpha books earned +9.8% and +10.3% a year; the three
meaningless orderings earned +8.8% to +11.9%. **The alpha books sit inside the placebo's spread,
below two of its three seeds.** Month by month, with deposits taken out, A20 trailed placebo seed 1
by 3.3 points a year (t −1.5) and seed 3 by 2.2 points (t −0.9). The ranking added nothing the
frame does not already deliver with no information at all.

## The crash: the question this method existed to ask

The parent's best case was that high-alpha names, held at market risk, would fall less in a crash.
They did not. In 2008 A20 lost 43%, *more* than SPY (−36.5%), more than its own low-alpha control
(−40.3%), and more than every placebo seed (−32% to −39%). The 2001-2002 bear market was the same:
A20 lost 13% and 23%, the control 2% and 12%. Three years of beating the market at average risk
said nothing about how a stock behaves when the market breaks.

## The gap over the control is gone

Month by month, deposits out:
- A20 minus L20: **−0.9 points a year** (t −0.3). The parent's +2.0 points (t 0.9) came from the
  switch hiding the crash months, when the high-alpha names fell harder.
- From 2009 on: +2.2 points a year, t 0.5. Noise.

The control did have a far deeper worst fall (70% against 58%), from the 2007-2009 run and its
1998-style air pockets: low-alpha stocks are the long-term laggards and they keep lagging when the
giants lead. But on returns there is nothing between them.

## The walk-forward and 2009-2015

The fold test reads 3 of 4, but it is not good news: in two of the four folds the selection
picked the **control** (L20), once winning 2003-2005 and once losing 2006-2008 badly (−38.4% vs
SPY −24.6%). A selection that keeps choosing the opposite of the idea is not evidence for the idea.

2009-2015 is the one bright spot, and it is not the method's. With deposits out, A20 earned about
+18.4% a year and A40 +18.0% against SPY's +14.8% over the same months. But the placebo seeds did
+15.9% to +21.3%, so this is the no-switch frame earning its keep in a rising market, not alpha.
(The switched books of this frame, which sat in cash in early 2009, all trailed SPY there.)

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed on every success condition except beating SPY on the deposits: the 2008
fall was not shallower than the control's or the placebo's, the gap over the control did not reach
a t of 2 (it turned negative), and the result landed inside the placebo spread. The expected
failure happened almost word for word: a 2008 fall in the 45-55% range (43% in the year, 58% peak
to trough), the gap over the control vanishing once crash months counted, the result inside the
placebo spread. The one part that did not happen is "2009-2015 behind SPY": without a switch, the
frame was ahead there, for the frame's reasons.

Beta (Sera note 3): the alpha books carried slightly less market risk than SPY (0.91-0.96), the
control slightly more (1.08), the placebo about the same (0.97-1.04). So the alpha books did not
lose to the placebo by carrying less risk in a rising market; they lost to it with about the same.

## Compared with the parent

M0188-A20 behind the switch: +12.3% a year on the deposits, worst fall 20.5%. M0194-A20 without
it: +9.8%, worst fall 57.7%. Everything that made the parent look good was the switch. The
beta-band coskewness book (M0184-B20, same frame, same band, no switch) earned a little more
(about 1.3 points a year, deposits out, t −0.7) and fell less in 2008.

**My opinion:** close this family. Three-year CAPM alpha among stocks at market risk is not a
signal in this frame: it loses to a meaningless ordering, it loses to its own opposite once the
crash months count, and it falls harder than the market when the market breaks. M0188's apparent
edge was the switch, which the lab has measured many times on its own. I would not spend another
variant on alpha persistence (not a longer window, not a sleeve beside SPY: a sleeve of nothing is
still nothing). The useful thing this run adds is the placebo comparison: it is now the fourth
ranking in a row that the meaningless order matches or beats, which says the next idea worth an id
must change the frame (how many names, how they are weighted, how big the companies are), not the
ranking inside it.
methods.verdict: Without the market switch the high-alpha picks fell 43% in 2008, more than SPY and more than their low-alpha opposite, and did no better than the same book filled in a meaningless order

methods.name: Stand-out losers among the big companies, with a fast way back in: salience in the 100 most traded members, out under SPY's 200-day average, back above its 50-day
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0192 (Cosemans & Frehen 2021, JFE 140, 460-483)
methods.hypothesis: M0192's salience book (buy the members whose stand-out days last month were losses) beat plain reversal by about 5 points a year and SPY by 2.8 on dev, but trailed SPY by 3-4 points a year over 2009-2015 and fell 29-34%. Two frame problems, not signal problems: equal slots across all screened members lean small against SPY's big-company drift (insight 91), and the 200-day switch kept the book in cash through the spring-2009 rebound that the no-switch arm used to lead SPY by 4.4 points a year in 2009-2015. Published 2021, so the dev window is pre-publication but inside the paper's sample. Variation: the same salience score (theta 0.1, delta 0.7, 21 sessions, measured against the equal-weighted average of the names scored), ranked only inside the 100 screened members with the highest 20-day dollar volume, 40 names at 2.5% with a keep band of 80, unfilled slots in SPY, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Switch 'fast': cash only while SPY closes under both its 200-day and its 50-day average (out under the 200-day, back in on the first close over the 50-day). Variants, every one with its switch set explicitly: B100-FAST (the idea), B100-SLOW (plain 200-day switch), B100-NONE (no switch), ALL-FAST (no busiest cut, every screened member), and two controls on the B100-FAST frame: REV-B100-FAST (plain one-month reversal) and PLC-B100-FAST (the same pool filled in a fixed hash order, a placebo). Judged against SPY TR and against the placebo and the equal-weight placebo book M0187 (+10.3-11.0% a year funded with its switch). Success: B100-FAST beats SPY TR on the deposits with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, DSR >= 0.90, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive 2009-2015 edge, and a clear gap over both its reversal and placebo controls; its beta to SPY is reported.
methods.expectedFailure: The big-company pool shrinks the salience spread: salience effects are larger in small, attention-poor stocks, and the 100 busiest names are the most watched in the market, so the gap over the placebo may close to nothing. Narrowing to 100 names also leaves 40 slots drawn from a pool of 100, so the book is 40% of a near-index basket and its return sits close to an equal-weight big-company book (RSP-like), which still lags SPY's cap-weighted drift in 2013-2015. The fast re-entry whipsaws: a first close over the 50-day average in a bear market (late 2001, spring 2002, mid and late 2008) buys a bear-market rally, and the 200-day exit fires again only after the next leg down, so B100-FAST may fall more than B100-SLOW and past 25%. The no-switch arm falls past 50% in 2008 as M0192's did. Monthly turnover on 40 small slots at Gotrade's minimum fees eats a one-month effect. If B100-FAST does not lead SPY in 2009-2015 and beat its placebo, the salience family is a pre-2009, small-company effect and should be left.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 -- result: the big-company pool and the fast way back in did not fix the 2009-2015 lag, and the idea version earned exactly what a placebo earned

**What was tried.** The parent method (buy the members whose loudest days last month were losses, the "salience" score) beat SPY over 1996-2015 but trailed it by 3-4 points a year over 2009-2015. Its analysis blamed the frame rather than the signal: equal slots across every screened member lean towards smaller companies, and the usual "step aside when SPY is under its 200-day average" switch kept the book in cash through the spring-2009 rebound. So this method kept the score and changed the frame. It ranked only the 100 most heavily traded members and held 40 of them, with a held name kept while it ranks in the best 80. It added a fast switch: cash only while SPY closes under both its 200-day and its 50-day average, so the book goes out on the usual signal and comes back on the first close over the 50-day. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly deposits.

**Assumptions written before the run.** (1) The fast switch is read without memory: in cash when SPY is under both averages, invested otherwise. In a rising market that exits at the same moment as the 200-day switch. After a fall it re-enters on the first close over the 50-day. (2) In the pooled versions, each day's "market" for the salience score is the plain average of the 100 names being scored. (3) The placebo is re-drawn monthly, so a held name stays about 80% of the time.

**Results on the owner's deposits.** The yearly rate is money-weighted: the rate a savings account would need to pay to turn the same deposits into the same final balance. SPY earned 7.2% a year on the same deposits. Beta is how much the book moved per 1% move in SPY, month by month, with the deposits taken out.

| version | your money / yr | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY | beta 1996-2015 (2009-2015) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B100-FAST (the idea: 100 busiest, fast switch) | 7.3% | 40.8% | 1.55 | 0.64 | -3.5 pts/yr | 0.62 (0.73) |
| B100-SLOW (plain 200-day switch) | **9.2%** | **19.5%** | **1.95** | **0.906** | -5.3 pts/yr | 0.45 (0.48) |
| B100-NONE (no switch) | 7.4% | 56.4% | 1.60 | 0.42 | +0.2 pts/yr | 1.00 (1.08) |
| ALL-FAST (every screened member, fast switch) | 9.0% | 50.7% | 1.38 | 0.68 | +1.5 pts/yr | 0.67 (0.85) |
| control: REV-B100-FAST (plain one-month bounce) | 6.1% | 43.7% | 1.43 | 0.59 | -4.1 pts/yr | 0.59 (0.66) |
| control: PLC-B100-FAST (placebo, fixed random order) | 7.2% | 36.7% | 1.62 | 0.61 | -3.3 pts/yr | 0.64 (0.74) |
| yardstick: the equal-weight placebo book M0187, with switch | 10.3-11.0% | 19-22% | 2.4-2.8 | 0.90-0.94 | -- | 0.43-0.47 |

**The idea failed against its own placebo.** The idea version, B100-FAST, earned 7.3% a year. The same pool, band, slots and switch filled in a meaningless fixed order earned 7.2%. That is no gap at all, and the placebo fell less (36.7% against 40.8%). Among the 100 busiest names, the salience score adds nothing you can see. It still beat plain bounce-buying by about 1 point a year, much less than the 5 points it had in the full screen. This is what the expected failure predicted: the most-watched stocks are where a "investors overreact to stand-out days" effect should be weakest.

**The fast switch made things worse.** With the fast switch the worst fall was 40.8%. With the plain 200-day switch it was 19.5%. Coming back in on the first close over the 50-day average bought the bear-market rallies of 2001-2002 and 2008, and the exit only fired again after the next leg down. That was the expected whipsaw. It did not even buy back the 2009-2015 lag: -3.5 points a year against -5.3 for the plain switch. Only the version with no switch at all kept level with SPY in those years (+0.2), at a 56% fall.

**The one eligible version, and why it goes no further.** B100-SLOW passed every go-live screen on dev. It earned 9.2% a year against 7.2%, fell at most 19.5% (under the owner's 25% real-money limit), and its gains were 1.95 times its losses. Its luck check was 0.906 against the bar of 0.90, at N = 128 (the lab's count of distinct methods tried, floored at the measured participation ratio). In words: after 128 tries, a result this good would come from luck slightly less than one time in ten. That is just inside the owner's bar. But:
- it won only **1 of 4** walk-forward folds (it beat SPY in 2006-2008 and lost in 2003-2005, 2009-2011 and 2012-2014), so the hard gate will refuse to promote it;
- it trailed SPY by **5.3 points a year over 2009-2015**, worse than the parent, and by 7.0 on the survivorship-check store (the same history with most of the dead companies added back);
- on that store it earns 8.0%, and all 6 versions earn less there;
- it is still below the meaningless equal-weight placebo book M0187 with the same switch, which earned 10.3-11.0%.

So its dev lead is the frame: equal weights plus a 200-day switch that sat out 2002 and 2008. It is not the score. **No buy signal**: it clears (a) dev-eligible, but fails (c) folds (1 of 4) and (d) the 2009-2015 edge.

**Beta.** The switched books ran at a beta of about 0.45-0.65 to SPY. They sit in cash in the big down months and miss the big rebound months. The no-switch book ran at 1.0. Low beta plus equal weights is the shape of every frame-driven result in recent batches. The salience books here have the same beta as their placebo, which says again that the score is not steering the risk.

**Hypothesis and expected failure.** The hypothesis failed. The busiest-member pool did not lift 2009-2015, which got worse with the plain switch. The fast switch failed on crashes, and the idea did not beat its placebo. Every part of the expected failure happened: the spread shrank in big names, the fast re-entry whipsawed, and the no-switch arm fell past 50%. One thing the expected failure did not foresee: the version without the busiest cut (ALL-FAST) was the only switched book ahead of SPY in 2009-2015, by 1.5 points. So the small names were where the 2009-2015 edge came from, not what was blocking it. But that book fell 51%.

**My opinion:** Stop the salience family here. The parent's edge over plain bounce-buying was real in the full screen, but it lived in the smaller, less-watched members and before 2009. In the big names, where SPY's drift lives, it is indistinguishable from a random order. The only way it kept up with SPY after 2009 was with no brake, at a fall twice the owner's limit. The eligible plain-switch version is a selection that the folds already refuse. The next thing worth the lab's time is not another salience frame. It is a standing rule: every new stock-picking book carries a same-frame placebo, and is judged on its gap over that placebo in 2009-2015.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1808, promotion step 0b)

Dev-eligible on B100-SLOW only (DSR 0.906), refused by the hard gate on its folds: 1 of 4 walk-forward folds, 2009-2015 edge -5.3% a year (-7.0% on the survivorship-check store). The fast-return variant tied its own same-frame placebo, and the eligible variant earned less than the reshuffling placebo behind the same switch. No test look spent.
methods.verdict: Buying big companies whose stand-out days were losses earned no more than the same picks in a random order (7.3% vs 7.2% a year, SPY 7.2%); the fast way back in fell 41%, and the one eligible version lost 3 of 4 test periods and trailed SPY by 5 points a year after 2009.

methods.name: Fear-exposed stocks weighted by size: does the fear signal pick anything once the equal-weight shape is gone?
methods.hypothesis: M0191's fear-exposed book (most negative daily VIX loading net of beta, quarterly, 40% keep band) beat SPY only in broad months and its fear-hedge control matched it, so its lead was the equal-weight shape. Weight the same 20 and 40 names by trailing 63-day average dollar volume (a size proxy; the store has no market caps), capped at 10% a name, with the paired fear-hedge control weighted the same way, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up; judge 2009-2015 first. Expected failure: once weighted toward the giants, the book is a noisy slice of SPY that trails it by its fees, and the gap to the control stays under a point a year, closing the family.

methods.name: Stocks that shrug off bond-yield moves: rank members by their sensitivity to the 10-year Treasury yield, after the market's own move
methods.sourceRef: D.E. Shaw research note on Treasury beta (caia.org/node/6853); Maio & Santa-Clara, short-rate innovations and CAPM anomalies; Driessen et al., Does interest rate exposure explain the low volatility anomaly? (Tilburg)
methods.hypothesis: Stocks differ in how they move when bond yields change, after allowing for the market: bond-like stocks (utilities, staples, steady payers) rise when yields fall, growth and cyclical stocks the other way. Several papers (2010s; so the whole dev window is before publication and any edge may have faded since) say rate exposure is priced and explains part of the low-risk premium. On the last close of each quarter, among members passing F4's $5 / $20M screen, regress 52 weekly log returns (marks 5 sessions apart) on SPY's weekly log return and the weekly change in the 10-year Treasury yield in percentage points (one shared fit, so the yield loading is net of the market), hold 20 names at 1/20 each, keep a holding while its rank fraction stays under 40%, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Variants, each with and without the SPY 200-day switch set explicitly (trend=None on the no-switch rungs): Y20, the 20 members whose prices rise most when yields fall (the bond-like side); Y20-OPP, the 20 with the most positive loading (the paired control, kept in the same pool so the walk-forward selection can pick against the idea); N20, the 20 with the smallest absolute loading (rate-neutral). Judged beside the meaningless placebo in the same frame (M0187, +8.8% to +11.9% a year on the deposits without the switch, +10.3% to +11.0% with it, SPY +7.2%), and each variant's beta to SPY is reported. Success: Y20 or Y20-SW beats total-return SPY and the placebo's range, worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive 2009-2015 edge, does not trail in the 2013 rate jump, and clearly beats Y20-OPP.
methods.expectedFailure: It is a sector bet and a falling-rate bet, not a priced exposure. A ranking probe run before this file was committed (rankings and in-window loadings only, no later returns) showed the bond-like side to be utilities and REITs in most years (2004-12-31: DUK, ED, AEP, EIX, FE, EXC...; 2013 and 2015: VTR, WELL, DOC, SPG, PLD, CMS, WEC, NEE) and the opposite side banks, life insurers and energy (SCHW, MET, PRU, LNC, ZION, BAC, RIG, FCX). Beta is not the main tilt: the bond side's average beta was 0.72 in 1999, about 1.0 in 2004, 2013 and 2015, and 2.0 on 2008-06-30, when the one-year fit put Fannie, Freddie, KeyCorp, Fifth Third and REITs on the bond side; the correlation between beta and the yield loading across members ran from -0.41 to 0.20. So: Y20 rides 1996-2015's falling yields through utilities and REITs, is hit in 2008 by the financials the 2007-08 fit picked up, and is hit in the 2013 rate jump (the taper scare, May-September) when REITs and utilities fell hardest; it fails 'beats SPY' in 2009-2015 or lands inside the placebo's range. Y20-OPP, a banks-and-energy book, loses 2008 badly. N20 behaves like the placebo, since a small loading carries no information, and that is its use: if N20 matches Y20, the ranking added nothing. Without the switch every book falls about 50% in 2008, like the placebo; with it the worst fall may pass 25% but DSR at N about 127 will not reach 0.90 unless the lead is well above the placebo's. The published evidence is mostly on portfolios sorted across all stocks; among big index members a 20-name equal-weight book is mainly the frame.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

Some stocks behave like bonds. When interest rates fall, they go up, even after you allow for
what the whole market did that week. Utilities and property companies (REITs) are the classic
case. Banks, life insurers and oil companies tend to do the opposite. Several research notes say
this "rate exposure" is rewarded and explains part of why calm stocks do well.

Each quarter the method measured, for every large index company that passed the lab's usual
price and trading screen, how much its weekly return moved with the weekly change in the 10-year
US Treasury yield over the past year, after taking out the market's own move. It then held 20
names at equal weight in the lab's standard frame: re-pick each quarter, keep a holding while it
stays in the top 40% of the ranking, park empty slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real
fees, 5M IDR topped up each month, 1996-2015.

Six versions, each with and without the switch that goes to cash when SPY is below its 200-day
average (set explicitly on every version):
- **Y20**: the 20 stocks that rise most when yields fall (the bond-like side). This is the idea.
- **Y20-OPP**: the 20 that rise most when yields *rise*. The paired control.
- **N20**: the 20 least moved by yields (rate-neutral).

A check of the rankings before the run (rankings only, no later returns) showed the bond-like
side to be mostly utilities and REITs, and the opposite side mostly banks, insurers and energy.
So this is partly a sector bet, and the pre-registration said so.

## Result, on the owner's deposits (SPY with the same deposits: +7.2% a year)

| version | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Y20 (idea) | +12.5% | 62% | 2.48 | 0.73 | 0.92 |
| **Y20-SW** (idea, switch) | **+11.8%** | **22.0%** | **3.08** | **0.955** | **0.40** |
| Y20-OPP (control) | +7.7% | 68% | 1.55 | 0.38 | 1.47 |
| Y20-OPP-SW | +10.8% | 33% | 2.51 | 0.82 | 0.62 |
| N20 (rate-neutral) | +7.4% | 54% | 1.70 | 0.48 | 0.88 |
| N20-SW | +9.2% | 24% | 2.46 | 0.89 | 0.41 |
| *placebo, no switch (3 seeds)* | *+8.8% to +11.9%* | *52-61%* | | | *0.97-1.04* |
| *placebo, switch (3 seeds)* | *+10.3% to +11.0%* | *19-22%* | | | *0.43-0.47* |

"Beta to SPY" is how much the book moves when SPY moves 1%. It is measured on monthly returns
with the deposits taken out. The placebo is the same frame filled in a meaningless order (the
lab's yardstick since the last batch).

**Y20-SW passed the lab's dev screen.** It beat SPY by 4.6 points a year on the deposits. It lost
at most 22% from a peak, under the 25% limit. It made about three dollars on winning trades for
every dollar lost (PF 3.08, bar 1.3). The luck test (DSR: how likely the result is real rather
than the best of many tries) scored 0.955 against the 0.90 bar, with the lab counting N = 130
independent tries. In the walk-forward test it won 3 of 4 later periods: 2003-05, 2006-08 (+10%
while SPY lost 25%) and 2009-11 (barely: +62.6% vs +60.8%). It lost 2012-14 (+50% vs +66%).

## Against the placebo, not just SPY

- **Without the switch the idea clearly beats its opposite and the placebo.** Y20 earned +12.5%,
  above every placebo seed (+8.8 to +11.9) and 4.8 points above its opposite. The rate-neutral
  book (+7.4%) did worse than the placebo, as expected: a small loading carries no information.
  Taken alone, this is the clearest gap between an idea and its control in the last several
  batches.
- **With the switch most of that gap goes away.** Y20-SW +11.8% against the best switched
  placebo seed +11.0% and its own switched opposite +10.8%. That is a lead of about one point a
  year over a book with no idea in it. The switch does most of the work: it is out of the market
  in 2001-02 and 2008, and its low beta (0.40, the same as the placebo's) is the time spent in
  cash.

## Where it fails: the years most like today

- **2009-2015, the first filter.** Y20-SW trailed SPY by 3.3 points a year in 2009-2015. The
  switch sold into the 2010 and 2011 dips, and SPY's big-company rally ran on without it. Y20
  without the switch led by 7.0 points there, but its +20.3% a year (deposits removed) sits inside
  the placebo's 2009-15 range (+15.9% to +21.3%), so the frame explains it.
- **The 2013 rate jump** (May-September, when yields rose a full point). The bond-like book
  trailed SPY only modestly, at +12.6% annualised vs +15.6%. The rate-rising book, as expected,
  did best (+38.7%). It was not the crash I feared, but it was the wrong side to be on.
- **Market breadth.** Every version made all its lead in "broad" months (when the average member
  beat the index) and lost in "narrow" months (a few giants carrying SPY): Y20-SW −1.0% narrow,
  +9.4% broad. That is the shape of every equal-weight book in this lab. The 36-month persistence
  reading was positive in only 6 of 202 windows on dev, so dev had almost no long narrow stretch
  like 2017-2024's.
- **Dead companies.** On the check history, which adds back most of the companies that failed or
  left the index, Y20-SW's lead falls from +4.6 to +2.1 points a year. Its luck score drops from
  0.955 to 0.84, below the bar, and its 2009-2015 gap widens from −3.3 to −5.7. Y20's lead falls
  from +5.3 to +1.9. So more than half of the lead came from companies missing from the
  usual data. The rate-neutral book improved, a sign that the yield ranking was picking names
  whose losers had left the data.

## The buy signal

The walk-forward report printed its "buy signal": dev-eligible, no failed relatives, 3 of 4 folds,
and a +7.0 point 2009-2015 edge. Read it carefully. That +7.0 is the record of the fold
picks, and in 2009-2015 the rule picked the no-switch book. The version that would actually be
promoted, Y20-SW, has a **negative** 2009-2015 edge (−3.3, −5.7 with dead companies). By the
spirit of condition (d), the promotable configuration does not clear it.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis held in part. The bond-like side beat the rate-rising side and the placebo
  without the switch, and the switched version cleared the dev screen. It failed the 2009-2015
  condition, and its gap over the switched placebo (under one point) is not the "clear gap" the
  pre-registration demanded.
- The expected failure largely happened. It was a utilities-and-REITs book riding twenty years
  of falling yields. 2008 was its worst year (−39.5% without the switch, worse than the placebo's
  −32% to −39%), because the 2007-08 fit had put Fannie, Freddie and regional banks on the bond
  side. It lagged in 2009-2015 with the switch. The 2013 hit was milder than predicted.

## My opinion

This is the first idea in several batches where the ranking beat its own opposite by a wide
margin, so rate exposure is a real pattern in this data and not noise. But the promotable
version is a switch plus a utilities-and-REITs lean that the falling yields of 1996-2015 paid for.
It is about a point a year above a meaningless book, below SPY in 2009-2015, and more than half its
lead disappears when dead companies are added back. I would not spend a test-window look on
Y20-SW: from 2016 yields stopped falling and then rose sharply in 2022, which is exactly when a
bond-like book suffers, and the dev data cannot show that. If the coordinator's gate admits it,
expect it to fail on "beats SPY". The direction worth one more try is the one that removes the
two things we know flatter it. Weight the bond-like 20 by trading value instead of equal
slots (no small-company lean), and judge it first on 2009-2015 against SPY and RSP. If that
lags, close the family.

### 2026-10-17 (Sera 20261017-1808, promotion step 0b: not promoted by Sera's decision)

(1) With a 15% ceiling and 20 names drawn from the screened members, a handful of giants can take half the book, so a seed's result may hinge on whether its hash happened to pick a Microsoft or a GE: the seed spread could widen until it says nothing. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

# The placebo book sized by company size: was the lead the equal slots?

## What this was

Not a strategy. A control experiment. The lab's "meaningless-order" book holds 20 index members
picked in a scrambled order that knows nothing about prices. It re-picks every quarter, parks any
empty slot in SPY and holds each name in an equal 5% slot. It beat SPY over 1996-2015 by as much
as four real rankings did. So the frame (the screen, the quarterly holding, the 20 slots) earns
the lead, not any ranking.

The question here was **which part of the frame**. The usual suspect is the equal slots. Equal
slots give a small company the same money as a giant, while SPY gives the giants most of the
money. When small companies do well, equal slots look like skill (insight 91).

So this method keeps the scrambled picks **exactly**, using the same code that chose them before,
and changes only how much money each pick gets. Each pick is sized by its average daily trading
value (price times shares traded) over the last 60 sessions. That is a size stand-in, because the
store has no reliable company values. No single name may hold more than 15% of the account. The
total in stocks stays what the equal book holds, and empty slots still go to SPY. Every variant
pays Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares, on the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up.

One assumption, written down before the run: trading value is partly how busy a stock is, not
only how big it is, so a stock in the news briefly gets extra weight.

## Result on the dev window (1996-2015), on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends, on the same deposits, earned **+7.2% a year**.

| book | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | luck test (DSR) | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| equal slots, scramble 1 (the control) | +11.9% | 52.3% | 2.12 | 969 | 0.817 | 1.02 |
| sized, scramble 1 | +11.5% | 59.0% | 1.85 | 961 | 0.809 | 1.11 |
| sized, scramble 2 | +8.1% | 62.4% | 1.79 | 970 | 0.374 | 1.11 |
| sized, scramble 3 | +10.9% | 52.3% | 2.10 | 929 | 0.695 | 1.02 |
| sized, scramble 1, with the switch | +11.1% | 26.9% | 2.61 | 821 | 0.955 | 0.44 |

The control reproduces the earlier placebo's scramble-1 book to the trade (+11.9%, 969 trades).
So the comparison is clean. The earlier equal-slot scrambles 2 and 3 earned +8.8% and +11.8%.

"Beta to SPY" is how much the book's monthly return moves for each 1% that SPY moves, measured on
the book without its deposits. 1.1 means it moved about 10% more than the market.

**Sizing by company size cost almost nothing.** Scramble for scramble, the sized books earned
0.4, 0.7 and 0.9 points a year less than their equal-slot twins (11.5 vs 11.9, 8.1 vs 8.8,
10.9 vs 11.8). Every one still beat SPY. With the switch, the sized book earned more than its
equal twin (+11.1% against +10.4%).

**The switched sized book passed every dev screen condition.** It beat SPY and fell at most 26.9%,
under the lab's 50% screen. That is just over the 25% limit for real money, so it would fail
there even before anything else. It made 2.6 times as much on winning trades as it
lost on losing ones. Its luck test (DSR, how likely the result is real rather than luck after all
the lab's tries) was 0.955, judged at N = 131 independent methods against the owner's 0.90 bar.
It is still evidence only. It is a scramble, and it won only 1 of 4 walk-forward periods. In
those periods the lab re-chooses its best variant on the past and scores it on the next three
years. It lost 2003-05, 2009-11 and 2012-14 to SPY and won only the crash years 2006-08, when the
switch sat in cash. The hard gate refuses it for that reason alone.

The unswitched books failed on their worst fall (52-62%, over the 50% limit) and on the luck test.
Their worst year was 2008 (-36% to -41%). The switched book's worst year was 2011 (-15%).

## By era

| book | 1996-2008, a year | SPY | 2009-2015, a year | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| equal, scramble 1 | +11.3% | +4.4% | +17.7% | +14.8% |
| sized, scramble 1 | +14.4% | +4.4% | +14.6% | +14.8% |
| sized, scramble 2 | +3.3% | +4.4% | +17.3% | +14.8% |
| sized, scramble 3 | +8.4% | +4.4% | +20.4% | +14.8% |
| sized, scramble 1, switch | +14.5% | +4.4% | +10.4% | +14.8% |

(These are the books' own yearly growth without deposits, month by month.) The unswitched sized
books held up in 2009-2015, the era that looks most like today: two of three beat SPY. The
switched one trailed SPY by about 4 points a year there, the same switch cost the lab has seen
on every book in this frame.

## The cross-check with the dead companies put back

The dev store prices only about half to three quarters of the index's past members. The missing
ones are mostly the companies that died. A *random* pick from that store is therefore a pick from
the survivors, which is a head start no skill earned. The survivorship-check store adds back most
of the missing members, dead ones included. On it:

| book | dev store | with dead companies | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| equal, scramble 1 | +11.9% | +9.5% | -2.4 |
| sized, scramble 1 | +11.5% | +7.7% | -3.7 |
| sized, scramble 2 | +8.1% | +9.3% | +1.2 |
| sized, scramble 3 | +10.9% | +9.1% | -1.9 |
| sized, scramble 1, switch | +11.1% | +9.7% | -1.4 |

So the missing dead companies were worth about **1.6 points a year on average** to these random
books, two to four times what the equal slots were worth. After both are taken out, a lead of
about 0.5 to 2.5 points a year over SPY is left. The books also move about 10% more than the
market (beta 1.02-1.11), and in a market that rose 7% a year that extra movement alone is worth
roughly half a point to a point.

## Why

Two things the lab blamed for this frame's lead turned out small, and one it underrated turned
out large.

- **The equal slots: small.** Random picks from the index's screened members are mostly
  mid-sized companies whatever you weight them by, and sizing them inside the book barely moves
  the needle. The lean that matters is in *who can be picked* (any member, with no tilt to the
  giants), not in how much each pick gets.
- **The missing dead companies: large.** A book that picks at random from a survivors-only
  list collects the survivors' head start. That is the biggest single piece found so far.
- **Market sensitivity: real but modest.** The unswitched books sit at beta 1.0-1.1, so they ride
  the market's rise a little harder than SPY.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**No.** I expected the sized books to fall back toward SPY (+7.5% to +9%). On the dev store they
kept most of the lead (+8.1% to +11.5%). The equal-weight lean is not what the frame earns.

Of the expected failures: (1) the seed spread did widen a little (8.1 to 11.5 against 8.8 to
11.9), but not enough to say nothing. (2) The busy-stock lean into the 1999-2000 bubble did not
show up as a worse fall for scramble 1 (it earned more in 1996-2008). Scramble 2's 1996-2008 was
weak, though, and its worst fall was the deepest (62%). (3) The monthly re-sizing did not add
trades (821-970 against 969). The unswitched books fell about 50-60% in 2008 as expected, and
the switched one trailed SPY in 2009-2015 as expected.

## Comparison with the parent

The parent placebo's switched scrambles earned +10.3% to +11.0%, with beta 0.43-0.47 and a worst
fall of 19-22%. The sized switched book sits in that band (+11.1%, beta 0.44) with a deeper fall
(26.9%), because a sized book puts up to 15% in one name. The frame's yardstick from that
analysis (about +11.5% before a ranking says anything) stands. On the survivorship-check store it
should be read about 1.5 points lower.

## My opinion:

Stop blaming the equal slots for this frame's lead. The lab has been treating "equal weight leans
small" as the explanation for every twenty-year win in this frame, and this run says that piece
is worth under a point. The bigger, cheaper explanation is the data: a random pick from a store
missing the dead companies is a pick from the winners. I would not spend more ids on placebos
that vary weighting. The next useful test is the *pool*: the same scramble restricted to the
100 most-traded members, which are roughly SPY's own big names. If that random book lands on SPY,
the frame's lead is "picking from the whole index instead of the giants" plus survivorship, and
every ranking in this frame should be judged against the survivorship-check store before it gets
any further. Separately, any real ranking in this frame should now quote its survivorship-check
number beside its dev number in its first analysis, since the placebo itself loses 1.5 points
there.


### 2026-10-17

### Sera 20261017-1835 — promotion attempt

M0198 is a placebo and was written never to be promoted. For the record, `lab promote M0198` also exits 2 on the folds (1 of 4); kin is clean. No look spent, no buy signal (2009-2015 lead −6.0 points against SPY for DV1-SW).
