### 2026-10-18

Sera 20261018-0517 reserves this for the owner's theme "books shaped like the market", and sharpens it: weight by REAL point-in-time market value (market.market_value, market_fields = ("shares",)), not dollar volume, one share class per company, with a pre-registered weight ceiling. Keep a dollar-volume arm only if cheap, for the bridge to M0122. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up (a -frac-gotrade preset). Run beside the meaningless control of the same shape: 20 size-weighted random members. Report both stores (dev and survivorship-check) and 2009-2015 against SPY.


### 2026-10-18

## What was tried

The parent method (the bond-like stock picker, M0197) ranks big index companies by how much they
rise when the 10-year US Treasury yield falls, after taking out the market's own move. It holds
the top 20 at **equal** weight, re-picks each quarter, and parks empty slots in SPY. Without a
crash guard it beat its own opposite (the 20 that rise when yields rise) by about 5 points a year.

But an equal-weight book quietly leans toward the smaller companies in the index, while SPY is
weighted by company size. This method asks: does the bond-like lead survive once the book is
shaped more like the market?

It keeps the parent's 20 picks exactly and weights each by its **real company size on that day**
(shares the company had filed by then times the price that day), with no company above 10% of the
account. Unknown sizes (about one pick in ten) take the middle size of the others; two share
classes of one company (Alphabet's two tickers) count as one company. Fractional shares, Gotrade's
real fees, the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly top-up.

Six versions:

- **Y20-MV10**: the bond-like 20, size-weighted, no guard. This is the idea.
- **Y20-MV10-SW**: the same behind the SPY 200-day switch (all cash when SPY is below its
  200-day average).
- **OPP-MV10**: the opposite side, size-weighted. The paired control.
- **Y20-DV10**: the bond-like 20 weighted by daily trading value instead of company size.
- **PLC1-MV10, PLC2-MV10**: the same 20-slot frame filled in a meaningless order, size-weighted
  the same way. The "placebo": what the frame earns with no idea in it.

## Result, on the owner's deposits (SPY with the same deposits: +7.2% a year)

| version | your money a year | equal-weight twin | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Y20-MV10 (idea) | +9.5% | +12.5% | 55% | 2.15 | 0.63 | 0.84 |
| **Y20-MV10-SW** (idea, switch) | **+9.2%** | +11.8% | **20.4%** | **2.57** | **0.906** | **0.39** |
| OPP-MV10 (control) | +6.2% | +7.7% | 71% | 1.40 | 0.35 | 1.41 |
| Y20-DV10 (by trading value) | +10.9% | +12.5% | 61% | 2.14 | 0.64 | 0.92 |
| PLC1-MV10 (placebo) | +10.3% | +11.9% | 53% | 1.85 | 0.78 | 1.00 |
| PLC2-MV10 (placebo) | +8.1% | +8.8% | 59% | 1.82 | 0.48 | 1.00 |

"Beta to SPY" is how much the book moves when SPY moves 1% (monthly, deposits taken out). The
"equal-weight twin" is the parent's recorded result for the same picks at equal weight (for the
placebo, the equal-weight placebo of the same seed).

**One version passed the lab's dev screen: Y20-MV10-SW.** It beat SPY by 2.0 points a year on
the deposits. It lost at most 20.4% from a peak, under the 25% limit. It made about $2.57 on
winning trades for every $1 lost (PF; the bar is 1.3). Its luck score (DSR: how likely the result
is real rather than the best of many tries) was 0.906. The bar is 0.90, with the lab counting
N = 145 independent tries when it ran. That is a pass by less than a hair.

**It will not be promoted.** In the walk-forward test (pick the best version on the past, score
it on the next three years) it won 2 of 4 periods. It won 2003-05 (+61% vs +52%) and 2006-08 (+13%
while SPY lost 25%: the switch sat in cash). It lost 2009-11 (+42% vs +61%) and 2012-14 (+34% vs
+66%). The hard gate needs a strict majority, so the promotion step refuses it.

## What sizing by company size did

- **It cost the idea more than it cost the placebo.** The bond-like book lost 3.0 points a year
  going from equal slots to size (+12.5% to +9.5%). The meaningless books lost 1.6 and 0.7 points
  (+11.9% to +10.3%, +8.8% to +8.1%). So the size weighting did not just remove a frame effect.
  It took away **more than half of what the ranking itself was adding**. The bond-like lead lived
  disproportionately in the *smaller* bond-like names: the small utilities and property companies.
- **The idea now sits inside the placebo's range.** +9.5% against +8.1% to +10.3% for random
  picks of the same shape. It is below placebo seed 1.
- **It still beats its opposite**, by 3.3 points a year (+9.5% vs +6.2%), down from 4.8 at equal
  weight. The opposite side (banks, insurers, energy) still fell 56% in 2008 alone.
- **Trading value beat company size** (+10.9% vs +9.5%), and was closer to the equal book. It
  leans toward the busiest names, which is not the same thing as the biggest.

## The years most like today

- **2009-2015, the first filter.** With deposits taken out, SPY earned +14.8% a year. The
  size-weighted bond book earned +14.6%: a tie. The placebo seeds earned +14.7% and +16.4%. The
  switched version earned only +8.6%. The switch sold the 2010 and 2011 dips and missed the
  rebound. On the lab's funded measure its 2009-2015 lead is −7.8 points a year. Only the
  trading-value version led here (+3.5 points).
- **2008.** The bond book without the guard fell 33% in the calendar year, a little better than
  its equal twin (−39%), because the 10% ceiling and the size weights put less on the regional
  banks and Fannie/Freddie that the 2007-08 fit had pulled onto the bond side. From its peak, with
  deposits removed, it still fell 48%. The switched version was flat in 2008.
- **The 2013 rate jump** (May-September). The bond book made +5.3%, SPY +6.2%, the opposite
  side +14.1%. A modest miss, as in the parent.
- **Narrow markets** (months when a few giants carried SPY). Even size-weighted, the bond book
  lost to SPY by 8.0% a year in narrow months and won by 12.9% in broad ones. A 10% ceiling on 20
  names still does not own what SPY owns: the giants it holds are whichever ones happen to be
  bond-like, not the ones carrying the index.

## Dead companies

On the check history, which adds back most of the companies that failed or left the index:

- Y20-MV10's lead over SPY falls from +2.4 to +0.9 points a year; its worst fall deepens from
  55% to 61%.
- Y20-MV10-SW's lead falls from +2.0 to +0.6 points; its worst fall rises from 20.4% to 22.8%;
  its luck score drops from 0.906 to 0.79, below the bar. Its 2009-2015 gap widens from −7.8 to
  −9.0.
- The opposite side collapses: +6.2% to +2.4% a year, worst fall 90%. It picked the banks that
  died.
- The placebo seed 1 loses 2.9 points; seed 2 gains 0.8.

So the bond-like side keeps a real gap over its opposite (5.6 points a year on the check history: +8.0% against +2.4%), but
over SPY there is under a point a year left.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis failed.** The success line asked for a 2+ point lead over both the opposite
  and the sized placebo, and no lag behind SPY in 2009-2015. It beat the opposite (by 3.3) but not
  the placebo (seed 1 did better), and the switched version trailed SPY badly in 2009-2015.
- **The expected failure mostly happened**, with one twist. I predicted the book would become
  its few biggest names at the ceiling and lose 1-3 points against its equal twin: it lost 3.0.
  I predicted the gap to the opposite would shrink: 4.8 to 3.3. I predicted the sized placebo
  would land within a point: it landed *above*. The twist: I expected it to trail SPY in
  2009-2015 because of a utilities lean; without the switch it tied SPY there instead, and only
  the switched version trailed.

## My opinion

The rate-exposure ranking is a real pattern in this data: the bond-like side beats its opposite
at equal weight, at size weight and on the check history with dead companies. But it is not a
way to beat SPY. Most of its lead came from small bond-like companies and the falling yields of
1996-2015. Once the book is weighted by size, it is no better than random picks of the same
shape. The one version that passed the screen did it with the switch, and the switch is exactly
what loses in 2009-2015. I would not run another equal-slot or size-slot variation of this family.
The one test left that is worth an id is the clean one: start from the market-shaped core (the
50 biggest companies at their market value) and tilt it toward or away from the bond-like names,
beside a random tilt. If that cannot beat the core and its random twin, close the family. I
expect it to land within a point of the core, which itself trailed SPY by about a point
(the dividend-tilt method run beside this one), so the honest bet is that the family closes.


### 2026-10-18

Sera 20261018-0517, Promotion step 0b: refused by the hard gate on the fold rule (2 of 4 walk-forward folds; kin clean). The eligible switched market-value variant cleared dev by a hair (DSR 0.906) but trailed SPY in 2009-2015 on both stores (-7.8 dev, -9.0 survivorship-check) and its survivorship-check DSR falls to 0.79. No look spent. Buy signal: no.


### 2026-10-20

**A correction, and it reverses this page's central sentence.**

The two placebo books above — the ones that gave this method its verdict — traded about 980 times
over the twenty years. The real book traded 433. They were more than twice as busy as the book
they were meant to imitate, and on Gotrade's fees that is worth several points a year. The
comparison was never a fair one.

Two placebos shaped like this book have since been drawn, matched to its own trading: 411 and 416
trades against 433. They earned **+7.1% and +7.1% a year** on the same deposits. The book earned
**+9.5%**.

So the book sits **above both**, by about **2.4 points a year** against each, and the two placebo
seeds now land 0.08 points apart instead of 2.2. Two published sentences are withdrawn:

- the verdict's *"did no better than random picks of the same shape"*, and
- *"The idea now sits inside the placebo's range. +9.5% against +8.1% to +10.3% for random picks
  of the same shape. It is below placebo seed 1."*

**This is a correction, not a reopening.** The rejection stands, on everything else, untouched:
the book fell 55% from a peak, its luck score is 0.63, and the one version that passed the dev
screen did so by a hair with the cash switch, trailed SPY badly in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4
later periods. The hard gate refuses it on the later periods either way, and no test-window look
was spent. What changes is the reason the owner is given: this book is rejected because it cannot
survive its own fall and does not hold up out of sample — not because its picks were
indistinguishable from random ones. They were not.

The success line written before the run asked for a 2-point lead over both the opposite side and a
placebo of the same shape, and no lag behind SPY in 2009-2015. Read honestly it now clears the
first two (+3.3 over the opposite, +2.4 over each placebo) and still fails the third, which is why
the hypothesis still reads as failed.

Nothing was re-run to find this: these are the same trials, measured against a fair opponent.
methods.verdict: Weighted by company size, the bond-like picks beat random picks of the same shape by about 2.4 points a year - a correction, because the random books this was first judged against traded more than twice as often as it did. It is still rejected, on everything else: the book fell 55% from a peak, and the version with the cash switch passed the dev screen only by a hair, trailed SPY badly in 2009-2015 and won only 2 of 4 later periods.

methods.name: Bond-like stocks with a gentler crash guard: half the book stays invested below SPY's 200-day average instead of all of it going to cash
methods.sourceRef: M0197 synthesis (Sera 20261017-1808); Treasury beta, caia.org/node/6853
methods.hypothesis: M0197's bond-like picks (the 20 screened members whose weekly returns rise most when the 10-year Treasury yield falls, net of the market, re-picked quarterly with a 40% keep band, empty slots in SPY) beat every placebo seed and their own opposite without a switch (+12.5% a year on the deposits vs +8.8% to +11.9%, SPY +7.2%) but fell 62% in 2008; behind the all-or-nothing SPY 200-day switch they fell 22% but trailed SPY by 3.3 points a year in 2009-2015 and led the switched placebo by under a point. The rate-beta papers are from the 2010s, so the dev window is before publication and any edge may have faded since. A gentler guard keeps half the bet on: full size while SPY closes above its 200-day average, every target at half weight (rest cash) below it (HALF); and HALF-FAST, full size again as soon as SPY closes above its 50-day average. Holdings are kept and only resized when the guard flips. Controls under the same guard and frame: N20-HALF (rate-neutral, smallest absolute loading) and a hash-order placebo over the same scoreable names (two seeds under HALF, one under HALF-FAST). Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly top-up. Success, written now: Y20-HALF or Y20-HALF-FAST beats total-return SPY on dev with a worst fall under the screen's 50% bar, a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, and beats its own same-guard placebo seeds by at least 2 points a year on the deposits.
methods.expectedFailure: Halving exposure halves the switch's protection without restoring the ranking's edge: the 2008 fall of the bond-like book was led by the financials the 2007-08 fit put on the bond side (Fannie, Freddie, regional banks), and half of a 62% fall compounded through a year below the 200-day is still about 35-40%, past design section 1's 25% even if it clears the screen's 50%. In 2009-2015 the half-size book recovers only half as fast in the 2009 rebound and the 2010-11 dips, so it lands between Y20 (+7.0 points vs SPY) and Y20-SW (-3.3), likely near zero, and the placebo under the same guard rises with it, leaving the gap to the placebo near M0197's one point rather than two. HALF-FAST adds whipsaw trades at real fees around the 50-day. DSR at N about 130 needs a lead well above the placebo's; the survivorship check halved M0197's lead and is likely to do the same here. And from 2016 yields stopped falling and rose sharply in 2022, the regime a bond-like book suffers in, which dev cannot show.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The parent method (the bond-like stock picker) ranks big index companies by how much they rise
when the 10-year US Treasury yield falls, after taking out the market's own move. Mostly that means
utilities and property companies. It holds the top 20 at equal weight, re-picks each quarter, and
parks empty slots in SPY. With no crash guard it beat every meaningless "placebo" book but fell 62%
in 2008. With the usual all-or-nothing guard (all cash whenever SPY is below its 200-day average) it
fell only 22%, but it trailed SPY in 2009-2015 and led the placebo by under a point a year.

This method tries a gentler guard. Below SPY's 200-day average the book does not go to cash: every
position is cut to half size and the other half waits in cash. The holdings stay the same; only
their size changes. A second version (HALF-FAST) goes back to full size as soon as SPY closes above
its 50-day average. As controls, the same guard ran on the rate-neutral ranking (stocks least moved
by yields) and on three placebo books: the same pool of stocks in a fixed, meaningless order (two
seeds under the half guard, one under the fast guard). Everything ran in fractional shares at
Gotrade's real fees, with 5M IDR topped up each month, 1996-2015.

Success was written down before the run: beat SPY with a worst fall under the screen's 50% bar, a
positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, and **a lead of at least 2 points a year over the same-guard
placebo seeds.**

## Result, on the owner's deposits (SPY with the same deposits: +7.2% a year)

| version | your money a year | worst fall | worst year | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead over SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Y20-HALF** (idea) | **+12.7%** | 38.0% | 2008 −20% | 3.21 | **0.914** | +3.2 pts |
| Y20-HALF-FAST (idea) | +12.1% | 49.7% | 2008 −29% | 2.78 | 0.844 | +4.5 pts |
| N20-HALF (rate-neutral) | +8.3% | 33.9% | 2008 −19% | 2.03 | 0.765 | −3.2 pts |
| PLC1-HALF (placebo) | +11.3% | 31.3% | 2008 −15% | 2.31 | **0.937** | −1.2 pts |
| PLC2-HALF (placebo) | +9.6% | 39.9% | 2008 −19% | 2.11 | 0.764 | −0.5 pts |
| PLC1-HALF-FAST (placebo) | +11.4% | 39.8% | 2008 −21% | 2.23 | 0.906 | +0.7 pts |
| *parent, all-cash guard* | *+11.8%* | *22.0%* | | *3.08* | *0.955* | *−3.3 pts* |
| *parent, no guard* | *+12.5%* | *62.1%* | | *2.48* | *0.73* | *+7.0 pts* |

"Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is dollars won on winning trades per dollar lost on losing ones;
the bar is 1.3. The luck score (DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many
tries. The lab now counts N = 133 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90.

**Y20-HALF passed the lab's dev screen.** It beat SPY by 5.5 points a year on the deposits. Its worst
fall was 38%, under the screen's 50% limit but well over the 25% real-money limit in design §1.
Gains vs losses was 3.21 and the luck score 0.914, just over the 0.90 bar.

**But a placebo passed it too, and that is the real result.** PLC1-HALF, a book that picks stocks in
an order that knows nothing about prices, also passed the screen, with a *higher* luck score (0.937)
and a smaller worst fall (31%). PLC1-HALF-FAST passed as well. The half guard plus the 20-name
equal-weight frame is enough to clear the screen with no idea in it.

## Which conditions failed

- **Lead over the placebo: failed.** Y20-HALF +12.7% against placebo seeds at +11.3% and +9.6%. That
  is 1.4 points over the better seed, short of the 2 points written down in advance. Against the
  average of the two seeds it is 2.2, so it depends on which placebo you pick, and that is exactly
  the kind of gap that is not evidence.
- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4 periods.** This test lets an earlier stretch choose the version, then scores
  it on the next three years. The lab picked the *placebo* in three of the four periods (2003-05,
  2009-11 and 2012-14), and lost both of the recent ones (2009-11: +51.5% vs SPY +60.8%; 2012-14:
  +58.0% vs +65.9%). It won 2006-08 with Y20-HALF-FAST (−19.7% vs SPY −24.6%). The hard gate needs
  a majority of at least four, so `lab promote` would refuse this method.
- **Dead companies.** On the check history, which adds back most of the companies that failed or
  left the index, Y20-HALF's lead falls from +5.5 to +2.8 points a year. Its worst fall deepens from
  38% to 45%, its luck score drops from 0.914 to 0.785, and its 2009-2015 lead shrinks from +3.2 to
  +0.7. On that history the placebos earn +9.5% and +9.7% against the idea's +10.0%, so the
  ranking is worth about half a point. The placebo with a different seed (PLC2) did not move at
  all, and the rate-neutral book barely moved. The bond-like ranking lost the most. As in the
  parent, the yield ranking leans toward companies whose failures are missing from the usual data.
- **Market breadth.** Every version earns its whole lead in "broad" months (when the average company
  beats the index) and loses in "narrow" months (a few giants carry SPY): Y20-HALF −5.6% narrow,
  +14.8% broad. The 36-month persistence reading was positive in only 6 of 202 windows on dev, so dev
  never saw a long narrow stretch like 2017-2024.

## Why

The half guard did what it was meant to do to the shape of the curve. It kept enough of the bet
on to recover the 2009-2015 lead the all-cash switch threw away (+3.2 points against −3.3) and
roughly halved the 2008 damage (worst year −20% against −40% unguarded). But the same thing
happens to any 20-name equal-weight book in this frame. The lift comes from being in the market
through the rebounds, not from which stocks are held. What is left of the ranking itself is about
1.4 points a year on the usual data and about half a point on the fuller data.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis held on two of its three conditions on the usual data: it beat SPY under the 50%
  bar, and its 2009-2015 lead was positive. It failed the one that matters most, the 2-point lead
  over its own placebo. On the fuller data the 2009-2015 lead is close to zero too.
- The expected failure mostly happened, with two surprises. The worst fall landed where I said
  (38%, inside the predicted 35-40%, over §1's 25%). The placebo rose with the idea, and the gap
  stayed near the parent's one point. The surprise in the idea's favour: the 2009-2015 lead came out
  positive (+3.2) rather than near zero. The surprise against it: a placebo cleared the whole dev
  screen, luck score included.

## My opinion

This direction is finished. The rate-exposure ranking is real when no guard is used, but every way
of making it survivable (all-cash switch, half guard, fast re-entry) brings it to within a point or
so of a meaningless book. The dead-companies check takes about half of what is left. I would close
the bond-like picker family and not spend a test-window look on any of its versions. The more useful
lesson is about the lab itself: a half-size guard on a 20-name equal-weight frame lets a placebo
pass the dev screen with a luck score of 0.937. Every future method in this frame must beat its
same-guard placebo by a margin set in advance before anyone takes its dev result seriously. The
next thing I would try is turning the placebo into a standing yardstick, like SPY: a lab report
that runs three placebo seeds in the same frame and guard as any method and prints the gap, so the
comparison does not depend on each method remembering to include one.


### 2026-10-17

### Sera 20261017-1835 — promotion attempt

`lab promote M0202` exited 2: the hard gate refused it on the folds (2 of 4, pick changed). Kin was clean, so the refusal is on the fold condition alone. Nothing was pre-registered and no look was spent. Sera also agrees with the child's own read: the same-guard placebo passed the screen too (DSR 0.937), the bond-like picks led it by only 1.4 points a year (about half a point with dead companies added back), and the survivorship store cut the lead from +5.5 to +2.8 with DSR 0.785. Buy signal: no (folds fail). The stock-treasury-beta family is closed for this lab on current data; reopening it needs the years after 2015 (the 2022 rate rise), which only a counted test look or new data can give.


### 2026-10-20

**Two of this page's conclusions rested on controls that traded more than twice as often as the
book. Both are withdrawn.**

The three placebo books above traded about 990 times over the twenty years. The books they were
imitating traded 440. A placebo that busy pays roughly twice the fees, and nothing drawn from the
comparison is safe.

Placebos shaped like these books have since been drawn — 423, 425 and 423 trades against 440 —
and they earned **+9.0%, +8.9% and +8.6% a year** on the same deposits, against the half-guard
book's **+12.7%** and the fast-re-entry version's **+12.1%**.

| the comparison | as published | against an honest placebo |
|---|---|---|
| the half-guard book's lead over a meaningless book of the same shape | +1.4 points a year | **+3.6 and +3.8 points** |
| the fast-re-entry version's lead | +0.8 points | **+3.5 points** |

**Withdrawn:** *"But a placebo passed it too, and that is the real result"*, and the verdict's
*"a meaningless book under the same guard passed it too; the bond-like picks led it by only 1.4
points a year."* Scored at the lab's present count of tries, the only placebos that ever cleared
the luck bar were the two over-trading ones (0.94 and 0.92). The three honest ones read 0.77, 0.76
and 0.65 against a bar of 0.90 — not one of them comes within 0.13 of it. The original comparison
also mixed luck scores taken at two different counts of tries, and was never valid on its own
terms.

**What survives is the more important half.** The recommendation written below — that every method
in this frame must beat a placebo under the same guard by a margin set in advance, and that the
placebo should become a standing yardstick like SPY — is unchanged, and the lab has since built
exactly that: a control whose trading is derived from the book it controls rather than chosen by
hand. The evidence that prompted the recommendation was wrong. The recommendation was right.

**And the rejection stands.** It never rested on the placebo. The book fell 38% from a peak, far
past the 25% the owner's rule allows for real money; its lead shrinks sharply once dead companies
are added back; and it won only 2 of 4 later periods, with the lab's own picker choosing the
placebo in three of the four. No test-window look was spent and nothing was re-run: these are the
same trials, read against a fair opponent.
methods.verdict: The half-size guard passed the dev screen, and the bond-like picks led a meaningless book of the same shape by about 3.6 to 3.8 points a year - corrected upward, because the earlier reading of 1.4 points, and the claim that a meaningless book passed the screen too, both came from controls that traded more than twice as often as the book. It is still rejected: it fell 38% from a peak, its lead shrinks once dead companies are added back, and it won only 2 of 4 later periods.

methods.name: The trend factor: one score from price moving averages over every horizon, from three days to four years
methods.sourceRef: Han, Zhou and Zhu (2016), A trend factor: any economic gains from using information over investment horizons?, Journal of Financial Economics 122(2)
methods.hypothesis: Each month-end, divide each screened member's 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000-day moving averages by its price; regress the next month's return on these 11 ratios across members, once for each of the last 12 months (all data at or before the decision date); forecast with the average of the 12 slope vectors; hold the 20 highest forecasts in equal 5% slots, monthly, keeping a holding while it ranks inside the top 40, unfilled slots in SPY, behind the SPY 200-day switch (F4's screen and switch, M0192's band). Han, Zhou and Zhu (published 2016, working paper from 2013) find the combined trend signal beats short-term reversal, momentum and long-term reversal separately in US stocks 1930-2014, because it lets the data weight each horizon. The dev window ends in 2015, so most of it predates the paper; this is in-sample for the paper. Arms: TF-N40 (40 names, band 80), TF-N20-NOSW (no switch). Control: HASH-N20, the same pool, band, slots, fill and switch in a fixed hash order (M0187's placebo). The plain 12-1 momentum contrast named when the idea was reserved is dropped: a momentum variant would tie the whole method to the test-failed momentum books through the behaviour test (hardgate D14); momentum is compared against the recorded real-fee momentum books instead. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly top-up. Success: beats SPY TR on dev with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, and beats the placebo by at least 2 points a year.
methods.expectedFailure: The forecast's slopes are dominated by the short averages (3-20 days), which is one-month reversal, and by the long ones, which is momentum; in large caps at real fees the reversal part churns 20 small slots every month and the lab's reversal books all trailed SPY. The 11 ratios are almost collinear, so 12 noisy least-squares fits on a few hundred names give slopes that flip sign month to month and the book trades like the placebo. The paper's spread is long-short and much of it lives in small, illiquid names the screen excludes. A published anomaly with a big paper fades (insight on M0050), and equal slots lean small against SPY's big-company drift (insight 91), so 2009-2015 is likely to lag SPY even if the twenty-year average wins. If it does win, it may simply be momentum by another route and inherit momentum's 2009 crash, which the 200-day switch meets late.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The trend factor (Han, Zhou and Zhu, 2016). Each month, for every screened index member, compare its price with eleven moving averages, from 3 days up to 1000 days (about four years). Fit, across all members, how well each of those eleven readings predicted the next month's return, once for each of the last 12 months. Average the 12 fits into one recipe and score every stock with it. Hold the 20 best scores in equal amounts, keep a holding while it stays in the top 40, park unused slots in SPY, and go to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5 million rupiah topped up every month. Four versions: the main book (20 names), a 40-name book, the 20-name book without the cash switch, and a **placebo**: the same frame, the same pool of stocks, but filled in a fixed meaningless (hash) order.

Assumption made before the run: the idea as reserved also named a plain 12-month momentum book as a contrast. I left it out, because one momentum version would make the whole method "kin" of the momentum books that already failed their test-window look (the lab's behaviour rule), and nothing here could ever be promoted. Momentum is compared below against the lab's recorded real-fee momentum book instead.

## Result vs SPY (1996 to 2015, with the monthly deposits)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 names | +9.7% | +7.2% | 29.1% | 1.48 | 0.81 |
| 40 names | **+10.4%** | +7.2% | **22.1%** | 1.67 | **0.899** |
| 20 names, no cash switch | +6.7% | +7.2% | 70.6% | 1.24 | 0.35 |
| placebo (hash order) | +7.9% | +7.2% | 23.9% | 1.45 | 0.75 |

- The 40-name book cleared every go-live condition except the luck check: its DSR is **0.899 against the bar of 0.90**, judged at N = 134 (one look per distinct method in the lab). In words: after 134 tries, about a 90% chance the result is not luck, a hair below what the owner asks. The bar is not "basically" met; it is missed.
- The 20-name book fell 29% at its worst (over the 25% screen) and its luck check reads 0.81.
- Without the 200-day switch the book fell 71% (2008 alone lost 53%) and earned less than SPY.

## The two checks that matter most

- **2009-2015, the best-covered years, it lost.** The walk-forward record is 2 of 4 folds: it won 2003-05 (+65% vs +52%) and 2006-08 (+11% vs -25%, the cash switch dodging the crash), and lost 2009-11 (+45% vs +61%) and 2012-14 (+36% vs +66%). Every edge it has was earned before 2009. That is the pattern the lab has seen again and again (insights 89, 91, 93), and it alone would block promotion: the hard gate needs a majority of folds.
- **The placebo test was half passed.** The 20-name trend book beat the same-frame placebo by 1.8 points a year (9.7% vs 7.9%), short of the 2 points written down in advance. The 40-name book is 2.5 points over the 20-name placebo, but the two differ in width as well as signal, so that is not a clean comparison. Most of the "beat SPY" comes from the frame (the cash switch and equal slots), which a meaningless order also enjoys.

## Why

The fitted recipe, averaged over 12 months, mostly leans on the longer averages: a stock well above its 200-1000 day averages scores high. That is momentum by another route. It caught the 2003-07 run in energy, materials and industrials (the 2005 picks were refiners, drillers and metals), and the cash switch kept it out of 2008. After 2009 the market was led by large, steady companies; an equal-weight book of 20 trend names among a few hundred members leans smaller than SPY and paid for it. The short averages (3-20 days, which is one-month reversal) add turnover at Gotrade's minimum fees without adding much.

Against the lab's real-fee residual momentum book (the realistic twin of the best momentum picker, same fees and deposits), the trend factor is clearly weaker: +10.4% a year at best vs +13.7%, a gentler worst fall (22% vs 21%: about the same), and that momentum book itself later failed its test-window look. So the eleven-horizon recipe did not find anything plain momentum lacked.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (beats SPY, wins 2009-2015, beats the placebo by 2 points) did not hold: two of its three tests failed. The expected failure was largely right: the edge was momentum-like, lived before 2009, and the placebo came close. The fear that noisy fits would make it trade like the placebo was only half right: it does beat the placebo, just not by enough.

**My opinion:** this direction is not worth more variants. The 40-name book's near-miss on the luck bar is tempting, but it loses both post-2009 folds by 15-30 points, and that is the window most like today; a wider book or a tweak would be fitting the old years harder. The useful lesson is that letting a regression weigh horizons, on large US stocks, rebuilds momentum and inherits its post-2009 weakness. What I would try next is the same eleven readings used as a *crash filter* rather than a ranking: hold the market (SPY) and step aside only when the cross-section's average short-versus-long reading turns sharply negative, which tests whether the trend information is worth more as timing than as stock picking, and does not bet against SPY's big-company drift.
methods.verdict: Rejected: beat SPY on the deposits (+10.4% vs +7.2% a year at best) but missed the luck bar (0.899 vs 0.90), lost both 2009-2014 periods, and beat a meaningless-order placebo by less than the 2 points promised

methods.name: Sell a momentum holding that falls on heavy trading: the residual-momentum book with a weekly loud-fall exit
methods.sourceRef: M0161 (quiet vs loud fallers) for the signal; M0007-N20-RAW / M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT for the host book; Conrad, Hameed & Niden 1994, J. Finance 49(4); Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014, Management Science 60(3); Lee & Swaminathan 2000, J. Finance 55(5) 'Price momentum and trading volume'
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-2014, so the volume-conditioned continuation of news-driven falls was public for most of the dev window. M0161 found big index members falling on above-normal share volume keep falling (its loud-fall book's worst fall 37% vs 24% for the quiet one). The residual-momentum book (M0007-N20-RAW at real fees and fractional shares, M0032: 13.7% a year on the owner's deposits vs SPY's 7.2%, worst fall 20.6%) skips the last month in its ranking, so a holding collapsing on news is invisible to it until the next re-pick. RULE: hold the same top-20 raw residual-momentum picks, ranked at the month's start with the SPY-200 switch read monthly, and at every weekly check drop to cash any holding whose ten-session standardised market-model residual is in the bottom tenth of the screened pool AND whose ten-session mean share volume is above its prior-year mean; no refill until the next monthly re-pick. Clock: weekly rank cadence, fractional, Gotrade's real fees (weekly-hold-frac-gotrade), because the split monthly/weekly preset only rescales total weight. Arms: LOUD (main), ANY (the bottom-tenth exit with no volume condition: the control for the volume split), QUIET (the other half: falls on below-normal volume, which M0161 says bounce, so it should do worst), NONE (the parent's picks on this weekly clock with no exit: the clean control). Predicted: the exit fires on roughly one holding a month; LOUD keeps NONE's return within a point a year and trims its worst fall by 2-4 points to under 20%; LOUD beats QUIET by at least a point a year (otherwise volume says nothing). Success: LOUD beats NONE on worst fall without losing more than a point a year, beats SPY on the deposits, and has a positive edge in 2009-2015. Assumptions: d's member list used for the anchor pick; decile and volume cut fixed at 10% and 1.0 from M0161, not tuned.
methods.expectedFailure: Short-horizon losers bounce on average, so selling a two-week loser is a reversal bet with the sign wrong; the volume condition is meant to keep only the news-driven falls, but if it does not separate them every exit arm trails NONE by 1-3 points a year, and QUIET and LOUD look alike. Fees: each exit is an extra sale of a $30-200 slot plus the cash drag until the re-pick. The brake will sell bottoms in V-shaped recoveries (spring 2009, autumn 1998) where the whole tape falls on heavy volume, though the residual and pool-relative cut should spare most market-wide falls. The momentum book already lagged SPY in 2009-2015 on dev, and an exit cannot add return there. Promotion is not available: this line runs through M0007, test-failed, and the book moves with the test-failed momentum books (hard gate kin), so any dev-eligible arm is a by-product and not a candidate.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

**What this tried.** The lab's best stock-picking book holds the twenty index members that have
risen most over the past year *after* taking out what the whole market did, re-picked once a month,
and steps aside when the market is below its 200-day average. It never looks at the last month,
so a holding that starts to collapse on bad news stays in the book until the next re-pick. The
quiet/loud study before this one found that big companies falling on **heavier-than-usual trading**
tend to keep falling. So this method checked the twenty holdings every week and sold any that was
among the worst tenth of the market over the last two weeks *and* trading above its normal volume.
The money then sat in cash until the next monthly re-pick.

Four versions, all at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares, on your 5 million rupiah a month:

| version | what it sells mid-month | your money a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NONE (control) | nothing | **13.2%** | 7.2% | 21.9% | 1.92 |
| QUIET | worst-tenth fallers on *light* trading | 12.5% | 7.2% | 19.8% | 1.88 |
| LOUD (main idea) | worst-tenth fallers on *heavy* trading | 10.9% | 7.2% | 20.4% | 1.74 |
| ANY | every worst-tenth faller | 10.3% | 7.2% | 19.9% | 1.72 |

The control is the parent book run on this weekly clock with no exit. It lands close to the
monthly real-fee version already recorded (13.7% a year, worst fall 20.6%), so the clock itself
changed little.

**Result.** Every version beats putting the same deposits into SPY, but **every exit made the
book worse**. The main idea, selling the loud fallers, cost 2.3 points a year (13.2% down to 10.9%)
to make the worst fall only 1.5 points shallower (21.9% to 20.4%). I predicted it would cost under
a point and save 2-4 points of fall. It missed both.

**The volume split pointed the wrong way.** I expected selling the *quiet* fallers to do worst,
because quiet falls are the ones that tend to bounce. It was the reverse: selling quiet fallers
cost only 0.7 points a year, and selling loud ones cost 2.3. Among stocks that have been rising
all year, a sharp drop on heavy trading was *more* likely to recover than a quiet one. It looks
like a crowded winner being shaken out for a few days, not bad news sinking in. The finding from
the study before this (loud fallers keep falling) was about the whole pool of fallers. It does not
carry over to last year's winners.

**Luck test (DSR).** This asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries.
The lab now judges at N = 137 independent methods against a bar of 0.90. LOUD scores 0.888 (just
under), ANY 0.863 (under), QUIET 0.911 and NONE 0.918 (both over). The two that clear it are the
versions that do least, which says the clearing comes from the parent book, not from this idea.

**Worst year and the falls.** Worst calendar year: 2011 for every exit version (LOUD −7.4%,
ANY −9.1%, QUIET −6.4%) and 2008 for the control (−4.7%). The exits made 2011 *worse*. That
summer the whole market fell hard on heavy trading, so the exits sold good holdings near the
bottom and sat in cash through the bounce, which is the V-shaped-recovery failure written down
before the run. Monthly deposits soften how these falls look, so the real falls without top-ups
were deeper than the funded numbers suggest.

**2009-2015, the years most like today.** Lead over SPY a year: NONE +0.8%, QUIET +0.3%,
LOUD −1.2%, ANY −1.2%. The main idea **lost to SPY** in those years.

**Check against the missing dead companies** (the survivorship-check store adds most of the index
members the normal data cannot price, including ones that went bust). This is the one place the
loud exit earned something. On that data the control drops to 11.9% a year with a worst fall of
24.7%. LOUD *rises* to 11.1% with a worst fall of 23.5%, and its 2009-2015 lead improves from
−1.2% to −0.2%. So the exit does catch some companies on their way to collapse, and the normal
data hides that, because it is missing most of the companies that died. Even so, on the fuller
data it still trails the control by 0.8 points a year and both versions break the 20% fall limit.

**Walk-forward folds.** 2 of 4 won: lost 2003-05 and 2009-11, won 2006-08 and 2012-14. The hard
gate needs a majority, so this would be refused. It would also be refused on kin: the residual
momentum line has relatives that failed the test window (M0021, M0022, M0029). As written before
the run, the two versions marked eligible (QUIET, NONE) are a by-product of the parent book, not
candidates. No buy signal.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis failed: LOUD did not keep the return within a
point, did not cut the fall by 2-4 points, and did not beat QUIET. The expected failure happened
mostly as written: selling short-term losers is a bounce bet with the sign wrong, the fees and the
cash drag cost real money, and V-shaped recoveries (2011 here) were where it hurt most. One part
did not happen the way I guessed: the volume condition did separate the two halves, but in the
opposite direction.

**My opinion:** Mid-month exits on this book are a dead end on the evidence we have. Three of three
exit rules cost more return than they saved in fall, and the best of them (QUIET) only looked
good because it sold the least. The one real signal is the fuller-data result, where the loud
exit catches dying companies. That is worth one more try, and only one: the same loud exit but
**refilled** at once with the next-best ranked stock, so the book stays fully invested. That
separates "the signal is wrong" from "sitting in cash for three weeks is expensive". If the refill
version still trails the control, single-stock exits on the momentum book should be closed, and
the honest answer to single-stock blowups stays what the width study found: hold more names.


### 2026-10-17

### Sera 20261017-1858 — promotion attempt

`lab promote M0204` exited 2 on both conditions: 2 of 4 folds (pick changed), and kin M0021, M0022, M0029 read test-failed (the residual-momentum parent book). The only eligible arms are the quiet-fall exit and the no-exit control, both carried by the parent book; the loud-fall exit itself cost 2.3 points a year to save 1.5 points of fall. No buy signal, no look spent.
methods.verdict: Selling holdings that fell hard on heavy trading cost 2.3 points a year to save 1.5 points of fall, and lost to SPY in 2009-2015; selling the quiet fallers hurt less, the opposite of the idea

methods.name: The trend readings as a market crash filter: hold SPY, step aside when the average stock sits far below its long averages
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0203 (the trend factor's moving-average readings, used to rank stocks); Zweig (1986), Winning on Wall Street, and percent-above-200-day breadth lore; Han, Zhou & Zhu (2016), A trend factor, JFE 122(2)
methods.hypothesis: Breadth timing is old (Zweig 1986; 'percent of stocks above their 200-day average' is a chart-room staple), so no fade argument is new here and the dev window sees it long after the crowd knew it. M0203 showed the moving-average readings, used to RANK stocks, rebuild momentum and lose to SPY after 2009 because an equal-weight pick of index members leans small. Used as TIMING instead they need not fight SPY's big-company drift: hold SPY at full weight, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, and go to cash only while the MEDIAN point-in-time index member trades under its own long moving average (close / SMA, median over at least 100 members with full history; a thinner cross-section keeps SPY). Variants, all thresholds fixed now: MED200 (median close/SMA200 under 1.00 -> cash); MED400 (the same on the 400-day average); MED200-95 (cash only below 0.95, deeper trigger to skip corrections); MED200-HYST (leave below 0.97 while held, return at 1.00 while in cash); BOTH200 (cash only when SPY is under its own 200-day average AND the median member is under its own); SPY200 (control: the lab's SPY 200-day switch alone, re-run on this window from 1996 so the paired difference is the breadth reading). The comparison point from the lab: M0084-MONTHLY (SPY's 200-day switch, from 1994) earned +9.1% a year on deposits vs +7.7% for SPY with an 18.9% worst fall, but lost 6 points a year to SPY in 2009-2015 because it sat out the 2009 recovery. SUCCESS: a breadth variant beats the SPY200 control on funded return AND on 2009-2015, beats SPY TR on the deposits, keeps the worst fall well under SPY's, and wins a majority of walk-forward folds. The trade count will be far under 100, so eligibility is not expected; the paired differences are the result.
methods.expectedFailure: Whipsaw: the median stock dips under its 200-day average in ordinary corrections (1998, 2010, 2011, 2015) as well as in bears, and each false exit sells low and buys back higher, which the lab's other market switches (M0084, M0113, M0097) all found costs more than the 2008 dodge saves once the window reaches 2009-2015. The breadth reading may also simply be SPY's switch in disguise -- the median member and SPY move together in every real bear -- so MED200 and SPY200 may differ by only a few flips, and BOTH200 by fewer. The 400-day reading is slow enough to exit 2008 late and return 2009 late, the worst of both. Survivorship leans the breadth reading healthy at every bottom (the dead companies are missing), so exits come late and returns early compared with true data. Trades will number a few dozen, so profit factor and DSR are close to meaningless and no variant should clear the luck bar or the 100-trade floor. Cash earns nothing in the simulator, so every switched variant's cost is an upper bound.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## The question

The lab's last idea, the trend factor (M0203), measured how far each stock's price sat above or
below its own long-run average price, and used that to **pick** stocks. Picking lost to SPY after
2009, mostly because a hand-picked list of index members leans toward smaller companies, and SPY
is driven by the giants.

This test used the same measurement for **timing** instead. The book holds only SPY (the S&P 500
tracker), at full weight. Once a month it looks at every company in the index and asks: is the
typical one (the median) trading below its own 200-day average price? If yes, the market is
"broadly sick", so sell SPY and sit in cash. When the typical company recovers, buy SPY back.

The hope: this broad reading might spot a real bear market more reliably than the usual rule,
which looks only at SPY's own price against its 200-day average.

Six versions, all fixed before any result. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, 5 million
rupiah added on the 25th of each month, 1996 to October 2015:

| version | goes to cash when… | money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| typical stock vs 200-day | median stock below its 200-day average | +7.0% | +7.2% | 37.5% | −6.4 pts |
| typical stock vs 400-day | the same, slower average | +6.5% | +7.2% | 42.4% | −6.5 pts |
| deeper trigger | median stock 5% or more below | +5.8% | +7.2% | 54.4% | −4.9 pts |
| slow out, quick back | out at 3% below, back at the line | +6.1% | +7.2% | 55.0% | −7.5 pts |
| both must agree | SPY **and** the median stock both below | +6.9% | +7.2% | 36.2% | −7.5 pts |
| **control: SPY's own rule** | SPY below its 200-day average | **+8.6%** | +7.2% | **18.9%** | −5.9 pts |

## Result: rejected, and the control beat every breadth version

None of the five breadth versions beat simply putting the same deposits into SPY. Every one of
them did worse than the plain old rule it was meant to improve on, on return (by 1.6 to 2.8
points a year) **and** on the worst fall (36-55% against 18.9%).

The worst fall here is measured on the book itself. Monthly top-ups refill a falling account and
make a fall look gentler than it was, so the table uses the unfunded figure.

The method's best version won 1 of the 4 later test stretches the lab scores (2003-2005,
2006-2008, 2009-2011, 2012-2014). It won only the 2008 crash stretch. The luck check (DSR: how
likely a result is real rather than luck after the lab's 138 tries, against a bar of 0.90) read
0.58 for the best breadth version. Every version also had 8 to 12 trades, far below the 100 the
gate needs, as I said it would before the run.

Rerun on the second price set that adds back most of the companies that later went bust, the
picture held. The 200-day breadth version's worst fall got deeper, from 37.5% to 46.8%, because
those dead companies drag the typical stock down earlier and make the signal noisier. Its
2009-2015 lag barely moved.

## Why: the breadth reading watched a different market from the one the book held

I printed the reading month by month (median stock against its 200-day average, next to SPY
against its own). From 2007 to 2015 the two agree almost every month: they both flagged
2008, mid-2010, late 2011 and August 2015. So in the years most like today, breadth was SPY's own
switch in disguise, which is the failure I expected.

The whole loss comes from **1999 to 2001**, where the two readings point in opposite directions:

- **Late 1999 to mid-2000:** the typical stock was already sliding (the median stock sat 10-17%
  under its average in early 2000), while a handful of giant tech names pushed SPY to its peak.
  The breadth book sold SPY and sat in cash through SPY's last bubble months.
- **Late 2000 to mid-2001:** the giants crashed and SPY fell hard, but the typical stock was
  *fine*. Smaller, cheaper companies were rising. The breadth reading said "healthy" for
  eleven months straight (median 2-12% above its line) while SPY was 5-15% under its own. The
  breadth book held SPY all the way down. That is where its 37-55% worst falls come from.

So the idea's own premise turned against it. The trend factor lost because "the typical stock"
is not what SPY is. Timing SPY with the typical stock fails for exactly the same reason: in a
market led by a few giants, the typical company is the wrong thermometer. The book held SPY
and should have watched SPY.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis (breadth beats SPY's own switch, and beats SPY in 2009-2015): failed.** It lost
  to the control everywhere, and lagged SPY by 5-7.5 points a year in 2009-2015, like every
  other market switch the lab has tried.
- **Expected failure:** partly right. "Breadth is SPY's switch in disguise" was right for
  2007-2015. "Whipsaw in corrections" was right too: 2010, 2011 and 2015 flipped both readings.
  But I did not foresee the real damage: in 2000-2001 the two readings split, and that one
  split decided the result. The deeper trigger and the slow-out version did worst, because they
  stayed in even longer.

## Compared with its relatives

- The **SPY-only switch measured on its own** (M0084, monthly, from 1994) earned +9.1% a year
  with an 18.9% worst fall. This method's control reproduced the same 18.9% fall and +8.6% on its
  slightly shorter window (from 1996, because this book reads index membership), so the setup is
  sound.
- **The trend factor** (M0203) lost to SPY by picking stocks. Using the same measure for timing
  lost too, for the same reason.
- **The "typical company vs the giants" switch** (M0097) also lost. Together these three say the
  same thing three ways: in this lab's data, any bet on the typical company over the
  giants, whether as picks, as a rotation or as a thermometer, has lost to SPY.

## My opinion:

Stop using the typical stock to time SPY. This direction is closed. The only version that held
up was the control, the lab's existing SPY 200-day switch, and that rule's 2009-2015 lag of about
6 points a year is already well measured. A rule that holds SPY should read SPY, or something that
moves SPY. If a thermometer is ever tried again, it should be weighted by company size, so it
measures what SPY measures (for example, the share of the index's *value* sitting above its
200-day average). That is a cheap test of whether 2000-2001 was the only problem. I don't expect
it to beat SPY's own switch by more than whipsaw costs. The more useful next step is the open
question from the lab's switch work: whether **anything** can cut the 2009 re-entry lag that
every switch pays. The breadth reading did not: it came back in June 2009, the same month as
SPY's own rule.
methods.verdict: Timing SPY by whether the typical stock is above its long-run average lost to SPY's own 200-day rule on every count: it held SPY through the giant-led 2000-2001 fall because the typical stock looked healthy
