M0187, M0193, M0197 and M0202 each showed the frame (20 equal slots, SPY filler, a market guard) earning most of a dev lead, and M0202's half-guard placebo passed the dev screen at DSR 0.937. Success: the report reproduces M0202's recorded placebo trials exactly and flags any picker whose lead over the best seed is under 2 points a year.

methods.name: The meaningless-order book drawn only from the 100 busiest members: does random picking among the giants land on SPY?
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0198 (the size-weighted placebo); reserved by Sera batch 20261017-1858
methods.hypothesis: Sizing the scrambled picks by trading value cost under a point a year (M0198), so the frame's lead is not the equal slots. The next suspect is the pool: picking from any screened member rather than from the big names that dominate SPY. Keep M0187's scramble, band, quarterly re-picks and SPY slots, but restrict the pool on each date to the 100 screened members with the highest 60-session trading value; 20 names, equal slots, seeds 1-3 with no switch (trend explicitly None), seed 1 behind the SPY 200-day switch, and seed 1 on a 50-name pool as a dose check; fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. Expected: the unswitched seeds land within about a point a year of SPY's funded +7.2% (against M0187's +8.8-11.9%) with beta near 1.0, and the 50-name pool closer still; then the frame's lead was 'pick from the whole index' plus the missing dead companies. If they keep a two-point lead, the screen and quarterly holding are worth naming. The survivorship-check store is read beside the dev one. Not a published anomaly; evidence only, never to be promoted.
methods.expectedFailure: Three ways this reads badly. (1) Twenty random names out of 100 giants is still a 20-name book: in 1999-2000 the busiest names were the bubble stocks (Cisco, Lucent, Worldcom), so a seed that drew them may crash harder than SPY and the seed spread may be too wide to say 'lands on SPY' or not. (2) Equal slots among giants still lean toward the smaller giants compared with SPY's weights, so a residual point of lead could be that lean, not the screen. (3) Membership in the pool churns with trading value, so held names drop out and the book trades more than M0187, paying Gotrade's fees for it. Expect unswitched worst falls near 50% in 2008 and the switched seed to trail SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

# Random picks among the giants: they land on SPY

## What this was

Not a strategy. A control experiment, the third in a row on the same question.

The lab's "meaningless-order" book holds 20 index members picked in a scrambled order that knows
nothing about prices. It re-picks every quarter, keeps a held name while it stays in the front 40%
of the scramble, parks empty slots in SPY, and holds each name in an equal 5% slot. Over 1996-2015
it beat SPY by about as much as four real rankings did. So something in that frame earns the lead,
not the rankings.

The last experiment kept the same scrambled picks and sized them by company size instead of equal
slots. It cost under a point a year, so the equal slots are not the lead.

This one changes only **who can be picked**. On each date the screened members are cut to the 100
busiest ones: the 100 with the most money traded per day over the last 60 sessions (price times
shares traded). That is the lab's stand-in for "the biggest companies", the ones SPY's money sits
in. Then the same scramble, the same keep rule, the same quarterly re-picks and the same equal
slots run on that cut. Every variant pays Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares, on the owner's
5M IDR monthly top-up. A fifth variant cuts the pool to the 50 busiest as a dose check: if the
lead lives outside the giants, a tighter pool should do worse still.

## Result on the dev window (1996-2015), on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends, on the same deposits, earned **+7.2% a year**.

| scramble | whole screened pool (earlier book) | 100 busiest (this book) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | +11.9% | +6.5% | -5.4 |
| 2 | +8.8% | +7.7% | -1.1 |
| 3 | +11.8% | +9.3% | -2.5 |
| 1, with the SPY switch | +10.4% | +8.2% | -2.2 |
| 1, 50 busiest only | | +5.5% | |

Averaged over the three unswitched scrambles: **+10.8% a year from the whole pool, +7.8% from the
100 busiest, against SPY's +7.2%.** Narrowing the pool to the giants took about three points a
year off a book that changed nothing else, and left it within about half a point of SPY. The
50-name pool did worse again (+5.5%), as the dose check predicted.

Other numbers, on the book without its deposits:

| book | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | luck test (DSR) | beta to SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 busiest, scramble 1 | 57.9% | 1.46 | 976 | 0.44 | 1.12 |
| 100 busiest, scramble 2 | 52.4% | 1.73 | 1013 | 0.37 | 1.04 |
| 100 busiest, scramble 3 | 52.9% | 1.72 | 978 | 0.60 | 1.00 |
| 100 busiest, scramble 1, switch | 25.4% | 1.96 | 846 | 0.80 | 0.49 |
| 50 busiest, scramble 1 | 64.8% | 1.40 | 983 | 0.27 | 1.10 |

"Beta to SPY" is how much the book's monthly return moves for each 1% SPY moves. 1.0 means it
moves like the market.

Every variant failed. Scramble 1 and the 50-name pool did not beat SPY at all. The unswitched books
all fell more than 50% at their worst (over the lab's 50% screen), in 2008, with a worst calendar
year near -32% to -36%. The switched book fell at most 25.4% and passed every screen but the luck
test: its DSR was 0.80 against the owner's 0.90 bar. DSR is how likely a result is real rather
than luck, given the 135 independent methods the lab has now tried (the N the luck gate judges at).
It also won only 1 of 4 walk-forward periods, the 2006-08 crash period when the switch sat in cash.

## By era

The books' own yearly growth without deposits, month by month:

| book | 1996-2008 | SPY | 2009-2015 | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whole pool, scrambles 1-3 (average) | +8.3% | +4.4% | +18.3% | +14.8% |
| 100 busiest, scrambles 1-3 (average) | +5.6% | +4.4% | +14.9% | +14.8% |
| 100 busiest, scramble 1, switch | +9.2% | +4.4% | +9.3% | +14.8% |
| 50 busiest, scramble 1 | +3.2% | +4.4% | +12.3% | +14.8% |

In 2009-2015, the years most like today, the 100-busiest books tied SPY (+14.9% against +14.8%);
the whole-pool books had beaten it by three and a half points. The switched book trailed SPY by
five and a half points there, the same cost of sitting in cash during a rising market the lab has
measured on every switched book in this frame.

## With the dead companies put back

The dev store is missing most of the index's past members that died. The survivorship-check store
puts most of them back. On it, the funded yearly return was:

| book | dev store | with dead companies | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 busiest, scramble 1 | +6.5% | +5.3% | -1.2 |
| 100 busiest, scramble 2 | +7.7% | +7.3% | -0.3 |
| 100 busiest, scramble 3 | +9.3% | +6.8% | -2.5 |
| 100 busiest, switch | +8.2% | +8.7% | +0.5 |
| 50 busiest | +5.5% | +4.6% | -0.9 |

Every dev re-run reproduced its recorded trial, so the side-by-side is sound. With the dead
companies back, the three unswitched scrambles average **+6.5% a year against SPY's +7.2%**:
random picks among the giants lose to the giants' own index once fees and the dead are counted.
The switched book is the one exception; it gained half a point, because it sat in cash through
much of the 2000-2002 and 2008 collapses where the dead companies did their damage.

## Why

Three experiments now pin the frame's lead down.

- **Equal slots versus company-size slots:** under a point a year (the last experiment).
- **The pool:** about three points a year (this one). Picking at random from the whole screened
  index means picking mostly mid-sized companies, because there are far more of them. Over
  1996-2008 those beat the giants: the biggest names of 1999-2000 were the bubble stocks, and they
  spent 2000-2002 deflating while mid-sized companies kept going. SPY puts most of its money in
  exactly those giants. A book drawn from the whole index was therefore a bet on mid-sized
  companies against big ones, not a stock pick. Draw from the giants only and the bet is gone, and
  so is the lead.
- **The missing dead companies:** about one to one and a half points a year on these books, more
  in the whole-pool books (the last experiment measured about 1.6).

So the frame has no edge of its own. What looked like the frame's lead was the mid-sized lean plus
the survivors-only data. Once the pool is the same companies SPY holds, a random 20 of them
moves like SPY (beta 1.0-1.1), earns about what SPY earns, and pays Gotrade's fees on about 1,000
trades for the privilege.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Yes. It predicted the unswitched seeds would land within about a point of SPY's +7.2% with beta
near 1.0: they landed at +6.5% to +9.3% (average +7.8%) with beta 1.00 to 1.12. It predicted the
50-name pool would sit closer to SPY; it sat below it instead (+5.5%). That is the same direction
pushed further, not a miss in kind: the 50 busiest held more of the 1999-2000 bubble leaders.

Of the expected failures: (1) the seed spread was 2.8 points, about the same as the whole-pool
books' 3.1, so the seeds still say something together, though no single seed is a verdict;
(2) any lean toward smaller giants did not show up as a lead; (3) the pool did churn a little more
(turnover 5.05-5.25 against 4.97-5.04), costing a little in fees. The predicted 2008 falls near 50%
and the switched book's lag in 2009-2015 both happened.

## Assumptions

The pool is the 100 busiest of the members that already pass the frame's screen ($5 price,
$20M a day traded), ranked by 60-session trading value, ties by symbol. Trading value is partly
how busy a stock is, not only how big. A held name that leaves the busiest 100 is replaced at the
next quarterly re-pick, not sooner.

**My opinion:** This line of control experiments has done its job and should stop here. The frame
the lab kept finding "skill" in was a bet on mid-sized companies, made on data that hides the ones
that died. That bet is exactly what lost to SPY from 2018 on. The useful thing to carry forward
is a better yardstick. From now on, any ranking that picks from the whole index should be judged
against this frame's scrambled book, not SPY alone. A ranking that picks among the giants should
be judged against this method's busiest-100 scramble, which is SPY with extra fees. The next real
trial should run a ranking inside the busiest-100 pool, where the yardstick is honest, and ask it to
beat both SPY and this scramble in 2009-2015. I would not spend another id on a placebo.
methods.verdict: Random picks among the 100 biggest names landed on SPY: the frame's old lead was a bet on mid-sized companies plus missing dead ones, not skill. Evidence only.

methods.name: Paper gains and paper losses: buy the stocks whose recent holders sit on the biggest unrealised gains
methods.sourceRef: Grinblatt and Han (2005), Prospect theory, mental accounting, and momentum, Journal of Financial Economics 78(2)
methods.hypothesis: Holders who sell winners too early and keep losers too long (the disposition effect) hold prices below value after gains and above value after losses, so stocks with a large capital-gains overhang drift up. Each month-end, estimate each screened member's reference price as the turnover-weighted average of its past weekly closes (up to 260 weeks, at least 156; week n weighs its turnover times the share of it not traded in any later week), compute overhang = 1 - reference/price, and hold the 20 highest in equal 5% slots, monthly, keeping a holding while it ranks inside the top 40, unfilled slots in SPY, behind the SPY 200-day switch (F4's screen and switch, M0203's band). Turnover is proxied, as the store has no share counts: weekly volume over the name's own average weekly volume times 2% (about 100% a year), so the timing of trading is the paper's but every name gets the same average turnover. Grinblatt and Han published in 2005 (working paper 2001); about half the dev window predates it. Arms: CGO-N40 (40 names, band 80) and CGO-LOW-N20 (the 20 largest paper losses, the paper's losing side, which should trail). Control: HASH-N20, the same pool, band, slots, fill and switch in a fixed hash order (M0187's placebo). The plain 12-1 momentum contrast named when the idea was reserved is dropped, as in M0203: a momentum variant would tie the method to the test-failed momentum books through the behaviour test (hardgate D14); momentum is compared against the recorded real-fee momentum books instead. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly top-up. Success: beats SPY TR on dev with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, beats the placebo by at least 2 points a year, and the high side beats the low side.
methods.expectedFailure: A large overhang mostly means the price rose a lot over the last one to three years, so the book is a slow momentum book under another name: it inherits momentum's 2009 crash (which the 200-day switch meets late) and, by the behaviour test, likely moves with the test-failed momentum books, which would make it unpromotable however it scores. The turnover proxy gives every stock the same average turnover, so it loses the part of the paper's signal that comes from heavily traded names refreshing their cost basis faster. The paper's spread is long-short across all US stocks, and much of the losing side's drift is in small, hard-to-short names the screen excludes; the long side alone in big index members may be close to the market. A published anomaly fades (insight on M0050), and equal slots lean small against SPY's big-company drift (insight 91), so 2009-2015 is likely to lag SPY even if the twenty-year average wins. The low-overhang contrast may not trail at all: deep paper losers in the index are also long-term losers, which reverse.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The **capital-gains overhang** (Grinblatt and Han, published 2005, working paper 2001). The idea: people who own a stock tend to sell too early when it's up and hold on too long when it's down (the "disposition effect"). That selling holds back stocks whose owners are sitting on gains, and the holding-on props up stocks whose owners are sitting on losses. As those gaps close, stocks where most owners are in profit should keep drifting up.

Each month, for every screened index member, I estimated the average price its current holders paid. That estimate leans on weeks with heavy trading, and it fades older weeks as later trading replaces those holders. I then measured how far today's price sits above that average. The 20 stocks furthest above it were held in equal amounts. A holding stayed while it ranked in the top 40, any unused slot sat in SPY, and the whole book went to cash while SPY was below its 200-day average. The book traded fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on a 5 million rupiah monthly top-up.

Four versions: the main book (20 names), a 40-name book, the **opposite** (the 20 stocks whose holders sit on the biggest losses), and a **placebo** (the same pool and frame, filled in a fixed meaningless order).

Assumptions written down before the run:
- The store has no share counts, so the paper's turnover (shares traded over shares outstanding) was replaced by each stock's weekly volume over its own average weekly volume, times 2% a week. The timing of trading is the paper's, but every stock gets the same average turnover.
- The reserved idea named a plain momentum book as a contrast. I left it out, as I did for the trend factor, because one momentum version would tie the method to the momentum books that already failed their test look.

## Result vs SPY (1996 to 2015, with the monthly deposits)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 names, biggest gains | **+13.9%** | +7.2% | 24.9% | 3.13 | **0.920** |
| 40 names, biggest gains | +12.0% | +7.2% | **20.8%** | 3.08 | 0.919 |
| 20 names, biggest losses (opposite) | +8.0% | +7.2% | 34.7% | 1.54 | 0.64 |
| placebo (meaningless order) | +8.0% | +7.2% | 23.9% | 1.47 | 0.72 |

- Both main books passed every dev condition, so the method is **dev-eligible**. The worst fall stayed under the 25% limit (24.9% and 20.8%). PF is gains over losses, and 3.1 means three dollars won for every dollar lost. The luck check (DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries. At N = 136 it read 0.92, above the bar of 0.90. That N is one look per distinct method, and `lab status` now reads 138.
- **It beat the placebo by about 6 points a year.** I had promised at least 2, so that held. It is the widest margin over a meaningless book the recent batches have recorded. The trend factor managed +2.5, and several recent ideas did not beat the placebo at all.
- **The high side beat the low side by about 6 points a year.** The paper's direction held.
- It traded remarkably little: 624 trades in twenty years, against 2,749 for the placebo in the same frame. The overhang moves slowly, so holdings stay put.
- The worst year was 2006, at only −1.3%. The worst fall came in the 2007-2009 bear market, when the 200-day switch moved to cash late.
- Walk-forward: it beat SPY in 3 of 4 later periods. It lost 2009-2011 (+54% vs +61%) and won 2003-05, 2006-08 (+9% vs −25%) and 2012-14.

## Where it fails

1. **2009-2015, the first filter.** The 20-name book trailed SPY by 0.9 points a year there, and the 40-name book by 2.8. The lab treats an idea that lags SPY in those years as not worth a variation, however good its average. Most of the edge was earned before 2009, above all in 2006-2008, when holding winners behind a cash switch dodged the crash.
2. **It is a momentum book under another name.** The hard gate refuses to promote it. What is left of its monthly return after the market's share is taken out moves with the tested momentum book M0002 (M0002-REL-85) at a correlation of 0.90, above the 0.85 line. That book lost its test-window look: +6.3% a year against SPY's +15.7% on the same deposits from 2015. The money lines up too. The real-fee residual-momentum book (M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT) earned +13.7% a year on the same deposits, against +13.9% here. The paper's claim that overhang *replaces* momentum looks true in our data in the plainest sense: this is the same bet.
3. **Missing dead companies.** On the survivorship-check store (adding most of the index members the dev store cannot price, dead companies included), the 20-name book fell from +13.9% to +13.1% a year. Its worst fall deepened from 24.9% to 27.2%, past the 25% limit. The luck check fell to 0.878, under the bar. The 2009-2015 lag widened to −2.6 points a year. The 40-name book held up better (+11.6%, worst fall 20.7%, DSR 0.892), but it also slipped under the luck bar and lagged SPY by 4.0 points a year in 2009-2015. The opposite book collapsed on the check store (+4.6%, −8.5 points in 2009-2015): some of its stocks that "bounced back" in the dev store are ones that actually died.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Partly. The overhang sorted stocks the right way: high beat low, and high beat the placebo clearly. The expected failure also happened almost word for word. I wrote that it would be "a slow momentum book under another name", would move with the test-failed momentum books and so be unpromotable, and would lag SPY in 2009-2015. All three came true. The turnover shortcut evidently did not ruin the signal, but there is no way to tell what the real share-count version would add.

**Buy signal:** not fired. It is dev-eligible with a majority of folds, but kin has failed (M0002) and the 2009-2015 edge is negative.

**My opinion:** This is the cleanest evidence yet that the lab's stock-picking edge comes from one place: owning what has gone up. The overhang adds nothing that momentum didn't already find. More overhang variants would just be more momentum, and the gate is right to refuse them. One thing is worth taking from it: the book barely trades (624 trades in twenty years). If a slow, low-turnover momentum book ever gets a new argued route past the momentum failure, this is the cheapest way to run it. The next idea should test the one part of the paper momentum *cannot* see. Among stocks with the same past return, does a bigger overhang still win? That means ranking on the overhang left over after taking out what twelve-month return explains. If the leftover beats the placebo and does not move with the momentum books, the disposition effect is real here. If not, the family is closed.


### 2026-10-17

### Sera 20261017-1858 — promotion attempt

`lab promote M0208` exited 2 on the kin condition, not the folds (3 of 4 folds): by behaviour (D14), M0208-CGO-N20's market-neutral monthly return moves with the test-failed M0002-REL-85 at 0.90 residual correlation, above the 0.85 line. The overhang score, built from turnover-weighted past prices, behaves like the momentum book that already lost its look. No buy signal either way: the 2009-2015 lead over SPY is −0.9 points (N20) and −2.8 (N40), and the survivorship store lifts N20's worst fall to 27.2% and drops its DSR to 0.878. No look spent.


### 2026-10-20

**The margin over a meaningless book is smaller than published, and the honest figure is a floor
rather than a measurement.**

The meaningless book above traded **2,749 times** in twenty years. The real book traded **624**.
It was more than four times as busy, which on Gotrade's fees is a heavy and invisible handicap —
and the whole point of this method was that it barely trades.

A fairly shaped control has since been drawn. It trades 455 times against the book's 624, and
earned **+9.5% a year** on the same deposits against the book's **+13.9%**. So *"it beat the
placebo by about 6 points a year"* is withdrawn, and the honest reading is **at least 4.3 points a
year**.

**Provisional, and a floor.** Even the new control is not a match: at 455 trades against 624 it
still trades about a quarter less than the book, so it is still under-paying the fee bill. A
control that paid the full bill would earn less, and the true margin would be **larger** than 4.3,
not smaller. The lab has not measured the exact number. The reason the control under-trades is
understood and is a property of this book rather than a mistake: this book keeps a name until it
drops out of the top 40, and a control cannot know how far a long-held name has drifted toward
that edge, so it lets go of names too slowly.

The promise written before the run was a lead of at least 2 points. It is still met, by a wide
margin, wherever the remaining uncertainty falls.

**Nothing else changes.** The method is still dev-eligible and still refused by the hard gate for
the reasons given above: it moves with the momentum book that already failed its test-window look,
it trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and it falls past the drawdown limit once dead companies are added
back. No look was spent and nothing was re-run: these are the same trials, read against a fairer
opponent.


### 2026-10-20

**The margin over a meaningless book is now a measurement rather than a floor — and the floor was
too high.**

The last entry said the lead was *at least* 4.3 points a year, and explained why it could be no
more precise than that: the fairest control the lab could draw still traded only 455 times against
the book's 624, so it was still under-paying the fee bill, and a control that paid the whole bill
would earn less, which would make the true lead wider.

A control that does pay the whole bill has now been drawn. It trades 596 times against the book's
624 and turns the book over at 1.03 times the book's rate — inside the match band on both counts,
which is what "the same shape" has to mean before a margin is worth quoting. It earned **+10.1% a
year** on the same deposits, against the book's **+13.9%**. So the lead is **3.7 points a year**,
and the word "at least" comes off it.

**The reasoning behind the floor was wrong, and it is worth saying which half.** The shape argument
held: the old control really was under-trading, and the new one really does trade like the book.
What did not hold was the assumption that a busier control must therefore earn less. It earned
**more** — 10.1% against the old control's 9.5% — so the extra fees it paid were more than covered
by what the extra buying and selling happened to land on. That is not a surprise this lab is
entitled to be shocked by: a meaningless book's return is close to arbitrary, and the lab has
measured before that the direction an honest control moves a margin in cannot be guessed ahead of
time. The honest conclusion is that *"at least 4.3"* was never a floor at all. It was the number
one particular badly-shaped draw happened to produce, and the fairly shaped draw produces 3.7.

**The promise written before the run was a lead of at least 2 points, and it is still met.**

**What changed in the drawing.** The old control had to guess what the book was holding before each
month's decision, because nothing in the machinery records it, and it guessed with a freshly taken
list of the twenty best names. That list is far too tidy: a name only leaves this book once it has
slipped out of the top forty, and a freshly taken top twenty is nowhere near that edge, while the
book's real holdings have been drifting toward it for months. The new control replays the book's
own rule forward from an empty book two months back, so it is holding a drifted set by the time it
has to count. It also replays the cash switch, which the old guess ignored entirely: in a month
when the book had sold everything and sat in cash, the old guess still imagined it holding twenty
names, and so read a handful of purchases where the truth was a full refill of twenty.

**How much each half was worth.** Measured before the new control was drawn, and on the book's own
twenty years: the old guess credited the book with 304 purchases where the truth was 624. Replaying
the cash switch alone lifts that to 446. Replaying one further month of drift on top lifts it to
592, within about five per cent of the truth — and replaying more months than that buys nothing, so
two is where it stops. The trading that actually results does not rise in the same proportion, and
that was written down before the run: the control is also forced to let go of any name that leaves
the index, which was already doing some of this work at 304 purchases. So 304 to 592 in estimated
purchases came out as 455 to 596 in trades actually made.

**Nothing else changes.** The method is still dev-eligible and still refused by the hard gate, for
the reasons given above: it moves with the momentum book that already failed its one look at the
later years, it trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and it falls past the drawdown limit once dead companies
are added back. No look was spent on the later years and the book's own recorded result is
untouched: this is the same book, read against a fairer opponent.
methods.verdict: Dev-eligible but refused by the hard gate: beat SPY on the deposits (+13.9% vs +7.2% a year) and a meaningless book of the same shape by 3.7 points a year - measured now rather than a floor, because the fairest control the lab can draw finally trades as often as the book does; the earlier figures of 6 points and of at least 4.3 are both withdrawn. It still moves with the momentum book that already failed its test and trailed SPY in 2009-2015.

methods.name: Momentum among the 100 busiest members, judged against the busiest-100 scramble
methods.hypothesis: M0207 showed a scrambled 20-name book drawn from the 100 busiest screened members lands on SPY (+7.8% funded vs +7.2%, beta 1.0-1.1, tied in 2009-2015; +6.5% with the dead companies back). That pool removes the mid-sized lean that flattered every whole-index ranking, so it is an honest arena. Rank only those 100 by 12-1 month momentum (F4's rank), 20 names, equal slots, quarterly re-picks with M0187's 40% keep band, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits; seeds are not needed, but run the M0207 scramble's frame byte for byte so the only change is the order. Pass bar for the lab's reading (not the gate): beat M0207's three unswitched scrambles (best +9.3%) and SPY in 2009-2015 on the survivorship-check store. Momentum is a published anomaly (1993) and has faded among large caps; expected_failure should say a giant-only momentum book may simply track SPY with more fees. The behaviour kin rule (D14) may tie it to the failed momentum books; read lab status before planning a promotion.

methods.name: Paper gains beyond the price rise: rank on the part of the capital-gains overhang that twelve-month return does not explain
methods.hypothesis: Grinblatt and Han (2005) say the capital-gains overhang subsumes momentum; M0208 built the overhang book and found it moves with the test-failed momentum book at 0.90 residual correlation, so in this store the two are the same bet. Test the part momentum cannot see. On each decision date, across the screened members that have an overhang, regress the overhang on 12-1 month return and on its square (the return winsorised at the cross-section's 5th and 95th percentiles, then standardised; at least 50 names or nothing is scored) and rank on the residual, so a stock gets in by having paper gains its own price rise does not account for. Hold the top 20 in equal 5% slots, monthly, in M0208's frame exactly: F4's screen, the SPY 200-day switch, a held name kept while it ranks inside the top 40, unfilled slots in SPY, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Measured before the run: the scored pool is 80 to 395 names from April 1996 on and the overhang's cross-sectional correlation with 12-1 return is about +0.63, so roughly 60% of the overhang's spread survives the regression. Arms: RESID-N40 (40 names, band 80), RESID-LIN-N20 (linear fit only, no square) and RESID-LOW-N20 (the most negative residuals, which should trail). Control: HASH-N20, the same pool, band, slots, fill and switch in a fixed hash order. Success: beats the placebo by at least 2 points a year, residual correlation with the momentum books under 0.85 so the hard gate's behaviour test lets it through, a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, beats SPY TR on dev with worst fall <= 25% and PF >= 1.3, and a majority of walk-forward folds. If it fails, the disposition-effect family is closed in this data.
methods.expectedFailure: The regression removes the part of the overhang that momentum explains, and that part may be the part that pays: the overhang's power in this store could be nothing but a slower, smoother reading of the price rise, in which case the residual book earns little and may not beat the placebo at all. Residuals are also where measurement error concentrates -- the turnover proxy gives every name the same average turnover, so a stock whose reference price is wrong for a data reason, not a behavioural one, lands high in the residual ranking; the book may end up holding the names whose cost basis the proxy mis-estimates. A stock with a big overhang and a flat twelve-month return has usually risen over two to five years and gone quiet lately, which is the long-term winner the long-term-reversal work says reverses, so the book may lean into names that mean-revert. Even if the behaviour test clears 0.85, the method still has to beat SPY in 2009-2015, where every equal-slot book in this lab has lost to SPY's big-company drift (insight 91), and a published anomaly fades (insight on M0050): Grinblatt and Han was a 2001 working paper, so only the window's first half predates the crowd. Finally the residual is a small number -- the overhang's spread is wide but its momentum-free part is narrow -- so the top 20 may be separated from the next 20 by noise, which would show up as high turnover and a result close to the placebo's.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What was tried

The previous method (M0208) bought the stocks whose owners were sitting on the biggest **paper
gains** — how far a share trades above the average price the people holding it actually paid. It
looked good: your money would have earned 13.9% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits put into
the market. Then it was refused, because once you take the market's own movement out of both, its
month-to-month pattern was 90% the same as a momentum book that had already lost its one real
out-of-sample test. In plain words: it looked like a new idea and behaved like an old failed one.

So M0208 ended by naming the one question that would settle it. **Among stocks that have risen by
the same amount over the past year, do the ones with bigger paper gains still do better?** If yes,
the paper-gains idea is real and separable. If no, "paper gains" was never anything but "the price
went up", and the whole family is closed.

This method asks exactly that. Every month, across the several hundred screened companies, I took
the paper-gain figure and statistically removed the part that each company's own twelve-month
price rise explains (and the part its rise-squared explains, so a curved relationship is removed
too). What is left over is the ranking. A stock gets in by having paper gains that its own price
rise does **not** account for.

Everything else is M0208's, unchanged, so only the signal differs: the same companies, the same
rule of standing aside when the market is below its 200-day average, the same twenty equal slots,
the same holding band, unused slots parked in the market, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees
on a 5 million rupiah monthly top-up.

Measured and written down **before** the run: the pool to rank is 80 to 395 companies from April
1996 onward, and paper gains and twelve-month rise are about 63% correlated across companies. So
roughly 40% of the paper-gain spread is the price rise and about 60% survives the removal. There
was genuinely something left to rank on.

Five versions: the main 20-name book, a 40-name book, a version that removes only the straight-line
part of the price rise, the **opposite** book (the 20 stocks whose paper gains are *smallest*
relative to their rise, which should trail if the idea is real), and a **placebo** — the same
companies, the same frame, picked in a fixed meaningless order.

## The result (1996 to 2015, on the monthly deposits)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check | times it traded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **main, 20 names** | **+8.0%** | +7.2% | 22.3% | 1.54 | 0.64 | 1,476 |
| 40 names | +9.2% | +7.2% | 19.8% | 1.85 | 0.78 | 2,119 |
| straight-line removal only | +9.6% | +7.2% | 20.4% | 1.68 | 0.78 | 1,478 |
| **the opposite book** | **+10.0%** | +7.2% | 31.1% | 1.52 | 0.82 | 1,394 |
| **placebo (meaningless order)** | **+8.0%** | +7.2% | 23.9% | 1.47 | 0.72 | 2,749 |

All five are **rejected**. Every one fails the luck check: the bar is 0.90 and the best of them
reads 0.82. The luck check (DSR) asks how likely a result is real rather than the best-looking of
many tries; it is judged at N = 151, which is one look for each distinct method the lab has ever
run, and both the bar and the N are the owner's settings, not mine.

But the rejection is the least interesting thing here. Three numbers are:

1. **The main book tied the placebo, and actually lost to it.** 7.99% a year against the placebo's
   8.01%. A meaningless ordering of the same companies in the same frame did marginally better than
   the signal. There is no gap to argue about and no version to tune.

## Addendum, same day: one limit on "the family is closed"

After this run finished, the session coordinating the batch pointed out something I should have
set out more carefully above, so I am recording it rather than leaving the stronger claim standing
unqualified.

Everything here measures unrealised gains the only way this data allows. The original research
asks how much of a company's stock changes hands each week as a fraction of all the shares that
exist. We do not have share counts in the development data, so the parent method replaced that
with each week's trading volume compared against the company's own average week, and assumed every
company turns over at the same average rate. That assumption keeps the timing of trading but
deliberately throws away the differences *between* companies — and differences between companies
are exactly the kind of place where a signal that momentum cannot see might live.

So the honest scope of this result is: **unrealised gains as we can currently measure them are
momentum and nothing else.** Whether unrealised gains measured properly, with real share counts,
have a momentum-free part worth owning is a question this run did not answer and could not. Share
counts are being added to the data by other work now in progress. When they land, the same
subtraction done here can be run once on the properly measured figure, and that is a genuinely
different measurement rather than a tweak of this one. I have queued it.

Until then, "closed" means closed on the proxy. I would not spend another method id on a *ranking*
built from the proxied figure.

M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (news days on 3x volume with an up gap, a three-day jump >= 4 points over SPY and >= 2 of the stock's own daily swings, the 20 biggest raw jumps held 60 sessions at 5% each, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) earned +12.3% a year on the owner's deposits vs +7.2% for SPY, DSR 0.914 at N=59, beat SPY by ~3.7 points a year in 2009-2015, and failed only the worst fall (23.8% funded, 1998). Earnings seasons cluster by industry, so a ranking by jump size can fill the book from one industry that just reported well: a hidden sector bet. Cap each Fama-French 12 industry at 3, 4 or 5 of the 20 slots (held names count first; slots the cap leaves empty go to SPY, as the frame's empty slots always have). The uncapped control is the parent's recorded trial M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (same frame, fees and deposits), not re-run. A hash-order control draws new names from the same live news-day pool in a fixed meaningless order (M0187's hash), uncapped and capped at 4, to ask whether ranking by jump size adds anything over 'any qualifying news day'. Variants: CAP3, CAP4, CAP5, HASH, HASH-CAP4. Expectation: CAP4 keeps most of the parent's edge (within ~1 point a year), the fall shrinks a little because a one-industry slump hits fewer slots, and 2009-2015 stays ahead of SPY; the hash books trail the score books by 1-2 points a year. If the capped books lose the edge, the edge was a sector bet. Success: a capped variant with worst fall under the bar, beating total-return SPY with DSR >= 0.90 and beating SPY in 2009-2015 and in a majority of walk-forward folds.
methods.expectedFailure: The parent's worst fall was 1998, a market-wide fall caught late by the monthly SPY-200 switch, not a one-industry slump; a sector cap cannot fix timing, so the fall likely stays above 20%. If the jump ranking's best picks cluster in tech in 1998-2000 and 2009-2013, the cap removes exactly the names that earned the edge and the excess over SPY shrinks, dragging the luck score under 0.90. A tight cap (3) leaves slots to SPY in hot seasons, drifting the book toward plain SPY. EDGAR's SIC is the latest, not point-in-time, so a few companies that changed trade sit in the wrong bucket. The hash control may earn as much as the ranked book, meaning the frame (news days at all, plus the SPY park) rather than the ranking carries the edge. And this is a published anomaly, so a strong dev result may have faded in 2016-2026; its kin (the momentum books that failed their looks) may move with it.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The parent is the lab's best "news-day" book (M0072-Z2-RAWRANK). It buys big stocks right after a day that looks like an earnings report: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal volume, a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's that was also big for that stock's usual swing. It holds the 20 biggest such jumps for about three months at 5% each, keeps empty slots in SPY, and goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average (checked monthly).

The worry: earnings seasons come in waves by industry. When one industry reports well, many of its companies jump in the same weeks, and a book that ranks by jump size could quietly fill up with that one industry. That would be a hidden bet on a sector, not on picking news days.

The lab can now read each company's industry (the government's SEC filing code, grouped into 12 broad industries the standard academic way). So this method capped each industry at 3, 4 or 5 of the 20 slots. Slots the cap left empty went to SPY, like any empty slot in this book. Beside them ran two controls: the same pool of news days picked in a fixed, meaningless order (a "placebo" order that knows nothing about prices), once uncapped and once capped at 4. The uncapped real book is the parent's own recorded trial, with the same fees and deposits. All five variants trade fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5M IDR monthly deposits. Everything was written down before any result.

## Was the book really a sector bet?

Not much. I counted the industries of the fresh picks at each month-end with the market switch on (170 months, 1996-2015):

- Uncapped, the biggest industry (business equipment: tech hardware and software) took 26% of the slots. The placebo order, drawing from the same news days, gave it 21%. So ranking by jump size leans toward tech by about 5 points, not a lot.
- The top industry held 5.5 of about 19 names on an average month. It held 8 or more in only 17 of 170 months.
- A cap of 4 cut tech to 19% and a cap of 3 to 16%, with almost no empty slots (18.6 to 18.9 names on average either way).

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, the owner's monthly deposits)

| variant | your money per year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall (funded) | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead over SPY a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parent, no cap (recorded trial) | +12.3% | +7.2% | 23.8% | 1.98 | 0.914 at N=59 | about +3.7% |
| cap 5 per industry | +12.1% | +7.2% | 23.6% | 2.01 | 0.899 | +3.0% |
| cap 4 | +11.8% | +7.2% | 24.9% | 1.94 | 0.888 | +2.0% |
| cap 3 | +11.0% | +7.2% | 25.5% | 1.85 | 0.872 | −0.5% |
| placebo order, no cap | +10.9% | +7.2% | 25.3% | 1.76 | 0.891 | −2.7% |
| placebo order, cap 4 | +10.7% | +7.2% | 24.0% | 1.75 | 0.858 | −1.4% |

**Rejected.** Every variant beats total-return SPY on the same deposits, by 3.5 to 4.9 points a year, and every one makes about twice as much on winners as it loses on losers (the bar is 1.3). Every fall is the same summer-1998 fall the parent had. Every one fails the luck bar. The lab now counts N=140 separate ideas tried, and the bar is a DSR of at least 0.90 (at least a 90% chance the edge is real, not the best of 140 lucky draws). The best, cap 5, reached 0.899, a hair under. Note the parent cleared 0.914 when the lab had tried 59 ideas; at 140 ideas the same numbers would score lower too.

Walk-forward (the lab picks a variant knowing only the past, then scores it on years it never saw): 3 of 4 folds beat SPY. It lost 2009-2011, where it had picked the placebo order.

## Survivorship cross-check

The dev data misses many companies that later died. Re-run on the check store that adds most of them back (report only, nothing recorded):

- cap 5: +12.1% → +11.3% a year, worst fall 23.6% → 26.7%, 2009-2015 lead +3.0% → +0.8%.
- cap 4: +11.8% → +11.1%, 2009-2015 lead +2.0% → +0.7%.
- cap 3: +11.0% → +8.7%, luck score 0.872 → 0.646.
- The placebo books barely moved, and even got a little better (+10.9% → +11.1%).

So with the dead companies added back, the real ranking and the placebo order earn about the same (11.0-11.3% a year). The ranking's extra edge on dev was partly the missing companies.

## Why

- **The cap costs money, step by step.** Uncapped +12.3%, cap 5 +12.1%, cap 4 +11.8%, cap 3 +11.0%. The names a cap removes are the 4th, 5th and 6th tech jumps of the month, and those were good picks. A tech news day with a big jump in a strong tech season is not a hidden mistake; it is part of what the ranking finds.
- **The 2009-2015 edge sits in the same names.** The lead over SPY in the best-covered years falls from about +3.7 points uncapped to +3.0, +2.0 and −0.5 as the cap tightens. Most of what this book earned after 2009 came from tech news days.
- **The ranking matters on dev, less so on the fuller data.** The placebo order on the same news days earned 1.4 points a year less than the real ranking on dev, and lost to SPY in 2009-2015. That says the frame (news days at all, plus the SPY park and the switch) carries most of the edge, and ranking by jump size adds a bit on top. On the check store that bit nearly disappears.
- **The cap does nothing for the worst fall.** The 1998 fall was the whole market, caught late by a switch checked once a month. Spreading across industries cannot help with that, exactly as the expected failure said.

## Hypothesis vs expected failure

The hypothesis said cap 4 would keep most of the edge (within about 1 point a year). It did: −0.5 points. It said the fall would shrink a little; it did not (24.9% vs 23.8%). It said the placebo books would trail by 1-2 points; they did on dev (1.4 points), not on the check store. The expected failure ("the cap removes the names that earned the edge, so the excess and the luck score shrink") happened, mildly. The "if the capped book loses its edge, the edge was a sector bet" test reads: the edge is mostly not a sector bet (cap 5 and cap 4 keep most of it), but the part after 2009 leans on tech.

## My opinion:

Sector caps are not the fix for this book. It was never heavily concentrated (one industry averaged a quarter of the slots), the cap costs money in proportion to how tight it is, and it does nothing for the 1998 fall, which is the book's real problem. The more useful finding is the placebo: drawing news days in a meaningless order earns almost as much, and as much on the fuller data. So the edge, if real, is in "buy a big stock after a strong earnings day and hold three months", not in which of those days you pick. I would stop varying the ranking and attack the timing instead: the fall comes from the monthly SPY-200 switch selling late. Next I would test this same news-day frame with the switch checked weekly, or a faster 100-day average, in fractional shares at real fees, and see if the 1998 fall drops while the 2009-2015 lead holds.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tested

The live coskewness book (the one that buys the stocks that fall hardest when the market swings hardest) came out 12 of its 20 names in oil and gas on 2026-10-17. The owner asked whether that is the risk a sector cap removes. This method asks a sharper question: **was coskewness's twenty-year lead over SPY really a hidden bet on one industry?**

Everything else is the parent book unchanged: the same large-company screen, three years of weekly returns, a re-pick every quarter, a holding kept while it stays in the top 40% of the ranking, empty slots in SPY, the whole book in cash while SPY is under its 200-day average, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, 1996 to 2015.

Industries are the twelve broad Fama-French groups (energy, money, business equipment, utilities, and so on), built from each company's SEC filing code. Two ways to take the industry out:

- **a cap**: walk down the ranking and skip any name whose industry already holds 3 (or 4) of the 20 slots; never bend the cap to fill a slot (an empty slot holds SPY).
- **within-industry**: score each stock against the other members of its own industry, so it is picked for being crash-prone *for an oil company* or *for a bank*, and allow at most 2 per industry.

The yardstick is the lab's placebo: the same pool of stocks in a fixed random order, capped the same way. If capped coskewness cannot beat capped random, the ranking adds nothing.

Assumptions written down before the run: an industry needs 5 scoreable names before its members get a within-industry score; companies with no known industry share one capped bucket; the filing code is the company's latest one, not the one it had at the time.

## How concentrated was the uncapped book?

Measured outside the run, at every quarterly re-pick from 1996 to 2015 (no cash switch, so every quarter counts):

| book | average share of its biggest industry | worst quarter |
|---|---|---|
| coskewness, 20 names, no cap | 34% | 50% (10 of 20) |
| random order, 20 names, no cap | 25% | 40% |
| coskewness, 40 names, no cap | 28% | 45% |
| coskewness, cap 3 of 20 | 15% | 15% |
| within-industry, cap 2 | 10% | 10% |

So yes: coskewness bunches names by industry more than chance does, about a third of the book in one industry on an average quarter and half of it at the worst. Over 1996-2015 the leaders were factories and machinery (18% of slots), technology (15%), banks and insurers (15%) and utilities (10%). Energy was not the usual leader in the dev years; the 12-of-20 oil book is a recent shape. In 2009-2015 the uncapped book leaned on banks (20%), technology (17%) and utilities (16%).

## Results against SPY (total return, same deposits)

| version | earned a year | SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cap 3 of 20 | +9.9% | +7.2% | 33.1% | 2.71 | 0.81 | −3.9% a year |
| cap 4 of 20 | +10.4% | +7.2% | 34.8% | 2.76 | 0.84 | −4.6% |
| within-industry, 2 per industry | +10.0% | +7.2% | 26.0% | 2.76 | 0.89 | −6.0% |
| **40 names, cap 6** | +10.1% | +7.2% | **20.4%** | 2.59 | **0.91** | −5.5% |
| control: random order, cap 3 of 20 | +9.6% | +7.2% | 21.8% | 2.55 | 0.89 | −3.9% |
| control: random order, 40 names, cap 6 | +10.0% | +7.2% | 20.8% | 2.36 | **0.93** | −3.5% |

"Worst fall" is the biggest drop from a peak with the deposits taken out; the screen's limit is 25%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is money made on winners over money lost on losers; the bar is 1.3. The luck test (deflated Sharpe ratio, DSR) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries; it was judged at **N = 139** methods in the lab against the owner's bar of **0.90**.

For comparison, the parent's uncapped books earned +10.8% a year (20 names) and +10.5% (40 names), with 2009-2015 leads of −4.0% and −5.6%.

Two variants passed the twenty-year screen: the 40-name capped coskewness book (luck score 0.91, worst fall 20.4%) and **its own random-order control** (0.93, 20.8%). The lab marks the method dev-eligible, but the hard gate refuses to promote it: the walk-forward test (pick the best version using only the past, then score it on the next three years) won **1 of 4** folds. It lost 2003-2005, 2009-2011 and 2012-2014 to SPY and won only 2006-2008, when the cash switch sat out the crash. The 40-name capped book on its own won 2 of 4, still not a majority. No failed test-window method moves like it (kin clean).

## Why

1. **The cap cost about half a point a year and changed nothing that matters.** Capped coskewness earned +9.9% to +10.4% where the uncapped parent earned +10.5% to +10.8%. The lead over SPY did not vanish, so the twenty-year lead was not *only* an industry bet. But it did not need the ranking either: the capped random book earned +9.6% and +10.0%, within half a point of capped coskewness, with a gentler fall. On this evidence coskewness adds roughly nothing over a random pick from the same pool. The lead belongs to the frame: equal weight across 20-40 big members, slots in SPY, and a cash switch that dodged 2008.
2. **The capped 20-name books fell harder, not softer** (33-35% against 32% uncapped). Forcing the book out of its favourite industries pushed it into the next most crash-prone names in other industries, which still crash together with the market. A cap spreads the names; it does not spread the risk, because coskewness is by construction a bet on the market's big weeks.
3. **2009-2015 is negative everywhere**: −3.5% to −6.0% a year behind SPY, coskewness and random alike. That is the lab's familiar story: an equal-weight book of index members loses to SPY's big-company drift in the years most like today. The within-industry book was the worst there (−6.0%), because it holds two names from every industry, including the ones that lagged.
4. **On the survivorship-check prices** (the same run with most of the companies that later died put back in), the 40-name capped book's worst fall deepens from 20.4% to 23.3%, and its 2009-2015 gap narrows to −3.4%. The random controls get worse there. Nothing flips into a pass.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Half. The uncapped book *was* more concentrated than chance (a third of the book in one industry on average), so the owner's instinct about the energy book is right: the live shape is a real risk. But removing it neither rescued nor killed the lead, and the expected failure happened almost word for word: capped books within half a point of their capped random controls, still behind SPY in 2009-2015, and the coskewness family still short of a fold majority.

My opinion: the coskewness ranking is not worth another variation. Five methods now say the same thing from different angles: the opposite end of the ranking, a random ranking and now a capped ranking all earn about the same, so the ranking is not what beat SPY. The one lasting lesson is about the cap itself: it is cheap (about half a point a year here) and it caps the single-industry risk the owner saw, so it belongs on any book the lab does promote, not as a source of edge. The next useful test is the frame, not the signal: the same 40-name equal-weight book against the equal-weight S&P 500, to see whether everything this family earned is just equal weighting plus the cash switch.

The 2009-2015 edge over SPY is negative on every version, from about −3.5 to −6.0 points a year. The hard gate refuses it on the folds condition; kin is clean. No test look was spent and none was attempted. No buy signal.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

The **calm big raisers** book buys big index companies that just raised their dividend by a quarter or more, keeping only the calmer half (daily price swing over the last three months at or below the middle of the group). Each name gets 5% of the money and is held while the raise is under six months old. The rest of the money sits in SPY. Everything steps into cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It re-picks monthly, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's deposits.

The question: is this book a hidden bet on a few industries? If it is, and those industries had a bad 2009-2015, a cap on how many names one industry can fill should help. Industries are the standard 12 broad groups (Fama-French 12), read from each company's SEC filing code.

Before writing the method I replayed the parent's recorded configuration (528 trades, reproduced exactly) to see what it actually held:

- It holds **9.5 names on average**, not 20. There are rarely 20 calm raisers alive at once, so about half the money is usually in SPY.
- **Banks and finance fill 25% of its slots and retailers 19%.** Utilities are only 4%, so the idea's guess ("utilities and banks") was half wrong: banks and shops are the real lean.
- One industry held more than 3, 4 or 5 names in 78, 45 and 22 of the 169 months the book was invested.

## Versions, fixed before any result

- **CTRL**: no cap, the parent book. It had to reproduce M0168-CTRL.
- **CAP3 / CAP4 / CAP5**: at most 3, 4 or 5 names from any one industry. A raiser the cap skips gives its slot to the next raiser in line. If none is left, the slot goes to SPY, as the parent has always done with empty slots. (The batch's other ideas leave empty slots in cash. This book parks in SPY, and switching to cash would change two things at once, so I kept SPY. That was my assumption.)
- **HASH**: a placebo. Each month it fills exactly as many slots as the raise book would, with the same switch and the same SPY parking. The names come from all screened index members in a fixed, meaningless order (a hash). Names already held go first.
- **HASH-CAP4**: the placebo with the cap of 4, to show what a cap does to any book of this shape.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year | trades | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CTRL | +10.6% | 18.7% | −2.6 pts | 528 | 3.52 | 0.950 |
| CAP3 | +10.2% | 18.7% | −3.1 pts | 459 | 3.78 | 0.941 |
| CAP4 | +10.3% | 19.1% | −3.1 pts | 500 | 3.48 | 0.943 |
| CAP5 | +10.6% | 19.6% | −2.8 pts | 519 | 3.48 | 0.949 |
| HASH (placebo) | +8.7% | 21.9% | −5.9 pts | 179 | 4.39 | 0.813 |
| HASH-CAP4 | +8.6% | 21.0% | −6.2 pts | 179 | 4.45 | 0.818 |

CTRL reproduced the parent exactly (528 trades, 18.7% worst fall), so the comparison is fair.

Industry mix (share of slot-months): CTRL banks 25%, shops 19%. CAP3 brought banks to 21%, CAP4 to 23%, CAP5 to 24%. The placebo's mix is different by nature (tech 20%, manufacturing 19%, banks 16%, shops 7%).

- **Against SPY:** the four raise versions all beat SPY by 3.1 to 3.4 points a year and pass every dev check. The **worst fall** (biggest drop from a peak) stays under the 20% limit. The two placebos beat SPY by only 1.4 to 1.5 points, fall 21-22% at worst, and fail the luck check.
- **Luck check (DSR):** judged at N = 142 independent tries in the lab, against the bar of 0.90. The raise versions clear it (0.941 to 0.950), so their lead over SPY on these years is unlikely to be luck. The placebos do not (0.81).
- **Walk-forward folds** (four later stretches the method never trained on): **2 of 4**, unchanged. It lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011 and won 2006-2008 and 2012-2014. The hard gate needs a majority, so this cannot be promoted. Kin was not checked further, because the folds already refuse it.
- **2009-2015**, the best-covered years and the most like today: the cap made the gap **worse**, from −2.6 to −3.1 points a year at caps of 3 and 4.
- **Survivorship check** (the same runs on a store that adds most of the dead companies the dev store lacks): every raise version loses 0.1-0.2 points of lead and about 0.6-0.9 points more in 2009-2015. CAP4 and CAP5's worst falls cross 20% there (21.0%, 21.4%), and so does CTRL's at exactly 20.0%.

## Why

**The cap removed good picks, not risk.** The raisers the cap skipped were the newest raises in an industry that was already full. Their slots went to SPY or to an older raiser. Fewer fresh raisers meant less of the signal and a little more SPY, so the lead shrank by up to 0.4 points a year. The worst fall barely moved, because the safety switch, not the industry mix, is what limits this book's falls. In 2008 the switch had already moved the book to cash before the banks fell hardest.

**The 2009-2015 gap is not about industries.** Banks were the book's biggest lean and had a poor 2009-2011, but cutting them did not help. That points again at the earlier diagnosis (M0096): the switch sold into the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and bought back higher. The book also holds only about half its money in stocks. Its edge over SPY is a slice of a slice.

**The placebo is the new finding.** At the same month-by-month exposure, with the same switch and SPY parking, random index members earned **1.9 points a year less** than the calm raisers. In 2009-2015 they were **3.3 points a year worse**. So the dividend-raise signal carries real information over random names, in the old years and in the best-covered ones. The frame (half in SPY, plus the 200-day switch) is what trails SPY after 2009, and the signal makes back part of that gap. Two caveats. The placebo keeps its holdings much longer (179 trades against 528), so it is not a perfect twin. And one seed is one draw, not a spread.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: no capped version beat CTRL, and none improved 2009-2015 or the folds. The cap's gain over CTRL (−0.4 to 0.0 points) was no better than the placebo's (−0.1), so a cap does nothing specific for the raise book. The expected failure happened as written: the folds stayed at 2 of 4 and the era gap stayed near −2.6. CAP5 was a near-null, and capped slots drifted toward SPY. One expected failure did **not** happen: the placebo did not earn as much as the raise book. That is good news for the signal.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

Every number here is at Gotrade's real fees, the same as the parent's, so no fee adjustment is needed. This is the seventh attempt on the calm big raisers. Switch bands (M0101), a quarterly exit (M0143), a switch cool-off (M0148), a keep band (M0168) and now an industry cap all left the folds at 2 of 4 and the 2009-2015 gap near −2.6 points.

**My opinion:** sector caps are a dead end for this book. It was never mainly a sector bet, and the cap only trims the signal. What this run did show is useful: the raise signal beats random names at the same exposure by about two points a year, and by more after 2009. What loses is the frame, about half in SPY behind a 200-day switch. The next try should keep the signal and change the frame. Simply dropping the switch is already known to fail: with SPY always held and the switch on the stock slots only (M0096-S70), the worst fall was 42.9%. So the next try is a gradual brake in place of the all-or-nothing switch: scale the stock slots down as SPY's own recent daily swing rises, instead of selling everything at the 200-day line. The 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips were sharp but short, and a swing-based brake trims into them instead of selling out and buying back higher. Pair it with the hash placebo again, so the signal's margin is measured rather than assumed. I would not try any more variations of the picks themselves.


### 2026-10-17

### 2026-10-17 — Sera 20261017-2050, Promotion step 0b

Dev-eligible on the uncapped control and all three capped versions, so Sera ran the durability check before any promotion. Walk-forward: 2 of 4 folds beaten (lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011), pick changed. The 2009-2015 edge over SPY is negative (about −2.6 points a year on the picked version, −3.1 with a cap). On the fuller price history every version keeps only a −0.1 to −0.2 point lead change, but the 4- and 5-per-industry caps cross a 20% worst fall there. The hard gate refuses it on the folds condition; kin is clean. No test look was spent and none was attempted. No buy signal.
methods.verdict: Rejected: capping how many dividend raisers one industry can fill cost up to 0.4 points a year and made 2009-2015 slightly worse; the book was never mainly a sector bet, though the raise signal does beat random names at the same exposure by about 2 points a year

methods.name: Winning industries, lagging members: buy last month's laggards inside the strongest industries
methods.sourceRef: Moskowitz & Grinblatt (1999) Do Industries Explain Momentum?; Hameed & Mian (2015) Industries and Stock Return Reversals, JFQA; Li & Turkington, Mapping Momentum (S&P 500)
methods.hypothesis: Momentum lives mostly at the industry level, while over one month a stock reverses against its own industry. Each month-end, among F4's screened members, label each with its Fama-French 12 industry (SEC EDGAR SIC; unknowns never picked), rank industries with at least 5 members by the equal-weight mean of their members' 6-1 or 12-1 return, give the 3 or 4 strongest an equal share of 20 slots (7/7/6 or 5 each, so a structural sector cap of 7 or 5), and inside each buy the members with the lowest last-month return relative to their industry. Equal 5% slots, re-picked monthly with no band, unfilled slots in SPY, cash under SPY's 200-day average. Variants: top-3 vs top-4 industries, 6-1 vs 12-1 industry window; control HASH-T3-W6, the same industries, allotment and switch with members in a fixed hash order (a plain industry-rotation book). Moskowitz and Grinblatt published in 1999 and Hameed and Mian's reversal in 2015, so most of the dev window predates the industry-momentum crowd and all of it predates the within-industry reversal paper. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade) on the owner's monthly top-up. Success: beats SPY TR on dev with worst fall <= 25%, PF >= 1.3, a majority of walk-forward folds, a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, laggard picks beat the hash control by at least 2 points a year, and the book does not move with the test-failed momentum books (residual correlation under 0.85).
methods.expectedFailure: Holding only 3 or 4 industries is a concentrated bet: when the leading industries turn (tech in 2000, financials and energy in 2008) the book holds 15-20 names in them and the 200-day switch meets the turn late, so the worst fall may break 25%. Industry momentum is a well-published 1999 anomaly and may have faded inside the window; 2009-2015's big-company drift (insight 91) works against equal slots in mid-sized laggards. The one-month reversal is a short-horizon effect that is strongest in small, illiquid stocks and is eaten by trading costs; in large index members at monthly re-picking and Gotrade's real fees on 20 small slots it may be gone, so the laggard picks may not beat the hash control. Last month's laggard inside a hot industry is sometimes the member with real bad news, which keeps falling. The 12-1 window ranks industries as momentum does, so the rotation may move with the test-failed momentum books (hardgate D14) and be refused on kin however it scores.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-17

## What was tried

Each month, the book sorted the big US stocks it may buy into 12 broad industries (Fama-French 12, built from each company's SEC filing code). It picked the 3 or 4 industries whose stocks had risen most over the last 6 or 12 months, skipping the latest month. Inside those industries it bought the stocks that had **lagged their own industry the most last month**. The idea comes from two research findings. A stock's winning streak is mostly its industry's streak. Over a single month, a stock that fell behind its peers for no industry-wide reason tends to catch up. So the book follows the industry's trend and buys its members on a dip.

It held 20 equal slots (7/7/6 across 3 industries, or 5 each across 4), so no industry ever held more than 7 of the 20. It picked fresh every month, kept unfilled slots in SPY, and went to cash while SPY was under its 200-day average. Trades were in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly top-up. A **control book** used the same industries, slot split and safety switch, but picked members in a fixed random order. It answers one question: do last month's laggards add anything over plain industry rotation?

## Result (dev window 1996 to Oct 2015, same deposits into SPY total return as the yardstick)

| variant | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| top 3 industries, 6-month | +9.7% | +7.2% | 24.1% | 1.50 | 0.81 |
| top 3, 12-month | +8.5% | +7.2% | 20.0% | 1.48 | 0.78 |
| top 4, 6-month | +9.1% | +7.2% | 24.5% | 1.44 | 0.74 |
| top 4, 12-month | +8.4% | +7.2% | 19.9% | 1.43 | 0.77 |
| **control: top 3, 6-month, random members** | **+10.0%** | +7.2% | 21.6% | 1.56 | 0.82 |

Every variant beat SPY over the full 20 years and stayed inside the 25% worst-fall limit. Every variant made well over 1.3 dollars of gains per dollar of losses. **All five failed one condition: the luck test.** The DSR (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many lucky tries. The lab now holds 141 independent methods (N = 141), and at that N the bar is 0.90. The best variant reached 0.82, the worst 0.74. A result this size could easily be the luckiest of 141 tries.

**Walk-forward: lost 3 of 4 folds.** Each fold picks a variant using only earlier years, then scores it on the next three years. The book lost 2003-2005 (+43% vs SPY +52%), 2009-2011 (+50% vs +61%) and 2012-2014 (+53% vs +66%). It won only 2006-2008 (−2% vs −25%), and that win was the 200-day safety switch moving the book to cash during the crash, not the stock picking. **Its edge in 2009-2015, the best-covered years and the most like today, was −5.7% a year.** It lost to SPY there.

The worst calendar year was 2007 (−11.7%, top-3 6-month). The worst fall, 24%, is on a book refilled by monthly deposits, so the fall without them was a little deeper still.

## Where the book sat

I replayed the picks month by month. Across 1996-2015 the slots were spread fairly wide: business equipment and tech about 15-17% of slot-months, energy 11-14%, then retail, manufacturing, health, banks, utilities and the "other" bucket at 7-11% each. Of 237 month-ends, 67 were spent in cash under the safety switch. The structural cap worked. No industry dominated the book over the 20 years, though in any one month 3 industries held all 20 slots.

## Why it failed

- **The laggard pick added nothing. It slightly hurt.** With the same industries and the same slot split, random members earned +10.0% a year against +9.7% for last month's laggards, fell less at their worst (21.6% vs 24.1%), and had a better gains-to-losses ratio (1.56 vs 1.50). The one-month catch-up the papers find does not show up in big index stocks re-picked once a month and charged Gotrade's fees on small slots. Some of last month's laggards were lagging for a real reason, and they kept falling.
- **What return there is comes from industry rotation plus the safety switch,** and both are old, crowded ideas. Industry momentum was published in 1999. By 2009-2015 rotating among 3 or 4 industries lost to SPY's steady big-company climb. The book held 20 equal slots in mostly mid-sized names, which is the shape insight 91 warns about.
- **Three or four industries at a time is a concentrated bet even with the cap.** The slot cap stops one industry from taking the book. It cannot stop the 3 chosen industries from all being wrong together after a turn.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed on its own test. Laggards had to beat the random control by at least 2 points a year, and they trailed it by 0.3. The expected failure largely happened as written. The reversal "may be gone" in large members at real fees: it was. Industry momentum "may have faded", and 2009-2015 "works against equal slots": the book lost to SPY in that era and lost 3 of 4 folds. One expectation did not happen. The worst fall stayed under 25% (19.9-24.5%), because the 200-day switch caught 2008.

## Compared with near misses

The lab's closest-to-eligible books are monthly momentum and low-volatility blends with MAR (return per unit of worst fall) around 0.8. They were mostly recorded at the old flat 0.1% fee, so their recorded numbers are not a fair comparison. On real fees this book's MAR of 0.37-0.46 is in the middle of the pack. It does not beat the momentum books it was meant to improve on, and it fails the same 2009-2015 test that sank them.

## My opinion

This direction is not worth more variants as a stock picker. The finding that matters is the control. Industry rotation alone did as well as anything here, and the within-industry laggard pick made it worse. The one-month reversal is not a usable signal in big US stocks at monthly re-picking and real fees, so another reversal variant (different lookback, different industry count) would be fishing. The sector labels themselves are the useful new tool. They are best used defensively, as a cap on books that already have a reason to work, which is what the sibling methods in this batch test. They are not a source of return on their own. If I tried one more thing from this line, it would be measuring each live book's sector tilt against SPY's own sector weights. That would show whether the books' 2009-2015 lag is a sector bet against big tech rather than a stock-picking failure.
methods.verdict: Rejected: buying last month's laggards inside the hottest industries did no better than random picks in the same industries, and it lost to SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: Index-shaped industry weights: a stock book whose slots follow the index's own industry mix
methods.hypothesis: Every equal-slot book in the lab lost to SPY in 2009-2015, and the industry-rotation book showed that random picks inside chosen industries do as well as clever ones, so the industry mix itself may decide the result. Measure it directly: split 20 slots across the 12 Fama-French industries in proportion to each industry's share of the screened pool's 20-day dollar volume (a size proxy, since the store has no market caps), fill each industry by a fixed hash order (control) and by the lab's best ranker (12-1 momentum, low volatility), monthly, fractional at Gotrade real fees. If the hash book tracks SPY in 2009-2015 while the equal-industry books lag, the lag was an industry bet against big tech, not a stock-picking failure. Report each variant's industry mix vs the pool's, the 2009-2015 edge, folds, and residual correlation to the test-failed books.

methods.name: News-day book filled freshest first: the most recent qualifying earnings days take the slots, not the biggest jumps
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008 (earnings-day drift; Bernard and Thomas 1989 showed the drift is strongest in the first weeks), so judge 2009-2015 first. M0213 showed that picking the filtered news days (3x volume, up gap, jump >= 4 points over SPY and >= 2 own daily swings) in a meaningless hash order earns about as much as ranking by jump size (+10.9% vs +12.3% a year on dev, about equal on the survivorship-check store), so the ranking adds little. The drift literature says the price keeps adjusting most in the days right after the news and fades over the quarter, so fill the 20 slots by recency instead: the news days with the fewest sessions since the event first, held names kept. Same frame as M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (60-session hold, 5% slots, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Variants: FRESH (newest first), STALE (oldest first, the mirror control), and FRESH with a 20 and 40 session hold. If freshness is the edge, FRESH beats STALE by more than the 1.4 points the jump ranking beat the hash order; if FRESH and STALE tie, the 60-session hold window itself is the whole edge. No sector cap (M0213 showed it only costs).

methods.name: Equal-weight frame vs the equal-weight S&P: is the coskewness family's lead just equal weighting plus the cash switch?
methods.hypothesis: Capped coskewness, uncapped coskewness, its opposite end and a random order all earned within about a point a year of each other over 1996-2015, so the shared frame (F4's screen, 40 big members at equal weight, quarterly re-pick with a 40% keep band, empty slots in SPY, SPY 200-day cash switch) is what beat SPY. Test the frame head-on: (a) the random-order 40-name book with an FF12 cap of 6 and the switch, (b) the same with no switch, (c) every screened member at equal weight with the switch, rebalanced quarterly. Judge each against total-return SPY and report its lead over an equal-weight S&P 500 built from point-in-time members on the same deposits. If the switch is the whole edge, (b) and (c)-without-switch trail SPY and the 2009-2015 era stays negative; then the family is a cash-switch bet, not stock picking. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees.

methods.name: Calm dividend raisers with a gradual swing brake instead of the 200-day switch
methods.hypothesis: M0215's placebo showed the calm-raiser signal beats hash-ordered members at the same exposure by about 1.9 points a year (3.3 in 2009-2015), while the frame -- half in SPY, all-or-nothing SPY-200 switch -- trails SPY after 2009 (M0096: the switch sold the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips). Dropping the switch breaks the drawdown bar (M0096-S70: 42.9%). Replace the binary switch with a gradual brake: scale the stock slots (and optionally the SPY park) by a target over SPY's 21- or 63-session realized volatility (allocator.VOLTARGET-style), so the book trims into sharp short dips instead of selling out and buying back higher. Variants: vol-target at two levels on the stock slots only, on the whole book, and the SPY-200 control; each beside an exposure-matched hash-order placebo. Fractional at Gotrade's real fees (-frac-gotrade). Success: worst fall at or under 20%, 2009-2015 gap under 1 point, majority of folds.

methods.name: The honest yardstick: the biggest index members held in proportion to their real market value, with and without the 200-day switch
methods.sourceRef: S&P 500 cap-weighting; Sera 20261018-0517 owner theme 'books shaped like the market'; insight 391; M0122 and M0198 (trading value as the size stand-in)
methods.hypothesis: Not a picker but the yardstick every picker needs. Now that the store carries point-in-time market value, hold each month the top N index members by real market value (one share class per company), weighted by market value with no name above 10% of the account, fully invested, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Arms: C50 (top 50, no switch), C100 (top 100, no switch, the closest to SPY's shape), C20 (top 20, no switch, concentrated), C50-SW (top 50 behind the SPY 200-day switch), E50 (the same top 50 at equal weight: the lab's usual shape on the biggest names), and R50 (50 members drawn in a fixed hash order that ignores size and price, cap-weighted: the meaningless control of the same shape). Predictions, written before any result: C100 and C50 track total-return SPY within about a point a year over 1996-2015 and within about a point in 2009-2015, with worst falls near SPY's 55% in 2008; C20 trails SPY after 2009 by more, because the 10% ceiling binds on the giants; C50-SW gives up return after 2009 to whipsaws but roughly halves the 2008 fall; E50 leads the cap arms before 2009 and trails after; R50 lands nearer the equal-weight arm than SPY, because without size ranking it holds mostly mid-sized members. Success is a yardstick that tracks SPY, not a book that beats it: no arm is expected to pass the gate, and none is for promotion (it would simply be SPY with fees). Cap weighting is not a published anomaly; it is the market itself.
methods.expectedFailure: The store, not the shape. About 44% of dev member-days have no market value (mostly members with no bars at all, many of them the companies that later died), so the biggest N is the biggest N the store can see; Berkshire reads too small in 2010-11 and Alphabet goes unknown from 2014. If C100 drifts from SPY by more than about a point a year -- above it because the missing names were the losers (survivorship), or below it because missing giants carried SPY -- the yardstick measures the store's holes and the verdict must say so; the survivorship-check store re-run then decides which. Second, fees: a 100-name book on a 20M IDR account means slots of about $15 at the start, where Gotrade's minimum charges bite hardest, so C100 may trail C50 on fees alone in the early years. Third, the 10% ceiling on C20 moves money from the biggest names to the rest every month and may trade more than the uncapped arms.
