Fourth, a 2009-2015 lag on C50 would mean the lab's measuring frame itself handicaps any member book against SPY, which is worth knowing even though it is the uncomfortable answer.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

**What this was.** Not a stock picker. A ruler. Each month, take the biggest index members by
their real company size (shares outstanding times price, as known that day), hold them in
proportion to that size like SPY does, with no company above 10% of the account. Fractional shares,
Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up. Six versions: the top 20, 50 and 100 by
size; the top 50 behind the 200-day switch (go to cash when SPY is below its 200-day average); the
same top 50 at equal weight; and 50 names drawn blindly (a fixed shuffle that ignores size and
price) then sized by company size, as a control.

The question: if the lab can build a book shaped like the market, does it track SPY? If yes, the
lab's long losing streak to SPY in 2009-2015 comes from equal slots and the switch. If no, the
store itself is missing part of the market, and every "beats SPY" in the lab carries that error.

**The answer: the ruler does not track SPY, and the store is the reason.**

| version | earned a year on the deposits | SPY, same deposits | 2009-2015 a year (SPY 16.6%) | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| top 50, size-weighted | 5.6% | 7.2% | 11.9% | 44.9% |
| top 100, size-weighted | 4.8% | 7.2% | 10.3% | 39.7% |
| top 20, size-weighted | 5.2% | 7.2% | 12.3% | 55.3% |
| top 50, behind the switch | 7.8% | 7.2% | 8.7% | 15.0% |
| top 50, equal weight | 6.9% | 7.2% | 14.4% | 48.1% |
| 50 blind picks, size-weighted | 6.7% | 7.2% | 14.0% | 46.2% |

I predicted the top 100 and top 50 would land within about a point a year of SPY, over twenty years
and in 2009-2015. They missed by 1.6 to 2.4 points over twenty years and by 4.7 to 6.3 points a year
in 2009-2015. The prediction failed badly, and in the way the expected failure described: the store,
not the shape.

**Why: two checks.**

1. *Fees are not the main cause.* I re-ran the top-50 and top-100 books by hand on the store's
   prices with no fees, no deposits and no cash drag, month-end to month-end, against SPY's price.
   Without fees they still trail SPY in 2009-2015: by 8.0, 4.2, 0.9, 4.1, 3.0 and 0.4 points in
   2009, 2010, 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015 for the top 50 (2011 was +1.9). That is about 2.7 points
   a year, and about 2 for the top 100. Before 2000 the same fee-free books *beat* SPY by 10-20
   points a year (1998: +46.8% against +27.0%). The rest of the funded gap is Gotrade's fees on
   many small monthly orders.
2. *The store cannot see some of the decade's biggest winners.* On 2012-12-31 the store has
   prices but **no company size** for Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS, Regeneron,
   Constellation Brands, Accenture, CME, Simon Property, Prudential, Ford and about twenty more.
   Most of them have more than one share class, or a share count the filings tag in a way the
   reader leaves out. And it has **no prices at all** for 147 of 525 members that day, Celgene,
   Alexion, Express Scripts, Walgreens, Time Warner, DirecTV, Activision and Electronic Arts among
   them. Many of 2009-2015's best large companies are therefore invisible to a size ranking. Before
   2000 the holes go the other way: the 268 members with no prices in 1998 are mostly the ones that
   later died or were bought (Enron, WorldCom's peers, Lucent, Compaq, Kmart...), so the store's
   "biggest 50" were the survivors, and the book beat SPY by more than any real index fund could.

The survivorship-check store, which adds prices for most of the dead members, made every version
worse (top 50: 5.6% to 4.0% a year, worst fall 44.9% to 64.6%). That fits the picture: put the
collapses back and the early-years lead shrinks. But that store does not fix the missing company
sizes, so the 2009-2015 gap stays (top 50: 11.9% to 11.3% against 16.6%).

**The other predictions.**
- *The switch halves the 2008 fall:* held, and more than that. 15.0% worst fall against 44.9%.
  *It gives up return after 2009:* held, badly. 8.7% a year in 2009-2015 against the unswitched
  11.9% and SPY's 16.6%. The switch's whole lead comes from 2000-2002 and 2008.
- *Equal weight leads before 2009 and trails after:* failed. Within the top 50, equal weight beat
  size weight in 2009-2015 too (14.4% against 11.9%). The biggest names were not the leaders of
  that era in this store, partly for real (Exxon, GE, IBM, Walmart and Microsoft lagged), partly
  because the giants that did lead are missing.
- *The top 20 trails more after 2009:* failed. 12.3%, slightly ahead of the top 50.
- *The blind control lands near equal weight:* held. 6.7% against 6.9%.

**The gate.** The switched top 50 passed the dev screen: 7.8% a year on the deposits against
SPY's 7.2%, worst fall 15.0% (under the 25% bar), gains 5.7 times losses (bar 1.3), and a luck
score (DSR) of 0.904 at N = 143, just over the 0.90 bar. DSR says how likely the edge is real
rather than the best of 143 tries; 0.904 is right on the edge. It is not a candidate. It won only 1
of 4 walk-forward periods (the 2006-2008 one, by going to cash), and it trailed SPY by 8 points a
year in 2009-2015. `lab promote` would refuse it on the folds, and the durability rule's 2009-2015
test fails as well. It is SPY with a crash brake, the same thing the lab's market-trend-switch
family already measured. The other five versions failed "beats SPY", the gains-vs-losses bar (or
the 100-trade minimum for the blind control) and the luck bar.

**What this means for the lab.** Every member book in this lab is measured against SPY on a store
that, in 2009-2015, cannot hold several of the companies that carried SPY. A book of index members
starts that era roughly 2 points a year behind before it picks anything, and before 2000 it starts
well ahead. Part of the "every edge was earned before 2009" pattern (insights 89, 91, 93) is this
tilt in the data, not a change in the market. It does not rescue any failed method: the test
window's losses were real money on real prices.

**My opinion:** This direction is finished as a strategy and was never meant to be one, but it is
the most useful ruler the lab has built, and it says the ruler is bent. The next step is to fix the
data, not to try another picker: fill the share counts for multi-class and odd-tag companies (Visa,
Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS, Alphabet after 2014), then re-run this same cap-weighted
top 100 as a new method. If it then tracks SPY within a point a year in 2009-2015, the lab gets a
store-matched benchmark to judge every member book against beside SPY. Until then, read any member
book's 2009-2015 shortfall knowing about 2 points a year of it is the store.


### 2026-10-18

Sera 20261018-0517, Promotion step 0b: refused by the hard gate on the fold rule (1 of 4 walk-forward folds). The only eligible row, the top 50 by market value behind the 200-day switch, earned its dev pass by sitting out 2008 and ran about 8 points a year behind SPY in 2009-2015. No look spent. Buy signal: no. The method's lasting value is as a ruler, and the ruler is bent by missing data (no share count for several multi-class or foreign-filer giants, no prices for some acquired names), so its 2009-2015 shortfall is partly the store's.


### 2026-10-20

**The blind control above barely traded, and the shortfall measured against it is withdrawn.**

The table puts the fifty biggest companies by size at **+5.6% a year** and fifty blind picks,
sized the same way, at **+6.7%** — a shortfall of **1.1 points a year** against a book with no
idea in it. That control traded **76 times** in twenty years against the real book's **360**, and
turned over half as much. It was not the same book with the idea taken out. It was a far stiller
book, and stillness is worth money here.

A control matched to this book's own trading has since been drawn: 371 trades against 360, within
three per cent. It earned **+6.0% a year**. The shortfall measured against it is **0.4 points a
year**, not 1.1.

**But this one does not come out clean, and it must not be read as if it did.** The replacement
matches the book's trading and still turns over **almost twice as much**. This book holds its
names in proportion to company size; a blind draw spreads money more evenly, so its weights drift
across the account's resize band at a different rate even when it is buying and selling the same
number of times. A control paying nearly twice the turnover is paying fees the book does not, so
0.4 is not a clean reading of anything, and the lab is not going to quote it as one. The honest
sentence is: **the fifty biggest by size trail a blind draw of their own shape by a small amount
that this lab has not pinned down, somewhere around 0.4 points a year, measured against a control
that over-pays turnover by about twice.**

**This changes nothing about the method.** It was never a strategy; it is a ruler, and the ruler's
reading is unchanged: this book does not track SPY, and the reason is the store, which cannot see
several of 2009-2015's biggest companies. The conclusion the lab takes from it — that a book of
index members starts that era roughly 2 points a year behind before it picks anything — comes from
the hand-run, fee-free comparison against SPY in the section above, and never touched the blind
control at all. No test-window look was spent and nothing was re-run.


### 2026-10-20

### 2026-10-20 (later the same day)

**The gap is no longer "somewhere around 0.4 points". It is about 4 points a year, and the
opponent that measures it is finally honest on both counts.**

Two days ago this page said the fifty biggest companies by size trail a blind draw of their own
shape by *"a small amount that this lab has not pinned down, somewhere around 0.4 points a year,
measured against a control that over-pays turnover by about twice."* The half that was missing has
now been built.

The blind opponent already changed hands as often as the real book — within three per cent. What
it did not do was hold its money the same way. The real book puts ten per cent of the account in
its largest company and a fraction of a per cent in its smallest; the blind opponent spread its
money far more evenly, so the same number of trades moved far more money, and it was paying a fee
bill the real book never pays. That is what "over-pays turnover by about twice" meant.

The new opponent takes the real book's own ladder of position sizes — the largest slot, the second
largest, and so on down — and pays it out to its own blindly chosen names, with the names it is
newly buying this month put at the bottom of the ladder, where a real top-fifty puts the company
that has just climbed into it. It now matches the book it measures on both counts at once: it
traded 372 times against 375, and it moved 1.01 times as much money. Four different ways of
handing out that ladder were measured first, on this same book, before any of this was recorded;
they ranged from one per cent away to fifteen times too much, and the one chosen is the one that
closed the gap.

**The reading, re-measured on one set of prices so both halves are comparable:** the fifty biggest
by size earned **5.9% a year** of the owner's money over 1996-2015. The honest blind opponent
earned **9.9%**. So the book trails a blind draw of its own shape by **about 4 points a year** —
ten times the figure this page carried, and the earlier one is withdrawn. The blind draw also beat
the market's own total return over the same deposits, which the real book did not.

**Read that with one thing in mind, because it is probably most of the gap and it is not stock
picking.** The blind opponent holds fixed proportions and is pushed back to them every month, so
it is forever trimming whatever has risen and topping up whatever has fallen. The real book does
the opposite by construction: it lets its biggest companies grow into larger and larger slots and
never trims them. That difference is a known source of return in its own right, and this lab has
already seen a smaller version of it here — the same fifty names held in equal slots earned more
than the same fifty held by company size. Matching how often an opponent trades, and how much
money it moves, does **not** make it a neutral opponent; this is the clearest case of that the lab
has recorded, and nobody should read these 4 points as evidence that picking blindly beats picking
by size. One blind draw is also one sample: the opponent's largest slot sits on a single name for
twenty years, and a second draw would settle how much of the 4 points is luck. That has not been
run.

**Nothing about the method moves.** It was never a strategy, it is a ruler, and no part of the
ruler's reading rests on the blind opponent: the conclusion that a book of index members starts
2009-2015 roughly 2 points a year behind comes from the fee-free comparison against the market
itself, further up this page. The gate still refuses this method, and for a reason that has
nothing to do with any of this — it lost most of the rolling stretches the gate re-checks it over, which it is asked
before anything about opponents is even read. No test-window look was
spent and nothing here is a reason to buy anything.
methods.verdict: Rejected as a strategy, useful as a ruler: the biggest members held by real company size trailed SPY by about 2 points a year, and by 5 to 6 in 2009-2015, because the store cannot see several of that era's biggest winners (Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Celgene...). The switched version passed the dev screen only by sitting out 2008; it lost 3 of 4 test periods.

methods.name: A market-shaped book that leans toward dividend raisers: every member at its market value, tilted by a dividend-raise score
methods.sourceRef: FTSE Russell factor-tilt method (cap weight x normal-CDF score, rescaled; 'Multi-factor indexes: the power of tilting'); MSCI factor tilt indexes; CEPR index-weight study via AAII (index weight negatively predicts return); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); insight 391 (dividend-raise signal real, frame trails)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1995 (dividend-change drift); factor tilting is index practice since about 2013, not an anomaly. Insight 391: the raise signal beat a random twin of its own frame by about two points a year, but the frame (equal 5% slots, the SPY-200 switch, the rest parked in SPY) trailed SPY in 2009-2015. Remove the frame. Core: the 50 biggest F4-screened index members by point-in-time market value (shares filed by that day x the close as printed), one share class per company (classes grouped by their shared share count, the more traded kept), weighted by market value, no company over 10%. Tilt: each weight x score^power, rescaled, re-capped; score = Phi(z), z = r / rms(r) clipped to +-3, where r is the latest dividend's change against the median of its up-to-four payments in the prior 400 days, dated by its declaration (else ex-date) and live 182 days; unchanged (within 1%), specials (over +100%), first payments, non-payers and names without a live dividend sit at a neutral 0.5; raises tilt up, cuts down. Variants (all monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, target-relative band, owner's deposits, no SPY parking): CORE (power 0: the market-shaped yardstick), TILT1 (power 1), TILT2 (power 2), RAND1 and RAND2 (the same day's non-neutral scores handed to hash-drawn names, quarterly), TILT2-T (TILT2 behind the SPY-200 switch). Success: TILT1 or TILT2 beats total-return SPY on the owner's deposits with the worst fall under the bar, beats its RAND twin, beats CORE, and does not trail SPY in 2009-2015. Assumptions: the tband preset rather than the plain monthly one, because a 50-name book of 1-2% weights would otherwise leave most deposits in cash; first payments neutral.
methods.expectedFailure: A tilt this gentle moves a 50-name market-value book less than a point a year from its core, and the core itself trails SPY: the top 50 is not the S&P 500 (it leaves out SPY's other ~50% and holds no names the dev store cannot price), the 10% ceiling bites on GE, Exxon, Microsoft and Apple in their peaks, and the deposits and fees on fifty names cost more than SPY's single order. The 1990s-2000s top 50 is GE, Exxon, Citi, AIG, Enron-era names: a bigger-is-better core lost hard in 2000-2002 and 2008, so CORE and the ungated tilts take a 45-55% fall, far over the bar; only TILT2-T has a chance at the bar and the switch is what made the old frame trail after 2009. Among the 50 biggest companies raises are routine (most raise 5-10% a year), so the score spreads little and the difference to the random tilt is noise. Banks raised the most before 2008 and cut the most in it, so a raise tilt may lean into the 2008 crash, and the cut penalty only arrives after the fall. A published anomaly whose dev edge, if any, may have faded; withholding tax on dividends is not modelled; market value is missing for members with no bars, which the dev store mostly lacks before 2005.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

## What was tried

The last batch found something odd about the **dividend-raise books**. Picking companies that just raised their dividend did beat picking random companies inside the same setup, by about two points a year. But the setup around those picks lagged SPY after 2009: equal 5% slots, money parked in SPY, and a switch to cash whenever SPY fell under its 200-day average.

So this method dropped that setup and started from the market's own shape:

- **The core**: the 50 biggest index companies by their real market value on each day (shares the company had reported by then × the price that day). Each is weighted by its size, and no company is allowed over 10%. Where a company lists two share classes (Google, Fox, News Corp) only one is kept.
- **The tilt**: each company's weight is multiplied by a score between 0 and 1. A company whose latest dividend (counted from the day it was announced, for six months) was a raise scores above 0.5. A cut scores below 0.5. No change, no dividend, a one-off special or a first-ever payment all sit at a neutral 0.5. The score comes from how big the change was compared with every other change that day, through a bell curve, which is how FTSE and MSCI build their "tilt" indexes. TILT1 uses the score once and TILT2 uses it squared, so the lean is stronger.
- **The random twins** (RAND1, RAND2): each day the real scores, same number and same values, go to randomly drawn companies instead.
- **TILT2-T**: TILT2 behind the SPY 200-day switch.

Every version re-picks monthly in fractional shares, pays Gotrade's real fees and runs on the owner's deposits (10M IDR, then 5M a month). No money is parked in SPY.

One assumption I made: I used the rule set that rebalances a holding once it is 20% off its own target. Under the account-wide 1% band, a book of fifty 1-2% weights would leave most deposits sitting in cash.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**. The middle columns are the dev store. The "check store" also has the companies that later died or were bought out, which the dev store cannot price.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year | check store: a year / worst fall | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CORE (no tilt) | +6.0% | 47.3% | −3.6 pts | +4.6% / 59.2% | 0.46 |
| TILT1 | +6.3% | 48.8% | −2.7 pts | +4.8% / 58.0% | 0.45 |
| TILT2 | +6.1% | 50.0% | −2.7 pts | +4.8% / 56.9% | 0.44 |
| RAND1 (random) | +6.1% | 51.7% | −3.0 pts | +4.4% / 62.3% | 0.44 |
| RAND2 (random) | +5.7% | 53.4% | −3.4 pts | +3.8% / 65.2% | 0.41 |
| TILT2-T (switch) | +7.1% | 19.0% | −8.2 pts | +6.5% / 19.0% | 0.84 |

**Every version lost to SPY.** The closest was TILT2-T at +7.1% against +7.2%. It also lost 3 of its 4 walk-forward tests: it won only 2006-2008, when the switch dodged the crash. It trailed SPY by 8 points a year in 2009-2015, because the switch sold in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and missed the rebounds. Its worst fall, 19%, was under the owner's real-money limit of 25%, but a book that does not beat SPY never reaches that question.

The ungated versions fell 47-53% from their peak, about as far as SPY did in 2008. That is twice the real-money limit, and they lost money in 2008 (about −30% that year).

**The luck check.** The lab has now tried 146 different methods, so a result needs a DSR of at least 0.90 to count as more than luck. The best version here scored 0.84 and the rest 0.41-0.46. None comes close, and none beat SPY anyway.

## Why

1. **The core itself is the handicap.** The 50 biggest companies, weighted by size, earned 1.2 points a year less than SPY (2.6 less on the check store). Today's giants were often tomorrow's laggards: GE, Exxon, Citi and AIG at the top in 1998-2007, Apple and Exxon in 2012. The 10% ceiling also trimmed GE and Microsoft at their peaks. SPY holds the other 450 companies too, and its slow drift toward big companies comes from smaller ones growing into giants. A top-50 book misses exactly that. This fits the outside study the idea row cited (a company's index weight predicts lower returns). The money columns include the 50 orders a month and their fees, which SPY pays only once.
2. **The tilt helps, but only a little.** TILT1 beat CORE by 0.3 points a year and beat its random twin by 0.2. TILT2 beat its random twin by 0.4. On the check store, both tilts beat both random twins by 0.4-1.0 points. The direction is the same as the last batch's finding: the raise signal carries some information. But among the 50 biggest companies, raises are routine and small, so a gentle tilt moves the result by tenths of a point. That is far from the 1.2-point gap the core starts with. In 2009-2015 the tilts cut the core's lag from 3.6 to 2.7 points a year, still well behind.
3. **Missing companies flatter every version.** On the check store every version earns 0.6-1.9 points a year less, and the ungated falls deepen by 7-12 points. The dead and bought-out giants (Enron, WorldCom, Lehman, Wachovia) were in the top 50 and are missing from the dev store.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The hypothesis needed a tilt to beat SPY, its random twin and the core, and to keep pace in 2009-2015. The tilt beat its random twin and the core by small margins, on both stores. It never beat SPY, and it lagged in 2009-2015. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the gentle tilt moved the book less than a point, the core trailed SPY, the ungated books fell about 50%, and the switched version only had a chance at the drawdown bar but lost the folds.

Compared with the sector-capped raise book (+10.6% a year, recorded at real fees), this market-shaped version gave up four points a year. So the old frame was not what held the raise signal back. The equal slots and the SPY park were adding return before 2009, not costing it.

## My opinion:

This direction is a dead end as built. A size-weighted top-50 core starts 1.2 points behind SPY, and no dividend tilt gentle enough to stay market-shaped can make that up. I would not run more tilt strengths on this core. What is worth one more run is the same tilt on a core that actually *is* the market: every index member with a known size, perhaps 300-450 names, with a ceiling. If the raise tilt still beats its random twin there, the signal is real and the only question left is whether fifty-plus tiny orders a month can pay for it. If the full-market core also trails SPY, that measures how much the dev store's missing companies and Gotrade's fees cost any market-shaped book, which is worth knowing before anyone builds another one.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a book shaped like the 50 biggest companies, leaning toward dividend raisers, earned +6.3% a year against SPY's +7.2%; the raise lean beat a random lean by a few tenths of a point, but the top-50 core itself trails SPY by more than a point

methods.name: Momentum picked inside each size band: four names from each fifth of the index by company size
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0047's finding that size weighting starves the mid-size picks; point-in-time market value from 2026-10-17; Sera 20261018-2051; placebo frame of M0187
methods.hypothesis: M0047 found that sizing the residual-momentum picks by company size cost 2.5-3.3 points a year and turned the 2009-2015 lead negative, which suggests the ranking's edge lives in the smaller and mid-sized names. Each month, split the screened members whose point-in-time market value is known (one class per company) into five equal-count bands by size and hold the top four raw residual-momentum names in each band (B5X4), equal slots, SPY 200-day gate, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up. Controls on the same sized universe: the plain top 20 (TOP20), the top 20 from the two smallest bands (SMALL2), the top 20 from the two biggest bands (BIG2), and a hash-order placebo with four names per band redrawn quarterly (PLC1-B5X4). Unknown sizes are dropped from every arm (assumption). Predictions, written now: SMALL2 earns the most and falls the deepest; BIG2 earns the least and lags SPY in 2009-2015; B5X4 sits between TOP20 and BIG2 on return with a shallower fall than TOP20; the momentum arms beat the placebo by 2+ points a year. If the small bands carry the whole edge, the honest construction is SPY as the core with a small-band momentum sleeve, not a size-bent book. Residual momentum was published in 2011 (Blitz, Huij and Martens) and the size effect in 1981 (Banz); expect fade after 2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The edge in this lab's dev store leans small partly because the store is missing about half the index members in the 1990s, mostly companies that later died, and those were mostly small: the small bands read the survivors, so SMALL2's lead may be a hole in the data (the survivorship-check store should shrink it most). Forcing four names from the biggest fifth means holding big companies with merely the best of a slow group's momentum, so B5X4 probably gives up a point or two a year against TOP20 without a much shallower fall, and in 2009-2015, when the giants led, BIG2 may track SPY but not beat it once fees are paid. The placebo will likely beat SPY on dev too, because the gate and the screen do most of the work (M0187). Every arm descends from the residual-momentum family, which has a test-failed method, so the hard gate is expected to refuse promotion whatever dev says; the value is the answer to where the edge lives.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

### What was tried

The lab's best stock picker ranks index members by "residual momentum": how strongly a stock has risen over the past year after taking out the part explained by the whole market. Last time (the size-weighted version) we learned that leaning the money toward the biggest picks cost 2.5 to 3.3 points a year. That suggested the edge might live in the smaller names. This method tested that directly. Each month it sorts the screened index members into five equal groups by company size (smallest fifth to biggest fifth) and picks from inside those groups. Every arm holds 20 names in equal slots, sits in cash when SPY is below its 200-day average, buys fractional shares, pays Gotrade's real fees, and adds Rp 5 million each month. Members with no known company size that day were left out of every arm, so all five arms pick from the same list (an assumption written before the run).

### Results, 1996 to 2015, on the owner's deposits

"Yearly" below is what the deposited money earned a year. The same deposits put into total-return SPY earned **+7.2% a year**.

| Arm | What it holds | Yearly | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Luck test (DSR) | 2009-2015 lead over SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain top 20 | best 20 of the whole sized list | **+13.5%** | 20.6% | 1.94 | 0.925 pass | +0.3 pts |
| Four per fifth | best 4 from each size fifth | +12.8% | 21.3% | 1.88 | 0.919 pass | -0.5 pts |
| Small two fifths | best 20 of the smallest 40% | +12.2% | 24.9% | 1.81 | 0.897 fail | 0.0 pts |
| Big two fifths | best 20 of the biggest 40% | +9.7% | 19.6% | 1.88 | 0.914 pass | **-6.1 pts** |
| Placebo, four per fifth | 4 random names per fifth | +7.8% | 21.1% | 1.60 | 0.732 fail | -6.8 pts |

The luck test (DSR) asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It is judged at N = 147 independent methods in the lab, against the bar DSR >= 0.90. Three arms passed the lab's dev screen. The small-band arm missed only the luck test (0.897, just under 0.90). The placebo missed badly.

Worst years: the top-20, four-per-fifth and big arms had their worst year in 2015 (-4.1%, -5.1%, -3.6%). The small arm's worst year was 1998 (-9.4%). The placebo lost 13.1% in 2015.

### Why

- **The ranking works in every size group, not just the small ones.** The four-per-fifth momentum book beat its own random-pick twin, built from the same size groups, by 5 points a year (+12.8% vs +7.8%). Its gains-vs-losses ratio was 1.88 against 1.60. So the size groups explain almost nothing. The ranking does the work.
- **Small names were not where the edge lived.** The small-only arm earned *less* than the plain top 20 and fell deeper (24.9%, against a 20.6% worst fall). The hypothesis was wrong. M0047's cost came from moving money onto the biggest picks, not from small picks being special.
- **Big names drag.** Limiting the ranking to the biggest 40% cost almost 4 points a year. In 2009-2015, when giant companies led the market, this arm trailed SPY by 6 points a year. That is about as badly as the random placebo did. Picking the "best momentum" among giants mostly meant holding giants that were not the ones carrying SPY.
- **2009-2015 is flat for everything.** No arm beat SPY in the best-covered years by more than a third of a point. This is the same wall every momentum book in the lab has hit.

### The dead-companies check (report only, nothing recorded)

The lab re-ran every arm on the second store, which adds prices for most of the index members the main store lacks, including companies that died.

- Plain top 20: yearly +13.5% -> +11.6%, worst fall 20.6% -> 25.0%, DSR 0.925 -> 0.839, 2009-2015 lead +0.3 -> -0.8 pts.
- Four per fifth: +12.8% -> +12.1%, worst fall 21.3% -> 23.0%, DSR 0.919 -> 0.882, 2009-2015 lead -0.5 -> -1.1 pts.
- Small two fifths: +12.2% -> +12.6% (it *rose*), worst fall 24.9% -> 24.7%.
- Big two fifths: +9.7% -> +10.1%. Placebo: +7.8% -> +7.6%.

The prediction was that the small arm would shrink most, because dead companies are mostly small. It did not happen: the small arm did not shrink at all. The arm that lost most was the plain top 20, which can pile into one size group. Forcing four picks into each fifth made the book sturdier against the missing companies: it lost 0.7 points a year where the plain book lost 1.8. On the second store, the four-per-fifth book is the better of the two.

### Hypothesis and expected failure

- Hypothesis "small bands carry the edge": **rejected**. The ranking earns about equally across sizes, and the plain top 20 is best on the main store.
- The prediction that "four per fifth" gives up a point or two against the top 20 without a much shallower fall: **held** (it gave up 0.7, and its worst fall was slightly deeper).
- The prediction that the big-band arm trails SPY in 2009-2015: **held**, and by more than expected.
- The prediction that the momentum arms beat the placebo by 2+ points: **held** (+5 points).
- The expectation that the small arm's lead is a hole in the data: **did not happen**.
- Walk-forward: on the lab's shared folds, the arm picked in training won only 1 of 4 folds against SPY (2 of 4 on the check store). The lab's promotion gate needs a majority. This method also descends from the residual-momentum family, which has a test-failed method. So the gate will refuse a promotion whatever these dev numbers say.

### Compared with the parent

The parent's equal-slot arm (M0047-EQ) earned +13.7% with a 20.6% worst fall. This method's plain top 20 earned +13.5% with the same fall. The small difference is the members with no known size, which this method leaves out. Splitting by size did not beat simply taking the best 20.

**My opinion:** Hunting for momentum by company size is settled, and it is a dead end as a return booster. The ranking is not a small-company trick, and the big-company version is worse than useless after 2009. The one useful thing found here is robustness. Forcing the picks across all five size groups lost less when the dead companies were added back. That makes "four per fifth" a better default shape for any future momentum book than the plain top 20. None of that fixes the real problem, though: no momentum book here beats SPY in 2009-2015. The next thing worth trying is to stop fighting SPY and own it. Put most of the money in SPY and run a small four-per-fifth momentum sleeve beside it, then judge whether the sleeve adds anything in 2009-2015. I do not expect this family to pass the promotion gate. The answer is still worth having.


### 2026-10-18

### 2026-10-18 (Sera 20261018-2051)

Not promoted. The lab's hard gate refuses this method on both of its conditions: its chosen version beat SPY in only 1 of the 4 walk-forward periods (a strict majority is required), and it descends from the residual-momentum family, three of whose methods have already failed their one look at the test years. No test-window look was spent. The useful finding stays: the momentum ranking works in every size group, so the next step is the version that keeps most of the money in SPY with a size-balanced momentum sleeve.
methods.verdict: Momentum works in every size group, not just the small ones; picking four per size fifth beat SPY by 5.6 points a year on 1996-2015 and held up better with dead companies added, but nothing beat SPY in 2009-2015

methods.name: The market-shaped book leaning toward bond-like stocks: every index company at its market value, tilted toward those that rise when yields fall, beside a random tilt
methods.sourceRef: M0201 (bond-like ranking at size weight) and M0197 (weekly 10-year yield loading); D.E. Shaw research note on Treasury beta (caia.org/node/6853); Maio & Santa-Clara; Driessen, Kuiper & Beilo; FTSE Russell factor-tilt method; M0222/M0226 (the tilted market core and its random twin)
methods.hypothesis: Treasury-beta pricing published in the 2010s; the dev window is before publication. The bond-like ranking (M0197's weekly loading on 10-year yield changes, net of SPY) beat its opposite at equal weight (+12.5% vs +7.7% on the deposits), at size weight under a 10% cap (M0201: +9.5% vs +6.2%) and on the survivorship-check store (+8.0% vs +2.4%), but as a 20-name book it was no better than a size-weighted random 20 (+8.1% to +10.3%). Test it as a tilt on the market's own shape. Core (refined from the reserved top-50: M0226 measured the top-50 core 1.2 points a year behind SPY and the whole screened market 0.2 ahead): every F4-screened index member with a known point-in-time market value, one class per identical share count, weighted by market value, no company over 5% (M0226's core through M0222's code). Score: M0197's 52-week weekly loading c, z = (c - cross-sectional mean) / sd over the core names with a loading, bond side -z, opposite +z, clipped +-3, score Phi(z), re-fit monthly; no loading or fewer than 20 loadings that day: neutral 0.5. Weight = value x score^power, rescaled, re-capped. Variants: CORE (power 0; should reproduce M0226-CORE), TILT1, TILT2, OPP2 (the opposite tilt, power 2), RAND1/RAND2 (the day's bond scores handed to the same names in a hash order, quarterly). All monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, target-relative band, owner's deposits, no SPY parking, no switch. Success: TILT1 or TILT2 beats total-return SPY on the deposits, beats CORE and both RAND twins by 1+ point a year, does not trail SPY in 2009-2015, and its gap to OPP2 survives the check store. The 2x2 that prices the opinion: TILT2 vs OPP2 is the signal, CORE is the no-opinion arm, RAND2 the cost of tilting at that strength with no information.
methods.expectedFailure: Size dominates the weights: a tilt of Phi(z)^2 moves a 5%-capped market book by tenths of a point a year, as the dividend tilt did on the same core (M0226: +0.1-0.3 over CORE, 0.2-0.8 over its random twin). The bond-like end of the market is utilities, staples, pharma and REITs; in 1996-2015 falling yields paid them, but in 2009-2015 they lagged a tech-led rally, so the tilt trails CORE there and CORE already trails SPY by about a point after 2009. On the check store the dead companies cost about a point a year and erase any lead. Ungated, every variant falls about 50% in 2008, twice the 25% bar; the bond tilt may soften that fall by a few points (bond-like stocks fell less), which is the one thing it could add. A falling-yield era favours this tilt on dev; 2022's rising yields are exactly when it would have hurt, so any dev edge is partly the era.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tried

Earlier runs found a real pattern: companies whose shares tend to **rise when long-term interest rates fall** ("bond-like" stocks: drug makers, food and household brands, utilities, and some big growth names) did better from 1996 to 2015 than companies that move the other way. But when the lab bought just 20 of them, sized by company size, the book did no better than 20 companies picked at random. A 20-name book is a bet on 20 names, whatever chose them.

So this run used the pattern only to **lean** a book that is otherwise shaped like the whole market:

- **The base (CORE)**: every index company the data can size, weighted by its market value, none over 5%. This is the same base as the dividend-lean run from 2026-10-18, which had beaten SPY by 0.2 points a year. (The reserved idea named a base of only the 50 biggest companies; that base had trailed SPY by 1.2 points, so a lean on it could only ever read as "less behind". I used the wider base instead and decided this before any result.)
- **The lean**: each month, every company's sensitivity to the 10-year Treasury yield is measured over the past year of weekly prices, after taking out the market's own move. Bond-like companies get a score above 0.5, the others below. Each weight is multiplied by that score (TILT1) or its square (TILT2, a stronger lean).
- **The opposite lean (OPP2)**: the same strength, toward companies that rise when rates rise (banks, energy, industrials).
- **Random leans (RAND1, RAND2)**: the same scores handed to companies in a random order, redrawn each quarter.

All re-weight monthly, buy fractional shares, pay Gotrade's real fees, and run on the owner's deposits (10M IDR, then 5M a month). No switch, no money parked in SPY.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**. The "check store" adds back most of the companies that later died or were bought out.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year | check store: a year / worst fall | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CORE (no lean) | +7.4% | 50.2% | −1.1 pts | +6.3% / 50.5% | 0.55 |
| TILT1 (bond-like) | +7.1% | 50.9% | −2.1 pts | +5.9% / 52.2% | 0.50 |
| TILT2 (bond-like, strong) | +6.9% | 50.4% | −2.7 pts | +5.6% / 51.8% | 0.49 |
| OPP2 (rate-rising, strong) | +6.3% | 60.1% | +0.0 pts | +4.8% / 67.9% | 0.35 |
| RAND1 (random) | +6.1% | 54.3% | −2.0 pts | +4.4% / 59.4% | 0.39 |
| RAND2 (random, strong) | +5.2% | 55.2% | −3.1 pts | +3.4% / 61.8% | 0.31 |

CORE reproduced the earlier whole-market base exactly (+7.4%, the same total return to the decimal), so the new code leaves the base untouched when the lean is off.

**Every lean did worse than no lean.** The base beat SPY by 0.2 points a year; the bond-like leans trailed it by 0.3 and 0.5 points and fell behind SPY. Every version fell about half its value in 2008-2009 (worst calendar year 2008, about −31% to −41%), twice the owner's real-money limit of 25%.

**Walk-forward**: TILT2 beat SPY in 1 of 4 three-year test periods (2006-2008, by losing less in the crash) and lost 2003-2005 and 2009-2011; the 2012-2014 pick, CORE, also lost.

**The luck check.** The lab has now tried 177 different methods, so a result needs a DSR of at least 0.90 to count as more than luck. The best here is 0.55. Nothing came close, and only the base beat SPY at all.

## Why

1. **The signal is real but points the wrong way after 2009.** The strong bond-like lean beat its opposite by 0.6 points a year on the main data and by 0.8 on the check store, and it fell 50% where the opposite fell 60%. So over twenty years, bond-like stocks were the better half. But in 2009-2015, the best-covered and most recent years, it reversed: the opposite lean kept pace with SPY and the bond-like lean trailed by 2.7 points a year. That is the falling-rate era ending its run: rates were already near zero, and the rally after 2009 was led by banks, industrials and tech that move with rates.
2. **Leaning costs more than it earns.** Pricing the habit: averaging the two opposite leans cancels the opinion and leaves only what leaning itself costs. That average (+6.6%) sits 0.8 points below the base (+7.4%), while the opinion is worth about 0.3 points each way (half the 0.6-point gap). The lean moves money away from the biggest companies, which was SPY's winning side in this period, and it trades more (1,891 trades for TILT2 against 1,265 for the base). So the rule is **dead, not badly dressed**: a cheaper way to lean would still not pay for the opinion.
3. **The random leans are a handicapped control.** They reshuffle at full strength every quarter and churned far more (the lab's shape check flags them: up to 41 times the base's turnover). TILT2 beating RAND2 by 1.7 points is mostly RAND2's extra trading, not evidence for the signal. The fair control here is the opposite lean, and against it the edge is 0.6 points.
4. **The missing dead companies cost every version 1.1-1.8 points a year**, more for the leans than for the base, so on the check store even the base trails SPY by 0.8.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. Success needed a bond-like lean that beats SPY, beats the base and both random leans by a point, keeps pace in 2009-2015, and keeps its gap to the opposite lean on the check store. Only the last part held (0.8 points on the check store). It lost to SPY, lost to the base, and trailed SPY by 2.7 points in 2009-2015. The expected failure happened as written: the lean moved the book by tenths of a point, the bond-like side lagged the tech-and-banks rally after 2009, the check store took about a point, every version fell about 50%, and the bond lean's one contribution was a softer fall than its opposite (but not than the base).

Compared with the parent (20 bond-like picks sized by company size, +9.5% a year, and its random twins +8.1% to +10.3%): the parent's lead came from being a concentrated 20-name book, which random 20s matched. With the concentration removed, the bond-like signal is worth minus a few tenths against the market's own shape.

## My opinion:

Close the treasury-beta family as a way to beat SPY. Four methods now say the same thing: the bond-like side beats its opposite over 1996-2015, but that is the falling-rate era, it reversed in the best-covered years, and it never beats either a random book of the same shape or the plain market. I would not run another strength or core. What is worth keeping is the yardstick: the whole-market base reproduces exactly and beats SPY by 0.2 points on the main data and trails by 0.8 on the check store, so any lean on it must clear about a point just to break even once the dead companies are back. The one idea from this run worth a trial is the reverse framing, a **rate-regime switch** between the two leans (bond-like when rates are falling, rate-rising when they are rising, judged on the past year's yield change), with the base as the no-opinion arm. I expect it to fail too, because the yield's own trend is a slow, published signal, but it is the only way left to use the 2009 reversal rather than be hurt by it.
methods.verdict: Rejected: leaning a market-shaped book toward stocks that rise when rates fall did worse than not leaning (+6.9-7.1% a year vs +7.4% for the plain market book and +7.2% for SPY), and it trailed SPY after 2009

methods.name: The honest yardstick, repaired: the size-weighted top 100 once multi-class companies have a size
methods.sourceRef: M0221 analysis; data-wish on multi-class share counts
methods.hypothesis: M0221's size-weighted top 100 trailed SPY by about 2 points a year without fees in 2009-2015, and Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast and UPS had no company size in the store. Once share counts are summed across classes, re-run the same top 100 and top 50 (10% ceiling, no switch, fractional, Gotrade fees) beside an equal-weight top 100. Prediction: the fee-free gap to SPY in 2009-2015 shrinks to about a point a year; whatever remains is the members with no prices at all, which only a fuller price history can close. If it tracks SPY, adopt its curve as a store-matched second yardstick for every member book. Sera 20261018-2051 adds: carry M0221's six arms unchanged (top 20, 50 and 100 by size, the switched top 50, the equal-weight top 50 and the blind-draw control) as the pre-registered twin on the repaired store, so the before-and-after comparison measures the data fix and nothing else; the equal-weight top 100 runs as this method's first amendment. Funded predictions against M0221's recorded trials: C100 and C50 gain 1 to 3 points a year in 2009-2015 (C50 from 11.9% toward 14%, C100 from 10.3% toward 13%, SPY 16.6%) and about half a point a year over 1996-2015; C20 gains the most in 2009-2015, because Visa, Mastercard, Meta and Berkshire enter a 20-name book at once; E50 and R50 move least, because they never weighted by size or never ranked by it. No arm is for promotion: success is a ruler that tracks SPY, and cap weighting is the market itself, not a published anomaly.
methods.expectedFailure: Most of the 2009-2015 gap was the members with no prices at all, not the members with no size: coverage of member-days rose only from 62-69% to 62-75%, and the unpriced names (Celgene, Alexion, Express Scripts, Walgreens, Time Warner, DirecTV, Activision, Electronic Arts) were among the era's best large companies. If C100 still trails SPY by 4 points a year or more in 2009-2015 (M0221 was 6.3), the repair closed a small part of the gap and the ruler stays bent until the prices arrive. Second, the switched top 50 may stay dev-eligible exactly as M0221's did, by sitting out 2008; that is not a candidate and the same fold rule refuses it. Third, fees on a 100-name book at about $15 a slot dominate the early years whatever the size data says. Fourth, folding Berkshire A into B and Visa B/C into A may raise those two to the 10% ceiling in the top 20, so C20's gain may be capped by its own ceiling.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

Unblocked: the missing data arrived. Company size now covers firms that split their shares into more than one class.

Until now our research data had no size at all for some of the biggest companies of 2009-2015 (Meta, Visa, Mastercard, Comcast, UPS, Ford, and Alphabet from 2014), and it counted only Berkshire Hathaway's expensive shares, which made Berkshire look a tenth of its real size. A book shaped like the market therefore started those years behind the S&P 500 before it chose anything. The counts are now read class by class from each company's own quarterly and annual reports to the SEC, and every figure is used only from the day it was filed.

How often an index company's size is known, before → after:
2009: 61.7% → 61.8%
2010: 65.1% → 65.1%
2011: 66.2% → 66.9%
2012: 64.7% → 69.0%
2013: 66.4% → 71.4%
2014: 67.7% → 72.8%
2015: 68.7% → 74.5%
Most of what is still missing is companies we have no prices for, not companies without a size. Trading days where we had a price but no size fell from about 45,000 to about 19,000.

Checks on 30 June 2014: Apple about $560 billion (unchanged), Meta about $173 billion, Visa about $132 billion, Berkshire Hathaway about $312 billion, and Alphabet's two share lines together about $391 billion. Meta, Visa, Mastercard, Alphabet and Berkshire now have a size on every trading day they were in the index from 2009 to 2015.

When a company has two share classes that both trade (Alphabet, Fox, News Corp), each line is now sized by its own shares, so a book weighted by size holds the company once at its true size, with no hand-kept list. One exception: before April 2014 Alphabet had only one class that traded, but our index lists it under both of its later names, and both show the same whole-company size, so a book should keep only one of the two.

The prices did not change, so every result recorded before still compares like for like. Still without a size: foreign companies that file a different annual report (such as Baidu or Check Point) and a few companies whose earlier reports were filed under another company. These are small next to the gap that closed.

It was blocked on: point-in-time share counts summed across share classes (Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS, Alphabet after 2014)


### 2026-10-18

### 2026-10-18 (Sera 20261018-2051)

Batch decision: this method is also the exact re-run of the honest yardstick on the repaired data. Besides its own arms, it carries M0221's six versions unchanged (top 20, 50 and 100 by size, the switched top 50, the equal-weight top 50, and the blind-draw control), so the before-and-after comparison measures the data fix and nothing else. The question it answers: did the roughly 2-point-a-year gap to SPY (5 to 6 points in 2009-2015) close once Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire and Alphabet have their real size? Pre-registered prediction: the gap halves; what remains is companies with no prices at all.


### 2026-10-18

**What this was.** A re-measurement, not a new picker. The ruler from M0221 (each month, hold the biggest index members in proportion to their real company size, no name above 10% of the account, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5M IDR monthly top-up) was run again on the same prices after one data fix: company size now covers firms with more than one share class (Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS, Ford, Alphabet after 2014). M0221's six versions run unchanged, so the only difference between the two runs is the size data. A seventh version, the same top 100 at equal weight, was pre-registered in the same commit and run straight after.

**The answer: the fix was real but small. The gap to SPY barely moved.**

The 2009-2015 lead over SPY a year, on the owner's deposits (negative means behind SPY):

| version | before the fix (M0221) | after the fix (M0225) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| top 50 by size | −4.7 | −4.3 | +0.4 |
| top 100 by size | −6.3 | −5.7 | +0.6 |
| top 20 by size | −4.3 | −3.8 | +0.5 |
| top 50 behind the switch | −7.9 | −7.7 | +0.2 |
| top 50, equal weight | −2.2 | −2.0 | +0.2 |
| 50 blind picks | −2.6 | −2.6 | 0.0 |
| top 100, equal weight (new) | – | −7.1 | – |

Over the whole 1996-2015 window, on the deposits: top 50 earned 5.8% a year (was 5.6%), top 100 5.1% (was 4.8%), top 20 5.5% (was 5.2%), against 7.2% for the same deposits in SPY. The switched top 50 earned 7.9% (was 7.8%), equal-weight top 50 7.0% (was 6.9%), blind picks 6.7% (unchanged), equal-weight top 100 4.5%.

**The fee-free check.** I re-ran the top 50 and top 100 by hand on the store's prices, month-end to month-end, with no fees, no deposits and no cash, against SPY's price (the same check M0221 made). The 2009-2015 gap to SPY was about 2.7 points a year for the top 50 and about 2 for the top 100 before the fix. After it, about 2.3 and 1.6. A gain of about 0.4 points a year. I predicted the gap would shrink to about a point. It did not.

Where the gap now sits: 2009 alone is most of it. In 2009 the top 100 by size rose 17.0% against SPY's 23.5% (price only). In 2010 it trailed by 3.5 points. From 2011 to 2015 it was within about 1.5 points of SPY every year, and ahead in 2011 and 2015. The repaired names make up 5% of the top 100 in 2009, rising to 14% by 2015, so the fix mostly helps the years when the gap was already small.

**Why the fix did so little.**
1. *Most of the missing market was never missing sizes. It was missing prices.* The fix cut trading days with a price but no size from about 45,000 to about 19,000, but coverage of index member-days rose only from 62-69% to 62-75%. The store still has no prices at all for many of 2009-2015's best large companies (Celgene, Alexion, Express Scripts, Walgreens, Time Warner, DirecTV, Activision, Electronic Arts). This was the expected failure I wrote down, and it happened.
2. *Part of the 2009 gap may be real.* The 2009 rebound was led by smaller and badly beaten companies, and the biggest names lagged. Even equal weight among the top 100 trailed SPY that year (20.7% against 23.5%, fee-free). From memory, the real S&P 100 also trailed the S&P 500 in 2009 by a few points. The store has no S&P 100 fund to check that against, so I cannot split the 2009 gap between the data and the market.
3. *On the owner's deposits, the gap is bigger than the fee-free one.* The top 100 trails by 5.7 points a year funded and about 1.6 fee-free. The difference is Gotrade's fees on a hundred small orders a month, cash between deposits, and the way a money-weighted rate counts a short stretch of years. I did not split it further. The equal-weight top 100 shows the fees most plainly. Fee-free it matched SPY in 2009-2015 (11.7% a year each). On the deposits it trailed by 7.1 points, because it re-trims a hundred equal slots every month at about 0.35% an order.

**Prediction by prediction.**
- *The fee-free 2009-2015 gap shrinks to about a point a year:* failed (2.3 and 1.6).
- *C50 and C100 gain 1 to 3 points a year in 2009-2015:* failed. They gained 0.4 and 0.6.
- *About half a point a year over 1996-2015:* roughly held (0.2 to 0.3).
- *C20 gains the most:* failed. 0.5, between the top 50 and top 100. Berkshire and Meta joined the top 20 (Berkshire 7th in 2012, Meta 11th in 2014), but under a 10% ceiling, with Visa and Mastercard just outside it.
- *Equal weight and the blind control move least:* held (0.2 and 0.0). They never weighted by size, or never ranked by it.
- *The equal-weight lead over size weight shrinks to under a point:* failed for the top 50 (still 2.3 points). For the top 100 it reversed, but only because of fees.
- *The switched top 50 stays dev-eligible by sitting out 2008:* happened, as expected.

**The gate.** The switched top 50 again passed the dev screen: 7.9% a year on the deposits against SPY's 7.2%, worst fall 15.0% (bar 25%), gains 5.6 times losses (bar 1.3), and a luck score (DSR) of 0.908 at N = 148, just over the 0.90 bar. DSR is the chance the edge is real and not the best of 148 independent tries. It is not a candidate. It won 1 of 4 walk-forward periods (2006-2008, by going to cash) and trailed SPY by 7.7 points a year in 2009-2015. The hard gate refuses it on the folds, exactly as it refused M0221's twin. It is SPY with a crash brake, which the market-trend-switch family already measured. All six other versions failed "beats SPY" and the luck bar (best 0.534). Most also failed gains vs losses (bar 1.3), the blind control failed the 100-trade minimum, and the top 20 fell 55% at its worst. The amendment's version was judged at N = 149.

**Worst falls.** All unswitched versions had their worst year in 2008: −27% to −32% on the deposits. Their worst fall from a peak was 33% to 55%, against about 55% for SPY. The deposits soften those yearly numbers, because new money kept arriving into a falling market.

**The survivorship-check store** (adds prices for most of the dead members): every version earned less, by 0.5 to 1.6 points a year, and the unswitched top 50's worst fall went from 45% to 65%. The 2009-2015 gap barely changed (−4.3 to −4.9 for the top 50). The dead companies explain the flattering 1990s, not the 2009-2015 shortfall.

**What this means for the lab.** The ruler is still bent, and now we know which way. About 0.4 points a year of the 2009-2015 shortfall was missing sizes, and that is now fixed. About 1.5 to 2 points a year fee-free remains. Most of it is in 2009 and 2010, and it comes from companies the store cannot price, plus possibly a real tilt of 2009 toward smaller names. Gotrade's fees on many small monthly orders add several points a year on top of that. A member book that trails SPY by 2 points a year in 2009-2015 on this store is roughly level with what a fee-free market-shaped book can do here. A member book that trails by 5 has no such excuse.

**My opinion:** Fixing more of the size data is no longer worth it. This run shows the share-class fix was real and worth only about 0.4 points a year. The next useful step is outside the store's members: put a real fund that tracks the biggest 100 companies (the S&P 100 fund, from 2000) and the equal-weight S&P 500 fund (from 2003) in the store as yardsticks. Run this same top-100 book against them. If it tracks the S&P 100 fund within a point a year, the store is fine and the 2009 gap was the market. If not, the remaining gap is the missing prices, and only paid survivorship-free data closes it. Until then, read any member book's 2009-2015 result with this ruler's 1.5 to 2 points a year of fee-free store drag in mind, not the 2.7 measured before.


### 2026-10-18

### 2026-10-18 (Sera 20261018-2051)

Not promoted, and never meant to be: it is a ruler. Its one eligible row, the switched top 50, passed the dev screen only by sitting out 2008 and beat SPY in 1 of 4 walk-forward periods, so the hard gate refuses it. Batch finding: the size fix closed only a sliver of the gap to SPY (about 2 points a year to about 1.6 before fees in 2009-2015). The rest is companies the store has no prices for, plus fees, so every "beats SPY" in the lab still carries a store handicap of roughly a point and a half a year in that era.


### 2026-10-20

**This book finally has a fair opponent, for the first time since it was written.**

The table above puts the fifty biggest companies by size at **5.8% a year** of the owner's money
and fifty blind picks at **6.7%**, and leaves the reader to draw the obvious conclusion. This page
has never actually stated that conclusion as a shortfall, and it was right not to: the blind
opponent in that table changed hands **73 times in twenty years** against the real book's **375**,
and moved less than half as much money. It was not the same book with the idea taken out. It was a
far stiller book, and stillness is worth money here — it is barely paying any fees at all.

A fair opponent has now been drawn, and it is the first this method has ever had. It is the same
kind of blind book, with two things changed and nothing else: the number of names it replaces each
month is the real book's own number, and the sizes it holds them at are the real book's own ladder
of sizes — the largest slot, the second largest, and so on down — with the names it is newly
buying each month placed at the bottom of that ladder, where a real top-fifty puts a company that
has just climbed into it. It traded **372 times against 375**, and moved **1.01 times** as much
money. On both counts at once it is now the same shape as the book it measures.

**The reading.** The fifty biggest by size earned **5.9% a year**. The fair blind opponent earned
**9.9%**. So this book trails a blind draw of its own shape by **about 4 points a year** — not the
0.9 the old table implies, and four times further the wrong way. The blind draw also beat the
market's own total return over the same deposits, which the real book did not.

**Read that with one thing in mind, because it is probably most of the gap and it is not stock
picking.** The blind opponent holds fixed proportions and is pushed back to them every month, so
it is forever trimming whatever has risen and topping up whatever has fallen. The real book does
the opposite by construction: it lets its biggest companies grow into ever larger slots and never
trims them. Rebalancing like that is a known source of return in its own right, and this page
already shows a smaller version of it — the same fifty names held in equal slots earned more than
the same fifty held by company size. Matching how often an opponent trades, and how much money it
moves, does **not** make it a neutral opponent. Nobody should read these 4 points as evidence that
picking blindly beats picking by size, and one blind draw is in any case one sample: the
opponent's largest slot sits on a single name for twenty years. A second draw would settle how
much of the 4 points is luck, and it has not been run.

**One more thing a reader of the twin should know.** This method exists to measure a data repair
by running the same book before and after it. On today's prices that before-and-after has closed:
the unrepaired twin's book and this one now produce the identical result, to four decimal places,
because the repaired share counts are in the shared data both of them read. The difference still
recorded between the two pages is a difference between two vintages of the data, not between two
books — which is worth knowing before any pair of figures from the two pages is subtracted.

**Nothing about the method moves.** It was never a strategy; it is a ruler, and the ruler's
reading is unchanged: once multi-class companies have a size, the market-shaped book still trails
the market by about 1.6 points a year before fees in 2009-2015, and the rest is companies the data
cannot price. The gate still refuses this method, and for a reason none of this touches — it lost
most of the rolling stretches the gate re-checks it over, which it is asked before anything about
opponents is read. No test-window look was spent, and nothing here is a reason to buy anything.
methods.verdict: The data fix was real but small: once multi-class companies have a size, the market-shaped top 100 still trails SPY by about 1.6 points a year before fees in 2009-2015 (was about 2). The rest is companies the store cannot price, and fees.

methods.name: The dividend-raise lean on the whole market: every index member at its real size, not only the 50 biggest
methods.sourceRef: M0222 (raise tilt on the top-50 market-value core) and its analysis; FTSE Russell factor-tilt method; Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); M0221 (cap-weighted top-N yardstick); M0047 (a size-weighted book needs a ceiling)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1995 (dividend-change drift); tilting is index practice since about 2013. M0222 tilted the 50 biggest companies by market value toward dividend raisers; the tilt beat a random tilt of the same strength by 0.2-0.4 points a year (0.4-1.0 on the survivorship-check store), but the top-50 core trailed SPY by 1.2 points a year, so the test said nothing about whether a raise tilt can beat the market. Run M0222's allocator unchanged except for the core: every F4-screened index member with a known point-in-time market value (top=1000, past any day's member count), one class per company, weighted by market value, no company over 5%. Same score (normal-CDF of the dividend change against its own prior payments, scaled by the day's rms change, neutral 0.5, raises up, cuts down), power 1 and 2, against CORE (power 0) and RAND1/RAND2 (the day's non-neutral scores handed to hash-drawn names). All monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, target-relative band, owner's deposits, no SPY parking, no 200-day switch (M0222's switched twin lost 3 of 4 folds and trailed by 8 points in 2009-2015). Success: TILT1 or TILT2 beats total-return SPY on the owner's deposits, beats its RAND twin and CORE, and does not trail SPY in 2009-2015. Also read: does CORE now track SPY within half a point a year? Assumptions: 5% ceiling (M0047's), the tband preset so deposits reach hundreds of sub-1% weights, first payments neutral.
methods.expectedFailure: Hundreds of small orders a month at Gotrade's minimum fees cost more than the tilt earns: on the owner's 5M IDR deposits a 0.2% weight is a sub-dollar order. M0221 already showed a wider cap-weighted core trailing more, not less (top-100 +4.8% a year against top-50's +5.6% and SPY's +7.2%). About 44% of member-days have no market value (mostly members with no bars at all, the companies that later died), so the core is the survivors' market, not SPY, and in 2009-2015 it lacks some of the era's biggest winners, so CORE trails SPY by 1-3 points. The tilt's spread grows with smaller names' bigger raises and cuts, but the weight it moves sits mostly in the giants, where raises are routine, so the tilt-minus-random gap stays at tenths of a point. Ungated, every variant falls 45-55% in 2008, twice the bar. A published anomaly; any dev edge may have faded; dividend withholding tax is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

## What was tried

The last run (the dividend-raise lean on the **50 biggest** companies) found two things. The lean toward companies that just raised their dividend beat a random lean of the same strength by a few tenths of a point a year. But the 50-company base itself trailed SPY by more than a point a year, so we could not tell whether the lean could ever beat the market.

This run kept everything the same except the base:

- **The base (CORE)**: every index member the data can size on that day (shares the company had reported by then × that day's price), not just the top 50. Hundreds of companies, each weighted by its size, none allowed over 5% (it was 10% with 50 names). Where a company lists two share classes, both identical in the data, only one is kept.
- **The lean (TILT1, TILT2)**: each weight is multiplied by a score from 0 to 1. A dividend raise scores above 0.5, a cut below, no change or no dividend sits at 0.5. TILT2 squares the score, so it leans harder.
- **The random twins (RAND1, RAND2)**: the same scores each day, handed to randomly drawn companies.

All versions re-pick monthly, buy fractional shares, pay Gotrade's real fees, run on the owner's deposits (10M IDR, then 5M a month), and park nothing in SPY. No 200-day switch: last run the switch dodged 2008 but trailed SPY by 8 points a year after 2009.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, on the same deposits: **+7.2% a year**. The "check store" adds back most of the companies that later died or were bought out, which the main data cannot price.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year | check store: a year / 2009-2015 | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CORE (no lean) | +7.4% | 50.2% | −1.1 pts | +6.3% / −1.7 pts | 0.56 |
| TILT1 | +7.7% | 51.2% | −0.6 pts | +6.4% / −1.9 pts | 0.56 |
| TILT2 | +7.7% | 50.4% | −0.7 pts | +6.5% / −1.9 pts | 0.57 |
| RAND1 (random) | +7.4% | 53.2% | −0.6 pts | +6.2% / −1.4 pts | 0.52 |
| RAND2 (random) | +6.9% | 53.4% | −1.1 pts | +5.7% / −2.2 pts | 0.46 |

**On the main data, four of five versions beat SPY, by 0.2-0.6 points a year.** That is the first market-shaped book in the lab to do so without a switch. But every one fell about half its value from its peak in 2008-2009 (50-53%), which breaks even the lab's loose screen (50%) and is twice the owner's real-money limit of 25%. The worst calendar year was 2008, at −32% to −34%.

**The lead does not survive the check store.** With the dead companies put back, every version earns 1.1-1.3 points a year less and all of them trail SPY by 0.7-1.4 points. All five also trailed SPY in 2009-2015, the best-covered and most recent years, on both stores.

**Walk-forward**: TILT2 beat SPY in only 1 of 4 three-year test periods (2006-2008, by losing less in the crash). It lost 2003-2005, 2009-2011 and, by a hair, 2012-2014.

**The luck check.** The lab has now tried 150 different methods, so a result needs a DSR of at least 0.90 to count as more than luck. The best here is 0.57. A half-point lead over twenty years with a 50% fall is well inside what luck produces.

## Why

1. **A wide enough base does track the market.** The 50-company base trailed SPY by 1.2 points; the whole-market base beats it by 0.2 on the main data and trails by 0.8 on the check store. So the main data can price the market's shape almost exactly when it holds enough names, and the remaining gap is the dead companies: about a point a year, the same size the lab measured on stock-picking books. That answers the run's first question. The 50-company base's lag came mostly from being too narrow, not from fees: the whole-market book paid for about 1,250 trades over twenty years and still kept pace.
2. **The lean is real but small.** TILT2 beat its random twin by 0.8 points a year, on both stores, and TILT1 by 0.2-0.3. Against the base with no lean, the lean adds 0.1-0.3 points. That matches the last two runs: the raise signal carries a little information, and a gentle lean turns it into tenths of a point. In 2009-2015 the gentle lean (TILT1) did no better than its random twin at all.
3. **Nothing here limits the fall.** A book shaped like the market falls like the market. SPY itself fell about 55% in 2007-2009. No dividend lean changes that, and the one tool that did (the 200-day switch) cost far more after 2009 than it saved.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. Success needed a lean that beats SPY, its random twin and the base, and keeps pace in 2009-2015. On the main data TILT1 and TILT2 beat SPY, the base and (TILT2 clearly) the random twin, but both trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and the lead turns into a loss once the dead companies are back. The expected failure was half right: the fees did not eat the lean (wrong), but the lean-minus-random gap stayed small, 2009-2015 lagged, and every version fell about 50% (right). The base came closer to SPY than I expected: within 0.2 points on the main data, not 1-3 behind.

Compared with the parent (the 50-company lean), the whole-market base added 1.3-1.4 points a year to every version on the main data, and about the same on the check store. The breadth was worth more than any lean.

## My opinion:

As a way to beat SPY, this direction is done: a market-shaped book with a dividend lean is SPY plus a few tenths of a point that the dead companies take back, with SPY's own 50% fall. I would not run more lean strengths on it. What this run is good for is a ruler: the main data can price the whole market's shape to within a fifth of a point, and its survivorship gap is about a point a year. That means any stock-picking book whose lead over SPY is under a point is probably the missing dead companies, and every future method should be judged with that in mind. The one follow-up worth a single run is the strong lean (TILT2 beat its random twin by 0.8 points on both stores) behind a fall control that does not sell into dips the way the 200-day switch does: scale the whole book down when the market's own recent swings are wide, and back up as they calm. If even that trails SPY after 2009, the dividend-raise family should be closed.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a dividend-raise lean on every index company at its real size beat SPY by half a point a year on the main data, but lost it once the dead companies were put back, trailed after 2009, and fell 50% in 2008

methods.name: Companies shrinking their share count: buy the index members that bought back the most stock over the past year
methods.sourceRef: Pontiff & Woodgate (2008) JF 63(2) 921-945, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v63y2008i2p921-945.html; Daniel & Titman (2006) composite issuance; McLean & Pontiff (2016) decay
methods.hypothesis: Firms that reduce their shares outstanding (buybacks) beat firms that issue shares, a published effect (Pontiff and Woodgate 2008; Daniel and Titman 2006) the lab can test only now that the store carries point-in-time share counts from SEC filings (from 1996, per listed class from 2009). Each month, for every index member with a bar that day, compare the share count public today with the one public 365 days ago, carried across splits, and score the log change; skip a member whose two figures were counted under 180 days apart or whose ratio sits within 3% of a common split ratio (a missed split) or outside 0.5-3.0 (a units error in a filing), and keep one listing per company. Book: the 20 biggest shrinkers, equal slots, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up (monthly-hold-frac-gotrade). Arms: S20 (no switch), S20-SW (behind the SPY 200-day switch), S40 (the 40 biggest shrinkers, broader and closer to the market), I20 (the 20 biggest issuers, the opposite book) and R20 (20 names from the same scored pool in a fixed hash order: the placebo of the same size). Window: 1997-2015 (a year of counts first). Predictions written before any result: S20 beats I20 by 2 or more points a year and beats R20; S20 beats total-return SPY over 1997-2015 by a point or two, mostly from 2000-2008 when issuers (the dot-com offerings) collapsed; in 2009-2015 the gap over SPY shrinks to about zero.
