methods.expectedFailure: Four ways, in order of likelihood. (1) The buyback tilt is a disguised big-mature-company tilt that tracks SPY with an equal-weight drag, so S20 lands near R20 and both lag SPY after 2009 -- the lab's usual 2009-2015 shortfall -- and the issuer book is the only one that differs (it lags). (2) Data, not markets: share-count gaps sit on the firms the store cannot see (the dead ones, which were disproportionately heavy issuers), so I20 looks better than it was and the shrink-minus-issue spread is understated; a split the guard does not catch (a 5-for-4, say) puts a false issuer or shrinker in the book now and then. (3) The 2008 fall: shrinkers in 2007-2008 included the banks that bought back stock right before collapsing, so without the switch the worst fall is near SPY's and breaks the 20% limit. (4) Decay: the anomaly was public from 2006-2008 and buybacks became the default way for US companies to return cash, so the signal is crowded by 2010 and the 2009-2015 era shows nothing. Any of these is a rejection; none is a reason to tune the 365-day window or the guards afterwards.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-18

## What was tried

Companies that buy back their own stock shrink their share count. Companies that sell new stock
grow it. A 2008 paper (Pontiff and Woodgate) found the shrinkers beat the issuers. The lab could
not test this before 2026-10-17, because it had no share counts. Now it does.

Each month the book compared every index member's share count with its count a year earlier,
corrected for stock splits. It held the 20 that shrank the most, in equal slots, in fractional
shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly top-up. Five versions:

- **S20**: the 20 biggest shrinkers.
- **S20-SW**: the same, but it holds cash whenever SPY is below its 200-day average (the "switch").
- **S40**: the 40 biggest shrinkers.
- **I20**: the 20 biggest *issuers*, the opposite book.
- **R20**: 20 names drawn at random from the same pool, as a luck control.

One thing was fixed before the run, after a check of pool sizes only (no returns were read): a
handful of filings were off by a factor of a thousand. A share count stated in thousands one year
and in units the next looks like a 99.9% buyback. Any one-year change outside half to triple is
skipped as a units error.

## Result

The "money earned a year" figures below count each deposit from the day it was paid in. SPY on the
same deposits earned **+7.2% a year** over 1996-2015.

| version | earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S20 shrinkers | +13.0% | 58.7% | 2.66 | 0.853 |
| **S20-SW shrinkers + switch** | **+10.3%** | **25.8%** | 2.43 | **0.937** |
| S40 shrinkers | +11.2% | 59.2% | 2.76 | 0.758 |
| I20 issuers | +9.2% | 72.7% | 1.94 | 0.404 |
| R20 random | +7.7% | 65.1% | 1.47 | 0.448 |

**S20-SW passed every dev-window condition and is marked dev-eligible.** It beat SPY by about 3
points a year. Its worst fall was 25.8%, under the lab's screen. That fall is just *over* the 25%
real-money bar in design §1, so it would not clear that bar as measured here.

**Luck test.** DSR is the chance the result is real rather than the best of many lucky tries. The
lab has made N = 149 distinct tries, and the bar is 0.90. S20-SW scored 0.937, so it clears. The
other four versions do not.

**The ordering came out the way the paper predicted.** Shrinkers (+13.0%) beat the random draw
(+7.7%), and the random draw roughly matched SPY. The issuers (+9.2%) sat in between and had the
deepest fall, 73%. Shrinkers beat issuers by about 3.8 points a year, above the 2 points predicted.

## Where it is weak

- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4 periods won.** This check picks a version using only earlier years, then
  scores it on later years it has not seen. It won 2003-05 (+80% vs +52%) and 2012-14 (+79% vs
  +66%). It lost 2006-08 (−28% vs −25%) and 2009-11 (+38% vs +61%). In 2009-11 the switch kept it
  in cash through the rebound. The promotion gate needs a majority of periods, so **`lab promote`
  will refuse this method.** That is the gate working, not a bug.
- **2009-2015 is split.** These are the best-covered years. The book without the switch led SPY by
  +3.8% a year (S20) and +4.2% (S40). The switched version *lagged* by 4.0% a year: the switch
  costs more in a steady bull market than the 2008 fall it saved. So the signal itself held up in
  the best-covered years, but the one eligible version did not.
- **Missing companies.** The lab re-ran everything on a check history that adds back most of the
  companies that died or left the index. On it S20 earns +11.8% (was +13.0%) and S20-SW +9.6% (was
  +10.3%). S20-SW's luck score drops to 0.895, just under the bar. The big change is the
  *issuers*: they jump from +9.2% to +12.7%, driven by a few huge winners among the added names
  (skew 4.5). On the fuller history **the shrinker-over-issuer gap mostly disappears.** The
  shrinkers still beat SPY and the random draw, but the "issuers lose" half of the story does not
  survive.
- **Narrow vs broad markets.** Every version made its money in months when most stocks moved
  together. In months when a few giants carried the index, every version lost to SPY, by 7 to 14
  points a year. That is the equal-slot handicap the lab sees everywhere.

## Why it might work

A buyback means management thinks the stock is cheap and has the spare cash to act on it. It also
returns cash that would otherwise be spent on empire-building. Issuers often sell stock when it is
expensive: the dot-com offerings, and acquisitions paid in stock. Before 2009 the issuers' fall was
the clearest part of the effect. After that, buybacks became routine for large US companies, so a
shrinking share count says less about any one company.

## Hypothesis vs result

- Held: shrinkers beat issuers by more than 2 points and beat the random draw. The switch cut the
  2008 fall a lot (to 26% from 59%).
- Did not hold as predicted: the switch did not get the fall under 20%, and it cost about 4 points
  a year in 2009-15.
- Expected failure (1), a disguised big-company tilt: partly. The random draw tracked SPY and the
  shrinkers clearly beat it, so the signal is more than a tilt. But all versions trail in
  narrow-market months.
- Expected failure (2), data holes: yes, in a direction I did not expect. Adding the missing
  companies helped the issuers, not hurt them.
- Expected failure (3), the 2008 fall: yes. Without the switch the worst fall is 59%.
- Expected failure (4), decay after publication: no. The plain book led SPY by about 4 points a
  year in 2009-15.

## My opinion

This is one of the more honest results the lab has produced. The random control matched SPY, the
real signal beat it, and the plain shrinker book kept its lead in the best-covered years. But the
one version that passes the gate does so only because of the 200-day switch. The switch is exactly
what lost the 2009-11 period and made the walk-forward a coin flip. I would not promote this, and
the gate will not let me. The direction is worth more trials, aimed at the fall rather than the
pick. Keep the plain shrinker signal, and control the fall with something that does not sit out
whole rebounds: a weight ceiling plus a book that is half SPY, or a faster exit than the 200-day
line. Also try the shrinker filter inside a book shaped by company size, so it stops fighting the
big-company drift. I would not spend effort on the issuer side. The fuller history says that half
of the story was partly a hole in the data.


### 2026-10-18

### 2026-10-18 (Sera 20261018-2051)

Not promoted. The switched buyback book passed the dev screen, but the lab's hard gate refuses it: the version picked from earlier years beat SPY in only 2 of the 4 walk-forward periods, and a strict majority is required. No test-window look was spent. The family is clean (nothing in it has failed a look), so the follow-up, half SPY and half the biggest shrinkers, is free to run.


## Correction, 2026-10-20 — the random draw this page compares against barely traded

The comparison above is withdrawn. It is not wrong about which book won; it is wrong about by how
much, and the reason is the opponent.

The random draw quoted at +7.7% a year held its names almost permanently. Set beside the shrinker
book it is meant to blind-test, it traded 41 times against 608 and turned over about an eighth as
much. That is not a blind version of this book. It is a different and far cheaper strategy, and it
escaped a fee bill the shrinker book pays in full.

Drawn honestly — the same pool, the same switch, the same twenty slots, and its churn matched
month by month to what the shrinker book actually does — the blind draw earns **+9.1% a year**
rather than +7.7%, while trading within one percent of the shrinker book on both counts. So the
lead falls from about **5.2 points a year to about 3.9**.

**The honest draw earned MORE, not less, and that was predicted the other way round.** This
amendment said in advance that a control trading fifteen times as often would be dragged down by
fifteen times the fees and the lead would widen past 5.2 points. It did the opposite. The extra
fees were real and the draw still came out ahead of them, so the gap between this book and a blind
one was never as much about fees as the page assumed. The prediction is reported as it landed and
not re-drawn.

**What this does not change.** Buying the companies that shrink their own share count still beats
an equally busy blind draw from the same pool, and still beats the market. What changes is the
size, and one more thing worth seeing: the honest blind draw also beats the market, at +9.1%
against +7.2%. So roughly two of the shrinker book's points over the market come from the frame it
sits in — the pool and the safety switch — and not from picking shrinkers at all.

No verdict moves. This was found by re-drawing every handicapped control in the lab on 2026-10-19
and 2026-10-20, and the sentence that the shrinkers beat the random draw by five points a year
should not be quoted again.
methods.verdict: Buyback shrinkers beat SPY and a random draw; the switched version passes dev, but wins only 2 of 4 test periods and the issuers-lose half fades with dead companies added

methods.name: Buyback shrinkers as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: half SPY, half the 20 biggest share-count shrinkers, no 200-day switch
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0227 (S20 as the sleeve); Pontiff & Woodgate (2008) JF 63(2) 921-945, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v63y2008i2p921-945.html; core-satellite shape of P7a F9, M0030 and M0096
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008. M0227's plain shrinker book (the 20 index members whose split-adjusted share count fell most over a year) earned +13.0% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's +7.2% and beat both its opposite book and its hash-drawn placebo, but fell 58.7% in 2008; only the arm behind the SPY 200-day switch passed the dev screen, and that arm sat out the 2009-11 rebound and lost 2 of 4 walk-forward folds. Replace the timing with a market core: hold a fixed share of equity in SPY -- which owns the mega-caps an equal-weight book never does and never steps out of a recovery -- and run M0227's sleeve on the rest, monthly, fractional, at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's top-up, with the rebalance band measured against each holding's own target (the tband preset) so halving the parent's 5% slots to 2.5% does not also halve how often they are rebalanced. Arms: C50 (50% SPY, equal slots: the idea as reserved), C70 and C30 (the same at 70% and 30%, the dose-response), C50-SZ (50% SPY with the shrinkers weighted by real point-in-time market value, capped at 10% of the sleeve, so no shrinker weighs over twice an equal slot), C50-R (50% SPY with M0227's hash-drawn placebo in the sleeve: the same frame, names that know nothing about buybacks) and C50-SWS (50% SPY always held, the SPY-200 switch emptying the sleeve alone). Predictions written before any result. (1) The lead: C50 beats total-return SPY on the deposits by 2 to 3 points a year, roughly half the parent's 5.8-point lead, and C70 and C30 land near 1.5 and 4 points -- a lead that scales with the sleeve is the signal surviving dilution rather than a frame effect. (2) C50 beats C50-R by 1.5 points or more; if it does not, the half-SPY frame is doing the work. (3) The fall, stated against the reserved idea's own guess of 35-40%, which is arithmetically unavailable: the sleeve and SPY fell 59% and 55% in the same months for the same reason, so C50 falls about 55-57% and C70 and C30 both land near 55% too. Every ungated arm breaks the 20% bar; that is expected, pre-registered, and not a surprise to be explained afterwards. (4) The real question: 2009-2015 and the folds. The core should lift the 2009-2015 era above the parent's switched arm and win 3 of 4 walk-forward folds, because the one fold the switch lost outright (2009-11, +38% against SPY's +61%) was lost to cash, and a core that never leaves cannot lose it that way. (5) C50-SWS is the only arm that can reach the 20% bar: its fall should be near 30% (half of SPY's 55% plus a sleeve that leaves), still over the bar, and it should lose the 2009-11 fold less badly than the parent did. Success is (2) and (4) together: the signal survives dilution and the core buys back the folds. Success on (1) alone, with the folds still lost, is a rejection.
methods.expectedFailure: Five ways, in order of likelihood. (1) Dilution without repair: the core halves the lead and halves nothing else, so C50 lands near +10% a year with a 56% fall, still loses the 2006-08 fold, and the fold record does not move -- the switch was not what lost 2006-08, the 2008 crash was, and a core that holds SPY through it loses it too. Then the method is a worse M0227 and the family is out of ideas that do not involve timing. (2) The frame is the result: C50-R lands within half a point of C50 because half an account in SPY dominates twenty 2.5% slots, the buyback signal is no longer visible through it, and the method measures the core rather than the idea. (3) Size weighting makes it worse: M0047 and M0201 both measured that weighting picks by company size costs 2.5-3.3 points a year and does not soften the fall, and a 10% sleeve ceiling on 20 names is a weak brake, so C50-SZ should trail C50; it is here as a measurement, and if it wins it wins against two prior readings and deserves suspicion, not a variation. (4) Survivorship: M0227's shrink-minus-issue spread already faded once the dead companies were put back, and half of this book is SPY, which the check store prices correctly, so the check store should cut the lead by roughly half of whatever it cut from the parent -- and if the parent's whole lead was missing dead companies, this one's is too. (5) Decay: the anomaly was public from 2006-2008, buybacks became the default way US companies return cash, and the dev window's best-covered years are exactly the post-publication ones. An edge that is all pre-2009 is a dead edge whatever the twenty-year average says. None of these is a reason to tune the core share, the ceiling or the 365-day window afterwards.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What was tried

Companies that buy back their own shares beat the market in the lab's previous test (the buyback
book, M0227): it earned 13.0% a year on the owner's deposits where SPY earned 7.2%. But it fell
58.7% in 2008. The only version that passed the lab's screen was the one that sold everything
whenever the market was below its 200-day average — and that version sat out the 2009-11 recovery
and won only two of the four test periods.

So the timing rule was the problem. This method removes it and replaces it with something that
never steps out of a recovery: hold a fixed slice of the account in SPY itself, and run the same
buyback picks on the rest. SPY owns the giant companies that an equal-slot 20-stock book never
holds, and it is always invested.

Six versions, all monthly, all in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, all on the owner's
5 million rupiah monthly top-up:

- **C70, C50, C30** — 70%, 50% and 30% of the account in SPY, the rest in the 20 biggest buyback
  companies in equal slots. Nothing is ever timed.
- **C50-SZ** — half SPY, half buyback companies, but those weighted by company size instead of
  equally, with no single company over a tenth of that half.
- **C50-R** — the control. Half SPY, half twenty names drawn from the same pool by a fixed
  shuffle that knows nothing about buybacks. If this matches C50, the SPY half is doing the work.
- **C50-SWS** — half SPY held always, and the 200-day rule emptying only the buyback half.

## Result

All six failed. None is dev-eligible. The figures below count each deposit from the day it was
paid in; SPY on the same deposits earned **+7.2% a year** over 1996-2015.

| version | buyback half | earned a year | vs SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C70 | 30% | +8.6% | +1.4 | 52.0% | 2.76 | 0.654 |
| C50 | 50% | +9.7% | +2.5 | 55.1% | 2.71 | 0.730 |
| C30 | 70% | +11.0% | +3.8 | 56.7% | 2.66 | 0.797 |
| C50-SZ | 50%, by size | +8.8% | +1.6 | 52.6% | 2.53 | 0.656 |
| **C50-R (control)** | 50%, shuffled | **+7.1%** | **−0.1** | 59.9% | 1.47 | 0.463 |
| C50-SWS | 50% + timing | +8.5% | +1.3 | 33.3% | 2.44 | 0.820 |

**Every version broke the drawdown limit.** The owner's bar is a 20% worst fall. Even the lab's
looser internal screen is 50%, and five of the six broke that too. Only the timed version got
anywhere near sane, at 33.3%, and that is still well over the bar.

**The luck test.** DSR asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of many lucky
tries. The lab has now made **N = 154** distinct tries, and the bar is **0.90** — the owner's
setting since 2026-10-07, and not mine to move. The best score here was 0.820 (C50-SWS). Nothing
came close.

## What the method proved, and it is not nothing

**The buyback signal is real, and it adds up in proportion.** The lead over SPY scaled almost
perfectly with how much of the account was in buyback companies:

| buyback half | 30% | 50% | 70% | 100% (the parent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lead over SPY | +1.4 | +2.5 | +3.8 | +5.8 |

That is a straight line through four points. A result that appears only at one setting is usually
an accident; a result that grows in step with the dose is usually a mechanism. The prediction
written before the run was "about 1.5, 2.5 and 4 points", which is what came out.

**This ladder is the load-bearing evidence, and it needs no control to read.** The three versions
are the same machinery, the same fees and the same monthly re-pick, differing only in how much of
the account sits in buyback companies. If the SPY half were producing the lead, *more* SPY would
mean *more* lead. The opposite happens, every step of the way. And the versions that earned more
also traded more (turnover 1.08, 1.76 and 2.43 a year), so they paid higher fees to do it. Neither
the SPY half nor cheap trading can explain the ladder.

**The shuffled control, and an honest limit on what it proves.** C50-R — the same book with the
names shuffled — earned **+7.1% a year, slightly behind SPY's 7.2%**, with a far worse ratio of
gains to losses (1.47 against 2.71). But this control is weaker than it first appears, and the
tell is its trade count: **41 trades against C50's 608.**

The reason is that the shuffle is drawn once and never re-drawn. Its running order is a fixed hash
of the company's name with no date in it, so the control holds the same twenty names for twenty
years and only trades when one leaves the eligible pool. It is a *sticky* placebo, the kind the lab
has used before as M0193, and not the kind that re-draws each period, which is M0187. It was
inherited unchanged from the parent method's control, which has the identical 41 trades — and that
should have been caught when the arm was written, not afterwards.

So the gap between C50 and C50-R is picking **plus** the difference between re-picking monthly and
holding a fixed twenty. How much is that second term worth? It was measured rather than guessed.
At this method's turnover, Gotrade's real fees cost $11,300 over the window — 8.1% of gross trading
profit, and 0.3 percentage points of yearly return against a flat-fee assumption. The control
trades at roughly a seventh of that turnover, so it saves something in the region of a third to
half a point a year in fees.

**That runs against C50, not for it.** The control is the cheaper book, and C50 beat it by 2.6
points a year anyway, while paying the higher fee bill. So 2.6 points is a floor on what the
picking was worth, not a ceiling. What cannot be claimed from this control is that the SPY frame
contributed exactly nothing — sticky-versus-re-picked was never isolated. The ladder above is what
carries that conclusion; the control is consistent with it and no more.

## Where it failed, and why

**The fall. The idea as reserved predicted a worst fall "near 35-40%"; this was flagged as
arithmetically impossible before the run, and it was.** You cannot diversify away a fall by mixing
two things that fall at the same time for the same reason. The buyback book fell 59% in 2008 and
SPY fell 55%, in the same months. A half-and-half book falls about 56%, and C50 fell 55.1%. The
averaging works on the return; it does not work on the fall.

**The test periods: still 2 of 4, the same as the parent.** The lab trains on early years, picks a
version, and scores it on years it has never seen. This won 2003-05 and 2012-14, and lost 2006-08
and 2009-11 — exactly the parent's record.

But *how* it lost is informative, and this is the one number worth keeping:

| period | parent (timed) | this method | SPY |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2006-08 | −28% | −26.9% | −24.6% |
| 2009-11 | +38% | +47.0% | +60.8% |

In the 2009-11 recovery the parent trailed SPY by 23 points. The market core cut that to 13.8
points — it recovered about **40% of what the timing rule threw away**. That is the core doing
precisely the job it was given. It simply was not enough: the timing rule throws away more in a
rebound than a half-sized core can win back. And 2006-08 barely moved (−3 points of shortfall
became −2.3), which confirms the prediction written before the run — **2006-08 was lost to the
2008 crash, not to the timing rule**, and a core that holds SPY through the crash loses it too.

**The timed version is strictly worse than the parent's timed version.** Holding the core through
the crash instead of stepping fully out cost on every axis at once:

| | parent's timed book | this method's C50-SWS |
|---|---|---|
| earned a year | +10.3% | +8.5% |
| worst fall | 25.8% | 33.3% |
| luck test | 0.937 | 0.820 |

So "stay half invested during the timing signal" is a clearly measured dead end. If you are going
to use the 200-day rule at all, stepping all the way out beats stepping half out.

**And a second method found the same thing today, by a different route.** M0230's staged-re-entry
method (M0136) tested coming back into the market halfway first, on a book holding nothing but
SPY. It found that staging the re-entry closes only 11-15% of the gap in the 2009-2015 years, where
changing *when* the signal fires closes 43%. Two different methods, two different mechanisms, one
answer: **when you are out of the market, what matters is the trigger, not how much you hold.
Partial exposure loses to all-or-nothing.** Nobody should spend a third method id proving it again.

**Size weighting cost money again.** C50-SZ earned 0.9 points a year less than the equal-slot C50
and cut the fall only from 55.1% to 52.6%. That is the third independent reading in this lab
(after M0047 and M0201) that weighting picks by company size costs return without buying safety.
The prediction said it would trail; it did. Note this arm leans on the lab's market-value figure,
which is only trustworthy because the store's split list was rebuilt today (below) — without it
that number mixes today's share count with split-adjusted old prices.

**Narrow markets.** Every version, the control included, "pays only in broad markets" — it earns
when most shares rise together and loses when a few giants carry the index. That fragility scales
with the buyback half exactly as the lead does (−4.4% narrow at a 30% half, −9.9% at a 70% half),
so the core does buy narrow-market protection, proportionally. The years since 2015 have been the
narrowest in memory, which is the standing reason to distrust every lead in the table above.

## With the dead companies put back

The lab keeps a second copy of history that includes the companies that went bankrupt or were
bought — the ones the main data set simply cannot see. Re-running all six versions there is the
honest test of whether an edge was real or was just the survivors flattering themselves. Every
re-run reproduced its recorded result first, so the comparison is sound.

| version | lead over SPY, main data | with dead companies | 2009-2015 lead, honest data |
|---|---|---|---|
| C70 | +1.4 | +0.9 | −0.1 |
| C50 | +2.5 | +1.9 | **+1.1** |
| C30 | +3.8 | +2.9 | **+2.1** |
| C50-SZ | +1.6 | +1.3 | −0.4 |
| C50-R (control) | −0.1 | +0.2 | +0.3 |
| C50-SWS (timed) | +1.3 | +1.1 | **−2.6** |

Three things worth keeping.

**The edge shrinks but does not vanish.** Each real-pick version gave back 0.3 to 0.9 points a year
when the dead companies came back. That is the expected size and was predicted before the run.

**The ladder survives the honest data.** +0.9, +1.9, +2.9 for a 30%, 50% and 70% buyback half —
still a straight line, still in the right order. The buyback effect is not an artefact of missing
companies.

**And here the hypothesis actually won its real argument.** The whole point of this method was that
removing the 200-day timing rule should repair the 2009-2015 years, which are the best-measured and
the most like today. It did. The untimed versions keep a *positive* 2009-2015 lead even on the
honest data (+1.1 and +2.1), where the timed version is at **−2.6**. Removing the timing rule
repaired exactly what it was supposed to repair.

That makes the failure sharper, not softer. The untimed book earns its keep in the modern era and
is destroyed by its 55% fall; the timed book survives the fall and is destroyed by the modern era.
Nothing on offer here is both.

**One more thing the fold record was hiding.** The lab picks each test period's version by MAR —
return divided by worst fall — which structurally prefers the low-drawdown timed version. So for
the 2009-11 and 2012-14 periods the selection rule chose C50-SWS, the one arm with a negative
2009-2015 edge. The fold record did not improve partly because the rule kept choosing the version
this method was built to replace.

## A note on the data, because it nearly stopped this run

The lab's copy of the market had lost the two files that record how many shares each company had
and when stocks split. All three copies had lost them, and the day-old work that built them was
gone. Nothing was broken visibly — prices and every past result were intact — and the only alarm
was this method being refused, because it asked for company size and the lab correctly declined to
measure a hole in the data instead of the idea. Nothing was spent by that refusal. The files were
rebuilt from SEC filings and a fresh split list (539 of 539 companies, no failures), and the
rebuild was checked: Apple reads $629B, Berkshire $321B and Meta $253B at the end of September
2015, which are the right magnitudes, and **the price fingerprint did not move**, so every earlier
result in the lab remains comparable with these.

One check worth recording, because getting it wrong would quietly double a company's weight in the
size-weighted version. Before 2014, Google was listed twice under two ticker symbols, and both
lines report the *whole* company: on the last day of 2007 each reads $216.3 billion on an identical
share count. A book that weighted by company size and took both lines would hold Google at twice
its real size. The buyback method this one is built on keeps only one listing per identical share
count, and this method reuses that code unchanged, so the company is held once. It was checked
rather than assumed.

## Hypothesis vs result

- **Held:** the lead scaled with the dose, almost exactly as predicted (+1.4 / +2.5 / +3.8), and
  the ladder survived the honest data (+0.9 / +1.9 / +2.9).
- **Held, with a caveat found after the run:** the shuffled control failed to beat SPY, so the
  expected failure "the frame is the result" did not happen. But that control is sticky rather
  than re-drawn, so it under-tests the frame; the dose-response ladder, not the control, is what
  establishes that the picks earned the lead.
- **Held:** the fall landed at 55.1%, as written before the run, not the 35-40% the idea guessed.
- **Held:** size weighting trailed equal slots, as the two prior readings said it would.
- **Held:** 2006-08 was lost to the 2008 crash, not to the timing rule.
- **Held:** the dead companies cost 0.3 to 0.9 points a year, the predicted size.
- **Held, and this was the point of the method:** removing the timing rule repaired the 2009-2015
  years. The untimed versions lead by +1.1 and +2.1 there even on the honest data, where the timed
  version is at −2.6.
- **Did not hold:** the core did not win back a majority of the test periods. It recovered 40% of
  the 2009-11 shortfall and that was not enough. By the success rule written before the run —
  "success on the lead alone, with the periods still lost, is a rejection" — this is a rejection.

## My opinion

Reject this method, and I would not run another variation of this shape. But this run is more
useful than most rejections, because it split one problem into two and solved one of them.

**What is established.** The buyback signal is real, it is additive, and it is not an artefact of
missing dead companies — a four-point dose-response ladder that stays monotone on both data sets
says so, without needing a control to lean on. And removing the market-timing rule genuinely fixed
the modern era: untimed, this book leads SPY by 1 to 2 points a year in 2009-2015 on honest data,
where every timed version of it trails by 2.6. That was the method's actual thesis and it is the
one thing that came out right.

**What is closed.** Using SPY as the brake. The core cannot fix the fall, because the fall is the
2008 crash and SPY was in it — this was arithmetic before it was a measurement. Also closed:
half-timing. Stepping half out of the market is worse than stepping all the way out on return, on
fall, and on the luck test simultaneously, and a second method today reached the same conclusion
from the opposite direction. And a third reading now says weighting picks by company size costs
money without buying safety.

**What is left.** Exactly one problem, now cleanly isolated: this book earns its keep in the modern
era and falls 55% doing it. The fall is not a market-timing problem and it is not a weighting
problem — it is a *concentration* problem. In 2007-08 the biggest buyers of their own stock were
banks buying back shares immediately before they collapsed. A screen that ranks only on share-count
change will load up on one industry at exactly the wrong moment, and no amount of SPY beside it
helps, because SPY was falling too.

So the next thing to try is a cap on how much of the book can sit in one industry at once, inside
the picking rather than beside it. That is queued. I would also test the buyback signal as a tilt
on a book that is already shaped like the market, since this run proves the signal survives
dilution intact.

I would not spend another method on the core share, the ceiling, or the length of the lookback.
Those are dials, and this run swept one of them across four settings and got a straight line —
which means there is no setting of it that passes.
methods.verdict: Rejected: half SPY plus the biggest buyback companies beat SPY by 2.5 points a year and the buyback effect is real and survives the dead companies, but the book still fell 55% in 2008 and won only 2 of 4 test periods; a market core cannot brake a crash it is sitting in

methods.name: The strong dividend-raise lean on the whole market, turned down when the market's own swings are wide instead of switched off under the 200-day average
methods.hypothesis: M0226's squared raise lean on every sized index member beat its random twin by 0.8 points a year on both stores and SPY by 0.6 on dev, but fell 50% in 2008 and trailed SPY in 2009-2015; M0222's 200-day switch cut the fall to 19% but cost 8 points a year after 2009 by selling into dips. Scale the whole TILT2 book by a target volatility on SPY's own recent daily swings (e.g. 63-day, target 14%, capped at 100% invested, the rest in cash), checked monthly, so it de-risks gradually in calm-to-wild transitions rather than flipping on a price average. Same RAND2 twin under the same scaling. Expected failure: volatility peaks after the fall starts, so the scaling cuts late in 2008 and stays out of the 2009 rebound; the deposit flow and fees still make it a market-shaped book with a few tenths of a lean, and the dead companies take back about a point.

methods.name: Risk pays only near the high: the most volatile stocks among those closest to their 52-week high
methods.sourceRef: Chen, Chen, Tu, Wang & Wang (2026), 'Proximity to the 52-week high and the risk-return trade-off', Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control, S0165188926000321; reserved by Sera 20261019-0720; frame of M0015, placebo of M0187
methods.hypothesis: The paper finds a POSITIVE risk-return relation among stocks near their 52-week high and a NEGATIVE one among stocks far below it: investors anchor on the high, turning risk-seeking when the price is far below it (overpaying for volatile losers) and risk-averse when it is near (underpaying for volatile winners). That implies a conditional double sort this lab has never run: proximity first, risk second, with the sign of the risk tilt flipping between the two groups. Arms, all twenty equal slots, monthly, behind the shared SPY 200-day switch, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, drawn from the index members that pass F4's liquidity screen: NEAR-HIVOL, the twenty highest 60-session volatility names inside the top fifth by price-to-52-week-high ratio; NEAR-LOVOL, the same group's calmest twenty, the within-group control the paper says should lose; FAR-LOVOL, the calmest twenty inside the bottom fifth by proximity, the other side of the paper's claim; FAR-HIVOL, its control; NEAR-ALL, the twenty nearest their high across the whole pool, which is M0015-N20's ranking re-measured at real fees; and PLC1, a same-frame fixed-random-order placebo. The lab already knows plain 52-week-high proximity (M0015, MAR 0.58) and already knows that high-volatility picks lose outright (stock-lottery-avoidance, best MAR 0.45), so the whole question is whether CONDITIONING the risk tilt on proximity turns a losing signal into a winning one. SUCCESS: NEAR-HIVOL beats NEAR-LOVOL by 3 or more points a year, beats the placebo by 2, keeps a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015, and its worst fall stays under the dev screen; FAR-LOVOL beating FAR-HIVOL confirms the sign flip rather than a plain volatility effect.
methods.expectedFailure: NEAR-HIVOL only matches the placebo and FAR-LOVOL beats everything, which would mean the paper's effect is a small-cap long-short result that does not survive a large-cap long-only book at real fees, and the 52-week-high family should be closed. The mechanisms behind that: the high-volatility half of any cross-section in this universe is the lab's lottery-avoidance finding in disguise, and twenty of the most volatile names in any fifth is the deepest-falling book the frame can build, so NEAR-HIVOL most likely clears the dev screen on return and breaks it on the worst fall; and nearness ties at 1.0 in a strong market push the momentum tiebreak into the band definition, so the near band may quietly become a momentum band. The paper is dated 2026 but the anchoring effect it rests on has been published since 2004, so expect the dev window to flatter it and 2009-2015 to be the honest read. Check the survivorship-check store before concluding: the most volatile names are exactly where the dead companies the dev store cannot price are hiding, so NEAR-HIVOL and FAR-HIVOL should lose the most there.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What we tried

A 2026 paper (Chen, Chen, Tu, Wang and Wang) makes an unusual claim. It says risk does not pay
or fail to pay as a rule — it depends on where a stock sits against its own highest price of the
past year. Investors anchor on that high. When a stock is far below it they feel they are in a
hole, turn into gamblers, and overpay for the wild names; so wildness is punished there. When a
stock is sitting near its high they feel they have something to lose, turn cautious, and underpay
for the wild names; so wildness is rewarded there. Same measure, opposite sign, depending on the
group.

That is a claim this lab could test directly and never had. Both halves of it had already lost
here on their own: picking stocks purely for being near their yearly high (the "near the high"
picker) earned about what the index earned, and buying the wildest stocks outright has never
worked in this lab. So the whole question was whether **combining** the two — sort by proximity
first, then by wildness inside each group — turns two losing signals into a winning one.

Six versions, all fixed in writing before the run, all identical except for how they choose:
20 stocks, equal slots, reconsidered monthly, all in cash whenever SPY is below its 200-day
average, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's real 5 million rupiah monthly
top-up. Each month the eligible, liquid index members are ranked by how close they are to their
yearly high and cut into five equal groups.

| Version | What it holds | Your money earned | Worst fall | Gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NEAR-HIVOL** | the 20 wildest in the group **nearest** their high | **+10.0% a year** | 23.5% | 1.55 |
| FAR-LOVOL | the 20 calmest in the group **furthest below** their high | +8.3% | 38.5% | 1.66 |
| FAR-HIVOL | the 20 wildest in that same far group | +7.1% | 40.9% | 1.31 |
| PLC1 (placebo) | 20 names drawn at random from the same pool | +6.9% | 23.6% | 1.37 |
| NEAR-ALL | the 20 nearest their high, no wildness sort | +6.1% | 21.0% | 1.36 |
| NEAR-LOVOL | the 20 calmest in the group nearest their high | +4.9% | 39.7% | 1.47 |

The same deposits put into SPY with dividends reinvested earned **+7.2% a year**.

## The paper's claim held. Both halves of it.

This is the rare case where a published effect reproduced in this lab, in sign, on both sides:

- **Near the high, wild beat calm by 5.1 points a year** (+10.0% against +4.9%). We had promised
  beforehand to call it a hit only at 3 points or more. It cleared that.
- **Far below the high, calm beat wild by 1.2 points a year** (+8.3% against +7.1%). The sign
  flipped, exactly as the paper says it should. Weakly, but in the right direction.
- NEAR-HIVOL also beat the meaningless placebo by 3.1 points a year, where we had asked for 2.
  So this is not the trend switch and the liquidity screen doing all the work, which is the trap
  three earlier batches in this lab fell into.

NEAR-HIVOL also passed four of the owner's five go-live conditions outright: it beat SPY, its
worst fall of 23.5% stayed inside the 25% limit, its gains outweighed its losses 1.55 to 1, and it
traded 2,407 times. It failed one condition — the luck test.

## Why it is still a rejection

**The luck test.** DSR asks how likely it is that a result is real skill rather than the best of
many tries. NEAR-HIVOL scored **0.765**, where the owner's bar is **0.90**. The lab has now looked
at 153 distinct methods (that is the N the luck gate uses; the lab counts one look per method,
not per version). Roughly: about a 1-in-4 chance this is a lucky draw out of 153 tries. That is
too high for real money and the bar is not ours to move.

**And the luck test was right.** Here is the twenty years cut into three eras, measured on the
book alone with the monthly deposits stripped out, so a top-up never reads as a gain:

| Era | SPY with dividends | NEAR-HIVOL | Lead |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1996–2001 | +11.8% a year | +9.0% | **−2.8 points** |
| 2002–2008 | −1.4% a year | +11.2% | **+12.6 points** |
| 2009–2015 | +16.6% a year | +9.7% | **−6.9 points** |

The entire twenty-year win is one era: 2002–2008, the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. In
both bull markets it lost to simply holding the index. And the placebo tells us how much of even
that one era was just the trend switch: the placebo made +3.1% a year in 2002–2008 while SPY lost
1.4%, so being in cash under the 200-day average is worth about 4.5 of those 12.6 points on its
own. The picking is worth the other 8 — and only there. In 1996–2001 and 2009–2015 the picking
added or subtracted about one point and nothing more.

The walk-forward record says the same thing in a different language, and the agreement is exact.
The method won the two folds scored over 2003–2005 and 2006–2008, and lost the two scored over
2009–2011 and 2012–2014. **2 of 4.** A method that wins its twenty-year average and loses the
recent half of its folds is a selection, not an edge.

**2009–2015 is the lab's first filter**, because it is the best-covered stretch of data and the
most like today. Every single version here was negative against SPY in it, from −5.4 points
(FAR-HIVOL) to −9.7 points (NEAR-LOVOL). On that test the whole method is dead, and a 2026 paper
resting on an anchoring effect published in 2004 is exactly the kind of result we expect to have
faded by the time it is printed.

## The genuinely new thing: proximity is a survivorship-proof filter

The dev store cannot price about half of the index members of the 1990s, and the ones it is
missing are disproportionately the companies that went bust. We re-ran all six versions on the
check store, which adds most of those dead companies back. Almost every stock-picking book in this
lab loses 1 to 1.4 points a year when the dead come back. These did not behave alike at all:

| Version | On the usual data | With the dead companies back | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| NEAR-HIVOL | +10.0% | **+11.4%** | **+1.3 points better** |
| PLC1 (placebo) | +6.9% | +7.6% | +0.7 |
| NEAR-ALL | +6.1% | +6.7% | +0.7 |
| NEAR-LOVOL | +4.9% | +5.0% | 0.0 |
| FAR-LOVOL | +8.3% | +7.7% | −0.6 |
| **FAR-HIVOL** | +7.1% | **+3.6%** | **−3.5 points worse** |

And the falls: FAR-HIVOL's worst fall went from 40.9% to **56.1%** once the dead companies were
back in the pool, while NEAR-HIVOL's barely moved, 23.5% to 24.9%.

That is a clean, one-directional result and it makes sense. A company on its way to bankruptcy is
by definition a long way below its yearly high. So "near its high" quietly screens the dying out
before the wildness sort ever sees them, and "far below its high plus wild" is close to a
purpose-built screen for catching them. Buying wild stocks is only dangerous in the half of the
market that is already falling.

## Against the parent, at the same fees

The parent is M0015, the plain "near the high" picker, and its headline came from the old flat
0.1% cost assumption. Re-priced at Gotrade's real fees, its best version earns **+7.5% a year
against SPY's +7.9%** — it stops beating the index altogether. The NEAR-ALL arm here is the same
idea measured properly from the start and says the same: −1.1 points a year behind SPY. **Plain
proximity to the yearly high is not an engine at real fees.** It only became one here when a
wildness sort was applied inside it, and then only in 2002–2008.

## Did the predictions hold?

The hypothesis held in its mechanism and failed on its test. The sign flip is real, on both sides,
and NEAR-HIVOL beat its own control group and the placebo by the margins we had demanded. But we
had also demanded a positive lead over SPY in 2009–2015, and it was −6.9 points.

The expected failure was half wrong, usefully. We predicted NEAR-HIVOL would only match the
placebo (it beat it by 3.1 points), that FAR-LOVOL would beat everything (it came second), and
that holding 20 of the wildest names would break the drawdown limit (23.5% stayed inside 25%). The
one thing we got right was that the wild arms would suffer most with the dead companies back — and
even that split: only the *far* wild arm suffered. The near wild arm improved.

Assumption worth recording: in 1996 the screened pool was only 64–97 names, so a fifth of it held
12–19 slots rather than 20 and the rest sat in cash; from 1997 on every band filled. The two
whole-pool arms (NEAR-ALL, PLC1) never had thin bands, which flatters them slightly in 1996 alone.

## My opinion

**The direction is worth one more trial, but not this one, and not as a standalone book.**

Tuning NEAR-HIVOL — a different number of groups, a different volatility window, 30 names instead
of 20 — would be fitting a shape to one era. Its whole lead is 2002–2008 and the folds confirm it.
I would not spend another id on that, and I would close the standalone 52-week-high direction
here: both the plain version and the conditioned version now lose to the index in the modern half
of the data, at real fees.

What I would carry forward is the one result here that was not about returns. The proximity band
is the first filter this lab has measured that gets *better* when the dead companies come back,
and its mirror is the worst. That is a risk control, not a return engine, and we have been testing
it as the wrong thing. The honest next trial is to stop asking it to beat the market on its own
and ask it to improve a book that already has the market's shape: SPY as the core, with a sleeve
of near-the-high wild names as the satellite. That attacks the lab's real opponent — since 2018
every strategy tried has lost to SPY's big-company drift on the owner's deposits, and a 20-name
equal-weight book is betting against the market's shape before it picks a single stock. NEAR-HIVOL
is also the only arm in this run the breadth report called "pays in both" narrow and broad markets,
which is exactly the property a satellite needs and exactly what the four far-group and
whole-pool arms lacked. That is the trial I have queued.
methods.verdict: The paper's flip is real — wild stocks beat calm ones near the yearly high by 5 points a year and lose to them far below it — but the whole twenty-year win came from 2002-2008, and every version lost to the index in 2009-2015.

methods.name: A staged re-entry underneath a real stock book: buy the picks back in halves, not all at once
methods.hypothesis: M0136 measured the staged buy-back on a SPY-only book and found it is insurance: it halved what a hasty re-entry signal cost (2008 -10.7% to -5.4%, 2001 -8.8% to -5.5%) and, most importantly, took that signal's worst fall from 23.6% to 15.3% while RAISING its return 8.68% to 9.13% a year de-funded -- an improvement on both axes at once, which this lab almost never sees. On SPY it was still pointless, because the careful UP63 trigger it was competing with had no false start to insure against and simply paid the premium (9.85% to 9.56%). But SPY's falls are shallow. The near-miss stock books fail the real-money bar on DEPTH OF FALL, not on return: M0007-N20-RAW is +15.0% vs SPY +7.9% with a 19.6% fall (23.5% on the survivorship-check store), M0020-W-NOSTOP +15.3% with 19.3%, M0133-G20-UP63 +40.2% vs +32.4% with 22.7%. Every one of them sits behind the same 200-day switch M0136 just dissected, and the lab has already established the switch cannot be removed (it helped 22 of 22 variants whole-window). So put the staged ramp under a book that can actually qualify: hold the exit fixed at a fresh 200-day break, then rebuild the stock book in two steps -- half the target weights when the early trigger fires, full weights once SPY is above its 200-day average -- rather than reinstating the whole book at once. Variants, all on an existing near-miss configuration so the picks are not a new search: the parent book unchanged (control, must reproduce its recorded trial); HALF-UP63 and HALF-SMA50 ramps; a HOLD arm that does not trim the half back out when the early trigger reverses; and the same ramp on a second near-miss book to see whether the effect is the book's or the frame's. Use M0136's corrected blackout (one check, not six weeks -- see M0137's finding) if that has landed by then, and say which was used. SUCCESS: the staged book keeps the parent's return within half a point a year while cutting its worst fall by two points or more, which is the shape that moves a near miss across the drawdown bar. EXPECTED FAILURE: a stock book re-enters by buying 20-40 names, so a half-weight rebuild is 20-40 half-sized orders at Gotrade's worst fee tier, and the fee drag may eat the benefit that a single SPY order never paid; second, the near-miss books' deep falls happen while they are FULLY invested above the 200-day line (M0007's 19.6% is not a switch problem), in which case the ramp cannot touch them and the right lever is width or the exit, not the re-entry. Note the lab's measured width result cuts the other way and must be held alongside this: on the honest tape falls go 29.4% to 20.3% as names go 20 to 55, so a width change may dominate anything the ramp does.
methods.verdict: dropped before running: Re-homed by Sera: declared in family stock-momentum-risk-managed, which contains the test-failed M0002, so the hard gate's kin walk would have refused it on day one without ever running. Re-reserved with the same hypothesis under a kin-clean host (see the replacement id).

methods.name: Let the instalment rule act on ordinary dips: shorten the staged re-entry's six-week blackout to one check
methods.hypothesis: M0136's staged re-entry carried a guard that was not part of the idea being tested: a drop below the 200-day average within FRESH_EXIT_N = 32 sessions of an above-the-line reading counted as a fresh break and went all the way to cash, with no instalment allowed. The guard exists for a real reason -- without it a fall out of a fully invested position becomes a trim to a half position rather than a clean exit, and the exit is the half of the switch the lab has already decided to keep -- but 32 sessions is roughly six weeks, long enough to swallow an ordinary dip whole. It did: the market broke its 200-day average in August 2011 and recovered inside the year, the staged rule never took its half step, and HALF-UP63 earned -2.1% in 2011 and +9.8% in 2012, identical to the plain SMA200 control to the decimal, where M0113-UP63 earned -0.4% and +13.6%. Those two years are about 5.5 points of the roughly 10-point cumulative gap HALF-UP63 gives up to UP63 over 2009-2015; the halving itself accounts for about 4, all of it in 2009. So for most of the modern era the experiment measured the guard, not the idea -- and still beat deposit-matched SPY. The minimum blackout that preserves the clean exit is ONE monthly check: 23 sessions is the longest gap between two monthly checks, and anything at or above that guarantees the first below-the-line check after a break sells everything, which is all the exit needs. Variants, same SPY-only frame, same 253-bar lookback and sessions as M0084, M0113 and M0136 so all four are directly comparable: HALF-UP63 at 23 sessions and at 12 sessions (below one check interval, which deliberately lets a mid-month recovery ramp back in and shows what the guard was buying); the same two for HALF-SMA50; and the M0136-HALF-UP63 and M0113-UP63 controls re-run, which must reproduce their recorded trials or nothing else is readable. SUCCESS: a shortened blackout recovers most of the 5.5 points lost in 2011-2012 without deepening the worst fall past M0136's 18.9% or re-opening the 2008 hole that the 50-day arm fell into. EXPECTED FAILURE: the guard was load-bearing, and shortening it converts every short dip into a half-position round trip -- more trades at Gotrade's real fees, a shallower but more frequent bleed, and possibly a deeper 2008 because the May 2008 bounce now buys back sooner as well. The second, likelier failure is that even a full recovery of those 5.5 points leaves the staged rule behind M0113-UP63 at full size, since UP63 already earns +9.85% de-funded against HALF-UP63's +9.56% -- in which case sizing is settled for good and this family closes with a clean answer instead of a technicality. Either outcome is worth the id: the first makes M0233's stock-book ramp worth building properly, the second stops it being built on a bug.

methods.name: Unrealised gains measured with real share counts, with the price rise taken out
methods.hypothesis: M0210 showed that the capital-gains overhang's whole edge is its momentum content: with 12-1 return regressed out the book earned 8.0% a year against the same-frame hash placebo's 8.0%, the inverse arm earned 10.0%, and the behaviour correlation with the test-failed M0002-REL-85 fell from the parent's 0.897 to 0.528. But both M0208 and M0210 measure the overhang on a turnover PROXY, because the dev store had no share counts: weekly volume over the name's own average weekly volume times a flat 2% a week, which keeps the paper's timing and deliberately discards every cross-sectional difference in turnover. Grinblatt and Han's tau is weekly volume over shares outstanding, and cross-sectional turnover differences are precisely where a momentum-free component would live (a heavily traded name refreshes its holders' cost basis far faster than a sleepy one, so two stocks with the same 12-1 return can have genuinely different overhangs). shares.csv is being rebuilt into the dev store by the M0230 work. When it lands, re-run M0210's exact design with tau = weekly volume / shares outstanding on the decision date (market.shares_on, market_fields=('shares',)), one arm with the real tau and one with M0208's proxy as the matched control so the two are comparable name for name, plus the same-frame hash placebo. Success is the same bar M0210 missed: the residual book beats the placebo by at least 2 points a year with behaviour correlation under 0.85 and a positive 2009-2015 lead. Expected failure: ~57% of dev member-days have a share count and ~97% have one since 2009, so the early window will score fewer names than the proxy did and the two arms are not quite the same universe; and the proxy may turn out to have been the better estimator anyway, since a flat average is a low-variance guess where a noisy filed share count is not. If the real-tau residual also ties the placebo, the disposition effect is closed in this data for good and no further overhang id should be spent.

methods.name: How much of the family resemblance is the chassis? The same signal moved into three different frames
methods.hypothesis: Measured on M0210's run: the same-frame HASH placebo -- a book that ranks twenty companies by a hash of their ticker and has no opinion about anything -- reads 0.394 behaviour correlation against the test-failed M0002-REL-85, 0.689 against M0021-B70-RAW, 0.646 against M0022-W-TV14 and 0.709 against M0029-B70-RAW-FRAC. The hard gate's line is 0.85. So roughly seven tenths of what makes a new book look like a disproven one is bought by sharing the chassis alone: F4's screened universe, the SPY 200-day stand-aside switch, twenty equal slots, the keep-band and SPY in unfilled slots. More than a dozen dev-eligible methods are currently refused on kin (M0020, M0033, M0034, M0035, M0036, M0044, M0050, M0053, M0056, M0059 and others at 0.86-0.98) and every one of them shares that chassis. Test whether the chassis or the bet is doing the work: take ONE fixed signal with a known high reading -- M0208's plain capital-gains overhang, recorded at 0.897 against M0002-REL-85 -- and change only the frame, one element at a time. Arms: NOSWITCH (no 200-day stand-aside, cash when a slot is unfilled), CASHFILL (switch kept, cash instead of SPY in unfilled slots), N50-WIDE (fifty names, band 100, switch kept) and the matched BASE (M0208's frame verbatim, as the control). Then read hardgate.kin_matrix over every arm -- the full grid, not behavioural_kin's best-twin-per-failed-method, which reports one Twin per failed method and hides every other variant's own number. Success is a diagnostic, not a return: if an arm's correlation drops below 0.85 while the book still beats SPY TR on the deposits, then kin refusals in this lab are substantially about shared plumbing and the cheapest route past the gate is a different chassis, which would reopen a dozen refused methods as genuinely new candidates. Expected failure: the switch is most of the chassis, so NOSWITCH drops the correlation only by trading away the drawdown protection that made these books eligible at all -- it falls below 0.85 and simultaneously breaches the 25% fall bar, which is no escape, merely a worse book. Equally likely, every arm stays above 0.85, which would say the resemblance is the BET after all and the gate's dozen refusals are exactly right -- a finding worth as much as the other one and reached for the same single method id. Note this method will rank on a signal already shown to be momentum, so it is expected to be refused on kin itself; its value is the measured grid, not a promotion.

methods.name: SPY core with a near-the-high high-volatility satellite: keep the market's shape, add the one tilt that survives the honest tape
methods.hypothesis: M0232-NEAR-HIVOL (the twenty wildest names inside the fifth of the index closest to its 52-week high) was the only arm of six that beat SPY on the owner's deposits (+10.0% vs +7.2% a year), the only one the breadth report called 'pays in both' narrow and broad markets (+1.2% / +2.6%), and the only stock-picking book this lab has measured that EARNS MORE on the survivorship-check store (+10.0% -> +11.4%, worst fall 23.5% -> 24.9%) while its mirror FAR-HIVOL collapsed (+7.1% -> +3.6%, fall 40.9% -> 56.1%). But as a standalone twenty-name equal-weight book it lost to SPY by 6.9 points a year in 2009-2015 and its whole twenty-year lead came from 2002-2008 (folds 2 of 4, won 2003-2008, lost 2009-2014). The diagnosis is not the signal, it is the container: an equal-weight twenty-name book is betting against the market's shape before it picks a stock, and since 2018 that bet has lost for every strategy this lab has tried. So stop asking the tilt to be the whole book. Arms, all on M0030's core-satellite frame at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares on the owner's monthly top-up, with the SPY 200-day switch applied to the SATELLITE only so the core keeps compounding: C70-S30, C50-S50 and C30-S70 holding that much SPY and the rest in M0232-NEAR-HIVOL's twenty names; a pure-SPY control at the same fees and deposits; and the same three weights with the satellite filled by M0232-PLC1's hash-order placebo, so any lead has to come from the tilt and not from the mix. SUCCESS, and this is the only test that matters: a mix beats deposit-matched SPY TR in 2009-2015 by a positive margin, keeps its worst fall under 20%, and beats its own placebo mix by 1 point a year or more. EXPECTED FAILURE: the satellite's 2002-2008 edge is the only thing it has, so every mix lands between SPY and NEAR-HIVOL in exactly the proportion of its weight, which would prove the tilt adds nothing the core does not already own and would close the 52-week-high direction for good. Note the published-anomaly discount: the anchoring effect behind this dates to 2004 and the dev window can only show it before the crowd traded it.

methods.name: A staged re-entry underneath a real stock book: buy the picks back in halves, not all at once
methods.sourceRef: re-homed from the dropped M0233 (M0136's follow-up); host changed to M0133-G20-UP63 so the hard gate's kin walk can pass
methods.hypothesis: Re-homed by Sera from the dropped M0233, which named family stock-momentum-risk-managed and so would have been refused by the hard gate's kin walk on day one (that family holds the test-failed M0002) without ever running. The host is now M0133-G20-UP63: a near miss at MAR 0.74 that misses NO go-live condition, is already built on the UP63 trigger M0136 dissected, and whose kin walk is clean (M0133 -> M0110 -> M0108, all clean families, nothing test-failed). Hypothesis unchanged otherwise. M0136 measured the staged buy-back on a SPY-only book and found it is insurance: it halved what a hasty re-entry signal cost (2008 -10.7% to -5.4%, 2001 -8.8% to -5.5%) and took that signal's worst fall from 23.6% to 15.3% while RAISING its return 8.68% to 9.13% a year de-funded, an improvement on both axes at once that this lab almost never sees. On SPY it was still pointless, because the careful UP63 trigger it competed with had no false start to insure against and simply paid the premium (9.85% to 9.56%). But SPY's falls are shallow and the near-miss stock books fail the real-money bar on DEPTH OF FALL, not on return: M0133-G20-UP63 is +40.2% vs SPY +32.4% with a 22.7% fall. CRITICAL READING OF THE PARENT'S FINDING, and the thing that decides this method: staging only pays on a RECKLESS trigger. Do not simply bolt a ramp onto the host's existing careful UP63 trigger, which M0136 showed costs 0.3 points a year for nothing. The arm that matters is the host given an EARLY, reckless re-entry trigger (the 50-day cross) PLUS the ramp, against the host unchanged: the early trigger buys back months sooner, and the ramp is what makes its false starts survivable. Arms: the host unchanged as control, which must reproduce its recorded trial to the decimal or nothing else here is readable; HALF-SMA50 (the reckless-plus-insurance arm, the real test); HALF-UP63 (the careful-plus-insurance arm, expected to cost about 0.3 points, included so the parent's finding is re-confirmed under a stock book rather than assumed); a HOLD arm that does not trim the half back out when the early trigger reverses; and the same ramp on ONE other near-miss book whose kin is also clean, which rules out M0007 and M0020 (poisoned families) so pick from the kin-clean menu. Use M0136's corrected blackout (one check rather than six weeks) if M0234 has landed by then, and say which was used. SUCCESS: the staged book keeps the host's return within half a point a year while cutting its worst fall by two points or more, the shape that moves a near miss across the drawdown bar. EXPECTED FAILURE: a stock book re-enters by buying 20-40 names, so a half-weight rebuild is 20-40 half-sized orders at Gotrade's worst fee tier, and the fee drag may eat a benefit a single SPY order never had to pay; second, these books' deep falls may happen while they are FULLY invested above the 200-day line, in which case the ramp cannot touch them and the lever is width or the exit, not the re-entry. Hold the measured width result alongside this: on the honest survivorship-check tape falls go 29.4% to 20.3% as names go 20 to 55, so a width change may dominate anything the ramp does, and the two must be measured separately or the result is confounded.
methods.verdict: dropped before running: Dropped by Sera: the host is barred too. Re-homing M0233 onto M0133 fixed only the family-and-ancestry half of the kin walk; the hard gate also refuses on D14 behaviour, and M0133 is blocked because M0133-G20 moves with the test-failed M0002-REL-85 at 0.91. The M0136 child's survey is correct and this confirms it: the kin-clean dev-eligible set is dividend and macro books that fail on walk-forward folds, not on depth of fall, so the staged ramp has no patient among the methods it could legally be fitted to. Repair and patients do not overlap. The ramp should be built once as a reusable frame and fitted to whatever book clears the gate on its own merits, rather than spending an id on a barred host now. See insight 420.

methods.name: Buyback shrinkers with a cap on how much of the book sits in one industry at once
methods.hypothesis: M0230 isolated the problem: the buyback book earns its keep in the modern era (untimed, it leads SPY by 1.1 to 2.1 points a year in 2009-2015 even with the dead companies put back) and is killed only by a 55% fall in 2008. M0230 proved that fall is not fixable from outside the picking -- holding half the account in SPY moved it from 58.7% to 55.1%, because SPY fell 55% in the same months, and the 200-day switch that does fix it costs the 2009-2015 era (-2.6 points) and the walk-forward folds. So the fall has to be attacked inside the pick. The mechanism is concentration, not timing: in 2007-08 the heaviest buyers of their own stock were banks buying back shares immediately before they collapsed, so a screen that ranks only on share-count change loads one industry at exactly the wrong moment. Test the identical M0227 shrinker book (20 names, equal slots, monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's top-up, no market-timing switch) with one addition: no more than a fixed share of the book may sit in any one industry on any decision day, the overflow going to the next-best shrinkers outside that industry. Arms: a 20%, 30% and 40% industry cap, an uncapped control (M0227-S20's book re-run on the tband preset so the cap is the only difference), and a placebo that caps on a hash-assigned fake industry label of the same group sizes, to separate the cap from the act of spreading out. Prediction: the 20% and 30% caps cut the 2008 fall by 10 to 20 points to roughly 40-48%, cost under a point a year of return, keep a positive 2009-2015 edge, and beat the fake-industry placebo -- which would say the gain came from avoiding the banks and not merely from holding a wider book. Expected failure: still over the 20% bar even at a 20% cap, because 2008 was a fall in everything and a book fully invested in stocks fell with it whatever it owned; or the cap costs more return than it saves fall, because the top shrinkers cluster in one industry for a good reason; or the fake-industry placebo matches it, meaning the cap is just width and M0047-style width findings already cover it. A sector label is needed and the store has none -- if no point-in-time industry classification can be derived, this is blocked on data, and that refusal is itself the finding.

methods.name: The buyback signal as a lean on a market-shaped book, not a book of its own
methods.hypothesis: M0230 showed the buyback signal survives dilution intact and linearly: the lead over SPY was +1.4, +2.5 and +3.8 points a year at a 30%, 50% and 70% sleeve, extending to the parent's +5.8 at a full sleeve, and the ladder stayed monotone (+0.9, +1.9, +2.9) with the dead companies put back. A signal that scales that cleanly is a good candidate for a tilt rather than a book. M0230 used the signal to pick twenty names and sat them beside SPY, which left the 55% fall untouched because the twenty names were still an equal-slot book of twenty. Instead apply the signal the way index providers apply a factor tilt (the shape M0222 used for dividend raises): hold every screened index member weighted by its real point-in-time market value, then multiply each weight by a score built from its one-year share-count change, rescale, and cap any one company at 10%. The book is then shaped like the market and leans toward the buyback companies, rather than being twenty of them. Arms: no tilt (the market-shaped yardstick), a gentle tilt, a strong tilt, a random twin of each tilt that hands the same day's scores to hash-drawn names re-drawn quarterly -- explicitly the re-drawing placebo and not the sticky kind M0230 inherited by accident -- and the strong tilt behind the 200-day switch as evidence only. Prediction: the fall drops to roughly SPY's own 55% rather than the book's 59%, so the drawdown bar is still missed, but the 2009-2015 edge stays positive and the walk-forward folds improve, because the book stops fighting the market's shape. Expected failure: the honest reading from M0221, M0222 and M0225 is that a market-shaped core in this lab's data trails SPY by 1.6 to 2 points a year in 2009-2015 before any tilt, because the store cannot price several of that decade's biggest winners -- so the tilt would have to earn 2 points just to break even, and M0222's dividend tilt earned only a few tenths. If that repeats, the finding is that the ruler is bent and no tilt on it can pass, which is worth recording once and not three times.

methods.name: Buy the companies that just split their shares
methods.sourceRef: Ikenberry, Rankine & Stice (1996), What Do Stock Splits Really Signal?, JFQA 31(3) 357-375; Walker (2021), Post-split underreaction, IRFA
methods.hypothesis: A share split gives a shareholder nothing: two shares at $50 are the same stake as one at $100. So a board that pays to split is making a statement it will not otherwise make, that the price it is splitting from is a level the company can hold. Ikenberry, Rankine and Stice (1996) measured US splitters beating matched peers by about 8% over the following year. The research store carries the split ex-dates behind its own adjusted closes, so each monthly check can see which index members have split since a cut-off without reading anything dated after that day. Buy every eligible member whose ex-date fell in the trailing twelve months, equal weight with no name above 20%, behind the SPY 200-day trend gate, monthly, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. A six-month arm asks whether the drift is front-loaded, a twenty-name arm whether the freshest splitters carry it, a stale arm (split one to two years ago and not since) whether the date does any work at all, and a hash-order placebo built to match the split calendar's monthly count and twelve-month stickiness exactly whether the identity of the splitter matters or only the book's shape.
methods.expectedFailure: Two ways, both likely. First, the store knows the ex-date, not the announcement, and the announcement is the event: the shares begin trading split-adjusted three to six weeks after the board speaks, so most of the drift Ikenberry measured may already be priced before this method can buy. Second, the finding was published in 1996 and the dev window ends in 2015, so it can only show an edge from before the crowd traded it; worse, US splits collapsed after 2008 (11-27 a year across the store's members against 50-95 in the late nineties), so 2009-2015 -- the era this lab weighs most -- is a book of five to twenty names chosen from a nearly empty calendar, and any edge that survives there will be hard to tell from the luck of a handful of names. The most likely verdict is a good whole-window average earned entirely before 2001, with the placebo arm matching it once the book is thin enough that shape beats identity.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# M0241 — Buy the companies that just split their shares

## The idea

A share split hands a shareholder nothing. Two shares at $50 are the same stake as one share at
$100; nothing the company owns has changed. So when a board goes to the trouble of splitting, it
is doing something purely cosmetic, and finance researchers have long read that as a message:
a board splits when it thinks the price it is splitting down from is a level the company can
hold. Ikenberry, Rankine and Stice measured this in 1996 and found US splitters beat comparable
companies by about 8% over the year that followed.

Seer can finally ask this question because the price store quietly carries the split dates behind
its own adjusted prices. On any given month-end the lab can see which index members have split
since a cut-off, and nothing about the future leaks in: a split date is public the day it
happens.

The test bought every eligible index member that had split in the previous twelve months, equal
weight, no name above 20% of the account, only while SPY was above its 200-day average, trading
once a month in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the usual 5 million rupiah monthly
top-up. Five other arms were run beside it to try to break it.

## What happened

The main book earned **11.0% a year on the owner's money** over 1996-2015, against **7.2% a year**
for the same deposits dripped into SPY. It lost **20.2% from a peak** at its worst, inside the 25%
limit. Gains outweighed losses **3.2 to 1**. It made 586 trades. Its worst calendar year was 2015,
down 7.3%.

By the lab's own screen this is the first arm in a while to pass every condition at once, and the
lab marked the method **dev-eligible**.

**And it should not be promoted, and will not be.** The reason is below, and it is not close.

## The controls — this part is the good news

Three arms were built specifically to take the result away, and the first two failed to.

| arm | what it bought | money earned a year |
|---|---|---|
| twelve-month splitters | split in the last 12 months | **+11.0%** |
| six-month splitters | split in the last 6 months | +10.8% |
| twenty freshest | the 20 most recent splits | +11.2% |
| stale splitters | split 1-2 years ago, not since | +8.8% |
| shape-matched placebo | random names, same book shape | +9.1% |
| no trend gate | the main book, gate switched off | +9.8% |
| *the deposits in SPY* | | *+7.2%* |

The **placebo** is the one that matters. It was built to copy the splitter book exactly in every
respect except which companies it bought: the same number of names every month, the same habit of
holding each name about a year, the same turnover, the same screen, the same gate — but the names
drawn by a fixed scramble rather than by who split. It earned 9.1% a year. So of the 3.8 points a
year the splitter book beat SPY by, roughly **1.9 points came from the shape of the book** — being
a gated, equal-weight basket of a few dozen large US companies — and roughly **1.9 points came
from actually knowing who split.**

The **stale** arm is the second control, and it lands where the theory says it should. Companies
that split one to two years ago and not since earned 8.8% — the same as the placebo, within noise.
So the effect decays: being a company that splits is worth nothing; having split *recently* is
worth something. That is a dose-response, and it is much harder to fake than a single good
backtest. The split date is doing real work.

The **six-month** arm says the drift is not front-loaded: cutting the window in half earned
slightly less (10.8%) and fell further (22.7%). Twelve months — the horizon the 1996 paper
measured — is the right one. The **twenty freshest** arm was a statistical tie (11.2%).

## The trend gate: worth a lot, but not lately

Switching off the "only buy while the market is above its 200-day average" rule cost 1.2 points a
year *and* turned a 20% worst fall into a **58.7%** one. 2008 alone went from a mild year to
**−44.6%**. Over the whole twenty years the gate is not a drag on this book; it is most of its
safety and it adds return on top.

But the same arm says something uncomfortable that has to be reported beside it. **In 2009-2015
the ungated book beat SPY by 5.8% a year while the gated one lost to it by about 3%.** Since the
2009 bottom the gate has been a standing cost: it keeps stepping out of a market that keeps going
back up. That matches what the lab has found on momentum books — the gate helped in every variant
measured over the full window and in none of them after 2009 — and this run extends the same
pattern to an event-driven book.

So the gate earns its place on a twenty-year view and has been pure cost for the last third of it.
That tension is unresolved and is not this method's to resolve.

## It survives the honest tape — and that is the most surprising number here

The dev price store cannot price about half the companies that were ever index members, and the
ones it is missing are disproportionately the ones that died. So every result is re-run on a second
store that puts the dead companies back. Almost everything the lab has measured gets worse there:
the stock-picking books lose 1 to 1.4 points a year and fall 2.6 points deeper on average.

**This book got better.** With the dead companies restored it earned **11.2% a year instead of
11.0%**, and its worst fall *shrank* from 20.2% to **19.0%**. Every other arm got worse: the stale
arm lost 0.8 points, the ungated arm 0.7, the placebo 0.2. The splitter book was the only one that
gained, and its lead over the shape-matched placebo widened from 1.9 to 2.3 points a year.

The reason is almost tautological once you see it, and it is a point in the idea's favour. A
company that has just split its shares is a company whose price has gone up a lot. Those are not
the companies that quietly disappear. Putting the failures back into the universe adds names this
screen would never have bought, so it dilutes everything except this. The split signal is not an
artefact of missing dead companies — it is one of the very few things the lab has measured that is
*immune* to them.

## Why it still fails

The lab runs the same method over four separate stretches of history, each scored only on months
it was never fitted on. **The splitter book won 1 of those 4.**

| stretch | the book | SPY | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2003-2005 | +49.7% | +52.1% | lost |
| 2006-2008 | +15.9% | −24.6% | **won** |
| 2009-2011 | +54.7% | +60.8% | lost |
| 2012-2014 | +61.7% | +65.9% | lost |

Read that table honestly and the twenty-year average dissolves. The single stretch it won is
2006-2008 — the crash — and the thing that won it was the trend gate stepping out of the market,
not splits. In every stretch where the market simply went up, the book quietly trailed it.

Worse, in **2009-2015 the book earned about 3 points a year less than SPY** — and the second store
agrees, so this is not a data hole. That is the era with the best data and the one most like today,
and it is the lab's first filter. A method that loses there does not get a look at the test window
however good its average.

And the reason is visible in the data itself. **US companies stopped splitting.** Across the
store's members there were 50 to 95 splits a year in the late 1990s and only 11 to 27 a year after
2008. So the modern book is five to twenty names drawn from a nearly empty calendar, and the thing
that made the strategy work in 1997 — a wide, constantly refreshed basket of confident boards —
barely exists any more. Buying back fifty names is not an option when only fifteen companies split.

One more quiet warning. Over almost all of 1996-2015 the index did *not* persistently beat the
average of its own members (6 of 202 rolling windows), which means an equal-weight book had a
standing tailwind through the whole dev period. Since 2018 that has run the other way: the biggest
companies have carried the index. So this book was swimming downstream in the years it was
measured on, and upstream in the years the owner would actually have traded it.

## How likely is this to be real rather than luck

The lab's luck score (DSR) for the main arm is **0.916**, against the owner's bar of **0.90**, and
it is judged after **157** distinct methods have been tried. Read plainly: after accounting for
every idea this lab has searched through, there is roughly a 92% chance the twenty-year result is
a real pattern rather than the best of many coin flips. That clears the bar.

But the luck score only asks whether the *average* is real. It cannot see that the average is made
of one winning crash and three losing expansions. The fold table can, and it says selection. **When
