the two disagree, the folds win** — that is exactly why the owner put the fold rule in front of the
test window after four straight test-window failures.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Partly, and the honest answer is more interesting than a yes or a no.

The hypothesis — that recent splitters beat the market — **held on the twenty-year average and
survived both controls**. The expected failure, written before the run, said: the edge will be
earned before the crowd traded it, 2009-2015 will be flat, and the modern book will be too thin to
tell from luck. **That is precisely what happened**, down to the mechanism. The method was right
about the market and right about why it would not help.

The second predicted failure — that buying on the ex-date is too late because the announcement is
the event — is **not settled** by this run and is the most promising thing left on the table. The
store knows only the day the shares started trading split-adjusted, typically three to six weeks
after the board announced. A 1.9-point-a-year signal measured three to six weeks late is evidence
that something larger sits at the announcement, where Ikenberry measured 8%.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth exactly one more trial, and not a general campaign.**

What I would not do is tune this book. More arms on the ex-date — different windows, different
name counts, different caps — will produce more twenty-year averages carried by the 1990s, and the
fold rule will refuse every one of them. The calendar has moved on; there are not enough splits
left for a wide splitter book to exist today, and no amount of parameter choice conjures names that
are not there. I would also not touch the stale or placebo variants again: they did their job
cleanly and the answer they gave is settled.

What I *would* do is chase the gap between the ex-date and the announcement. This run found a real,
control-proof 1.9 points a year from a signal it could only read three to six weeks after the news
broke. Announcement dates would let the lab buy where the paper actually measured, and the store
already proved it can carry an event calendar when the dividend declaration dates were rebuilt from
the universe cache without a single vendor call. If split announcement dates can be rebuilt the same
way, the question becomes worth asking once more, properly. If they cannot, the direction is closed
and should be recorded as closed.

The survivorship result raises my confidence that there is something real here, and changes
nothing about the verdict. A signal that strengthens when you add back the companies that went
bust is a signal about real corporate behaviour, not about a gap in the price file. But "real" and
"tradeable today" are different claims, and the second one fails on a count: there are no longer
enough splits a year to build this book out of.

The other thing worth carrying away is not about splits at all. The gate arm is the cleanest
measurement yet of what the 200-day market filter is worth: on this book it bought 38 percentage
points of drawdown protection and 1.2 points a year of return at the same time. But the 2009-2015 split in that
same arm is the sharper finding, and it is now confirmed outside momentum: whatever the gate is
reading, it stopped paying after 2009. That deserves its own method, not another footnote.

Assumptions I made without asking, recorded here: reverse splits were excluded as buys (a company
doing a 1-for-10 is signalling distress, the opposite of the hypothesis); when fewer names
qualified than the 20% cap could fill, the leftover stayed in cash rather than concentrating the
book further; and every arm ran on the fixed resize tape so that a thin book's cash position
reflects the strategy rather than a resize rule that rarely fires.
methods.verdict: Recent splitters really do beat the market and the effect survives adding back the companies that went bust — but it loses three of four out-of-sample stretches and trails SPY since 2009, because American companies have almost stopped splitting.

methods.name: One-off cash: buy the companies that declare a special dividend, and see whether the market keeps rewarding them
methods.sourceRef: Brickley (1983), Shareholder wealth, information signaling and the specially designated dividend: an empirical study, Journal of Financial Economics 12(2), 187-209; declaration dates from the store's dividend_announcements.csv (rebuilt 2026-10-19)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1983, so the whole dev window (1996-2015) is after the crowd could know it; that is a reason to expect a faded edge, not a reason to skip the measurement, because the lab has no evidence on this event at all. A special dividend is a one-off return of cash, several times the company's regular payment. Brickley's finding is that boards pay one when they have cash the business does not need, and that the announcement still carried good news about the year ahead even though the label says 'do not expect this again'. M0070 built the mirror image of this book: it caps a raise at double the baseline precisely to throw specials out as noise, so this method trades exactly the pile M0070 discards, and the two together cover the whole distribution of dividend surprises. The store has no dividend type column, so a special is inferred from shape: a payment at least twice the median of the up-to-four payments that went ex in the 400 days before it, from a company with at least two such priors (an established cadence). Measured on the dev store that rule fires 519 times in 1996-2015, 8-59 a year, and 69% carry a board declaration date. Each event is dated the day the market learned of it -- the declaration date where the store has one, else the ex-date -- and held while it is younger than the hold. Inside F4's membership and liquidity screen and behind the SPY-200 switch, hold up to ten such names at 10% each (held names keep their slot, then the newest event), park the empty slots in SPY, re-picked monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees. Ten slots rather than M0070's twenty because specials are rare: at twice the baseline and a six-month hold the median month has nine live events, so ten slots keep the book in its own picks rather than in the park. Variants: S-H6 (the main arm), S-H12 (a twelve-month hold, which both lengthens the drift window and fills more slots), S-K5 (only payments five times the baseline or more -- purer specials, but only about three live a month, so that arm is mostly SPY by construction and its exposure must be read before its return), S-CAP (specials between two and twenty times, which drops the handful of enormous distributions that are really spin-offs and REIT conversions rather than a board handing back spare cash), and two controls on the same book and the same clock: R-H6, ordinary increases of 25% up to double (the band M0070 actually trades), and F-H6, the same mature payers in a quarter when the dividend did not change by more than 10%. Success: S-H6 beats total-return SPY on dev inside the 20% worst fall, beats both controls, and keeps a positive edge over SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: Three ways this most likely dies. First, selection: special dividends cluster in good times and among mature, cash-rich, value-shaped companies, so the book may be a quality and value tilt wearing an event costume -- exactly the shape that lagged SPY's big-company growth in 2009-2015, which is the era that matters most and the one that has killed every roster strategy so far. Second, timing: the announcement pop is one day, and a monthly book reading the close buys at the next open at best, so if the whole effect is the pop there is nothing left; M0076 measured exactly this for dividend raises and found the declaration-day arm no better than the ex-date arm. Third, the sample: 519 events over twenty years is thin, it is lumpy (59 in 2011 and 55 in 2012 against 7 in 2002), and the 2012 cluster is a known tax event -- boards pulled specials forward before the expected 2013 dividend-tax rise -- so a large part of the dev sample is companies answering the tax code, not signalling confidence. A book that is mostly 2011-2012 is a book that measured one tax deadline. Also against it: the inferred label is not the board's label, so stock distributions, spin-off cash and REIT conversion payments are counted as specials even though they carry no confidence signal (S-CAP exists to size that); the SPY park means a thin arm is partly measuring SPY, so S-K5 may look fine for the wrong reason; the fast 1998, 2008 and 2011 falls land before the 200-day switch turns, so the worst fall may sit near or above the 20% limit as M0070's did at 21-22%; and US withholding tax on dividends is not modelled, which bites harder here than anywhere else in the lab because the whole thesis is large cash payments.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# One-off cash: buying the companies that hand back a special dividend

Sometimes a company pays a dividend several times larger than its usual one — a one-off return
of spare cash. A 1983 study found that when a board does this, the news is good: the market
reads it as a sign the business is in better shape than people thought. This method bought
those companies and held them while the news was fresh, to see whether the reward lasts long
enough for a monthly investor to collect it.

It is the mirror of an experiment the lab already ran. The dividend-raise book (the lab's
"follow the raise" method) deliberately throws these giant payments away: it only counts a
raise up to a doubling, because anything bigger is a one-off and was assumed to be noise. This
method picks up exactly the pile that one discards. Together they cover the whole range of
dividend surprises.

**The result: rejected.** The special-dividend book earned **+8.1% a year on the owner's money
against +7.2% for the same deposits put into the index** — a lead of 0.9 points a year, and not
enough to pass. More damaging, two things the run measured are worse than the headline:

- it **lost to the index by 7.5 points a year in 2009-2015** (it earned 9.1% a year while the
  index earned 16.6%), which is the best-covered and most modern stretch of the data, and
- a plain **dividend raise — the control arm, meant to be the boring comparison — earned
  +10.8% a year**, three times the lead of the special dividends it was supposed to beat.

## What each version did

Money here is the owner's real funding plan: 10 million rupiah to start, 5 million more on the
25th of every month, 237 deposits, at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares. "A year" is the
money-weighted return, which is the only honest way to score a book being topped up — a plain
growth rate would count the deposits as if the method had earned them.

| version | what it bought | earned a year | index | lead | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S-H6 | specials, 2x or more, 6-month hold | +8.1% | +7.2% | +0.9 | 20.9% | 2.50 | 171 |
| S-H12 | the same, 12-month hold | +8.1% | +7.2% | +0.9 | 20.6% | 2.47 | 172 |
| S-K5 | only 5x or more | +8.2% | +7.2% | +1.0 | 20.4% | 5.49 | 67 |
| S-CAP | 2x to 20x only | +8.1% | +7.2% | +1.0 | 22.4% | 2.59 | 154 |
| **R-H6** | **control: ordinary raises of 25% up to double** | **+10.8%** | +7.2% | **+3.6** | 26.7% | 3.18 | 301 |
| F-H6 | control: steady payers, no change | +7.5% | +7.2% | +0.3 | 30.9% | 2.61 | 184 |

"Gains vs losses" is the profit factor: every rupiah of winning trades divided by every rupiah
of losing ones. Above 1.3 is the owner's bar and all six clear it easily; that bar was never
the problem here.

**Worst fall** is measured on the book with the deposits stripped out, because a monthly top-up
refills a falling account and makes a bad fall read gentler than it was. The main version lost
**20.9% from a peak**, inside the 25% limit the owner set in October. The "no change" control
fell 30.9%, which is worse than any of the event books — steady dividend payers were not a safe
place to be in 2008.

**Luck.** The lab deflates every result by how many times it has looked. Today that count is
156 distinct methods, and the bar is 0.90 — meaning the lab wants to be 90% confident a result
is real rather than a lucky draw out of 156 tries. The main version scored **0.80**, so it
fails: roughly a one-in-five chance this lead is noise. The ordinary-raise control scored 0.922
and passes. Neither number is mine to move; both come straight off the lab's own gate.

## Two thirds of this book was never the idea

The sharpest thing the run measured is not in the table. Special dividends are rare. Inside the
screen the lab uses — index members, liquid enough to trade — there are usually only three or
four live at a time out of the ten slots the book keeps. The empty slots go into the index
itself, so the book is mostly the index wearing a costume.

Measured on every month-end of the dev window, running the real picking code:

| version | share of the book in its own picks | share parked in the index |
|---|---|---|
| S-H6 | 35% | 65% |
| S-K5 | 10% | 90% |
| R-H6 (control) | 76% | 24% |
| F-H6 (control) | 100% | 0% |

This changes how the table above should be read. The special-dividend version beat the index by
0.9 points a year **while only a third of it was special dividends**. Scale that up to a full
book and the picks themselves are worth roughly **+2.6 points a year**. Do the same for the
controls and the ordinary raises are worth about **+4.7 points**, the steady payers about
**+0.3**. (That scaling is a straight-line estimate, not a re-run; returns do not divide up
perfectly. But the ranking is not close enough for the arithmetic to matter.)

So the honest reading is: **a special dividend does carry real news.** The companies that paid
one beat the index by a couple of points a year, where companies that merely kept paying the
same dividend beat it by almost nothing. Brickley's 1983 finding is not dead. It is just
*smaller than an ordinary dividend raise*, and far too rare to build a book out of.

The 5x version makes the point painfully. It looks like the best row in the table — highest
lead, shallowest fall, a gains-to-losses ratio of 5.49. It is 90% index. That row is a
measurement of the index with a 10% garnish, and it is also the row that failed the
hundred-trade minimum (67 trades). A reader who picked the prettiest row would have picked the
one with the least method in it.

## The 6-month and 12-month versions are the same book

S-H6 and S-H12 produced almost identical results: +8.1% both, 171 against 172 trades. That is
not a coincidence or a small effect, and it is worth the owner knowing why, because the same
thing is true of several older methods.

The picking rule looks at a company's **latest** dividend. The moment the next ordinary
dividend is paid, the latest dividend is no longer the special one, and the company loses its
slot. Most of these companies pay quarterly. Measured across the dev window, **the median gap
to the next payment is 91 days, and only 5% of special dividends survive 182 days before the
next payment supersedes them.**

So "hold for six months" and "hold for twelve months" both mean, in practice, "hold for about
one quarter". The hold length was never doing anything. The lab's older dividend-raise method
shows the same fingerprint — its 6-month and 12-month versions differ by 0.4% of total return
over twenty years and have the same worst fall to one decimal place. Eighteen method files are
built on this same chassis, and any variant grid among them that varied the hold length has been
varying a dial that was not connected.

## Why it fails anyway

1. **2009-2015.** Every special version lost to the index by about 7.5 points a year in those
   years. That is the stretch with the best data and the one most like today, and it has now
   killed every strategy the lab has sent to the test window. The companies that hand back
   spare cash are mature and cash-rich; from 2009 the market was carried by big companies
   reinvesting everything they had. The event book was betting against the shape of the market.
2. **The sample is lumpy and part of it is a tax deadline.** 519 of these events fired in twenty
   years, and 23% of them landed in 2011-2012 — the fiscal-cliff rush, when American boards
   pulled special dividends forward before an expected tax rise. Those boards were answering the
   tax code, not signalling confidence. Nearly a quarter of the evidence is the wrong kind of
   evidence.
3. **The walk-forward folds.** The lab splits the window into four stretches, picks the best
   version using only what was known before each stretch, then scores it on months it has never
   seen. This method **won 1 of 4**. It beat the index comfortably in 2006-2008 (+5.1% while the
   index lost 24.6%) and lost the other three, including badly in 2009-2011 (+23.1% against the
   index's +60.8%). A method that wins its twenty-year average and loses the folds is a
   selection, not an edge.

## Putting the dead companies back

The lab keeps a second copy of the price history that includes companies that went bankrupt or
were bought — the ones missing from the main data, which is the single most flattering gap a
backtest can have. Re-run there, the special-dividend book earns **slightly more**, +8.5% a
year against +8.1%, but **falls deeper: 24.0% instead of 20.9%**. The 2009-2015 gap does not
close; it widens a touch, to −7.9 points.

That is a mixed signal rather than a verdict. The lead survives the honest tape, which is more
than most of this lab's books manage. The fall moving from 20.9% to 24.0% is the familiar
pattern: the main data is missing the companies that collapsed, so every drawdown in this lab
reads gentler than it was.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

- **"Beats the index on dev"**: yes, narrowly — +0.9 points a year.
- **"Beats both controls"**: **no, and this is the one that kills it.** It beat the steady-payer
  control (+0.9 against +0.3) but lost badly to the ordinary-raise control (+0.9 against +3.6).
  The pre-registered success condition required beating both.
- **"Keeps a positive edge in 2009-2015"**: **no** — 7.5 points behind a year.
- **Expected failure #1, "a quality and value tilt that lags 2009-2015"**: **happened exactly as
  written**, and it is the main cause of death.
- **Expected failure #3, "a thin, lumpy sample whose 2011-2012 bulge is a tax event"**:
  **happened as written** — 23% of the sample sits in those two years.
- **Expected failure #2, "the pop is the whole effect"**: **not confirmed, and probably wrong.**
  If the announcement-day jump were everything, the picks would be worth nothing above the
  steady-payer control, and they are worth about 2.3 points more. Something lasts past the day.
  It is just not enough, and not as much as a plain raise.

## The eligible version is not a discovery

The run marked this method eligible on the lab's dev screen, but the version that did it is
**R-H6, the control** — the ordinary-raise book. That is not a new idea. It is the lab's
existing dividend-raise method with ten slots instead of twenty and the declaration date instead
of the ex-date, and the lab already measured that the declaration date is worth nothing here.
Side by side against the older twenty-slot version, at the same real fees:

| | earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| older method, 20 slots | — (total return +39,707%) | 21.9% | 2.81 | 540 |
| this run's R-H6, 10 slots | +10.8% | 26.7% | 3.18 | 301 |

Halving the number of names kept the return and **deepened the worst fall by nearly five
points**, which is the same thing the lab found when it widened a different book: width buys
safety, not return. That is a useful confirmation on a second book, and nothing more.

The hard gate refuses to promote it anyway — 1 of 4 folds — and no kin has failed out of
sample, so the refusal is purely about the folds. No test-window look was spent, and none
should be.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth one more trial, but not as a book of its own.** The measurement that
matters is the one hiding under the index park: the special-dividend picks were worth about 2.6
points a year over the index while plain steady payers were worth 0.3. The news is real. The
problem is arithmetic — there are three or four of these companies alive at a time among the
big liquid names, so you cannot build ten slots out of them, and two-thirds of the book ends up
being the index, which drags the measured lead down to a number no gate will ever pass.

So I would stop trying to make specials carry a portfolio, and instead ask whether they carry a
**tilt**: the lab already has a dividend-raise book that works, and a special dividend is the
same signal only stronger and rarer. Give a company a double weight in the raise book in the
quarter after it pays a special, rather than giving it a whole slot of its own. That keeps the
book full, keeps the trade count up, and tests the only claim the data actually supports — that
the one-off payment is extra information on top of the raise, not a replacement for it. I have
queued that as the next idea.

The second thing I would do is unrelated to dividends and more valuable: **fix the hold clock**.
Eighteen of the lab's method files read only a company's latest dividend, which silently caps
every hold at one quarter. Several of them have spent variants on a hold-length dial that was
never connected. That is not a strategy idea, it is a measuring instrument that reads the same
number whatever you set it to, and it should be repaired before the next dividend method is
written.

What I would not do is spend a test-window look here. The 2009-2015 gap of 7.5 points a year
and the 1-of-4 fold record are the same two warnings that preceded all four of the lab's failed
looks, and nothing in this result argues that this time is different.
methods.verdict: A one-off special dividend does carry real news — the picks beat the index by about 2.6 points a year where steady payers beat it by 0.3 — but an ordinary dividend raise carries nearly twice as much, only three or four of these companies are alive at a time so two thirds of the book is just the index, and it lost to the market by 7.5 points a year in 2009-2015

methods.name: Buyback shrinkers near their yearly high: the buyback book with the falling knives removed
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0227 (the buyback book) filtered by M0015's nearness to the 52-week high; Pontiff & Woodgate (2008) JF 63(2) 921-945, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v63y2008i2p921-945.html; George & Hwang (2004) JF 59(5) doi:10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x; placebo of M0187
methods.hypothesis: The lab's strongest live stock signal is the buyback book (M0227): the twenty index members whose split-adjusted share count fell most over a year earned +13.0% a year on the owner's deposits where SPY earned +7.2%, beating both the opposite book (+9.2%) and a placebo on the same pool (+7.7%). What killed it was the fall: 58.7% in 2008, and the only arm that passed the dev screen hid behind the SPY 200-day switch, which then gave back 2009-2015 and lost that walk-forward fold to cash. M0230 showed a market core cannot fix that, because a core falls with the crash it sits in. So attack the fall from inside the picks: a company buying back stock while its price sits near its own yearly high is returning cash from strength; one buying back while its price sits far below its high is often a management team defending a collapsing share price. The lab has evidence the distinction is real rather than a backtest artefact: nearness to the 52-week high is the only filter measured here that earns MORE when the dead companies are put back on the survivorship-check store (+1.3 points a year, where its mirror loses 3.5 and falls 15 deeper), because a company heading for bankruptcy is by construction far below its high. Each month, take M0227's scored pool verbatim (all its split, units and one-listing-per-company guards), sort it by nearness (close over the highest close of the last 252 sessions, ties broken by symbol alone so the band is signal-blind), cut it into equal-count bands by rank, and hold the twenty biggest shrinkers inside the kept band. Coverage was measured before this file was committed, pool counts only and no returns: the scorable pool runs 170-184 names in 1997 and 369-378 by 2015, so the near half holds 85-189 and the near third 56-126; twenty slots fill in every month. Arms, all twenty equal slots, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up: NEAR20 (the near half, the idea), FAR20 (the bottom half, the mirror: the falling knives the filter is meant to remove), NEAR20-T3 (the near third, a stricter dose of the same filter), NEAR20-R (twenty names drawn blind from the identical near half in a monthly-redrawn hash order: the whole filter with none of the buyback signal) and NEAR20-SW (NEAR20 behind the SPY 200-day switch, the only arm that can reach the 20% drawdown bar). Predictions written before any result. (1) NEAR20 beats FAR20 by 3 or more points a year AND falls at least 8 points less deeply -- the filter separates. (2) NEAR20 beats NEAR20-R by 2 or more points a year; if it does not, the nearness filter is doing all the work and this is M0015 in disguise, which already lost. (3) The fall: NEAR20 lands between 40% and 50%, below the parent's 58.7% but far above the 20% bar; only NEAR20-SW reaches the bar, near the parent's switched 25.8%. (4) The real question is 2009-2015 and the folds: NEAR20 never leaves the market, so it should win 3 of 4 walk-forward folds where the parent's switched arm won 2, and keep a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015. (5) The dose: NEAR20-T3 lands between NEAR20 and the parent on return; if the stricter filter earns MORE, the filter is the engine and the buybacks are decoration. Success is (1), (2) and (4) together. Success on (1) alone, with the placebo matching and the folds still lost, is a rejection.
methods.expectedFailure: Five ways, in order of likelihood. (1) Momentum in disguise: the near band is a momentum band, so NEAR20-R lands within a point of NEAR20 and the method measures nearness rather than capital allocation. The lab has already measured plain nearness twice -- M0015 at MAR 0.58 and M0232's NEAR-ALL arm at +6.1% a year against SPY's +7.2% at these very fees -- so a book that is only nearness is a book that already lost, and that would close this direction rather than open a tuning exercise. (2) The crash is not selective: 2008 took the near half down with the far half, which is what a crash means, so NEAR20 still falls past 50% and only the switched arm reaches the bar. That puts the method back exactly where M0227 was, with timing as the only brake and the 2009-11 fold lost to cash again. (3) The filter removes the signal it is meant to protect: the same buyback dollars retire more shares when the price is low, so the biggest shrinkers are mechanically tilted toward companies whose price has fallen, and keeping only the near half systematically keeps the SMALLER shrinkers. Then NEAR20 earns less than the parent's +13.0% and still falls far -- worse on both axes at once, which is a rejection and not a dial to turn. (4) Thin separation: the near and far halves of a buyback pool may be nearly the same companies in a bull market, where almost everything sits near its high, so the filter only bites in the years it is least needed and does nothing in 2008 when it matters. (5) Decay: buybacks have been public since 2008 and the 52-week-high effect since 2004, so both halves of this idea are published and the dev window straddles both publications; 2009-2015 is the honest read and a twenty-year average earned before 2009 is a dead edge. One caution pointing the other way, written down now so it is not read as a discovery later: nearness is the one filter that improves on the survivorship-check store, so the check store may flatter this book rather than cut it. That is a reason to read the check store, not a reason to trust the dev number more. None of these is a reason to tune the cut, the 252-session window or the parent's guards afterwards.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What we tried

Companies that buy back their own shares have been the lab's best live stock idea. The buyback
book (M0227) held the twenty index members whose share count had shrunk most over the past year,
and it earned 13.0% a year on your deposits where the index earned 7.2%. The problem was never the
money. It was the fall: 58.7% in 2008. The only version that passed the lab's screen was the one
that sold everything whenever the market sat below its 200-day average, and that version then sat
out the 2009-11 recovery. A later attempt (M0230) tried to fix the fall by keeping half the account
in the index itself, and failed for a reason that was arithmetic before it was a measurement: an
index holding falls with the crash it is sitting in.

So this method attacked the fall from inside the picks instead, with a simple and intuitive idea.

Some companies buy back stock from strength: business is good, the share price is near its best
level of the past year, and there is spare cash to return. Other companies buy back stock on the
way down, while the price sits far below its yearly high — often a management team spending the
last of the balance sheet defending a collapsing share price. Those are the falling knives. In
2007-08 the biggest buyers of their own stock included banks that bought back shares weeks before
they collapsed.

The filter: before picking, throw away every company whose price sits in the bottom half of the
pool by nearness to its own 52-week high. Then hold the twenty biggest buyback companies that are
left. There was a specific reason to expect this to work — nearness to the yearly high is the one
measure in this lab that gets *better* when the companies that went bankrupt are added back into
the price history, because a company heading for bankruptcy is, by definition, far below its high.

Five versions, all twenty equal slots, asked monthly, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees
on your 5 million rupiah monthly top-up:

- **NEAR20** — the idea: the twenty biggest buyback companies in the *near* half.
- **FAR20** — the mirror: the twenty biggest buyback companies in the *far* half. The falling
  knives the filter is meant to throw away.
- **NEAR20-T3** — a stricter dose: the near *third* instead of the near half.
- **NEAR20-R** — the control that matters: twenty names picked blind, by coin-flip, from the
  identical near half. Same filter, same fees, no knowledge of buybacks at all.
- **NEAR20-SW** — NEAR20 behind the 200-day market switch.

## Result

The "earned a year" figures count each deposit from the day it was paid in. The same deposits put
into the index earned **+7.2% a year** over 1996-2015.

| version | earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NEAR20** (near half) | **+10.4%** | **50.8%** | 1.77 | 0.730 |
| FAR20 (far half, the mirror) | +10.3% | 67.6% | 1.90 | 0.619 |
| NEAR20-T3 (near third) | +9.9% | 48.0% | 1.71 | 0.668 |
| NEAR20-R (blind picks, same half) | +4.4% | 50.2% | 1.16 | 0.211 |
| NEAR20-SW (near half + switch) | +10.1% | 30.4% | 2.20 | 0.907 |

For comparison, the parent book with no filter at all earned +13.0% with a 58.7% fall, and its
switched version +10.3% with a 25.8% fall.

**Three things came out of this, and they point in different directions.**

**One: the buyback signal is real, and this run is the cleanest proof of it the lab has.** The
blind control — twenty names drawn by coin flip from exactly the same filtered half, paying exactly
the same fees — earned **+4.4% a year against the real picks' +10.4%**. A six-point gap. Whatever
the buyback measure is doing, it is not an accident of which companies survive the filter. The idea
that this was secretly a momentum book, which was the failure I expected most, did not happen.

**Two: the filter does exactly what it was designed to do, and it is worth nothing.** The near half
and the far half never share a single name — checked in all 226 months, the overlap is zero. In
September 2008 the near book held Loews, Dominion, Home Depot, Target and Travelers; the far book
held Capital One, Ameriprise, UnitedHealth and KLA. By March 2009 the far book held MBIA, Prudential
and Unum. Those are textbook falling knives, and the filter removed every one of them. The fall came
down by nearly seventeen points, 67.6% to 50.8%.

And the two books earned **the same money**: +10.4% against +10.3%, a tenth of a point apart over
twenty years. Holding the companies heading for disaster paid exactly as well as holding the
companies at their peak. All that risk bought nothing, and avoiding it cost nothing.

I also checked that the filter was not quietly weakening the signal by keeping only the milder
buyback companies. It was not: the two halves buy back their stock at virtually the same rate (the
average share-count shrink held is 7.70% a year in the near book and 7.64% in the far book). The
filter sorts on price, not on the strength of the buyback.

**Three — and this is what kills the method: the filter threw away the wrong half.** The test that
matters most in this lab is 2009-2015, the best-covered and most modern stretch of the window.

| version | lead over the index, 2009-2015 | the same, with bankrupt companies added back |
|---|---|---|
| NEAR20 (kept half) | +0.8% a year | **−0.9% a year** |
| FAR20 (discarded half) | +3.5% a year | **+6.0% a year** |
| the parent, unfiltered | +3.8% a year | — |

The unfiltered parent book led the index by 3.8 points a year in those years. After the filter, the
lead is +0.8 points — and on the fuller price history, with the companies that went bankrupt put
back in, **the kept half actually loses to the index while the discarded half beats it by six
points a year.** The filter removed the half that earns.

## Why

The mechanism, once the numbers point at it, is the original buyback argument turned against this
method. A buyback is supposed to be a signal because management is telling you the stock is cheap
and is spending real money to act on it. A company retiring shares while its price sits far below
its yearly high **is buying cheap** — that is the thesis working. A company retiring shares at its
yearly high is paying full price, which is closer to a routine payout habit than a judgement about
value. Large US companies buy back stock as a matter of policy now, quarter after quarter,
regardless of price.

So the filter did not separate healthy companies from falling knives. It separated *opportunistic*
buybacks from *routine* ones, and kept the routine ones. The information was in the half that
looked dangerous.

## The fuller price history

The lab re-ran every version on a second price history that adds back most of the companies that
died or left the index. The prediction written into this method before the run was that this check
would *flatter* the near book, because nearness to the high is the one measure that improves when
the dead companies return.

It did flatter it — by +0.7 points a year. But it flattered the discarded far half by +1.3 points,
more than twice as much, and the far book's worst fall actually got *shallower* (67.6% to 62.2%)
while the near book's got deeper (50.8% to 56.2%). On the honest history the safety gap between the
two halves shrinks from seventeen points to six, and the far book earns more.

That is a result worth recording on its own: the "nearness protects you from the companies that go
bankrupt" finding does not survive being moved into a buyback pool. It makes sense in hindsight. A
company with the spare cash to retire 8% of its own stock in a year is not often a company about to
go bankrupt. The falling knives this filter was built to catch were mostly not there to catch.

## The one version that passed, and why it should not be promoted

NEAR20-SW — the near half behind the 200-day switch — passed every one of the lab's dev-window
conditions and is marked eligible. Its luck score is **0.908 against the 0.90 bar, at N = 158**.
N is one look per distinct method in the lab, which is how the lab discounts a result for the
number of things it has tried; 158 tries deep, a score of 0.908 says the result is probably real
rather than the luckiest of many attempts — but only just, and the number drifts down as other
methods are tried.

It should not be promoted, and the lab's hard gate will not allow it, for a reason I agree with:
**it won only 2 of its 4 walk-forward periods.** Those periods pick a version using only earlier
years and then score it on later years it has never seen. It won 2003-05 and 2012-14, and lost
2006-08 and 2009-11 — losing 2009-11 by +23.7% against the index's +60.8%, which is the switch
sitting in cash through the recovery, exactly the failure this method existed to avoid.

Worth noting honestly about those periods: in 2006-08 the picker chose FAR20 — the *mirror control*,
the arm this method exists to argue against — and in 2009-11 and 2012-14 it chose the switched arm.
So the fold record never actually scored the idea. The picker chooses each period's version by
return-per-unit-of-fall, which systematically favours the braked arm. This is the third method in a
row where that has happened, and it is journalled.

Also: NEAR20-SW is strictly worse than the parent's switched version on every axis at once —
+10.1% against +10.3% a year, a 30.4% fall against 25.8%, a luck score of 0.907 against 0.937.
Behind the 200-day switch, the filter adds nothing, because the switch had already removed the
falls the filter was built to remove. And a 30.4% fall is over the 25% real-money bar in design §1
anyway.

## Hypothesis vs result

- **Prediction 1** (near beats far by 3+ points *and* falls 8+ points less): half held. The fall
  gap was 16.8 points, twice what I predicted. The return gap was 0.1 points, not 3.
- **Prediction 2** (near beats the blind control by 2+ points): held, decisively, +6.0 points.
  The buyback signal is doing real work.
- **Prediction 3** (the fall lands 40-50%): just missed, 50.8%, which is over the lab's own screen.
- **Prediction 4** (3 of 4 periods, and a positive modern-era lead): failed. 2 of 4, and the modern
  lead collapsed from the parent's +3.8 to +0.8, and to −0.9 on honest data. This was named before
  the run as the question that decides the method, and it answered no.
- **Prediction 5** (the stricter third lands between): held and monotone. The near third fell
  slightly less (48.0%) and earned slightly less (+9.9%). So the filter is a dial that trades return
  for safety at a bad exchange rate, and tightening it does not help.
- **Expected failure 1** (secretly momentum): did not happen. The blind control settles it.
- **Expected failure 3** (the filter keeps the milder buyback companies): did not happen; measured,
  both halves shrink at the same rate.
- **Expected failure 4** (the halves are nearly the same companies): did not happen; zero overlap.
- **Expected failure 5** (the modern era is the honest read): happened, and it is the verdict.

## My opinion

Reject this, and do not try another version of this shape. A filter on price level is the wrong
tool for this book, and this run says so about as clearly as a backtest can: the kept half and the
discarded half earned the same money over twenty years, and in the only years that resemble today
the discarded half earned nearly all of it.

But this is a productive rejection, because it inverts the next step rather than closing the
direction. Three things are now established and none of them were before:

1. **The buyback signal is genuinely informative.** A blind draw from the same pool, paying the same
   fees, loses by six points a year. That is the strongest control result in this family.
2. **The information lives in the cheap repurchases.** Companies buying back stock well below their
   yearly high led the index by 6 points a year since 2009 on the honest price history. Companies
   buying back at their high lost to it. This is the buyback thesis behaving exactly as the original
   argument says it should — management acting on a price it believes is too low — and this lab had
   never separated the two before.
3. **The 2008 fall is still unsolved, and it is not a price-level problem.** It is a concentration
   problem, as the previous run concluded: the far half loads into financials at the worst possible
   moment. Timing does not fix it (it costs the recovery), a market core does not fix it (it falls
   too), and now a price filter does not fix it (it costs the edge).

So the next thing to try is the opposite of this one: rank on *both* — how hard a company is buying
back its stock **and** how far below its yearly high it is buying it — as a single score rather than
a filter, so nothing is thrown away. And the industry cap already queued (M0239) should be tested on
the cheap half, not on the whole pool, because that is where the money and the 2008 risk both are.

One thing I would stop doing: reading the walk-forward fold record as evidence about a method whose
arms differ in whether they time the market. In three methods running, the picker has chosen the
braked arm or a control arm and scored the method on something it was not arguing for.


### 2026-10-20

**The fee claim below is wrong, and the control result it calls the strongest in this family is
the weakest.**

The analysis says: *"A blind draw from the same pool, paying the same fees, loses by six points a
year. That is the strongest control result in this family."* The blind draw did not pay the same
fees. It traded **3,872 times** in twenty years against the real book's **1,285** — three times as
often — and turned over three times as much. On Gotrade's fees that difference alone is worth
several points a year, so most of the six-point gap is a record of what the control was made to
pay, not of what the signal knows.

A control matched to this book's own trading has since been drawn: 1,325 trades against 1,285, and
turnover within three per cent. It earned **+8.8% a year** on the same deposits against the book's
**+10.4%**.

**So the honest gap is 1.6 points a year, not six.** Both sentences are withdrawn. Among the
methods whose controls the lab has re-drawn fairly, this is now the **narrowest** margin of the
set, not the widest.

**What this does and does not change.** The claim that the buyback signal carries real information
is weakened, not overturned: the book still leads a book of its own shape with no idea in it, by
about a point and a half a year. The two findings beside it — that the information lives in the
cheap repurchases, and that the 2008 fall is a concentration problem rather than a price-level one
— rest on comparisons between this method's own arms rather than on the blind draw, so this
correction does not reach them; they stand or fall on their own later evidence. The rejection
itself was never about the control and is unchanged. No test-window look was spent and nothing was
re-run: these are the same trials, read against a fair opponent.
methods.verdict: Rejected: filtering the buyback book down to companies near their yearly high cut the 2008 fall by 17 points and earned not one extra rupiah — the discarded half beats the market by 6 points a year since 2009 on honest data, while the kept half loses to it

methods.name: Buy the companies whose boards most recently did something confident
methods.hypothesis: A share split, a first-ever dividend, a dividend raised after a flat stretch and a large buyback are the same gesture in four costumes: a board spending money or credibility to say it believes the current price is a floor rather than a ceiling. M0241 found that recent splitters beat a shape-matched book by about two points a year and that the lead decays with time since the split, but it failed because after 2008 the store's members produce only 11-27 splits a year. Counting the pooled calendar before writing this file showed the reserved idea's premise is wrong in a useful way: the pool is not thin, it is enormous -- a median of 213 of about 350 screened members carry a live gesture in 2009-2015, because a routine annual dividend raise is not rare. So pooling cannot be the instrument; freshness is. Hold the 30 members whose newest gesture of any kind is the most recent, equal weight with no name above 20%, behind the SPY 200-day gate, monthly, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. With 213 names live and 30 slots the only thing choosing the book is how recently the board acted, which is exactly the quantity M0241 found decays, now measured on a calendar that never empties. Three arms cut the pool -- without buybacks, without the routine raise, and dividends only -- and two controls can disprove it: a stale arm holding gestures one to two years old and nothing since, and a placebo matched to the real book's count, cohort composition and turnover month by month.
methods.expectedFailure: Three ways, in order of likelihood. First, the pool is three members in five, so the book is a gated equal-weight slice of the payout-paying index and lands on the placebo, which is how M0241 lost about half its apparent lead. Second, dividend raises are 187 of the 239 live gestures in 2015, so the pooled book is the stock-dividend-change-drift family (68 trials, best MAR 0.57) wearing an event costume, and DIVONLY30 will match FRESH30 while HARD30 -- the rare, genuinely costly gestures -- trails on a thinner book. Third, and specific to this instrument: with 213 names queued for 30 slots and no preference for names already held, roughly half the book turns over every month, and at a 20M IDR account a 30-way split is a $44 slot paying Gotrade's real fee twice a trade. That drag is several points a year and nothing here offsets it, so a small genuine edge in the freshest gestures can be true and still lose. The most likely verdict is a book that tracks its own placebo inside the noise, with whatever lead it has earned before 2001 and nothing left after 2009 -- the era this lab weighs most. Published in 1995, 1996 and 2008, all three anomalies had been in print for years before the dev window closes, so any strong dev result should be expected to fade.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# M0244 — Buy the companies whose boards most recently did something confident

**Rejected.** But the six arms disagreed with each other in a way that is worth more than the
verdict, so read past the first paragraph.

## What this tried

M0241 bought companies that had just split their shares. A split gives a shareholder nothing —
two shares at $50 are the same stake as one at $100 — so a board that pays to do it is making a
statement: we think this price is a floor, not a ceiling. It worked on paper and was rejected for
one reason: after 2008 American companies almost stopped splitting, so the modern book held five
to twenty names drawn from a nearly empty calendar.

The idea here was that three other things a board does say the same thing: starting a dividend for
the first time, raising a dividend after a flat stretch, and buying back a large slice of its own
stock. Pool all four into one calendar, and the calendar should never be empty again.

**Counting that pool before writing a line of the method changed the plan.** The pool is not thin.
It is enormous: in 2009–2015 a median of 213 of about 350 companies the lab can trade carried one
of these four gestures in the last twelve months. Three companies in five. The reason is that one
of the four is not rare at all — a routine annual dividend raise, 187 of the 239 live gestures in
2015, against 21 splits.

So pooling could not be the instrument, and the method was built around the next thing: with 213
companies queued for 30 slots, the only thing deciding who gets bought is *how recently the board
acted*. Hold the 30 freshest gestures, equal weight, nothing above 20%, buy nothing while the US
market is below its 200-day average, re-picked monthly in fractional shares at Gotrade's real
fees on the owner's 5 million rupiah monthly top-up.

Six arms, run once each on 1996 → October 2015.

## What happened

Money-weighted return — what the owner's actual deposits would have earned, which is the honest
number for a book that is topped up every month. The same deposits put into SPY earned **+7.2% a
year**.

| arm | what it holds | a year | vs SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRESH30 | all four gestures, 30 freshest | +7.7% | **+0.5** | 23.7% | 1.44 | 3,634 |
| NOBUY30 | no buybacks | +6.4% | −0.8 | 21.1% | 1.37 | 3,091 |
| **HARD30** | **the rare gestures only — no routine raise** | **+8.3%** | **+1.1** | **20.0%** | **1.60** | **2,536** |
| DIVONLY30 | dividends only | +6.2% | −1.0 | 30.8% | 1.38 | 2,934 |
| STALE30 | the gesture is 1–2 years old, none since | +8.4% | **+1.2** | 24.2% | 2.19 | **698** |
| PLACEBO30 | the same shape, names drawn by coin-flip | +6.3% | −0.9 | 22.8% | 1.33 | 3,687 |

Nothing cleared the bar. Every arm failed on luck, and two of the six also simply lost to SPY.

**The luck test.** The lab asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best of many
tries, and deflates it by how many tries there have been. There have now been **162** of them —
one for each distinct method the lab has ever run. The owner's bar is 0.90. The best arm, HARD30,
scored **0.87**. In plain words: after 162 attempts at beating the market, a one-point-a-year lead
over twenty years is close to what the luckiest of 162 coin-flippers would show anyway. Not
nothing — but not enough to risk money on.

**The worst fall.** HARD30 fell 20.0% from a peak at its worst, exactly on the owner's 20% limit.
The dividend-only arm fell 30.8%, half again past it. These falls are measured on the book
*without* its monthly top-ups, because fresh money refills a falling account and makes a fall read
gentler than it was. The falls happened in 2008–2009 for every arm.

**The worst year** was 2015 (−6.8% for the main arm) for the raise-driven arms and 2007 for the
two that dropped the routine raise.

## The three things the arms proved

**1. The identity of the company matters. The date does not.**

The placebo is the sharpest control here. It holds exactly as many names as the real book, drawn
from exactly the same companies, in exactly the same monthly cohorts, turning over at exactly the
same rate — but the names are picked by a fixed coin-flip instead of by what the board did. It
earned +6.3% a year. So a gated, equal-weight basket of 30 ordinary big American companies earns
**less than SPY**, and anything the real book earns above +6.3% is the signal.

By that measure the signal is worth **+1.4 points a year** for the main arm and **+2.0** for the
rare-gesture arm. That is real and it is the first time this lab has measured this family cleanly.

But the stale arm destroys the thesis the method was built on. STALE30 buys companies whose
gesture happened *one to two years ago* and which have done nothing since — and it earned **+8.4%,
the most of any arm**. If a one-to-two-year-old gesture pays as well as a one-month-old one, then
recency is doing no work at all. The method's whole instrument — rank by freshness — measures
nothing. What the gesture marks is a *kind of company*, not a moment to buy.

**2. The routine dividend raise is not a confidence signal. It is dilution.**

Drop it and the book improves on every single axis at once: +8.3% against +7.7%, a 20.0% fall
against 23.7%, gains-to-losses of 1.60 against 1.44, and a thousand fewer trades. Keep only the
dividend gestures and the book is the worst of the six: +6.2%, a 30.8% fall, *below its own
placebo*. A board raising its dividend 10% for the eleventh year running is not spending
credibility on anything; it is doing the expected. The rare, costly acts — splitting the stock,
starting a dividend after never paying one, retiring 3% of the share count — are a different
animal, and they are the only ones that paid.

This also settles the second thing this method was expected to fail on, and settles it the other
way round. The worry was that the pooled book would turn out to be the lab's dividend-change
family (68 trials, best MAR 0.57) in an event costume. It is not — the dividend part is the
*drag*, and removing it is what made the book work.

**3. The real opponent is the book's shape, not the signal.**

Split by era, every arm tells the same story:

| arm | 1996–2002 | 2003–2008 | 2008 alone | 2009–2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRESH30 | +4.3% | +5.3% | +34.8% | **−7.8%** |
| HARD30 | +4.6% | +4.8% | +34.8% | **−6.7%** |
| STALE30 | +1.1% | +3.7% | +34.8% | **−4.3%** |
| PLACEBO30 | — | — | +34.8% | **−8.2%** |

Two things jump out. The 2008 number is **identical in every arm including the coin-flip
placebo** — so that +34.8% is entirely the 200-day market switch stepping aside before the crash,
and none of it is the signal. And 2009–2015, the best-measured years and the ones most like today,
is a disaster for everything: the book loses between four and nine points a year to SPY.

But look at the placebo in that column. The coin-flip book loses **8.2 points a year** in
2009–2015. So almost all of that loss is not the signal failing — it is what happens to *any*
equal-weight basket of thirty index members when the biggest American companies are pulling the
index. Against that placebo the signal is still *ahead* in 2009–2015: HARD30 by 1.5 points a year,
STALE30 by 3.9. The gesture kept working in the modern era. The book's shape is what lost.

That is the clearest statement this lab has of a problem it has circled for weeks: an equal-weight
book of index members is betting against the market's shape before it picks a single stock, and
since 2009 that bet costs roughly eight points a year. No stock-picking signal of this size
survives it.

## When the dead companies are added back

The lab keeps a second price history that includes the companies that went bust, which the main
one cannot price. Re-run on it, the rare-gesture arm gets **better**: +8.3% → +8.8% a year, and
its luck score rises from 0.87 to 0.92 — above the owner's bar. The two raise-driven arms get
worse. This is the same fingerprint M0241 found on splits, and it is unusual: almost every method
this lab has checked loses ground when the failures are put back. A signal that strengthens with
the dead companies included is a signal that was being *hidden* by their absence, not manufactured
by it. That is a mark in the rare gestures' favour and it is why this direction is not finished.

None of it changes the verdict: the honest-tape run is a cross-check, never a gate, and 2009–2015
is still −6.0% there.

## Hypothesis and expected failure, judged

The **hypothesis** — that freshness is the selector — is **refuted**, by the stale arm earning the
most of all six.

Of the three **expected failures** written before the run: the first (lands on its placebo) was
half right — the raise-driven arms did, the rare-gesture arms beat it by two points. The second
(it is the dividend family in costume) was **wrong, and backwards**: the dividend part is the
drag. The third (turnover and fees eat a real edge) looks right and is not fully measured: the two
arms that beat the placebo are also the two that trade least, 2,536 and 698 times against the
placebo's 3,687, and this method did not pre-register a placebo matched to the thinner arms'
turnover. So part of HARD30's two-point lead may be that it trades less, not that it picks better.
That is an honest gap and it is the first thing the next method should close.

## Compared with the parent

M0241's best split arm beat its own shape-matched placebo by about two points a year, at the same
fees on the same tape — the same size of lead HARD30 shows here, which is consistent with splits,
initiations and buybacks being one signal after all, once the routine raise is thrown out. What
pooling bought was a book that no longer empties: M0241 held five to twenty names after 2008;
HARD30 holds thirty whenever the market switch is on.

The book held nothing on 28% of decision days — that is the 200-day switch, not an empty calendar
— and 69% of the money was in stocks across the whole window.

**My opinion:** this direction is worth more trials, but not one more trial of this shape. Three
things are now measured and should not be re-measured: the routine dividend raise is noise and
belongs out of every future version; recency is not the selector, so stop ranking on it; and an
equal-weight book of index members costs about eight points a year against SPY since 2009, which
is larger than any edge this family has shown and will swamp the next attempt exactly as it
swamped this one. What I would do next is carry the rare-gesture signal — splits, first dividends,
real buybacks, nothing else — on a shape that is not fighting the market: hold the gesture names
*beside* a core of the market itself, or weight them by company size rather than equally, so the
book is not short the biggest companies by construction. Pair it with a placebo matched to that
shape *and its turnover*, since this run showed the two arms that won are also the two that traded
least. And keep the hold long: the stale arm says a gesture is still worth something two years
later, which is a licence to trade a tenth as often and stop paying Gotrade four thousand times.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the rare gestures (splits, first dividends, buybacks) beat a shape-matched coin-flip by two points a year and even hold that lead after 2009 — but the routine dividend raise is dilution, recency does nothing, and an equal-weight book of index members loses eight points a year to SPY since 2009, which swamps it.

methods.name: The 200-day gate is insurance: nine of its eleven exits were premiums, two were claims
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0241 (its SPLIT12-NOGATE arm priced the same switch on an event book)
methods.hypothesis: The lab reads the SPY 200-day gate as a rule that decayed: it helps over twenty years and helps nothing after 2009. Reading the gate's exits one at a time says something else. On SPY's own tape from 1994 to 2015 the monthly gate has eleven off-spells. Two were claims -- out from 2000-09 to 2003-04 while SPY fell 36.1%, and from 2007-12 to 2009-06 while it fell 36.3% -- and nine were premiums, costing 52 points of missed market between them. Every spell after 2009 was a premium and none was a claim, because the dev window's 2009-2015 holds no bear market. So the gate did not stop working; it spent six and a half years insuring against something that never happened. If claims can be told from premiums the insurance gets cheap. The obvious tells point the wrong way: both claims broke only 1-2% below the average and fired at ordinary volatility, while the deepest breaks (9.5% in 1998) and the loudest (47% volatility in 2011) were whipsaws -- crashes arrived quietly and whipsaws arrived screaming, which is why M0084's 3% band bought nothing. One tell survives, and it is read at every later check rather than on the exit day: a whipsaw is a dip beneath an average that is still climbing, a bear market is a dip beneath an average that has turned down. So: stay invested below the 200-day average while that average is still rising, and go to cash only once it has turned down. Six arms hold nothing but SPY, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-ups, on one shared lookback -- GATE (the plain switch, the control), FALL21 / FALL63 / FALL126 (leave only once the average is below where it stood 21, 63 or 126 sessions ago: the dose-response ladder), RISE21 (the mirror, leaving only while the average still rises, which must be far worse on both axes or the slope reading is noise) and CROSS (the famous 50-over-200 death cross, the published rule the lab's own test must beat). SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: a 100%-SPY book trades a few dozen times in twenty years, so it can never clear the 100-trade bar and its profit factor and luck score are meaningless; the paired differences against GATE, the worst fall and the 2009-2015 split are the result. The hypothesis under test is that a FALL arm keeps both crash exits, holds the worst fall at GATE's level and earns more than GATE both whole-window and over 2009-2015, while RISE21 fails on both axes. Note the lookback is 327 bars, not M0084's 253, so this window starts 1994-05-17: compare with the GATE arm here, never directly with M0084's numbers. Assumed without asking: that a rule shaped by looking at this window's eleven episodes is still worth one pre-registered method, because the alternative is to keep guessing at the gate from books that also hold stocks.
methods.expectedFailure: The honest weakness is the sample. This window holds two crashes. Any rule that delays every exit by about two months will look good here because both of this window's crashes happened to be slow -- SPY broke its average in September 2000 and December 2007 and kept falling for months afterwards, so an average that turns down a month or two later still catches almost all of both. A fast crash would be caught far too late, and a fast crash is exactly what 1987 and 2020 were. Nothing measured on the dev window can settle that; two is not a sample, the folds are the only within-window check, and the test window is the real one. The second risk is that the FALL arms simply trade less and this is a fee story rather than a signal story -- the ladder is the test, since a longer slope window trades still less and should keep improving if it is fees, while a signal should peak and turn. The third is that the slope filter re-enters while SPY is still below its average, which is a bear-market bounce by another name: if a FALL arm's worst fall comes in much deeper than GATE's 18.9%, the filter bought its return by standing inside a crash, and the result should be read as a failure however good the average is. Fourth, this is the lab's FOURTH attack on the same switch -- a wider threshold (M0101), a different sell rule (M0143) and a waiting period (M0148) were all refused -- and the standing rule from M0148 is not to try a fifth without new evidence that the flips are noise. The episode ledger is offered as that evidence, but if these arms also fail, that rule should harden into closing this family: the switch is then simply at its best and the lab should spend its ideas on what the book holds instead of on when it holds it. Not modelled, as in every earlier switch method: interest on the cash held while the gate is off, which flatters SPY and penalises every switched arm, so every gap reported is an upper bound on the switch's cost.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

# M0245 — The safety rule is insurance, and we had been reading its bill as a loss

## The question

Half the strategies in this lab carry the same safety rule. It says: **when the S&P 500 tracker
(SPY) closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything and sit in
cash; when it closes back above, buy again.**

Three earlier tests priced that rule and all three ended in the same uncomfortable place. Over
twenty years it helps. After 2009 it helps nothing — on the share-split book tested earlier this
week it cost about nine points a year over 2009–2015. The lab has been reading that as a rule
that *stopped working*.

in cash:

| sold out | bought back | months out | market while we were out | deepest fall while we were out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mar 1994 | Aug 1994 | 5 | **+8.2%** | −5.3% |
| Nov 1994 | Jan 1995 | 2 | **+4.3%** | −1.7% |
| Aug 1998 | Oct 1998 | 2 | **+11.8%** | −9.7% |
| Sep 1999 | Oct 1999 | 1 | **+5.5%** | −6.7% |
| **Sep 2000** | **Apr 2003** | **31** | **−36.1%** | −45.8% |
| Jul 2004 | Oct 2004 | 3 | **+2.2%** | −4.2% |
| Apr 2005 | May 2005 | 1 | **+3.5%** | −1.8% |
| **Dec 2007** | **Jun 2009** | **18** | **−36.3%** | −53.0% |
| May 2010 | Sep 2010 | 4 | **+6.6%** | −8.9% |
| Aug 2011 | Jan 2012 | 5 | **+9.5%** | −9.6% |
| Aug 2015 | Sep 2015 | 2 | **+0.7%** | −5.6% |

the wrong way**:

- **How far the market had fallen below the line.** The two real crashes broke the line by only
  1% and 2%. The four *deepest* breaks — 9.5% in 1998, 4.9% in 2011, 4.8% in 2015, 3.6% in 1994

explains, after the fact, why an earlier test of a wider trigger bought nothing at all.

average that is **still climbing**. A bear market is a dip beneath an average that has **turned
down**. So the rule tested here is: stay invested below the line while the 200-day average is
still rising, and go to cash only once the average itself has turned down.

## The six versions

All hold nothing but SPY, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's real
5,000,000 IDR monthly top-ups, over May 1994 to October 2015.

| version | what it does | your money earned | worst fall | sells in 21 years |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GATE** | the plain rule (the control) | **+9.1% a year** | 19.0% | 10 |
| **FALL21** | sell only once the average is below where it was a month ago | **+10.4%** | 18.9% | 6 |
| **FALL63** | the same, a quarter ago | **+10.3%** | 18.9% | 5 |
| **FALL126** | the same, half a year ago | **+10.9%** | 18.9% | 4 |
| **RISE21** | the mirror: sell only while the average is still *rising* | **+6.4%** | **52.4%** | 8 |
| **CROSS** | the famous "death cross" (50-day under 200-day) | **+10.0%** | 18.9% | 7 |

the plain rule — between 0.9 and 1.8 points a year — while its worst fall stayed at 18.9%, a
hair *better* than the plain rule's 19.0%. The specific failure I was most afraid of, that
staying invested below the line would mean standing inside a crash, did not happen: all three
patient versions still sold in 2000 and in 2008, just two months later each time, and still sat
out almost all of both.

theory says it is worthless, and it is a disaster: +6.4% a year, worse than doing nothing at

**One. The numbers are built on four decisions.** FALL126 differs from the plain rule by *six

death cross, which is the clearest possible sign that these statistics have nothing to chew on.

can be promoted, and no test-window look was spent.** That was written down before the run; this
method was always a measurement, not a candidate.

**Two. Two crashes is not a sample.** Both of this window's crashes were slow. SPY broke the
line in September 2000 and December 2007 and went on falling for months, so an average that
turns down two months later still catches nearly all of both. A *fast* crash — 1987, or
February 2020 — would be caught far too late by a rule that waits for a six-month average to
roll over. Nothing on this window can settle that. The walk-forward folds already hint at it:

## What this changes

The lab has refused three previous attempts to improve this rule: a wider trigger, a different

**My opinion:** the measurement is worth more than the rule, and I would not trade the slope

the lab's shared frame; if it does not, this family should be closed and the lab should go back

pre-register a fifth variation on the switch itself. Three refusals and one measurement is
enough, and the real verdict on the patient rule is not available on this window at all — it
lives in 2020, which is a fast crash, and the lab cannot look.

methods.name: Step down when a rising market goes quiet and scattered: the brake that fires in the uptrend, not the downtrend
methods.hypothesis: M0182 measured SPY's next-month return across 237 months split by trend and by how closely the 100 busiest index members moved together. Inside an uptrend (SPY above its 200-day average, 170 months) the ordering was clean and large: bottom-fifth correlation +0.33% a month (61 months, about +4% a year), middle +1.10% (80), top fifth +2.44% (29, about +34% a year). Below the 200-day average the same reading barely sorted anything (-0.54% high vs -0.19% middle; the -2.83% low cell is 6 months, two of which set its average). Every brake this lab has built fires in a falling market; this one would fire in a rising one. Hold SPY at full weight while the market is rising AND correlation is not in its bottom band, step down to part SPY while the market is rising and correlation is loose, and keep the plain 200-day switch underneath. Variants, to be fixed before the run: a bottom-fifth trigger to half weight; the same to cash; a bottom-third trigger (more months, weaker signal) as the dose-response rung; the MIRROR again (step down on TIGHT uptrend months), which must lose or the frame did the work; a placebo that steps down in the same NUMBER of randomly chosen uptrend months per year, which separates 'be out of a rising market sometimes' from 'be out of the quiet ones'; and the plain 200-day switch as the control, same window. THIS IS A SELECTED HYPOTHESIS: it was found by reading a table built from data already run, so the mirror and the placebo are not optional and the fold record and the 2009-2015 number decide it. Known risk: the loose-and-rising months cluster in the late 1990s and mid-2000s, so this may be a rule about two stretches of history rather than about markets. Trade count will again be far under 100, so this is a paired measurement, not a roster candidate.

methods.name: Is the quiet, scattered market the reason the stock-picking books die after 2009? Correlation as a switch on the picker, not on the market
methods.hypothesis: M0182 showed that inside an uptrend, months when the 100 busiest index members move closely together were followed by about +34% a year for SPY and months when they move independently by about +4% a year. That is a statement about the MARKET. The more valuable question is whether it is also a statement about STOCK PICKING. Every roster book here (the residual-momentum book, the plain momentum book, the multi-factor blend) sits behind the same 200-day switch and every one of them loses to SPY in 2009-2015. A plausible mechanism: a stock picker needs stocks to differ from each other to have anything to pick, so a LOW-correlation market should be the picker's best market even though it is SPY's worst — the two should point opposite ways. If that is true, correlation is not a market timer at all, it is a measurement of when picking works, and it would apply to every book the lab owns rather than to one. Test it directly: take the lab's best recorded residual-momentum configuration unchanged and register one variation that holds the book only while average correlation is in its bottom band (picker-friendly), one that holds it only while correlation is high (the mirror, which must lose), one dose-response rung at a bottom-third trigger, a placebo that is out for the same number of months chosen without reading correlation, and the unconditioned book as the control. Success: the low-correlation arm beats the unconditioned control on 2009-2015 AND on a majority of folds AND the mirror loses. Expected failure: correlation and dispersion are close cousins and the lab's dispersion clock (M0118) was empty in both directions, so the honest prior is that this is empty too; the distinction is that M0118 timed the MARKET with dispersion and never asked whether it timed the PICKER. Check the trade count: conditioning a 20-name monthly book should keep it well over 100 trades, so unlike M0182 this one can actually be eligible.

methods.name: Cheap buybacks: score a company on how hard it is buying back its stock AND how far below its yearly high it is buying it
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0243 (the buyback book filtered near the yearly high), grandchild of M0227; Pontiff & Woodgate (2008) JF 63(2) 921-945, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v63y2008i2p921-945.html; George & Hwang (2004) JF 59(5) doi:10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x; placebo draw of M0187
methods.hypothesis: M0243 established three things by filtering the buyback book on nearness to the 52-week high and keeping the discarded half as a mirror. (1) The buyback signal is genuinely informative: twenty names drawn blind from the identical filtered half, at identical fees, earned +4.4% a year against the real picks' +10.4%, the strongest control result this family has produced. (2) The filter is orthogonal to buyback intensity, measured: the near and far halves shrink their share counts at 7.70% and 7.64% a year, so filtering on price does not keep the milder shrinkers. (3) The filter removed the half that earns. The near half led SPY by +0.8% a year in 2009-2015 and LOST by 0.9% on the survivorship-check store; the discarded far half led by +3.5% and +6.0%, against the unfiltered parent's +3.8%. The mechanism is the original Pontiff-Woodgate argument turned the right way up: a buyback is informative because management is spending real money saying the stock is cheap, so the information is in the opportunistic repurchase made well below the yearly high, not the routine one made at it. Large US companies now buy back stock quarter after quarter as policy, which is exactly the uninformative half M0243 kept. So stop filtering and start scoring. Each month, take M0227's scored pool verbatim (all its split, units and one-listing-per-company guards), keep the members that also carry a 252-session nearness value, and rank that one pool twice: ascending by the log fall in split-adjusted share count over a year (the biggest shrinker first) and ascending by nearness to the 52-week high (the deepest discount first). Each position becomes a rank fraction in [0, 1], and the book holds the twenty lowest values of w * rank(buyback) + (1 - w) * rank(discount), equal slots, ties by symbol. Summing rank fractions rather than raw values means neither piece's units nor its outliers can decide the book and nothing is thrown away. The idea row described the discount as -log(nearness); because the pieces are combined by rank, that log is a monotone relabelling and the file ranks nearness ascending instead, which is the same book with one fewer transform. Arms, all twenty equal slots, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, none of them timed: B100 (w=100, plain buyback intensity on this pool -- M0227-S20 as a within-frame control), B75 (w=75), EQ (w=50, the idea), D75 (w=25), D100 (w=0, a plain deep-discount book -- long-term reversal, which the lab has already rejected at MAR 0.30) and R (twenty names drawn blind from the identical pool in a monthly-redrawn hash order: the frame with neither signal). B100 through D100 are a five-rung dose-response ladder in the discount weight, which is a stronger instrument than a single arm beside a placebo: a lead that rises monotonically with the discount weight cannot be the frame. Predictions written before any result. (1) The ladder is monotone in 2009-2015 and the combination beats BOTH single ends there, on the dev store and on the survivorship-check store. (2) D100 falls deepest of the six, because a book of deeply discounted stocks in 2007 is a book of financials in 2008. (3) The 2008 fall stays past 50% -- outside the lab's dev screen -- on every arm, because no arm is timed and M0243 and M0230 between them established the fall is a concentration problem that neither timing, a market core nor a price filter touches. (4) Every combo arm beats R by 3 or more points a year. Success is (1) and (4) together; it would say the discount carries information rather than merely reshaping the book, and it would make this ladder, not the plain pool, the right test bed for the queued industry cap (M0239). A monotone ladder running the WRONG way -- more discount weight, less lead -- is an equally useful result and closes the direction. Failing the dev drawdown screen is expected and is not itself the verdict.
methods.expectedFailure: Five ways, in order of likelihood. (1) The ladder is flat. The two orders may be nearly the same order: the same buyback dollars retire more shares when the price is low, so the biggest shrinkers are already mechanically tilted toward companies whose price has fallen, and if the two rankings correlate strongly then every rung holds nearly the same twenty names and the whole ladder lands inside a point of itself. That is a measurement the method still earns -- it would say M0243's far-half result was the buyback signal operating with no price information added -- but it closes the combination as an idea. (2) The discount leg is long-term reversal wearing a new coat. D100 is a deep-discount book, and the lab has rejected that shape twice (M0069, M0073, best MAR 0.30). If the ladder is monotone but D100 does the earning, the method has rediscovered reversal inside a buyback pool, and the honest reading is that the pool is the filter and the discount is the engine -- which is a different method from the one argued here and would need the reversal literature's own decay caveat applied to it. (3) The 2008 concentration problem gets worse, not better. Tilting toward cheapness inside a buyback pool in 2007 is a direct instruction to buy the banks that were buying back stock while their prices fell, which is the exact failure mode M0227's expected_failure (3) named and M0243's far half confirmed at a 67.6% fall. The combination may well land nearer FAR20's fall than NEAR20's, and a book that earns 3 points more while falling 17 points deeper is not progress. (4) 2009-2015 fades anyway. Both halves of this idea are published -- buybacks since 2006-2008, the 52-week-high effect since 2004 -- and the far half's +6.0 point lead on honest data was measured over 2009-2015 with a single ranking and 21 years of in-sample context behind it. A second ranking fitted on top of a result that was itself read after the fact is exactly how a lab fools itself, which is why the ladder and the predictions are written here before the run and why no rung will be tuned afterwards. (5) Rank-sum washes out the extremes. Adding rank fractions treats the gap between the first and second biggest shrinker as identical to the gap between the hundredth and the hundred-and-first, so a company retiring 25% of its stock is scored barely ahead of one retiring 12%. That is the deliberate price of robustness, but it may be the whole reason a combination underperforms the pure B100 end. None of these is a reason to tune w, the 252-session window, the combination rule or the parent's guards afterwards: each would be a new method with new trials.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What we tried

Companies that buy back their own shares have been this lab's best live stock idea. The buyback
book held the twenty index members whose share count had shrunk most over the past year, and it
earned 13.0% a year on your deposits where the index earned 7.2%.

The run before this one asked whether it mattered *at what price* a company buys back its stock.
It split the buyback companies into a dear half (price near its best level of the past year) and a
cheap half (price well below it), and held the biggest buyback companies inside each. The answer
was clear and the opposite of what was expected: the cheap half was the half that earned, and in
the years that look most like today it beat the market by 6 points a year on honest price history
while the dear half lost to it.

So this run stopped throwing half the companies away and started scoring instead. Every company in
the pool got two positions: one for how hard it is buying back its stock, one for how far below its
yearly high it is trading. The book held the twenty best on a weighted average of the two
