positions, and the weight was turned through five settings — a ladder — so you can see what each
ingredient is worth rather than guessing:

- **B100** — all buyback, no price. The buyback book, unchanged.
- **B75** — three parts buyback, one part cheapness.
- **EQ** — equal parts. The idea itself.
- **D75** — one part buyback, three parts cheapness.
- **D100** — all cheapness, no buyback.
- **R** — twenty names picked blind from the same pool, as a luck control.

All six hold twenty names in equal slots, are asked monthly, and trade in fractional shares at
Gotrade's real fees on your 5 million rupiah monthly top-up. None of them times the market: two
market-timed versions of this family already sit in the lab and both are blocked, and mixing a
timed version in with untimed ones corrupts the lab's own period-by-period check — a mistake the
previous run asked not to repeat.

## Result

Two price histories are shown. "Usual" is the lab's normal one. "Honest" adds back most of the
companies that have since gone bankrupt, been bought out or vanished — the ones the usual history
cannot price, and which are, by definition, the ones that were in trouble. Where the two disagree,
believe the honest one. All figures count each deposit from the day it was paid in; the same
deposits put into the index earned **+7.2% a year** over 1996-2015.

| version | what it holds | earned a year (usual / honest) | lead over the index 2009-2015 (usual / honest) | worst fall (usual / honest) | luck test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B100 all buyback | 100% buying back, 10.4% of shares retired | +13.3% / +12.2% | +3.7% / **+3.5%** | 58.6% / 55.2% | 0.874 |
| B75 | 100% buying back, 8.2% retired | +10.7% / +11.7% | +5.7% / **+8.1%** | 69.4% / 67.4% | 0.607 |
| **EQ equal parts** | 99% buying back, 6.3% retired | +10.5% / +11.3% | +6.9% / **+11.8%** | 74.9% / 74.5% | 0.510 |
| D75 | 85% buying back, 4.4% retired | +17.6% / +12.3% | +18.3% / **+11.7%** | 73.9% / 79.7% | 0.776 |
| D100 all cheapness | only 32% buying back | +19.0% / +17.9% | +23.3% / **+11.4%** | 73.2% / **84.4%** | 0.658 |
| R blind picks | 51% buying back (the pool's own mix) | +7.7% / +8.4% | +1.1% / +1.1% | 54.2% / 61.2% | 0.372 |

**Every version is rejected, and not narrowly.** The lab's working limit on a fall is 50%; the best
of these falls 55%, the worst 85%. The luck test asks how likely a result is to be real rather than
a fluke after 159 separate attempts across the whole lab; the bar is 0.90 and the best version here
reaches 0.874. Nothing is close. The worst calendar year for every version was 2008, between −31%
and −44%.

## What the ladder actually says

Read the two whole-window columns and the ladder looks like a failure: the two pure ends earn the
most and every mixture earns less. That reading is wrong, and the reason it is wrong is the whole
value of this run.

The whole-window figures are dominated by the years before 2009, and by one effect: **the lab's
usual price history flatters a cheapness book enormously, because the cheapest stocks are exactly
the ones that were about to die, and the usual history cannot price the ones that did.** Look at
what happens to each version when the dead companies are put back:

| version | lead over the index 2009-2015, usual → honest |
|---|---|
| B100 all buyback | +3.7% → +3.5%  (barely moves) |
| B75 | +5.7% → +8.1%  (improves) |
| EQ equal parts | +6.9% → **+11.8%**  (improves most) |
| D75 | +18.3% → +11.7%  (loses 6.6 points) |
| D100 all cheapness | +23.3% → **+11.4%**  (loses 11.8 points — half of it was an illusion) |

And here is why, measured directly from what each book holds. Reading down the ladder, the share of
the book that is actually buying back stock stays at 100%, 100%, 99%, 85% — and then collapses to
**32%** at the pure-cheapness end. The pool itself is 51% buyback companies, so the all-cheapness
book does not merely ignore buybacks; it actively *avoids* them. It is a book of distressed
companies, and when you add the distressed companies that actually died, half its apparent edge
disappears, its fall deepens from 73% to 85%, and its gains-to-losses ratio collapses from 3.04 to
1.75. Its honest return is carried by a handful of enormous bounces in near-dead companies — not
something a 20 million rupiah account could ever have held through.

So the honest answer, in the years that matter most:

> **A buyback book earns three times more when you tilt it toward cheap stocks — from 3.5% a year
> over the index to 11.8% — and tilting further, past the point where the companies are still
> buying back, buys nothing and costs a great deal.**

The buyback requirement is not the engine. It is the **safety catch**. A company retiring 6% of its
own shares is spending real cash and is not about to go bankrupt, so requiring it lets you buy
cheapness without buying the dying. That is exactly why the equal mixture is the one version whose
character barely changes when the dead companies come back (its fall moves 74.9% → 74.5%, its
gains-to-losses 2.06 → 1.99) while the pure-cheapness version falls apart.

Why did mixing look so bad over the whole window, then? Because the two rankings are almost
unrelated — their rank correlation is −0.09, and the all-buyback and all-cheapness books share only
**1.1 names out of 20**. Averaging the positions of two unrelated rankings produces a book that sits
in the top tail of neither. That is a genuine cost, and over 1996-2008 it outweighed everything
else. It does not outweigh the survivorship correction in the modern era.

## Hypothesis vs result

- **Prediction 1** (the ladder is monotone and the mixture beats both pure ends, in 2009-2015, on
  both histories): **half held, and the half that held is the important one.** On the usual history
  it failed — the all-cheapness end ran away with +23.3%. On the honest history it held: the equal
  mixture's +11.8% is the best rung on the ladder, ahead of both +3.5% and +11.4%. The margin over
  the cheap end is 0.4 points, which is noise; the margin over the buyback end is 8.3 points, which
  is not.
- **Prediction 2** (the all-cheapness version falls deepest): **failed on the usual history** — the
  equal mixture fell deepest there, 74.9% against 73.2%. **Held on the honest one**, 84.4%, and
  by the largest margin of the six. Another case of the dead companies being where the risk hides.
- **Prediction 3** (every version breaks the 50% fall limit): **held**, all six, 55% to 85%.
- **Prediction 4** (every scored version beats the blind control by 3 or more points a year):
  **held for four of the five, and failed for the idea itself.** The equal mixture beat the blind
  draw by 2.8 points on the usual history and 2.9 on the honest one — just short. The scoring is
  working, but the equal mixture is the rung where it works least over the whole window.
- **Expected failure 1** (the two rankings are really the same ranking): **did not happen**, and the
  measurement is the cleanest thing in this run. They are independent and share one name in twenty.
- **Expected failure 2** (the cheapness half is just "buy what has fallen", which this lab already
  rejected): **happened at the far end and only there.** The all-cheapness version is that book, it
  holds 32% buyback companies, and it behaves exactly as that shape behaves on honest data — a
  lottery ticket. It does not describe the middle of the ladder, which stays 99% buyback companies.
- **Expected failure 3** (tilting toward cheap makes the 2008 problem worse): **happened.** Every
  mixture falls further than the plain buyback book, 69-75% against 58.6%.
- **Expected failure 4** (2009-2015 fades anyway): **did not happen.** +11.8 points a year on honest
  data in the best-covered era is the largest modern-era lead this family has produced.
- **Expected failure 5** (averaging positions washes out the extremes): **happened**, and it is the
  mechanical explanation for the whole-window shape.

## Where this leaves the lab's own checks

- **Period-by-period check:** 4 of 4 periods won, on both price histories — the first time this
  family has managed that. But the lab's picker chose a different version for the last period than
  for the first three, so the record describes the family and not one tradable rule.
- **Narrow versus broad markets:** every version pays only when the average stock beats the index.
  That is the standing weakness of every equal-weighted book in this lab and it is not news.
- **No buy signal.** The owner's data-purchase trigger needs a version that passes the lab's
  screen first. None does, by a wide margin. Nothing here argues for buying survivorship-free
  price history yet.

## My opinion

The combination, as built here, is dead: averaging two unrelated rankings is a bad way to use both,
and the drawdowns — 55% to 85% — are so far outside anything you could hold that no amount of
tuning closes the gap. This method is rejected and I would not run another rank-average.

But I think this run has found the most useful thing the buyback family has produced, and it is not
what the previous run concluded. The previous run said the information lives in the cheap
repurchases. That is half right in a misleading way. **Cheapness is what earns; the buyback is what
keeps the cheapness survivable.** Buying cheap stocks is a known way to make money and a known way
to go broke, and the measurements here separate those two for the first time in this lab: the pure
cheapness book loses half its modern edge and gains 11 points of fall when the dead companies come
back, while the same book with a buyback requirement attached barely moves and ends up leading by
the same amount. Requiring that management is spending real cash is a bankruptcy screen that costs
nothing.

What I would do next, and it is a single decisive experiment rather than another dial: inside the
cheapest third of the pool, hold the biggest buyback companies, the biggest share *issuers*, and a
blind draw — three books on the same cheap names. If the buyback book beats the issuer book there,
the buyback signal carries information on top of cheapness and this family is worth continuing with
a proper brake. If all three land together, then buybacks are purely a survival filter with no
return content, and the honest conclusion is that this family is deep value in disguise and should
be closed and folded into whatever the lab does about falls. I have queued that as the next method.

The thing I would not do is attack the 2008 fall first. Every brake this lab owns has now been tried
on this family — market timing costs the recovery, an index core falls with the crash, a price
filter costs the edge — and the queued industry cap is worth one run but will not turn a 75% fall
into a 25% one. Settle what the signal is before spending more ids on how to survive it.
methods.verdict: Rejected on a 55-85% fall, but it found the family's real mechanism: cheapness is what earns and the buyback is what keeps it survivable — tilting the buyback book toward cheap stocks tripled its modern-era lead on honest data, from 3.5% to 11.8% a year

methods.name: A special dividend as extra weight inside the raise book, not a book of its own
methods.hypothesis: M0242 measured that a special dividend carries real news — scaled to a full book its picks were worth about +2.6 points a year over SPY where the steady-payer control was worth +0.3 — but there are only three or four live specials among big liquid index members at a time, so a ten-slot book was 35% picks and 65% SPY park, and the measured lead collapsed to +0.9. The ordinary-raise control on the same chassis filled 76% of its slots and earned +3.6. The arithmetic says: stop asking specials to carry a portfolio, and ask whether they are extra information on top of a raise. Take M0070's R25 big-raise book (up to 20 F4-screened members, SPY-200 switch, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) and give a name a double slot weight in the quarter after it declares a special dividend of twice its regular payment or more, with the book renormalised so it stays fully invested. The book stays full, the trade count stays above the 100 minimum, and the only thing being tested is the increment. Controls, pre-registered: the plain R25 book at single weight (the parent), and a sham tilt that doubles the weight of an equal number of raise names drawn without reference to any special, so the comparison separates 'specials are extra information' from 'concentrating the raise book helps'. Success: the tilt beats the plain R25 book by a point a year or more AND keeps the same or shallower worst fall, with the sham tilt sitting between them or below. Expected failure: at three or four specials among twenty names a double weight moves about 15% of the book, which may be too small to see above the noise; and M0242 found the special signal lags badly in 2009-2015, so a tilt may import that lag into a book that already has one.

methods.name: A dilution-matched control for any book that parks its empty slots in the index
methods.hypothesis: M0242's four special-dividend arms each beat SPY by about a point a year while being 35%, 35%, 33% and 10% their own picks — the rest was the SPY park. A lead of +0.9 from a 35%-filled book and a lead of +0.9 from a full book are completely different findings, and the lab currently prints them the same way. Worse, the 90%-parked arm had the prettiest row in the table (shallowest fall, gains-to-losses 5.49) purely because it was mostly the index. Build the matched control the M0241 placebo work argues for: a book on the same chassis, same F4 screen, same SPY-200 switch, same monthly clock and real fees, that on each decision date fills exactly as many slots as M0242-S-H6 filled on that same date — reading the count from the real book's own calendar, not an average — with names drawn by a stable hash rather than by any event, and parks the rest in SPY identically. Running it beside the real arm splits the +0.9 lead into the part that is 'this shape of book, two thirds index, re-picked monthly behind a trend switch' and the part that is 'special dividends'. Variants should also sweep the fill rate deliberately (a dose-response ladder: 10%, 35%, 70%, 100% filled with the same drawn names), because more SPY giving less lead excludes the frame by construction the way M0241's ladder did. Success: the real arm's lead over the matched placebo is positive and roughly equal to the 2.3-point gap M0242 estimated by straight-line scaling, which would confirm the scaling the analysis relied on. Expected failure: a hash-drawn book inside the F4 screen behind the SPY-200 switch may itself beat SPY by a point a year, in which case the whole special-dividend lead was the frame and the estimate in M0242's analysis was too generous.

methods.name: The price of risk as a timing signal: hold more of the market when insurance against its swings is expensive
methods.sourceRef: Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou (2009), Expected Stock Returns and Variance Risk Premia, Review of Financial Studies 22(11) 4463-4492
methods.hypothesis: Bollerslev, Tauchen and Zhou (2009) found that the variance risk premium -- what the option market charges for variance, less the variance that actually turns up -- predicts stock returns at the quarterly horizon, and does it better than the dividend yield or the price-earnings ratio. The store has no options but it has the fear index and SPY's daily bars, which is all the paper's own empirical proxy needs: implied variance is the fear index squared and expected future realised variance is proxied by the realised variance just past (the no-change forecast), so the premium is VIX(d) squared less 252/22 times the sum of the last 22 squared daily SPY log returns, both annualised, read from rows dated on or before d. The level means nothing on its own, so the rule reads the premium's rank inside its own trailing 252 sessions: top third SPY at full weight, middle third half weight, bottom third cash, decided once a month in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up. Variants: LADDER (the idea), MIRROR (the falsification arm, the same three rungs reversed -- if it does as well, the ladder is measuring the shape of a part-invested book and not the premium), BINARY (full in the top two thirds, cash in the bottom third, which prices the half-weight middle rung on its own), HOLD (control: SPY at full weight always, same rules and same fees, so the paired difference is the signal alone), SPY-200 (control: the 200-day switch the lab already trusts, on the same monthly rules), and LADDER-CASH (the ladder with idle cash credited the 13-week Treasury bill yield -- one lever away from LADDER and the only difference). A ranking probe run before this file was committed (rungs and dates only, no returns) found the month-end rungs split 35% cash, 26% half and 39% full over 1994-2015, with the rung changing in 151 of 260 month steps, so the signal is busy and not degenerate. Assumed: no fresh fear index or too little history means full weight, not cash, so every arm's early window is identical; the premium is read on day d's close and traded at the next open; idle cash earns nothing except in LADDER-CASH. Success: LADDER beats HOLD on funded return with a shallower worst fall, beats MIRROR clearly, and beats SPY-200 on at least one of return and depth of fall, with a positive 2009-2015 edge. Eligibility is not expected: a one-instrument book has far fewer than 100 round trips and cannot clear the luck bar at N=158, so the paired differences are the result.
methods.expectedFailure: The reserved idea row expected this rule to be fully invested into crashes, because the premium is highest in crises. The probe says the opposite and that correction is written here before any return is known: with trailing realised variance as the forecast, the premium goes deeply NEGATIVE in a crash -- October 2008 is the lowest reading in the window -- because realised variance explodes above the fear index once the fall is already happening. So the ladder is a defensive signal, and its real failure mode is the one every reactive risk rule in this lab has had: it sells after the drop and buys back after the rebound. The probe's 151 rung changes in 260 months is a flip roughly every other month, each paying Gotrade's fees on a 20M IDR book, and most of those flips are noise in a rising market. Expect the ladder to cut the 2008 fall and to give the saving back across 2009-2015, the years this lab weighs most, where it is in cash or half weight about 61% of months during the longest rally in the window. March 2009 is the sharpest warning in the probe: the ladder reads full in January and February 2009 and then CASH at the end of March, one rung change at the exact bottom. A second, quieter failure is that the premium and the 200-day switch may be the same signal twice -- both go defensive after a fall -- in which case LADDER-SPY-200 differences are noise and the idea adds nothing to what the lab already owns. A third: the paper is from 2009, so the 2009-2015 half of the window is post-publication and the edge there is the faded one. The half-weight rung is the most likely thing to be worthless -- a 26%-of-months rung that splits the difference should earn about half the ladder's gap to HOLD and nothing more, which BINARY will show. Finally, idle cash earning nothing penalises every arm but HOLD, and in 1994-2007 Treasury bills paid 4-5%, so a book in cash a third of the time is charged more than a point a year that a real account would have earned: LADDER-CASH measures exactly that, and if the whole of LADDER's gap to HOLD is closed by it, then this lab's verdicts on the 200-day switch, the fear-spike gate and every other cash-holding rule are all overstated.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What was tried

When you buy insurance against the stock market swinging about, you pay more than the swings
usually turn out to cost. That gap — what insurance costs minus what the swings actually cost —
is the **price of risk**. A 2009 study (Bollerslev, Tauchen and Zhou) found that when this gap is
unusually wide, the next few months tend to be good ones to own shares, and that it predicted
returns better than the old standbys like dividend yield.

The lab has no options data, but it does not need any: the study's own calculation uses the fear
index (the market's published guess at how much it will swing) squared, minus how much the market
actually swung over the past month. Both come straight out of the store. So each month-end this
method worked out that gap for SPY, compared it with its own readings over the past year, and set
how much of the account to hold:

- gap in the **top third** of its own past year → **all** of the money in SPY
- **middle third** → **half** in SPY, half in cash
- **bottom third** → **all cash**

Six versions, all in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5,000,000 rupiah a
month, 1994 to 2015:

| | what it does |
|---|---|
| **LADDER** | the idea above |
| **MIRROR** | the same three steps **upside down** — all in when the gap is narrowest. The falsification test. |
| **BINARY** | the middle step removed: all in for the top two thirds, all cash for the bottom third |
| **HOLD** | control: SPY, always, same rules and same fees |
| **SPY-200** | control: the lab's usual safety switch — out when SPY is below its average price of the last 200 trading days |
| **LADDER-CASH** | the ladder again, but idle cash earns the 3-month Treasury bill rate |

Before any of this was run, a check of the **rankings only** — which step the rule lands on each
month, never what happened next — was committed with the method. It found the steps split 35% all
cash, 26% half, 39% all in, with the step changing in 151 of 260 months. It also found something
that **contradicted the written-down expectation**: the gap goes deeply *negative* in a crash
(October 2008 is the lowest reading in twenty-two years), because once the market is actually
falling, the real swings overshoot what the fear index predicted. So this is a **defensive**
signal, not the "buy the fear" signal the idea was reserved as. That correction was written into
the method file before the run, not after it.

## Result

Everything is money-weighted: what the owner's actual deposits would have earned, not a headline
number that counts deposits as profit. The fall is measured on the book with the deposits taken
out, so a monthly top-up cannot make a crash look gentler than it was.

| version | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | round trips | invested | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **LADDER** | +6.0% | +7.7% | 33% | 2.93 | 54 | 51% of the time | 0.50 |
| **MIRROR** | **−1.2%** | +7.7% | 46% | **0.85** | 56 | 47% | 0.03 |
| **BINARY** | +5.6% | +7.7% | 36% | 2.36 | 54 | 64% | 0.41 |
| **HOLD** | +7.9% | +7.9% | 55% | — | 0 | 99% | 0.56 |
| **SPY-200** | **+9.2%** | +7.7% | **19%** | 599 | 11 | 71% | **0.90** |
| **LADDER-CASH** | +6.8% | +7.7% | 30% | 2.93 | 54 | 51% | 0.68 |

"Gains vs losses" is the profit factor: money made on winning trades divided by money lost on
losing ones; above 1.3 is the bar. "Luck score" is the deflated Sharpe ratio — the chance the
result is real rather than a lucky draw after this many tries. Every number above was judged at
**N = 160**, meaning 160 distinct methods have now been looked at, against a bar of **0.90**,
which has been the owner's risk appetite since 7 October 2026. Neither number is the lab's to
move. Four test-window looks have been spent in this lab's life and **this run spent none**.

**The ladder failed.** It earned 6.0% a year where the same deposits in SPY earned 7.7% — 1.7
points a year worse, for twenty-two years. It also missed the trade-count condition (54 round
trips, not 100) and the luck bar (0.50, not 0.90). Rejected.

## But the signal is real, and that is the finding

Look at the mirror. Turning the same three steps upside down did not produce a similar number or
a slightly worse one. It produced **−1.2% a year** — losing money across twenty-two years in which
the market roughly quadrupled — with a profit factor of 0.85, meaning the losing months took more
money than the winning months made. The two versions trade at almost the same rate (56 round trips
against 54) and spend almost the same time invested (47% against 51%), so the shape of the book is
the same. **The whole 7.2-point-a-year difference between them is which way round the signal is
read.**

That is the cleanest falsification result this lab has produced. A signal that carries nothing
would have the mirror land near the ladder. This one punishes the wrong direction severely, and it
keeps doing so in the modern era: over 2009–2015 the ladder trailed SPY by 3.9 points a year while
the mirror trailed it by **16.2**. A twelve-point gap in the years after the study was published
is not a faded anomaly.

## So why did it still lose?

Because knowing *which* months are better is not the same as knowing *whether to be in the market
at all*, and this rule was built as an on/off switch.

The ladder was invested 51% of the time and earned 6.0% a year. Buy-and-hold was invested 99% of
the time and earned 7.9%. Per unit of time actually in the market, the ladder earned **about 46%
more**. It is picking its months well. But the US market rises in roughly six months out of ten,
so sitting out a third of all months costs a great deal, and a modest advantage in *which* months
cannot pay for it. The rule has a good opinion and an unusable floor.

Fees are not the explanation. 54 round trips in 21.6 years is about two and a half a year, and
turnover of 5.6 times the account over the whole window is low — Gotrade's fees on that are small
next to a 1.7-point annual gap. It is being out of the market that costs the money.

The half-weight middle step did roughly what it was predicted to do. Removing it (BINARY) kept the
book invested more (64% against 51%) and earned slightly *less* (5.6% against 6.0%) with a deeper
fall (36% against 33%). So the middle rung is mildly useful, not decorative — but it is worth
about half a point a year, not the two points the rule needs.

## The cash finding, which matters beyond this method

Money sitting in cash earns nothing in every backtest this lab has ever run. **LADDER-CASH** is the
same rule with idle cash paying the 3-month Treasury bill rate, which is what a real account would
have earned. It changed the answer: 6.0% → **6.8%** a year, and the worst fall 33% → 30%.

So **0.8 points a year of this method's shortfall was never the method's fault** — it was an
accounting choice. Every verdict this lab has written about a rule that steps aside into cash — the
200-day switch, the fear-spike gate, every risk brake — is harsher than the truth by something of
that order.

But there is a sting, and it is the more useful half: **over 2009–2015 the credited and uncredited
versions are identical, both trailing SPY by 3.9 points a year.** Treasury bills paid nothing after
2008, so the whole 0.8-point correction is earned in 1994–2007 and none of it in the years this lab
weighs most. The bias is real, it is worth re-reading old verdicts for, and it rescues nothing in
the modern era.

## The safety switch won again, and that is awkward

The control nobody was testing came out best. The plain 200-day switch, on the same monthly
rules and the same real fees, earned **+9.2% a year against SPY's +7.7%**, with the worst fall cut
to 19% — inside the owner's 25% real-money limit — and a luck score of **0.903**, which clears the
0.90 bar. It failed one condition only: 11 round trips, not 100.

Two things should be said plainly about that. First, it is a twenty-two-year average and the fold
record is poor: it won 1 of 4 walk-forward folds, and its only winning fold is 2006–2008, the
crash. Second, over 2009–2015 it trailed SPY by **5.9 points a year** — *worse* than the variance
ladder's 3.9. So the switch's whole advantage is one crash, which the lab already knew (M0084,
M0113), and in the era most like today the new signal is the less destructive of the two defences.

A caution for whoever reads the fold line on this method's page: the walk-forward scored
**SPY-200**, the control, because the folds pick each method's best variant by return-per-unit-of-
fall and the control has the best. It did not score the ladder. That is a known rough edge, not a
statement about the idea.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis asked for the ladder to beat HOLD with a shallower fall, beat the mirror clearly,
and beat the 200-day switch on at least one of return and depth. It got **one of three**: it beat
the mirror decisively. It lost to HOLD on return (though it did halve the fall, 33% against 55%)
and lost to the switch on both.

The expected failure was written in three parts and all three landed. The ladder did cut 2008 (its
worst year is 2001 at −14%, not 2008) and did give it back in the rally. It was in cash or half
weight most of 2009–2015 and trailed by 3.9 points there. The half-weight rung was worth about
half a point. The idle-cash penalty was real and was measured.

One part of the written expectation was wrong in an interesting way. The prediction was that the
premium and the 200-day switch would be "the same signal twice". They are not. Their 2009–2015
records differ by two points a year in the ladder's favour and their worst-fall behaviour is
different (the switch cut the fall to 19%, the ladder only to 33%). They are two different
defences with different costs, which is what makes combining them worth a trial.

## My opinion

**This direction is worth more trials, and I would not have said that before seeing the mirror.**

The lab has spent a lot of ids on signals that turned out to be noise, and the usual tell is a
control arm that does just as well. This is the opposite case: the falsification arm lost money
outright, and kept losing in the post-publication era where faded anomalies go to die. There is
information in the price of risk. The implementation threw it away by converting a good opinion
into a cash position.

Two follow-ups, in order of how much I would spend on them.

**First, raise the floor.** The ladder is right about *which* months and wrong to leave the market.
Run the same three steps with the money never fully out: 100% / 75% / 50% instead of 100% / 50% /
0%, with a 100% / 85% / 70% rung and the original as the third step of a dose-response ladder. If
the information is real — and the mirror says it is — a book that stays invested and merely leans
should land *above* buy-and-hold, because it keeps the market's drift and still tilts. If the
raised-floor version does not beat HOLD either, the information is too weak to use at any dose and
the family should be closed. That is a clean, decidable test and it is queued as the next idea.

**Second, use the premium to decide when to come back, not when to leave.** The lab already
established (M0113) that the 200-day switch's exit is the valuable half and its re-entry is the
expensive half — the same slow average that correctly gets you out keeps you out through the
recovery. The ranking probe showed the price of risk reading "all in" in January and February 2009,
months before SPY crossed back above its 200-day line. That is a non-price re-entry trigger, which
is exactly what M0113 went looking for among price triggers and did not find. Keep the 200-day
exit; buy back when the price of risk recovers into its top third.

What I would **not** do is tune this ladder's thresholds. Moving the cut-offs from thirds to
quarters or lengthening the one-year reference window is the kind of change that finds a better
number without finding a better idea, and the lab counts every one of those tries against every
future result.
methods.verdict: Rejected: stepping out when the price of risk is low cost 1.7 points a year, but the upside-down version lost money outright, so the signal is real and the on-off switch is what wasted it

methods.name: Inside the cheapest third: do buybacks tell you anything a low price has not already told you?
methods.hypothesis: M0248 measured three things inside M0227's share-count-readable pool, all on both stores. (1) The two rankings are near-orthogonal: rank correlation -0.09, and the pure-buyback and pure-discount 20-name books share 1.1 names out of 20, stable across all three eras. (2) Averaging their rank fractions earns LESS than either end over the whole window (10.5%/yr equal-weight vs 13.3% pure buyback and 19.0% pure discount), because each signal's money is in its own tail and the average holds compromises. (3) In 2009-2015 on the survivorship-check store the picture inverts and becomes the real finding: the lead over SPY runs +3.5, +8.1, +11.8, +11.7, +11.4 points a year as the discount weight rises, while the share of the book that is actually buying back stock runs 100%, 100%, 99%, 85%, 32% against the pool's own 51%. The pure-discount end loses 11.8 points of its dev-store lead when the dead companies are restored and its fall deepens 73.2% -> 84.4% with profit factor 3.04 -> 1.75 and kurtosis 14 -> 85; the equal mixture loses nothing (fall 74.9% -> 74.5%, PF 2.06 -> 1.99). So cheapness is the engine and the buyback requirement is a bankruptcy screen that makes cheapness survivable -- NOT, as M0243 concluded, that the information lives in the cheap repurchases. The open question that decides whether this family continues is whether buybacks carry any RETURN information conditional on cheapness, or only survival information. Answer it by double sort rather than rank-sum, so both signals stay in their own tail. Cut M0227's scored pool (all its split, units and one-listing-per-company guards, intersected with members carrying a 252-session nearness value) to its cheapest third by nearness, then inside that band hold 20 names three ways: the biggest one-year share-count shrinkers (CHEAP-S), the biggest issuers (CHEAP-I) and a monthly-redrawn blind hash draw (CHEAP-R). Mirror the cut on the dearest third (RICH-S, RICH-I) so the conditional spread is read in both bands and the band effect is separated from the signal effect. All twenty equal slots, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's top-up, none timed. Predictions to write in the file: (a) CHEAP-S beats CHEAP-R by 3+ points a year on BOTH stores in 2009-2015 if buybacks add return information; (b) CHEAP-S beats CHEAP-I by 3+ points, which is the sharper test because both are cheap; (c) CHEAP-S survives the restoration of the dead companies far better than CHEAP-I and CHEAP-R, which is the survival-screen prediction and should hold even if (a) and (b) fail; (d) every cheap-band arm falls past 50%, because M0248 established the fall is unrelated to the price filter. If CHEAP-S, CHEAP-I and CHEAP-R land within 2 points of each other on both stores while (c) still holds, the honest reading is that the net-share-issuance family is deep value with a bankruptcy screen attached, carries no return signal of its own, and should be closed -- and the screen itself becomes the reusable finding, worth bolting onto any cheapness book the lab builds later.

methods.name: Put the patient safety rule under a real stock book, where it has enough trades to be judged
methods.hypothesis: M0245 measured the shared 200-day safety rule exit by exit and found it is insurance: nine of its eleven exits between 1994 and 2015 were false alarms costing 52 points of missed market, and only two were real crashes. It also found one way to buy less of the insurance. Waiting for the 200-day average itself to turn down before selling - rather than selling the moment price crosses it - skipped five of the nine false alarms, kept both crash exits (just two months later each time), earned 0.9 to 1.8 points a year more on the owner's deposits and held the worst fall at 18.9%, a hair better than the plain rule's 19.0%. Its mirror, selling only while the average still rises, collapsed to +6.4% a year and a 52.4% fall, which is the strongest evidence shape this lab can make on its own data. But the whole result rests on four to six selling decisions in twenty-one years, because every M0245 arm held nothing but SPY. Four decisions cannot clear the hundred-trade bar, cannot produce a meaningful profit factor and cannot produce a meaningful luck score, so the method was correctly rejected as a measurement rather than a candidate. The open question is therefore not whether to try a fifth switch variant - it is whether the patient rule survives contact with a book that actually picks stocks and therefore actually trades. Take the residual-momentum book, the one whose best variant the owner's roster already mirrors, and run it unchanged except for the gate: one arm on the lab's plain 200-day gate (the control, which must reproduce the recorded parent trial), one arm with the exit held back until the 200-day average has fallen below where it stood 126 sessions earlier, one at 21 sessions, one on the 50-over-200 death cross (the free published rule M0245 found captures most of the benefit), and the mirror arm selling only while the average still rises, which must fail. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-ups, the parent's own cadence and name count, so every paired difference is the exit rule alone. SUCCESS: a patient arm that beats the plain-gate control on the owner's deposits by at least half a point a year without pushing the worst fall past the control's, and whose 2009-2015 lag to simply holding SPY is smaller than the control's. FAILURE, and it is the likely one: the book trades hundreds of times, so the gate's handful of flips is a much smaller share of what happens to it, and the whole 1-to-1.8-point gain washes out into noise - which would say the patient rule is a SPY-only curiosity and this family should finally be closed.

methods.name: Lean, never leave: the price of risk as a weight dial with a floor that never reaches cash
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0251 (the variance risk premium ladder), lab journal 2026-10-19
methods.hypothesis: M0251 showed that the price of risk -- the fear index squared, less the realised variance just past, ranked inside its own trailing 252 sessions -- carries real information: its upside-down arm earned -1.2% a year where the ladder earned +6.0%, a 7.2-point gap on the same book shape and the same trade rate, widening to 12 points over 2009-2015. What wasted that information was the bottom rung. The ladder sat entirely in cash in 35% of months (recorded exposure 0.512 against buy-and-hold's 0.992) and the US market rises in roughly six months out of ten, so a modest advantage in WHICH months cannot pay for sitting out a third of them; measured per unit of time invested the ladder earned about 46% more than buy-and-hold. So this method moves ONE dial, the floor, and imports M0251's signal from M0251's own frozen module so the reading cannot drift: floor f gives rungs 1.0 in the top third, (1+f)/2 in the middle third and f in the bottom third, evenly spaced by construction, decided once a month in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up. Arms: FLOOR70 (f=0.70, the lean 30 points wide), FLOOR50 (f=0.50, 50 points), FLOOR25 (f=0.25, 75 points), FLOOR00 (f=0.00, 100 points -- M0251-LADDER's shape re-run on this chassis so the ladder is internally comparable), HOLD (f=1.00, always fully invested) and MIRROR50 (f=0.50 reversed). HOLD is re-run rather than read off M0251's row because an allocator's lookback sets its start date: M0251's HOLD ran on the TIMING allocator, which needs one bar, so it started hundreds of sessions earlier and was scored against a different SPY benchmark (367.6% against the ladder's 323.7%), and a difference taken across two windows is not a paired difference. Every arm here carries the same 274-bar lookback, the same start date and the same benchmark. MIRROR50 is the one pair matched on all three of weighting arrangement, exposure distribution and fee bill: at f=0.5 the reflection is exact, the same three weights in the same months assigned the opposite way round. Every floor-against-HOLD difference deliberately moves exposure, because exposure is the treatment, and is therefore an estimate of unknown sign rather than a bound. Assumed: no fresh fear index or too little history is full weight, not the floor; the premium is read on day d's close and traded at the next open; idle cash earns nothing (M0251 priced that at 0.8 points a year before 2008 and nothing after). Success: a raised-floor arm beats HOLD on the funded money-weighted return, since it keeps the market's drift and merely leans, AND the curve is monotone in f, so more lean means more lead. Eligibility is not expected and is not the point: an arm with a floor above zero never closes its position, so it will record zero closed round trips and an undefined profit factor and be scored failed on both, which is a property of the shape and not a result (measured on M0182-HI-HALF). The readable result is the dose curve.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely outcome is that the information is too weak to survive dilution. At a 70% floor the lean is only 30 points wide, so whatever edge the full ladder had is cut to roughly a third of it while the market's drift is restored in full; if the premium's advantage is of the order of a point or two a year, the raised-floor arms will land within noise of HOLD and the dose curve will be FLAT. A flat curve is the decidable answer the parent asked for: it would say the signal cannot be used at any dose on this chassis, and the family should be closed rather than tuned. A second, more interesting failure is that the curve is monotone the WRONG way -- more lean, less return -- which would mean M0251's 7.2-point gap to its mirror was bought entirely by being out of the market during the two crashes and not by picking months at all, and that the lab has been crediting a crash hedge to a signal. Third, the raised floors keep the book invested through 2008, so every arm's worst fall climbs back towards buy-and-hold's 55%: FLOOR70 should fall about 70% as far as buy-and-hold does at the worst, around 40%, which is far outside the owner's 25% real-money limit, so an arm that finally beats SPY on return may breach the depth rule instead. Fourth, and the reason this may be a risk dial rather than an engine, the return benefit and the drawdown benefit may sit at opposite ends of the floor curve, in which case no single floor does both and the honest verdict is that the premium buys shallower falls at a price in return -- which is what M0251's own numbers already hint at, since its SPY-200 control beat the ladder on return AND depth at once. Fifth, the comparison itself is weaker than it looks: HOLD trades almost nothing, so it banks the owner's deposits only through the rebalance band, while the leaning arms trade every few months and pay Gotrade for it; part of any gap will be the fee bill and part the deposit channel, and only the MIRROR50 pair holds those fixed. Sixth, this is a post-2009 anomaly in its second half: the paper is from 2009, so the 2009-2015 era is the faded one, and that era is the first filter this lab applies. Finally, at f=1.0 HOLD should reproduce a plain buy-and-hold almost exactly; if it does not, the chassis itself is doing something and every other number here is suspect.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-20

## What was tried

Insurance against the stock market swinging about costs more than the swings usually turn out to
cost. That gap — what the insurance costs, minus what the swings actually cost — is the **price of
risk**. The parent method found that this gap carries real information about which months are good
ones to own shares. It also threw that information away, by converting a good opinion into an
on/off switch: when the gap was in the bottom third of its own past year, the parent sold
everything and sat in cash, which it did in about a third of all months. The US market rises in
roughly six months out of ten, so sitting out a third of them is expensive.

This method changes **one thing and nothing else**: how much money is allowed to leave. The signal,
its one-year reference window and its two cut-offs are the parent's, imported from the parent's own
frozen file rather than retyped, so there is no chance of a transcription slip making this a
different rule wearing the same name. A **floor** says how much of the account must stay invested
no matter what, and the three steps are evenly spaced above it:

| floor | top third of readings | middle third | bottom third |
|---|---|---|---|
| **70%** | all in | 85% | 70% |
| **50%** | all in | 75% | 50% |
| **25%** | all in | 62.5% | 25% |
| **0%** | all in | 50% | all cash — the parent's shape |
| **100%** | all in | all in | all in — the control: never lean at all |

Plus one falsification arm: **the 50% floor read upside down**, which holds 50% when the signal
says "all in" and all in when it says "get out". At a 50% floor that is an exact mirror — the same
three weights, in the same months, assigned the opposite way round — so it is matched on the
weighting arrangement, on how much time it spends invested (73.6% against 75.3%) and on how often
it trades (2.71 turns a year against 2.82). It is the only pair here where all three are held
fixed. Everything else deliberately moves how much is invested, because that **is** the treatment.

Monthly decisions, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5,000,000 rupiah a month,
March 1994 to October 2015. Every arm shares one 274-day warm-up, so all six start on the same day
and are scored against the same SPY. The parent's own always-invested arm could not be reused for
that reason: it ran on a different engine with a one-day warm-up, started years earlier, and was
measured against a different SPY (367.6% against 323.7%). A difference taken across two different
windows is not a difference.

## Result

Everything below is money-weighted: what the owner's real deposits would have earned, not a
headline number that counts deposits as profit. The fall is measured with the deposits taken out,
so a monthly top-up cannot make a crash look gentler than it was.

| version | floor | your money a year | vs SPY | worst fall | invested | 2009–2015 vs SPY | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HOLD** | 100% | **+7.7%** | −0.0 | **55.0%** | 99% | +0.0 | 0.57 |
| **FLOOR70** | 70% | +7.2% | −0.4 | 48.3% | 85% | −1.0 | 0.60 |
| **FLOOR50** | 50% | +6.9% | −0.8 | 43.5% | 75% | −1.8 | **0.61** |
| **FLOOR25** | 25% | +6.4% | −1.2 | 37.3% | 63% | −2.9 | 0.59 |
| **FLOOR00** | 0% | +6.0% | −1.7 | **33.2%** | 51% | −3.9 | 0.51 |
| **MIRROR50** | 50%, flipped | **+3.4%** | −4.3 | 46.6% | 74% | **−8.2** | 0.28 |
| SPY, same deposits | — | +7.7% | — | — | 100% | — | — |

"Luck score" is the deflated Sharpe ratio: how likely the result is real rather than a lucky draw
after this many tries. Every number was judged at **N = 167** — one look per distinct method the
lab has now examined — against a bar of **0.90**, the owner's risk appetite since 7 October 2026.
Neither number is the lab's to move. The best arm reached 0.61. **Four test-window looks have been
spent in this lab's life and this run spent none.**

Every arm is rejected. None beats SPY. None has 100 closed round trips. None clears the luck bar.
And every one of them falls far past the owner's 25% limit — the gentlest lean still loses 48% at
its worst.

**Two checks passed before anything else can be read.** The always-invested arm earned +7.656%
where the same deposits straight into SPY earned +7.681%: a gap of two and a half hundredths of a
point, which is the whole cost of running buy-and-hold through this machinery. The chassis is
clean. And the 0% floor reproduced the parent's ladder **to the last digit** (+5.981097782%), which
is what it means to say only the floor moved.

## The curve is steep, and it points the wrong way

The written-down expectation was that a raised floor would land **above** buy-and-hold: keep the
market's drift, merely lean. The opposite happened, and it happened in a perfectly straight line.
Every point of floor given up costs return and buys depth:

- **return**: −0.4, −0.8, −1.2, −1.7 points a year at floors of 70, 50, 25 and 0.
- **worst fall**: −6.7, −11.5, −17.7, −21.8 points at the same four floors.

There is no best floor. The curve has no hump, no interior sweet spot, nothing to tune. It runs
monotonically from "lean hardest, earn least, fall least" to "never lean, earn most, fall
furthest". The exchange rate is roughly **13 to 16 points off the worst fall for every one point of
yearly return given up**, and it gets slightly worse the harder you lean.

So the honest description of this idea is not an engine. It is a **risk dial**: a knob that trades
return for calm at a fixed, knowable price. That was written down beforehand as the fourth way this
could fail, and it is what happened.

## Why it cannot work at any setting — the part worth keeping

The mirror arm makes the arithmetic exact. Reading the signal the right way and reading it upside
down are two books with the same shape, so their average is a book with the shape and none of the
opinion. Split each arm into those two halves:

| | the opinion is worth | the shape costs | net |
|---|---|---|---|
| **50% floor** | **+1.8%** a year | −2.5% a year | −0.7 |
| **0% floor** (the parent) | **+3.6%** a year | −5.3% a year | −1.7 |

Both halves **halve when the lean halves**. The opinion is worth 3.6 points at full lean and 1.8 at
half; the shape costs 5.3 at full lean and 2.5 at half. The ratio between them barely moves: 0.68
and 0.70.

That is the finding, and it closes the question the parent left open. **Diluting the rule dilutes
what it earns and what it costs by the same factor, so the ratio never improves — and the ratio is
about 0.7, which is less than one.** There is no floor at which this pays, because the floor is not
the variable that decides. You cannot fix a rule that gives back 10 units for every 7 it earns by
turning it down.

The cost is not fees. At a 50% floor the book sits a quarter of the time out of the market, and a
quarter of SPY's own per-unit-invested return over these years is about 2.5 points a year — which
is the whole of the shape cost, leaving no room for a large fee term. The money is lost to being
absent, not to trading. (The shape figure does bundle both; they were not separated by a dedicated
arm, so read it as an estimate, not a bound.)

## The signal did not fade. The way of using it got more expensive

A 2009 paper is a prime suspect for a faded anomaly, and this lab's first filter is whether an edge
survives 2009–2015. It did — the opposite of fading:

- Over 2009–2015 the mirror arm lost **8.2 points a year** to SPY where the straight arm lost 1.8.
  The opinion was worth **+3.2 points a year** in that era, nearly twice its +1.8 over the whole
  window.
- But in the same era the shape cost **5.0 points a year**, twice its whole-window 2.5 — because
  2009–2015 is the longest rally in the window and that is exactly when being out hurts most.
- Ratio: **0.64**. Slightly worse than the twenty-year 0.70.

So the strongest years for the signal are also the most expensive years to express it, and the
second effect is the larger one. That is a much more interesting failure than decay.

Breadth tells the same story from another angle. In months where a few big names carried the index,
every leaning arm is level with SPY (+0.2%). In broad months — 138 of the 237 — they lose
progressively more the harder they lean: −1.2, −2.1, −3.3, −4.5. The lean only ever helps by being
absent, and most months are not months to be absent in.

## Other things worth recording

- **The survivorship check was free and uninformative, by construction.** This book holds one
  exchange-traded fund and no company shares, so re-running it on the store that adds back the
  companies that died changed every number by exactly 0.0. That is the right answer and it is worth
  stating: survivorship bias cannot touch a method that never picks a company.
- **Blending is very slightly better than its parts.** The raised floors earn about 0.09 points a
  year more than a straight line between buy-and-hold and the parent's ladder would predict, and
  fall 0.1 to 1.4 points less deep. That is an ordinary rebalancing bonus from mixing two things
  that do not move together. It is real, it is in the right direction, and it is two orders of
  magnitude too small to matter here.
- **How much is invested is a straight line in the floor**, to within 0.2 of a percentage point at
  every rung (51.2%, 63.3%, 75.3%, 84.9%, 99.1%). The dial does exactly what it says and nothing
  else, which is why the whole method reads as arithmetic rather than as a search.
- **The automated control-shape check reported nothing**, correctly: these are dose-response arms,
  which that check deliberately does not shape-match, because an arm that is supposed to differ is
  the experiment. The shape matching here was done by hand on the mirror pair and is quoted above.
- **Walk-forward: 2 of 4 folds.** The two it lost are 2006–2008 (where the always-invested arm was
  picked and matched SPY to within a tenth of a point) and 2012–2014 (where a leaning arm was
  picked and trailed badly, 36.8% against 65.9%). That is the same story again: the fold chooser
  picks on risk-adjusted return, so it picks a leaning arm, and a leaning arm loses a rally.
- **The lab already owns a better version of this trade.** The parent's own 200-day trend control
  earned +9.2% a year with a 19% worst fall. It beats every arm here on **both** axes at once. A
  dial that pays return for calm is dominated outright by a rule that gets both for free.

## My opinion

**This direction is finished in this shape, and I would close the floor question rather than spend
another id on it.** Not because the signal failed — it did not; the mirror lost 8.2 points a year
in the modern era, which is as strong a sign of real information as this lab has produced — but
because the arithmetic of expressing it is now measured and it does not close. The opinion is worth
about 0.7 of what the expression costs, that ratio is flat across the whole dose range, and in the
era that matters most it is slightly worse. Turning the dial cannot fix a ratio.

**What I would try instead is the one change that makes the cost zero: lean without leaving.** Every
point lost here was paid for by having money out of the market. The signal never needs money out of
the market — it is an opinion about how *risky* the coming months are, not about whether to
participate. So express it by changing **what** is held at a constant 100% invested, not **how
much**. The lab's executable version of that is a rotation between the two exchange-traded funds the
owner can already trade without new permissions: hold the Nasdaq-100 fund when the price of risk is
in the top third and the S&P 500 fund when it is in the bottom third, with a blend in the middle.
Always fully invested, so the shape cost is structurally zero, and the lean is expressed in how
jumpy the holding is rather than in how much of it there is. The exposure swing of that rotation is
far smaller than 100 points, so the opinion is worth far less than 3.6 points a year — but it is
being bought for nothing instead of for 5.3, and a small number beating zero is the only arrangement
in which this signal can ever pay. That is queued as the next idea.

The second thing I would **not** do is tune the signal — the cut-offs, the one-year window, the
one-month realised variance. The parent said so and this run is the evidence for it: the problem was
never where the thirds sit. It was that every version of this rule, at every dose, pays for its
opinion with time out of a market that rises.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the floor dial is a straight line from 'lean hardest, earn least, fall least' to 'never lean' — the signal is real but the opinion is worth only 0.7 of what being out of the market costs, at every dose

methods.name: Keep the 200-day exit, buy back when the price of risk recovers
methods.hypothesis: M0113 split the 200-day safety switch into its two halves and found the exit is the valuable one and the re-entry the expensive one: the same slow average that correctly gets the book out keeps it out through the recovery, costing 6 points a year across 2009-2015. It then tried six re-entry triggers and every one of them was read off SPY's own price, so every one could fire inside a bear-market bounce; the best (a positive 63-session return) bought back barely sooner than the control. M0251 supplies the thing M0113 did not have: a re-entry trigger that is not a price. The price of risk -- the fear index squared, less the realised variance just past, ranked inside its own trailing year -- read its top third in January and February 2009, months before SPY crossed back above its 200-day average, because once a crash stops getting worse, insurance stays dear while realised swings fall away. M0251 also proved the signal is not noise: its upside-down arm lost money outright, a 7.2-point-a-year gap on the same book shape. So: hold the 200-day exit fixed and unchanged (monthly check, SPY under its 200-day average goes to cash, exactly M0251-SPY-200's recorded +9.2% a year, 19% worst fall, 11 round trips), and move ONLY the way back in. Variants: SMA200 (the control, which must reproduce the recorded switch trade for trade or the machinery is wrong), VRP-TOP (back in when the price of risk reaches its top third while still under the 200-day line), VRP-MID (back in at its middle third, a looser trigger), VRP-HALF (back in at HALF weight on the middle third and full on the top third, so the re-entry is graded rather than a jump), and VRP-AND (back in only when BOTH the price of risk is in its top third AND SPY is back above its 200-day line, the strictest arm, which should be worse than the control and bound the experiment from below). Monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's top-up. Success: an arm keeps the 2001, 2002 and 2008 exits and the worst fall inside 25%, and closes at least half of the switch's 5.9-point 2009-2015 gap to SPY. Expected failure: the price of risk is itself a reactive signal -- M0251 found it goes deeply negative DURING a crash -- so its recovery into the top third may be the same information the 200-day crossing carries, only noisier, in which case VRP-TOP buys back into 2002 and the first half of 2008 and gives up the exits the switch exists for. M0251's probe holds the sharpest warning: the ladder read its top third in January and February 2009 and then its BOTTOM third at the end of March 2009, the exact bottom, so a re-entry on this trigger can be reversed one month later at the worst possible moment. Trade counts stay in the tens, so profit factor, the 100-trade condition and the luck bar are all unreachable here and the paired differences against the control are the only readable result; say so rather than reporting an eligibility failure as news. Note kin: the parent M0113 is rejected, not test-failed, and this book holds only SPY, so its curve carries no stock-picking kin.

methods.name: The rare confidence signals, held beside a core of the market itself instead of spread evenly
methods.hypothesis: M0244 measured two things that should decide the next attempt. First, the rare board gestures work: splits, first-ever dividends and real buybacks beat a shape-matched coin-flip book by about two points a year, and unlike almost everything else in this lab they keep that lead after 2009 (the rare-gesture arm beat its placebo by 1.5 points a year in 2009-2015, the stale arm by 3.9). Second, the shape they were carried in loses eight points a year to SPY over the same years: the coin-flip placebo, holding thirty index members in equal slices behind the 200-day switch, was 8.2 points a year behind the market in 2009-2015 purely by construction. The signal is real and the vehicle is wrong. So carry the same three rare gestures -- never the routine dividend raise, which M0244 showed is dilution -- on a shape that does not short the biggest companies. Three arms worth trying: the gesture names weighted by company size rather than equally (share counts are available point-in-time from 1996, with a weight ceiling as M0047 requires); the gesture names as a tilt of a fixed size beside a core held in SPY itself (M0222 and M0230's chassis), so the book owns the market and overweights the gesture names rather than replacing it; and a size-weighted placebo matched to both the count and the turnover of whichever wins, because M0244's placebo was matched to the fresh arm's turnover and not to the thinner arms that actually beat it. Drop recency as the selector: M0244's stale arm, buying gestures one to two years old, earned the most of six arms on a fifth of the trades, so rank on something else or do not rank at all and hold everything that qualifies.

methods.name: How long is a board confidence signal worth holding? A hold ladder at real fees
methods.hypothesis: M0244's stale arm -- companies whose split, first dividend or buyback happened one to two years ago and which have done nothing since -- earned +8.4% a year against SPY's +7.2%, the best of its six arms, on 698 trades against the fresh arm's 3,634. That is a fivefold difference in trading cost for a better result, and it says the lab has never actually measured how long these signals last. Run the hold itself as a dose-response ladder on the rare gestures only (splits, first-ever dividends, buybacks at or beyond a 3% share-count fall; no routine dividend raises, which M0244 showed are dilution): hold each qualifying name 91 days, 365 days, 730 days and 1,095 days, same screen, same 200-day switch, same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the book size held constant so only the hold changes. If the ladder is flat or rising with the hold, the right instrument is a slow book that trades a few dozen times a year, and every version of this family built so far has been paying Gotrade for nothing. Mandatory control: a coin-flip book matched to each rung's own count AND its own turnover, because M0244 could not separate 'picks better' from 'trades less' -- its placebo matched the fast arm and the two arms that beat it were the slow ones. Note for whoever builds it: the raise and initiation scan must walk back through every payment in the window, as M0244's does, not read only the latest one as M0070's chassis does, or the hold dial is inert above about 91 days and the whole ladder measures nothing.

methods.name: A price band on the 200-day safety gate, on a book that holds stocks: is the band worth anything once the gate is only read once a month?
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0072-Z2-RAWRANK (its book unchanged); the band is m0101.band_on verbatim, as M0084 already reuses it; Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992), Simple technical trading rules and the stochastic properties of stock returns, JF 47(5), for the banded moving-average rule
methods.hypothesis: Published 1992 (the banded moving-average rule), so nothing in the band is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies to it; what is new is the question. A study on 2026-10-19 found that a price band around the SPY 200-day gate -- leave only once SPY closes b percent under its 200-day average, return only once it closes b percent over -- beat the bare gate on every axis, and asked for a method. The lab has already answered half of that twice and recorded the answers, and every figure here is the MONEY-WEIGHTED return on the owner's own monthly deposits, which is the only honest headline for a funded book -- what the lab prints as 'your money earned', against the SAME deposits put into SPY, which earned 7.19% a year over M0101's and M0072's window and 7.69% over M0084's. On a book that holds stocks, M0101-BAND-3 earned 10.44% a year against M0101-CTRL's 10.62% and fell 20.39% against 18.71%, on 525 trades against 528 and turnover 4.727 against 4.780; M0101-BAND-5 earned 10.10%. So on a stock book the band COST 0.18 points a year at 3% and 0.52 at 5%, fell 1.68 points deeper at both, and barely changed how much the book traded. On SPY alone read monthly, M0084-BAND3-M earned 8.73% against M0084-MONTHLY's 9.13% and fell 20.69% against 18.89%: the band cost 0.40 points and fell 1.80 deeper. But the lab also recorded, and never read, the other half. On SPY alone read WEEKLY the bare gate earned just 4.35% a year -- more than three points BELOW its own deposits in SPY -- and fell 33.13%, while the same band read weekly earned 7.78% and fell 18.92%, on turnover 0.861 against 3.383. Read weekly the band is worth +3.42 points a year and 14.22 points of worst fall; read monthly it is worth -0.40 and 1.80 points worse. That is a 3.82-point swing in the band's worth, in money, from the reading cadence alone, already recorded. (Every difference in this paragraph is taken at full precision from the recorded money-weighted returns, so it can be re-derived exactly; differencing their two-decimal printed forms instead gives +3.43, 14.21 and 3.83.) The cadence grid measured for this file (SPY alone, dev store, one-session lag, signal held as read at each rank session) says the same thing as a smooth function: band 3% minus bare gate is +1.82 points a year and 8.4 points of worst fall better when the gate is read daily, +2.53 and 15.5 better read weekly, and -0.12 and 1.7 points WORSE read monthly. The monthly bare gate beats the daily 3% band on every axis in the original study's own table. The mechanism is not new: a band suppresses flips shorter than the band is wide, a monthly reading suppresses flips shorter than a month, and they are substitutes -- which is why the study's band left exactly the eleven episodes insight 452 counted AT ITS MONTHLY CHECKS. So the question worth one method id is not 'does the band win', which the lab has answered twice, but 'IS THE BAND'S WORTH A FUNCTION OF HOW OFTEN THE GATE IS READ, ON A BOOK THAT HOLDS STOCKS'. Six arms hold M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's book verbatim -- the standardised earnings-day jump kept at two of the stock's own daily swings and ranked by the raw jump, F4's five-dollar and twenty-million screen, 20 slots at 5%, SPY in the empty ones, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-ups -- and move only the band and the cadence: M-B0 (monthly, no band: the paired bare gate and the ladder's zero dose, which must reproduce the host's recorded trial), M-B15, M-B30 and M-B60 (monthly, 1.5%, 3% and 6%: the dose-response ladder across the measured plateau), W-B0 and W-B30 (the same book and the same two signals read weekly). The lookback is M0072's 253 bars exactly, so every arm is scored from 1996-01-03 on the same sessions and each paired difference is the gate alone. THE PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION, written before the run: (W-B30 minus W-B0) much greater than (M-B30 minus M-B0), which is itself about zero, on return AND on worst fall; and the monthly ladder flat or gently downward in the band across 0, 1.5, 3 and 6 percent rather than humped. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY. This method is bought to settle a cadence question the lab has been reasoning past, and a null on the monthly pair is a result that corrects a standing document. If instead the monthly pair shows a real gap on a book of stocks, then the handover's finding survived contact with stock selection and the lab has a genuinely better gate, which would be worth far more than one id. Assumed without asking: that M0072 is the right host because it is one of three promotable, kin-clean books and the only one whose engine counts its hold in sessions rather than calendar months, so it can carry a weekly arm honestly.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely outcome is simply NOTHING on the monthly pair -- M-B30 within a few tenths of a point of M-B0 on return and within a point or two on worst fall, and the ladder across 0, 1.5, 3 and 6 percent flat or drifting down rather than rising. That is what the cadence grid predicts and what M0101 already recorded on a different book, and if it happens this method has bought a null. The null is still worth the id, because the lab is currently carrying a committed study and a journalled insight whose headline compares the band against a baseline no book in the lab runs, and nothing short of a pre-registered paired measurement on a real book corrects that. Second, the walk-forward folds pick each fold's variant by MAR, so they will favour whichever arm trades least -- M0245's folds picked its slowest rung in three of four, and the lab has written that down. A fold majority won by M-B60 is therefore weak evidence for the band and should be read as evidence about turnover; read the folds arm by arm, not just the headline. Third, the weekly arms run on a rule set that is not in the promotion presets, so they can never be promoted no matter what they show; they are diagnostic, and a result that lives only in them is a measurement the lab cannot act on. Fourth, even if the weekly band does win, it may be a FEE story rather than a signal story: the band cuts the gate's own flips by about a factor of four, a weekly book pays Gotrade on every re-pick, and the fee term was the second-largest container in the 824-trial shortfall sweep. The ladder is the only defence against that reading -- a fee story should keep improving monotonically as the band widens and trading falls, while a signal story should peak and turn. But note what is already measured about that: the band cut turnover only at the WEEKLY cadence, 0.861 against 3.383 on the weekly SPY book, a 75% cut. On both recorded MONTHLY books it cut essentially nothing -- 4.727 against 4.780 on M0101's stock book, a 1.1% difference on 525 trades against 528, and 0.826 against 0.826 on SPY. So the brief's premise that the band cuts turnover sharply is a weekly-cadence fact and not a monthly one, the four monthly arms here are expected to differ from each other in shape by well under 1%, and any difference between them is therefore the gate's TIMING rather than its cost. If instead the monthly arms do separate on turnover, something in this book interacts with the band that SPY alone and M0101's book did not, and that itself is the finding. Fifth, the dev window holds exactly TWO crashes, and the whole of the band's measured advantage comes from holding each of them as one exit instead of fragmenting it and buying back inside the fall. Two is not a sample; both of this window's crashes happened to be slow, and a fast crash is what 1987 and 2020 were. Nothing measured on dev can settle that, the folds are the only within-window check, and no test-window look is spent here. Sixth, the host book's own recorded worst fall is 23.80%, over the real-money bar already, so no arm is expected to clear every go-live condition and the band is not being asked to fix that. Finally, as in every switch method the lab has run: interest on the cash held while the gate is off is not modelled, which flatters SPY and penalises every gated arm equally, so each gap reported is an upper bound on the gate's cost and the paired differences are unaffected.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What was asked, and what was done

A study written earlier the same day found that giving the safety rule a "clear break" margin —
leave the market only once it has fallen a few percent below its one-year average, and come back
only once it has risen a few percent above — beat the plain safety rule on every measure. That
study watched the market every single day. None of your books do. They all look once a month, and
hold whatever they saw until the next look.

So this method put the margin on a book that actually picks stocks — the earnings-jump picker,
carried over unchanged — and ran six versions of it. Four look once a month, with no margin, then
a 1.5%, 3% and 6% margin. Two more run the same book but look once a week, with no margin and
with the 3% margin. Nothing else differs between any of them. Every number below is what your
money earned on your own monthly deposits, against the same deposits put into the market index,
which earned 7.2% a year over the same stretch.

## The four comparisons that matter

**Checked once a month, the margin is worth nothing.** The 3% margin earned 11.8% a year against
12.3% for no margin at all — it cost you half a point a year — and it fell 24.0% from a peak
against 23.8%, a quarter of a point deeper. Slightly worse on both measures, which is as close to
nothing as a result gets.

**Checked once a week, the same margin is worth a great deal.** It earned 10.0% a year against
5.3% without it — nearly five points a year — and its worst fall was 29.7% against 35.5%, almost
six points shallower. Better on both measures, by a lot.

**Checking monthly instead of weekly, with no margin at all, is worth more than the margin ever
is.** The monthly version earned 12.3% a year against the weekly version's 5.3% — seven points a
year — and fell 23.8% against 35.5%, nearly twelve points shallower. This is the largest single
effect anywhere in this method, and nobody was looking for it.

**With the margin in place, the gap between checking monthly and weekly shrinks to a quarter of
what it was.** The 3% margin monthly earned 1.7 points a year more than the 3% margin weekly and
fell 5.7 points less — against seven points and twelve points when neither had a margin. The
margin closes most of the damage that checking too often does.

## The ladder: more margin does not buy more

The four monthly versions, in order of how wide the margin is:

| margin | your money earned | worst fall | trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | 12.3% a year | 23.8% | 1208 |
| 1.5% | 11.2% a year | 23.8% | 1241 |
| 3% | 11.8% a year | 24.0% | 1205 |
| 6% | 9.1% a year | 28.2% | 1182 |

No width of margin beats having none. The money wanders within about a point for the first three
and then drops off sharply at 6%; the worst fall only ever gets deeper, never shallower. The
response is not humped — there is no sweet spot in the middle that beats the ends — and it is not
a clean straight line either. It is simply flat-to-falling.

That shape matters for the reason the ladder was built. A straight, steady improvement as the
margin widens would have meant the margin was only saving trading costs. A rise and then a fall
would have meant it was genuinely improving the timing. This is neither: on a monthly schedule the
margin does not do anything worth measuring, in either direction.

## The prediction written down before the run

Before any of this was run, the method committed to one sentence: that the margin's worth checked
weekly would be far greater than its worth checked monthly, which would itself be about zero, on
both the money and the worst fall. **It held, on both measures.** The margin is worth 5.3 points a
year more when the book looks weekly than when it looks monthly, and 6.0 points more of worst
fall. The monthly half came in at half a point against it, which is "about zero" by any reading.

## The reproduction check

The no-margin monthly version is the host book run again under a new name, and it had to come back
the same or nothing else here could be trusted. It came back **identical to every digit recorded**:
the same 12.3314% a year, the same 23.8026% worst fall, the same 1208 trades, the same amount of
trading, the same share of time invested, the same ratio of gains to losses. That is better than
expected — re-runs usually drift slightly — and it means every comparison above is the safety rule
alone, with nothing else moving.

## How each version did against the market, and what it failed

Against the same deposits put into the index, which earned 7.2% a year:

| version | your money earned | worst fall | what it failed |
|---|---|---|---|
| no margin, monthly | 12.3% | 23.8% | nothing — passed the research screen |
| 1.5% margin, monthly | 11.2% | 23.8% | the luck test |
| 3% margin, monthly | 11.8% | 24.0% | nothing — passed the research screen |
| 6% margin, monthly | 9.1% | 28.2% | the luck test |
| no margin, weekly | 5.3% | 35.5% | beating the index; the gains-to-losses bar; the luck test |
| 3% margin, weekly | 10.0% | 29.7% | the luck test |

The luck test asks how likely a result this good is to be real rather than a lucky draw after many
tries. The lab has now tried 163 methods, and the bar you set on 7 October last year is that a
result must be at least 90% likely to be real. The no-margin monthly version comes in at 92.8% and
the 3% margin monthly version at 91.0%, so both clear it. The 1.5% version reaches 86.5%, the
weekly 3% version 83.8%, the 6% version 78.8%, and the weekly no-margin version only 41.6% — a
coin-flip.

Separately from the research screen, your own rule for real money is that a book must never have
lost more than a quarter of its value from a peak. Two versions clear that: no margin at 23.8% and
the 3% margin at 24.0%, both uncomfortably close to the line. The other four breach it — the 6%
margin at 28.2%, the weekly 3% margin at 29.7%, and the weekly no-margin version at 35.5%.

## The worst years

The no-margin monthly version's worst calendar year was 2005, down 4.6%. The 3% margin's was 1998,
down 6.3%. The 6% margin's was 2008, down 7.7%, and the weekly no-margin version's was 2007, down
11.3%. One caution on all of these: your monthly deposits keep refilling the account while it is
falling, so every fall here reads gentler than it would have felt with no new money going in.

## What the out-of-sample stretches said

The book was re-tested on four separate stretches it had never seen, each one trained only on what
came before it. It won three of the four. The stretch covering 2003 to 2005 picked the 3% margin
and lost to the index; 2006 to 2008 picked the 6% margin and won; and both 2009 to 2011 and 2012 to
2014 picked the **no-margin** version and won.

That last detail is worth pausing on. The expectation written down beforehand was that these
stretches would drift toward whichever version traded least, because of how they choose — which
would have made a win by the widest margin weak evidence. That is not what happened: two of the
four stretches chose the version with no margin at all. So the stretches are not quietly flattering
the margin. If anything they are the opposite.

## Why this method cannot be accused of a mis-matched comparison

A common way a result like this goes wrong is comparing a book against a made-up random version of
itself that trades a completely different amount — then the difference is just the trading, not the
idea. This method does not have one, deliberately. The four monthly versions are a ladder of doses
of one treatment, and the zero-dose rung is the comparison. The lab's shape check reads all four as
exactly that, assigns them no shape ratio, and cannot object to them.

And a drawn-at-random version would have been the wrong shape here anyway. A coin-flip switch
flipping at the same rate the safety rule goes off would flip about four times a year against the
real rule's roughly two, and on a twenty-name book every flip is around forty trades — so it would
have landed near seven times the trading of the thing it was supposed to be comparable to, far
outside what the check accepts.

One more thing the trading figures settle. On the monthly schedule the four versions traded within
