half a percent of one another — 1208, 1241, 1205 and 1182 trades. So whatever the margin is doing
on a monthly schedule, it is not saving money on trading; it is only shifting *when* the rule acts.
On the weekly schedule it did cut trading, by 19% — but far less than the 75% cut the same margin
produced on the index alone, which means even the weekly gain is mostly better timing rather than
lower costs.

## Why

A margin and a slow schedule do the same job. A margin ignores every move smaller than the margin
is wide. Looking only once a month ignores every move that starts and finishes inside a month.
Those are overwhelmingly the same moves. Once you are doing one of them, the other has almost
nothing left to suppress — and your books have been doing the slow schedule all along.

That is the whole result. The earlier study was not wrong about what it measured; it measured a
margin against a rule checked every day, and against *that* the margin genuinely helps. But you
never ran the rule that way. Against the rule you actually run, the margin is a small, consistent
cost.

The weekly versions are what prove the mechanism rather than merely asserting it. Forced to look
every week, the book bleeds badly — 5.3% a year against 12.3%, and a 35.5% fall — because it keeps
reacting to moves that reverse before the month is out. Put the margin on it and most of that
damage goes away. The margin is a real tool. It is a tool for a problem your books do not have.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did the expected failure happen

The hypothesis held, in full and on both measures. The margin's worth is a function of how often
the rule is read, and it is worth essentially nothing at the schedule your books run.

The expected failure also happened, and it was the main one: the monthly comparison came back as a
null, half a point against the margin. Two of the other warnings did not come true. The
out-of-sample stretches did not drift toward the least-trading version — they chose the no-margin
version twice. And the worry that a weekly win would turn out to be a trading-cost story is
weakened, because weekly trading only fell 19% while the money improved by nearly five points a
year; that is too large a gain for too small a cost saving.

One thing to flag that was not predicted. The version that passed everything and triggered the
lab's signal to go buy better price history is the **no-margin** one — which is the host book over
again under a new name. The margin did not earn that. The book did, and it had already earned it.

## What this does not settle

The stretch this was measured on contains exactly two market crashes, and both of them were slow.
A margin's whole case is that it treats a crash as one exit instead of several, and a fast crash is
a different animal. Nothing measured here can speak to that, and no part of the untouched
out-of-sample window was spent to find out.

The two weekly versions also run on a trading schedule that is not among the ones a book can be
promoted on. They were always diagnostic, and they did their job — but no amount of success there
could have turned into a book you actually run.

My opinion: the margin is finished as an idea for your books, and I would not spend another method
id on it. The monthly comparison is a null on a book that holds stocks, which is now the third time
the lab has measured this and the second time on real stock picking, and the ladder shows no width
that helps. The genuinely valuable thing this run found was not about margins at all: checking the
safety rule monthly instead of weekly is worth seven points a year and twelve points of worst fall
on this book, which is larger than almost any edge the lab has ever measured, and it had been sitting
unnamed in the records the whole time. That is what I would chase next — not by widening anything,
but by asking the obvious follow-up question: if monthly beats weekly by this much, does checking
even less often beat monthly, and where does it turn? Every book in the lab reads its safety rule at
whatever speed it happens to re-pick stocks, which nobody ever chose deliberately. That looks like a
free decision the lab has been making by accident for its entire history, and it costs one method id
to find out. I would also stop quoting any count of how often the safety rule went off without
saying how often it was being checked, because the same rule gives wildly different counts at
different speeds and two documents on your site currently disagree for exactly that reason.
methods.verdict: A clear-break margin on the safety rule is worth nothing on a book that holds stocks once the rule is only checked monthly: it cost half a point a year and fell slightly deeper, while the same margin checked weekly was worth nearly five points — the margin and the monthly schedule suppress the same thing, and the books already have the schedule.

methods.name: Say how often the safety rule was checked whenever its exits are counted
methods.hypothesis: Eleven exits and a hundred and fifty-one flips are the same safety rule read at two different speeds, not a discrepancy: the monthly count and the daily count are both correct and neither is comparable to the other. One standing insight reports the eleven and a later one reports the hundred and fifty-one, and because the journal cannot be edited the two currently contradict each other on the owner's site. Append a correction row saying that every count of how often the rule went off must carry the speed it was read at, and that the number to use is the one matching the cadence of the book being discussed. This costs no method id and removes a contradiction the owner can see.

methods.name: How often should a book read its safety gate? A dose-response ladder in the SPY-200 gate's reading interval, from weekly to yearly, on a book that holds stocks
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0258-M-B0 (its book and its bare gate unchanged; M0258-M-B0 is itself M0072-Z2-RAWRANK); Faber (2007), A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, JWM 9(4), for the long-moving-average switch and for evaluating it at a fixed interval rather than continuously
methods.hypothesis: Published 2007 (the long-moving-average switch), so nothing in the rule is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies to it; what is new is the question, which is not whether to use the gate but HOW OFTEN TO LOOK AT IT. Every figure here is the MONEY-WEIGHTED return on the owner's own monthly deposits -- what the lab prints as 'your money earned' -- because these books are funded with a monthly top-up and the curve-shape columns beside them are not returns at all; SPY's figure is the SAME deposits put into SPY. M0258 ran on 2026-10-19 to settle whether a price band helps this gate, and the answer was no, but it carried two arms that differed in one thing only -- the rule set's cadence -- and those two measured the largest single effect in the method. M0258-M-B0, the book behind its own bare gate re-picked MONTHLY, earned 12.33% a year of the owner's money and fell 23.80%, on 1208 trades with gains 1.98 times losses. M0258-W-B0, the SAME book and the SAME bare gate re-picked WEEKLY, earned 5.32% a year and fell 35.49% on 1923 trades. The same deposits in SPY earned 7.19%. So reading the gate monthly rather than weekly was worth +7.01 points a year and 11.69 points of worst fall with nothing else moving -- against -0.40 points for the price band at the monthly cadence and a constant 3.6 points a year for the whole gate premium after 2009, measured across all 824 trials. The cadence is worth roughly twice the gate itself. AND NOBODY EVER CHOSE IT: there is no cadence lever on a gate anywhere in this lab, because the allocator is only called on decision sessions, so every book inherits its gate's reading interval from however often it happens to re-pick stocks. The prior grid measured for this file on the dev store (SPY ALONE, 200-bar warmup, one-session lag, the reading held as read at each rank session; UNFUNDED, so plain CAGRs that are NOT comparable with the money-weighted figures above) reads: monthly native 9.08% a year and a 19.0% fall; monthly anchored at k = 1 the identical 9.08% and 19.0%; k = 2 8.56% and 19.7%; k = 3 6.71% and 24.5%; k = 6 8.39% and 25.9%; k = 12 7.06% and 19.4%; weekly native 5.51% and 34.6%; weekly anchored at k = 1 8.49% and 19.0%. It reproduces the lab's own recorded SPY-only trials -- its monthly fall of 19.0% against M0084-MONTHLY's recorded 18.89%, its weekly 34.6% against M0084-WEEKLY's 33.13% -- and shares no code with the simulator. THE CONFOUND, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. The two axes are the same event as the chassis stands: run_book calls the allocator only on decision sessions, with data_date = prev_session(session), and the gate is read inside that call, so the rule set's cadence sets BOTH how often the gate is read and how often the book re-picks, and M0258's +7.01 is the sum of the two and names neither. Slower than the re-pick IS separable and promotable: nothing stops an allocator reading the gate at an earlier date, and anchoring it to a month-end grid leaves TradeRules untouched, so every slow arm still runs on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, which IS in sim.rules.PRESETS. Faster than the re-pick is NOT separable, by construction: a monthly book cannot act on a reading taken between its rank sessions, and a reading it never acts on changes no target and no trade, so making it act weekly IS a rule-set change which also re-picks weekly. That is a property of the simulator rather than a gap in this design, and no arrangement of params can undo it. So the confound is DECOMPOSED. With A = M-NATIVE (monthly re-pick, monthly gate), B = W-NATIVE (weekly re-pick, weekly gate) and C = W-G1 (weekly re-pick, MONTHLY gate): (A - B) = (A - C) + (C - B), where the first bracket is re-pick frequency with the gate held monthly and the second is the gate's reading cadence with the re-pick held weekly. The first bracket is clean because at a weekly rank session in month M, arm C's anchor is the newest month end on or before its data date -- THE SAME MONTH-END SESSION arm A read at its own rank session that month. Arm C does not approximate arm A's reading; it reuses it, and the dedicated test module asserts that session by session rather than asserting it in prose. On the unfunded SPY-alone prior the split is +3.58 total, of which +0.59 is re-pick frequency and +2.99 is the gate's reading cadence -- 84% of the gap is the gate, on an instrument with no stock picking at all. THE ANCHOR, with month_index(d) = (d.year - 1970) * 12 + (d.month - 1): the newest bar a <= data_date that is the last session of its calendar month and has month_index(a) % k == k - 1, falling back to data_date when none is on hand. Phase k - 1 makes the grid calendar-natural: k = 3 is the calendar quarters, k = 12 is December only. It is never later than data_date, so every anchored arm is strictly SAFER on look-ahead than the native reading the lab already runs, and the fallback never fires inside the dev window -- measured on the store's whole SPY tape, k = 12 is unresolvable only on the first 233 sessions, all of them before 1993-12-31, and the dev window opens on 1996-01-03. SIX ARMS hold M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's book verbatim -- the standardised earnings-day jump kept at two of the stock's own daily swings and ranked by the raw jump, F4's five-dollar and twenty-million screen, 20 slots at 5%, SPY in the empty ones, a 60-session hold, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-ups -- and move only the cadence and the reading interval: M-NATIVE (monthly, native: the ladder's fastest rung, which must reproduce M0258-M-B0), M-G3 (quarterly), M-G6 (half-yearly), M-G12 (yearly, barely a gate at all), W-NATIVE (weekly, native: must reproduce M0258-W-B0) and W-G1 (weekly re-pick with a MONTHLY gate: the decomposition arm). The anchored k = 1 rung on a monthly book is NOT an arm and costs no trial: a monthly book's data_date is always a calendar month end, so it resolves to data_date itself and is identical to M-NATIVE, which the test module asserts on every decision session and the prior grid's first two lines show measured. PROMOTABILITY IS A FACT ABOUT sim.rules, NOT AN OPINION: lab promote requires membership of sim.rules.PRESETS, MONTHLY_HOLD_FRAC_GOTRADE is a member so all four monthly arms can reach paper, and WEEKLY_HOLD_FRAC_GOTRADE is NOT a member -- it is M0063's one-off rule set, declared under its own comment saying no preset of its id exists -- so BOTH WEEKLY ARMS ARE DIAGNOSTIC FOREVER whatever they show, and minting a preset mid-run would be scope nobody asked for. And the slow rungs live in the allocator's params rather than in a cadence because sim.rules.Cadence is Literal['daily', 'weekly', 'monthly']: there is no quarterly and no yearly rule set, and there cannot be one without moving _CADENCE_ORDER, _first_of, is_rank_session, every TradeRules canonical text and the web mirror -- which is exactly what keeps the slow rungs promotable, since the rule set they run on is still the preset. M0072 IS THE HOST because the cadence axis is only clean on a book whose event hold is counted in SESSIONS: M0072 keeps the newest event with i - hold < t <= i - 1 for 60 sessions, so the same event is live for the same 60 sessions whether the book looks four times or sixty, while M0197's chooser keys its re-pick on data_date.month and would measure two things at once. THE PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION, written before the run: (1) THE LADDER DOES NOT HUMP -- no rung above k = 1 beats M-NATIVE on money, the turn is AT k = 1, and M-G3, M-G6 and M-G12 each come in at least a point a year below M-NATIVE, flat-to- falling rather than rising then turning and not necessarily monotone in the middle; as a SHAPE, THE AXIS TURNS AT MONTHLY AND FALLS AWAY ON BOTH SIDES, since M0258 already measured the fast side at -7.01 points a year and 11.69 points of worst fall, which is a sharper and more falsifiable claim than 'a best speed exists somewhere between weekly and yearly' -- one slow rung beating M-NATIVE on money falsifies it outright; (2) THE FALL DEEPENS BEFORE IT SHALLOWS -- M-G3 and M-G6 fall deeper than M-NATIVE's 23.80% because a quarterly or half-yearly reading is late to both of the window's exits, with at least one slow rung past 28%, while M-G12 falls no shallower than M-NATIVE because a December-only reading is close to no gate at all; (3) THE DECOMPOSITION SPLITS TOWARD THE GATE -- both brackets positive and (C - B) at least half of the +7.01, point estimate 4 to 6 points a year, leaving (A - C) at 1 to 3, with the same ordering on worst fall; (4) W-G1 BEATS W-NATIVE ON BOTH AXES by at least 3 points a year and at least 6 points of worst fall; (5) THE REPRODUCTIONS ARE EXACT -- M-NATIVE returns M0258-M-B0's recorded row to the digit, 12.3314% a year and a 23.8026% worst fall on 1208 trades, and W-NATIVE returns M0258-W-B0's, and if either drifts then every paired difference here is void and the run is a null. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY. Prediction 1 coming true is the most useful outcome even though it changes nothing the owner does: it converts an accident into a decision and retires 'read the gate less often' as a direction. Prediction 1 failing would be worth far more than one id, because every monthly book in the lab would then be leaving points on the table through a change that needs no new rule set and no new preset. Assumed without asking: that the right host is M0072-Z2-RAWRANK, because it is the book M0258 already measured the +7.01 on, so this method's two native arms are reproductions rather than new baselines.
methods.expectedFailure: First and most likely: the ladder is simply FLAT-TO-FALLING and the headline is 'monthly is already right'. M-G3, M-G6 and M-G12 all come in under M-NATIVE, no rung turns, and the method has bought the knowledge that a lever nobody chose happens to sit near its best value. That is a null in the sense that nothing changes, and it is still worth the id, because the lab is currently carrying a recorded analysis whose closing paragraph asks this exact question and a journalled insight that reports gate-flip counts without saying how often the gate was being checked -- and nothing short of a pre-registered ladder closes either. Second, THE WALK-FORWARD WILL FLATTER THE SLOWEST RUNG. lab walkforward picks each fold's variant by MAR, and MAR favours whichever arm trades least; the slow rungs flip the gate less -- 22 flips at k = 1 against 9 at k = 12 on the unfunded prior -- so the folds are structurally biased toward M-G12. M0245's folds picked its slowest rung in three of four and the lab has written that down. A fold majority won by M-G12 is therefore evidence about turnover FIRST and about the cadence second, and the folds must be read arm by arm rather than by their headline; M0258's folds, which chose its no-band arm twice of four, are the counter-example that keeps this honest. Third, THE WEEKLY ARMS CAN NEVER BE PROMOTED. They run on weekly-hold-frac-gotrade, which is not in sim.rules.PRESETS, so whatever the decomposition shows lives in a measurement the lab cannot act on; only the four monthly arms could ever reach paper, and the decomposition's value is explanatory rather than operational. Fourth, A SLOW RUNG THAT WINS MAY BE WINNING ON FEES RATHER THAN ON TIMING. A gate that flips less trades less, and on a 20-name book every flip is around forty orders at Gotrade's real schedule; the fee term was the second-largest container in the 824-trial shortfall sweep. The ladder is the only defence against that reading -- a fee story improves monotonically as the reading slows and trading falls, while a timing story peaks and turns -- so the trade counts and turnover of the four monthly arms must be reported beside their returns and not after them. Note what the unfunded prior already says about this: the share of time invested barely moves across the ladder, 71.9% at k = 1 against 67.9% at k = 12, so the slow rungs are not simply sitting in the market more. Fifth, THE DEV WINDOW HOLDS EXACTLY TWO CRASHES AND BOTH WERE SLOW. A reading interval's whole effect is WHEN it notices, and a quarterly reading that looks fine against two slow falls could be catastrophic against a fast one; 1987 and 2020 are what fast looks like and neither is in this window. Nothing measured on dev can settle that, the folds are the only within-window check, and no test-window look is spent here under any outcome -- four are spent and all four failed. Sixth, THE 2009-2015 ERA IS WHERE A SLOW GATE SHOULD LOOK BEST AND IT IS THE ERA THAT MATTERS LEAST FOR SAFETY. A nearly always-on gate wins a window with no crash in it, so M-G12 flattering itself on the second half while falling hard in 2008 would be the expected shape of a bad answer, not a good one, and the two eras must be read together. Seventh, the host book's own recorded worst fall is 23.80%, already at the real-money bar, so no arm of this method is expected to clear every go-live condition and the cadence is not being asked to fix that. Eighth, the k = 1 identity is load-bearing and asserted on a 473-session synthetic fixture rather than on the dev tape: if sim.rules._first_of ever stopped making a monthly book's data_date a calendar month end, M-NATIVE would silently stop being the ladder's k = 1 rung and the ladder would have a hole at its fastest end. The test module asserts the identity on every decision session it can see, which is the strongest check available without spending a trial on a rung that is provably a duplicate. Finally, as in every switch method the lab has run: interest on the cash held while the gate is off is not modelled, which flatters SPY and penalises every gated arm equally -- and it penalises the FAST readings most, since they sit out most often, so each gap this method reports between a fast and a slow reading is a LOWER bound on how well the fast reading really did. The paired differences within one cadence are unaffected.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-19

## What was asked, and what was done

Every book in this lab has a safety rule: when the market as a whole is below its own
two-hundred-day average, the book stops holding stocks and sits in the index instead. Nobody
has ever chosen **how often that rule gets looked at**. A book only makes decisions on the days
it re-picks its stocks, and the safety rule is read on exactly those days — so a book that
re-picks weekly happens to check its safety rule weekly, and a book that re-picks monthly
happens to check it monthly. That was never a decision. It was a side effect.

Last run showed it was an expensive side effect. The same book, with the same safety rule,
earned 12.3% a year when it checked monthly and 5.3% a year when it checked weekly — seven
points a year apart, with nothing else moved. That is larger than the whole safety rule is
worth. So this run asks where the best checking speed actually is.

Six versions of one book were run over twenty years, 1996 to 2015, on the owner's real monthly
deposits at Gotrade's real fees. Everything about them is identical — the same stocks, the same
screens, twenty slots, the same sixty-day holding period — except how often the book acts and
how fresh a safety reading it acts on:

- **checks once a month** (the book as it stands today)
- **checks once every three months** — the end of March, June, September, December
- **checks twice a year** — the end of June and December
- **checks once a year** — the end of December only
- **checks weekly**
- **re-picks weekly but acts on the monthly reading** — the version that separates the two

The benchmark throughout is the same deposits, on the same days, put into the index instead:
**7.2% a year**. Every percentage below is what the money actually earned on those deposits.

## The comparisons that matter

Checking monthly rather than weekly was worth **+7.0 points a year** and a worst fall
**11.7 points shallower** — 12.3% a year against 5.3%, and a worst fall of 23.8% against 35.5%.
That is the figure from last run, and it reproduced to the digit.

Checking less often than monthly was worth nothing at all. Not one of the four slower versions
beat the monthly one. Three months cost 3.6 points a year, twice a year cost 0.2, once a year
cost 3.7.

And every slower version fell **deeper**, not shallower. The book that checks monthly fell
23.8% at its worst. Three months fell 33.6%, twice a year 30.3%, once a year 25.6%. Reading the
safety rule less often made the book less safe on every single setting, which is the thing a
safety rule exists to prevent.

## The ladder

| how often it checks | your money earned | worst fall | trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| once a month | **12.3%** a year | 23.8% | 1208 |
| once every three months | 8.8% a year | 33.6% | 1184 |
| twice a year | 12.1% a year | 30.3% | 1202 |
| once a year | 8.6% a year | 25.6% | 1099 |

**The ladder is not a ladder.** It is neither humped nor monotone — it zig-zags, and it turns
at the fastest rung. Monthly is the best of the four on money, and the shallowest of the four
on the worst fall, and nothing slower recovers it.

The two-month setting was not run. It is the seventh version and the method is capped at six,
so it was measured beforehand on the index alone as a prior and is left for a follow-up. Read
this as a four-rung ladder, not a five-rung one with a hole in it.

**The zig-zag is the real finding, and it is sharper than it looks.** The slower settings read
a strictly nested set of dates: December only is inside June-and-December, which is inside
March-June-September-December, which is inside all twelve months. So the twice-a-year version
reads **a strict subset of the dates the three-month version reads** — strictly fewer readings,
every one of them also taken by the faster version — and it earned 3.3 points a year *more*
while falling 3.3 points *less deep*.

Reading fewer times cannot, by itself, make a book earn more than reading those same times plus
some others. So whatever is moving these numbers is not **how often** the rule is read. It is
**which months** it happens to be read in. Across twenty years this window contains two slow
crashes, and whether a given calendar grid happens to take a reading just before or just after
each of them is worth several points a year. That is luck about dates, dressed up as a setting.

## Splitting the seven points

Of the **7.0 points a year** that checking monthly beat checking weekly:

- **1.0 point** came from picking stocks less often
- **6.0 points** came from reading the safety rule less often

And of the **11.7 points of worst fall**:

- **2.3 points** came from picking stocks less often
- **9.4 points** came from reading the safety rule less often

So roughly **six-sevenths of it is the safety rule, not the stock picking.** The slow, expensive
thing about a weekly book was never that it churns its names — it is that it panics at the
market's weekly noise, selling out and buying back on wobbles a monthly reading never sees.

The way to read this split: a third version was run that re-picks its stocks weekly but acts on
the month-end safety reading. At every weekly decision it reuses the exact reading the monthly
book took that month — not an approximation of it, the same session. So the gap between it and
the weekly book isolates the reading speed, and the gap between it and the monthly book isolates
the picking speed. The two halves add to the whole exactly, with no remainder: the split is a
decomposition, not a second measurement. The halves cannot both be wrong and still sum.

That weekly-picking, monthly-reading version earned 11.3% a year with a 26.1% worst fall — it
recovers almost all of the monthly book's advantage without changing how often it trades names
at all.

## The prediction written down before the run

Five things were written down and committed before any of this ran.

1. *No slower setting beats monthly; the turn is at monthly, and the axis falls away on both
   sides.* **Held.** Nothing slower beat it, and the fast side was already measured at seven
   points worse. The one clause that missed: each slow rung was predicted to come in at least a
   point a year below monthly, and the twice-a-year rung came in only 0.2 below.
2. *The fall deepens before it shallows, with at least one slow setting past 28%.* **Held**, and
   more strongly than predicted — two of them went past 30%, and the yearly one still fell
   deeper than monthly rather than shallower.
3. *The split goes toward the reading, with the reading worth 4 to 6 points and the picking 1 to
   3.* **Held**, at the top of the predicted range: 6.0 and 1.0.
4. *The weekly-picking, monthly-reading version beats the weekly one by at least 3 points a year
   and 6 points of fall.* **Held**: 6.0 points and 9.4 points.
5. *Both reproductions are exact.* **Held** — see below.

Four of five held outright and the fifth held on its falsifier and missed on a margin. This is
the outcome that changes nothing the owner does, and it was the one predicted. What it buys is
that it is now a decision rather than an accident: monthly is where the lab had landed by
chance, and monthly turns out to be right.

## The reproduction check

The fastest version here is the existing book run again under a new name, and it came back
**identical on all six measures** — the same money earned, the same worst fall, the same 1208
trades, the same turnover, the same share of time invested, the same ratio of gains to losses.
The weekly version reproduced the weekly book from last run the same way, on all six. Nothing in
the machinery moved between the two runs, so every paired difference above is a real difference
and not drift.

One number does read differently, and it is not the book changing. The luck score — the check
that asks whether a result could be the best of many tries rather than a real edge — is computed
against the whole pile of attempts the lab has made. The lab has now made one more attempt than
it had last run, so the bar is fractionally higher. The fastest version scores 0.928 against the
recorded 0.928: unchanged in practice. Two of the six versions clear the luck bar — the monthly
one and the twice-a-year one. The other four do not, which is itself worth noticing: the versions
that do not clear it are the ones whose results came from reading a handful of calendar dates.

## What the out-of-sample stretches said

The lab splits the twenty years into four stretches, trains on what came before each, and scores
the version it would have chosen on months it had never seen. Two of the four beat the index.

The warning has to come first, because it decides how to read this. The lab picks each stretch's
version by a return-to-worst-fall ratio, and that ratio structurally favours whichever version
trades least — which here is always a slow one. So a stretch choosing a slow setting is evidence
about trading volume before it is evidence about safety.

And that is exactly what happened. Three of the four stretches picked a slow setting — the yearly
one once, the twice-a-year one twice — and only the last picked the monthly one. **Of the three
slow picks, two lost to the index.** The one that won was the stretch containing the 2008 crash,
where any safety rule at all wins. The single stretch that picked the monthly setting won.

So the stretches did drift toward the slow settings exactly as feared, and the drift cost them.
Read the headline — two of four — knowing that the selection rule handed three of the four
stretches a version this run has just shown to be worse.

## The shape check

Each version was compared against the shape of the version it controls, to catch a comparison
between two books that do not trade alike. All six passed: every one is a rung of the same
ladder, holding the same book at the same size with the same holding period, so each is its own
control and there is nothing mismatched to flag. Nothing was refused.

## Why

A safety rule based on a two-hundred-day average is slow by construction. It is trying to tell a
real downturn from a wobble, and two hundred days of averaging is what does the telling. Reading
that slow signal *quickly* adds nothing — the signal has not changed since yesterday — but it
does add the chance to act on it, and acting costs money twice: once in fees, and once in selling
near a low and buying back near a high. That is the six points. A weekly book is not better
informed than a monthly one; it just has more chances to flinch.

But slowing the *reading* past monthly does not continue the trick, because it stops being a
speed and starts being a date. Once the book only looks four times a year, what matters is not
the interval but whether one of those four dates lands before or after a crash. That is why the
numbers stop behaving like a dial and start behaving like a coin — and why reading twice a year
beat reading four times a year while reading once a year lost again. There is no mechanism that
makes two readings better than four; there is only the accident of which two.

The turn, then, is at monthly, and the reason it is at monthly is that monthly is the slowest
reading that is still a *rate* rather than a *date*. Twelve readings a year are enough that no
single one of them carries the result.

The fee numbers confirm this is timing and not cost. Reading once a year pays $37,600 in real
Gotrade fees over the twenty years against $57,200 for monthly — nearly $20,000 saved — and still
earns 3.7 points a year less. The saving is real and it is swamped. Measured as a share of gross
trading profit the slow versions are actually *worse*: 15.5% for yearly and 15.1% for quarterly
against 11.5% for monthly, because their profits shrank faster than their fees did.

## What this does not settle

- **Only two crashes, and both were slow.** This window holds 2000-02 and 2008, and both unfolded
  over months. A checking interval's entire job is *when it notices*, and a quarterly reading that
  copes with two slow falls could be ruinous against a fast one. 1987 and 2020 are what fast looks
  like and neither is in this window. Nothing measured here can speak to that.
- **The sub-monthly end cannot be cleanly separated.** A book that only acts monthly cannot act on
  a reading taken between its decision days — a reading it never acts on changes nothing. So
  making it read weekly necessarily makes it trade weekly. That half of the axis is confounded by
  how the simulator is built, not by how this was designed, and no arrangement of settings undoes
  it. The decomposition above is the honest way around it, and it is the reason the weekly-picking,
  monthly-reading version exists.
- **The two weekly versions can never be traded.** They run on a weekly schedule that is not one
  of the broker-priced schedules a book can be promoted on. Whatever they show stays a
  measurement. The four monthly versions, slow readings included, all run on the ordinary monthly
  schedule and could all reach paper trading.
- **Nothing of the untouched window was spent.** Four looks at it have been used and all four
  failed; this method spent none, under any outcome, and the count is still four.

## My opinion

**Keep checking monthly. Change nothing.**

The honest summary is that the lab had already stumbled into the right answer, and this run turned
a guess into a measurement. That is worth the method id on its own — "read the safety rule less
often" was a live direction with a seven-point result pointing at it, and it is now closed.

What I would actually take from this is the other half. Six of the seven points were the *reading*,
not the picking. That is a fact about every book in the lab, and it says something useful about any
future book that wants to trade frequently: it is not the churn that will hurt it, it is that a
fast book reads a slow safety signal too often and flinches at noise. A weekly book that keeps its
weekly picking but reads its safety rule monthly got back 6.0 of the 7.0 points and 9.4 of the 11.7
points of fall. If a weekly schedule ever becomes tradeable, that is the shape to build.

I would not spend a method id chasing the zig-zag. Twice-a-year beating three-months is a calendar
accident, and the way to prove that is a second host book rather than a finer grid on this one — if
the zig-zag is real it will repeat, and if it is luck about dates it will scramble. That is worth
queuing, not worth running next.

And I would not spend one on the two-month setting. It was the version that did not fit, its prior
sits between the two neighbours rather than above them, and the ladder came back flat-to-falling
with the turn at the fastest rung — exactly the shape in which a missing middle rung has nothing
to add.
methods.verdict: Reading the safety rule once a month instead of once a week is worth seven points a year and twelve points of worst fall, six-sevenths of it from the reading rather than the stock picking; reading it less often than monthly pays nothing and makes every version fall deeper, because past monthly it stops being a speed and becomes an accident of which calendar dates get read.

methods.name: Past monthly, is a safety gate's reading speed real or is it just which month you happen to look? The same reading interval at different calendar dates, on a second book
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0260 (its anchored-gate machinery and its four monthly rungs carried, the host book replaced by M0088-C-LIVE-63's); Faber (2007), A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, JWM 9(4), for the long-moving-average switch and for evaluating it at a fixed interval rather than continuously
methods.hypothesis: Published 2007 (the long-moving-average switch), so nothing in the rule is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies to it; what is new is the question. Every figure here is the MONEY-WEIGHTED return on the owner's own monthly deposits -- what the lab prints as 'your money earned' -- except where a line says UNFUNDED, which marks the SPY-alone prior grid and nothing else. WHAT M0260 LEFT OPEN. M0260 swept how often a book reads its SPY 200-day gate, on M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's earnings-jump book. Below monthly the answer was clean: reading weekly cost 7.01 points a year and 11.69 points of worst fall, 85% of it the gate's reading cadence rather than the book's re-pick frequency. Above monthly it was not: monthly 12.33% and a 23.80% fall, quarterly (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec) 8.78% and 33.64%, half-yearly (Jun/Dec) 12.10% and 30.34%, yearly (Dec) 8.64% and 25.64%. Twice a year beat four times a year by 3.3 points of money and 3.3 points of fall -- AND THE TWICE-A-YEAR GRID IS A STRICT SUBSET OF THE FOUR-TIMES GRID. Reading strictly fewer of the same dates cannot beat reading those dates plus others on any theory where the INTERVAL is what matters, so past monthly the axis had stopped being a speed, and M0260 could not say what it had become because every rung of its ladder carried exactly one phase. THE PRIOR GRID, measured on the dev store before a word of this file was written by docs/backtests/2026-10-20-gate-reading-phase.py (SPY ALONE, a 200-bar average, a one-session lag, a monthly acting calendar, the reading held as taken; UNFUNDED, so plain CAGRs that are NOT comparable with the money-weighted figures above), holds the interval fixed and moves the phase across all three phases of a quarterly reading, all six of a half-yearly one and all twelve of a yearly one: quarterly spans 6.36% to 9.43% (3.07 points) and -27.2% to -19.0%; half-yearly spans 6.03% to 9.76% (3.73 points) and -27.2% to -19.4%; yearly spans 4.47% to 9.02% (4.55 points) and -51.8% to -19.4%, a 32.4-point span of worst fall; the native monthly reading every book in the lab runs today is 8.19% and -19.0%. M0260's whole slow ladder spans 3.69 points of money from its best rung to its worst, so HOLDING THE INTERVAL FIXED AND MOVING ONLY THE PHASE MOVES THE RESULT BY AS MUCH AS, OR MORE THAN, CHANGING THE INTERVAL AT ALL. The grid reproduces M0260's zig-zag in its own shadow (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec 6.36% against Jun/Dec 8.17%, the same sign and nearly the same size as the funded 8.78 against 12.10) and reproduces the lab's recorded SPY-only trials (native monthly fall 19.0% against M0084-MONTHLY's recorded 18.89%). The sting is that the BEST phase of every interval beats native monthly -- 9.43%, 9.76%, 9.02% against 8.19% -- while the AVERAGE phase of every interval loses to it (7.52%, 7.90%, 7.06%): there is always a slower reading that looks better than monthly, there is no way to know in advance which, and picking it after the fact is the definition of fitting the window. THE ANCHOR, with month_index(d) = (d.year - 1970) * 12 + (d.month - 1): the newest bar a <= data_date that is the last session of its calendar month and has month_index(a) % k == phase, falling back to data_date when none is on hand. M0260's anchor is this one at phase = k - 1, and the test module asserts that equality against M0260's own frozen function on every session of the smoke tape. It is never later than data_date, so every anchored arm is strictly SAFER on look-ahead than the native reading, and the fallback never fires inside the dev window: the prior walked all 237 monthly decision sessions from 1996-01-03 at all 21 (k, phase) pairs and found zero fallbacks, zero late anchors and at worst 526 SPY bars behind an anchor. THE HOST IS M0088-C-LIVE-63, not M0072, or the method would measure the same book twice: the calm big dividend-raisers book carried verbatim -- M0076's ex-date event with a raise of 25% or more, the calmer half of the live raisers by a 63-session daily swing, F4's five-dollar and twenty-million screen, 20 slots at 5%, SPY in the empty ones, a 182-day event hold, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-ups, behind the same bare SPY-200 gate. Its recorded dev row (trial 289) earns 10.62% a year of the owner's money against SPY's 7.19%, falls 18.71%, makes 3.52 of gains per 1 of losses on 528 trades and reads DSR 0.945, so it is eligible, it is UNDER the 20% fall bar M0072's host is not, and it is the lab's strongest kin-clean book (M0088-C-LIVE-63, M0101-CTRL, M0107-HOST and M0122-CALM-EQ are one book in four wrappers, identical to the digit). IT QUALIFIES FOR THIS AXIS and that was checked in its own code first: the handover's constraint is that the host's event hold must be an interval rather than a calendar grid, because a book whose re-pick grid IS a calendar grid would alias with the gate's reading grid; M0197's chooser keys on data_date.month and cannot host this axis at all, while M0088's hold is live_event's (data_date - e).days >= hold_days, an interval measured from a company's own ex-date, and the book re-picks monthly at every rung and never changes that. One honest caveat: US ex-dates do cluster on the calendar quarters, so this book's refresh rhythm is not perfectly blind to a quarterly grid -- a reason to read the quarterly arm with care, and no objection at all to the k = 12 pair, whose two dates are six months apart. THE SIX ARMS all hold that book verbatim on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade and move only the date the gate is read at: NATIVE (every month end: the zero rung and the reproduction), Q-MJSD (k=3 phase 2, Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec: M0260's quarterly rung on a second host), H-JD (k=6 phase 5, Jun/Dec: M0260's half-yearly rung), H-MS (k=6 phase 2, Mar/Sep: the SAME interval as H-JD, the other dates), Y-DEC (k=12 phase 11, Dec: M0260's yearly rung) and Y-JUN (k=12 phase 5, Jun: the same interval as Y-DEC, six months away). Four of the six are M0260's ladder rung for rung on a differently-picked book, which is the generalisation test; the other two hold an interval fixed and move the phase, which is the test M0260 could not run; the two questions share four arms, which is how both fit inside MAX_VARIANTS = 6. H-MS IS NOT AN ARBITRARY SECOND PHASE, IT IS Q-MJSD'S OTHER HALF: the months 2, 5, 8, 11 split exactly into {5, 11} = Jun/Dec and {2, 8} = Mar/Sep, so the quarterly grid is precisely the union of the two half-yearly grids and the quarterly arm's anchor is always whichever half-yearly anchor is NEWER -- proved session by session on all 237 scored decision sessions by the prior's Job B. So an interval story predicts Q-MJSD >= max(H-JD, H-MS), M0260 measured Q-MJSD < H-JD on its own host, and a Q-MJSD that loses to BOTH halves here leaves no interval story alive on either host. Y-JUN is the maximal phase shift at the slowest interval, six months from December, and on the unfunded prior the pair reads 7.67% / -30.8% against 6.77% / -19.4%: nearly the same money, 11.4 points apart on the fall. THE LOOKBACK IS 454 AT EVERY RUNG -- max(CALM.lookback(book), 200 + 254) -- because reading a 200-bar average at an anchor up to twelve months old needs 200 + gap bars and the worst gap over every scored session at every phase was measured at 234; 254 is deliberately M0260's own margin so the two ladders are scored under identical arithmetic. Widening from the host's 253 does not move the first scored session, because dev.candidate_window binds on MEMBERSHIP_START (1996-01-02) for any lookback up to 739; the standing rule is 'never cross 739', not 'never widen', and 454 is also inside the 473-session smoke fixture's cap. THE PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION, written before the run: (1) THE PHASE IS WORTH AT LEAST AS MUCH AS THE INTERVAL ON A REAL BOOK -- |H-JD minus H-MS| is at least 1.5 points a year of the owner's money, and Y-DEC against Y-JUN is at least 5 points of worst fall; both pairs read the gate exactly as often as each other, so any gap at all is the dates, and the claim is falsified by both pairs landing inside a point of each other; (2) THE TURN AT MONTHLY GENERALISES -- NATIVE beats all four anchored M0260-phase arms on money; (3) THE ZIG-ZAG REPRODUCES RATHER THAN SCRAMBLING, and this CONTRADICTS the idea row that reserved this id, which predicted a scramble and was written before anyone measured a phase grid: the gate's on/off path at a given (k, phase) is a property of SPY and the calendar ALONE and is byte for byte the same path on every book in the lab, so two long-equity books behind the same path share most of their monthly return pattern and the ordering should largely carry over -- concretely, H-JD beats Q-MJSD on money here as it did on M0072's book (12.10 against 8.78) and in the unfunded shadow (8.17 against 6.36), and a reversal would mean M0260's zig-zag was about M0072's holdings after all and prediction 1 is all that survives; (4) THE NESTING PARADOX SURVIVES -- Q-MJSD does not beat BOTH of its own halves on money even though its reading is the fresher of the two at every moment, which is the cleanest possible demonstration that freshness is not what is being paid for past monthly; (5) AT LEAST ONE SLOW ARM FALLS DEEPER THAN 24% against NATIVE's recorded 18.71%, and I expect the deepest to be a k = 12 arm; (6) THE REPRODUCTION IS EXACT -- NATIVE returns M0088-C-LIVE-63's recorded row digit for digit, 10.62% of the owner's money, an 18.71% worst fall, 528 trades, turnover 4.78, exposure 0.704 and gains 3.52 times losses, and if it drifts then every paired difference here is void and the run is a null. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: predictions 1 and 4 coming true would retire an entire direction, because nobody should then ever again spend a method id on 'read the gate every N months' when the N is not the lever and the lever that is there -- which month -- is unknowable in advance and fits the window when chosen after the fact. Assumed without asking: that M0088-C-LIVE-63 is the right second host, because it is the lab's strongest kin-clean dev-eligible book, its signal (a dividend raise) shares nothing with M0072's (an earnings-day price jump), and its hold is an interval rather than a calendar grid; and that the two phase arms should be chosen structurally (the complement half, and the maximal shift) rather than for how their phases scored on the prior grid, so that the method cannot be accused of picking a phase to win.
methods.expectedFailure: First and most likely: THE TWO PHASES OF AN INTERVAL LAND ON TOP OF EACH OTHER once the book is a funded, fee-paying stock book rather than SPY alone. The prior's phase spreads are measured on a weight path with no picking in it, and a book that is only 70% invested and holds twenty names may wash the dates out. That would be a clean null, it would mean the interval IS the dial after all and M0260's zig-zag was noise in one book, and it would be worth the id because a finer interval ladder would then be worth building -- which on the current evidence it is not. Second, THE DEV WINDOW HOLDS EXACTLY TWO CRASHES AND BOTH WERE SLOW, so any phase result is a statement about where 2000-2002 and 2007-2009 happened to sit in the calendar. A phase that reads the gate each November looks catastrophic on this tape (-51.8% on the prior) largely because of where the 2008 exit fell relative to each November; 1987 and 2020 are what a FAST fall looks like and neither is in this window. That is not a flaw in the finding -- it is the finding: if a two-crash window can move a yearly reading by 32 points of worst fall depending on which month it is taken, then no yearly reading is a rule anyone can trust. But it does mean the SIZE of the phase effect is not transportable, only its existence. Third, THE HOST'S OWN DIVIDEND RHYTHM IS NOT PERFECTLY BLIND TO A QUARTERLY GRID. US ex-dates cluster on the calendar quarters, so Q-MJSD and H-MS and H-JD all read the gate at dates near which this book's own holdings refresh. The k = 12 pair is immune (six months apart, one reading a year) and is therefore the arm pair the first prediction should be judged on if the two disagree. Fourth, THE WALK-FORWARD WILL FLATTER THE SLOWEST ARMS. lab walkforward picks each fold's variant by MAR and MAR favours whichever arm trades least; the slow rungs flip the gate less (28 flips at the native reading against 5 to 12 at a yearly one on the prior), so the folds are structurally biased toward Y-DEC and Y-JUN. M0245's folds picked its slowest rung in three of four and M0260's picked a slow rung in three of four, two of which then lost. A fold majority won by a yearly arm is evidence about turnover FIRST. Fifth, SIX ARMS ON ONE BOOK IS A WIDE SEARCH AND THE LUCK GATE WILL SAY SO. The host's own recorded DSR is 0.945 at the N in force; every arm here is the same book with a different reading date, so an arm that happens to draw a lucky phase will look eligible for exactly the reason this method exists to expose. Any arm that clears the screen must be read as a draw from a distribution whose spread this method has measured, and NOT as a configuration to promote -- promoting the best phase of a slow reading would be the single most on-the-nose way to fail the lesson. Sixth, THE REPRODUCTION MIGHT DRIFT. The native arm runs the host's code through a new allocator id and a new params class; if its row does not come back digit for digit against trial 289 then something in the overlay is not the host, every paired difference here is void, and the run must be reported as a null rather than patched. Seventh, as in every switch method the lab has run: interest on the cash held while the gate is off is not modelled, which flatters SPY and penalises every gated arm equally -- and it penalises the arms that sit out most, so each gap this method reports between a mostly-invested phase and a mostly-out one is a LOWER bound. The paired differences within one interval are unaffected, because two phases of one interval sit out for similar fractions of the tape. Eighth, this method cannot and does not settle what the RIGHT reading date is, only that the date matters; any arm that wins here is winning on this window's two crashes and nothing in the dev store can say whether it would win on a third.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-20

# Which month you look at the safety switch matters more than how often you look

**The short version.** Last night's run (M0260) found that a book should read its safety switch
once a month, and that reading it less often gave strange, jumpy answers — twice a year beat four
times a year, even though twice a year is just two of those same four dates. This run asked why,
on a different book, and the answer is clean: **past once a month, the switch's reading interval
is not a dial at all. It is a lottery over which calendar months get read, and the prize money in
that lottery is bigger than the whole interval question.**

Six versions of one book. Nothing moved but the date the switch was read at.

| version | months the switch is read | your money earned | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | share of time invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **every month** (what the lab runs today) | all twelve | **+10.62% a year** | **18.7%** | 3.52 | 528 | 70.4% |
| twice a year | June, December | +10.57% | 23.2% | 3.47 | 507 | 73.2% |
| once a year | June | +10.14% | 27.4% | 3.38 | 518 | 78.1% |
| once a year | December | +8.76% | 19.2% | 3.19 | 471 | 68.1% |
| four times a year | Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec | +8.41% | 23.0% | 2.62 | 526 | 69.1% |
| twice a year | March, September | +7.36% | 24.7% | 2.40 | 516 | 65.4% |

The same monthly deposits put into SPY earned **+7.19% a year** over the same stretch. Every
number in that table is the money-weighted return on the owner's own monthly top-ups — what the
lab calls "your money earned" — not the curve's growth rate, which counts the deposits as gains.

## The one number this method was bought for

**Two versions that read the switch exactly as often as each other, and differ only in which
months, are 3.21 points a year apart.** June/December earned 10.57%; March/September earned 7.36%.
Same interval, same book, same switch, same fees, same deposits. The only difference is the date.

Put that beside the interval question M0260 asked. Across the four readings M0260 measured —
every month, four times a year, twice a year, once a year — this book spans **2.21 points a year**
(10.62% down to 8.41%). So **moving only which month you look at is worth 45% more than moving how
often you look at all.**

On worst fall the gap is wider still. The two once-a-year readings, identical in every respect
except that one looks each December and the other each June, fell **19.2% and 27.4%** — 8.2 points
apart. The whole interval ladder spans 4.5 points of fall. The date is worth nearly twice the
interval there too.

## The four-dates-versus-two-dates paradox, settled

March/June/September/December reads *every date* that June/December reads, plus two more. It is
the fresher reading at every single moment of the twenty years — the lab's prior grid proves that
session by session. On any theory where the interval is what matters, reading a superset of dates
cannot do worse.

It did worse: **8.41% against 10.57%, and 2.16 points a year is not a rounding difference.** That
is the same sign and nearly the same size as M0260 found on a completely different book
(8.78% against 12.10%), and as the switch read on SPY alone with no stock picking in it at all
(6.36% against 8.17%). Three books, three times, the same direction.

And now the missing half is measured. March/June/September/December is exactly June/December plus
March/September. Its result, 8.41%, sits between its two halves (7.36% and 10.57%) and within
half a point of their plain average, 8.97%. **Adding dates to a sparse grid does not sharpen the
reading. It averages two lottery tickets.**

One honest complication, because the lattice is not tidy. June/December (10.57%) beat *both* of
its own halves, June-alone (10.14%) and December-alone (8.76%), while four-times-a-year sat
between its halves on money and fell *less* than either of them. So adding dates sometimes lands
between the halves, sometimes past both, and it does different things to the return and to the
fall at the same time. **There is no monotone structure anywhere in the sparse grids.** The only
thing that is reliably best is the full one: reading every month won on return *and* on worst fall
*and* on gains-versus-losses, against all five sparser readings.

## Does M0260's answer generalise? Yes, on a book picked by a completely different rule

M0260 ran on a book that buys stocks after a big earnings-day price jump. This run ran on a book
that buys big companies right after they raise their dividend by 25% or more, keeping the calmer
half of them. The two share no signal at all. The four readings they have in common ordered like
this:

| reading | earnings-jump book (M0260) | dividend-raisers book (here) |
|---|---|---|
| every month | 12.33% | 10.62% |
| twice a year, Jun/Dec | 12.10% | 10.57% |
| four times a year | 8.78% | 8.41% |
| once a year, December | 8.64% | 8.76% |

The top two reproduce in order, and in both books they are a near-tie — 0.23 points apart there,
0.05 here. The bottom two swap places, but they sit 0.14 and 0.35 points apart, which is inside
the noise of either book. **The ordering carried over almost perfectly**, which is exactly what
should happen once you see the mechanism: the switch's on/off path at a given set of dates is a
property of SPY and the calendar alone. It is the *same* path on every book in the lab. Two books
that are both long US shares behind the same path share most of their month-to-month pattern.

That contradicts the prediction written into this method's own queued idea row, which guessed the
ordering would scramble on a second book. This run's pre-registration said so before anything ran,
and gave the reason. The scramble theory is now dead: the slow readings are not noisy, they are
*systematic* — and what they are systematic about is the calendar, not the interval.

## Why reading more often wins, mechanically

A switch read every month is close to the market. A switch read once or twice a year is a stale
promise about a market that has since moved. In the twenty-year window the dev store covers, there
were exactly two bear markets, both of them slow. A sparse grid either happened to have a reading
date shortly before one of those falls — in which case it sat out and looks brilliant — or it did
not, in which case it rode the fall down with no protection and only noticed months later.

The share-of-time-invested column is the fingerprint of that. March/September sat invested 65.4%
of the time and earned 7.36%; June-only sat invested 78.1% and earned 10.14%. The better-looking
sparse readings are mostly the ones that happened to stay switched on through the rising decade
after 2009, and they paid for it in 2008: June-only fell 27.4% and had its worst calendar year in
2008 at −8.9%, while December-only fell only 19.2%. **The sparse readings are not buying safety or
returns. They are buying a different mix of the two, picked by an accident of the calendar.**

Reading every month is the one setting that does not make that trade. It earned the most *and*
fell the least *and* made the most gains per unit of losses, all at once, while sitting invested
only 70.4% of the time. That is timing doing work, not exposure.

## Is it real, or luck?

The lab now counts **165** independent looks (one per distinct method, which is the owner's policy
since 2026-10-08). After deflating for that many tries, the deflated Sharpe ratio — a measure of
how likely a result is real rather than a lucky draw — reads **0.956** for the every-month version
and **0.945** for June/December, both over the **0.90** bar the owner set on 2026-10-07. The other
four fail it: 0.823, 0.738, 0.884 and 0.896.

Read that the right way round, though. The every-month version *is the host book itself*, run
again through this method's machinery, and its 0.956 is simply the dividend-raisers book's own
long-standing result. The two versions that clear the luck bar are the two that read the switch
most often. Every sparse reading fails it. **A method built to show that sparse readings are a
lottery produced exactly one lottery ticket that looks like a winner — June/December — and the
lesson of the method is that you must not cash it.**

## The reproduction, and why every comparison above is trustworthy

The every-month version returned the host book's recorded row to every printed digit: +10.624% a
year of the owner's money, an 18.705% worst fall, 3.5231 of gains per 1 of losses, 528 trades,
4.7805 turnover, 70.4% invested, MAR 0.568. Identical to trial 289, recorded on 2026-10-11. (Its
deflated-Sharpe figure reads 0.9557 against the old row's 0.9446 only because the lab has run more
methods since, and that number is always scored at the count in force on the day.) So every paired
difference reported above is the switch's reading date and nothing else.

## What this does *not* settle

**The worst fall is still over the real-money bar on four of six versions**, and the two that are
under it are the two that read the switch most often. The owner's bar is 25% since design §18; on
the lab's own screen, four versions fail the luck test anyway.

**This book loses to SPY in the years that matter most.** Over 2009–2015 — the best-covered era
and the one most like today — *every single version* trailed SPY: −2.6% a year for the every-month
reading, and −5.8%, −4.2%, −6.3%, −6.6% and −3.1% for the rest. That is in line with what the lab
measured across all 824 trials (the safety switch costs about 3.6 points a year after 2009, when
there was no bear market for it to catch), but it is still the first filter, and this book does not
pass it. Nothing here is a reason to put money on the dividend-raisers book.

**The folds say selection, not edge.** The lab's walk-forward check — which re-picks the best
version at each fold boundary knowing nothing of the future — won **2 of 4** folds, lost
2003–2005 and 2009–2011, and won 2006–2008 and 2012–2014. A method that wins its twenty-year
average and loses half its folds is a selection, not an edge. The hard gate refuses promotion on
exactly that count, and it is right to.

**The buy signal did not fire.** Survivorship-free price history is still not worth paying for.

**And the size of the phase effect is not transportable.** Both of this window's crashes were slow
ones. 1987 and 2020 are what a fast fall looks like and neither is in the dev window. That a
two-crash window can move a once-a-year reading by 8 points of worst fall depending on which month
it is taken is not a flaw in the finding — it *is* the finding — but it means we know the effect
exists, not how big it would be on a third crash.

## The dead companies do not explain it

Re-running all six versions on the survivorship-check store — the dev store plus prices for most
of the companies the dev store cannot price, the ones that died included — moved almost nothing.
June/December went 10.57% → 10.8%, March/September 7.36% → 7.4%, so the 3.21-point phase gap
**widened slightly to 3.4 points**. The once-a-year fall gap went 8.2 points → 7.1. Every version's
2009–2015 shortfall got half a point worse, and every version's gains-versus-losses got worse by
0.4 to 0.85 as the dead names came back, which is the usual shape.

That is exactly what should happen. The switch reads SPY, and SPY is the same on both stores, so a
finding about *when the switch is read* has no reason to depend on which companies the book held.
It is a timing effect, and the honest tape says so.

## The pre-registered predictions, scored

Six were written down before the run. **All six came true.**

1. The phase is worth at least as much as the interval — predicted at least 1.5 points a year
   between the two twice-a-year readings and at least 5 points of fall between the two
   once-a-year readings. Measured **3.21 points** and **8.2 points**.
2. The turn at once-a-month generalises — every-month beat all five sparser readings on money.
   Measured, and it beat them on worst fall as well.
3. The zig-zag reproduces rather than scrambling — June/December beats four-times-a-year.
   Measured, 2.16 points, third book in a row.
4. The nesting paradox survives — four-times-a-year does not beat both of its own halves.
   Measured: it lost to one by 2.16 points.
5. At least one sparse version falls past 24%, and the deepest is a once-a-year one. Measured:
   24.7% and 27.4%, and the deepest is June-only.
6. The reproduction is exact. Measured, to every printed digit on six fields.

## My opinion

This direction is finished, and that is worth more than one more trial would have been. The lab
should never again spend a method id on "read the safety switch every N months". The N is not the
lever. The lever that is actually there — *which* month — is unknowable in advance, swings the
result by more than the N does, and can only be picked after the fact, which is the textbook
definition of fitting the window. Both M0260 and this run arrived at the same operating answer
from opposite directions: **read the switch every month, which is what the lab has been doing by
accident since its first trial.** Two books, one SPY-only prior, six pre-registered predictions,
and an honest-tape cross-check all agree. Close it.

The one thing I would *not* do is promote June/December, even though it clears the luck bar at
0.945 and is a legal configuration on a preset that exists. It earns 0.05 points a year less than
reading every month and falls 4.5 points deeper, and this method's entire finding is that its
0.945 is a draw from a distribution whose spread it has just measured at 3.2 points. Promoting the
lucky phase of a sparse reading would be the single most on-the-nose way to fail the lesson. The
hard gate would refuse it anyway — 2 of 4 folds — and for once the gate and the argument agree.

What I would try next is the question this one keeps bumping into and cannot answer: the whole
phase effect here is about *where the exits fell in the calendar*, and the dev window contains
exactly two of them, both slow. The useful follow-up is not another gate dial. It is to ask whether
anything at all distinguishes a reading date that was lucky from one that was not — specifically,
whether a reading taken a fixed number of *sessions* after the previous one, with no calendar in it
anywhere, removes the phase spread entirely. If it does, the lesson sharpens from "read it every
month" to "never let a market rule sit on a calendar grid", which would apply to far more of the
lab than this gate. That is the idea queued below.

## Mechanics, for the audit record

Method M0261, six dev trials #854–#859, run 2026-10-20 on dev store `640fc25e5c7b`, git sha of the
pre-registration commit `7cb6201`. Host configuration `M0088-C-LIVE-63` (trial #289), carried
verbatim; allocator `M0261` overlays only the date `f_factor.trend_on` is asked at. Arms are
(k, phase) pairs on the month-end grid `month_index(a) % k == phase`: NATIVE (native), Q-MJSD
(3, 2), H-JD (6, 5), H-MS (6, 2), Y-DEC (12, 11), Y-JUN (12, 5). Lookback 454 at every rung
(max anchor gap measured at 234 sessions over the window's 237 decision sessions at all 21 grids).
Prior grid: `docs/backtests/2026-10-20-gate-reading-phase.py`, committed before the run, UNFUNDED,
SPY alone. Test-window looks used: 4 before, 4 after — none spent, and none will be.
No promotion: `lab promote` refuses on the fold majority (2 of 4), and the method's own
pre-registration argued against promoting a phase arm regardless.
methods.verdict: Which month the safety switch is read matters more than how often: two readings taken equally often, six months apart on the calendar, differ by 3.2 points a year — more than the entire weekly-to-yearly interval ladder — and only reading it every month wins on return and on worst fall at once.

methods.name: Is a safety gate's slow-reading spread the calendar's fault or rarity's? The same gate read every N trading days, with the start slid across the period
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0261 (its anchored-gate overlay, its host book and its 454-bar lookback all carried, the grid's coordinate replaced); Faber (2007), A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, JWM 9(4), for the long-moving-average switch itself
methods.hypothesis: Published 2007 (the long-moving-average switch), so nothing in the rule is a new anomaly and no fade argument applies to it; this method changes nothing about what the gate says or how often it is asked, only the COORDINATE its dates are counted on. Every figure here is the MONEY-WEIGHTED return on the owner's own monthly deposits -- what the lab prints as 'your money earned' -- except where a line says UNFUNDED, which marks the SPY-alone prior and nothing else. WHAT M0261 LEFT OPEN. M0261 measured, on M0088-C-LIVE-63's calm big dividend-raisers book at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, that two readings of the SPY-200 gate taken EXACTLY as often as each other but on different calendar months differ by 3.21 points a year of money (Jun/Dec 10.57% against Mar/Sep 7.36%), and that two once-a-year readings six months apart differ by 8.2 points of worst fall (Dec 19.2% against Jun 27.4%) -- both LARGER than the whole weekly-to-yearly interval ladder, which spans 2.21 points of money and 4.5 of fall on the same book. So past monthly the reading axis is not a speed, and two sentences fit that evidence while prescribing opposite things. (A) THE CALENDAR IS THE PROBLEM: a month-end grid is an arbitrary human convention, the dev window's two crashes sit at particular places in it, and a rule firing on a SESSION COUNT would spread far less as its start slid -- in which case several lab books that re-pick monthly or measure calm over windows ending at month ends are all standing on a grid nobody chose, and the whole lab needs auditing. (B) RARITY IS THE PROBLEM: a gate asked twice a year is a stale promise whatever grid it sits on, the spread is the irreducible variance of reading rarely, and a session grid will spread just as wide -- in which case the lesson is narrow and already known, read the gate every month, and no other book needs auditing. THE IDEA ROW'S DESIGN WAS BROKEN AND THE PRIOR CAUGHT IT BEFORE A LINE OF THE METHOD WAS WRITTEN. The row specified a 126-session period on the grounds that a session count has 'no calendar anywhere in it'. That is false. The NYSE ran 248 to 254 sessions in each whole year of the dev window and averaged 251.8, so 126 sessions is half a year to within a fifth of a session: a 126-session reading drifts -0.2 sessions a year, which is to say it does not drift, and measured over 1994-2015 its offset 0 reads ONLY in June, July and December while its offset 63 reads ONLY in March, April, September and October. A 126-SESSION GRID IS A CALENDAR GRID WEARING A SESSION LABEL, and running it alone could only have produced a near-tautology. A period coprime with the year's session count does drift: 131 sessions drifts -10.2 sessions a year and sweeps all twelve calendar months, at 1.92 readings a year against 126's 2.05 and the calendar half-yearly grid's 2.00 -- the same rarity, no calendar lock. So this method runs BOTH periods and the comparison it is bought for is between a calendar-LOCKED session grid and a calendar-FREE one at matched rarity, with M0261's calendar grid as the third reference. That change is forced by an arithmetic fact about the exchange calendar, not by any return: the drift job reads no prices at all. THE UNFUNDED PRIOR, measured on the dev store in ONE sweep in ONE process by docs/backtests/2026-10-20-gate-reading-sessions.py before this file existed (SPY alone, a 200-bar average, a one-session lag, a monthly acting calendar, the reading held as taken; UNFUNDED, so plain CAGRs NOT comparable with the money-weighted figures above), and reproducing all seven numbers M0261's own prior quotes to the digit as its proof it reads the same tape: SESSION period 126 (LOCKED), 126 offsets, range 5.78 points, standard deviation 1.38, mean pairwise gap 1.55, fall sd 9.0; SESSION period 131 (FREE), 131 offsets, range 5.26, sd 1.31, mean pair gap 1.51, fall sd 8.1; CALENDAR half-yearly, 6 phases, range 3.73, sd 1.34, mean pair gap 1.78, fall sd 2.8; CALENDAR yearly, 12 phases, range 4.55, sd 1.32, mean pair gap 1.59, fall sd 9.1. FOUR GRIDS AT FOUR DIFFERENT COORDINATES AND THEIR STANDARD DEVIATIONS ARE 1.31, 1.32, 1.34 AND 1.38 -- a span of seven hundredths of a point on figures of one and a third. The range is not the statistic to read and the sd is, because a 131-offset grid out-ranges a 6-phase grid for free: more draws spread wider whatever the mechanism. On the statistic that does not grow with the draw count, removing the calendar entirely changes nothing, so on the unfunded shadow the answer is (B) and it is not close. THE SIX ARMS all hold M0088-C-LIVE-63's book verbatim on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade and move only the date the gate is read at, strictly backwards: NATIVE (the zero rung and the reproduction), LOCK-0 (period 126 offset 0, reads Jun/Jul/Dec, unfunded 8.55% / -27.0%), LOCK-63 (period 126 offset 63, reads Mar/Apr/Sep/Oct, unfunded 6.69% / -27.2%), FREE-0 (period 131 offset 0, all twelve months, unfunded 9.11% / -19.4%), FREE-33 (period 131 offset 33, unfunded 8.67% / -20.8%) and FREE-65 (period 131 offset 65, unfunded 6.21% / -43.4%). THE HEADLINE STATISTIC IS THE MAXIMALLY SEPARATED PAIR AT EACH PERIOD AND IT IS DRAW-MATCHED BY CONSTRUCTION: LOCK-0 against LOCK-63 is two draws, FREE-0 against FREE-65 is two draws, and M0261's funded Jun/Dec against Mar/Sep was two draws; half a period apart is exactly how Jun/Dec and Mar/Sep sit on a six-month grid, so all three pairs have the same shape. FREE-33 is a third point, there only so the free pair's gap can be seen to be representative or not, and is never part of the headline. The offsets were fixed on that structural argument -- maximal separation plus one quarter point -- and written into the prior script BEFORE the period-131 grid was computed, so no offset here was chosen for how it scored. THE LOCKED PAIR IS THE BRIDGE, NOT A THROWAWAY: unfunded its gap is 1.86 points, which is to the hundredth M0261's own unfunded Jun/Dec against Mar/Sep gap of 1.86, as it should be since offset 0 reads Jun/Jul/Dec and offset 63 reads Mar/Apr/Sep/Oct; M0261 measured that same calendar pair FUNDED at 3.21 points, so the locked arms give a direct same-shape handle on how much funding and stock picking amplify a date gap on this exact book -- 1.7 times, if LOCK reproduces it. THE GRID COUNTS FROM A FIXED CALENDAR EPOCH (the first NYSE session of 1990) AND NOT FROM 'THE SYMBOL'S FIRST BAR' as the idea row wrote it, because the lab hands an allocator a lookback window on one path and a full history on another, so 'the first bar' is a different bar in the two paths and the same configuration would score differently depending on which path ran it; session_index reads the published exchange calendar and no price, and sliding the epoch only relabels which offset is called zero. THE LOOKBACK IS 454 AT EVERY RUNG -- max(CALM.lookback(book), 200 + 254) -- deliberately M0261's own number so the two ladders are scored under identical arithmetic; the probe measured the worst anchor gap at 130 sessions over all 237 monthly decision sessions at all five anchored arms, with zero fallbacks and zero late anchors, so 330 bars is the true requirement and 454 carries 124 of margin; widening from the host's 253 does not move the first scored session, because dev.candidate_window binds on MEMBERSHIP_START (1996-01-02) for any lookback up to 739, and 454 is inside the 473-session smoke fixture's cap. A NEW ALLOCATOR ID is spent because PhaseParams holds gate_months and gate_phase and giving it a period field would move every recorded config digest that carries it, M0261's six rows included. THE PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION, written before the run: (1) (B) WINS ON A REAL FUNDED BOOK TOO -- the calendar-free pair's gap |FREE-0 minus FREE-65| is at least 2.0 points a year of the owner's money, at least two thirds of M0261's 3.21, and the three free arms' standard deviation is at least 0.9 points; this is the claim the method is bought for and it is FALSIFIED by the free pair landing inside 1.0 point, which is the only outcome that would justify auditing the rest of the lab's calendar grids; (2) THE FREE GRID SPREADS AT LEAST AS WIDE AS THE LOCKED ONE, as it did unfunded (2.90 against 1.86), and a funded free pair that spreads LESS is evidence for (A) the shadow missed and must be reported as such rather than explained away; (3) THE LOCKED PAIR REPRODUCES M0261'S CALENDAR PAIR to within 1.0 point of its funded 3.21, and if it does not then the unfunded-to-funded amplification is not stable on this book and every cross-method gap in prediction 1 is softer than it reads; (4) NATIVE STILL WINS ON BOTH AXES AT ONCE, beating all five anchored arms on money and falling less deep than all five, as it did in M0261 (10.62% and 18.71%); (5) AT LEAST ONE FREE ARM FALLS DEEPER THAN 28% against NATIVE's 18.71%, and I expect FREE-65, which unfunded falls 43.4% against the locked pair's 27.0% and 27.2%, because a drifting grid can land a reading just before a slow slide and hold it where a month-end grid is at least pinned to a month boundary; (6) THE REPRODUCTION IS EXACT -- NATIVE returns M0088-C-LIVE-63's recorded row digit for digit, 10.62% of the owner's money, an 18.71% worst fall, 528 trades, gains 3.52 times losses and exposure 0.704, as M0261-NATIVE did at trial 854, and if it drifts every paired difference here is void and the run is a null. SUCCESS IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT ELIGIBILITY: prediction 1 coming true closes M0261's question narrowly -- the spread is rarity, the fix is read the gate every month, no other book needs auditing -- while prediction 1 failing would mean the lab is standing on an arbitrary human convention in a dozen places and would be the most expensive finding of the batch. Either way an arm that clears the screen is a draw from a distribution this method has measured, NOT a configuration to promote, and no test-window look is spent here under any outcome. Assumed without asking: that replacing the idea row's single 126-session period with a locked/free pair of periods is a refinement rather than a different method, because the row's own stated purpose was to take the calendar out and 126 demonstrably does not; and that 131 is the right free period because it is the nearest period to 126 that is coprime with the year's session count while holding the readings-a-year inside 4% of the calendar grid's.
methods.expectedFailure: First and most likely: THE FREE PAIR SPREADS AS WIDE AS THE LOCKED ONE AND THE METHOD SIMPLY CONFIRMS WHAT THE SHADOW ALREADY SAID. That is a success for the prediction and a thin result for the lab -- it closes a question rather than opening a direction, and nobody should then spend another id on where a gate's dates are counted from. I am writing it down as the expected failure because 'the prior already answered it' is exactly the kind of result that tempts a write-up into overclaiming. Second, THE DEV WINDOW HOLDS EXACTLY TWO CRASHES AND BOTH WERE SLOW, so every number here is a statement about where 2000-2002 and 2007-2009 happened to sit relative to each grid. FREE-65's 43.4% unfunded fall is one reading landing badly before one slide; 1987 and 2020 are what a FAST fall looks like and neither is in this window. The EXISTENCE of the spread transports; its SIZE does not. Third, THE HOST'S OWN DIVIDEND RHYTHM IS NOT BLIND TO THE CALENDAR. US ex-dates cluster on the calendar quarters, so the LOCKED arms read the gate at dates near which this book's own holdings refresh, while the FREE arms do not -- which means the locked-versus-free comparison carries a second difference besides the one it is measuring. It cuts AGAINST the free arms spreading wider, so prediction 2 coming true survives it; prediction 2 FAILING could be this and not the calendar, and the analysis must say so rather than claim (A). Fourth, THE FREE GRID IS ONLY FREE OVER A LONG WINDOW. 131 sessions drifts ten sessions a year, so across any five-year stretch a free arm still reads in roughly the same season; the calendar is removed over twenty years and merely blurred over five. A walk-forward fold is five years, so the fold record cannot separate locked from free at all and must not be read as if it could. Fifth, THE WALK-FORWARD WILL FLATTER THE SLOWEST ARMS. lab walkforward picks each fold's variant by MAR and MAR favours whichever arm trades least; the anchored arms flip the gate 7 to 14 times against the native reading's 28 on the prior, so the folds are structurally biased toward them. M0245's folds picked its slowest rung in three of four and M0260's picked a slow rung in three of four, two of which then lost. A fold majority won by an anchored arm is evidence about turnover FIRST. Sixth, SIX ARMS ON ONE BOOK IS A WIDE SEARCH AND THE LUCK GATE WILL SAY SO. The host's own recorded DSR is 0.945 at the N in force; every arm here is the same book with a different reading date, so an arm that draws a lucky offset will look eligible for exactly the reason this method exists to expose, and promoting it would be the single most on-the-nose way to fail the lesson. Seventh, THE REPRODUCTION MIGHT DRIFT: the native arm runs the host's code through a new allocator id and a new params class, and if its row does not come back digit for digit against trial 854 then something in the overlay is not the host, every paired difference is void, and the run must be reported as a null rather than patched.
