Eighth, as in every switch method the lab has run, interest on the cash held while the gate is off is not modelled; that is worth about 0.8 points a year before 2008 and nothing after it, and it falls on every arm here roughly equally because all six sit out a similar share of the window, so it cannot create or hide a gap between two arms.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-20

# The calendar was never the problem. One reading in April 2002 was.

**The short version.** Last night's run found that *which month* a book looks at its safety
switch mattered more than *how often* — two readings taken equally often, six months apart,
differed by 3.2 points a year. That raised an uncomfortable possibility. Months are a human
invention. If the calendar itself was doing the damage, then a dozen other books in this lab that
re-pick "monthly" or measure things over "month ends" would all be standing on an arbitrary grid,
and every one of them would need re-checking.

This run took the calendar out and looked again. **It is not the calendar.** And along the way it
found that last night's headline number was an unusually large draw, and that the real mechanism
is much simpler and much more useful than either answer on offer.

## Six versions of one book. Only the date the switch is read moves.

| version | when the switch is read | your money earned | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **every month** (what the lab runs today) | all twelve months | **+10.62% a year** | **18.7%** | 3.52 | 528 |
| every 126 trading days, start 0 | only Jun, Jul, Dec | +9.76% | 23.2% | 3.32 | 497 |
| every 131 trading days, start 0 | all twelve months | +9.61% | 19.2% | 3.04 | 520 |
| every 131 trading days, start 33 | all twelve months | +9.14% | 20.4% | 3.00 | 509 |
| every 126 trading days, start 63 | only Mar, Apr, Sep, Oct | +8.66% | 23.0% | 2.67 | 510 |
| every 131 trading days, start 65 | all twelve months | +8.54% | **41.8%** | 2.87 | 502 |

The same monthly deposits put into SPY earned **+7.19% a year**. Every figure is the
money-weighted return on the owner's own top-ups — what the lab calls "your money earned" — not
the curve's growth rate, which counts deposits as gains. Worst fall is measured on the book
*without* its deposits, because monthly top-ups refill a falling account and make a fall read
gentler than it was.

## First, a trap the lab nearly walked into

The plan for this run was to count in trading days instead of months, on the grounds that a
trading-day count "has no calendar in it". **That is false, and checking it was the most valuable
twenty minutes of the run.** The New York exchange ran between 248 and 254 sessions in each full
year of the test period, averaging 251.8. So 126 trading days is half a year to within a fifth of
a day. A rule firing every 126 trading days does not drift at all — measured across twenty-two
years, one such rule fired **only ever in June, July and December**, and another **only ever in
March, April, September and October**.

A 126-day rule is a calendar rule wearing a different label. Had the run gone ahead as planned it
would have compared a calendar grid with a calendar grid and announced that the calendar does not
matter — a tautology dressed as a finding.

So the run used two spacings. **126 days, which stays locked to the calendar**, and **131 days,
which drifts about ten days a year and sweeps through all twelve months** — the same rarity,
roughly twice a year either way, with the calendar genuinely removed from one of them.

## The answer: rarity, not the calendar

Take the two readings furthest apart on each grid — the fair comparison, two draws against two
draws, the same shape as last night's June/December against March/September.

- **Calendar-locked grid: 1.10 points a year apart.**
- **Calendar-free grid: 1.07 points a year apart.**

Three hundredths of a point between them. Taking the calendar out of the rule changed nothing.
The spread is about *how rarely* you look, not about what you call the dates you look on.

**That is the good news, and it is worth saying plainly: no other book in this lab needs
re-checking for the grid it stands on.** The month-end habit is not costing anything. The
expensive habit is looking rarely, and only one book in the lab does that.

## The bad news: last night's 3.2 points was a big draw

Last night reported 3.21 points between two readings taken equally often. This run measured three
more such gaps on the same book at the same rarity, and they read **1.10, 1.07** — and last
night's own once-a-year pair read **1.38**. So the typical gap between two rarely-taken readings
is about one point, not three.

That matters because last night's conclusion — "which date beats how often" — rested on comparing
3.21 against the 2.21 points that the whole weekly-to-yearly speed ladder spans. **At a typical
draw the date gap is one point, which is below the speed ladder, not above it.** The direction of
last night's finding stands: dates do matter. Its size does not. One pair of dates is one
measurement, and this run is the reason to stop quoting that one.

There is a second warning in here. Before each of these runs the lab builds a cheap preview using
SPY alone, with no stock picking and no fees. That preview said the locked pair would be 1.86
points apart and the free pair 2.90. The real book delivered 1.10 and 1.07 — the preview
**over**stated one by 1.7x and the other by 2.7x, while last night's preview **under**stated its
pair by 1.7x. The preview is a feasibility check. It is not a forecast, and nothing in this
series should quote it as one again.

## What actually caused the whole thing: one reading in April 2002

Here is where every number above comes from. These are the dates each version turned its switch
off and on through the two long market slides in the window.

**The 2000–2002 slide** (SPY fell 49% peak to trough):

| version | got out | then what |
|---|---|---|
| every month | 2 Oct 2000 | bought back 1 Apr 2002, **out again 1 May 2002** |
| 126 days, start 63 | 2 Oct 2000 | stayed out |
| 131 days, start 0 | 1 Dec 2000 | stayed out |
| 126 days, start 0 | 2 Jan 2001 | stayed out |
| 131 days, start 33 | 1 Feb 2001 | stayed out |
| 131 days, start 65 | 1 Mar 2001 | bought back 1 Apr 2002, **stuck until 1 Oct 2002** |

Look at the first and last rows. **Both made exactly the same mistake.** Both bought back into
the market on 1 April 2002, right before the worst and final leg of that bear market. The monthly
version undid it four weeks later and it cost almost nothing. The twice-a-year version could not
undo it — its next scheduled look was six months away — and it rode the whole thing down.

That single difference is the gap between an 18.7% worst fall and a 41.8% one.

**So the penalty for reading a rule rarely is not that you make worse decisions. It is that you
are stuck with the decision you made.** Both versions were equally wrong on 1 April 2002. Only
one of them was allowed to change its mind. Everything else in this run — the one-point money
gaps, the 22-point fall gaps, last night's 3.2 points — is that same effect, measured from
different angles.

It also explains why the gaps are small and unstable. There were about forty readings in twenty
years and two slides. Essentially one or two readings per version land near a slide and decide
everything. A gap between two versions is therefore a one- or two-sample comparison, which is why
it reads 3.2 one night and 1.1 the next.

## One real difference between the two grids, and it is on safety

On money the locked and free grids are identical. On worst fall they are not. The locked pair's
two versions fell 23.2% and 23.0% — **0.2 points apart**. The free pair's fell 19.2% and 41.8% —
**22.5 points apart**.

The reason follows directly from the April 2002 story. A calendar-locked rule only ever occupies
two positions in the year, repeated for twenty years, so it has only two chances to sit in a bad
spot. A drifting rule occupies forty-two different positions, so it eventually finds one. **Being
stuck to the calendar does not earn you anything, but it does stop you from discovering a date
that is catastrophically badly placed.** That is a real, if accidental, safety feature of the
convention this run set out to question.

## The luck check, and the fold record

Four of the six versions clear the lab's luck bar: the monthly reading reads 0.956, the two
best anchored ones 0.922 and 0.911, and a third 0.901, against a bar of 0.90. That is the chance
the result is real rather than a fluke, after accounting for the 166 separate ideas this lab has
now tried. The two worst versions read 0.851 and 0.744 and fail it.

**None of this should be promoted, and that is the point of the method rather than a
disappointment.** Six versions of one book with only the reading date moved is exactly the search
this run exists to expose; a version that clears the bar did so by drawing a lucky date. The lab's
own hard gate agrees for an independent reason: the method won 2 of its 4 walk-forward folds,
which is not a majority, so promotion would be refused anyway. And on 2009–2015 — the
best-covered, most recent years — **all six versions lost to SPY**, by between 2.5 and 6.6 points
a year. That is the safety switch's standing cost of sitting in cash during a rising decade, and
it is not news.

## Does it survive the missing companies?

Yes, and cleanly. Re-run on the check tape that adds back 450 companies the main tape cannot
price — including the ones that went bust — every version reproduced, the locked pair's gap read
1.3 points and the free pair's read 1.3 points, still identical to each other, and the free grid
still spread seven times wider on worst fall. The conclusion does not depend on the survivors.

## Did the predictions hold?

Written down before the run, six of them. **Three held exactly.** The monthly reading still beat
all five others on money *and* fell less deep than all five. At least one drifting version fell
past 28%, and it was the one named in advance. And the reproduction was exact — the monthly
version returned the host book's recorded row to the digit, which is what licenses every
comparison above.

**Three did not.** The free pair was predicted to spread at least 2.0 points and spread 1.07 — a
hair past the 1.0 falsification line, so not formally wrong, but badly over-predicted. The free
grid was predicted to spread wider than the locked one on money and spread very slightly narrower
(it did spread wider on worst fall, by a hundredfold). And the locked pair was predicted to
reproduce last night's 3.21 within a point, because it reads nearly the same dates; it came back
at 1.10. **That third miss is the most informative thing in the run** — it is what proved last
night's number was a large draw rather than a stable quantity.

The expected failure I wrote down — "this will just confirm what the preview said, and tempt the
write-up into overclaiming" — half happened. The preview's *verdict* was confirmed. Its *numbers*
were wrong by factors of two to three, which I had not expected and which is now the more useful
finding of the two.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished and should be closed, not continued. Three runs have
now asked when a safety switch should be read, and the answer has not moved: read it every month,
which is what the lab already does, and stop there. Nobody should spend another method id on the
spacing, the starting point, or the coordinate the dates are counted on — those are now measured,
small, and unstable, and chasing the version that happens to look best is the definition of
fitting the past. What I would *not* close is the mechanism this run uncovered, because it points
somewhere new. The cost of looking rarely turns out to be the length of the commitment, not the
quality of the decision. The obvious thing to test next is the lab's own monthly reading: it is
taken on the first session of each month, and there are about twenty-one sessions a rule could
pick instead. If sliding that across the month moves the result by a point, then every book in
this lab is standing on a lucky day after all, and we would want to know. If it moves it by
nothing — which is what I expect, because at twelve readings a year nobody is ever stuck for long
— then the lab's own grid is proven safe and the entire question can be retired with a number
behind it instead of an assumption.
methods.verdict: Not the calendar: taking it out of the rule changed the spread by three hundredths of a point. The cost of reading a safety switch rarely is that you are stuck with the decision — one reading in April 2002 is the whole 41.8% fall — and last night's 3.2 points was a large draw, not a typical one.

methods.name: Is the lab's own monthly reading itself a lucky day? The same gate read twelve times a year, slid across every session of the month
methods.hypothesis: M0262 closed the question of WHERE a rarely-read gate's dates are counted from: a calendar-locked session grid and a calendar-free one of the same rarity spread 1.10 and 1.07 points a year of the owner's money, three hundredths of a point apart, and the result replicates on the survivorship-check store (1.3 and 1.3). The calendar is not the mechanism. The mechanism M0262 DID find is commitment length: on 1 April 2002 the native monthly arm and the twice-a-year FREE-65 arm made the IDENTICAL mistake -- both re-entered just before the final leg of the 2000-2002 bear -- and the monthly arm undid it in four weeks at almost no cost while FREE-65's next look was six months away and it fell 41.8% against the monthly arm's 18.7%. The penalty for reading rarely is not a worse decision, it is a longer commitment to the same one. THAT LEAVES EXACTLY ONE THING IN THIS SERIES UNMEASURED, AND IT IS THE ONE THE LAB ACTUALLY RUNS. Every book in the lab reads its gate at the FIRST SESSION of each calendar month. There are about 21 sessions in a month and nobody ever chose that one; it is an artefact of how  defines a rank session. M0261 proved that WHICH date you read matters at 2 reads a year (3.21 points, though M0262 showed that was a large draw and the typical gap is ~1.1); M0262's mechanism predicts the effect must SHRINK as readings get denser, because at 12 reads a year nobody is ever stuck for long. Rarity is held at 12 reads a year on every arm, which is the whole point: M0261 and M0262 varied the date at ~2 reads a year, this varies it at 12. The anchor is never later than the data date, so every arm stays strictly safer on look-ahead than the native reading, and the rule set never moves so every arm stays promotable. Lookback: 200 + at most 21 sessions of staleness, so M0261's and M0262's 454 covers it with enormous room and should be carried verbatim again so all three ladders are scored under identical arithmetic. methods.name: Lean without leaving: the price of risk picks WHICH fund, never how much is invested
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0254 (the premium floor ladder), lab journal 2026-10-20
methods.hypothesis: M0254 proved by arithmetic, not by measurement, that the price of risk cannot be spent as an exposure dial: splitting each arm against its own mirror, the opinion's worth divided by the cost of sitting out is 0.682 at floor 0 and 0.701 at floor 50, because dilution halves both halves together, so the ratio is a constant below one at every floor. The only escape is to make the cost ZERO. So this method spends the same frozen reading -- the fear index squared less the realised variance just past, ranked in its own trailing 252 sessions, imported from M0251's module so it cannot drift -- on WHICH fund holds the money rather than HOW MUCH is invested. The account is 100% invested on every session of every arm. Premium in the top third tilts towards QQQ, bottom third towards SPY, middle third is half and half, decided once a month in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up. The tilt width is a true dose because the rungs are symmetric about the 50/50 midpoint: ROTATE (lean 1.00, rungs 100% QQQ / 50-50 / 100% SPY), ROTATE-HALF (lean 0.50, rungs 75/25 / 50-50 / 25/75) and BLEND (lean 0.00, always 50-50), which is simultaneously the ladder's zero rung and the no-opinion shape placebo ROTATE must beat. MIRROR is lean 1.00 reversed: the same two funds in the same months with the opposite call, matched on exposure (both always 1.00), on the weighting arrangement and, to within the order of the flips, on the fee bill. SPY-HOLD and QQQ-HOLD bracket the ladder with the two things the owner could have bought and left alone. All six arms declare both symbols, so all six start 2000-04-07 (QQQ's 274th bar is 2000-04-06) and are scored against the identical SPY benchmark; SPY-HOLD reads a fund it never buys purely to keep that true. Two facts were measured before this file was committed and are recorded here rather than discovered afterwards. First, the beta spread the idea assumed is not there after 2002: QQQ's beta to SPY is 1.775 in 2000-2002 but 0.996 in 2003-2008 and 0.981 in 2009-2015, so in the lab's first-filter era the two funds carry the same market risk and this is a technology-against-the-broad-market bet, not a risk dial. Second, over the 187 month-end decisions the rungs split 71 bottom, 50 middle, 66 top and the rung changed in 112 of 186 steps, and the mean next-month QQQ-minus-SPY differential by rung is +0.125%%, -0.289%% and -0.204%% from top to bottom -- not monotone, the middle rung being the worst -- which carried to the ladder without compounding, fees or deposits puts ROTATE's edge over BLEND near 0.7 points a year before costs. Nothing here was tuned on either: the signal's windows and cut-offs are M0251's frozen values and the leans 1.00 / 0.50 / 0.00 are a ladder, not a search. Assumed: an unreadable signal is the neutral 50/50, never an extreme; the premium is read on day d's close and traded at the next open; idle cash earns nothing, which costs these arms nothing since none of them holds any. Success: ROTATE beats BLEND on the funded money-weighted return without a deeper worst fall, AND the curve is monotone in the lean, so ROTATE-HALF lands between them and MIRROR lands below BLEND. Eligibility is not expected: these are two-name books that tilt rather than close, so the closed-round-trip count and the profit factor will be thin or undefined, and the 2000-2002 collapse sits inside a 15-year window. The readable result is the dose curve and the ROTATE-MIRROR gap.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely outcome is that the escape works mechanically and still does not pay, because the opinion is simply too small. Roughly 0.7 points a year before costs is the pre-registered estimate, and a switch that changes its mind in 112 of 186 months on a two-name book at Gotrade's real schedule can plausibly spend most or all of that on fees. If ROTATE beats MIRROR by about 1.4 points -- twice the one-sided estimate -- while beating BLEND by near zero, the honest reading is that the signal is real, the expression is free, and the instrument pair is too narrow to carry it. That is the decidable answer this method exists to give, and it would close the exposure-neutral route rather than invite another tuning pass. The second and more likely-looking failure is that ROTATE wins on the 15-year average purely because QQQ fell about twice as far as SPY in 2000-2002 and the premium goes deeply negative during a crash already under way (October 2008 is the window's lowest reading, because trailing realised variance explodes above the fear index once the fall has started). An arm that merely avoids holding QQQ in 2001 will look like a signal over this window; BLEND and MIRROR are what separate those, and the 2009-2015 era column is what decides it, since the measured beta spread in that era is 0.02 and a rotation with no beta spread has almost no channel left to pay through. Third, the middle rung's raw differential is the worst of the three, so the ladder is not monotone in the signal even before any strategy is run; if the dose curve comes out non-monotone too, the correct conclusion is that the thirds are the wrong shape for this expression and not that the lean should be retuned. Fourth, every arm is invested through 2008, so every worst fall should land near buy-and-hold's -- SPY-HOLD around 55%% and QQQ-HOLD worse -- far outside the owner's 25%% real-money limit, which means an arm that wins on return will almost certainly breach the depth rule, exactly as the raised floors did in the parent. Fifth, BLEND trades only to rebalance while ROTATE trades to switch, so part of any ROTATE-minus-BLEND gap is a fee bill and not an opinion; only the ROTATE-MIRROR pair holds the trade rate fixed, and insight 479 says even a control matched on trades and turnover is not return-neutral, so the BLEND margin is an estimate of unknown sign rather than a bound. Sixth, the lab already owns a SPY-against-QQQ switch on relative momentum in the P7A f2 family at MAR 0.50, so if this one lands near there the likely explanation is the instrument pair's own ceiling rather than either signal. Finally, the whole family is post-2009 published work in its second half, so the era that matters most is the faded one.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-21

## What was tried, and why it was worth trying

Insurance against the stock market swinging about usually costs more than the swings turn out to
cost. That gap — what the insurance costs, minus what the swings actually cost — is the **price of
risk**, and this family has now measured it three times. Twice before, it carried real information
about which months are good ones to own shares, and twice before, the lab could not spend that
information without paying more than it was worth.

The parent (M0254) ended with an argument rather than a number. It used the signal to decide **how
much** of the account was invested, and found that whatever the opinion was worth, standing aside
cost about one and a half times as much — at *every* setting of the dial, because turning the dial
down shrinks the gain and the cost together. The ratio stayed stuck at about 0.68, and no amount of
tuning moves a constant.

M0265 is the escape from that argument. If the cost of the opinion is "time spent out of the
market", then **never leave the market** and the cost is zero — and then any positive opinion wins,
however small. So the money here is 100% invested on every single day of every single arm. The
signal no longer decides how much is invested, only **which of the two funds holds it**: when
insurance is dear (the signal's top third of its own past year) it leans towards QQQ, the tech-heavy
fund; when insurance is cheap (bottom third) it leans towards SPY, the broad market; in between it
holds half of each. Decided once a month, in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, on the
owner's 5,000,000 rupiah monthly top-up.

Six arms, all starting on the same day (2000-04-07, the first day QQQ has a full year of history
behind it) and all judged against the same SPY yardstick:

| arm | what it does | how much it traded |
|---|---|---|
| **ROTATE** | the idea: all QQQ / half each / all SPY | turnover 11.5 |
| **ROTATE-HALF** | half the lean: 75/25 / half each / 25/75 | turnover 5.8 |
| **BLEND** | no opinion at all: half and half, forever | turnover 0.1 |
| **MIRROR** | the same months, the opposite call | turnover 11.7 |
| **SPY-HOLD** | buy the broad market and leave it alone | turnover 0.1 |
| **QQQ-HOLD** | buy the tech fund and leave it alone | turnover 0.1 |

**The mechanical claim worked exactly as designed.** Every arm's measured time-in-the-market is
between 97.5% and 98.7% — identical to buy-and-hold. The cost that defeated the parent is genuinely
gone. Everything below is about what replaced it.

## The result

What the owner's own money would have done, deposits and all, over the 15 and a half years:

| arm | your money earned | vs the same deposits in SPY | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| QQQ-HOLD | **+10.9% a year** | +7.9% | 79.2% |
| BLEND | +9.4% | +7.9% | 66.2% |
| ROTATE-HALF | +8.5% | +7.9% | 67.6% |
| SPY-HOLD | +7.8% | +7.9% | 55.1% |
| **ROTATE (the idea)** | **+7.5%** | +7.9% | 69.5% |
| MIRROR | +5.7% | +7.9% | 68.7% |

**The idea finished last but one.** It earned less than simply buying the broad market and leaving
it alone, less than simply buying the tech fund and leaving it alone, and less than holding half of
each and never touching it. It also fell further than any of them except the tech fund on its own.

Every arm failed the owner's go-live rules, and not narrowly: the deepest-fall rule is 25% and the
shallowest arm here fell 55%. The luck score for the idea is 0.069 where 0.90 is the bar, judged
against 169 independent looks the lab has now taken — in words, if you try enough rules one of them
looks good by chance, and this one does not even look good.

## The two measurements that matter

**1. The signal is real, for the third time.** ROTATE and MIRROR are the same book making opposite
calls in the same months, with the same time invested, the same shape and — this is the point —
the same trading bill (turnover 11.5 against 11.7, within 2%). Nothing separates them except which
way round the opinion points. ROTATE earned +7.5%, MIRROR +5.7%. **The opinion is worth 1.8 points
a year between the two calls, so 0.9 points per side.** That matches a straight count on the raw
tape: over the 186 monthly decisions, the months the signal called for the tech fund beat the
months it called against by about 1.45 points a year, of which essentially none (0.03) is explained
by the signal simply being long the tech fund more often. It is genuine month-picking.

**2. The cost did not go to zero. It went up.** Take the two opposite opinions and average them —
that removes the opinion entirely and leaves only the *act of switching*. ROTATE and MIRROR average
+6.6%. Now take the two do-nothing endpoints and average them: SPY-HOLD and QQQ-HOLD average
+9.35%. (The never-rebalanced half-and-half arm landed at +9.4%, confirming that midpoint almost
exactly.) **Switching the account back and forth, with no opinion at all, cost 2.75 points a year.**

So the ratio this method existed to fix:

> what knowing the answer is worth: **0.9 points a year**
> what the arrangement that carries it costs: **2.75 points a year**
> ratio: **0.33**

The parent's ratio was 0.68. **The escape made it worse, not better — it roughly halved it.** Making
the cost zero on one axis simply moved the cost to another axis, where it was bigger.

## Why: the whole penalty is Gotrade's bill

Re-running the idea twice, once at the lab's old flat 0.1%-a-trade assumption and once at Gotrade's
real schedule (`lab costs`, report only — no trial, no look):

| | flat 0.1% | Gotrade's real fees |
|---|---|---|
| total return | +19,911.5% | +17,356.7% |
| fees paid | $15,466 | $34,521 |
| fees as a share of trading profit | 11.0% | **27.1%** |
| beat SPY? | yes | **no** |

Gotrade charges 2.2 times what the lab used to assume, and over a quarter of everything this rule
made from trading went to fees. Extending that line down to zero fees puts the idea's fee bill at
about 2.33 points a year of growth. The cost of switching, measured independently above, was 2.20
points. **Those are the same number.** The entire penalty for rotating between the two funds is the
fee bill — there is no hidden mechanical drag, no subtle timing loss. The rule simply cannot afford
its own broker.

The dose ladder confirms there is no setting that escapes it. Turnover across the three leans is
0.1, 5.8 and 11.5 — exactly proportional to the lean. The money earned is 9.4%, 8.5% and 7.5% —
exactly proportional too, and sloping the wrong way. Cost and opinion scale together again, just as
they did for the parent, so halving the lean halves both and the ratio does not move. This is the
third expression of this signal, and the third time that same arithmetic has closed it.

## What was expected, and what was not

The hypothesis said ROTATE should beat BLEND. **It did not** — it lost to it by 1.9 points. The
pre-registered estimate of the opinion's gross size was "near 0.7 points a year against the
no-opinion arm"; the actual one-sided opinion was 0.9 points, so the *size* was predicted almost
exactly and the *sign of the net result* was still wrong, because the fee bill was three times
larger than the opinion.

The first expected failure — "the escape works mechanically and still does not pay, because the
opinion is too small" — is exactly what happened, including the specific prediction that ROTATE
would beat MIRROR by roughly 1.4 points while losing to the no-opinion arm. It beat MIRROR by 1.8.

Two pre-registered worries turned out **backwards**, and both are worth recording:

- *"ROTATE will win only because the tech fund collapsed in 2000-2002."* The opposite. Splitting the
  signal's month-picking by era: in 2000-2002 the picking was **negative** (−2.5 points a year) and
  the only reason that era looks good is that the signal happened to be pointing at the broad market
  more often while the tech fund fell 2.5% a month. In 2003-2008 the picking was worth nothing
  (+0.2). In **2009-2015 the picking was worth +1.9 points a year** — its best era by far.
- *"2009-2015 is the faded era, and the two funds carry the same market risk there, so there is no
  channel left."* Also backwards. The two funds do carry the same market risk after 2002 (measured
  beta 0.98 against 1.78 in the dot-com years), so this is not a risk dial — and the signal paid
  anyway, through picking months rather than through risk. **This signal has not faded.** It is
  strongest in the most recent, best-covered era, which is unusual in this lab and is the single
  most encouraging fact on this page.

## Two caveats on the numbers

**The no-opinion arm did not behave as its name suggests, and the lab caught it.** BLEND was
designed as a half-and-half book rebalanced monthly; its measured turnover of 0.1 says it bought
half and half once in 2000 and then drifted. The lab's own control-shape check refused it for
exactly this (it trades 0.00x and turns over 0.01x what the arm it controls does), so any sentence
of the form "the idea lost to its control by 1.9 points" is quoted against an opponent that paid no
fees at all. **The verdict does not rest on it.** The two clean comparisons — the mirror, which is
matched on fees and shape, and the two do-nothing endpoints, which are simply what the owner could
have bought instead — say the same thing and are not handicapped. The drifting half-and-half arm
landing within 0.05 points of the endpoints' average is a cross-check, not the evidence.

**The fold record on this page is about the wrong arm.** The walk-forward picked SPY-HOLD — a
control arm, not the idea — and scored it 1 of 4. That is the lab's known habit of letting the
best-looking variant be a control, and here it means the fold line is really asking "does buying
SPY beat buying SPY", which it answers by rounding error (52.0% against 52.1%). Ignore it.

## My opinion:

**This direction is closed, and I would not spend another method id on it.** Not because the signal
failed — it did not, and this run is the cleanest evidence yet that it is real and, unusually for
this lab, not fading — but because the lab has now tried all three ways to spend it and hit the same
wall each time. As an on/off switch it paid for sitting in cash. As a dimmer it paid for sitting
partly in cash. As a fund-chooser that never sits in cash at all it pays Gotrade instead, and
Gotrade is the most expensive of the three. The opinion is worth roughly 1 to 1.4 points a year;
every arrangement that delivers it costs between 2 and 3.

I checked the obvious remaining lever before closing it, so that nobody spends an id on it later:
reading the signal less often to cut the fees. Holding each call for two, three, six or twelve
months instead of one, the month-picking in the 2009-2015 era is +0.2, +0.0, −3.0 and −1.7 points a
year against +1.9 at one month. **The opinion lives at the monthly horizon and does not survive being
slowed down**, so cutting the fee bill by trading less often cuts the edge faster than it cuts the
cost. That is the same trap a third time, and it is now measured rather than assumed.

What I would do instead is take the chassis and throw away the signal. This run has quietly built
something the lab did not have: a **priced, always-invested switch between the only two funds the
owner is allowed to buy**. It costs 2.2 points a year to operate and it never sits in cash. That is
now a yardstick — any market opinion worth more than about 2.5 points a year of month-picking will
pay on it, and anything worth less will not, and we no longer have to run a method to find out which.

The lab already owns one opinion that clears that bar: the 200-day trend rule, whose premium has
been measured at a constant 3.6 points a year across all 824 trials, and which has always been paid
in *cash* — the single most expensive way to hold it, and most of the reason the lab's books lag
after 2009. Paying it in SPY instead of cash, on this chassis, is the obvious next method: above the
line hold the tech fund, below it hold the broad market, never cash. The trend rule changes its mind
far less often than this signal did (which is where the fee bill comes from), its opinion is more
than twice as large, and the arrangement is now priced. That is queued.

And one thing the owner can decide that no amount of lab work can: **this whole family is capped by
the fact that only two funds are permitted.** The gap between SPY and QQQ is narrow, which is why a
real opinion worth 1.4 points could not clear a 2.2-point toll. A permitted third fund with a wider
gap would earn more per switch at the same fee, and would move the ratio in a way that no tuning
can. That is a one-sentence decision, not a research programme, and it is the cheapest thing on this
page.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the escape from the parent's arithmetic worked mechanically -- the money never leaves the market -- and made the ratio worse, because switching funds at Gotrade's fees costs 2.75 points a year where the opinion is worth 0.9

methods.name: Split the drift trigger's gain: is it the cash it releases, or the trimming itself?
methods.sourceRef: M0127, which measured +0.49 points a year of money-weighted return from moving the rebalance band off the account and onto the holding and said plainly that it could not split that gain between the cash it released and the trimming it enabled; M0109 for the neutral 50-name base book; insight 479 for the 1.25 points a year the weighting arrangement was worth on identical names and identical trades; insight 481 for the rule that an unsplit margin may not be called a floor in either direction
methods.hypothesis: M0127 measured that moving the rebalance band from 1 percent of the account to a share of the holding is worth +0.49 points a year of money-weighted return on a 50-name book whose picks are identical across every arm, and it could NOT say how much of that was which of two channels, because they move together: average exposure rose 88.65 to 98.57 percent across the ladder AND the book began genuinely trimming winners to feed laggards at the same time. This method separates them by holding exposure FIXED on both sides. On M0127's own allocator -- M0109's unbraked 50 most-traded index members at equal weight, no gate, no brake, no stock picking -- with one field added, a scale that multiplies every target weight so that a book may deliberately hold cash, six arms run in ONE sweep on ONE store: the loose equity-basis band at scale 1 (the control, economically M0127-E1), the band of 0 at scale 1 (economically M0127-T00, the unsplit margin re-measured inside this sweep), the band of 0 at the calibrated scale (the treatment), the 20-percent-of-target band at scale 1 and at its own calibrated scale (the second matched pair, on the rule the lab actually runs), and the loose band at the same calibrated scale as the treatment (the ruler, which moves exposure about 8.9 points with the trimming held still and so prices a point of exposure on this book directly). THE CALIBRATION IS PRE-REGISTERED AND READS NO RETURN: scale equals the recorded average exposure of M0127-E1 divided by the recorded average exposure of M0127's arm at that band, both from trials run on 2026-10-20 on this store, giving 0.899329 at band 0 and 0.921402 at the 20-percent band, which after the engine floors each name's weight to a millionth predict average exposures of 0.886430 and 0.886456 against the control's 0.886458. PREDICTIONS, written now. (1) The match holds: the control and both matched arms land within half a point of 88.6 percent average exposure. (2) The two scale-1 arms reproduce M0127's rows 875 and 879 to the digit; a mismatch is a bug in the scaling and must be chased before anything is read. (3) Most of the +0.49 was cash: the matched treatment is expected to beat the control by between 0.0 and +0.2 points a year, and a LOSS is an equally clean result meaning trimming winners to feed laggards costs money on a book of large momentum-heavy names. (4) Insight 479's 1.25 points is not expected to be confirmed here, because that number compared two DIFFERENT target weightings while this holds the target weights identical and moves only whether the book is pushed back to them. (5) The trimming arm trades about 18 percent more money a year and pays Gotrade's per-order minimum on every drift trade, so its gross worth exceeds whatever the net difference shows and turnover must be quoted beside return. (6) With exposure matched the trimming arm should still fall further than the control, and that gap is now attributable to buying the faller rather than to being more invested. (7) No arm is a candidate: the base book loses to a deposit-matched SPY and falls 57 percent, and the scale field and band rungs have no preset, so every arm is unpromotable by construction. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's funding plan. Success is a measurement, not a candidate.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the exposure match does not hold. A band and a weight scale both move exposure and they interact, so the calibration may land an arm a point or two off the control, in which case the analysis must report the residual exposure gap and REFUSE to publish a split rather than quote one. The second is that the two arms earn the same within noise. That is not a failure of the method but it IS the outcome being pre-registered as acceptable: if the matched treatment and the control land on top of each other, the whole of M0127's gain was cash and the trimming is worth nothing on this book, which is a real and publishable result and must be stated as such rather than dressed up as a near miss. The third is that the two routes to the split disagree -- the direct matched difference and the ruler's exposure slope multiplied by M0127's 9.92-point exposure gap -- in which case neither number may be quoted as the answer and the disagreement itself is the finding, because it would mean the return is not linear in exposure on this book and every exposure-matched control the lab draws in future needs a wider tolerance. The fourth is paths: the two matched arms agree on AVERAGE exposure but not on the shape of their cash -- the control's idle money is drifting cash it cannot deploy, the treatment's is a deliberate near-constant buffer re-set monthly -- so two books can average the same exposure and still have been differently invested in 2008, and that residual is a caveat the analysis must carry rather than hide. The fifth is survivorship: the dev store prices no delisted names and a rebalancing rule buys fallers, so the trimming arms are structurally flattered by the dead companies' absence and the widest arm must be survivorship-checked with the result quoted beside the dev column. The sixth is that the whole difference turns out to be the per-order minimum fee on tiny drift trades, in which case this is a measurement of a 20,000,000 IDR account's order economics rather than of rebalancing, and the verdict must say so.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-21

# M0266 — was the rebalancing worth anything, or was it just the cash?

## This is a ruler, not a strategy

Nothing here is a candidate and nothing is being proposed for your money. The book used below
holds the fifty most-traded big American companies in equal amounts and does no stock picking at
all. Every version of it lost to simply buying SPY with the same deposits, and the gentlest of
them still fell 53% from a peak — more than twice the 25% you allow. It exists to settle one
question that a measurement last October could ask but could not answer.

## The question left open

Last October a ruler called M0127 found a rule inside the simulator that nobody had chosen on
purpose. When a holding drifts away from the size it is supposed to be, the simulator only trades
it back if the gap is big enough to be worth a trade — and "big enough" was measured against one
per cent of the **whole account** rather than one per cent of the holding. In a fifty-name book
that is half a holding, so in practice nothing was ever traded back.

Fixing it was worth **+0.49 points a year** of your own money's return. But that measurement could
not say *why*, because fixing it changed two things at once:

* **It released cash.** Under the old rule a monthly deposit could buy a brand-new holding but
  could never top up an existing one, so the account carried money it never chose to leave idle.
  Across the five versions the share of the account actually invested rose from **88.6% to 98.6%**.
  Over twenty years in which the market went up, being more invested pays all by itself.
* **It started trimming.** The same fix is what first lets the book sell a little of whatever has
  grown too big and buy a little of whatever has shrunk. That is a genuinely different thing, and
  this lab has elsewhere estimated it to be worth real money.

Those two always move together, so the +0.49 could not be divided. This method divides it.

## The trick: hold the cash still and let only the trimming move

Six versions of the identical book. Same fifty names, same dates, same equal shares, same
fractional trading, same real Gotrade fees, same 10 million rupiah start and 5 million a month,
all six run in a single pass over one copy of the price data.

The new ingredient is a **deliberate cash buffer**. A version that trims is told to aim at holding
only about 89% of its money in shares rather than 100%, chosen precisely so that it ends up as
invested, on average, as the version that never trims. Then the two differ in the trimming and in
nothing else.

**The size of that buffer was fixed before a single return was calculated**, and this is the whole
reason the answer can be trusted. It was computed from two numbers recorded last October — how
invested the patient version was, and how invested the busy version was — divided one by the
other. No return, no worst fall and no fee bill went anywhere near the calculation, and the figure
was written into the method file and committed to the repository before the run started. Had it
been tuned afterwards, the experiment would have been fitted and worthless.

| version | trigger | aims to hold |
|---|---|---|
| **L** | 1% of the whole account — the old rule, never fires | all of it |
| **T00** | nothing at all: every holding reset to its share every month | all of it |
| **T00M** | the same full monthly reset | about 89% — matched to L |
| **T20** | a fifth of the holding — the rule the lab uses today | all of it |
| **T20M** | the same fifth-of-a-holding rule | about 89% — matched to L |
| **LS** | 1% of the account, same as L — still never fires | about 89% |

`LS` is the measuring stick. It trims exactly as little as `L` does while sitting about ten points
lower in the market, so it prices **one point of being invested** on this book directly, with the
trimming held still. That gives a second, independent route to the same answer.

## First: the match held

This is the precondition, and if it had failed there would be no answer to publish.

| version | share of the account invested |
|---|---|
| L | 88.646% |
| T00M | 88.674% |
| T20M | 88.766% |

The two trimming versions landed **within 0.03 and 0.12 of a point** of the control, against a
pre-registered tolerance of half a point. The calibration worked.

Two other checks passed on the way. The three unmatched versions reproduce last October's
measurements **to every recorded digit** — same total return, same worst fall, same gains-to-losses
ratio, same 1,338 trades — which proves the new cash-buffer ingredient does nothing at all when it
is switched off. And all of it ran on the identical copy of the price data, so none of the
differences below is an artefact of the data being rebuilt in between.

## The answer

| version | invested | money moved a year | your money a year | worst fall | 2009–2015 a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L** — never trims | 88.6% | 2.86x | **+6.46%** | **57.2%** | +16.16% |
| LS — never trims, less invested | 78.5% | 2.56x | +5.79% | 52.9% | +14.35% |
| **T20M** — trims, same cash as L | 88.8% | 2.77x | **+6.47%** | **56.1%** | +15.82% |
| **T00M** — resets monthly, same cash as L | 88.7% | 3.04x | **+6.36%** | **55.4%** | +15.41% |
| T20 — trims, fully invested | 96.2% | 3.00x | +6.92% | 59.2% | +17.12% |
| T00 — resets monthly, fully invested | 98.6% | 3.38x | +6.95% | 59.5% | +17.12% |
| SPY, same deposits | — | — | +7.19% | — | +16.60% |

Read the three bold rows. Once the cash is held still, **the trimming is worth nothing.** Letting
the book trim with the fifth-of-a-holding rule changed your money's return by **+0.02 points a
year**. Going all the way to a full monthly reset changed it by **−0.10 points a year** — slightly
worse, not better.

So on this price history the split of last October's +0.49 points is:

> **the cash: about +0.59 to +0.66 points a year. The trimming: between −0.16 and +0.02 points a
> year — zero, and if anything faintly negative.**

The measuring stick agrees. One point of being invested was worth 0.066 points a year of your
money on this book; the old rule left 9.92 points of the account idle; 9.92 × 0.066 is +0.66
points a year, which is **more than the whole +0.49 that was observed**. Both routes to the answer
land in the same place and they agree to within **a tenth of a point a year on every column
measured**. The disagreement this method pre-registered as a possible failure did not happen here.

**And no fee bill is hiding a positive effect underneath.** The obvious escape — "trimming really
does pay, but Gotrade's per-order minimum eats it" — is closed by `T20M`, which moved **3.3% less**
money a year than the control and still only matched it. It is a cheaper book that earns the same.
There is nothing for fees to have eaten.

## The surprise: the trimming makes the fall shallower, not deeper

Last October's reading was that trimming **deepened** the worst fall by 2.4 points (57.2% → 59.5%),
with the explanation that rebalancing keeps buying whatever is falling, so in a market that grinds
lower it keeps buying on the way down. **That explanation is measured false here.**

With the cash held still, trimming made the worst fall **1.7 points shallower** (57.2% → 55.4%),
and the worst year, 2008, went from −37.8% to −37.3%. The measuring stick says the same thing from
the other side: one point of being invested costs 0.42 points of worst fall, so the ten extra
points of exposure should have deepened the fall by about 4.2 points on their own. Only 2.4 showed
up. The missing 1.8 is the trimming, pulling the other way.

This cannot be the cash buffer flattering the result. The buffer is only 0.03 of a point bigger
than the control's own idle cash, which at 0.42 points of fall per point of exposure is worth
about a hundredth of a point — not 1.7. And it runs *against* the control, which automatically
de-risks in a crash: the control's idle cash is money it cannot deploy, so as its holdings fall
the idle share rises by itself. The trimming version keeps buying back in and still fell less.

So the honest reading is the reverse of last year's: **being more invested is what deepened the
fall; trimming, on its own, softened it.**

## The era that matters most says trimming actively costs

2009–2015 is the best-covered stretch of the window and the one most like today, and it is where
this lab sends every idea first. Stripping the deposits out so the eras can be compared fairly,
here is what the trimming alone was worth, in points a year:

| trimming, with the cash held still | whole window | 1996–2002 | 2003–2008 | 2009–2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| full monthly reset | +0.16 | **+1.00** | −0.03 | **−0.74** |
| the fifth-of-a-holding rule | +0.17 | +0.73 | −0.13 | **−0.34** |

The trimming's entire gain lives in **1996–2002** — the dot-com boom and bust, when the most-traded
list was Cisco, Intel, JDS Uniphase and Qualcomm and there were enormous winners to trim. In
2009–2015 it **loses** 0.74 points a year. Both routes agree again: the measuring stick puts the
modern-era trimming effect at −0.80, the direct comparison at −0.74.

That is also why the two ways of counting your return disagree in sign. Counted without deposits
over the whole window, trimming looks worth +0.16 a year; counted on the money you actually had —
most of which arrived late, in the years where trimming loses — it is −0.10. **The money-weighted
answer is the one that matters, and it is the negative one.**

## The honest price history: the match broke, so no split is published there

Everything above is measured on the lab's ordinary price data, which prices no company that died.
A rebalancing rule buys whatever has fallen, so the trimming versions ought to be flattered by the
absence of the companies that fell all the way. That was written down beforehand as the most
likely way this result would be wrong, so all six versions were re-run on the check copy of the
history, which puts most of the dead companies back.

**The first thing to report is that the calibration did not survive the move.** The buffer sizes
were computed from exposures measured on the ordinary data; on the honest data the same buffers
left the trimming versions **0.90 and 0.75 of a point less invested** than the control, past the
half-point tolerance this method set for itself. The method said in advance that in that case it
would report the gap and refuse to publish a split rather than quote one, so that is what happens:
**there is no split for the honest price history.** The two routes also disagree there by 0.27
points a year, which on its own would forbid a number.

What can honestly be said is the direction, and it is worth saying because it is the opposite of
the worry:

| | ordinary data | honest data |
|---|---|---|
| the whole book, your money a year | +6.46% | +4.17% |
| worst fall | 57.2% | 72.1% |
| trimming's effect on your money a year | −0.10 | +0.21 |
| trimming's effect in 2009–2015 | −0.74 | −0.23 |
| trimming's effect on the worst fall | −1.7 pts | −3.4 pts |

Putting the dead companies back costs this book 2.3 points a year and deepens its worst fall by
15 points — it is a much worse book than the ordinary data suggests, and all six versions earn
less. But **trimming is not the thing that was being flattered.** With the dead companies back,
trimming looks slightly *better* over the whole window, not worse. The pre-registered survivorship
worry was wrong in direction.

Two things do survive both copies of the history, and they are the findings I would stand behind:
**trimming costs money in 2009–2015** (−0.74 and −0.23), and **trimming makes the worst fall
shallower** (−1.7 and −3.4 points). The whole-window sign is not robust and should not be quoted.

## Why

Trimming a winner to feed a laggard is a bet that what has gone up will come back down relative to
what has gone down. On a book of fifty large, liquid, heavily-traded American companies over
2009–2015, that bet was simply wrong: the big winners kept winning, and selling a slice of them
every month to buy more of the laggards gave money away. In 1996–2002 the same bet paid, because
the companies that ran up hardest fell hardest. It is not a free source of return; it is a view
about things reverting to the middle, and that view has been out of favour for the whole modern
era.

The shallower fall is the other side of the same coin. Never trimming lets a winner grow into a
slot the book never agreed to, and a concentrated book falls further when that winner turns. The
trimming buys a little safety and charges a little return — an honest trade, just not one that
makes money.

## Did the predictions hold

Seven were written down before the run.

1. **The match holds** — yes on the ordinary data, to 0.03 and 0.12 of a point against a half-point
   tolerance. **No on the honest data**, by 0.90 and 0.75 of a point, which is why no split is
   published there.
2. **The unmatched versions reproduce last October exactly** — yes, to every recorded digit, and
   all six reproduced again inside the survivorship check.
3. **Most of the +0.49 was cash; trimming between 0.0 and +0.2** — the direction was right and the
   size was wrong in the honest direction. Trimming came in at −0.10 to +0.02, at or just below
   the bottom of the pre-registered range. The alternative written down as equally acceptable —
   "trimming is worth nothing on this book" — is what happened.
4. **The 1.25-points-a-year estimate from elsewhere is not confirmed here** — correct, and the
   reason stands: that number compared two *different* target sizes, while this holds the target
   sizes identical and moves only whether the book is pushed back to them. Re-imposing a slot you
   already chose is a far smaller thing than choosing a different slot. That earlier number is not
   refuted; it answers a different question.
5. **The trimming version trades about 18% more** — wrong, and usefully so. The full-reset version
   moved only 6.0% more money, and the fifth-of-a-holding version moved 3.3% **less** than the
   control, because shrinking the book shrinks every ranking-driven order too. This is what closes
   the fee escape.
6. **The fall still gets deeper with trimming** — **wrong, and reversed.** It gets 1.7 points
   shallower on the ordinary data and 3.4 on the honest data. This is the most useful thing the
   method produced.
7. **No version is a candidate** — correct. All six were rejected.

And of the six ways this was expected to fail, the survivorship one fired in the opposite
direction to the one predicted, and the exposure-match one fired on the honest data only.

## The gate numbers

All six versions failed, and none was close. Each lost to a deposit-matched SPY (+6.36% to +6.95%
a year against SPY's +7.19%) and each fell far past the lab's 50% screening limit for a dev
result, let alone your own 25% limit for real money — 52.9% at best, 59.5% at worst, and 66% to
73% once the dead companies are put back. The four trimming versions also failed the
gains-to-losses test at 1.25–1.27 against a bar of 1.30; the two non-trimming versions passed it
at 1.31.

On luck: the lab judges a result by how likely it is to be real rather than a fluke after
everything that has been tried, and the bar is **0.90**. The lab has now looked at **171 distinct
methods**, and against that many tries the best of these six scores **0.41** — and 0.23 on the
honest price history. Nowhere near. That is exactly as expected: these are rulers, not attempts to
win, and a book with no stock picking in it has nothing to be lucky about.

On the fold record: 1 of 4 out-of-sample stretches won. For a measurement that is not a mark
against it — the question was never whether this book beats the market.

## What it cost, and a lesson for next time

This method spent six recorded trials and raised the lab's method count by one, which lifts the
luck bar very slightly for every future idea. Three of those six — the unmatched versions — turned
out to reproduce last October's numbers exactly, digit for digit. They were run because a ratio
drawn across two separate passes over the data is not a comparison, and because they are the proof
that the new cash-buffer ingredient is inert when switched off. That proof was worth buying once.
It need not be bought again: the next exposure-matched experiment on this book can quote the
recorded numbers directly and spend three fewer trials, provided it checks the data fingerprint
matches first.

The more expensive lesson is the one the honest price history taught. **A buffer calibrated on one
copy of the history does not stay calibrated on another.** Any future exposure-matched experiment
that wants an answer on both copies has to calibrate separately for each, which means measuring
the control's exposure on both before fixing either buffer.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and that is a good outcome rather than a disappointing one. The
question "what is rebalancing worth on a wide book" now has an answer — **close enough to nothing
that it should not be chased** — and the practical consequence is immediate, though it is not the
one last October's verdict implied. The rule the lab switched to on 12 October is worth keeping,
but **not for the reason it was adopted**. It is worth keeping because it stops the account sitting
in cash it never chose to hold. The trimming it also enables is a slight drag on return in the
modern era on both copies of the history. Nobody should go looking for a better rebalancing rule
on this chassis; there is no money under that stone.

What I would chase instead is the one effect that came out positive on **both** copies of the
history and got *stronger* on the honest one: **trimming makes the fall shallower.** That is a
safety effect, measured on identical names, identical dates and identical average cash, and
safety is the thing this lab is short of — four of four looks at the real test window have failed,
and every roster strategy breached the drawdown rule. But "trimming" is still two actions bolted
together: selling a slice of the winners, and spending the proceeds on the laggards. My strong
suspicion is that **all of the safety comes from the selling and all of the modern-era cost comes
from the buying**, because capping a winner is what stops the concentration, while topping up a
faller is the bet that has been wrong since 2009. A book that trims its winners back to their slot
and puts the proceeds in cash rather than into the laggards would separate them in one run, and if
that suspicion holds it is a genuinely useful dial: a point and a half to three points of worst
fall for nothing. I have queued it as the next method.

I have also queued a second, smaller one. The measuring stick put a price on idle cash — 0.066
points a year of your money per point of the account left out of the market, and 0.42 points of
worst fall — but that price collapsed to 0.008 on the honest data over the same stretch, while the
top ten points of exposure were clearly worth far more than either figure. That is not a constant,
it is a curve, and the lab draws exposure-matched controls all the time on the assumption that it
is a straight line. A ladder of five buffer sizes on this same book, run on both copies, would map
it properly and tell every future control how wide its tolerance needs to be.

One last warning, worth repeating because this is the second case of it in a week: when an
experiment changes how a book *holds* its money rather than which names it picks, almost every
number the lab records is useless. All six versions here reported exactly **1,338 trades** while
their idle cash ranged from 1.4% to 21.5% and their returns spread over 1.2 points a year. Read
how much of the account was invested, and how much money moved. Nothing else will tell you
anything.
methods.verdict: The rebalancing was never the point, the cash was: with both books equally invested the trimming is worth nothing, it costs money in the modern era on both price histories, and it makes the worst fall shallower rather than deeper.

methods.name: Pay the trend rule's premium in shares, not cash: above the 200-day line hold QQQ, below it hold SPY
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0265 (the premium picks the fund), lab journal 2026-10-20
methods.hypothesis: M0265 found no signal but left a priced instrument: an always-invested monthly switch between the only two funds the owner may buy, exposure 0.975-0.987 on every arm, costing 2.75 points a year of funded money-weighted return which lab costs showed was entirely Gotrade's fee bill. This method puts the lab's oldest and largest market opinion on it. The 200-day trend gate's premium is a constant 3.6 points a year swept over all 824 recorded trials and helped 22 of 22 variants whole-window, and it has only ever been spent in CASH -- which insight 462 priced as ~3.6 of a wide book's 8.2-point post-2009 shortfall, eleven exits after 2009 and eleven false alarms in a decade with no bear market. So: same opinion, same chassis, never cash. SPY strictly above the mean of its last 200 closes holds QQQ; below it holds SPY; decided once a month in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up. THE ARITHMETIC THAT MOTIVATES THIS IS NOT PORTABLE AND BOTH HALVES OF IT ARE CORRECTED HERE BEFORE THE RUN. The 3.6 points was measured as cash against invested, where the alternative instrument has beta zero; here the alternative is a fund whose beta to SPY M0265 measured at 0.98 after 2002. The worth of an opinion depends on the spread of the instruments available to express it, so it was measured through THIS pair before this file was committed, on nothing but the two funds' closes over the 191 month-end decisions this window yields (1999-12-31 to 2015-10-16; QQQ's 200th bar is 1999-12-21): the mean next-month QQQ-minus-SPY log differential is +0.2373%% in the 126 months the gate is above and -0.7120%% in the 64 below, a spread of +0.9492%% a month, which annualises to GATE +1.89 points against buying SPY and leaving it, MIRROR -2.88, so GATE minus MIRROR is +4.77 and the ONE-SIDED OPINION IS +2.38 POINTS A YEAR, NOT 3.6. A third of the premium is gone to the narrowness of the pair. The toll is corrected the other way and moves further: M0265's signal changed its mind in 112 of 186 months, this gate in 13 of 190, and the toll it measured was almost all fees on those rotations, so 13/112 of 2.2 points is about 0.25 points a year and the chassis is 8.6 times cheaper under this signal than under the one it was priced with. Opinion 2.4 against toll 0.25 says the whole window pays. The era split says it will not matter: GATE minus MIRROR is +24.61 points in 2000-2002 when the gate was below for 78%% of months and QQQ lost 27 points a year, -1.14 in 2003-2008, and +0.78 in 2009-2015 -- so every point of the whole-window opinion is the dot-com unwind, and in the lab's first-filter era the opinion is +0.39 one-sided against a 0.25 toll, a coin flip. Beside it in the same row, QQQ bought once and left alone beat SPY by 6.16 points a year in 2009-2015 while the gate, stepping out of QQQ a fifth of the time, captured 3.47. Assumed: an unreadable gate is the neutral 50/50, never an extreme; the gate is read on day d's close and traded at the next open; idle cash earns nothing, which costs these arms nothing since none holds any. Success, stated so it can fail: GATE beats MIRROR by about 4.8 points whole-window and by about 0.8 in 2009-2015, the gap halves at half lean so the dose is a line through the origin, and -- the only test that would make this a direction worth continuing -- GATE beats QQQ-HOLD in 2009-2015. Eligibility is not expected: these are two-name tilting books so closed round trips and the profit factor will be thin or undefined, and every arm is invested through 2000-2002 and 2008, so every worst fall should land near buy-and-hold's.
methods.expectedFailure: The pre-registered expectation is that this LOSES, and the shape of the loss is named here so the result cannot be re-read favourably afterwards. The whole-window numbers will probably look like a win -- the measured differentials put GATE about 4.8 points a year above MIRROR and about 1.9 above buying SPY, against a fee toll near 0.25 -- and that win is one era. 2000-2002 contributes +24.61 points of the GATE-minus-MIRROR gap, 2003-2008 contributes -1.14, and 2009-2015 contributes +0.78. A rule that was paid once, in the window's first three years, and was flat to negative for the thirteen years after it, is a crash rule that happened to catch its crash, and quoting its twenty-year average as an edge is precisely the mistake insight 462 corrected about the cash gate. The decisive comparison is therefore not GATE against SPY-HOLD but GATE against QQQ-HOLD, and in 2009-2015 the gate is pre-registered to lose it by about 2.7 points a year, because nine of its eleven post-2009 exits were false alarms and here a false alarm costs the QQQ-minus-SPY gap rather than the whole market's rise -- the identical failure to the cash gate's, merely cheaper. Second, the dose may not halve. The gate is binary and the rungs are symmetric, so a GATE-minus-MIRROR gap at lean 0.5 that is not close to half the gap at lean 1.0 means the difference is being made by fees or by the resize band rather than by the opinion, and the correct conclusion then is that the chassis is noisier than the signal and not that the lean should be retuned. Third, every arm is fully invested through two collapses, so SPY-HOLD should fall around 55%% and QQQ-HOLD far worse, which means any arm that wins on return will almost certainly breach the owner's 25%% depth rule -- the same way the parent's raised floors did. Fourth, the window is not the parent's: the gate needs 200 bars where M0265's signal needed 274, so this starts 1999-12-21 and sees three and a half extra months containing the dot-com top, which makes the 2.75-point toll a reference from a neighbouring window and never a paired number. Fifth, insight 479 says a control matched on trades and turnover is still not return-neutral and insight 481 says an under-shaped control's margin has unknown sign, so even MIRROR -- which here is matched on every axis the lab checks -- is a measurement and not a bound. Sixth, hardgate D14 reads this book's curve against kin, and the P7A f2 family already switches SPY against QQQ on relative momentum at MAR 0.50; a correlated-kin refusal is likely whatever the numbers say, and the market-trend-switch family this method is filed under already holds 42 trials whose best MAR is 0.58. Finally, this is a two-name always-invested book, so insight 495 applies: trade count will not describe it and the readable meters are exposure and turnover.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-21

# Paying the trend rule in shares instead of cash

The lab has one market opinion it trusts more than any other. When the American market is above
its own 200-day average, it tends to keep rising; when it falls below, it tends to keep falling.
Measured across all 824 trials the lab had recorded, obeying that rule was worth about 3.6% a year.

But the lab has only ever obeyed it one way: **by going to cash.** And that is the most expensive
way to hold any opinion. Sitting in cash through 2009 to 2015 — a near-unbroken rise with no
crash in it at all — cost about 3.6% a year on its own, and the rule's eleven exits in those years
were eleven false alarms. The opinion paid for itself and then handed the money straight back.

So this method asked the obvious question. **Keep the opinion, lose the cash.** The owner is
allowed to buy exactly two funds: the broad American market, and the tech-heavy one. Above the
line, hold the tech fund. Below it, hold the broad market. Never cash, not for a single day.
Decided once a month, in fractional shares, at the fees we really pay.

## What was promised before the run, and what arrived

This method's great advantage is that almost every number was written down **before** it ran, and
most of them were written down after being measured on the two funds' prices alone — no strategy,
no fees, no deposits. So this is a scorecard, not a story.

| written down beforehand | what actually happened |
|---|---|
| The opinion is worth about 4.8% a year, not 3.6% | 4.84% a year. **Right.** |
| The trading cost is about 0.25% a year, not 2.75% | 0.2% a year; fees ate 3.4% of trading profit against the previous method's 27.1%. **Right.** |
| Half the dose should give half the result | Full dose 1.03%, half dose 0.48%. **Right, almost exactly.** |
| It will look like a win over twenty years | It does: 9.2% a year against the market's 7.7%. **Right.** |
| It will still lose to simply buying the tech fund and never touching it | It loses by 1.4% a year. **Right.** |
| Every version will fall much too far | Falls of 55% to 82%. **Right.** |

Six out of six. The method did exactly what its own pre-registration said it would, which is the
best outcome available to a method that was registered to fail.

**It was rejected.** Every one of the six versions breached the lab's depth limit, and none made
the hundred completed trades the go-live rules ask for. The best version's luck score is 0.19
where the owner's bar is 0.90 — meaning that after 170 distinct attempts in this lab, a result
this good is far more likely to be chance than skill. The four-period hold-out check split 2–2.

## The one thing that was NOT predicted, and it is the finding

The opinion was worth 4.84% a year. The owner's money earned **1.03% a year** from it. Nearly
four fifths of a correctly measured, correctly priced edge simply did not arrive.

Here is where it went. The rule's entire payout in this window happened in one stretch:

| years | what obeying the rule was worth, in total |
|---|---|
| 2000–2002 | **+61.4%** |
| 2003–2008 | −6.4% |
| 2009–2015 | +6.3% |

Everything is the dot-com crash. That part was expected and was written down. What was not written
down is what it collides with: **by the end of 2002 the owner had paid in only 21% of his money.**

The owner's real plan is a small start and a top-up every month for sixteen years. A rule that
earns its keep in years one to three of that plan is earning it on a fifth of an account. A rule
that costs nothing in years four to sixteen is costing nothing on four fifths of one. The
arithmetic is correct and the money is still not there, because the money was not there yet.

This is the sharpest version of something the lab already half-knew. A twenty-year average
assumes twenty years of equal-sized money. The owner does not have that and never will.

## The harsher test, and it fails it too

A fair question: is this rule actually doing anything, or does it just happen to hold the better
fund most of the time? The tech fund beat the broad market by 6.2% a year from 2009 to 2015, and
the rule holds it about two thirds of the time. Perhaps that is the whole story.

So twenty thousand fake rules were drawn, each one a coin flip that changes its mind as rarely as
the real rule does and favours the tech fund as often — same temperament, no information. Over
2009 to 2015 the real rule earned 3.47% a year over the broad market. **The average fake rule
earned 3.87%.** The real one lands at the 38th percentile of its own placebos: worse than a coin
flip with the same habits. Over the full window it reaches the 85th percentile, which is still not
enough to call it real, and all of that comes from 2000–2002 again.

In the years that resemble today, the rule knows nothing. What it has is a *preference for the
tech fund*, and that preference is worth money only because the tech fund happened to win.

## Did the mirror work?

Yes, and this is worth recording because the lab has been burned by bad controls. Every comparison
here is against the same rule read upside-down — same months, same two funds, same fees, same
amount of money moved, opposite call. The lab's control-shape check passed all six arms with
nothing to flag, which has been rare.

There was also a structural discovery. The usual fix for a weak control is to draw a random one
that trades on the same days. **With only two funds and an on/off switch, that control cannot
exist**: anything that changes its mind on exactly the same days is either the rule or its exact
mirror, and nothing else. So the mirror is not a convenient control here, it is the only one. That
is why the fake-rule test above had to be done as arithmetic rather than as a seventh version.

## Two meter-readings worth keeping

The half-dose versions recorded **zero trades and no gains-to-losses figure**. They are not inert
— they moved 0.83 of the account a year and earned 9.2%. They simply always hold a slice of both
funds, so nothing is ever fully sold, and the trade counter only counts complete round trips.
Read how much money moved, never the trade count, on a book like this.

And the account was 98.8% invested on every single version. The promise to never hold cash was
kept exactly. That part of the design worked perfectly; it just did not matter.

## My opinion:

**This closes the shape, and I would not spend another method id anywhere near it.**

The lab has now spent this gate's opinion four ways: as cash in every book it owns, as a dimmer on
how much to invest, as a tilt between two funds on a different signal, and now as the fund choice
itself. The last one is the cheapest arrangement that exists — the fee bill fell by a factor of
eight and the account never left the market — and it still did not pay. That is not a tuning
failure. There is nothing left to make cheaper.

Two things are now settled and should stop being re-asked. First, **the trend rule is a crash
rule.** Its value is concentrated in crashes and it is worth roughly nothing otherwise, so any
measurement of it over a window containing a crash will overstate what it does for the next
fifteen years. Second, and more useful to the owner than anything about this rule: **a crash rule
and a monthly savings plan are a bad match.** Protection pays in proportion to what is being
protected, and in the owner's plan that amount starts near zero and grows for years. The lab
should stop valuing timing rules by their twenty-year average and start valuing them by what they
do to money that is actually there — which is the money-weighted number, not the headline one.

What I would try next is the opposite question, and it is the one the placebo test kept pointing
at. The rule added nothing after 2009; what added 6.2% a year was *holding the tech fund*. The
lab has never once asked whether that is a durable thing or a decade-long accident, and it has
never had a reason to ask because no method was allowed to simply hold it. It now has two
recorded, funded, honest baselines in the same window — the broad market at 7.6% and the tech
fund at 10.6% — and the gap between them is bigger than almost every edge the lab has ever
chased. That is queued as the next idea, and it should be measured as a question about the gap's
durability, not as another switch.

The other thing worth saying to the owner directly is the one no amount of lab work can settle,
and this run is the second method in two days to run into it. **Only two funds are permitted, and
they move almost identically.** A rule that swaps between two nearly identical things pays full
price for almost no difference. Permitting a third fund that behaves differently from both would
widen every switch idea the lab can test, at the cost of one decision.
methods.verdict: Rejected: the trend rule's opinion survived being moved out of cash and into the fund choice, and the owner's money still only saw a fifth of it, because all of it was earned in 2000-2002 when only a fifth of his money was in.

methods.name: Is the tech fund's lead over the broad market durable, or was it one decade
methods.hypothesis: M0267 spent an id proving a timing rule knows nothing, and in doing so recorded two honest, funded, same-window baselines the lab has never had side by side: on 1999-12-22 to 2015-10-16, at the owner's real deposits and Gotrade's real fees, the broad market earned 7.6 percent a year of money-weighted return and the tech fund 10.6. That 3.0-point gap is wider than almost every edge the lab has ever chased, and the placebo sweep in M0267 showed it is the ENTIRE source of value in every arm that method ran: twenty thousand uninformed sticky switches averaged +3.87 pts/yr against the broad market after 2009 purely by leaning towards the tech fund, and the real trend rule managed only +3.47. The lab has never asked whether that gap is durable because, until M0265 built the always-invested two-fund chassis, no method was allowed to simply hold one fund and be scored. It now is. So ask the question directly and stop asking it sideways. Arms should be the two buy-and-leave endpoints (which M0267 already recorded, so their digests are spent and this method must carry a different shape) plus the structural alternatives that do NOT require a market opinion: a fixed split rebalanced monthly at several ratios, which is a dose ladder in how much tech exposure is carried; and critically a ratio chosen ONCE at the window's start versus one chosen by a backward-looking rule, since the second is the one that would be available in real life. The decisive measurements are (a) the gap era by era, including whether 2003-2008 and 2000-2002 reverse it, which M0267's own figures say they do -- the tech fund LOST 27 points a year to the broad market across 2000-2002 and the whole-window lump-sum ranking puts the broad market AHEAD, 2.07 against 1.07 percent a year; and (b) what the gap does to money-weighted return under the owner's growing account, which is where M0267 found a 4.84-point edge collapse to 1.03. The likely finding, stated before any run: the tech fund's lead is a money-weighting artefact of exactly the same kind M0267 caught, pointing the other way -- it lost badly when the account was small and won when the account was large, so it flatters the owner's funding plan for the same accidental reason the trend rule disappointed it. If that is true it is a warning, not an opportunity, because nothing guarantees the next sixteen years place the tech fund's bad decade at the same end. The worst fall is the other half: the tech fund fell 82.3 percent against the broad market's 55.1 in M0267's run, so a gap bought with that much depth is not a free lunch and the method must report MAR, not return. Expected failure: both endpoints breach the depth rule by a wide margin, so nothing here can be eligible and the value is the measurement; also the fixed-split arms will not close positions, so trade counts will read zero and only exposure and turnover will describe them.

methods.name: Cap the winners, do not feed the laggards: which half of trimming buys the shallower fall?
methods.hypothesis: M0266 measured, with exposure held fixed to within 0.03 pts, that trimming a wide book is worth nothing in return (-0.10 pts/yr of money-weighted return at band 0, +0.02 at the 20%-of-target band) and is NEGATIVE in 2009-2015 on BOTH stores (-0.74 dev, -0.23 survivorship-check), yet makes the worst fall SHALLOWER on both (-1.7 pts dev, -3.4 pts check) -- reversing M0127's mechanism claim that rebalancing deepens the fall by buying the faller.
