But trimming is two actions welded together: SELLING a slice of whatever has outgrown its slot, and SPENDING the proceeds on whatever has shrunk below it. The hypothesis is that the safety comes entirely from the selling (an uncapped winner becomes a concentration the book never agreed to, and a concentrated book falls further when that winner turns) and the whole 2009-2015 cost comes entirely from the buying (topping up a faller is a mean-reversion bet that has been wrong for the entire modern era). Separate them on M0266's own chassis -- M0109's unbraked 50 most-traded index members at equal weight, one allocator, one params object, the scale field M0266 added -- with a trim-only rule set: a holding that has grown beyond its band is sold back to its slot, a holding that has fallen below its band is LEFT ALONE and the proceeds sit in cash. Four arms: the never-trim control, trim-and-feed at the 20%-of-target band (M0266-T20M, re-measured in this sweep), trim-only at the same band, and trim-only at band 0. CRITICAL: trim-only changes exposure by construction -- it only ever sells -- so the exposure match CANNOT be inherited from M0266 and must be re-derived, and insight 527 says it must be derived separately for each store. Calibrate the trim-only arms' scale UPWARD on the unbraked book's exposure alone, before any return, and refuse to publish a split if the realised exposures miss by more than half a point. Expected to fail by the trim-only arms drifting far enough in exposure that no fixed scale can match them, since a sell-only rule's cash share depends on how much the book has run. If the suspicion holds the payoff is a real dial: 1.5 to 3 points of worst fall for approximately zero return. No arm is a candidate; the base book loses to SPY and falls 57 percent.

methods.name: The price of idle cash is a curve, not a slope: map it before drawing another exposure-matched control
methods.sourceRef: M0266, which priced a point of being invested for the first time and found the number eight times smaller on the survivorship-check store than on the dev store over the same range, and whose own exposure calibration failed to transfer between the two; M0127 for the band rungs; M0109 for the neutral 50-name base book; insight 527, which says the lab has no basis for any exposure tolerance at all
methods.hypothesis: Every exposure-matched control this lab draws assumes return is a straight line in how invested a book is, and M0266 measured that line for the first time and found it bent. Its ruler priced a point of the account left out of the market at 0.0661 points a year of money-weighted return on the dev store over the 78.5-to-88.6 percent range, and at 0.0078 on the survivorship-check store over the 79.9-to-89.4 percent range -- the same book, the same dates, the same cash step, a factor of eight apart -- while the worst-fall slope held up at 0.42 and 0.61. Inside the dev store the top of the range is already visibly steeper than the bottom. So map the curve rather than assume it. Six arms, one dial: M0266's allocator subclassed unchanged under a new allocator id, M0127's band of zero on every arm so the trimming is held constant throughout, and six target-weight scales fixed on round numbers at 1.00, 0.94, 0.88, 0.82, 0.76 and 0.70, evenly spaced 0.06 apart. THERE IS NO CALIBRATION AND THAT IS THE DESIGN: M0266's buffer was computed to hit an exposure measured on one store and that is precisely what failed to transfer, so this ladder aims at no exposure at all. The scales are fixed, the realised exposure is read per store, and each store's curve is drawn against its own x values, which means a transfer failure cannot occur by construction. Band zero rather than the loose band because the loose band caps exposure at 88.6 percent at full weight and therefore cannot reach the 88.6-to-98.6 percent stretch where M0266 found the bend and where real books live. The ladder distinguishes two shapes: the additive straight line the lab assumes today, where a control one point off may be corrected by subtracting a constant slope, and a line through the origin, where return is simply exposure times what the fully invested book earns and a control must be corrected by dividing rather than subtracting. The second predicts 0.0705 per point on dev against 0.0596 measured, and 0.0466 on the check store against 0.0078 measured, so it is close on one store and wrong by six times on the other. My actual prior is a third shape: the slope is the book's return per unit of exposure minus what cash buys back in smoothness, the second term grows with the book's violence, and that is why the honest tape's return slope nearly vanished while its worst-fall slope did not -- the same book falls 57 percent on one store and 72 on the other. PREDICTIONS, written now. (1) Realised exposure is strictly decreasing in scale on both stores and lands on dev within half a point of 98.6, 92.7, 86.8, 80.9, 74.9 and 69.0 percent; if it is not monotone the x axis is broken and nothing may be read. (2) The top rung reproduces M0266-T00 to the digit on dev, because the subclass changes only the allocator id. (3) The curve is readable on dev, where adjacent rungs should differ by about 0.35 points a year, and marginal on the check store, where they would differ by 0.05; at least one sign flip between consecutive rungs is expected there and none on dev. (4) The curve is convex on dev, the top pair steeper than the bottom pair, against M0266's two pairs which point the other way by a hair on two different bands. (5) Worst fall against exposure is close to straight on both stores, near 0.42 and 0.61 points per point, so an exposure-matched control is far safer as a safety claim than as a return claim. (6) Turnover falls with scale while fees rise as a share of equity, because a smaller book pays the per-order minimum on more of its orders, which bends the bottom of the curve down for a reason that is not a market reason. (7) No arm is a candidate: the base book loses to a deposit-matched SPY and falls past 50 percent, and the scale field has no preset, so every arm is unpromotable by construction. THE DELIVERABLE, defined now so it cannot be chosen afterwards: fit the global straight line through each store's six points, compare every rung pair's measured return difference with the one that line predicts, and publish as the tolerance the largest exposure gap over which the error stays under 0.10 points a year. If consecutive local slopes disagree in sign on the dev store, no tolerance is published and the deliverable becomes the opposite instruction: match exposure exactly rather than correct for it. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's funding plan. Success is a measurement.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the curve is too noisy to read on the survivorship-check store, and I am expecting it rather than hoping against it. At the 0.0078 points a year per point M0266 measured there, consecutive rungs six points of exposure apart differ by 0.05 points a year, which is the same size as the path jitter between two books that hold the same names in different amounts through 2008. If consecutive rungs disagree in sign on that store, the honest reading is not that the curve bends in some interesting way but that there is no usable curve there at all, and the published answer must then be that an exposure-matched control on the honest tape has to match exactly, because nothing in the record supports correcting for a gap of any size. The second failure is the same thing on dev, which would be worse and would mean five rungs over thirty points of exposure on one book are five points rather than a function; in that case the method publishes no tolerance and says the lab must match exposure exactly. The third is that the whole shape turns out to be the fee schedule rather than the market: a book at 70 percent of full weight places orders 30 percent smaller and pays Gotrade's per-order minimum on a larger share of them, so the bottom rungs are penalised for a reason that has nothing to do with being out of the market, and if the bend sits entirely in the cost column then this is a measurement of a 20,000,000 IDR account's order economics and the verdict must say so rather than dress it as a market finding. The fourth is paths again, the caveat M0266 carried and this method inherits: every rung holds its buffer as a deliberate near-constant share re-set monthly, which is not the shape of the drifting idle cash a real book carries, so the curve prices a DELIBERATE buffer and may not transfer to a book whose cash is an accident. The fifth is that the dev and check stores disagree so completely that no single sentence covers both, in which case the deliverable is per-store and the lab must be told plainly that it may not carry an exposure correction from one copy of the history to another -- which is already the lesson M0266 paid for once. The sixth is that the ladder confirms the straight line everyone assumed, over the whole thirty points, on both stores. That would be a dull result and a genuinely useful one, and it must be reported with the same emphasis as a bend rather than buried as a non-finding.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-21

# M0270 — what does it really cost to leave money sitting in cash?

## This is a ruler, not a strategy

Nothing here is a candidate and nothing is being proposed for your money. The book used below
holds the fifty most-traded big American companies in equal amounts and does no stock picking at
all. Every one of the six versions lost to simply buying SPY with the same deposits, and the
gentlest of them still fell 46% from a peak — nearly twice the 25% you allow. It exists to put a
number on something the lab has been assuming for months without ever measuring it.

## The assumption that needed checking

The lab constantly compares two versions of a book that differ in one rule. For that comparison to
mean anything the two have to be **equally invested** — if one quietly sits on more cash it will
earn less for a reason that has nothing to do with the rule being tested. So the lab builds
matched pairs: it gives one version a deliberate cash buffer until both hold the same share of
their money in shares.

Underneath that practice is an assumption nobody had tested: **that return changes smoothly and
evenly with how invested a book is.** If a book one point less invested earns a fixed amount less,
a small mismatch can be corrected and a comparison survives it. If the relationship is lumpy,
every matched pair the lab has ever drawn is standing on soft ground.

Last October a measurement called M0266 put the first two points on that line, and they were
alarming. On the ordinary price data one point of the account left in cash looked worth **0.066
points a year**. On the check copy of the history — the one that puts the companies that died back
in — the identical step looked worth **0.0078**, eight times smaller. Two pairs of versions, and
they disagreed by a factor of eight. This method was built to settle it with a ladder instead of
two points.

## The ladder

Six versions of the identical book, differing in exactly one thing: how much of the account each
deliberately aims to hold in shares. **100%, 94%, 88%, 82%, 76%, 70%** of full weight — six round
numbers, evenly spaced, fixed in the method file and committed to the repository **before a single
return was computed**.

That last point is the design. M0266's buffer was *calculated* to hit a particular share measured
on one copy of the history, and when it was moved to the other copy the buffer missed by more than
the tolerance M0266 had set itself — so M0266 honestly refused to publish an answer for that copy.
This ladder aims at no share at all. It sets round numbers, runs them, and *reads* what each one
ended up holding, separately on each copy. A design that never aims at a target cannot miss one.

**The rungs landed where the file said they would.** Predicted, before the run: 98.6, 92.7, 86.8,
80.9, 74.9, 69.0 percent of the account invested. Measured: 98.57, 92.68, 86.78, 80.88, 74.97,
69.07. Every one within 0.07 of a point. And the top rung reproduced M0266's fully invested
version **to every recorded digit** — same total return, same worst fall, same gains-to-losses
ratio, same 1,338 trades — which proves the ladder's machinery is the same machinery, just
re-labelled.

## The answer: it is a straight line, and M0266's factor of eight was an artefact

| version | invested | money moved a year | fees paid | your money a year | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S100 | 98.57% | 3.38x | $19,933 | **+6.95%** | 59.6% |
| S094 | 92.68% | 3.17x | $18,392 | +6.60% | 57.1% |
| S088 | 86.78% | 2.97x | $16,914 | +6.24% | 54.6% |
| S082 | 80.88% | 2.77x | $15,488 | +5.88% | 51.9% |
| S076 | 74.97% | 2.57x | $14,119 | +5.50% | 49.2% |
| S070 | 69.07% | 2.37x | $12,807 | **+5.11%** | 46.2% |
| SPY, same deposits | — | — | — | +7.19% | — |

Six points, perfectly ordered, no reversals anywhere. **The price of a point of idle cash on the
ordinary data is 0.0623 points a year**, and a straight line drawn through all six points is never
off by more than **0.029 points a year** on any pair of rungs — including the widest pair, which
spans 29.5 points of exposure.

The same ladder on the honest copy of the history, which prices the companies that died:

| version | invested | your money a year | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| S100 | 98.38% | +4.71% | 73.2% |
| S094 | 92.53% | +4.51% | 70.6% |
| S088 | 86.64% | +4.30% | 67.8% |
| S082 | 80.74% | +4.08% | 64.8% |
| S076 | 74.85% | +3.85% | 61.6% |
| S070 | 68.95% | +3.61% | 58.2% |

Also perfectly ordered, also straight — never off by more than **0.034 points a year** over the
same 29.5-point span. **The price of a point there is 0.0375 points a year.**

So the headline is the dull one, and the dull one is the useful one. **The relationship is a
straight line on both copies of the price history, over the whole range tested.** The method wrote
down in advance that this was one of the ways it could "fail", and that a dull confirmation had to
be reported with the same emphasis as a dramatic bend. It is being reported that way.

And **M0266's factor of eight is not real.** The true gap between the two copies is 0.0623 against
0.0375 — a factor of **1.66**, not eight. M0266's 0.0078 was a single two-point reading taken on
two versions that had themselves missed their intended cash levels, and the ladder's five
consecutive readings in that same stretch of the honest data all sit between 0.034 and 0.041.
Nothing anywhere near 0.0078 appears. On the ordinary data, by contrast, M0266's two-point reading
of 0.066 sits within 5% of this ladder's 0.062, so the disagreement is not about which version of
the book was used — it is that two points cannot measure a slope when one of them has drifted.

## There is a gentle bend, and it is not the broker's fees

The line is straight to a thirtieth of a point, but it is not perfectly straight. Reading the
ladder rung by rung, the top is slightly shallower than the bottom:

| stretch of the account invested | ordinary data | honest data |
|---|---|---|
| 92.7% → 98.6% | 0.0590 | 0.0343 |
| 86.8% → 92.7% | 0.0606 | 0.0354 |
| 80.9% → 86.8% | 0.0623 | 0.0374 |
| 75.0% → 80.9% | 0.0639 | 0.0394 |
| 69.1% → 75.0% | 0.0656 | 0.0414 |

**The more cash you already hold, the more the next point of it costs you.** The bend is 11% from
top to bottom on the ordinary data and 21% on the honest data — real, consistent in direction on
both, and far too small to break a comparison.

The obvious suspect was the broker. A book at 70% of full weight places orders 30% smaller and
pays Gotrade's per-order minimum on more of them, so the bottom rungs might be penalised for a
reason that has nothing to do with being out of the market. That was written down in advance as a
way this result could be a fake. **It is not.** Running all twelve versions again with the fees
switched off entirely, the bend is the *same size*: 0.0669 at the top to 0.0743 at the bottom, a
rise of 11%, identical to the version that pays. Fees shift the whole line down by about **0.009
points a year per point of exposure** — being more invested does cost more to run, about an eighth
of what it gross earns — but fees do not bend it.

What does bend it is arithmetic you would expect: a book that resets a fixed cash share every
month is a constant blend of something volatile and something flat, and the return of such a blend
curves gently downward as the volatile share rises. The honest copy of the history holds the same
book on a more violent tape — it falls 73% rather than 60% — and it has **both the lower slope and
the stronger bend**, which is exactly what that explanation predicts.

## The number that actually matters: it changes by 34 times between eras

This is the finding with teeth, and it was not what the method went looking for.

Stripping the deposits out so the periods can be compared fairly, here is what one point of the
account left in cash cost in each stretch of the window:

| stretch | what the market did | price of a point of cash |
|---|---|---|
| 1996–2002 | SPY +6.6% a year | 0.076 points a year |
| 2003–2008 | SPY +2.3% a year | **0.005 points a year** |
| 2009–2015 | SPY +15.0% a year | **0.173 points a year** |
| whole window | SPY +8.1% a year | 0.062 points a year |

(The market figures in this table are SPY's own return over each stretch with no deposits in it,
which is why the whole-window one reads +8.1% rather than the +7.19% in the table above — that one
is what SPY would have done with your actual monthly deposits, most of which arrived late.)

In 2003–2008, which contains both a long bull market and the 2008 crash, holding cash was very
nearly **free** — the drag in the good years and the shelter in the bad year cancelled almost
exactly. In 2009–2015, a rising decade with no bear market in it at all, the same point of cash
cost **thirty-four times as much**. The 2009–2015 column is also the straightest of the lot: the
six rungs are spaced 1.02, 1.02, 1.02, 1.03 and 1.02 points apart, which is as close to a ruler as
this lab ever gets.

This lines up with a model the lab already uses without having checked it. The shortfall report
prices time spent out of the market at the era's own market return — for 2009–2015 it uses 16.6%
a year, which is 0.166 points per point of cash. The ladder measures **0.173**. Those agree to
within 4%, so that model is now measured rather than assumed, *for an era claim*. For a
whole-window claim the same model would say 0.081 where the truth is 0.062 — a third too high. The
model is right for an era and wrong for an average.

## What this means for every matched comparison the lab draws

This is the deliverable, and it was defined in the method file before any return was computed.

1. **The straight line is safe.** Over the whole 30 points tested, on both copies of the history,
   with fees on and with fees off, a straight line never mis-states a difference by more than
   0.034 points a year. Correcting for an exposure gap is legitimate.
2. **But the slope has to be measured in the same setting as the claim.** It is 0.062 for a
   whole-window claim on the ordinary data, 0.038 on the honest data, 0.005 in 2003–2008 and
   0.173 in 2009–2015. A slope carried from one era, one copy of the history or one book to
   another is wrong by up to 34 times. **This is the rule that was missing.**
3. **The tolerance, in plain numbers.** If a comparison is quoted to a tenth of a point a year,
   two versions may differ in how invested they are by **1.6 points** for a whole-window claim on
   the ordinary data, **2.7 points** on the honest data, and only **0.6 points** for a 2009–2015
   claim. That last one is the strict case, and 2009–2015 is the era this lab sends every idea to
   first.
4. **Correct by subtracting, never by dividing.** The tempting shortcut — "a book 10% in cash
   earns 90% as much" — over-states the cost by 13% on the ordinary data and 28% on the honest
   data, because of the gentle bend. Subtract the measured slope times the gap.
5. **A matched comparison supports a safety claim far better than a return claim.** The worst fall
   moves 0.451 points per point of exposure on the ordinary data and 0.509 on the honest data —
   only 13% apart, against 66% apart for return. Falls behave almost identically across copies of
   the history; returns do not.
6. **M0266's own refusal was right for the wrong reason.** Its matched versions were 0.90 and 0.75
   of a point off on the honest data, which it treated as past tolerance. At the slope now
   measured there, those gaps are worth 0.034 and 0.028 points a year — comfortably inside a tenth
   of a point. The real reason it could not publish was that its two routes disagreed by 0.27
   points a year, and that disagreement is now explained: one of the two routes was the two-point
   reading that this ladder shows to be wrong.

## The gate numbers

All six versions were rejected and none was close. Each lost to a deposit-matched SPY (+5.11% to
+6.95% a year against SPY's +7.19%), and four of the six also broke the lab's 50% screening limit for a
dev result. Every one of the six broke your 25% limit for real money by a wide margin — 46.2% at
best, 59.6% at worst, and 58% to 73% once the dead companies are put back. All six also failed the
gains-to-losses test, at 1.25–1.28 against a bar of 1.30.

On luck: the lab judges a result by how likely it is to be real rather than a fluke after
everything that has been tried, and the bar is **0.90**. The lab has now looked at **172 distinct
methods**, and against that many tries the best of these six scores **0.41**. Nowhere near, and
exactly as it should be — a book with no stock picking in it has nothing to be lucky about.

On the fold record: **0 of 4** out-of-sample stretches won. For a ruler that is not a mark against
it; the question was never whether this book beats the market.

## What was predicted, and what happened

Seven predictions were written before the run. Five held, two were wrong, and the two that were
wrong are the interesting ones.

1. **The rungs land where predicted** — held, every one within 0.07 of a point.
2. **The top rung reproduces M0266's fully invested version to the digit** — held exactly.
3. **Readable on the ordinary data, marginal on the honest data, with at least one reversal
   there** — half wrong. It is readable on *both*, and there is **no reversal anywhere**, on
   either copy, with fees on or off. The honest data turned out to have a slope five times larger
   than M0266 had measured, which is why it is legible.
4. **The curve bends the other way — steeper at the top** — **wrong, and cleanly so.** It is
   steeper at the *bottom*, on both copies, with fees on and off. I predicted this against the
   existing evidence on purpose and wrote that the file would say so afterwards. It says so.
5. **The fall axis is the well-behaved one** — held, and more strongly than expected.
6. **Fees bend the bottom down** — wrong. Fees shift the line without bending it.
7. **No version is a candidate** — correct. All six rejected.

Of the six ways this was expected to fail, the one that fired was number six: the ladder confirmed
the straight line everyone had assumed. The method committed in advance to reporting that as a
finding rather than burying it as a non-result.

## What this cost and what it did not buy

Six recorded trials and one more method on the lab's count, which lifts the luck bar very slightly
for every future idea. It did not spend a test-window look and nothing here goes near one.

One check was deliberately skipped. The lab's own cross-store report was not run on this method,
because it does not carry the two columns this method is about — how invested each version was,
and how much money each moved — and the sweep written for this method does carry them, on both
copies, in one pass. Running it as well would have added a journal entry saying less than the
paragraphs above. The reproduction check it would have performed was done directly instead: the
top rung matches M0266's recorded row to the digit.

## My opinion:

The lab can keep drawing exposure-matched controls, and it should stop quoting a single slope when
it does. The shape is fine — a straight line is good to a thirtieth of a point over thirty points,
on both copies of the history, which is far better than the method expected. What is not fine is
the habit of treating the price of idle cash as a constant. It is 0.005 in one era and 0.173 in
another, and the lab's standard first filter, 2009–2015, is the most expensive era of the three.
Any comparison that is quoted for 2009–2015 and matched on a whole-window slope is under-correcting
by nearly three times.

The practical rule I would adopt is short: **match exposure to within half a point and stop
correcting at all.** The measurement says half a point costs 0.09 points a year even in the
expensive era — inside the tenth of a point this lab quotes to — and a tolerance that needs no
slope cannot be wrong about which slope to use. M0266's half-point rule, chosen by instinct, turns
out to have been exactly right; it just had no evidence behind it until now.

The thing I would chase next is the arithmetic that fell out of the era table. The lab has a
long-standing figure for what its market-timing switch costs: a flat 3.6 points a year since 2009,
measured across every trial the lab holds and treated as a mysterious constant of the switch. Divide it by
the 0.173 points this ladder measures, and it is **21 points of exposure** — which is about how
much of the time a 200-day rule sits in cash during a decade with no bear market in it. If that
holds, the switch's famous premium is not a property of the switch at all. It is the switch's time
out of the market, multiplied by the price of a point of cash in the only era anyone has been
measuring. That would mean the lab has been trying to tune a rule when the only thing it can
actually change is how long the rule stays out. I have queued it as the next method, and it is
cheap: the switch's cash share is already recorded for every gated trial the lab holds.
methods.verdict: The line is straight on both price histories and M0266's factor of eight was a two-point artefact; what is not constant is the slope, which runs from 0.005 to 0.173 points a year between eras, so match exposure to half a point rather than correcting for it.

methods.name: Is the safety switch's famous premium anything but its time in cash? A re-entry-delay ladder on an opinion-free book
methods.sourceRef: M0270, which priced a point of cash at 0.1732 points a year over 2009-2015 on this exact book; insight 463, the 3.6-points-a-year constant swept across 824 trials; insight 532, the hypothesis; insight 516, the real gate at the 38th percentile of 20,000 uninformed imitators with its own habits; insight 529, the lab clustering by its gate rather than by its ideas; insight 533, that a slope read from two points is not a measurement
methods.hypothesis: The lab treats 3.6 points a year as a constant of the shared SPY 200-day switch: swept across all 824 recorded trials since 2009, barely moving from book to book, and most of the typical post-2009 shortfall. M0270 has now priced the other half of that arithmetic on the same opinion-free 50-name book, in the same era, on the same store: one point of the account held in cash cost 0.1732 points a year over 2009-2015. Divide and the switch is worth 20.8 points of exposure. Measured off SPY's own bars before this ran, the plain gate is out of the market on 15 of 82 monthly decisions over 2009-2015 -- 18.29 percent, about 18 points of a 98.6-percent-invested book -- and 18.0 times 0.1732 is 3.12 points a year. The premium and the time in cash agree to within half a point with no backtest at all. SO THE HYPOTHESIS IS THAT THE SWITCH'S COST IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE SWITCH: it is how long the rule stays out, priced at what being out was worth in the era, with no judgement in it. Two independent results already point the same way. Twenty thousand uninformed sticky switches drawn at the real gate's own transition rate put the real gate at the 38th percentile of its own imitators over 2009-2015. And the lab's books cluster by the gate they share rather than by the ideas inside them, at 0.633 against 0.064, with the lab-wide resemblance collapsing from 0.288 to 0.070 once the gate-alone book is projected out. THE RECORDED TRIALS CANNOT SETTLE IT, because every gated book here sits behind the same rule read on the same monthly dates and four of the five live books go to cash on the identical 28.3 percent of their decision days: exposure is a constant there, not a lever. So this method makes exposure the independent variable. One book -- M0266's allocator, subclassed from M0270's own subclass so all three cannot drift apart, the 50 most-traded index members at equal weight, band zero, no picking, no brake, full scale -- behind the lab's shared gate, with one dial: a re-entry delay of 0, 6, 16, 30 and 42 sessions of continuous gate-on required before the book comes back, plus the gate switched off entirely as the no-opinion arm. Every arm leaves the market on exactly the same days for exactly the same reason; they differ only in how long they wait, so time in cash moves deliberately while the signal is held fixed. Measured in advance off SPY's bars and reading no return at all, the five gated rungs are out on 18.29, 23.17, 28.05, 34.15 and 39.02 percent of 2009-2015 decisions -- five steps of 4.9, 4.9, 6.1 and 4.9 points, so the rungs are evenly spaced in the x axis, which is cash, rather than in the dial. That is a 21-point lever on five points, which is what insight 533 demands after M0266 read an eight-fold store gap off two. The ladder stops at 42 sessions because the smoke fixture that catches dead allocators stops it there, and shrinking a frozen fixture to fit one experiment is the wrong trade; a ladder anchored close to the gate's own operating point also extrapolates back to the no-gate arm better than one stretched far past it. THE DELIVERABLE, fixed now. Fit the straight line through the five delay rungs in points of cash against de-funded lead; its slope is the price of episodic cash at the gate's own boundary. Extrapolate it back to the no-gate arm's cash level and compare the prediction P with that arm's measured lead A. P equal to A means the gate's own 18 points of cash are priced exactly like the delay's and the switch's decision carries no information. A below P means the gate's cash was cheaper than the delay's, so the exit decision does carry information and three lines of evidence this week were misread. A above P is anti-skill and would be reported as such. The headline residual is the gate's measured cost minus 0.1732 times its own points of cash, and the hypothesis predicts zero. The noise band is internal and is not borrowed: the root-mean-square residual of the five rungs about their own fitted line, because every rung is the same book on the same tape with one dial moved, and M0270's rung-pair errors on this chassis ran 0.000 to 0.034 points a year. A residual within half a point a year confirms the hypothesis; one of a point or more, with a rung scatter under 0.2, falsifies it and says the switch has real timing skill worth about that much a year; in between the answer is 'mostly cash, with a residual too small to tune against'. PREDICTIONS. Realised exposure is strictly decreasing in delay and lands within 2 points of 98.6, 80.5, 75.7, 70.9, 64.9 and 60.1 percent over 2009-2015, the era the claim is about, with exposure re-measured over that era's own sessions rather than taken from the whole-window average a trial records; if it is not monotone the x axis is broken and nothing may be read. The no-gate arm reproduces M0270-S100 to the digit on dev, which is what licenses using 0.1732 at all. If the hypothesis holds exactly the 2009-2015 leads are plus 0.52, minus 2.60, minus 3.44, minus 4.27, minus 5.31 and minus 6.14 points a year, where the '3.6 is a constant' reading would instead put the plain gate at minus 3.08. The prediction I am least sure of is that the delay slope comes out ABOVE 0.1732, because the delay buys its cash in the weeks just after the market crosses back above its own average and in a decade of recoveries those weeks were strong; if it lands near 0.1732 anyway the hypothesis survives in its strongest form. The whole window goes the other way, carries 2000 and 2008, and is reported anyway without being allowed to touch the 2009-2015 claim. Turnover is near-constant across the rungs and falls slightly at the long end because a delay can swallow an episode and save a round trip; the no-gate arm pays no gate round trips at all, so zero-fee twins of all six arms are run outside the registry to split the gate's cash from the gate's fees, exactly as M0270 did, and trade count is a dead meter on this host and is printed for completeness only. Both stores are loaded in one process with both fingerprints printed, because a ratio across two store vintages is not a comparison. No arm is a candidate: the base book loses to a deposit-matched SPY and falls past 50 percent, and the delay field has no preset and no resolver entry, so eligibility would be reported and would still not be promoted. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's funding plan. Success is a measurement.
methods.expectedFailure: THE LIKELIEST FAILURE IS THAT THE DELAY'S CASH IS NOT THE GATE'S CASH, and the ladder answers a neighbouring question instead of the one asked. A re-entry delay buys its extra cash in the weeks immediately after the market crosses back above its own average -- early recoveries, which in 2009-2015 were the strongest weeks on the tape. The gate's own cash is bought while the market is below that average. If those two kinds of cash turn out to be priced very differently, the back-extrapolation from the delay rungs to the no-gate arm is an extrapolation across a boundary rather than along a curve, and the honest reading is that the ladder priced the re-entry margin and not the switch. The method must then say so, and the residual against M0270's 0.1732 -- which is cash spread evenly over every session rather than bunched into episodes -- becomes the primary number instead of the extrapolation. THE SECOND FAILURE IS THE SHAPE OF THE CASH rather than its timing. M0270's 0.1732 was measured on cash held as a constant fraction every day; this method's cash is all-or-nothing, in episodes. Two books with the same average exposure and different cash shapes do not have to earn the same return, because compounding is not linear along a path, and nothing in the lab has ever measured that difference. If the no-gate arm's measured lead sits far from the delay line for that reason, the finding is about the shape of cash and not about the switch's judgement, and it would be a real finding that nonetheless does not answer the question. THE THIRD is fees. The no-gate arm never pays a gate round trip, and insight 462 already split the equal-weight book's post-2009 shortfall into 3.6 points of gate and 3.8 of fees, so the one step this method most needs to be clean is the one most polluted. The zero-fee twins are the answer and they are run for all six arms, but if the gross and net ladders disagree about the sign of the residual then the method has not settled anything and must say which half it believes and why. THE FOURTH is that 2009-2015 is 82 monthly decisions and five re-entries. Five episodes is not a sample; one unusually good or bad re-entry moves the whole delay slope, and a residual of half a point could be one month in 2011. The analysis must report how much of the residual rides on the single largest episode, and if one episode carries most of it the verdict is 'not settled on this era' rather than a number. THE FIFTH is that the base book is not a book anyone would trade: it falls past 50 percent and loses to SPY at every rung, so its 2009-2015 lead is a small difference between two large and violent numbers, and the price of cash measured on it may not be the price of cash on a 20-name momentum book that actually picks. That is the cost of using an opinion-free chassis, it is deliberate, and the across-the-lab half of the analysis -- a gate-off sweep over recorded gated books, which costs no method id -- exists precisely to check whether the arithmetic holds where the lab actually lives. THE SIXTH is the dull one and would be the most useful: the residual comes out at zero, the switch is confirmed to be a cash dial, and the lab has spent six method ids this month tuning a dial that was never connected to the price. That must be reported with the same emphasis as a surprise rather than buried as a non-finding.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-21

# M0271 — Is the safety switch's famous cost just its time in cash?

## What this asked

For a year the lab has carried one number about its safety switch — the rule that sells
everything when the market closes below its own one-year average. Across all 824 trials ever
recorded, the switch looked like it cost **3.6 points a year since 2009**, and that figure barely
moved from one strategy to another. It read like a stubborn property of the switch.

Last week a separate experiment (M0270) measured the other half of that arithmetic directly: on a
deliberately opinion-free book, one point of the account held in cash cost **0.1732 points a year**
over 2009–2015. Divide 3.6 by 0.1732 and you get 20.8 points of cash — which is almost exactly how
much of the time the switch sits out in a decade with no crash. The hypothesis was therefore that
**the switch's cost is not about the switch at all**: it is how long it stays out, multiplied by
what being out was worth, with no judgement in it. If that were true, every attempt this lab has
made to tune the switch has been adjusting something that does not set the price.

This method tested it by moving time-in-cash on purpose while holding the signal fixed. One book —
the fifty most-traded index members at equal weight, no stock picking, no brake, which is the same
chassis M0270 measured the price of cash on — ran six ways. One with the switch off entirely. Five
with the switch on, differing only in how long the book waits after the market crosses back above
its average before buying again: no wait, then six, sixteen, thirty and forty-two trading days.
Every version sells on exactly the same days for exactly the same reason. They differ only in
patience, so time in cash becomes a dial rather than an accident. The five waits were chosen from
the switch's own calendar before anything ran, so they are evenly spaced in cash — out of the
market on 18.3%, 23.2%, 28.1%, 34.2% and 39.0% of the monthly decisions in 2009–2015.

## The headline: the hypothesis is wrong, and not by a little

**The switch is not a cash dial. It is a large, real timing rule — and it has been wrong in
opposite directions in different decades, by amounts that dwarf what its cash is worth.**

| era | what the switch actually cost | what its time in cash should have cost | the difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1996–2015, whole window | it **earned 2.16** points a year | it should have **cost 1.73** | **−3.89** |
| 1996–2002 | it **earned 4.58** | should have cost 2.67 | **−7.25** |
| 2003–2008 | it **earned 6.78** | should have cost 0.14 | **−6.92** |
| 2009–2015 | it **cost 6.71** | should have cost 3.49 | **+3.22** |

Read the last column as the part of the switch that is judgement rather than cash. A negative
number means the switch sat out at worse-than-average moments, which is what a working safety rule
does. A positive number means it sat out at better-than-average moments, which is what a broken one
does. **Both appear, and both are far larger than the measurement's own noise**, which this method
measures internally at 0.35 to 0.52 points a year from how tightly its five waiting rungs sit on
their own straight line.

The same answer comes back on the second copy of the price history, which includes the companies
that went bust (2009–2015 difference +2.66 instead of +3.22), and with trading fees switched off
entirely (+3.30 instead of +3.22). So it is not survivorship and it is not Gotrade's fee schedule.

## The numbers the lab records

All six versions are funded the owner's way — 10 million rupiah to start and 5 million on the 25th
of every month — and pay Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares.

| version | wait | your money earned | SPY TR, same deposits | worst fall (no deposits) | gains vs losses | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no switch | — | +6.9%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 55.2% | 1.25 | 0.409 |
| the switch, plain | 0 days | **+9.0%/yr** | +7.2%/yr | **17.8%** | 2.69 | 0.876 |
| wait 6 days | 6 | +6.3%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 17.8% | 2.09 | 0.583 |
| wait 16 days | 16 | +5.6%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 17.8% | 2.06 | 0.554 |
| wait 30 days | 30 | +4.6%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 17.8% | 1.88 | 0.388 |
| wait 42 days | 42 | +3.7%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 17.8% | 1.72 | 0.304 |

Five of the six lose to a deposit-matched SPY and all six are rejected. The plain switch is the only
one that beats SPY, keeps the fall inside the 20% limit and clears the profit bar — it fails on one
condition only, the luck score.

**The luck score, in words.** It asks how likely a result is to be real rather than a lucky draw
after everything the lab has tried. The owner's bar is 0.90. The lab has now looked at 173 distinct
strategies, and that count is what the score is deflated by — every new idea raises the bar for
every old one. The plain switch scores **0.876**: close, and still short. The waiting versions score
0.30 to 0.58, which is nowhere near. Nothing here was ever a candidate anyway: the underlying book
holds fifty names with no opinion about any of them, it loses to SPY without the switch, and the
waiting dial has no entry in the live trading rules, so none of these could be promoted even if
they passed.

**Worst years.** Without the switch, 2008 cost 42.5%. With it, the worst calendar year is 2015 at
−6.4%. That is the switch earning its keep, and it is why the fall drops from 55% to 18%.

**Walk-forward.** Scored over four non-overlapping stretches, the plain switch beat the market in 1
of 4 — it won 2006–2008 by 42 points and lost the three rising stretches. That is the same story the
era table tells, and it is the modal fold record in this lab rather than a near miss.

## Why: the switch sat out the best months of the decade

Logs add, so the 2009–2015 gap can be split exactly. Comparing the no-switch book with the plain
switch month by month:

* **94% of the gap is the months the switch was out.** Only 6% is everything else — the extra fees
  it pays and the different fifty names it owns after each round trip. So this is genuinely about
  being out of the market, not about churn.
* **The book ran at about 28% a year in the 16 months the switch sat out, against 14% a year in the
  65 months it stayed in.** The switch chose to be absent at double the book's normal rate of pay.
  SPY itself ran at 24% against 15% in the same split, so this is a market-timing failure and not a
  stock-picking one.

That gives the clean three-way split of the switch's 6.71 points a year of 2009–2015 cost on this
book:

| where it went | points a year |
|---|---|
| simply holding 20 points of cash | 3.49 |
| holding that cash in lumps at the switch's own boundary rather than spread evenly | 1.79 |
| the switch's own choice of which lumps | 1.44 |

The middle row is new and matters on its own: **even uninformed cash costs 1.6 times more when it
arrives in all-or-nothing lumps near a trend boundary than when it is spread evenly over every
day** (0.2832 points a year per point against 0.1732 on the same book, same store, same years). Part
of what the lab has been calling "the switch's cost" is the shape of its cash, not its opinion.

**And the honest caveat on the third row.** There were four out-episodes in 2009–2015, and one of
them — staying out from February to June 2009, through the bottom and the first leg of the recovery
— carries 1.54 of the 2.28 points of episode cost, which is 68%. Four episodes is not a sample. The
*direction* of the judgement term is solid and repeats on both copies of the history; the *size* of
it rests on one call. A 200-day rule is structurally guaranteed to be late back in after a crash, so
that call is not bad luck — but one instance cannot price it.

## Does this hold where the lab actually lives?

The chassis here picks nothing, which is the point and also the limit: what it costs to sit out a
month is whatever that particular book would have earned in it. So the same measurement was repeated
on twelve recorded strategies spanning twelve different ideas — residual momentum, risk-managed
momentum, portfolio construction, the 52-week high, seasonality, short-term reversal, long-term
reversal, lottery avoidance, the price-delay screen, coskewness, treasury beta and a core-satellite
blend — each run as recorded and again with the switch removed and nothing else touched. No trial
was recorded, no window was spent, nothing was written.

| era | measured cost ÷ what cash explains, median of 12 | range |
|---|---|---|
| whole window | **−0.80** (the switch *earned*) | −2.90 to +0.65 |
| 1996–2002 | −0.23 | −3.48 to +2.16 |
| 2003–2008 | **−53** | −72 to −27 |
| 2009–2015 | **1.42** | 0.59 to 3.05 |

A ratio of 1 would mean the hypothesis is exactly right. It is never 1. In 2009–2015 — the era the
3.6-point figure is about — nine of the twelve cost more than cash explains, by 42% on the median.
In every other era the cash model gets the *sign* wrong.

**And the sharpest number in the whole method.** Across those twelve books, what the switch
actually cost in 2009–2015 ranges from 0.60 to 10.37 points a year — a seventeen-fold spread. What
the cash model predicts for the same twelve ranges from 0.92 to 3.47, and for the eleven fully
invested ones only 2.83 to 3.47, a spread of 1.23 times. **The famous constancy of the 3.6 is the
constancy of the formula, not of the switch.** Gated books all sit out the same days because they
share the same rule, so "(1 − exposure) × the market's return" hands back nearly the same number
every time — by construction. The thing it is supposed to be estimating varies by seventeen times.

## Did the pre-registered predictions hold?

* **The no-switch version reproduced M0270's fully-invested rung to the digit** — same return
  (+6.949%), same fall, same 1,338 trades. That is what licenses using M0270's 0.1732 here at all,
  and it held.
* **Realised cash was monotone in the waiting dial** on both windows and landed within 2 points of
  what the switch's own calendar predicted. The x axis is sound, except in 1996–2002 where the 30-
  and 42-day waits saturate at the same value and no slope should be read.
* **The waiting slope came out above 0.1732**, as predicted and for the predicted reason: 0.2832 on
  the dev store, 0.2452 on the survivorship-check store.
* **The predicted 2009–2015 leads were wrong, and that is the finding.** The hypothesis said the
  plain switch would land at −2.60 points a year and the "3.6 is a constant" reading said −3.08. It
  landed at **−6.19**.
* **Four of the six written-down failure modes fired.** The delay's cash is indeed not the switch's
  cash (so both references are reported, not one). The shape of cash is a real and separate effect
  (1.79 of the 6.71). Four episodes is not a sample, and one of them carries two thirds of the
  judgement term. Fees were ruled out rather than assumed. Only the "dull confirmation" ending did
  not happen.

## Against the parent and the near misses

M0270 is the parent and nothing here contradicts it: its 0.1732 is reproduced as the baseline and
its straight line holds. What changes is what the lab may do with it. M0270 said a point of cash
costs 0.1732 in that era. This method says **you may not run that backwards**: knowing a rule holds
20 points of cash tells you almost nothing about what the rule costs, because the rule chooses
*when*, and when is worth between −7 and +3 points a year depending on the decade.

Insight 463 is not wrong about its own arithmetic — it said plainly that its 3.6 was arithmetic
rather than a finding about any strategy. What this method retires is the habit that grew around it:
quoting the model's output as the switch's measured cost. Insight 516 (the switch losing to 20,000
uninformed imitators over 2009–2015) and insight 529 (the lab clustering by its switch rather than
by its ideas) both survive and are, if anything, strengthened for that era — but neither of them
licenses the whole-window claim, and this method shows the whole-window claim is the opposite.

## My opinion

This direction is worth more trials, and it changes which trials are worth running.

The useful finding is not that the switch is good or bad. It is that **the switch's value is an era
variable with a range of ten points a year, and the lab has been treating it as a constant of about
three and a half.** Every shortfall attribution this lab has published since 463 used that constant.
On the twelve-book sample the constant is too small by 42% in 2009–2015 and has the wrong sign in
every other era, which means the leftover that those attributions assigned to "the picking" has been
systematically mis-stated — too generous to the picking after 2009, far too harsh before it. I would
re-run the shortfall sweep with a measured gate column rather than a modelled one before another
word is written about what this lab's stock-picking is worth. That costs no method id and no look.

The second thing I would do is price the shape of cash on its own. The 1.79 points a year that came
from cash arriving in lumps rather than evenly is, as far as I can tell, a quantity nobody here has
ever measured, and it sits inside every timing comparison the lab has made. A ladder that holds the
same average cash in lumps of one, three, six and twelve months would settle it in one method, and
it would tell us how much of *every* timing rule's bill is simply the lumpiness of switching.

What I would **not** do is go back to tuning the switch. Six method ids this month went into when to
read it, how often, with what band and in what phase, and the answer each time was a fraction of a
point. The thing that actually moves the number is which months it sits out, and the biggest single
contribution in the owner's own era is one five-month absence in 2009 that a 200-day rule cannot
avoid by construction. The honest conclusion is that a trend switch is a very good crash insurance
policy with a premium that is large, variable and payable in exactly the years the owner's money is
in the account — and that the way to improve it is to change what the book does while it is out, not
when it goes out.
methods.verdict: Rejected, and it refutes what it was built to test: the safety switch is not a cash dial. Whole window it earned 2.2 points a year where its time in cash says it should have lost 1.7; since 2009 it cost 6.7 where cash explains 3.5. The famous 3.6 is the constancy of the formula, not of the switch.

methods.name: Does the exposure slope hold on a book that picks stocks, or only on a book that does not?
methods.hypothesis: M0270 measured the price of a point of idle cash on ONE book: M0109's fifty most-traded index members at equal weight, no gate, no brake, no stock picking. It came out at 0.0623 points a year per point of exposure on the dev store, 0.0375 on the survivorship-check store, and 0.005 to 0.173 depending on the era -- straight to 0.034 points a year over the whole 29.5-point range on all four curves measured, with a gentle concave bend of 11 to 21 percent that survives the fees being switched off. Every one of those numbers is a property of THAT book and that tape, and the lab draws exposure-matched controls on books that look nothing like it. The open question is whether the slope travels. The mechanism M0270 proposes -- a monthly-reset mix of a volatile book and flat cash, whose return curves gently downward as the volatile share rises -- predicts that the slope is roughly the book's own return minus a term that grows with its violence, so a CALMER book should show a slope closer to its own return and a flatter bend, and a more violent one the reverse. That is a prediction with a sign, and it is testable without a new chassis: run the identical six-rung ladder on a second book with a genuinely different temperament -- the relative-strength roster book at its own best width, which picks stocks and falls differently -- and read whether the slope lands where its own return and volatility say it should. If it does, the lab gains a FORMULA rather than a table: estimate the slope from a book's own recorded return and fall, and the half-point matching rule becomes a fallback rather than the only safe answer. If it does not, the honest conclusion is that every book needs its own ladder and the lab should stop correcting exposure gaps entirely. Expected to fail by the picking book's exposure being hard to move cleanly -- a book with a gate already holds cash for a second reason, and the scale dial and the gate interact, so the realised rungs may not be evenly spaced and the x axis may stop being a clean dial. Pre-register what happens then: report the realised spacing and refuse to publish a slope rather than quote one fitted to uneven rungs.

methods.name: Come back in quarters, not all at once: a partial re-entry ladder against the switch's structural lateness
methods.hypothesis: M0271 measured where the shared SPY 200-day switch's 2009-2015 bill actually goes: 94 percent of it is the months the book is absent and only 6 percent is churn and the rebuilt book; the book would have earned about 28 percent a year in the 16 months the switch sat out against 14 percent in the 65 it stayed in; and ONE absence, February to June 2009, carries two thirds of the judgement cost. That absence is not bad luck. A rule that waits for price to clear its own 200-day average is guaranteed by its own arithmetic to be late back after a deep fall, because the average it waits for has been dragged down and takes months to be cleared, and the deeper the crash the later it is. M0271 also showed that six methods' worth of tuning WHEN the switch is read (cadence, phase, band, session grid, confirmation) each moved a fraction of a point, because none of them touches the lateness. The untouched dial is what the money does while the switch is out: today, nothing. So hold the exit decision exactly as it is and change only the RE-ENTRY SHAPE. Five rungs on one book, on M0271's own opinion-free 50-name chassis so the result is comparable to its ladder arm for arm: the plain switch (all out, all back at once, the reference and the no-opinion arm is the gate-off book M0271 already recorded); then a ladder that restores a quarter of the book for each 21 consecutive sessions the gate has been on, so a four-month climb is needed for a full return; a half-and-half version restoring 50 percent immediately and 50 percent after 42 sessions; a version that holds SPY itself at half weight while out rather than cash; and a version that holds the long-dated Treasury series while out. All five share the identical exit calendar, so the comparison is purely about the absence. PREDICTIONS WRITTEN NOW: the quarter ladder recovers at least half of the 1.4 points a year M0271 attributed to the switch's own choice of months, because most of that is the spring of 2009 and a ladder is partly invested through it; the SPY-at-half-weight arm recovers more return but gives back most of the fall protection, because the thing it holds is the thing it was hiding from; the Treasury arm is the one I expect to look best on both axes over 1996-2015 and to look much worse after 2009, because long bonds paid in both crashes and nothing since; and all five remain worse than the plain switch WHOLE WINDOW, because 2008 is 34.8 points of lead that only full cash collects. The trap to avoid: M0271's own warning that cash in lumps costs 1.6 times cash spread evenly, so a partial ladder changes the SHAPE of the absence as well as its content and the analysis must price the two separately rather than crediting the signal with both. An allocator cannot read its own weight, so each rung must recover its position from price, which M0231's partial-weight work already shows how to do.

methods.name: Price the lumpiness of cash on its own: the same average cash in absences of one, three, six and twelve months
methods.hypothesis: M0271 found, as a by-product, a quantity this lab has never measured and which sits inside every timing comparison it has ever made. On the opinion-free 50-name book over 2009-2015, a point of the account kept in cash EVERY DAY cost 0.1732 points a year (M0270's measurement). A point of cash arriving instead as an all-or-nothing absence around the SPY 200-day boundary cost 0.2832 -- sixty per cent more for the same average amount of cash, measured across five evenly spaced rungs that sit on a straight line to within half a point a year. That matters because the lab's habit is to subtract the plain cash figure from a timing rule's measured cost and call the remainder judgement. On M0271's book the remainder was 6.71 points a year, of which 3.49 is cash, 1.79 is the LUMPINESS of that cash and only 1.44 is the rule's actual choice of months -- so two thirds of what reads as a verdict on judgement is really a verdict on the shape of absences, and the shape is a property of switching at all rather than of switching well. M0271 could not separate the two cleanly because its lumps were all anchored to one boundary and all of similar length. So: hold the average cash FIXED and vary only the lump length. Five arms on M0271's chassis, each holding the same average share of the account in cash over the window but delivering it in absences of about one, three, six, twelve and twenty-four months, drawn on a fixed calendar that reads no market data at all so there is no signal anywhere in the design -- a deterministic rotation, not a random one, so the arms are reproducible and the draw cannot be the finding. PREDICTIONS: the cost per point of cash rises monotonically with lump length, because a long absence is more likely to straddle a run of strong months and the sequence of returns matters to a funded book; the rise is steeper in 2009-2015 than in 1996-2002 and nearly flat in 2003-2008, mirroring the era slopes M0270 measured; and the one-month arm lands within a tenth of a point of M0270's evenly-spread 0.1732, which is the check that the chassis has not drifted. The deliverable is a correction table -- cost per point of cash by lump length and era -- that any future timing comparison can subtract BEFORE it attributes anything to a signal. Trap: a fixed calendar that happens to align with month ends or quarter ends can pick up a seasonal effect by accident, so the rotation must be offset and the offset swept as a sanity arm.

methods.name: Companies that stopped growing their balance sheet: buy the index members whose total assets grew least over the past year
methods.sourceRef: Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) Asset Growth and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns, J. Finance 63(4); Fama-French (2015) CMA factor; McLean & Pontiff (2016) post-publication decay
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008, so the only years this lab can test it on (October 2010 to October 2015, where the SEC panel carries a balance sheet a year apart for 270-380 index members) are all after publication. Cooper, Gulen and Schill report that low year-on-year growth in total assets beats high growth among large companies as well as small; Fama and French made it a factor in 2015. Signal: each month, for each index member with a bar, the newest total-assets figure filed by that day against the one for the balance-sheet date a year earlier (within 20 days), filed by that day too; skip members whose newest balance sheet is over 200 days old or whose ratio sits outside 0.2-5.0 (a units error), one listing per company. Arms: L30 (the 30 lowest growers), H30 (the 30 highest, the opposite book), L30-PLC (L30's size and entry count drawn blind from the same pool: the no-opinion arm) and L60 (the 60 lowest). Equal slots, monthly, fully invested, no switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up; SPY is held before October 2010, so the whole-window row differs from SPY only after it. Predictions written before any result, on the de-funded monthly curve from 2010-10 to 2015-10: L30 beats H30 by 2 or more points a year; L30 beats L30-PLC by a point or more; L30 ends within a point a year of total-return SPY, ahead or behind. Unpromotable by construction (three walk-forward folds, one with picks): run as evidence on whether older fundamentals are worth buying.
methods.expectedFailure: Four ways, in order of likelihood. (1) Decay and crowding: the effect was published in 2008 and made a Fama-French factor in 2015, and the conservative-minus-aggressive factor earned close to nothing in US large caps over 2010-2015, so L30 lands near the placebo and behind SPY, the gap being the lab's usual equal-weight shortfall against a market led by a few fast-growing giants -- which are exactly the high-asset-growth names this book avoids. (2) The low-growth book is a disguised value-and-distress tilt: shrinking balance sheets belong to utilities, energy write-downs, and companies selling divisions, so the 2014-2015 oil fall hurts it and H30 (growth, healthcare and tech acquirers) wins. (3) It is the buyback book re-dressed: buybacks shrink assets, so L30 may hold many of the shrinking-share-count book's names; the analysis compares their picks month by month. (4) Five years is one regime and about 60 monthly decisions; any gap under 3 points a year is inside the noise. Any of these is a rejection; none is a reason to tune the 365-day window, the band or the book size afterwards.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tested

A well-known finding from 2008 says companies whose total assets (everything on the balance sheet) grew least over the past year go on to beat companies that grew fastest. This method checked that among big US index members. The SEC filings the lab holds only start in 2009, and a balance sheet a year apart exists for most members only from late 2010. So the book picked stocks only from **October 2010 to October 2015**. Before that it simply held SPY, so its twenty-year numbers are SPY's own until 2010.

Four books, all bought monthly in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's monthly top-up:
- **L30**: the 30 members with the lowest asset growth (the idea itself)
- **H30**: the 30 with the highest (the opposite book, which the paper says should lose)
- **L30-PLC**: 30 names drawn blind from the same pool, with the same number of new names each month as L30 (the no-opinion book)
- **L60**: the 60 lowest growers

## Results, October 2010 to October 2015 (deposits taken out)

| book | yearly return | vs SPY (+14.3%) | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| L30, lowest growers | +17.8% | +3.5 pts | 22.9% (2011) |
| H30, highest growers | +17.2% | +2.9 pts | 18.7% (2011) |
| L30-PLC, blind draw | +14.0% | −0.3 pts | 16.2% (2011) |
| L60, 60 lowest | +15.4% | +1.1 pts | 18.8% (2011) |

Year by year, L30 against H30: 2011 −2.1% vs −5.8%, 2012 +19.2% vs +8.6%, 2013 +44.9% vs +43.8%, 2014 +10.3% vs +15.6%, 2015 to October +0.9% vs +15.9%. The low growers won two years and the high growers won the last two.

**The idea predicts L30 well ahead of H30. It was ahead by only 0.6 points a year**, against the 2 or more I wrote down beforehand. The lab's mirror check reads the gap between the two books as "no signal" (+0.07 points a year over the whole window, +0.23 over 2009-2015).

Both extremes beat the blind draw by about 3-4 points a year. That is not asset growth: the same lead shows up whichever way the ranking points. Both extremes hold unusual companies. They fell harder in 2011 and rose harder in 2012-2013, and in a steadily rising market a jumpier book earns more. It is a bet on movement, not on the balance sheet.

## The dead companies take away what was left

The dev store is missing many companies that later died. The survivorship-check store adds most of them back. Re-run there:
- L30's lead over SPY in 2009-2015 drops from **+2.7 to −0.7 points a year**. Over the whole window its yearly money return falls from +8.3% to +6.8%, which is now behind SPY's +7.2%.
- H30 drops much less (2009-2015 lead +2.2 → +1.2), and the blind draw hardly moves (−0.2 → −0.5).

So most of the low-growth book's apparent edge came from shrinking companies that happened to survive. A company whose assets are shrinking is often a company in trouble, and the ones in trouble that went under are exactly the ones missing from the dev store. Critics of the 2008 paper made this objection (missing delisting returns), and here it shows up plainly.

## The gate

- Beats total-return SPY: L30, H30 and L60 pass on the dev store, but only from 2010. On the store with the dead companies, L30 fails.
- Worst fall: all four show 55% because they held SPY through 2008. That fall belongs to SPY, not the picker, but the 50% screen fails on it all the same. The worst fall while picking was 22.9% (L30, 2011), above the 20% go-live limit.
- Luck test (DSR): 0.468 for L30 at N = 174 independent tries, against the 0.90 bar. In plain words, after 174 methods tried, a result this size is about as likely to be luck as not.
- Walk-forward folds: 1 of 4, and the one win went to the blind draw. The hard gate needs a majority of at least four. This method could never have been promoted, and I said so before the run.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis failed: low growers did not beat high growers by 2 points a year (0.6), though L30 did beat the blind draw (by about 3.8 points, see above).
- Expected failure (1), decay, half happened: the asset-growth spread was about zero, but the books did not trail SPY on the dev store.
- (2), a distress tilt, is what the survivorship check found, though not through the oil fall I guessed. The shrinkers that died are the missing piece.
- (3), the buyback book re-dressed, did not happen. In a typical month L30 shared 4.8 of the buyback book's 20 names, and H30 shared 7.5 of the share-issuers' 20. They are related ideas but not the same book.
- (4), five years is one regime, holds: about 60 monthly decisions, and the 0.6-point gap is noise.

## Assumptions I made

Ran with the coverage floor lowered to 0.20, because the filings cover only about 31% of the dev window. Before October 2010 every book held SPY (the same rule the accounts-only picker used). The blind draw is the lab's matched draw. The mirror report does not count it as an always-invested arm because it trades about 2.2 times a year, but it is this book with the opinion removed, and that is how I compare against it.

**My opinion:** Asset growth is dead here. In the only years the lab can see, the low and high growers finished level. The small lead the low growers had over SPY turned negative once the companies that died were put back. I would not spend another id on asset growth or buy older fundamentals for it. The lesson worth acting on is that **both extremes of a balance-sheet ranking beat the blind draw by 3-4 points**. That looks like "unusual, jumpier companies earned more in a rising 2010-2015", not stock-picking skill. The next useful method asks this directly: hold the most volatile index members against the calmest and against the blind draw, on the same frame, and check whether the "extremes win" pattern is just market sensitivity (beta). If it is, the lab has a cheap, general explanation for many near misses that won only in rising years.
methods.verdict: Rejected: low and high asset growers finished level in 2010-2015, and the low growers' small lead over SPY turned negative once the companies that died were put back

methods.name: Cheap companies whose accounts are getting stronger: a financial-health score among the cheapest index members
methods.sourceRef: Piotroski (2000), Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers, Journal of Accounting Research 38 (supplement) 1-41
methods.hypothesis: Published 2000, so the whole dev window is after publication and any edge here survived being known; the lab can only measure it in 2010-2015, where two comparable annual reports exist in the SEC panel for 200-330 index members (measured before the run: 209 on 2010-03-31, 304 on 2011-06-30, 334 on 2015-06-30; 16 at the end of 2009). Piotroski's nine yes/no tests of improving health separate the cheap companies that are recovering from the ones the market has correctly written off. Eight are buildable here: positive profit, positive operating cash flow, rising return on (year-end) assets, cash flow above profit, a rising equity share of assets (the panel has no debt tag, so this stands in for falling leverage), no rise in diluted shares, rising gross margin, rising asset turnover; the current-ratio test is dropped (no current assets or liabilities in the panel) and a test with a missing input is dropped for that company, the score being the fraction passed of those available, at least six. Pool: F4-screened members ($5, $20M a day) with a fiscal year under 16 months old, its prior year visible, positive book equity and a known company size of at least $500M (smaller is a share count in the wrong units), one listing per company. Cheapness is book equity over company size; the cheap third is the frame. Twenty equal slots, monthly, incumbents kept while within the best forty of their arm's order (the buffer stands in for quarterly rebalancing so the fee does not decide). Before the panel scores 150 companies every arm holds SPY, so 1996-2009 is SPY's own curve and the method cannot reach four walk-forward folds: it is not promotable by construction and is run as evidence. Arms: HI20 (the idea), LO20 (the mirror, Piotroski's short leg), R20 (the cheap third in a yearly-redrawn hash order: the opinion-free arm that prices acting on the score), CHEAP20 (cheapest first, no score), HIALL20 (the score over the whole pool, no cheapness). Predictions, fixed now, judged on the recorded monthly curves sliced 2010-04 to 2015-10 against SPY's: (1) HI20 beats LO20 by at least 3 points a year; (2) HI20 beats R20 by at least 2 points a year, so acting on the score pays for its trading; (3) HI20 beats SPY total return over the slice; (4) HI20 beats HIALL20, so the score needs the value frame as the paper says. Success is (1), (2) and (3) together, on the dev store and on the survivorship-check store.
methods.expectedFailure: Four ways, most likely first. (1) Large companies were not the paper's ground. Piotroski's edge lived in small, thinly followed, hard-to-short value stocks, where accounting news reaches the price slowly; index members are covered by dozens of analysts and their 10-Ks are read the day they land, so HI20 and LO20 land within noise of each other. (2) 2010-2015 was a decade in which value lost to growth and cheap stocks as a group trailed SPY, so even a working score lifts HI20 above R20 and CHEAP20 without lifting it above SPY: the frame is the opponent, not the signal. (3) The score is coarse: with six to eight tests it takes a handful of values, so the top twenty is decided as much by the cheapness tie-break as by health, and HI20 drifts toward CHEAP20. (4) Five and a half years is thin: a 3-point gap between two twenty-name books over 66 months is within what luck makes, so even a clean pass on (1)-(3) is suggestive, not proof. Whatever happens, the whole-window row fails the worst-fall screen on SPY's own 2008 fall and the walk-forward gate on folds; that is the construction, not the verdict.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tested

Piotroski's 2000 idea. Take the cheapest third of big US companies, measured as what their accounts
say they own against what the market says they are worth. Then use a simple health check on the last
two annual reports to keep the ones that are getting better. The check is eight yes/no questions:
is it profitable? is cash coming in? is profit rising against its assets? is the profit backed by
cash? is the balance sheet getting safer? did it avoid printing new shares? are margins and sales
per dollar of assets rising? The paper found the healthy cheap stocks beat the sick ones by about
23 points a year in 1976-1996, mostly among small companies.

The lab's SEC filing data only has two comparable annual reports from March 2010 on (about 210
index members then, 330 by 2015). So every arm held SPY until then. The 1996-2009 part of each
curve is SPY's own, and the real test is **April 2010 to October 2015, about five and a half
years**. I said so before the run. These trials are evidence, not candidates. The run also needed
`--allow-coverage 0.30`, because the filing data covers 31.5% of the dev window, below the usual
80% floor. That was a known limit and the hypothesis states it.

Five arms, each holding twenty names in equal slots, at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares,
on the owner's monthly top-up:

- **HI20**: the healthiest companies in the cheap third (the idea)
- **LO20**: the sickest companies in the cheap third (the mirror)
- **R20**: twenty from the cheap third drawn at random once a year (no opinion at all)
- **CHEAP20**: the cheapest twenty, with no health check
- **HIALL20**: the healthiest twenty from all companies, cheap or not

## Results, 2010-04 to 2015-10

Monthly curves with the deposits taken out, compared with the lab's recorded SPY curve:

| arm | a year | vs SPY | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| HI20 (the idea) | 12.5% | −0.0 | 20.4% |
| LO20 (mirror) | 9.6% | −3.0 | 21.4% |
| R20 (no opinion) | 12.1% | −0.5 | 21.2% |
| CHEAP20 | 9.3% | −3.2 | 30.9% |
| HIALL20 | 13.7% | +1.2 | 12.8% |
| SPY | 12.6% | — | 16.1% |

Year by year, HI20 minus LO20 was −6.5, +1.4, +12.3, +10.4, −1.3 and +2.8 points (2010-2015).
HI20 minus R20 was −7.8, −4.4, +6.0, +7.9, −0.9 and +3.9. Two good years, 2012 and 2013, carry
the whole gap.

**The predictions I wrote before the run:**

1. HI20 beats LO20 by at least 3 points a year. It beat it by **2.9**. Missed, barely.
2. HI20 beats R20 by at least 2 points a year, which would show acting on the score pays for its
   trading. It beat it by **0.4**. **Failed.**
3. HI20 beats SPY over the slice. It **tied** SPY, 12.5% against 12.6%. **Failed.**
4. HI20 beats HIALL20. It lost by **1.2**. **Failed.** The health check did better *without* the
   cheapness filter, which is the opposite of what the paper says.

Success needed (1), (2) and (3) together. None of the three held.

**On the survivorship-check store**, which puts back most of the companies that later died, every
arm earns less. HI20's 2009-2015 lead goes from +0.2 to −1.2 points a year. HIALL20, the one arm
that looked good, goes from +1.0 to **−1.3**. Every arm trails SPY there.

## The lab's own checks (whole 1996-2015 window, by construction)

- Every arm's worst fall is 55%, which is SPY's own 2008 crash. The arms were holding SPY then, so
  the drawdown screen fails for all of them. That comes from the construction, not the idea.
- Luck check (DSR, the chance the result is skill rather than luck after the lab's tries) at
  N = 176 independent methods: 0.33 to 0.44, against the 0.90 bar. All fail.
- Walk-forward: 1 of 4 folds on the dev store and 0 of 4 on the check store. The three early folds
  are SPY against SPY, so this was never going to pass.
- Status: rejected.

## Why

- **Big companies are watched too closely.** Piotroski's edge was in small, thinly followed value
  stocks, where good news in the accounts takes months to reach the price. Index members' annual
  reports are read the day they come out. The health check still sorts a little: high beat low by
  2.9 points. But most of that is luck-sized over 66 months, and it does not pay for trading on it
  (HI20 against R20 is only +0.4).
- **The cheap third was the opponent.** 2010-2015 was a bad stretch for value. Simply buying the
  cheapest twenty (CHEAP20) lost 3.2 points a year to SPY and fell 31% at its worst, because the
  cheapest big companies then were insurers, banks and energy names. The health check pulled HI20
  back to even with SPY, but it could not overcome the frame. This was expected failure (2), and it
  happened.
- **The health check without cheapness looked better, until the dead companies came back.**
  HIALL20 is close to a profitable-and-improving quality screen. It led SPY by 1.2 points with a
  smaller fall on the dev store. On the store with the dead companies restored, that turned into a
  1.3-point loss. Part of its edge was the missing failures.
- **The score is coarse.** With six to eight tests, the score takes about 15 values, and within a
  value the cheapness tie-break decides. That is expected failure (3). HI20's picks lean toward the
  cheapest healthy names, mostly financials.

## Data notes

Stryker's 2013 share count is filed in the wrong units (378 shares), which made it look 350,000
times cheaper than it was. I caught this before pre-registering and excluded any member worth under
$500M. The panel has no debt or current-asset tags, so two of Piotroski's nine tests could not be
built as written. One was replaced by a proxy (equity's share of assets) and one was dropped.

## My opinion

This direction is closed for big companies. The health check sorts cheap stocks a little, but not
by enough to pay for trading on it or to beat SPY, and the one arm that looked good lost its edge
once the dead companies came back. I would not run another Piotroski variant on index members. The
one thing worth keeping is a question: does a quality screen (profitable, improving, cash-backed)
help *inside a book that already holds the market's big names*, as a tilt rather than a
replacement? That avoids betting against SPY's big-company drift, which is what sank the cheap
third. I am queueing it with a 2009-2015 and check-store-first bar. I expect it to land within a
point of SPY.
methods.verdict: Picking the healthiest of the cheapest big companies only tied SPY over 2010-2015, barely beat a random pick from the same cheap group, and fell behind SPY once failed companies were put back

methods.name: Earnings news confirmed twice: take a large-for-the-stock earnings-day jump only when the company's reported earnings also beat the same quarter last year
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0072-Z2-RAWRANK; Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok (1996), Momentum strategies, J. Finance 51(5); Bernard & Thomas (1989), J. Accounting Research 27; Foster, Olsen & Shevlin (1984), The Accounting Review 59
methods.hypothesis: Published 1984-1996 (the earnings surprise and the price reaction as separate drifts) and 2008 (the earnings-day jump), so the dev window can only show an edge from after the crowd knew it. M0072-Z2-RAWRANK beat SPY on dev (+12.3% a year vs +7.2% on the owner's deposits, luck score 0.914) and beat SPY in 2009-2015, failing only the worst fall (23.8%). Its signal is the price reaction alone.
