Adding the accounts' own reading of the quarter -- standardised unexpected earnings from SEC EDGAR diluted EPS (this quarter minus the same quarter a year earlier, over the spread of up to eight earlier such changes), gated on the filing date and matched to the jump as the newest quarter that ended before the jump day, counted only if it was filed no more than 5 days before the jump -- should keep the jumps that are really earnings news and drop the ones the earnings contradict. EDGAR's XBRL starts in 2009 and a surprise needs nine quarters, so the filter can act only from about 2011; this runs knowingly below the 80% panel-coverage floor (lab run --allow-coverage) and is judged on 2012-2015, where the arms differ, against the control in the same years. Four arms on M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's frame exactly (monthly, 20 slots of 5%, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's monthly deposits): OFF (the parent's book, panel never read: the no-opinion arm, a re-run that should reproduce the parent's recorded trial), VETO (drop a jump only when its quarter is known and negative; unknown passes, so identical to OFF before ~2011), CONFIRMED (keep only known-and-positive; before ~2011 the book is SPY behind the switch) and CONTRADICTED (the mirror: keep only known-and-negative). I expect CONFIRMED > VETO > OFF > CONTRADICTED on the 2012-2015 book return. Success for the idea: VETO beats OFF in 2012-2015 and CONFIRMED beats CONTRADICTED there; success for the gate: a variant with worst fall under the screen, beating total-return SPY, DSR >= 0.90.
methods.expectedFailure: The gate will very likely reject every arm on the 1998 fall, which no earnings filter can touch (no panel before 2009): VETO inherits OFF's 23.8%, and CONFIRMED is SPY behind the switch for fifteen years, so it will not beat SPY over the whole window. The real question lives in about four years, with perhaps 20-40 live jumps a month, so the difference between arms may be within noise. Most big up-gaps on heavy volume in large caps are earnings beats already, so CONTRADICTED may hold only a handful of names and VETO may barely differ from OFF. The 10-Q often arrives weeks after the release, so on many pick dates the quarter is still unknown; CONFIRMED then waits a month to buy, losing the early part of the drift the jump book lives on. The year-on-year surprise is a crude stand-in for the analyst consensus the price actually reacted to, and a published anomaly, so even a clean 2012-2015 win may have faded since.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tried

The parent book (the "news-day" book, M0072-Z2-RAWRANK) buys big stocks right after a day that looks like an earnings report: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal volume, a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's, and a jump that was large for that stock's normal swing. Up to 20 names at 5% each, the rest in SPY, cash while SPY is under its 200-day average, re-picked monthly. Its signal is the price move alone.

The idea: a price jump on a busy day might be earnings, or it might be a takeover rumour, an upgrade or a product launch. The company's own filed accounts give a second, independent reading of the same quarter. So for every jump I looked up the quarter it reported in SEC filings and asked: did diluted earnings per share beat the same quarter a year earlier, by more than is usual for this company? (This is "standardised unexpected earnings": the year-on-year change in EPS divided by how much that change normally wobbles over the last two years.) A jump the accounts agree with is news confirmed twice; one they contradict is a price move the earnings don't explain.

How a quarter is matched to a jump: on each pick date, take the newest quarter in the filings that ended before the jump day, and count it only if it was filed no more than 5 days before the jump (an older filing was already old news on the day). Anything else is "unknown", never a sign.

Four arms, fixed before any result, all on the parent's exact frame (fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's 5M IDR monthly deposits):

- **OFF**: the parent's book, earnings never read. The no-opinion arm.
- **VETO**: drop a jump only when its quarter is known and the earnings fell short. Unknown passes.
- **CONFIRMED**: keep a jump only when its quarter is known and the earnings beat.
- **CONTRADICTED**: the mirror. Keep only jumps whose earnings fell short.

**The data limit, stated up front.** The SEC's machine-readable filings start in 2009, and a surprise needs nine quarters of history, so the filter can only act from about 2011. The lab's coverage check refused the run at 31.5% coverage (the floor is 80%), and I ran it knowingly with the floor lowered to 30%, as pre-registered. Before 2011, VETO is the same book as OFF, and CONFIRMED and CONTRADICTED are SPY behind the 200-day switch. **The real test is 2012-2015**, about four years.

How often was there a reading? Sampling four pick dates a year, a pick date had about 40 live jumps. In 2012-2015 about 45% had no matched quarter (not an earnings day, or the filing not out yet), about 37% were confirmed and about 18% contradicted. So all three filtered arms held real names.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015)

| arm | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OFF | +12.3% | +7.2% | 23.8% | 1.98 | 0.919 | passes |
| VETO | +11.1% | +7.2% | 23.8% | 1.79 | 0.887 | fails luck bar |
| CONFIRMED | +8.0% | +7.2% | 18.9% | 2.34 | 0.801 | fails luck bar |
| CONTRADICTED | +8.7% | +7.2% | 18.9% | 4.36 | 0.848 | fails luck bar |

OFF reproduces the parent's recorded trial exactly (same return, same trades), which confirms the frame is the parent's and that the earnings plumbing changes nothing when it is switched off. It is "eligible" only because it **is** the parent's book under a new name: it adds no new evidence, and the method should not be promoted on it. The walk-forward check (pick a variant knowing only the past, score it on the next three years) won 1 fold of 4, because it kept picking a filtered arm. `lab promote` refuses anything under a majority, so M0277 cannot be promoted.

The luck score is judged at N = 175 (one look per distinct method in the lab), against the 0.90 bar. Only OFF clears it, and OFF is the parent.

The worst fall for OFF and VETO is the parent's 1998 fall, which no earnings filter can touch (there is no data before 2009). CONFIRMED and CONTRADICTED fall 18.9% because for 15 years they are SPY with the switch.

## The years that decide it: book return without deposits

| | OFF (no opinion) | VETO | CONFIRMED | CONTRADICTED |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2012 | +9.6% | +0.7% | +4.9% | +16.3% |
| 2013 | +39.8% | +43.2% | +32.5% | +26.5% |
| 2014 | +14.4% | +11.9% | +6.8% | +11.3% |
| 2015 (to Oct) | +1.0% | -4.6% | -3.3% | -4.4% |
| **2012-2015 a year** | **+16.1%** | **+11.9%** | **+9.9%** | **+12.4%** |
| 2009-2015 lead over SPY a year | +2.3 | -0.4 | -7.2 | -5.8 |

I expected CONFIRMED > VETO > OFF > CONTRADICTED. The order came out **OFF > CONTRADICTED > VETO > CONFIRMED**, nearly reversed.

- **Throwing out the contradicted jumps cost money.** VETO against OFF: -3.6 points a year over 2012-2015, worse in 30 of 46 months and better in 14. That is about two standard errors (t = -2.0, and -2.1 over 2010-2015), the strongest number in this run. On 2009-2015 it turned the parent's lead over SPY (+2.3 points) into a small loss (-0.4).
- **Confirmed against contradicted is a coin flip.** Contradicted-only beat confirmed-only by 2.3 points a year in 2012-2015, but at t = 0.9, with 22 better months and 22 worse. The sign of the accounting surprise tells you nothing about which jump drifts further.
- Both narrow books held few names (on average about 3 confirmed and 1.5 contradicted over the window, more in 2012-2015) and lagged SPY in 2009-2015 even with the parked money removed, so neither is a book worth having.

## Why

The price jump already *is* the better surprise measure. A three-day jump on triple volume is the market's reaction to the gap between the news and what it expected: analyst forecasts, guidance, the margin story. The year-on-year EPS change is a crude stand-in for that expectation. A company whose earnings are still below last year's but far better than feared jumps on the news and keeps drifting, and the year-on-year measure calls that jump "contradicted". Vetoing it throws away exactly the kind of surprise that matters most: a turnaround the accounts don't show yet. The veto also adds churn: a name bought on its jump can be sold a month later when its 10-Q arrives with a weak year-on-year number (VETO made 45 more trades than OFF).

The academic result (price reaction and earnings surprise each carry their own drift) was measured on all stocks, mostly small ones, and before 1996. In large index members in 2012-2015, with the crude year-on-year surprise, the second signal adds nothing and the filter built on it subtracts.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: confirming the jump with the accounts did not help, and vetoing contradicted jumps hurt. The expected failure was right on several counts: the gate rejected the filtered arms, the deciding window was only four years and the confirmed-versus-contradicted gap was inside the noise. It was wrong that VETO would barely differ from OFF: it differed, in the wrong direction. Pre-registered success needed VETO > OFF and CONFIRMED > CONTRADICTED in 2012-2015; neither happened.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

This is the third attempt to improve the news-day book's picks: the volatility brake (M0066), the own-swing filter (M0072) and now the earnings check. The own-swing filter helped a little; the earnings check hurts. The parent is still the best version of this family, and its only failing is the 1998 fall, which is about the safety switch, not the picks.

**My opinion:** stop trying to filter the news-day book's picks with accounting data. The price reaction already contains the surprise, and a year-on-year EPS number is a worse copy of it. The clean result here, that vetoing on the accounts loses about 3.6 points a year at two standard errors, is worth keeping as a lesson: a second signal that measures the same thing worse dilutes the first. The productive direction for this family is still the one M0072 named: keep the picks exactly and fix the 1998 fall with a faster safety exit. One different use of the accounts might be worth one more method: take jumps on days the accounts call unknown (no matched quarter), since those are the non-earnings news days, and test whether they drift as well as earnings jumps. That separates "earnings news" from "any news" directly, which this run could not.


### 2026-10-22

## Coordinator's note (Sera, 2026-10-22): no test look

The only arm that cleared the dev screen is the unfiltered control, which is the parent book re-run unchanged: identical return, identical trades. It adds no new evidence, so spending a test-window look on it would be spending it on the parent under a new name. Its walk-forward record is also 1 of 4 periods, and the gate needs a strict majority of at least four, so the promotion step would refuse it anyway. Every filtered arm, which is the idea this method was about, failed the luck bar. Not promoted.
methods.verdict: Checking each earnings-day jump against the company's filed earnings made the book worse (about 3.6 points a year lost in 2012-2015); only the unchanged parent book passed, so nothing new to promote

methods.name: Jumpy versus calm index members: is 'both ends of a ranking win' just market sensitivity?
methods.sourceRef: Black, Jensen & Scholes (1972); Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) Betting Against Beta, JFE 111(1); Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006) idiosyncratic volatility; lab M0275
methods.hypothesis: Published 1972 (flat beta-return line) and 2014 (betting against beta), so the dev window 1996-2015 is long after the first and mostly before the second. In M0275 the 30 lowest and 30 highest asset growers both beat a matched blind draw by 3-4 points a year over 2010-2015 and finished 0.6 points apart: the ranking carried no signal and the lead came, the hypothesis says, from holding unusual, more market-sensitive names in a rising market. Signal: each month, for each index member with a bar, beta to SPY and daily volatility over SPY's last 252 sessions (at least 200 paired daily returns), one listing per company. Arms: HB30 (30 highest beta), LB30 (30 lowest beta), HB30-PLC (HB30's size and monthly entry count drawn blind from the same pool: the no-opinion arm), HV30 and LV30 (30 highest and lowest volatility). Equal slots, monthly, fully invested, no switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Predictions written before any result, on de-funded monthly returns: HB30 beats HB30-PLC in 2003-2007 and in 2009-2015 and loses to it in 2000-2002 and in 2008, ending within 2 points a year of it over 1996-2015 with a worst fall at least 15 points deeper; LB30's worst fall is the shallowest of the five and its twenty-year return is within 2 points a year of HB30's; the volatility arms tell the same story as the beta arms. If HB30 leads the placebo by 3 points or more in 2009-2015, the lab's near misses that led SPY there are suspect of a high-beta lean.
methods.expectedFailure: Nobody expects an eligible arm here; the method is a diagnostic. Ways the prediction itself can fail: (1) the jumpy end does not win 2009-2015 at all -- the 2011 and 2015 sell-offs and the long rally of the calm, dividend-paying names in 2011-2014 favoured low beta, so the 'unusual names in a rising market' story for M0275 would be wrong and its both-ends lead needs another explanation; (2) the high-beta book is dominated by the 1999-2000 technology bubble and its collapse, so its twenty-year number is one episode, not a property; (3) LB30 beats the placebo by a wide margin before 2009 and nothing after (the low-risk anomaly was crowded once Frazzini-Pedersen and the low-volatility ETFs arrived in 2011-2014) -- a published anomaly fading; (4) all arms trail SPY on the owner's deposits through fees on 30 equal slots and the equal-weight lean against the big-company drift. None is a reason to tune the 252-session window or the book size.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What this was for

The asset-growth picker (M0275) had a puzzle: its 30 slowest-growing companies and its 30
fastest-growing companies *both* beat a blind draw of 30 names from the same pool by 3-4 points a
year in 2010-2015. When both ends of a ranking win, the ranking is not what paid. This method
tested the suspicion that what both ends shared was **market sensitivity** ("beta": how hard a
stock moves when the market moves; beta 1.5 means it tends to move 1.5% when SPY moves 1%).
It sorted index members on their last year's beta, and on their last year's day-to-day swings
(volatility), and held each end beside a blind draw. Nobody expected an arm to qualify; it was a
diagnostic.

## The answer to the question: yes, it was market sensitivity

Measured on M0275's own monthly results, October 2010 to October 2015 (deposits removed):

| book | moved with SPY (beta) | extra return a year once that is allowed for |
|---|---|---|
| asset growth, slowest 30 | 1.19 | +0.7% |
| asset growth, fastest 30 | 1.05 | +2.0% |
| blind draw of 30 | 0.92 | +0.8% |

SPY averaged about 14% a year in those months. A book that moves 1.19 times the market, against a
draw that moves 0.92 times it, earns about (1.19 - 0.92) x 14 = 3.8 points more just by leaning
into a rising market -- which is the whole of the slow-growers' lead. Once the lean is taken out,
they did what a random 30 did. The fast-growers keep about a point, well inside the noise of five
years. **M0275's "both ends win" was a bet on the market going up, dressed as a stock pick.**

## The five arms (1996-2015, real Gotrade fees, the owner's 5M IDR a month)

Yearly growth with deposits removed, and worst fall from a peak on the same basis:

| arm | 1996-99 | 2000-02 | 2003-07 | 2008 | 2009-15 | 20 years | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPY with dividends | +25.4% | -14.4% | +12.5% | -36.4% | +14.9% | +7.9% | 50% |
| 30 jumpiest by beta (HB30) | +39.7% | -22.9% | +19.9% | -46.0% | +21.6% | +11.5% | 72% |
| 30 calmest by beta (LB30) | +9.9% | +4.5% | +19.9% | -22.7% | +14.4% | +11.1% | 29% |
| blind draw (HB30-PLC) | +15.1% | +0.9% | +17.1% | -35.1% | +14.1% | +9.7% | 50% |
| 30 most volatile (HV30) | +29.1% | -19.4% | +31.9% | -50.7% | +29.4% | +15.1% | 69% |
| 30 least volatile (LV30) | +5.6% | +8.0% | +9.6% | -18.6% | +12.8% | +8.0% | 30% |

On the owner's deposits (money-weighted, the way the owner would feel it) every arm earned more
than the same deposits in SPY (+7.2% a year): HB30 +10.1%, LB30 +10.8%, the draw +8.6%, HV30
+15.1%, LV30 +8.3%.

**Every arm was rejected.** The gate's conditions:
- The jumpy arms broke the dev screen's 50% fall limit: HB30 fell 77% at its worst (funded),
  HV30 74%, even the blind draw 56%. All of it is 2000-2002 and 2008.
- The luck test (DSR: how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries) was
  judged at N = 178 distinct methods against the bar of 0.90. LB30 came closest at **0.892**,
  just under; LV30 0.751; HB30 0.411; HV30 0.576; the draw 0.581.
- LB30's fall was 34% funded, 29% with deposits removed -- inside the dev screen, but well
  above the 25% the owner's real-money bar allows.

## Did the predictions hold?

- *HB30 beats the draw in 2003-07 and 2009-15, loses it in 2000-02 and 2008, ends within 2 points
  of it with a worst fall 15+ points deeper*: **held on every count.** +2.8 and +7.5 points in the
  rising stretches, -23.8 and -10.9 in the falls, +1.8 a year over twenty years, worst fall 22
  points deeper.
- *LB30's twenty years within 2 points of HB30's*: **held** (11.1% against 11.5%). This is the
  old finding of Black, Jensen and Scholes: the calmest stocks earned as much as the jumpiest with
  less than half the fall. LB30 moved only 0.38 times the market yet earned an extra 8% a year
  over what that sensitivity alone would give -- the long side of "betting against beta".
- *LB30 has the shallowest fall of the five*: held, barely (29% against LV30's 30%).
- *Volatility tells the same story as beta*: **only half.** The calm volatility arm matched the
  calm beta arm on falls, but HV30 beat HB30 by 3.6 points a year over twenty years and by 8
  points in 2009-15 -- its 2003 (+135%), 2009 (+91%) and 2013 (+60%) are rebounds of beaten-down
  names. That is lottery-like recovery, not beta, and it is exactly where the missing dead
  companies matter most (see the survivorship check below).
- *If HB30 leads the draw by 3+ points in 2009-15, the lab's near misses are suspect*: it led by
  7.5 points. **The warning fires.** But it fires through one year: 2009's +73% against +33%.
  From 2010 to 2015 HB30 earned 14% a year against the draw's 11% and SPY's 13%, with a 2011 of
  -16% -- and over October 2010 to October 2015, after allowing for its beta of 1.73, it was 9.6 points a year *behind* where its
  sensitivity should have put it.
- Expected failure (3), the low-risk effect fading after 2011: **did not happen.** LB30's extra
  return after allowing for its low beta was 9.6% a year in 2009-15, higher than over the whole
  window. What it did not do is beat SPY: its return in 2009-2015 (+14.4% a year) trailed SPY
  (+14.9%) because a book that moves 0.3 times a market rising 15% a year starts 10 points behind.

## Why

A stock's beta is mostly what kind of business it is: banks, chip makers, homebuilders and
miners swing with the economy; utilities, food and drug companies and REITs do not. Holding the
30 jumpiest is a leveraged bet on the economy that the owner cannot otherwise make (no margin at
Gotrade) -- and the market does not pay for that leverage fairly: the jumpy book earned no more
over twenty years than the calm one. The calm book wins in falls and loses in rallies, and with
2009-2015 being one long rally, it drifted level with SPY there. Both lessons are thirty and
fifty years old; the lab's dev window reproduces them cleanly.

The useful lesson is about the lab, not the market: **any equal-slot stock book whose beta is
above the blind draw's will look like it has skill in 2009-2015**, because that era rose 15% a
year with only small dips. M0275 was one such book. The walk-forward gave LB30 three folds of
four; the one it lost was 2012-2014, a calm rally.

## Survivorship

The dev store is missing about half the index members of the 1990s, mostly the companies that
later died. Re-running every arm on the survivorship-check store (the same prices plus most of
the dead companies) changes the story for the jumpy books, as feared, and not for the calm ones.
Money-weighted yearly return on the owner's deposits, against SPY's +7.2%:

| arm | dev store | with the dead companies | worst fall (funded) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 jumpiest by beta | +10.1% | **+3.7%** | 77% -> **93%** |
| 30 calmest by beta | +10.8% | +12.8% | 34% -> 35% |
| blind draw | +8.6% | +11.8% | 56% -> 57% |
| 30 most volatile | +15.1% | **+10.4%** | 74% -> **85%** |
| 30 least volatile | +8.3% | +8.2% | 35% -> 37% |

The jumpy books' twenty-year record was partly the missing dead companies: the stocks that swing
hardest are the ones most likely to go bust, and a store without them only ever shows the
survivors' rebounds. With them back, the high-beta book trails SPY by 3.5 points a year and
falls 93% at its worst -- and its luck score drops from 0.41 to 0.16. The most volatile book loses
5 points a year. The calm books barely move.

LB30's luck score on the check store is 0.920, above the 0.90 bar, but this is not evidence for
it: the check store is a cross-check and never a gate, its return series there carries a few
extreme single days (skew rose from 0.5 to 4.2), which flatters the luck score's formula, its
2009-2015 shortfall against SPY on the report's own measure went from 2.6 to 3.0 points a year, and its walk-forward record fell
from 3 of 4 folds to 1 of 4.

## Mirror pairs

`lab dressing` reads HB30 against LB30 as "no signal": over twenty years they finish 0.2
points apart on prices, which is the flat-beta-line finding itself. The habit cost is unpriced by
that report because its opinion-free arm must trade almost never, and this method's blind draw
trades as often as the book it controls (that was its purpose: to price the churn, not to remove
it). The blind draw against HB30 is the pricing that matters here: the beta opinion was worth
+1.8 points a year for 22 more points of fall.

## My opinion:

The question is answered and the answer is useful: the asset-growth "both ends" lead was market
sensitivity, and the lab should stop crediting any 2009-2015 lead before checking the book's beta
against its blind draw. I would build that into the lab as a report rather than spend method ids
on more beta sorts: the jumpy end is dead as a strategy (no extra return, falls of 70%), and the
calm end, though it earns a real extra return per unit of risk, cannot beat SPY in a rising
decade without leverage the owner does not have. The one direction worth a single more method is
the calm book *as a partner for SPY* -- half calm stocks, half SPY -- which keeps the calm book's
extra return while moving roughly 0.7 times the market; I expect it to tie SPY in 2009-2015 with
a much shallower 2008, which would make it a candidate on falls, not on return. The most volatile
arm's big number is the one I trust least, and the survivorship check above is why.
methods.verdict: The calm and the jumpy index members earned about the same over twenty years; the jumpy ones fell three times as far and lost to SPY once dead companies were counted. The asset-growth picker's 2010-2015 lead was this lean, not skill.

methods.name: Non-earnings news days: take a large-for-the-stock jump only when no earnings filing explains it
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0277 / M0072-Z2-RAWRANK; Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam (2008), SSRN 909563; Chan (2003), Stock price reaction to news and no-news, J. Financial Economics 70
methods.hypothesis: Published 2003 (news days drift, no-news days reverse) and 2008 (the earnings-day jump), so the dev window can only show an edge from after the crowd knew it. M0277 found the sign of the year-on-year earnings surprise adds nothing to the news-day book, and that about 45% of 2012-2015's live jumps had no matching earnings filing. If the jumps no earnings report explains drift as well as the earnings jumps, the book's edge is a slow reaction to any big news, not post-earnings drift, and the earnings data is not needed. Two splits, each a mirror pair beside the unchanged book (OFF, the no-opinion arm, M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's frame exactly: monthly, 20 slots of 5%, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's monthly deposits). FILED/UNFILED: a jump is filed when the newest fiscal period that ended before it was first reported to the SEC between 5 days before and 45 days after the jump; unfiled when that period was reported outside that span and no newer quarter was pending (the period ended at most 100 days before the jump); the company must have filed something 100+ days before the jump; otherwise unknown and dropped from both. EDGAR's XBRL starts in 2009, so this pair is SPY behind the switch until about 2010 and is judged on 2011-2015; it runs knowingly below the 80% panel-coverage floor (lab run --allow-coverage 0.30, as M0277 did). SEASON/OFFSEASON: price only, the whole window: a jump is in season when the stock had a session at 2x its 60-day median volume within 7 sessions of the same point 1, 2, 3 and 4 quarters earlier in at least three of the four, off season in at most one, unknown at two. I expect UNFILED and OFFSEASON to drift about as well as their mirrors (within 2 points a year of each other on the book return), which would say the edge is any news. Success for the idea: OFFSEASON's 1997-2015 book return within 2 points a year of SEASON's or better, and UNFILED's 2011-2015 within 2 points of FILED's or better; success for the gate: a variant with worst fall under the screen, beating total-return SPY, DSR >= 0.90.
methods.expectedFailure: OFF is the parent's book again (it should reproduce M0277-OFF) and inherits the 1998 fall of 23.8%; every arm that keeps a subset of the parent's jumps likely falls about as far in 1998 and holds fewer names, so the gate may reject them all on the worst fall or the luck bar. Chan (2003) found news-less big moves reverse, and an off-season gap on heavy volume in a big company is often a takeover bid (a one-off jump with no drift after it) or an index-inclusion day, so OFFSEASON may drift less, not as well. Only roughly one jump in four may be off season, so OFFSEASON may hold few names and be mostly SPY; the price calendar is a proxy and will misfile companies that moved their report date. The filing split is judged on about five years with perhaps 15-25 live jumps a pick date per arm, so its difference may be inside the noise; the 45-day match window can call a deal announced in the first weeks after a quarter end an earnings jump. A published anomaly, so even a clean win may have faded since.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tried

The parent book (the "news-day" book, M0072-Z2-RAWRANK, re-run inside M0277 as its OFF arm) buys big stocks right after a day that looks like big news: a jump at the open on at least 3 times normal volume, a three-day gain at least 4 points better than SPY's, and a jump that was large for that stock's normal swing. Up to 20 names at 5% each, the rest in SPY, cash while SPY is under its 200-day average, re-picked monthly.

M0277 showed that the sign of the earnings surprise does not help pick among these jumps. This method asks the next question: **does it matter whether the news was an earnings report at all?** If jumps on other news (upgrades, deals, product days) drift as well as earnings jumps, the book's edge is a slow reaction to any big news, and the earnings data is not needed.

Two independent ways to split the jumps, each with its mirror, beside the unchanged book (fixed before any result):

- **OFF**: the unchanged book. The no-opinion arm.
- **FILED / UNFILED** (SEC filings, usable from about 2010): a jump is "filed" when the company's newest quarter that ended before the jump was first reported to the SEC between 5 days before and 45 days after the jump. "Unfiled" when that quarter had been reported earlier and no newer quarter was still waiting to be reported: a news day in the middle of the quarter. Anything else is unknown and left out of both. Before about 2010 both arms are SPY behind the 200-day switch. Ran knowingly below the panel-coverage floor (31.5%, allowed at 0.30), as M0277 did.
- **SEASON / OFFSEASON** (price only, the whole window): big companies report in the same weeks every year and leave volume spikes. A jump is "in season" when the stock had a session at 2x its normal volume near the same date 1, 2, 3 and 4 quarters earlier in at least three of the four; "off season" in at most one; unknown at two.

Assumption written down before the run: the thresholds were set a priori; a count-only check (no returns) before the commit showed both splits hold names and agree with each other (86% of filed jumps read in season; 63% of unfiled jumps read off season).

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, the owner's monthly deposits, Gotrade's real fees, fractional shares)

| arm | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OFF | +12.3% | +7.2% | 23.8% | 1.98 | 0.920 | passes (the parent again) |
| FILED | +8.4% | +7.2% | 24.9% | 1.91 | 0.793 | fails luck bar |
| UNFILED | +9.3% | +7.2% | 18.9% | 3.66 | 0.874 | fails luck bar |
| SEASON | +9.1% | +7.2% | 27.6% | 1.65 | 0.817 | fails luck bar |
| OFFSEASON | +7.3% | +7.2% | 19.1% | 2.19 | 0.723 | fails luck bar |

The luck score (how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries) is judged at N = 179 looks, against the 0.90 bar. Only OFF clears it, and OFF reproduces M0277-OFF and the parent exactly (same return, same 1,208 trades): no new evidence. Walk-forward (pick an arm knowing only the past, score it on the next three years) won 2 of 4 periods, not a majority, so the promotion gate would refuse it anyway.

## Book return without deposits

| | OFF | FILED | UNFILED | SEASON | OFFSEASON |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1997-2015 a year | +12.3% | +8.9% | +9.6% | +10.0% | +7.7% |
| 1997-2008 a year | +8.9% | (SPY only) | (SPY only) | +9.0% | +6.8% |
| 2009-2015 a year | +18.5% | +9.9% | +11.9% | +11.8% | +9.5% |
| 2011-2015 a year | +12.7% | +8.0% | +10.8% | +6.4% | +7.3% |

**The two halves of each split are about equal.**

- Unfiled minus filed, 2011-2015: +2.4 points a year (t = 0.7, better in 30 of 58 months). The non-earnings news days did *at least* as well as the earnings days.
- Off season minus in season, 1997-2015: -2.5 points a year (t = -1.2); in 2011-2015 +0.5 (t = 0.15). Within noise.

Pre-registered success for the idea needed both gaps within 2 points or better. The filing split met it. The calendar split missed it by half a point over the whole window, at a t of about -1. My reading: the label "earnings or not" does not separate jumps that drift from jumps that don't. Chan (2003)'s worry, that news-less moves reverse, did not show up here: these are all news days, earnings or not.

**But every narrowed arm lost to the whole book.** Against OFF, per year:

- FILED -4.3 points in 2011-2015 (t = -2.3); UNFILED -1.9 (t = -0.6)
- SEASON -5.7 in 2011-2015 (t = -3.1) and -2.3 over 1997-2015; OFFSEASON -4.8 over 1997-2015 (t = -2.1)

## Why

The exposure report (re-runs, no trial) shows what each arm actually held. OFF asked for 13.6 names on average; FILED 4.5, UNFILED 2.1, OFFSEASON 4.8, SEASON 11.9. Every filter shrinks the pool and the empty slots go to SPY. In 2009-2015 the parent's own picks led SPY by about 2 points a year, so swapping picks for SPY costs money. The narrowed books' own picks also did worse than SPY there (FILED -10, UNFILED -11, OFFSEASON -13 points a year on the picks alone), so the smaller pools were not even better picks, just fewer.

One thing I cannot fully explain: SEASON kept 12 of 13.6 names and still lost 6 points a year in 2009-2015 at t = -3. The jumps it dropped were the off-season ones *and* the in-between ones (two of four past quarters spiking). Off-season alone was weak, so the strength seems to sit in the in-between group, or in which names held their slots first. This is one split of the pool, found after the fact; I would not build on it without a fresh pre-registration.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis (non-earnings news drifts as well as earnings news) held on the filing split and nearly held on the calendar split. The expected failure was right that the gate would reject the narrowed arms, and that they would hold few names and be mostly SPY. It was wrong that off-season jumps would be weaker because they are takeovers: they were about as good as in-season jumps over the 2011-2015 years.

## Compared with the parent

Six arms across M0277 and M0279 have now tried to keep only part of the news-day book's jumps: by the sign of the earnings surprise, by whether a filing explains the jump, and by the reporting calendar. All six lost to the unfiltered book. The parent remains the best version; its only failing is the 1998 fall (23.8%), which is about the safety switch, not the picks.

**My opinion:** stop slicing the news-day book's jump pool. Two methods and six arms say the same thing: the drift is about big news of any kind, and the book's value is in holding as many of those jumps as it can find, not in choosing which ones. The useful lesson runs the other way: if non-earnings news drifts too, the pool should be *widened*, not narrowed. The next try should loosen the event (for example a lower volume bar, 2x instead of 3x, so more mid-quarter news days qualify) and keep everything else, to see whether a fuller book of news days beats the 13-name one. The 1998 fall still needs its own fix (a faster safety exit), separately from the picks.


### 2026-10-22

### Sera 20261022-1954: not promoted

Sera's decision: no test-window look. The only eligible arm, M0279-OFF, is the parent news-day book re-run unchanged (same return, same 1,208 trades as M0277-OFF and M0072-Z2-RAWRANK), so it carries no new evidence, and its walk-forward record is 2 of 4 folds, which the hard gate refuses (it needs a majority of at least four). Nothing was attempted around the gate.
methods.verdict: Jumps on non-earnings news drifted about as well as earnings jumps, but every filtered book lost to the unfiltered one; only the unchanged parent book passed, so nothing new to promote

methods.name: A quality tilt on the market itself: hold the big companies, but lean toward those whose accounts are improving
methods.hypothesis: M0276 found the account-health check sorts big companies a little (healthy beat sick by 2.9 points a year in 2010-2015) but a cheap-stock frame cost more than the check earned, and a check-only twenty-name book (HIALL20) led SPY by 1.2 on the dev store and lost 1.3 once dead companies were restored. The expensive part was leaving SPY's big-company shape. So keep it: hold the largest index members by company size (capped weights, M0047's ceiling), and tilt each weight up or down by the health score, never dropping a name, with low turnover because the score moves once a year. Judge on 2010-2015 de-funded against SPY and on the survivorship-check store first; arms with the tilt on, off (plain size-weighted core), and reversed. Expected to land within a point of SPY; published 2000, crowded.

methods.name: Lean with the rate trend: a market-shaped book that tilts toward bond-like stocks while 10-year yields are falling and toward rate-rising stocks while they are rising
methods.sourceRef: M0224 (bond-like lean on the whole-market core) and its analysis; M0197 (weekly 10-year yield loading); D.E. Shaw research note on Treasury beta (caia.org/node/6853); Maio & Santa-Clara; Driessen, Kuiper & Beilo
methods.hypothesis: Treasury-beta pricing published in the 2010s; the rate-trend read is decades old. M0224's bond-like lean beat its opposite by 0.6 points a year over 1996-2015 (0.8 on the check store) but reversed in 2009-2015 (opposite lean +0.0 vs SPY, bond lean -2.7). Use the reversal: on the whole-market base (every sized member at market value, one class per identical share count, 5% ceiling, monthly, fractional, Gotrade fees, target-relative band; M0224's core, scores and cap unchanged), lean power 2 toward the bond-like side when the 10-year yield is below its level 12 months ago and toward the rate-rising side when it is at or above it; a stale (over 7 days) or missing yield leans nowhere. Arms: SWITCH, MIRROR (the reverse rule), BOND2 (always bond), OPP2 (always opposite) and CORE (no lean, the no-opinion arm); BOND2/OPP2/CORE should reproduce M0224's TILT2/OPP2/CORE. Success: SWITCH beats CORE and total-return SPY on the owner's deposits, beats MIRROR, does not trail SPY in 2009-2015, and its gap to MIRROR holds on the check store. Assumption: 12 months and the level comparison are fixed now, not searched.
methods.expectedFailure: The yield's 12-month trend is slow and public, and stock prices move before it does: by the time a year of falling yields is visible, bond-like stocks have already re-priced. The lean costs about 0.8 points a year in churn and in weight moved off the biggest companies (M0224), and switching sides adds turnover on top, so SWITCH trails CORE even if it beats MIRROR. 2009-2015 had mostly falling-then-flat yields with sharp rises in 2009, 2013 and 2015, so the switch spends that era mostly on the bond side, the side that lost then. Ungated, every arm falls about 50% in 2008, twice the 25% bar; nothing here touches that.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tried

The last run (the bond-like lean on the market-shaped book) found that companies whose shares rise when long-term interest rates fall ("bond-like": drug makers, food and household brands, utilities) beat the opposite kind over 1996-2015, but **the other way round** in 2009-2015. A fixed lean is a bet on one interest-rate era. So this run let the lean follow the rates themselves:

- **SWITCH (the rule)**: each month, if the 10-year Treasury yield is below where it was a year ago, lean the book toward bond-like stocks; if it is at or above, lean toward the rate-rising ones (banks, energy, industrials).
- **MIRROR**: the reverse rule, to check whether the yield's trend carries any information at all.
- **BOND2 / OPP2**: always lean one way (the last run's strong leans, re-run here).
- **CORE**: never lean. This is the arm with no opinion in it, and it is what prices the cost of leaning.

The base is unchanged from the last run: every index company the data can size, weighted by company size, none over 5%, re-weighted monthly, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's deposits (10M IDR, then 5M a month). BOND2, OPP2 and CORE reproduced the last run's numbers to the decimal, so the new code changes only which way the book leans.

How often the switch leaned each way: in 1996-2008 the yield was falling on 97 of 156 month-starts; in 2009-2015 on 60 of 82. So in the recent years the switch was mostly on the bond-like side, the side that lost then. I wrote that down before the run.

## Results, 1996-2015, on the owner's deposits

SPY with dividends reinvested, same deposits: **+7.2% a year**. The check store adds back most of the companies that later died.

| version | your money a year | worst fall | 2009-2015 vs SPY, a year | check store: a year / 2009-2015 | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SWITCH (follow the yield) | +6.5% | 50.4% | −2.9 pts | +5.0% / −4.2 | 0.43 |
| MIRROR (against the yield) | +6.2% | 60.1% | −0.3 pts | +4.8% / −0.8 | 0.37 |
| BOND2 (always bond-like) | +6.9% | 50.4% | −2.7 pts | +5.6% / −3.7 | 0.50 |
| OPP2 (always rate-rising) | +6.3% | 60.1% | +0.0 pts | +4.8% / −0.8 | 0.35 |
| CORE (no lean) | +7.4% | 50.2% | −1.1 pts | +6.3% / −1.7 | 0.55 |

**Every lean lost to SPY and to not leaning.** The switch earned 0.9 points a year less than the plain book and 0.7 less than SPY. It even lost 0.4 points a year to just always leaning bond-like, and it did worst of all in 2009-2015, the years it was built to fix. Every version fell about half its value in 2008-2009 (worst calendar year 2008, −31% to −42%), twice the owner's 25% limit.

**Walk-forward**: the best variant beat SPY in 1 of 4 three-year periods (2006-2008, by falling less) on both stores.

**The luck check.** The lab has now tried 181 different methods, so a result needs DSR 0.90 or more to count as more than luck. The best here is 0.55, and that is the arm with no lean. Nothing came close.

## Why

1. **The yield's trend knew almost nothing.** Following it beat going against it by only 0.3 points a year over twenty years. Half that gap, about 0.15 points a year, is what the rule "knows". In 2009-2015 it knew less than nothing: following the yield trailed the reverse rule by 2.6 points a year. Stock prices move on rate news the day it happens; a year-long trend in the yield is old news by the time it is visible.
2. **Leaning costs about a point a year, whichever way.** Average the switch and its mirror and the opinion cancels. What is left (+6.35%) sits about 1.05 points below the no-lean book (+7.4%). That is the habit: weight moved off the biggest companies, which were SPY's winners, plus about half again the trading (1,901 trades against 1,265). A 0.15-point opinion cannot pay a 1-point habit. The rule is **dead, not badly dressed**: a cheaper way to lean would still not pay for what it knows.
   (The lab's automatic pricing tool reported this pair as "unpriced" because the no-lean book re-weights monthly and so trades more than the tool's "always invested, never trading" threshold. CORE is the right yardstick here: same base, same rules, same fees, only the lean removed. I priced it by hand from the recorded numbers above.)
3. **The switch flips at the wrong times.** Yields bottomed and turned up in 1999, 2003-2006, 2013 and 2014. Each time the switch moved to rate-rising stocks a year late, after they had already moved. Then it moved back to bond-like stocks when the yield trend turned down, again late.
4. **The dead companies cost every version 1.1-1.5 points a year** on the check store. Even the no-lean book trails SPY there.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. Success needed SWITCH to beat CORE and SPY, beat MIRROR, keep pace with SPY in 2009-2015 and keep its gap to MIRROR on the check store. It beat MIRROR by 0.3 points on the main data and 0.2 on the check store, and failed everything else. It trailed SPY by 2.9 points a year in 2009-2015. The expected failure happened as written: the trend was too slow, the lean's cost (about 0.8-1 point) outweighed the opinion, and the switch spent 2009-2015 mostly on the losing bond-like side.

Compared with the parent: this is the same lean with a timing rule added, and the timing rule made it worse than both its fixed leans' better half (BOND2 +6.9% vs SWITCH +6.5%).

## My opinion:

Close the treasury-beta direction completely, fixed or timed. Five methods now say the same thing. Over twenty years the bond-like half did a little better than its opposite, and that was the falling-rate era. A slow rate trend can't time it. Any lean on the market-shaped book pays about a point a year before it earns anything. The one useful thing left is the lesson for every future lean on this base: the no-lean book only beats SPY by 0.2 points on the main data and trails by 0.8 on the check store, so a lean has to know more than a point a year to be worth anything. Next I would stop leaning the market book on slow signals and test whether that base can be made cheaper instead. Re-weighting it quarterly or only on deposits would cut its 1,265 trades, and turnover is the dial the lab has measured as expensive.
methods.verdict: Rejected: switching the lean between bond-like and rate-rising stocks by the 10-year yield's trend earned less than not leaning (+6.5% a year vs +7.4% for the plain market book and +7.2% for SPY), and did worst in 2009-2015

methods.name: Moving-average distance: buy index members whose 21-day average sits furthest above their 200-day average
methods.sourceRef: Avramov, Kaplanski & Subrahmanyam (2021), Moving Average Distance as a Predictor of Equity Returns, Review of Financial Economics 39(2):127-145 (SSRN 2018); https://alphaarchitect.com/moving-average-distance/
methods.hypothesis: Anchoring: investors under-react when a stock drifts away from its own long-run price level, so the ratio of its 21-session to its 200-session moving average (MAD) predicts next month's return across stocks. The paper (SSRN 2018, so the whole 1996-2015 dev window predates the crowd) reports about 9% a year long-short alpha over 1977-2018, strongest on the long side, surviving momentum and 52-week-high controls. Test: each month, among sized index members with 253 bars (one listing per company; fewer than 50 and the month holds SPY), rank by MAD and hold 20 in equal slots, a held name kept while inside the top 40, fully invested, no switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. Arms: TOP20; BOT20 (the mirror); TOP20-PLC (TOP20's size and entry count drawn blind from the same pool, its band replayed six months back: the no-opinion arm that prices the habit); RESID20 (MAD with 12-1 momentum and 52-week-high proximity regressed out each month); TOP20-SW (TOP20 behind the SPY 200-day switch, the habit-on twin). Predictions written before any result: TOP20 beats BOT20 and the placebo by 2 or more points a year over 1996-2015; RESID20 beats the placebo by at least 1 point a year, or MAD is momentum renamed; TOP20 leads SPY in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: In order of likelihood. (1) It is momentum in a new coat: a top-MAD stock has risen over the year and sits near its high, so TOP20's de-funded monthly returns move with the test-failed momentum books at 0.85 or more, the hard gate calls it their kin, and it cannot be promoted however good its dev numbers -- while RESID20, the arm that would escape that, ties the placebo because what MAD adds beyond momentum is small and noisy. (2) The momentum crashes: TOP20 holds 1999-2000 technology into the 2000-2002 fall and the high-beta laggards' rebound of 2009 hurts it, so its worst fall without a switch breaks the 25% bar, and TOP20-SW passes the fall test only by paying the switch's cash drag in a rising 2009-2015. (3) 2009-2015 is the first filter and every equal-slot book in this lab has trailed SPY there; a book of recent winners among index members is no exception, and the paper's value-weighted alpha came disproportionately from smaller stocks than these. (4) The mirror BOT20 may beat TOP20 in 2009 alone by enough to blur the twenty-year contrast. Any of these is a rejection, not a reason to tune the 21 and 200 windows afterwards.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-22

## What was tested

The idea is from Avramov, Kaplanski and Subrahmanyam (working paper 2018, published 2021). Compare a stock's average price over the last month (21 trading days) with its average over the last 200 days. When the short average sits far above the long one, the paper says the stock keeps rising next month, because investors are slow to let go of the old price level. We ranked the index members the lab can size (171 companies in early 1996, 390 by 2015) and held 20 in equal slots. A held name stayed while it ranked in the top 40. The book traded monthly in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, with the owner's monthly top-up. The whole 1996-2015 test period comes before the paper, so a crowd trading on it cannot have killed the edge here.

## Results (money-weighted, on the owner's deposits, against the same deposits put into SPY with dividends: +7.2% a year)

| arm | a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) | 2009-2015 vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Top 20 by distance (TOP20) | +11.9% | 57.7% | 1.55 | 0.727 | −2.1 |
| Bottom 20, the mirror (BOT20) | +15.8% | 69.0% | 2.36 | 0.603 | +19.1 |
| Blind draw, same size and churn (TOP20-PLC) | +8.8% | 60.4% | 1.49 | 0.571 | +1.0 |
| Distance with momentum and nearness-to-high removed (RESID20) | +8.4% | 71.4% | 1.33 | 0.464 | +1.4 |
| Top 20 behind the SPY 200-day switch (TOP20-SW) | **+16.0%** | **31.8%** | 2.26 | **0.949** | **−3.3** |

TOP20-SW is the only arm that passed the lab's screen (dev-eligible): it beat SPY, its worst fall of 31.8% is inside the screen's limit, and it is 0.949 on the luck check, above the 0.90 bar at N=180. That N counts one look per distinct method in the lab. Its worst calendar year was 2011 (−12.8%). It also beat SPY in 3 of 4 walk-forward folds. The fold it lost was 2009-2011 (+21% against SPY's +61%), when the switch had it sitting in cash during the rebound.

**It cannot be promoted, and nothing below changes that.** The hard gate reads it as kin of the momentum book M0002, which already failed the test window: their monthly moves, with the market's share taken out, track each other closely. That was failure (1) in my pre-registered list, and it happened. The edge was also negative in 2009-2015 (−3.3 points a year), the years most like today, so the buy-data signal does not fire either.

## What the arms say

- **Is there a signal at all?** Yes, a little. TOP20 beat its blind draw by 3.1 points a year on the same churn and fees (the draw matched its trade count and turnover; `lab control` found no shape problem). The prediction asked for 2 points or more, so that part held.
- **Is it anything more than momentum?** No. Strip out what 12-month momentum and nearness to the yearly high explain, and the leftover (RESID20) earned 8.4% against the blind draw's 8.8%. It also traded more and fell deeper. My test said that if this arm tied the draw, MAD is momentum under a new name. It tied the draw.
- **The mirror won, which the paper says should not happen.** On the dev store BOT20 beat TOP20 by 3.9 points a year. Almost all of that came from 2009-2015 (+19.1 points against SPY), when the stocks that had fallen hardest in 2008 bounced back. On the survivorship-check store, which adds back the companies that later died, BOT20 dropped to +11.5% a year and its worst fall deepened from 69% to 85.6%. TOP20 rose to +15.3% there. On the more honest prices the paper's ordering returns, top above bottom by 3.8 points. The dev store's missing dead companies were flattering the buy-the-fallen book. Insight 149 measured the same thing: the store's holes hurt books that buy losers most.
- **The switch did most of the work.** TOP20 against TOP20-SW is the same book with the market filter off and on. The switch took the worst fall from 57.7% to 31.8% and the return from 11.9% to 16.0% a year, because it sat out 2000-2002 and 2008. The cost showed up in 2009-2015, where the switched book trailed SPY by 3.3 points a year (dev) and was roughly even on the check store (+0.8). This is the same pattern as every momentum book behind the switch in this lab.
- **Narrow and broad markets.** TOP20-SW was ahead of SPY in both kinds of month (+11.8 narrow, +8.3 broad), but on the lab's own record that reading does not separate good methods from bad ones.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- The hypothesis held partly. Top beat the blind draw, but it did not beat its mirror on the dev store, the residual arm failed, and TOP20 lost to SPY in 2009-2015.
- Failure (1), momentum in a new coat, happened exactly: the gate calls it kin of a failed momentum book, and the residual arm tied the draw. Failure (2) happened too. Without the switch the worst fall was 58%, and the switched book's cash cost it the 2009 rebound. Failure (3), trailing SPY in 2009-2015, happened as well. Failure (4) happened on the dev store but went away once the dead companies were added back.

## Compared with the lab's momentum books

At real fees this book looks like the lab's 12-month momentum books (M0002, M0007, M0020). It has a similar worst fall behind the switch, the same 2009-2015 shortfall, and close co-movement. MAD is a smoother way of measuring how much a stock has risen over the past year and how close it sits to its yearly high, and the cross-section shows that it ranks almost the same names.

**My opinion:** This direction is closed in the form tested here. Moving-average distance is momentum measured differently. The only arm that passed the screen is a momentum book behind the market switch, which the lab has already paid for twice in test-window looks, and the hard gate correctly refuses it. I would not spend more ids on window lengths (10/100, 50/200): those are tweaks of the same trend reading. The one result worth following is on the losing side. After a crash, the members furthest below their long average bounced hard, and that held partly on the check store too (+15.9 points a year in 2009-2015), though with a ruinous 85% worst fall. The next useful question is whether that rebound can be caught with the fall controlled: the mirror book behind the same switch, priced against a switched blind draw. I have queued that idea. I expect it to fail, because buying the fallen after the market recovers is the slow long-term-reversal family the lab has already rejected, but the test is cheap and it answers a question the mirror raised.


### 2026-10-22

### Sera 20261022-1954: hard gate refused, not promoted

Sera's decision: no test-window look. M0282-TOP20-SW is dev-eligible (DSR 0.949, 3 of 4 walk-forward folds), but the hard gate refuses it on the kin condition: by behaviour it moves with M0002, which already read test-failed. That is a block on the whole family, not on this arm. Its 2009-2015 edge was also negative on the dev store (-3.3 a year), so the durability check would have refused a look on its own. No buy signal. Nothing was attempted around the gate.
methods.verdict: Picking stocks whose short-run average sits far above their long-run average is momentum by another name. Behind the market switch it beat SPY on the old data and fell at most 32%, but it moves with a momentum book that already failed, trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and cannot be promoted.

methods.name: Calm stocks beside SPY: how much of the market should sit next to the low-beta book?
methods.sourceRef: Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) Betting Against Beta, JFE 111(1); Black, Jensen & Scholes (1972); the core-satellite frame of M0030 and M0104; lab M0278
methods.hypothesis: Betting against beta was published in 2014, at the very end of the dev window, and its central claim is that the calm book's extra return can only be collected by leveraging it up to the market's sensitivity. In M0278 the 30 lowest-beta index members earned about 8 points a year more than their 0.38 market sensitivity alone entitles them to (9.6 points in 2009-2015, so the effect had not faded after publication), fell only 29% at worst against SPY's 50%, and kept their record when the dead companies were put back. They trailed SPY in 2009-2015 only because a book moving a third of a rising market starts far behind. The owner cannot borrow, so the substitute for leverage is to buy the missing market sensitivity outright: hold SPY itself beside the calm book. A 50/50 mix moves about 0.69 times the market while keeping roughly half the excess return. Arms: a three-rung dose ladder on the SPY share (C70-LB 70%, C50-LB 50%, C30-LB 30% SPY beside the calm 30), which together with SPY itself at 100% and the recorded M0278-LB30 at 0% makes five rungs; C50-PLC, 50% SPY beside a blind draw of 30 from the same pool matched to the calm book's own size and monthly entry count (the no-opinion arm); and C50-HB, 50% SPY beside the 30 JUMPIEST members (the mirror). All monthly, fully invested, no switch, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, on M0278's own preset so the 0% rung stays comparable. Predictions written before any result, on de-funded monthly returns: C50-LB ties SPY within one point a year over 2009-2015 and its 2008 fall is at least 10 points shallower than SPY's; C50-LB beats C50-PLC by 3 or more points a year over the twenty years; the ladder is monotone, so return per point of worst fall (MAR) rises as the SPY share falls from 100% to 0%; and C50-HB falls at least 15 points deeper than C50-LB while earning no more.
methods.expectedFailure: The most likely failure is that the SPY half pays nothing extra while the calm half's monthly rebalancing fees and its 2009-2015 lag leave the mix one to two points a year behind SPY in exactly the era most like today, making it a candidate on falls alone -- and a book judged on falls has to survive 2008, where a 50/50 of a book that fell 23% and a market that fell 36% cannot do much better than 30%, well above the owner's 20% bar even though the lab's dev screen allows 50%. Three more ways it can fail: (1) the ladder is not monotone, because a mix of two imperfectly correlated books earns a rebalancing bonus that peaks in the middle rather than at an end, so the dose reading would be a shape artefact rather than a dose; (2) C50-PLC lands within a point of C50-LB, which would say that what pays next to SPY is holding thirty index members at all -- the equal-weight shape M0275 and M0278 already caught -- and not the calm sort; (3) the luck test refuses every arm, since the calm book alone reached only 0.892 against the bar of 0.90 at N=178 and diluting it with SPY lowers the Sharpe ratio the luck test reads. None of these is a reason to tune the 252-session window, the book size or the rungs after the fact.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## The question

An earlier method found something that looks like a free lunch. The thirty calmest companies in
the index — the ones that barely move when the market moves — earned more over twenty years than
the thirty jumpiest, and fell less than half as far. That is the oldest known oddity in investing:
calm stocks pay better than how calm they are says they should.

But the calm book has a catch. It only moves about a third as hard as the market does. In a decade
when the market climbs 16% a year, a book that moves a third as hard starts a long way behind every
January — and sure enough, the calm book *lost* to SPY from 2009 to 2015 even while it was earning
its extra.

The textbook fix is to borrow money and buy more of the calm book. The owner cannot borrow: Gotrade
is cash-only. So this method asked the obvious substitute. **Instead of borrowing to get more market
movement, just buy the market.** Hold SPY itself next to the calm thirty. A half-and-half mix moves
about two thirds as hard as the market while, in theory, keeping about half the extra return.

The real question was not "does calm work" — that was already answered. It was **"what is the right
amount of SPY to hold next to it?"** So the SPY share was turned like a dial, five settings wide.

## The answer: none. Zero SPY is best, and it is not close

Three settings were run here. The two ends already existed: SPY on its own, and the calm book on its
own, both measured earlier on exactly the same fees, the same monthly deposits and the same years,
so all five lines below are the same measurement.

| how much SPY | how much calm | your money earned a year | worst fall | lead over SPY a year | lead in 2009-2015 | lead in 2008 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **100%** (SPY alone) | 0% | +7.2% | 55.0% | — | — | — |
| 70% | 30% | +7.5% | 49.4% | +0.2 pts | **−1.1 pts** | +3.9 pts |
| 50% | 50% | +8.8% | 44.2% | +1.4 pts | **−1.2 pts** | +6.7 pts |
| 30% | 70% | +9.4% | 39.6% | +1.9 pts | **−1.9 pts** | +11.0 pts |
| **0%** (calm alone) | 100% | +10.8% | 34.1% | +3.2 pts | **−2.6 pts** | +15.7 pts |

Read any column top to bottom and it moves one way, every single step. Every slice of SPY you take
out of the mix earns you more money, loses you less in the worst fall, and pays you more in 2008 —
and costs you more in 2009-2015. There is no sweet spot in the middle, no setting where the mix is
better than both ends. The dial is a straight line, and the good end of it is the end with no SPY
in it at all.

**That is the whole finding, and it is a finding about arithmetic, not about the market.** Borrowing
multiplies the calm book's extra return. Mixing with SPY only *averages* it away. Half the calm book
gives you half the extra (+1.4 against +3.2 — almost exactly half), because SPY brings market
movement and nothing else with it. The textbook fix needs borrowing to work; the cash-only
substitute for borrowing is not a substitute at all. It is just a slower walk back to owning SPY.

If anything the mix is slightly *worse* than a straight average, because the two halves have to be
traded back to their shares every month and that costs fees. The 70%-SPY setting is the clearest
case: it earned a lead of 0.2 points a year, and its return per point of worst fall (0.15) is
actually a touch *below* plain SPY's. A small slice of calm names next to a big slice of SPY buys
nothing and pays the trading bill anyway.

## Every version was rejected, and the reason is the same for all five

The luck test asks how likely a result is to be real rather than the best-looking of many tries. It
is scored at **N = 183** — one look for each distinct method the lab has run — against the owner's
bar of **0.90**. The five versions scored 0.46 to **0.82**. The best of them, the 30%-SPY mix, is
0.08 short. Nothing here is eligible.

Two versions also broke the lab's own screening limit on falls (50%): the blind-draw version fell
51.7% and the jumpy version 64.4%.

## Where the money actually came from: one year

The right-hand columns of the table are the uncomfortable part. **Four fifths of the calm mix's
entire twenty-year lead was earned in the years 2003-2008, and about a third of it in 2008 alone.**
The half-and-half mix beat SPY by 6.7 points during 2008 and by 11.0 points at the 30%-SPY setting.

Take 2008 away and there is very little left. In the seven years from 2009 — the years with the best
data and the ones that look most like today — every single setting of the dial **lost** to SPY, and
lost by more the more calm names it held.

So the calm book is not an engine. **It is insurance.** It pays out in a crash and charges a premium
the rest of the time. That is a perfectly respectable thing for an investment to be, but it is not
what the owner is looking for, which is a rule that beats SPY.

## Was it the calm sort, or just owning thirty index companies?

This is the question the lab now asks of every method, so one version held 50% SPY next to **thirty
names picked blind** — drawn by a hash from exactly the same pool, kept at the same size, and made
to trade on the same days as the real calm book (824 trades against 844, a very close match). No
skill in it at all.

| 50% SPY plus… | your money earned a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | lead over SPY a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the calm thirty | +8.8% | 44.2% | 2.93 | +1.4 pts |
| **thirty names picked blind** | +8.3% | 51.7% | 1.80 | +0.9 pts |
| the jumpy thirty | +9.2% | 64.4% | 2.23 | +2.3 pts |

**On money, the calm sort beat the blind draw by about half a point a year — and that is too small
to believe.** To check how small, I measured the lab's own blind draws against each other. Nine
groups of recorded versions exist that are identical in every way *except* which hash number was
used to pick the names — pure luck of the draw, no difference in idea. Changing only that number
moved the twenty-year yearly return by between 0.06 and 2.70 points, with a middle value of 1.40,
and **seven of the nine moved by more than the 0.56 points that separates the calm mix from its
blind twin here.** Honestly stated: *next to SPY, the calm sort's advantage in return over picking
thirty names at random is smaller than the noise of which thirty names you happened to draw, and
cannot be measured with the evidence here.*

What **can** be measured is the other two columns, which barely move when the draw changes. The calm
thirty fell **7.5 points less** than the blind thirty and turned in 2.93 of gains for every 1 of
losses against the blind draw's 1.80. The calm sort buys safety. It does not demonstrably buy return.

A separate breakdown of the 2009-2015 shortfall says the same thing from the other direction. Of the
1.2 points a year the half-and-half mix lost to SPY in those years: 1.1 points was money sitting in
cash rather than invested, 0.3 points was fees, the shape of the book (SPY plus thirty index names
at all) was worth **+2.2 points**, and picking the *calmest* thirty rather than any thirty cost
**−1.9 points**. The shape helped; the skill hurt. The same caution applies, and with force — that −1.9 is measured
against a single blind draw, and the draw-to-draw spread just measured is of the same size. Treat
its direction as a signpost and its size as unestablished.

## The jumpy version is the warning, again

The mirror version — 50% SPY next to the thirty *jumpiest* names — beat SPY by 2.3 points a year,
more than any calm version, and by 4.2 points a year in 2009-2015, the only version here to win
that era at all. It also fell **64.4%**, nearly two thirds of the account.

That is not skill. It is the thing the previous method warned about: in a decade that rises steadily,
anything that moves harder than the market looks clever. The lab's breadth report agrees — all five
versions read "pays only in broad markets", and it says so about almost every method, which is why
the useful line underneath it is the one reporting that a broad-market tailwind was sustained in
only 6 of 202 three-year stretches. Leaning on it is leaning on weather.

## Did the predictions hold?

Written down before any result:

- *The mix ties SPY within a point a year in 2009-2015* — **just failed.** It was 1.15 points behind.
- *Its 2008 fall is at least 10 points shallower than SPY's* — **half held.** Its worst fall of the
  whole twenty years was 10.8 points shallower (44.2% against 55.0%), but the calendar year 2008
  alone was only about 6 points better.
- *The calm mix beats the blind-draw mix by 3 or more points a year* — **clearly failed.** It beat it
  by 0.56 points, which is inside the noise of a single draw.
- *The dial is monotone: return per point of fall rises as SPY comes out* — **held, completely.**
  0.14, 0.15, 0.20, 0.24, 0.32 across the five settings. This is one of the cleanest dose readings
  the lab has recorded, and it is the finding.
- *The jumpy mix falls at least 15 points deeper while earning no more* — **half held.** It fell 20
  points deeper, but it earned **more**, not less.

Of the three ways the method said it could fail, two happened: the blind draw landed within a point
(it did), and the luck test refused everything (it did). The third — that the dial would be lumpy
rather than smooth, so the dose reading would be an artefact — **did not happen at all.** The dial
was perfectly smooth.

## One housekeeping note, written down so it is not repeated

The blind-draw version was built correctly and matched its target closely, but the lab's control
checker reported "no control arm" for this method. It recognises a control by the words in its
description, and the phrase used here — "blind draw" — is deliberately not on its list, because it
had never appeared in a method file before. The arm is real and the numbers above are sound; the
automatic check simply could not see it. The method file cannot be edited now (its contents are
sealed once it runs), so the fix belongs to the next method that writes one: use the word *placebo*,
or declare the target outright once the lab adds the field for it.

## Comparison with the parent

The parent measured the calm thirty on its own and rejected it: 0.892 on the luck test against a bar
of 0.90, and a fall of 34%, well past the 25% the owner's real-money rule allows. This method asked
whether SPY could fix the one thing holding it back. The answer is that SPY makes it worse on every
axis except the one nobody was worried about.

One thing did improve. The calm book alone fell 34.1%; at 30% SPY it falls 39.6% and at 50% it falls
44.2% — so no setting of this dial gets anywhere near the owner's 25% limit either. The limit is not
reachable by diluting. It would have to come from the calm book itself holding fewer, calmer names,
or from something that steps aside.

## My opinion:

**This direction is finished, and I would not spend another method id on mixing a stock book with
SPY.** The result is not a near miss; it is a clean, five-point straight line saying that dilution
moves you toward SPY on every measure at once, which is exactly what dilution is supposed to do. The
lab now has a measured answer to a question it will be tempted to ask again — "should we hold some
SPY alongside?" — and the answer is no, for any book whose edge is stronger than SPY's, and trivially
yes for any book whose edge is weaker, in which case just hold SPY. There is no version of this worth
a trial.

What I would try instead comes from the one number here that is solid. The calm sort reliably buys
**falls and gains-vs-losses**, not return: 7.5 points shallower and 2.93 against 1.80 versus a blind
draw, in columns that barely move when the draw changes. So calmness is a safety filter, which is
exactly what the lab learned about proximity to the 52-week high. The question worth asking next is
whether **calmness works as a filter on somebody else's picks** rather than as a ranking of its own:
take a book that already earns a lead, drop the names in the jumpiest quarter of the market, and see
whether the fall shrinks by more than the return does. That costs nothing extra to hold and does not
need SPY in the mix.

And one honest warning for whoever runs it. Everything the calm sort demonstrably bought here was
bought in 2008. The dev window contains exactly one crash of that kind, so a rule that pays only in
crashes has a sample size of one, however good its twenty-year average looks. I would want that rule
to show its worth in 2000-2002 as well before believing it.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-0843: the mirror prices backwards, and the habit cannot be priced

Verified: five trials, all rejected on the luck bar, leads over the lab's SPY line of +0.34, +1.57
and +2.23 as the SPY share falls from 70% to 30%, falls of 49.4%, 44.2% and 39.6%. Monotone in
every column, as reported. The dilution finding is sound and reusable.

The automatic mirror check found no reversed pair here, which is the same blind spot journalled as
577. Split by hand, the calm half-and-half arm against its jumpy twin:

  whole window    what the sort knows  -0.44 pts on the prices, -0.22 on the money
  2009-2015       what the sort knows  -2.67 pts on the prices, -2.39 on the money
  what the habit costs                 unpriceable, on both columns and both windows

**BACKWARDS on return.** The jumpy half-and-half arm beat the calm one, by a little over the whole
window and by nearly two and a half points a year on the owner's money after 2009. So the beta sort
is upside down as a return ranking, and the run's own shortfall decomposition agrees from the other
side: the calm selection itself is worth -1.92 points a year over 2009-2015, with the +2.24 coming
from the shape.

That is not a contradiction of the run's conclusion, it sharpens it. Calmness ranks forwards on
safety -- 44.2% against 64.4% worst fall -- and backwards on return. "It buys safety, not return"
is the right sentence, and the mirror is the measurement that makes it defensible rather than a
reading of one arm.

Two cautions attach to the backwards half. First, this lab has measured that the dev price history
flatters jumpy stocks specifically, because the companies it omits are the ones that swung hardest
before dying, so a high-beta arm beating a low-beta one on this tape is the expected artefact and
not news. Second, the gap is -0.22 points on the money whole-window, which sits well inside the
seed noise this very run measured at a median of 1.40 points. The 2009-2015 figure of -2.39 is the
only one of the four outside it.

**The habit is unpriceable here**, and that is a finding about the batch rather than about this
method. The pair's midpoint has to be measured against an arm that is always invested and barely
trades; this method's nearest candidate is the blind-draw twin, which turns over 824 round trips.
So what the arrangement costs -- fees, churn, the cash it sits in -- is not recoverable from this
file. The lab's standing count is that 22 of 28 recorded pairs can never be priced, and this is a
twenty-ninth. None of the four methods in this batch registered a priceable mirror.
methods.verdict: Holding SPY beside the calm stocks only waters them down: every slice of SPY added earned less, fell further and paid less in 2008, and no setting beat SPY after 2009.

methods.name: Wider news-day pool: take large-for-the-stock jumps on 2x normal volume, not only 3x
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0279 / M0277 on M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's frame (Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara & Venkatachalam 2008, SSRN 909563); the 3x volume bar is M0063's and has never been varied
methods.hypothesis: Published 2008, so the dev window can only show an edge from before and just after the crowd traded it, and a strong dev result is likely to have faded; 2009-2015 is judged first. M0277 and M0279 tried six ways of keeping only part of the news-day book's jumps (by the sign of the earnings surprise, by an SEC filing explaining the jump, by the stock's own reporting calendar) and all six lost to the unfiltered book, by 2 to 6 points a year in 2009-2015, because they held 2 to 5 names where the unfiltered book held about 13.6 of its 20 and parked the difference in SPY. So the book may be short of jumps, not short of selectivity. On M0072-Z2-RAWRANK's frame exactly (monthly, 20 slots of 5%, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, 60-session hold, up gap, 4-point market-adjusted three-day jump, own-swing filter z >= 2, ranked by the raw jump, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's monthly deposits), turn the one filter nobody has varied -- the event's volume bar, 3x the 60-day median since M0063 -- and nothing else. Five rungs, a ladder and not a pair: NOVOL (no volume bar at all), VOL20 (2x), VOL25 (2.5x), VOL30 (3x, the parent's bar unchanged, the no-opinion reference rung every other rung is read against) and VOL40 (4x, stricter, the other direction of the same dial). The rungs nest, so names held rises monotonically as the bar falls. I expect the book return to rise as the bar falls from 3x toward 2x, because the 20 slots fill closer to full and the slots the parent leaves empty earn SPY's return rather than the picks' -- and if the drift is about any big news rather than about the volume of the news day, the extra jumps should drift about as well. Success for the idea: average names held rises above 16 at 2x and the 2009-2015 book return at 2x or 2.5x beats VOL30's by at least 1 point a year, with the response monotone in the bar across at least four of the five rungs. Success for the gate: a variant with a worst fall under the screen that beats total-return SPY with DSR >= 0.90.
methods.expectedFailure: Lower-volume gaps are weaker news: a 4-point three-day move on ordinary volume is as likely to be a drifting sector or a thin tape as a real announcement, so the extra jumps may drift less and dilute the book instead of filling it, making the response flat or the wrong way round. The parent's own worst fall (23.8%, summer 1998) is untouched by this dial and is mostly the market's fall behind a late monthly switch, so every rung probably breaks the worst-fall screen and the gate may reject all five. A wider pool also means more competition for 20 slots and more turnover, and turnover is the expensive dial at Gotrade's real fees on a $22-70 slot, so a fuller book can earn less after costs even when its picks are no worse. NOVOL may reproduce M0071's finding that volume carries no edge of its own, in which case the whole dial is inert and the ladder is flat -- which is still the answer to the question. And because the rungs nest, the five arms are heavily overlapping rather than independent, so a monotone-looking response can come from a handful of shared names.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## What was tried

The "news-day" book buys big companies straight after a day that looks like big news: the stock
gaps up, trades at least three times its normal volume, and gains at least 4 points more than SPY
over the three days around it — and the jump has to be large measured against that stock's own
normal swing. It holds up to 20 names at 5% each, parks the rest in SPY, sits in cash while SPY is
under its 200-day average, and re-picks monthly.

Two earlier methods tried six different ways of keeping only *part* of those jumps — by whether
the earnings surprise was positive, by whether an SEC filing explained the jump, by whether the
jump fell in the company's usual reporting week. All six lost to the unfiltered book, by 2 to 6
points a year in 2009-2015, and the reason looked simple: each filter cut the book from about 13.6
names down to 2-5, and the empty slots went to SPY during a decade SPY spent rising.

So I asked the opposite question. Maybe the book is **short of jumps, not short of fussiness**.
The one filter nobody has ever varied is the volume bar: "three times normal volume" has been a
fixed constant since the first version of this book, chosen once and never tested. I turned that
one dial and nothing else, five times rather than twice, because two points cannot read a slope:

- **no bar at all** — any up gap with a big enough jump, volume ignored
- **2x** normal volume — the widest setting the idea asked for
- **2.5x**
- **3x** — the parent's bar unchanged. This is the reference rung: the same book with no opinion
  about volume expressed, so the cost of every other rung is read directly against it
- **4x** — stricter, the other direction of the same dial

The rungs nest: every jump the 4x book sees, the 3x book also sees, and so on down. Assumption
written down before the run: the five settings were fixed in advance and no result was looked at
before committing them.

## The premise was wrong at the source

Before any return: **how many names did each setting actually hold?**

| volume bar | names it asked for | of the days it was allowed to trade |
|---|---|---|
| none | 14.3 | about 20 of 20 |
| 2x | 14.3 | about 20 of 20 |
| 2.5x | 14.1 | about 20 of 20 |
| **3x (parent)** | **13.6** | **about 19 of 20** |
| 4x | 11.4 | about 16 of 20 |

Removing the volume bar entirely moves the book from 13.6 names to 14.3. Seven tenths of one name.

The "13.6 of 20" that started this whole idea was never empty slots. The book sits in cash on 28.3%
of its decision days, because the 200-day switch is off — and 13.6 is just 19 names averaged over a
year in which it was allowed to trade only 71.7% of the time. **The book was essentially full all
