along.** The earlier filtered arms really were starved at 2-5 names; the unfiltered book never was.
I built this method on a number I misread, and the exposure report answered it in one line.

## Results (dev window 1996-2015, the owner's monthly deposits, Gotrade's real fees, fractional)

| volume bar | your money a year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score | 2009-2015 lead | gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | +12.1% | +7.2% | **37.0%** | 2.05 | 0.787 | +0.7% | fails fall + luck |
| 2x | +11.5% | +7.2% | 28.1% | 1.96 | 0.756 | +1.3% | fails fall + luck |
| 2.5x | +11.6% | +7.2% | 26.3% | 1.98 | 0.826 | +2.4% | fails fall + luck |
| **3x (parent)** | **+12.3%** | +7.2% | **23.8%** | 1.98 | **0.920** | +2.3% | **passes** |
| 4x | +12.0% | +7.2% | 24.1% | 1.98 | **0.925** | +0.7% | **passes** |

The luck score is how likely the result is real rather than the best of many tries; the bar is 0.90,
the owner's setting since 2026-10-07, and it is judged at N = 182 — one look per distinct method in
the lab, which is what the lab's own policy counts, not one per trial row.

**Returns barely move: 11.5% to 12.3%, a range of eight tenths of a point across the whole dial.**
But the worst fall moves enormously, and it moves in a straight line:

> **37.0% → 28.1% → 26.3% → 23.8%** as the bar rises from nothing to 3x, then flattens at 24.1%.

Four clean rungs in a row, the fifth turning the corner. The luck score follows the same shape
(0.787 → 0.756 → 0.826 → 0.920 → 0.925), and so does return-per-unit-of-fall (0.33 → 0.41 → 0.44 →
0.52 → 0.50).

So the volume bar is **not a pool-size dial at all. It is a safety filter.** It buys almost no
return and it halves the worst fall. And the parent's 3x — a constant picked once, years ago,
without any search — sits at or within a whisker of the best setting on every axis at once. That
is the second time this lab has found an inherited constant already standing on the optimum.

My pre-registered success test wanted names held above 16 at the 2x setting and a 2009-2015 gain of
at least a point. Names held went to 14.3, not 16. The 2009-2015 reading went the wrong way: +1.3%
at 2x against the parent's +2.3%. **The hypothesis failed on both halves, and the expected failure
is what happened** — lower-volume gaps are weaker news and dilute the book rather than filling it.

## Why, mechanically

A 4-point three-day move on ordinary volume is not usually an announcement. It is a sector drifting,
or a thin tape, or nothing. The volume test is what separates "the market is reacting to something"
from "the price wandered". Drop it and you keep every real news day you had, plus a tail of
look-alikes that bring no drift and a great deal of extra downside — the no-bar book falls 37%,
half again as far as the parent, for two tenths of a point *less* return.

One surprise worth recording: turnover does not fall as the pool widens, it **peaks in the middle** —
707 trades with no bar, 1,150 at 2x, 1,214 at 2.5x, 1,208 at 3x, 1,072 at 4x. The mechanism is the
hold rule: a name keeps its slot while its news day is younger than 60 sessions, and a *fresh*
qualifying event restarts that clock. With no volume bar, events are so common that held names keep
being re-triggered and simply never leave. The book stops trading because nothing ever expires.

## The honest-tape check, and why it overrules the dev window

Re-run on the survivorship-check store — the same window with the dead companies put back, the ones
the dev store cannot price — the picture changes, and it changes **in a second straight line**:

| volume bar | a year, dev → honest tape | 2009-2015 lead, dev → honest tape |
|---|---|---|
| none | +12.1% → **+8.8%** (−3.3) | +0.7% → **−4.5%** |
| 2x | +11.5% → +10.3% (−1.3) | +1.3% → −0.4% |
| 2.5x | +11.6% → +10.6% (−1.0) | +2.4% → +0.8% |
| **3x (parent)** | +12.3% → +10.7% (−1.6) | **+2.3% → −0.1%** |
| 4x | +12.0% → **+12.5% (+0.6)** | +0.7% → **+1.8%** |

**The lower the volume bar, the more of the book's apparent edge was the missing dead companies.**
The no-bar book gives back 3.3 points a year and its modern-era edge collapses to −4.5%. The
strictest book is the only arm in the method that earns *more* with the dead companies back.

That makes sense of the whole result: heavy volume is a proxy for *being alive*. A company the
market is actively trading on a news day is a company that still exists. A 4-point move on ordinary
volume is disproportionately a thin, fading name — exactly the kind the dev store happens to price
while the ones that actually died are absent. The volume bar was quietly doing survivorship work all
along, which is why loosening it looks free on dev and is expensive on the honest tape.

This now joins a very short list: filters that earn more, not less, when the dead companies come
back. It is a safety filter, never an engine.

## The buy signal fired — and I do not believe it

`lab walkforward` reports that this method cleared all five durability conditions, and printed the
buy signal: the moment survivorship-free price history is worth paying for. I am reporting it
because the rule says report it loudly. I am also reporting, in the same breath, why the coordinator
should not act on it.

**First: the arm it fired on is the parent's book, not this method's idea.** The arm the gate would
pre-register is the 3x rung — which is the reference rung, the unchanged parent. Its recorded trial
is bit-for-bit identical to three trials the lab already holds: same +47,105.4% return, same 1,208
trades, same 23.8% fall, and the same equity curve down to the hash. Four different configuration
digests, four method ids, **one book**:

| recorded as | trial | digest | curve |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0072-Z2-RAWRANK | #283 | 2a2a1c53d6 | caa33dc4844b |
| M0277-OFF | #914 | 2f275ac73a | caa33dc4844b |
| M0279-OFF | #934 | 0ff600f4a3 | caa33dc4844b |
| M0284-VOL30 | #952 | ec71756966 | caa33dc4844b |

**Second, and this is the part that matters beyond this method: that one unchanged curve has
collected three different fold verdicts.**

| recorded under | folds won | which arm the selector scored | majority? |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0277 | 1 of 4 | the earnings-confirmed arm, all four folds | no |
| M0279 | 2 of 4 | the season / filed / unfiled arms | no |
| **M0284** | **3 of 4** | **the parent book itself, all four folds** | **yes** |

Nothing about the book changed. Walk-forward picks each fold's arm by the best training-period MAR
*within that method file*, and in the two earlier files some filtered sibling always out-scored the
parent book in training — so the gate never actually scored this book at all. It was scoring the
siblings and attaching their record to the method. In my file every sibling rung is worse than the
3x rung at every fold, so the selector stayed on the parent book, and the parent book won 3 of 4.

Two readings, and both are true. The charitable one: this book had genuinely never been fold-tested
before, and the first time it was, it passed. The uncharitable one: a method's fold record is a
property of the company its arm keeps, and a book can be walked through the gate by registering it
beside weaker siblings. Neither is a reason to spend a look today, and the second is a defect worth
fixing.

**Third, the check the signal's last condition exists to approximate says no.** Condition (d) asks
for a positive edge in 2009-2015 precisely so the edge is not an artefact of the missing dead
companies. On the honest tape that edge is **−0.1%**, and the fold majority falls to 2 of 4. The
dev-window reading it fired on was +2.3% with its own noise at 3.0 points a year — the report itself
calls that indistinguishable from zero. The signal fired on the one tape that cannot answer its own
question.

**Fourth, the selector would promote the wrong arm anyway.** `lab promote` picks the best eligible
dev trial by MAR: 0.52 for the 3x rung against 0.50 for the 4x rung. So it names the arm that gives
back 1.6 points a year on the honest tape, over the one arm in the method that gains 0.6. The dev
window's own ranking points at the most survivorship-dependent rung.

Kin is clean — no pair reaches the 0.85 bar against the four books that already failed out of
sample, though the 4x rung at 0.77 against the two blend books is closer than the number suggests.

One audit note: the same curve's luck score has drifted 0.914 → 0.919 → 0.920 across its four
recordings, because it is scored against the lab as the lab stood on each run date. The stored
number is a record of that day, not a verdict about the book.

## Comparison with the parent

The 3x rung reproduces M0072-Z2-RAWRANK exactly, so there is no fee asymmetry to correct for — the
parent already ran at Gotrade's real fees, and the two are the same configuration under a different
allocator id. Against M0279, the method directly above this one: M0279 found that *narrowing* the
pool costs 2-6 points a year. This method finds that *widening* it costs almost nothing in return
and up to 13 points of extra fall. Put together, the book sits on a plateau in the middle and falls
off both edges — the pool is right where it is, and the search for a better one through this dial is
finished.

**My opinion:** this direction is done, and I would not spend another method id on the pool width of
this book. The dial is measured end to end, in one straight line each way, and the answer is that
the 3x bar is already the best setting on every axis. But the run was worth it twice over for what
it found beside the point. The first is that the volume bar is a *liveness* filter, not a news
filter — it is the thing standing between this book and the dead companies, which is why the honest
tape rewards the strict end and punishes the loose end monotonically. That is a reusable idea: every
book in the lab that screens on a price move alone is exposed in the way the no-bar rung is, and
pairing a volume condition with a price condition may be a cheap, general survivorship brake worth
testing on a book that has nothing to do with news days. That is the variation I have queued. The
second is a problem the lab should fix before it spends look number five: a method's fold record
depends on which siblings happen to share its file, and today the same unchanged curve reads 1 of 4,
2 of 4 and 3 of 4 in three places, one of which fires the buy signal. The fold gate should score the
arm it would actually promote, on its own curve, independent of the menu — otherwise the way to pass
it is to register weak siblings, and that is the exact mechanism the gate exists to prevent. Do not
buy data on this firing. If the owner ever does take this book to a look, take the 4x rung, not the
3x one the selector names.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator decision, sera-20261023-0843: the buy signal fired and no look was spent

`lab walkforward M0284` cleared all five conditions and printed BUY SIGNAL. I verified each of
the child's four counter-arguments against the database rather than taking the report, and I am
not promoting. The reasoning, so the next batch does not have to rediscover it:

**1. The arm `promote` would pre-register is the parent's book, not this method's idea.**
Verified directly: trials #283 (M0072-Z2-RAWRANK), #914 (M0277-OFF), #934 (M0279-OFF) and #952
(M0284-VOL30) carry the same total return to fourteen digits (471.0543445417878), the same 1208
trades, the same 0.23802572713684836 fall and the same curve hash caa33dc4844b under four
different config digests. One book, four method ids. This method's own idea -- a looser volume
bar -- lost at every rung it was turned to. So the eligible arm is the unchanged parent, and a
look spent here would be spent on evidence this method did not produce. That is the same shape
as D18's control-arm clause: when a method's own idea cannot beat the thing it was registered
against, the finding is that the idea failed, not that the incumbent is ready for the owner's
money.

**2. The condition the buy signal exists to protect reverses on the honest tape.** The signal
fired on a 2009-2015 edge of +2.3 points a year, which `lab walkforward` itself prints as
indistinguishable from zero (SE 3.0). The two-store check recorded in journal entry 563 puts the
same arm at -0.1 points over the same years once the companies that failed or were bought are
put back, and its fold record at 2 of 4 rather than 3 of 4. Step 0b's rule is that a negative
2009-2015 edge means no look. The better-covered reading is the negative one.

The lab has spent four looks on two distinct books and all four failed on `beats SPY TR`. This
would be the fifth, on a book whose honest-tape edge over the best-covered years is negative.

**3. If this book is ever taken to a look, it should be the 4x rung, not 3x.** `promote` ranks by
dev MAR and would name VOL30 (0.52) over VOL40 (0.50). VOL40 is the only rung in the method that
gains when the dead companies are added back (+12.0 to +12.5% a year, 2009-2015 edge +0.7 to
+1.8), while VOL30 gives back 1.6 points. Ranking by dev MAR picks the arm that the dev store's
own omissions flatter most.

**4. The fold record here is the most honest one this book has had, which is worth saying out
loud.** The child's one-line summary -- that one curve carries three fold records -- is loose,
and the journal entry it filed (566) gets it right: in M0277 every fold scored M0277-CONFIRMED
and in M0279 the folds scored SEASON, FILED, FILED and UNFILED. The shared book was never the arm
under test. In this file every fold picked VOL30, with no pick change and `stable: yes`, so this
is the first time the book itself was fold-tested -- and it won 3 of 4. That reads in the book's
favour. It does not change the decision, because point 2 stands on its own, but a future batch
should not cite "sibling-dependent folds" as evidence against this particular book. The real
finding there is about the gate, and it is queued as M0289.

What survives from this method is not the book but the dial: the volume bar is a liveness filter,
not a pool-size dial, and the looser it is set the more of the dev edge turns out to have been the
missing dead companies. That is journal entry 565 and it generalises to any price-only screen,
which is M0288.
methods.verdict: Widening the news-day pool was the wrong question: dropping the volume bar adds 0.7 of a name and doubles the worst fall, and on the honest tape the loosest book gives back 3.3 points a year while the strictest gains 0.6 — the volume bar is a safety filter, not a pool-size dial

methods.name: The fallen after the storm: the members furthest below their 200-day average, bought only while SPY is above its own 200-day average
methods.hypothesis: M0282's mirror arm (the 20 sized members whose 21-day average sits furthest below their 200-day average) beat the top arm on the dev store by 3.9 points a year, almost all from the 2009-2015 bounce (+19.1 points a year vs SPY; +15.9 on the survivorship-check store), but fell 69% (86% on the check store) because it held the fallen straight through 2000-2002 and 2008. Test whether the bounce can be kept without the fall: the same pool, band (top 40), equal slots, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, behind the SPY 200-day switch. Arms: BOT20-SW; BOT20-SW-PLC (a matched blind draw behind the same switch, the no-opinion arm); TOP20-SW (M0282's eligible arm re-run, for a same-frame comparison); and BOT20 with no switch (the habit-off twin). Prediction: BOT20-SW beats its switched draw by 2+ points a year and leads SPY in 2009-2015 on both stores. Expected failure: this is long-term reversal, which the lab has rejected (M0069, M0073); the switch re-enters after the bounce has begun, so it misses the steepest part of the rebound, and the check store's dead companies take back the rest. Read the result on the survivorship-check store before believing any lead.

methods.name: How often must a book be re-weighted? The market's own shape and the lab's equal slices, each re-set every month and once a year
methods.sourceRef: M0281's CORE arm and M0224/M0226, which built the whole-market base; M0266 (with exposure held still, trimming winners to feed laggards is worth nothing on a 50-name equal-weight book); M0127 (the rebalance band measured against the holding); insight 462 (fees on 15 turns a year were 3.8 of the equal-weight placebo's 8-point gap); insight 492 (cash in lumps costs more than cash spread evenly)
methods.hypothesis: The whole-market base -- every F4-screened index member with a known point-in-time market value, one listed class per identical share count, no company over 5%, monthly, fractional, Gotrade's real fees, the band measured against each holding's own target -- beats deposit-matched SPY by 0.2 points a year (+7.4% vs +7.2%). The dial never turned on it is how often it is re-weighted, and M0266 found that with exposure held still the trimming itself is worth nothing. A size-weighted book, though, barely needs re-weighting by arithmetic: market value is share count times price, so its weights drift the way its targets drift, and only issuance, index changes and the ceiling separate them. So the dial is turned on two shapes at once, a 2x2 of shape and cadence over identical names, with one field between each pair. MONTHLY and ANNUAL weight by market value and re-set every month or each January; EQ-MONTHLY and EQ-ANNUAL give the same names one equal slice each on the same two cadences; EQ-DEPOSIT shares EQ-ANNUAL's January anchor but never sells to fund a buy, spending each month's deposit on the names furthest below an equal slice; SPY is the endpoint with no opinion in it, the same deposits buying total-return SPY at the same fees with the band at zero. On a non-anchor month a book is its anchor's weights carried forward by each name's own price change, so nothing trades but an index exit and a name over the 5% ceiling. MONTHLY should reproduce M0281-CORE's +7.4%, a built-in check that the carry code leaves the base alone. Predictions, written before any result: ANNUAL lands within about 0.3 points a year of MONTHLY, because the shape rebalances itself; EQ-ANNUAL beats EQ-MONTHLY by a point or more, because the equal shape does not; and EQ-DEPOSIT beats EQ-ANNUAL, because the deposit buys the laggards for free. Nothing here is a candidate: the base falls about 50% in 2008, twice the 25% bar, and no cadence touches that. Success is a measurement -- what the lab's habitual equal-slice shape pays to be held in place, on a book where the market's own shape pays nothing.
methods.expectedFailure: Three ways this answers nothing. (1) The 20% target band on a book of several hundred sub-1% weights may already suppress nearly every drift trade, in which case all four book arms land on top of each other and the finding is about the band, not the cadence; turnover, order count and average exposure must be quoted beside return either way. (2) The equal arms slice a 20-million-rupiah account about 240 ways, so a slot starts near six dollars and a 20%-of-target drift trade is a one-dollar order. Gotrade's per-order minimum then swallows it, or the engine refuses it as too small, and the equal cadence gap becomes a measurement of a small account's order economics rather than of rebalancing. That is still a real answer for the owner, but the verdict must say which it is. (3) A slower cadence leaves the month's deposit in cash for up to eleven months, and cash in lumps costs more per point of absent exposure than cash spread evenly (insight 492), so an annual arm may lose on exposure what it saves on fees; EQ-DEPOSIT exists precisely to separate those two. Beyond that: the base's small lead over SPY is the missing dead companies and the coverage hole, not fees, so no cadence closes it; rebalancing buys the faller and the dev store prices no delisted names, so the often-re-weighted arms are structurally flattered here and the check store should move them down relative to the annual ones; and the carry rule is price drift only -- dividends are credited to cash and redeployed by the band like any other money -- so a carried weight is a few tenths of a percent off a truly untouched book's, far inside the 20% band but not zero.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0286 — how often must a book be re-weighted, and what does holding it in place cost?

## This is a ruler, not a strategy

Nothing here is a candidate and nothing is being proposed for your money. Every version below
fell between 50% and 58% from a peak, twice the 25% you allow, and the luck score of the best of
them is 0.68 against the 0.90 bar. The six versions exist to settle one question: a book has to
be nudged back into shape from time to time, and nudging costs money in fees. How often is
often enough, and what is the nudging actually buying?

## The two shapes

All six versions own the same companies: every member of the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 that the
store can price, that trades at least $20M a day and costs at least $5, and whose real size is
known — about 240 companies in 2005, about 330 by 2010. Only the **amounts** differ.

- **By size** (MONTHLY, ANNUAL): each company held in proportion to what it is actually worth,
  with no single one over 5% of the account. This is the market's own shape — what SPY does.
- **Equal slices** (EQ-MONTHLY, EQ-ANNUAL, EQ-DEPOSIT): the same companies, the same money split
  evenly. This is the shape nearly every other book in this lab holds.

And each shape was re-set either **every month** or **once each January**. In between a January
re-set nothing is traded at all: the holdings simply drift with their own prices, and the only
sales are a company leaving the index or one growing past the 5% ceiling. EQ-DEPOSIT is the
third way: it never sells to fund a purchase, and instead spends each month's 5,000,000 rupiah
deposit on whichever names have fallen furthest below an equal slice. The sixth version, SPY,
buys nothing but SPY with the same deposits and the same broker fees — the version with no
opinion in it at all.

## What happened

Money-weighted return on your real deposit plan, 1996 to October 2015, at Gotrade's real fees:

| version | your money earned | same deposits into SPY | trading per year | share invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MONTHLY — by size, re-set monthly | **+7.4%** | +7.2% | 27% of the book | 91.4% |
| ANNUAL — by size, re-set each January | **+7.4%** | +7.2% | 10% | 91.5% |
| EQ-MONTHLY — equal slices, monthly | **+10.2%** | +7.2% | 56% | 97.1% |
| EQ-ANNUAL — equal slices, each January | **+9.7%** | +7.2% | 23% | 94.5% |
| EQ-DEPOSIT — equal slices, deposit only | **+10.3%** | +7.2% | 38% | 97.5% |
| SPY — just buy SPY | +7.7% | +7.7% | 7% | 99.4% |

(The SPY version opens in 1994 rather than 1996, because it reads no index membership and so
needs no run-up: that is why its own SPY line reads 7.7% and not 7.2%. Compare each version with
the SPY line on its own row, never across rows.)

MONTHLY reproduced the recorded whole-market base to every digit it was checked against — same
total return, same 1265 round trips, same 91.43% invested as M0281-CORE, M0224-CORE and
M0226-CORE. That was the built-in check that the new "leave it alone" code does not disturb the
old behaviour, and it passed exactly.

## Finding 1: on the market's own shape, re-weighting is free and worthless

Re-setting the size-weighted book once a year instead of every month cut its trading by almost
two thirds — 27% of the book changing hands each year down to 10%, 1265 round trips down to 251
— and changed what your money earned by **nothing at all**: +7.4% either way, to the first
decimal, with the worst fall a tenth of a point shallower and the share of money invested
identical to two decimal places.

This is not a surprise and it was predicted before the run, because it is arithmetic rather than
a discovery. A company's size is its share count times its share price. If you hold companies in
proportion to their size and you touch nothing, every holding's share of your account moves
exactly the way its target moves. The book re-balances itself. Only three things can pull it off
target — a company issuing or buying back shares, a company joining or leaving the index, and
the 5% ceiling — and together those are small. Measured directly before the run: after six to
eight months of drift, only 1% to 4% of holdings had moved far enough off target for the
simulator to bother trading them, against 19% to 22% on the equal-slice book.

So if you ever hold a book shaped like the market, re-weight it once a year. Monthly is pure
cost with no benefit, and here the cost happened to be small enough to hide.

## Finding 2: on equal slices, the re-weighting IS worth something — but it is the cash, not the trimming

The equal-slice book behaved the opposite way, and this is where the prediction written before
the run was **wrong**. The prediction was that the yearly version would beat the monthly one by
a point or more, because it trades less and trading costs money. It lost instead: +9.7% against
+10.2%, half a point a year worse despite doing a fifth of the trading.

The third version says why. EQ-DEPOSIT never sells to re-balance either — it is exactly as
hands-off as EQ-ANNUAL — but it spends each month's deposit on the names that have slipped
furthest below an equal slice. It earned **+10.3%**, the best of the six, while trading a third
less than EQ-MONTHLY (38% of the book a year against 56%, 842 round trips against 1248).

Line the three up by how much of the account was actually in the market rather than sitting in
cash:

| version | invested | earned | trading |
|---|---|---|---|
| EQ-ANNUAL | 94.5% | +9.7% | 23% |
| EQ-MONTHLY | 97.1% | +10.2% | 56% |
| EQ-DEPOSIT | 97.5% | +10.3% | 38% |

The return follows the invested share and ignores the trading. Each extra point of the account
kept invested was worth about 0.2 points a year, which is squarely inside the range this lab has
measured for a point of exposure elsewhere. The yearly book was not punished for failing to trim
its winners; it was punished for leaving up to eleven months of deposits in cash with no rule
that would spend them. Give it a rule that spends them and it catches up and passes.

This confirms, on a different book and a different shape, what M0266 found in October: once you
hold the invested share still, trimming winners to feed laggards is worth nothing. The lab has
now seen that twice, on a 50-name equal book and on a 240-name one.

**The practical form of it:** the cheapest honest way to run an equal-slice book is to never sell
to re-balance at all, and let the monthly top-up do the whole job. That is also the easiest thing
to actually do by hand at Gotrade, and it is the version that earned the most.

## Finding 3: the equal shape beat the market's shape by about three points a year — and that is the uncomfortable part

Over identical companies, equal slices earned +10.2% to +10.3% against +7.4% for size weighting.
In 2009-2015 — the best-covered years and the ones most like today — the gap is wider still: the
equal-slice book beat SPY by **3.5 points a year** while the size-weighted book **lost to SPY by
1.1 to 1.3**. On the survivorship-check store, where most of the companies that died are priced
back in, the equal book keeps +2.5 points a year in 2009-2015 and the size-weighted book falls
to −1.7.

Three reasons not to get excited.

**It is a bet on breadth, and it says so plainly.** Split the 237 months into those where a few
giant companies carried the index and those where the average company did the work: the
equal-slice versions earned +13% a year in the broad months and **lost 8% to 9% a year in the
narrow ones**. The years your money has actually been invested — 2018 onward — were famously
narrow, carried by a handful of very large American companies. A book that loses 9% a year when
that happens is the wrong book for the era we are in, whatever it did in 1996-2015.

**It fell much harder.** 57.7% from a peak against 50.2%, and a worst year of −36.7% in 2008
against −32.0%. Both are far outside what you allow, but the equal book is the worse of the two.

**It costs the most where the account is smallest.** Splitting 20,000,000 rupiah about 240 ways
is a slot near six dollars. These results say that worked anyway, but it works by fractional
orders and a 20%-of-slot patience rule, and it is the kind of thing that breaks quietly when
account sizes or fee minimums change.

## On luck, and on the gate

Every version failed the screen. The best luck score here is 0.68 against the 0.90 you require
since October 2026 — meaning that after 185 distinct method attempts in this lab, a result this
good would turn up by chance often enough that it cannot be called real. Every version also broke
the fall limit (50% to 58% against 25%) and the gains-versus-losses test.

A word on that last one, because the numbers look alarming: the profit factor reads 0.31 to 0.84,
which normally means a book that loses more than it makes. It does not mean that here. These
books almost never sell, so the only *completed* trades are the handful of companies that dropped
out of the index — mostly losers — while every gain is still sitting unrealised in a holding that
was never sold. The measure is not meaningful on a buy-and-hold book, and the returns above are.

Walk-forward came out 3 of 4 periods beaten, which would clear the fold condition, but no version
is dev-eligible so nothing is promotable and no buy signal fires. Survivorship-free price history
is still not worth paying for.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Three predictions were written down before the run. The first — that the yearly size-weighted
book would land within 0.3 points a year of the monthly one — held exactly (0.0). The second —
that the yearly equal book would beat the monthly one by a point or more — was **wrong and
backwards**: it lost half a point, and the third version showed why (idle cash, not fees). The
third — that deposit steering would beat the plain yearly book — held (+10.3 against +9.7).

Of the three ways the run was expected to answer nothing: the band did not flatten everything
(the equal arms separated cleanly); the six-dollar slots did not break the equal book (though the
fee minimum is still the suspect behind the small size-weighted numbers); and the idle-cash
worry turned out to be the *entire* story on the equal side rather than a caveat on it. The
survivorship warning landed too — every version earned 0.9 to 1.2 points a year less with the
dead companies priced back in, and the often-re-weighted ones lost slightly more than the yearly
ones, as predicted, though only slightly.

This method registers no mirror or reversed arm, so the lab's dressing check has nothing to
split; that is correct here. The question was never "is a signal real" — there is no signal. It
was "what does a habit cost", and the no-habit endpoints (the January book, which never trims,
and SPY, which holds one thing) are both in the run.

## One small extra

Buying SPY monthly with your deposits, at Gotrade's real fees, earned −0.0 points a year against
the same deposits into SPY at no fees, over 21 years. Broker fees on a single monthly purchase of
one liquid ETF are, to one decimal place, free. Whatever beats SPY has to beat it on the strategy
and not by shaving costs, because there are no costs there left to shave.

## My opinion:

The cadence question is settled and I would not spend another method on it. On a size-weighted
book re-weighting is arithmetic noise — do it once a year, or once a decade. On an equal-slice
book the right answer is better than either of the ones I registered: never sell to re-balance,
and let the monthly deposit do the whole job. That version earned the most, traded a third less
than the monthly one, and is the easiest to execute by hand. I would adopt "deposit-steered, no
re-balancing sales" as the default shape for every equal-slice book this lab builds from here,
and I think that is worth a short note to you rather than another experiment: it is a free
improvement on the frame, not a strategy.

What I would spend a method on next is the uncomfortable part of Finding 3. Equal slices beat
the market's own shape by three points a year over the same companies, and by 4.6 points in
2009-2015, and the lab has spent a year assuming the opposite — that equal weighting was a
handicap the roster was quietly paying. That assumption came from books that also had a market
switch and 15 turns a year attached to them, and when those were separated out in October the
weighting itself priced at under one point. This run says it is worth more than that and in the
right direction. But it is a bet on the average company beating the giants, it loses 9% a year
when it doesn't, and the era we are actually living in is the one where it doesn't. The method I
want next asks that directly: hold the same names, slide the weighting continuously from pure
size to pure equal in five rungs, and read the 2009-2015 column and the narrow-month column
together. If the best rung is partway along and holds up in narrow months, that is a frame change
worth having. If the whole gain lives at the equal end and dies in narrow months, then the lab's
old assumption was right for the wrong reason, and we should say so and stop.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-0843: verified, with one open term in the headline gap

Everything reported reproduces. MONTHLY matches #923 M0224-CORE, #754 M0226-CORE and #948
M0281-CORE at 1265 trades and exposure 0.914323363572897, identical to fifteen digits, so the
chassis is the one the lab already trusts. The six funded leads over SPY are +0.21, +0.22, +2.99,
+2.50, +3.10 and -0.02 as reported. Nothing is dev-eligible: the falls run 50-58% and the luck
reading 0.52-0.68 against a 0.90 bar, so there is no promotion and no buy signal here, correctly.

Findings 1 and 2 hold as stated and are the keepers. Cadence really is inert on a size-weighted
book -- +7.40% against +7.41% for two thirds less trading -- and the equal-slice cadence gap really
is idle cash rather than trimming: the deposit-driven arm carries the January arm's no-selling
discipline at the monthly arm's exposure and wins outright, which is a second confirmation of M0266
on a different book.

**The open term.** The caution in finding 3 is right to insist the breadth split travels with the
2.8-point equal-versus-size gap. There is a second term it does not yet account for, and it runs
the same way. The two arms do not hold the same amount of money in the market: the size-weighted
arms sit invested 91.4% of the time and the equal-slice arms 97.1%, a 5.7-point gap. This run's own
finding 2 priced a point of exposure at roughly 0.19 points a year on this very chassis. Applied
naively that is about a point of the 2.8, or two fifths of it, before weighting has explained
anything at all.

I am not asserting that correction, because the lab has already been burned reading a slope off two
points, and because the price of a point of exposure is an era rather than a constant -- near zero
in 2003-2008 and about 0.17 in 2009-2015. The honest statement is that the 2.8-point gap has at
least three ingredients: exposure, breadth regime, and whatever is left for the weighting itself,
and this run separates none of them. The lab has been here before: an 8-point equal-weight gap
decomposed into 3.6 of gate, 3.8 of fees and 0.9 of actual weighting, and the shape got the credit
for years.

So the gap is not reportable as a weighting result. M0292 is the right instrument and should carry
an exposure column and a turnover column beside its five rungs, so that the exposure term is
measured across the dial rather than assumed away. Recorded so the synthesis quotes the caveat and
not the headline.


### 2026-10-23

## Correction, sera-20261023-1049: the open term is measured, and the 2.8 is withdrawn

My check above said this run's 2.8-point equal-versus-size gap had an unmeasured exposure term,
that the two arms sat at 91.4% and 97.1% invested, and that the gap was therefore not reportable
as a weighting result. M0292 ran the dial in five rungs the next day and measured it.

The exposure term is real and it slides with the rung: 91.22% at pure market value to 97.52% at
equal slices, a 6.30-point spread, not a flat offset. The mechanism is the one that makes this
method unable to finish the job -- market value is shares times price, so at the size end a
holding's weight drifts exactly the way its target drifts, the monthly deposit finds no gap to
fill, and the cash banks. Weighting and exposure are collinear on this chassis by construction.

The reportable figure is a bound. The end-to-end gap is 2.73 points a year; a point of exposure
has never been worth more than 0.17 points a year here and is worth about nothing in 2003-2008,
so exposure carries between 0 and 1.07 points of it. **The weighting term is 1.6 to 2.7 points a
year, and the unqualified 2.8 should not be quoted.** M0300 pins every rung to one exposure and
closes it.

Nothing about this run's own numbers changes: the cadence findings stand, the deposit-steered arm
is still the best equal arm, and this record is not edited. The correction is to what the 2.8 was
taken to mean.


### 2026-10-23

## Correction to the correction, sera-20261023-1305: the 2.8 stands

M0300 pinned every rung of this dial to one level of invested money -- exposure spread 0.080
points where it had been 6.30 -- and the end-to-end gap barely moved, 2.73 to 2.59 points a year.
Its bridge arm prices a point of exposure on this chassis at 0.0128 points a year, so the 6.30-
point spread was worth about 0.08, not the 1.07 the earlier ceiling allowed.

So the exposure term is about zero. With each ladder's own fee slope removed the two runs agree at
2.82 and 2.86 points a year.

The earlier coordinator correction withdrew the unqualified 2.8 and replaced it with a bound of
1.6 to 2.7. The bound was honest and the true value lies inside it, but the instruction attached
-- that the 2.8 should not be quoted -- is now wrong and is itself withdrawn. **The weighting term
is about 2.6 to 2.9 points a year, and it is not about being invested.** Quote that.

Nothing in either record is edited; this is the third entry in the chain and the one measured on
purpose.
methods.verdict: Rejected as a strategy, kept as a ruler: a book shaped like the market re-weights itself, so doing it monthly instead of yearly costs trading and earns nothing; an equal-slice book does need the help, but what it needs is the cash, not the selling — never selling to re-balance and letting the monthly deposit do the whole job earned the most of all six and traded a third less.

methods.name: Many speeds, graded exposure: a trend vote across horizons instead of one on-off 200-day line
methods.sourceRef: Faber 2007, A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation (SSRN 962461), for the switch and for the parameter-stability claim this method tests; Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012, Time Series Momentum (JFE 104:2), for the same insensitivity across one-, three-, six- and twelve-month look-backs; M0271, whose re-entry-delay ladder measured episodic cash at 0.2832 points a year per point over 2009-2015 on this exact book and store, and whose verdict asked for the shape of cash to be priced on its own; M0270, which measured evenly spread cash at 0.1732 on the same book; M0266 for the opinion-free 50-name chassis; M0281 for the measured warning that turning a losing timing rule down leaves its ratio invariant; insight 523, the rule that a reversed pair needs a no-opinion third arm; docs/backtests/2026-10-23-graded-trend-vote.py, the unfunded prior grid
methods.hypothesis: Faber reports broad parameter stability from a three-month trend out to beyond twelve, with the 200-day and 252-day versions statistically indistinguishable, and Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen report the same across one to twelve months. If several horizons are each individually defensible but disagree on different days, a vote across them GRADES exposure instead of switching it, and this lab has just measured the two numbers that decide whether that is worth anything. M0270 priced a point of the account held in cash spread evenly over every session at 0.1732 points a year of de-funded lead over 2009-2015 on this exact book, store and era; M0271 priced the same point bought in all-or-nothing episodes at 0.2832. Cash in lumps costs about 1.6 times what the same average cash costs spread out, so a graded gate should buy the same protection out of cheaper cash. The opposite reading is that grading is dilution wearing a story, and dilution halves the good half and the bad half together and leaves the ratio invariant at about 0.69. THE OBVIOUS EXPERIMENT CANNOT TELL THOSE APART, AND THE PRIOR GRID SHOWS WHY. Measured on SPY's own closes, monthly and unfunded, before this file was written: the literature's own 50/100/200/252 vote earns 6.36 percent a year against the single 200-day gate's 8.07 and falls 21.24 percent against 19.03 -- worse on both axes. But every horizon set centred on 200 instead lands within half a point of the gate (150/250 at 8.00, 125/175/225/275 at 7.58, eight horizons spanning 125 to 275 at 7.87), while every set centred near 150 loses one and a half points. Nearly the whole of the published vote's shortfall is its CENTRE OF GRAVITY and not its grading: the 50-day average is simply a worse timer than the 200-day one on this tape, and a vote including it replaces the gate's opinion with a faster one rather than grading the gate's own. SO THIS METHOD HOLDS THE MEAN HORIZON FIXED AT 200 AND MOVES ONLY HOW FINELY THE SAME AVERAGE OPINION IS EXPRESSED. The instrument is k whole-session horizons evenly spaced across 125 to 275, every set summing to exactly 200 times k: k=1 is 200 alone, which is the lab's own shared gate and therefore the degenerate first rung of this family rather than a foreign comparison; k=4 is 125/175/225/275 with five exposure levels; k=8 is 125/146/168/189/211/232/254/275 with nine. THE LADDER IS EXPOSURE-MATCHED BY CONSTRUCTION, WHICH IS BETTER THAN AN EXPOSURE-MATCHED CONTROL: read off SPY's bars in advance, the three rungs sit at 73.42, 72.68 and 73.15 percent of monthly decisions invested, a spread of 0.74 points, worth about 0.13 points a year at the era price of cash and reported beside every rung difference. A difference between these rungs cannot be dilution because there is nothing left to dilute. That is why the idea row's exposure-matched control has moved: it is spent on the published 50/100/200/252 set, which really does run 2.85 points less invested, as a single 200-day switch capped at 0.961207 of the book when it is on -- LIT4's average exposure over K1's, read from the same bars -- so the dilution question is asked on the one arm where it is real. The sixth arm is the gate switched off entirely, always invested, the no-opinion endpoint insight 523 asks for and the thing that makes the cost of the HABIT recoverable rather than cancelling across a pair. The host is M0270's opinion-free book -- M0266's 50 most-traded index members at equal weight, band zero, no picking, no brake, full scale -- chosen because the two prices of cash this hypothesis rests on were measured on it, because the no-gate arm reproduces M0270-S100 and M0271-OFF to the digit and the k=1 arm reproduces M0271-D000, and because a book with no opinion of its own cannot interact with the gate's. The price is that the base book loses to a deposit-matched SPY and falls past 50 percent, so no arm is a candidate and none will be promoted; eligibility would be reported and still not acted on. PREDICTIONS, written now. The no-gate and k=1 arms reproduce their recorded twins to the digit, and a mismatch is a bug chased before anything else is read. Realised exposure lands within 2 points of 98.6, 72.4, 71.7, 72.1, 69.6 and 69.6 percent, and if the three centred rungs do not land within a point of each other the graininess ladder may not be read as one. GRADING AT A FIXED CENTRE IS NEARLY INERT AND THAT IS THE HEADLINE I EXPECT: on SPY alone the three rungs span 0.49 points a year and are not monotone in k, which is the signature of noise rather than a dial, and the structural reason is that a centred vote is fully invested on 66.7 percent of decisions and fully out on 20.3, agreeing with the single gate on 87 percent of them. A rule that is the same rule seven times out of eight cannot be worth much. THE FUNDED ANSWER SHOULD BE WORSE FOR THE GRADED ARMS THAN THE PRIOR, BY AN AMOUNT THIS METHOD MEASURES: weight changes at monthly decisions run 21 of 236 for k=1, 55 for k=4, 56 for k=8 and 115 for the published set, so grading roughly triples the churn and the published set quintuples it, and on a 50-name book at Gotrade's real fees a quarter-weight move still places fifty orders and still pays the per-order minimum on most of them. I expect the graded rungs to lose 0.3 to 1.0 points a year more than the prior says; zero-fee twins of all six arms are run outside the registry to split the churn from the market. The published set loses to the centred four-horizon set -- same k, same five levels, only the centre and span differ -- by about 1.22 points a year, and it loses to its own dilution control too, which would make the published vote strictly worse than simply turning the single switch down. Worst fall barely moves across the centred ladder, three times 19.03 on the prior, because the deep falls happen when every horizon agrees and a vote with every member voting the same way IS the single gate. And the gate's habit costs about five points a year in 2009-2015 on the unfunded prior (12.72 for always-invested against 7.43 to 7.82 for every gated rung), which swamps everything else here and must be said in those words rather than buried under a 0.3-point ladder. THE DELIVERABLE, fixed now so it cannot be chosen afterwards: G is the de-funded lead of the finest rung minus the lead of the incumbent, at a matched centre and a matched exposure, quoted whole window and over 2009-2015 beside the 0.74-point exposure residual that produced part of it. G within 0.3 points a year CONFIRMS that a graded trend vote is the single switch wearing a finer dress and the lab should stop considering ensembles of one rule; G at or above 1.0 with a monotone ladder FALSIFIES that and the next method runs the same ladder on a book that picks; G at or below -1.0 says the all-or-nothing shape is doing work nobody has credited it with. Between those the answer is too small to tune against and the method says so. Both stores in one sweep with both fingerprints printed. Fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's funding plan. Success is a measurement.
methods.expectedFailure: THE LIKELIEST FAILURE IS THAT THE WHOLE LADDER COMES OUT INSIDE THE NOISE AND THE METHOD CANNOT TELL 'GRADING IS WORTH NOTHING' FROM 'THIS BOOK CANNOT MEASURE 0.3 POINTS A YEAR'. The prior's three centred rungs span 0.49 points a year on SPY alone with no fees and no picking; on a funded 50-name book that falls past 50 percent, path jitter between two arms holding the same names in different amounts through 2008 is of that order. The honest answer then is a bound -- 'grading is worth less than X a year on this chassis, and X is as small as this lab can currently measure' -- and not a finding either way. The internal noise band is the only honest yardstick: every rung is the same book on the same tape with one dial moved, and M0270's rung-pair errors on this chassis ran 0.000 to 0.034 points a year, so a ladder scatter near a twentieth of a point is expected and a spread much larger than that is real. The lab-wide 3.1 points a year of year-to-year noise is a different quantity about different books and is NOT the yardstick here. THE SECOND FAILURE IS THAT THE EXPOSURE MATCH FAILS IN THE RUN even though it holds on SPY's bars. The decision-session shares are computed on SPY alone; the realised exposure of a funded book also carries its fill path, its cash drag between decisions and its deposits, and those need not be identical across arms whose weights differ. If the three centred rungs land more than a point apart in realised exposure, the graininess ladder has become an exposure ladder and must be read as one, with M0270's era price applied and the residual stated rather than the difference quoted raw. THE THIRD IS THAT GRADING'S COST IS ENTIRELY THE FEE SCHEDULE AND NOT THE MARKET. A quarter-weight move on a 50-name book places fifty orders of a quarter the size and pays Gotrade's per-order minimum on more of them, so the graded rungs are penalised for a reason that has nothing to do with trend following. The zero-fee twins exist to split that, but if the gross and net ladders disagree about the SIGN of G then this method has measured a 20,000,000 IDR account's order economics rather than a market fact, and the verdict must say so in those words rather than dress it up. THE FOURTH IS THAT THE CENTRED LADDER IS TOO CONSERVATIVE TO BE THE TEST ANYONE MEANT. Holding the mean horizon at 200 is what makes the experiment clean, and it is also what makes the vote agree with the single gate on 87 percent of decisions. A reader could fairly say the method has defined the ensemble down to something that could not possibly differ. The answer is that the wide set is registered too, beside its own dilution control, so the published refinement is measured in its own terms as well -- but if LIT4 turns out to be the only arm that moves, then what this method has really measured is the 50-day horizon and not grading at all, and it must be reported under that name. THE FIFTH IS THAT THE BASE BOOK IS NOT A BOOK ANYONE WOULD TRADE. It falls past 50 percent and loses to SPY at every rung, so every lead here is a small difference between two large and violent numbers, and what grading is worth on it need not be what grading is worth on a 20-name book that picks. That is the deliberate price of an opinion-free chassis and it is why the deliverable is a bound on G rather than a recommendation. THE SIXTH IS THE ONE THAT WOULD HURT MOST: the ladder comes out monotone and positive, grading is worth a point a year, and the lab learns it on a chassis where no arm can be promoted and must spend another method id to find out whether it survives on a book that picks. That would be a good result arriving expensively, and the right response is to queue that method rather than to regret this one. THE SEVENTH is the dull one and would be the most useful: G comes out at zero, the graded vote is the single switch wearing a finer dress, and the practitioner literature's favourite refinement of the Faber rule is confirmed to be decoration. That must be reported with the same emphasis as a surprise rather than buried as a non-finding, because it closes a direction this lab would otherwise keep paying ids to re-open.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0287 — Many speeds, graded exposure: does a vote across trend horizons beat one on-off line?

**Rejected.** Grading the safety switch costs about a point a year, buys nothing in safety on the
dev price history, and makes the worst fall up to 6 points **deeper** on the fuller one. The
published version of the idea is the worst arm in the method and the only one that loses to SPY.

## The idea in one paragraph

The safety switch the lab uses everywhere is one line: if the market closes above its own 200-day
average, be invested; if not, hold cash. The best-known refinement is to stop treating that as a
yes-or-no question. Ask several averages of different lengths, count how many say yes, and hold
that share of the book — all of it, three quarters, half, a quarter, or nothing. The case for it is
arithmetic this lab measured itself only two days ago: a point of cash held evenly all the time
cost 0.17 points a year in 2009–2015, while the same point of cash taken in all-or-nothing lumps
cost 0.28. Lumpy cash is about 1.6 times as expensive. A graded switch holds the same average cash
in smaller pieces, so it should buy the same protection more cheaply.

## The trap, found before anything was run

The obvious experiment is the literature's own set of lengths — 50, 100, 200 and 252 days — against
the single 200-day line. Run on the market index alone, before this method's file was written, that
pair reads: the vote earns 6.36% a year against the single line's 8.07%, and falls 21.2% against
19.0%. Worse on both counts. It would have been read as "grading fails" and it would have been the
wrong conclusion, because **two things change at once**. Moving the probe over sets of lengths
centred on 200 instead separated them:

| lengths used | average length | earned | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 alone (the lab's switch) | 200 | 8.07% | 19.03% |
| 150 / 250 | 200 | 8.00% | 19.41% |
| 125 / 175 / 225 / 275 | 200 | 7.58% | 19.03% |
| eight lengths from 125 to 275 | 200 | 7.87% | 19.03% |
| 50 / 100 / 200 / 252 (the published set) | 151 | 6.36% | 21.24% |

Every set centred on 200 lands within half a point of the single line. Every set centred near 150
loses a point and a half. **The 50-day average is simply a worse market timer than the 200-day one,
and a vote that includes it replaces the switch's opinion with a faster one rather than grading the
switch's own.** So this method held the average length fixed at 200 and moved only how finely the
same opinion gets expressed.

## What was run

Six versions of one deliberately opinion-free book — the 50 most-traded index members at equal
weight, no stock picking, no brake — so that nothing but the switch could move. Fractional shares,
Gotrade's real fees, the owner's real 5,000,000 rupiah monthly top-up, 1996 to October 2015.

| arm | what it is | your money earned | worst fall | gains per 1 of losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K1 | the lab's switch: 200 alone, in or out | **+9.0%** | 20.4% | 2.69 |
| DIL | the same switch, turned down to hold 96% when it is on | **+8.7%** | **19.7%** | 2.70 |
| K8 | eight lengths, 125–275, nine exposure levels | +8.1% | 20.4% | 2.54 |
| K4 | four lengths, 125–275, five exposure levels | +7.8% | 20.4% | 2.51 |
| FULL | no switch at all, always invested | +6.9% | 59.5% | 1.25 |
| LIT4 | the published 50/100/200/252 vote | +6.0% | 21.3% | 1.99 |

The same deposits put into SPY earned **+7.2%**. Two arms lost to it: the always-invested book and
the published vote.

## The answer

The number this method was built to produce, fixed in writing before the run, is the gap between
the most finely graded arm and the plain switch, both centred on 200 and both holding the same
average amount of cash. It came out at **−1.11 points a year**. The pre-registered line was that
anything past 1 point means the all-or-nothing shape is doing real work. It is past it.

Three things make that solid rather than a fluke:

* **The two arms really do hold the same amount of cash.** Measured after the fact, the three
  centred arms sat invested 70.82%, 70.39% and 70.65% of the time — a spread of 0.43 points, inside
  the half-point tolerance the lab publishes for this. So the gap is not one arm simply being more
  invested than another. It cannot be dilution, because there is nothing left to dilute.
* **It is not the fees.** Re-run with every fee set to zero, the gap is −1.04 instead of −1.11. Fees
  explain 0.07 of it. This was the failure I expected most and it did not happen: grading's cost is
  a market effect, not an artefact of a small account paying a minimum charge on more orders.
* **It holds on the fuller price history too**, where it reads −1.39.

## Why grading costs money: it cannot be all the way out when that is what matters

Break the twenty years into eras and the cost is not spread evenly at all.

| era | what grading cost (per year) | what was happening |
|---|---|---|
| 1996–2002 | −2.24 | the dot-com crash |
| 2003–2008 | −0.55 | |
| 2008 alone | −2.45 | the financial crisis |
| 2009–2015 | −0.52 | no bear market at all |

**Grading is nearly free in the one stretch where the switch was useless, and expensive in exactly
the years the switch earns its keep.** 2008 shows the mechanism at its clearest. Through that year
the single switch was out of the market 100% of the time and fell 0%. The graded arms held a sliver
— just under 2% — and fell 2.2%. That tiny difference cost 2.45 points.

The reason is structural. For a vote to reach zero, *every* length has to agree, and the longest
ones only turn down well after the fall is under way. So a graded switch is never fully out at the
moment of maximum danger; it gets there late, having carried part of the book down the slide. The
all-or-nothing shape, which looks crude, is what lets the switch leave the room in one step.

## The dev prices hide the harm. The fuller prices do not.

On the dev price history the three centred arms fall 17.816%, 17.818% and 17.817% — a spread of
**two thousandths of a point**. Grading buys literally no safety there.

Re-run on the survivorship-check history, which restores most of the companies that went bankrupt
or were bought, the same three arms fall **17.5%, 23.8% and 21.1%** — a spread of 6.3 points.
Grading does not just fail to buy safety on the honest tape; it costs up to 6 points of extra fall.
This is the same pattern the lab has seen before: a safety claim that looks neutral on the dev
prices because the companies that actually died are missing from them.

## The published version, taken apart

The published 50/100/200/252 vote lost **3.11 points a year** to the single 200-day switch, and
that splits almost exactly in half:

* **1.52 points for grading the exposure at all** (the single switch → four lengths centred on 200)
* **1.59 points for dragging the average length from 200 down to 150** (centred four → the published
  four)

It also lost 2.71 points to the dilution control — the single switch simply turned down to hold the
same average amount of cash. So the published refinement is beaten by the crudest possible
alternative: leave the rule alone and just hold a bit less of the book.

## How likely is this to be real rather than luck?

The lab's luck measure (DSR — how likely a result is real rather than a lucky draw after many
tries) was judged against **184 looks** at the moment these trials were recorded, one per distinct
method in the lab; the lab now stands at 185. The bar is 0.90.
The best arm here reads 0.878 and the worst 0.414. **Every arm fails the luck bar**, so none of
them is a candidate and none will be promoted — which was written into the pre-registration before
the run, because the base book was chosen for being opinion-free rather than for being good. It
loses to SPY when always invested and falls 59.5%. That is the deliberate price of a clean
measurement.

The method also won only 1 of its 4 walk-forward stretches. Worth noting that 2 of 4 is the usual
outcome in this lab, so 1 of 4 is genuinely poor.

## The elephant: the switch itself costs far more than any of this

Whatever grading is worth, the switch's own habit is worth ten times more, and in both directions.
Over the whole twenty years the switch earned **+2.16 points a year** over never using it, and made
the worst fall **37 points shallower** (20.4% against 59.5%). In 2008 alone it was worth **+40.8
points**.

But over 2009–2015 — the best-covered years, the ones most like today, and the era the owner's own
money lives in — the switch **cost 6.71 points a year**. Its time in cash explains at most 5.70 of
that even at the expensive lumpy price, so a point a year is unexplained by cash at all. That
matches what the re-entry-delay ladder found two days ago: the switch is not a cash dial.

A single five-month absence in 2009 is most of it, and no 200-day rule can avoid that by
construction. Tuning the switch finer does not touch it.

## Did the hypothesis hold, and did the expected failure happen?

The hypothesis was that grading buys the same protection out of cheaper cash. **It did not hold,
and it failed in the opposite direction** from the one the arithmetic suggested. The lumps-versus-
evenly-spread price gap is real — the lab measured it — but it does not apply here, because the
graded arm does not convert lump cash into evenly-spread cash. It converts *decisive* cash into
*late* cash, and late cash during a crash is the most expensive kind there is.

Of the seven written-down failure modes, the one that fired was the fourth, partly: the published
wide set is the arm that moves most, so some of what this method measured is the 50-day length
rather than grading. The centred ladder settles that, and both halves are reported above rather
than merged. The two I expected most — that the whole ladder would vanish into noise, and that
grading's cost would turn out to be the fee schedule — **both failed to fire**, which makes the
result stronger than I expected it to be. The one I called "dull and most useful" did not happen
either: grading is not neutral decoration, it is actively costly.

One prediction was wrong in detail and should be recorded as such. I predicted the three centred
arms would be "nearly inert", spanning well under a point. They span 1.11. The market-index-only
prior under-stated the effect roughly five-fold, which is a warning about that kind of prior in
general: a weight path on the index alone does not reproduce what the same rule does to a book of
fifty names, even when the rule reads nothing but the index.

The ladder is **not** a dose-response. Going from one length to four costs 1.52 points; going from
four to eight gives 0.41 back. Same sign and shape in every era and on both price histories. So the
cost is in having in-between levels at all, not in how many of them there are. There is no dial here
to turn — only a thing to do or not do.

## Against the parent and the near misses

The parent is the re-entry-delay ladder, and this method agrees with it and extends it. That one
showed the switch is not a cash dial; this one shows the switch's *shape* — leaving in one step
rather than several — is part of what it is for, not an implementation detail. Two arms reproduce
that method's recorded rows to twelve digits (the no-switch arm and the plain-switch arm, same
return, same fall, same trade count), which is what licenses reading everything else here.

Nothing in this method comes near the lab's closest-to-eligible trials; it was never meant to. The
base book is a measuring instrument.

## My opinion:

**This direction is closed and should stay closed, and I would spend the saving elsewhere.**

Ensembles of one rule are not worth another method id. The result is clean, it holds on both price
histories, it survives having the fees removed, it is exposure-matched by construction, and the
mechanism is understood rather than merely observed: a vote cannot be decisive, and the switch's
whole value is in being decisive at the two moments in twenty years when that mattered. Any future
proposal that averages several versions of the same timing rule is answered by this method, and a
reviewer can point at the 2008 column and stop.

What I would do next follows from the elephant rather than from the ladder. The switch's value
ranges from +40 points in 2008 to −6.7 points a year in 2009–2015, and the lab has now spent seven
method ids this month on *when* to read it, *how often*, in what phase, with what band, with what
delay, and now at what graininess. Every one of those answers came back a fraction of a point. The
one thing nobody has changed is **what the book does while it is out**. It sits in cash. In
2009–2015 that cost nearly seven points a year, and holding cheap broad exposure instead of nothing
— even a quarter of the book — would be a genuinely different rule rather than another dial on the
same one. That is the method I have queued.

The second thing I would do costs no method id at all: the dev-versus-fuller-price-history split on
worst fall here (0.002 points against 6.3) is large enough that I would not trust *any* safety claim
made on the dev prices alone without re-running it on the fuller ones first. That is a habit change,
not an experiment.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-0843: the verdict stands, the headline number does not

Everything structural in this run verifies. The two reproduction anchors are exact to fourteen
digits against trials this lab already held: M0287-FULL (250.32044936670573, 1338 trades) equals
#898 M0270-S100 and #904 M0271-OFF, and M0287-K1 (317.1788319736869, 1330 trades) equals #905
M0271-D000. The exposure match is real: 70.82%, 70.39% and 70.65% for K1, K4 and K8, a 0.43-point
spread, inside the half-point tolerance the lab publishes. So the result is not dilution, which is
the failure this method was designed to rule out, and it ruled it out properly. Separating the
centre of gravity from the grading before committing the file was the right call and is the most
valuable thing in the run.

**The correction.** The analysis reports the headline gap -- the most finely graded arm against the
plain switch -- as -1.11 points a year, and reads it as past the pre-registered 1-point line. The
recorded trials do not give that number on either column the lab stores:

  money-weighted (the column the pass/fail screen reads)   K8 - K1 = -0.929
  de-funded CAGR                                            K8 - K1 = -0.725
  money-weighted, four horizons instead of eight            K4 - K1 = -1.208

The -1.11 is closest to the era table aggregated by calendar years: seven years at -2.24, six at
-0.55 and seven at -0.52 average -1.13. That aggregation weights every year equally, and the
owner's account did not hold equal money in every year. The cost of grading is concentrated in
1996-2002 and in 2008, which is exactly when the account was smallest, so weighting by years
over-states what grading would have cost the owner. On the money the gap is -0.93 and the
pre-registered line was **not** crossed by the most finely graded arm. It is crossed by the
four-horizon arm, at -1.21.

This is the lab's recorded front-loading problem wearing its other face: most leads here are
earned before most of the money arrives, and so are most costs.

**Why the verdict is unchanged.** Every graded arm earns less than the plain switch on the money
column; the dev falls are identical to two thousandths of a point; the check-store falls spread
6.3 points the wrong way; and all six arms fail the luck bar at N=184. The direction is unambiguous
and the mechanism -- a vote cannot be all the way out until every horizon agrees, and the long ones
turn late -- is demonstrated cleanly at 2008. Grading the switch is dead either way. What changes
is only the size of the claim a later batch may quote: about nine tenths of a point on the owner's
money, not one and a tenth, and the pre-registered threshold should be read on the money column
rather than on an equal-weighted average of eras.


### 2026-10-23

## Admitted to paper as the roster's always-invested control (owner, 2026-10-23)

Owner override after his calculate-assets run of this method's gate-off arm. M0287-FULL joins the
paper roster as FULL50-FR-GT (migration 023), replacing MVW-FR-GT, which is retired beside it.

**It is a control, not a candidate, and the entry says so in its first sentence.** C has been on
this roster permanently since the Gotrade rebuild as the daily-trading control, because measuring
how bad daily trading would have been is itself the finding. This is the complement: how bad, or
good, never stepping aside would have been. Every other book on the board defends itself with a
market switch, a brake or a weighting scheme, and nothing there has ever measured the absence of
that going forward.

**Not a lab pass, and not a near miss either.** This method is rejected and this arm failed every
dev condition: it loses to a deposit-matched SPY TR (+250.3% against +257.2%, 6.9% a year against
7.2%), falls 59.5% against the screen's 50% and the owner's 25% real-money bar, makes a profit
factor of 1.25 against 1.30, and reads a recorded DSR of 0.414 at its recorded N=184 on 1,338
trades. No test-window look is spent by the admission and none ever will be on this arm.

**What put it on the board is the other window.** Over 2018-04-02 to 2026-10-08, on the owner's
real deposits at Gotrade's real fees, it ended at Rp 1,558,671,049 -- 24.6% a year against SPY's
20.4%, the only arm of this batch's four methods to beat the market -- while falling 33.3%. The
dev verdict above was earned in 1996-2002 and in 2008. A book with no defence wins a decade with
no long bear market in it and loses the one that has two, and the owner's money has never lived
through a fall of that kind. The entry is how the roster finds out which kind of decade it is in.

**One engine change travelled with it.** The arm runs the band-zero tape, where every holding is
traded back to its slot each month, and that is what the 24.6% was earned on. The tape lived
inside M0127's method file, and a roster entry can only name a rules preset, so the preset was
added to sim.rules field-for-field equal to M0127's object (asserted in the suite) and M0127 was
left exactly as committed. Admitting the book on the roster's usual preset instead would have put
a different book on the board wearing this one's number.
methods.verdict: Grading the safety switch costs about a point a year, buys no safety on the dev prices and up to 6 points of deeper fall on the fuller ones: a vote can never be all the way out at the moment that matters, and 2008 is where the whole cost sits.

methods.name: A traded-volume floor as a general survivorship brake on a price-only stock screen
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0284 (its volume-bar ladder and the dev-minus-check-store line it produced), carried onto M0032's chassis -- M0007-N20-RAW in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits (Blitz, Huij & Martens 2011, Residual momentum, J. Empirical Finance 18(3), 506-521)
methods.hypothesis: M0284 turned the news-day book's event volume bar five ways and found a second, independent straight line nobody asked for: dev store minus survivorship-check store, funded, a year, ran -3.3 points with no bar, -1.3 at 2x, -1.0 at 2.5x, -1.6 at 3x and +0.6 at 4x. The strictest rung is the only arm in that method that earns MORE with the dead companies put back, and its 2009-2015 lead went from +0.7% to +1.8%. The reading is that a volume condition is a liveness proxy and not a news proxy: a company the market is actively trading still exists, so a price move on ordinary volume is disproportionately a thin, fading name of the kind the dev store prices and the check store exposes. If that is general rather than a quirk of event books, it must transfer to a screen with no events in it. This runs it on M0032's chassis verbatim -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 monthly trend switch, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits -- adding one requirement to the pool and moving nothing else: a pick must not be in the worst-traded dv_pct percent of that day's own eligible names by 20-day mean dollar volume. Five rungs, a ladder and not a pair, because two points cannot read a slope: DV00 (no floor, the reference arm with no opinion in it, which must reproduce M0032's recorded trial bar for bar), DV20, DV40, DV60 and DV80. The cut is cross-sectional and not a fixed dollar bar on purpose: dollar volumes grew by more than an order of magnitude across the dev window, so an absolute bar is a disguised date filter whose ladder would measure the era. I measured the geometry before writing this file, over all 238 decision months: the dial binds hard and monotonically (names shared with the no-floor book are 20.00, 16.36, 12.69, 8.47 and 4.40 of 20), and -- unlike all six filters M0277 and M0279 tried -- it does not starve the book, holding 20.00, 20.00, 20.00, 20.00 and 19.87 names on average, so M0279's 2-to-6-point cost of parking empty slots cannot be the explanation for anything seen here. The measurement that matters is NOT the dev return: it is the dev-minus-check-store gap, rung by rung, which lab survivorship prints. Success for the idea: that gap narrows monotonically as the floor rises across at least four rungs and sits within half a point of zero at the top rung, while under 1 point a year of dev return is given up. Success for the gate, separately: an arm with a worst fall under the screen that beats total-return SPY with DSR >= 0.90, on the check store as well as dev.
methods.expectedFailure: The effect may be specific to event books. A news day's volume spike is a different animal from a momentum name's ordinary turnover -- M0284's dial asked whether TODAY was busy for this stock, while this one asks whether this stock is busy compared to its peers -- so the transfer may simply not happen and the ladder be flat in the gap, which would mean the liveness reading was a coincidence of the news chassis. The second way it fails is that a dollar-volume floor is a crowding tilt as much as a liveness one: it pushes the book toward the names everyone is already trading, and a crowded name is where a published edge fades first, so the strict rungs may lose dev return steadily even while their survivorship gap closes -- and since residual momentum was published in 2011, inside this window, the fade is the base case and 2009-2015 is where it would show. Third, the floor tilts toward the largest companies, and insight 91 says the dev store's edge sits with the smaller index members, so the strict rungs may converge on SPY's own big-company drift and beat nothing. Fourth, the whole chassis inherits M0007's worst fall near 19-20%, which this dial has no reason to touch, so the drawdown screen may reject every rung regardless of what the gap does. And fifth, even a clean monotone result here is evidence about how to BUILD books and not a candidate: the check store is a cross-check and not a gate, so an arm that only looks better there can never be promoted on that basis.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## What was tried

An earlier experiment (the wider news-day pool) was asking whether a book built on big news days
was being too fussy. It turned one dial — how busy a stock's trading had to be on the news day —
and on the way it turned up something nobody had asked for. The lab keeps two copies of market
history: the everyday one, and an honest one that puts back the companies that went bust or were
bought out. The looser that volume dial was set, the more of the book's apparent edge disappeared
when the dead companies were put back. The strictest setting was the only one that earned *more*
on the honest tape.

The reading was that asking for volume is really asking **"is this company still alive?"**. A
company the market is actively trading still exists. A price move on sleepy volume is more often a
thin, fading name — exactly the kind the everyday tape quietly drops and the honest tape exposes.

That was found on a book about news events. This method asks whether it is a general truth about
building any stock book, or just a quirk of news. So it was carried to a book with no events in it
at all: the residual-momentum book the paper roster trades, which simply buys the twenty stocks
that have climbed most on their own merits, re-picked monthly, behind the usual safety switch that
sits the book out when the market is below its long-run average.

One requirement was added and **nothing else was moved**: a stock may not be in the least-traded
part of that day's own candidate list. Five settings, from "no requirement at all" up to "only the
most-traded fifth qualifies". Measuring five points rather than two is deliberate — the lab has
been fooled before by reading a slope from a single pair.

Two choices worth naming. The bar is **relative to the other candidates that day**, not a fixed
dollar amount, because trading volumes grew more than tenfold across these twenty years, so a
fixed bar would quietly be a date filter and the whole ladder would measure the calendar rather
than liveness. And it uses dollars traded rather than company size, because the lab's company-size
figure is known to be broken while its dollars-traded figure is sound.

## Checks that the experiment is clean

Three things were verified before reading any result, because the last few attempts at filtering a
book all failed for the same boring reason and it would have been easy to repeat.

- **The "no requirement" setting reproduces the existing book exactly** — the same total return to
  sixteen digits, the same 1,607 trades, the same worst fall, the same gains-to-losses. So the new
  code is the same arithmetic, and every difference further up the ladder is the dial and not a
  bug.
- **The dial really bites.** Of the twenty names held, the number shared with the no-requirement
  book falls 20.0 → 16.4 → 12.7 → 8.5 → 4.4 as the bar rises. At the top setting the book is
  almost entirely different stocks.
- **It never leaves the book sitting in cash.** This is the one that mattered. Every previous
  filtering attempt starved the book — it asked for twenty names, found three, and parked the rest
  in the index, which cost 2 to 6 points a year and swamped whatever the filter was trying to say.
  Here the candidate list has 262 names for 20 slots, so the book still holds 20.0, 20.0, 20.0,
  20.0 and 19.9 names on average, and the share of time invested barely moves (69.4% down to
  68.6%). **Nothing below can be explained by money sitting idle.**

## What happened

Against the same deposits put into the index, which earned +7.2% a year, every setting won on the
everyday tape:

| bar | a year, everyday tape | a year, honest tape | difference | worst fall | 2009-15 vs index, honest tape |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | +13.7% | +12.0% | **−1.7** | 20.6% | −0.2% |
| 20% | +14.0% | +12.3% | **−1.7** | 22.8% | −0.0% |
| 40% | +12.6% | +12.7% | **+0.0** | 23.0% | **+0.4%** |
| 60% | +10.8% | +10.6% | **−0.2** | 22.0% | −5.7% |
| 80% | +8.3% | +10.2% | **+1.8** | 20.9% | −6.6% |

**The honesty gap swings from −1.7 points to +1.8 points as the bar rises.** The earlier news-day
experiment swung from −3.3 to +0.6 — the same shape, and a similar size, on a completely
different kind of book. So the finding generalises: **a volume requirement is a liveness filter on
any price-based stock screen, not a news trick.** That is the question this method was registered
to answer, and the answer is yes.

## But the idea failed its own test, and I should say so plainly

Before any of this was run, success was written down as: the gap closes step by step across at
least four settings, lands within half a point of zero at the top, and costs less than 1 point a
year. All three clauses failed.

- The gap does not close tidily. It goes −1.7, −1.7, +0.0, −0.2, +1.8: two rises, one flat step
  and one step backwards.
- The top setting does not land near zero, it sails past it to +1.8.
- And the price is not under 1 point a year. It is **5.4 points** a year: the strictest book earns
  +8.3% where the unfiltered one earns +13.7%.

So as a recipe — "add this bar to your book and it will be more honest for almost nothing" — the
idea is rejected. Buying 3.5 points of honesty for 5.4 points of return is a bad trade.

## The thing actually worth knowing

The interesting result is not in the column I pre-registered. Read the honest tape **on its own**,
ignoring the everyday one:
