> On the everyday tape the bar looks like a pure cost: +13.7% with no bar, +12.6% at the 40%
> setting. On the honest tape the order **reverses**: +12.0% with no bar, **+12.7%** at the 40%
> setting — the best of all five.

The everyday tape systematically flatters the unfiltered book and punishes the filtered one, and
it does it by enough to invert which one you would choose. That is a warning about the lab's main
data set, not about this method.

The 40% setting is also **the only one of the five with a positive edge in 2009-2015 on the honest
tape** (+0.4%). Those are the best-covered years and the most like today, and they are the lab's
first filter. Every other setting is negative there — the no-bar book included.

## Why: the mechanism

The market-breadth report explains the cost, and it is the cleanest five-step response in this
method. As the bar rises, the book's return in months when **a few big companies carried the
index** climbs +5.6% → +6.5% → +8.2% → +9.1% → +11.4%. In months when **gains were widely
spread**, it falls +6.4% → +5.9% → +3.5% → +0.6% → −4.7%.

So the bar does exactly what was feared: it herds the book into the biggest, most-traded names.
Those names win when the index is being carried by a handful of giants and lose when gains are
broad. The strictest setting stops being a stock-picking book and becomes a large-company bet. The
lost 5.4 points a year is not a fee or a cash drag — it is this tilt.

That also explains why the honesty gap closes. Dead companies are overwhelmingly small and thinly
traded. Refusing to buy thin names is refusing to buy the companies that later disappear. The
protection is real, but it is bought by giving up the part of the market where this book earns.

## Did the predictions hold?

The hypothesis held in direction and failed in size, as above. Of the five ways it was expected to
fail, written down before the run:

- **"The effect may not transfer at all."** Did not happen. It transferred clearly.
- **"A volume bar is a crowding tilt toward names everyone already trades."** Happened, and is now
  measured: that is the breadth table.
- **"It tilts to the largest companies, where this book has no edge."** Happened; same table.
- **"The worst fall will reject everything regardless."** Did not happen — the falls stayed
  between 20.6% and 23.0%, inside the 25% limit the owner set on 2026-10-14.
- **"Even a clean result is advice about building books, not a candidate."** Exactly right, and it
  is the conclusion.

## The luck test, and why none of this can be taken further

Three settings (none, 20%, 40%) cleared every go-live condition and are marked eligible. The luck
score asks how likely a result is to be real rather than a fluke, after accounting for how many
distinct ideas the lab has tried. N is 187 — one look per method, not per trial — and the bar is
0.90, the owner's setting since 2026-10-07. The three scored 0.923, 0.925 and 0.905; the two
strictest scored 0.853 and 0.729 and failed on that alone.

Two warnings about those numbers. The 40% setting's 0.905 is **borderline**, and a borderline luck
score is not a property of the strategy — it reads the whole lab's population, so it drifts when
unrelated methods land beside it. And the eligible marks are partly a moved goalpost: the
no-requirement setting is the same book, to sixteen digits, as one recorded in the lab on
2026-10-08 that was marked **failed** at the identical 20.6% fall. Nothing improved; the drawdown
limit moved from 20% to 25% on 2026-10-14. It would be wrong to read "eligible" here as progress.

**None of this will be taken to the test window.** The hard gate refused promotion, on two
independent grounds, and there is no override:

1. The method wins only **2 of its 4** walk-forward folds. A book that wins its twenty-year
   average but loses the folds is a selection, not an edge.
2. Its **kin have already failed the test window** — the multi-factor blend and the weekly-brake
   and residual books (three of them). They are three looks on what is substantially one book, and
   this method rides the same chassis.

So no counted look is spent, and the buy signal for survivorship-free data does **not** fire: it
needs a fold majority, and this has none.

## One honest limit on the measurement

The bar is relative to the day's candidate list, and the honest tape has 989 companies where the
everyday one has 539. So putting the dead companies back does not only add names to choose from —
it also **moves where the bar sits**. The gap in the table therefore mixes the liveness effect
with a change in the pool the percentage is taken of, and these numbers cannot separate them. A
fixed dollar bar would avoid it, but would reintroduce the calendar problem that made the
relative bar the right choice. The clean way to settle it is a bar pinned to a fixed rank — "the
200 most-traded names", the same count on both tapes — and that is the next idea, queued below.

## My opinion

This direction is worth more trials, but not this book, and not this dial as a return-improver.

What has now been shown twice, on two unrelated chassis, is that **how heavily a stock trades is
the lab's cheapest available proxy for whether its edge is an artefact of missing dead companies.**
That is a genuinely useful tool, and it is free — it needs no new data. I would start using it as a
diagnostic on every stock-picking method the lab already holds: run the ladder, read which way the
honesty gap moves, and treat a book whose edge evaporates under a volume bar as suspect before
spending anything else on it. That is worth more than any single method.

What I would not do is keep paying 5.4 points a year for it. The breadth table says the cost is a
large-company tilt, and a tilt is a design choice that can be made far more cheaply — by capping
how much the book may hold in the thinnest names rather than refusing them outright, which keeps
the small-company exposure where the edge actually lives while still declining the genuinely
moribund.

The next thing I would run is the fixed-rank version, because the one real weakness in this
measurement is that the bar moves between the two tapes, and until that is pinned down the 3.5
point swing is suggestive rather than settled. If a fixed-rank bar reproduces the swing, the
finding is solid and should change how the lab reads every stock screen it owns.

I would also say clearly: this method produced no candidate and never could have. Its chassis has
kin that already failed out of sample, so the gate was always going to refuse it. That was known
and written down before the run, and the method was worth running anyway, because what it was
built to measure is not a candidate but a fact about the lab's data.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1049: verified, no promotion, and the goalpost note is right

Reproduces exactly. M0288-DV00 is M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT to sixteen digits -- total return
554.9227319691738, 1,607 trades, fall 0.20649523233479192 -- so the chassis is the one the lab
already trusts and the ladder's zero rung is the parent unchanged.

**No promotion, and two independent refusals rather than one.** `lab walkforward` reads 2 of 4
folds on the selector and names the kin refusal in the same line: M0021, M0022 and M0029 have
already failed the test window. Either clause alone would refuse it. The buy signal does not
fire. No look was spent and none will be on this family -- the kin walk closes it permanently,
which is the mechanism working, not an obstacle to route around.

**The goalpost observation is correct and I checked it rather than taking it.** The identical
fall of 20.6495% is recorded on M0032 as `failed: max DD <= 20%` and on this method's DV00 as
eligible with nothing failed. Nothing about the book improved between those two rows. The owner's
drawdown condition moved from 20% to 25% on 2026-10-14 by a dated revision (design section 18),
and three arms here read "eligible" on numbers that failed a fortnight earlier for that reason
alone. The child said so in its own analysis rather than letting the word do the work, which is
the behaviour this lab is for. Note that the lab's own dev SCREEN is a separate and much looser
number -- `metrics.DEV_MAX_DRAWDOWN` is 0.50 -- so what moved is the owner condition, and the two
must not be collapsed back together.

**What the method actually bought.** The liveness reading generalises: the dev-minus-check-store
gap per year runs -1.7, -1.7, +0.0, -0.2, +1.8 across the rungs here against M0284's -3.3, -1.3,
-1.0, -1.6, +0.6 on a completely different chassis. Same shape, same size, unrelated book. That
is two independent confirmations that demanding heavy trading is a test of whether the company is
still alive rather than a test of news.

**And the headline is the reversal, not the gap.** On the dev store the floor is a pure cost
(13.7% to 12.6% a year at the 40% rung); on the check store it is a gain (12.0% to 12.7%), and
that rung is the only one of five with a positive 2009-2015 lead there. A size or liquidity
comparison settled on the dev store alone can therefore pick the wrong arm, and the bias is not a
constant that can be subtracted. That belongs beside every width, size and liquidity result the
lab holds.

The caveat the child declined to paper over is the right one to carry: the floor is a percentile
of each day's pool, and the check store has 989 symbols against dev's 539, so restoring the dead
names also moves where the bar sits. The 3.5-point swing mixes liveness with pool composition.
M0298's fixed-rank bar at identical K on both tapes is the instrument that separates them, and
until it runs the reversal is a direction rather than a magnitude.


### 2026-10-23

## Correction, sera-20261023-1305: the honest-tape reversal is withdrawn

M0298 asked this method's question a second way -- a fixed COUNT of names instead of a share of
each day's pool -- and two of the conclusions above do not survive.

Withdrawn: that on the check store the arm order reverses, with the 40% rung earning +12.7%
against the no-bar book's +12.0%; and that the 40% rung was the only one of five with a positive
2009-2015 lead there. On the fixed-count ladder the no-bar book is the best arm on the honest tape
and every rung is negative over 2009-2015.

The cause is arithmetic, not judgement, and it was the caveat this run itself raised and could not
resolve. The bar here is a PERCENTILE of each day's candidate pool. The check store prices nearly
twice as many companies, so "drop the least-traded 40%" keeps about 243 names there against 150
for a fixed "keep the top 150". A share-based bar silently loosens as the pool grows, so the two
tapes were never being asked the same question. Any reader comparing this method's two stores was
reading a bar that changed between them.

What stands, and stands stronger: the liveness swing itself. The dev-minus-check-store gap here
was 3.5 points; M0284's was 3.9 and M0298's fixed-count ladder is 3.4, monotone across all five
binding rungs. Three experiments, two chassis, two opposite bar definitions, one answer.

methods.verdict: Rejected as a recipe but the finding transferred: a busy-trading bar is a general liveness filter, not a news trick — it swung the honest-tape gap 3.5 points, and on the honest tape the 40% setting is the best of the five, but it costs 5.4 points a year by herding the book into big companies

methods.name: Make the fold gate score the arm it would promote, not the arm its siblings name
methods.hypothesis: This is a lab-rules idea, not a strategy, and it should be settled before the fifth test-window look is spent. M0284 recorded a trial whose equity curve is bit-identical to three already in the lab (M0072-Z2-RAWRANK #283, M0277-OFF #914, M0279-OFF #934, M0284-VOL30 #952: same +47105.4%, same 1208 trades, same 23.8% fall, same curve hash caa33dc4844b, four different config digests). That one unchanged curve carries three different fold records: M0277 1 of 4, M0279 2 of 4, M0284 3 of 4 - and only the third is a majority, which is what fired the buy signal. The cause is that walkforward picks each fold's arm by best training MAR WITHIN the method file: in M0277 the selector named CONFIRMED at all four folds, in M0279 SEASON/FILED/FILED/UNFILED, and in M0284 every sibling rung was worse than VOL30 so the selector finally named the book itself. So the book was never fold-tested in the first two files; the gate scored the siblings and filed the answer under the method. Consequence: hardgate condition (F) and the buy signal's (c) can both be moved by the choice of siblings, and the cheapest way to pass is to register a favourite beside weak company. Nobody did that deliberately here and it happened anyway. Proposal to measure first and then argue in a commit to lab/hardgate.py: compute the fold record of the arm promote would actually name (best dev-eligible by MAR, the D11 own-folds column already does this) and require the majority on THAT curve independent of the menu, keeping the picks-selector record as reported evidence rather than as the gate. Measure before changing: re-score every recorded method both ways and count how many of the 81 dev-eligible methods change verdict, and specifically whether any method already promoted or already test-failed would have been refused. If the two rules agree almost everywhere, the change is cheap and should be made; if it flips many, the lab needs to know which of its past refusals were menu artefacts. Note D11 already records an own-folds column (M0284 reads 3 of 4 there too), so the data may already exist and this may be a one-line change to which column gates. EXPECTED FAILURE: the own-arm record may be systematically easier to pass, since it drops the selector's own out-of-sample error and asks only whether one fixed curve beat SPY in most folds - which is closer to a backtest than to a forward test, and would weaken the gate rather than strengthen it. The honest fix may then be to require BOTH records to carry a majority, which is stricter than today on every method. Either way the current state, where an unchanged curve reads 1, 2 and 3 of 4 in three places, is not defensible.

methods.name: Which leg carries the cost: grade the exit, grade the re-entry, or both
methods.hypothesis: M0287 measured that grading a trend gate's exposure costs 1.11 points a year whole window on the opinion-free 50-name book, at a matched centre (mean horizon 200) and a matched average exposure (70.82 / 70.39 / 70.65 percent, a 0.43-point spread), gross and net of fees alike (-1.04 and -1.11, so fees explain 0.067). It also proposed a MECHANISM and did not test it: that the cost is entirely in the EXIT leg, because a vote cannot reach zero until every horizon agrees and the long ones only turn down well after a fall is under way, so a graded rule is never all the way out at the moment of maximum danger. The evidence offered for that was the 2008 column -- the plain gate 0 percent invested and 0 percent fall, the graded arms 1.96 percent invested and a 2.25 percent fall, costing 2.45 points -- plus the era pattern, -2.24 in 1996-2002 and -2.45 in 2008 against -0.52 in the bear-market-free 2009-2015. That is suggestive and it is not a measurement, because every M0287 arm graded BOTH legs at once. This method separates them with a 2x2 on the identical chassis, identical store and identical mean horizon of 200: DECISIVE-DECISIVE (the lab's shared gate, which reproduces M0287-K1 and M0271-D000 to the digit and is the ladder's zero rung), GRADED-EXIT (the four-horizon vote on the way down, snapping to fully invested the moment the 200-day line is regained), DECISIVE-EXIT (fully out the moment the 200-day line is lost, the four-horizon vote on the way back in), and GRADED-GRADED (M0287-K4's rule, which reproduces its recorded row and anchors the 2x2 against a known number). Plus the always-invested no-opinion arm insight 523 requires, and the plain gate at the graded arms' average exposure as the dilution control. The two legs are defined off a single state variable -- whether the book was invested at the previous decision -- which the allocator may not read directly (insight 511: held is a set of symbols, not weights), so the leg is resolved from the 200-day line's own history on SPY's bars rather than from the book, and that is the one piece of machinery this method has to get right. Success is a decomposition, not a candidate: no arm on this chassis can be promoted. If GRADED-EXIT carries essentially the whole -1.11 and DECISIVE-EXIT carries essentially none, M0287's mechanism is confirmed and the lab learns something transferable -- that a timing rule may be smoothed on the way IN for free, which is the half that every practitioner smooths last. If both legs carry roughly half, the mechanism story is wrong and the cost is simply that in-between weights are worse than either end. If DECISIVE-EXIT carries the cost, the finding inverts and the re-entry is what must be decisive, which would contradict M0271's delay ladder and would be the most interesting outcome of the three.

methods.name: Stop tuning when the gate goes out and change what the book holds while it is out
methods.hypothesis: Seven method ids this month have moved WHEN the shared SPY 200-day gate is read (M0245 confirmation, M0258 band, M0260 cadence, M0261 phase, M0262 session grid, M0271 re-entry delay, M0287 graininess) and every answer came back a fraction of a point against the gate's own value, which M0287 measured at +2.16 points a year and 37 points of worst fall whole window, +40.8 points in 2008 alone, and MINUS 6.71 points a year over 2009-2015. The one thing nobody has changed is what the book holds while the gate is out: it holds cash, in every gated book in the lab, always. M0287 priced that directly on the opinion-free 50-name chassis -- 20.14 points of cash over 2009-2015 costing 6.71 points a year, where even M0271's expensive episodic price of cash explains only 5.70, leaving a point a year that is not cash at all. The dev store carries tradeable bars for TLT, IEF, SHY, BIL, GLD, XLP and XLU, so the alternatives are testable today with no new data: while the gate is out, hold long Treasuries, intermediate Treasuries, gold, consumer staples or utilities instead of nothing, each as its own arm, against the all-cash incumbent and the always-invested no-opinion arm. THE CONSTRAINT IS STATED UP FRONT AND IS NOT A REASON TO SKIP THIS: a non-default ETF needs the owner's input and can never be eligible, so every non-cash arm here is EVIDENCE ONLY and the method must say so in its own hypothesis and verdict. That is precisely why it is worth running -- if parking in intermediate Treasuries recovers most of the 6.71 points without giving back the 40.8 points of 2008, that is not a lab candidate, it is a decision to put in front of the owner with a number attached, and the lab currently has no number at all. The expected failure is specific and likely: Treasuries and equities were negatively correlated through 2000-2002 and 2008 and positively correlated in parts of 2009-2015, so the arm that rescues the crashes may be the same arm that does nothing in the era the money lives in, and the honest answer would then be that there is no single parking place that works in both. Gold's own 2009-2015 collapse makes it the arm most likely to look good whole window and worst in the era that matters, which is exactly the shape insight 89 warns about, so the era column decides this method and the twenty-year average may not.

methods.name: Slide the weighting from pure size to pure equal in five rungs over the same names, and read the narrow-month column beside 2009-2015
methods.sourceRef: M0286 (the re-weighting cadence 2x2: equal slices beat market value by 2.8 points a year over identical names, 4.6 in 2009-2015, and the equal arms lose 8-9% a year in narrow months); M0281/M0224/M0226, which built the whole-market base; M0222 (the market-value core and the per-company ceiling); M0266 (the price of a point of exposure is an era, not a constant); insight 91 (the lab's old reading that favouring the smaller members is a handicap); insight 462 (the equal-weight placebo's 8-point gap decomposed to 3.6 gate, 3.8 fees, under 0.9 pool and weighting); insight 500 (a two-point slope read is wrong: turn the dial five times)
methods.hypothesis: M0286 measured, on identical names at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits, that equal slices beat market-value weights by 2.8 points a year over 1996-2015 and by 4.6 points in 2009-2015, and that the lead survives the survivorship-check store. That contradicts the lab's year-old assumption and goes further than insight 462, which priced the weighting itself at under 0.9 points once the gate and the fees were taken out. But a two-point read cannot rank a dial, and M0286's own check named two terms riding along with the 2.8: a 5.7-point exposure gap between the two shapes, and a breadth split in which the equal arms earn +13% a year in broad months and lose 8-9% in narrow ones -- and 2018-2026 was narrow. So the switch becomes a dial, turned five times over identical names with one field moving: each name's weight is its market value raised to a power, rescaled and capped at 5%. EQUAL (power 0) gives every name the same weight; P25, P50 and P75 are the rungs; SIZE (power 1) is the market's own shape. All five run M0286's EQ-DEPOSIT cadence -- a January anchor, never a sale to fund a buy, the month's deposit handed to the names furthest below target -- because M0286 found that is the cheapest shape and the one that holds exposure nearly still across shapes, so the ladder moves weighting and not time in cash. EQUAL should reproduce M0286-EQ-DEPOSIT, a built-in check that the power code leaves the equal end alone. The sixth arm, SIZE-NOCAP, is not a rung: it is power 1 with the 5% ceiling lifted, the one arm that prices the cap at the rung where it binds hardest, so any curvature in the return curve can be attributed to the weighting rather than to the cap re-spreading the excess. Predictions, written before any result: the funded return curve is monotone and rises toward EQUAL; the narrow-month annualised spread is monotone the other way and crosses zero between P50 and P75; the worst fall rises monotonically toward EQUAL; exposure is flat to within a point across the five rungs; and SIZE-NOCAP lands within about half a point a year of SIZE, because the dev window's biggest member rarely reaches 5% of the index. Nothing here is a candidate: every rung should fall roughly 50-58% in 2008, twice the bar, and a weighting dial does not touch that. Success is a measurement -- whether the dial is a curve with an interior best rung, or a step function between the two ends M0286 already has.
methods.expectedFailure: The rungs may not separate. Market value is distributed so unevenly across index members that raising it to 0.25 may already be most of the way to equal weighting, in which case EQUAL, P25 and P50 land on top of each other, the dial is a step function near the size end, and five rungs bought what two already said. The cap is the second trap and the reason SIZE-NOCAP is registered: market value raised to a power is not a clean size tilt once the 5% ceiling re-spreads the excess, and the ceiling binds hardest at power 1, so part of any curvature belongs to the cap; if SIZE and SIZE-NOCAP differ by more than the gap between two neighbouring rungs, the ladder is measuring the cap and the verdict must say so. Third, the narrow-and-broad split is computed on the dev window's own months, 2009-2015 contained no bear market and few genuinely narrow stretches, and the column may rest on too few months to rank six arms by -- a monotone-looking narrow-month curve could be noise with a slope. Fourth, the dev store cannot price about 40% of member-days and the missing names skew small, so every rung nearer the equal end is flattered here; the survivorship-check store must be read for ALL six arms, not only the ends, and if the ladder's slope flattens there then the slope was partly the coverage hole. Fifth, the deposit cadence spends each month's money on the names furthest below target, which is a size-dependent habit in itself: at the size end the under-weight names are the big ones and at the equal end they are the small ones, so the cadence is not perfectly neutral across the dial, and an exposure column that moves across rungs is the symptom. Finally the whole exercise is about a book that falls 50-58% in 2008 and can never be a candidate, so a monotone answer changes what the lab believes about weighting and still promotes nothing.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0292 — Sliding the weighting from "equal slices" to "the market's own shape", five rungs at a time

## What was asked

Last run (M0286) found something the lab had believed the opposite of for a year. Take the same
companies, at the same moment, bought the same way, and the only difference being how much money
goes into each one. Give every company an identical slice and you earned 10.3% a year. Give each
company a share matching its size — the way the market itself is shaped, the way an index fund
does it — and you earned 7.4%. Nearly three points a year, from nothing but the split.

That was a two-position switch, and a switch cannot tell you the shape of a slope. This lab has a
scar from exactly that mistake: an earlier run read "eight times" off two points and five rungs
later the honest answer was 1.66 times. So this method replaced the switch with a dial and turned
it five times.

The dial: each company's slice is its size raised to a power. At power 0 every company gets the
same slice. At power 1 each gets its full size, which is the market's own shape. The quarter
steps in between are a continuous slide from one to the other, over identical companies, with
nothing else moving. A sixth arm removed the 5%-per-company limit at the size end, to check
whether that limit was secretly doing the work.

## What happened

Your money, after Gotrade's real fees, with 5 million rupiah going in on the 25th of every
month, 1996 to 2015. The same deposits into SPY earned 7.2% a year.

| Slice rule | Your money earned | Worst fall | Share of time invested | Trading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal slices (power 0) | **+10.3%** | 57.5% | 97.5% | most |
| power 0.25 | +9.5% | 56.1% | 96.3% | |
| power 0.5 | +8.9% | 54.3% | 94.8% | |
| power 0.75 | +8.2% | 51.6% | 92.3% | |
| The market's shape (power 1) | +7.5% | 50.0% | 91.2% | least |
| …with the 5% limit removed | +7.5% | 50.0% | 91.0% | least |

**There is no best rung in the middle.** The line is straight. Every quarter-turn toward equal
slices bought about 0.7 points a year of extra return and cost about 1.9 points of extra fall.
Nothing bends, nothing peaks, nothing turns. The owner is not choosing a setting; he is choosing
a point on a trade-off, and every point on it costs the same.

The equal end also reproduced last run's figure to the last digit — same return, same fall, same
842 trades — which is the check that the new code did not quietly change the old answer.

## The 5% limit was not doing the work

A company's weight was capped at 5% so no single name could dominate. That cap could have been
bending the curve instead of the weighting. It was not: removing it moved the answer by 0.09
points a year, against 0.60 points between the two closest rungs. A check run before this method
was registered had already shown the cap never binds at all below the top rung, and touches at
most 1.8% of the book at the top one. The curve is the weighting.

## Where the extra return came from, and what it cost

Split the twenty years into eras. Every column is monotone — the dial moves all of them at once,
in lockstep, with no exceptions.

| Slice rule | 1996-2002 | 2003-2008 | **2008 alone** | 2009-2015 | Narrow months | Broad months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal slices | +4.2% | +2.4% | **−1.7%** | **+3.5%** | **−8.8%** | +13.0% |
| power 0.25 | +3.9% | +1.7% | −0.6% | +2.4% | −6.6% | +9.9% |
| power 0.5 | +3.6% | +1.2% | +1.1% | +1.3% | −4.0% | +6.7% |
| power 0.75 | +3.2% | +0.7% | +3.4% | +0.1% | −1.1% | +3.2% |
| The market's shape | +3.2% | +0.5% | **+4.8%** | **−1.0%** | **+1.6%** | +0.4% |

(All against SPY, with the deposits stripped out so a top-up is never counted as a gain. "Narrow"
months are the ones where a few giant companies carried the market; "broad" months are the rest.)

**The crash is where the dial reverses.** In 2008 the market's own shape beat SPY by 4.8% and
equal slices lost to it by 1.7% — a six-and-a-half point swing, in the one year that matters most
for whether the owner can hold on. Equal slices earn their premium in the calm and hand a chunk
of it back in the fall.

**And the two worries are one worry.** The lab has tracked two separate concerns about equal
slices: that they lose when the market narrows, and that their edge might not survive into the
modern era. Both columns cross zero at the same rung, power 0.75. They are not two facts. They
are one fact measured twice. Equal slices win exactly when the average company beats the giants,
and that is all they do.

Measured directly on these two books: over the twenty years the average company beat the giants
in 55% of months, by 0.21% a month. In 2009-2015 it was 58.5% of months and 0.34% a month. In
2008 it was 50% of months and **minus** 0.50% a month. That monthly number, compounded, is the
entire premium. There is no other ingredient.

## The honest caveat, and why it does not sink the finding

These arms do not hold the same amount of money in the market. The equal end sits invested 97.5%
of the time, the size end 91.2% — a 6.3-point gap that slides with the dial. I predicted this
would be flat and it was not; the reason is mechanical. The money that arrives each month is
handed to whichever holdings are furthest below target. At the size end a company's weight drifts
almost exactly the way its target drifts, because a company's size *is* its share count times its
price — so there is rarely a gap to fill and cash piles up. At the equal end the gaps reopen
constantly and every deposit finds a home.

So part of the gap is simply being invested more. How much? Not most of it. For exposure alone
to explain the ladder, each point of extra time invested would have to be worth 0.43 points a
year on average across the five rungs — 0.28 to 0.66 depending on which pair you read. The
highest rate ever measured on this very chassis is about 0.17, in the single era most favourable
to it, and in 2003-2008 the same rate was near zero. Exposure would have to be worth about two
and a half times its best-ever measured price, across a window two-thirds of which priced it
near nothing. It cannot carry the ladder.

Taking that best-case rate and applying it to the whole 6.3-point exposure gap gives at most 1.1
points — and that is deliberately generous, since it charges the whole window at the rate of its
most favourable era. So the weighting itself is worth **1.6 to 2.7 points a year**. That is a
real narrowing of last run's unqualified 2.8, and it still points the same way.

One more thing runs *against* the finding and therefore strengthens it: the equal end trades more
(turnover 0.38 against 0.18) and so pays more in fees. It wins anyway, after paying them.

## The honest tape says the same thing

The dev store cannot price about 40% of the companies that were in the index, and the ones it
misses are disproportionately the ones that went bust. The check store prices most of them back.
I expected the ladder's slope to flatten there, because a book that spreads money evenly across
everything is the one most exposed to the companies that failed.

It did not flatten. It did not move at all.

| Slice rule | Lead over SPY, dev | Lead over SPY, honest tape | 2009-2015, dev | 2009-2015, honest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal slices | +3.1% | **+1.9%** | +3.5% | +2.5% |
| power 0.25 | +2.3% | +1.2% | +2.4% | +1.6% |
| power 0.5 | +1.7% | +0.5% | +1.3% | +0.6% |
| power 0.75 | +1.0% | −0.3% | +0.1% | −0.7% |
| The market's shape | +0.4% | −0.8% | −1.0% | −1.6% |

Every arm lost about 1.1 to 1.2 points a year once the failed companies were priced back in —
the standard haircut this lab sees. But the *gap between the ends* is 2.7 points on the dev store
and **2.7 points on the honest tape**, to the decimal. The haircut is a level, applied equally to
every rung; the dial's effect is untouched by it.

That matters more than the headline. It means the equal-weight premium is **not** an artefact of
the missing dead companies — the single most common way this lab's findings have died. All six
arms reproduced their recorded dev numbers exactly, so the comparison is sound.

What the honest tape does change is who beats SPY at all. On it, only the three rungs nearest
equal slices still beat the deposits-into-SPY benchmark; power 0.75 and the market's own shape
both lose to it. And the best number on the ladder is +1.9% a year, not +3.1%.

The one arm that behaved differently was the one with the 5% limit removed: it lost 1.8 points
instead of 1.1, and its 2009-2015 figure fell from −1.0% to −3.1%. Concentrating without a limit
is more fragile when the companies that failed are put back on the tape. That is a reason to keep
the limit, not a reason to doubt the ladder — and it is a side arm, not a rung.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Mostly, and the misses are worth naming.

- **Monotone return curve rising toward equal** — held exactly.
- **Monotone worst fall rising toward equal** — held exactly.
- **The cap worth under half a point** — held (0.09).
- **Equal reproduces last run** — held to the digit.
- **Narrow-month spread crosses zero between power 0.5 and 0.75** — *wrong by one rung.* It
  crosses between 0.75 and 1.0. The direction and the monotonicity were right, the location was
  not.
- **Exposure flat across the rungs to within a point** — *wrong, and it was the important one.*
  It moved 6.3 points. This was written down beforehand as the fifth way the method could fail,
  and it happened.

Two expected failures did *not* happen, and both were ones I rated likely. The rungs separated
cleanly, with no two sitting on top of each other — the dial is real. And the slope survived the
honest tape unchanged, which I had explicitly predicted it would not.

A note on method: the lab's dressing check refused this method, correctly, because no two arms
reverse each other. That is the right refusal. A five-rung dose-response ladder is a stronger
instrument than a mirror pair, and its "no opinion" endpoint is built in — the market's own shape
is what you get for holding the same companies with no view about size at all.

## Against the bar

Nothing here is a candidate and the registration said so before the run. Every rung falls 50-58%
from a peak against a 25% limit — twice over. Gains against losses run 0.46 to 0.78 where 1.3 is
needed. The luck reading is 0.56 to 0.68 against a bar of 0.90, judged against 188 distinct
methods tried: after that many attempts, a result this size is more likely to be chance than
skill, and the lab says so. Three of four time-slices beat SPY — on the dev store and on the
honest tape alike — which is a pass on that one condition alone and changes nothing else.

So: six trials, no promotion, no counted look spent, and the method is rejected — as designed.
It was registered as a measurement, not a candidate.

## My opinion:

The dial question is settled and I would not spend another method on it. The answer is a straight
line with no sweet spot: equal slices earn more, fall harder, and the whole of the difference is
one bet — that the average company beats the giants. There is no clever middle setting that keeps
the return and drops the risk, and anyone who goes looking for one on this chassis will find a
straight line again.

What this changes is how the lab should talk about equal weighting. The old assumption (insight
91) said equal slices were a handicap the roster paid. Last run said they were worth 2.8 points.
Both are too simple. The correct statement is conditional: equal slices are worth about 1.5 to
2.7 points a year *while broad months outnumber narrow ones*, and they are a liability when that
reverses — which it did in 2008, and which the owner's own 2018-2026 window largely was. The
honest recommendation is that the lab stop treating "equal versus size" as a free choice and
start treating it as a market-breadth bet with a known price.

What I would spend a method on next is the only question this one opens that it cannot answer. The
exposure confound is now measured but not separated, because on this cadence the dial moves
weighting and exposure together by construction. Break that link: run the same five rungs on a
cadence that forces every rung to the *same* exposure — re-weight on a fixed schedule so each
arm is fully invested — and the residual is the weighting term, clean, with no appeal to an
era-dependent exposure price. That would turn today's "1.5 to 2.7 points" into one number, and it
is the last thing standing between this lab and a settled answer on the oldest assumption it has.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1049: verified, and it closes the term I opened on M0286

Reproduces exactly: M0292-EQUAL is M0286-EQ-DEPOSIT to fifteen digits -- return
368.8530704793742, 842 trades, exposure 0.9751872211300118 -- so the power code leaves the earlier
answer untouched and the ladder's zero rung is that book unchanged.

The ladder is monotone on every axis the trials record, in both directions at once:

  EQUAL   +10.28%  fall 57.5%  exposure 97.52%  turnover 0.38
  P25      +9.51%  fall 56.1%  exposure 96.34%  turnover 0.29
  P50      +8.86%  fall 54.3%  exposure 94.81%  turnover 0.22
  P75      +8.15%  fall 51.6%  exposure 92.29%  turnover 0.18
  SIZE     +7.55%  fall 50.0%  exposure 91.22%  turnover 0.18

No interior optimum anywhere. Every rung falls 50-58% against the owner's 25% bar, so the
rejection is as pre-registered and nothing here is a candidate.

**The open term is measured and it was real.** My check on M0286 said its 2.8-point equal-versus-
size gap had at least three ingredients -- exposure, breadth regime and the weighting itself --
and that none of them was separated. Exposure is NOT flat across this dial: it slides from 91.22%
to 97.52%, a 6.30-point spread moving with the rung. The child predicted flat and recorded being
wrong, which is the right way to be wrong.

The mechanism is the reason, and it means this method cannot finish the job: at the size end a
holding's weight drifts the way its target drifts, because market value IS shares times price, so
the monthly deposit finds no gap to fill and cash banks instead. Weighting and exposure are
collinear here by construction.

What can still be said is a bound, and it is worth more than the headline it replaces. The
end-to-end gap is 2.73 points a year. A point of exposure has never been worth more than 0.17
points a year on this chassis and is worth about nothing in 2003-2008; at 0.17 the 6.30-point
spread carries 1.07 points, leaving 1.66 for the weighting, and at zero it carries none, leaving
2.73. **So the weighting term is 1.6 to 2.7 points a year.** Quote that range. The unqualified 2.8
is withdrawn. M0300, which pins every rung to the same exposure, is the instrument that closes it.

**The survivorship result is the strong one and it is unusual for this lab.** Every arm loses 1.1
to 1.2 points a year with the dead companies restored, and the end-to-end gap is 2.7 points on the
dev store and 2.7 on the check store. The haircut is a flat level charge; the dial's slope is
untouched, and the fold record is 3 of 4 on both tapes. Nearly every other survivorship finding
this lab holds changes the RANKING -- M0288's liquidity floor reverses sign between stores,
M0283's calm book reverses -- and this one does not. A dial whose slope survives the honest tape
is a different and better class of result than one whose level does.

The caveat belongs beside it: on the honest tape only the three rungs nearest equal still beat
SPY, the best lead is +1.9% rather than +3.1%, and the uncapped size arm loses 1.8 points instead
of 1.1, with its 2009-2015 lead going -1.0 to -3.1. The 5% cap earns its keep, and it was checked
rather than assumed -- lifting it moved 0.09 points against a 0.60-point smallest-rung gap.


### 2026-10-23

## Correction to the correction, sera-20261023-1305: the 2.8 stands

M0300 pinned every rung of this dial to one level of invested money -- exposure spread 0.080
points where it had been 6.30 -- and the end-to-end gap barely moved, 2.73 to 2.59 points a year.
Its bridge arm prices a point of exposure on this chassis at 0.0128 points a year, so the 6.30-
point spread was worth about 0.08, not the 1.07 the earlier ceiling allowed.

So the exposure term is about zero. With each ladder's own fee slope removed the two runs agree at
2.82 and 2.86 points a year.

The earlier coordinator correction withdrew the unqualified 2.8 and replaced it with a bound of
1.6 to 2.7. The bound was honest and the true value lies inside it, but the instruction attached
-- that the 2.8 should not be quoted -- is now wrong and is itself withdrawn. **The weighting term
is about 2.6 to 2.9 points a year, and it is not about being invested.** Quote that.

Nothing in either record is edited; this is the third entry in the chain and the one measured on
purpose.
methods.verdict: Rejected as designed: the size-to-equal dial is a straight line with no best setting — equal slices earn 2.7 points a year more and fall 7.5 points deeper, the whole of it a bet that the average company beats the giants, and the slope survives the honest tape unchanged.

methods.name: Calmness as a safety filter on someone else's picks, not a ranking of its own
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0283 / M0278 (Black, Jensen & Scholes 1972; Frazzini & Pedersen 2014, Betting Against Beta, JFE 111(1)) applied as a filter to M0197-Y20-SW's book (D.E. Shaw Treasury-beta note, caia.org/node/6853); the blind-drop arm M0059 never registered
methods.hypothesis: M0283 measured what the calm sort reliably buys and what it does not. Against a blind draw of the same shape it bought 7.5 points of shallower worst fall and gains-vs-losses of 2.93 against 1.80, both steady when the draw's seed changes, and at most 0.56 points a year of return, which sits inside the 0.06-2.70 point seed-to-seed spread measured across the lab's nine seed-only draw groups -- so the return advantage is unreadable rather than small. That is the signature of a safety filter, not an engine, the same shape proximity-to-the-52-week-high showed; and M0283 closed the engine reading from the other side, since every slice of SPY held beside the calm book earned less and fell further, monotonically. So stop ranking on calmness and start filtering with it. CHOOSING THE HOST IS THE WHOLE RISK, so it is named and argued here. The host is M0197-Y20-SW, the bond-like book: among F4-screened members, one shared yearly fit of 52 weekly log returns on SPY's and on the weekly change in the 10-year Treasury yield; hold the 20 names that rise most when yields fall, equal slots, re-ranked quarterly with a 40% keep band, behind the SPY 200-day switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up. It was chosen for four reasons: (1) lab status lists it as promotable now, so no family, ancestor, ingredient or behavioural twin of it has test-failed and a win here can actually be promoted -- unlike M0059, which ran this very filter on a momentum book whose kin have already lost four looks; (2) it leads SPY clearly, +11.8% a year on the deposits against +7.2%, worst fall 22.0%, gains 3.08x losses, luck score 0.955, 3 of 4 folds; (3) its pool is every screened member, hundreds of names, so dropping a quarter still leaves far more than 20 candidates and the book stays exactly 20 names fully invested -- a drop changes WHICH names, never HOW MANY, which is the confound that sank M0277's and M0279's six pick filters on the thin news-day pool, where every filter emptied slots into SPY through a rising decade; and (4) the host already computes the market beta this filter needs and throws it away -- its fit returns beta and the yield loading together and ranks on the loading alone -- so the filter adds no new estimate, no new window and no new free parameter. M0197's own pre-registered fear is why it should bite: on 2008-06-30 its fit put Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, KeyCorp, Fifth Third and REITs on the bond-like side at an average beta of 2.0. Five arms, all on the host's exact configuration: REF (nothing dropped, the no-opinion reference, which must reproduce M0197-Y20-SW bar for bar); HI25 (drop the jumpiest quarter of the pool before ranking, the idea); HI50 (drop the jumpiest half, the dose rung); LO25 (drop the CALMEST quarter, the mirror); and BLIND25 (drop the same count by a fixed per-symbol hash, the arm with no opinion in it, which prices what dropping any quarter costs). The blind draw is sticky, one hash per symbol with no date in the key, because a beta quartile is a slow-moving property and a re-drawn placebo churns about fourteen times harder and would price turnover instead of selection. BLIND25 is the arm M0059 never registered, which is why its verdict -- 'softened the fall only by cutting the return' -- cannot distinguish a calm filter from the plain arithmetic of swapping a quarter of the names. Predictions, written now, on returns with the deposits taken out: REF reproduces M0197-Y20-SW's recorded trial (same return, same trade count), and if it does not the whole comparison is void and the analysis says so; HI25's worst fall is at least 2 points below REF's 22.0%; HI50's fall is no deeper than HI25's, so the dose is monotone; HI25 gives up less than 1 point a year of funded return against REF, so the fall shrinks by more than the return does; HI25 beats BLIND25 on the worst fall by at least 1.5 points, without which the shrink was the swapping and not the calmness; and LO25 falls deeper than REF. Success for the gate: a filtered arm still beats total-return SPY with gains at least 1.3x losses and a luck score of 0.90 or better, at a shallower fall than REF and with a positive 2009-2015 edge.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the dial is simply inert, and for a reason the host already wrote down: M0197's own ranking probe found the correlation between a member's market beta and its yield loading running from -0.41 to 0.20 across years, negative in most of them. Negative means the bond-like end of the pool is ALREADY the calm end, so the jumpiest quarter is made of names the book was never going to buy, and all five arms land within a point of each other. That would be a real finding -- the host has done its own filtering -- but not a win. Second, the host's 22.0% fall is what is LEFT after the SPY 200-day switch, so most of it is the market's own fall during the weeks before a monthly switch reads, and no pick filter can touch that; the lab has measured the same thing on the news-day book, where better picks never moved a switch-shaped fall. Third, the one episode where the filter should earn its keep, 2008, is the one where a trailing beta is least likely to work: by mid-2008 Fannie, Freddie and the regional banks had not yet collapsed, so their trailing one-year beta may still read near one and the filter would leave them in. A backward-looking safety measure against a forward-looking crash is the standard way this kind of filter disappoints. Fourth, HI50 tilts the book hard into utilities and REITs, which is precisely the 2013 taper-scare exposure M0197 feared, so the dose rung may fall FURTHER in 2013-2015 and lose the 2009-2015 era outright -- and 2009-2015 is the lab's first filter, the best-covered years and the ones most like today. Fifth, BLIND25 may match HI25: with a deep pool of mostly bond-like names, removing any quarter leaves twenty near-identical utilities and the blind arm reproduces the idea arm, which is the equal-weight-placebo trap insight 462 caught. Sixth, betting against beta was published in 2014, at the very end of the dev window, so a strong dev result here is likely to have faded -- though the lab's own evidence is that the calm sort's SAFETY half survived the dead companies being put back, and the safety half is all this method asks for. None of these is a reason to tune the quarter, the half, the 252-session fit or the host after the fact.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## The question

An earlier experiment found that sorting stocks by how calmly they move is a strange kind of
signal. It buys a much shallower fall, reliably. It does **not** buy more money — the extra return
it seemed to earn was smaller than the gap between two coin tosses. That is the shape of a **safety
belt**, not an engine. You do not steer with it. You wear it.

So this method stopped using calmness to *choose* stocks and started using it to *veto* them. Take
a book that already beats the market, look at the whole list of candidates it ranks each quarter,
throw away the jumpiest quarter of that list before it picks, and see what happens.

**Which book to bolt it onto was the whole risk, so it was argued before anything ran.** The host
chosen was the bond-like book: among big index members, hold the twenty whose prices rise most when
bond yields fall, twenty equal slices, re-ranked quarterly, sitting in cash while the market is
below its own one-year average. It earns +11.8% a year on the owner's monthly deposits against the
market's +7.2%. Three things made it right:

* **nothing in its family has ever failed a real out-of-sample test**, so a win could actually go
  forward. An earlier method ran this same calm filter on a momentum book, got a promising answer,
  and could never use it — momentum books here have already lost four such tests.
* **its candidate list is hundreds of names long**, so throwing away a quarter still leaves far
  more than twenty. The book stays exactly twenty names, fully invested. This matters more than
  anything else: a drop changes *which* names, never *how many*. Two earlier methods ran six
  filters on a book with a short candidate list; all six lost, and the reason was not the filters
  but that each left slots empty and parked the money in the market index through a rising decade.
  The design worked: every version asked for **14.3 names on average and held no pick on 28.3% of
  its decision days — identical to the first decimal across all fifteen versions.**
* **the host already measures calmness and throws the number away.** Its quarterly maths produces
  each company's jumpiness alongside the bond-sensitivity it ranks on, then ignores it. So the
  filter invented no new measurement and added no new setting to tune.

Fifteen versions ran in three batches under one method id, because twice the lab pointed out
something the design had missed. The follow-ups cost no new method id and did not move the luck bar.

## What happened: the first five

| version | money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| drop nothing (the reference) | **+11.8%** | 22.0% | 3.08 | 0.956 |
| drop the jumpiest quarter | +10.8% | **20.3%** | **4.16** | 0.964 |
| drop the jumpiest half | +8.3% | 25.2% | 3.36 | 0.838 |
| drop the *calmest* quarter (the mirror) | +12.0% | 22.3% | 2.49 | 0.955 |
| drop a quarter *blindly* (the control) | +12.0% | 23.5% | 3.30 | 0.969 |
| the market, same deposits | +7.2% | — | — | — |

The reference reproduced the host's own recorded result to the last digit — same return, same fall,
same 447 trades — so every comparison below is like for like.

Read the mirror first; it is the cleanest thing here. On **gains versus losses** the three versions
line up exactly with how calm the book is: drop the jumpy names, 4.16; drop nothing, 3.08; drop the
calm names, 2.49. Turn the dial one way it goes up, the other way it goes down. That is a signal.

But the **money** column runs the other way. The calmest book earned least, the jumpiest earned
most. Calmness costs return, and this is the fourth method in a row to say so.

And look at the **jumpiest half**. If this were a dose — more filtering, more safety — that row
should have been the safest. It was the worst: it fell *further* than doing nothing (25.2% against
22.0%), gave up three and a half points a year, and failed the luck test. Dropping half the list
corners the book in utilities and property companies, and a book in a corner is not a safe book.
**The idea is not a dose you can turn up.**

## Then the lab caught two things, and the method was rebuilt twice

**First: the crash had been sitting it out.** All five versions scored the *identical* advantage in
2008, to the decimal. Of course they did — the host goes to cash when the market is below its
one-year average, and it was in cash through 2008. The one real crash in twenty years was spent out
of the market, so the safety belt had never been shown a crash. Four more versions ran with the cash
rule switched off. None is a candidate — a book that falls sixty per cent is nowhere near what the
owner would accept — and none was meant to be. They are evidence about one question:

| version, cash rule off | loss in 2008 | worst fall | money a year |
|---|---|---|---|
| drop the *calmest* quarter | −40.8% | 66.8% | +13.4% |
| drop nothing | −39.5% | 62.1% | +12.5% |
| drop a quarter blindly | −34.1% | 59.4% | +13.1% |
| **drop the jumpiest quarter** | **−24.5%** | 56.4% | +11.2% |

Shown a real crash, the filter cut the 2008 loss from 39.5% to 24.5% — **fifteen points** — and the
mirror went the other way, as a real signal must.

**Second, and this one hurt: all of that was measured against one coin toss.** The blind control was
a single reshuffle. So six more versions ran — three more blind reshuffles on each side of the cash
rule — purely to find out how far a reshuffle wanders on its own. It wandered further than expected,
and the honest thing is to say which claims it killed.

| claim | against one reshuffle | against four | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| shallower fall, cash rule on | 3.2 points better | reshuffles ran 20.4%–23.5%; filter 20.3% | **withdrawn** |
| shallower fall, cash rule off | 3.0 points better | reshuffles ran 55.2%–59.4%; filter 56.4% | **withdrawn** |
| smaller 2008 loss | 9.6 points better | reshuffles ran −28.5% to −34.1%; filter −24.5% | **survives, at 4.0** |
| better gains vs losses | 0.86 better | reshuffles ran 2.96–3.44; filter 4.16 | **survives, at 0.72** |

**The worst-fall claim is gone.** One reshuffle happened to fall 20.4%, a hair shallower than the
filter's 20.3%. Shuffling the list at random buys the whole of what the filter appeared to buy.
Anyone reading only the first table would have believed something that is not there.

There was also a sting nobody predicted. The *return cost* was supposed to be the unreadable part —
the lab's rule of thumb is that anything under about 1.5 points a year drowns in reshuffle noise. It
was the opposite. The four reshuffles earned +11.5% to +12.0% a year, a spread of half a point, and
the filter earned +10.8% — **below the worst of them.** The cost is real and steady. The *saving*
was the noise.

## The honest tape, where the picture improves and the noise doubles

The practice data is missing about four companies in ten that actually sat in the index, and the
missing ones are overwhelmingly those that went bankrupt or were bought. There is a fuller set of
prices with most of them put back. All fifteen versions were re-run on it.

| version | money a year | change | worst fall | change | gains vs losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| drop the *calmest* quarter | +9.9% | −2.1 | 25.4% | **+3.1 deeper** | 2.04 |
| drop nothing | +9.2% | −2.6 | 23.5% | **+1.5 deeper** | 2.21 |
| drop the jumpiest quarter | +9.4% | −1.4 | **21.1%** | **+0.7 deeper** | **3.09** |
| drop the jumpiest half | +9.0% | **+0.7** | **19.6%** | **−5.6 shallower** | 3.14 |
| four blind reshuffles | +8.7% to +10.7% | — | 21.2% to 28.7% | — | 2.12 to 2.59 |

Read the change-in-fall column top to bottom: **+3.1, +1.5, +0.7, −5.6.** The calmer the book, the
less it is hurt by putting the dead companies back — in perfect order, and the same order appears
again with the cash rule off (+5.7, +5.0, −2.7). The reason is not subtle: companies that go
bankrupt are jumpy before they die, so a filter that throws out the jumpy quarter has already thrown
most of them out. This is the fingerprint the lab found once before, on the filter that keeps stocks
near their one-year high — **the only kind of rule that earns more when the dead companies return is
a safety filter**, and the practice data *understates* it rather than inventing it.

Two things to be careful about, though, because this is where it would be easy to oversell.

**The reshuffles are twice as noisy on the honest tape.** Their worst falls span 7.5 points here
against 3.1 on the practice data, and their returns span 2.0 points against 0.5. So the filter's
21.1% fall is below all four reshuffles — but only 0.1 below the best of them, which is exactly the
margin that evaporated last time. And "the filter beats doing nothing here" (+9.4% against +9.2%) is
a two-tenths gap inside a two-point spread. **That is not a result; it is a coin landing on its
edge, and I am not claiming it.**

**What does hold on both sets of prices is gains versus losses.** 4.16 against a reshuffle best of
3.44 on the practice data; 3.09 against a reshuffle best of 2.59 on the fuller one. The mirror sits
below every reshuffle on both (2.49 and 2.04). Same direction, clear margin, twice, on different
prices. That is the one thing here I would defend.

And one more that only shows up on the fuller prices: with the cash rule off, the filtered book
falls **53.7%** where the four reshuffles fall 59.0% to 66.1% — below all of them by five points,
and it is the only version of any kind whose worst fall gets *shallower* when the dead companies
return. On the practice data that same comparison sat inside the reshuffle range. The crash
protection is real; the practice data was hiding it.

## The luck test, and why nothing here goes forward

The luck test asks how likely a result is to be real rather than a fluke given how many ideas the lab
has tried. The bar is 0.90 and the count is 189 — one per distinct method, printed by the lab, not
chosen here. Most versions clear it comfortably (0.951 to 0.969); the jumpiest-half version fails at
0.838. But a good luck score on a book that cannot go forward is a number without a job.

**The version the lab would put forward is the one that does nothing.** Promotion automatically
picks a method's best version by return-per-unit-of-fall, and the do-nothing reference ties for
best. That version *is* the host book restated — same return, same fall, same 447 trades. Spending
the lab's fifth-ever real-world test on it would buy information already owned. Three of the four
tests spent so far went to variations of a single book; that mistake is not worth repeating.

In the end the lab refused it anyway, for an honest reason. Before the controls were added this
method won 3 of the 4 rolling out-of-sample checks and was listed as ready. **After the six blind
reshuffles joined the pool it won 2 of 4, and the gate now refuses it.** A reshuffle won two of the
folds. Adding honest controls took a method *off* the ready list — the opposite of what its author
would want, and precisely what the lab is for.

There is no buy signal for real survivorship-free data either. That needs a positive edge in
2009-2015, the best-covered years and the ones most like today. Every version is negative there
(−2.1% to −6.4%), and the lab's own error bar on that edge, ±3.1 points, cannot tell it from zero.
Worth noting *why*: with the cash rule off, 2009-2015 turns **positive** (+7.0% for the reference).
The whole shortfall is the cash rule sitting out a rising decade, not the picks.

## Did the predictions hold?

Thirteen were written before any result. **Six held, seven did not** — and the pattern in the misses
is the useful part. Every *direction* was right: the mirror went the right way, the control was
beaten on gains-versus-losses, the calm books suffered least when the dead companies came back.
Every *size* was predicted too large: 2 points of fall became 1.7, 8 became 5.7, 4 became 3.0. The
one prediction about *shape* — that more filtering means more safety — was simply wrong.

Of six ways this was expected to fail, two happened: the cash rule really did own the fall, and
dropping half really did corner the book and lose the modern decade. Three did not: the dial was not
inert, the jumpiness measure *did* catch the 2008 banks despite looking backwards, and the control
did not match the filter on gains-versus-losses.

## Why it behaves this way

A safety filter and a cash rule are both insurance, and **this book was already insured.** The cash
rule claims first: it was out of the market through 2008 and handed every version the same advantage
there. Behind it the filter has almost nothing left to protect, so it goes on paying its premium — a
point a year of forgone return — for a claim it can no longer make. Switch the cash rule off and the
filter suddenly has a job and does it well: fifteen points of 2008, four of them beyond any
reshuffle, and on the fuller prices a worst fall five points below every reshuffle.

That is the real finding, and it is not about calmness. **Two safety devices on one book do not add
up. The faster one takes the claim; the slower one keeps paying the premium.** This lab owns several
of each and has been quietly stacking them.

**My opinion:** the filter is worth more trials, but not on this host and not as a fall-reducer. Two
things survive an honest control. It improves gains-versus-losses, on both sets of prices, with the
mirror below every reshuffle both times — that one I would defend. And it earns its keep in an
actual crash: fifteen points of 2008, and with the dead companies back a worst fall below every
reshuffle by five points. Two things I am withdrawing. Behind a cash rule it does **not** make the
worst stretch shallower — a random reshuffle does that just as well — and it is **not** a dose,
because turning it up corners the book and makes everything worse. The return cost, which I expected
to be noise, turned out to be the steadiest number in the experiment: about a point a year, every
way I measured it.

What I would do next, in order. **First, stop bolting safety onto books that already have a cash
rule.** This method spent most of its evidence discovering its host was already insured, and the lab
has several hosts in the same position. The sharp question is not whether the filter helps *behind*
a cash rule — it barely can — but whether a filtered book can **replace** one. On the numbers above
that book falls about 54% and could never be promoted as it stands, which is the honest reason to
ask the question properly rather than assume the answer. **Second, every honest control in this lab
should be four draws, not one.** A single reshuffle supported a 3.2-point claim that four reshuffles
erased for about a minute of compute — and the reshuffles are twice as noisy on the fuller prices as
on the practice data, so every single-draw control already recorded here is less reliable than it
looks. I would not trust one again. **Third, the unambiguous win deserves its own follow-up**: a
rule that earns more when the dead companies come back is pointing at something the practice data
systematically hides, and only two rules in this lab have ever done that.


### 2026-10-23

### Correction, same day

The section above says the version the lab would put forward is the one that does nothing. That
was true when it was written and is no longer true, and the truth is worse.

Once the six extra coin tosses were recorded, the lab re-ranked this method's fifteen versions by
return-per-unit-of-fall and the winner is **a coin toss** — the third blind reshuffle, at 0.57,
ahead of the do-nothing reference and every filtered version. So if this method were promoted, the
rule pre-registered and sent to a real-world test would be *throw away a quarter of the candidate
list at random, decided by a hash of the company's ticker*.

It will not be promoted — the gate refuses it on the out-of-sample folds, and two of the four folds
were themselves won by reshuffles. But it is worth saying plainly what happened, because it is the
sharpest version of this method's whole lesson. A ranking that sorts on return-per-unit-of-fall and
nothing else cannot tell an idea from its own control. When we put honest controls in the pool, they
do not sit quietly at the bottom waiting to be beaten; sometimes they win, and the machinery has no
way of noticing that the winner was the thing the experiment registered in order to beat.


### 2026-10-23
