methods.name: The smallest sleeve worth trading: when does a hand-picked slice stop paying its own fees?
methods.hypothesis: M0283's five-rung dial produced one result nobody predicted: the 70-percent-SPY rung, holding only 30 percent in a hand-picked thirty-name sleeve, returned 0.15 per point of worst fall -- slightly WORSE than holding SPY alone at about 0.14 -- while the 50 and 30 percent rungs rose cleanly to 0.20 and 0.24. The sleeve's signal was identical at every rung; only its share changed. The obvious reading is that below some share a sleeve cannot pay its own trading bill, because Gotrade's per-order floor is charged per name regardless of how small the slot is, and a thirty-name sleeve at 30 percent of the book means slots a third the size paying the same floor. If that reading is right the threshold is a property of the fee schedule and the name count, not of the signal, so it should sit in the same place for sleeves built on completely different ideas -- and it would be a standing rule for every core-and-satellite design the lab tries. Arms: one sleeve idea run at sleeve shares of 20, 30, 50 and 70 percent beside SPY (four rungs, because M0283 showed a two-point read would have missed the turn entirely), plus the same ladder on a second, unrelated sleeve idea to test whether the threshold moves with the signal. Prediction written before any result: return per point of fall is flat or falling from 20 to 30 percent and rises monotonically above it, the turn sits within one rung of the same share for both sleeves, and narrowing the sleeve from thirty names to ten at the SAME share moves the turn down, because ten fatter slots pay fewer floors. Run lab names and lab turnover alongside, since both already price this schedule.

methods.name: The industry's biggest name leads: do its smaller peers follow next month?
methods.sourceRef: Hou (2007) Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-Lag Effect in Stock Returns, RFS 20(4); Lo & MacKinlay (1990) When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction?, RFS 3(2)
methods.hypothesis: News reaches an industry's biggest, most-watched company first and its smaller peers with a lag, so last month's return of the largest member should predict this month's return of the others. The stock's own past return is never read, so the book cannot be momentum renamed. Each month-end, among F4's screened members, label each with its Fama-French 12 industry (SEC EDGAR SIC; unknowns never picked), call an industry's most-traded member by 20-day dollar volume its leader (the lab's market-cap figure is broken, dollar volume is not), keep industries with at least 5 pool members, rank them by their leader's last-month return, give the 3 strongest an equal share of 20 slots (7/7/6, a structural sector cap), and buy the other members of those industries in a fixed hash order — the within-industry choice carries no opinion in any arm, because M0216 already measured that a clever one adds nothing. Equal 5% slots, re-picked monthly with no band, unfilled slots in SPY, cash under SPY's 200-day average. Arms: FOLLOW-T3 (the idea), FADE-T3 (its mirror, the weakest leaders' industries), MATCHED-T3 (the control that matters: three industries drawn blind, the same split, switch and member order, so the bellwether signal is separated from the shape of a three-industry rotation book), FOLLOW-T3-NOGATE and MATCHED-T3-NOGATE (the 2x2 that prices the switch's habit, so the mirror pair does not join the 22 that cannot be priced), and SMALL-T3 (rank industries by their least-traded member instead: if it does as well, nothing is leading anything). Success: FOLLOW-T3 beats MATCHED-T3 by more than the lab's measured blind-draw noise of about 1.5 points a year, the ladder runs the right way against FADE-T3, and the lead survives on the survivorship-check store. Hou published in 2007, so most of the dev window predates the crowd, and the fade warning applies. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits.
methods.expectedFailure: The leader's last-month return is just its industry's last-month return, the followers are just that industry's members, and the whole lead is the three-industry rotation bet M0216 already priced at roughly nothing — its rotation book lost to SPY by 5.7 points a year in 2009-2015 and lost 3 of 4 walk-forward folds. If that is what happens here, FOLLOW-T3 and MATCHED-T3 will land inside the 1.5-point blind-draw noise band, SMALL-T3 will do about as well as FOLLOW-T3, and the mirror FADE-T3 will not be clearly worse. The second likely failure is the era: three concentrated industries re-picked monthly in equal slots is the book shape insight 91 warns about, so even a real lead before 2009 should vanish against SPY's big-company drift afterwards. The third is cost: 20 slots re-picked every month on a hash order churns hard, and Gotrade's fees on a $35 slot are several times the old flat assumption.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0295 — The industry's biggest name leads: do its smaller peers follow next month?

## What this tried

A well-known piece of research (Hou, 2007) says news reaches an industry's biggest,
most-watched company first and reaches its smaller rivals a few weeks later. If that is true,
how the biggest name in an industry did **last month** should say something about how its
smaller rivals do **this month**.

So each month-end the book did this. It took the screened pool of index members (at least $5 a
share, at least $20 million traded a day). It labelled each with its industry, using the twelve
broad industry groups economists use, read from the company's own filings as of that date. In
each industry it named the single most heavily traded company the **leader** — the one everyone
watches. It ranked industries by how their leader did over the last month, picked the three
best, split 20 equal slots across them (7, 7 and 6), and bought the industry's *other* members.
The leader itself was never bought: it is the signal, not a holding. The stock's own past return
was never read anywhere, so this book cannot be momentum wearing a new name.

**Inside a chosen industry, members were picked by a fixed coin-toss order — in every arm.**
That was deliberate. A sister method already measured that choosing cleverly inside a chosen
industry adds nothing, so re-buying that answer would have wasted the method. Here the only
thing that differs between arms is *how the three industries were chosen*.

Six arms, so the result could not hide:

- **Follow** — the idea: the three industries whose leader rose most last month.
- **Fade** — its mirror: the three whose leader fell most.
- **Blind draw** — the control that matters: three industries picked by coin toss, with the
  identical slot split, the identical safety switch and the identical coin-toss member order.
- **Follow, no switch** and **Blind draw, no switch** — the same two always invested, so what
  the safety switch costs could be priced instead of silently cancelling out.
- **Smallest leads** — the mechanism probe: rank industries by their *least* traded member. If
  that works too, nothing is leading anything.

Everything in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's real plan of 5 million
rupiah a month.

## Result (dev window 1996 to Oct 2015; yardstick is the same deposits into SPY total return)

| arm | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | gains vs losses (PF) | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Blind draw (control)** | **+7.6%** | +7.2% | 28.2% | 1.36 | 0.81 |
| Follow (the idea) | +7.3% | +7.2% | 33.9% | 1.43 | 0.57 |
| Blind draw, no switch | +6.9% | +7.2% | 58.1% | 1.20 | 0.47 |
| Follow, no switch | +6.5% | +7.2% | 59.9% | 1.25 | 0.27 |
| Fade (the mirror) | +5.5% | +7.2% | 27.6% | 1.28 | 0.48 |
| Smallest leads | +5.0% | +7.2% | 27.7% | 1.23 | 0.53 |

**Every arm is rejected.** The top two rows are the whole method: the coin toss beat the idea by
0.35 points a year. The idea had to win by at least 1.5 points — the lab's own measured noise
from a blind draw — and it finished on the wrong side of zero instead.

Two conditions to be clear about. The idea's worst fall of 33.9% passes the lab's loose internal
screen (50%), but it is well past the 25% the owner set for real money, so this book would never
have been fundable even had it won. And no arm came near the luck bar.

## The finding that matters: a clean mirror that means nothing

Judge the idea against its mirror alone, which is how most of this lab's timing rules have been
settled. Follow earned +7.3% and Fade +5.5% — a 1.75-point spread running the right way. The
lab's own splitter prices that as **+0.87 points a year of "what the opinion knows"** over the
full window, growing to **+2.15 points a year after 2009**. On that evidence alone this reads as
a confirmed signal.

It is not. **The coin toss sits above both of them.** Picking three industries at random earned
more than following the leader. The 1.75-point spread is not the idea earning money — it is the
mirror *losing* money. Buying the industries whose biggest name just fell is a genuinely bad
idea, and that is all the spread says. Every opinion about which industries to hold cost
something here: follow cost 0.35 points a year against the coin toss, fade cost 2.14, and
ranking by the smallest member cost 2.62.

This generalises, which is why it is the headline. **A rule and its mirror will show a positive
gap whenever the two sides are unevenly bad.** The gap only becomes evidence of knowledge once
the straight arm also clears a blind draw of the same shape. Without that third arm this method
would have been written up as a working lead-lag signal.

One practical note for the lab's own tools: the splitter would not accept either of the
always-invested arms as the "no-opinion" endpoint, because it wants a book that barely trades
(turnover at most 0.15 a year) and these turn over sixteen times a year. For a stock screen the
useful no-opinion arm is not a buy-and-hold endpoint at all — it is a blind draw of the same
shape, which is what was registered here and what the splitter cannot currently read.

## What the safety switch was worth (the 2x2)

| | with the switch | always invested | the switch is worth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Follow | +7.3% | +6.5% | +0.8 points a year, and 26 points less fall |
| Blind draw | +7.6% | +6.9% | +0.7 points a year, and 30 points less fall |

Nearly identical for the idea and for the coin toss. Over the full window the switch does not
interact with the picking: it is a flat benefit paid to any 20-name book, and it is what keeps
the worst fall near 28% instead of near 59%. None of that belongs to this idea.

## The honest-tape check, which complicates the story

Re-running every arm on the survivorship-check tape — the same window with the companies that
went bankrupt or were taken over put back — moved things, and not all in the same direction:

| arm | dev tape | honest tape | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Follow | +7.3% | **+7.3%** | −0.0 |
| Fade | +5.5% | +6.6% | +1.1 |
| **Blind draw** | **+7.6%** | +6.4% | **−1.2** |
| Smallest leads | +5.0% | +5.2% | +0.2 |

With the dead companies back, the order reverses: the idea becomes the best arm and the coin
toss drops below it by 0.9 points. The mechanism is plausible — a blind draw across industries
picks up dying companies, while tilting toward industries whose giant just rose systematically
avoids them. But 0.9 points is well inside the lab's own measured blind-draw noise of about 1.5
points, and the control was run on a **single** coin-toss seed, where one seed alone is worth
2.0 to 2.6 points. So this is not a result. It is a reason not to close the question.

The more interesting number is the era. Look at the **gate-off** pair in 2009-2015, the
best-covered years and the ones most like today:

| arm, always invested | 2009-2015 lead over SPY, dev tape | honest tape |
|---|---|---|
| Follow, no switch | **+3.0%** | **+3.5%** |
| Blind draw, no switch | −1.1% | −0.8% |

A gap of about 4 points a year in the idea's favour, in the era that matters, on both tapes.
Against that, the same pair over the whole twenty years has the coin toss ahead by 0.4 points —
so if the gap after 2009 is real, the signal must have been *negative* before 2009 by roughly
2.8 points a year. A sign that flips across eras is usually noise, and a 4-point gap measured
over under seven years against one coin-toss seed is comfortably inside what one seed can
produce. The two tapes are not an independent replication either: same dates, mostly the same
names. This is a thread to pull, not a finding.

## Why it failed

- **The leader's last month is the industry's last month.** The biggest, most-traded company in
  an industry *is* most of that industry's move. Ranking industries by their leader's last month
  is very nearly ranking them by their own last month — a one-month industry bet, which the lab
  priced at roughly nothing in the sister method. The lag the research describes lives in weekly
  data among small, barely-followed firms. Everything in this pool is a large US index member
  with analysts covering it, so there is no information left travelling slowly between them.
- **It hurt most where today's market lives.** In months where a few big names carried the index
  — the shape of 2009 onward — the idea lost 8.1% a year to SPY where the coin toss lost only
  1.4%. Chasing industries whose giant just rose is a concentrated bet against the market's own
  shape. (This cuts against the gate-off era reading above, and is one more reason to treat that
  reading as unproven.)
- **Three industries is concentrated however they are chosen.** The idea's worst fall was 33.9%,
  five points worse than the coin toss. A 20-name book spread over three industries can have all
  three wrong at once.
- **Churn.** Sixteen full turns of the book a year at real fees on $35 slots. The control pays
  exactly the same, so churn does not explain the gap between arms — but it is a large part of
  why no arm cleared the luck test.

## The luck test

The DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the luckiest of many tries. The lab counts
186 independent methods, and at that N the bar is 0.90 — the owner's setting since October 2026,
not mine. The best arm reached 0.81, the idea 0.57, the worst 0.27. None is close. Note which
arm scored highest: the coin toss.

## Walk-forward: 1 of 4 periods

Each period picks the best-looking arm from earlier years only, then scores it on the next
three. It won only 2006-2008 (+5.8% against SPY's −24.6%), and that win was the safety switch
sitting in cash through the crash, not the picking. It lost 2003-2005, 2009-2011 and 2012-2014.
**In three of the four periods the arm chosen on past evidence was a control arm, not the idea.**
The selection process preferred the coin toss too. The honest tape gives the same 1 of 4.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed its own pre-registered test: the idea had to beat the blind draw by 1.5
points a year and it lost to it on the dev tape. The expected failure happened almost word for
word — "the leader's return is just the industry's return, and the whole lead is the
three-industry rotation bet already priced at nothing." Two things written in advance were
wrong, both instructively. I expected the mirror to be "not clearly worse": it was clearly
worse, which is exactly what made the mirror look like a signal and the blind-draw control
indispensable. And I expected the honest tape to take the edge away, since a signal about small
fading companies should give its edge back: instead it took 1.2 points off the *control* and
left the idea untouched.

## Compared with its nearest sibling

The sister method that bought laggards inside the strongest industries earned +9.7% a year with
its own random-member control at +10.0% — the same pattern, control slightly ahead. Put the two
together: **choosing industries, and choosing inside them, are both worth nothing or less in
large US stocks re-picked monthly at real fees.** Three industries chosen by any rule tested so
far do about as well as three chosen by coin toss, and essentially the whole return of these
books is the 20-name spread plus the safety switch.

## My opinion

The lead-lag idea as a monthly stock picker is dead, and I would not spend another method id on
a book that ranks industries by one designated company's last month. The mechanism needs weekly
data and small, uncovered firms, and this lab has neither.

But I would spend one method on the loose thread, because it is cheap and the lab keeps running
into the same measurement problem. The thread is this: **always invested, the follow book led
the blind draw by about 4 points a year in 2009-2015 on both tapes, while trailing it over the
full twenty years.** I do not believe it yet, and the reason I do not believe it is precisely
measurable: the control was one coin-toss seed, and one seed alone is worth 2 to 2.6 points. So
the next method should register the identical gate-off follow book against **five or six
blind-draw seeds** instead of one, and read the era gap against the spread of the draws rather
than against a single draw. If follow sits inside the spread of seeds, this line closes for
good, which is a real result. If it sits clearly above all of them in 2009-2015, the lab has
found something that works in the era it cares most about, and the pre-2009 sign flip becomes
the thing to explain.

That experiment is worth running for a second reason that outlives this idea. The lab has
twenty-eight recorded mirror pairs and can price only a handful, and this run shows that for a
stock screen the missing arm is not the always-invested endpoint the splitter asks for — it is a
**shape-matched blind draw, run on several seeds**. Getting that convention right is worth more
than any one industry signal.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1049: verified, and the fold record is worse than reported

Every number reproduces from the recorded trials. On the owner's money against SPY's +7.19%:
MATCHED-T3 the blind draw +7.65%, FOLLOW-T3 the idea +7.26%, FADE-T3 the mirror +5.51%. The blind
draw really does sit above the idea, and FOLLOW minus FADE is 1.75 points to the digit. Nothing
is near the luck bar; the best arm reads 0.805 at N=186.

`lab dressing`, split by hand because the automatic check finds no reversing pair here, prices the
mirror at **+0.87 points a year of "what the opinion knows" on the money, +2.15 after 2009**, and
reports the habit as unpriced. So the pair reads exactly like a confirmed signal, and it is not
one. That is the finding and it generalises: **a mirror gap is positive whenever the two sides are
unevenly bad.** It becomes evidence only once the straight arm also clears a blind draw matched to
the book's own shape. The lab holds 28 mirror pairs and can price 6, and every one of the 28 has
been read without this second condition.

**The fold record is worse than the report says.** The child wrote that 3 of the 4 folds selected a
control arm. The recorded picks are MATCHED-T3-NOGATE, MATCHED-T3, MATCHED-T3 and SMALL-T3 -- **4
of 4**. In not one fold did the lab's own selection rule prefer the idea to a control registered
to beat it. That is the strongest available form of "the idea did not beat its own placebo", and
it agrees with the headline rather than softening it.

**The tooling gap is real and I confirmed the mechanism.** `lab/dressing.py` picks its
habit-pricing endpoint with `exposure >= EXPOSURE_BAR and turnover <= TURNOVER_BAR`, and
`TURNOVER_BAR = 0.15` a year. This method registered two always-invested arms precisely so the
habit could be priced; they turn over 20.77 and 21.44 a year, two orders of magnitude above the
bar, so the tool reports "the method never registered an always-invested arm" when in fact it
registered two. No monthly-rebalanced stock screen can ever satisfy that test -- these books turn
16 to 21 times a year by construction. For a stock picker the no-opinion arm is not a buy-and-hold
endpoint; it is a blind draw wearing the book's own shape. Feature-wish 584 has it.

**The live thread is correctly left open.** On the survivorship-check store the order reverses --
FOLLOW holds +7.3% while MATCHED drops to +6.4% -- and gate-off over 2009-2015 FOLLOW leads
MATCHED by +4.1 points a year on dev and +4.3 on the check store. The child does not believe it
and nor do I: one seed's draw noise on a book this size is 2.0-2.6 points over twenty years, and
this is a sub-seven-year slice measured against a single draw. M0296 is the right instrument,
and its real value is not this thread but the error bar itself -- the lab has never had one for a
twenty-name three-industry book over a seven-year slice, and has been quoting such slices for
months.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a blind draw of three industries beat following the biggest name's lead, and the clean-looking mirror was the mirror losing, not the idea winning.

methods.name: Read the industry-lead-lag book against a spread of blind draws, not one
methods.hypothesis: M0295 left exactly one number unresolved. Always invested, with the safety switch off in both arms, its industry-follow book led its single blind-draw control by about 4.1 points a year over 2009-2015 on the dev store and 4.3 on the survivorship-check store, while trailing that same control by 0.4 points a year over the whole twenty years. A sign that flips between eras, measured over a 6.75-year slice against ONE coin-toss seed, is the exact shape of draw noise: seed alone is worth 2.0-2.6 points a year on a twenty-year window, and a seven-year slice is noisier still. So this method turns the single control into a population. It registers six more blind draws — seeds 2 through 7, identical in every other respect, on the same engine, the same three-industry split, the same Fama-French 12 taxonomy, the same opinion-free member order, the same real Gotrade fees, and the safety switch off in every arm. Read beside the two already recorded gate-off arms of M0295 that this engine produced, that gives one follow book against seven draws. Success: the follow book sits clearly ABOVE all seven draws over 2009-2015 and outside their range over the full window, in which case the lead is real and the pre-2009 sign flip becomes the thing to explain. The second deliverable does not depend on the first: the spread of seven draws is the lab's first measured error bar for a twenty-name three-industry book, whole-window and over the 2009-2015 slice, and every shape-matched control the lab reads from now on can be sized against it.
methods.expectedFailure: The follow book sits INSIDE the spread of the seven draws over 2009-2015, which closes the industry lead-lag line for good: choosing three industries by their biggest member's last month would then be worth nothing that a coin toss is not, in the era the lab cares most about, having already been worth nothing over the full window. That is the likely outcome, because M0216 priced industry rotation at roughly nothing after 2009 and because a 4-point gap on a 6.75-year slice is inside what a single seed can produce. The second expected failure is about the instrument rather than the idea: the six draws may land so close together — same pool, same screen, same slot count, same monthly re-pick, only the industry labels shuffled — that the error bar comes out implausibly narrow, because three industries drawn from the same nine or ten eligible ones overlap heavily by construction and the draws are not really independent books. If that happens the spread understates true draw noise and must be reported as a lower bound, not as the error bar. Third: every arm is always invested through 2008, so all seven will fall far past the 20% limit and none will be dev-eligible. That is expected and is not a result; this method is an instrument, and its product is a measurement, not a candidate.

### 2026-10-23

# M0296 — one book read against nineteen coin tosses

## What this was for, and why it is not a stock picker

Its parent asked whether an industry's biggest, most-watched company leads its smaller
neighbours: if the big name moved last month, do the others follow this month. That idea was
rejected. But it left one number hanging. With the safety switch turned off in both arms, the
idea's book beat its single coin-toss control by about four points a year over 2009-2015, while
losing to the same control by 0.4 points a year over the full twenty years. A result that changes
sign between eras, measured over seven years, against **one** coin toss, is exactly what pure
luck looks like.

So this method did not try to pick stocks. It rebuilt the same book eighteen more times with
nothing changed but the coin — which three industries get bought — and asked where the real rule
sits among them. Nineteen coin tosses in all, counting the one the parent had already run. Every
arm is always invested, so time spent in cash cannot colour the era comparison. Every arm pays
Gotrade's real fees on the owner's real monthly deposits of 5 million rupiah.

Six tosses were registered first. When they came back the rule was ahead of all six in 2009-2015,
and six is far too few to mean anything, so twelve more were registered in a second commit —
before any of them were run — with the reading rule fixed in advance: run every seed, report the
rule's rank among the full population, drop nothing. Adding controls is the one direction that
cannot flatter a result: more coin tosses can only make "better than all of them" harder.

## Result 1: how wide the coin's own range is

Over the twenty years, the same book built nineteen times with nothing changed but the coin
earned anywhere from **1.5% to 9.1% a year** on the owner's money. SPY earned 7.2%. That is a
**7.5-point spread between the luckiest and the unluckiest version of an identical rule**. The
middle of the nineteen is 5.3% and the typical distance from it is 1.8 points. Three of the
nineteen beat SPY; sixteen lost to it.

This is the measurement the lab has been missing, and it is worth more than any strategy this
run could have found. When two versions of a book like this differ by two points a year, that
difference is smaller than the coin's own swing and carries no information whatever. The lab has
been reading such gaps as findings for months, including the four-point gap that caused this run.

## Result 2: what the coin moves, and what it leaves alone

The coin does not only move the return. Across the nineteen:

- **worst fall from a peak: 49.0% to 69.7%** — a 20.7-point swing;
- **worst single year: −23.5% to −55.0%** — a 31.5-point swing;
- gains-to-losses ratio: 1.04 to 1.29;
- risk-adjusted return (Sharpe): 0.21 to 0.60, nearly a factor of three.

And what it barely moves at all:

- **number of trades: 4,011 to 4,120** — a 2.7% spread;
- **portfolio turned over: 20.6 to 21.4 times a year** — a 4.1% spread.

So the bill is fixed by the shape of the book, and every measure of how well it did is at the
mercy of the coin. The lab has been working from the opposite belief — that a book's worst fall
and its gains-to-losses ratio are steady enough to read when its returns are not. That belief was
measured on books that keep a safety switch, and the switch caps every version's fall at roughly
the same place, which is what made them look steady. Take the switch away and the fall is as
noisy as the return.

## Result 3: the rule itself, and the question it finally answers

**Over the full twenty years** the rule lands 4th of 20 on the dev data and 6th of 20 on the
honest tape that puts the dead companies back. Respectable, unremarkable, and well inside what
the coin produces by itself. The parent's "the control beat the idea by 0.4 points a year" was
noise, as suspected: against a 7.5-point spread, 0.4 points is nothing.

**Over 2009-2015** the rule is **1st of 20 on both tapes**. On the dev data it earns 3.0 points a
year more than SPY where the best of nineteen coin tosses manages +0.8 and the average is −3.0.
On the honest tape it earns 3.5 points more than SPY where the best coin toss manages −0.8 and
the average is −4.0. The gap is **larger with the dead companies put back**, which is the one
direction that argues against a hole in the data.

That is exactly the pre-registered success condition, and on its own it would be the strongest
result this line has produced.

**It does not survive the other half of the window.** The same rule, measured the same way over
**1996-2008, ranks 17th of 20** — worse than sixteen of the nineteen coin tosses, a full standard
deviation below their average. First of twenty in one era and seventeenth of twenty in the other,
with nothing remarkable over the two together, is not a mechanism that arrived in 2009. It is one
long coin toss, read twice.

And the era was not chosen fresh. It was chosen because the parent noticed the rule looked good
there. The nineteen draws control for the luck of *which industries* the coin picks; they cannot
control for the luck of *which seven years* someone chose to look at after seeing the answer. The
companion era settles that, and it says the opposite.

## Against the lab's go-live bar

None of the eighteen trials is eligible and none was ever going to be: always invested through
2008, every one falls between 49% and 70% from its peak, against the owner's 20% limit, and
fifteen of the eighteen also lose to SPY outright. The luck score (DSR — how likely a result is
real rather than the best of many tries) runs from 0.08 to 0.64 against a bar of 0.90, judged at
N = 190 and 191, where N is one look per distinct method in the lab. Nothing here is close, and
nothing here was meant to be: this method is a measuring instrument and its product is a number,
not a candidate.

The twelve extra draws cost the lab nothing. They were recorded as amendments under the same
method id, so no new method id was spent and the luck bar everyone else is judged against did not
move.

## Compared with the parent

The parent ran one coin toss and read a four-point era gap against it. With nineteen, that gap is
real as a gap — the rule genuinely is the best of twenty in that era — and meaningless as
evidence, because the same rule is near the bottom in the other era and in the middle overall.
The parent's own verdict, that the lead-lag idea is dead as a monthly stock picker, stands; what
this run adds is that the one loose thread it left is not a thread.

## My opinion

The industry lead-lag line is closed and I would spend nothing further on it. One era first of
twenty, the other seventeenth of twenty, the whole fourth of twenty: that is a coin, and the only
reason it looked otherwise is that the lab had never measured how wide its coins swing.

What is worth more trials is the instrument. Two things came out of this run that apply to
everything the lab does. The first is the number: on a twenty-name book re-picked monthly at real
fees, the coin alone is worth 7.5 points a year of twenty-year return, 21 points of worst fall
and 32 points of worst year, while the trading bill barely moves. Every two-arm comparison in the
lab's record should be re-read against that, and most of them will stop saying anything. The
second is a rule of arithmetic the lab has been ignoring: "it beat all k of its controls" can
never be worth more than a one-in-(k+1) chance, so a single control arm buys a one-in-two claim
and is therefore worth nothing at all, six buys one-in-seven, and nineteen is the smallest
population that reaches the one-in-twenty the rest of the lab is judged by. A great many recorded
comparisons in this lab rest on a single control.

So the next thing I would run is the same instrument on the chassis the lab actually cares
about: the same twenty-name book **with** the safety switch, which is what every near miss on the
leaderboard is. The error bar measured here is for the switch-off version. Until the switched
version has one too, every "beat its placebo by N points" in the record is an unlabelled number,
and I would rather spend a method id learning the width of the lab's own ruler than on one more
idea measured with it.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1305: the error bar is real, and it is bigger than most of what the lab has reported

Eighteen trials verified from the recorded rows, on M0295's own allocator object so the engine is
literally the same code the two gate-off arms it is read against ran on. Every figure reproduces:

  money-weighted return   1.528% to 9.056% a year   range 7.528   sd 1.791
  worst fall             48.952% to 69.683%         range 20.732  sd 6.049
  profit factor           1.038 to 1.289            range 0.252
  Sharpe                  0.212 to 0.603
  deflated Sharpe         0.080 to 0.635
  trades                  4,011 to 4,120            range 2.7%
  turnover a year         20.584 to 21.401          range 4.0%

**Nineteen identical rules, differing in nothing but the coin, span seven and a half points a year
and twenty points of worst fall.** That is the number this lab has been missing. Almost every
margin it has reported on an ungated stock book -- and all four of the counted looks it has spent
-- was smaller than this, and was compared against nothing or against one draw.

**The cost meters are seed-stable and the performance meters are not**, which is the clean half of
the result: trades move 2.7% and turnover 4.0% across the whole population while return moves
sevenfold. A fee or churn comparison between two draws is readable; a return or drawdown
comparison is not.

**One standing note is corrected by this.** The lab has been carrying "fall and profit factor are
seed-stable" and a draw-noise figure of 2.0 to 2.6 points. Both were measured on GATED books,
where the market switch caps every arm's fall in the same months and suppresses the spread. With
the gate off the fall is as noisy as the return -- twenty points of it. The old figure is not
wrong, it is narrower than it looked and belongs only to gated books; the ungated number is this
one, and the two must not be used interchangeably.

**The arithmetic is the part to propagate.** Under the null the idea arm is exchangeable with its
draws, so "beats all k controls" has a one-sided p of exactly 1/(k+1). One control gives 0.5 and
establishes nothing whatever. Six gives 0.143. Nineteen gives 0.050 -- the smallest population
that reaches the bar the rest of this lab is held to. And widening a control population after a
favourable result is the one direction that cannot be fishing, because more draws only make
"above all of them" harder to achieve. That gives the lab a rule it can apply immediately and
cheaply, and M0307 should apply it to every single-control comparison on the shelf.

**On the signal itself the child's reading is right and its own instrument killed it.** FOLLOW
ranks 1 of 20 over 2009-2015 on both stores, with z around +2.9 to +3.0 -- which looks decisive
until the companion era is read, where it ranks 17 of 20, and 4 of 20 over the whole window. The
nineteen draws control for luck in picking industries; nothing here controls for luck in picking
the years, and 2009-2015 was chosen precisely because M0295 had noticed it looked good there.
First in one era and near-last in the other is a coin read twice. I did not re-derive the per-era
ranks from the curves; they are reported as the child measured them, and nothing turns on them --
the line is closed either way and no look was spent.

**No buy signal, and it could not have fired.** Nothing here is dev-eligible or could be: every
arm is always invested through 2008, falls 49-70% against the owner's bar, 15 of 18 lose to SPY
outright, and the deflated Sharpes run 0.08 to 0.64 against a 0.90 bar.
methods.verdict: Rejected, and the line is closed: with nineteen coin tosses instead of one, the industry-leader rule is first of twenty in 2009-2015 and seventeenth of twenty before it — a coin read twice, not a signal. The lab now has its first error bar: the coin alone is worth 7.5 points a year of return and 21 points of worst fall.

methods.hypothesis: M0295 showed a mirror pair can read as a clean signal while a blind draw of the same shape beats both arms: the gap was the mirror losing, not the idea winning. Swept on 2026-10-23, the lab holds 35 reversed pairs across 27 methods and can price only 8; 20 of those 27 methods have no control arm of any kind, and four of the twenty are dev-eligible. This method buys the missing arm for the four of them whose chassis the matched draw is exact on -- band-free, equal-slot, monthly F4 books -- and asks whether a mirror gap systematically over-states what a stock screen knows. Each draw takes its parent's own pool, book size, monthly entry count, switch, slot weights, SPY filler and fees, and replaces only the choice of names, with a date-free keep hash and a month-keyed entry hash. Arms: D93-S1 and D93-S2 (two seeds against M0093-LO5-S60-N20-T, dev-eligible, mirror gap +3.04 points a year on the prices), D58-S1 and D58-S2 (two seeds against M0058-ILL20-T, dev-eligible, +1.76), D91-S1 (against M0091-LO5-N20-T, rejected, mirror -0.36 and so already backwards) and D69-S1 (against M0069-L60-N20, rejected, ungated, +1.20). Predictions, written before any result: (1) for at least two of the four books the straight arm's lead over its own blind draw is SMALLER than the half-gap lab dressing prices from its mirror, which is what over-statement looks like; (2) M0093 still beats its draw, because a lowest-scaled-spike ranking is a real low-volatility tilt rather than an empty opinion, but by under 3 points a year; (3) the two seed pairs differ by less than 1.5 points a year, the lab's own measured blind-draw noise, so the single-seed reads on M0091 and M0069 can be read at all; (4) each draw's worst fall lands within 5 points of its parent's and its profit factor within 0.3, because those axes are seed-stable and the shape is matched by construction. No arm here is a strategy; every one is a placebo and none may be promoted.
methods.expectedFailure: The headline failure is that the sweep finds nothing: all four straight arms beat their draws by about what their mirrors implied, M0295 was a one-off, and the convention matters only going forward. That is the honest outcome and is pre-registered as such. Second, the seed pairs may differ by more than 1.5 points a year, in which case the single-seed reads on M0091 and M0069 are unreadable on return and the method can only report the fall and the profit factor for them. Third, a draw may clear the lab's screen outright: a blind twenty-name book behind the SPY 200-day switch inherits whatever that switch is worth (insight 462 prices it near 3.6 points a year in 2009-2015), so an eligible placebo would be a finding about the screen and not a strategy, and promoting it is forbidden. Fourth, M0069's draw inherits a book that fell over 70%, so nothing on that row will be near a go-live bar whichever way it lands. Fifth, lab control cannot resolve a control that lives in a different method from the arm it controls, so these six arms will report as unresolved and the comparison has to be made by hand from the recorded trade and turnover counts; that is a gap in the tool, not in the draws.

### 2026-10-23

# M0297 — The missing third arm: a blind draw for the stock screens that only ever had a mirror

## What this tried, and why none of it is a strategy

Every arm in this method is a **coin toss**. That is the point.

When the lab tests a stock-picking rule it usually registers the rule and its **mirror** — the
same book buying the opposite names. If the rule earns more than its mirror, the gap reads as
proof that the ranking knows something. Last week a method (the industry lead-lag book) showed
that proof can be empty: the rule beat its mirror by 1.75 points a year, which looked convincing,
and then a **blind draw of the same shape** — same number of names, bought and sold on the same
days, from the same pool, paying the same fees, chosen by a coin toss — beat *both* of them. The
gap was the mirror being bad, not the rule being good.

So: was that a one-off, or has the lab been over-reading its mirrors for years?

Swept on 23 October, the lab holds **35 mirror pairs across 27 methods**, and **20 of those 27
methods have no coin-toss arm at all**. Their only evidence is the kind that just failed.

This method buys the missing arm for four of those books. It could not be done by editing them —
a method's file is sealed once its results are recorded — so the repair had to be a new
pre-registration. One method id, four books.

**A correction to my own pre-registration.** The hypothesis says "four of the twenty are
dev-eligible". The correct count is **nine**: the illiquidity book, two dividend-raise books, the
lottery-spike book, three coskewness books, the steady-alpha book and a market-sensitivity book.
I had counted only the ones whose mirror gap was both unpriced and positive. The four books
repaired here were chosen for a different and unchanged reason — their machinery is the only kind
the matched draw copies exactly — so nothing else in the method moves. But the sentence was
wrong, and the real backlog is more than twice what it claimed.

## The four books and their coin tosses

| book | what it ranks on | status |
|---|---|---|
| scaled-lottery-spike | the 20 members whose biggest recent day was smallest next to their own normal swing | dev-eligible; its best arm clears every bar |
| illiquidity | the 20 big members that trade thinnest for their size | dev-eligible |
| raw-lottery | the same, unscaled (the parent of the first one) | rejected |
| long-term losers | the 20 that fell furthest over three to five years, skipping the last year | rejected |

Each coin toss copies its book exactly: same screen, same 20 slots, same monthly re-pick, same
safety switch, same spare-cash-into-SPY rule, same real Gotrade fees on the owner's 5 million
rupiah a month. At each monthly decision it counts how many names the real book is **adding**,
keeps all but that many of its own names, and draws that many fresh ones out of a hash. Nothing
in it ever reads a price ranking.

**The copies are honest, and that is the one thing here measured beyond doubt.** All six traded
between 0.93 and 1.00 times as often as the book they copy, and turned their money over between
0.92 and 1.00 times as fast — inside the band the lab calls a clean match on both axes. Trade
counts and turnover are the only numbers in this whole exercise that a coin toss cannot move
(the lab measured them at 2.7% and 4.1% across nineteen draws of one book). So the race was not
rigged in either direction, and the **retrofit works**: a missing control can be bought for a
sealed method, cheaply, as a new pre-registration.

## Result (dev window 1996 to Oct 2015; the yardstick is the same deposits into SPY, +7.2% a year)

| book | the rule | its mirror | the coin toss(es) |
|---|---|---|---|
| scaled-lottery-spike | **+10.7%** | +4.8% | +7.3% and +5.3% |
| illiquidity | **+12.8%** | +8.1% | +12.5% and +9.7% |
| raw-lottery | +7.1% | +8.1% | **+7.3%** |
| long-term losers | +9.0% | +7.3% | **+9.9%** |

And the same four books re-run on the honest tape — the check store that puts back most of the
companies the dev store cannot price, the ones that went bankrupt or were taken over:

| book | the rule | its mirror | the coin toss(es) |
|---|---|---|---|
| scaled-lottery-spike | **+9.4%** | +3.4% | +6.0% and +5.3% |
| illiquidity | **+22.3%** | +8.4% | +9.4% and +7.4% |
| raw-lottery | **+7.8%** | +4.7% | +5.6% |
| long-term losers | +6.8% | +6.3% | **+8.1%** |

## The honest reading, which is thinner than the tables look

A sister session measured, the same day, how wide a coin toss's own luck is: **nineteen draws of
one book spanned 7.5 points a year of return and 21 points of worst fall.** And it settled the
arithmetic: beating *k* coin tosses can never support better odds than **1 in (k+1)**. One toss
is a 1-in-2 coin flip and establishes nothing; two is 1-in-3. The lab's usual bar is 1-in-20,
which needs nineteen.

So, plainly: **no single one of the four comparisons below is established.** Two of my books got
two tosses and two got one. I bought coverage instead of power, which I would do again given that
the power experiment landed the same day on another book — but the per-book readings are
directional, not proven, and anyone quoting one of them as settled is repeating the mistake this
method exists to name.

What the four say, with that caveat attached to every row:

| book | mirror claimed the ranking is worth | coin toss says, dev | coin toss says, honest tape |
|---|---|---|---|
| scaled-lottery-spike | +2.96 | **+3.4 to +5.4** | **+3.4 to +4.1** |
| illiquidity | +2.32 | +0.3 to +3.1 | +12.8 to +14.8 |
| raw-lottery | −0.48 | −0.2 | +2.2 |
| long-term losers | +0.84 | **−0.9** | **−1.3** |

- **The scaled-lottery-spike book is the one that holds up.** It beat both its tosses on both
  tapes, by three points a year or more every time. Its mirror had under-stated it. With two
  tosses the odds are still only 1-in-3, but it is the only book here whose sign never wavered.
- **The long-term-losers book is the one that fails**, and it fails the same way the lead-lag
  book did: its mirror said the ranking was worth +0.8 points a year, and a coin toss of its own
  shape earned **more** than it on both tapes. One toss, so 1-in-2 odds — but the sign is the
  same on two different sets of prices, which one toss alone would not guarantee.
- **The illiquidity book cannot be read at all.** Its lead over its tosses is +0.3 on one tape
  and +14.8 on the other. That is not a measurement, it is two different questions.
- **The raw-lottery book flips sign between tapes** (−0.2, then +2.2). Also unreadable.

**So the mirror and the coin toss disagree in direction on one of four books on the dev tape and
two of four on the honest tape.** That is the finding, stated at the strength the evidence
supports: mirror gaps are not reliable, and the lab has 20 methods resting on them.

## Why the illiquidity book explodes on the honest tape, and why that is a warning

It earns 12.8% a year on the dev store and **22.3%** on the honest tape. Nothing else in the lab
moves like that; the biggest previously measured move in that direction was 1.3 points.

The reason is almost certainly its screen. Alone among the lab's books, the illiquidity book
**removes the traded-volume floor entirely** — it has to, because its whole idea is to buy the
names that trade thinnest. A sister session measured on the same day that a volume floor is a
**liveness filter**: companies get quiet before they die, so refusing quiet names is refusing the
ones that vanish. A book with no floor at all is the maximum possible exposure to exactly the
companies the dev store is missing.

That does not make 22.3% a discovery. It makes it a number that has to be explained before it is
believed: the thinnest-traded names are also where reconstructed price history is least
trustworthy, and a book whose returns treble when you add back the dead and the delisted is
telling you about your data as much as about the market. **I would not spend a test-window look
on this book on the strength of that number.** Its 2009-2015 record is negative on both tapes
(−1.7 and −0.9), which is the lab's first filter and it does not pass it.

## A coin toss passed the lab's screen — the strongest single result here

One of the six, the first toss of the illiquidity book, came back **eligible**: it cleared every
go-live condition and scored 0.960 on the luck test, above the 0.90 bar, on a search that has now
made 193 distinct attempts. It earned 12.5% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%,
fell 31.3% at its worst, and made 5.17 of gains for every 1 of losses.

**It picked its twenty stocks by coin toss.** Nothing in it read a price, a ranking or a company.

This needs no error bar — it is a single existence proof, and one is enough. It was written down
as a possible outcome before the run. Two things make it possible: the safety switch these books
sit behind, already priced at roughly 3.6 points a year through the 2009-2015 rally, and the
floorless pool described above, which is a better pool than a normal blind draw gets.

**It must never be promoted, and it will not be.** The hard gate would refuse this method anyway
— it won only 2 of its 4 walk-forward folds, short of the majority required — but that is luck,
not the reason. The reason is that a pre-registration is a promise about a *rule*, and this arm
has none.

It also lands on a defect the lab found three days ago on another method: the lab's own "best
eligible arm" picker has no idea what a control is, so **this method's headline arm on the site
is a coin toss**. That is now two methods in a week.

## The lab's control checker gave this a false all-clear

When the run finished, the lab printed:

> no control arm to report: every one of them matches its book's shape
> Every control arm matches the arm it controls on both axes.

All six arms **are** coin-toss controls, and the checker had correctly recognised all six as
such. What it could not do was work out **which book each one controls**, because each controls a
book in a *different method* — which is the only way a missing control can ever be added, since a
method's file is sealed once it has run. Unable to resolve them, the checker dropped all six, and
its empty-case sentence then asserted the opposite of the truth.

Here the copies really were well shaped; I measured all six by hand. But the next method in this
position could be badly shaped and would get the same green light. Logged as a risk and a tool
request.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

1. **"For at least two of the four books the mirror over-states what the ranking knows."**
   **Held, at exactly two** on the dev tape — illiquidity (2.32 claimed, 1.67 delivered) and
   long-term losers (0.84 claimed, −0.89 delivered). On the honest tape it is two as well, but a
   different two. Held in letter; the instability underneath it was not predicted.
2. **"The scaled-lottery-spike book still beats its coin toss, by under 3 points a year."**
   **Half held.** It beat it, on both tapes — but by more than three points, not less, and more
   than its mirror had claimed. Right about direction, wrong about size, wrong in the book's
   favour.
3. **"The two pairs of coin tosses differ by less than 1.5 points a year."** **Failed, both** —
   2.0 and 2.8. And the sister measurement published hours later makes clear how badly this
   prediction was framed: on a book with no safety switch the true spread is 7.5 points. My
   books are all switched except one, so 2.0-2.8 is plausibly the *switched* chassis's width,
   which nobody had measured. That is worth having, and it is two draws per book, so it is a
   hint and not a number.
4. **"Each coin toss's worst fall lands within 5 points of its book's."** **Failed for three of
   four**, and the whole premise was wrong: the fall is not a stable axis. It moved 2.2-2.4
   points between my two tosses of one book, flipped sign between tapes on two books, and the
   sister measurement found a 21-point spread across nineteen draws of an unswitched book. I had
   intended to fall back on the fall where the return was unreadable. **That fallback does not
   exist** and the earlier note in the lab's memory that said it did has been corrected.

The pre-registered failure modes: the "headline failure" (nothing moves) did **not** happen; the
"a coin toss clears the screen" failure **did**; and the "the checker cannot resolve a
cross-method control" failure **did**, in a worse form than predicted — a false all-clear rather
than an honest "cannot tell".

## Why a mirror misleads: the mechanism

A rule and its mirror are two *opinions*, not an opinion and the absence of one. Both pick twenty
names from the same few hundred on the same days and pay the same fees. The gap between them is
the distance between two opinions, and that distance is wide whenever **either** is wrong — with
nothing in the pair to say which.

The coin toss is the only arm with no opinion in it. It is the zero. Lay the three on a line and
the long-term-losers book looks like this on the dev tape: mirror +7.3 … rule +9.0 … **toss
+9.9**. Both opinions sit *below* the zero. The mirror gap is real, both arms are bad, and the
ranking's supposed edge is the coin toss's edge minus a penalty for having an opinion at all.
That shape is invisible to any amount of mirror arithmetic. Only the zero reveals it.

## My opinion:

**This direction is worth more trials, but not more of this shape of trial.** Running one or two
coin tosses against four different books was the wrong trade: it produced four unproven readings
where nineteen tosses against one book would have produced one proven one. The sister session
that did exactly that, on the same day, is the model, and the arithmetic is not negotiable —
beating *k* tosses is worth 1-in-(k+1) and nothing more.

What I would do next, in order.

**First, finish the one book that looks real.** The scaled-lottery-spike book beat both its
tosses on both tapes by three points or more. That is the best candidate in this method by a
distance, and it is already dev-eligible with an arm that clears every bar. It deserves nineteen
tosses, not two. If it survives that, the lab has its first stock screen whose edge has been
measured against the zero rather than against its own mirror — and I would say so loudly, because
the lab has never had one.

**Second, do not spend a look on the illiquidity book.** Its 22.3% on the honest tape is a data
question, not a finding; its 2009-2015 record is negative on both tapes; and the lab's own screen
just handed an eligible verdict to a coin toss drawn from its pool. Everything about that book
currently says "the pool is doing the work".

**Third, treat the remaining sixteen unrepaired mirror methods as unproven rather than wrong.**
This run shows the retrofit is cheap and mechanically exact — the six copies matched their books
to within 7% on both cost meters — so the work is doable. But it should be done one book at a
time with a proper population of tosses, and the honest tape should be run alongside, because two
of my four books flipped sign between the two sets of prices.

**Fourth, and the thing I would fix before any of that:** the lab cannot currently say "this arm
controls that arm in another method". That single missing field is what turned a correct check
into a false all-clear here, and it is also what makes every future retrofit unreadable by the
tool that exists to read it.


### 2026-10-23

# M0297 — correction, same day: what the safety switch was actually worth here

Two places above say the safety switch is worth "roughly 3.6 points a year", and use that to
explain why a coin toss passed the lab's screen. **That number is borrowed and it is wrong for
these books.** It came from a measurement of a different book, and the lab has already recorded
that it is not a constant. I should have measured it rather than quoted it, so I have now
measured it, on the two books here that have both a switched-on and a switched-off arm.

| arm | with the switch | always invested | the switch is worth |
|---|---|---|---|
| illiquidity, the 20 thinnest | +12.7%/yr, fell 26.4% | +12.1%/yr, fell 67.5% | **+0.6 points a year, and 41 points less fall** |
| illiquidity, the 20 most liquid | +8.1%, fell 17.6% | +6.7%, fell 57.4% | +1.4 points, and 40 points less fall |
| raw-lottery, the 20 calmest | +7.1%, fell 30.1% | +6.4%, fell 44.8% | **+0.7 points, and 15 points less fall** |
| raw-lottery, the 20 jumpiest | +8.1%, fell 33.8% | +3.5%, fell 82.4% | +4.6 points, and 49 points less fall |

So on these books the switch bought between half a point and four and a half points a year, and
on the two that matter here it bought **under a point**. The "3.6" does not apply.

**This makes the explanation of the eligible coin toss better, not weaker.** The switch did not
hand it a return. It handed it a **shallow fall** — 41 points of one. Look at the two illiquidity
rows: always invested, that pool earns about the same money and falls 67%. Behind the switch it
earns about the same money and falls 26%. Our go-live test divides return by worst fall, so
turning a 67% fall into a 31% fall is what carried the coin toss over the bar, not any extra
earnings.

Which sharpens the warning. **Our screen can be passed by a shallow fall bought from a switch,
sitting on top of a pool that earns well, with no idea anywhere in the book.** The two
ingredients were a pool with the liquidity rule switched off and a market switch that caps the
fall. Neither is a strategy and both are inherited by anything that runs on that chassis.

Everything else above stands. The gate figures here are from the lab's own switch-off report on
the dev store; no new trial was recorded and no test-window look was spent.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1305: every structural number re-derived, and DO NOT PROMOTE

I re-ran the sweep rather than taking it. `lab dressing --all` prints its own header: **35
reversed-arm pairs across 27 methods**, out of 193 methods with recorded dev trials. I then ran
`lab control` against each of those 27 and counted the ones answering "no control arm to report":
**20 of 27**. Of those twenty, **nine are dev-eligible** -- M0058, M0083, M0088, M0093, M0179,
M0184, M0185, M0188, M0293 -- which is the child's list exactly. Its pre-registration said "four";
that was a miscount it caught and corrected in its own analysis rather than leaving to be found.

**The eligible coin toss is real and I confirmed it two ways.** M0297-D58-S1 records funded
12.48% a year against SPY's 7.19%, fall 31.33%, profit factor 5.17 and a deflated Sharpe of 0.960
at N=193, with nothing in its failed column. `store.best_dev_eligible` returns it, so the arm this
method would put forward -- and the arm the site shows as its headline -- picks its twenty names
out of a hash.

**The sharper demonstration is sitting beside it, and it is the error bar landing on the
eligibility decision itself.** M0297-D58-S2 is the SAME rule at a different seed: 9.69% a year,
deflated Sharpe 0.898. Two draws of one random rule, 2.79 points a year apart, straddling the 0.90
bar -- one clears every condition the lab has, the other fails. That is M0296's 7.5-point spread
expressed as a pass and a fail, and it is the most compact argument in the batch that an
eligibility verdict near the bar carries no information.

**No promotion, and the gate agrees.** The hard gate refuses on folds (2 of 4) and `lab
walkforward` fires no buy signal. But the danger this raises is not promotion, it is display: for
the second time in a week (M0293 was the first) `best_dev_eligible` names a control as a method's
best arm, so a reader of the site sees a coin toss presented as the method's result. That is a
reporting defect with real consequences and it is the thing to fix.

**The honesty caveat is correct and must travel with every per-book number here.** With one or two
draws per book the one-sided p is at best 1/3 by the arithmetic M0296 established today, so **no
individual book's reading in this run is established**. What is established is the structural
count above, the shape match (all six copies 0.93-1.00x trades and 0.92-1.00x turnover, so the
retrofit itself works), and the existence proof of an eligible coin toss, which needs no error bar.
The long-term-losers book losing to its own draw -- mirror claimed +0.84, draw says -0.89 on dev
and -1.32 on the honest tape -- is the M0295 pattern reproduced on an unrelated book from an
unrelated paper, and it is suggestive at p = 1/2 rather than shown.

**The tool defect is worth the owner's attention.** `lab control` resolves a control's target only
within its own method, so a cross-method control always reads `unresolved` -- and cross-method is
the only shape a retrofit can take, because `source_sha` seals a method's file. Both reports then
sign off "every control arm matches the arm it controls": once at `lab run` through the empty-table
message, and once in the standalone report printed directly beneath a table of six unresolved rows.
A false all-clear in two places, on the check that exists to catch exactly this.

My recommendation stands with the child's: do not spend a test look on M0058 until M0309 separates
the illiquidity anomaly from a data artefact. Its 2009-2015 edge is negative on both tapes, and its
+9.5-point jump between stores is far outside anything else recorded in that direction.
