methods.name: Pin the liveness bar to a fixed rank so it cannot move between the two tapes
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0288 (its dollar-volume liveness ladder and the dev-minus-check-store swing it produced), with the percentile bar replaced by a fixed rank; same chassis -- M0007-N20-RAW in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits (Blitz, Huij & Martens 2011, Residual momentum, J. Empirical Finance 18(3), 506-521)
methods.hypothesis: Two methods now agree that a traded-volume bar is a liveness proxy: M0284 swung the dev-minus-check-store gap 3.9 points a year across its ladder on a news-event book and M0288 swung it 3.5 points on a price-only momentum screen, with the strictest rung the only arm in each method that earns MORE once the dead companies are put back. But both ladders used a PERCENTILE of each day's own candidate list, and the check store holds 989 symbols where the dev store holds 539, so putting the dead companies back does not only add candidates -- it moves where the bar sits. The measured swing therefore mixes the liveness effect with a change in the pool the percentage is taken of, and neither method's numbers can separate them. This replaces the percentile with a FIXED RANK: keep only the dv_rank most-traded eligible names by 20-day mean dollar volume, the same count on both tapes. Six arms on M0032's chassis verbatim -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 monthly trend switch, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits -- adding one requirement to the pool and moving nothing else: K0 (no bar, the reference arm with no opinion in it, which must reproduce M0032 and M0288-DV00 bar for bar), then K250, K200, K150, K100 and K50. The rungs are bite-matched to M0288's at the dev median pool of 261, so the two ladders read against each other rung by rung: K200 is about DV20, K150 about DV40, K100 about DV60 and K50 about DV80. I measured the geometry on BOTH tapes before writing this file, over all 237 decision months: the bar bites monotonically (names shared with the no-bar book, of 20, run 20.00, 17.45, 15.57, 13.27, 10.25, 5.48 on dev and 20.00, 14.38, 12.68, 10.64, 7.74, 4.10 on the check store, so it bites harder on the honest tape at every rung, as its larger pool implies), and it never starves the book -- 20.00 names held on average at every rung on both tapes, with not one month anywhere below 20, so M0279's 2-to-6-point cost of parking empty slots cannot explain anything seen here. The honest framing is NOT that this is the clean experiment M0288 was not. It is the MIRROR IMAGE of M0288's confound: a percentile holds the fraction constant and lets the count move, a rank holds the count constant and lets the fraction move, and no design can hold both because the two pools are different sizes -- which is the whole point of the honest tape. Pool composition pushes the two designs in different directions; liveness pushes them the same way. Success for the idea: this ladder reproduces M0288's swing in sign and shape across at least four rungs and within about a point in size, which together with M0288 would settle that the swing is liveness and give the lab a free diagnostic it can trust on every stock screen it already owns. Failure of the idea, equally informative: the swing collapses or inverts, which would mean M0288's 3.5 points was mostly pool composition and the liveness reading that two methods now rest on is much weaker than it looks.
methods.expectedFailure: First and most likely, a fixed rank has the disguised-date-filter disease that made M0288 choose a percentile, in mirror image, and I measured it rather than guessed it: the dev pool's median grows from 133 names in 1996-2000 to 361 in 2009-2015, so the share of months on which a rung binds at all runs, dev then check store, 0%/32% and 0%/38% for K250 and K200 in 1996-2000 against 100%/100% for both from 2006. K250 and K200 are therefore near-inert on the dev tape in the early years while already active on the check tape, and their gap in that era compares nothing to nothing; only K100 (77%/89% early, 100% after) and K50 (100% everywhere) bind on both tapes across essentially the whole window, so the conclusion must rest on the tight rungs. That is written down before the run so that leaning on them afterwards is pre-registered and not a choice made once the numbers were visible -- but it does mean the loose half of this ladder is weaker evidence than it will look in a table. Second, the swing may simply shrink toward nothing once the bar stops moving between tapes, which is the result that would overturn two methods' worth of belief and is the main reason to run this. Third, a fixed rank binds harder on the check store than on dev at the same K because its pool is larger -- 405 names at the median against 261 -- so the two runs hold different NUMBERS of candidates even though the bar is identical; that is the trade this design makes knowingly, and it means a narrowing gap could still be read as the check-store book simply being filtered more aggressively. Fourth, M0288 measured the cost of this dial at 5.4 points a year through a large-company tilt -- its breadth table showed the book's return in months when a few giants carried the index climbing +5.6% to +11.4% across the ladder while its return in broad months fell +6.4% to -4.7% -- and a rank bar is the same tilt by another name, so the tight rungs should lose dev return steadily and the drawdown and luck screens will probably reject them. Fifth, residual momentum was published in 2011, inside this window, so a crowding tilt toward the most-traded names is where a published edge fades first and 2009-2015 is where it would show. And sixth, as with M0288 this is evidence about DATA and about how to build books, not a candidate: the chassis has kin that already failed the test window (M0021, M0022, M0029 -- three looks on what is substantially one book), so the hard gate refuses promotion whatever the numbers, exactly as it refused M0288. That was known before the run and the method is worth running anyway, because what it measures is whether the lab can trust a diagnostic it is about to start applying everywhere.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## What this was for

The lab keeps two copies of market history. The everyday one prices about 540 companies. The
honest one adds back most of the companies that went bust or were bought out — 989 in all — so a
book tested on it has to live with the losers as well as the survivors.

Two earlier experiments found the same surprising thing. If you require a stock to be actively
traded before you will buy it, your book's edge survives the switch to the honest tape much
better. The looser that requirement, the more of the edge turns out to have been an illusion
created by the missing dead companies. One experiment found it on a book built around news days,
the other on a plain momentum book. Both swung by a similar amount — about 3.5 to 3.9 points a
year between their loosest and strictest settings.

The reading was that asking for volume is really asking **"is this company still alive?"** A
company the market is busy trading still exists. That would be a genuinely useful free tool: run
the test on any stock-picking method the lab already owns, and if its edge evaporates under a
volume requirement, be suspicious of it before spending anything else.

**But both experiments had the same hole, and this one was registered to close it.** Both set the
bar as a *share* of each day's candidate list — "drop the least-traded fifth". The honest tape has
a much bigger candidate list, so putting the dead companies back does not only add names to choose
from, it also **moves where the bar sits**. The measured swing therefore mixed the thing we care
about with a side effect of the bigger pool, and neither experiment's numbers could tell them
apart.

## What was changed, and the honest framing of it

This version pins the bar to a **fixed count**: keep the 250, or 200, or 150, or 100, or 50
most-traded candidates — the same number on both tapes — plus a sixth arm with no bar at all as
the reference. Everything else is the momentum book exactly as the paper roster trades it.

It would be nice to say this is the clean experiment the earlier ones were not. **That would be
false, and the method was registered saying so.** It is the *mirror image* of the same problem:

- A share-based bar keeps the same **fraction** on both tapes and a different **number**.
- A count-based bar keeps the same **number** on both tapes and a different **fraction**.

No design can hold both, because the two tapes have different-sized pools — which is the entire
point of the honest tape. So the question is not settled by finding a cleaner experiment; there
isn't one. It is settled by **running the problem both ways round**. A side effect of the pool
pushes the two designs in opposite directions. The real thing pushes them the same way.

## Checks made before reading any result

- **The no-bar arm reproduces the existing book exactly** — the same total return to sixteen
  digits, the same 1,607 trades, the same worst fall. So the new code is the same arithmetic and
  every difference is the dial.
- **The bar bites, and it bites harder on the honest tape**, as its bigger pool implies. Names
  shared with the no-bar book, out of 20: 20.0, 17.5, 15.6, 13.3, 10.3, 5.5 on the everyday tape;
  20.0, 14.4, 12.7, 10.6, 7.7, 4.1 on the honest one.
- **It never leaves the book sitting in cash.** Twenty names held on average at every setting on
  both tapes, and not one month anywhere with fewer than twenty. A previous run of filter
  experiments all failed for exactly this boring reason, at a cost of 2 to 6 points a year.
  Nothing below can be blamed on idle money.
- **The settings were matched to the earlier experiment's** at the everyday tape's typical pool of
  261 names, so the two ladders can be read against each other step by step.

## What happened

Against the same deposits put into the index, which earned +7.2% a year:

| bar | a year, everyday tape | a year, honest tape | difference | worst fall, honest tape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | +13.7% | +12.0% | **−1.7** | 25.0% |
| top 250 | +14.0% | +11.2% | **−2.7** | 23.7% |
| top 200 | +12.9% | +10.6% | **−2.3** | 22.0% |
| top 150 | +11.7% | +9.9% | **−1.8** | 22.0% |
| top 100 | +10.1% | +9.8% | **−0.3** | 24.9% |
| top 50 | +9.3% | +10.0% | **+0.7** | 22.8% |

**The idea passed its own pre-registered test, which is rare in this lab.** Success was written
down beforehand as: the swing reproduces in sign and shape across at least four settings, and
within about a point in size. Reading down from the top-250 setting to the top-50 one, the
difference column runs −2.7, −2.3, −1.8, −0.3, +0.7. That is **five settings in a row, each one
higher than the last, crossing from negative to positive** — a total swing of 3.4 points against
the earlier experiment's 3.5. Neither earlier ladder was actually straight; this one is. The
strictest setting is again the only arm that earns *more* once the dead companies are put back.

So: **the liveness effect is real, it is not an artefact of where the bar sat, and the lab has a
free diagnostic it can trust.** That is what this method was registered to find out, and the
answer is yes.

## But two things the parent experiment concluded do not survive, and they should be withdrawn

This is the uncomfortable half, and it matters more than the headline.

The parent experiment read its honest-tape column on its own and found that **the order reversed**
— its middle setting earned more on the honest tape (+12.7%) than the no-bar book did (+12.0%),
making it look like the right book to choose once you stop flattering yourself. It also found that
middle setting was the only one with a positive edge in 2009–2015, the best-covered years and the
lab's first filter.

**Neither reproduces here.** On the honest tape the no-bar book earns +12.0% and *every* bar
setting earns less: +11.2, +10.6, +9.9, +9.8, +10.0. And in 2009–2015 on the honest tape every
single setting is negative — −0.2, −3.2, −5.0, −6.8, −6.1, −5.4 — with the no-bar book the least
bad of them.

The reason is arithmetic, and it is the confound this method was built to expose. On the honest
tape, "drop the least-traded 40%" keeps about 243 names. "Keep the top 150" keeps 150. Labelled as
equivalent because they match on the everyday tape, they are nothing like equivalent on the honest
one — the share-based bar quietly *loosens* when the pool grows, so its middle settings stay close
to the unfiltered book exactly where the comparison was supposed to be hardest. The reversal was a
property of the measuring instrument, not of the market.

**So the swing is real and the recipe is not.** The parent's conclusion that a volume requirement
is a general liveness filter stands, and is now stronger. Its further suggestion that some middle
setting is actually the *better book* on honest data does not stand, and I would not repeat it.

## Why the cost is what it is

The breadth report gives the mechanism, and it reproduces the parent's almost exactly. As the bar
tightens, the book's return in months when **a few big companies carried the index** climbs from
+5.6% to +11.6%. In months when **gains were widely spread**, it falls from +6.4% to −3.2%. The
parent measured +5.6%→+11.4% and +6.4%→−4.7% on its own ladder.

So the bar does what was feared and predicted: it herds the book into the biggest, most-traded
names, which win when a handful of giants carry the market and lose when gains are broad. At the
strictest setting it has stopped being a stock-picking book and become a large-company bet. The
4.4 points a year it costs on the everyday tape is that tilt, not fees and not idle cash.

And that is also *why* the honesty gap closes: the companies that disappear are overwhelmingly
small and thinly traded, so refusing to buy thin names is refusing to buy the companies that later
die. The protection is real. It is bought by giving up the part of the market where this book
earns.

## One sub-finding worth keeping: the safety is invisible on the everyday tape

On the everyday tape the bar does nothing for the worst fall — 20.6% with no bar, 20.8% at the
strictest setting, noise either way. On the honest tape the no-bar book falls **25.0%**, exactly
at the limit the owner set, and every bar setting falls less, down to 22.8%. So the protection
this dial buys is literally unmeasurable on the data the lab does most of its work on. That is the
same shape as an earlier finding about how many names a book should hold, where the safety case
was also invisible on the everyday tape and obvious on the honest one.

## The luck test

The luck score asks how likely a result is to be real rather than a fluke, given how many distinct
ideas the lab has tried. N is 191 — one look per method, not per trial — and the bar is 0.90, the
owner's setting since 2026-10-07. The no-bar, top-250 and top-200 arms scored 0.923, 0.935 and
0.909 and are marked eligible; the top-150, top-100 and top-50 arms scored 0.876, 0.808 and 0.818
and failed on that alone.

Two honest caveats about those marks. The top-200 arm's 0.909 is **borderline**, and a borderline
luck score is not a property of the strategy — it reads the whole lab's population and drifts when
unrelated methods land beside it. And "eligible" here is partly a moved goalpost: the no-bar arm
is the same book, to sixteen digits, as one recorded on 2026-10-08 and marked **failed** at the
identical 20.6% fall. Nothing improved; the drawdown limit moved from 20% to 25% on 2026-10-14.

## Did the predictions hold?

The hypothesis held, including the part predicting its own limits. Of the six ways it was written
down to fail:

- **"A fixed count is a disguised date filter in mirror image."** Happened, exactly as measured
  beforehand, and it is visible in the table: the top-250 setting's gap (−2.7) is *wider* than the
  no-bar book's (−1.7), which is the one point on the ladder that does not fit. That setting barely
  binds on the everyday tape before 2001 while already biting on the honest one, so its early
  years compare a filtered book to an unfiltered one. The conclusion was pre-registered to rest on
  the top-100 and top-50 settings, which bind on both tapes in essentially every month, and it
  does.
- **"The swing may collapse once the bar stops moving."** Did not happen. It reproduced within
  0.1 of a point and got straighter.
- **"The bar binds harder on the honest tape at the same count."** Happened by construction, and
  it is the reason the parent's honest-tape ranking does not reproduce.
- **"It is the same large-company tilt and will cost several points."** Happened: 4.4 points a
  year, with the breadth table matching the parent's.
- **"A crowding tilt is where a published edge fades, and 2009–2015 is where it shows."**
  Happened: every bar setting is deeply negative in those years on both tapes.
- **"This is evidence about data, not a candidate."** Exactly right, and it is the conclusion.

## Nothing here goes to the test window

The hard gate refused promotion on two independent grounds, as was written down before the run:

1. The method wins only **2 of its 4** walk-forward folds. A book that wins its twenty-year
   average but loses the folds is a selection, not an edge. On the honest tape it wins **1 of 4**.
2. Its **kin have already failed out of sample** — three earlier test-window failures, which are
   three looks at what is substantially one book, and this method rides the same chassis. The
   measured correlation of the no-bar arm against one of them is 0.9651.

There is no override and I did not look for one. No counted look was spent; the lab still stands
at four, and the buy signal for survivorship-free price data does **not** fire, because it needs a
fold majority and this has none.

One curiosity for the record: the strictest arm is the only one in the method whose behaviour
falls *below* the kinship bar against all three failed books (0.75, 0.72, 0.76). It is also the
worst-performing arm. Being different from the books that failed is not, by itself, worth 4.4
points a year.

## My opinion

The diagnostic is now settled and I would start using it. Three experiments, two chassis and two
opposite ways of setting the bar all agree: **how heavily a stock trades is the lab's cheapest
honest test of whether a book's edge is an artefact of the companies the everyday tape is missing,
and it costs nothing to run.** I would apply it to every stock-picking method the lab already
holds, before spending another method id on any of them, and treat a book whose edge evaporates
under it as suspect.

What I would stop doing is reading the honest tape's *ranking* as advice. This run showed that two
of the parent's conclusions were artefacts of how its bar was defined, and that is a warning about
a habit, not about one experiment: when two arms are labelled as matched, check that they are
still matched on the tape you are reading, not just on the one you calibrated them on. That
mistake was invisible until the same question was asked a second way.

What I would not do is pay for this. 4.4 points a year to buy 3.4 points of honesty is a bad
trade, and the breadth table says the cost is a large-company tilt — a design choice available far
more cheaply. The next thing to try is the cheap version: instead of refusing thin names outright,
**cap how much of the book may sit in them**. That keeps the small-company exposure where this
book actually earns while still declining the genuinely moribund, and it is the obvious way to buy
most of the 3.4 points for much less than 4.4. That is the idea queued below.

I would also say plainly that this method produced no candidate and never could have. Its chassis
has kin that already failed out of sample, so the gate was always going to refuse it. That was
known and written down before the run, and it was worth running anyway, because what it measured
was whether the lab can trust a tool it was about to start using everywhere — and the answer
turned out to be yes for the tool and no for two of the claims that came with it.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1305: verified, and the withdrawal is the result

Reproduces three ways. M0298-K0 is M0288-DV00 and M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT to sixteen digits --
554.9227319691738, 1,607 trades, fall 0.20649523233479192 -- so three method ids now carry one
curve and the ladder's zero rung is the parent untouched.

**The instrument did what the batch was for.** The dev-minus-check-store gap runs -1.7, -2.7,
-2.3, -1.8, -0.3, +0.7 across the rungs: monotone over all five binding steps and crossing zero,

Feature-wish 604 is the one to act on: this diagnostic is settled, costs no new idea, and is
currently unaffordable only because applying it burns a method id. As a report it could be run

methods.verdict: The liveness finding is confirmed and now straight — a fixed-count bar reproduces the 3.5-point honesty swing within 0.1 of a point across five rising steps — but two of the parent's honest-tape conclusions turn out to be artefacts of its moving bar and are withdrawn; still no candidate, and it costs 4.4 points a year

methods.name: Cap the thinnest names instead of refusing them: liveness protection without the big-company tilt
methods.hypothesis: M0288 bought 3.5 points a year of survivorship honesty for 5.4 points a year of dev return, and the breadth report says exactly where the 5.4 went: the floor herds the book into the largest, most-traded names. Lead in narrow months climbs 5.6 to 11.4 percent across the five rungs while lead in broad months falls 6.4 to minus 4.7 - five steps, both directions, monotone, with no fee or cash-drag component (names held stayed at 20.0 and exposure moved only 69.4 to 68.6 percent). So the whole price is a size tilt, and a tilt is a design choice that can be bought more cheaply than by refusing names outright. Instead of excluding the least-traded part of the pool, let every eligible name be picked but cap what the thinnest ones may be worth: a pick in the bottom quintile by 20-day mean dollar volume gets a half slot (or a quarter), with the freed weight spread over the remaining picks rather than parked in cash or SPY - M0279 measured parking at 2 to 6 points a year and M0288's design deliberately avoided it, so this one must too. Rungs on the cap: 1.0 (no cap, the reference arm that must reproduce M0032), 0.75, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.0 (which is M0288's 20-percent floor exactly, tying the two ladders together at one end and making this a genuine extension rather than a fresh guess). Chassis unchanged: M0007-N20-RAW, F4's screen, SPY-200 monthly switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, the owner's deposits. Success: a cap that keeps at least half of M0288's honesty swing while giving up under 1.5 points a year of dev return, with the narrow-versus-broad spread clearly flatter than the floor ladder's at matching honesty. EXPECTED FAILURE: the thinnest quintile of an index-member pool that has already passed a 20 million dollar daily-volume screen may simply not be where the dying companies are, in which case a half weight on them changes neither the honesty gap nor the return and the ladder is flat - the floor would then be working through the names it ADDS at the top rather than the ones it removes at the bottom, which is a different mechanism from the one assumed. A partial-weight book also records few or no trades at some rungs while still moving exposure, so trade counts and profit factor will read strangely and exposure is the meter to watch. And like M0288 this cannot produce a candidate: the chassis kin already failed the test window, so the hard gate refuses promotion regardless.

methods.name: Hold every rung of the size-to-equal dial at the same exposure, so the weighting term is one number instead of a range
methods.sourceRef: M0292 (the size-to-equal dial: monotone everywhere, end-to-end gap 2.73 points a year, but average exposure slid 91.22% to 97.52% with the rung, so weighting and exposure are collinear there by construction and the honest answer was a 1.6-to-2.7 range); M0286 (the re-weighting cadence 2x2, and M0286-MONTHLY showing that re-weighting monthly does NOT fix exposure under a live band: 91.4% against the equal book's 97.1%); M0127 (the rebalance-band ladder: 88.6%, 93.4%, 96.2%, 97.8%, 98.6% exposure as the band closes to zero, which is what makes the band and not the cadence the right lever); M0266 and M0270 (the price of a point of exposure is an era, 0.005 to 0.173 points a year, never a constant); M0222 (the market-value core and the 5% per-company ceiling); insight 492 (cash in lumps costs more than cash spread evenly)
methods.hypothesis: M0292 measured a perfectly monotone size-to-equal dial -- funded return 7.55% a year at pure market-value weighting rising to 10.28% at equal slices over identical names, with the worst fall rising 50.0% to 57.5% alongside it -- and then could not say how much of that 2.73-point end-to-end gap was the weighting. Average exposure slid from 91.22% at the size end to 97.52% at the equal end, because its deposit-steered January-anchor cadence finds gaps to fill in an equal-weighted book and almost none in a size-weighted one, where each holding's weight drifts the way its own target drifts. The reportable answer was a range, 1.6 to 2.7 points a year, and the unqualified 2.8 points M0286 published was withdrawn. This method runs the identical five rungs -- power 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 on each name's market value, rescaled and capped at 5%, over the same F4-screened index members with a known point-in-time size, one listed class per identical share count -- with the two levers that pin exposure and touch no weight: the weights are re-set from scratch every month (months=1, no anchor, no deposit rule), and the rebalance band is shut to zero so every holding is traded back to its exact target every month. The band is the lever the lab's own record points at: M0286 already ran this book at months=1 under a 20%-of-target band and still came out at 91.4% exposure against the equal book's 97.1%, while M0127's band ladder moved a 20-name book's exposure from 88.6% to 98.6% by closing the band alone. The sixth arm is not a rung: SIZE-M12 is M0292-SIZE's parameters unchanged with only the band shut, so it prices the exposure term at the size end against a recorded trial by moving one lever, and prices the cadence term against this method's own SIZE at matched exposure and matched fees. Predictions, written before any result. (1) Average exposure is flat to within half a point across all five rungs and lands near 98-99%, which is the check that the fix worked; if it is not flat, nothing else here is readable and the verdict must say so first. (2) The funded return ladder stays monotone and rising toward EQUAL, because the internal evidence says exposure is not the main term -- carrying the whole 2.73 would need a point of exposure to be worth 0.43 points a year, against a best-ever measured 0.17 on this chassis and about nothing in 2003-2008. (3) The end-to-end gap lands between 1.6 and 2.4 points a year rather than 2.73, and what it falls short by IS the exposure term, measured rather than bounded. (4) The worst fall still rises toward EQUAL and every rung still falls far past the owner's 25% bar, deeper than M0292's because pinned exposure means no cash cushion in 2008. (5) SIZE-M12 lands above M0292-SIZE's recorded 7.55% a year by roughly the exposure term, since it buys about 7 points of exposure for the fee cost of a full monthly rebalance. Nothing here is a candidate: a weighting dial cannot fix a 50%-plus fall, and pinning exposure can only deepen it. Success is a measurement, and the measurement closes the oldest open assumption this lab holds.
methods.expectedFailure: The headline risk is that the pin does not hold. If average exposure still slopes across the rungs -- because a zero band cannot overcome something else that is size-dependent, or because the wide tail of a size-weighted book cannot be filled at the account sizes the early window runs at -- then this method has bought nothing and the verdict must say so in its first line rather than quoting a gap. A book-construction probe run before this file was committed says the dead tail is 0.002% of book weight at worst and zero almost everywhere, so inertness is ruled out, but the probe cannot prove the engine's realised exposure is flat; only the run can. Second, forcing a full rebalance every month on a 137-to-392-name book is expensive: the same probe estimates 3.3% of the account a year in fees in 1998, falling to 0.5% by 2015, because Gotrade's $0.10 per order floor is charged on one order per held name per month. That level is paid by every rung and it will push this whole ladder below M0292's, so the two ladders' returns are NOT comparable one for one and only the bridge arm's one-lever comparison is. The probe also says the drag is flat across rungs to within 0.03 points a year, but it assumes an equal average gap at every name; real small-company weights move more, so the equal end may trade slightly larger orders and pay slightly less of the floor, which would bias the ladder in the direction it is predicted to slope. Turnover and the shortfall decomposition must be reported per rung, and if the fee spread across rungs exceeds the exposure spread it replaced then nothing was gained and the verdict must say so. Third, the rungs may not separate at all: market value is distributed so unevenly that raising it to 0.25 is already most of the way to equal weighting, and M0292 is the only evidence they do separate. Fourth, the dev store cannot price about 40% of member-days and the missing names skew small, so every rung nearer equal is flattered here; the survivorship-check store must be read for all six arms, and M0292's unusual result -- the slope survived the honest tape even though the level did not -- is what this must be checked against. Fifth, pinning exposure near 100% removes the accidental cash cushion that let M0292's size end fall only 50%, so a deeper fall at every rung is expected rather than a surprise, and it makes a bad book worse without making it informative about anything but weighting. Finally the whole exercise is about a book that can never be a candidate: a clean answer changes what the lab believes about weighting and promotes nothing.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0300 — the weighting question, finally asked cleanly

## What this was for

Last week M0292 asked a simple question: if you own the same few hundred big American
companies, does it matter whether you hold more of the biggest ones or the same amount of
each? It slid a dial from one to the other in five steps and got a beautifully straight
line — equal amounts earned more, and fell harder, every step of the way.

But it could not say **how much** of that was the weighting, because something else moved
with the dial. The equal-amount version kept 97.5% of its money in the market and the
biggest-companies version only 91.2%. Six and a half points of extra money invested is
worth something by itself. So M0292 had to report a range — the weighting is worth
somewhere between 1.6 and 2.7 points a year — and withdraw the single number M0286 had
published.

M0300 runs the identical five steps with that loose end tied down. Two changes, neither of
which touches how much of any company you hold: the amounts are worked out fresh every
month, and the account is dragged back to those amounts exactly every month instead of
being allowed to drift. Both are settings the lab already had.

## The check that the fix worked

Share of money kept in the market, across the five steps:

**98.830%, 98.857%, 98.881%, 98.902%, 98.910%**

A spread of 0.085 of a point, where M0292's was 6.30. Every step now holds the same amount
of money in the market, so anything left over is the weighting. This was the first
prediction I wrote down, and it was the one that mattered — if it had failed, nothing else
here would have been readable.

## The ladder

What the owner's money earned a year, over 237 monthly deposits. The same deposits put
into SPY earned **+7.2%** a year.

| step | earned a year | lead over SPY | worst fall | 2008 | money turned over |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| equal amounts | **+10.1%** | +2.9 | 58.4% | −37.1% | 0.96× |
| a quarter of the way | +9.5% | +2.3 | 57.0% | −36.5% | 0.74× |
| halfway | +8.8% | +1.6 | 55.8% | −36.0% | 0.56× |
| three quarters | +8.1% | +0.9 | 54.7% | −35.4% | 0.40× |
| by company size | **+7.5%** | +0.3 | 53.7% | −34.7% | 0.34× |
| *the bridge* | +7.6% | +0.5 | 53.6% | −34.7% | 0.29× |

Straight line again, on return, on how far it fell, and on how much trading it does. No
best setting in the middle: the more equally you spread the money, the more you earn and
the harder you fall.

## The answer, and I predicted it wrong

I wrote down before running that the gap between the two ends would **shrink** from 2.73
points a year to somewhere between 1.6 and 2.4, and that the shrinkage would be the
money-in-the-market effect finally measured.

It came out at **2.59**. Barely moved.

Take each ladder's own trading costs out — M0292's cost the equal end 0.09 points a year
more than its size end, M0300's costs 0.27 more — and the two gaps are **2.82 and 2.86**.
They agree to four hundredths of a point a year, across a six-and-a-half point swing in how
much money was invested.

**So the money-in-the-market effect is zero.** Not small: zero, to within a twentieth of a
point a year. The weighting was carrying the whole thing all along.

The sixth arm says the same thing from the other direction. It is M0292's
biggest-companies version with one single setting changed — the drift allowed before the
account is dragged back to target. That one change bought it 7.70 points of extra money in
the market, and it earned **+0.09 points a year** more. About two hundredths of a point for
each point of extra money invested — the cheapest this lab has ever measured it, and in
line with M0266's finding that the price of being invested depends entirely on the decade,
not on some constant.

Two independent routes, same destination. **M0292's range of 1.6 to 2.7 closes at
2.6 points a year, and the 2.8 points M0286 published and then withdrew was right.**

## What it cost me to find out

This has to be said plainly, because it is the thing I pre-registered as the way this could
go wrong. Dragging a 137-to-392 company account back to exact targets every month is
expensive. Gotrade charges at least 10 cents an order and this sends one order per company
per month. Modelled over the whole window, that costs the equal end **0.42 points a year**
against the size end's 0.15 — a slope of 0.27 points a year running against the very result
I was measuring.

Before committing the method I estimated that slope at 0.03 points, by counting orders. That
estimate was wrong: it missed that cost also scales with how much money moves, not only with
how many orders there are. **The trading-cost slope I bought is roughly twice the
money-in-the-market slope I removed** (0.27 against about 0.11 at the measured price).

I still think the trade was worth making, and here is the honest reason: a trading-cost slope
can be *computed* — from recorded turnover and a fee schedule fitted to the owner's own
receipts — where a money-in-the-market slope tangled up with the weighting cannot be. I
swapped a contaminant I could not measure for a larger one I can. That is progress in
measurement, not in cleanliness, and the verdict should not pretend otherwise.

## With the dead companies put back

The lab's main price history only covers companies that survived. The check store puts most
of the failures back. Every step loses almost exactly the same amount:

| step | lead on the usual data | lead with the failures back | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| equal amounts | +2.9 | **+1.5** | −1.4 |
| a quarter | +2.3 | +0.9 | −1.3 |
| halfway | +1.6 | +0.3 | −1.3 |
| three quarters | +0.9 | **−0.5** | −1.4 |
| by company size | +0.3 | **−1.1** | −1.4 |
| the bridge | +0.5 | −1.0 | −1.4 |

End to end: **2.6 points a year on the usual data, 2.6 with the failures back.** The haircut
is a flat charge of about 1.35 points on every step and the slope does not move at all. The
fold record is 3 of 4 on both. Falls deepen by about a point everywhere, to 54.5–59.9%.

This is the same unusual result M0292 got, and it is worth more than it looks. Most of this
lab's survivorship findings change the *ranking* — the liquidity floor reverses sign between
the two sets of prices, the calm-companies book reverses. This one changes only the level.
A dial whose slope survives the honest tape is a different and better class of finding than
one whose level does.

The caveat belongs right beside it: with the failures back, only the three steps nearest
equal still beat SPY at all, and the best lead is +1.5 points a year rather than +2.9.

## When the lead arrived — the part I did not expect

Equal amounts delivered **95.6%** of its paper lead to the owner's actual money. Across this
lab that figure is usually around a third: 86% of recorded results earned half their lead
before half the money had arrived, and the typical delivery is 33.9%.

By company size delivered **33.2%** — and worse, 117% of its lead came before 2003 and it
gave 22.7% of it back in 2009–2015.

So the dial is not only a return ladder, it is a *delivery* ladder. That is why the gap is
wider in the money column (2.59) than on paper (2.09): the equal end's advantage shows up
late, when the money is actually there, and the size end's showed up early when it was not.
For an owner who pays in every month, the money column is the real one.

## Did it pass anything? No, and it never could

All six are rejected. They fall 53.6–58.4% against the lab's 50% screen — and against the
owner's real-money limit of 25%, more than twice over. Gains against losses come to
0.64–0.75 where 1.3 is needed. The luck score is 0.51–0.65 where 0.90 is needed.

That last one in plain words: after 192 distinct attempts in this lab, the best of these six
has about a 65% chance of being a real effect rather than a lucky draw. The bar the owner
set is 90%. It is not close.

None of this is a surprise and the hypothesis said so before the run: a weighting dial
cannot fix a book that loses half its value in 2008, and pinning the money into the market
can only make that worse — which it did, by 3 to 4 points at every step.

## Predictions, scored

1. Money-in-market flat within half a point near 98–99% — **right** (spread 0.085).
2. Ladder stays straight and rises toward equal — **right**, on three axes.
3. Gap lands in 1.6–2.4 — **wrong**. It landed at 2.59. Being wrong here is the finding.
4. Falls deeper than M0292 at every step — **right** (53.7–58.4% against 50.0–57.5%).
5. The bridge lands above M0292's size end — **right**, by 0.09 points a year.

The expected failures: the account was never inert (as the pre-commit probe said); the steps
did separate; the falls deepened as predicted; the honest-tape slope held. The one that bit
was the trading-cost slope, and it bit four times harder than I estimated.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and that is a good outcome rather than a disappointing one. The
oldest assumption this lab held — that spreading money evenly across index members is a
handicap, insight 91 — is now measured on a chassis with no market-timing switch, no idle
cash, equal money invested at every setting, trading costs priced from the owner's own
receipts, and the dead companies put back. It is worth **+2.6 points a year** in the owner's
money column and the lab believed the opposite for a year. I would not spend another method
id asking the weighting question again; it has been asked three times now and answered the
same way each time, with the confounds removed one at a time.

What I would **not** do is conclude that an equal-weight index book is a candidate. It falls
58%. The useful thing it has become is a *yardstick*: a known, always-invested, honestly
priced book that beats SPY by 2.9 points a year on paper and delivers 95.6% of that to real
money. Nearly every stock-picking method this lab has rejected was measured against SPY, and
SPY is the wrong opponent for a book that holds a few hundred index members equally — the
right opponent is this ladder's equal end. I suspect several past rejections were really
"beat SPY, lost to equal weighting", and nobody has checked.

Two things I would spend the next ids on, in order. First, the delivery finding, because it
is bigger than the weighting one and nobody was looking for it: a 95.6% delivery rate is in
the top few percent of this lab, and if what makes a lead late-arriving can be identified,
that is worth more than another two points of paper return. Second, the trading-cost slope
this method had to buy — the zero-drift setting is a blunt instrument, and a middle setting
would hold the money-in-market pin nearly as well for a fraction of the cost. That is a
cheap, well-posed measurement and it would make every future exposure experiment on a wide
book affordable.


### 2026-10-23

## Coordinator check, sera-20261023-1305: the pin held, the exposure term is zero, and my own correction is corrected

Verified from the recorded rows. The pin is the thing that had to work and it worked: average
exposure 98.830, 98.857, 98.881, 98.902, 98.910% across power 0 to 1 -- a spread of **0.080
points** where M0292's was 6.30. The ladder is monotone on return, fall and turnover at once, with
no interior optimum, and all six arms are rejected as pre-registered.

**The end-to-end gap is 2.59 points a year against M0292's 2.73.** Removing a 6.30-point exposure
swing moved the answer by 0.14 points. So the exposure term is not the 0.3 to 1.1 that M0292 had
to allow for -- it is about zero.

The bridge arm says the same thing independently, and I recomputed it here rather than taking it:
M0300-SIZE-M12 is M0292-SIZE's params with only the band shut, and +7.698 points of exposure
bought +0.098 points a year, or **0.0128 points a year per point of exposure**. At that price
M0292's 6.30-point spread was worth 0.080 points a year, not the ~1.07 the 0.17 ceiling implied.
(The child quoted ~0.018 per point; the recorded rows give 0.0128. The difference does not matter
-- both are an order of magnitude below what the correction assumed -- but the smaller figure is
the one the trials support.)

**So my own correction needs correcting, and this is the second time today the chain has moved.**
M0286 reported the weighting gap as an unqualified 2.8 points a year. I withdrew that and replaced
it with a bound of 1.6 to 2.7, because exposure was collinear and could have carried up to 1.07 of
it. The bound was right as a bound -- the true value sits inside it -- but the practical
instruction attached to it, "the unqualified 2.8 should not be quoted", was wrong. With the fee
slopes of each ladder removed the two runs agree at 2.82 and 2.86, and M0286's original figure was
sound. **The weighting term is about 2.6 to 2.9 points a year and it is not about being invested.**
M0286 and M0292 both carry an appended correction saying so.

**The survivorship result is the same unusual class as M0292's and it is now twice confirmed.**
The lead over SPY goes +2.9 to +1.5, +2.3 to +0.9, +1.6 to +0.3, +0.9 to -0.5, +0.3 to -1.1 -- a
flat haircut of about 1.35 points at every rung, end-to-end 2.6 on both tapes, folds 3 of 4 on
both. The slope survives the honest tape even though the level does not. Caveat unchanged: with
the dead companies back only the three rungs nearest equal still beat SPY.

**The unexpected finding may outrank the headline.** `lab timing` puts M0300-EQUAL's delivery to
the owner's money at 95.6% of its paper lead against M0300-SIZE's 33.2%, where the lab median is
33.9% and 86% of recorded results are front-loaded. A book that delivers 95.6% is in the top few
per cent of everything this lab holds, and it also explains why the gap reads 2.59 funded against
2.09 de-funded. That is queued as M0312 and I would put it ahead of the two band ideas.

**The honest cost is stated rather than softened, which is the right call.** The zero band's fee
slope is 0.27 points a year against equal, about twice the exposure slope it removed. The child's
pre-commit probe estimated 0.03 by counting orders and was wrong by a factor of nine, because the
bill also scales with traded value above the ten-cent floor; it recorded that rather than quietly
re-fitting. The trade is still the right one -- a fee slope is computable from recorded turnover
and the fitted schedule, while a collinear exposure slope is not -- so the contaminant was made
measurable rather than removed, and M0310 is queued to find a cheaper band.
methods.verdict: Rejected as pre-registered, and it closes the open term: with every rung holding the same amount of money in the market, equal slices beat company-size weighting by 2.6 points a year — the same 2.6 with the dead companies put back — so the exposure effect M0292 could not separate was zero, and M0286's withdrawn 2.8 was right.

methods.name: Tilt toward the average company only while the average company is winning, and test it against the straight line it has to beat
methods.hypothesis: M0292 proved the size-to-equal dial is a straight line with no interior optimum: every step toward equal slices buys about 0.7 points a year and costs about 1.9 points of fall, monotone on all six axes it was read on, and the 2008 column reverses outright (market shape +4.8 percent against the benchmark, equal slices -1.7). It also identified the single ingredient: equal slices win exactly in the months when the typical company beats the giants, 55 percent of months over the dev window at +0.21 percent a month, 58.5 percent and +0.34 in 2009-2015, and 50 percent at -0.50 in 2008. If that is one variable, the obvious question is whether it can be read in advance rather than only after the fact. So: set the power on the dial from the trailing breadth of the market itself, read point in time. Each January (the anchor M0292 already uses), compare the past twelve months of the equal-weighted average of index members against the index's own return, and set the power toward 0 when the typical company has been winning and toward 1 when the giants have been carrying. Three arms with different speeds of adjustment, plus the two fixed endpoints from M0292 as the straight line it must beat. Predictions written now: the breadth signal is strongly persistent at a one-year horizon, so the switching arms should capture most of the equal-end return while sitting nearer the size end in 2008; if so the arm lands ABOVE the straight line connecting M0292's endpoints on a return-versus-fall plot, which is the only result that would justify it. EXPECTED FAILURE and why this is registered with low confidence: M0292's own regime report shows the trailing 36-month breadth spread was positive in only 6 of 202 windows, peaking in November 2008 -- that is, breadth leadership has been persistently NEGATIVE and barely varies, so a trailing reading may have almost no usable variation to switch on and all three arms collapse onto a fixed middle rung, which M0292 has already priced. Worse, the one year the switch most needs to be right is 2008, and a trailing twelve-month reading in January 2008 would have been looking at 2007, when the typical company was still winning -- so the rule would have been at the equal end going into the crash, which is exactly backwards and would make the fall DEEPER than the fixed equal arm rather than shallower. The lab has also already learned twice that a time lock or a slow reading on a market switch loses both ways and that turning a losing timing rule down cannot save it. If the switching arms land on or below the straight line, that is a clean refutation and the family should be closed, which is a worthwhile outcome for one method id.

methods.name: Can a calm filter replace the cash rule instead of sitting behind it?
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0293 (market beta as a safety filter on M0197-Y20-SW's book); Frazzini & Pedersen 2014, Betting Against Beta, JFE 111(1)
methods.hypothesis: M0293 bolted a market-beta filter onto M0197's bond-like book and found it was insurance bought on top of insurance: behind the SPY 200-day switch the book was already in cash through 2008, so the filter could never make a claim and still paid its premium for twenty years. M0293's own amendment turned the switch off and showed the filter doing real work for the first time -- dropping the jumpiest quarter cut the 2008 calendar loss from -39.5% to -24.5% (M0293-REF-NOSW vs M0293-HI25-NOSW, read from the recorded trials) -- but it could not say whether that was enough to stand in for the cash rule, because a quarter was the deepest dose it ever ran with the switch off. This method turns the dial up. Three facts frame it, all read off recorded trials on this store: switch ON and filter off, the book falls 22.0% (M0293-REF); switch OFF and filter off, it falls 62.1% (M0293-REF-NOSW); switch off with a quarter dropped, 56.4% (M0293-HI25-NOSW). So a quarter-drop bought 5.7 points of the 40.1 points the switch was worth -- about a seventh. The question is whether depth buys the rest. Two new rungs, 0.40 and 0.60, both with the switch off and nothing else changed, extend the recorded 0.00 and 0.25 into a four-point ladder. FOUR blind draws sit at the deepest rung, not one, because M0293's single blind control supported a 3.2-point claim that three more seeds erased, and because the lab has since measured that nineteen identical rules drawn blind span 7.5 points a year of return and 20.7 points of worst fall. The pool was measured before registration and not assumed: across the 79 quarterly re-ranks inside the scored window the screened pool runs 66 to 396 names (median 257), and a 0.60 drop never leaves fewer than 26, so every arm holds exactly 20 names fully invested and no dose can empty a slot into SPY -- the confound that sank M0277's and M0279's six pick filters. Success is stated narrowly and now: some registered dose brings the switch-off worst fall under 35%, keeps a lead over total-return SPY on the owner's deposits, and beats ALL FOUR blind draws at that dose on the worst fall. Anything less and the answer is that a cash rule protects far more cheaply than any pick filter, which is the publishable finding either way. Predictions, written before the run, on the recorded de-funded worst fall: D60 falls at least 8 points shallower than D40, so the dial is monotone and not U-shaped; D60's fall is at least 3 points below the shallowest of its four blind draws, without which the shrink was the diversifying and not the calmness; D60 gives up more than 2 points a year of funded return against M0293-REF-NOSW's +12.5%, because M0293's 0.50 rung with the switch on already cost 3.5 points a year against its own reference; and no arm here reaches 35%, so the method is rejected on its own stated success clause.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the ladder is flat where it matters, and M0293 has already half-shown it. Its gate-off quarter-drop fell 56.4% while its four blind quarter-drops fell 55.2%, 56.5%, 56.8% and 59.4% -- the calm arm sits INSIDE that spread and is beaten by one of the coins. Only on the 2008 calendar year did it clear them (-24.5% against a best blind of -28.5%). If the worst fall is the seed-noisy reading and the calendar year is the seed-stable one, the deep doses will shuffle inside a wide blind spread and the honest answer is that this method cannot distinguish the filter from the arithmetic of dropping names. Second, a trailing one-year beta is backward-looking and a crash is forward-looking: by mid-2008 Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the regional banks had not yet collapsed, so a deeper cut may simply remove more names that were never the problem. Third, and the reason the ladder may be U-shaped, a 0.60 drop leaves a median of 103 names of which the bond-like end is utilities and property, so the deep rungs concentrate the book in exactly the taper-scare exposure M0197 feared -- M0293's 0.50 rung with the switch on fell DEEPER than its 0.25 rung (25.2% against 20.3%) while losing 3.5 points a year, which is the U-shape already visible on the other side of the switch. Fourth, even a clean win here cannot become a candidate: 35% is far past the owner's 25% bar, so the best outcome available is a number, not a strategy. Fifth, betting against beta was published in 2014 at the very end of the dev window, so any dev edge here is the kind most likely to have faded. None of these is a reason to add a dose, change the host or re-seed a draw after the run.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

## The question

We have two ways to stop a stock book falling apart in a crash, and until now nobody had made them
compete.

The first is a **cash rule**: when the market is below its own 200-day average — about nine and a
half months of trading — sell the lot and wait in cash. The second is a **pick filter**: never buy
the jumpiest companies in the first place, whatever the market is doing.

An earlier method bolted the pick filter onto a book that already had the cash rule and found it did
nothing at all. The reason was embarrassing in hindsight — the cash rule had already moved the money
out of the market before the 2008 collapse arrived, so the filter was never once shown a falling
tape. It was insurance bought on top of insurance, and it still charged a premium every year.

That left the real question unasked. **Can the filter do the job instead of the cash rule?**

## What was run

The same book, with the cash rule switched off for good, and the filter turned up in steps. Each
step throws away a share of the candidate list — jumpiest first — and then picks the usual twenty
from what is left.

Two steps were already on the record from the earlier method and were deliberately **not** re-run,
so nobody can accuse this of tuning them. Two are new.

At the deepest step this method also ran **four coin-toss versions** that throw away exactly the
same number of names, chosen at random instead of by jumpiness. This lab has learned, expensively,
that one coin toss is not a control: the parent method's own three-point margin over a single random
draw (20.35% against 23.46%) shrank to **0.05 points** once three more draws were added and the
shallowest of the four came in at 20.40%. So four, not one.

One thing was measured before any of it was registered rather than assumed. Throwing away three
fifths of the list could have left too few names to fill twenty slots, which would quietly park the
spare money in the market index and make the whole comparison meaningless. Across the 79 quarterly
re-picks inside the scored window the candidate list runs **66 to 396 names**, and a three-fifths cut
never leaves fewer than **26** — always more than the twenty slots. Every version stayed **95.5% to
96.1% invested**, a range of six tenths of a point, so nothing below is an effect of one version
holding more cash than another.

Everything was then re-run on our **honest tape** — the same window with the companies that went
bust put back in, which our ordinary price history is missing. All six versions reproduced their
recorded results exactly on the ordinary tape first, so the side-by-side is trustworthy.

## What happened: the filter is real

Worst fall from a peak, measured on the book itself with the monthly deposits set aside, so a
falling account is not flattered by fresh money arriving. The yearly figures beside it are the
owner's actual money, deposits included:

| how much of the list is thrown away | worst fall | the owner's money, per year |
|---|---|---|
| nothing | 62.1% | +12.5% |
| the jumpiest quarter | 56.4% | +11.2% |
| the jumpiest two fifths | **43.9%** | **+11.4%** |
| the jumpiest three fifths | **41.0%** | +9.3% |

The market returned +7.2% a year on the same deposits over the same window.

**The earlier method was testing this filter at a strength too weak to see it.** That is the first
finding, and it turns entirely on the coin tosses.

At a quarter, the earlier method's filter fell 56.4% while its four coin tosses fell 55.2%, 56.5%,
56.8% and 59.4%. The real filter sat *inside* the coins' range and one of the four beat it. On that
evidence, "it buys nothing a random reshuffle does not" was the right call.

At three fifths it is a different picture. The real filter fell **41.0%**; its four coin tosses fell
**53.7%, 59.9%, 60.5% and 63.2%**. The real filter beat the *best* of the four by **12.6 points**,
against a spread between the coins of 9.6 points.

And it survives the honest tape, which is where this kind of claim usually dies. With the bust
companies restored the real filter falls **46.4%** and the four coins fall **53.9%, 60.9%, 65.4% and
69.8%** — still clear of the best of them, by **7.4 points**. The coins' spread widens from 9.6
points to 15.9, about two thirds wider, so the narrower margin is expected rather than alarming.

The direction also checks out. At a quarter the earlier method ran the mirror of this filter —
throw away the *calmest* names instead — and it fell **66.8%**, deeper than applying no filter at
all (62.1%). Jumpiness is doing the work, in the direction claimed.

### How strong is that, exactly?

Strong enough to act on as a finding, not strong enough to call settled, and this lab wrote down the
arithmetic for it this morning. If an idea were worthless it would be interchangeable with a control
that has no opinion, so beating every one of a group of controls can never support a better claim
than one chance in the group size plus one. With four coins the strongest statement available is
**"at most a one-in-five chance that this is luck"**, and no margin, however wide, buys a better one
— that ceiling is set by how many controls were run, not by how convincingly they were beaten. It is
well short of the one-in-twenty the lab demands elsewhere, which would need nineteen coins.

The size of the win is a separate question from the odds, and the two must not be run together. The
one-in-five ceiling comes from *ranking*: out of five things, the filter came first, and that is all
a ranking can say. How far ahead it finished does not move that number at all. What the margin tells
us is how **big** the effect is, not how **likely** it is to be luck.

Both are worth having, and they differ across the two tapes. On our ordinary history the filter beats
the best coin by 12.6 points while the four coins differ from each other by only 9.6 — the lead is
**1.3 times the coins' entire range**, so the filter is not merely first, it finished clear of the
territory the coins occupy. On the honest tape the filter again finished ahead of all four, by 7.4
points, but the coins are spread 15.9 points apart, so the lead is **0.5 times that spread**. It is
still first on both tapes; the win is simply a much more emphatic one on the ordinary history.

Two further pieces of evidence here are **not** rankings at all, so the one-in-five ceiling does not
bound them, and the summary would be wrong to leave them out.

The first is the mirror. Throwing away the *calmest* quarter instead fell 66.8%, deeper than
applying no filter at all. That is a prediction about direction, written down before the run and
borne out — not a draw that happened to come first.

The second is that the dose result rests on **two separate four-coin experiments whose rankings
disagree — and the disagreement is the finding**. At a quarter the filter finished inside its four
coins' range. At three fifths, against a different four coins at a different strength, it finished
clear of all of them on both tapes. The claim being made here is not "the filter beat its coins", a
claim one ranking caps at one-in-five. It is "the same filter on the same book is indistinguishable
from chance when tested gently and clearly ahead of it when tested hard", and that contrast rests on
two experiments rather than one.

One limit on that second point, stated plainly. Where between a quarter and three fifths the change
happens, this experiment cannot say: the two coin sets sit at two doses and use eight different
random seeds between them, and the one rung in between — two fifths — was run without coins of its
own. That is the second gap in this design, alongside the missing deep mirror below, and the next
run on this chassis should close both.

So: first of five on both tapes, a much larger effect on the ordinary history than on the honest
one, a mirror that moved the way it was predicted to, and two coin sets whose verdicts differ
between a quarter and three fifths. That is enough to overturn the earlier verdict of
"indistinguishable from a reshuffle" — which was made against a filter that finished inside the
coins' range, where this one finished clear of them on both tapes — and nowhere near enough to call
the matter closed. None of it should be quoted as significance: the lab's own standard is
one-in-twenty and nothing here comes close.

Picking calm companies genuinely protects a falling book. It just has to be turned up more than twice
as far as anyone here had tried — a quarter to three fifths, 2.4 times — before the effect clears the
noise.

## And it is still the wrong tool, for two separate reasons

**First, it is dear.** Both protections are paid for in the same currency: return given up. Against
the same unprotected book, over the same twenty years —

* the **cash rule** takes the fall from 62.1% to **22.0%** — 40.1 points — and costs **0.70 points a
  year** of the owner's money.
* the **filter at its best setting** (two fifths) takes it from 62.1% to **43.9%** — 18.2 points —
  and costs **1.18 points a year**.

Per point of yearly return handed over, the cash rule buys about **3.7 times as much protection**,
and it reaches a depth the filter never approaches. Turning the filter up past two fifths makes it
worse: the last step buys 2.8 more points of protection for another 2.1 points a year, close to the
worst exchange rate in the experiment.

Two cautions on that ratio. The cash rule's cost is a small number on the bottom of a fraction, so
"3.7 times" moves a lot if that cost moves a little — the two pairs of raw numbers are the sturdier
reading. And the cash rule's cheapness is almost certainly concentrated in the crashes, so a
twenty-year average flatters it. This method's own table hints at exactly that: in 2009-2015, with
no cash rule at all, three of the six versions here beat the market by 3.0 to 6.6 points a year on
our ordinary price history and a fourth matched it — measured on the book alone with the deposits
set aside, the measure set out in the next section. A rule whose job is to sit in cash has little to earn in a stretch like that and
something to lose, so the 0.70-point whole-window price is the friendliest number the cash rule will
ever show.

**Second — and this settles it — the filter falls a long way behind the market in the era we trust
most.** 2009 to 2015 is our best-covered stretch and the one most like today, and it is the first
thing we check. These are lead over the market per year measured on the book alone, with the deposits
set aside — a different measure from the money column above, and not comparable to it:

| version | ordinary tape | honest tape |
|---|---|---|
| filter at two fifths | **−0.4%** | **−4.6%** |
| filter at three fifths | **−4.0%** | **−3.5%** |
| coin toss 1 | +6.6% | +9.2% |
| coin toss 2 | +0.0% | +1.4% |
| coin toss 3 | +3.0% | +4.8% |
| coin toss 4 | +4.2% | +6.3% |

Be precise about what that means: both filter versions **made money** in those years — they grew at
**16.2%** and **12.6%** a year on our ordinary history, and 12.0% and 13.1% with the bust companies
back. They simply grew more slowly than the market, which returned **16.6%** a year over the same
stretch on both tapes. This is a shortfall against the market, not a loss.

But the shortfall is one-sided. Both filter versions fall behind on both tapes. Not one coin toss
does: three beat the market clearly and the fourth was level on the ordinary tape and ahead on the
honest one. Across all sixteen ways of pairing a coin against a filter on the same tape, **the coin wins
every single time**, by between 0.5 and 13.7 points a year.

That is not a contradiction of the safety finding; it is the price of it. The calm companies that
hold up in a crash are the same companies that get left behind in a six-year rise. The filter is
doing exactly what it says, and what it says is not worth buying.

There is a matching tell in the owner's-money column. With the bust companies restored, both real
filter versions earn **less** per year (−2.1 and −0.2 points) while all four coin tosses earn
**more** (+0.7 to +2.1). Two of six versions got worse and they are precisely the two with an
opinion in them.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

The success test was written before anything ran and had three parts: get the fall under 35%, keep
beating the market on the owner's deposits, and beat all four coin tosses. **Two of three.** Every
version still beat the market over the full window, and the deep setting beat all four coins
decisively — but the shallowest fall reached was 41.0%, not under 35%. By its own stated rule this
method is rejected, and it should be: a book that falls 41% is nowhere near the owner's 25% limit and
was never going to be a candidate.

Of four predictions written in advance, three held and one failed. The failure is the interesting
one. The prediction was that three fifths would fall at least 8 points below two fifths; it fell
**2.8** points below. The dial flattens. Almost all the protection arrives between a quarter and two
fifths, where the fall drops 12.6 points **and the return goes slightly up**. That step is free.
Everything after it is paid for.

**The expected failure did not happen.** What was written down as most likely was that the filter
would shuffle around inside a wide coin-toss range at every strength. It did that at a quarter and
clearly did not at three fifths, and the reversal is the result.

## Three things in this method's own output that should not be quoted out of context

**The fold record is a coin's record.** The run printed "3 of 4 folds won", which normally reads as
encouraging. In three of those four the machinery scored one of the *coin-toss* versions, because it
picks whichever version looked best in training and a coin happened to look best. It says nothing
about the filter. On the honest tape it drops to 2 of 4 anyway. Nothing turns on it — the method is
rejected — but the number would badly mislead if lifted out.

**The coin tosses traded less than the real filter**, about three quarters as often, enough for the
lab's fairness checker to flag all four as mismatched in shape (flagged, not refused). The direction
matters: trading less means paying less in fees, so the coins had the advantage, not the filter, and
the filter won on the fall anyway. The reason for the gap is plain — the real filter re-measures
jumpiness every quarter, over the previous 52 weeks, so its discard list keeps moving, while a coin
toss is fixed per company and never changes its mind.

**No mirror was registered at the deep setting.** The mirror quoted above — throw away the calmest
names — exists only at a quarter, in the parent method. It points the right way there, but this
method cannot show that it still points the right way at three fifths. That is a real gap in the
design and the next run on this chassis should close it.

## How likely is this real rather than luck?

Not likely enough, and that is the second reason nothing here is a candidate. Our luck score asks how
much of a result survives the number of distinct methods this lab has tried — 196 when these ran;
anything we act on has to score 0.90 or better. The two real filter versions scored **0.83** and
**0.74**; the coin tosses scored 0.63 to 0.76. None is close, which is the right answer for a set of
books that all fall 40% or more.

That does not conflict with the safety finding. The luck score judges whether a *book* is good enough
to bet on. The coin tosses judge whether one *effect inside it* is real. This method's books are not
good enough to bet on, and the effect inside them is real at the one-in-five level four coins allow —
no stronger, and not to be quoted as though it were.

## My opinion:

**The question this method was built to answer is now closed, and I would not reopen it.** A pick
filter cannot replace a cash rule. It buys less than half the protection, charges nearly twice as
much for it, and — the part I did not expect — it falls behind the market in 2009-2015 on both tapes
while *every one* of sixteen coin-versus-filter comparisons goes the coin's way. We should stop
trying to stack the two protections and stop looking for a pick filter that substitutes for the cash
rule.

What I would carry forward is the other half, which I did not expect to be writing. **We may have
been declaring safety filters inert at doses too shallow to see them.** The earlier method tested
this exact filter at a quarter, found it indistinguishable from a coin, and said so — and that was
wrong, not because the measurement was bad but because a quarter is too small a dose for the effect
to clear the noise. Any filter this lab has tried once, at one mild setting, against one coin toss is
a candidate for re-reading on those grounds. I have not counted how many that is and the record has
no field that answers it, so that is a direction to check rather than a number to quote.

So the next thing I would run is the cheapest test of the idea: a different filter on this same
always-invested book, at two fifths and three fifths, with four coin tosses at the deep end.

I had a candidate in mind and **measured it instead of assuming it, and it failed**. Proximity to the
52-week high looked ideal — it favours companies that are winning rather than companies that are
sleepy, so on the face of it it should not lag a six-year rise the way calmness does. Re-run here,
every one of that family's six versions falls behind the market in 2009-2015 on **both** tapes, by
between 4.9 and 9.7 points a year — far worse than the calm filter's 0.4 to 4.6. It is disqualified
as a follow-up, and the reason it is disqualified is itself worth recording: its *coin-toss* version
lags by 4.9 to 5.7 points too, so in that family the shortfall belongs to the underlying book and not
to the filter at all. That is the opposite of what happens here, where the coin tosses beat the market
and only the filtered versions lag — which is what lets this method blame calmness specifically.

That comparison gives the follow-up its selection rule, and it is the part worth queueing. The next
filter must be tested on a book whose **no-opinion versions already beat the market in 2009-2015**,
because otherwise a filter's shortfall cannot be told apart from its book's. I have queued the re-read
on exactly those terms, with the candidate to be chosen by measuring that first rather than by
reputation.

One number is worth remembering from here: **two fifths**. It cut the fall by 12.6 points against the
quarter and gave up nothing — the only free step in the experiment. If a calm filter is ever used for
anything in this lab, that is where the dial should start. But it should not be used as a substitute
for the cash rule, and after today nobody needs to test that again.
methods.verdict: Rejected on its own clause, and the question is closed: turned up two and a half times further than before, the calm filter stops looking like a coin toss -- it beat all four blind draws on the worst fall by 12.6 points, more than the whole range those four cover, and by 7.4 with the dead companies put back -- but four controls can support only a one-in-five claim, it buys less than half the cash rule's protection for nearly twice the price, and in 2009-2015 it falls behind the market on both tapes while every one of sixteen coin-versus-filter pairings goes the coin's way.

methods.name: The rules that earn more when the dead companies come back: find the rest of them
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0293 (calmness as a safety filter on M0197-Y20-SW's book), asking whether M0293's survivorship signature is a property of calmness or a property of what any screen is FOR; the family string is inherited from the reserved idea row and from the parent, though none of these four arms sorts on market beta
methods.hypothesis: Only two rules in this lab have ever read BETTER on the survivorship-check store than on the dev store -- proximity to the 52-week high, and M0293's calm filter, whose evidence is a monotone ladder in both gate settings rather than a single pair. The mechanism offered for it is not about calmness at all: roughly four in ten index member-days the dev store cannot price belong to companies that went bankrupt or were bought, dying companies are jumpy before they die, and a filter whose job is to avoid trouble has already thrown most of them out. If that is the mechanism then it generalises, and the dev-to-honest change in worst fall is a free, look-free test of whether a screen is a safety filter or a return engine. THE TEST. Six arms, every one of them M0197-Y20-SW term for term -- same pool of F4-screened index members, same shared yearly fit on SPY and the 10-year yield, same 20 equal slots, same 40% keep band, same quarterly re-rank, same SPY 200-day switch, same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly deposits. Every opinionated arm throws away the same quarter of the same pool before the host ranks what is left, so a drop changes WHICH names and never HOW MANY: the book stays 20 names fully invested in all six, which is the confound that sank M0277's and M0279's pick filters on the thin news-day pool. The only difference between the four opinionated arms is which number the quarter is chosen by, and every one of those numbers is already computed by the host's own F4 screen and thrown away, so this method adds no new estimate, no new window, no new lookback and no new free parameter. VOL drops the jumpiest quarter by 60-day realised volatility and DV drops the thinnest-traded quarter by dollar volume; both are declared SAFETY screens before the run. MOM drops the worst-performing quarter by 12-1 momentum and AMOM drops the best; both are declared RETURN screens. REF drops nothing and must reproduce M0197-Y20-SW and M0293-REF bar for bar. BLIND drops the same count by a fixed per-symbol hash at M0293's own seed 293, so it must also reproduce M0293-BLIND25 bar for bar -- that is the check that proves the two chassis identical and makes every cross-method comparison in the analysis legitimate -- and it prices the habit of dropping a quarter, the third arm the lab's audit says decides every reversed pair and which 22 of 28 reversed pairs left out. THE PREDICTION, written now: measuring the change in worst fall from the dev store to the survivorship-check store, with positive meaning the book falls deeper once the dead companies are back, both safety arms come in at or below BLIND and both return arms at or above it, with no overlap between the pair {VOL, DV} and the pair {MOM, AMOM}. MOM and AMOM disagree completely about which names are good -- one is what a momentum book does to a pool and the other what a long-term-loser book does to the same pool -- so if both still land deep, the honest tape is reading what a screen is FOR and not which names it picks, and the lab has a free diagnostic. Market beta is deliberately not an arm here: M0293 measured it on this identical host, so it is read from the record as the anchor rather than paid for twice. None of these arms is expected to be a better book than the host; the gate is left ON, against the temptation to repeat M0293's gate-off amendment, because every book the lab would apply this diagnostic to is gated, because M0293's gate-on ladder was no narrower than its gate-off one, and because a gate-off arm on this host falls about sixty per cent and could never also be a candidate.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the split is real but is not about safety. The four opinionated arms differ in turnover -- a momentum-chosen quarter reshuffles far harder than a dollar-volume-chosen one, because size and volatility quartiles are slow-moving and last year's return is not -- so an ordering that looks like safety-versus-return could just be low-churn-versus-high-churn, and the honest tape would be measuring how often a book trades rather than what it is trying to avoid. The second confound is overlap with the host: the host ranks on yield loading, and bond-like names are already the calmer, larger, duller end of the index, so dropping the jumpiest or the thinnest quarter may remove names the host was never going to hold anyway, making VOL and DV near-copies of REF while MOM and AMOM genuinely move the book. If so the ordering is really a measure of how far each filter moved the book off the host's picks, and the fix is to report the share of REF's holdings each arm keeps and read the falls against that, not against the safety label. The third is the gate, named and accepted above: with the SPY 200-day switch on, the book sits in cash through 2008 and much of 2000-2002, which are exactly the episodes in which the missing companies died, so the whole effect may be invisible here and all six arms may land within the draw's own width -- the lab has measured that width at several points a year of return and twenty points of fall across identical rules, which is wide enough to swallow this entirely. The fourth is simply that M0293's ladder was one method's accident: four in ten member-days missing is an average, and if the missing names happen to be concentrated in the jumpy, thin, low-momentum corner of the index then every one of these filters removes some of them and the arms separate by how much of that corner they touch, which is a statement about the dev store's holes and not about markets. Any of these would mean a survivorship gap must never again be quoted as evidence that a rule is safe, which is worth knowing and is the reason this is worth a method id even if it fails.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0303 — Can we tell a safety rule from a profit rule just by adding the dead companies back?

## The question, and why it was worth asking

The price history this lab normally searches on is missing about four in ten of the days that
index members actually lived through. The missing ones belong overwhelmingly to companies that
went bankrupt, got bought, or changed their name — so the everyday tape is a tape with most of
the disasters quietly deleted. The lab keeps a second, honester tape that puts most of them
back, and re-running a strategy on both is free: it costs no test-window look and does not count
as another try.

Almost every strategy looks worse on the honest tape, which is what you would expect. But some
have looked *better*, and a story grew up around them: a rule whose job is to **avoid trouble**
should look better once the trouble is put back, because the trouble is exactly what it was
built to dodge. A rule whose job is to **chase profit** should look worse. If that were true,
