the lab would get something valuable for nothing — a free honesty test that says whether a new
rule is really a safety belt or an engine wearing a safety belt's jacket. Answering that
question has cost a whole method id twice already.

This method was built to test that story properly, and the story does not survive.

## How it was built

Six versions of one strategy, identical in every respect but one. All six are the bond-like
book: among screened index members, hold the 20 whose prices rise most when interest rates fall,
equal slices, re-picked every quarter, behind the rule that moves to cash when the market is
below its 200-day average, fractional shares at the real Gotrade fees on the owner's actual
monthly top-up of 5,000,000 IDR (237 of them, on a starting 10,000,000 IDR).

Before ranking, five of the six throw away a quarter of the names they could have picked from.
The pool is hundreds of names deep, so throwing a quarter away changes **which** names get held
and never **how many** — the book is still 20 names in all six versions. That matters, because
the most common way this kind of test goes wrong is that the filter quietly empties slots into
cash and you end up measuring the cash. It did not happen here: the share of time invested is
0.680 to 0.689 across all six, essentially identical.

The only difference is what the discarded quarter is chosen by, and every one of those numbers
was already being worked out by the strategy's own screen and thrown away — so nothing new is
estimated, no new window, no new setting to tune.

| version | what it throws away | declared, before the run, as |
|---|---|---|
| REF | nothing | no opinion |
| BLIND | a quarter picked by a fixed hash of the ticker | no opinion |
| VOL | the jumpiest quarter, by 60-day wobble | **safety** |
| DV | the least-traded quarter | **safety** |
| MOM | the worst-performing quarter over the past year | **profit** |
| AMOM | the best-performing quarter over the past year | **profit** |

The prediction was written and committed before anything ran: both safety versions should come
out at or shallower than BLIND, both profit versions at or deeper, and the two groups should not
overlap.

Two checks first. REF reproduces the host strategy exactly — 22.0% worst fall, 3.08 gains per
unit of loss, 447 trades, to every digit. BLIND reproduces the parent method's own blind version
exactly, on **both** tapes. So this is genuinely the same machine, and comparing across the two
methods is legitimate rather than an accident of two similar setups.

## What happened on the everyday tape

All six beat SPY over 1996–2015 on the owner's deposits: between +10.3% and +12.0% a year
against SPY's +7.2% for the same money paid in on the same days. All six clear the lab's luck
bar of 0.90, with scores of 0.935 to 0.968. Those scores were set against 197 distinct attempts,
the count on the day this ran; another method has since registered and the count is 198 today,
at which all six are still clear. The method is marked dev-eligible.

Two of them would nonetheless fail the owner's own real-money rule, which allows a 25% fall:
VOL fell 28.2% and AMOM 25.9%. The lab's internal screen is a much looser 50%, which is why they
were not thrown out automatically. None of this matters much, because this method was never
meant to be a strategy to trade — it was built as a measuring instrument, and it is reported as
one.

## What happened when the dead companies came back

This is the experiment. The number is the change in the worst fall from a peak when the missing
companies are added: positive means the strategy falls further once you stop hiding the
disasters.

| version | declared as | change in worst fall | change in yearly return |
|---|---|---|---|
| VOL | safety | **−7.10 pts** | **+0.59 pts** |
| BLIND | no opinion | −2.30 pts | −1.93 pts |
| MOM | profit | −0.79 pts | −0.27 pts |
| REF | no opinion | +1.48 pts | −2.60 pts |
| AMOM | profit | +2.21 pts | −0.78 pts |
| DV | safety | **+4.74 pts** | −1.27 pts |

The prediction is wrong, and not narrowly. The two versions declared **safety** before the run
finished at the two opposite ends of the table. They are 11.8 points apart — a wider gap than
the entire rest of the table put together — and they completely surround the two profit
versions, which land quietly in the middle. There is no clustering, no separation, and no
diagnostic. On this evidence, how a rule behaves when the dead companies come back tells you
nothing whatever about what the rule was built to do.

## And then it got worse: the measurement has no error bar

The obvious next question is how much of that table is just noise. The parent method had already
registered the thing needed to answer it — four versions of the blind draw that differ **only**
in the seed of the hash that picks the quarter. Same strategy, same host, same number of names
dropped, no opinion in any of them. Re-run on both tapes, their changes in worst fall are:

  −2.30, +2.67, +3.85, +5.42

**Four identical rules spread over 7.71 points.** That is the width of the coin. Nothing
narrower than that can be read at all on this meter.

Now put the original story's evidence against that width. The ladder that started all of this —
throw away the calmest quarter, throw away nothing, throw away the jumpiest quarter — reads
+3.11, +1.48, +0.74. It is a perfectly ordered ladder, exactly as advertised, and it is **2.37
points wide inside a 7.71-point coin**. All three rungs sit inside the range that four
meaningless rules produced on their own.

The same measurement with the cash rule switched off tells a slightly different and more
interesting story. There the ladder spans 8.38 points and the blind draws span 8.77, so the
ladder is again no wider than its own coin — but the containment breaks in exactly one place:
the jumpiest-quarter rung lands at −2.70 against a draw floor of +0.51, escaping on the
favourable side. It does not join the two survivors described below, because it still lost 0.79
points a year. That one rung is the only place in the parent's whole record where something
pokes out from under the noise, and what it points at is jumpiness, not safety.

This method's own six versions say it again from the other side. REF and BLIND have no opinion
in them at all — one drops nothing, the other drops a quarter at random — and they are 3.8
points apart.

Two sibling methods settled this month both found that the cash switch makes a book fall far
less deep **without making its versions any more alike**; one of them added that the worst fall
is the meter the switch steadies least. This result is the natural next step: if the worst fall is
the least stable meter the lab owns, then the *difference* of that meter between two price
histories inherits the instability of both readings. I could find no published measurement of
how wide that difference's own noise is. It is 7.71 points.

So the honest verdict is not "the diagnostic exists but points the wrong way". It is that the
change in worst fall between the two tapes **cannot reliably tell two identical rules apart**,
so it was never going to tell a safety rule from a profit rule. The story was built on a ladder
that was never measured against its own control.

Of this method's four opinionated versions, exactly one escapes the coin's width: VOL, at −7.10.
The other three sit inside it and should be read as saying nothing at all.

## How common is "looks better on the honest tape", really?

The premise behind this whole idea was that only two rules in the lab's history had ever read
better once the dead companies were added back. That premise is false, and the evidence was
already sitting on disk. Across the 78 strategy versions the lab has recorded on both tapes
measured the same way — on the owner's deposits — the tally is:

- **22 of 78** earned *more* a year on the honest tape.
- **23 of 78** fell *less* from their peak.
- **3 of 78** did both at once.

(Those 78 were measured on an earlier build of the two price histories than this method's own
versions were. Each population is an internally consistent comparison of one history against
the other and nothing here divides one by the other, but they are not the same build.)

So roughly three in ten look better on one meter or the other. One strategy reading better is
not a rare event that needs explaining — it is close to a coin flip on either meter taken alone,
and the lab should stop treating it as a signature of anything.

## The one thing that did survive

Take the one population where a proper error bar exists: the twelve distinct versions of **this
one strategy** measured on both tapes with the cash rule on, four of which are blind draws
spanning those 7.71 points. Exactly two of the twelve escape the draws' range on the fall *and*
earn more a year:

- **VOL** here: throw away the jumpiest quarter by 60-day wobble. Fall improves 7.10 points
  (28.2% → 21.1%), return improves 0.59 points a year, and its luck score goes **up**,
  0.945 → 0.969. It is also the only one of the six whose lead over SPY in 2009–2015 gets
  *better* on the honest tape, −4.16% → −3.47%, where the other five all get worse.
- **The parent's HI50**: throw away the jumpiest *half*. Fall improves 5.62 points
  (25.2% → 19.6%), return improves 0.68 points a year.

Two caveats, both of which matter. First, these are two **different** measures of jumpiness —
VOL sorts on recent wobble in the price, HI50 on how hard the stock swings with the market — at
two different strengths, so "the same idea at two doses" is doing more work than it has earned;
a proper ladder has to hold the measure fixed and move only the strength. Second, HI50's
honest-tape figure was measured once, in this session, and has no second source in the lab's
record, unlike the blind draws and this method's own arms.

With those caveats, the finding is narrower and more useful than the one predicted: it is not
"safety filters read better on the honest tape". It is **"throwing out a lot of jumpy companies
reads better on the honest tape"** — the stated mechanism taken literally, since the companies
the everyday tape is missing are companies that got violent before they died. What a rule
physically removes is everything; what it was designed for is nothing. And the gentler rungs of
the same family earn nothing readable, which is what makes it look like a question of strength.

Set against that, the three versions that improved on both meters lab-wide are an earnings-jump
book, a long-term-loser book and a dividend-raise book. None of them is a jumpiness screen. So
the mechanism above is a hypothesis this method makes attractive, not one it establishes.

The least-traded screen, DV, makes the point from the other direction. It was declared a safety
rule on good grounds — the lab has found elsewhere that demanding busy stocks closes the gap
between the two tapes — and it came out the single worst version in the table, 4.74 points
deeper. A plausible reason, offered as a guess and not a measurement: dying companies often
trade *heavily* on the way down, so a rule that discards the quietest names keeps the distressed
ones. Whether that is right is a question for another method.

## The usual checks

Hypothesis: did not hold. Expected failure: partly. The churn worry was real but turned out not
to matter — the profit versions do trade harder (2.95 and 2.80 turns a year against 2.32 to 2.42
for the rest), but across the lab's 102 recorded pairs the correlation between a version's
**number of trades** and its change in worst fall is −0.055, which is nothing. The "the safety
filters barely move the book" worry was half right: of the five filters, DV shifts the book
least — less than a random draw does — while VOL shifts it most, so that worry applies to one of
the two safety versions and not the other.

Against the parent: this method's REF and BLIND reproduce the parent's to every digit, so the
comparison is clean, and the conclusion is that the parent's survivorship ladder — quoted as
unusually sharp evidence — sits inside its own control's width and should not be quoted that way
again. That takes nothing away from the parent's main result, which was about what its filter
does in a crash on the everyday tape and was measured against those same blind draws.

Not promotable, and that is correct. The hard gate refuses it at 2 of 4 walk-forward periods, a
strict majority being required, with no related strategy having failed out of sample. The
data-buying signal does not fire either: beyond the periods, every one of the six versions has a
**negative** lead over SPY in 2009–2015, the best-covered and most modern stretch — between
−3.34% and −4.16% a year on the everyday tape. That is the condition that matters most and it
fails for all six. (On the honest tape five of the six get worse still; VOL is the single
exception noted above, and one arm improving does not make the method's case.)

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and I would stop it rather than vary it. The specific idea — read
the gap between the two tapes as a safety detector — is not weakly supported, it is refuted by
its own control, and no rearrangement of filters will fix a meter whose noise is 7.71 points
wide when the effects being chased are 2 points. I would also go further than this method's own
scope: the lab should treat *any* single-strategy comparison between the two tapes as unreadable
unless several blind draws of the same shape are run beside it, and the places where such a gap
has already been cited as evidence of safety deserve re-reading in that light.

What I would spend the next method id on is the one thing that came out of this alive. Throwing
away a large slice of the jumpiest names improved the fall *and* the return on the honest tape,
twice, and both times by more than the coin is wide — the opposite of the usual result, where
the honest tape takes something away. It is worth finding out whether that is a question of
strength by running one single jumpiness measure at a quarter, a half and two thirds on both
tapes, with blind draws **at each strength** so every rung arrives with its own error bar. A
blind draw that discards half is not the control for a real screen that discards a quarter,
because how much you throw away is itself part of the effect. That is the next idea queued.

The second thing worth doing costs nothing and is a tooling matter rather than a market one:
this method's blind version is a textbook no-opinion control, and the lab's tools did not
recognise it as one, because the check that prices "what the habit costs" insists the comparison
version be invested essentially all the time. Only 11 of the lab's 1,070 recorded runs on this
window clear that bar, and all eleven hold index funds rather than individual shares. Nearly two
in three recorded runs sit between half and four fifths invested — 685 of 1,070 — which is what
a strategy that steps aside to cash looks like. For all of those the question is unanswerable by
construction, and the tool reports it as the author's omission rather than its own limit.
methods.verdict: The honest tape cannot tell a safety rule from a profit rule: the two filters declared safest finished at opposite ends of the table, and four identical blind draws spread 7.71 points — wider than the whole ladder this idea was built on.

methods.name: Cap the book's weight in thin names instead of refusing them
methods.hypothesis: M0298 and M0288 agree that a traded-volume bar buys roughly 3.4-3.5 points a year of honesty (dev-minus-check-store gap) on M0032's chassis, and both agree on why it costs so much: the breadth report shows the book's return in narrow months climbing +5.6% to +11.6% while its broad-month return falls +6.4% to -3.2%, i.e. the bar herds the book into the largest, most-traded names and stops being a stock picker. The cost is 4.4 points a year at the strictest rung (M0298) and 5.4 at M0288's. But a refusal is the bluntest possible instrument: a name either qualifies or it does not, and the book is then equal-weighted over whatever survives. Insight 91 says the dev store's edge sits with the SMALLER index members, so refusing thin names throws away exactly the part of the market this book earns in. The cheaper design keeps every name eligible and instead CAPS how much of the book may sit in the thin ones: rank the 20 picks by 20-day mean dollar volume as usual, then limit the combined weight of the bottom-traded half of the book to cap_pct of equity, pushing the freed weight onto the better-traded picks rather than onto cash or onto different stocks. The book still holds 20 names, still picks them on residual momentum alone, and never declines a pick -- so the pool, the turnover and the time invested are all held at the no-bar arm's values and cannot explain any difference, which is the confound that made M0279's filters unreadable and that M0288 and M0298 each had to rule out by hand. Rungs: cap at 50% (no bind, the reference arm with no opinion in it, since the bottom half of an equal-weight book of 20 already holds exactly 50%), then 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%, the last being nearly a refusal in weight terms, plus the strict top-50-names refusal arm from M0298 carried over as the endpoint the ladder is trying to beat. Success: at least one cap rung recovers a majority of M0298's 3.4-point honesty swing for materially less than its 4.4-point dev cost, which would turn a settled diagnostic into an affordable design rule. Measure the gap rung by rung with lab survivorship, exactly as M0288 and M0298 did, and read the breadth table to confirm the large-company tilt is weaker than under a refusal. EXPECTED FAILURE: the thin names may carry the honesty risk in proportion to their weight, in which case a cap buys honesty and cost in the same ratio as a refusal and the ladder is simply M0298's in different units, with nothing gained. Second, an allocator cannot read its own current weight (only the set of symbols held), so the cap has to be imposed as a target weight recomputed from scratch each decision session rather than as a brake on an existing position, which is clean here but means the rung is a re-weighting and not a trade rule. Third, this chassis's kin have already failed the test window (M0021, M0022, M0029), so the hard gate refuses promotion whatever the numbers -- this is again evidence about how to build books, not a candidate, and it should be run knowing that.

methods.name: Complete the two-by-two: the fixed-count bar on the news-day book
methods.hypothesis: The liveness finding now rests on three runs: M0284 (news-day book, share-of-pool bar, swing -3.3 to +0.6), M0288 (momentum book, share-of-pool bar, -1.7 to +1.8) and M0298 (momentum book, fixed-count bar, -2.7 to +0.7, and the first of the three to be monotone). That is three cells of a two-by-two of chassis against bar definition, and the missing cell is the news-day book under a fixed-count bar. It is worth filling for a specific reason rather than for symmetry: M0298 showed that the share-of-pool bar does not merely add noise, it systematically MISLEADS, because the check store's larger pool makes the same label a gentler requirement there. That is what made M0288's honest-tape ranking reverse and made its middle rung look like the best book, both of which M0298 withdrew. M0284's conclusions were drawn from the same instrument and have never been re-read with a bar that holds still -- and M0284 is the run the whole liveness reading originally came from, so if its numbers carry the same artefact the lab should know before leaning on them further. Carry M0284's chassis verbatim and replace its event volume bar (a multiple of the name's own recent volume) with a fixed count of the most-traded eligible names on the event day, at rungs chosen after measuring the event-day pool's size on BOTH tapes first, the way M0298 did -- the news book's pool is far thinner than the momentum book's, so the rungs must come from that measurement and not be copied across. Include the no-bar reference arm with no opinion in it. Success: the swing reproduces in sign and size on this chassis too, which would make the liveness reading invariant to both the chassis and the instrument and close the question for good; and separately, whether M0284's own honest-tape readings survive the change, as M0288's did not. EXPECTED FAILURE: M0284's event-day pool may be too thin for a fixed count to have room to move -- if the median event-day pool is only a few dozen names, every useful rung either binds on nothing or starves the book, and M0279 measured the cost of empty slots at 2 to 6 points a year, which would swamp the signal. Measure the pool on both tapes BEFORE writing the file and block or redesign the idea if the rungs cannot be made to bind without starving it. Second, M0284's dial asked whether TODAY was busy for this stock while M0288's and M0298's asked whether this stock is busy relative to its peers, so a cross-sectional count on the news chassis is a genuinely different question and a flat result would not cleanly falsify anything. Third, this is evidence about data and not a candidate, as all three predecessors were.

methods.name: Finish the gated coin: the switch-on draw population from seven to nineteen
methods.hypothesis: M0296 measured how far pure chance moves a twenty-name three-industry book re-picked monthly at real fees, and the answer was large: nineteen identical rules differing only in a coin toss spanned 7.5 points a year of money return on the owner's deposits, 20.7 points of worst fall and 31.5 points of worst year, while trades varied 2.7 percent and turnover 4.1 percent. Every one of those nineteen was ALWAYS INVESTED, and that is not the chassis the lab uses. Every near miss on the leaderboard keeps the SPY 200-day switch, and the switch is what flattens the fall: M0295's gated arms fall 27.6 to 33.9 percent where its switch-off arms fall 58.1 and 59.9. M0307 began the gated half of this measurement and got seven draws into it. Seven is not enough to put beside nineteen, because the range of a sample grows with the size of the sample: a seven-draw gated range read against a nineteen-draw switch-off range comes out narrower even when the two distributions are identical, which is the very conclusion the measurement is supposed to be able to refute. This method runs the missing twelve — M0295's engine with inner=GATED, side=matched, leader=largest, three industries, seeds 8 through 19 — so the gated population reaches nineteen and can be read against M0296's nineteen seed for seed. The pre-registered null is dilution by time invested: the gated arms hold exposure 0.694 against 0.964, so if the switch does nothing but keep the book out of the market the spread ratio should be 0.720 on every meter. The hypothesis is that the worst-fall ratio comes in clearly below 0.720 while the money-return ratio sits near it, and that the nineteen-draw gated spread is materially wider than the seven-draw one. Success is not a strategy and no arm is expected to be eligible: the deliverable is the width of the ruler the lab has used on every gated comparison in its record, whether it can be derived from the one it already has, and how badly a short draw population understates it.
methods.expectedFailure: The expected failure is that the gated draws cluster so tightly on the fall — because the switch takes every one of them to cash in the same months, and the deepest part of every draw's 2008 is a month the switch sits out — that the fall spread comes out near zero and the SHAPE of the distribution rather than its width becomes the finding. That would be worth knowing on its own: it would mean the lab may read a fall difference between gated twins and may never read a return difference, and it would retire the worst fall as a discriminator between gated books. The second likely failure is the opposite and worse: the ratio lands near 0.720 on every meter at once, the switch turns out to be a pure exposure dial with no effect on draw noise beyond arithmetic, and these twelve runs will have bought a multiplication the lab could have done from M0296 for nothing. The third is that seeds 8-19 land inside the range M0307's seven already covered, so the population saturates and the gated bar is a lower bound however many seeds are spent — in which case the only safe ruler for a gated comparison remains the switch-off one, and the lab must go on treating every single-control claim as the one-in-two claim it is.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0306 — Finish the gated coin: the switch-on draw population from seven to nineteen

## What this tried

Almost every promising strategy in this lab keeps one safety rule: get out of the market when
SPY is below its 200-day average, come back when it is above. Call it the switch.

Last week the lab measured, for the first time, how much pure luck moves a result. It built
nineteen versions of the same twenty-stock book that were identical in every way except one — a
coin toss decided which three industries each version bought. Nothing in any of them was a
prediction. The answer was sobering: those nineteen identical rules earned between 1.53% and
9.06% a year on the owner's deposits, and fell between 49.0% and 69.7% from their peaks. A gap of
7.5 points of yearly return and 20.7 points of fall, from nothing but the coin.

That ruler has been used ever since to judge whether one strategy really beat another. But every
one of those nineteen versions had the switch **off** — they stayed invested the whole time. The
strategies the ruler is used on all keep the switch on. Nobody had checked whether the ruler
transfers.

A sister run (the gated-width exploration) started that check and got seven versions into it.
Seven is not enough to compare with nineteen, and the reason is arithmetic rather than
fussiness: **the more times you toss a coin, the further apart the best and worst results will
be.** Comparing a seven-toss spread against a nineteen-toss spread finds the seven "narrower"
even when nothing is different. This run supplied the missing twelve, so there are now nineteen
switch-on versions to set against the nineteen switch-off ones, coin for coin, on the same
hashes.

## What happened

**The switch makes every version fall far less deep. It does not make them any more alike.**

| | switch off (19) | switch on (19) |
|---|---|---|
| money earned on the owner's deposits | 1.53% to 9.06% a year | 4.39% to 9.53% a year |
| worst fall from a peak | 49.0% to 69.7% | 20.0% to 43.0% |
| worst single year | −55.0% to −23.5% | −17.3% to −5.4% |
| gains vs losses | 1.038 to 1.289 | 1.184 to 1.519 |
| share of time invested | 96.3% | 69.3% |

Read the fall row twice. With the switch off the gap between the luckiest and unluckiest version
is 20.7 points. With the switch on it is **22.9 points** — slightly *wider*. Every version got
about 30 points shallower (30.4 points on average), but the spread between them did not shrink at
all.

Before any of this ran, the method wrote down the dullest possible explanation of any narrowing
and turned it into a number. The switch does not know about the coin: it reads SPY and nothing else, so all
nineteen versions step out and back in on essentially the same dates and differ only in what
they hold while invested. Their time invested varies by less than half a point
(69.05% to 69.48%), and the switch-off versions — which have no switch at all — vary by just as
much (96.05% to 96.51%), so that sliver is fill mechanics rather than the coin moving the
switch.

So the switch-on versions have only 69.3% as much time to differ as the switch-off versions'
96.3%, and pure arithmetic predicts a spread **0.720** times as wide. Measured:

| | spread with switch on, divided by spread with switch off |
|---|---|
| money earned | **0.683** — almost exactly the arithmetic prediction of 0.720 |
| worst fall | **1.105** — no narrowing at all |
| worst single year | **0.378** — real narrowing, much more than arithmetic |
| gains vs losses | 1.330 — wider |
| turnover | 1.170 — wider |

So on the money, the switch steadies the result by nothing beyond keeping the book out of the
market for a third of the time. On the worst single year it genuinely helps, and by a lot: it
takes every version out of 2008, so no version can have a catastrophic calendar year. But on the
**worst fall from a peak** it helps not at all. That combination is the finding, and nobody
predicted it.

The mechanism is consistent once you see it. The switch protects against the one long, deep,
market-wide decline. What it cannot protect against is being whipsawed — selling after a dip,
missing the bounce, buying back higher — and how badly that hurts depends entirely on which
twenty stocks the coin handed you. With the switch off, the deepest fall is 2008 for every single
version, so they are all dragged toward the same number. With the switch on, 2008 is handled and
the deepest fall is whatever private accident each version suffered. The versions are no longer
anchored together, so their falls spread out just as far around a much better average.

**The consequence the owner should care about.** His rule says a strategy may not fall more than
25% from a peak. Of the nineteen switch-on versions — identical rules with no opinion in them,
differing only by a coin toss — **ten passed that test and nine failed it.** With the switch off,
none of the nineteen passed. So the switch moves a book from "never qualifies" to "a coin
decides", and the coin's say is not small: it is the whole decision. Twelve of the nineteen also
cleared the gains-to-losses bar of 1.3, and six of the nineteen beat SPY. None of this is skill.
There is no skill anywhere in these books.

**How badly a short set of coin tosses misleads.** Measured on this method's own versions, the
first seven understated the full nineteen-version spread by:

- money earned: 2.44 points instead of 5.14 — understated by 52%
- worst fall: 15.6 points instead of 22.9 — understated by 32%
- worst single year: 8.5 points instead of 11.9 — understated by 29%
- gains vs losses: 0.144 instead of 0.335 — understated by 57%

Any error bar built from a handful of controls is a floor, not a measurement, and it can be off
by half.

**The best-covered years.** Over 2009-2015 — the stretch with the most complete data and the one
most like today — every single switch-on version lost to SPY, by between 2.92 and 11.87 points a
year. The switch-off versions ran from −6.12 to +0.80. This is the known cost of sitting in cash
through a decade that mostly rose, and it is large. The spread here was also wider with the
switch on (8.95 points against 6.92), which is the same story as the fall.

**What it says about the industry lead-lag idea.** The book that started this family — buy the
smaller companies in the industries whose biggest name rose most last month — can now be placed
inside its own population of coin tosses rather than against a single one. With the switch on it
ranks 7th of 20 on money earned and 16th of 20 on the fall: middle of the pack and below middle
on safety. Its rejection stands, and the earlier line that "a blind draw beat it" was reading one
coin toss. In the 2009-2015 stretch it does better, 2nd of 20, which is interesting but is one
rank in one era and sits inside the spread this very method just measured.

## The luck test

None of the nineteen is eligible and none was meant to be. The lab's luck test asks how likely a
result is to be real rather than a fluke after everything the lab has tried; it is scored out of
1 and the owner's bar is 0.90. At the time these ran, the lab counted 195 distinct attempts. The
best of the twelve new versions scored 0.886 and the worst 0.251 — all below the bar, which is
the correct answer for books that contain no idea. That the best coin toss gets within 0.014 of
the owner's luck bar is itself worth noticing.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No, and the part it got wrong is the part that mattered.

The hypothesis said the switch would narrow the spread of falls by clearly more than time out of
the market explains — a ratio well below 0.720. The measured ratio is **1.105**. The switch
narrows the spread of falls by nothing. The hypothesis was right about the money, where the
measured 0.683 sits near the predicted 0.720, but that half was the easy half and was written as
the null rather than the claim.

The written expected failure was that the falls would cluster so tightly that the spread came out
near zero. The opposite happened. The second expected failure — that every meter would land near
0.720 and the run would buy only a multiplication — did not happen either; only the money did
that. What actually happened was a third thing: one meter obeys arithmetic, one meter narrows
hard, and one meter does not narrow at all, so there is no single gated error bar and there never
was going to be.

The amendment's hypothesis held: nineteen versions really did spread much further than seven, by
29% to 57% depending on the meter, so stopping at seven would have misstated every one of these
numbers in the same direction.

## Comparison with the parent

The parent measured the switch-off ruler on nineteen coin tosses and published 7.5 points of
money and 20.7 points of fall. This method measured the switch-on ruler the same way on the same
nineteen coins and got 5.14 points of money and 22.9 points of fall. The parent's numbers were
not wrong; they were simply about a chassis the lab does not use. Both are measured at the same
real Gotrade fees on the same monthly deposits, so the comparison is clean, and because the same
coins were used in both, the versions can be read as nineteen matched pairs: the switch added
1.33 points of yearly money on average and removed 30.42 points of fall, but the amount it
removed varied from 9.7 points to 46.7 depending on the coin.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and it earned its keep. The lab now knows that it has not one error
bar but three, that two of them are wider behind the safety switch than in front of it, and that
the worst fall — the meter the owner's most important rule is written on — is the one the switch
does least for. The practical rule I would adopt immediately: **never treat a difference in worst
fall between two gated books as evidence unless it exceeds about 20 points.** On the dev window
that is nearly every comparison the lab has ever made on safety, and it means the lab has almost
certainly been reading noise as safety for months.

What I would not do is spend more method ids on industry draws. The population is complete at
nineteen and more coins would only sharpen a number that is already clear enough to act on.

What I would do next, and it is the obvious follow-up, is check whether this transfers. These
nineteen books pick three industries at random; the strategies actually on the leaderboard are
twenty-name momentum books. The fall-spread finding has a mechanism behind it — the switch
removes the shared 2008 anchor and leaves private whipsaw accidents — and that mechanism does not
care what the book ranks on, so I expect it to hold. But "I expect it to hold" is exactly the
sentence this lab exists to distrust, and the whole value of the finding depends on whether the
20-point rule applies to the books the owner might actually buy. That is the next run, and it is
queued as M0313: nineteen blind draws of a twenty-name momentum book behind the identical
switch, plus the same nineteen with the switch off, so the two fall spreads can be read on the
chassis the near misses actually use.

I would also stop quoting any error bar drawn from fewer than about fifteen controls. The
measurement here says a short population understates the truth by a third to a half, always in
the direction that makes a result look more impressive than it is.
methods.verdict: The safety switch makes every version of a book fall thirty points less deep without making them any more alike, so the lab has no single error bar and the worst fall is the meter the switch steadies least.

methods.name: The coin's width behind the switch
methods.hypothesis: Behind the SPY 200-day switch the coin is narrower than the lab's only measured error bar says, and markedly narrower in the fall than in the return. The seven gated draws should span less of the twenty-year money return than the same seven hashes span ungated, and should span far less worst fall, because the switch stands the whole population in cash through the episodes where blind draws diverge most — a draw's fall is decided mostly by which names it happened to hold into 2008, and a book that is out of the market in 2008 cannot express that difference. If that holds, the lab has been holding the wrong yardstick: its recorded idea-versus-control claims are overwhelmingly gated, the only width it has measured is ungated, and using the ungated width to audit them would retire real findings as noise. Success for this method is not eligibility — no arm here has an opinion and none should be eligible — but a usable gated width, stated as a range and a typical distance from the middle on both the return and the fall, that the audit in the analysis can then apply to the lab's own record.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that the gated width in RETURN barely narrows. The switch is a common factor: it moves every draw into cash on the same days, so it may subtract roughly the same amount from all seven and leave the picking noise — which is what the seeds actually differ in — untouched. The fall would still compress, but a bar that narrows on one axis and not the other is harder to use than one number, and the honest report would then be two separate bars rather than a tidier one. The second failure is subtler and worse: seven gated draws may land so close together that the measured range is dominated by whichever single seed happens to sit furthest out, in which case this buys a lower bound on the gated width rather than the width, exactly as M0296 feared for its own first seven. The third is that three industries drawn from roughly ten eligible ones overlap so heavily that gated draws are near-duplicates of each other, and the bar produced is too narrow to be safe to audit with — which would be a finding, but a disappointing one, because it would mean the only safe bar is still the ungated one. If any of the three lands, the analysis falls back to the idea row's own fallback and flags the comparisons that rest on a single control arm, which needs no width at all: beating one control can never support better than a one-in-two claim, whatever the gap looks like.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0307 — The coin's width behind the switch

## What this was for

Last week a sister method proved something uncomfortable. It took one stock-picking rule, stripped
every opinion out of it, and ran nineteen copies that differed in nothing but a coin toss deciding
which industries to buy. Those nineteen identical, opinion-free books earned between 1.5% and 9.1%
a year on the owner's deposits — a spread of 7.5 points a year from luck alone. That gave the lab
its first error bar, and it was badly needed: for months the lab had been reporting "the idea beat
its control by three points" without any idea of how big a gap luck alone can produce.

But all nineteen of those copies ran with the safety switch **off** — always invested, never
stepping aside. The lab is not like that. Almost every method the lab has ever recorded keeps the
switch that moves the book to cash when the market is below its long-term average, and almost every
"idea beat its control" claim in the record is a switched-on book against a switched-on control.
Measuring those claims against a switched-off error bar is the wrong ruler, and it is wrong in the
expensive direction: if the switched-on coin is narrower, the wrong ruler quietly throws away
findings that were real.

So this method bought the missing half of the ruler. Six more coin-toss books, identical in every
respect to six of the originals — same rule, same twenty names, same industries, same coin — with
the safety switch **on**. Together with one switched-on copy the lab already had, that makes two
groups of seven over the *same seven coin tosses*, differing in exactly one thing. Nothing was
re-run; no new idea was tested. None of these seven books has an opinion about anything, and none
was expected to pass. The product was meant to be a number.

## What happened

**The switched-on coin is less than half as wide — in return.** The same seven coin tosses spanned
5.97 points a year of the owner's money with the switch off, and only 2.44 points with it on. The
typical distance from the middle fell from 1.92 to 0.86. On the fuller twenty-year group of
nineteen switched-off copies the spread is 7.53 points. So for a switched-on book, the noise floor
is roughly **two and a half points a year**. The lab has been holding a ruler between two and a
half and three times too long for most of what it measures: two and a half times when the copies
are matched one for one, which is the fair comparison, and three times against the seven-and-a-half
figure the lab actually had on its books — part of that extra width being simply that nineteen
copies spread wider than seven, with no dial changed at all.

**But the fall does not behave the same way, and here I was wrong.** I wrote before the run that
the switched-on coin would be "markedly narrower in the fall", reasoning that a book sitting in
cash through 2008 cannot express which names it happened to hold. The first half of that was right
and the second half was not. The switch cut the *size* of the worst fall enormously — from 57.4% on
average down to 26.7% — but it did not narrow the *spread* of it at all. Seven switched-off copies
spanned 14.4 points of worst fall; the same seven switched on spanned 15.6 points, slightly wider.
Measured against the number you are actually comparing, the switched-on fall is far noisier: 15.6
points of scatter around an average of 26.7% is a scatter of well over half the number itself,
where switched-off it was about a quarter. **A safety switch makes the fall shallower without
making it any more predictable.** Two books running the same rule, differing only in luck, can fall
20.8% or 36.4%. Any claim that one book is safer than another by a handful of points is, behind a
switch, almost certainly noise.

**The switch pays, on books with no opinion whatsoever.** Because the seven pairs are matched coin
toss for coin toss, the switch's own contribution is readable directly: it improved the owner's
yearly return in **seven cases out of seven**, by 1.4 points a year on average, and cut the worst
fall by about 31 points every time. That is a clean measurement of what the safety switch is worth,
with the stock-picking entirely removed. It also shows the switch's payoff is *not* a fixed number
— across the seven it ranged from 0.07 to 3.6 points a year, depending purely on which names the
coin happened to pick.

**And this is the uncomfortable part.** Four of the seven switched-on coin tosses beat SPY on the
owner's actual deposits. The best of them earned 9.1% a year against SPY's 7.2%, fell only 20.8%,
and reached a luck score of 0.887 against a bar of 0.90 — it failed the lab's screen on that one
number and nothing else. With the switch off, only two of nineteen coin tosses beat SPY and the
best luck score was 0.635. So the safety switch is most of what makes a book with no idea in it
look like a strategy. And this book is not even unusual in that. The lab has itself registered 115 arms as
placebos — books built on purpose to have no opinion — and **eleven of them have already cleared
the entire screen outright**, with luck scores from 0.904 to 0.963. A coin toss passing every test
the lab applies is not a freak event; it has happened eleven times.

## The audit this method was queued to do

The original plan for this method was a report: walk every recorded comparison in the lab, work out
how far the idea beat its control, and flag every gap small enough to be luck. That plan wrote down
its own problem — the error bar might not carry across from one kind of book to another. It does
not carry cleanly, and now we know by how much: the one dial tested here moves it by a factor of
two and a half. So the audit below applies the switched-on bar to switched-on comparisons and the
switched-off bar to switched-off ones, which is the best the lab can currently do. It is an
approximation, and the right word for the results is "flagged", not "disproved".

A gap between two books is a difference, so the right noise scale for it is a little wider than the
scale of one book — about 1.2 points a year for switched-on books and 2.7 for switched-off. Which
of the two applies is decided by how much time the book actually spent in the market, a figure the
lab records for every run: books below 85% invested get the switched-on bar, the rest the
switched-off one. That is a physical measurement rather than a reading of the method's settings,
which matters because several methods express their switch in ways a settings-reader misclassifies.

Measuring all 57 idea-versus-control comparisons the lab can resolve automatically, across 30
methods — 31 of them switched-on books, 26 always invested:

- **43 of the 57 (75%) are inside two standard deviations of the coin.** They may still be real,
  but the lab's own record cannot tell them apart from luck.
- **26 of the 57 (46%) are inside one standard deviation.** These are indistinguishable from noise.
- The typical gap claimed anywhere in the lab is **1.98 points a year** — below the switched-on
  coin's own two-sigma scale.

Where exactly the line between switched-on and always-invested books is drawn does move these
numbers, and honesty requires saying by how much. There is a range of placements that still sort
the two reference groups correctly, and across the whole of it the two-standard-deviation figure
runs from 63% to 88%, and the one-standard-deviation figure from 35% to 58%. The 75% and 46% quoted
above sit near the middle of both. So the precise percentage is a choice, and I am not going to
pretend otherwise — but **the shape of the answer is not a choice**: on every admissible placement,
a clear majority of the lab's recorded comparisons fall inside the coin's own range, and the number
that survive it is somewhere between seven and twenty-one out of fifty-seven. The guess written
into this method's backlog entry was "two thirds or more"; that holds at the placement used here
and across most of the range, and dips just below two thirds only at the most extreme placement.

**There is a second finding here that needs no error bar at all, and it may be the more important
one.** Beating one control can never support a better claim than one-in-two, beating six
one-in-seven, and reaching the one-in-twenty standard the lab judges everything else by takes
nineteen. Counting every method in the lab that has ever run:

- 197 methods have a recorded result, as counted on the day this was written; the number grows
  almost daily, which is itself part of the problem.
- **184 of them ran six arms or fewer.** Even pretending every arm but one was a control — which is
  far more generous than the truth — the strongest claim any of them could support is about
  one-in-six.
- **Not one method in the lab has the twenty arms a one-in-twenty claim requires.** The widest ever
  run is eighteen, and that was the error-bar method itself, whose arms were *all* controls.

So the lab holds its methods to a one-in-twenty standard on luck and has never once built a control
population capable of reaching it. That is not a flaw in any individual method; it is a flaw in the
shape of the experiments.

## The honest-tape check

Re-running all six new books on the fuller price history — the one that includes companies that
later died — the switched-on coin's width barely moves: 2.4 points a year becomes about 2.6. **The
new ruler is not an artefact of missing data**, which is the main thing that could have invalidated
it. The spread of the worst fall actually narrows there, from 15.6 points to about 8.8.

What does shrink is the coin's flattery. On the dev prices four of seven coin tosses beat SPY; on
the fuller tape only one of six clearly does, and the best book's lead over SPY drops from 1.9
points a year to 0.7. The dev window makes a no-opinion book look better than it is, and that is
worth remembering every time a method posts a modest lead there.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

Half of it, cleanly. The return half was right and is the useful half: the switched-on coin is 2.44
points wide where the switched-off coin is 5.97. The fall half was wrong in the way I least
expected — the switch shrinks how far you fall without shrinking how much that varies. The first of
my three written-down failure modes (that the return width would barely narrow) did not happen. The
second (that seven draws would be dominated by one outlier, giving a floor rather than a width)
partly did: the widest switched-on book, at 9.12%, is alone at the top, and with seven draws this
number is better read as a lower bound on the true width than as the width itself. The honest-tape
agreement makes me more confident than seven draws alone would.

Every arm failed the lab's screen, exactly as pre-registered. Six trials recorded, status rejected.
These six were scored against a count of 194 previous attempts, the figure in force at the moment
they ran; sibling methods have landed since — three of them while this very analysis was being
checked — so the lab's current count is 197 and still climbing. The bar is 0.90 either way. Four test-window looks were already spent before this method
began and none was touched by it.

## My opinion

This direction is worth more trials, and it is worth them more than most stock-picking ideas
currently queued. The reason is leverage: every method the lab runs from now on is measured against
a yardstick, and the lab has now discovered that the yardstick it owned was the wrong length for
most of its own record. Fixing a measuring instrument improves every future measurement, which no
individual strategy does.

Three things I would do next, in order. First, and most urgently, I would stop treating worst-fall
comparisons between a book and its control as meaningful at all behind a safety switch — the
scatter is larger than the gaps routinely claimed, and that is a correction the lab can apply today
for free. Second, I would widen this switched-on group from seven to nineteen, the way the
switched-off group was widened, because seven draws give a lower bound and the lab deserves the
real number for the setting it actually uses; that is one method id and no new idea. Third, I would
change the shape of future experiments rather than keep auditing old ones: a method that registers
one idea and one control cannot support a claim the lab would act on, no matter how large the gap
looks, and that is arithmetic rather than opinion. Registering four or five cheap coin-toss arms
beside an idea costs one method id and converts an unreadable result into a readable one.

I would not spend further ideas on refining the audit itself. It has told us what it can: a clear
majority of the lab's recorded idea-versus-control gaps — three quarters at the fairest reading,
and a majority on any reading — are inside the coin's own range, the typical claimed gap is smaller
than the noise, and no method has ever had enough controls to reach the standard the lab demands. The remedy is in how the next experiment is built, not in further
measurement of the old ones.
methods.verdict: Rejected as pre-registered — no arm had an opinion. It bought the lab a missing ruler: behind the safety switch seven identical coin tosses span 2.44 points a year against 5.97 for the same seven without it, so a clear majority of the lab's recorded idea-beats-control gaps — three quarters at the fairest reading — sit inside the coin's own range; the switch makes the fall shallower but no more predictable, and four of the seven coin tosses beat SPY on the owner's money.

methods.name: Nineteen blind draws of the scaled-lottery-spike book: the first stock screen in the lab measured against a real control population
methods.hypothesis: M0297 gave M0093-LO5-S60-N20-T (dev-eligible, MAR 0.445, DSR 0.921) two shape-matched blind draws and it beat both on BOTH stores: +3.4 to +5.4 pts/yr on dev and +3.4 to +4.1 on .research-sv, where its mirror had priced the ranking at only +2.96. It is the only one of M0297's four books whose sign never wavered across seeds or stores. But two draws support a one-sided p of 1/3 and nothing better (M0296's arithmetic: beating k controls is worth 1/(k+1)), so the claim is directional, not established. This idea runs NINETEEN draws of that one book, reaching p=0.05 -- the bar the rest of the lab is judged by -- using the same matched-draw chassis M0297 proved exact (all six of its copies landed 0.93-1.00x trades and 0.92-1.00x turnover against the books they copied). Method: one allocator, nineteen seeds, the arm id M0093-LO5-S60-N20-T as the hash tag, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, the owner's deposits. Read: where the real book ranks among the twenty curves, on dev and on .research-sv separately, plus M0296's era discipline -- rank it over 1996-2008 as well as 2009-2015, because M0296's rule was 1st of 20 in the era someone had been looking at and 17th of 20 in the era nobody had. Success: the real book is above all nineteen draws on dev AND above all nineteen on the check store. Anything less and the lab's first properly controlled stock screen is a negative result, which is worth exactly as much. Secondary payoff: nineteen draws of a GATED book is the error bar M0296 could not supply -- it measured 7.5 pts/yr and 21 pts of fall with the switch OFF, and M0297's two gated pairs hint at 2.0-2.8 pts and 2.2-2.4 pts with it on. Expected failure: the real book finishes inside the pack, in which case its 2009-2015 record (negative on both stores, -2.5 and -5.9) was the honest signal all along and the twenty-year lead was the switch plus the draw's luck. Second expected failure: the gated spread turns out near the ungated 7.5 pts, which would put every two-draw and four-draw margin in the lab, M0293's and M0297's included, back inside the noise.

methods.name: Is the illiquidity book buying an anomaly or buying bad data? Put the volume floor back one rung at a time, on both tapes
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0058; two-store reading from M0297, fixed-rank bar from M0298
methods.hypothesis: The thin-stock book is the only book in the lab that earns dramatically more once the dead and delisted companies are put back: M0297 measured M0058-ILL20-T at +12.8%/yr money-weighted on the dev store against +22.3% on the survivorship-check store, a +9.5 point jump, where the largest move previously recorded in that direction is +1.3 points. Its two shape-matched blind draws moved the other way, so the jump lives in the ranking, not the pool or the chassis. M0058 is also the only lab book with no dollar-volume floor at all, and M0284/M0288/M0298 measured that such a floor is a general liveness filter -- companies go quiet before they die -- so a floorless book is the maximum possible exposure to exactly the names the dev tape is missing and whose reconstructed history is least trustworthy. This runs the identical Amihud-ranked 20-name book behind a fixed-rank liveness bar at six rungs (no bar, then the 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 most-traded names of the day's eligible pool) and reads the two-store gap at each rung. A fixed count rather than a percentile because the eligible pool is 223 names on dev against 406 on the survivorship store at the end of 1998 and 408 against 519 in 2015 (measured this session from each store's bars against point-in-time membership), so a percentile bar would cut a different number of names on each tape; the rungs are M0298's own so the two ladders can be compared setting for setting. Success for the anomaly reading: the gap stays large at every rung, so illiquidity genuinely pays more once the dead are back. Success for the artefact reading: the gap collapses as the bar tightens, which says the +9.5 points was concentrated in names too thin to price honestly, and the parent's dev-eligible status is a hole in the tape. The K50 rung is the built-in null: the 50 most-traded names are nearly the same companies on both tapes, so any gap surviving there is not about thinness.
methods.expectedFailure: The ladder is monotone and uninformative because tightening the bar simply deletes the strategy: an illiquidity book behind a liquidity floor is a contradiction, and at the tight rungs the 20 'most illiquid of the 100 most traded' are just ordinary large companies, so every rung below 150 collapses toward the parent's own most-liquid control and the return falls away for a reason that has nothing to do with survivorship. If the return and the gap fall together at the same rate, the ladder cannot separate the two readings and the honest finding is that this book cannot be made honest -- in which case its id should not be spent on a test look. Separately, the parent is already a poor candidate on evidence the lab is allowed to see: its 2009-2015 record is negative on both tapes (-1.7 and -0.9 points), it fails the lab's first filter, and M0297 showed a coin toss drawn from its floorless pool clearing every go-live condition at DSR 0.960. Nothing here is expected to produce a candidate; the deliverable is the shape of the gap.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# The thin-stock book was buying bad data, and one notch of a volume filter proves it

## What this was asking

The lab holds one book that behaves unlike anything else in it. The thin-stock book — it buys the
twenty big-company shares that trade least for their size — earns about 12.7% a year on our normal
price history and about 22.3% a year on the "honest" history, the one that puts back the companies
that went bust or were taken over and that our normal history simply does not have. Putting the
dead companies back usually makes a strategy look *worse*, though the lab has already corrected
itself on how usual that is: of the 102 strategy settings in its stored comparison, 23 move the
other way, which its own journal records as closer to a coin flip than a rare event. So a positive
gap is not by itself remarkable. The size of this one is. It gained 9.5 points a year.

For scale, with a caveat that matters. The lab's stored comparison of 102 strategy settings across
its own pair of histories averages −0.5 points — the expected direction — and its single most
positive case is +1.51 points. That stored grid was measured on an earlier vintage of both
histories than this run used, so the comparison is indicative rather than exact. Even allowing for
that, +9.5 is several times larger than anything else the lab has on record, in a direction where
results are supposed to shrink.

Two very different things predict exactly that. Either thin shares genuinely pay a large premium
that our incomplete history hides — or the thinnest shares are precisely the ones whose prices the
honest history had to reconstruct, and the book is harvesting reconstruction errors.

This run separates them. It takes the identical book and puts a liveness filter in front of it —
keep only the most actively traded names, then pick the thinnest twenty of those — and turns that
filter up one notch at a time: no filter, then the 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 busiest names. Each
setting then runs on *both* histories. If thin shares really pay, the 9.5-point gap should survive
the filter. If the gap is bad data, it should die as soon as the filter removes the names that are
too thin to price honestly.

The filter is a fixed count rather than a percentage on purpose. The pool of eligible companies is
223 names on our normal history against 406 on the honest one at the end of 1998, and 408 against
519 in October 2015 (measured in this session by reading each history's own price file against
point-in-time index membership). A percentage would cut a different number of names on each history
every year, and the ladder would not be a ladder.

## The answer

The gap exists at one setting only — the setting with no filter at all.

| filter | normal history | honest history | gap | fall (normal / honest) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | +12.7%/yr | **+22.3%/yr** | **+9.5 pts** | 26.4% / 28.1% |
| busiest 250 | +12.2% | +8.3% | −3.9 pts | 32.6% / 32.2% |
| busiest 200 | +10.7% | +10.3% | −0.4 pts | 30.5% / 30.7% |
| busiest 150 | +10.7% | +8.5% | −2.2 pts | 28.4% / 29.3% |
| busiest 100 | +8.5% | +6.6% | −1.9 pts | 27.6% / 27.7% |
| busiest 50 | +9.8% | +8.5% | −1.2 pts | 24.4% / 24.0% |

SPY earned +7.2% a year on the same deposits in every one of these runs. All six settings
reproduced their recorded result on the normal history exactly, so every row is a fair comparison.

One notch of the filter turns +9.5 into −3.9, and it never comes back. Every filtered setting is
*negative*, averaging about −2 points. That is the ordinary direction for this lab and close to its
ordinary size: across the 102 settings in the stored grid the average is −0.5 points and the worst
is −2.57.

## Why this is conclusive and not just suggestive

Look at what that first notch does to each history separately. On our normal history, going from no
filter to "busiest 250" costs **0.6 points** a year — 12.75 down to 12.18. On the honest history the
same change costs **14.0 points** — 22.27 down to 8.30.

That asymmetry is the whole finding. The filter removes the names outside the 250 busiest. On our
normal history those names are largely missing in the first place, so removing them changes almost
nothing. On the honest history they are present — and they were carrying the entire excess. The
extra return was never in the strategy. It was in the names only one of the two histories has.

A concrete reading of the same thing, on the last day of 2009: the first notch removes 95 names
from the normal history's pool and 254 from the honest one, and 97 of those 254 are companies the
normal history does not carry at all.

The shape of the returns says it again. A measure called kurtosis says how much of a result comes
from a few freak days rather than from steady earning. Across the eleven other cells in this grid
it sits between 8.0 and 11.3, which is normal for a stock book. In the one cell where the 9.5
points lives — no filter, honest history — it is **420.7**, and the lopsidedness of the returns is
+14.8 where every other cell is between −0.35 and −0.19. In plain words: that result is a handful
of enormous single days, not twenty years of patient premium. The moment the filter removes the
thinnest names, the freak days disappear and the excess return disappears with them, at the same
notch.

I then looked at the honest history directly. It carries 450 companies our normal history does not
have at all. Thirty-nine of those 450 produce at least one day where the share price rose by more
than half in a single session, 98 such days between them; on eight of those days, across six
companies, the price actually more than doubled. The worst is a single company whose price goes
from $0.57 to $27.80 on 10 February 2004 — a rise of 4,802% in one day — with 19 days above the
half-again mark in its record. I checked what the store itself says about that company's share
splits: it records exactly one, in March 2007, and nothing anywhere near February 2004. So the
49-fold jump is not an adjusted split being read correctly — it is either a bad price or a split
the reconstruction missed. Either way, no share rose 49-fold in a single session and no strategy
earned that money.

I should be careful about one thing, because my first guess was wrong. The very largest nonsense
prices in the honest history — one name trades at millions of dollars a share in 1998 — are in
**both** histories, identically; I checked the two files line by line for that company and they do
not differ. So the problem is not that the honest history is sloppier in general. It is narrower
than that: the honest history adds a set of thin, mostly dead companies, and some of those
additions are badly reconstructed. The filter removes exactly that set.

I have not traced the 9.5 points to named holdings day by day; that would need the book's daily
record, which this report does not produce. What is measured is that the gap lives only where those
names live, dies the instant they are excluded, and carries the freak-day signature while it lives.

## Did it beat SPY, and is it real?

The unfiltered setting beats SPY on the normal history: +12.7% a year against +7.2% for the same
monthly deposits put into SPY, and it clears the lab's luck test at 0.942 against a bar of 0.90,
judged against 198 independent looks. (That test asks how likely a result is to be real rather than
luck, after allowing for how many different ideas the lab has tried.) On the honest history it
scores 0.996.

**Those numbers are exactly the trap this run was built to find.** They are the score of a book
whose returns are a few reconstruction errors. The luck test measures whether a pattern could have
come from chance; it cannot tell whether the prices were real.

What actually rules it out:

- **The 2009-2015 test.** The lab's first filter is the best-covered and most modern stretch of the
  dev window. This book loses to SPY there at **every one of the six settings on both histories** —
  twelve readings out of twelve, from −0.3 to −10.3 points a year. The unfiltered setting is −1.7.
- **The fold test.** Split into four periods and scored only on months it had never seen, it wins
  2 of 4. The lab requires a majority, so promotion is refused outright by the hard gate, and the
  signal to go and buy survivorship-free price history does not fire.

And one correction to how I first wrote this up. I claimed the worst fall broke a 20% limit at
every setting. **There is no 20% limit in force.** The owner's real-money bar has been 25% since
the design revision, and the lab's own development screen is 50%; neither is breached in a way the
record flags, which is why the unfiltered setting records no drawdown failure at all. The honest
statement is narrower: the falls run 24.4% to 32.6% on the normal history, so five of the six
settings would breach the owner's 25% real-money bar, and the tightest filter (24.4%, and 24.0% on
the honest history) would clear it. That removes one of the three reasons I originally gave. The
other two stand, and the fold majority is a hard gate, so the conclusion does not move.

No candidate here, and no reason to spend a test-window look. Four looks are spent and this run
spent none.

## The side-effect worth knowing

Adding the filter at all multiplies the trading by between 2.7 and 4.1 times. The unfiltered book
makes 365 trades in twenty years; at "busiest 250" it makes 1,001, and at "busiest 150" it makes
1,504, its busiest setting.
Nothing about the strategy changed — only which names are allowed in. Shares drift across the
cut-off from month to month, and the book has to follow them. A filter that looks free on paper is
not free: it hands you a churn bill before it hands you any safety.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis offered two outcomes and the data picked one cleanly: the gap collapses as the
filter tightens, so the 9.5 points was concentrated in names too thin to price honestly.

One correction to my own pre-registration, which is frozen as written and cannot be edited. It says
the largest gain previously recorded in this direction was 1.3 points, attributed to a book that
buys shares near their one-year high. That figure was carried over from the idea that prompted this
run and I did not check it before registering it. Measured here across the lab's stored
survivorship files, the largest positive gap is **+1.51 points**, and it belongs to a
dividend-timing book, not the one-year-high book. No book of the one-year-high family appears in
any stored grid at all. The correction makes this run's +9.5 slightly less extreme and changes none
of its conclusions.

The expected failure was that the ladder would be uninformative because tightening the filter
simply deletes the strategy. That half-happened — the filtered settings earn between 8.5% and
12.2% a year against the unfiltered 12.7%, and the two tightest give up the most — but it did
**not** spoil the reading, for a reason worth recording. The gap is a
difference between two histories *at the same setting*, so whatever the filter costs the strategy
cancels out of it. And the gap dies in the first notch, where the strategy has barely been touched
at all (−0.6 points). The ladder worked.

I registered no separate placebo arm, on the grounds that the earlier run had already drawn two
coin-toss books of this exact shape from the unfiltered pool and both moved the *other* way between
the two histories, and that the tightest rung is its own null, since the 50 busiest names are
nearly the same companies on either history. The lab's own control checker agrees there is nothing
to price here: it reports that no two arms differ in exactly one reversing setting, which is correct
for a dose ladder.

## Compared with the parent

The parent is the same book with no filter. This run does not merely come close to it — the
unfiltered setting reproduces it **exactly**, to the last decimal on return, worst fall and trade
count, because it is the same configuration re-registered under a new engine name. (The parent is
sometimes quoted at 12.8%; its own recorded number is 12.7%, and this run matches that.)

The parent was called a small-company bet in disguise. That reading was right about the strategy
and too kind about the evidence: a meaningful part of what made it look good on the honest history
was not a small-company bet at all, it was broken prices.

Both ran at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares, so no part of this comparison is a fee
artefact.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished, and I would close it rather than vary it. The thin-stock
book fails the 2009-2015 test at every setting on both histories and loses its folds; and the one
number that ever made it interesting turns out to be a measurement error. Do not spend a look on it.

But the run found something worth more than the method it killed. We have been using the honest
history as the lab's truth-teller — the thing that tells us whether an edge was real or an artefact
of missing companies — and it contains badly reconstructed price series that can manufacture an
edge out of nothing. It did so here, convincingly enough to clear the lab's luck test at 0.996.
Every honest-history reading the lab has taken was taken on some build of that same reconstructed
tape — at least two builds exist, this run's and the older one behind the stored grid, and only the
current one is still on disk, so the check has to be run against whichever build is live. What I would do
next, and have queued, is build a sanity filter for the honest history — flag any price series that
makes single-day moves no real share makes, and re-check which of our past honest-history
conclusions move when those series are left out. That is a tooling job, not a strategy idea, and it
protects every future reading rather than one book.
methods.verdict: The thin-stock book's standout result was bad data: one notch of a liveness filter turns its 9.5-point gain on the fuller price history into a 3.9-point deficit, and what is left behind carries the mark of a few broken prices rather than a premium.

methods.name: Find the cheapest drift setting that still pins exposure on a 300-name book
methods.hypothesis: M0300 pinned average exposure across five weighting rungs to within 0.085 points by shutting the rebalance band to zero -- every holding dragged back to its exact target every month -- and that is what made the weighting term measurable. But the pin was bought at a price that is not flat across rungs: modelled over the whole window the zero band costs the equal end 0.42 points a year against the size end's 0.15, a 0.27-point slope running against the very result being measured, because an equal-weighted book has more drift to correct. That slope is roughly twice the exposure slope it removed (about 0.11 points at the bridge-measured price of 0.018 per point of exposure). A pre-commit probe estimated the fee slope at 0.03 points by counting orders -- one order per held name per month at every rung alike -- and was wrong by a factor of nine, because the bill also scales with traded value above the /usr/bin/zsh.10 per-order floor, and traded value is exactly what differs across rungs. The band is not a switch, it is a dial, and the lab has only ever turned it on a 20-name book: M0127 measured 88.6%, 93.4%, 96.2%, 97.8% and 98.6% average exposure at bands of 1% of equity, 33%, 20%, 10% and 0% of target, and the presets for 33, 20, 10 and 0 already exist, so this costs no new chassis. Run one weighting rung -- the equal end, because it is where both the exposure gain and the fee cost are largest -- across the full band ladder, and run the size end at the two extreme bands as the second line of the grid so the SLOPE of the pin can be read rather than only its level at one rung. Predictions written now: average exposure rises monotonically toward the shut band at both rungs, as it did on the 20-name book, but the equal end starts far higher than the size end at every loose band and the two converge as the band closes -- the convergence IS the pin, and where it becomes complete is the answer. Turnover and modelled fee drag rise monotonically toward the shut band at both rungs, faster at the equal end. The useful number is the band at which the exposure gap between the two rungs falls under half a point while the fee slope is still under 0.1 points a year; I predict that band is near 10% of target rather than 0, which would make every future exposure experiment on a wide book roughly four times cheaper than M0300's. EXPECTED FAILURE: the convergence may not happen until the band is genuinely shut, because the mechanism that opens the exposure gap is that a size-weighted holding's weight drifts the way its own target drifts and so never clears any band at all, in which case no interior band pins anything and the answer is that M0300's price is simply what the pin costs. The band also interacts with the deposit: on a monthly-deposit account a loose band means the month's money has nowhere to go and banks as cash, so the band dial and the cash dial are the same dial, and a reading that looks like a rebalancing result may be a deposit-steering result instead -- which is why the size end must be on the grid, since it is the rung where the deposit finds no gaps. Finally this is a measurement about measurement: it promotes nothing, it earns nothing, and it is only worth an id because every future wide-book exposure experiment pays M0300's price until someone turns this dial.

methods.name: Score the lab's rejected stock screens against the even-spread book instead of against SPY
methods.hypothesis: M0300 closed the weighting term: holding the same dollar amount of each screened index member beats holding them at their market value by 2.6 points a year in the owner's money column, 2.6 again with the dead companies restored, at pinned exposure (98.83 to 98.91 percent across five rungs), with fees priced from the owner's own receipts and no market-timing switch anywhere in the chassis. The even-spread arm earns +2.9 points a year over SPY total return on paper and hands 95.6 percent of that to the money. That makes it something the lab does not currently have: a known, always-invested, honestly-priced, survivorship-checked yardstick that is NOT the market. And it exposes a measurement problem across the whole lab. Almost every stock-picking method here was scored against SPY total return, but most of them hold 20 to 50 index members in equal slots -- so their book SHAPE already carries the even-spread tilt that is worth 2.6 points a year by itself, before any picking. A method that beat SPY by 2 points may therefore have LOST to its own shape by 0.6, and been recorded as evidence that its signal works when the signal was actually a drag. Insight 462 already decomposed one equal-weight placebo's 8-point gap into 3.6 gate, 3.8 fees and under 0.9 pool-and-weighting, but that decomposition was computed on a gated, banded chassis where exposure and weighting were tangled; M0300's chassis has neither confound. So: re-score, as a report rather than a method, every dev-eligible stock screen against a shape-matched even-spread arm drawn from M0300's own equal rung -- same screened pool, same name count as the method's own calendar produces (insight 505: derive the control's width from the real book's calendar, never from a round number), same fees, same pinned exposure, no gate -- and count how many leads survive. Predictions written now: a clear majority of the 84 dev-eligible methods lose more than half their recorded SPY lead when the opponent is the even-spread book rather than the market; the ones that survive are concentrated in the families that do NOT hold equal slots of index members; and at least a handful cross from positive to negative, which would mean the lab has been carrying rejected-for-the-wrong-reason and eligible-for-the-wrong-reason rows side by side. EXPECTED FAILURE: the comparison may not be constructible one-for-one, because a 20-name screen and a 392-name even-spread book differ in width as well as in weighting, and M0229-era work showed width alone is worth points -- so a shape-matched control has to match the width too, and at 20 names the even-spread book is a different object from M0300's equal rung and may not carry its 2.6 points at all. If the yardstick's advantage turns out to be mostly width rather than weighting, then this re-scoring measures width and the right answer is to say so and stop. Second, the gate: most eligible methods run behind the SPY 200-day switch and M0300's chassis has none, so a fair comparison must either put the gate on the yardstick or take it off the method, and insight 523's warning applies -- without the habit-off arm the comparison prices the gate, not the picking. Third, this is a re-reading of recorded curves and cannot create new evidence; it can only redistribute credit, and if it moves nothing the honest report is that the shape tilt was already priced out by the existing controls.

methods.name: What makes a lead late-arriving: sort the lab by delivery rate and find the shared ingredient
methods.hypothesis: M0300 turned up something nobody was looking for and it may matter more than the weighting answer it was built to give. The even-spread rung delivered 95.6 percent of its paper lead to the owner's actual money; the market-value rung delivered 33.2 percent, and earned 117 percent of its lead before 2003 while giving 22.7 percent of it back after 2009. Across this lab the ordinary figure is the second one: 86 percent of recorded results earned half their lead before half the money had arrived, median delivery 33.9 percent, and eight trials win on paper and lose on the money outright. A 95.6 percent delivery rate is therefore in the top few percent of everything recorded, and it arose on a book nobody designed for it.
