That asymmetry is worth more to an owner who pays in every month than another two points of paper return, because an early edge lands on a small account and the subsequent fade lands on a big one -- which is precisely the shape of the 0-for-2 out-of-sample record, where all four roster strategies lost to deposit-matched SPY over 2018-2026. The lab already has the meter (lab timing, which prints paper lead, money lead, delivered share, and the share of the lead earned in each era beside the share of money that had arrived) and it has been run one trial at a time. Run it over every recorded dev trial, sort by delivered share, and ask what the top and bottom deciles have in common: family, gate or no gate, turnover, exposure, name count, weighting scheme, and whether the signal is a timing rule or a stock screen. Predictions written now, so this is falsifiable rather than a fishing trip: gated books deliver worse than ungated ones, because a switch's best years are the famous crashes and the crashes are early in this window; high-turnover books deliver worse, because fees scale with the account and the account is biggest late; and the single strongest predictor is not any of those but simply whether the edge lives in 2009-2015, which is the only era in which 100 percent of the money has arrived. If that last one holds, delivery rate is not a new fact but a restatement of the lab's existing first filter, and the honest report says so and the idea costs nothing further. EXPECTED FAILURE: delivery is mechanically tied to when an era's returns happened to be good, so a book that merely held more equity late will read as a good deliverer without any property worth copying -- the analysis must separate when the LEAD arrived from when the MARKET rose, and lab timing's per-era lead-rate column is the only thing that can do it. The sample is also not independent: the lab clusters by gate rather than by idea, 67 clusters at the 0.85 bar, so a decile may be one book wearing eleven hats and any count of methods must be a count of clusters instead. And the whole exercise re-reads recorded curves, so it can create no new evidence and must not be allowed to produce a promotion argument -- its only legitimate output is a rule for choosing between candidates that already look alike on paper.

methods.name: Does the fall-width finding transfer to a momentum book behind the same switch?
methods.hypothesis: M0306 measured nineteen opinion-free draws of a three-industry book on the gated chassis against the same nineteen run ungated, and found the SPY 200-day switch cuts every draw's worst fall by about 30 points (mean -30.42; 20.0%-43.0% gated against 49.0%-69.7% ungated) while narrowing the SPREAD of falls not at all: a ratio of 1.105 against a dilution-by-time-invested null of 0.720. On money the ratio was 0.683, near the dilution null; on worst single year 0.378, a real compression. The proposed mechanism — the switch removes the one anchor every ungated draw shares (2008) and leaves each gated draw's deepest fall to be its own private whipsaw accident — does not depend on what the book ranks on, so it should hold for any re-picked, re-entering book behind the identical switch. But M0306's draws are three-industry rotations, and the books on this lab's leaderboard (M0007, M0020, M0022) are twenty-name momentum-shaped books built on the F4 chassis. This method draws six twenty-name books from that exact chassis — its 12-1 momentum eligibility window, its SPY-200 trend gate, its equal slots, re-picked monthly — with the pick replaced by a month-keyed hash so no ranking opinion survives, and runs the identical six seeds gated and ungated. Success is not a strategy and no arm is expected to be eligible: the deliverable is whether the gated fall spread on this chassis is also near or above the ungated one (M0306's practical rule generalises, and no worst-fall difference between two gated momentum-shaped books under about 20 points is readable evidence) or whether it narrows here (the non-narrowing was a property of three-industry draws specifically, and a momentum-shaped control needs its own ruler).
methods.expectedFailure: A hash-ordered momentum-shaped book is not a momentum book at all once the ranking is removed, so if the F4-screened pool at any month end is not much larger than twenty names, different seeds could draw heavily overlapping books and produce a spread too narrow to read anything into, on either side of the switch. The second likely failure is sample size: six draws per side is a lower bound on the true spread exactly as M0307's first seven were, so a six-draw ratio near 1.0 or near 0.72 is suggestive rather than conclusive, and only a wider draw (the queued follow-up) can turn a lower bound into the width. The third is that the mechanism is real but weaker on this chassis: a momentum screen already excludes the worst-behaved names (price and liquidity floors, a 12-1 window), so the 'private whipsaw accident' M0306 describes may have less room to differ seed to seed than it does among three blindly drawn industries.

methods.name: Does the switch's fall-spread invariance survive a less concentrated book?
methods.hypothesis: M0306 measured, on a twenty-name book drawn blind from three Fama-French industries, that the SPY 200-day switch cuts every draw's worst fall by about 30 points on average while leaving the SPREAD of those falls no narrower than with the switch off (22.9 points gated against 20.7 ungated, a ratio of 1.105 where dilution by time invested alone predicts 0.720). The proposed mechanism was that the switch removes the one shared anchor every draw has in common -- 2008 -- and leaves each draw's deepest fall to its own private whipsaw accident, which the switch cannot flatten because it reads only the market, never the book. A three-industry draw concentrates all twenty slots into three sector bets, which is exactly the shape that would make private accidents large and idiosyncratic. This method rebuilds the identical measurement with the same twenty slots spread over six industries instead of three (4/4/3/3/3/3 instead of 7/7/6) -- three switched-on draws and three switched-off draws, matched seed for seed. If sector concentration is what drives the private-accident spread, the six-industry switched-on/switched-off fall-spread ratio should sit clearly below the three-industry book's 1.105, because a less concentrated draw should leave less idiosyncratic risk for the switch to fail to flatten. Success is not a strategy and no arm is expected to be eligible: the deliverable is whether concentration is an ingredient in M0306's finding or whether the finding is a property of the switch alone, independent of how a gated book is built.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is that three draws each way is too thin to read a direction at all: M0307 already flagged seven draws as a lower bound on the three-industry book's width, and three is half that. The measured ratio could land anywhere within a wide band purely from which three hashes happened to be drawn, in which case the honest report is 'not resolved at this sample size' rather than a number, and a widening amendment (the way M0296 went 7 to 13 to 19) would be the next step rather than a verdict. The second failure is about the instrument rather than the mechanism: the Fama-French 12 taxonomy has roughly ten to twelve industries eligible on any given date, so a six-industry draw covers more than half the eligible pool and any two draws share several industries by construction -- far more overlap than a three-industry draw has. A narrower measured spread at six industries could then be a pool-exhaustion artefact (the draws are closer to being the same book) rather than evidence that diversification tames idiosyncratic whipsaw risk, and this method cannot tell the two apart on its own; it would need a universe larger than twelve industries to settle, which this lab's Fama-French taxonomy does not have. The third possibility is that the ratio simply does not move from M0306's 1.105, in which case concentration is not the ingredient, the shared-anchor-removal story needs no sector-risk term at all, and M0306's practical rule -- never treat a gated worst-fall gap under about 20 points as evidence -- applies to every shape of gated book the lab is likely to register, not only three-industry ones.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

# M0314 — Does the switch's fall-spread invariance survive a less concentrated book?

## What this was for

A sister method, M0306, found something uncomfortable last week. Almost every promising strategy
in this lab keeps one safety rule: get out of the market when SPY is below its 200-day average,
come back when it is above — call it the switch. M0306 built nineteen copies of a twenty-stock
book that differed in nothing but a coin toss deciding which three industries each copy bought,
and ran them with the switch on and with it off. The switch cut every copy's worst fall by about
30 points, as expected. What was not expected: the SPREAD between the luckiest and unluckiest
copy did not shrink at all — it was actually slightly wider with the switch on (22.9 points)
than off (20.7 points). The proposed reason: the switch keeps every copy out of the one shared
disaster — 2008 — but it cannot stop a copy from having its own private bad luck afterwards,
and once the shared disaster is removed, the copies are no longer all anchored to the same worst
year, so they spread out more freely around a much better average.

This method's id was originally reserved to repeat that exact measurement, but M0306 already
finished it today before this run started. Re-running the identical thing a second time under a
different name would have spent a method id to re-answer a question the lab already has an
answer to, so this run asks a different question that M0306 raised but could not answer on its
own: is that "no narrowing" result about the switch in general, or about this particular shape of
book — twenty names concentrated into only three industries? A book spread over six industries
instead of three holds the same twenty names but in smaller, more varied groups (four, four,
three, three, three, three instead of seven, seven, six). If a book's own bad luck comes mostly
from a few concentrated sector bets going wrong together, a less concentrated book should show
*less* of the "no narrowing" effect. Three switched-on and three switched-off blind draws were
run at six industries, matched coin for coin, to check.

## What happened

| | three industries (M0306, 19 draws) | six industries (this method, 3 draws) |
|---|---|---|
| money earned a year, switch on | spread 5.14 pts | spread 0.57 pts |
| money earned a year, switch off | spread 7.53 pts | spread 1.12 pts |
| money ratio (switch on ÷ switch off) | 0.683 | 0.51 |
| worst fall, switch on | spread 22.9 pts | spread 7.03 pts |
| worst fall, switch off | spread 20.7 pts | spread 7.08 pts |
| **fall ratio (switch on ÷ switch off)** | **1.105 — no narrowing, slightly wider** | **0.99 — also no narrowing** |
| time spent invested, switch on | 69.3% | 69.3% |
| time spent invested, switch off | 96.3% | 96.3% |

All nineteen-draw figures above are the full population: one draw already on record plus the
eighteen this lab added across two follow-up runs.

**The headline: six industries gave the same answer as three.** The switch cut the average worst
fall from 54.2% to 25.1% — a cut of 29.0 points, almost identical to M0306's 30.4-point cut on the
three-industry book. But the SPREAD of those falls across the three coin tosses barely moved: 7.03
points with the switch on, 7.08 points with it off, a ratio of 0.99. That is not the "clearly
narrower" result the hypothesis asked for. If concentration were the ingredient driving M0306's
finding, spreading the same twenty slots over twice as many sectors should have made the switched-
on spread visibly tighter relative to the switched-off one. It did not. The point estimate sits
even closer to "no narrowing at all" than the three-industry book's own 1.105.

**The mechanism M0306 proposed still shows up, unmistakably, in the shape of the failures.** All
three switched-off copies had their single worst year in 2008 (falls of −31.6%, −26.0%, −33.6%).
All three switched-on copies had their worst year somewhere else entirely — 1998, 2000, and
2015 — with no two the same. That is exactly M0306's story: the switch removes 2008 as the shared
disaster and leaves each copy to its own private accident. That part of the mechanism replicates
cleanly at six industries. What does not replicate is the expectation that removing concentration
would shrink those private accidents enough to narrow the spread.

**The money side compressed more than simple time-out-of-market explains, at both concentrations.**
Dividing by the time each side spent invested, dilution alone predicts a ratio of about 0.72 for
money (0.693 time invested divided by 0.963) — identical at six industries to M0306's three-
industry book, because the switch reads only the market and does not know how many industries a
book holds. The measured money ratio here was 0.51, further below the dilution prediction than
M0306's 0.683 was. With three draws a side this could easily be noise rather than a real
difference between three and six industries.

## A technical note on how this result was recorded

While this method's six backtests were running, two other experiments in this lab were running
their own backtests in the same shared database at the same time. The first time this method's
results were saved, the run reported success and the six results were confirmed present and
correct. A few moments later, a fresh check of the same database showed this method's six results
gone, and a different experiment's six results occupying the exact same place in the record
instead — with no error reported by anything, on either side. Exactly how that happened is not
something this session could pin down: the database is built to make a saved result impossible to
overwrite or delete, so the loss most likely happened underneath that protection rather than
through it, for instance if the whole saved file was briefly replaced rather than one result being
changed. What is certain is what was observed directly: present, then gone, then someone else's in
its place. The method was re-run immediately afterward, the six backtests produced byte-identical
numbers to the first attempt (as they should, since nothing about the inputs changed), and this
second copy was checked again right away and confirmed to still be there. The numbers in this
analysis are from that confirmed, still-present copy. This is a real weakness in how the lab
currently handles several experiments running at once, separate from anything this method set out
to measure, and it is being flagged to the people running the other experiments so a result is not
silently lost without anyone noticing a second time.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

No. The hypothesis needed the six-industry switched-on/switched-off fall-spread ratio to sit
"clearly below" the three-industry book's 1.105, on the reasoning that a less concentrated book
leaves less idiosyncratic risk for the switch to fail to flatten. The measured ratio, 0.99, is
numerically a little below 1.105, but it is nowhere near the kind of drop that reasoning would
predict (something closer to the 0.72 dilution floor), and with only three draws a side it cannot
be told apart from "did not move at all." The first written-down expected failure — that three
draws a side would be too thin to read a direction — is the one that happened. The analysis
cannot rule in concentration as an ingredient, and it cannot cleanly rule it out either; what it
can say is that the "no narrowing" behaviour is not something that three industries alone
produced and six industries cures, at least not within what three draws a side can detect. The
second written-down failure mode — that six-of-roughly-ten-or-twelve industries overlap so much
that draws become near-duplicates of each other and understate true spread — cannot be
distinguished from the first on this data; both would look like "the spread came out small."

## Comparison with the parent

M0306 measured the three-industry book's switched-on/switched-off fall ratio at 1.105 from
nineteen draws a side, and separately noted that even seven draws understated the true width by
roughly a third. This method's three-draws-a-side figure of 0.99 is, if anything, consistent with
M0306's own warning: a short draw population is a floor, not a measurement, and three is thinner
than the seven M0306 already called too thin. The qualitative finding both methods share — the
switch removes the one year every copy would otherwise fall hardest in, and nothing stops the
rest from scattering — holds at both three and six industries, which is the one thing this run
adds with confidence: it is not a property of three-industry books specifically.

## My opinion:

This direction is not worth another method id on its own. A three-draw-a-side comparison was
always going to be too thin to resolve a question this subtle, and it was. Widening this run's own
population the way M0296 went from seven to nineteen would answer whether concentration matters,
but I do not think it is the highest-value use of the next method id, because M0306 already
established the practical rule that actually protects the owner — never read a gated worst-fall
gap under about 20 points as evidence — and that rule does not need to know whether the
underlying mechanism depends on concentration to be followed safely. What I would spend the next
id on instead is the sibling direction already running concurrently, checking whether the whole
finding transfers to the momentum-ranked books the lab actually considers buying, because that is
the result the rule gets applied to. If that comes back inconclusive too, widening the
concentration question would become worth the id; until then it would be spending a scarce
resource to sharpen a number the lab is not short of an answer for. The database collision
described above is the other thing worth acting on, separately from any method: it means every
number this lab produces while more than one experiment runs at once needs to be checked against
the database directly rather than trusted from a single run's own report, until someone fixes the
underlying cause.
methods.verdict: Not resolved: a less concentrated six-industry book cuts the worst fall by about the same 29 points as the three-industry one did, but three draws a side are too thin to say whether spreading the names over more sectors narrows how much the falls still vary from each other.

methods.name: Does the coin get wider as the book gets narrower
methods.hypothesis: A blind draw's spread scales with how few names it holds, because each pick is a larger share of a narrower book: M0307 measured the gated coin at width 20 and found funded CAGR spanning 32.0%-33.9% and max drawdown 20.8%-36.4% across six seeds plus the recorded seed-1 arm. If noise scales the way diluting independent picks predicts, the same six seeds at width 10 should span MORE than that on both axes and at width 40 should span LESS, with the ordering 10 > 20 > 40 holding on both return and drawdown and not just on one. Success is that ordering, stated as a usable scaling factor (for instance, how many points of spread one more halving or doubling of width buys or costs) that the audit M0307 queued can apply to a method of any width instead of assuming every book scatters like a twenty-name one. No arm here is trying to beat SPY and none is expected to be dev-eligible; the deliverable is the scaling rule, not a candidate.
methods.expectedFailure: The likeliest failure is the one flagged above: at width 40 each industry must fill up to 14 slots from hash-ordered followers that ``MIN_MEMBERS=5`` never guaranteed exist, so unfilled slots fall to SPY and the width-40 arms end up partly invested in the market itself rather than in fourteen independent picks per industry. If that happens the width-40 spread will narrow for the wrong reason — forced SPY exposure smoothing the result, not forty names diluting it — and the scaling read will overstate how much a genuinely wide, fully-filled book would narrow. The second failure is that the switch dominates again exactly as M0307 found for the width/switch dial: the SPY 200-day gate may compress every width's drawdown toward the same floor (time in cash in 2008 regardless of how many names are held), so the drawdown axis shows no width ordering at all while the return axis does — a bar that scales on one axis and not the other, which is harder to use than a single scaling factor. The third is that six seeds per width is still too few: M0307 itself warned that seven gated draws can be dominated by whichever single seed sits furthest out, and that risk applies at each of three widths independently, so a non-monotonic reading (20 wider than 10, say) may be seed-count noise rather than evidence against dilution. If any of the three lands, the fallback is to report the scaling as a loose direction and a known lower/upper bound rather than a precise factor, and to flag M0307's audit as still needing the ungated chassis swept the same way before any number here is applied to an ungated method.

methods.name: A sanity filter for the honest tape: find the reconstructed price series that make moves no real share makes, and re-read what the lab concluded without them
methods.hypothesis: M0309 showed the survivorship-check store can manufacture an edge. Its thin-stock book earned +22.3%/yr there against +12.7% on the dev store, cleared the luck bar at DSR 0.996, and the whole gap died at the first rung of a fixed-rank liveness bar, with the honest-tape no-bar curve carrying kurtosis 420.7 and skew +14.8 against 8.0-11.3 and -0.35 to -0.19 in the other eleven cells of the same grid. Measured this session: the sv store adds 450 symbols the dev store lacks entirely; 39 of them have at least one single-day close-to-close rise above 50% (98 days in total), 6 of them have 8 days that more than double, and CBE rises 0.5671 -> 27.7978 on 2004-02-10, a 49x print that is a split-reconstruction failure rather than a market event. Note the control: the most extreme prints in the whole store (MCIC at millions of dollars a share) are byte-identical in BOTH stores, so this is specifically about the EODHD-reconstructed additions, not about the tape in general. Every survivorship reading the lab owns -- the 102-pair stored grid, insight 149's roster measurement, and every  call since -- was taken on this tape, and  is the lab's designated check on whether an edge is real or an artefact of missing companies. This idea is tooling, not a strategy: build a detector for implausible reconstructed series (single-day moves beyond what a split-adjusted equity makes, prices that jump orders of magnitude and stay, series whose level is discontinuous at a split date), expose it as a store-level report and an optional exclusion list, then re-run  on the methods whose honest-tape conclusions the lab has already acted on and report which of them move. Success: the detector flags a small, auditable set and at least one recorded honest-tape conclusion changes sign or size enough to matter. Expected failure: the bad series are too few to shift any aggregate, in which case the finding is that M0309's book was uniquely exposed because it ranks ON thinness and everything else is safe -- which is itself worth knowing, and would restore confidence in every other survivorship reading.
