methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-23

test analysis content
methods.verdict: test dry run

methods.name: Does the dose lesson generalise? A second pick filter at depth, on a host whose blind draws already beat the market
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0302 (calm filter at depth, gate-off); selection rule derived from M0232's measured 2009-2015 record
methods.hypothesis: M0302 found two things at once. The calm filter is real at depth -- at three fifths it beat all four blind draws on the worst fall by 12.6 points on dev and 7.4 on the survivorship-check store, where at a quarter it had sat inside its own blind spread and been beaten by one draw. And it is useless anyway, because in 2009-2015 both filtered arms fell behind SPY on both stores (they grew 16.2%/12.6% a year on dev against SPY's 16.6%, so a shortfall and not a loss) while all four blind draws did not, and across all sixteen coin-versus-filter pairings the coin won every time. This idea tests whether the DOSE lesson generalises to a second filter, holding the chassis fixed: same always-invested host, same two deep rungs, four blind draws at the deepest rung, and a mirror arm at the deep rung too -- the gap M0302 left, since it could only show its mirror at a quarter, inherited from its parent. THE SELECTION RULE IS THE POINT, and it was learned by measuring. The obvious candidate was proximity to the 52-week high, chosen because it favours winning companies rather than sleepy ones and so looked unlikely to lag a long rise. Measured here with lab survivorship M0232 --no-journal, all six of its variants fall behind SPY in 2009-2015 on BOTH stores by 4.90 to 9.72 points a year -- far worse than the calm filter's 0.42 to 4.57 -- so it is disqualified. The reason matters more than the disqualification: M0232-PLC1, its own placebo, lags by 5.74 and 4.90 points, so in that family the shortfall belongs to the host book and not to the filter at all. That is the opposite of M0302, where every blind draw BEAT SPY in 2009-2015 (+0.03 to +6.56 on dev) and only the filtered arms lagged, which is precisely what let M0302 blame calmness itself. So the rule for this follow-up: pick a filter whose host's NO-OPINION arms already beat SPY in 2009-2015 on both stores, verified before the method file is written, because otherwise a filter's shortfall cannot be separated from its host's and the experiment answers nothing. M0197's gate-off book satisfies this and is the default host. Success: the deep rung beats all four blind draws on the worst fall AND holds a non-negative 2009-2015 edge on both stores. The honest expectation is that it buys protection and pays for it in the same era, because calmness in a fall and participation in a rise may be one property with the sign flipped for every filter and not only this one -- in which case the finding is that the dose lesson generalises while the bull-market tax is unavoidable, and the pick-filter-as-protection line closes for good.

methods.name: How much jumpiness must a book throw out before the honest tape pays it back? The strength ladder, with error bars this time
methods.hypothesis: M0303 killed the general claim that a screen built for safety reads better once the dead companies are added back: its two declared safety screens finished at opposite ends of the table, 11.8 points apart, and four identical blind draws on the same host spread 7.71 points, wider than the 2.37-point ladder the idea was built on. But two rules in that twelve-version population escape the draws' range on the worst fall AND earn more a year, and both throw away a lot of jumpy names: drop the jumpiest quarter by 60-day realised volatility (fall 28.2% to 21.1%, a 7.10 point gain, and +0.59 points a year, with the luck score rising 0.945 to 0.969 and the 2009-2015 lead the only one of six to improve on the honest tape) and M0293-HI50, drop the jumpiest half by market beta (fall 25.2% to 19.6%, +0.68 points a year). With the switch off, M0293-HI25-NOSW also clears the gate-off draws on the fall at -2.70 against a floor of +0.51, though it loses 0.79 points a year. Three data points, all jumpiness, all at a serious dose; the gentle rungs clear nothing. THE FLAW THIS MUST FIX: those are two different jumpiness measures at two different strengths, so 'a dose effect' is not yet earned. Hold the measure fixed and move only the strength. On the identical M0197-Y20-SW host at Gotrade's real fees, drop 25%, 50% and 65% of the pool by 60-day realised volatility, and read every rung on the dev store and the survivorship-check store together. THE REQUIREMENT THAT MAKES THIS WORTH AN ID: each rung carries its own error bar, because M0303's whole finding is that this meter has one and nobody had measured it. Register blind draws at the SAME strength as each rung -- a blind draw dropping half is not the control for a real screen dropping a quarter, since how much you throw away is itself part of the effect. Six variants will not hold three strengths plus their draws, so either run two strengths with two draws each plus the no-drop reference, or run three strengths and add the draws by amendment. Success: the gain in worst fall grows monotonically with strength, and the top rung sits outside its own same-strength draws on both the fall and the return. Failure, likelier and still worth the id: the gain does not grow with strength, or the top rung sits inside its own draws, in which case the two survivors were two lucky draws out of the roughly three in ten that look better on the honest tape by chance, and the lab should close the book on survivorship gaps as evidence about any single strategy.

methods.name: Widen the six-industry draw population to a size that can actually settle whether concentration matters
methods.hypothesis: Three draws a side could not tell whether spreading a book over six industries instead of three changes how much the safety switch's worst-fall spread narrows; the measured ratio (about 0.99) was close to the three-industry book's 1.105 but the sample is too thin to trust. Widening the six-industry population the way the three-industry one was widened -- more seeds on both the switch-on and switch-off sides -- would let the comparison be read with a real error bar instead of a single noisy point.

insights.title: Volatility scaling buys drawdown at a near-linear price in return
insights.body: Scaling top-20 momentum to a 10-12% own-volatility target cut max DD from 22% to 11-13% but also CAGR from 16% to 6-7.6%, because a ~22%-vol book is held at about half exposure all the time, not just in crashes. The frontier passes near DD 13% at SPY's CAGR. To beat SPY under DD 15% we need more return per unit of risk, or de-risking that triggers only in dangerous regimes.

insights.title: Delisted stocks and fundamentals
insights.body: The store has no delisted names (survivorship makes stock results optimistic) and no fundamentals, so value, quality, profitability and earnings-surprise strategies, the best-documented factors after momentum, cannot be tested. A point-in-time source such as Sharadar or a CRSP/Compustat-like feed would unlock them and make every stock result more honest.

insights.title: The 15% max-DD bar over 1996-2015 includes two -50% crashes
insights.body: The dev window contains the 2000-02 and 2008-09 bear markets. Any strategy with meaningful equity exposure must sidestep most of both to stay under 15%, so the gate rewards crash avoidance above everything else. Expect winners to be regime-switching or heavily de-risked designs, and expect their test-window (2015-2026, one sharp 2020 crash) behaviour to differ.

insights.title: Weekly risk checks with monthly re-ranking
insights.body: M0001's weekly variant re-ranked and re-scaled together, which more than doubled turnover and cut PF to 1.49. A rule set that re-ranks monthly but re-scales exposure weekly would test whether faster risk control helps without the whipsaw cost. That needs a new TradeRules cadence split (rank cadence vs resize cadence).

insights.title: M0005 promoted to the paper roster as FND
insights.body:
Promoted to the paper roster as `FND`.

Variant: `M0005-ALL`. Roster object: `FUNDAMENTAL`. Frozen spec digest: `4a9dacc37478bf4d17b3ba35cbebd9e0c3f8759f122c4596f7cd9d076d8ef530`.

The roster row is `status='active'` with no `paper_start`: the next paper night freezes the spec and starts its own clock, so the paper record begins at the promotion and claims nothing earlier. `backtest.registry.REGISTRY` was not appended to -- a promoted method reaches the roster through the roster's own resolver, so the lab's multiple-testing count is unchanged by this.

insights.title: FND, a company-fundamentals picker, now trades on paper, and paper is its real test
insights.body:
Most strategies Sera has tried pick stocks by how their price has moved. This one is different: each month it picks the 20 big US companies whose own reports look best. It favours companies that are cheap next to what they own, earn well on their money, make healthy profits on what they sell, and recently beat what was expected of their earnings. Those four signals have a long track record in finance research.

**Why it went to paper even though the history test marked it "rejected".** The company reports Sera can read only start in 2015. The history test runs from 1996 to 2015, so for 19 of those 20 years the strategy had nothing to go on and just sat in cash. That's why it "failed": it never really got to play. The idea wasn't proven wrong. It was never tested.

Waiting is the only fair test left. From here on, FND trades every night with pretend money, its rules are locked, and nothing before its first night counts. That's also why it isn't a candidate for real money: it hasn't earned it yet.

**What to watch:** month by month, does it keep up with or beat SPY, and how far does it fall in a bad month? A few good months could be luck. A year of steady results would mean something.

insights.title: A slow signal does not get better by checking it more often
insights.body:
The lab has a stock picker that cuts its own exposure when the market gets choppy. It measures choppiness over the past three months. We wondered whether checking that measure weekly instead of monthly would catch crashes faster, so we built the ability to pick stocks on one schedule and set exposure on another, and tried every combination.

Checking weekly did not help. It made things slightly worse. The reason is simple once you see it: a three-month average barely moves in a week. Reading it every Monday gives back almost the same number it gave a month ago, so the faster schedule learns nothing new. What it does do is create four times as many chances to shuffle the book around that same unchanged number, and each shuffle costs a little. The worst fall improved by less than one point, from 11.0 percent to 10.3 percent, while yearly growth dropped from 6.1 percent to 4.8 percent. We paid more than we got.

The cleanest proof sits in the version with the market-trend filter switched off. Measured monthly and measured weekly, it scored identically. With nothing else in front of it, re-reading the choppiness number weekly changed literally nothing.

The useful lesson is a rule of thumb for everything the lab builds next. How often it is worth re-checking something is decided by how fast that something actually moves, not by how often we are willing to trade. Pair a three-month measure with a monthly schedule. If we want a genuinely faster reaction, we need a measure that genuinely moves faster, such as one built from the last few weeks rather than the last few months.

One thing did come out of it worth keeping. Splitting the two schedules let us settle an old question: the heavy trading in the weekly version came almost entirely from re-choosing which stocks to hold, not from adjusting how much to hold. Re-choosing costs about eight times as much trading as re-sizing. That is now a measured fact rather than a guess.

insights.title: Spreading money more cleverly is not the same as holding less of it
insights.body: We took the stock picker that buys the twenty strongest risers and, instead of splitting the money evenly between them, worked out from a year of daily prices which mix of those same twenty moves around the least, and bought that mix. It worked as mathematics and failed as safety. The month-to-month wobble of the account dropped by about a fifth. The worst fall, which is the thing the owner actually cares about and the thing our rules measure, dropped from 22.2% to 21.6% - almost nothing - while the yearly rate of return fell from 16.2% to 13.7%. We paid two and a half points of return for half a point of safety. The lesson is that wobble and worst fall are two different risks and a clever split only touches the first one. An ordinary month is made of twenty stocks disagreeing with each other, and a clever split smooths that out. A bad month is made of twenty stocks all falling together, and then there is no clever split, because they were all the same bet to begin with. The proof is the version we ran with the safety switch turned off: it fell 54% at its worst and lost 41% in 2008, slightly worse than just owning the market through the crash. The earlier method that simply held half its money in cash fell 18% in the same test. Holding less protects you. Holding the same amount, arranged more intelligently, does not. What to do about it: stop trying weighting schemes inside a single-theme book. Risk parity and its cousins would hit the same wall for the same reason. Safety in this kind of portfolio has to come from owning less of it at the right moments, or from owning something genuinely different, not from rearranging the same bet.

insights.title: The crash that keeps blocking us is 2006, and our safety switch never saw it
insights.body: Every version of the strongest-risers picker that uses the market safety switch - hold stocks while the market is above its 200-day average, otherwise sit in cash - has its worst moment in the same five months: March to August 2006. Not the dot-com bust, not 2008. In those five months the market itself fell at worst 7.6% and never once dipped below its 200-day average, so the safety switch stayed in the on position the entire time and the book rode it all the way down, losing about 18%. What crashed in 2006 was not the market. It was the theme: the energy, materials and emerging-market names that had all climbed smoothly for a year unwound together in May. This matters because it reframes the problem. We have been trying to make the book safer in general, when what actually blocks us is one specific kind of event that our one safety switch is blind to by construction - a crash in what we own while the market around it is fine. Worse, the clever-split experiment made 2006 worse rather than better, because the optimiser leans toward whatever has been calmest over the past year, and in 2006 the calmest names were exactly the smooth one-way climbers that broke hardest. A year of quiet upward drift looks like safety to the arithmetic and is in truth a crowded trade. What to do about it: give the book a second safety switch that watches the book itself rather than the market. When the account is more than some distance below its own previous high, cut back until it recovers. That is pointed straight at the event that keeps stopping us, and unlike holding permanent cash it costs nothing in the calm years. It is queued as the next trial.

insights.title: Taking the market's move out of a stock's score is the cheapest safety we have bought so far
insights.body:
Until now, every way we found to make the strategy fall less has cost about as much return as it saved. Shrinking positions when markets get jumpy cut the worst fall from 22% to 13%, and it cut the yearly return from 16% to 8% doing it - roughly one point of return for one point of safety.

The market-adjusted picker is the first exception. Before ranking stocks on how much they rose over the past year, it subtracts the part of each rise that the whole market explains, and ranks on what is left - the company's own story. It stays just as fully invested as before, buys the same number of names, and still turned a 22.2% worst fall into a 19.6% one while giving up only 1.2 points of yearly return. That is about half price.

Why it works: a stock that rose mostly because the market rose is a bet on the market, not on the company. A book full of those bets is a leveraged market bet in disguise, and it falls hardest exactly when the market turns. Removing that part of the score leaves a book of genuine company winners that does not all move together.

What to do about it: this is a better starting point, not a finished strategy, because 19.6% is still well over the 15% limit. The right next move is to put our existing position-shrinking overlay on top of this better book rather than on the old one - we would be spending a 15% yearly return down to about 11% instead of spending a 16% one down to 8%. That is the first combination where the arithmetic reaches the limit with something left over for the owner.

insights.title: A buy-only strategy's crash is the market's crash, so a cleverer stock score cannot prevent it
insights.body:
The research papers behind this experiment report that market-adjusted momentum largely cures the sudden collapses that plague momentum strategies. We tested that claim directly by removing our market-trend safety switch and letting the stock score fend for itself. It fell 51% from its peak and lost 34% in 2008 - no better than the plain version.

The reason is a mismatch we should remember. Those papers study a portfolio that buys winners and sells losers short at the same time. Its collapses really are a momentum-specific event: after a bad market the losers it is short are the jumpy, high-market-sensitivity names, and when the market rebounds those explode upward and the short side blows up. We never sell short. We only buy. So our collapses are simply the market's collapses, arriving through the stocks we hold, and no improvement to how we choose stocks can remove them.

What to do about it: keep treating the market-trend switch - being in cash when the market is below its long-term average - as the one thing that controls our worst falls, and treat every stock-scoring idea as a way to earn more while invested, never as a substitute for it. Also, when a paper promises crash protection, check first whether it is protecting the short side we do not have. Usefully, the test also showed where our remaining risk actually sits: with the switch on, 2001, 2002 and 2008 were all flat, and the deepest fall of the whole twenty years came from one fast shock in the autumn of 1998 that the switch reacted to too late.

insights.title: The falls that hurt this strategy happen in calm markets, not crashes
insights.body:
A momentum strategy that buys the twenty strongest stocks and sits in cash when the market is below its 200-day average has almost no bad years. Over 1996-2015 its worst calendar year was about minus three percent, and 2001, 2002 and 2008 came out flat, because it was in cash through those crashes.

Its losses come from somewhere else entirely. The four worst spells were March to August 2006, the summer of 1998, the spring of 2010 and the autumn of 2011. In every one of them the market was fine and the particular stocks the strategy had crowded into reversed. Spring 2006 is the clearest: commodity and emerging-market names had run hard, the market stayed comfortably above its 200-day average so the cash switch never tripped, and the holdings unwound anyway.

This matters because the usual safety device is a brake tied to how much the holdings have been bouncing around lately. That brake cannot help here. The jump in bounciness and the loss are the same event, and a three-month measurement needs weeks to notice it, so the brake comes on after the money is gone. It protected against long bad stretches, which is real, and did nothing about sharp ones.

What to do about it: stop trying to predict these falls from past bounciness and react to the fall itself. A brake that watches whether the stocks currently held are below their own recent high can move on day one of a reversal instead of six weeks in. That is the next thing worth testing.

insights.title: Turning a strategy down is not the same as making it safer, and the lab keeps proving it
insights.body:
The lab has now run three versions of the same experiment: take the strongest stock picker it has, and shrink how much money it puts to work when things look risky. The unshrunk picker grew 16.2 percent a year and fell 22.2 percent at its worst. Shrinking it all the time gave 7.6 percent and 12.9 percent. Shrinking it only when the holdings were unusually jumpy gave 12.6 percent and 18.4 percent.

Line those up against how much money each one actually kept in stocks on an average day, and the picture is stark. Every single version gave up roughly the same amount of fall for each unit of money it put at work: around thirty-five, in those units, whether it braked hard, softly, cleverly, or not at all. The brake was not removing risk. It was turning the whole thing down, and return and risk came down together in step.

The one real gain is smaller and worth keeping: braking only when the holdings are jumpy for themselves earns more per unit of money at work than braking all the time, about 24 against 21 in the same units. A well-aimed brake is better than a permanent one. It is just a refinement on a dial, not an escape from it.

The risk this creates for the lab is spending run after run on that dial. Because the trade is so close to a straight line, where any setting lands can now be read off in advance, and the honest answer is that no setting of it produces a strategy that is better rather than smaller. The remaining problem is the quality of the stock picking itself, not what is done with the picks afterwards.

insights.title: The lab's own searching is raising the bar it has to clear
insights.body:
Before any strategy is allowed near real money, the lab asks how likely its result is to be genuine rather than the best of many lucky tries. The more things have been tried, the better a result has to be. That count has now reached eighty-five, and the bar has moved with it.

Working from where this run landed, a strategy of this shape now needs a reward-per-unit-of-wobble score of about one a year to clear the bar. The best this lab has ever recorded is 0.89, from the plain momentum picker with no brake on it. This run's best was 0.87. Everything tried so far sits just under the line, and roughly every seventy further trials pushes the line a little further away.

The important part is where that score does not come from. Across this whole family of experiments the score barely moved: 0.89 with no brake, 0.81 braked all the time, 0.87 braked only in jumpy spells. Adjusting how much money is at work changes the return and the swings together and leaves their ratio alone. So no amount of further work on brakes, targets or triggers will clear this bar.

What will clear it is picking better stocks: a signal that earns more for the risk it takes. That points the next runs at the queued work on momentum measured against what the market did anyway, and on weighting holdings by how they move together rather than equally. It also argues for being sparing with trials, because every one spent raises the bar for the ones after it.

insights.title: Sera 20261006-1137: three ways to make a winner safe, and only changing what we buy worked
insights.body:
Three sessions ran side by side, each trying a different way to make the same winning
strategy safe enough to use. The strategy is the one that keeps coming back: buy the twenty
stocks that rose most over the past year, refresh the list monthly, and sit in cash whenever
the market itself is below its long-run average. It makes about 16% a year against the
market's 8%. It has one flaw, and the whole lab is now organised around that flaw: at its
worst it fell 22% from a peak, and our limit is 15%.

There are only three places you can intervene. You can change how much you hold and when
(braking). You can change how the money is split between the names you hold (weighting). Or
you can change which names you pick in the first place (the score). This batch tried one of
each, deliberately, so that a failure would tell us something a success could not.

**Braking and weighting both failed, and failed for the same reason.** The first session
braked only when the basket itself turned jumpy, leaving it fully invested in calm spells.
The second kept the same twenty names and the same full investment, but worked out from the
past year of prices which mix of them moves together least, and held that mix instead of
equal amounts. Both beat the market comfortably. Neither got the worst fall below 17%.

The second session produced the cleanest evidence of the batch. Its clever splitting did
exactly what it promised: the day-to-day wobble dropped by almost a fifth, with every penny
still invested. The worst fall barely moved, from 22% to 21.6%. **Wobble and worst fall are
not the same risk**, and we have now paid to learn that in the only way that counts. The
first session found the matching fact from the other side: across all nine braked versions
we have ever run, the worst fall shrinks in exact proportion to how much you were holding.
Turning the strategy down does not make it safer. It just makes it smaller, and the return
goes down by the same proportion.

**Both sessions then independently found the same culprit, which nobody was looking for.**
The falls that block us are not the crashes. 2001, 2002 and 2008 are quiet in these results,
because the market was below its average and we were in cash, exactly as designed. The damage
is done in March to August 2006, in August 1998, and in the spring of 2010 and 2011 — stretches
where the market was calm, above its average, never triggered our safety switch, and our basket
of recent winners fell apart anyway. In 2006 the market fell at most 8% and never broke its
average, while the basket lost about 18%. These are not market crashes. They are the crowd
getting out of last year's winners all at once. **Our one safety switch watches the market, and
this risk is not in the market.** That is the single most useful thing this batch found.

**The third session is the one that worked, and it worked by changing the score.** Instead of
ranking stocks on how much they rose, it ranked them on how much they rose *after taking out
the part the whole market explains* — the stock's own story, with the market's tide removed.
Nothing else changed: same number of names, same monthly refresh, same safety switch, same
full investment. It returned 15% a year against the market's 8% at a worst fall of 19.6%, and
that is the best return-per-unit-of-fall this lab has ever recorded, in a brand new family
that went straight to the top on its first attempt. It is still 4.6 points outside the limit,
so it is not usable. But it is the only thing in three batches that improved the trade-off
rather than sliding along it. One footnote worth keeping: the textbook refinement of this
idea, which rescales each stock's score by how erratic it is, made things worse every time.
The plain version won.

**So: changing what we buy is alive. Changing how much we hold, or how we split it, is dead.**
We should stop spending runs on risk overlays. Three batches have now established that they
move the strategy along a fixed line rather than lifting it off that line.

**A new obstacle has appeared, and it is one we create ourselves.** Every result is discounted
for how many things we have tried — 85 experiments now — because the more ideas you test, the
likelier it is that the best one is luck. We are close to the point where the remaining gap is
this discount rather than the drawdown. On this batch's evidence it needs a strategy whose
quality score reaches about 1.0; the market-adjusted scorer reached 0.94, the best we have ever
had and better than the 0.89 one session believed was our ceiling. It is reachable, but only
by a genuinely better score. No amount of risk management will get there, because risk
management does not move that number at all. **The honest reading is that our own searching is
raising the bar we have to clear, and only better ideas, not better safety nets, can clear it.**

**What would unlock the most.** We do not need new data to attack the real obstacle; we need a
second safety switch that watches our own basket instead of the market. Both failing sessions
converged on the same design without talking to each other: brake when the basket itself is
down from its own recent peak, rather than when it looks jumpy. The reason braking on jumpiness
fails is now understood — jumpiness arrives *with* the fall, not before it, so the brake is
still off while the loss is being made. A basket's distance below its own high is visible
immediately. Beyond that, the thing we genuinely lack is any direct measure of how crowded a
trade has become, which is what actually causes these unwinds; nothing in our data sees it.

**What the next batch should try.** First, the market-adjusted scorer combined with modest
braking — this is the one combination whose arithmetic plausibly closes, because it starts from
a better trade-off than anything else we have, and the braking line it would slide down crosses
our limit while still beating the market. Second, the own-basket brake, which two sessions
recommended independently and which attacks the 2006-style unwind directly. Third, one cheap
run holding 30, 40 and 50 names instead of 20: simply holding more names has cut the worst fall
from 33% to 20% as we widened from 5 to 20, and we have never looked past 20. Spreading wider
may be a better brake than any of our clever ones, and it costs one run to find out.

No test-window look was spent this batch. Our one chance to check against unseen data is still
untouched, which is right, because nothing yet deserves it.

insights.title: A stop-loss on a momentum strategy sells at the bottom of the bounce
insights.body: We tried cutting back the stock-picking strategy whenever the stocks it held had fallen 8% from their recent best, getting down to a quarter invested by a 16% fall. It made things worse. Checked every week, the worst fall grew from 22% to 30%, and yearly return dropped from about 16% to about 10%. The reason is that the falls in these winning stocks are usually sharp dips that recover within weeks: the brake sold after the damage was done and bought back only after half the recovery had already happened, locking in a loss every time. Lesson: for this kind of strategy, reacting to losses after they happen is a cost, not a protection. Safety has to come from what we hold, not from when we run away.

insights.title: Checking risk weekly quietly re-runs the market switch too
insights.body: When a strategy keeps its monthly stock picks but adjusts how much it holds every week, the weekly check also re-asks whether the market is above its long-term average. If the market dips below for a single week, everything is sold and not bought back until the next month. That adds extra sell-low trips we never meant to test. A control test in this run that should have done almost nothing did just as badly as the real brake, which points at this hidden effect. Every 'check risk weekly' result so far mixes the two, so we should measure the weekly check by itself before trusting any of them.

insights.title: A safety brake that looks at last month, not last quarter, finally kept a winning strategy inside the limit
insights.body: We took the best stock-picking strategy we have and added a brake: when its stocks have been swinging hard, it holds less of them and keeps the rest in cash. With the brake judging the swings over the past three months, the strategy still fell 15.4% at its worst, just over the 15% limit. Judging them over only the past month, the worst fall dropped to 14.1% and the yearly return went up, from 9.3% to 10.8% (SPY made 7.9%). The reason is timing. The fall that always hurts is the sudden 1998 shock, which came after a calm spring. A three-month reading still remembered the calm and kept the strategy fully loaded; a one-month reading saw the jitters of July and cut back before August. It also relaxes faster after a storm, so the money gets back to work sooner. This is the first strategy in the lab to pass all four of the owner's rules on 20 years of history. It is not promoted yet, because the lab's own luck check (how likely this is real after 90 tries) reads 0.90, not the 0.95 it needs.

insights.title: Stocks near their yearly high fall less, but they also stop the strategy from earning
insights.body: We tried picking the stocks trading closest to their highest price of the past year, instead of the ones that rose most. The worst fall shrank (to between 15.6% and 18%, against about 20% for our best stock-picker), which supports the idea that crashes come from stocks that bounced up from far below their high. But yearly return fell from about 15% to 8-10%, barely above simply holding the S&P 500's 7.9%. In strong markets dozens of stocks sit right at their high, so ranking on it stops telling strong stocks from merely steady ones. The lesson: closeness to the high is better used to rule stocks out than to pick them. Next we keep the best picker and only let it choose among stocks near their high.

insights.title: Every new try makes the next winner harder to trust
insights.body: The best result so far missed only one bar: the luck check, which asks whether a result could simply be the best of many attempts. Each experiment the lab runs raises that bar a little, because more tries mean more chances to get lucky. So the way to pass is not to keep turning dials on the same strategy, which adds tries and gains little, but to test one clear question at a time with as few versions as possible. Future experiments on this strategy should use one or two versions, not five.

insights.title: Sera 20261006-2027: the first all-rules pass, held back only by the luck test
insights.body:
This batch tried the three ideas the last batch asked for, and for the first time one strategy
passed every rule the owner set on the twenty years of history we test on. It is not usable yet,
and the reason is now the most important thing to understand about this lab.

**The one that worked.** Start from the best stock picker we had: each month, buy the twenty
stocks whose rise over the past year owes the most to their own story rather than to the market
lifting everything, and sit in cash when the market is below its long-run average. On its own it
made 15% a year but fell 19.6% at its worst, past our 15% limit. This session added a brake: when
the basket has been swinging wildly over the past month, hold less of it. Every earlier brake we
tried looked at the last three months and reacted too late, after the damage was done. Looking at
only the last month reacts in time. The result: 10.8% a year against the market's 7.9%, a worst
fall of 14.1%, gains about twice the size of losses, and nearly 1,600 trades. That clears the
return rule, the fall rule, the gains-to-losses rule and the enough-trades rule, all at once.
A gentler setting of the same brake passed too, but beat the market by only a hair.

**Why it still is not allowed near money.** Before anything is promoted, the lab asks how likely
it is that a result this good is the luckiest of all the things we have tried, rather than a
real edge. We have now tried a hundred variations. Against that count, this strategy scores 0.90
on a scale where we require 0.95. It is close, and it is the closest thing to a genuine pass we
have ever had, but the rule exists precisely so that we do not fool ourselves on the hundredth try.
Every further experiment raises that bar a little more, so each next run has to be chosen for
what it can teach, not fired off in hope.

**The brake on our own losses made things worse.** The second session cut back whenever the stocks
it held fell 8%. Two sessions last batch had recommended exactly this, and it failed badly. Checked
every week, the worst fall grew from 22% to 30%. The reason is that dips in this kind of strategy
usually snap back within days: the brake sold near the bottom, missed the rebound, then bought
back higher. Checked every month, it hardly ever fired. Selling because you are down is the
classic stop-loss, and on a strategy built on trends that recover, it sells at the worst moment.

**Stocks near their yearly high are calmer but earn less.** The third session tried a different way
of choosing stocks altogether, picking the ones trading closest to their highest price of the past
year, an idea from a well-known 2004 finance paper. It was a genuinely good brake: the worst fall
dropped to 15.6%, barely over the limit, without holding any cash. But the return dropped to
roughly what the market makes, so there was nothing left to show for the extra safety. Good at
falling less, poor at making money.

**What looks alive.** Picking stocks on their own story, with the market's tide removed, is now
clearly our best engine, and a fast one-month brake is the first brake that has ever paid its way.
Together they made the lab's first all-rules pass. "Near the yearly high" is useful as a filter on
which stocks to consider, even though it is a poor way to choose among them.

**What looks dead.** Stop-loss style braking on our own losses. Slow, three-month volatility
brakes. Re-checking risk every week, which also turned out to re-run the market-trend switch more
often than intended and caused extra whipsaw.

**What would unlock the most.** Nothing new in data this time. The obstacle is the luck test, and
only two things move it: a stronger result, or fewer wasted tries. More history would help most of
all, because a longer track record makes any real edge easier to tell apart from luck.

**What the next batch should try.** First, the winning combination with a still faster brake,
reading the last two weeks instead of the last month, to see whether reacting sooner lifts return
without giving back safety. Second, the market-adjusted picker restricted to stocks near their
yearly high, so the calm-stocks filter supplies the safety and the strong picker supplies the
return. Third, rather than adding more variations of the same picker, look for a genuinely
different source of return that could be blended with it, because two independent edges score
better on the luck test than one edge tuned many times.

No look at the held-back test years was spent. Nothing qualified, because the luck test blocked
the one strategy that passed everything else, which is exactly what that test is for.

insights.title: An automatic sell order under each stock hurts a hold-for-months momentum strategy
insights.body: We gave the best stock-picking book a safety exit: sell any stock that falls 15%, 20% or 25% below what we paid. It made the worst fall no smaller (and at 20% and 25%, slightly bigger) and cost up to 2.4 points of return a year. The reason is that this book's big falls are the whole market falling together, not one stock collapsing. On those days many safety exits fire at once, often at a gap-down opening price, so the selling happens near the bottom, and the money sits in cash until next month's re-pick while prices bounce back. One stock collapsing on its own costs the book little, because each stock is only 5% of the money. For the owner: for the monthly methods, a resting Stop Sell under each holding is not worth placing; the brake that holds less when the whole basket gets jumpy is what actually protects them.

insights.title: Raw residual momentum under an own-volatility target (M0007-N20-RAW + M0001 overlay) starts paper trading as RM-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name RM-FR, taking the place of FND. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: Checking the momentum book every week instead of every month costs nothing
insights.body: We ran the best stock-picking book with a weekly check that keeps the same monthly list but nudges every holding back to an equal share each week. It came out the same as checking once a month: about 15% a year either way, the same worst fall and the same luck score. So a weekly signal can be added to this book without paying extra in costs or lost return, which opens the door to ideas that need to react faster than once a month. The weekly safety exit we were testing at the same time did not work: selling a falling stock and buying it back a week later during a market-wide drop just sold it again lower.

insights.title: A brake that checks weekly how wildly the stocks swing makes the best book safer at no cost
insights.body: The braked momentum book on paper decides once a month how much to hold, based on how wildly its stocks swung over the past month. Checking that same brake every week, while still picking the stocks once a month, cut its worst fall from 14% to 12% with almost no loss of return, and only 4 more trades in 20 years. It works because it trims all holdings a little as the swings grow, before most of a fall, and adds back as they calm, without selling any particular stock. Everything that sold after prices fell (safety exits under each stock, a brake on the whole basket, a weekly market switch) did worse, because it sold near the bottom and missed the rebound. For the owner: a weekly check of this kind is worth doing; it means adjusting how much you hold once a week, not picking new stocks.

insights.title: RM's book with its volatility brake re-read every week starts paper trading as RMW-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name RMW-FR, taking the place of RM-FR. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: The luck bar moved to 0.90 and the drawdown bar to 20%: three trials now clear the gate
insights.body:
The two bars you set moved today, and the gate admits something for the first time. This note records the change and what it did. It supersedes the 2026-10-06 batch summary below it, which quoted the luck bar as 0.95 — correct on the day it was written, and kept as written.

**What changed.** On your instruction, the luck bar went from 0.95 to 0.90 and the drawdown limit from 15% to 20%. Both are your dials and both moved by your call, not by anything the lab inferred. A third lever was built and deliberately not pulled: how the luck test counts how many things we have tried. That count is now an inspectable policy with its evidence attached, left at its existing setting — every one of the 110 trial runs counted as an independent try. The measured alternatives are on record (23 if you count each idea once, about 2 if you count by how much the trials actually overlap), so the lever can be moved later as a deliberate decision rather than a silent one.

**What it did.** Two methods moved from rejected to eligible, and exactly three trials now clear every rule at once: M0020-W-NOSTOP, M0022-W-TV14 and M0022-W-TV16 — the three highest-MAR books in the lab. Before today, nothing could ever reach eligible, so the promotion path was unreachable and the test window had never been spent. It still has not been: no held-back test year was looked at in making this change.

**What it did not do.** The strategy the last summary was about — the market-adjusted picker with the one-month brake, M0011's best variant — is still blocked. It is closer than that summary said, and blocked by a different margin than it claimed. Its recorded score was 0.8974 when it was judged against 90 tries. Re-scored today against 110 tries and the 0.90 bar, it reads **0.8844**, and the only rule it misses is the luck test. So the conclusion in the older note stands even though its arithmetic no longer does: that strategy is not usable, and nothing became usable by accident while the page said otherwise.

**Older verdicts are now comparable.** Until today a trial's luck score was frozen at the number of tries in force on the day it ran, so two trials judged months apart were measured against different bars and could not be ranked honestly. Every verdict is now re-derived at the current count when it is read, which is why several recorded scores above differ from what the database holds. The recorded values are untouched — all 110 of them — and are quoted with the count they were taken at whenever the subject is what the database holds.

**Half the lab had never been luck-tested.** 54 of the 110 trials were imported without the inputs the luck test needs, so they paid the full cost of being counted as tries while receiving no verdict in return — ineligible by a gap in the data rather than on merit. Their inputs have now been recovered and they have real verdicts. One of them, F9-SPY200M70-MOM30, passes every one of your conditions at the new 20% limit; on the luck test it reads 0.8567 and does not clear the bar. It stays out — but now on a test it received rather than on a missing number. Recovering those inputs did not change how many tries the lab counts, so it did not raise the bar for anything else.

**The margin to watch.** M0022-W-TV16 clears the luck bar by 0.016. On today's rate of exploration it would fall back below the bar after roughly 33 more trial runs. The lab now warns when the best luck-only candidate is within 0.03 of the bar and names the count that would sink it, so the next version of this squeeze is visible before it happens rather than 110 trials after.

insights.title: Residual momentum: rank on market-model residual returns, not total returns starts paper trading as RAW-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name RAW-FR. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: Momentum, own-vol scaling only in high-vol regimes (asymmetric scale) starts paper trading as MOM-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name MOM-FR, taking the place of F4-MOM12-N20-TREND-FR. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: Minimum-variance weighting of the momentum book starts paper trading as MVW-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name MVW-FR, taking the place of F1-SPY-SMA200-M-FR. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: Half the companies in the index before 2002 are missing from our prices
insights.body:
Half of the companies that were in the index before 2002 are simply not in our price data, and we had never measured how big that hole was until today. It is big: of the 1,041 companies that belonged to the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 at some point in our test years, 522 have no prices at all. In 1996 we can price 236 of the 487 companies that were actually in the index. By 2015 that is 409 of 527.

The reason is mundane. Our prices come from a free source, and free sources keep the companies that still exist. When a company is bought, merged away or goes bankrupt, it stops being a customer of anyone and quietly disappears from the record. Thirty-two of our missing names end in the letter Q, which is the marker American exchanges put on a company that has filed for bankruptcy.

Why this should worry a reader of our results: a method that buys last year's winners would, in real life, sometimes have bought a company that went on to collapse. Our data cannot show us that mistake, because the collapsed company is not in it. Every past result we publish is therefore measured on a field of survivors, and the further back in time you look, the more the losers have been quietly swept off it.

We checked today whether that is what produces our good results, and the answer appears to be no. If the missing bankruptcies were flattering us, our methods should look best in the oldest years, where the data is worst. They do not. Our books look weakest in 1996 to 2001, where only half the index is priced, and strongest in 2002 to 2008, where coverage is middling. That is the opposite of what the flattery story predicts.

This is not proof that the hole is harmless. Data coverage improves steadily with time, so we cannot fully separate "better data" from "different market", and the check has limited power. What we can say is that the obvious worry does not show up in the direction or the size it should.

What it would take to close the hole: a paid subscription to a price history that keeps dead companies. That is the one kind of market data almost nobody gives away, for the same reason the hole exists. We are not buying one yet, because today's check did not find the damage it would repair, and rebuilding our data from a new source would reset every measurement the lab has recorded so far. The decision should wait until something actually hinges on it.

The real answer to this worry is not better history at all. It is that our five books now trade forward, night by night, on companies that are alive today and may not be in five years. A forward record cannot be flattered by survivors, because nobody knows yet who the survivors are.

insights.title: Our books earn their keep in crashes, and give some back in calm years
insights.body:
Splitting our twenty test years into three stretches shows something our single headline numbers hide completely: our best books do not beat the market by picking better stocks in good times. They beat it by losing much less in bad times, and they give some of that back when nothing goes wrong.

The three stretches, each against simply holding the market with dividends reinvested:

From 1996 to 2001 the market made 11.9% a year and at its worst fell 30%. Our books made between 12.6% and 18.1% a year and fell between 11% and 16%.

From 2002 to 2008 the market LOST 1.4% a year and at its worst fell 40%. Our books made between 6.8% and 9.4% a year and fell between 10% and 15%. This stretch is where almost all of our advantage comes from.

From 2009 to 2015 the market made 16.7% a year and at its worst fell 16%. Three of our four books made about 14.5% a year, which is less than the market, though they still fell only about 10%. One, the unbraked book that ranks on a stock's rise beyond what the market explains, made 19.3%.

Read that middle row again, because it is the whole story. A stretch containing two crashes is where our methods earn their keep. The thing they are really selling is not cleverness about which stocks go up; it is staying out of the way when everything goes down, which these books do by moving to cash when the market falls below its one-year average.

The honest consequence is that in a long calm rise, three of our five will trail simple market-buying, and we should expect that rather than be alarmed by it. The question to ask of them is not "did it beat the market this year" but "did it fall far less when the market fell", because that is the trade we are actually making. A reader watching only the running total in a good year will conclude these methods are broken, and will be wrong.

One book came through all three stretches ahead of the market: the unbraked one, at 17.8%, 9.4% and 19.3% a year against the market's 11.9%, minus 1.4% and 16.7%, while never falling more than 16% where the market twice fell more than 30%. It is on paper now, and it is the one to watch hardest, both because it looks best and because a book that wins in every stretch is also the kind of result that most deserves suspicion until forward trading confirms it.

insights.title: A vanishing company would have to lose more than everything before it explains our edge
insights.body:
Our price history is missing 522 companies that were once in the index and have since vanished,
and the worry has always been that the strategies look good only because the companies that went
to zero are invisible to them. We cannot buy the missing prices, so we asked the question
backwards: how much would each of those companies have had to lose on the day it disappeared
before the strategy's advantage over the market disappears too?

Companies were killed off at random inside the ranking universe, at a rate measured from our own
index membership rather than guessed: 4.0% a year is the rate at which the universe lost a company
whose prices we never had, and 5.1% a year is the rate at which it lost any company at all, both
measured across about ten thousand company-years. Each strategy was re-run a hundred times at each
assumed loss.

The answer: the loss would have to be more than everything the company was ever worth - which is
impossible, since a shareholder cannot lose more than the whole of what they hold. All four
strategies still beat the market even when every single vanishing company is assumed to go to zero,
every time, for twenty years. So the missing companies do not explain the advantage. Two of the
four - the weekly-brake book and the min-variance-weighted book - come close enough that this
conclusion rests on the measured 4.0% a year rather than the more pessimistic 5.1%; at the
pessimistic rate the min-variance book would stop beating the market if every vanishing company
lost about 86% of its value on the way out, which is still far worse than a realistic set of
departures, because most companies leave the index by being bought, not by dying.

One thing worth separating out. Even when every vanishing company is sold whole at the last price
anyone saw - no loss at all - the strategies still earn between a third of a percentage point and
nine-tenths of one a year less than they do untouched, simply because there are fewer companies
left to choose from. That is the price of a thinner pool, not the price of a delisting, and it is
already there before any loss is assumed.

Two things this cannot tell us, and they matter. First, the simulated company dies with no warning,
so the strategy gets no chance to sell on the way down - in reality its trend rules would have been
pushing it out for weeks. That makes this an upper bound on the damage: the real answer is kinder
than the one above. Second, of the 522 missing companies only 404 actually left the index inside
the period we tested, and those are the ones we simulated. The other 118 were still in the index on
the last day and are simply absent from our prices - they died later and were dropped from the
record afterwards. Nothing we inject can model them, because what is missing there is twenty years
of prices, not a death. Their cost is a thinner pool to choose from, and it stays unmeasured.

This cost nothing: it recorded no trial, so the luck test's trial count is unchanged; it spent none
of the held-back test period; and it left the price store untouched.

insights.title: Adding a calm partner did more than any brake: the luck score jumped from 0.91 to 0.95
insights.body: Every earlier try at making the momentum picker safer sold stocks after a fall, and each one paid for it on the rebound. This time we left the picker alone and gave it a partner: a second book holding the 20 calmest big stocks, each book running a fixed share of the money. In the momentum picker's ten worst months it lost about 8% a month, while the calm stocks lost about 2%. That gap is the whole effect. With 70% in momentum and 30% in calm stocks, the portfolio grew 12.6% a year against the market's 7.9%, and lost at most 14% from a peak, where the market lost about 55%. Its gains were also steadier, which is what the lab's luck test rewards. The surprise is where the help came from. The calm stocks did not save us in the 2000-02 or 2008 bear markets, because the market filter already had us in cash then. They helped inside rising markets, in sudden shocks like August 1998, when the hot stocks fell hard and the dull ones barely moved. The lesson: a second, different engine beats a better brake.

insights.title: Each book's bad stretch landed where the other was doing well
insights.body: Alone, the calm-stock book had an ugly patch: it lost about a quarter of its value from spring 1998 to early 2000, as investors dumped utilities and food companies to buy tech. The market filter never noticed, because the market itself was rising. Inside the blend, that patch hardly showed, because the momentum picker was riding the same tech boom and gained 56% in 1999. A strategy whose worst stretch nobody would accept on its own can still be a very good partner, as long as its bad times fall where the other book's good times are. Worth checking for every rejected method in the lab: not 'is it good alone?' but 'does it hurt at different times from our best picker?'

insights.title: Blend the residual-momentum book with a calm-stock book: two different engines in one portfolio is pre-registered for its one test-window look
insights.body: Sera picked M0021-B70-RAW -- this method's best variant on the practice years -- and wrote down, before looking, exactly what it will test. The note is docs/lab/prereg/M0021.md and it goes into git before the test runs. The unseen years can be looked at once per setup, so writing the choice down first is what stops a disappointing answer from quietly becoming a different question.

insights.title: Checking the market switch more often made our best stock picker worse, not safer
insights.body: Our best stock-picking book goes to cash when the market drops below its long-run average, and it checks this once a month. We tried checking every week, and adding quicker warning signs, hoping to dodge sudden crashes like the one in 1998. It did dodge 1998. But when the market drifts sideways around its average, as in 2000, 2007, 2010 and 2015, a weekly check keeps selling after small dips and buying back a little higher. Our book holds the market's most volatile stocks, so every one of those round trips costs extra. Return fell from about 15% a year to 11%, and the worst fall grew from 19% to between 22% and 30%. Checking less often is the better choice here, because it ignores the noise. The book's real worst fall (mid-2006) happened while the overall market looked fine, so no market switch could have caught it. The fix has to watch our kind of stocks, not the market.

insights.title: The lab's safety check cannot test quick market switches
insights.body: Before a new idea runs, the lab tries it on a small made-up market to prove it is coded correctly. That made-up market rises and falls in a smooth wave, and it only checks a few dates. On the one date that counts, any market switch faster than about 80 trading days reads 'stay out', so the check sees nothing to verify and blocks the idea. Two versions of this test (a 50-day switch, and an exit when the market is 6% off its three-month high) had to be dropped before running. A made-up market with a longer stock history, or a few more checking dates, would let quick switches be tested.

insights.title: A stock's lucky month last year mostly tells you how jumpy it is
insights.body: We tried buying, each month, the 20 big-company stocks that did best in that same calendar month a year earlier, an idea from a well-known study that some stocks have their own good months. It made 10.6% a year against SPY's 7.9%, but its worst fall was 22%, over the 20% limit. The picks turned out to be mostly the most volatile stocks: a stock with a huge month last year is usually just a stock with huge months. They soared in the 1999 and 2003 rallies and lost 18% in the single month of August 1998. Worse for us, this book rose and fell with our momentum books in the same months, so adding it to them as a second engine did not soften their worst falls at all. The lesson: a new idea only helps as a partner if its bad months are different from the books we already have, and the place to check that is the month-by-month record, not the yearly return.

insights.title: Let a method remember 20 years of a stock without starting its test 20 years late
insights.body: The seasonality study we wanted to test looks at how a stock did in the same month over the last 10 to 20 years. Our lab cannot run that today. The rule that says how far back a method may look at any stock is the same rule that decides when its test may begin, so a 20-year memory would push the start of the test to 2013 and leave almost nothing to judge. We tested only the one-year version instead, which is much noisier. If the lab let a method read a long history of each stock while still starting its test in 1996, a whole family of slow-moving ideas would open up: multi-year seasonality, and the tendency of stocks that lagged for three to five years to recover. It would also need a longer practice data set for the lab's own checks, which today hold only about two years of made-up prices.

insights.title: Our best book failed its real-world test mostly because a small account cannot buy whole shares of today's stocks
insights.body:
The strategy that pairs the momentum picker with a calm-stock book had the best record in our twenty test years, so it got its one look at the last ten years. It failed: 3.3% a year, against 13.6% a year for simply holding the market.

Looking closer, the stock picking was barely tested. On average only about a fifth of the money was ever invested. Our pretend account starts at about 1,450 dollars and splits that across 40 stocks, roughly 22 to 51 dollars a stock. The rules only buy whole shares, and since 2016 most index stocks cost more than that per share. Those picks were simply skipped and the money sat in cash. In the older history, prices are adjusted down for later splits, so almost everything fit and this problem never showed up.

What to do: test these books in fractional shares, which the broker accepts and which our pretend-money books already use. Before any book gets its one look at recent years, check that it could actually have bought what it picked. This look is spent and cannot be retaken.

insights.title: The lab still treats fractional shares as unconfirmed, so a fractional book can never pass
insights.body: You confirmed that the broker accepts fractional limit orders, and our pretend-money books already trade that way. The lab's gate still lists fractional shares as an input you have not confirmed, so any strategy tested in fractional shares fails automatically. Most of our strategies cannot fill their whole-share slots at today's prices with a small account, so every whole-share result from the recent years will understate the strategy. Clearing fractional shares in the gate is your call. Once it is cleared, the lab can test the momentum plus calm-stock pairing the way it would actually trade.

insights.title: Sera 20261007-2056: a second engine beat every brake, then a small account in whole shares sank its real-world test
insights.body:
This batch tried three different ideas. One gave the best result the lab has ever had on our twenty years of history, and then failed its one look at the last ten years, for a reason that has little to do with picking stocks.

**What we tried.**
- Pairing the momentum picker with a calm-stock book. 70% of the money goes to the twenty stocks with the strongest run of their own (after removing the market's move), and 30% to the twenty calmest index stocks. On 1996 to 2015 it grew 12.6% a year against the market's 7.9%, fell at most 14% from a peak, and had the strongest luck score yet. The two books hurt at different times, so each covered for the other. That beat every brake and safety exit we have tried, all of which sell after a fall.
- A faster, weekly market switch for the momentum book. It dodged the 1998 crash but kept jumping in and out in sideways markets, and its worst fall got bigger (22 to 30%). The book's real worst fall, in 2006, came from momentum stocks alone collapsing while the market was fine, and no market switch can see that.
- Buying the stocks that did best in this same calendar month last year. It beat the market but fell 22% at its worst, and it moved almost in step with the momentum books, so it adds nothing as a partner.

**The look at the last ten years.** The pairing got its one look at 2016 to today and failed: 3.3% a year against the market's 13.6%. But only about a fifth of the money was ever invested. Our pretend account starts near 1,450 dollars spread over 40 stocks, and the rules buy whole shares only. Since 2016 most index stocks cost more per share than a slot holds, so most picks were never bought. The older history hides this, because its prices are adjusted down for later splits. So this look says little about whether the idea works, and it cannot be retaken.

**Alive:** mixing different engines whose bad stretches do not line up. That is the clearest lesson the lab has learned. **Dead:** faster market switches, per-stock stop losses, and last-year same-month seasonality.

**What would unlock the most:** letting the lab count fractional shares as allowed, since the broker accepts them and the pretend-money books already use them. Until then, any strategy holding many stocks with a small account will look worse in recent years than it really is. A longer memory for each stock, without pushing the start of the test back, would let the 20-year seasonality idea run properly.

**Next batch:** the same pairing in fractional shares; a three-engine book that adds stocks near their yearly high; the calm partner next to plain momentum; and a switch that reads the momentum stocks' own health instead of the market's. Before any book is promoted, check that it could actually buy what it picked.

insights.title: Even fully invested, our best older-history book trailed the market by six points a year since 2016
insights.body:
We reran the momentum plus calm-stock pairing in fractional shares, so every pick was actually bought. It was invested most of the time and still grew only 7.4% a year since late 2015, while simply holding the market grew 13.6%. Its worst fall was about 25%, over our 20% limit.

The last ten years were carried by a handful of giant technology companies. An equal-share book of forty stocks owns only a sliver of them. Its calm half sat in utilities and food companies that lagged, and its momentum half held 2022's winners just as the market swung back to tech in 2023. Our market filter also stepped out after each fall and came back in after the rebound had started.

Our strategies were built to dodge crashes, and the older history rewarded that. The risk in the last decade was being left behind by the leaders, not crashing. The momentum half is the same engine two of our pretend-money books use, so their month-by-month record against the market is the thing to watch.

insights.title: Sera 20261007-2056, updated: in fractional shares the pairing was fully invested and still trailed the market since 2016
insights.body:
This updates the batch summary just below it, which blamed the failed look on whole shares and left fractional shares as your call. You confirmed that the broker trades fractional shares, so the lab now counts them as allowed, and we reran the pairing that way.

**What happened.** The momentum plus calm-stock pairing, in fractional shares, still passed every rule on 1996 to 2015: 13.5% a year against the market's 7.9%, with an 18% worst fall. On its look at late 2015 to today it was invested most of the time, so this time the account size explains nothing. It grew 7.4% a year against the market's 13.6% and fell about 25% at its worst. It failed for real.

**What it taught.** Our strategies were built to dodge crashes, and the older history paid well for that. The last ten years were different. The risk was being left behind while a few giant technology companies carried the market, and an equal-share basket of forty stocks owns only a sliver of them. The pairing trailed the market by twenty points or more in 2019, 2023 and 2024.

**What that means for the pretend-money books.** Two of them run the same momentum engine as this pairing. Their month-by-month record against the market is now the most important thing to watch.

**What changed in how we work.** Every strategy that holds many stocks is now built and tested in fractional shares, and nothing gets its one look at recent years until we have checked that it could actually buy what it picks. Two of the lab's twenty-two-year history of looks have now been spent, both on this pairing.

**Next:** hold the market itself as the core, so the leaders are always owned, and add momentum on top as a smaller extra. After that, the ideas already queued: a three-engine book, the calm partner next to plain momentum, and a switch that reads the momentum stocks' own health.

insights.title: Holding the market itself keeps up in good years, but it does not make a book steadier
insights.body:
We built a book that keeps half its money in the market itself and half in our best stock picker, stepping both out when the market drops below its 200-day average. On 1996 to 2015 it grew 12.7% a year against the market's 7.9%, and its worst fall was about 19%, inside our 20% limit. Unlike our earlier mixes, it kept up in strong years such as 1999 and 2013, which is exactly what our strategies lacked after 2016.

It still fell just short on the luck test, 0.87 against a bar of 0.90. The market and our momentum stocks rise and fall at the same moments, so mixing them adds return but not steadiness, and steadiness is what the luck test rewards. The calm-stock pairing was steadier because calm stocks fell at different times.

Holding the market also only works with the safety switch. Without it, the same book lost a third of its value in 2008.

insights.title: Residual momentum: rank on market-model residual returns, not total returns: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +15.0% at the assumed fee, +13.5% at the real fees (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 19.6% and 19.8%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 2.16 and 2.00.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $2,245 and $4,921.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Real fees cost this book a point and a half a year; fractional shares handed back more
insights.body:
The residual-momentum book was the lab's best result on paper, and the obvious worry was that it
only looked good because the lab was pretending trading is nearly free. It is not pretending any
more, and the idea survived.

Run again with every slot actually bought, with the fee schedule fitted to the owner's own order
receipts, and with 5 million rupiah arriving on the 25th of every month: the money earned 13.7% a
year, against 7.2% a year for those identical deposits put into the market on those identical days.
Both sides got the same money at the same time, so that is a like-for-like answer and it is the only
one a funded run has.

Two things moved in opposite directions and that is the useful finding. Real fees cost about one and
a half points of yearly return — fees went from eating roughly a twentieth of the gross trading
profit to roughly a sixth — which the book absorbs because it trades about eighty times a year
rather than eighty times a week. Fractional shares then handed back more than that, because the
share of money actually invested rose from about 62% to about 69%: at the account sizes the owner
really starts from, whole shares were leaving a tenth of the money permanently in cash. Realism is
not a one-way tax; it changed the answer in both directions, and the net was slightly positive.

The method still fails one go-live condition — its worst fall, by about half a point. Worth
recording plainly: that fall is not an artifact of the deposits. The engine measures a funded run's
fall on the path a single unchanging dollar would have traced and divides each deposit out of the
day it lands on before working out any daily figure, precisely so deposits cannot make a strategy
look safer or steadier than it was. So the fall came out deeper than the unfunded version's, not
shallower, which is what more money invested should do. The only figures left contaminated are the
total and yearly ones, which are kept as the recorded shape of the curve and must never be read as
performance.

The lesson for where to search next: stop treating the fee question as the open risk on this family.
It is answered. The open risk is the fall, and the lab already has a measured price for buying it
down on this exact book.

insights.title: Four of four test looks failed, and the dev window cannot see why
insights.body:
Four of four test-window looks have now failed on "beats SPY TR", and all four strategies on the
paper roster lost to a SPY fed the owner's identical deposits over 2018-2026, every one of them
falling further than the 20% the roster's own risk rule allows. This note is what the diagnosis
turned out to be, including the part that refutes the first guess.

**The first guess was wrong, and it is worth writing down why.** M0007's dev analysis had already
noticed that stripping the market's move out of a ranking means refusing the high-beta names that
lead a narrow melt-up; it cost the method 1999-2000 and nothing else, and was filed as a virtue.
The obvious conclusion was that 2023-2025 was that same weather, and that a panel splitting dev
results into narrow and broad months would have caught it before promotion. That panel now exists
(`lab regime`) and it does not catch it. Measured month by month, the dev window is 41% narrow and
2023-2026 is 54% -- close enough that almost every recorded method reads "pays in both", including
the one that went on to lose. The month labels do not discriminate.

**What does discriminate is how long narrowness lasts.** The extremes are the same in both eras:
the twelve narrowest dev months run +2.1% to +5.2%, the twelve narrowest of 2023-2026 run +2.0% to
+4.5%. What moved is the average -- dev -0.66% a month, 2023-2026 +0.60% -- because the broad
months that used to pay an equal-weighted book back stopped arriving. On a constant-coverage
measurement the trailing three-year mean peaked at +0.68% a month in December 2025, above the
dot-com peak of +0.53%, and has been positive almost unbroken since late 2023. Across 1996-2015 it
cleared +0.17% once, in 6 of 202 three-year windows.

**The uncomfortable consequence.** The dev window does not contain this regime at any strength, so
no cleverer dev statistic could have predicted it. A sustained positive spread is a standing
headwind for any equal-weighted or beta-stripped book -- at half a percent a month that is six
points a year, every year, with no broad spell to recover in -- and the lab has been selecting
methods that are, without ever saying so, bets against it. The defence is not a better dev gate.
It is the test window, used earlier and more often than once per method at the very end.

**A data problem worth fixing first.** The dev store serves 539 of 1061 requested symbols. Breadth,
and anything else measured across the member universe, is computed on that surviving half.

**What the next batch should try.** Ideas whose edge does not depend on the typical stock keeping
up with the index: cap-aware or cap-tilted weighting inside the picks rather than equal weights; a
relative-drawdown brake that reverts to the index when the active bet has trailed it badly for a
year; and a blend of total and residual momentum rather than choosing between them. And before any
of those, a second benchmark that separates the two claims a method is really making -- RSP, the
equal-weighted index, so "my stock-picking is good" stops being confounded with "equal-weighting
beats cap-weighting this decade".

insights.title: Four free datasets, one purchase worth making, and why none of it is the binding constraint
insights.body:
Four free datasets would unlock work this lab cannot currently do. None needs a paid subscription,
an API key, or a vendor relationship; all four need a loader in `research_store` and a file beside
`fx.csv` in the store. Listed in the order I would do them.

**1. RSP, the equal-weight S&P 500 (yfinance, since 2003).** One extra ticker in the store's ETF
set. Today every verdict in the lab turns on `beats SPY TR`, which silently asks two questions at
once -- is the stock-picking good, and does equal-weighting beat cap-weighting this decade -- and
answers them with one number. Four of four test looks have now failed that condition, and nobody
can say which half failed. RSP separates them, and it is the cheapest item on this list by a wide
margin. The store currently serves SPY, QQQ, IWM, BIL, GLD, TLT, XLK, XLP and XLU; this is a tenth.

**2. FRED daily macro (free, no key): T10Y2Y, BAA10Y, DGS10, DFII10.** Every method here shares one
risk control -- a 200-day SPY trend gate -- which is a function of the very price it is meant to
protect against, and which this lab's own notes call too slow. The term spread and the BAA credit
spread are exogenous, daily since the 1960s, and tend to move before equity prices rather than
after. Reserved as M0038.

**3. CBOE VIX and VIX3M daily closes (free).** The term structure inverts at the start of a shock
rather than in the middle. M0007's deepest fall was not 2008 or 2000 -- the trend gate sat both of
those out -- but the six weeks after June 1998, when the gate had not yet turned off. That is
precisely the shape a term-structure gate is supposed to catch. VIX3M starts 2002-09, so it is only
testable on the back half of the dev window. Reserved as M0039.

**4. FINRA consolidated short interest (free, twice monthly).** Eleven flavours of momentum in this
lab and no measure of how crowded any pick is, when crowding is the documented mechanism behind
momentum crashes. Needs a point-in-time join on the settlement date, never the publication date.
Reserved as M0040.

**What is NOT on this list, and why.** Market cap: already computable from the EDGAR panel in the
store (shares outstanding with filed dates, 863 symbols) -- but only from 2006, because XBRL filing
became mandatory around 2009. Before 2006 there is none, so a cap-weighted anything is testable on
the back half of the dev window and the whole test window, and not before.

**The one thing worth paying for.** The dev store serves 539 of 1,061 requested symbols. yfinance
does not carry delisted tickers, and the losers are exactly the names that get delisted, so the
