universe is survivor-biased in the direction that flatters momentum. This is a correctness problem
and it may be inflating every dev result on the books, not a feature request. Survivorship-free
daily history -- Sharadar, Norgate, or CRSP with academic access -- is the only purchase I would
argue for before any signal data.

**And the caveat that applies to all of it.** Every new data family multiplies the ideas worth
trying, which raises N, which deflates every method's luck score. The lab went 0 for 4 out of
sample with the data it already has. Adding datasets without changing how methods are *evaluated*
mostly buys new ways to overfit; see the walk-forward proposal in docs/plans/.

insights.title: Raw residual momentum under an own-volatility target (M0007-N20-RAW + M0001 overlay): what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +9.9% at the assumed fee, +8.2% at the real fees (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 12.3% and 12.4%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 2.06 and 1.87.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $469 and $1,190.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A size brake cannot protect you from a fall it only learns about afterwards
insights.body:
The safety brake tested here measures how jumpy your twenty picks have been over the past month, and buys less of each when they are jumpy. Five strengths were tried on the real-fee book. The brake plainly did something: it cut the share of your money in the market from 69% to 66, 65, 63 and eventually 57 percent. But the worst fall hardly moved - 20.65% without it, then 19.98, 20.00, 19.94 - and simply sat there no matter how much more was applied, until the heaviest fast setting finally dragged it to 16.4%.

The reason is the date. In every version the worst fall is the same one: the summer of 1998, peaking at the end of June and bottoming at the end of August. It was fast, and it arrived after a calm stretch. A brake that looks backwards at the past month measured that calm, concluded nothing was wrong, and was switched fully off on the way down. It then woke up afterwards, when the picks were visibly jumpy - which is precisely when the rebound arrives. So it took none of the fall and some of the recovery.

The numbers carry a fingerprint of this. As the brake tightened, the book's results became more lopsided towards bad days rather than less: a lopsidedness reading of minus 0.32 with no brake, worsening steadily to minus 0.59 with one. Real protection would move that the other way. This moved it the wrong way because it was reliably absent for the falls and reliably present for the recoveries.

What to do about it: stop tuning this dial. Five settings were tried and all five failed in the same direction, so a sixth will not help. The falls that set the record in this family are fast ones that begin in calm weather, which means the tool has to react to the market's own sudden move within days, or else react to the account actually losing money, rather than try to forecast jumpiness from last month. Both of those are now queued.

insights.title: Passing the fall limit by three ten-thousandths of a point is not passing it
insights.body:
Three of the five versions tested today clear your 20% worst-fall rule with falls of 19.98%, 20.00% and 19.94%. The middle one is 19.9997%. It clears your rule by three ten-thousandths of a percentage point.

These are recorded as passes, because they are passes and the rule is not the lab's to move. But they should not be read as a method that solved the problem. A margin that small is smaller than the effect of a single different fill, or one day's price being a cent different. The honest description is that the safety brake was aimed at a fall it could not see, missed it, and the fall happened to land a hair under the line anyway.

Why this matters more than usual: all four test-window looks spent so far have failed, and every one of them failed on this same fall rule. The dev window is the old history the lab searches on; the test window is the recent decade, kept sealed and spendable only once per method. A method whose margin on the old history is literally zero has no margin at all on a decade that contains 2020. Spending the fifth look on it would be repeating the same experiment and expecting a different answer.

The version actually worth protecting is the heavier one, which came in at a 16.4% fall - 3.6 points of room - while still earning 9.8% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits put into the market. It gives up return, but it is the only one of the five whose pass would survive a slightly different world.

insights.title: When two versions rank the same, the lab should spend its one look on the safer one
insights.body:
Promotion is the step that spends a method's single, irreversible look at the sealed recent decade. The lab chooses which version of a method to send by ranking them on return per unit of fall, and takes the top one. That choice is made automatically and cannot be overridden from the command.

Today it picks badly, and the example is clean. The lightest brake scores 0.62 on that ranking; the heavy fast one scores 0.60. Two hundredths apart - well inside noise, and nobody would claim one is genuinely better than the other on that evidence. But on safety they are not remotely equal. The first clears your 20% fall rule by two hundredths of a point. The second clears it by 3.6 points. If this method goes forward, the lab will automatically spend the look on the fragile one, purely because a tie-level difference in one score broke in its favour.

The suggestion: when the top versions are within noise of each other on the ranking, break the tie by how much room each has against the go-live rules, not by the third decimal place of the score. A version sitting on the limit and a version sitting well inside it are different bets, and the one thing the lab cannot buy back is a spent look.

Narrower version of the same fix, if the above is too fuzzy to define: let the promotion step accept a named version, so a run that has just analysed all five can say which one deserves the look and have its reasoning recorded in the pre-registration. Right now the analysis can say it in words while the machinery does the opposite.

insights.title: Why I did not spend a look on the braked version of your best book
insights.body:
Your best book so far misses one rule and one rule only: at its worst it fell 20.65% from a peak, where your limit is 20%. This batch tried to buy those six tenths of a point down with a brake that holds money back when the book's own holdings have been jumpy lately. Four of the five brake settings came back passing every rule, and the lab's own ranking would have put one of them forward for its single look at the unseen years. I decided not to spend it. The reasoning is written here so it can be argued with later.

Three of the four passes clear the limit by almost nothing: 19.98%, 20.00% and 19.94% against a 20% line, the middle one by three ten-thousandths of a point. That is not a method solving a problem. It is the same fall measured with slightly less money in the book, landing on the right side of the line by luck. All four looks at the unseen years spent so far have failed, and every one of them failed on this exact rule. Spending the fifth on a version with no room to spare is the same bet a fifth time.

The deeper reason is what the brake turned out to be doing. It really does hold money back, taking the book from 69% invested down to 66, then 65, then 63. And yet the worst fall barely moves. The fall it was bought for is the fast summer of 1998, and a brake that measures how jumpy the last month has been is switched off going into a fast fall and switched on during the recovery that follows. It takes none of the fall and some of the rebound. Measured as return earned per unit of fall suffered, every single brake setting is worse than no brake at all.

And the one setting that genuinely does cut the fall, down to 16.4% with real room to spare, gets there by sitting 56% in cash instead of 69%. What killed all four previous looks was a decade in which being out of the market cost far more than being in it ever cost in falls. So the heavy brake trades away the rule that is failing on the practice years in exchange for the failure that has actually happened, four times out of four, on the real ones.

The honest reading is that this is a useful negative result rather than a candidate. Those six tenths of a point cannot be bought by holding money back, because the fall is a timing problem and not a sizing problem. Two better-aimed ideas came out of it and are queued: a fast crash gate that reacts in days rather than a month, and a brake that reads the account's own fall as it happens instead of forecasting it.

The rule I will apply from here, so this is not just one judgement call: a look gets spent when a version has real room on the condition that binds it, and is not more exposed than its parent to the thing that has already failed. This one has neither.

insights.title: Stocks that climb quietly keep climbing; stocks that jump give it back
insights.body:
Every stock picker this lab has built so far asks the same question: how much did this stock go up in the past year? Eleven versions of that question, and not one of them ever asked how it got there. A stock that drifted up two cents a day for a year and a stock that sat still for eleven months and then leapt 40% on one announcement look exactly the same to all of them.

They do not behave the same afterwards. I built two books from the same forty candidates on the same days with the same fees, and the only difference was which twenty I kept. Keep the twenty that climbed most quietly and your money grew 12.1% a year. Keep the twenty that climbed in jumps and it grew 9.8%. On the deposits you actually make, that is 572,000 dollars at the end against 435,000 — a third more money, bought by nothing except asking how the gain was earned.

The reason is visible in the trading. The quiet book bought and sold 1,203 times; the jumpy book 1,582 times, a quarter more. Each of those extra trades is a stock bought right after it spiked, then faded and had to be sold at a loss. A quiet climber is usually still climbing a month later, so it stays in the book. The explanation people give for this is attention: nobody reacts to a 0.2% day, so the news gets absorbed into the price slowly and the drift continues. One enormous day is impossible to miss, everyone piles in at once, the price overshoots and then settles back.

I expected this to be dead in a universe of 539 huge, heavily watched American companies — the research says the effect lives in small, ignored stocks. It is not dead. It is worth more than two points a year even there.

What it did not do is make the book any safer, and that is why it is not going on your roster. Every version still fell about 22% from a peak, past your 20% limit. The falls all happened in six-week market-wide crashes — August 2011, August 1998 — and in a crash like that it makes no difference at all which twenty names you own. Picking better names and falling less are two separate problems, and this only solves the first one.

insights.title: Measure the path of the same thing you ranked on, or the measurement says nothing
insights.body:
The same smoothness test that was worth more than two points a year on one stock picker was worth exactly nothing on another, and working out why looks like the most useful thing to come out of this run.

The first picker ranks stocks on how much they rose over the past year. Sorting its candidates by whether they rose quietly or in jumps separated them cleanly: 12.1% a year against 9.8%.

The second picker — the one behind the book you already trade — ranks stocks on how much they rose after the whole market's move is taken out of the number. Sorting its candidates the same way separated nothing at all: 11.90% against 11.99%, which is the wrong way round and well inside noise.

My first guess was that the second picker already prefers quiet stocks, so there was nothing left to sort. I checked that on 76 dates spread across twenty years instead of assuming it, and the guess was wrong: its candidates were slightly less quiet on average than the first picker's, and the spread among them was slightly wider, so there was more to sort on, not less. The two pickers only agree on about 18 of their 40 candidates, so they really are looking at different companies.

What I think went wrong is that I counted the wrong days. The second picker judges a stock on its move with the market stripped out, but I counted up days and down days on its raw price, market move included. For a stock chosen because its market-adjusted climb was steady, the up-and-down pattern of its raw price is mostly the market's pattern, not the stock's. I measured the smoothness of one thing and used it to sort by another.

The fix is small and worth running: count the up and down days of the market-adjusted move, the same stream the picker is built on. If matching them brings the separation back, it is a cheap quality gain on the book you already have, and the lower churn pays for itself in fees. If it does not, then the effect genuinely is absent for that kind of winner, which is also worth knowing. Either way the general lesson stands on its own: when you measure how smoothly something was earned, measure it on the same returns you ranked on.

insights.title: Choosing better names has never once made the book fall less
insights.body:
This is the fifth or sixth time the lab has tried to fix the one thing standing between your best book and going live — it falls about 21% from a peak and your limit is 20% — by changing which stocks it buys. It has never worked, and this run shows why in a way that is hard to argue with.

Five different ways of choosing twenty names were run side by side, all on the same machinery, the same fees and the same deposits. The money they made ranged from 9.8% a year to 12.1%. The worst fall ranged from 22.2% to 22.8%. The choosing changed the earnings by two and a half points and the falling by half a point of noise.

Looking at when the falls happened explains it. One book's worst fall ran from 7 July to 22 August 2011 — the debt-ceiling fight. Three others fell hardest between mid-July and the end of August 1998 — Russia defaulting and a large hedge fund collapsing. These are six-week, everything-drops events. The book has a safety switch that steps fully aside when the market is below its 200-day average, but a 200-day average takes months to turn, so in all of these cases the book was still fully invested when it hit. And when everything drops 15% in six weeks, owning a better twenty stocks is worth almost nothing.

The practical consequence: stop trying to buy the last point of fall with the stock picker. It is the wrong tool. Falling less comes from owning less — holding back some of the money when the book itself has turned jumpy, or when it has lagged the market for a while. Those brakes have a known price, measured this week: near the limit, roughly a point and a half of yearly return for every point of fall removed, which is expensive but at least it is real. The stock picker's job is to earn more, and it is good at that; it should be judged on earnings and left alone on falls.

insights.title: Sharing out money in proportion to size turns a twenty-stock book into a one-stock bet
insights.body:
The stock picker everyone knows from the roster holds twenty names and puts the same amount of money in each. That even split is quietly a decision, and nobody ever chose it on purpose, so we tested the obvious alternative: give the bigger, more heavily traded names more of the money, the way a stock market index does.

It backfired, and the reason is worth remembering for every future idea.

Inside a list of twenty stocks the sizes are wildly lopsided. Measured across 170 rebalances, the most heavily traded name in the book trades about thirteen times as much as the typical one, and in the worst month sixty-one times as much. So handing out money in proportion to that number does not produce a gentle lean toward the big names. It produces a single enormous holding. On the last day of 1999 this rule put sixty-one percent of the whole account into Qualcomm. By the end of March 2000 it held Cisco and Qualcomm together at nearly three-fifths of the money, at the exact peak of the dot-com bubble. In June 2014 it was three-quarters Apple and Meta. On an average month it had twenty-seven percent of everything in one stock and behaved like a book of nine names, not twenty.

The result followed from that. It earned more in a good year and fell twenty-nine percent at its worst, against twenty-one percent for the even split, and its deepest slide was precisely the five months from New Year 1999 into the dot-com crash, while every other version's worst moment was back in the 1998 Russia scare. The rule did not stumble into that crash; it aimed at it, because in a book that buys what has been rising, the stock being traded hardest is by definition the most crowded trade of the moment.

Putting a ten percent ceiling on any one holding looked like the obvious repair and came out worst of all: the lowest return of the five versions and still a twenty-five percent fall. The money pushed off the biggest name simply moved to the second and third most crowded ones, so it kept all the danger and threw away the one thing crowding had ever paid for.

The thing to carry forward is general, and it applies before anyone writes the next idea. A whole market index is spread out because it owns five hundred companies and its largest is about four percent of it. A pick of twenty weighted the same way is a bet on one company. Any rule that shares out money in proportion to a very lopsided quantity inside a small book is a concentration rule wearing a diversification costume, and it should be judged as one.

There was one quiet positive. Turning the dial the other way, deliberately putting less money into whatever the crowd is trading hardest, beat the even split on every measure at once: slightly more money a year, a slightly smaller worst fall, steadier along the way, and a better odds-of-being-real score. The gain is small, about three tenths of a percentage point a year, and it does not rescue a book that keeps failing the fall limit by half a point. But it is free, it is simple, and it is worth folding into the next attempt rather than running on its own.

insights.title: The company-value figure the lab computes is wrong, and wrong by a different amount for every company
insights.body:
This turned up by accident while checking something else, and it matters more than the method that uncovered it.

The lab's price history is adjusted for stock splits, which is normal and correct. When a company splits its shares four for one, every price before that day is divided by four so that a chart of returns stays smooth. Apple's closing price on 16 October 2015 is therefore stored as 27.76 dollars, where the price people actually paid that day was 111.04, because Apple split four for one in 2020. Daily trading volume is adjusted to match, so anything built from price times volume comes out right. We checked: the stored and the real daily turnover for Apple agree to within three percent.

The problem is a figure the lab builds by a different route. To work out what a company is worth, it multiplies the number of shares the company reported to the regulator by that adjusted price. The share count is a real, unadjusted number from a filing. The price is an adjusted one. Multiplying the two gives a figure that is neither. Apple's worth on 30 June 2014 comes out of the lab as twenty billion dollars. The real figure was around five hundred and sixty billion.

What makes this genuinely dangerous rather than merely untidy is that the error is not the same for everybody. Microsoft and Exxon, which never split again after the data starts, come out exactly right. Apple is out by a factor of about twenty-eight. So whenever the lab lines companies up against each other and ranks them by what they are worth, it is ranking them partly by whether they happened to split their shares at some point in the future. That is backwards in time: it lets information from after the test date leak into a decision made before it, which is the one mistake this whole lab is built to avoid.

Two places this reaches today. The method that picks stocks on company accounts uses this figure as the divisor in its cheapness test, and that family scores worst of anything in the lab. We cannot say the broken figure is why, and the direction of the damage is not obvious either, because the companies that split their shares tend to be the ones that rose a lot, so they are being made to look cheap exactly when they were expensive. Either way the ranking is not measuring what it claims to measure. The second place is any future idea that wants to weigh its holdings by company size, which is a direction the lab keeps being drawn to.

What to do about it: the lab needs to keep an unadjusted price alongside the adjusted one, or equivalently keep each company's cumulative adjustment factor, so that anything multiplying a share count by a price can undo the adjustment first. Until that exists, no result that ranks companies by what they are worth should be believed, and no new idea should be written that reads that figure.

insights.title: We cannot say how big a company was before 2009, and that blocks a whole line of ideas
insights.body:
Every test in the lab runs over 1996 to 2015, because the years after that are held back as the one honest exam each idea gets. The company filings the lab holds, which is where share counts come from, only begin in 2009. The regulator did not require companies to file their numbers in a machine-readable form before then, so there is simply nothing there.

That gap blocks a specific and recurring question. Several times now an idea has wanted to know how big a company is, not just how its price has moved: to lean the book toward the larger names, to work out whether a stock is cheap relative to what it owns, or to tell a genuine giant apart from a smaller company that happens to be busy that month. Any such idea that insisted on a real share count would hold nothing at all for thirteen of the twenty test years, and its result would be a measurement of when the regulator changed its filing rules rather than of the idea.

The workaround used this time was to lean on how much money changes hands in a stock instead, which the lab has going back to 1993. We measured how good a stand-in that is over the 2010 to 2015 stretch where both exist: the two put the candidate list in roughly the same order about seven tenths of the way, where one would be identical and zero unrelated, but they put thirty-five to forty percent of the money on different names. So it is a cousin, not a substitute, and the test that followed answered a related question rather than the one that was asked.

What would fix it is a historical series of shares outstanding for American companies going back to the mid-1990s. Commercial databases carry exactly this, and so do some academic datasets. It does not need to be fast-moving or precise to the day; a quarterly figure with the date it became public would be enough, because that is all the current data gives us after 2009 anyway. With it, three things become possible that are not possible today: a genuine test of whether leaning the book toward larger companies pays, a cheapness ranking that is not distorted, and the ability to tell crowding apart from size, which this round showed are very different things and currently get measured by the same number.

One caution for whoever fetches it. The lab's prices are adjusted for later share splits, so a share count must never simply be multiplied by a stored price. That mistake is live in the lab today and has its own entry in this journal.

insights.title: The insurance made the thing it insures against worse
insights.body:
We tested a simple safety idea: when our stock picker has fallen behind the plain market over the previous twelve months, move part of the account into the market itself until it catches up. The idea came from a real problem. All four of our one-shot tests on recent years failed the same quiet way -- not by crashing, but by trailing the market for years while nothing about their own behaviour looked wrong. Nothing we build watches for that.

Six versions were registered before any result, from a cautious one that only acts when the picker is fifteen points behind to an aggressive one that moves the whole account at ten. Every one of them lost money against doing nothing, costing between a tenth of a point and a point and a sixth a year. The worst fall did not improve by even a hundredth of a point. And then the measurement that settles it: on the very thing the switch was built to prevent -- the worst the account ever did over twelve months compared with simply buying the market -- every single version came out worse than leaving it alone, and the version that acted hardest came out worst of all.

The reason is the useful part, and it is not bad luck. The picker's worst stretch on the old history ran from early May to late July 2006, when it lost a fifth of its value. Over the twelve months before that peak it was ahead of the market by nearly twelve points, and still ahead by six a month into the fall. So the switch was off through the entire drop, correctly off by its own rule. It turned on ten days after the bottom -- and then sat in the market through the recovery it had just sold.

That is the shape of this kind of picker, not an accident of one year. It owns whatever has already run furthest, so it falls hardest right after it has done best. Judging it on the last twelve months therefore guarantees you sell after the loss and buy back after the rebound. Stepping into the market at the moment you are furthest behind locks the shortfall in and hands away the catch-up, which is exactly why the insurance made the symptom worse.

What to do about it. Stop looking for a switch that reacts to the picker falling behind: by the time that is visible, the money is already gone. Read beside its two sister experiments from the same week, the picture is clear -- changing which names you pick moved the worst fall by six tenths of a point across five completely different pickers; changing when you hold less moved it not at all; and the only thing that did move it, down to a sixteenth from a fifth, was holding less all the time, in good markets as well as bad, which cost about two points of yearly return. The worst fall only moves when you hold less always, not when you hold less sometimes. The more promising new question is the mirror of this one: the picker is at its most dangerous when it is furthest ahead, and unlike falling behind, that is something you can see while it is happening.

insights.title: The new go-ahead check cannot read any method built since the fees became real
insights.body:
The lab just gained a check that asks, before any method is allowed its one look at the unseen years, whether its edge survives in the stretch of history where we can price the most companies. It is a good check and it is about to give wrong answers, so this is worth fixing before anyone trusts it.

The check works by taking each method's recorded account curve, cutting it into three eras, and comparing each slice against the market over the same months. That works for the older methods, which were run as a single lump sum paid in at the start. It does not work for anything built since the lab started charging real fees, because those runs also pay in 5 million rupiah every month for twenty years, and the recorded curve counts every one of those deposits as if it were a gain. The market comparison it is measured against gets no deposits at all.

Run as it stands today, the check reports this batch's methods beating the market by seventy to eighty points a year in the early era. That is not performance. That is 148,000 dollars of the owner's own money being counted as profit on one side of a comparison and not the other. Every method the lab builds from here on will be funded, so this is not an edge case; it is the normal case from now on.

Two ways to fix it, either is fine: feed the comparison the same deposits on the same days, the way the main engine already does when it reports what your money actually earned, or slice the money-weighted return instead of the raw curve.

Until it is fixed, the only honest way to read the era check on a funded method is to compare funded methods with each other, never against the market, because they all received identical deposits and the distortion cancels. That is how this batch's verdict was reached, and it is a workaround, not a fix.

insights.title: A gate meant for company filings is blocking strategies that never read them
insights.body:
This one is plumbing, but it quietly rules out a whole class of ideas, so it is worth a line in the journal.

The lab holds company filings for only about a third of the companies it can price, because the regulator did not require machine-readable filings until 2009. To stop anyone building a method on that thin a base, the lab refuses any strategy that asks to see market-wide information whenever filing coverage is under eighty percent.

The trouble is what counts as asking. The refusal fires on the request itself, not on what the strategy actually looks at. A strategy that never touches a single filing, and only wants to know which companies were in the index on a given day, is turned away exactly like one trying to work out what a company is worth.

It bit this batch. The step-aside brake needed to know what the index held on each rebalance date, which is information the lab has in full and which has nothing to do with filings. It had to approximate instead, using the membership list as at the data date rather than the date being tested. The distortion was measured and small, the two lists agreeing ninety-four to ninety-eight percent a year apart, and it touched only the brake's trigger and never the stocks the book actually bought. But it is a real compromise that was not necessary.

The fix is to key the gate on whether a strategy genuinely reads the filings, rather than on whether it asked to see anything market-wide at all. That would unblock overlay ideas generally, which is where several of this batch's queued follow-ups live, and it costs nothing in honesty: a strategy that does read filings would still be refused on thin coverage exactly as it is now.

insights.title: Sera 20261009-1503: four ways to stop the big fall, and only one of them works
insights.body:
Your best book earns good money and breaks one rule. Run the way you actually trade it -- every pick actually bought, Gotrade's real fees paid, 5 million rupiah arriving on the 25th of every month -- your money earned 13.7% a year where the same deposits put into the market earned 7.2%. At its worst it fell 20.65% from a peak. Your limit is 20%. Six tenths of a point is the only thing standing between it and your rules.

This batch sent four ideas at those six tenths of a point from four different directions. All four failed, and failing in four different ways taught us more than one success would have.

**The rule the batch found.** Pick better stocks: the fall does not move. Give the good picks more money and the weak ones less: the fall does not move. Hold back money when the stocks look jumpy: the fall does not move. Step aside into the market when you have been trailing it for a year: the fall does not move -- all six settings of that one came back at 20.6%, the same number to one decimal place, which is as close to a flat no as a measurement gets.

There was exactly one exception, and it is the whole lesson. One setting of the hold-back-money idea did cut the fall, to 16.4%, with real room to spare. The difference is that it holds back money all the time, not only when something looks wrong. So: the worst fall only moves when you hold less all the time, not when you hold less sometimes. Every clever trigger failed; only the blunt permanent one worked. And it costs about four points of yearly return to do it, which takes your money from 13.7% a year down to 9.8%.

**Why every trigger failed.** The falls that bind are six-week, market-wide crashes, and a signal read once a month cannot see one coming. The worst fall in your book ran from early May to late July 2006 and began with the book 11.8 points AHEAD of the market over the previous year, still 6 points ahead a month into the fall. Every trigger was switched off the whole way down, and the step-aside brake turned on ten days after the bottom and then sat in the market through the recovery it had just sold. Measured properly, that brake made the very thing it was built to prevent worse on every single setting: the worst year-long shortfall against the market went from 43.6% without it to as bad as 51.5% with it. Insurance that reliably worsens the thing it insures is not mispriced, it is backwards.

**The genuinely good news, and it is real.** Among last year's winners, the stocks that climbed quietly -- up a little on most days -- beat the stocks that got to the same place in a few big jumps, by 2.3 points a year on your money, with gains outrunning losses 2.09 to 1.72 and a quarter less buying and selling. This was tested the honest way: the opposite version was written down in advance as the thing that should lose, and it lost. That is a new and genuine way of choosing stocks, and it is the first idea in this lab that asks HOW a stock earned its year rather than how much. It does not fix the fall -- nothing in this batch fixes the fall -- but it is worth building on.

**A warning worth keeping.** One idea asked what happens if you give the biggest, busiest names more of the money, the way an index does. Inside a list of twenty stocks the sizes are so lopsided that this is not a gentle lean, it is a single enormous bet: 61% of everything in one stock at the end of 1999, nearly three-fifths in two names at the exact peak of the dot-com bubble, three-quarters in two names in 2014. On average 27% in one stock, behaving like a book of nine names rather than twenty. It fell 29%. Leaning the other way -- deliberately away from the crowded names -- quietly beat the even split on return, on steadiness and on the luck test, at the same fall. Avoiding the crowd looks more promising than joining it.

**A data fault found by accident, which matters beyond the method that found it.** The lab works out what a company is worth by multiplying the share count a company reported to the regulator by the stored share price. The share count is a real, unadjusted number. The price has been adjusted for every share split since, including splits that happened years after the date being tested. Multiplying the two gives a figure that is neither. Apple on 30 June 2014 comes out as 20 billion dollars against a real 560 billion. Companies that never split again come out exactly right. So the error is different for every company and depends on the future. Anything the lab has judged on how cheap a company is has been dividing by this number. It needs fixing at the data level before any value-based idea is trusted.

**The go-ahead signal: no, not this batch.** The new rule says a method may use one of its irreplaceable looks at the unseen years only when it is eligible on today's bars, beats most of a walk-forward test, and still earns its keep in the stretch of history where we can price the most companies. Nothing cleared it. One method did come out formally eligible, and I chose not to spend its look -- the reasoning is written up separately, but briefly: the version the lab would have put forward clears the fall limit by three ten-thousandths of a point, which is not a margin, and the only version with real room buys that room by sitting 56% in cash, which is precisely what beat the last four attempts. I checked that against the record rather than guessing: in the most recent and best-covered stretch of history, the stretch most like the years we are being judged on, that cash-heavy version is the second worst of this batch's six and trails the unbraked book by nearly five points a year. The walk-forward part of the test cannot be run at all yet because the tool does not exist, and the coverage part quietly mis-reads any funded method, which is now all of them. Both are written up as things to fix. Until they are, no look gets spent.

**What the real fees did.** Everything here was run at your real fees, so there are no pretend-fee results to discount. Fees turned out not to be the obstacle this time: the brake changes how much of each stock you buy, not how often you trade, so it placed exactly the same 1,607 trades as the unbraked book. The sharper fee lesson came from re-pricing an older method: at real fees its edge over the market shrank to almost nothing, three tenths of a point a year. The same idea run the way you actually trade -- fractional shares, so every pick is really bought -- put ten more points of your money to work and turned that rounding error into a genuine 2.6-point edge. Fractional shares are not a detail; they are the difference between an idea that works and one that does not.

**What the next batch should try.** Stop attacking the fall with cleverness and attack it with speed: a gate that reacts in days rather than once a month, and a brake that reads your account's own fall as it is happening instead of trying to forecast it. Both are queued. Second, build on the drizzle finding, measuring the path of the same thing being ranked rather than mixing the two. Third, the mirror of the brake that failed: trim toward the market when the book is furthest AHEAD of it, since that is when the falls actually started. And before any of it, fix the walk-forward tool, because the real lesson of the last five months is that one look at the end is not enough evidence to bet on.

insights.title: The go-ahead check now reads funded methods, and here is how we know
insights.body:
Insight 72 reported that the era check could not read any method built since the fees became real,
because a funded run's recorded account curve counts every monthly deposit as if the book had
earned it, and the market it is compared against receives no deposits at all. The report was right
and the fix is in.

Both readers now take the deposits back out before they measure anything: the regime panel and the
coverage-era script. A recorded curve is normalised to the opening cash, so one deposit is simply
the monthly amount divided by the opening amount -- a half, for 5 million a month against a 10
million start -- and no exchange rate enters the arithmetic, because the run converted both at one
rate. Each month's return is then measured on what the book did with the money it already had.

**How we know it is right, rather than merely different.** M0032 is the owner's best book run with
three pieces of realism switched on and nothing else changed, so its regime profile should sit
beside its parent's. Before the fix it could not be read at all. After it, M0032 reads +5.6% in
narrow months and +6.4% in broad, against its parent M0007-N20-RAW at +6.6% and +7.7%. And the
coverage-era table is unchanged to the last decimal, which is the other half of the check: all four
roster entries were lump-sum runs, so taking deposits out of them must do nothing, and it does
nothing.

**What it changes about reading this batch.** The workaround insight 72 recommended -- compare
funded methods only with each other, never with the market -- is no longer necessary. The market
column is now honest for funded methods too.

One thing the batch surfaced that is worth keeping: with the deposits gone, the size-tilted book
reads +18.1% in narrow months against +0.4% in broad, where every other method in the lab is
roughly even between the two. That is the first method on the books whose edge is openly a bet on
a few large companies leading, and it points the opposite way to the rest of the shelf. It was
rejected on its worst fall, not on that, and the direction is worth another look.

Also fixed in passing: a drawdown printed with a plus sign, which read like a gain.

insights.title: Walk-forward: the lab can now ask whether its own choosing would have chosen well
insights.body:
The lab can now ask a question it could never ask before: not "did this method do well over twenty
years", but "would the rule we use to choose it have chosen well, again and again, on years it had
not seen". `lab walkforward` answers that from the database alone -- no backtest, no research
store, no look spent -- because every recorded trial already carries its monthly account curve.

**What it does.** Four folds across the dev window. In each, it picks the variant the lab's own
rule would have named knowing nothing past the train end, then scores that pick on the three years
after it. A method that wins its twenty-year average and loses three folds out of four is not a
method, and nothing here could notice that until today.

**Does it work? Partly, and the honest number is three out of four.** Of the four methods already
known to have failed the real test window, three won only two folds out of four and would have been
flagged before a look was spent: the weekly-braked book, the asymmetric-scaling book, and the
two-book blend. The fourth, the fractional blend, won three of four and slips through. Three out of
four is not a gate and it is measured on the same four failures that motivated building it, which
is a small and slightly circular sample. It is still the first thing in this lab that would have
said no in advance.

**And it taught us something by firing wrongly.** Run as first built, the buy-the-data signal fired
on three methods. Every one of the three belonged to a family that had *already* failed out of
sample. The worst case was the raw residual-momentum book, which the lab still records as eligible
for the simple reason that no formal look was ever spent on it -- while its own realistic twin, the
one that trades the way the owner actually trades, lost 415 million rupiah to the same deposits put
into the market over 2018 to 2026. The status column said candidate; the evidence said disproven.

So the signal gained a fourth condition: no method may be a buy candidate while another method in
its family has failed the test window. With it, the answer across the whole lab today is **no buy
signal** -- which is what the evidence says. Survivorship-free price history is not worth buying
yet, and the rule for when it will be is now written down in three places that execute rather than
one that is read.

**What to take from it.** Twelve of thirty-three methods beat the market in a majority of folds, so
this is not a filter that rejects everything. But every method that currently clears the fold test
is a variant of a family already disproven on the years that count. The lab's problem is not that
its ideas fail the new check; it is that its surviving ideas are all cousins. The next batch should
be judged on whether it brings a mechanism this shelf has never tried, not on whether it squeezes
another tenth of a point out of momentum.

insights.title: Old results stopped matching because the starting amount changed, not the prices
insights.body:
On 9 October the lab looked as if its own records could not be trusted. Re-running one recorded method gave a 545% return where the record said 660%, and the lab's 152 results had been saved against three different versions of the price history -- including the market yardstick every method is judged against. Before changing anything we measured what had actually moved.

**The price history never changed.** The three versions differ only in the separate file of company accounts (earnings and balance sheets), which was added on 5 October and widened the same day. Leave that file out and all three are the same price history to the last byte. Every method that trades on prices alone, and the market yardstick, has been tested on one unchanging history since 4 October.

**What changed was the starting amount.** On 8 October the simulated account's opening sum moved from 20 million rupiah to 10 million, to match the owner's real account. Nothing recorded which sum each result had started from, and because the simulation buys whole shares, a smaller account buys a different number of shares and ends somewhere else. That alone explains 545% against 660%: the re-run started with 10 million, the record with 20 million. The rule turned out to be exact for all 152 results: every result that started with one lump of money began at 20 million, and every result fed the monthly top-up began at 10 million.

**Re-run from their own starting sum, the old results match exactly.** All 54 of the original results from 4 October, the market yardstick among them, come out the same as their records to the sixth decimal with the same number of trades, on today's data, with today's 10 million default left alone. Started at 10 million, all 54 came out different; started at their own 20 million, none did. Every variant of M0007 and of M0011 matches too, and the 660% re-run now reads 660%. The earlier note that the yardstick "ends 1.83% higher" on today's data was not a change in the data: the yardstick reproduces once it starts from its own sum.

**So how far did the drift reach on a method, not just on the market?** Nowhere. Once the starting amount is honoured, nothing in the record moved, and none of today's verdicts changes.

**What each way of fixing it would have cost.** Freezing the price history and treating a rebuild as a deliberate event strands nothing. Re-running the yardstick strands nothing, but is unnecessary because it already reproduces. Refusing to compare any two results saved under different version labels would have closed every road to promotion, because the yardstick carries the 4 October label and every newer method a later one, though the prices are identical. Refusing only when the prices themselves differ strands nothing today. Recording enough to re-run each result strands nothing, and needed exactly one number the lab had never kept: the starting amount.

**What the lab does now.** Every result, old and new, carries its starting amount and a label for the price history alone, with the company accounts left out. The 152 existing results were filled in from the rule above and marked as filled in; not one recorded result was changed. Every re-run of a recorded result starts from its own sum. The go-ahead check refuses to compare a method with the market yardstick unless both ran on the same price history, and refuses when it cannot tell; the two report-only readouts warn instead of refusing. A new run on a rebuilt price history is refused before it starts. No method can be promoted today, before or after.

**One thing left undone on purpose.** Re-running the old results also recovers the inputs the luck test needs, which the oldest results never stored. Saving them would change how three things read, though not any status: one of the original 4 October families, currently rejected (H-P7A-F9), would become eligible to be judged again, and the luck score of M0007's best variant would rise from 0.952 to 0.978 and M0011's from 0.943 to 0.973. That is a judgement about the lab's verdicts rather than about whether its records hold, so it is left for the next round of exploration to decide.

insights.title: Let the strategies see the dividend calendar the lab already owns
insights.body: The lab keeps a full record of every cash dividend the stocks paid since 1993, but it only uses that record to put the payouts into the account's cash. The part of the lab that chooses what to buy is shown prices only, so it cannot know which companies are about to pay. That blocked a well-known idea from a 2013 finance paper: stocks tend to rise a little in the month they are expected to pay a dividend, because many investors buy them for the payout. Nothing new has to be bought or downloaded to test it. The fix is plumbing: hand the dividend dates to the stock pickers, letting each one see only payouts already announced by the day it decides. Once that exists, the dividend-month idea can be run as written, and so can others, such as favouring steady payers or avoiding stocks just after their payout.

insights.title: Momentum's reward comes overnight, not during the trading day
insights.body: We split each stock's daily move in two: the jump from last night's close to this morning's open, and the move during the trading day. Then we ranked last year's winners on each half alone. Picking the stocks with the biggest overnight jumps earned your deposits 16.9% a year from 1996 to 2015. Picking the ones with the biggest daytime gains earned 8.1%, barely above the 7.2% the same deposits made in the market. A 2019 study found the same split in US stocks, and it held in our large-company universe too. The catch is that overnight jumps cluster in stocks that make news, and those fall together in a panic. Overnight-only picking lost 30% at its worst. Using overnight jumps only to choose among the plain winners kept most of the gain (15.1% a year) with a 23% worst fall. That is still above the 20% limit, but by less than 3 points. What to do: keep this signal and put the lab's fall-limiting tools on top of it.

insights.title: The overnight measure counts every dividend as a small loss
insights.body: Our price history is not adjusted for dividends. On the morning a stock starts trading without its dividend, the price opens lower by about the dividend amount. The overnight ranking reads that drop as a loss, so it leans slightly away from companies that pay big dividends. The lab already has the dividend dates and amounts, but a strategy's ranking cannot see them; only the account bookkeeping can. Letting rankings read dividends would remove this bias here, and in every momentum ranking that compares prices a year apart.

insights.title: A size brake costs about one point of yearly return for every point of fall it saves, on every book tried
insights.body: The lab has now put the same brake on two different stock books: shrink the book when its own recent swings get large, and keep the rest in cash. Both times the price was the same, about one point of yearly return for each point taken off the worst fall. On the steady-climbers book, the brake that got the worst fall from 22.3% to 19.2% (under the 20% limit) took yearly growth from 12.0% to 8.7%. The lighter settings were nearly useless, because the 1998 crash came faster than a one-month reading of the swings could notice. The hope was that a calm, slow-trading book would be cheaper to brake. It was not. The lesson: this brake is a fixed-price trade of return for safety, not a free fix. The lab should stop testing it as the way to rescue a book that is just over the fall limit.

insights.title: The promotion gate checks the method's track record, not the version that would be promoted
insights.body: Before a strategy gets its one real test on recent years, the lab checks it in four separate stretches of history and asks whether it beat the market in most of them. The steady-climbers book with its hardest brake passed that check at three of four. But the three wins came from the lighter versions, which the check picks when they looked best at the time. The braked version that would actually be promoted beat the market in only one of the four stretches, and it trailed the market by seven points a year from 2009 to 2015. Those are the years the lab's data covers best and the years most like today. The gate as written would let it through. Since four of four promoted strategies have already failed on beating the market, the coordinator should treat this one as a likely fifth failure. A stricter gate would also score the exact version being promoted, in each stretch.

insights.title: Two long-only stock pickers never really disagree
insights.body: We tried to find a partner for the momentum book: a book that buys last month's biggest fallers among calm, healthy stocks. Textbooks say this bounce effect pays off exactly when momentum loses. In our data it didn't: month by month the two books moved together about two-thirds of the time (a correlation of 0.65, where 1 means lockstep). In momentum's 25 worst months the bounce book lost too, just less (2.6% on average against 6.2%). The reason is simple. Both books own large US stocks and nothing else, so when the market falls they both fall, whatever their picking rule. A half-and-half mix did cut the worst fall from about 21% to 17%, but only by giving up about 3 points of return a year, and all of its edge over the market came from the momentum half. Lesson for the search: looking for diversification among stock pickers is mostly wasted effort here. A real partner has to hold something other than stocks, or hold less of them, on a rule the market's own trend doesn't drive.

insights.title: A strategy that passes on paper can be half a strategy that already failed
insights.body: The half-and-half mix of the bounce book and the momentum book passed every go-live rule on the practice years: 10.6% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2% for the market, a worst fall of 17%. But its edge comes entirely from the momentum half, and momentum's own family has already failed its one look at the recent years. The safety check that blocks relatives of failed strategies only follows family names and parent links. A mix that contains a failed engine as an ingredient slips past it, and here only the separate year-by-year check (it won 2 of 4 periods) stopped it. It would be worth teaching that check to also look inside mixes.

insights.title: A volatility brake punishes a book whose edge is jumpiness
insights.body: The overnight winners picker earns its extra return from stocks that jump on news between one day's close and the next day's open. Putting the lab's weekly volatility brake on it did bring its worst fall under the 20% limit (from 22.8% to 18.8%), but it cut the yearly return on the owner's deposits from 15.1% to 10.5%. That is a worse trade than the brake has given on any calmer book. The reason: these stocks are jumpy in good months too, so the brake keeps part of the money in cash while the book is quietly winning. It also broke the book's durability. Without the brake it beat SPY in 3 of 4 out-of-sample checks and stayed ahead in 2009-2015. With it, only 2 of 4, and it fell behind SPY by almost 4% a year in 2009-2015. What to do: stop adjusting how much this book holds. If its big falls get fixed at all, it should be by changing which stocks it picks, for example skipping stocks whose overnight gain came from one or two huge jumps.

insights.title: Sera 20261009-2105: momentum is earned at night, and the brake throws that away
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch, and no look spent.** Nothing cleared all four conditions. The closest was the overnight-winners book: it beat the market in three of four walk-forward tests and still earned its keep in 2009-2015, the best-covered years, but it falls 22.8% at its worst, over your 20% limit. When we fixed the fall, the other two conditions broke.

**What we tried.** Five ideas, each one a way of choosing stocks the lab had never used:

- Pick last year's winners by how much they gained overnight, between one day's close and the next day's open, instead of by their whole gain.
- The same overnight book with a brake that holds back money when the book gets jumpy.
- Buy last month's biggest fallers among calm, rising stocks and wait for the bounce.
- The quiet-climber book from the last batch, the stocks that rose a little on most days, with the same brake on top.
- Buy the stocks that are about to pay their dividend.

**The real find: momentum is earned at night.** A recent study says that almost all of the reward for holding last year's winners arrives overnight, while during the trading day the same stocks drift the other way. Our data agrees, clearly. Picking winners by their overnight gains earned 15.1% to 16.9% a year on your real deposits at Gotrade's real fees, against 7.2% for the same deposits put into the market. That is the best this lab has ever measured on your real funding. Picking by daytime gains alone, the control we wrote down in advance as the version that should lose, earned 8.1%, barely ahead of the market. The luck test puts the overnight book at 0.97 and 0.96, well clear of the 0.90 bar. It is also the only new idea this batch that still beat the market in 2009-2015 (+1.1 points a year), which is exactly where every earlier failure was already losing.

**But the fall did not move, and the brake broke the good part.** Every overnight version fell more than 20%, in the summer-1998 shock that sets the fall for every momentum book in this lab. Adding the brake brought it under the limit (19.0% at its best), but it cost about four and a half points a year, taking your money from 15.1% down to 10.6%. Worse, it lost exactly the evidence that made the book interesting: the braked version wins only two of four walk-forward tests and trails the market by 3.8 points a year in 2009-2015. The brake trims the book when it gets jumpy, and the overnight book earns its money by being a little jumpy. This is the third batch in a row to learn the same lesson: a brake costs roughly one point of yearly return for every point of fall it saves, on every book we have tried.

**The other three.**

- The quiet-climber book under the brake did pass the twenty-year rules, but only at the hardest brake setting: 8.7% a year, a 19.2% worst fall, and a luck score of 0.901 against a 0.90 bar. The gate would have let it through. I chose not to spend one of our irreplaceable looks at the unseen years on it. The exact version that would be tested wins only one of four walk-forward tests and trails the market by about seven points a year in 2009-2015. Every one of the four looks spent so far failed on beating the market, and this one points the same way. A failed look would also permanently close the quiet-climber idea, which is still the newest stock-picking idea we have.
- The bounce book on its own only matched the market (7.5% against 7.2%), fell 27%, and moved with the momentum books rather than against them. It passed the rules only when blended half-and-half with the old residual-momentum book, and the gate refused that blend: two of four walk-forward tests, and residual momentum already failed its look.
- The dividend idea could not be tested. The lab holds every dividend date, but a strategy cannot see them yet. That is plumbing, not a bad idea, and it is written up as the most valuable feature to add.

**The gate.** It refused the bounce blend and the braked overnight book, both on the walk-forward condition, not on family history. It would have taken the quiet-climber book; that one was my judgement, and the reasoning is on its page. No look was spent.

**What Gotrade's real fees did.** Everything ran at your real fees in fractional shares on your real monthly top-up, so nothing here is flattered by pretend costs. The overnight book trades less than the plain momentum book (about 800 to 1,100 trades over twenty years against 1,160), so fees are not what holds it back.

**Alive:** the overnight signal, and the quiet-climber signal as a way of choosing stocks. **Dead:** volatility brakes as the fix for the fall, which has now been shown five ways, and the bounce trade among large companies.

**What the next batch should try.** First, keep the overnight picks and attack the fall without a brake. That means a cleaner signal (steady overnight drift rather than one big gap, now queued), or holding the market instead of cash when the trend switch is off, so the book's worst stretch is shared with the market rather than added on top of it. Second, let strategies see the dividend calendar. That one change unlocks the dividend-month idea and also fixes a small flaw in the overnight measure, which currently reads every dividend as a small overnight loss. Third, stop spending effort on brakes.

insights.title: The overnight edge is spread over many ordinary nights, not a few big jumps
insights.body: The overnight momentum picker buys last year's strongest stocks whose gains came mostly between the close and the next open. We tried leaving out each stock's 3 or 5 biggest overnight jumps before ranking, expecting to lose the earnings-news effect. Return barely moved: 15.0% a year on your deposits instead of 15.1% (SPY: 7.2%). So the edge is a steady habit of rising overnight, not a handful of earnings surprises. What did not change was the worst fall, about 23%, set in the summer of 1998 when every strong stock fell at once. Choosing 20 of the 40 strongest stocks more carefully cannot dodge a fall that hits all 40. The next fix has to change what the book is exposed to in a crash, for example favouring strong stocks that move less with the market.

insights.title: In big companies, last month's winners that traded quietly beat the ones everyone was trading
insights.body: A 2022 study says a stock that rose last month keeps rising when it is heavily traded, because the market is still digesting news. We tried it on the large index companies Seer can buy, and got the reverse. Winners from the busiest fifth earned 6.5% a year on the owner's monthly deposits, less than the 7.2% the same deposits made in SPY. Winners from the quietest fifth earned 8.2%. The likely reason: among big, well-followed companies, a burst of trading after a good month means the crowd has already arrived, so the move is late and tends to fade, while a gain that came without fuss is still under-noticed. An older study (Lee and Swaminathan, 2000) found the same thing. The quiet-winner edge is not usable on its own: it came from the 1990s and turned negative in 2009-2015. But it is a hint that a sudden surge in trading is a warning sign for a momentum pick, worth testing as a filter on the longer twelve-month momentum signal.

insights.title: The steady-climber picks stopped working after 2009; the cash switch was doing all the work
insights.body: The steady-climber picker buys twenty stocks whose past year's rise came in many small up days. It looked good because a market-trend switch moved it to cash when the market fell below its long average. This run took the switch away to see what the picking alone is worth. Era by era, against SPY: about 9 points a year ahead in the late 1990s, 1 point ahead in 2002-2008, and 2.3 points behind in 2009-2015. The edge faded in step with how complete our price data is, which is a warning sign that early wins may partly come from the dead companies our free data is missing. Without the switch, the worst fall was 60%. The lesson: when a strategy has both a stock picker and a market-timing switch, test the picker alone before trusting it. Here the picker had nothing left in the modern era.

insights.title: Hold the market, not last year's winners, right after a crash
insights.body: When the market bounces back from a crash, last year's best stocks tend to lag badly, because they were the defensive names that held up while the beaten-down ones rebound hardest. In this run, the version that held SPY instead of its stock picks while the market was below its long average was the only one that kept up with SPY in 2009-2015, mostly by owning the market in the spring 2009 rebound. That suggests a general rule worth testing on the lab's better pickers: for the months right after the market turns back up, hold SPY itself, then switch to the stock picks once the rebound is established. It would not fix the 2008 fall, which still needs cash, but it could recover a few points a year the switch currently loses.

insights.title: Thinly traded big companies are just small companies in disguise
insights.body: We tried buying the index stocks whose prices move most for each dollar traded, a well-known source of extra return in research. Over 1996 to 2015 it earned about 5 points a year more than SPY on the same monthly deposits, and a check for luck said the average was real. But almost all of that came before 2009. In 2009 to 2015, the years our data is most complete, it lagged SPY by about 7 points a year, and it won only one of four tests on years it had not trained on. The reason: inside the index, the thinly traded names are simply the smaller ones, so this was a bet that small companies beat big ones. That bet paid in the early 2000s and has not paid since big companies took over the market. Any idea that quietly favours smaller members should be checked against the 2009 to 2015 years first.

insights.title: Plain momentum books can slip past the family check under a new name
insights.body: Two ideas queued this batch, "quiet twelve-month winners" and "momentum among the most heavily traded members", are plain momentum books filed under brand-new family names, with the new stock-picking method as their parent. The gate's family check only follows family names and parent links. A plain momentum book filed this way is not linked to the momentum books that already failed their one real test, so the check would not block it. Nobody meant to dodge the gate, but the way ideas are filed lets it happen by accident. Until the check learns to recognise what a strategy actually holds, the coordinator must judge any such idea as a relative of the failed momentum books before promoting it. A cleaner fix: when an idea is queued, its family should be set by the main thing it ranks on (momentum, here), not by the idea that inspired it.

insights.title: Sera 20261009-2125: every twenty-year edge this batch was earned before 2009
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch, and no look spent.** None of the four ideas passed the twenty-year rules, so nothing came near the four conditions, and nothing reached the gate. Since nothing was put forward, the gate refused nothing.

**What we tried.** Four new ways of choosing stocks, each tested on your real deposits at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares:

- The overnight-winners book from last batch, but preferring stocks that rise a little on most nights over stocks carried by one or two big overnight jumps.
- The quiet-climber book with its market switch changed: hold the market instead of cash when the market is weak, or switch the timing off altogether, to see what the stock picking is worth on its own.
- Last month's winners among the stocks everyone is suddenly trading. A 2022 study says these keep going.
- The big companies that trade most thinly for their size. A well-known 2002 study says these pay extra.

**What the batch taught.**

- *The overnight edge is a steady habit, not a few lucky nights.* Leaving out each stock's biggest overnight jumps barely changed anything: 15.0% a year on your money against 7.2% for the same deposits in the market. That makes the overnight signal look sturdier. But the worst fall stayed around 23%, above your 20% limit. In the summer of 1998 every strong stock fell at once, and picking more carefully among them cannot dodge a fall that hits all of them.
- *The quiet-climber picks have nothing left on their own.* With the market switch off, the picks trailed the market by 2.3 points a year after 2009 and fell as far as 60%. All of the book's edge came from the switch moving it to cash in 2008. That idea is now closed.
- *Among big companies, a surge of trading is a warning, not a green light.* The study's busy winners lost to the market (6.5% a year against 7.2%). The quiet winners did a little better (8.2%), but that was luck-test thin and gone after 2009. This matches an older 2000 study: when the crowd has arrived, the move is late.
- *Thinly traded big companies are small companies in disguise.* They beat the market by 5 points a year over twenty years, and the luck check said the average was real. But they won only one of four tests on unseen years and trailed the market by about 7 points a year in 2009-2015. It was a bet on smaller companies that has not paid since 2009.

**One pattern runs through all four.** Every idea that looked good over the full twenty years earned its edge before 2009 and lost it afterwards. The years after 2009 are the ones our data covers best and the ones most like today. The overnight book is the one exception: it still beat the market slightly in those years. This is the lab's strongest warning so far. A good twenty-year average proves little here; the 2009-2015 years are the real exam.

**Alive:** the overnight signal, still the only stock-picking idea that holds up after 2009. **Dead:** the quiet-climber picks without their switch, buying winners because they are suddenly busy, and favouring thinly traded or smaller members.

**What Gotrade's real fees did.** Everything ran at your real fees from the start, so no result here is flattered. The busy-winners book traded most (2,500 to 3,400 trades in twenty years) and fees were part of why it fell behind. The thin-stock book traded rarely (about 300 to 500 trades), so fees did not hold it back.

**What the next batch should try.** First, attack the overnight book's 1998 fall by changing what it is exposed to in a crash, not by braking it and not by picking more carefully among the same stocks: for example, overnight winners that move least with the market (now queued). Second, test holding the market instead of cash in the months right after a crash, when last year's winners lag the rebound (now queued). Third, let strategies see the dividend calendar, still the most valuable missing feature. Fourth, look first at 2009-2015 before believing any twenty-year number.

**A note on how ideas get filed.** Two of the follow-up ideas this batch queued are plain momentum books given new family names. The safety check that blocks relatives of strategies that already failed their real test only follows family names and parent links. So a renamed momentum book could get past it. I have flagged both on their pages. If either one ever passes, it will be judged as a relative of the momentum books that already failed.

insights.title: Two momentum ideas now filed as momentum, and the gate now reads how a strategy moves
insights.body: The two queued ideas "quiet twelve-month winners" and "momentum among the most heavily traded members" both pick stocks by how much they rose over the past twelve months. That is plain momentum, so their family now says so: they are filed with the lab's plain-momentum family, the same one as the original twelve-month momentum test, instead of the new names they were queued under. Their parents are unchanged. This changes no verdict today: neither idea has run yet, and nothing in that family has failed its real test. What closes the hole Sera found is a change to the gate itself. It now compares how a strategy's month-to-month results move, once the market's own ups and downs are taken out, with the strategies that already failed their one real test; a strategy that moves almost in step with one of them (a match of 0.85 or more on a scale where 1 is identical) counts as its relative, whatever it is called. Measured on the lab today, the original twelve-month momentum strategy matches one failed strategy at 0.97, while unrelated ideas such as sector rotation, low-volatility stocks or company fundamentals stay well below the line. So a filing name can no longer let a momentum strategy slip past by accident. One thing to keep: when one of these ideas is written up and run, the runner copies the family from the method file, so the file must keep the plain-momentum family.

insights.title: A calendar trick that trades every month cannot pay Gotrade's fees
insights.body: We tested an old finding: most of the stock market's yearly gain arrives in the few days around the turn of each month. The test held SPY, and for those five days each month moved part of the money into the stocks that swing hardest with the market, then moved it back. Every version lost to simply holding SPY, and the more money it moved, the worse it did: from about 2 points a year behind for a quarter of the money, to about 9 points behind for all of it. Moving money out and back once a month costs about 1.2% of the amount moved at Gotrade's fees, roughly 14% of it a year. The best the turn of the month ever offered was about 0.3% a month on the whole market, and the extra from riskier stocks is about half that. On top of that, from 1996 to 2015 those days were no better than an ordinary week in the middle of the month. The lesson goes beyond this one idea: any trick that needs extra trading in and out every month must earn well over 1% per trip before it can help, so the lab should favour ideas that trade at most once a month.

insights.title: A stock's jump keeps going when heavy trading came with it, and mostly stops when it did not
insights.body: The earnings-day book buys big companies after a day when they opened higher on three or more times their usual trading volume, which is what an earnings report usually looks like in daily prices. A control book bought the same kind of jumps on ordinary volume, when there was probably no news. Over 1996-2015 the news version grew the owner's deposits by 5.0% a year and the no-news version by 2.9%. In 2009-2015 the gap was 9.9% against 4.2% a year. The lesson: the volume is what makes the jump worth following, because it marks the market changing its mind about a company, and that change takes weeks to finish. Future ideas that buy on recent jumps should keep a news filter like this one.

insights.title: Checking the trend switch every week cost far more than it saved
insights.body: The same earnings-day picker, behind the same rule of stepping into cash while SPY is under its 200-day average, earned 11.6% a year when it looked once a month and 5.0% when it looked every week. The weekly book lost 17% in 2000, 8% in 2011 and 6% in 2015, while the monthly one finished those years up. In each of those years SPY kept crossing its average, and a weekly check sold the whole book on every dip and bought it back on every recovery, paying fees and locking in losses each time. Any book with a market switch should check it slowly unless it has a reason not to, and a faster switch should be tested on its own before it is trusted.

insights.title: A weekly real-fee trading schedule the promotion step can accept
insights.body: This run had to build its own weekly schedule at Gotrade's real fees, because the lab only has monthly ones ready for promotion. The weekly versions lost this time, so nothing is blocked today. But if a weekly book ever wins, it cannot be promoted until a named weekly real-fee schedule exists. Adding one now would avoid a stall later.

insights.title: Chasing dividends lost; dodging them won
insights.body: We tested a well-known finding: stocks rise in the month they are about to pay a dividend, because dividend lovers buy ahead of the payment. On twenty years of index stocks it did not pay. Every book that bought next month's payers lost to SPY once Gotrade's fees were counted, and all fell between 29% and 58% at their worst. The surprise was the comparison book: the same kind of high-dividend stocks, but held only in months they do NOT pay. It beat every dividend-chasing version and beat SPY by about a point a year. Chasing payment dates means selling nearly the whole book every month, and the minimum fee per order eats a small account alive. Any extra return from the dividend month was gone after 2009, two years before the study was even published.

insights.title: The lab credits every dividend in full, but the owner keeps only 70-85% of it
insights.body: When a backtest holds a stock on its dividend date, the simulated account receives the whole dividend in cash. The owner's real account loses the US withholding tax first: 30%, or 15% if the tax-treaty form is on file. For a book like SPY, which yields about 2% a year, that costs about half a point a year. For a high-dividend book it is worse. The dividend-month books collected 5-7% a year in dividends, so the missing tax is worth 1-2 points a year. That is enough to turn a near-tie with SPY into a clear loss. Every high-dividend result in the lab is flattered by this. The fix is to take the tax off each dividend in the simulation, at the rate the owner actually pays.

insights.title: Take the dividend tax off in the simulation
insights.body: Add a withholding rate to the trading rules, so each simulated dividend is credited at 70% (or 85%) and not 100%. SPY, the yardstick, pays the same tax in the same run, so the comparison stays fair. Books that collect more dividends than SPY then pay for it, and books that avoid payment dates get the credit they earn. The owner's real rate (15% or 30%) should be confirmed from a Gotrade dividend statement before the number is fixed.

insights.title: Pairs trading without the short side is the losing half of the trade
insights.body: The pairs book looked for two stocks that had moved together for a year, waited for them to drift apart, and bought the one that fell behind, betting the gap would close. The original 2006 study also sold the stock that ran ahead, and that turned out to be where the money was: gaps mostly close because the leader falls back, not because the laggard catches up. Holding only the laggard, the book made about 1% a year on the money in those stocks, and every version lost to simply holding SPY, by 4 to 6 points a year from 1996 to 2015, and again in 2009-2015. A stock that lags a close partner usually lags for a reason. For an account that can only buy, strategies that profit when two prices come back together should be treated as off the table unless the buy side alone is shown to earn money.

insights.title: Checking the market's 200-day average every week costs about three points a year
insights.body: The pairs book kept most of its money in SPY and moved it all to cash whenever SPY closed below its 200-day average, checked every week. The version without that switch earned 5.8% a year; the same book with it earned 2.5%. The switch did keep it out of the 2008 crash, but most weeks it bought and sold the whole account on small crossings that reversed quickly, and every round trip paid fees. Earlier lab tests found the same pattern: the 200-day rule checked once a month beat SPY at a smaller worst fall, while the daily check lost to it. Any book that adds a market switch should check it monthly, or should show it survives the whipsaw, before trusting it.

insights.title: A database update in the main folder can break a strategy run that is saving its results
