insights.body: During this batch, one strategy run failed while saving its results, with a read-only database error. Nothing was recorded; the child ran it again and the second run saved normally. The likely cause is the coordinator updating the main folder with git while the run was writing: git can swap the database file for a new copy, and the open run then loses its write access. No result was lost or changed, but a swap at the wrong moment could drop a write that had not been committed. Until this is fixed, the coordinator should commit with lab stage and push, and avoid pulling into the main folder while a child may be writing, unless main has actually moved.

insights.title: Sera 20261009-2241: heavy trading on a jump day is the first new edge outside momentum
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch, and no look spent.** No idea passed the twenty-year rules, so none could be put forward, and the gate refused nothing. The closest was the earnings-day book below. It cleared three of the four conditions the buy signal needs, but it fell 25% at its worst, so it is not eligible.

**What we tried.** This batch stayed away from momentum on purpose. Every idea close to passing in earlier batches is related to the momentum strategies that already failed their one real test, so a variation of any of them could never be promoted. All four ideas ran on your real deposits, at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares:

- Hold the market, but for the four trading days around each month's turn, move part of it into the most market-sensitive stocks.
- Buy the stocks that are about to pay their dividend this month. This needed a small engineering job first: strategies can now see each stock's dividend calendar, the missing feature the last batch asked for.
- Buy big companies right after a jump in price on unusually heavy trading, the footprint an earnings announcement leaves, and hold for a while.
- Pairs trading without the short side: find two stocks that usually move together, and when one falls behind its partner, buy the one that fell behind.

**What the batch taught.**

- *Heavy trading on the day of a jump is a real signal, and it is new to the lab.* Re-picked once a month, the earnings-day book turned your deposits into 11.6% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits in the market. It also beat the market in 2009-2015, the years that look most like today (17.7% against 14.8% a year). It passed the luck check, and it beat the market in three of four runs on years it had not been tuned on. Its month-to-month moves do not follow the failed momentum strategies. Its control picked the same kind of jumps on ordinary trading volume, and it did much worse, so the heavy volume is where the edge lies. It failed one rule: it fell 25% at its worst, in the summer of 1998, against your 20% limit.
- *Checking the market's trend every week cost about three points a year.* Two strategies found this separately. Each switches to cash when the market drops below its 200-day average. Checked weekly, the switch flips in and out too often, and every flip pays fees. Checked monthly, the same earnings-day picks went from losing to the market to beating it.
- *The dividend-month premium runs the wrong way here.* Buying stocks just before their dividend lost to the market after fees: 5-7% a year against 7.2%, and 3 points a year behind in 2009-2015. Its control, which benched each stock in the month it pays, did best of all (8.3% a year), though not well enough to pass. The lab also still credits every dividend in full, while you keep only about 70-85% of it after US tax, so dividend-heavy books look slightly better here than they would really be.
- *The turn of the month is a dead end at these fees.* Moving money twice a month cost about 1.2% of the amount moved each month, far more than those four days ever earned. In 1996-2015 they were no better than an ordinary mid-month week.
- *Pairs trading needs its short side.* Buying only the laggard lost to the market by 4-6 points a year. It never beat the market in any run on unseen years, and it trailed in 2009-2015. The money in pairs trading comes from betting against the partner that ran ahead, which your account cannot do.

**Alive:** the earnings-day book, the first strategy in a long while that is not a relative of the failed momentum books and that still beats the market after 2009. The overnight signal from earlier batches is alive too, but it moves too much like momentum to be promoted. **Dead:** turn-of-month trading, buying before the dividend, and long-only pairs.

**What Gotrade's real fees did.** Everything ran at real fees from the start, so nothing here is flattered by cheap trading. Fees killed the turn-of-month idea outright and made every weekly market switch expensive. The dividend book traded 12,000-16,000 times in twenty years, and fees were a large part of why it lost.

**What the next batch should try.** First, the earnings-day book with a brake that cuts how much of the money is invested when the book gets jumpy, aimed only at the 1998 fall, with the monthly picks unchanged (queued). If it gets under the 20% limit without losing its edge, it is the first candidate in months the gate could actually let through. Second, bench dividend payers in the month they pay (queued). Third, take the dividend tax off in the simulation, so dividend-heavy books are measured the way you would really hold them. Fourth, stop checking the market switch weekly, in any strategy.

insights.title: In big companies, heavy trading on its own predicts nothing; the direction of the news is what counts
insights.body: A well-known 2001 study found that a stock trading far more than usual tends to rise over the next month, because the busy week brings it to more investors' attention. The lab tried this on S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 companies, keeping only busy weeks where the price barely moved. It tied SPY (7.3% a year against 7.2%) and failed the luck test. Worse, the opposite book, holding the quietest stocks, did a little better (7.8%). This is the second time the lab has seen quiet beat busy among big stocks. The likely reason: a big company is already watched by everyone, so a busy week brings no new buyers, and a busy week with no price move is usually routine fund trading, such as an index rebalance. What does work is the earnings-day book: heavy trading together with a big jump up. Heavy volume is useful only as a sign that real news arrived, read together with which way the price went. Future ideas should treat volume as a filter on a price signal, never as a signal on its own.

insights.title: Buying the long-term losers is a crash-and-rebound bet, not a steady edge
insights.body: We tried the classic 'buy what fell the most over five years' idea on big American companies. Over twenty years it beat the market by about 3 points a year, but nearly all of that came from two moments: the tech crash of 2000-2002, when unloved old-economy companies held up, and the wild rebound of 2009, when the most battered companies jumped hardest. In ordinary years it trailed the market, and at its worst it lost about 70% of its value, against about 50% for the market. The lab's records also lack the companies that went bankrupt, and among long-term losers those are exactly the ones a real buyer would have been stuck with, so even the small edge is flattered. The lesson: a strategy whose twenty-year average comes from one or two dramatic episodes is not something to hold month after month. It is a disguised bet on the next crash and rebound.

insights.title: A big dividend raise is a real signal, but dividend payers as a group lose to SPY after 2009
insights.body: We tried buying big US companies right after they raised their dividend and holding them for six months. Companies that raised by a quarter or more beat steady payers, whose dividend did not change, by about two points a year in every period from 1996 to 2015. So a big raise does tell you something about the company. But a book made of dividend payers in equal slots leans toward steady, value-style companies, and from 2009 that whole group trailed SPY, which the biggest growth companies carried. The big-raise book still lost to SPY by about three points a year in 2009-2015, and most of its lead in 2002-2008 came from stepping into cash during the crashes, which every book with that rule gets. Smaller raises of 10% are too common among big companies to mean anything. The lesson: treat a big dividend raise as a small tilt inside a book shaped like the market, not as a book of its own.

insights.title: Dividend announcement dates would let event books act weeks earlier
insights.body: The research data records each dividend on the day the stock stops carrying the next payment. The company announces it two to six weeks earlier, and that announcement is when the news reaches the market. Any book that reacts to a dividend change sees it weeks late, after the quickest part of the price move. A dividend history with the announcement date (some paid data vendors keep it, and the companies' own filings state it) would let the lab test the idea as the research describes it. It only matters if the big-raise tilt earns a second look.

insights.title: A volatility brake can't stop a fall that starts quietly, and it costs the rebound after
insights.body: The earnings-day stock book lost about a quarter of its value in 1998, and the loss started as a slow slide in April while markets were calm. We added a brake that shrinks the book when its recent swings get big. The swings stayed small through the slide, so the brake only kicked in near the bottom. Even the hardest brake left a 20% fall, still over the limit. Then, after 2008, the brake held the book partly in cash through the 2009 recovery, because recent swings were still large. That cut 2009 from about +50% to about +21%. In 2009-2015 every braked version ended up behind SPY, where the unbraked book had been 3 points a year ahead. This is the second book where the brake failed this way, so it is not a fluke: a brake that reads the past month is too slow for a sudden fall and too late for the rebound. The same run had good news: checking the 'is the market in a downtrend?' switch once a month instead of every week doubled the weekly book's return on the owner's money (5% to 11% a year), because a weekly check kept selling everything on small dips and buying it back. What to try next: a crash exit that reacts within days to a sharp market drop, but only buys back in at a monthly check.

insights.title: Sera 20261010-1651: a dividend raise and an earnings jump are signals; heavy trading alone is not
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch, and no look spent.** None of the four ideas passed the twenty-year rules, so none could be put forward and the gate had nothing to refuse. The closest, the dividend-raise book below, failed two of the four buy-signal conditions: it lost to the market in 2009-2015 and beat it in only two of four runs on years it had not been tuned on.

**What we tried.** We stayed away from momentum again, and all four ideas ran on your real deposits, at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares:

- The earnings-day book from last batch (buy big companies after a price jump on heavy trading), now with a brake that invests less when the book gets jumpy. It was aimed only at its one failure, a 25% fall in summer 1998.
- Buy the big companies that fell furthest over the past three to five years, betting that the market overreacted and they will bounce back.
- Buy big companies right after they raise their dividend, and hold them for months.
- Buy big companies after a week of unusually heavy trading that did not move the price, to see whether heavy trading alone is the signal.

**What the batch taught.**

- *A volatility brake cannot stop a fall that starts quietly.* The 1998 fall came out of calm markets, so the brake only reacted once most of the damage was done, and it then kept money out of the 2009 rebound. The braked earnings-day books still fell 20-23% at their worst, and they lost to the market in 2009-2015. A side finding matters more: the same book with weekly picks but only a monthly check of the market trend turned your deposits into 10.9% a year against 7.2% in the market. Its worst fall was still too deep (27%).
- *Heavy trading on its own predicts nothing in big companies.* The heavy-trading book tied the market (7.3% against 7.2% a year), and its comparison book of the quietest stocks did slightly better. That settles last batch's question: the edge in the earnings-day book comes from the up jump that arrives with the heavy trading, not from the trading itself.
- *Buying the long-term losers is a crash-and-rebound bet, not a steady edge.* Every version beat the market over twenty years, but only by riding the 2000-2002 crash recovery and the 2009 rebound. It trailed in calm years and fell about 70% at its worst (34% even with the market-trend switch). These results also look better than reality, because the losers that went bankrupt are missing from our price history.
- *A big dividend raise is a real signal, but it is not enough today.* Companies that raised their dividend by a quarter or more beat the market by almost four points a year, passed the luck check, and made almost three times as much on winning trades as they lost on losing ones. But they fell 21.9% at their worst (limit 20%), and they lost to the market by about three points a year in 2009-2015, when dividend payers as a group trailed the big growth companies. Small raises did no better than companies whose dividend did not change.

**Alive:** big dividend raises (as a tilt beside a market core, queued), and the earnings-day book with a slow monthly trend check, if its worst fall can be cut without a volatility brake (a fast crash exit with slow monthly re-entry, queued). **Dead:** heavy trading as a signal on its own, and buying long-term losers among big companies.

**What Gotrade's real fees did.** Everything ran at real fees from the start. Fees were not what decided this batch. The heavy-trading book replaced almost all its holdings every month, and that churn, paid at real fees, is part of why it only tied the market.

**What would help most.** Dividend announcement dates: the lab only sees the date a dividend is paid out, which comes weeks after the raise is announced, so part of the move is already gone when the book buys. The lab also still credits every dividend in full, while you keep only 70-85% after US tax, so dividend books look slightly better here than they really are.

**What the next batch should try.** The earnings-day book behind a fast crash exit with slow monthly re-entry. Big dividend raisers as a small tilt beside a half-market core. Earnings-day jumps measured against each stock's own normal daily swing. Long-term losers that have already started to recover in the past year. And, as always, at least one fresh idea from outside momentum.

insights.title: Strategies can now see the day a dividend was announced, not just the day it was paid out
insights.body: The lab used to learn about a dividend only on its ex-date, usually three weeks after the company announced it, so a book that buys after a dividend raise always bought late. The announcement dates are now in the research history: about 94% of the dividends from 1996 to 2015 have one, and 96-99% of those after 2015, so the real test and paper trading are covered as well. They come from a one-month download from a data vendor, and the half-month gap is typical: companies announce a median of about 20 days before the ex-date. A dividend with no known announcement date is still treated as known only from its ex-date; no date is ever guessed. The dividend-raise idea should be run again, buying on the announcement day.

insights.title: Knowing about a dividend cut three weeks earlier changed nothing for our monthly books
insights.body: We tested whether the dividend announcement dates we bought make existing books better. We added a rule that drops any stock whose board cuts or stops its dividend, and ran two books with the rule hearing about cuts either on the announcement day or about 19 days later on the ex-dividend date. The difference was under a tenth of a point a year, and it went in opposite directions on the two books, so it is noise. Even the rule itself barely mattered: it changed fewer than 2 in 100 trades. Big companies rarely cut, our books already step out of the market in crashes when most cuts happen, and a book that trades once a month usually acts on the same day whichever date it hears about it. One thing did show: in 2009-2015 the rule cost the news-day book about a point a year, because the companies that cut in 2009 were the ones that later bounced. The data's value, if any, is in books that act on the announcement day itself, not in a monthly filter.

insights.title: For big companies, the first dividend is old news by the time it is declared
insights.body: Old studies found that when a company pays its first ever dividend, its price jumps about 3% that day and keeps rising for months. We checked the 91 times a big S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 company did this between 1996 and 2015. On the day the board announced it, the price barely moved (a typical gain of 0.4% more than the market). In the two weeks between the announcement and the day the dividend was paid out, the stocks did no better than the market. A year later, fewer than half had beaten the market; the average looked good only because of a few big winners. The old studies were about small companies decades ago, where a first dividend was real news. For a company like Microsoft or Cisco, analysts see it coming months ahead. This is the fourth test in a row where knowing the announcement date two weeks early changed results by less than a quarter of a point a year. The announcement dates are not useful as an earlier alarm clock; if they help at all, it will be as a way of telling disciplined payers from the rest.

insights.title: Checking the market's trend every week costs more than it saves
insights.body: Several of our strategies step aside into cash whenever the S&P 500 drops below its average of the last 200 days. Checked once a month, this rule dodged most of the 2008 crash. Checked every week, the same rule kept jumping in and out of the market in choppy years like 2011, paying trading fees each time and selling near the lows. In this test the weekly versions fell about 30% at their worst, against 28% for the monthly one, and earned 4 points a year less. The dividend-raise test earlier today showed the same thing. Any future strategy that wants to react to news within a week should still check the market's trend only once a month. The lab cannot do that split yet, so it is worth building.

insights.title: Knowing about a dividend raise three weeks sooner did not help
insights.body: The owner bought a month of data that tells us the day each dividend was announced, which was usually about three weeks before the day it went ex. We tested it in the cleanest way we could: the same dividend-raise book, run twice, once seeing each raise on its announcement day and once on the later ex-date, in three matched pairs. Every pair came out slightly worse with the earlier date: 10.3% a year against 10.9% for the monthly book, on the owner's deposits, with SPY at 7.2%. The gaps are small enough to be chance, but none of them went the hoped-for way. The reason is that the price jumps on the day of the announcement itself, before any book that trades at the next open can buy, while the slow months-long drift afterwards is caught just as well three weeks later. So for books like ours the useful part of a dividend raise is that it happened, not when we heard. The data is still worth having for a different question: how the stock reacted on the announcement day, which the ex-date alone could never tell us.

insights.title: Re-checking a slow signal every week costs about five points a year
insights.body: The same dividend-raise book, re-picked every week instead of every month, earned about 5 to 6% a year instead of about 10 to 11%, and fell around 32% at its worst instead of 21%. The weekly version kept stepping in and out of the market on the 200-day trend switch, nearly doubling its trades and paying Gotrade's fee on every small slot each time. A faster clock only pays for a signal that changes fast; a dividend raise plays out over months. Keep slow ideas on a monthly clock.

insights.title: Knowing the dividend announcement date early was worth almost nothing to a slow signal
insights.body: We bought a month of dividend announcement dates so the lab could act on a dividend raise the day the board announces it, instead of waiting three to six weeks for the day it actually pays out. In three matched pairs of books, identical except for which of the two dates they used, the announcement-date books came out ahead by between a tenth and a half of a percentage point a year. That is too small to tell apart from luck, and in the 2009-2015 years two of the three pairs went the other way. The likely reason: whatever the market does with a dividend raise, it mostly does on the announcement day itself, and a book that holds for two months gains little by getting in a few weeks sooner. If the announcement data is going to earn its keep, it will be in fast uses, such as buying within days of a raise and holding only weeks, or selling the moment a cut is announced, not in signals that are held for months.

insights.title: Checking the market's 200-day trend every week costs about three points a year by itself
insights.body: One of this run's books almost never found anything to buy, so it sat in SPY nearly all the time, stepping out to cash whenever SPY fell below its average price of the last 200 trading days, and it checked that every week. It still earned only 3.9% a year on the owner's deposits, where simply holding SPY earned 7.2%. The gap is the switch itself: near the line it flips in and out, each time paying fees, selling after a dip and buying back after a bounce. It lost money in 2010, 2011 and 2015, years the market ended flat to up 15%. The earnings-day book showed the same thing: run weekly it earned 5.0% a year, run monthly 11.6%. Any future book that uses this safety switch should check it monthly, or only act when SPY is clearly through the line, and the lab should measure that switch on its own before blaming the stock picks for a loss.

insights.title: Knowing the dividend announcement date did not help a short-term dividend book after 2001
insights.body: We tested the new announcement dates head to head. One book bought big companies the day after their board declared a dividend; its twin bought the same companies only on the day the dividend was paid out (the only timing we had before), and both held for three weeks. Over 1996-2015 the announcement timing gained about 1 point a year, which is within the noise. All of that came in 1996-2001, when it was worth about 5 points a year. In 2009-2015, the years most like today, it was about 2 points a year worse. Both books lost badly to SPY anyway: holding stocks for three weeks means about 300 round trips a year, and Gotrade's fees on those cost roughly a tenth of the account every year, far more than the few tenths of a percent the dividend window earns. What to do: use the announcement dates only on slow signals, such as acting on a big dividend raise or a dividend cut the day it is declared, never to trade the short window around the payment.

insights.title: Announcement dates told the dividend-raise book nothing new, three tests in a row
insights.body: The owner's month of announcement data gives the day each dividend was declared, about three weeks before it goes ex. Three tests have now asked whether that day helps: buying the raise earlier, catching first-ever dividends earlier, and this one, keeping only the raises the market cheered in the two days after the news. Every time, the old ex-date version did as well or better. Here the announcement-day reaction filter earned about one point a year less than the same filter measured on the ex-date, whether or not the undated dividends were counted. Even the cheered-raise filter itself did not pay: raises the market shrugged off still drifted up afterwards, beating SPY on their own, so throwing them out just left more money in SPY. The lesson is that the slow climb after a big dividend raise is what this kind of book earns, and the news-day move is too noisy to sort raises by. The announcement data is still worth keeping for other questions, but not for when or how this book hears of a raise.

insights.title: A late dividend announcement is not bad news; boards just keep untidy calendars
insights.body: We tested whether a company that announces its dividend later than its usual rhythm is in trouble. It is not, at least among big companies from 1997 to 2014. Late announcers beat the market over the next three and six months by about as much as every other steady dividend payer did. Announcement dates wander a lot: by the same yardstick, about 170 companies a year looked late on their announcement calendar, against about 30 on their payment calendar. Selling on that warning cost the best dividend book about half a point a year in fees and lost gains. This is the fifth test of the bought announcement dates as a timing signal, and none has earned half a point a year. The steady, useful part of dividend behaviour is the payment calendar the lab already had; the announcement dates should be treated as background, not as a trigger.

insights.title: The dividend announcement dates add nothing a calendar guess does not already give
insights.body: The owner bought a month of dividend announcement dates to see if knowing a dividend was coming, rather than guessing it from past payment dates, would improve our strategies. Five separate tests now give the same answer: no. The last one was the cleanest. We took the plain twelve-month momentum book and only reshuffled its monthly picks: a small push up for stocks with a dividend coming in the next five weeks, a push down for stocks that just paid. Knowing the dividend from the board's announcement earned about 0.7 points a year less than simply guessing the next payment from the usual gap between past ones. It was also worse on the worst fall and on the luck test, and it tied in 2009-2015. The reason is simple. Big companies pay on a steady quarterly schedule, so the guess lands within days of the real date, and the announcement-day jump in price is over before we could buy. What to do: stop testing announcement dates against ex-dates, and spend the data budget on prices of companies that later disappeared, which the lab cannot guess.

insights.title: Two dividend books with almost no stocks in common earned the same: the pool decides, not the ranking
insights.body: The steady-dividend picker ranked big companies two ways: by how regularly the board announces its dividend, and by how evenly the payments are spaced. The two 20-stock books shared only 0 to 4 names at any time, yet they ended within half a point a year of each other in every era. So inside the pool of big companies that pay steady, uncut dividends, the ranking is cosmetic. What the book really holds is old, big, value companies: banks, oil majors, industrials. That pool did well in 2002-2008 (mostly thanks to stepping out of the 2008 crash), fell about a quarter from its peak during the 1998-2000 tech run while the market rose, and trailed SPY by 5 to 7 points a year in 2009-2015. Any future dividend idea should be tested as a small tilt inside a book shaped like SPY, or it will mostly measure value against growth, a bet that has lost since 2009.

insights.title: Sera 20261010-1742: the dividend announcement dates did not improve our methods
insights.body:
**The verdict on the dividend announcement dates: they did not improve results.** Eight new methods each ran their rules twice on the same stocks over 1996-2015. One copy acted on the day the board announced a dividend. The other waited for the day the dividend went ex, which was all the old data could see. Over 20 such side-by-side pairs, the announcement-day copy did better in only 4, and in each of those by 0.4 points a year or less. It did worse in 15 and tied in 1. On average it earned about 0.3 points a year *less* of the owner's money. No single gap was bigger than about one point a year either way. The 2009-2015 years were the same story: ties or small losses. The walk-forward check agreed, with the announcement-day copy ahead in at most one of four periods for most methods. Because each pair holds nearly the same stocks, this comparison is sharper than a normal backtest. We can be confident that the true value of the dates for our kind of book is somewhere between "nothing" and "a few tenths of a point a year". It is not a hidden edge worth chasing. The data itself is sound: whenever a method's ex-date copy re-ran an earlier book, it matched that book exactly.

**Why the head start was worth nothing.** The dates show the news about three weeks earlier. But the price moves on the announcement day itself, before our next chance to buy at the open, and then barely drifts until the ex-date. Acting earlier mostly meant buying right after the jump, plus a few more trades. The dates were tried in every way we could think of: as an earlier buy signal for big dividend raises, first-ever dividends and raises that came with an earnings jump; as a cut alarm and as a late-declaration warning on books we already have; as a short hold from announcement to ex-date; as a quality filter for boards that declare on a steady schedule; as a filter on how the market reacted to the news; and as a free tie-breaker inside the 12-month momentum book. None of them helped. Late announcers turned out to do no worse than punctual ones, and dividend cuts were too rare among big companies to move a book.

**The buy signal: no buy signal this batch.** One method cleared the development bars: big dividend raisers that the market cheered, timed on the ex-date. It earned +10.8% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's +7.2%, with a worst fall of 19.9%. The hard gate refused to promote it on the walk-forward condition, since it beat SPY in only 2 of 4 periods. Its family has no failed test look, so that was not the reason. It also trailed SPY by 3.4 points a year in 2009-2015, the years with the most complete data. So it fails two of the four conditions, and no test-window look was spent. That was the only refusal this batch. Everything else was rejected outright.

**What the batch taught about the dividend family.** Big dividend raises are still the strongest dividend signal we have, at about +10-11% a year against SPY's +7.2%. But every version falls 20-22% at its worst and loses to SPY after 2009. Dividend payers as a group were simply on the wrong side of the market's big-growth-company run.

**What fees did.** Gotrade's real fees decided two results. Holding stocks only in the three weeks from announcement to ex-date meant about 300 round trips a year, which cost 8-12% of the account a year and turned a small raw edge into a 5-8 point loss to SPY. Separately, a trend switch checked weekly instead of monthly cost 3-5 points a year in false alarms, a finding that applies to every book we run.

**What would unlock the most.** Not more dividend data. The earnings-jump books are our other live signal, and today they guess earnings days from volume spikes. Real earnings dates with the size of the earnings surprise would test that signal directly. The EODHD key keeps working until 2026-11-10, so it is worth checking now whether the same plan carries an earnings calendar, before the key expires.

**What the next batch should try.** Price the trend switch's check frequency on its own (weekly, monthly, or with a buffer band). Try the big-raise book weighted by trading size, and a calmer big-raise book aimed at a worst fall under 20%. Try the momentum book split into two halves that re-pick a fortnight apart. All of these are judged first on 2009-2015.

insights.title: Buy the long-term losers: big index members that fell furthest over the past three to five years, skipping the last year: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +9.8% on the usual history, +8.5% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 33.8% and 39.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.3% a year before and −4.3% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 1 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.3 points a year less. 4 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Survivorship check: adding back the dead companies cost our strategies about half a point a year, and pushed momentum's worst falls past 20%
insights.body:
**The answer: on average the missing dead companies barely moved our results, about half a point a year, but they did hide deeper falls in the momentum strategies.** Until now every strategy was tested on a price history that was missing about four in ten of the days a company sat in the big US indexes, mostly the companies that later went bankrupt, were bought or disappeared. This month we bought that missing history, cleaned it carefully (real collapses kept in, data errors taken out), and re-ran 102 versions of 22 strategies on both histories with the same money and the same monthly top-ups. Every version first reproduced its old result exactly on the old history, so the differences come only from the added companies. Nothing was added to the lab's trial count and no hidden-years look was spent.

**Buying long-term losers was the sharpest test.** This strategy buys the big companies that fell furthest over the past three to five years. If dead companies were hiding anywhere, it would be here, because the worst losers are exactly the ones that went on to die. On the fuller history its best version earned 7.3% a year instead of 9.8% (SPY: 7.2%), and its version with a trend filter earned 8.5% instead of 9.8%, with its worst fall going from 34% to 39%. Two of its five versions no longer beat SPY, and the other three now beat it by about a point or less. It won only one of its four walk-forward periods instead of two. The missing dead companies were flattering this idea by about one and a half points a year.

**The momentum books** (26 versions) lost 1.1 points a year on average (from 1.8 points worse to 0.2 better). Two of them stopped beating SPY, both of which had been within a point of it. The bigger change is the worst fall: it got deeper by 2.6 points on average, and nine versions that had stayed inside the 20% worst-fall line went over it. That includes our best momentum book, which still grows 13.6% a year against SPY's 7.9%, but whose worst fall went from 19.6% to 23.5%.
**The momentum plus calm-stock blends** (4 versions) lost about 1 point a year; one stopped beating SPY, and none crossed the 20% line.
**The earnings-jump book** (5 versions) lost 0.6 points a year on average, and it now wins only one of its four walk-forward periods instead of three.
**The dividend-date strategies** (62 versions) barely moved, 0.1 points a year on average. One stopped beating SPY and one started; two crossed the 20% worst-fall line. Their results stand as they were.

**Did any verdict change?** Yes, in three ways. Six versions stopped beating SPY and one started; all six had been less than two points a year ahead of SPY. Eleven versions that kept their worst fall inside 20% now fall further than that, and none moved the other way, which matters because a 20% worst fall is one of the bars for real money. And several strategies won fewer of their four walk-forward periods: the earnings-jump book and the dividend-cut alarm went from three to one, two momentum strategies and one blend from three to two, and long-term losers from two to one.

**How the fuller history looks.** It prices 89% of the index days instead of 59%. 2009-2015 is now 97 to 99% covered, against 65 to 76% before. 111 members are still missing even after we searched for their old ticker codes, about 5% of the index days, so a small part of the hole remains.

**What remains uncertain.** 1996 and 1997 are still thin (under half the days priced), because the bought histories for dead companies mostly start on the last day of 1997. Any edge that lives in those two years is not checked. The 111 members still missing are mostly companies whose ticker a different company now uses, so a little survivorship bias is still left in both histories.

**What this changes in how we work.** The fuller history stays a second opinion. It does not decide which strategy may be tried on the hidden years. That rule changes only through a separate, argued change, made after reading these numbers. Every future strategy can be checked against it, and the next batch should do so before trusting any momentum result whose worst fall sits just under 20%, or any result built on buying fallen or troubled companies.
