insights.title: The news-day book's worst fall was half the picks and half the safety switch
insights.body: The earnings-day book buys big stocks right after a news jump and keeps the rest of its money in SPY. Its one flaw is a fall of about 22% in 1998, over the 20% limit. This run measured each jump against how much that stock normally moves, which helped a little: the fall shrank by up to two points and the picks earned slightly more. Reading 1998 month by month showed why it was not enough. From April to August the market fell about 12% while the book fell about 22%, fully invested the whole time. 1998 was a year when a handful of giant companies carried the index and most other stocks sank, and a book that gives 20 news-day names equal slices loses ground in a year like that. Then the safety switch, which steps out to cash when the market is below its long-term average, only acted at the very bottom and missed the rebound. Fixing the picks alone or the switch alone can each only win back about half. A book that leans toward the biggest companies and also leaves faster in a crash is the combination worth testing.

insights.title: A surprise score is a good filter but a bad ranking
insights.body: Measuring a news-day jump against the stock's normal daily swing is a sensible way to decide whether the news was really surprising. Used as a filter (throw out the routine big days of naturally jumpy stocks), it improved the book: about 12.3% a year on the owner's deposits, against 11.6% before and 7.2% in SPY. Used to decide which stocks get the slots, it hurt: the same filter ranked by the surprise score earned only 10.7%, because the score favours the calmest stocks, and calm stocks lagged in the big rebound years like 2009. The lesson for future pickers: let a 'how unusual was this' score decide what is allowed in, and let the size of the move decide what goes first.

insights.title: Among big companies, the lottery-ticket stocks were not the losers
insights.body: A 2011 study found that stocks with a recent huge one-day jump go on to do worse, because people overpay for a lottery-like thrill. We tested it on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 from 1996 to 2015. The book that skipped the jumpers and held the 20 calmest names roughly tied SPY (7.1% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2%). It fell 30% at its worst, well past the 20% limit. The book that held the 20 biggest jumpers did better, at 8.1% a year. Among big companies, a stock with big up days is mostly just a jumpy stock, and jumpy stocks earned more over these years. The overpaying effect seems to live in small, thinly traded shares the owner's list does not include. One caution: companies that later died are missing from our price history, and lottery-type stocks die most often, so the jumpers' lead may be partly a gap in the data. What to do: stop treating calmness as an edge on its own. It only made a low-volatility book that lagged the 1999 and 2009-2015 rallies.

insights.title: The fear index's warning came late in 2008 and early in every false alarm
insights.body: We tried stepping out of the market whenever short-term fear rose above longer-term fear, a sign traders read as the start of a shock. In 2008 that sign only appeared after Lehman Brothers failed, when the market was already down about 20% and the ordinary 200-day average had turned long before. So it saved little: the gated SPY still lost 45% from top to bottom, against 51% for plain SPY. In the calmer years 2009-2015 it fired on every short scare (2010, 2011, 2014, 2015), sold after the first drop and bought back after the bounce, and earned 10% a year where plain SPY earned 17%. The best days often come right after fear peaks, so a fear-triggered exit misses them. Lesson: fear readings are a poor reason to sell; if they help at all, it is as a sign that the worst has passed.

insights.title: Cutting a book weekly but only buying back monthly costs about 4 points a year
insights.body: The big-dividend-raise book earned about 12% a year (before the owner's deposits) when it was checked once a month. Checked weekly, with everything else the same, it earned under 8% and fell deeper at its worst (23% instead of 17%). The reason is a quirk of how the book is run: a weekly check can sell the whole book on a warning mid-month, but the book can only buy back at the start of the next month. Every false alarm then costs up to a month out of the market, and in 2009-2015 false alarms were frequent. Any future book that checks for danger weekly should also be allowed to come back weekly, or it should simply stay on a monthly check.

insights.title: A calm filter fixes the worst fall but not the years that matter
insights.body: The book that buys big companies right after a large dividend raise used to fall 22% at its worst, just over the 20% limit. Keeping only the calmer half of those companies (the ones whose price moved least day to day over the last few months) cut that to about 19% and still earned around 10.5% a year against SPY's 7.2% on the same deposits. The jumpy half fell 27%, so how much a stock swings really does predict how hard it falls. But the calm half is mostly utilities, food and household-goods companies, and from 2009 to 2015 they rose more slowly than SPY, which was led by big growth companies. So the book passes on its twenty-year average and still loses in the stretch most like today. Lesson: a filter on which dividend stocks to hold can make a book safer, but it cannot turn a slow corner of the market into a fast one. The next test should change how much of the money sits in SPY, not which dividend stocks are chosen.

insights.title: Sera 20261011-1815: our books lose whenever a few giant companies lead the market
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch.** Four new strategies were tried, and none of them is ready for a look at the hidden years. One came close on its twenty-year numbers, but the lab's safety gate turned it away because it beat SPY in only two of four test periods and fell behind SPY in 2009-2015, the years with the most complete data. That was the only time the gate refused something this batch, and the reason was the test periods, not a failed relative. The other three were rejected outright.

**What was tried, in plain words.**
- *Calm big dividend raisers.* Our best dividend strategy buys big companies right after a large dividend raise, but its worst fall was 22%, over the 20% limit. Keeping only the calmer half of those companies brought the worst fall down to about 19%. It still earned about 10.6% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2% in SPY. Measured fairly, though, it lost to SPY by about 2.6 points a year from 2009 to 2015. The calm half is mostly utilities, food and household-goods companies, and those rose more slowly than the big growth companies that led the market in those years. With the dead companies added back to the price history, its worst fall goes back to 20%.
- *News-day jumps judged against each stock's normal swing.* The earnings-day strategy buys a stock after a big jump on heavy trading. This time a jump only counted if it was large for that particular stock. That helped a little: about 12.3% a year against SPY's 7.2%, and it beat SPY in three of four test periods. But the 1998 fall still reached 22-24%. In 1998 a handful of giant companies carried the market while most other stocks sank, and a book that gives 20 mid-sized names equal slices lost ground. The lesson worth keeping: a "how unusual was this" score is a good way to decide what is allowed in, but a poor way to decide what goes first.
- *Skipping lottery-ticket stocks.* A well-known 2011 study says stocks with a recent huge one-day jump go on to do worse. Among big US companies we found the opposite. The calmest 20 names roughly tied SPY (7.1% against 7.2%) and fell 30% at their worst, while the 20 biggest jumpers did better at 8.1%. The effect seems to live in small, thinly traded shares the owner cannot buy here.
- *Leaving the market when fear spikes.* We tried selling SPY whenever short-term fear on the options market rose above longer-term fear. In 2008 that warning came only after the crash was well under way, so it saved little. In 2009-2015 it fired on every small scare, sold after the drop and bought back after the bounce, and earned about 10% a year where simply holding SPY earned 17%. Every version lost to the same book with no switch.

**What looks alive and what looks dead.** Alive, but stuck on the same wall: the dividend-raise book and the news-day book both beat SPY over twenty years, and both lose ground either in 1998 or in 2009-2015, when a few giant companies led the market. Dead: fear-index switches, and the lottery-stock idea among big companies. The common thread is clear now. Our books spread money in equal slices across mid-sized names, and they lose whenever the giants run the market. That is the very kind of market the owner is living in today.

**What fees did.** Gotrade's real fees were in every test. No strategy lost its edge to them this batch. The fear switch's frequent in-and-out trading did add to its loss, though, and one side finding applies to every book: cutting a book weekly but only buying back monthly cost about 4 points a year.

**What would help most.** A true company-size number for the years before 2009, so a book could lean toward the giants by real size rather than by how much they trade.

**What the next batch should try.** The news-day picks sized toward the giants instead of equal slices. The calm dividend raisers as a smaller sleeve beside a large SPY core. A lottery measure scaled to each stock's own swing, to settle whether it was ever more than jumpiness. A switch that leaves on the 200-day average but comes back once fear has calmed.

insights.title: Big companies cut their dividend too rarely to build a book on it
insights.body: We tried buying large US companies six to eighteen months after they cut or stopped their dividend, once their price had started to recover. In most years only two to eight such companies qualified, so most of the money just sat in SPY, and the result depended almost entirely on the 2009-2010 rebound after the financial crisis. Without the market safety switch, the cutters themselves earned 5.3% a year where SPY earned 7.2%, and fell 54% in 2008. Waiting for the price to climb back above its long-run average made things worse, not better: by then the fastest part of the rebound was gone. Some of the 'cutters' had not been in trouble at all; they had simply changed how they pay (one switched to a single yearly payout). Together with the earlier test that benched cutters, this says a dividend cut, on its own, tells us little about a big company's next year. The one question left is the opposite bet: whether these stocks bounce in the first few months after the cut.

insights.title: Busy is not big: leaning the news-day book toward the most-traded stocks made its worst fall deeper
insights.body: The news-day book buys stocks right after an earnings-style jump. Its one flaw is a fall of about 22% in 1998, when a handful of giants carried the market. The guess was that giving more money to the biggest companies, the way the S&P 500 does, would soften that fall. Without share counts before 2009, the lab measured size by how much money trades in a stock each day. It went the wrong way: the fall deepened to 23.5-24.5%. The most heavily traded news-day stocks in 1998 were the fast, popular names, not the steady giants, and they fell hardest when the market cracked; the same tilt rode the 1999 tech boom up and gave it back in 2007. And when the book was allowed to pick only from the 100 most-traded stocks, the fall was smallest but the edge was gone: from 2009 to 2015 it trailed the S&P 500 by about 5 points a year. Two lessons. Trading volume is a poor stand-in for company size, so a real size measure needs real share counts. And this book earns its edge in the stocks the index gives little weight to; that cannot be sized away, only accepted or dropped. The fall itself belongs to the slow monthly safety switch, which is the next thing to change.

insights.title: Timing the average company against the giants caught some of their runs, but too late to pay
insights.body: We tried holding an equal mix of big companies only while the average one was beating SPY, and SPY the rest of the time. In the months when a few giants carried the market, the switch cut the loss against SPY from about 10 points a year to about 6, so the reading does notice when the giants take over. It notices late, and it gives part of that back by sitting in SPY when the average company recovers. The best version only tied SPY over 1996-2015, and every version fell more than 55% in 2008 because neither side of the switch protects against a crash. Worth keeping: the reading as a warning light for books that already earn something. Not worth keeping: the switch as a strategy of its own.

insights.title: A sample picked by rank churns, and the fees eat it
insights.body: To keep the book small, we held every fifth company from a list of the 100 most traded. That list reshuffles a little every month, so a company moving from 15th to 16th place dropped out and its neighbour came in, for no reason the idea cared about. The 20-name book traded about twice as often as a book holding all 100 names, paid Gotrade's minimum fee on each small order, and earned less than half as much. Any future book that samples from a ranked list should keep a name until it moves well away from its slot, not the moment its rank shifts by one.

insights.title: The safety switch, not the dividend raisers, is what loses to SPY after 2009
insights.body: We tried the calm dividend-raiser book with a big slice of plain SPY beside it, hoping the SPY slice would catch the giant companies that led 2009-2015. It made things worse. The more of the money sat in SPY behind the rule that sells everything when SPY drops below its 200-day average, the further behind SPY it fell in 2009-2015: about 5.6 points a year for the version that was mostly SPY, 2.7 for the version that was all dividend raisers. That rule sold during the 2010, 2011 and 2015 dips and bought back higher each time. So in those years the raisers were actually doing better than the market behind the same rule; the rule was the drag. The same rule is also where the book earned its lead: sitting in cash through 2008 is worth about 6 points a year over 2002-2008. Without the rule the book lost 43% at its worst in 2008, far past the 20% limit. The lesson for every book in the lab that uses this rule: its long-run average mixes a big win in 2008 with steady losses since, and a gentler version of the rule is worth testing before blaming the stock picks.

insights.title: Sera 20261011-1838: the safety switch, not the stocks, is what loses to SPY after 2009
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch.** Four new strategies were tried. One passed every check on its twenty-year numbers, but the lab's safety gate turned it away: it beat SPY in only two of four later test periods, and it fell behind SPY in 2009-2015, the years with the most complete data. That was the only refusal this batch. It was refused for its test periods, not because a related strategy had already failed. The other three were rejected outright. No look at the hidden years was spent.

**What was tried, in plain words.**
- *Calm dividend raisers next to a big slice of SPY.* Last batch's calm dividend-raiser book stayed inside the 20% worst-fall limit but lagged SPY after 2009. The idea was that putting half or more of the money in SPY would catch the giant companies that led those years. Half SPY, half raisers earned about 9.6% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2% in SPY, with a worst fall of 19%. But it lagged SPY in 2009-2015 by even more than before, about 4.4 points a year. The more of the money sat in SPY, the worse it did in those years. That pointed at the real cause, the batch's most useful finding: the rule that sells everything when SPY drops below its 200-day average sold in the dips of 2010, 2011 and 2015 and bought back higher each time. In those years the dividend raisers themselves were roughly keeping up. The safety switch was what lost.
- *News-day picks sized toward the giants.* Last batch's news-day book fell 22% in 1998, when a few giants carried the market. Here it gave more money to the stocks that trade the most, as a stand-in for company size. That made the fall worse, 24-25%. In 1998 the busiest stocks were the fast, popular names, not the steady giants, and they fell hardest. How much a stock trades is not how big the company is.
- *Buying big companies after a dividend cut, once they recover.* Too few big companies cut their dividend to fill a book, two to eight in most years. The result rested almost entirely on the 2009 rebound. It roughly tied SPY (7.3% against 7.2%) and lost to it after 2009.
- *Switching between the average big company and SPY*, depending on which had led over the last few months. The reading does notice when the giants take over, but it notices late. At best it tied SPY, and every version fell more than 55% in 2008, because neither side of the switch steps out of a crash. One version also traded far too often, because it held names by their place on a ranked list that reshuffles every month.

**What looks alive and what looks dead.** Dead: leaning toward big names by trading volume, buying dividend cutters, and timing the average company against the giants. Alive: the calm dividend raisers, because this batch suggests their recent lag belongs to the safety switch and not to the stocks. That makes the switch itself the next thing to test. It sits under nearly every strategy in the lab, and if it loses about three points a year to whipsaw in calm markets, many past results were paying that cost.

**What fees did.** Gotrade's real fees were in every test. They mattered most for the strategy that held names by their ranked place: it traded about twice as often as a version holding all 100 names, paid the minimum fee on each small order, and earned less than half as much. No method lost an edge it would otherwise have had.

**What would help most.** A true company-size figure for the years before 2009. This batch showed that trading volume is a poor stand-in for size.

**What the next batch should try.** A slower safety switch: checked monthly, or one that only acts when SPY is clearly through its 200-day average, priced on SPY alone first and then under the calm dividend raisers. The news-day book with an exit that steps aside when SPY slips under a shorter average. Buying a big company in the month it cuts its dividend, to see whether punished companies bounce.

insights.title: Calm big raisers behind a gentler safety switch: leave only when SPY is 3% under its 200-day average, return only when 3% over: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 4 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.6% on the usual history, +10.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.7% and 20.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −3.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 2 of its 4 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Three different ways of picking calmer winners all bought the same trade: a point less fall for a point less return
insights.body: The overnight momentum book buys last year's strongest stocks whose gains came mostly between one day's close and the next day's open. It earns about 15% a year on the owner's deposits, but at its worst it fell about 23%, over the 20% limit, in the summer 1998 shock. Three tries have now attacked that fall from three directions: a brake that sells when swings get large, picking the stocks that rose most steadily, and, this time, leaving out the strong stocks that move most with the market. All three land on one line. The version that finally got under the limit (19.8%) earned 10.6% a year, almost exactly where the brake landed (about 19% and 10.5%). And every cut cost the most in 2009 to 2015, the years most like today, where this version trailed SPY by 2.7% a year. What this says: the deep fall belongs to holding strong stocks in a momentum crash, not to which strong stocks you hold, so filtering inside the pool cannot fix it. The next try should add something that holds up when momentum crashes, such as a large plain-SPY share, rather than remove more stocks.

insights.title: Waiting for a beaten-down company to recover trades the crash loss for the rebound gain
insights.body: We tried buying big companies that had fallen hard over five years, but only once their shares had started rising again. The idea was to avoid catching companies still in free fall. It worked in 2008: those picks fell about as much as SPY instead of far more. But in 2009 the companies that bounced back hardest were exactly the ones still falling the year before, and the filter had left them out. Picking the still-falling ones won 2009 by 36 points; the recovering ones lost it by 21. Over a full cycle the two roughly cancel, and since 2009 no version beat SPY. The lesson: among big US companies, the reward for buying long-term losers is the payment for holding them through the worst of a crash. A rule that removes that pain also removes the reward. Every version also made its money in the 2000-2002 tech crash, when unloved old-economy companies held up. That happened whichever losers were picked, so it is about the market's mood then, not about any picking skill.

insights.title: A long record of dividend raises did not protect against 2008: the longest records belonged to banks
insights.body: We tried holding big companies that had raised their dividend every single year for five, seven or ten years. That is the idea behind the well-known Dividend Aristocrats, which are said to have fallen far less than the market in 2008. Without a safety switch, our version fell almost 60% from its peak, more than SPY itself. The reason is who had the longest records just before the crisis: Wells Fargo, US Bancorp, State Street, KeyCorp, Fifth Third, Freddie Mac, GE and property trusts. These steady payers had never had a bad year until 2008, when they collapsed and cut. Our screen only checked once a year, so a company that cut in the middle of 2008 stayed in the book until the next January. The lesson: a good past record is not a cushion. The published index protects itself by dropping a company the moment it cuts and by its own weighting, not by the streak alone. With the usual rule of stepping aside when SPY is below its 200-day average, the same book earned 1.5 points a year more than SPY and fell at most 21%. That is close, but still over the 20% limit.

insights.title: In 2010-2015 the market's dips were real falls that bounced fast, so no trend switch could dodge them cheaply
insights.body: The dividend-raise book steps into cash when SPY falls under its 200-day average. We tried four ways of reading that line: the plain one, a 3% cushion each side, a 5% cushion, and the famous month-end version. All four left the market in the same three dips of 2010, 2011 and 2015. Those were real falls of 10 to 19 percent, deep enough to cross any cushion. Each one then recovered within months. A cushion only made the book come back later, and the lag to SPY in those years grew from 2.6 to 5.0 points a year as the cushion widened. The lesson: a trend switch earns its keep in a long crash like 2008 and pays for it in every quick bounce. The years most like today were all quick bounces. Tuning the line does not change that. Only a faster way back in could.

insights.title: Sera 20261011-1912: the safety switch loses in quick bounces, and no tuning of it fixes that
insights.body:
**No buy signal this batch.** Four new strategies were tried. One passed every check on its twenty-year numbers, but the version that passed was the unchanged starting point from last week, not anything new, and the lab's safety gate turned it away again: it beat SPY in only two of four later test periods and fell behind SPY in 2009-2015, the years with the most complete data. That was the only refusal this batch. It was refused for its test periods, not because a related strategy had already failed. The other three were rejected outright. No look at the hidden years was spent.

**What was tried, in plain words.**
- *A gentler safety switch for the calm dividend raisers.* Last batch found that the rule which sells everything when SPY drops below its 200-day average, and not the stocks themselves, was what lost to SPY after 2009. So this time the switch only acted when SPY was clearly through the line: 3% or 5% beyond it, or checked once a month. It did not help. The dips of 2010, 2011 and 2015 were real falls of 10 to 19 percent, deep enough to cross any cushion, and each bounced back within months. A cushion only made the book come back later. Its lag to SPY in those years grew from about 2.6 to as much as 5 points a year, and the 3% and 5% versions fell just past 20% at their worst. A switch earns its keep in a long crash like 2008 and pays for it in every quick bounce, and the recent years were all quick bounces.
- *Overnight winners, leaving out the ones that move most with the market.* The overnight momentum book earns about 15% a year but fell 23% in 1998. Dropping its most market-sensitive stocks got the fall under 20% only by cutting the return to about 10.6% a year, the same trade the earlier fixes made. It trailed SPY by about 2.7 points a year after 2009. The deep fall comes from holding strong stocks when momentum crashes, not from which strong stocks are held.
- *Long dividend-raise streaks* (new this batch, the idea behind the well-known Dividend Aristocrats). Big companies that had raised their dividend every year for five to ten years, with no safety switch, fell almost 60% in 2008, worse than SPY. Just before the crisis the longest streaks belonged to banks and lenders such as Wells Fargo, State Street and Freddie Mac, which had never had a bad year until they collapsed. A long record is not a cushion. The published index protects itself by dropping a company the moment it cuts, which our version did not do.
- *Turnaround losers.* Big companies that fell hardest over five years, bought only once their shares had started rising again. That avoided the worst of 2008 but missed the 2009 rebound, when the biggest winners were exactly the ones still falling the year before. No version beat SPY after 2009, and all fell more than 27% at their worst.

**What looks alive and what looks dead.** Dead: tuning the 200-day safety switch with cushions or monthly checks, filtering inside the overnight momentum pool, holding dividend streaks without an instant exit on a cut, and waiting for long-term losers to turn. Still alive but stuck: the calm dividend raisers, which beat SPY over twenty years and keep losing in 2009-2015. This batch says the cost is in how slowly the switch comes back, not in where it leaves, so a faster way back in is the one direction left for it.

**The safety gate.** The gate refused one strategy this batch, on its record over later test periods (two of four), not on a failed relative. Every strategy that passed its twenty-year numbers is now refused by the gate. That is the lab working as designed: a good twenty-year average has not been enough.

**What fees did.** Gotrade's real fees and fractional shares were in every test. No strategy lost an edge to them this batch. The streak book traded rarely and paid little.

**What would help most.** A true company-size figure for the years before 2009, so a book could lean toward the giants that led 2009-2015 by real size.

**What the next batch should try.** The calm dividend raisers that leave on the 200-day line but come back as soon as SPY closes above a shorter average. The dividend streaks with an instant exit the day a smaller payment is announced, behind the usual switch. The overnight winners as half of a book whose other half is plain SPY. Long-term losers as a small cushion beside a large SPY core.

insights.title: Choosing steadier companies moves the return a lot and the worst fall barely at all
insights.body:
The steady-company picker was built to attack the one rule that has killed every promising strategy here: never lose more than 20% from a peak. It bought, each month, the twenty big companies whose own share price had fallen least from its own high over the past year. Five versions ran, deliberately spanning the best and worst the idea could do: the twenty steadiest, the forty steadiest, a longer eighteen-month memory, the twenty that had fallen hardest as a deliberately bad control, and a plain spread of equal money across the forty most-traded names.

The spread in return between the best and worst of those was wide, about 2.5 points a year. The spread in worst fall was almost useless. Every single version, including the steadiest one, fell between 42% and 79% from its peak. The steadiest book fell 42.5%, more than twice the limit it was designed to respect.

That is the finding, and it is bigger than this one idea. Choosing better companies is a powerful lever on how much money is made and a weak lever on how far the account falls. The reason is that the deep falls do not come from owning the wrong companies, they come from owning companies at all on the days when every company falls together. In 2008 there was nowhere in the index to stand, and the measure that was supposed to find shelter had instead found banks, insurers and utilities, because those had been the steadiest names through 2006 and 2007.

What to do about it: stop expecting any stock-picking rule to deliver the 20% limit on its own. The limit is a question about how much of the money sits in shares when the market breaks, not about which shares. Every future idea aimed at the drawdown rule should be judged on that basis before an identifier is spent on it.

insights.title: Spreading money evenly across the biggest companies lost to the market, and fell much harder
insights.body:
An open question has been sitting in this journal for a while: when a strategy buys twenty or forty companies and puts the same amount of money in each, is it quietly betting against the shape of the market itself? The market index puts far more money into its largest companies. A strategy that gives a giant and a mid-sized company the same slot is making a bet on the smaller one, whether or not it meant to.

This run finally measured it, because one of its five versions was put in purely as a yardstick: take the forty most heavily traded big companies in the index, give each an equal share of the money, re-pick monthly, and do nothing clever at all.

It earned 5.8% a year on the owner's deposits where the market itself earned 7.2%, and it fell 62% from its peak where the market fell far less. So the answer is clear and unflattering: over 1996 to 2015, equal-weighting the biggest companies cost about 1.4 points a year and roughly doubled the damage in a crash. The market's habit of concentrating money in its largest companies is not a flaw to be corrected, it is a large part of why the market is hard to beat.

What to do about it: any future strategy that holds equal slots now carries a known handicap of roughly a point and a half a year, which it must earn back from its stock picking before it is even level with doing nothing. That handicap should be stated when a result is judged, and a strategy that only just beats the market while equal-weighting is in fact picking stocks quite well and giving most of it back to the weighting. It is also worth testing the obvious alternative directly: the same picks, but with the money distributed the way the market distributes it.

insights.title: The dividend-raiser book never beat the market; the spare cash parked in the market did
insights.body:
For six methods now we have been testing a book that buys big companies right after they raise their dividend. Its best version earned 10.6% a year on the owner's deposits where the market earned 7.2%, and we kept trying to fix the one thing it got wrong, which is that it has lagged the market since 2009.

This run finally took the book apart, and the answer is uncomfortable. The book only ever finds enough fresh dividend raisers to fill about four of its twenty slots. More than half the money has nowhere to go, so the design quietly parks that spare money in the market itself, and steps the whole lot into cash whenever the market is in a downtrend. That parking is where the money came from. When we remove it and let the dividend picks stand alone, they lose to the market in every stretch of the twenty years we can test: by about four and a half points a year in 1996 to 2002, and by more after 2009. Turning the safety switch on or off barely changes that.

So the strategy we have been refining was really a timed holding of the market with a dividend-stock sidecar attached, and the sidecar was costing money rather than making it. Everything that looked like skill at picking dividend raisers was the market doing the work.

Two things follow. The family should close: no further rule about which raisers to buy can rescue picks that have no edge in the first place. And any future strategy that parks its spare money in the market has to be measured twice, once with the parking and once without, because otherwise we cannot tell the picks from the parking. This one fooled us for six methods.

insights.title: Sell each stock when it turns down, not the whole book when the market does
insights.body:
Most of our strategies carry the same safety rule: when the market as a whole is below its one-year average, sell everything and sit in cash. It has one job, which is to keep us out of a crash like 2008, and it does that job. But it has also been the single biggest reason our strategies have lagged since 2009, because it sold the ordinary dips of 2010, 2011 and 2015 whole and bought back at higher prices. We tried softening it and that made things worse.

This run tried a different machine for the same job. Instead of one decision about the whole market, make twenty small decisions: refuse to hold any individual stock that is trading below its own one-year average, and leave that slice of the money in cash until that stock recovers. The book then empties gradually, a name at a time, and refills a name at a time.

As a brake it is clearly better. It cut the worst fall from 26% to 13%, the lowest this family has managed. In 2008 it lost 5% where the market lost 35%. It costs about one point of return a year. Best of all, once it is in place the old market-wide switch adds nothing at all: with both rules running, the worst fall was identical to the per-stock rule alone, and the extra switch only cost return. They do the same job and the per-stock one does it better.

As a way of choosing which stocks to own it is worth nothing. We tested that separately, by handing the money freed up by the rule to the surviving stocks instead of leaving it in cash, so the book held the same amount and only the names changed. It made no difference. All the benefit is holding less money during falls, none of it is picking better names.

So the per-stock exit is a general-purpose brake that has never been tried on a strategy that actually has an edge. The obvious place is the residual-momentum book, which beats the market by three to seven points a year in testing and fails, or nearly fails, only on how far it falls. That is the next experiment and it is queued.

insights.title: Measure a strategy's picks separately from the spare money it parks in the market
insights.body:
Several of our strategies have a rule for spare money: when they cannot find enough stocks to buy, they put the leftover into the market itself and hold it there. It is a sensible rule and it is not cheating. The problem is that it hides which half of the strategy is working.

The dividend-raiser family ran for six methods before anyone noticed that it only ever filled about four of its twenty slots, and that the market holding filling the other sixteen was carrying the entire result. Once we took that holding out, the dividend picks lost to the market in every era we can test. Six method slots and dozens of trials went into refining picks that never had an edge.

The lab should make this impossible to miss. Two things would do it. First, every strategy report should show how much of the money was actually invested in its own picks, averaged over the run, next to the return. Second, any strategy that parks spare money in the market should be re-run automatically with that parking turned off, as a free side-by-side report that spends no test budget and counts as no extra try, the same way we already re-run strategies against the real trading fees and against the missing dead companies. If the picks cannot beat the market without the parking, that is the first thing to know about them, not the last.

insights.title: The dividend-raise family's edge was the market money parked inside it, not its picks
insights.body:
The dividend-raise family is closed, and closing it leaves the lab with a harder problem than
the one it has been working on.

Six methods and thirty-five variants have now been run on the idea that companies announcing a
big dividend raise keep doing well afterwards. Every one of them ended in the same place: good
twenty-year averages, a negative lead over the market from 2009 onward, and two of four later
stretches won. Three separate rounds blamed the safety switch — the rule that sells the whole
book when the market falls below its long-run average — and set about fixing it. The last round
concluded that no gentler or slower version of the switch helps.

This round took the switch out and found the answer was never in the switch at all. The
dividend picks only ever filled about four slots in ten; the rest of the money sat in the market
itself, timed by the switch. Measured with that parked money removed, the dividend picks lose to
the market in every single era — behind by 4.4 points a year in 1996-2002, ahead by only about a
point in 2003-2008, and behind again by 5.7 points from 2009. The timed market holding was
worth about nine points a year in the early stretch; the switch on top of it was worth about
four tenths of a point. So the family's apparent edge was a market holding wearing a dividend
costume, and three rounds of work went into tuning the costume.

The risk this records is not about dividends. It is that a book which parks idle money in the
market can hide picks that lose, for years, behind a result that looks like an edge — and this
lab had no routine check that would catch it. A method should not be able to report a lead over
the market without also reporting how much of its money was actually in its own picks, and what
those picks did on their own. That check is now queued as a feature wish.

It also sharpens what the lab is short of. The one genuinely good thing this round produced is a
far better brake: selling each holding when that share price turns down, rather than selling
everything when the market does, cut the worst fall from 26% to 13%, turned a 14% loss in 2008
into a 5% one, and cost under a point a year — and it makes the old market-wide switch
redundant rather than useful alongside it. But a brake only protects an edge; it cannot create
one. The only books in this lab whose picks demonstrably beat the market belong to the momentum
and residual-momentum families, and all of those are permanently closed because versions of them
have already failed out of sample. Every family still open now needs to prove its picks beat the
market with no parked market money and no gate at all, before anything is built on top of them.
That, not the drawdown rule, is the lab's binding problem from here.

insights.title: The safety rule does not cost money by sitting in cash. It costs money by changing its mind
insights.body:
Half the strategies here carry the same safety rule: sell everything when the market tracker closes below its average price of the last 200 days, buy back when it closes above. Until now it was always tested bolted onto a stock picker, so nobody could say what the rule itself was worth. This test held nothing but the market tracker and changed only how often the rule was read.

Read once a week, the owner's money would have grown at 4.4% a year. Read once a month, the exact same rule, 9.1% a year. That is a gap of 4.7 points a year for nothing but reading more often.

The surprise is where the gap comes from. The two versions use the same rule, and it says the same thing on the same days: out of the market on 1,562 of the 5,469 trading days, for both. Both ended up invested about 71% of the time. Trading fees explain only 0.7 of the 4.7 points, which I checked by re-running everything with the fees switched off. The other 4 points is simply buying and selling at worse prices, because the weekly version turned the whole book over four times as often inside that same 71%.

Why: a real crash lasts months, so a monthly check catches it just as well as a weekly one. A weekly check only reacts faster to dips that were about to end, which means selling near the bottom and buying back higher.

What to do: stop building strategies that check this rule weekly. Several of the strategies already judged and shelved here were carrying a 4.7-point handicap that had nothing to do with their own idea, and their verdicts are not safe. Any one worth another look should be re-run on the monthly reading first.

insights.title: The safety rule is insurance, and the premium is six points a year in the years most like today
insights.body:
Measured on its own, with no stock picking to hide behind, the safety rule's entire twenty-two-year advantage comes from three calendar years. It sat in cash through all of 2001, all of 2002 and all of 2008, and so avoided falls of 17%, 22% and 35%. That is worth a lot.

It pays for those three years everywhere else. It gave up 18 points in 2009 alone, because the same slow average that got it out in 2008 kept it out while the market turned. It gave up another 19 points across 1998, 2003, 2010 and 2015. Add it all up over 1994 to 2015 and the rule wins by a nose: 9.6% a year against 8.8% for just holding the market.

Now split the record by era. In 2009 to 2015 — the stretch most like the one the owner is actually investing in, and the one with the best data — every version of the rule lost to simply holding the market, by between 6 and 11 points a year. The best version gave up 5.9 points a year.

A second reading says the same thing. The rule earns about 5.6 points a year over the market in months when a few giant companies carry the index, and loses about 1 point in months when the typical company keeps up. That is the shape of an insurance policy: it pays out in a panic and bleeds the rest of the time.

What to do: treat this rule as insurance with a price tag, not as a free safety feature. Six points a year is a very expensive premium against a crash that may not come. Before putting it in any new strategy, ask whether the owner would knowingly pay six points a year for it. The honest answer so far is no.

insights.title: We never count the interest the cash earns while a strategy sits out of the market
insights.body:
When a strategy steps out of the market, its money sits as dollars earning nothing in every test this lab has ever run. In real life it would earn interest. The safety-rule test above sat in cash 29% of the time over twenty-two years, and for most of that period US short-term interest rates were 3 to 5 percent a year. So every strategy with a step-aside rule has been scored worse than it deserved, probably by around a point a year across the 1990s and 2000s.

I could not put a number on it. The research store can hold a file of market-wide daily series, Treasury yields included, but the copy these tests run on does not have that file. The only other route is to park the idle money in a Treasury-bill fund, and the fund the lab knows about has no prices before May 2007 — which is precisely the wrong half of the window, because rates were near zero from 2009 onward.

What to do: add Treasury-bill yields to the research store and let an idle-cash rule earn them. It is a small change with a wide reach: every step-aside strategy in the lab would be re-scored slightly kinder, and the comparison against simply holding the market would finally be fair in both directions. It will not rescue the safety rule — the era where it loses hardest is the era where cash paid nothing — but it would stop the lab quietly penalising every strategy that ever steps aside.

insights.title: Correction: the safety rule's weekly penalty does not transfer from one strategy to another
insights.body:
An earlier note today said that reading the safety rule weekly instead of monthly costs 4.7 points a year, and that several shelved strategies were therefore carrying a handicap that had nothing to do with their own idea. The first half is right. The second half overstates it, and the lab already held the evidence against it. I am correcting it here rather than quietly, because the overstatement would have sent us re-running a batch of old strategies for nothing.

The 4.7 points was measured on a book that held nothing but the market tracker, so the rule was the entire book. The late-declaration dividend strategy is the one other clean case where the same rule was read at both speeds on otherwise identical settings and real fees. There the cadence was worth only half a point to one point a year — its monthly versions earned 10.4 to 11.1% and its weekly versions 9.9 to 10.3%.

The reason is simple. A flip-flop costs whatever it sells cheap and buys back dear. When the book is all market tracker, a flip-flop sells and rebuys everything. When the book is twenty calm dividend payers it was going to re-pick anyway, the forced sale overlaps with trading it would have done regardless, and calm stocks fall less than the index in exactly the dips that trigger the flip-flop.

So the rule's cost scales with how much of the money the rule itself is holding: near the full 4.7 points when the book is parked in the market behind it, around one point when the book is in its own stock picks.

What to do: make monthly the default for new strategies, but do not re-run the shelved weekly ones as a batch hoping the frame was the problem. The ones worth revisiting are only those that spent most of their time parked in the market rather than in their own picks — for those, the test was measuring the safety rule more than the idea. What does hold everywhere is the other half: in every paired test here, reading the rule more often also made the worst fall deeper, by about 4 points on a stock book and by 14 points on this one.

insights.title: Protecting against falls is cheap over twenty years and ruinous in the years that matter most
insights.body:
A new experiment put one simple safety machine on a plain book of big, heavily traded companies: the further the book sits below its own best level of the past year, the more of it is moved into cash, in a straight line, until at a 20% fall it is all in cash. No judgement calls, no all-or-nothing switch.

Over the full twenty years it looks like the best bargain this lab has found. It cut the worst fall from 50% to 17%, and it charged about 1.3 points of return a year for that. A gentler setting charged 0.6 points a year and still held the worst fall to 24% instead of 50%.

Then look at when the bill came due. Almost all the protection was earned in two crashes, 2000 to 2002 and 2008. Almost all the cost was paid in the recoveries between and after them, and the worst single stretch was 2009 to 2015, where the safety machine gave up ten points a year. That stretch is the one we trust most, because the data covers it best and it looks most like today.

The reason is that a machine which reacts to falls is late in both directions. Being late to sell costs little, because the first part of a crash is already over. Being late to buy back costs a great deal, and it costs it every single time the market dips and bounces rather than crashing. Between 2009 and 2015 the market dipped and bounced over and over, and the book was never more than 15% down in that whole stretch, so the machine kept selling into drops that never needed protecting against and kept buying back higher.

One number captures it. The protected book's worst stretch began in October 2007 and did not end until June 2010. It was never deeply down, but it was still down more than a year after the unprotected version had already hit bottom and started climbing.

What to do about it: stop the machine reacting to small falls at all. If it sits idle until the book is 15% down and only then starts moving money to cash, it would have been close to dormant through all of 2009 to 2015, while still cutting hard in 2000 and 2008 when falls reached nearly half. That is the next thing to try, and it is queued.

insights.title: A safety machine can be driven off a cheap stand-in instead of the real account, and it barely notices
insights.body:
A machine that reacts to how far an account has fallen has an awkward problem: the part of the system that chooses what to buy is never shown the account's balance. So the fall it reacts to has to be rebuilt from share prices alone.

That rebuilt version is cruder than the real thing in three ways. It pays no trading fees. It knows nothing about the monthly deposits going in. And it does not know which companies were actually in the index on any past date, so it just ranks every company whose prices we hold.

I expected the two to drift apart, and for the machine to end up reacting to falls the real account never had. They did not drift. Month by month the stand-in and the real book moved together almost perfectly. Over twenty years both grew at the same 7.8% a year. Their readings of how far down the book was differed by about one point on average, and out of roughly fifty months where either called the book more than 10% down, they agreed on forty-eight.

Two things follow. First, this kind of safety machine is cheap to build and does not need the account's own records to work. Second, and more useful, it is portable: because it is driven by prices alone, the same machine can be bolted onto any of the lab's strategies without rebuilding it each time.

There is a caution attached. A stand-in driven off its own braked account would be useless, because once it has moved money to cash the account stops falling, so the fall never heals and the money never goes back in. This one deliberately tracks the unprotected book instead, which is what makes it recover sensibly. Any future version has to keep that property.

insights.title: There is no way to check a safety machine daily, only weekly
insights.body:
The owner's strategies can be set to re-pick their holdings monthly and to adjust how much is invested either monthly or weekly. There is no setting for adjusting daily.

That became a real limit in this experiment. The idea being tested was a machine that watches how far the book has fallen and moves money to cash in proportion. Watching that daily is the natural version, and the one most likely to protect well, because a bad fall can happen inside a week. The best available was weekly.

As it turned out, weekly versus monthly barely mattered here: checking weekly rather than monthly cost about 0.4 points of return a year and bought 1.7 points of protection. So the daily version probably would not have changed the verdict. But we cannot say that, we can only guess it, and the next safety machine may well be one where the speed of reaction is the whole point.

What would fix it is a fourth trading setting: re-pick holdings monthly, adjust how much is invested every day. The machinery to run it already exists; what is missing is a named, approved setting, which is what the rules require before a strategy can graduate to paper trading. Worth adding before the next experiment of this kind.

insights.title: Sera 20261012-0832: four ways to stop the falls, all of them work, none of them pay — and our best-looking family never had an edge
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Nothing cleared the four conditions together, and nothing came close
enough to argue about. Survivorship-free price history is still not worth buying.

This round went after the rule that has killed almost everything we have found: the limit that
says a strategy may never lose more than a fifth of its value from its peak. Every strategy that
has beaten the market on average has died on that rule, and the only tool we had for it was a
switch that sells everything when the market turns down. So we built four different machines for
holding on to money in a fall and measured all four.

The short answer is that all four machines work, and not one of them pays.

The switch that sells everything when the market turns down, measured on its own with nothing
else in the book, turns a 55% worst fall into a 19% one. From 2009 to 2015 it earned under 11%
a year while simply holding the market earned 16.6%. Its entire twenty-two-year advantage comes
from three years: 2001, 2002 and 2008. It hands back eighteen points in 2009 alone by sitting in
cash through the turn. It is insurance, and the premium is about six points a year in exactly the
kind of years we have been living in since.

Selling each share when that share turns down, rather than selling the whole book when the market
does, is clearly the better machine. It cut one book's worst fall from 26% to 13%, turned a 14%
loss in 2008 into a 5% one, and cost under a point a year. It also makes the old market-wide
switch pointless: running both together leaves the worst fall exactly where the per-share rule
alone put it, and costs a further fifth of a point. If we keep any fall-protection at all, this is
the one to keep.

Trimming the book in proportion to how far the account has fallen below its own high did the same
job at a similar price — a 50% worst fall became 17% for about 1.3 points a year — and lost ten
points a year from 2009 doing it.

Choosing companies that do not fall much does not work at all. Ranking the big, heavily traded
names by how far each had fallen from its own high in the past year is a genuinely good signal
for returns: the mildest fallers earned two points a year more than the hardest fallers. But every
version of that book, from the best to the deliberately worst, still fell between 42% and 79%.
A company's own past fall tells you nothing about the day every company falls together. Protecting
against falls is an exposure decision, not a stock-picking one.

The most important thing this batch found was not about falls at all, and it is uncomfortable.
Our dividend-raise family — six strategies and thirty-five variations, the one we have spent three
rounds tuning — never had an edge. The dividend picks only ever filled about four slots in ten;
the rest of the money sat in the market itself, timed by the switch. Take that parked money out
and measure the picks alone, and they lose to the market in every single era: behind by 4.4 points
a year in the late nineties, ahead by barely a point through the 2000s, behind by 5.7 points from
2009. The timed market holding was worth about nine points a year early on. The switch on top of
it was worth four tenths of a point. We were tuning the costume, not the body. That family is now
closed.

What that leaves is a harder problem than the one we started the batch on. A brake protects an
edge; it cannot create one. The only strategies in this lab whose picks demonstrably beat the
market belong to the momentum families, and every one of those is permanently closed because
versions of them have already failed on unseen data. The families still open turn out, when you
take the parked market money out, not to have a picking edge at all. So the question for the next
rounds is not how to stop the falls. We know how to do that now, and we know what it costs. The
question is whether there is any group of shares we can choose that beats simply owning the market,
held plainly, with no parked cash and no safety switch underneath it to flatter the result.

What the gate did. It refused the one strategy that reached eligibility, and it was right to:
that eligibility came only from a control arm we included deliberately to reproduce an earlier
result, and the strategy won only two of the four later stretches with an unstable choice of
version. It was refused on the fold test, not on family history. No test-window look was spent
this batch; we have still used four in total.

What the fees did. Less than you would guess, and the batch finally separated the two. Checking
the safety switch every week instead of every month costs 4.7 points a year — but only 0.7 of that
is Gotrade's fees. The other four points is simply getting worse prices by trading four times as
often on the same decisions. The switch does not cost money by sitting in cash; it costs money by
changing its mind. One honest correction came out of this mid-run: that 4.7 figure applies when the
switch is holding all of the money, and shrinks to well under a point in a real twenty-share book,
so it is not grounds for re-framing every strategy we own.

Three things in our own tooling are now costing us real accuracy. First, and worst: idle cash earns
nothing anywhere in our tests. We have no interest-rate history in the dev data at all. Every
strategy that steps out of the market is therefore penalised for doing so, by something like
three quarters of a point a year — which means the safety switch is being judged more harshly than
it deserves, and some of this batch's verdicts against it are partly our own measurement. Fixing
that is the single highest-value data job on the list. Second, nothing makes a strategy report how
much of its money was actually in its own picks; had it done so, we would have caught the dividend
family five strategies ago instead of on the thirty-fifth variation. Third, a safety rule can only
be checked weekly in our machinery, never daily.

For the next batch: stop building brakes and go looking for picks. Take each family that is still
open, strip out every parked holding and every switch, and ask the one question plainly — do these
shares, on their own, beat owning the market? Anything that cannot answer yes is not worth a brake.

insights.title: Idle cash can now be priced, but nothing pays it yet: the interest rule is still missing
insights.body:
Insight 178 asked for two things and today only the first is done.

**Done: the data.** The ten market-wide series are back in both research stores, from a free
source instead of the paid month whose cache was deleted. Over the dev window the 13-week
Treasury-bill yield covers 4,969 of 4,984 trading days, and over the test window all 2,758. The
store's price files are untouched, so none of the 354 recorded trials is affected, and both
stores rebuild to the same bytes from the same cache. A strategy can now read the interest rate
as a signal, and the two older strategies that needed these series are reproducible again.

**Not done: paying the interest.** Nothing in the simulator credits interest on money the book is
not holding in shares. Idle cash still earns exactly zero, which is the distortion insight 178 was
actually about: over the dev window the bill rate averaged 2.6% a year, 5.5% through the 1990s and
essentially nothing after 2009, and the safety-rule test that sat in cash 29% of the time was
charged the full twenty-two years of that at zero. The arithmetic on that one strategy is about
three quarters of a point a year.

**The reason it was not simply switched on, which is a decision rather than an omission.** The
simulator is shared by the lab's backtests and by the live paper books, and the lab compares
trials on the price files alone -- a change in how cash behaves is invisible to that check. So if
interest were credited unconditionally, every new trial would quietly stop being comparable with
the 354 already recorded, with nothing in the database to mark the break. That is the same shape
as the funding bug of 2026-10-08, where a return column silently meant two different things.

**What it should look like instead.** Interest should be an explicit part of a trading rule set,
the way the real Gotrade fees are: a named rule that a method opts into, defaulting to off, so
old trials keep meaning what they meant and any new trial that earns interest says so in its
configuration. Then the handful of step-aside strategies worth re-scoring can be re-run as
declared variations and compared against their own twins, rather than against a past that was
measured under different rules.

**What it is worth.** It will not rescue the safety switch: the era where that rule loses hardest,
2009 onward, is exactly the era where cash paid nothing, so the re-scoring helps it most in the
years it was already winning. The value is honesty rather than rescue -- today the lab quietly
penalises every strategy that ever steps aside, and cannot say by how much.

insights.title: Same-month seasonality: buy the stocks that did best in this calendar month last year: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 56.0% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +10.5% a year against the market's +7.9%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +12.3% a year, which is +4.4% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +2.6% a year against the market as recorded, +4.4% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +6.1% a year against the market as recorded, +7.6% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +4.7% a year against the market as recorded, +5.5% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −4.7% a year against the market as recorded, −1.7% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 3 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: What the five live books actually picked, and what was only the market
insights.body:
The question was simple and the lab had never been able to answer it: of the money each of the five
surviving books actually held, how much was ever in names the book chose for itself, and what did
those names earn against the market once the money parked in the market and the safety brakes were
taken away? Every book was re-run four ways over the same twenty years, on the same starting money
and the same monthly top-up, changing nothing but what it was allowed to hold.

The answer, book by book. The seasonality book held a little over half its money in its own names
and beat the market by two and a half points a year as it ran, four and a half with the brakes off.
The bounce book held the most of its own names of any of the five, and it is the one the brakes
barely touch — what it earns is simply what its picking earns, about three and a half points a year
ahead. The market-core book is the only one that parks anything, and it is the surprise: only about
a third of its money was ever in its own names, and those names, given the whole book, beat the
market by seven and a half points a year, better than the book as it actually ran. The money it
parks in the market was holding it back, not holding it up. The quiet-blend book and the overnight
book both park nothing, and for both the brake is expensive: each gives up between three and four
points a year of lead to save about the same in worst fall.

So the live space is not empty, and it is not what the dividend family was. There, the parked
market money was carrying picks that had no edge of their own. Here, three of the five books park
nothing whatsoever, and the one that does park is diluted by it rather than propped up.

Two cautions matter more than the good news. The five books are far less separate than they look:
almost all of them stop buying on the same signal, the market falling below its long-term average,
read on the same dates, and that single shared rule is what produced a thirty-five point lead in
2008 for every one of them. That is one trade shared five ways. The lab's own control for it shows
it has been a drag every year since 2009. And over the most recent stretch, 2009 to the end of the
development window, every book as it actually ran is behind the market, and even with the brakes
removed only two of them get back above it, by under three points a year. Whatever is chosen next
should be judged on the recent years first, because that is where all five are weakest.

One thing the measurement could not do, and it should be said plainly: a safety rule that works by
holding nothing at all cannot be switched off this way. When a book says "not today" it hands back
no names, and nothing can invent the basket it would otherwise have bought. So instead the share of
days each book held nothing is reported alongside — about twenty-eight in every hundred for four of
the five, which is that same shared signal firing.

None of this was recorded as a new try. The count of tries did not move, the budget of looks at the
held-out years was not touched, and no book's verdict changed. It was a measurement of what the lab
already had.

- With the rule it held nothing at all on 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold; without it, 0.0%.

- 2009-2015: −4.7% a year against the market as it stands, −0.1% with the rule off.
