insights.title: Overnight-picked winners under a weekly volatility brake: the 1998 fall is the only thing left to fix: what its market safety rule was worth
insights.body:
Most of the methods this lab still holds stop buying whenever the market is below its own long-term average, and they all read that same rule on the same dates. The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, once as it stands and once with that one rule switched off and nothing else changed. The numbers below are for its best version.

- As it stands it earned +10.2% a year against the market's +7.2%; with the rule off, +8.7%.
- Its worst fall was 17.5% with the rule and 37.1% without it.
- With the rule it held nothing at all on 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold; without it, 0.0%.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +3.0% a year against the market as it stands, +1.5% with the rule off.
- 1996-2002: +5.4% a year against the market as it stands, +2.7% with the rule off.
- 2003-2008: +7.0% a year against the market as it stands, +4.4% with the rule off.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as it stands, +14.9% with the rule off.
- 2009-2015: −4.9% a year against the market as it stands, −2.8% with the rule off.

Over the whole history the safety rule was worth +2.1% a year on average across this method's versions. In the 2008 crash alone it was worth +22.2%. From 2009 to the end of the history it cost +1.1% a year.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Six new trials, and the luck hurdle did not move
insights.body: The lab recorded six new development trials today, three on each of two books it already held, and the hurdle those trials are judged against stayed exactly where it was: 74. It counts books, not trials, so adding versions to a book the lab already has is free, and only a brand-new book raises the bar for every book at once. The count of development trial rows went from 354 to 360; that is a different number and it is not the hurdle. The held-out years were not touched: the look budget reads 4, as it has since it was last spent.

insights.title: The brakes buy the risk limit, and the market switch is one 2008 trade four books share
insights.body:
Two things were measured today, and they point in opposite directions from what we expected.

**The brakes are what keep these books inside your risk limit, and taking them off does not buy a
strategy you can hold.** The two books with the only recent edge in this lab were both re-run with
their safety mechanism removed. Both earned a lot more — your money would have grown about 15% a
year instead of about 10%, against 7.2% for the same deposits in the market. Both then fell too far:
20.6% on one and 22.4-22.8% on the other, against your 20% limit. That was predicted in writing
before either ran, and it held. So the finding is not that we found something and it broke a rule.
It is that the lab now holds, as a recorded measurement rather than an inference, the fact that its
best recent idea exists only above the line you drew. One of them misses by six tenths of a point.

**The shared market switch is not the drag it looked like — it is a bargain that stopped paying.**
The 200-day rule that four of the five live books share was priced across all 22 recorded versions
that carry it. Over the whole window it helped every single one: 22 of 22, worth +2.1% a year on
average. In 2008 alone it was worth +31%. And since 2009 it has helped none of them: 0 of 22, at a
cost of −3.2% a year. That unanimity is the point. It is one rule, read on one index, on the same
dates, so it is not twenty-two pieces of evidence — it is one trade that four books share, which
paid enormously once and has cost a little every year since.

What that means together: removing the switch is not the fix. Every version we ran with it off was
worse on return AND on worst fall at the same time — 66.7% and 61.4% on one book, 37.1% on the
other. The switch is buying the drawdown your limit requires. The brake is doing the same, and
costing about four and a half points a year to do it. Those are two prices you can look at and
judge. Neither is a strategy to promote, and no intermediate setting was tried for either, because
choosing one after seeing these numbers is tuning to a result.

The one durability reading worth keeping: the overnight book wins 3 of 4 walk-forward folds and is
stable across them, which is the strongest showing of the two. It still promotes nothing, because
every version of it that earns the return breaks the limit.

insights.title: The market switch across the whole lab: the collapse holds, the unanimity does not
insights.body:
Earlier today the market switch was priced across the five books still in service: 22 recorded
versions carry it, it helped every one of them over the whole window, and it has helped none of
them since 2009. The same question has now been put to the whole lab — every version of every book
that carries the switch, 228 of them — and the wider answer changes one part of that and confirms
the rest.

**What held.** The switch is still one trade, and still the same one. In 2008 alone it helped 226 of
the 228 versions, worth about +33% that year. Since 2009 it has helped 10 of 228, at a cost of about
−4.4% a year. The collapse is not a quirk of the five books we happen to still hold; it is
everywhere in the lab, and it is the same rule read on the same index on the same dates, so it
remains one piece of evidence rather than 228.

**What did not hold.** The unanimity did. Across the five live books the switch helped every version
over the whole window, which read like an unusually clean result. Across the whole lab it helps
about three versions in four — 174 of 228, worth +1.3% a year rather than +2.1%. So the "every
single one" was partly an accident of looking at five books. The direction is unchanged and the case
for keeping the switch is unchanged; the strength of the claim is weaker than it looked, and it is
better to find that out from our own wider sample than from the owner's money.

**Nineteen versions look as though they have no safety rule and sit in cash anyway.** That was worth
checking, because a version that quietly stops buying while declaring no rule is exactly the kind of
thing that makes a measurement wrong without announcing it. None of them turned out to be a missed
rule. Six belong to a book whose picks need company accounts that only begin in 2009, so it holds
nothing in the earlier years for want of data. Three run their own crash rule, read weekly instead
of monthly, and their own settings refuse to carry the market switch as well. Five belong to the
book whose entire purpose is to price the switch on its own — it holds the market when the switch is
on and cash when it is off, so switching it off would just be holding the market, which that book
already records as its own control. Two use a per-share version of the rule, dropping holdings one
at a time rather than selling everything at once, and also already record the comparison. Three
carry a falling-account brake and no market rule at all, by design. In every case the comparison
worth making either does not exist or is already on file.

**Why this could only be measured now.** The tool that prices the switch was reading each book's
original list of versions and not the later additions, so today's six new versions — the ones this
morning's work recorded — were reported as missing from their own books and were never priced. That
is fixed, and the wider run above is the first one that sees the whole lab. It changes none of the
numbers in this morning's note: those came from the recorded trials themselves, not from this tool.

insights.title: A safety rule you cannot tune lost to one you can, on both counts at once
insights.body:
Most of the strategies in this lab share one safety rule: sell everything when the S&P 500 tracker falls below its average price of the last 200 trading days, buy back when it rises above. Every post-mortem has eventually blamed that rule, and the standing complaint is that it reads the price chart, so it could have been quietly tuned until the past looked good.

This test put the complaint to the strongest possible alternative: a calendar. Sell in May, buy back on Halloween. It cannot be tuned, because it never looks at a price at all. There is no window length, no threshold, no reading schedule to choose, and both versions tried here were named in print long before the years they were tested on.

Measured on exactly the same days, the same deposits and the same real fees, the calendar lost on both counts at the same time. The 200-day rule made the owner 1.4 points a year MORE than simply holding the index and cut the worst fall from 55 percent to 19 percent. The calendar made 1.4 points a year LESS and still left a 36 percent fall. The narrow version that only steps aside in September and October was worse again, 2.0 points a year behind with a 42 percent fall.

Why it matters: the complaint about the 200-day rule can now be answered with a number instead of an opinion, and the answer is that the rule earns its place. The reason the calendar fails is worth remembering on its own. Summers are positive on average, so a rule that sits them out has to be paid for in disasters avoided, and twenty-two years contained only three worth avoiding: 2001, 2002 and 2008. Strip those three out and the other nineteen summers made 5.6 percent each, with nothing to step aside from.

What to do about it: stop treating the 200-day rule as the weak link that needs replacing, and do not spend another idea on a calendar rule of any kind. A rule that acts on a handful of calendar occasions has a handful of observations behind it, and the luck check will refuse it long before real money is at risk.

insights.title: Holding the twenty busiest big companies in equal amounts lost to simply buying the index
insights.body:
This test needed a plain, honest book to lay the calendar rule on top of, so it used one with no stock-picking claim at all: the twenty index members that trade the most dollars a day, held in equal amounts, refreshed monthly, with no safety rule of any kind. It was meant to be scenery. It turned out to be the most useful thing the test produced.

Over 1996 to 2015, on the owner's real deposits and real fees, that book made 5.7 percent a year while the same deposits put into the index tracker made 7.2 percent. Its worst fall was 74 percent, against the tracker's 55 percent. So: a point and a half a year worse, and roughly twenty extra points of fall, for holding the same kind of companies in equal slices instead of letting the big ones be big.

Why it matters: this is the clearest measurement the lab has of something the owner's own money runs kept hinting at. The index tracker is not merely a benchmark to beat, it is a particular bet, and the bet is that the largest companies keep getting larger. Every strategy here that holds twenty or thirty names in equal slices is quietly betting the other way, and now we know what that side bet costs before any stock picking has happened.

What to do about it: treat it as a starting handicap. Any book that holds twenty-odd big names in equal amounts begins a point and a half a year behind, and its picking rule has to earn that back before it has earned anything at all. The next question, already queued, is whether the penalty comes from the equal slices themselves or simply from holding too few names, which a run at thirty, forty and fifty names will settle.

insights.title: The lab's summary screen reports the wrong number for how many times we have looked
insights.body:
Every result in this lab is marked down for how many times we have gone looking, because the more ideas you try, the more likely the best one is luck. Since early October that count has been one per idea tried, not one per variation of an idea, and it is currently seventy-five.

The lab's summary screen still prints a different number in that slot. Today it says three hundred and seventy-two, which is the count of individual variations ever run, under a label saying it is the number the luck check uses. The results themselves are judged correctly against seventy-five. Only the summary line is wrong.

Why it matters: anyone reading the summary to judge how trustworthy a result is, including whoever writes the next analysis, will take the headline number and reach for the wrong conclusion, in either direction. The gap is nearly fivefold. The whole point of the luck check is that it is not negotiable and not confusing.

What to do about it: have the summary print the number the check actually uses, and keep the count of variations on a separate line with its own plain label, so both facts are available and neither is mistaken for the other.

insights.title: Cash earns nothing in our tests, which quietly punishes every strategy that steps aside
insights.body:
When a strategy here sells everything and waits, the money it is holding earns exactly zero until it buys back. In the real world that money sits in a brokerage account earning interest, and over most of 1994 to 2007 American short-term interest paid three to five percent a year.

For most strategies this barely matters, because they are out of the market for a few weeks at a time. For the ones built around stepping aside it matters a great deal. The calendar rule tested here is out of the market for six months of every year, so roughly one and a half to two and a half points a year of real income is missing from its column. The 200-day safety rule sat in cash for most of 2001, 2002 and 2008. Those are the exact years those rules are supposed to be judged on.

Why it matters: it means every number this lab has published for a rule that goes to cash is too low, and nobody knows by how much. Today that does not change any verdict, because the strategies being compared all hold cash and all lose the same income, so the ranking survives even if the levels do not. But the moment one strategy is compared with another that stays invested, the comparison is tilted, and the tilt grows with how long the cautious one waits.

What to do about it: pay interest on idle cash in the simulator, using the published short-term government rate for the day. The lab already stores those rates for other purposes, so the information is on hand. Until that exists, any analysis of a strategy that spends months in cash should say in plain words that its reported return is a floor, not an estimate.

insights.title: Where the monthly top-up goes: buy the laggard instead of topping everything up evenly: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 97.1% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +6.2% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +6.2% a year, which is −1.0% against the market.
- On 0.0% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: −1.0% a year against the market as recorded, −1.0% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: −1.3% a year against the market as recorded, −1.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: −2.7% a year against the market as recorded, −2.7% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: −3.3% a year against the market as recorded, −3.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: +1.5% a year against the market as recorded, +1.5% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 1 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: When a rule and its exact opposite both lose money, the rule is empty — not backwards
insights.body:
We tested a timing rule: own a basket of big companies in the months when those companies are moving far apart from each other, and own the market instead when they all move together. The thinking is that months when companies scatter are the months when choosing between them is worth doing. It lost. Against simply holding the basket every month and never consulting the rule at all, it cost 1.6 points a year of the owner's money.

That alone would be an ordinary failure. The useful part is that we also ran the identical rule read backwards — own the basket when companies move together — and that lost too, 1.1 points a year. Both directions lose.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. A rule that loses might simply be pointing the wrong way, and a wrong-way rule is a gift: you flip it and you have a winner. A rule whose opposite also loses cannot be fixed by flipping, by a longer lookback or by a different threshold, because there is nothing in it to flip. All it can do is make you trade, and trading costs money whichever way you face. We swept four settings of this one and they landed in a band barely one point wide, with the do-nothing version sitting above every one of them.

I would like this to become a habit: whenever we price a new on-off rule, run it backwards in the same batch. It costs one of the six slots we get per idea, it cannot be done afterwards without spending a fresh idea, and it is the difference between learning that something does not work and learning that it never will.

insights.title: A plain book of fifty big companies loses to the market by half a point a year — before any clever idea is added
insights.body:
To test whether it helps to avoid companies the index has only just bought, I needed a plain book to compare against: the fifty most heavily traded companies in the index, equal money in each, re-chosen monthly, run on your real deposits at Gotrade's real fees. That plain book is the finding.

Over twenty years it earned 6.5% a year on your money where the same deposits into the market earned 7.2%, and at its worst it fell 57% from its peak. It lost half a point a year, every year, just by spreading money evenly instead of leaning toward the biggest companies the way the market does.

The lab already suspected this for the years after 2018. This says it was true through the whole 1996 to 2015 stretch as well, once the money is counted the way you actually deposit it rather than as a single lump at the start.

Why it matters: almost every stock-picking book the lab has built is, underneath its signal, some version of this plain book. So a picking rule is not competing from a standing start — it is starting half a point a year behind the market and carrying a 57% fall. Several of the methods that came closest to passing are only ahead by about that much, which means their edge may be the weighting fight rather than the picking.

What to do about it: before trusting any near miss, check whether it still wins when its book is weighted toward the bigger companies instead of evenly. I have queued exactly that test as the next idea.

insights.title: Companies are a drag in their first year inside the index and winners by their third
insights.body:
When a company is added to a big index, every index fund has to buy it at once. The research says that forced buying lifts the price and that the company gives it back afterwards. I could test this directly, because the lab has always known the exact date each company joined.

It held up, on the timetable the research describes. Among the fifty most heavily traded members, the ones added within the previous twelve months went on to earn about 5.6 percentage points a year less than the rest of the book.

But the sign flips if you wait longer. Companies added two to three years earlier actually beat the rest of the book in the 2009 to 2015 years, by between 7 and 14 points a year. They are a drag while they are new and leaders once they have settled in, which makes sense: the index tends to add companies that are growing, and growth takes a few years to show up in the share price.

Why it matters: it means any rule built on how long a company has been in the index has a narrow window of about a year where it points the right way, and points the wrong way on either side of it. Avoiding new members for three years throws away winners, and that is exactly what happened — the three-year version was the worst of the five tried.

What to do about it: do not build another avoidance rule on this. The honest number is that only about one or two of fifty holdings are ever new enough to matter, so even a genuine 5.6-point drag on them moves a whole book by about a seventh of a point a year. The effect is real-shaped and far too small to pay for anything. If the idea comes back, it should come back as a short-term trade around the joining date itself, not as a filter on a long-term book.

insights.title: Reshuffling which companies you hold may be costing us more than any market-timing rule ever saved
insights.body:
This turned up by accident, in the version of the test that was only there as a yardstick.

Two of our experiments have now held a basket carved out of the same hundred most-traded big companies, with the same fees, the same monthly rhythm and the same twenty years. One held twenty of them and earned the owner 3.2% a year. One held fifty and earned 6.0%. Nearly three points a year of difference, from nothing but how finely the same hundred companies were sliced. That is a bigger gap than any of the market-timing rules we have carefully priced, including the famous one about the market's 200-day average.

I do not think it is really about owning more companies. The trade counts point somewhere else. Both baskets pick their names by taking every second company, or every fifth, off a list ranked by how heavily each is traded — and that ranking reshuffles every month. Companies drop in and out of the slice constantly, and each one of those is a complete buy and sell that bought us nothing. The twenty-name basket made 3,479 trades over twenty years; the fifty-name basket made 5,888.

If that is the real cause, the fix is free and applies to every book we run, not just this one: hold your whole shortlist instead of taking a sample of it that gets redrawn every month. A company would then only be sold when it genuinely drops off the shortlist.

I have deliberately not claimed this is proven. The obvious comparison — a hundred-name basket with no timing rule on it — does not exist in our records; the one hundred-name run we have had a timing rule attached, so it is not a fair yardstick. The next experiment is built to settle it properly, by separating how many companies you hold from how often you resample which ones.

insights.title: The check that adds back the companies that died is missing from this machine
insights.body:
The lab's main price history can price 539 of the roughly 1,061 companies that were ever in the index, and the ones it cannot price are mostly the ones that failed and were thrown out. That makes every result slightly too flattering, because the losers are invisible.

There is a second set of prices built to answer this — it adds back most of the dead companies so a method can be re-run with the failures included. It is not on this machine, and neither is the downloaded price data it is built from, so this method could not be checked against it.

Why it matters more here than usual: this method's entire subject was how long companies stay in the index. A missing-dead-companies problem is at its very worst for a question about who leaves. I had promised this check in writing before the run, so I am recording that it was not done rather than letting it pass quietly.

It does not change the verdict. Adding the dead companies back has, every time it has been measured, made results worse and never better, and this method was rejected by a wide margin. But if anyone picks this direction up again, that check has to come first, not last.

What to do about it: rebuild that second set of prices on this machine before the next time a method needs checking, so a promise like this one can be kept the same day it is made.

insights.title: Cash waiting to be spent cost more than spending it badly
insights.body:
Every strategy this lab has tried differs in which stocks it buys. None had ever varied where the owner's new money goes. So one dull book of twenty big, heavily traded companies was run five times, identical in every way except what the monthly top-up was spent on.

The intuitive rule turned out to be the worst of the sensible ones. Sending each month's money to whichever holding had fallen furthest behind sounds prudent: it puts the book back into equal slices without selling anything. In fact it earned 1.1 percentage points a year less than the opposite rule, and fell three points further at its worst. It lost on safety and on return at the same time, which means it was not buying safety with return, it was simply worse.

The reason shows up in 2008. A holding that has fallen furthest below its slice is not a bargain waiting to bounce; it is the company in the most trouble. A rule that automatically posts fresh money to whatever is falling fastest feeds the fire, once a month, for as long as the fall lasts.

But the biggest number in the whole experiment was not about steering at all. The version that simply left the deposit in cash until a brand-new name came along was only 77 percent invested, where every other version was 96 or 97 percent. That idleness cost 1.5 percentage points a year over twenty years. It bought one thing: a gentler 2008, because cash does not fall. It paid for that cushion in every other year, including the stretch since 2009 that most resembles today.

So the lesson is an ordering. Getting the money invested promptly is worth about 1.5 points a year and needs no judgement at all. Choosing which holding to put it in is worth about 0.7, and the obvious choice is the wrong one. Spend the deposit, spread it over what is already owned, and stop treating uninvested cash as harmless.

insights.title: The rebalancing rule in every strategy file may never actually run
insights.body:
The simulator only adjusts a holding when it has drifted more than one percent of the whole account away from the size it is supposed to be. That threshold is written as a share of the account, not as a share of the holding.

The consequence had not been noticed. A book of fifty equal holdings gives each one two percent of the account, so a holding must drift fifty percent out of line before anything happens. Measured across the whole dev history, that threshold is crossed in one tenth of one percent of holding-months. In plain terms: a fifty-name book is never rebalanced, no matter what its strategy file says it does.

The lab's own record already showed this without anyone reading it that way. The drawdown-brake study ran the same fifty-name book on a monthly re-sizing clock and on a weekly one, and the two made the identical one thousand three hundred and thirty-eight trades. The weekly clock changed nothing because there was nothing for it to do.

Only when a book is cut to twenty names does the threshold start to bite, and at twelve names it bites properly. That is why this experiment had to use a narrow, riskier book than it wanted to.

The fix to consider is to measure the threshold against the holding's intended size rather than against the account, so that a fifty-name book rebalances on the same relative drift that a twelve-name book does. This is not a trading idea and it would not make anything win on its own. It matters because several conclusions in this lab rest on re-sizing machinery that, at realistic book sizes, has not been running. Before any further conclusion is drawn about rebalancing, that should be priced.

insights.title: Sera 20261012-1842: the lab has been losing a race it never knew it had entered
insights.body:
Four fresh ideas this round and all four were rejected. That is the ordinary outcome and it is not the news. The news is that three of them, each testing something completely different, tripped over the same thing on the way past, and it has nothing to do with picking stocks.

THE HANDICAP EVERY STRATEGY HERE PAYS BEFORE IT STARTS. Each experiment needed a plain comparison book: hold a basket of big American companies in equal amounts, adjust monthly, no cleverness at all. Nobody had ever written down what that plain book actually earns on your real deposits at your real fees. Three separate runs now agree. It earns roughly half a point to a point and a half a year LESS than simply buying the market tracker, and it falls harder: 57 percent in 2008 against the tracker's 55, and 74 percent for a narrower twenty-company version. Holding companies in equal amounts, instead of in the proportions the market itself holds them, is a standing handicap. Every strategy in this lab begins that far behind and has to win the gap back with its stock-picking before it can show a profit over the market. Several of our closest near misses beat the market by about the size of that handicap, which raises a question we cannot dodge: were they winning on their picking, or only on their shape?

A SECOND HANDICAP, HIDING IN OUR OWN MACHINERY. One experiment measured something nobody went looking for. Our trading simulator only adjusts a holding once it has drifted off its target by more than one percent of the entire account. That sounds like a small threshold. But in a book of fifty companies each one is only two percent of the account, so a holding has to grow by half again before anything happens at all. Put plainly: every book here that holds twenty or more companies is in practice almost never rebalanced, whatever its own rules say it does. We read the code and confirmed it. Nobody introduced this carelessly; it is a threshold that was sensible for a concentrated book and quietly stopped being sensible as the books grew. It also means some of what we recorded as 'the weekly version against the monthly version' was measuring nothing, because the faster clock had nothing to do.

WHAT DIED, CLEANLY. Stepping aside by the calendar rather than by the chart: 'sell in May' cannot be fitted to the past because it never looks at the past, which was its whole appeal, and it lost anyway, costing 1.4 points a year and still leaving a 36 percent fall, where the ordinary 200-day rule gained 1.4 points and held the fall to 19. Three summers out of twenty-two carry its entire result. Timing the book on how far apart companies are moving: it cost money, and the valuable part is that running the rule backwards cost money too, so the rule is empty rather than upside-down, and we know it in one run instead of owing ourselves another. Leaving out companies the market index has only just bought: the effect is real, those companies did trail the rest by about 5.6 points a year, but only about one holding in forty is ever that new, so the book gained two tenths of a point. Real, and far too small to matter.

ONE PRACTICAL THING YOU CAN USE NOW. The deposit experiment asked where each month's top-up should go and found the popular intuition backwards: putting it into whatever had fallen furthest did worse than putting it into whatever had risen, and fell three points further besides, because in a crash the laggard is usually the sick company. But the bigger number was not about steering at all. The version that let the deposit sit in cash was only 77 percent invested against 96 for the others, and paid a point and a half a year for the privilege. Getting the money invested promptly matters about twice as much as being clever about where it goes.

WHAT IS ALIVE. Portfolio shape: not a new signal, but the arrangement of the money. How many companies to hold, how to size them, and how often to swap the list. One run found that holding fifty companies beat holding twenty by about three points a year, larger than any timing rule we have ever measured, and the trading counts point at how often the list is reshuffled rather than at how concentrated it is. Six follow-ups are queued and five of them aim here.

SHOULD YOU BUY THE CLEAN HISTORICAL DATA YET? No. No buy signal this round, and not close. Nothing this batch produced came near being good enough, and nothing already on the shelf moved. Your one-per-strategy look at the held-back years is untouched: four spent in the lab's whole life, none of them this round.

WHAT THE GATE DID. It refused everything, as it has since we tightened the rule. Fifteen strategies currently look good enough on the practice years and the gate turns down every single one: nine because a close relative already failed on genuinely unseen data, six because they win only two of four unseen stretches. No promotion was even attempted this round because nothing new got close. A round where the gate refuses everything is itself a finding, and it is this: the shelf is stale, and anything new on it will have to come from a genuinely different direction rather than another variation of what is already there.

FEES. Fees decided nothing this round, and we checked rather than assumed. In the timing experiment the arm that traded the MOST was the arm that won; in the deposit experiment the arm that traded LEAST lost by the most. Two unmeasured things cut the other way and should be said out loud: cash earns no interest in our tests, which quietly punishes any strategy that steps aside, worth perhaps one and a half to two and a half points a year to a rule that sits out half the year; and we could not run the check that adds back companies which went bust, because that data is not on this machine, which matters more than usual for the experiment about newly added companies.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST, in order: interest on idle cash; the bust-companies check data restored to this machine; and a rebalancing threshold measured against a holding's own target instead of against the whole account.

NEXT ROUND should stop hunting for new signals and settle the shape question instead: what equal amounts actually cost us, whether sizing companies by how heavily they trade repairs it, and whether our best near misses were ever winning on their picking at all.

insights.title: Our best near misses were winning on their picks, not on holding equal amounts
insights.body:
Our best near misses were winning on the stocks they picked, not on holding equal amounts of twenty names.

We split their lead into three parts by running them beside two plain books on the same money, fees and deposits. The stocks the momentum book picked added about four and a half points a year over a plain twenty-stock book that also steps aside when the market falls below its 200-day average. That market switch added about four points a year over the same plain book that stays invested all the time. Holding equal amounts of the twenty biggest names, always invested, cost about one and a half points a year against simply holding the market.

It mostly survives adding back the companies that later went bust. The picks still add about three and a half points a year, though every book earns less and the momentum book's worst fall gets deeper. The catch is the years since 2009, the stretch most like today. There the momentum book was only about a point a year ahead of the market, and level with it once the dead companies are added back. Most of the edge was earned before 2009.

Paying interest on idle cash added about half a point a year to the books that sit in cash part of the time, and almost nothing to a book that is always invested.

The new rule for when a holding is far enough off target to trade changes nothing for a twenty-stock book, because each name's slot is big enough that the old and new thresholds are the same. It would matter for books of fifty names or more, where each slot is small.

What to do: stop tuning twenty-stock momentum books, since what they do is now well measured and their worst fall is still past the limit. The next useful test is a fifty-stock momentum book, where spreading the bets may soften the worst fall and where the fixed rebalancing rule actually comes into play.

insights.title: Letting a model combine our signals picked worse than simply holding the most-traded big companies
insights.body: We trained a learning model once a year, on only what was known at the time, to rank the big US companies on seven signals we already use, and bought its top picks each month at Gotrade's real fees. Over 1999 to 2015 its top twenty grew 1.7% a year against 3.4% for a plain book of the twenty most-traded companies, and 9.0% against 14.5% after 2009. The less the model trusted itself, the better it did, which is what a model chasing noise looks like. Behind the usual market switch it nearly matched the S&P 500 (7.0% a year against 7.2% on the same deposits), but that was the switch's doing, not the model's. Learning tools do not fix this lab's real problem, the 2008-sized fall, and here they did not even pick better stocks.

insights.title: Company accounts data only starts in 2009, so a model cannot learn from it for most of our history
insights.body: The version of the learning model that also read companies' published accounts picked exactly the same stocks as the version without them until 2010, because there were no accounts in our data before 2009. From 2010 to 2015 it did half a point a year better, which over under six years is noise. To learn anything real about company accounts we would need accounts data that goes back to the 1990s, recorded as it was known at the time.

insights.title: Correcting ourselves: we tested one learning model, not whether learning can help
insights.body:
An earlier entry here ended by saying that learning tools do not fix this lab's real problem, the 2008-sized fall. That sentence claimed more than the test behind it can carry, and this entry narrows it. The journal only ever adds, so the earlier note stands exactly as it was written and this one says what it should have said.

What we actually tried was one kind of learning model, asked one question: out of the twenty most heavily traded big American companies, which will do best over the next month. It was only ever allowed to buy, never to bet against anything, and it held every name it picked in equal amounts. It paid Gotrade's real fees. And it was built out of the same seven signals this lab already computes, each of which had already failed on its own. A model of that sort can only recombine what it is handed. It cannot invent a signal nobody gave it.

The second half of the old sentence holds, and we are not softening it. On that test the model picked worse than simply holding the twenty most-traded big companies, and the less it trusted its own forecasts the better it did. For this kind of model, on these signals, among big companies, buying only, after our real fees, there is no stock-picking skill to be had. That is a real result.

The leap from there to the fall does not hold. The model was never asked to see a fall coming; it was asked to rank next month's winners. It was never allowed to decide how much of the money should be in the market at all, which is still the job of our one old safety rule, the one that steps aside when the market falls below its 200-day average. And it never saw small companies or the other side of a trade, which is where the published research that suggested this idea finds most of its edge in the first place. None of that was tested here, so none of it was ruled out.

So the honest version of the claim is narrower and duller than the one we wrote. Recombining the signals we already have, among big companies, buying only, after fees, adds nothing to our stock picking. Whether a model pointed at the fall itself, asked how much to hold rather than what to hold, can do better is still an open question, and it is the one worth asking next.

insights.title: A model that chose how much to own, not what to own, beat having no brake at all and lost to the one brake we have
insights.body:
We asked whether a model could learn how far a basket of big, heavily traded companies was about
to drop over the following three months, and then use that guess to decide how much of the basket
to own — more of it when calm was expected, less when a fall was, the rest left in cash. The point
was to go after the thing that keeps stopping us. Nearly two thirds of everything we have ever
tried beats the market over our twenty-year practice run, but under a quarter of it keeps the worst
drop to a fifth or less, and all four of the strategies we have spent a real out-of-sample look on
failed on returns rather than on the fall. Against that we have exactly one brake — stop buying
while the market sits below its long-run average — and nothing has ever improved on it.

Two things came back, and they point opposite ways. Owning the same twenty companies with no brake
at all was the worst thing in the run: it fell 74% at its deepest and turned the monthly deposits
into 4.9% a year. The model's sizing cut that deepest fall to 29% while earning the same 4.9% a
year, so as a replacement for having no brake it worked, and it was not a fluke of one year — it
held anywhere between a quarter and all of the basket depending on the date, and it did pull back
through 2008. But the plain brake, on exactly the same twenty companies, cut the fall further
still, to 21%, and earned 8.2% a year — better than the market gave the same deposits. So the model
was beaten on the fall and on the money at the same time, by the simplest rule we own. Running the
model behind the brake as well gave the shallowest fall of the five, 18%, and the thinnest return,
4.7%. The likeliest reason is that the model pulled back in a great many calm years too, and
sitting in cash through a stretch where the market roughly quadrupled is expensive. None of the
five cleared our bar, and scored on four separate stretches of history instead of one long average
they won only one of the four — in the two most recent stretches the better arm was the plain brake,
not any version of the model.

What this settles is narrow. It tested one way of guessing a fall — the worst drop over the coming
quarter, learned from signals we already had, on big American companies, bought and held long only,
after the fees we really pay, with idle cash earning nothing. It says that this guess, used this
way, is worse than the brake we have. It does not say that trying to forecast the fall is the wrong
idea, and it is no endorsement of the brake either: most of that brake's reputation still rests on
a single year.

insights.title: How much shelter can you actually buy by picking stocks? About half of what is needed
insights.body:
The owner's rule says a strategy must never lose more than a quarter of its value from its peak. Over the twenty years this lab studies, simply owning the market lost 55% of its value at the worst moment, in 2008. So the question that has been hanging over the lab is whether a careful choice of companies can close that gap.

This run measured it properly for the first time. It ranked every big, heavily traded company in the index by how much of the market's bad days it actually joined in - add up what the stock did on the days the market fell, divide by what the market did on those same days - and built books from the two ends of that ranking.

The ranking is real. Line the books up by how exposed they were built to be, and their worst falls come out in exactly that order: 40%, 41%, 43%, 74%, 91%. The book deliberately filled with the most market-exposed names fell more than twice as far as the sheltered one and earned barely half as much. That is not an accident of one crash; it holds across twenty years.

But the best shelter that twenty years of hindsight could find anywhere in the index still fell 40%. The market fell 55%. The limit is 25%. Choosing names covers about half the distance and then stops, because in a real crash every large company falls together and a book that is always fully invested has nowhere to stand.

What to do about it: stop asking selection to solve the fall. The remaining half of the gap can only come from owning less during the fall - a rule that steps out of the market, a cash reserve, or a brake that cuts the book when it is losing. Those are different lines of work, and this result says they are the only ones that can finish the job.

insights.title: The companies that fall hardest are the ones that lead the way back, and since 2009 that has been the better trade
insights.body:
The same run that measured how much shelter money can buy also measured what it costs, and the cost turned out to be larger than the benefit in the years that matter most.

Over the last seven years of the window, 2009 to 2015 - the best-covered years in the lab's data and the ones most like today - owning the market earned 15% a year. The books built out of the most sheltered companies earned 3 to 6 points a year less than that. The books built out of the most market-exposed companies earned 5 to 8 points a year more.

The reason is simple once it is said out loud: the companies that fall hardest in a crash are largely the same companies that lead the recovery out of it. Buying shelter means standing aside while that recovery happens. Over the full twenty years the two effects roughly cancel, which is why a sheltered book can still show a small lead on average. But that average is stitched together from two opposite eras, and the owner's money lives entirely in the second one.

One book in this run went the other way on purpose: it held the twenty companies with the most of the market's good days and the fewest of its bad ones. It beat the market by 3 points a year over twenty years and by nearly 8 points a year after 2009, which is the best post-2009 figure this lab has recorded. Its one defect is that it fell 74%.

What to do about it: treat any calm, low-swing or low-fall screen as a bill to be paid rather than a free improvement, and make every future strategy that uses one show it is not quietly selling the recovery. And run the opposite book - the one that leans into the swing - behind the market-trend switch that has been measured to help every strategy it has been tried on. That combination has not been tested, and this is the first evidence in the lab that it might be the right shape.

insights.title: A safety rule that sells in time can still be bad at buying back, and that half is fixable
insights.body:
Half the strategies here share one safety rule: when the market tracker closes below its average price of the last 200 trading days, sell everything; when it closes back above, buy again. A test last week showed the rule's whole twenty-two-year advantage is the three crashes it sits out, and that it pays for them most heavily right after a crash, because the same slow average that correctly got it out keeps it out through the recovery. In 2009 that cost it nearly eight points.

This test froze the selling half and changed only the buying-back half, six ways, on a book holding nothing but the market tracker so nothing else could cloud the answer. One version came out clearly ahead: buy back when the market's return over the last three months turns positive. It earned 9.7% a year on the owner's real deposits where the old rule earned 9.1% and simply holding the market earned 7.7%. In the years since 2009 it made 12.6% a year against the old rule's 10.7%, and its worst fall over those years was slightly shallower, so the extra return was not bought with extra risk.

The reason is worth keeping. Three of the six versions bought back whenever the price rose above a short average, and that is exactly what a bear-market rally looks like, so they climbed back into the middle of 2008 and 2001 and lost around ten and fifteen percent in years the old rule sat out for nothing. Asking instead for an actual positive three-month return is a different question: inside a real crash the last three months are almost never up, so the money stayed out, but once a bottom has genuinely passed, three months turns positive long before a two-hundred-day average does. A sixth version proved the point backwards by accident: it waited for a twenty-day price high, which after a long fall is harder to reach than the old rule, so it came back even later and cost nearly ten points a year in the modern stretch.

Two cautions. The improvement is real but small: it recovers about a third of what the safety rule costs after 2009, not half, and the best version is still four points a year behind simply holding the market over those years. And a book holding only the market tracker trades a handful of times a decade, so none of these versions can ever qualify for real money; they are a measurement of a frame, not a candidate.

What to do about it: the frame is shared by roughly half the lab, and the lab already knows the safety rule cannot just be switched off, because every version tried without it was worse on return and on depth of fall at the same time. So the rule stays, and the next test should put this faster way back in underneath a real stock-picking book that can clear the trade count. If two points a year survive on top of actual picks, it is a change worth making everywhere.

insights.title: The shared safety rule should let a strategy choose how it buys back, not just when it sells
insights.body:
Right now the safety rule that roughly half this lab's strategies sit behind is a single switch with one setting: out when the market tracker is below its two-hundred-day average price, in when it is above. Selling and buying back are the same test, and a strategy cannot ask for one without the other.

This run showed that is the wrong shape. The selling half is good and the buying-back half is expensive, and separating them is worth about two points a year on the owner's deposits with no extra depth of fall. But to test that at all, a whole new strategy file had to be written with its own copy of the switch, because the shared one has no way to express an asymmetric rule.

The wish is small and concrete: let the shared safety rule carry two settings instead of one, a leaving test and a returning test, with the returning test defaulting to the leaving test so that every strategy already recorded keeps its exact numbers and nothing in the existing record moves. Then any future book can ask for the slow careful exit with the faster quarter-return re-entry by naming it, instead of re-implementing it.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: the lab has nearly fifty strategies carrying this switch and every post-mortem since the news-day book has blamed it. If the fix turns out to be one shared setting, it can be applied to all of them at once and re-measured cheaply. If each book has to carry its own copy, it will be applied to one or two and the rest will stay mis-framed.

- 2009-2015: −0.7% a year against the market as recorded, −0.7% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 2 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Hold your shortlist, do not resample it: separating how many names a book owns from how often it swaps them: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +8.6% on the usual history, +6.4% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 59.3% and 61.9%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +1.5% a year before and +0.4% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.2 points a year less. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Half of a hundred-name account was sitting in cash, and nobody chose that
insights.body:
Every test this lab has ever recorded uses one rule to decide when a holding gets topped back up to its intended size: top it up once it has drifted away by one percent of the whole account. That sounds harmless until you notice what it means for a book that owns a hundred companies. Each holding in such a book is one percent of the account to begin with, so it can never drift a full one percent of the account below where it should be. It is arithmetically impossible, at any account size. A monthly deposit therefore cannot reach any company the book already owns. New money gets invested only when a company drops off the shortlist and is replaced.

Measured on the basket that owns all hundred: only fifty-one percent of the account was ever invested. Half the owner's deposits sat in cash for twenty years. The identical basket, with the top-up rule changed to measure the shortfall against the holding's own size instead of the whole account, was ninety-six percent invested and earned three point one points a year more. Same companies, same dates, the same eight hundred and fifty-nine trades. The only difference was whether the money got in.

The number depends on how busy the book is, not on anything its designer decided. The fifty-name version that barely trades was eighty-seven percent invested; a fifty-name version that churns half its holdings every month was ninety-six percent. So a book that trades little quietly turns into a part-cash position, which makes its worst fall look gentler than the idea deserves and makes its return look worse. The all-hundred basket's thirty-eight percent worst fall, the mildest in the whole experiment, was not caution. It was an accidental cash pile.

What to do about it: nothing in the record needs rewriting, because every recorded result used the same rule and they remain comparable with each other. But any book that is meant to go to real money should be measured again on the rule that actually invests the deposits, and the near misses are the place to start. The best of them clears every condition except the luck bar, holds seventy names and trades about eleven a month, so it is very likely holding cash it was never meant to hold. A book that is more invested earns more, and earning more is exactly what the luck bar is waiting for.

insights.title: A basket of the biggest companies only beats the market because the failures are missing
insights.body:
The lab keeps two price histories. The everyday one prices five hundred and thirty-nine companies: the ones that survived long enough to be priced. The check history prices nine hundred and eighty-nine, including the ones that went bankrupt or were swallowed and disappeared. Re-running a finished experiment on the second one costs nothing and settles a specific question: was the edge real, or was it the absence of the losers?

Six versions of a very simple idea were tested here. Take the hundred most heavily traded big American companies, own them equally, rebalance monthly, pay the real fees, add five million rupiah a month. Vary only the shape: own all hundred, or the busiest fifty, or the busiest twenty, or a thinned-out sample of them. On the everyday history the best version earned eight point six percent a year on the money paid in, against SPY's seven point two, and it was ahead in every stretch of the twenty years including the most recent one.

On the check history it earns six point four percent and loses to SPY. Its winnings barely exceed its losses at all. Its lead in the modern years drops from one and a half points to under half a point. And not one of the six beats SPY any more. Every single one of them also falls further than it did, by three to twelve points, with the twenty-giants version falling eighty-one percent.

Why this construction in particular: it owns everything on its shortlist. It makes no attempt to avoid anything. So every company that failed and vanished from the records is a loss it never took, and there is nothing else in the idea to offset that. This is the shape of book most flattered by a history of survivors, which is precisely why it was worth checking.

The practical consequence is that three experiments can now be closed together. Owning an equal slice of the big American companies, with or without a rule for when to step aside, is not a way to beat the market. It is a way to be the market minus the companies that died. The lab should stop spending ideas on it.

insights.title: Ask the computer a slower question and it answers much better
insights.body:
Our first attempt at a learning model asked it to guess which big companies would do best over the next month. It picked worse than simply buying the twenty most heavily traded companies, and the giveaway was that the least clever version of the model beat the cleverest one. A month of a share price is almost all noise, so there was nothing to learn and the clever version was learning the noise.

This run changed exactly one thing and nothing else: the model was asked about the next twelve months instead of the next month. Same information, same training schedule, same book, same fees, same safety switch, same years. The money it earned went from 6.7% a year to 10.5% a year over 2000 to 2015, and from 9.4% to 15.9% a year over 2009 to 2015. Its worst fall got shallower too, from 21% to 15%. A three-month version sat neatly in between, so the pattern runs the right way at every step.

Something else flipped. With the monthly question, taking cleverness away from the model helped. With the yearly question, cleverness helped instead. Put together, the two runs say the problem was never the model. It was the question we were asking it.

Worth doing about it: whenever this lab asks a computer to learn something about shares, ask it about a span of a year, not a month. It costs nothing but a year of waiting for the first answer, and here it was worth several points a year.

insights.title: Taking every fifth name off a monthly list rebuilds three-quarters of the portfolio for nothing
insights.body:
Two earlier experiments built a portfolio from the hundred most heavily traded big companies by sorting that list and taking every second name, or every fifth name, down it. The twenty-name one earned three point two percent a year on the owner's deposits and the fifty-name one earned six point zero, and the obvious reading was that owning more companies is worth nearly three points a year. That would have been one of the largest effects this lab has ever found.

It was not that. The list is re-sorted every month, by how much money changes hands in each company. A company drifting from fifth place to sixth is sold, and whoever is now fifth is bought. Nothing has been decided; the portfolio has simply been shuffled because a boundary moved. Measured here, that shuffling replaces half the fifty-name portfolio and seventy-three percent of the twenty-name portfolio every single month. The versions that own the top of the list outright, selling a company only when it really drops out of the group, replace four to six percent a month instead.

Running all of them inside one experiment, on one shortlist with one set of fees, shows what the shuffling costs. At fifty names, not shuffling was worth about a point a year, which is roughly what the extra trading fees come to. At twenty names it was worth four point eight points a year, which is four times more than fees can explain. The rest is not churn at all: the top twenty are the twenty giants, while every fifth name runs all the way down to the hundredth, and over this window the giants won. The shuffled twenty-name version's winnings barely exceeded its losses, which is what a portfolio looks like when most of its activity is noise.

Two lessons. Never build a portfolio by sampling a ranking that gets rebuilt on a schedule: either own the top of it or own all of it, because sampling it adds turnover that is pure cost and composition that was never chosen. And when a comparison changes two things at once, the lab cannot tell which one mattered, so the old three-point claim about owning more companies should not be quoted again.

insights.title: A good-looking result that is really one safety rule wearing a disguise
insights.body:
This run produced the first learning model in the lab to pass every go-live condition at once: it beat the index with dividends, its worst fall was 20% against the 25% limit, its gains outweighed its losses, and its luck score cleared the bar. On the face of it that is the best news this family has ever had.

Looking at where the money actually came from tells a different story. In 2001, 2002 and 2008 the book returned almost exactly nothing, because the safety switch had stepped it out of the market while the index fell 17%, 21% and 36%. Those three sidesteps are the whole twenty-year advantage. In the years since 2009, which are the best measured and the most like today, the book earned 15.9% a year while simply holding the index earned 16.6%. It lost. Every other version in the batch lost by more.

There are two further warnings. On fuller price history that includes the companies which later went bankrupt or were bought, the worst fall grows from 20% to 23% and the luck score drops from 0.912 to 0.839, below the bar it had just cleared. And when the window is cut into four stretches and the book is scored only on months it has never seen, it wins two and loses two. Both losses are rising markets, where the picking had to carry its own weight and could not. The lab's rules refuse to promote it for exactly that reason, and that refusal is correct.

Worth doing about it: when a book looks smooth, check whether the smoothness is picking or timing. Here it is timing. The owner should read the headline number as the safety switch saving him from three bad years, not as the model knowing which shares to buy.

insights.title: Sera 20261014-1206: half the account was in cash, and the questions we thought were settled were measured on that tape
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch, and nothing was promoted. Four ideas ran, one came out eligible on
paper, and the safety gate refused it because it won only two of four out-of-sample stretches. Of
the four, one found something that changes how we should read almost every result this lab already
holds.

The big one: half of a hundred-name account was sitting in cash, and nobody chose that. Two of the
six books tested this batch held exactly the same companies on exactly the same days and traded
exactly the same number of times. The only difference was the rule that decides when a holding has
drifted far enough from its target to be worth correcting. One of them was 96% invested. The other
was 51%. That is worth three points a year, and it is not a strategy difference — it is the tape
quietly leaving half the money uninvested. The cause is that the drift rule is measured against the
whole account rather than against the holding, so in a book of many small positions it can never
fire, and the monthly deposit only ever reaches the market when something is bought or sold for
another reason. The less a book trades, the more of it sits in cash.

That matters well beyond the book it was found in. Every comparison this lab has ever made between
a book that trades often and a book that trades rarely has been comparing two things at once:
how often it trades, and how much of the money was actually invested. The rarely-trading book looks
calmer in a crash partly because a large part of it was in cash, and earns less for the same reason.
We now have a tape that invests properly, and the two questions the lab thought it had already
answered — how many companies to hold, and how often to trade — are both queued to be asked again
on it. The answer that put twenty names in the roster was measured on the old tape.

The second finding is a warning about a whole family. A book that simply holds the hundred busiest
big companies appears to beat the market by a point and a half a year. Re-run on the fuller price
history that includes the companies that went bankrupt or were bought, it loses to the market
instead, and every version of it falls further — one of them by twelve points more. A book that owns
everything on its list owns every failure too, and our main history is missing about four in ten of
the days companies actually sat in the index. The apparent edge was the missing dead companies. Two
older methods in the same shape should be read the same way, and the family does not deserve another
attempt.

The third is about safety rules, and it is the most useful thing here for a future book. Our rule
for stepping out of the market when it turns down is good at selling and expensive at buying back.
Tested on its own, coming back in when the market has actually gained ground over the last quarter
earned more than coming back when the price crosses a line, and did not pay for it in the crashes —
it was flat through 2008 and gained far more in the 2009 recovery. Asking for a line to be crossed
buys into false starts; asking for realised gains waits for the turn to be real. Coming back even
later is worse still, so the finding is pinned on both sides. On its own this is worth about two
points a year, and it is now queued to be tried underneath an actual stock-picking book, where it
could matter for money rather than as a frame.

The fourth asked whether a computer model can pick stocks better if you ask it a slower question.
It can, and by a lot: asking it to rank next year instead of next month was worth four to six points
a year and made a learned model clear our bars for the first time. It also reversed what we thought
we knew — with the fast question the simplest model won because there was nothing to learn; with the
slow question the more flexible model wins because there is. But the win is mostly our safety rule
rather than the model's picking: in the recent years that look most like today it still lost to
simply holding the index, and on the fuller price history its safety score drops below our bar. Our
best hand-built signal still earns more than either computer model, on the same tape and the same
fees. The honest summary is that the horizon was the lever, not the machinery.

One idea from the shelter experiment is worth flagging as the liveliest thing queued. Choosing
companies that sit out the market's bad days does work — the measure sorted twenty years of falls
in exactly the right order — but it only takes the worst fall from the market's 55% down to about
40%, which is half the distance we need and the cheap half. The price is steep: in the recovery
years those sheltered books ran three to six points a year behind the market, while the most exposed
ones ran five to eight points ahead. The companies that fall hardest lead the way back. Any future
idea reaching for a calm or low-fall screen has to show it is not simply re-buying that trade. The
interesting twist is the one book built on the gap between how much a company joins the rises and
how much it joins the falls: it beat the market by three points a year overall and by nearly eight
in the recent era — the opposite direction to every other edge in this lab, all of which were earned
before 2009. Its only flaw is a very deep fall, which is exactly what our safety rule is measured to
fix. That is queued next.

On costs: nothing this batch lost its edge to fees specifically, because the books that failed
failed by much wider margins than fees. But the cash-drag finding is a cost finding in disguise —
the money that was not invested earned nothing at all, which is worse than any fee we pay.

What the next batch should do: ask the two settled questions again on the tape that actually invests
— how many names, and how often to trade — because the current answers are confounded. Put the
quarter-return re-entry under a real book. And give the shared safety rule the ability to buy back on
a different test than it sells on, which today requires a whole new method file each time and is the
single change that would let about fifty existing methods be re-measured at once.

- Of all the money it held, 51.4% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +10.9% a year against the market's +7.2%.

- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned +0.7% a year, −6.5% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- 1996-2002: +6.3% a year against the market as recorded, −3.3% from its own picks alone.

insights.title: Waiting for the market to actually make money beats waiting for a price to cross a line
insights.body:
Most of our best books sell everything when the market index drops below its average price of the last 200 days, and buy back when it climbs above that average again. The buying-back half is slow: after a crash, a 200-day average takes months to turn, so the book sits in cash watching the recovery happen.

We swapped only that buy-back, on two books that pick real stocks, for a different question: have the last three months actually made money? Nothing else changed, and each book was run twice side by side on the same days with the same deposits and fees, so the difference is the rule alone.

The twenty-stock book earned a point a year more. The blend of momentum and calm stocks earned 0.66 of a point more. And it was close to free: the twenty-stock book's worst fall went from 20.65 percent to 20.67 percent, two hundredths of a point, where we had predicted it would get one to three points worse. The books also sat out of the market almost as much as before, so this is not simply being invested more often — it is being invested at better moments.

The best part is that three months turns out to be a genuine sweet spot rather than a number we happened to pick. One month was worse than changing nothing at all: it kept buying false recoveries, deepened the worst fall by more than five points, and cut the ratio of gains to losses from 2.03 to 1.78. Six months was also worse than changing nothing, because it is nearly as slow as the average it was meant to replace. Having a worse answer on each side is much better evidence than a number sitting on a slope.

What to do about it: this is a rule about when to re-enter the market, and roughly half our books share the old version of it. It is worth carrying to books whose track record is still open — but not to these two, whose close relatives have already failed a real out-of-sample test.

insights.title: How fast a strategy trades decides whether its old results can be trusted
insights.body:
Yesterday we found a setting in the simulator that had been quietly leaving money in cash. It tops a holding back up only once the holding has drifted a long way from its target, and 'a long way' was measured against one per cent of the whole account instead of against the size of the holding. In a book holding a hundred stocks each stock is one per cent of the account, so the trigger could never be reached and the monthly deposit never got spent on anything already owned. That basket sat half in cash, and fixing it was worth three points a year.

The worry was that this had spoiled every result in the lab. It has not, and today's run shows why. The same fix was applied to the momentum book the paper account is built on, at thirty-five, fifty and seventy stocks. The cash it was leaving behind came to four tenths of a point, seven tenths, and one and a half points. Twenty to thirty times less than the basket.

The reason is simple once you see it. A deposit can reach your holdings two ways: the top-up rule, or just buying and selling in the normal course of things. The basket almost never traded, so the broken rule was the only road in, and it was closed. The momentum book replaces most of what it owns every few months and sells the lot three separate times when the market turns down, so its deposits were already being spent and the rule had nothing left to do.

What to do about it: when you look back at an old result and wonder whether it was measured fairly, the question to ask is not how many stocks it held. It is how often it traded. Slow, always-invested strategies holding a lot of names are the ones whose numbers were dragged down. Fast ones, and any strategy that steps aside when the market falls, can be read as they were recorded. That turns a worry about hundreds of old results into one short list to re-check.

insights.title: If a good quarter is a better reason to buy, a bad quarter may be a better reason to sell
insights.body:
Every experiment we have run on the market safety rule has frozen the selling side and changed only the buying side. The reason was a real finding: when we priced the two halves separately, the selling half was the one earning its keep, so we left it alone.

But there is a gap in that reasoning. Finding that the selling half is the good half is not the same as finding that it is expressed in the best way. Nobody has asked whether the selling rule itself could be better stated.

The new result makes the question worth asking. On the buying side, asking whether the last three months actually made money beat asking whether today's price sits above a slow average, and it beat it on two different books and at a setting with a worse answer on either side of it. The selling side currently uses exactly the kind of rule that lost: today's price against a slow average. A rule based on what the market actually did over the last quarter might sell earlier in a real decline, and might generate fewer false alarms in a choppy market that dips below a line and bounces straight back.

It costs nothing new to build, because both pieces already exist in the lab. The important part is where to test it: not on the momentum books, whose close relatives have already failed their one real test and which therefore can never be promoted however well they score, but on a book whose record is still open. That is queued as the next experiment.

insights.title: Owning more stocks did not make the falls any gentler
insights.body:
The usual reason to hold more stocks is safety: spread the money across seventy companies and no single disaster can hurt you much. Today that was measured properly for the first time on the momentum book, at twenty, thirty-five, fifty and seventy names, with every version equally invested so the comparison was fair.

The worst falls were 20.6 per cent, 19.6 per cent, 20.7 per cent and 19.9 per cent. Flat, and not even in order. Three and a half times as many companies bought no protection at all.

The reason is that this strategy already has a rule that steps entirely out of the market when the market itself turns down, and that rule has already removed the falls that spreading out could have helped with. What is left are the drops that happen while it is still invested, and those hit everything at once. Owning seventy momentum stocks instead of twenty does not save you from a market that falls on everything.

Meanwhile the cost of widening was real: seventy names earned 10.9 per cent a year on the deposits against 13.7 per cent for twenty, so widening gave up nearly three points a year and bought nothing. We checked whether that was just the extra trading fees — it is not. The fee bill is about one dollar in seven of gross profit whichever width you choose, and the total bill actually gets smaller as the book widens, because a wide book turns over fewer dollars even though it writes more tickets. The picks simply get weaker as you go further down the ranking.

What to do about it: keep the paper account at twenty names, and treat any future idea whose selling point is 'hold more names so it falls less' as unlikely to be worth testing, unless the strategy has no market-exit rule at all. That last case is still genuinely open and is the next thing worth running.

insights.title: This momentum book's whole advantage was earned before 2009
insights.body:
The momentum book the paper account is built on earned 13.7 per cent a year on the owner's deposits over 1996 to 2015, against 7.2 per cent for the same money put into an American index fund. That is the headline, and it is the reason the strategy is on the roster.

Today the same book was measured over 2009 to 2015 alone — the stretch our price history covers best and the one most like the market now — at four different widths. Against the same deposits in an index fund it came out at plus half a point at thirty-five stocks, minus 1.9 points at fifty and minus 2.1 points at seventy. Then the same runs were repeated on the price history that includes the companies that went bankrupt or were taken over, which the main history leaves out. The one positive number turned negative: minus 1.7 points. Every single reading of the modern era, on the fuller history, is a loss to the index fund.

This is not news about width. It is news about the strategy. Nearly all of its twenty-year advantage was earned in the first thirteen years, and in the most recent and best-measured stretch it did not beat simply buying the index. The lab has now spent four looks at untouched recent data on strategies from this same family, and all four failed. This is what that failure looks like before it happens.

What to do about it: do not read a long-run average as a promise. When a strategy is judged from here on, the 2009-onward stretch should be looked at first and the twenty-year figure second, because the early years are the ones carrying it. And the current paper roster deserves the same reading — the money behind it is real.

insights.title: Teaching the stock picker to forget made it worse, by exactly as much as you made it forget
insights.body:
The lab's learned stock picker retrains once a year on everything it has ever seen, back to 1996. That seemed suspicious: by 2012 it is still carrying lessons from the 1990s technology boom, and the two out-of-sample checks it had failed were both rising markets, which is what an old grudge against big popular companies would look like.
