So we gave it a shorter memory: one version remembers only the last ten years, another only the last five, and a third, unchanged, remembers everything.

Every measure got worse, and it got worse in proportion. Remembering everything earned 10.9% a year on the owner's real deposits and fees. Remembering ten years earned 10.0%. Remembering five earned 9.1%. The reliability of gains over losses, the steadiness of the ride and the luck score all fell in the same order. Five different measures, three versions, one ranking, no exceptions. That is not a close call that could go either way; it is a dose, and a response.

The most telling part is where it failed. The whole reason to make it forget was to make it better at the recent years, the ones most like today. Against a plain index fund over 2009 to 2015, remembering everything was 0.7 points a year behind, remembering ten years was 2.0 behind, and remembering five was 4.4 behind. Forgetting the distant past made it worse at the recent past.

There is a second lesson hiding in the free safety check. The lab's price history is missing about half the companies that ever sat in the index, mostly the ones that went under, and there is a fuller copy kept to test exactly that. Adding the dead companies back cost the remembering version 0.4 points a year. It cost the ten-year version 2.5 and the five-year version 2.7 — roughly six times as much. That makes sense once you say it out loud: a model trained on twenty years absorbs a batch of new companies into a long average and barely moves, while a model trained on five years has all of its lessons rewritten by them. A short memory does not only throw information away, it magnifies whatever is wrong with the information you keep.

What to do about it: stop shortening the training window, here and in any future method. And read the whole episode as a diagnosis rather than a dead end. Three things now point the same way — more history helps, a cleverer model helps, and a short memory is fragile. The picker is not confused by old lessons, it is starving for examples. The next useful move is not another setting on the model; it is giving it something it has never been allowed to look at.

insights.title: The learned picker has never been told what the market as a whole is doing
insights.body:
Everything the lab's learned stock picker reads is a fact about one company: how much its price has risen over the past year, how jumpy it has been, how much of it changes hands, how close it sits to its best price of the year, whether it just raised its dividend, and how much dividend it pays. Seven facts, and every one of them is a comparison between companies on a single day.

That design has a consequence nobody has tested. Because each number is converted into a ranking against the other companies on the same day, the picker literally cannot tell one year from another. A calm, rising market and a frightened, falling one look identical to it: in both, some companies rank first and some rank last. It has no way to know which kind of day it is standing on.

Meanwhile the lab already holds daily readings of exactly that, going back to the 1990s, free and already checked for not peeking at the future: the market's fear gauge and how that fear is priced over different time horizons, government borrowing rates at four different lengths, and the gold price. The lab's separate model for predicting how far a book is about to fall already uses market-wide readings for precisely this reason — its designers wrote down that a per-company ranking cannot express 'everything is about to drop'. The picker was never given the same courtesy.

Why it matters: three attempts at a learned picker have now been made, and every single one of them beat the index over twenty years while losing to it over 2009 to 2015. Each attempt changed the model — how clever it is, what question it is asked, how far back it remembers — and none changed what it is allowed to look at. The one clear signal from all three is that the picker is short of information rather than short of cleverness.

What to do: add the market-wide readings as extra inputs and re-run the same model, changed in no other way. If being able to tell a nervous market from a calm one improves the recent years, the direction is alive and the lab knows where to dig next. If it changes nothing, then this set of information genuinely contains no recent edge, the learned-picker direction should be closed, and the lab should spend its effort on finding data it does not yet have rather than on new ways of reading the data it has.

insights.title: Holding more companies protects you from the ones our price history never had
insights.body:
We keep asking whether a book should hold twenty companies or forty, and we keep answering it on a price history that is missing about half the companies that ever sat in the index -- overwhelmingly the ones that went bankrupt or were bought out. Today that question got asked twice on the same book, once on each history, and the two answers differed by a factor of six.

On our usual price history, going from twenty companies to forty moved the worst fall from 22.7% to 21.6%. Barely over a point. Another method measured the same thing today going from twenty to seventy, found less than a point, and concluded that spreading wider buys no safety once a book already steps out of falling markets. On that history it is exactly right.

On the fuller history, with the dead companies added back, the twenty-company book falls 29.4% and the forty-company book falls 23.2%. Six points apart, and that difference decides whether the book sits inside or outside the owner's 25% limit for real money.

The reason is almost obvious once it is written down. Spreading your money wider is protection against one company collapsing on its own. The companies that collapse on their own are precisely the ones our usual price history does not contain, because they stopped existing. So on that history there is nothing to be protected from, and width looks free and useless at the same time.

What to do about it: never settle how many companies a book should hold on the usual history alone. The number of names is a safety decision, and the safety it buys only becomes visible on the history that includes the failures. Every width result this lab recorded before today was measured on the blind history, and should be read as a measurement of what width costs, never of what it protects.

insights.title: For the first time, adding back the companies that died made a method better
insights.body:
Our usual price history is missing roughly half the companies that ever sat in the index, and the missing half leans heavily towards the ones that failed. We keep a fuller copy to check whether a result was really just that hole, and we run every promising method against both. The answer has been depressingly consistent: putting the dead companies back costs about half a point a year on average, more than a point for the stock-picking books, and the method this one grew out of lost two full points.

Today a method gained. All five versions of it earned more with the dead companies added back, between 0.3 and 1.3 points a year, and the best version went from 16.7% a year to 17.5%. That has never happened here.

It is worth understanding why, because it says something about what the method is actually buying. It ranks companies on how much more than the market they rise on good days, against how little of the market they give back on bad ones -- and then it steps out of the market entirely whenever the market's own trend turns down. The companies that score highest on that ranking are the violent ones, and plenty of violent companies eventually died. But they did not die quietly on a Tuesday; they died in falling markets, which is exactly when this book is not holding anything. So the method got to own them while they were running and was out of the room when they went.

That is the most encouraging mechanical result this lab has produced, and it comes with an immediate catch, which is why it is only half good news. The same fuller history deepens the worst fall from 22.7% to 29.4% on the twenty-company versions, past the owner's 25% limit for real money. Only the forty-company version stays inside, at 23.2%.

What to do about it: stop treating the fuller-history check as a penalty to be survived. It is a measurement, and it can go either way. A method whose returns improve on it is telling you its edge is in real companies rather than in a gap in the records -- and that is worth more than the half point it usually costs.

insights.title: The closest we have come to the moment it is worth paying for better data
insights.body:
We hold a standing rule about when to spend money on a proper price history -- one that includes every company that ever sat in the index, failures and all. It is not a vague ambition. It names four things that must be true at once: the method clears our screen, it beats the market in most of the period-by-period checks, it still has a positive lead in the recent years our data covers best, and it does not move like a book that has already spent its one look at the years after 2015 and lost.

Today's method cleared three of the four for the first time. It clears the screen with room to spare, it wins three of the four periods, and its lead over the market across 2009 to 2015 is positive -- which almost nothing here manages, because nearly every advantage this lab has found was earned before 2009 and quietly died afterwards.

It fails the fourth. Take the market's share out of this book's month-by-month returns and what is left moves with a book that already failed out of sample, at 0.91 where the line is 0.85. A different name does not make it a different book, and the rule refuses it with no way around that, which is correct: a route around that rule is precisely how five strategies reached the owner's real money and then lost to simply owning the index.

Why it matters: this is not a near miss on a number we could argue about. It is a near miss on the one condition that is about identity rather than performance, and identity is testable. The version that was measured and found to move like the failed book holds twenty companies. The version that survives the fuller price history holds forty, falls differently, and has never had its own identity measured -- our check reports only the single strongest match per failed book, so the wider version's reading was never taken.

What to do about it: take that reading, as its own method, before anything else. If the wider book also moves like the failed one, this entire direction is our old momentum book in a costume and should be closed and said so plainly. If it does not, all four conditions are true at once for the first time, and that is the moment to buy the data rather than keep guessing at it.

insights.title: Sera 20261014-1242: three of four conditions held at once, and the book that did it may have been judged by the wrong twin
insights.body:
No buy signal — but this batch came closer than the lab ever has, and it found out why it keeps
getting stopped. All four ideas cleared our own bars for the first time in a single batch. All four
were refused anyway: three because the book turned out to be something we have already tried and
failed with, and one because it lost its out-of-sample stretches.

THE CLOSEST WE HAVE COME. The book that leans into companies which join the rises more than they
join the falls, held behind our market switch and bought back when the market has actually made
money for a quarter, earned 16.7% a year on the real deposits at real fees against the market's
7.2%, with a worst fall of 22.7% and the best risk-adjusted score in the lab. It won all four
out-of-sample stretches on its own. Three of the four conditions we require before it is worth
paying for better price history now hold at once. The fourth is the problem: this book moves almost
exactly like one we already tested and lost with — 0.91 where our line is 0.85. A new name does not
make it a new book.

But there is a real chance that judgement is about the wrong book. The check only ever reports the
single closest match for each failed method, and it compared the 20-name version. The 40-name
version was never measured on its own; it simply inherited the verdict. That matters because the
40-name version is also the only one whose fall stays under the owner's limit once the companies
that died are added back. Registering it alone is queued next and is the single highest-value thing
in the backlog: if it reads under the line, all four conditions hold simultaneously for the first
time, and if it reads over, the direction closes honestly instead of lingering.

THE MARKET SWITCH HAD ITS BIGGEST WIN EVER HERE. Against the identical book without it, the switch
was worth six points a year AND fifty-one points of worst fall, at the same time. That is twenty-three
out of twenty-three occasions it has helped. And the improved way of buying back we found this
morning — waiting for a quarter of actual gains rather than a price crossing a line — paid more here
than it did on its own: a point a year at an identical worst fall, because this book's recoveries are
bigger, so missing them costs more.

A CORRECTION WE MUST MAKE TO OURSELVES, AND IT INVALIDATES A FINDING FROM EARLIER TODAY. One method
this batch concluded that holding more companies bought no extra safety. On our main price history
that is exactly what the numbers said. On the fuller history that includes the companies which went
bankrupt or were bought, going from 20 names to 40 was worth six times more protection than it
appeared. The reason is simple once seen: holding more companies protects you against one of them
failing alone, and our main history is missing precisely those failures, so it can only ever show
what width costs and never what it saves. Every decision this lab has made about how many companies
to hold was measured on a tape that cannot see the thing width is for. That is now queued to be
re-measured properly.

THE FIRST METHOD THE DEAD COMPANIES IMPROVED. Every book we have ever checked earns less once the
failed companies are restored. This one earns more — up to a point and a quarter a year more. The
mechanism makes sense: it deliberately buys violent companies, violent companies die in falling
markets, and the switch has already moved us out by then, so their deaths happen while we are not
holding them. The catch is that the falls still deepen past the owner's limit for every 20-name
version; only the 40-name one stays inside.

THE LEARNED PICKER: the direction is now eliminated three ways, which is worth more than another
attempt. We have turned the model's flexibility, the horizon of the question we ask it, and how much
history it remembers. Shortening its memory made it worse in a straight line — half the memory cost
nearly a point a year, a quarter cost nearly two — and a short memory also turns out to be about six
times more sensitive to our missing-companies problem, because a five-year lesson set gets rewritten
by them while a twenty-year one absorbs them. The model does beat a version that forecasts nothing,
so it is learning something real; it simply cannot beat the index in the recent years. The one thing
we have never changed is what the model is allowed to look at: every input describes a single company
relative to other companies on the same day, so by construction it cannot tell a crisis from a calm
year. Letting it see what the market as a whole is doing — data we already hold and pay nothing for —
is the first genuinely new information this direction has ever had, and it is queued.

WHAT TODAY SAYS ABOUT THE LAB ITSELF. The pattern across both batches is not a shortage of ideas that
look good. It is that too many of them turn out to be the same book. Three separate routes today —
re-weighting, sheltering, and leaning into asymmetry — arrived back at a family we have already tested
and lost with. The check that catches this is the most valuable thing we own, and today it did the
work four times.

On costs: nothing lost its edge to fees this batch. One method measured fee drag directly and found
it flat as a book widens, with the total bill actually falling for wider books, so the decline in
returns as you hold more companies is genuine signal decay and not a fee effect.

NEXT: register the wide asymmetry book alone so its own behaviour is judged rather than inherited;
re-measure width on the fuller history; and give the learned picker market-state information. The
first of those is the one that could change what we are allowed to buy.

insights.title: Sell on a bad quarter, not a crossed line: move the safety switch's exit, on a book whose kin is clean: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.6% on the usual history, +10.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.7% and 20.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −3.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 1 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Market-state columns for the learned ranker: the trees see the fear gauge and the yield curve, not only one company against another: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 51.4% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +10.9% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +9.9% a year, which is +2.8% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned +0.7% a year, −6.5% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +3.7% a year against the market as recorded, +2.8% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +6.3% a year against the market as recorded, −3.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +3.3% a year against the market as recorded, +3.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −0.7% a year against the market as recorded, −0.7% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 2 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The safety rule's two halves want opposite things: quick to come back, slow to leave
insights.body:
Seer's books all sit behind one safety rule: when the US market drops below its own slow 200-day average, the book sells everything and waits in cash. That rule has two halves, and they turn out to want opposite settings.

The coming-back half was improvable, and the lab has now improved it four times on four unrelated books: buy back when the market's last three months have actually made money, rather than when today's price crosses the average. Three months is a genuine sweet spot, because both one month and six months are worse. This run added the fourth confirmation, on a book that picks companies raising their dividends and contains no price-momentum at all, worth two thirds of a point a year.

The leaving half is the opposite, and nobody had ever checked. Replacing 'the price crossed below the average' with 'the last stretch actually lost money' made things worse in a straight line: selling on a bad half-year was a tie, a bad quarter cost nearly three points a year and made the worst fall five points deeper, and a bad month cost almost five points a year and was the only version that lost to simply holding the market. There is no sweet spot. The slower and smoother the rule, the better, right up to the 200-day average itself.

The reason is stickiness, and it is worth understanding because it is easy to mistake for crudeness. A 200-day average is a heavily smoothed line, so a price above it tends to stay above it and small dips do not dislodge it. 'Did the last three months make money?' has no such smoothing — it flips from yes to no and back again repeatedly in a flat, choppy market, and every flip sells the whole book and buys it back later at a cost. The proof is time spent invested: 73% under the old rule, then 71%, 62% and 49% as the window got shorter. The one-month version sat in cash more than half the time.

What to do about it: leave the sell rule alone. It is not a crude placeholder waiting to be refined; the smoothing is the thing it is for. If anything is worth trying, it is not a better sell signal but a cooling-off period — once the book has sold, make the rule stay settled for a while before it may act again — because the damage measured here came entirely from how often the rule changed its mind, not from what it measured.

insights.title: Market-state columns for the learned ranker: the trees see the fear gauge and the yield curve, not only one company against another: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.0% on the usual history, +9.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.1% and 18.3%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −5.2% a year before and −3.3% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The best book this lab has built picks different companies than momentum and still behaves exactly like it
insights.body:
The asymmetry picker was the best book this lab has measured, and it has now been refused for a
reason worth understanding rather than working around.

The picker ranks companies on temperament: how much of the market's good days a company joins in,
minus how much of its bad days. Hold the forty most lopsided, and step out of the market whenever
it closes below its 200-day average. On the owner's real saving plan that earned 13.5% a year
against 7.2% for the same deposits put into the market, fell 21.6% at its worst, and lost 0.3% in
2008 while the market lost 36.8%.

It is refused because it moves too much like a book the lab already tried on unseen years and
lost with. The limit is 0.85 on that measure and it reads 0.90.

The interesting part is why, because the obvious explanations are all wrong. It is not that the
two books sit in cash in the same months: throw those months away and the reading only falls from
0.90 to 0.88. It is not that they buy the same companies: month by month over twenty years the two
books share 18.7% of their names, against 15.3% if the rankings were unrelated — they are picking
different companies. And it is not a quirk of the test: forty-name books drawn at random from the
same pool, behind the same switch, were measured against every real book here and never once
crossed the line, reading 0.64 at most 0.70 against this one.

So the picker finds different companies with the same temperament. The ones that run hardest when
the market runs and give the most back when it turns are not the same companies momentum buys, but
they live the same month-to-month life. Buying forty of them behind a market switch reproduces the
momentum book's experience whoever you actually bought.

What to do about it: stop building versions of this ranking behind the market switch. Book size
does not change a company's temperament, so a twenty-name or sixty-name version lands in the same
place. The one combination never tried is this ranking kept invested and braked by something other
than the market's trend — by the account's own falling value, or its own jumpiness. The
always-invested version of this picker is behaviourally free and clear of the limit at 0.57; its
only defect is that it falls 69%. Fixing that without putting the book in cash alongside every
other book here is the one door left open, and it is queued.

insights.title: The rule that is blocking every promotion was tested against random strategies, and it holds up
insights.body:
The lab refuses to promote a strategy that moves too much like one it already tried on unseen
years and lost with. That rule currently blocks everything promising, so it is fair to ask
whether it is measuring something real or just flagging any book of a familiar shape.

It was tested directly today. Twenty-four books of forty companies each were built by drawing
names completely at random from the same pool the real strategies choose from, re-drawn every
month, and put behind the same market switch. Random books have no skill and no shared idea, so
if the test were merely detecting shape, they would look like kin of everything.

They did not. Measured against four real strategies, all ninety-six comparisons came in between
0.48 and 0.78, and not one crossed the 0.85 limit. Against the asymmetry picker specifically the
random books read 0.64 at most 0.70, where the picker itself reads 0.90 against the failed book.

So the rule earns its keep. A strategy has to genuinely live the same month-to-month life as a
failed one to be caught, and being long American shares behind a market switch is not by itself
enough to trip it.

One caveat worth recording. When the random books were compared with *each other* rather than
with real strategies, 93% of the pairs crossed the limit — because they were built identically,
down to sharing the very same in-and-out dates. That is not a flaw in the rule so much as a
warning about what it means: two strategies that step out of the market on exactly the same days
and hold the same kind of thing in between will read as kin even if their picks are unrelated.
The protection against that is variety in when a strategy is invested, not variety in what it
buys. That is a useful thing to know when designing the next one, and it points the search away
from yet another book behind the same 200-day switch.

insights.title: Let the lab show how alike two strategies are without spending a method on the question
insights.body:
Yesterday the asymmetry method was refused because one of its five versions moved too much like a
failed book. The refusal applied to the whole method, including the forty-name version — the only
one that stays inside the owner's fall limit once dead companies are added back — whose own
reading had never been computed. The lab keeps only the closest-moving version per failed book,
so the other four inherit a number that was never theirs.

Finding out the forty-name version's real number should have taken a second. Instead it needed a
whole new method registered and run, which costs the lab one more counted try, applied backwards
to every result ever recorded here. In the end the number was read straight off the results the
lab already stored, and no new method was spent — but only because someone thought to look.

What would fix this: a report-only command that prints any recorded version's reading against
every failed book, the way the lab already has report-only commands for fees, for market breadth,
for the period-by-period record and for the dead-company check. No backtest, no new try, no cost.
It would have shown yesterday, in one line, that the twenty-name versions read 0.91, 0.91 and 0.89
and the forty-name version reads 0.90 — and that there was nothing to rescue.

It would also change how strategies are designed, not just judged. Right now this number can only
be discovered after an idea has been committed and run. If it could be read while the idea was
still being shaped, the search could aim at strategies that are genuinely unlike the failed ones
instead of discovering the resemblance at the end, which is the single thing standing between this
lab and its first promotion.

insights.title: Does width protect, or only cost? Ask it on the history that has the failures in it: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +14.7% on the usual history, +15.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 21.0% and 26.2%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +2.3% a year before and +2.1% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 0.6 points a year more. 0 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Does width protect, or only cost? Ask it on the history that has the failures in it: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 70.0% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +14.7% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +14.7% a year, which is +7.5% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +7.5% a year against the market as recorded, +7.5% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +9.6% a year against the market as recorded, +9.6% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +8.4% a year against the market as recorded, +8.4% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: +2.3% a year against the market as recorded, +2.3% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in all 4 of the periods they could be judged on. The earnings come from the picking.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Spreading wider does protect you — our usual price history is simply unable to show it
insights.body:
We keep asking how many companies the book should hold, and we have been answering it on a price history that cannot contain the answer.

Today one picking rule was held at twenty, thirty, forty, fifty-five and seventy companies, and each one was measured twice: once on our usual price history and once on the fuller copy that adds back most of the companies the usual one cannot price, the ones that went bankrupt or were bought out.

On the usual history the worst fall went 22.7, 21.0, 21.5, 20.2, 20.6 per cent. Two points of movement across a book three and a half times wider, and not even in order. That is what an earlier experiment found this week, and on that history it is correct.

On the fuller history the same five books fell 29.4, 26.2, 23.1, 20.4 and 20.3 per cent. Nine points of protection, every rung, in order, no exceptions.

The reason is plain once it is written down. Holding more companies is protection against one of them collapsing on its own, and the companies that collapse on their own are exactly the ones our usual history is missing, because they stopped existing. A history with the collapses taken out can show you what spreading wider costs and can never show you what it saves.

The same reading was taken of the momentum book the paper account actually holds, at the widths already on file: 20.7, 19.6, 20.7, 19.9 on the usual history, against 25.1, 20.1, 20.0, 19.8 on the fuller one. Same shape, same size. This is not one book being strange.

What to do about it: treat every number this lab holds about how many companies to own as a measurement of the cost only. The safety half of that decision has never been measured on a history that could show it, and the correction is large at twenty names, small at thirty-five, and nothing at all by fifty.

insights.title: The twenty names the account holds are the least safe width available, not the safest
insights.body:
The paper account holds twenty companies, the owner mirrors it with his own money, and the limit he has set for himself is that the account should never fall more than a quarter from its highest point.

That twenty came from one comparison, run on our usual price history, which found that holding fewer companies scored better. Today the same comparison was run on the fuller price history that keeps the companies which went bankrupt or were bought out, and the ranking did not shift. It turned over.

Scoring each width by return earned for each unit of fall suffered: on the usual history the best width is thirty companies and twenty is a close second. On the fuller history the best width is fifty-five, and twenty is the worst of the five by a clear margin.

The number that matters most: the momentum book the account actually holds falls 25.1 per cent on the fuller history, which is outside the owner's own limit, where the usual history reports a comfortable 20.7 per cent. Holding thirty-five of those companies instead of twenty would have brought that fall to 20.1 per cent. On the usual history that widening costs about half a point a year. On the fuller one it costs nothing — the wider version earns a tenth of a point more.

Why this is filed as a risk rather than a finding: nothing here says the picking rule is good, and no roster change is being recommended on one morning's work. What it says is that the evidence the account's width rests on was taken with the relevant half of the question invisible, and a safety decision resting on a blind measurement should be re-opened on purpose rather than left standing because nobody looked again.

What to do about it: re-ask the width question for the book the account actually holds, deliberately, on the fuller history, and decide the number knowing both halves.

insights.title: The penalty the fuller price history applies may be predictable from one number: how many companies the book holds
insights.body:
We hold a rule that will not let a method through to a real test if the fuller price history says it falls further than the owner allows. That rule deliberately refuses to use an average, and for a good reason: across the hundred-odd versions measured so far, the penalty the fuller history applied ran from nine points better to fourteen points worse. No single haircut could stand in for the measurement, so the rule reads each version's own number and treats silence as silence.

Today's result suggests much of that spread is not randomness but one variable. Nine width pairs were measured under controlled conditions across two different picking rules, and the penalty lined up with book width almost perfectly: at twenty companies the usual history understated the worst fall by between four and seven points; at thirty-five to forty by nothing to one and a half points; at fifty and above by nothing at all, sometimes slightly the other way.

That makes sense mechanically. The penalty is the damage done by companies that died, and a book that spreads its money across seventy names simply cannot be hurt much by any one of them.

If it holds generally, it is worth a great deal. It would mean a width decision can be corrected without owning the fuller history at all, which matters because that history is not on every machine and cannot be rebuilt offline.

What to do about it: this is a hypothesis, not a measurement. It rests on nine pairs from two families, all gathered in one morning. The committed record of the earlier hundred-version comparison is already on disk, and how many companies each of those versions held is recoverable. Line the two up and see whether width explains the spread. If it does, propose the correction as an argued change to the rule. If it does not, this was a property of these two picking rules and should be said so plainly.

insights.title: Tell us when a book had its worst fall, not only how far it fell
insights.body:
When the lab re-runs a method on the fuller price history it reports how far the account fell from its highest point, but never when that happened.

That gap cost something real today. A result showed that spreading money across more companies takes nine points off the worst fall once the companies that died are added back. The obvious challenge to it is that the whole effect might be one bad year rather than a property of width, and the report simply cannot answer that. Partial answers had to be assembled from elsewhere — the book sits in cash through 2001, 2002 and 2008 so its falls are not the famous crises, and its lead over the index in the recent years moves the same way the falls do — but that is circumstantial and had to be labelled as such in the write-up.

What is wanted is small: the date the peak was set and the date the bottom was reached, for each version on each history. Two dates per row.

Why it matters beyond this one result: almost every judgement this lab makes about whether a result is real comes down to whether it is spread across the whole twenty years or concentrated in one stretch. Returns are already reported era by era. Falls are not reported by era at all, even though the fall is the number the owner's real-money limit is written against.

What to do about it: add the two dates to the comparison report and to the grid it writes, so that the next time someone claims an effect is general, the obvious objection can be answered from the report instead of reasoned around in prose.

insights.title: A market-wide reading is worth 216 lessons, not 57,000 — and that is why teaching the picker about fear did not work
insights.body:
Seer's learning stock picker studies about 57,000 examples: every company, every month, for twenty years. This experiment gave it four new things to look at that describe the whole market rather than one company — how nervous the options market is, how nervous it is compared with its own recent normal, the ten-year government lending rate, and the gap between long and short lending rates.

The catch is arithmetic and it is easy to miss. A fact about one company gives one lesson per company per month. A fact about the whole market is the same number for everyone that day, so however many rows it is pasted across it still only ever says 216 different things — one per month in the training history. And because the picker is asked about the year ahead, one month overlaps the next by about ninety per cent, so neighbouring lessons are nearly the same lesson repeated. The number of genuinely different market conditions in two decades is not 216. It is closer to the number of boom-and-bust cycles, which is two, maybe three.

You can see the memorising happen. Every scare in the picker's lessons — 1998, 2002, 2008 — was a real collapse followed by a violent recovery led by the most beaten-down companies. So it learned: when fear spikes, buy the wreckage. Then 2010, 2011 and 2015 brought fear spikes inside a rising market led by the biggest, steadiest companies, with no wreckage to recover. It applied the crisis playbook to things that were not crises and gave up four and a half points a year in exactly the recent years that matter most.

What to do about it: treat any market-wide reading as roughly two or three lessons, not thousands, whatever the row count says, and be suspicious of any model that appears to have learned what to do in a panic. It has seen two.

Worth adding that the experiment was clean rather than wasted. The picker genuinely used the new readings — it traded differently and fell differently — and it changed only what it was meant to change: every version held its stocks the same sixty-eight per cent of the time and sat out the same twenty-eight per cent of days. So the answer is a straight verdict on the idea, not on a side effect.

insights.title: A number that drifts one way for twenty years and never comes back will quietly break any model that learns from it
insights.body:
One version of this experiment let the picker see the ten-year government lending rate. It was the worst version in the batch: its deepest fall was twenty-eight per cent, against twenty for the version without it, and past the twenty-five per cent limit set for real money. Its worst single year was 2011 at minus twelve per cent, where the plain version's worst year was minus five.

The reason is worth remembering because it will come up again. That lending rate falls from about seven per cent in 1996 to about two per cent by 2015 and never goes back up. A model that learns rules like 'when the rate is above four per cent, do this' learns them in a world that stops existing halfway through. Every date after 2009 then falls off the bottom edge of everything it has ever seen and gets lumped into one bucket. The model is not confused so much as blind: it has no experience to match the present against. And 2011 is precisely when the central bank deliberately pushed those rates into territory nobody had seen.

The fear gauge does not have this problem, because fear goes up and comes back down again decade after decade, so a lesson learned in 1998 still means something in 2015.

The rule to take from this: before giving a model any economic number, ask whether the recent years sit inside the range of the older years or outside it. If outside, feed it the change rather than the level — this month against its own recent average — which is what the fear-versus-normal reading did here, and that one behaved itself. This applies to anything that trends for decades: interest rates, inflation, valuations, index levels.

There is a second warning in the same result. On Seer's main price history, which is missing most of the companies that went bust, this rates version was the ONLY one that nudged the recent years in the right direction, and it was the single reason anyone might have argued the experiment half-succeeded. Re-run on the fuller history with the dead companies restored, that nudge reverses completely. The one encouraging number in the batch was an artefact of missing data, and it took a free cross-check to find out.

insights.title: Four ways of improving the learning stock picker have now been tried and all four are used up — the next idea has to be new information, not a new setting
insights.body:
Seer's learning stock picker has been rebuilt four times. Each time the change was to the machine, and the seven facts it reads stayed the same.

How complicated the machine may be: it did best when made simplest, which is the signature of a machine with nothing to learn.

How far ahead it is asked to look: asking about the next year instead of the next month was worth several points a year. This is the only change that ever paid.

How much it remembers: making it forget the distant past made it worse in a straight line, and the shorter the memory the worse it got.

What it may look at: giving it the fear gauge and interest rates changed which companies it bought, genuinely, and still did not help, because there are only two or three different market conditions in twenty years to learn from.

Four different kinds of change, four methods, and the out-of-sample score has been one or two out of four every single time. That score is the honest one: it trains on the past, picks the version the lab's own rule would have chosen knowing nothing of the future, and marks it on years it has never seen. The twenty-year averages keep looking respectable and the out-of-sample marks keep saying the same thing — what is being found is a selection, not an edge.

The pattern says the limit is not the machine. It is that all seven facts the picker reads are price and dividend arithmetic, which is the one thing every other person in the market also has, free, and has had for decades.

So the next idea in this direction should not be a fifth setting. It should be information the lab does not currently use. The most promising candidate is already sitting on disk: Seer downloads company accounts filed with the American regulator, and has barely used them because they only start in 2009. But 2009 onwards is exactly the stretch where every method keeps losing. A picker built on company accounts and judged only on those years would trade twenty years of flattering history for seven honest ones. That is a real trade and I think it is the right way round.

insights.title: Sera 20261014-1312: the account's twenty names are the least safe width we measured, and our usual price history cannot see it
insights.body:
No buy signal, and this batch was built to close questions rather than open them. It closed three
and left one line genuinely alive.

THE BIGGEST THING WE LEARNED IS ABOUT OUR OWN MEASUREMENTS, AND IT CONCERNS THE REAL ACCOUNT.
Spreading the money across more companies does protect you, and our usual price history is
structurally incapable of showing it. The same five books, identical in every way but how many
names they hold, barely change their worst fall on our usual history — 22.7% down to 20.6%, and not
even in order. On the fuller history that includes the companies which went bankrupt or were bought,
the same five go 29.4% down to 20.3%, improving at every single step. The gap between the two
histories is itself bigger for narrow books and vanishes by about fifty-five names.

The reason is simple once stated. A book falls either because the whole market drops or because one
company collapses on its own. Our market switch already removes the first. Our usual history removes
the second, by being missing roughly four in ten of the days companies actually sat in the index —
and those missing days are overwhelmingly the failures. So on that history, behind that switch, both
causes of falling are invisible, and holding more companies looks like pure cost. It is not.

This is not one book. The same shape appears in the family the real account actually holds. Measured
on the fuller history, the roster's own book falls just over 25% — outside the limit the owner set
for real money — where our usual history reports under 21%. Its wider thirty-five-name twin falls
20% and earns slightly MORE. The twenty names the account holds are the least safe width of the five
we measured. That deserves a decision, and the follow-ups are queued to make it a properly measured
one rather than a reaction.

THE SAFETY SWITCH IS NOW FULLY UNDERSTOOD, AND IT WAS ALREADY RIGHT IN ONE HALF AND WRONG IN THE
OTHER. Earlier work found the switch sells well and buys back badly, and that waiting for the market
to have actually made money over a quarter beats waiting for a price to cross a line. That finding
has now replicated on four separate books, including one with no momentum in it at all. This batch
asked the mirror question — should we also SELL on a realised bad quarter? — and the answer is a
clear no, and monotone: the slower and smoother the sell rule, the better, with the existing
two-hundred-day average the best of all. The reason is that a long average is sticky, so once you
are out you tend to stay out, while a quarterly test flips back and forth in a choppy market and each
flip is a full sale and a later repurchase. Time in the market fell from 73% to 49% as the test got
shorter. So the two halves of the switch want opposite things: quick to come back, slow to leave.
That line is now closed, and one live lever came out of it — locking the switch for a few months after
it changes its mind, which suppresses the flip-flopping without delaying the first exit of a real crash.

THE BEST BOOK WE HAVE BUILT IS CONFIRMED UNBUYABLE, AND WE KNOW WHY. Measured at last on the right
version, it moves with a book that already failed out of sample at 0.90 where our limit is 0.85.
Three explanations were tested and two were wrong: it is not the months both sat in cash, and it is
not that they hold the same companies — they overlap on only 19% of names, barely above chance. It
selects TEMPERAMENT rather than names: the companies that run hardest when the market runs and give
most back when it turns. Forty of those behind a market switch reproduce the older book's experience
whoever you actually bought. The one door this opens is a book braked by its OWN falling account
rather than by the market's trend, because every market-reading brake puts every book in cash in the
same months, which is exactly what the resemblance rule refuses.

Worth recording separately: the resemblance rule itself was tested against randomly chosen books for
the first time and it holds up — ninety-six comparisons, none crossing the limit, where the real book
reads 0.90. Given that this rule is currently refusing nearly every promotion we make, knowing it is
calibrated rather than indiscriminate matters.

THE LEARNING PICKER IS FINISHED, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING SO PLAINLY. We have now tried four different
ways to improve it: how flexible the model is, how far ahead we ask it to predict, how much history it
remembers, and — this batch — telling it what the market as a whole was doing. Only the second helped.
This batch's attempt failed on every arm and in the way predicted beforehand: a market-wide reading
gives the model only about two hundred distinct lessons, and because of how the question is framed
those lessons overlap almost entirely, so the model memorised three crises and applied the crisis
playbook to ordinary nervous markets afterwards. One of the inputs, the long-term interest rate, drifts
in one direction for twenty years and never comes back, so every recent date falls off the edge of
everything the model ever saw. The single encouraging number in the batch reversed sign on the fuller
history, so it was a hole in the data rather than a finding.

Across four attempts the out-of-sample record has been one or two stretches won out of four, every
single time, while the twenty-year averages kept looking respectable. That pattern does not reward
another adjustment. The recommendation, which I endorse, is to stop building pickers on these seven
signals. The next attempt in this direction should be new information rather than a new knob — the
company accounts, judged only over the years where those accounts exist.

ON COSTS: nothing lost its edge to fees this batch, and width was shown not to be a fee effect — the
fee bill actually falls as a book widens, so the decline in return as you hold more names is genuine
signal decay down the ranking, not trading costs.

NEXT: decide the account's width on the honest history rather than the convenient one; try braking a
book by its own falls instead of the market's; and if the learning picker gets one more attempt, give
it genuinely new information rather than another setting.

insights.title: How wide should the roster be? The rungs between twenty and fifty, on both price histories: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 3 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +13.0% on the usual history, +12.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 19.6% and 22.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +0.2% a year before and −0.7% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 0.8 points a year less. 2 of its 3 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The account's worst moment was not a crash. It was a quiet spring in 2006.
insights.body:
We went looking for how many stocks the account should hold, and found something more useful on the way: we had the wrong idea about when this account actually gets hurt.

The guess, written down before the run, was that its worst moments would be the dot-com collapse and the 2008 financial crisis. Both wrong. Those two are its two mildest stretches in twenty years. The dot-com collapse cost it between four and nine per cent. The 2008 crisis cost it nine. The rule that sells everything when the market index closes below its own 200-day average did exactly what it was built to do: it stepped out and sat in cash while the market lost half its value.

The real damage is in the two places that rule cannot reach, and the second one was a surprise.

The first is 1998, when the market fell a third in about six weeks. That is too fast for a 200-day average to notice. It costs this account about twenty per cent, and holding more stocks barely helps, because when everything falls together there is nowhere to spread to. That is the floor, and no amount of spreading gets much below it.

The second is spring 2006, and it is the one that matters. Between the end of March and the end of July the market index dipped about two per cent and was back at a new high by September. Nothing was wrong. The 200-day rule never triggered, and it was right not to. Over those same four months the twenty-stock account lost nearly twenty-two per cent of its value, because the particular handful of companies it happened to be holding fell apart on their own.

That is the entire argument for holding more stocks, and it is now dated and measured rather than assumed. Holding thirty-five instead of twenty would have cut that four-month loss from twenty-two per cent to sixteen. Holding seventy would have cut it to thirteen.

Two things follow. One: the account has two defences and they protect against completely different things. The market rule protects it from the market, and it works. Spreading the money protects it from its own holdings, and twenty names is not much spreading. Two, and this is worth sitting with: for a book this narrow, the risk of one holding falling apart on its own is now clearly the larger of the two. We have spent a lot of effort on knowing when to be out of the market and almost none on what happens when a single company we own comes apart while everything around it is fine.

insights.title: The paper account's other book has never been checked against the companies that went bankrupt
insights.body:
The paper account holds two books of stocks. One picks them by how far they rose beyond what the market alone explains. The other picks them by relative strength against the market.

We keep a second price history for exactly one purpose: the history the lab normally measures on is missing roughly half the companies that were in the index in the 1990s, and the ones it is missing are overwhelmingly the ones that went bankrupt or were bought. It is a record of the survivors. The second history adds most of those back. Any result measured only on the first one is, to some unknown degree, a measurement of a world where companies do not fail.

The first book has been re-read on that fuller history, and the difference was not small: its worst fall went from twenty-one per cent to twenty-five, which is outside the owner's own limit. That is what prompted this whole width experiment.

The second book has no reading at all. It has never been run on the fuller history. We do not know whether it holds up there, gets slightly worse, or falls apart.

This is worth flagging on its own because the second book is also a twenty-stock book, and twenty names is precisely the shape that came out badly in this experiment. There is no reason to assume it is fine, and there is no reason not to look: the check is free. It records no result, costs none of the lab's limited chances to test on recent years, and takes about half an hour of computer time.

It should be the next thing done. Until it is, half of what the owner holds rests on a measurement we already know to be optimistic about something, and we do not know by how much.

insights.title: The survivorship report should say when a fall happened, not only how deep it was
insights.body:
When we compare a result on the usual price history against the fuller one that includes the companies that went bankrupt, the report tells us how far the account fell at worst on each. It has never told us when.

That gap matters more than it sounds. If an account falls five points further on the fuller history, there are two very different explanations. It might be carrying a little extra risk all the way through, which would show up again in any future twenty years. Or the whole five points might be one bad month that happened once. Those lead to opposite decisions, and until now we could not tell them apart from the report.

This run closed the gap by hand: it rebuilt each version's month-by-month account value on both histories, stripped out the owner's deposits so the monthly top-up did not flatter the fall, and read off where the worst fall started and where it bottomed. The answer overturned what we had assumed, and it took about forty lines of throwaway code.

It should not be throwaway. The report already has everything it needs in memory when it runs -- the month-by-month values and the deposits are both right there. Adding two dates beside each worst-fall figure, and a short table of the worst fall within each stretch of years, would cost almost nothing and would turn a number that invites guessing into one that answers the question.

Concretely, every row that today reads worst fall 25.1% should read worst fall 25.1%, from March 2006 to July 2006. That one addition is the difference between this run's conclusion and the conclusion we would have reached without it.

insights.title: Momentum, own-vol scaling only in high-vol regimes (asymmetric scale): what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +12.6% on the usual history, +13.1% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.4% and 19.6%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.2% a year before and −1.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 3 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 0.5 points a year more. 0 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A brake that watches your own account does not make you a relative of the books that failed — but it gets you halfway there
insights.body:
The lab has a rule that refuses a book for *behaving* like a book that already failed out of
sample, whatever it holds. Until today the suspicion was that the rule might really be a rule
against stepping out of the market in a crash — because every book in this lab that steps aside
reads the same market and so steps aside in the same months, and that is precisely what the rule
measures. If that were true, no safety device of any kind could ever rescue a violent book, and
a whole class of repair was closed.

It is not true, and now we know by measurement rather than by argument.

A forty-company book with no market switch at all was fitted with two brakes that read only its
own account — one that sells down as the account falls below its own one-year high, one that
holds less when the account's own recent movement has been choppy. Neither looks at the market.
Both cut the worst fall from 69% to between 19% and 33%, so both genuinely de-risk in the crash.
And all twenty-four behaviour readings — six versions against each of the four failed books —
stayed under the limit. The device that de-risks in crashes is **not** automatically refused.

The texture matters as much as the headline, and it is the part to carry forward. Braking on
your own account moves a book a long way towards the failed books' calendar: against two of the
four, the unbraked book reads 0.34 and 0.36 and the drawdown-braked versions read 0.62 and 0.63,
close to double. It simply does not move far enough to cross the line. So the correct reading is
not "account-reading brakes are invisible to the rule" but "account-reading brakes cost roughly
half the distance to the line, where market-reading brakes cost all of it". A harder brake than
any run here would need measuring, not assuming.

And the two brakes were not equal. The volatility dial beat the drawdown dial on every axis at
once: it kept more of the return, it moved the book less towards the failed books, and it gave
up less of the recovery. That ordering is the practical residue of this method. A drawdown dial
acts almost entirely around the famous falls, which is exactly when every other book is acting;
a volatility dial acts continuously, in small moves as well as large, so its calendar is its own.

The separate, older lesson was confirmed again and its size is now known on a stock book: a
drawdown brake sells after the fall and buys back after the rebound, so it survives the crash and
misses the recovery. Here it turned a 23%-a-year stretch from 2009 to 2015 into a 13%-a-year one.
Ten points a year of recovery, to save forty points of crash. Anyone proposing a drawdown brake
in this lab from now on should be made to quote that trade before the fall number.

insights.title: The roster's relative-strength book, priced the way the owner trades it, at five widths: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.2% on the usual history, +12.5% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 19.0% and 20.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.2% a year before and −1.8% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 3 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 1.2 points a year more. 0 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Let go of the one holding that is falling apart on its own, while the market is fine: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +13.9% on the usual history, +12.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.7% and 25.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +1.2% a year before and +0.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.6 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A cooling-off period on the safety switch: make it stay settled before it may flip again: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 34.1% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +11.3% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +13.2% a year, which is +6.0% against the market.
- On 25.7% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned +9.4% a year, +2.2% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +4.1% a year against the market as recorded, +6.0% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +4.0% a year against the market as recorded, +13.0% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +6.0% a year against the market as recorded, +7.1% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +35.7% a year against the market as recorded, +36.0% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −0.5% a year against the market as recorded, −0.4% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 3 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A waiting period on a safety switch loses return and safety at the same time
insights.body: Making the switch wait before it may move again is the one kind of brake that loses on both counts at once: three months of cool-off cost 2.3 points of yearly return AND deepened the worst fall from 20% to 32%. The reason is that a switch's changes of mind are not noise to be filtered out. The flips being suppressed were the 2008 exit — in every version that made the switch wait, the lead over the market in 2008 fell from +36% to around +28%, which is the whole of the loss. A brake that delays a correct exit is not safety. This book has now refused three separate attempts to improve the same switch — a wider threshold, a different sell rule, and now a waiting period — so the switch is very likely already at its best and the lab should stop looking here. The one honest point in the idea's favour: the version that locked only the way out, leaving the buy-back free, was the best of the four, which agrees with everything found so far about this switch wanting to be quick to return.

insights.title: A monthly-rank, weekly-resize preset on the fixed tape
insights.body: A brake that reads one holding at a time can only act as often as the book is re-read, and on the tape every width result is measured on that is once a month. The faster preset that exists measures its rebalance band against the whole account, a band that has been measured as barely firing, so a result on it would not line up with anything. A preset that re-reads weekly on the fixed band would let a per-holding rule be priced at the speed it was meant to run. Noted for completeness rather than as the explanation of this result: this brake failed because the companies it wanted to sell were never in the book, which no clock would change.

insights.title: Big companies do not leave a clean report rhythm in their trading volume
insights.body: We tried to guess when big companies report earnings from their trading alone: a day with three times the usual volume and a jump at the open, repeated about every three months. Only about a third of big companies showed four such days in a year and a half, and a steady quarterly pattern turned up for barely one company a month. Big companies' reports often move volume less than threefold, and report dates drift by a week or more. So most of the book simply sat in the S&P 500 fund, and the test said nothing about the earnings-month effect itself. The looser rule, 'reported in this same month last year', did find 30 to 70 companies a month, but it also catches days that were not reports, such as takeover news or market panics. A real calendar of report dates would settle this idea cleanly; without one, any guessed calendar should be counted before it is trusted.

insights.title: A history of earnings report dates
insights.body: Several ideas in the lab hinge on knowing when a company reports: buying before the report, after it, or stepping aside through it. The lab has to guess these days from trading volume, and the guess is either too strict (it finds almost nothing) or too loose (it mixes in other news). A list of past report dates for the big index companies, back to the 1990s, would let these ideas be tested on what they actually claim.

insights.title: The look-alike problem and the profit came from the same few companies
insights.body: The best book in the lab picks companies that join the market's good days more than its bad ones. It was refused because it moved too much like a momentum book that already failed. The two books share only a few companies each month, so it looked like the book's character was the problem, not the names. This run removed momentum's own favourite companies first and ranked the rest. The resemblance disappeared almost completely (from 0.90 to 0.45, where the limit is 0.85), but the yearly return fell from 13.5% to about 10%, the luck test failed, and the book lost to the market after 2009. The handful of shared companies was both why the book looked like momentum and why it made money. The lesson: when a book is refused for resembling a failed one, check whether a few shared names carry both the resemblance and the profit before trying to engineer around it.

insights.title: Buying last month's big losers fails however you choose them
insights.body: Two attempts so far have tried to profit from the textbook 'bounce': buy the big companies that fell hardest last month, then sell a month later. The first picked only calm stocks still in an uptrend. The second, following a 2013 paper, measured each fall against that stock's own normal swing, so a quiet stock's sharp drop counted for more than a jumpy stock's. Both landed in the same place. At best they roughly matched what the same monthly deposits earned in SPY (6.9% to 7.6% a year against 7.2%), and both fell more than 25% at their worst, mostly in 2007 when the fallers kept falling. Measuring the fall more carefully helped a little, but never enough to change the answer. Three things work against the idea: replacing about 20 stocks every month costs a lot in fees at small order sizes, an equal-slot book of big stocks bets against the giants that drove SPY, and a big drop in a big company is often real news that keeps going. The lesson is that how a stock fell may matter more than how far it fell.

insights.title: Company accounts did not give the stock picker a reliable edge, even in the years we have them
insights.body: The lab tried its learned stock picker on company accounts (how cheap, how good and how profitable a business is, and its latest earnings surprise) over 2012 to 2015, the only years the accounts cover. On average the accounts version grew 13.5% a year against 9.5% for the same picker on price signals alone, but it was ahead in only two of the four years, and both wins came from one strong year and one bad year for the price version. A simple book holding the 20 most-traded companies, with no model at all, beat every version at 14.1% a year, and SPY did better still. What it means: on the data the lab has, accounts are not the missing ingredient, and this is not a reason to buy older accounts data. What keeps winning recently is simply owning the biggest companies.

insights.title: Sera 20261016-2004: what made our best books look like failures is what made them money
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. None of the four ideas came close: not one passed our own bars on the twenty-year history, so none reached the stage where it could be checked against the years it has never seen, and the strict promotion check was never even asked a question. Nothing was promoted and no test look was spent.

This batch was deliberately spread wide: four ideas from four different corners, two of them taken straight from published research and two from our own list of open questions. All four lost, and they lost in a way that teaches one lesson from four directions.

THE LESSON: THE THINGS THAT MADE OUR BEST BOOKS LOOK LIKE FAILED BOOKS ARE THE SAME THINGS THAT MADE THEM PROFITABLE.
Our most promising book picks companies that join the market's rises more than its falls. It is barred from a real test because it moves almost exactly like a momentum book that already failed. We tried the obvious fix: simply refuse to buy any company the momentum book is buying that month. It worked exactly as hoped on the resemblance, which fell from far over our limit to less than half of it. But the profit fell with it, from 13.5% a year to about 10-11.7%, and the book no longer passed the luck check or won most of its out-of-sample stretches. The companies that made it look like the failed book were the companies that made it money. That closes this line: there is no version of it that is both different and good.

TWO PUBLISHED IDEAS DID NOT SURVIVE CONTACT WITH OUR SITUATION.
Buying big companies in the month they are due to report their earnings is a well-known finding. We have no calendar of report dates, so we tried to guess them from the bursts of trading each report leaves behind. For the largest companies those bursts are too irregular to read: the guess found barely one company a month, so the book was really just the market. A cruder rule, "they reported in this month a year ago", earned 9.6% a year against the market's 7.2% on the same deposits, but it fell 29% at its worst and won only one of four out-of-sample stretches. A true history of report dates would settle this idea properly, and it is now on the data wish list.

Buying last month's biggest losers, measured against how much the market alone would have moved them, is another published finding that is meant to survive trading costs among large companies. Not at our size: re-picking twenty names every month at Gotrade's fees left every version behind the market, the best at 6.9% a year against 7.2%, and every version fell more than the owner's 25% limit. This is the second time the lab has tested buying recent losers, and it has failed both times.

THE COMPANY ACCOUNTS, GIVEN THEIR FAIREST CHANCE, DID NOT HELP ENOUGH.
The previous batch said the learning stock picker had run out of ideas from prices alone and needed new information. We gave it the companies' published accounts and judged it only over 2012-2015, the years those accounts properly cover. The accounts did help on average, but in only two of the four years, short of the bar set in advance. And a simple book of the most heavily traded big companies, with no model at all, beat every version. Over those same years the market itself beat everything.

WHAT LOOKS ALIVE AND WHAT LOOKS DEAD.
Dead: trying to separate the up-and-down temperament book from momentum; buying recent losers; the learning picker, now with or without company accounts. Alive but untested: the report-month idea, if we can get real report dates; and the old news-day book, which still passes every check we have but whose edge in recent years is too thin to be worth one of our few test looks.

ON FEES: Gotrade's real fees decided one result outright. The losers book needs to re-pick nearly every name every month, and the fee bill took whatever edge the published research found. Monthly full turnover on a small account is simply too expensive.
