NEXT: the most valuable single thing is new data rather than a new rule, a real history of when companies reported their earnings, because it would let us test the report-month idea honestly. Without it, the next batch should look for ideas that trade rarely, since this batch showed again that anything which turns over the whole book each month starts several points behind.

insights.title: Same-month seasonality: buy the stocks that did best in this calendar month last year: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +10.5% at the assumed fee, +8.4% at the real fees (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 15.1% and 15.5%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 1.65 and 1.52.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $1,620 and $3,744.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Same-month seasonality: buy the stocks that did best in this calendar month last year: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +10.5% at the assumed fee, +8.4% at the real fees (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 15.1% and 15.5%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 1.65 and 1.52.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $1,620 and $3,744.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Trading less paid more than picking better: holding a stock until it falls well out of the top added almost two points a year
insights.body: The high-dividend book was run two ways on the same signal, once a year. The first sold everything that left the top 20 and bought the new top 20. The second kept a company until it fell out of the top 40. The second earned 9.0% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.3% for the first. It made about half the trades and fell a little less in 2008. Nothing about the stock-picking changed; it simply stopped paying Gotrade's fees to swap stocks that were only slightly worse for ones that were only slightly better. Re-ranking the same book every month instead of every December cost another 0.7 points a year. This matters beyond dividends: every book in this lab so far re-picks every month, and a small account pays for each swap. Any slow-moving book tried from now on should be built with a keep band like this from the start.

insights.title: Three different 'safe dividend company' books have now lost to SPY in 2009-2015
insights.body: The calm big dividend raisers, the long dividend-raise streaks, and now the highest dividend yields all lagged SPY in the years after 2009, which are the best-covered years and the most like today. The high-yield book made about 44% over 2012-2014 while SPY made 66%. These companies are mostly utilities, telecoms, energy, tobacco and property, and the market after 2009 was led by big tech companies that pay little or no dividend. Whatever the selection rule, a dividend book misses the part of the market that did the work. A fourth version of this would not help; only putting such a book beside SPY rather than instead of it might. Also, the lab does not take dividend tax off (15-30% for an Indonesian holder), which would remove most of the small lead the safer high-yield version had.

insights.title: Beaten-down companies as a small crash cushion beside SPY: 80% SPY, 20% the five-year losers, rebalanced monthly: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 4 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.9% on the usual history, +7.8% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 54.5% and 54.5%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +0.1% a year before and +0.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 4 of its 4 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Stop fighting the market's shape: the same fifty members, weighted by how heavily they trade instead of equally: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +6.5% on the usual history, +4.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 57.2% and 72.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −0.4% a year before and −2.3% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 1 of 4 periods won to 2 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.3 points a year less. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A small slice of stocks beside the market cannot cushion the market's crashes
insights.body: We held 80% of the money in the S&P 500 fund and 20% in companies that had fallen hardest over five years, hoping those beaten-down names would soften the market's crashes, as they did during the 2000-2002 tech crash. They did not. Every version lost about 55% at its worst in 2008, the same as the market alone. Over twenty years each earned only a few tenths of a point a year more than the market. A control slice of the opposite companies, the five-year winners, earned the same and did better after 2009. So the small extra return came from spreading money evenly across twenty stocks and rebalancing each month, not from picking beaten-down ones. In a real crash nearly every stock falls together, so a cushion has to be something that is not a stock, or something bought only after the fall has already happened.

insights.title: How much a stock trades is a measure of excitement, not of size
insights.body: We tried sizing a plain fifty-company book the way SPY is built, with more money in the bigger companies. The lab cannot measure company size reliably, so it used how much money changes hands in each stock every day. That turned out to measure the crowd's excitement more than size. At the end of 1999 it put almost half the money into five technology stocks just before they collapsed, with 13% in Qualcomm alone, a company far smaller than General Electric or Exxon. At the end of 2007 it leaned into the big banks. The book got a little closer to SPY's return but its worst fall went from 57% to 73%. There is still a real lesson underneath. On the price history that includes the companies that died, giving every company an equal share costs about 3 points a year against SPY before any stock picking starts, much more than we thought, and leaning toward bigger companies wins some of that back. So the handicap is real; this was just the wrong way to measure size.

insights.title: The trend switch cost the dividend book more in good years than it saved in bad ones
insights.body: The big-dividend-raise book behind the usual rule (sell when SPY drops below its 200-day average) made 7% a year from 2009 to 2015. The same book with no rule at all made 18%. The rule kept selling in the 2010, 2011 and 2015 scares and buying back after the bounce. A different rule did better: stay invested unless the bond market has warned of a recession in the last two years, which it did in 2000 and 2006. That rule dodged both big bear markets and still made 15% a year in 2009-2015. It shows the price rule's real cost is its false alarms, and that a signal from outside the stock market can tell a scare apart from a real downturn. The catch is that the bond signal fired only twice in twenty years, which is too few to trust on its own.

insights.title: The yield-curve warning was right twice before 2015 and wrong in 2022-2024
insights.body: Before 2015 the yield curve inverted twice, in 2000 and 2006, and a bear market followed each time. A rule that went to cash for two years after each warning looks brilliant on that record. Since then the curve inverted again from late 2022 into late 2024, the longest stretch on record, and no bear market came. This is public bond-market history, not something the lab measured. Over those years the same rule would have sat in cash through a strong rally. A signal that fires once a decade cannot be judged on two right calls. Any version of this rule needs a way out that does not wait two years, such as buying back once prices recover, before it deserves a counted look.

insights.title: Sera 20261016-2034: trading less helps, but it does not create an edge
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. One idea passed our own bars on the twenty-year history, a switch that steps out of the market for two years after the yield curve gives its warning. But the strict promotion check refused it a look at the unseen years: re-picked fairly inside each of four separate stretches of history, it won only two, and in 2009-2015 it trailed the market. Nothing was promoted and no test look was spent. The refusal came from the stretches alone; none of its relatives has failed a test.

This batch took the last batch's advice and tried only ideas that trade rarely: a yearly book of high-dividend companies, a small slice of beaten-down companies beside the market, the fifty busiest big companies sized by how much they trade, and the yield-curve switch.

THE LESSON: TRADING LESS HELPS, BUT IT DOES NOT CREATE AN EDGE.
The clearest new fact is about fees. Holding a dividend company until it falls well out of the top forty, instead of re-picking all twenty every year, was worth almost two points a year, more than any choice about which companies to pick. Rare trading is now the lab's default for new books. But a cheap book still needs a reason to beat the market, and three of the four had none that survived a crash.

THE DIVIDEND BOOK BEAT THE MARKET ON AVERAGE AND FELL APART IN 2008.
The twenty highest-yielding big companies earned 9.0% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2% for SPY, but they fell 62% in 2008, because the banks looked their most generous just before they cut. Behind the usual safety switch the worst fall shrank to about 26%, but it failed the luck check and lost both stretches covering 2009-2014. That makes three different "safe dividend company" books that have lost to SPY after 2009.

A SMALL SLICE BESIDE THE MARKET CANNOT CUSHION THE MARKET'S CRASHES.
Keeping 80% in SPY and 20% in the companies that fell furthest over five years fell as far as SPY did, about 55%, and earned no more than a slice of past winners did. What little lead it had came from equal slots and monthly rebalancing, not from buying losers.

HOW MUCH A STOCK TRADES MEASURES EXCITEMENT, NOT SIZE.
Weighting the fifty busiest big companies by their trading closed part of the gap to SPY (6.9% a year against 7.2%) but piled into whatever the crowd was chasing, nearly half the money in five technology companies at the end of 1999, and deepened the worst fall to as much as 73%. The check with the vanished companies put back showed that equal slots cost even more than we thought, about three points a year behind SPY. Matching the market's shape properly needs a true company-size figure, which we lack before 2009.

THE YIELD-CURVE SWITCH WAS RIGHT, BUT ONLY TWICE.
It stepped aside before both great bear markets, and on the dividend-raise book it earned 12.6% a year against 7.2% and passed the luck check. But two calls in twenty years is two events, not a pattern, and the warning is known to have gone wrong in 2022-2024, when the curve inverted and no crash came. The gate was right to refuse it.

ALIVE AND DEAD. Dead: high-dividend books as a market-beater; small slices of anything beside SPY as crash protection; trading activity as a size measure. Alive: the yield-curve warning as a second key beside the price switch rather than on its own, and the stay-until-well-out-of-the-top rule, applied to any book with a real edge.

ON FEES: the band rule's two points a year is the batch's most useful result for real money. Every future book should be built with it, and older monthly books should be re-asked with it.

NEXT: give the yield-curve warning an early way back in, so one wrong call costs months rather than two years; try the stay-in-the-band rule on the lab's best monthly books; and the data that would unlock the most is a true history of company size before 2009, which would let a book follow the market's shape instead of fighting it.

insights.title: News-day picks sized toward the giants: the filtered earnings-day book weighted by trading value instead of equal slots: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 3 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +12.4% on the usual history, +11.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 24.6% and 27.5%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +1.7% a year before and +1.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 3 of 4 periods won to 2 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.0 points a year less. 3 of its 3 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Buy signal: M0092 cleared the durability gate
insights.body: The news-day book sized toward the bigger companies is the first method to clear all four conditions of the buy signal: it passed our bars on the twenty-year history (luck score 0.911 against 0.90), none of its relatives has failed a test, it beat SPY in 3 of 4 separate stretches of history, and it led SPY by 1.7 points a year in 2009-2015, the years our price history is most complete. By the lab's own rule this is the moment a survivorship-free price history becomes worth buying. But the free check we already own, the same history with most of the vanished companies put back, weakens it sharply: it wins only 2 of the 4 stretches, its luck score falls to 0.81, its worst fall deepens to 27.5% (the real-money limit is 25%), and its lead almost disappears in years when a few giants carry the market. So its one look at the unseen years was not spent this batch; the family's repairs go first. Buying data now would mostly confirm what the check store already shows.

insights.title: Selling a dividend raiser when it turns jumpy is a good exit, not wasted trading
insights.body: The calm dividend-raiser book re-checks its holdings every month and sells any that have become jumpier than the middle of the group. That looked like wasted fees, so this test let holdings stay until they were much jumpier, or never re-checked them at all. Trading fell by up to 14%, but the yearly return did not change (10.5-10.6% against SPY's 7.2%). The winning trades shrank relative to the losing ones, and with no re-check at all the worst fall grew from about 19% to 20.5%. A raiser whose price starts swinging hard is often about to fall, so the monthly re-check was earning its fees. The lesson: a keep-it-longer rule only helps when the sell rule is reacting to noise. On a yield book it helped; on this book the sell rule was reacting to real trouble. Six tries have now tuned this book from every side, and none has fixed its lag behind SPY in 2009-2015. Stop tuning it.

insights.title: Slow-to-react big companies: rank index members by how late their price catches up with the market: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:

insights.title: Slow-to-react companies did beat quick ones, but the safety switch threw away their best recent years
insights.body: A new picker bought the big companies whose share prices catch up with market news a week or a month late, an idea from a 2005 study that says investors overlook them. Ranked that way, the twenty slowest earned about 1.8 points a year more than the twenty quickest under the same rules, so the ranking means something. But most of the lead over SPY came from the lab's usual frame (equal slots plus moving to cash when SPY is below its 200-day average), which the opposite ranking also enjoyed. The surprise was 2009-2015: with no switch, the slow reactors beat SPY by about 7 points a year; behind the switch they barely kept level, because the switch stepped out in the 2010 and 2011 scares and missed the rebounds. Without the switch they fell 64% in 2008, far too much to hold. The lesson: for a quiet, defensive kind of stock list, an on-off brake may cost more in recoveries than it saves in crashes, and a gentler brake that turns the book down gradually is worth testing.

insights.title: Measure a stock's big day against its own normal, and the lottery effect appears
insights.body: Last time we skipped stocks with big recent jumps and ended up with a dull book of utilities that only tied SPY, while the jumpy stocks it skipped did better. This time a jump was judged against how much that stock normally moves: a 4% day is huge for a soup maker and ordinary for a chip maker. With that one change, the stocks with the most unusual recent spikes earned about 6 points a year less than the quiet ones, and 2 points less than SPY, from 1996 to 2015. So people really do overpay for a sudden shock, but you only see it once you stop confusing 'shocked' with 'jumpy'. The catch: the quiet book still trailed SPY from 2009 to 2015, earned its whole lead in months when most stocks rose together, and lost two of four unseen-years tests. The signal is real; holding twenty equal slices of index members is what keeps losing to the giants.

insights.title: A bond-market warning cannot be told apart from a false alarm by price alone in time to matter
insights.body: The yield-curve watch sits in cash after the bond market signals a coming recession. This run added a way back in: after a year, buy back once the market shows it is not falling. Waiting a year proved too long to make a false alarm cheap. When the curve gave a false warning in 1998, the gate still missed most of the 1998-1999 rally, earning about 11% a year where the market made about 25%. Waiting less is no fix either. The version that bought back as soon as the market rose above its 200-day average did so in early 2002, in the middle of a bear market, and lost about 6 points a year over 2000-2002 compared with just staying out. The stricter proof, a new one-year high, never fired at all in 1996-2015, so on those years it was the old gate, trade for trade. The lesson: the twenty years the lab can test hold only two real warnings and one false one, which is too few to tune when to come back. Whether a way out helps can only be learned from years the lab has not yet looked at.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1530: the first buy signal, and why its look was held
insights.body:
BUY SIGNAL: for the first time, one book cleared all four conditions, but we held its test look. It is the book that buys big companies right after a strong earnings-day jump, giving more money to the bigger ones. It passed our bars on the twenty-year history (luck score 0.911 against 0.90). None of its relatives has failed a test. It beat SPY in 3 of 4 separate stretches of history, and it led SPY by 1.7 points a year in 2009-2015, the years our price history is most complete. By the lab's rule, that is the moment a full price history including the companies that later vanished becomes worth buying.

We already own a partial version of that history. On it, the same book won only 2 of the 4 stretches, its luck score fell to 0.81, and its worst fall deepened to 27.5%, past the 25% real-money limit. Its lead also nearly disappears in years when a few giant companies carry the market, and 2016-2026 has been the most extreme run of those on record. So we did not spend its one look at the unseen years. A failed look would also close the whole earnings-day family, and two repairs aimed at this book's 1998 fall are still waiting. Buying data now would mostly confirm what the free check already shows.

THIS BATCH: four new ideas from four different corners. All four passed our own screen on the twenty-year history, and all four won only 2 of the 4 separate stretches. So the strict promotion check would have refused every one on that rule alone; none had a failed relative. Nothing was promoted and no test look was spent.

THE LESSON: A TWENTY-YEAR AVERAGE THAT BEATS SPY IS NOW EASY TO FIND AND ALMOST WORTHLESS ON ITS OWN. Every idea beat SPY over twenty years, by 3 to 5 points a year on the owner's deposits. Every one lost to SPY in 2009-2015 except the earnings-day book, and every one split its stretches two-two. The safety switch that steps out below the 200-day average does most of the work in 2000-2002 and 2008 and then costs money in the long rise after 2009. Four very different stock-picking ideas sitting behind the same switch end up looking alike.

WHAT EACH IDEA SHOWED.
Holding dividend raisers longer: keeping a calm dividend raiser until it falls well out of the book cut trading by up to 14% and earned exactly the same, 10.6% a year against SPY's 7.2%. Selling a raiser when it turns jumpy turned out to be a good exit, not wasted trading. The two-points-a-year saving from holding longer, found last batch on high-dividend companies, does not carry over to a book that already trades little.
Slow-to-react companies: companies whose price catches up late with market news did beat quick ones, by about 1.8 points a year, as the published research says. But without the safety switch the book fell 64%, and with it most of the lead came from the switch.
Skipping lottery-like stocks: measuring a company's biggest recent day against its own normal swing finally made the lottery effect show up. The spiky companies we skipped earned only 4.8% a year, and the book that avoided them earned 10.7%. But the book trailed SPY after 2009, by 5.7 points a year once the vanished companies are put back.
The yield-curve warning with an early way back in: buying back once SPY regained its 200-day average walked straight into the 2002 fall. The safer rule, waiting for a new one-year high, never fired and simply copied the old switch. A bond-market warning cannot be told apart from a false alarm by price alone in time to matter.

ALIVE AND DEAD. Dead: the early way back in after the yield-curve warning; holding dividend raisers longer. Alive but not yet good enough: the lottery-spike measure, now that it is measured properly; slow reactors, if a gentler brake can replace the on-off switch; the earnings-day book, which is the strongest thing in the lab after the momentum books, if its 1998 fall can be repaired.

ON FEES: the band rule cut trading without moving the return, so on a book that already trades little the fees are not where the edge is lost. No old flat-fee method needed re-pricing this batch.

DATA: the most useful purchase is still a complete price history that includes the companies that later vanished. It is now justified by our own rule, but the free partial check says it would most likely sink the one book that triggered it. A true history of company size before 2009 remains the other big unlock.

NEXT: repair the earnings-day book's 1998 fall first: a fast crash exit with slow monthly re-entry, and a weekly slow-slide exit. Promote it only if a version holds its majority of stretches on both price histories. After that: the spike filter on only the busiest companies, slow reactors behind a gentle brake that scales toward SPY as their swings grow, and the yield-curve warning as a half-cash dial instead of a full switch.

insights.title: Skipping spiky stocks does not help among the biggest, busiest companies
insights.body: One idea in the lab skips stocks that just had an unusually big jump compared with their normal moves. Across all big index members it beat the market over twenty years but lagged in the recent years. We guessed the lag came from leaning toward the smaller companies, so we tried the same rule on only the 150 most-traded companies. It got worse: it lagged the market by almost 6% a year from 2009 to 2015, instead of 2.5%, and the gap between the calm stocks and the jumpy ones shrank by more than half. The most-watched stocks rarely stay mispriced after a jump, so the rule has little to work with there. Its recent-years lag came from holding equal amounts and stepping to cash, not from which stocks it picked. Lesson: this kind of signal lives in the less-watched names, and the only fair next test keeps the market's own weighting and uses the signal just to leave a few stocks out.

insights.title: A brake that watches past swings is too late for a crash that starts calm
insights.body: The slow-to-react company picker fell 64% in 2008 with no protection. This time, instead of the all-or-nothing safety switch, it got a gentle dial: each month the book shrank its positions in proportion to how wildly its own stocks had been swinging lately. It still fell 31-39% at its worst, about as far as with the switch (33%), and it did no better in 2009-2015, the years most like today. The reason is timing. These quiet companies were calm right up to September 2008, so the dial read 'safe' and the book entered the crash nearly fully invested. After the crash the dial kept the book small through the sharp 2009 rebound. Any brake that only looks backwards has this problem, whether it is a switch or a dial. And a book that is calm right before a fall is exactly the kind such a brake protects worst. What to take from it: stop trying new backward-looking brakes on books that fall more than 25%. A lower worst fall has to come from what the book holds, not from a brake bolted on afterwards.

insights.title: A crash exit that waits a month to come back trades one saved crash for many bad round trips
insights.body: The earnings-news book was given a fast exit: go to cash the week the market falls 8% from its high, and come back only at the next month's start. It worked in 1998: the book left in early August, missed the rest of the crash, and turned a small losing year into a 15% gain. But most sharp market drops bounce back within weeks. In 2000 and 2007 the exit sold after each drop, sat in cash while the market recovered, bought back at the next month's start near the top, and was hit by the next drop. Its worst fall grew from 25% to 33%, and faster triggers did worse still, two of them losing to plain SPY. The lesson: a rule that is slow to come back only pays when a fall keeps going, and nobody can tell which falls will keep going while they happen. If an exit is tried again, the way back in should follow the market's recovery, not the calendar.

insights.title: A control built into a method can sink its fold record
insights.body: The low-correlation book was registered alongside its opposite, the stocks most tied to the market, as a control. When the lab re-plays history to check a method, it picks whichever version looked best up to each cut-off date. Because the late-1990s bubble flattered the control, it was picked in all four re-plays and then lost three of them. The real book, on its own, would have won three of four. The method was refused for its control's record. Controls are still worth running, but as their own method, or in a re-play that is told to skip them, never as a version the lab can choose.

insights.title: Big companies that move least with the market beat SPY, but partly thanks to missing companies
insights.body: Inside the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, a book of the 40 stocks least tied to the market's daily swings (taken from calm, middling and jumpy stocks alike) earned about 12% a year from 1996 to 2015 where SPY earned about 7%, and fell at most 24% where SPY fell 50%. The opposite book, the stocks most tied to the market, trailed SPY badly after 2009. That matches the paper's idea that investors overpay for stocks that move with everything. But when prices for companies that later died are added back, the lead after 2009 turns slightly negative, and the book also earns its edge only in months when the average stock beats the giants, which has rarely been true since 2018.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1607: every repair aimed at one bad year broke a different year
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. One new idea passed our own bars on the twenty-year history: a book of big companies that move least with the rest of the market. But the strict promotion check refused it on its stretches of history. Inside each of the four separate stretches, the fair way of choosing a version kept picking the opposite book, the companies that move most with the market. Picked that way, it won only 1 of 4. On the history with the vanished companies put back, its lead in 2009-2015 also turns into a loss. The refusal came from the stretches alone; none of its relatives has failed a test. Nothing was promoted and no test look was spent.

The book that fired last batch's buy signal still has not earned its look. This batch's repair for it made things worse, so its look stays held.

This batch followed up on last batch's leads: a crash exit for the earnings-day book, a gentler brake for the slow-to-react companies, the lottery-spike filter on only the busiest companies, and one new idea from published research.

THE LESSON: EVERY REPAIR AIMED AT ONE BAD YEAR BROKE A DIFFERENT YEAR.
The earnings-day book's worst moment was the 1998 crash. A weekly exit that sells as soon as the market cracks did fix 1998. But in 2000 and 2007 it sold near the bottom of a dip and bought back higher a month later, twice. Its worst fall deepened from about 25% to 30-33%, and the faster versions lost to SPY outright. The same happened to the slow-to-react book: swapping the on-off safety switch for a dial that shrinks the book as its swings grow fell just as far, 31-39%, and kept none of its lead after 2009. A crash rule tuned on the crashes we know is a guess about the next one, and the history keeps saying the guess costs more than it saves.

WHAT EACH IDEA SHOWED.
The lottery-spike filter on only the busiest companies: narrowing the pool to the 150 most-traded companies shrank the gap between the calm and the spiky companies from 6 points a year to about 2.6. The book barely beat SPY over twenty years and trailed it by 5.7 points a year after 2009. The spike effect lives mostly in the less-watched companies.
Companies that move least with the market: the best version earned 12.0% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, with a worst fall of 24%, the cleanest numbers of the batch. But in the years before each test stretch, the companies that move most with the market looked better. An idea that only wins when you already know which side to back is not yet an edge. The published research warns that this effect is mostly about small companies, and among the giants that is what we found.
The slow-to-react companies: they only pay when small companies lead the market, which is why their lead vanished after 2009.

ALIVE AND DEAD. Dead: crash exits bolted onto a book (now tried three ways in this lab), the spike filter among the busiest companies, and the gentle brake on slow reactors. Alive but unproven: the earnings-day book as it stands, with its look still held; and low correlation, but only tested honestly with its opposite kept in the race.

A WARNING FOR THE NEXT BATCH: the obvious follow-up to the low-correlation book is to run it again without its opposite as a competitor, so the stretch test can no longer pick the opposite. That would pass the check by construction. It is exactly the kind of trick the strict check exists to stop, and the lab will not run it that way.

ON FEES: no method lost its edge to Gotrade's fees this batch, and no old flat-fee method needed re-pricing.

DATA: the most valuable thing is still a complete price history that includes the companies that later vanished. Three of this batch's four ideas lost a point or more a year once the vanished companies we can recover were put back.

NEXT: stop repairing crashes and look for edges that hold in 2009-2015 on both price histories. Candidates: the earnings-day book with a price-based way back in that waits for the market to settle, a blend of slow reactors with the biggest companies so it does not depend on small companies leading, and the low-correlation book on the 200 busiest companies with its opposite kept as a competitor.

insights.title: Stocks that fall hardest in the market's worst weeks won the twenty years and lost the recent ones
insights.body: A published idea says investors shun stocks that drop hardest when the market makes its biggest moves, so those stocks should pay more over time. Among large US companies from 1996 to 2015 they did: a 40-stock book of them earned about 10.5% a year on the owner's deposits where the same money in SPY earned 7.2%, and its worst fall was 23% behind a market-trend switch. But every bit of that lead came from the late-1990s boom and the 2003-2007 recovery. From 2009 to 2015, the years most like today, it trailed SPY by more than 5% a year. In a test that re-picks the best version using only the past, the opposite book (the stocks that hold up best in big weeks) looked better before every stretch, and the winner flipped back and forth. That is what a passing market mood looks like, not a lasting reward. Adding the dead companies back did not hurt it, so the missing data did not create the result. The lesson repeats one from the low-correlation book earlier today: risk-shaped stock picks among big companies tend to win one era and give it back in the next.

insights.title: A safety switch on a plain big-company book earns the same lead as the clever books built on it
insights.body: We paired the slowest-to-react companies with the 20 biggest, busiest companies, both stepping into cash when SPY falls under its 200-day average. As a control we also ran the big-company half alone: no stock-picking idea at all, just the giants plus the switch. Over 1996-2015 that control earned +10.3% a year against SPY's +7.2%, the same lead as the pair (+10.5%). Nearly all of it came from sitting in cash through 2001-2002 and 2008. In 2009-2015, the years most like today, the control trailed SPY by 4.6 points a year, because the switch jumped out in the 2010 and 2011 scares and missed the rebounds. What it means: when a switched book shows a twenty-year lead, much of that lead is the switch, not the picks. Judge any switched book against this plain switched big-company book, not only against SPY.

insights.title: Hedging small companies against giants overshoots: the giants side is much stronger
insights.body: The slowest-to-react companies make money when the average company beats the index and lose when a few giants carry it. Putting half the money in the biggest companies was meant to balance that out. Instead the pair flipped: it now makes money only when giants lead (+12 points a year in those months) and lags when the average company leads. A book of the busiest giants swings far harder with that tide than a book of quiet smaller names does in the other direction, so splitting the money evenly does not split the bet evenly. Any future hedge like this should size the halves by how strongly each one moves with the tide, not by equal money.

insights.title: Owning the companies that move least with the market paid before 2009, not after
insights.body: Two tries now bought the big companies whose prices move least in step with the market as a whole, once from all index members and once from only the 200 most heavily traded. Over 1996 to 2015 both beat SPY, about 11 to 12% a year against 7%, and the busiest-names version held up even after the lab added back prices for companies that later failed. But almost all of the lead was earned from 1998 to 2008, when these defensive names (utilities, food, drug makers, oil) sat out the dot-com crash. From 2009 to 2015, the years most like today, the busiest-names version trailed SPY by about 2 points a year. And each time the lab replayed history and asked which version looked best so far, it chose the opposite book, the companies most tied to the market, four times out of four. A strong twenty-year average can be real and still belong to the wrong decade. The lab is dropping correlation as a way to pick stocks.

insights.title: Exit on the crash, come back on the recovery: the filtered news-day book leaving when SPY is 8% under its high and returning once it is back within 4%: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 4 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.9% on the usual history, +11.1% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 23.4% and 27.4%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +0.8% a year before and +0.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 0.8 points a year less. 4 of its 4 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A crash exit on a stock-picking book either fires too often or barely matters
insights.body: Three tries put a fast exit on the news-day stock book: leave when the market drops sharply. The quick versions left on every dip that snapped back (2000, 2007) and bought in again higher each time, so they cost more than they saved. The best version this time leaves only when the market is 12% below its high. It fired only a handful of times in twenty years, earned about what the book with no exit earned (11.9% a year against 12.0%), and shaved about two points off the worst fall. A version that leaves at 8% and comes back once the market is within 4% of its high fixed the deep 2007-2009 fall (33% down to 26%) but still got whipsawed through 2000. The book's real weakness is not crashes. It trails the market's biggest companies in calm bull years, which is why it lost two of its four out-of-sample periods. More exits will not fix that, so the next try should change what the rest of the money sits in, not when to leave.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1625: when the opposite book stays in the race, the opposite book keeps winning
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Three of the four ideas passed our own bars on the twenty-year history, and the strict promotion check refused all three on the same rule: none of them beat SPY in a majority of the four separate stretches of history. None had a failed relative. Nothing was promoted and no test look was spent. The earnings-day book that fired the buy signal two batches ago still has not earned its look. This batch's version won only 2 of 4 stretches on both price histories, so the look stays held.

THE LESSON: WHEN WE KEEP THE OPPOSITE BOOK IN THE RACE, THE OPPOSITE BOOK KEEPS WINNING.
Two of this batch's ideas came from published research that says a certain kind of company is overlooked and pays more: companies that move least with the market, and companies that fall hardest when the market falls hardest. Each idea was run beside its opposite as a fair competitor. Both beat SPY over twenty years, by 3 to 4 points a year on the owner's deposits. But before each of the four test stretches, a fair look at the years so far said the opposite book was the better bet, every single time, and the opposite book then usually lost. Both of these research ideas made their money mostly around 2000-2002, when unloved companies rebounded while the giants crashed, and both trailed SPY from 2009 to 2015. A twenty-year lead that comes from one episode is not an edge we can count on.

WHAT EACH IDEA SHOWED.
Companies that move least with the market, now among only the 200 busiest: +11.2% a year against SPY's 7.2%, a worst fall of 24%, and they held up even with the vanished companies put back. But they won only 1 of 4 stretches and trailed SPY after 2009. Two tries now; this direction is closed.
Companies that fall hardest with the market: +10.5% a year against 7.2%, a worst fall of 23%, 2 of 4 stretches, and 5.6 points a year behind SPY after 2009.
Slow-to-react companies paired with the giants, so one half pays whichever kind of company is leading: the worst fall shrank to 20%, but the giants half alone earned as much as the pair. The lead was the safety switch, not the pairing.
The earnings-day book with a price-based way back in after a crash: coming back only once the market had recovered fixed the deep 2007 fall. But the version that won did so by almost never firing, so it is really the plain book again. Three batches of crash repairs on this book have found nothing better than leaving it alone.

ALIVE AND DEAD. Dead: correlation as a way to pick companies, crash exits on the earnings-day book, and pairing slow reactors with the giants. Still alive, barely: the plain earnings-day book, whose look is held, and the idea of a small slice of good picks beside a large share in SPY that never switches out, which the next batch should test properly.

A FINDING ABOUT THE LAB: across the last three batches, twelve ideas ran, eight passed our twenty-year bars, and only one won a majority of the separate stretches. That one is the earnings-day book, and it lost its majority once the vanished companies were put back. The strict check is doing its job: twenty-year winners are cheap, and stretch-by-stretch winners are very rare.

ON FEES: no method lost its edge to Gotrade's fees this batch.

DATA: a complete price history including the vanished companies is still the most valuable purchase, and a true history of company size before 2009 would let a book follow the market's shape.

NEXT: stop sitting the whole book behind the on-off safety switch, because that switch is where most of these leads really come from. Test small slices of the best picks beside a never-switching SPY core (earnings-day picks, slow reactors), and the market-wide correlation of stocks as a timer for SPY itself rather than as a way to pick companies.

insights.title: Picking the crash-prone stocks and picking their opposite earned the same
insights.body: Two tries at the coskewness idea bought the stocks that fall hardest when the market swings hardest, and compared them with books that bought the opposite stocks. With each book's risk level held fixed, the two earned the same month by month, within a twentieth of a point a year. The twenty-year lead both had over SPY came from holding 20 to 40 ordinary large companies in equal amounts, which wins when the average stock beats the giants and has lost to SPY since 2009. The headline yearly figures still made the idea look three points better than its opposite, only because the opposite book fell harder in 2008 when the account was largest. The lesson for reading any result here: compare an idea with its own opposite month by month before believing the yearly figure.

insights.title: Crash-prone stocks as a small sleeve: the negative-coskewness picks as a minority beside a SPY core, no market switch: what the missing companies did to it

insights.title: Coskewness closed as a stock picker
insights.body: Ranked within beta buckets, the most crash-prone stocks and their opposite earned the same month by month, and the hard gate refused the only eligible variant on 0 of 4 folds. The twenty-year lead over SPY belonged to the equal-weight 20-40 name frame, not to the coskewness ranking. A further coskewness variant would be the same book under a new name.

insights.title: Putting most of the money in SPY does not shrink a stock book's worst fall
insights.body: The owner asked whether the crash-prone stock picks could keep their gains while falling less than 25%. We kept 60 to 70 percent of the money in SPY and put only the rest into those stocks, with no rule for stepping out of the market. The book then simply behaved like SPY: it moved one-for-one with it and fell 52 to 54 percent in 2008, about as much as SPY did. The extra return over SPY shrank to about a third, in step with the share of money in the picks. The fall comes from owning stocks through a crash, not from which stocks are owned. Only stepping out of the market got the fall under 25 percent (18 percent here), and that step-out cost about 5 points a year against SPY from 2009 to 2015, as it has every time in this lab. So a smaller bet is not a cheaper way to the 25 percent limit. It is the same bet, made smaller.

insights.title: Show how closely every strategy follows the market
insights.body: For this batch we worked out by hand how much each strategy moves when SPY moves (its beta). It explained most of the results. Books that held stocks all the time moved one-for-one with SPY. Books that stepped out of the market moved only about 0.4 for 1. A strategy whose lead over SPY comes from holding riskier stocks in a boom, or from sitting out a crash, looks just like one that really picks well, until the number is printed next to it. The lab should print each strategy's beta to SPY, and its lead over SPY once that beta is accounted for, beside every result and on every method page. Then a lead that is only extra market risk would be visible before any idea is spent on it.

insights.title: Among big companies, the crash-prone stocks really do earn more, but only for riding out crashes
insights.body: We asked whether stocks that fall hardest in the market's worst weeks earn extra among the large, heavily traded companies that make up most of SPY, not just among smaller ones. They do, and by more than across the whole index: the crash-prone twenty beat the crash-resistant twenty by about five points a year over 1996-2015. But that extra is pay for holding stocks that move more than the market. Held straight through, the book fell 57% in 2008 (74% once companies that later died are added back). Stepping aside when the market dropped below its 200-day average cut the fall to about a quarter but left the book trailing SPY by six points a year from 2009. Giving bigger companies bigger slots changed almost nothing. Lesson: this premium cannot be timed away; the only open question is whether it survives among stocks that do not swing more than the market.

insights.title: Smoothing the crash-sensitivity signal made it look better in advance and do worse afterwards
insights.body: The lab tried the coskewness idea again with a calmer measurement: five years of history instead of three, and each stock's score averaged over a year. Coskewness is how a stock behaves in the weeks the market swings hardest. Trading fell by three quarters, and before each test stretch the lab's own rule now preferred the idea instead of its opposite. But the idea then lost two of the three stretches it was chosen for: 2009-2011 badly, because the market switch missed the rebound, and 2012-2014 by a hair. Without the switch, the idea and its opposite earned almost the same (7.6% against 7.4% a year). Both lost 7 to 12 points a year to SPY in months when a few giants carried the index. So once the signal is smoothed, what remains is a bet that the average stock beats the giants, and the switched version's good twenty-year average comes from dodging two crashes. A steadier measurement did not make the premium steadier, which suggests there was no steady premium to measure among large US companies.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1707: the crash-prone-stocks idea, taken apart
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two of the four methods passed the first screen, and the lab's hard gate turned both away because they lost to SPY in most of the four stretches they were tested on one at a time. No test look was spent.

The owner asked two things about the crash-prone-stocks idea: is its lead real stock-picking or just a riskier book, and can the version that never switches to cash keep its upside with a worst fall inside 25%? The honest answers are "neither" and "no".

Is it stock-picking? No. When we compared stocks that swing about as much as each other, the stocks that fall hardest in the market's worst months earned the same as the stocks that hold up best, month after month. The gap was a few hundredths of a percent a year, which is nothing. Is it simply a riskier, high-swing book? Also no, and that is worth saying plainly: the original never-switching book moved almost exactly with the market, not more. Its twenty-year lead over SPY came from the way the book is built (twenty to forty stocks held in equal amounts, reshuffled each quarter), not from which stocks it chose. That same shape has trailed SPY since 2009, when the biggest companies led the market. So the edge was neither real picking nor extra risk. It was the equal-weight shape, and that shape has been losing for a decade.

Can the no-switch upside be kept with a fall inside 25%? No. Every version that stayed fully in stocks fell more than 50% in 2008, and putting 60-70% of the money into SPY itself did not help, because SPY fell just as hard. The fall comes from being in stocks through 2008, not from the picks. The market switch does cut the fall to about 18-23%, but every switched version then trailed SPY from 2009 on, which is the same trade-off the lab has found in every family it has tried.

What each method tried:
- Ranking within equal-risk groups: the picks and their opposites earned the same. Refused by the gate, winning none of its four test stretches.
- A steadier, slower signal: it traded about a quarter as often and was chosen more consistently, but won only the 2006-2008 stretch (when the switch dodged the crash) and lost the two after 2009. Its worst fall, 27%, was also over the 25% real-money bar. Refused by the gate.
- Only the busiest companies, sized toward the bigger ones: the picks beat their opposites by about five points a year, but only by holding stocks that swing more than the market. It fell 57% unprotected, trailed SPY from 2009 when protected, and did worse once failed companies were added back. Rejected.
- A small sleeve beside SPY: it only watered the picks down. Rejected.

Both refusals were on the same condition: losing the majority of the test stretches. Neither was refused because a related method had already failed its final test. All prices here use Gotrade's real fees on fractional shares and the owner's monthly top-up. Fees did not decide anything this time; the slower signal cut trading by three quarters and still lost.

What is dead: crash-prone stocks as a way of picking stocks, in any form. Four methods and around twenty versions say the same thing, so the family is closed. One idea still sitting in the queue (the same ranking among the busiest, calmer companies) is the comparison the first method already ran, so it should not be launched.

What looks alive, and what would help most: three batches in a row have found a "control" book that did as well as the idea. That points at the equal-weight shape itself, so the most useful next experiment is a placebo: the same twenty-stock quarterly frame filled in a fixed, meaningless order, as a yardstick that any future idea must beat before it claims a lead. Two fresh directions are also queued: stocks that keep beating SPY after allowing for how much they swing, and stocks that react most to sudden jumps in market fear. A standard report of each book's swing against SPY would have made this batch's question quicker to answer, and that has been asked for.

insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.0% a year before and −4.2% after.
