This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A book filled in random order passed the lab's first screen
insights.body: We took the exact setup the last three ideas used (20 index stocks in equal slots, re-picked every quarter, spare money in SPY, out to cash when the market is under its 200-day average) and filled it in a meaningless scrambled order. All three scrambles earned 10.3 to 11.0% a year on the owner's monthly deposits, where SPY earned 7.2%. They fell at most 22% from a peak and passed the luck test. That is as good as the coskewness books and their opposite-end controls. So those ideas added nothing: the setup itself beats SPY over 1996-2015, mainly by owning average-sized index members in a period that favoured them, plus the dead companies missing from our data. It still trailed SPY by 2 to 4% a year in 2009-2015. The only rule that caught it is the walk-forward check (it won 2 of 4 later periods), which keeps it off paper. From now on, an idea in this setup has to beat the scrambles, not just SPY.

insights.title: Show a random-order yardstick beside SPY
insights.body: Most of the lab's stock-picking books share one setup, and that setup alone beats SPY on the old data whatever order the stocks are picked in. The method pages compare each book only with SPY, so a book that is really just the setup looks like a winner. It would help if each such book's page also showed the random-order books in the same setup (about 10.3 to 11.0% a year on the owner's deposits for 20 names with the market switch), and said whether the idea cleared that range. An idea that lands inside it found nothing.

insights.title: Which of last month's losers you buy matters: the ones whose bad days stood out beat plain bounce-buying by about 5 points a year
insights.body: The lab has tried buying last month's biggest losers several times, hoping they bounce, and it never beat SPY. This time it ranked them differently: by how much each stock's worst days stood out next to what the average big company did that same day. Investors seem to overreact to a loss that looks dramatic beside the market. With everything else identical (same stocks, same 20 slots, same fees, same rule for stepping aside in falling markets), that ranking earned 9.7% a year on the owner's deposits, where the plain bounce book earned 4.9% and SPY 7.2%. The stocks whose stand-out days were gains did worse, as the theory says. It still is not good enough for money: it fell 29-34% at its worst, its luck check fell just short, and it lost to SPY over 2009-2015. But it is the first sign in this corner of the lab that the signal itself is real.

insights.title: A default setting quietly added a market switch to a book that was meant to have none
insights.body: The steady-beaters book was planned to stay invested through every crash, so we could see how its stock picks held up in 2008. The stock screen it borrowed has a built-in rule that moves everything to cash when SPY drops under its 200-day average, and the book picked up that rule without anyone asking for it. All five versions sat in cash through 2001-2002 and 2008, so the worst fall was about 20% instead of the 50% or more a fully invested book takes in 2008. The record is still honest: it describes what really ran. But it answers a different question. A test is only as good as its settings, and a quiet default can change the answer more than the idea itself. The no-switch version is queued so the original question gets a clean answer, and new books built on that screen should set the switch on purpose, on or off.

insights.title: The step-aside rule saved this book in 2008 and then cost it the rebound
insights.body: Without the rule that moves to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average, the stand-out-losers book lost 77% from its peak in the 2008 crash, because stocks with dramatic losses kept falling. With the rule it lost about 29-34%. But over 2009-2015 the version without the rule beat SPY by 4.4 points a year, and the versions with it trailed SPY by 3-4 points. The beaten-down stocks bounced hardest in spring 2009, exactly while the rule still kept the book in cash. A signal that buys fear needs a faster way back in than the slow average that takes it out.

insights.title: Stocks that kept losing ground to the market kept losing it when the biggest companies led
insights.body: Among stocks that move about as much as the market, we ranked each one by how far it had run ahead of or behind the market over three years, after allowing for its market risk. Over 1996-2015 the leaders beat the laggards by only about 2 points a year, too little to tell from luck. But they differed sharply in the bad stretches. The laggards fell 12% in 1998 and 14% in 2007, while the leaders made money in both years, so the laggards' worst fall was twice as deep. The laggards earned only in months when the average stock beat the giants, and lost about 5% a year when a few big names carried the index. So this ranking is less a way to earn more and more a way to avoid the stocks that sink when the market narrows. That might make it useful as a small side portion next to SPY, not as a whole portfolio.

insights.title: Keep comparison books out of the walk-forward's choice
insights.body: This method carried two comparison books on purpose, the opposite end of the signal and a plain bounce book, so the result could be told apart from simpler ideas. The walk-forward check, which picks the best version on earlier years and scores it on later ones, picked one of those comparison books in two of its four rounds. That makes the walk-forward record describe a book nobody would trade. A way to mark a version as a control, so it is reported but never picked, would make paired controls free to use.

insights.title: Stocks that suffer when fear jumps: rank by sensitivity to daily VIX changes and own the least exposed: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.7% on the usual history, +10.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 32.1% and 31.9%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.8% a year before and −2.4% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 3 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Among big US companies, being hurt by fear jumps is not rewarded
insights.body: A 2006 study said stocks that get hurt when the market's fear gauge jumps should earn more, because investors overpay for the ones that act like insurance. The lab tested it on the big companies of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 from 1996 to 2015. The fear-exposed book beat SPY, but so did its opposite, the fear-hedge book, by almost the same amount, and from 2009 the hedges did better. Both made all their gains in months when the average stock beat the index, which is the shape of any equal-weight book, not a reward for fear. With the failed and delisted companies added back, most of the lead disappeared. Why it matters: on most days a jump in fear and a fall in the market are nearly the same event, so 'fear exposure' mostly re-measures how jumpy a stock is, and in 2007-08 it even mistook oil and steel stocks for calm ones just before they crashed. Measures built on the market's own swings keep turning into bets on jumpy stocks and on 2008, here and in the earlier crash-with-the-market books.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1752: a meaningless book matched the stock pickers
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. No method beat SPY in a majority of the four separate stretches it was tested on, and none had a positive lead over SPY in 2009-2015. The lab's hard gate turned away both methods that passed the first screen, each on that same condition (losing the majority of the test stretches); neither was refused because a related method had failed its final test. No test look was spent.

The headline lesson is a yardstick, and it is an uncomfortable one. We built a deliberately meaningless book: the same twenty stocks-in-equal-amounts, reshuffled each quarter, with the same switch to cash when SPY falls below its 200-day average, but the stocks chosen in a fixed random order that means nothing. It grew about 10-11% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, fell at worst 19-22%, and passed the lab's first screen. It did as well as the crash-prone-stocks books and their opposites from the last batch. So for the last several batches, the lead over SPY that looked like stock-picking was mostly the frame: equal amounts in twenty or so stocks, plus the cash switch. That frame has lost to SPY since 2009, when the biggest companies led. From now on, an idea in this frame has to beat the meaningless book, not just SPY.

The other three ideas say the same thing in different words:
- Stocks that kept beating SPY over three years after allowing for how much they swing: it passed the first screen at about 12% a year with a worst fall of 20%, but the best picks beat their opposite by only two points a year (not distinguishable from luck), it won only two of four test stretches, and it trailed SPY in 2009-2015. It also ran behind the cash switch even though its plan said it would not, because of a default setting the build did not override. That is a lab hazard: other methods meant to run without the switch should be checked for the same slip.
- Stocks that suffer least when market fear jumps: the opposite book did just as well, the lead mostly disappeared once failed companies were added back, and without the switch the worst falls were 60-81%. Rejected.
- Stocks whose stand-out days last month were losses (an idea from a 2021 study): this one did separate from its opposite and from plain bounce-buying, by about four to five points a year, which is the most real-looking signal of the batch. But it trades every month, fell 29% at worst, missed the luck bar, and trailed SPY by about three points a year in 2009-2015. Rejected.

Gotrade's real fees mattered most for the stand-out-days book, which made over four thousand trades in twenty years; the slow quarterly books were barely touched by fees.

What looks dead: any equal-weight twenty-stock book that only shows its lead against SPY. What looks alive, faintly: the stand-out-days signal, because it beat both of its comparison books, and possibly among the biggest, busiest companies, where the 2009-2015 market was won.

What would help most: a standard placebo line beside SPY in every report, so a frame's free lead is visible at a glance, and a standard measure of how much each book swings with the market. Both have been asked for.

Next batch: the switch-free version of the steady-beaters idea (the question this batch failed to ask), the stand-out-days signal among the hundred busiest companies, the fear signal with picks sized toward bigger companies instead of equal amounts, and a "sticky" meaningless book that does not reshuffle, to see how much of the low-correlation book's lead was simply trading less.

insights.title: A sticky placebo: the same frame in a fixed random order that is not re-drawn each quarter, 20 and 40 names: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.3% on the usual history, +9.9% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.3% and 21.6%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −1.8% a year before and −3.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.4 points a year less. 3 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Stocks that beat the market for three years were not safer when it crashed
insights.body: The steady-beaters book picked the stocks that had run furthest ahead of the market over three years while moving about as much as the market does. Run with no safety switch, so it stayed invested through every crash, it lost 43% in 2008, more than SPY's 37% and more than a book of the worst three-year laggards (40%). The earlier version had looked calm only because a switch had moved it to cash in 2008. Over twenty years it earned about 10% a year on the owner's deposits against 7% for SPY, but the same 20-slot book filled in a meaningless order earned 9% to 12%, so the picking added nothing. This is the fourth ranking in a row that a meaningless order matches. The lesson: inside this 20-stock, equal-slot, quarterly frame, the frame earns the lead and the ranking is decoration. The next ideas should change the frame itself (how many stocks, how they are weighted, how big the companies are) rather than try another ranking inside it.

insights.title: Stand-out losers among the big companies, with a fast way back in: salience in the 100 most traded members, out under SPY's 200-day average, back above its 50-day: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +9.2% on the usual history, +8.0% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 19.5% and 18.8%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −5.3% a year before and −7.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.3 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Trading less does not make a random book better; the low-correlation picker's lead is not about fees
insights.body: The lab built a book that picks its twenty stocks in a fixed, meaningless order and then hardly ever trades: about 210 trades in twenty years, a quarter of what the earlier random book made. It earned about the same, +10 to +11% a year on the owner's deposits against +7.2% for SPY, and three of its four switched versions passed the lab's first screen. So paying Gotrade less is not what lifts a book in this setup. The one ranking that stands clearly above every random version is the picker of companies that move least with the market, at +13.3% a year, and it also moved less with SPY than any random book. That makes it the one idea in this family worth a fair follow-up: compare it with a random book drawn only from calm, low-sensitivity companies, so that the only difference left is the thing it claims to rank on.

insights.title: Among the busiest big companies, the stand-out-days signal was no better than a random order
insights.body: The salience picker buys stocks whose loudest days last month were losses, betting that investors overreacted. Across all the index members it beat plain bounce-buying by about 5 points a year. Restricted to the 100 most heavily traded companies, it earned 7.3% a year on the owner's deposits. The same slots filled in a fixed random order earned 7.2%, and SPY earned 7.2%. The overreaction this signal reads seems to live in the smaller, less-watched members, before 2009. That is exactly where it cannot help against SPY's big-company drift today. A 'get back in fast after a fall' rule (back in once the market closes over its 50-day average) made it worse: it bought the bear-market rallies of 2001-2002 and 2008 and fell 41% at its worst.

insights.title: Every stock picker should carry a placebo of its own frame
insights.body: Three batches running, the frame (equal slots, a market brake, a monthly or quarterly re-pick) has earned most of what the stock pickers earned. This method registered a placebo with the identical pool, slots and brake, and the idea tied it exactly. That told more in one run than five comparisons with SPY. The lab should build a same-frame placebo into the method template. It should also show 'lead over its own placebo, 2009-2015' beside 'lead over SPY' on every method page, so the owner sees at a glance whether a ranking adds anything.

insights.title: Buy signal: M0197 cleared the durability gate
insights.body: The Treasury-yield book cleared all four buy-signal conditions in lab walkforward on 2026-10-17: (a) dev-eligible at the bars in force (M0197-Y20-SW: the 20 members whose prices rise most when the 10-year yield falls, behind the SPY 200-day switch; DSR 0.955 at N=130, worst fall 22.0%, PF 3.08, 447 trades); (b) kin clean; (c) 3 of 4 walk-forward folds beaten, pick changed; (d) 2009-2015 edge +7.0 points a year. Its paired opposite (Y20-OPP-SW) failed the luck bar at 0.817 and fell 32.9%. Survivorship-free price history is now worth buying for this method before a test look or real money. Open questions Sera is checking before any promotion: the pre-registered falling-rate trap (yields fell most of 1996-2015), the survivorship-check store, and the same-frame placebo.

insights.title: Stocks that shrug off bond-yield moves: rank members by their sensitivity to the 10-year Treasury yield, after the market's own move: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.8% on the usual history, +9.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 22.0% and 23.4%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.3% a year before and −5.7% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.5 points a year less. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Buy signal: M0197 cleared the durability gate, but its promotable version did not earn its 2009-2015 edge
insights.body: The bond-like stock picker set off the lab's buy signal for survivorship-free price data. It passed the dev screen with the switch on: it beat SPY by 4.6 points a year, its worst fall was 22%, it made three dollars on winners for every dollar lost, and the luck test scored 0.955 against a 0.90 bar. No failed relative. It beat SPY in 3 of 4 later test periods. The signal also reported a 7 point edge in 2009-2015. That edge belongs to the no-switch book the walk-forward rule picked for those years. The switched book that would actually be promoted trailed SPY by 3.3 points a year in 2009-2015, and by 5.7 points once dead companies are added back. Adding them back also cut its overall lead from 4.6 to 2.1 points and its luck score to 0.84, below the bar. It led the meaningless placebo book by under a point a year. Read the signal as a weak one: the free evidence already says most of this lead is the switch, the frame and the missing dead companies. If clean data is bought, test this book's 2009-2015 years first.

insights.title: Stocks that rise when interest rates fall really did beat the ones that rise when rates rise, from 1996 to 2015
insights.body: The lab ranked big US companies by how their price moved with the 10-year Treasury yield, after allowing for the market. The bond-like side (mostly power utilities and property companies) earned 12.5% a year on the owner's deposits. The opposite side (banks, life insurers, oil) earned 7.7%, and SPY 7.2%. That is the widest gap between an idea and its own opposite in several batches. A book filled in a meaningless order earned 8.8% to 11.9%. The catch: US yields fell for almost the whole of 1996-2015, so this is partly a bet that rates keep falling. From 2016 they stopped, and in 2022 they rose faster than at any time in forty years, the worst case for a bond-like book. A pattern measured in a falling-rate era should not be trusted to survive a rising one.

insights.title: Buy signal qualified: the variant a look would test fails its own success test
insights.body: The buy signal on the Treasury-yield book fired on its walk-forward picks, whose 2009-2015 edge (+7.0 points) came from the no-switch book that falls 62%. The one variant the hard gate would promote, the switched book, trails SPY by 3.3 points a year in 2009-2015, leads the meaningless placebo by under a point, and drops under the luck bar once dead companies are added back. Sera did not spend its look. The buy-signal rule reads the picks, not the promoted variant, so it can fire on a method whose promotable variant fails condition (d); the owner may want the rule to read the promoted variant too (lab/walkforward.py, an owner-decided change).

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1808: a buy signal with a catch, on bond-like stocks
insights.body:
The buy signal fired this batch, but with a catch, and the lab chose not to spend the test look. The idea: own the stocks whose prices rise most when long-term bond yields fall, after allowing for the market's own move (steady, bond-like companies). On the lab's free evidence it cleared all four buy-signal conditions: it passed the first screen, nothing related to it has failed a final test, it won three of its four separate test stretches, and the stretches' picks beat SPY by about seven points a year in 2009-2015. That is the point at which a cleaner price history, with the failed companies included (a one-month download, roughly 30 to 150 US dollars), becomes worth buying.

The catch: the seven-point lead in 2009-2015 came from the version without the cash switch, which fell 62% in 2008 and cannot be traded. The version that could be traded, with the switch, trailed SPY by about three points a year in 2009-2015, beat the meaningless placebo book by less than a point a year, and dropped under the luck bar once failed companies were added back. Its own plan, written before it ran, said it had to win 2009-2015 and clearly beat the placebo; it did neither. So the lab did not spend its one look on it. A look on a version that had already failed its own written test would be a look spent on hope. Buying the cleaner data is still the right next step if this idea is to be pursued, and the first thing to re-check on it would be exactly that version.

There is real news underneath. Without the switch, the bond-like stocks beat every placebo seed and beat their own opposite by about five points a year. That makes it only the second idea in three batches to separate cleanly from both its opposite and the meaningless book. The worry stated in its plan still stands: yields fell for most of 1996-2015, so a bond-like book may simply have ridden falling rates, and it lost the 2012-2014 stretch. The years since 2015, which include the steep rate rise of 2022, would be the honest test.

The other three, in brief:
- A meaningless book that keeps the same stocks instead of reshuffling them traded a quarter as often and earned the same. Trading less is not what the frame's lead is made of.
- Steady beaters without the cash switch fell 43% in 2008 and did no better than the meaningless book. The small lead they showed last batch came entirely from the switch they ran by mistake.
- Stand-out losing days among the hundred busiest companies tied their own meaningless book, and the one version that passed the screen won only one of four stretches. Refused by the hard gate on that condition, the folds.

The hard gate refused one method this batch, on the folds. It would have admitted the bond-yield book; the lab declined that one by its own judgment, not by the gate. Gotrade's fees decided nothing this time.

What is dead: steady beaters, and stand-out days as a big-company signal. What is alive: the bond-yield idea, on cleaner data. The lab also needs two rule changes, both the owner's to make: the buy-signal check should read the version that would actually be tested, not just the stretch picks, and the hard gate should refuse placebo books outright, so a meaningless book can never spend a look by luck.

Next batch: the bond-yield book with a gentler crash guard than the all-or-nothing switch, and its rate-neutral cousin; a size-weighted meaningless book, to separate the equal-weight lean from the frame; and fresh ideas that are judged against the placebo from the start.

insights.title: Stocks that fall on quiet trading bounce back; stocks that fall on heavy trading keep falling
insights.body: We bought big index stocks that had fallen hard over two weeks, then split them by how heavily they were traded during the fall. The ones that fell on below-normal trading earned 7.7% a year on the owner's deposits and fell 24% at worst. The ones that fell on above-normal trading earned 6.5% a year and fell 37% at worst. SPY earned 7.2% on the same deposits. A heavy-volume fall is usually real news, and news keeps working on the price; a quiet fall is more often noise that gets reversed. The split is real, but it does not save the strategy: from 2009 to 2014 the quiet-fall book trailed SPY by 7 to 10 points a year, because holding last fortnight's losers at equal size bets against the giant companies that carried the market. The useful lesson is about selling, not buying: a stock you own that drops on heavy trading is telling you something, and that is worth testing as an exit rule inside a book that already beats SPY.

insights.title: Bond-like stocks with a gentler crash guard: half the book stays invested below SPY's 200-day average instead of all of it going to cash: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.3% on the usual history, +9.5% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 31.3% and 39.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −1.2% a year before and −1.8% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 1 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.8 points a year less. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Letting the data weigh every price horizon just rebuilt momentum, with momentum's weak years
insights.body: The trend picker compared each stock's price with eleven averages, from three days to four years, and let a fitted recipe decide which ones mattered. Over 1996-2015 its best version turned monthly deposits into about 10.4% a year where SPY made 7.2%, but nearly all of that came before 2009. In 2009-2011 and 2012-2014 it trailed SPY by 15 and 30 points. A version that picked stocks in a fixed meaningless order, with the same cash switch and the same equal slots, made 7.9% a year, so a good part of the win was the frame, not the picking. The recipe leaned on the long averages, which is the same thing as buying recent winners, and it did no better than the lab's plain momentum picker at the same fees. Lesson: mixing price horizons does not escape the post-2009 problem; the next trend idea should time the market rather than pick stocks.

insights.title: A gentler crash guard lets a meaningless stock picker pass the lab's first screen
insights.body: We tried keeping half the money invested when the market turns down, instead of moving all of it to cash. It worked for the bond-like stock picker: it beat SPY by about five points a year on the monthly deposits and passed the lab's first screen. But a control book that picks its 20 stocks in a random, fixed order also passed, with a slightly better luck score and a smaller worst fall. So the guard and the 20-stocks-at-equal-weight setup earn most of the gain on their own, whatever is picked. The real picks beat the random ones by only about 1.4 points a year, and by about half a point once companies that later failed are added back to the history. What to do: never judge a picker in this setup against SPY alone. It has to beat a random picker run under the same rules by a margin written down before the test.

insights.title: Run the random-picker check on every method automatically
insights.body: The last several batches only caught 'the setup did the work, not the idea' because each method happened to include its own random-order control. A lab report that re-runs any stock picker with its picks replaced by three random orders, keeping the same rules, crash guard, fees and deposits, and prints how far the real picks beat them, would make that comparison standard instead of optional, like the comparison with SPY already is. It would spend no test look and add no trial.

insights.title: Equal slots were not why random picks beat SPY; missing dead companies mattered more
insights.body: The lab has a book that picks 20 index members in a scrambled, meaningless order, and it beat SPY over 1996-2015 by as much as several real strategies did. The usual explanation was that holding every pick in an equal slot quietly favours smaller companies. This time the same scrambled picks were sized by how much each company trades, a stand-in for size, so the bigger names got more money. The book earned only 0.4 to 0.9 points a year less than its equal-slot twin, and still beat SPY in every version. Re-run with the companies that later died put back into the data, the same random books lost about 1.6 points a year on average, two to four times what the equal slots were worth. What is left after both is a lead of roughly half a point to two and a half points a year, partly because these books move about 10% more than the market does. So when a strategy in this lab beats SPY over twenty years, the first question should be how it does with the dead companies put back, not whether it favours small companies.

insights.title: A random pick from a survivors-only list is a winning pick
insights.body: Our price history covers about half of the index's past members in the 1990s and three quarters by 2014, and the ones missing are mostly companies that went bust or were bought cheaply. Any book that picks from the members we can price is picking from companies we already know survived. A book that picked at random lost about 1.5 points a year of its lead once the dead companies were added back. Every strategy that picks broadly from the index carries this head start. The cross-check against the fuller data should be read in a strategy's first analysis, not only before promotion.

insights.title: The bond-like stocks idea is closed: with a gentler guard it did no better than a meaningless book under the same guard
insights.body: Two tries at stocks that rise when bond yields fall: with the all-or-nothing cash switch it trailed SPY after 2009, and with a half-size guard it passed the first screen but so did a meaningless book under the same guard, which it led by only about a point and a half a year (half a point once failed companies are added back). It won only two of its four separate test stretches, so the lab's gate refused it. Without data after 2015, there is nothing left to try in this direction.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1835: nothing beat the meaningless book by much
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two methods passed the lab's first screen, but neither beat SPY in most of its four separate test stretches, and neither had a clear lead over SPY in 2009-2015 once the failed companies were added back. The lab's hard gate refused both, each on that same condition (the test stretches); neither was refused because a related method had failed its final test. No test look was spent.

The lesson of the batch: the meaningless book is now the real opponent, and nothing beat it by much. Since last batch, every idea has been run beside a book with the same rules but stocks picked in a fixed random order. All four ideas this time came within about two points a year of that book, or below it.

- Bond-like stocks (the ones that rise when long-term bond yields fall), now with a gentler crash guard that keeps half the money invested when SPY drops below its 200-day average instead of moving all of it to cash. It earned about 12.7% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, with a worst fall of 38%, and passed the first screen. But a meaningless book under the same half guard also passed, and the bond-like picks led it by only about a point and a half a year, half a point once failed companies were added back. It won two of its four test stretches. This direction is now closed; only the years after 2015, with the steep rate rise of 2022, could reopen it.
- The meaningless book again, this time putting more money in bigger, busier companies instead of equal amounts in each. It kept almost all of its lead: about 11% a year against SPY's 7.2%, under a point less than the equal-amounts version. So the lead is not just a lean toward smaller companies. What hurts it most is adding back the companies that later failed: that took one and a half to four points a year off it. It is a yardstick and was never meant to be traded.
- The trend factor from a 2016 research paper: one score built from how far each stock's price sits from its averages over every span from three days to four years. It earned about 10.4% a year on the deposits with a worst fall of 22%, but it fell just short of the luck bar, lost both 2009-2014 stretches, and beat its own meaningless book by under two points. Letting the data weigh each time span mostly rebuilt plain momentum, including momentum's weak years.
- Buying big stocks after a quiet two-week fall: stocks that fell on light trading did bounce back better than stocks that fell on heavy trading, by about a point a year and with much smaller falls. But it earned only 7.7% a year against SPY's 7.2%, just missed the luck bar, and lost badly to SPY from 2009 to 2015.

What looks alive: very little that is new. The light-trading-versus-heavy-trading split is real, and the next step is to use it as an exit inside a book that already works: sell a momentum holding the day it falls on heavy trading. What looks dead: bond-like stocks on this data, the trend factor as a stock picker, and short-term bounce-buying as a book of its own.

Gotrade's fees decided nothing this batch; every method was built in fractional shares at the real fees from the start, and no separate fee check was needed.

What would unlock the most: price history after 2015, which only a counted test look or bought data can give, and a price history that includes the companies that failed, since that is what keeps taking the leads away. The lab also needs a standing report that sets every idea beside its own meaningless book automatically, so no one has to build the comparison by hand.

Next batch: the heavy-trading exit inside the residual-momentum book; the trend readings used as a crash warning for SPY rather than to pick stocks; the automatic meaningless-book report; and fresh ideas from outside price-and-volume patterns, such as dividends and company filings, judged against the meaningless book from the start.

insights.title: The meaningless-order book drawn only from the 100 busiest members: does random picking among the giants land on SPY?: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +8.2% on the usual history, +8.7% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 25.4% and 24.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −7.1% a year before and −6.8% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 4 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Paper gains and paper losses: buy the stocks whose recent holders sit on the biggest unrealised gains: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 4 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +12.0% on the usual history, +11.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.8% and 20.7%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.8% a year before and −4.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 4 of its 4 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Random picks among the biggest companies just earn what the market earns
insights.body: The lab has a 'scrambled' book: 20 index stocks chosen in a meaningless order, re-chosen every quarter. Picked from the whole index, it beat the S&P 500 fund by about three and a half points a year over 1996-2015, as much as several real stock-picking rules did. Picked only from the 100 biggest, busiest companies, the same scrambled book earned +7.8% a year against the fund's +7.2%, and moved almost exactly like the market. Put the companies that later died back into the data and it fell to +6.5%, below the fund. So the old lead was never skill. It was a bet that mid-sized companies would beat the giants, which paid in 2000-2008 when the giants of the dot-com bubble deflated, and it was flattered by data that leaves out the companies that died. That bet has lost since 2018. What to do: judge any stock picker against a scrambled book drawn from the same pool of companies, not against the market alone. A picker that only beats the market by choosing smaller companies has found the size bet, not an edge.

insights.title: The trend readings as a market crash filter: hold SPY, step aside when the average stock sits far below its long averages: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +8.6% on the usual history, +8.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.9% and 18.9%.

insights.title: Buying stocks whose owners are in profit is the same bet as buying stocks that went up
insights.body: We tried a well-known idea from behavioural finance: people sell winners too early and hang on to losers, so stocks where most owners sit on a paper gain should keep rising. We estimated what each stock's current owners paid and held the 20 stocks trading furthest above that price. It worked on the 1996-2015 history: about 14% a year on the owner's monthly deposits against 7% for SPY, with a worst fall of 25%. It beat a book filled in a meaningless order by about 6 points a year, more than any recent idea. But the result moves almost exactly with the plain momentum book (buy what went up), which already failed its real test on 2016-2026. It also earned almost the same money as that book and fell behind SPY in 2009-2015. So this is not a new edge; it is momentum seen from another angle. The lab rightly refuses to promote it. The one open question is whether the owners' paper gain still matters between two stocks that rose by the same amount.

insights.title: The typical stock is the wrong thermometer for SPY
insights.body: We tried holding the S&P 500 tracker and stepping aside whenever the typical company in the index was trading below its own long-run average price, a classic way of measuring how broadly a market is falling. From 2007 to 2015 it gave the same signal as simply watching SPY's own price, so it added nothing. In 2000 and 2001 it gave the opposite signal. A few giant technology companies were collapsing and dragging SPY down hard, while the typical, smaller company was rising, so the reading said all was well and the book rode SPY down. Its worst fall was 37% or more, where watching SPY itself limited the fall to 19%. The lesson matches what the stock-picking tests found: SPY is moved by its biggest companies, and anything built on the typical company, whether picks or timing, is measuring a different market. A rule that holds SPY should watch SPY, or a reading weighted by company size.

insights.title: Among last year's winners, a loud drop tends to bounce back, not keep falling
insights.body: Across all big index members, a stock that falls hard on heavier-than-usual trading tends to keep falling. We tried to use that to protect the lab's best stock-picking book: each week, sell any of its twenty holdings that had one of those loud drops. It backfired. Selling the loud fallers cost about 2.3 points a year and made the worst fall only 1.5 points shallower. Selling the quiet fallers instead cost less than a point. For a stock that has been rising all year, a sudden heavy-volume drop looks more like a crowd of holders being shaken out for a few days than like bad news sinking in, and it often comes back. The general lesson is that a pattern found across the whole market can flip inside a narrow group, so every exit rule needs testing on the book it will protect. There was one encouraging sign: on the fuller price history that includes companies that later went bust, the loud exit did catch some of them on the way down and nearly matched the plain book. That is why one more version, which refills the sold slot straight away, is queued.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-1858: good-looking books keep turning out to be momentum in disguise
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. The strongest new idea, buying the stocks whose recent buyers are sitting on the biggest paper gains, won three of its four separate test stretches and beat its own meaningless book by about six points a year. But it trailed SPY in 2009-2015, and the lab's hard gate refused it for a different reason: it turned out to move almost in step with the momentum book that already failed its final test. The gate refused two methods this batch: that one because it was too close a relative of a failed book, and the heavy-trading exit because it lost most of its test stretches (and its parent family had also failed). No test look was spent.

What the batch taught: the books that look good keep turning out to be momentum, or the equal-amounts setup, in disguise.

- Paper gains (a 2005 research idea: people sell their winners too early, so stocks whose holders are sitting on gains keep drifting up). It earned about 13.9% a year on the owner's deposits against SPY's 7.2%, with a worst fall of 25%. It beat both its opposite and its meaningless book by about six points a year, the cleanest separation the lab has seen in several batches. But what is left of its returns once the market's move is taken out tracks the plain momentum book at 0.90 (the lab's limit is 0.85). In 2009-2015 it trailed SPY by one to three points a year, and adding back the failed companies made its worst fall deeper and dropped it under the luck bar. The signal is real, but it is momentum's signal measured another way.
- Selling a momentum holding when it falls on heavy trading. Last batch found that heavy-trading falls tend to keep falling. As an exit, though, it cost about two points a year to save one and a half points of worst fall. Selling the quiet fallers hurt less, the opposite of the idea. The book was best with no exit at all.
- The trend readings as a crash warning for SPY: step aside when the typical stock sits below its long-run average. It lost to SPY's own simple 200-day rule on every count. In 2000-2001 the typical stock looked healthy while the giants fell, so it stayed in through a long fall.
- The meaningless book, picking only from the 100 busiest companies. It landed on SPY, tying it in 2009-2015. That settles where the meaningless book's old lead came from: a lean toward mid-sized companies plus the missing failed companies, not skill.

What looks alive: the paper-gains signal, but only if it can be separated from momentum; the next try asks what it adds once momentum is taken out. What looks dead: breadth timing of SPY, heavy-trading exits, and random picking among the giants as anything more than a yardstick.

Gotrade's fees decided nothing this batch; every method was built in fractional shares at the real fees from the start.

What would unlock the most: price history after 2015, and a price history that includes the companies that failed. Both keep shrinking or erasing every lead the lab finds. A standing comparison of each new idea against momentum, as well as against the meaningless book, would catch disguised momentum before a whole run is spent on it.

Next batch: paper gains with momentum taken out; momentum among the 100 busiest companies judged against the busiest-100 meaningless book; the heavy-trading exit with an instant refill; and ideas from outside price patterns altogether, such as dividends.

insights.title: Buying last month's laggards inside the hottest industries added nothing over random picks
insights.body: Research says a stock that falls behind its own industry for a month tends to catch up, while whole industries keep their trends for months. A book built on both ideas picked the three or four strongest industries and bought their worst stocks of the past month. It beat the S&P 500 over 1996-2015 (about 9.7% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2%), but a twin book that picked random stocks in the same industries did slightly better (10.0%) and fell less at its worst. So the one-month catch-up does not survive in big US stocks bought once a month and charged Gotrade's fees. What return there was came from riding strong industries plus the rule that goes to cash when the market is below its 200-day average, and that combination lost to the S&P 500 in 2009-2015, the years most like today. The new industry labels are worth keeping as a safety cap on other books, not as a way to pick stocks.

insights.title: The news-day book was never a hidden tech bet, and a random pick of news days earns almost as much
insights.body: The lab's best earnings-day book buys big stocks after a strong earnings-style day. The worry was that it quietly fills up with one industry whenever that industry has a good reporting season. Now that the lab knows each company's industry, we checked: tech took about a quarter of the slots, against a fifth when the same news days are picked at random, and one industry held eight or more of the twenty names in only 17 of 170 months. Limiting each industry to 3, 4 or 5 names cost money in steps (12.3% a year uncapped, 12.1%, 11.8%, 11.0% as the limit tightened, SPY 7.2%) and did nothing for the book's worst fall in 1998, which was the whole market. The bigger surprise was the random-order control: picking from the same news days in a meaningless order earned 10.9% a year, and on the fuller data that adds back companies that later died it earned as much as the real ranking (about 11%). So whatever edge there is lives in buying after strong earnings days at all and holding three months, not in choosing which of those days to buy. Future work on this book should stop polishing the ranking.

insights.title: A sector cap spreads the names, not the crash risk
insights.body: The crash-prone stock picker really did bunch up by industry: on an average quarter a third of its 20 names came from one industry, and at worst half, where a random pick from the same stocks put a quarter in its biggest industry. Capping each industry at 3 or 4 names fixed the bunching and cost only about half a point a year. But it did not make the book safer: the capped book fell 33-35% at its worst, a little more than before, because it swapped crash-prone oil or bank stocks for crash-prone stocks in other industries, and those still fall together when the market falls. A random pick capped the same way earned about as much with a gentler fall. So a cap is a cheap guard against one industry dominating a book, worth keeping on anything the lab promotes, but it is not a source of extra return and not a crash shield.

insights.title: The dividend raisers beat random names; the safety-switch frame is what trails SPY
insights.body: A book that holds big companies right after they raise their dividend has beaten SPY on paper from 1996 to 2015, but trails it from 2009 on. This run tested whether that was a hidden bet on banks and shops, which filled almost half its slots. Capping each industry at a few names did not help: it cost up to 0.4 points a year and made 2009-2015 slightly worse, because the names it skipped were fresh raisers, the very thing the book is built to buy. The more useful result came from a placebo: the same book, same cash and SPY share month by month, same safety switch, but filled with index members in a meaningless fixed order. It earned about 1.9 points a year less than the raisers, and 3.3 points a year less in 2009-2015. So the dividend-raise signal does carry information. What trails SPY after 2009 is the frame around it: about half the money in SPY and an all-or-nothing sell switch at the 200-day average that sold into the short dips of 2010, 2011 and 2015. Future work on this book should change the frame, not the picks.

insights.title: Measure every stock-picking book against a random-names twin of the same shape
insights.body: Beating SPY says little when half a book's lead can come from its shape alone: how much sits in cash or SPY, the safety switch, and equal slots. This run built a twin that copies a book's exposure month by month but picks random index members, and it showed the dividend-raise signal adds about two points a year on top of that shape. The lab would judge ideas more fairly if every stock-picking method were automatically paired with such a twin, so the score is the margin over its own random twin rather than over SPY alone. A few seeds rather than one would turn that margin into a range.

insights.title: Sera 20261017-2050: an industry limit spreads the names but does not fix the books
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two methods passed the lab's first screen: the crash-prone picks with an industry limit, and the dividend raisers with an industry limit. The lab's hard gate refused both for the same reason. Neither beat SPY in most of its four separate test stretches (the crash-prone picks won one, the dividend raisers two), and both trailed SPY in 2009-2015. Neither was refused because a related method had failed its final test. No test look was spent.

Does an industry limit help? No. This batch asked one question four ways: would stopping a book from filling up with one industry make it hold up after 2009? The lab can now tell which of twelve broad industries each company belongs to, from its SEC filings. In every case a limit of 3, 4 or 5 names per industry out of 20 cost a little money, from a few tenths of a point to about one and a half points a year. It never improved the 2009-2015 years.

- The earnings-day book (big stocks bought after a strong news day) was never a hidden one-industry bet. Tech took about a quarter of its slots, against a fifth for random picks of the same news days. The limit cost money in steps: 12.3% a year with no limit, then 12.1%, 11.8% and 11.0% as it tightened, against SPY's 7.2%.
- The dividend-raise book leaned on banks and shops, not utilities. Limiting them cost up to 0.4 points a year and made 2009-2015 slightly worse, because the names it skipped were exactly the fresh raisers the book exists to buy. The useful finding was elsewhere. A twin book with the same cash, the same SPY share and the same safety switch, but filled with random companies, earned about two points a year less, three in 2009-2015. So the dividend-raise signal is real. What trails SPY is the frame around it: the safety switch and the money parked in SPY.
- Buying last month's laggards inside the hottest industries, a sector-rotation idea from published research, did no better than random picks inside the same industries (9.7% against 10.0% a year) and lost to SPY in 2009-2015. Closed.

Is the energy-heavy crash-prone book an example of the risk a limit removes? Partly, and the part it removes is not the part that hurts. That book really does bunch up: on an average quarter a third of its 20 names came from one industry, and at worst half, where random picks put a quarter in their biggest industry. Today's paper book holds 12 of 20 in oil and gas. A limit spreads the names, and it cost only about half a point a year. It did not make the book safer. The limited 20-name book still fell 33-35% at its worst, a little more than before. It swapped crash-prone oil and bank stocks for crash-prone stocks in other industries, and those still fall together when the market falls. The risk in that book is that it holds stocks that crash with the market, whatever their industry. Spreading it across industries does not change that. A random pick limited the same way did as well as the real one.

What looks alive: the dividend-raise signal, if a gentler frame can replace the all-or-nothing safety switch. What looks dead: industry limits as a fix for 2009-2015, sector rotation by last month's laggards, and the crash-prone picks as a stock picker.

Gotrade's fees decided nothing this batch. Every method was built in fractional shares at the real fees from the start.

What would unlock the most is still price history after 2015, and a history that includes the companies that failed. The industry labels themselves are rough. They use each company's latest industry, not the one it had at the time, but that matters little here: no book turned out to depend on the labels. The lab would also judge every idea more fairly with a standing random-names twin of the same shape for each one, which this batch built by hand three times.

Next batch: the dividend raisers with a gradual brake instead of the 200-day switch; whether the crash-prone family's lead is just equal amounts plus the cash switch, measured against an equal-weighted S&P 500; the earnings-day book filled with the freshest news days first; and a book whose industry mix follows the index's own.

insights.title: Leaning a momentum book toward big companies takes away its edge, not its risk
insights.body: The lab's best stock picker holds twenty names with equal money in each. SPY instead gives money by company size, and since 2018 its biggest companies have won. So we gave the same twenty picks money in proportion to company size, with a cap of 10% or 20% on any one name. From 1996 to 2015 the owner's money would have grown 11.2% a year with the 10% cap against 13.7% with equal slots (SPY: 7.2%). The worst fall barely changed with the 10% cap (20.0% against 20.6%) and got deeper with the 20% cap (24%). In 2009 to 2015, the years most like today, the size-weighted books trailed SPY by 2 to 3 points a year while equal slots still led by about 1. The reason: the biggest names in a momentum list mostly rose because the whole market rose, and the picker's edge is in the mid-sized companies that rose on their own. Giving the big names more money moves it away from where the edge is. To capture SPY's big-company drift, hold SPY itself and keep the picker as a smaller side bet; do not bend the picker toward big companies.
