- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −8.2% a year before and −9.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 0.6 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Weighting a 20-stock pick by company size took away the idea's edge, not just the small-company lean
insights.body: The bond-like stock picker (stocks that rise when interest rates fall) earned 12.5% a year on the owner's deposits with 20 equal slots, against 7.2% for SPY. Weighted instead by each company's real size, capped at 10% a company, it earned 9.5%. Random picks in the same frame, weighted the same way, earned 8.1% and 10.3%. So size weighting cost the idea 3 points a year but cost random picks only 1 to 1.6: most of what the ranking added lived in the smaller bond-like companies, the small utilities and property firms. Two lessons. First, before trusting any stock-picking idea, run it size-weighted beside a size-weighted random twin; an edge that only shows up in equal slots is mostly a small-company bet. Second, size-weighting 20 picks does not make a book shaped like the market: in months when a few giants carried SPY, this book still lost to it by 8% a year, because the giants it owned were whichever ones happened to be bond-like, not the ones carrying the index. A book shaped like the market has to start from the biggest companies themselves and lean from there.

insights.title: A book shaped exactly like the market still trails SPY in our data, because our data misses some of the market's biggest winners
insights.body: We built the simplest possible market copy: the biggest index members, each held in proportion to its company size, like SPY itself. It should have matched SPY. Over 1996-2015 it trailed by about 2 points a year, and in 2009-2015 by 5 to 6 points a year (about 11 percent a year against SPY's 16.6). Without any fees it still trailed by about 2.7 points a year in those years. The reason is in the data: in 2012 the lab knows prices but not company size for Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS and Regeneron, and has no prices at all for Celgene, Express Scripts, Walgreens and Time Warner. Several of that decade's best big companies are invisible. Before 2000 the hole runs the other way: the companies that later collapsed are missing, so the same market copy beat SPY by 10 to 20 points a year. Why it matters: any book of index members starts 2009-2015 a couple of points behind SPY before it picks a single stock, and starts the 1990s well ahead. Part of the lab's pattern of edges that faded after 2009 is this tilt in the data, not only a change in the market. What to do: fill in the missing company sizes, then build this ruler again and judge member books against it beside SPY.

insights.title: Company size for firms with more than one share class
insights.body: The lab's new company-size figure is blank for many large firms that issue two or more kinds of shares or report their share count per class: Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast, UPS, Ford, Alphabet after 2014, and about twenty more in 2012 alone. These include several of the biggest winners of 2009-2015, so any book that ranks or weights by size leaves them out and drifts below the market. The fix is to add up the share count across classes (or take the total from the filing's cover page) and value each listed class at its own price. Once done, the plain size-weighted top 100 should be re-run to see if it finally tracks SPY.

insights.title: Holding only the 50 biggest companies, sized like the market, trails SPY by more than a point a year
insights.body: We built a book from the 50 largest companies in the index, each weighted by its real size, with no company above a tenth of the money. From 1996 to 2015, on the owner's monthly deposits, it earned 6.0% a year where SPY earned 7.2%. It fell 47% at its worst, about as far as the market. On the second set of prices, which also has the companies that later died, it earned only 4.6%. The giants of one decade were often the laggards of the next (GE, Citi, AIG), and SPY's long climb comes partly from smaller companies growing into giants, which a top-50 book never owns. A lean toward companies raising their dividend added only a few tenths of a point on top of that and beat a random lean by about as much. So a book that copies only the top of the market starts behind SPY, and a gentle signal cannot close the gap. The next market-shaped book should hold the whole index, not its top.

insights.title: Sera 20261018-0517: following the market's shape does not close the gap after 2009
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Four methods ran and three passed the lab's first screen in one form or another. The lab's hard gate refused all three for the same reason: none beat SPY in most of its four separate test stretches. The momentum one also has relatives that already failed their final test. All three trailed SPY in 2009-2015. No test look was spent.

Does following the market's shape fix the post-2009 gap? No, not in the lab's data, and part of the reason is the data itself. This batch asked one question four ways: if a book gives money to companies by their size, the way SPY does, instead of in equal amounts, does it stop trailing SPY after 2009? The lab can now tell how big each company was on any past day.

- The plainest possible copy of the market, the biggest index members each held by their size, should have matched SPY. It did not. It trailed by about 2 points a year over twenty years and by 5 to 6 points a year in 2009-2015, even with no fees at all. The lab's data cannot yet see the size of several of that decade's biggest winners, among them Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast and UPS. It has no prices at all for some big companies later bought out. Before 2000 the hole runs the other way: the companies that later collapsed are missing, and the same copy beat SPY by a wide margin. So any book built from index members starts 2009-2015 a couple of points behind SPY and starts the 1990s well ahead. Part of the "edges that faded after 2009" pattern is this tilt in the data, not only a change in the market.
- Holding only the 50 biggest companies by size also trailed SPY, by more than a point a year. It fell 47% at its worst, as far as the market did. The giants of one decade were often the laggards of the next, and a top-50 book never owns the smaller companies that grow into giants.

Does any picker add anything on top of the market's shape? Very little, and less than it adds in equal slots.

- The lab's best momentum picker, given money by company size instead of equal amounts, lost 2.5 to 3.3 points a year and fell no less deeply. Its edge lives in mid-sized companies that rise on their own; the big names in its list mostly rose because the whole market rose.
- The bond-like stocks book (stocks that rise when interest rates fall), weighted by size, landed inside the range of random picks weighted the same way. Weighting by size cost the idea 3 points a year but cost random picks only 1 to 1.6, so most of what the idea added was in the smaller bond-like companies.
- Leaning the 50 biggest companies toward dividend raisers beat a random lean, but only by a few tenths of a point. That is far too small to close the core's gap to SPY.

The lesson that cuts across all four: an edge that shows up only with equal amounts in each name is mostly a lean toward smaller companies, and every future idea should be run size-weighted beside a size-weighted random twin before it is trusted. The practical shape this points to is SPY itself as the core, with any picker as a smaller side bet beside it, rather than a picker bent toward big companies.

What looks alive: holding SPY as the core with a small side bet, and the dividend-raise lean spread across the whole index rather than only its top. What looks dead: weighting a stock picker's own picks by company size, the bond-like stocks book as a picker, and books of only the very biggest companies.

Gotrade's fees decided nothing this batch. Every method was built from the start to buy fractional shares at the real fees. The market copy trailed SPY by almost as much with no fees at all.

What would unlock the most: a company size for firms that have two or more kinds of shares, so the market copy can finally be checked against SPY. After that, as always, a price history that includes the companies that failed or were bought out.

Next batch: the market copy rebuilt once those company sizes are in; the dividend-raise lean over every index member at its real size; momentum picked inside each size band, so the picker cannot quietly lean small; and SPY as the core with the best equal-amount picker as a small side bet.

insights.title: Momentum picked inside each size band: four names from each fifth of the index by company size: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +13.5% on the usual history, +11.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.6% and 25.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +0.3% a year before and −0.8% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 1 of 4 periods won to 2 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.8 points a year less. 3 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The momentum ranking is not a small-company trick
insights.body: We split the index into five groups by company size and let the lab's best stock ranking pick four names from each group. The book still beat the same deposits in SPY by about 5.6 points a year from 1996 to 2015. The same groups filled with random names barely beat SPY at all. Holding only the smaller companies did not earn more, and it fell deeper (25% at its worst against 21%). Holding only the biggest companies earned the least, and from 2009 to 2015 it trailed SPY by 6 points a year, as badly as random picks. Spreading the picks evenly across sizes also held up better when the companies that later died were added back to the history. It lost under a point a year, where the plain best-20 book lost almost two. The lesson: the ranking earns across all sizes. A size-balanced spread is the sturdier shape. Neither one solves the main problem, because no momentum book here beats SPY in the years most like today.

insights.title: Companies shrinking their share count: buy the index members that bought back the most stock over the past year: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.3% on the usual history, +9.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 25.8% and 26.4%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −4.0% a year before and −4.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 0.7 points a year less. 2 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The honest yardstick, repaired: the size-weighted top 100 once multi-class companies have a size: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 7 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.9% on the usual history, +7.4% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 15.0% and 17.2%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −7.7% a year before and −8.4% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 0.5 points a year less. 7 of its 7 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Fixing company sizes closed only a sliver of the gap to SPY
insights.body: We repaired the size of companies with more than one kind of share (Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Comcast and others) and ran the market-shaped ruler again on the same prices. Before fees, a book of the hundred biggest members held by size now trails SPY by about 1.6 points a year in 2009-2015, down from about 2. On the owner's real deposits and fees the gain was half a point at most. Most of what is left sits in 2009 and 2010. It comes from big companies our data has no prices for at all (Celgene, Express Scripts, Walgreens, Time Warner and others), and perhaps from a real 2009 rally in smaller companies. So a stock book that trails SPY by about 2 points a year over 2009-2015 here is close to what a book shaped like the market can do on this data. One that trails by 5 has no such excuse.

insights.title: Add real index funds as yardsticks the data can be checked against
insights.body: Our ruler can only be checked against SPY, which holds all 500 companies. We cannot tell whether the biggest hundred companies really trailed the S&P 500 in 2009 or whether our data is missing some of them. Adding the price history of the fund that tracks the 100 biggest companies (from 2000) and the equal-weight S&P 500 fund (from 2003) would settle it. If our top-100 book tracks the real top-100 fund, the data is sound and the gap was the market. If not, the gap is the missing companies, and only paid price history for them can close it.

insights.title: Companies buying back stock beat the market, but the ones selling stock did not clearly lose
insights.body: The lab tested a 2008 finding: companies that shrink their share count by buying back their own stock do better than companies that sell new stock. On 1996-2015 the 20 biggest buyers-back earned 13% a year on the owner's deposits, where SPY earned 7% and 20 companies drawn at random earned 8%. The buyback signal also kept its lead in 2009-2015, the years the lab's data covers best, which most ideas here do not. The other half of the story is weaker. When the lab added back companies that later died or left the index, the book of heavy stock-sellers went from 9% a year to 13%. A few of the added names were huge winners. So 'sellers lose' was partly a gap in the data. Two lessons. A buyback is a real, lasting signal worth building on. And the fall is the problem: without a brake this book lost 59% at its worst in 2008. The usual brake, stepping out when SPY drops below its 200-day average, cut the fall to 26%, but it sat in cash through the 2009-2011 rebound and lost about 4 points a year to SPY in those good years.

insights.title: The dividend-raise lean on the whole market: every index member at its real size, not only the 50 biggest: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.7% on the usual history, +6.5% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 50.4% and 50.4%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −0.7% a year before and −1.9% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.3 points a year less. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A book holding the whole market by company size keeps pace with SPY in this lab's data, so a lead under a point a year is probably the missing dead companies
insights.body: We built a book that holds every index company the data can size, each in proportion to its real market value, re-weighted monthly at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's deposits. It earned 7.4% a year against 7.2% for SPY over 1996-2015. Holding only the 50 biggest had trailed SPY by more than a point, so the earlier gap came from being too narrow, not from fees or from the data being unable to copy the market. Then we re-ran it with most of the companies that later died or were bought out put back: it dropped to 6.3%, about a point behind SPY. That point is the cost of the data missing the losers. It matters for every strategy in the lab: a stock picker that beats SPY by less than about a point a year on this data may simply be benefiting from never having owned the companies that failed. A dividend-raise lean on top of this book added only a few tenths of a point, and the book still fell about half its value in 2008, as SPY did.

insights.title: Sera 20261018-2051: the market-shape fix, buybacks, and size-balanced risers
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Three of the four ideas passed the first screen on the 1996-2015 history, and the lab's promotion gate turned all three away, because none of them beat SPY in most of the separate time periods the lab checks one after another. No look at the held-back test years was spent.

What we tried. First, the ruler again: a book shaped like the market, the biggest companies held in proportion to their size, re-run now that the data finally knows the real size of companies with more than one kind of share (Visa, Mastercard, Meta, Berkshire, Alphabet). Second, the biggest companies leaning toward those that raised their dividend, this time across the whole index rather than only the top fifty. Third, last year's strongest risers picked four at a time from each fifth of the index by company size. Fourth, a new idea from published research: companies that shrank their number of shares over the past year by buying back their own stock.

What the batch taught. The data fix was real but small. The market-shaped book still trails SPY by about one and a half points a year before fees in 2009-2015, down from about two. What is left is mostly companies our data has no prices for, and fees on many small orders. Every result in the lab is still measured against that handicap in those years. A book holding the whole market by company size does keep pace with SPY on the main data, which is reassuring about the lab's frame, but it falls about a point a year behind once companies that later died are put back in.

Riser picks work in every size group, not only among small companies. Picking four per size fifth made about 12.8% a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2% for SPY, and held up better than the plain picks when dead companies were added back. But no version beat SPY in 2009-2015, it won only one of the four time periods, and its family has already failed the test years before.

Buyback companies beat SPY and beat a random draw of the same size: about 10.3% a year against 7.2%, worst fall 26%, with the 200-day safety switch on. It won two of the four time periods, one short of the majority the gate needs. The other half of the published idea, that companies selling new shares do badly, did not hold once dead companies were put back.

The dividend-raise lean added half a point a year on the main data and lost it once dead companies were back in. It fell about half in 2008. That direction now looks dead.

Alive: buybacks, and riser picks as a smaller sleeve beside SPY rather than the whole book. Dead: dividend-raise leans on market-shaped books. The ruler has done its job; the remaining gap is a data problem, not a method problem.

The buy signal. Nothing cleared all four checks (passes the screen, no failed relative, wins most time periods, and beats SPY in 2009-2015). The gate refused three methods this batch, all three on the time-period check, and the riser picks also because their family has failed before. Every promotion refused is a finding: the long-run averages keep looking good while the period-by-period record does not.

Fees. Every book this batch was built from the start in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up, so nothing lost an edge it never measured. Fees explain much of why the 100-name ruler trails: a hundred small orders a month cost more than they earn.

What would unlock the most: prices for the index companies our data still cannot see, and real index fund prices (the S&P 100 and equal-weight funds) as rulers to check the data against.

Next batch: half SPY with half buyback companies; SPY as the core with a size-balanced riser sleeve; the dividend-raise lean with risk-based sizing instead of the 200-day switch only if nothing better is queued; and a fresh published idea.

insights.title: Risk pays only near the high: the most volatile stocks among those closest to their 52-week high: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.0% on the usual history, +11.4% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 23.5% and 24.9%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −6.9% a year before and −6.4% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 1.3 points a year more. 2 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Buying back in halves is insurance: it only pays if your signal is reckless
insights.body:
Seer's safety rule sells everything when the market drops below its 200-day average, and the expensive half of that rule is deciding when to buy back. We tested paying for the buy-back in instalments: half the money on an early signal, the rest only once the market has genuinely reclaimed its 200-day average, so a false start costs half as much.

It works, and it works exactly as advertised — but only on a signal that makes false starts. The hasty signal (buy back as soon as the market crosses above its 50-day average) fires on bear-market bounces, so it keeps walking back into crashes: all at once, it lost 10.7% in 2008 and 8.8% in 2001, and its worst fall over twenty-two years was 23.6%, at the February 2009 bottom. Paid in halves, the same signal lost 5.4% in 2008 and 5.5% in 2001, earned slightly more over the whole stretch, and its worst fall became 15.3% — eight points shallower, and no longer in a crash at all. Its deepest hole is now the choppy autumn of 1998.

The careful signal got nothing. Buying back only when the last three months are positive almost never fires inside a crash, so it had no false start to insure against — and it paid the premium anyway, giving up about a third of a point a year and a chunk of the 2009 recovery for protection it did not need.

That is the lesson, and it generalises past this one rule: sizing and timing are substitutes, not partners. Making the position smaller is a way of being less wrong when your signal is wrong. If the signal is already careful, a smaller position just means less of the thing you got right. And a repaired careless rule still finished behind a careful rule used at full size, so there was no way through.

What to do about it: stop looking for a better buy-back on a book that holds only the market, and take the one genuinely useful number — eight points off the worst fall, with no loss of return — to where it would matter. The strategies closest to qualifying for real money fail on how deep they fall, not on what they earn.

insights.title: 52-week-high momentum: rank on nearness to the yearly high, not past return: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +9.7% at the assumed fee, +7.5% at the real fees (SPY: +7.9% and +7.9%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 16.8% and 18.2%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 1.54 and 1.41.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $1,856 and $3,993.

At the real fees it no longer beats SPY: the edge it showed was smaller than the fees it would have paid. At the real fees it falls short on beating SPY.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A safety guard switched our own experiment off for five years, and it still beat the market
insights.body:
Every experiment carries choices that are not the idea being tested, and this one had a big one. To keep the comparison fair, the staged buy-back was forbidden from acting for about six weeks after the market dropped below its 200-day average. The reason was sound: without that blackout, a fall out of a fully invested position would quietly become a trim to a half position instead of a clean exit, and the exit is the half of the safety rule we already know is worth keeping.

But the blackout turned out to be the loudest thing in the room. In August 2011 the market dipped below its 200-day average and recovered before the year was out — a short, ordinary scare. The staged rule was still inside its blackout, never took its half step, and earned exactly what the plain do-nothing safety rule earned in 2011 and 2012, to the decimal. For those two years the staging simply did not exist. Those two years account for more of the gap to the all-at-once rule than the halving itself does.

So the honest reading of the result is narrower than it first looks: for most of the modern stretch we did not measure a staged buy-back at all, we measured the old rule with extra steps — and it still beat the market on the owner's deposits over the full period.

The testable claim: shorten the blackout to a single monthly check instead of six weeks and the instalment rule gets to act on ordinary dips, not only on generational bottoms like 2009. That should recover most of those five points. If it does not, the sizing question is genuinely settled rather than settled on a technicality.

The wider point is worth remembering whenever a result looks flat: before concluding an idea does not work, check that the machinery actually let it run. A guard written for a good reason can quietly spend half the test window doing nothing, and a flat result is then a measurement of the guard, not of the idea.

insights.title: A strategy's edge and its family resemblance died together, which is the proof we could not get before
insights.body:
The lab keeps finding stock-picking rules that look good over twenty years and then turn out to move almost exactly like a rule that already failed its one real test. Until now that was a suspicion we could raise but never settle: the two books behave alike, but does the new one actually earn its money the same way, or does it just happen to rise and fall on the same days?

This run settled it for one idea, and the method is worth remembering. The idea was that stocks whose owners are sitting on large unrealised gains drift upward, because people sell winners too early. Bought plainly, that rule earned 13.9 percent a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2 for the same money in the market — and resembled the failed momentum book at 0.90 on a nought-to-one scale, where 0.85 is the line.

So I removed the overlap arithmetically. Each month, before ranking, I subtracted from every company's unrealised-gain figure the part its own twelve-month price rise explains. The rest of the strategy was left untouched, so only the signal changed.

Two things moved at once. The family resemblance fell from 0.90 to 0.53, well clear of the line — the removal genuinely worked. And the money fell from 13.9 percent a year to 8.0, which is precisely what a meaningless ordering of the same companies earned in the same frame. The gain and the resemblance left together, one for one.

That is the proof. The unrealised-gains rule was not a new bet that happened to move like momentum. It was momentum, measured a slower way. There was nothing underneath it.

What to do about it: when a strategy scores well and is then refused for moving like something that already failed, this test is now the cheap way to find out whether the complaint is fair. Strip the candidate of its overlap with the failed idea, run it once on the development years, and watch what happens to the money. If the edge leaves with the resemblance, the refusal was right and the idea is finished. If the edge survives while the resemblance drops, we have found something genuinely new — and that would be the first time. It costs one ordinary run and no part of the test-window budget.

insights.title: Most of what makes two strategies look like relatives is the chassis they share, not the bet they make
insights.body:
Every strategy in this run was measured against the four books that have already failed a real out-of-sample test, to see how much it moves like them. One of those strategies was the placebo: it picks twenty companies by scrambling their ticker symbols. It has no opinion about anything.

The placebo resembled the three failed blend-style books at 0.69, 0.65 and 0.71 on a nought-to-one scale. The line at which the lab treats a new strategy as the same bet as a failed one is 0.85.

So a book that is deliberately meaningless already sits most of the way to the line. It gets there by sharing the plumbing: the same few hundred large companies to choose from, the same rule of standing aside when the market is below its 200-day average, the same twenty equal slots, the same habit of parking unused slots in the market itself. Those choices decide most of when a book goes up and down. Only the last fifteen points of the scale are about what it actually ranks on.

This does not mean the line is set wrong. A meaningless book never crosses it, which is exactly the calibration we want, and the genuinely-momentum books sit at 0.90 to 0.98 — far above the plumbing's level. The test is doing its job.

But it does change where to look next. More than a dozen strategies in the lab are currently refused for resembling a failed one, and all of them share that same chassis. If seven tenths of the resemblance is the chassis, then a real escape route is more likely to come from changing the frame — no stand-aside rule, cash instead of the market in unused slots, a different number of holdings — than from inventing yet another way to rank the same companies inside the same frame. That is worth one experiment before the next promotion is attempted, because it would tell us whether a dozen refusals were about the bet or about the chassis.

insights.title: The price history keeps losing the files that are not fingerprinted, and we only find out when a method needs one
insights.body:
The lab's price history is kept in a folder of files on this machine. Most of those files are checked against a fingerprint every time a method runs, so if one of them changed or went missing we would know at once. But a few files sit outside that check, and the company share counts are one of them. They went missing some time after the 13th of October, and nothing noticed until a method asked for them this morning.

This is the third time the same thing has happened. The market-wide price series and the dividend announcement dates have both vanished the same way before, on a rebuild. The pattern is clear: whenever the store is rebuilt or copied, the files that are not fingerprinted are the ones that quietly do not come along.

Why it matters more than it sounds. The share counts were refreshed on the 18th of October specifically to fix companies with more than one kind of share, such as Alphabet, Berkshire, Meta, Visa and Mastercard. Three of the last batch's four methods were built on that fix, and one of them existed only to measure it. Losing the file does not corrupt any result we have already recorded, because it was never part of the fingerprint, but it does mean a method that needs company sizes cannot run at all until it is rebuilt, and rebuilding it takes most of an hour of fetching data from the internet. Worse, if a rebuild quietly produces the older, unfixed share counts, a method would run perfectly happily against exactly the broken sizes we spent a batch repairing, and the numbers would look fine.

The lab refused to run rather than measure missing data, which is the system working as intended. The gap is that it refused at the moment of use, not at the moment of loss.

What should change: the files that sit outside the fingerprint should either be brought inside it, or checked for at the start of every run, so that a missing one is noticed when it goes missing rather than days later when a method happens to need it. Until then, after any rebuild or copy of the price history, check that the share counts, the market-wide series and the dividend announcement dates are all still present, and that the share counts still know the companies with more than one kind of share.

insights.title: A stock near its yearly high is a stock that is not dying, and that makes it safe to buy wild ones
insights.body:
Half the companies in the index of the 1990s are missing from our usual price data, and the missing ones are mostly the companies that went bust. We keep a second, honest copy of history with most of them put back, and almost every stock picker we test loses about a point a year of its return when they come back.

This month we ran six versions of one idea side by side on both copies, and for the first time the results split in opposite directions. The version that buys the wildest, most jumpy stocks from among those trading closest to their own highest price of the past year earned MORE on the honest data, not less: ten percent a year became eleven point four, and its worst fall barely moved, from twenty-three and a half percent to twenty-five. Its mirror image, the version that buys the wildest stocks from among those trading furthest BELOW their yearly high, collapsed: seven point one percent a year fell to three point six, and its worst fall went from forty-one percent to fifty-six.

The reason is almost too simple to state. A company heading for bankruptcy is, by definition, a long way below its best price of the last year. So asking 'is this stock near its yearly high' quietly throws the dying ones out before you choose anything else, and asking for the wildest stocks far below their high is close to a purpose-built net for catching them.

What to do about it: stop treating closeness to the yearly high as a way to pick winners. On its own it has now lost to simply holding the market twice, once in its plain form and once here. Treat it instead as a safety filter to put in front of a signal we already trust, especially any signal that likes volatile stocks. It is the only filter we have measured that gets better, not worse, when the dead companies are put back in the data, and that is the opposite of what a result built on a hole in the data looks like.

insights.title: The fix we found cannot be tested on the strategies it would most help
insights.body:
The staged buy-back did one thing well: on a hasty re-entry signal it took the worst fall from 23.6% to 15.3% and raised the return at the same time. That is the exact shape the lab needs, because the strategies closest to qualifying for real money fail on how deep they fall, not on what they earn.

The problem is that every one of those strategies is already barred. The momentum and blend books near the top of the leaderboard all inherit from, or move in step with, books that have already spent their one out-of-sample look and lost it. The lab's rule is that a new name is not a new book: if what is left of a strategy's monthly swings, after the market's own share is taken out, moves in lockstep with a book that already failed, it counts as the same book and cannot be promoted. Four failed books block roughly a dozen of the best-looking candidates that way. So putting the staged ramp underneath them would produce a nicer number that can never be acted on.

The strategies that are not barred are mostly dividend-timing books, and they do not have deep falls to cut. The repair and the patients do not overlap.

What follows from this is a change of plan rather than a dead end. The staged ramp is not a strategy, it is a frame — a way of getting back into the market that any book could wear. It should be built once, as a shared piece that a future candidate can be fitted with, and tested the day a book clears the gate on its own merits. Building it now against a barred host would be spending an idea on a result nobody is allowed to use.

The wider lesson is one the lab keeps relearning: a good fix found in the wrong place is not yet progress. Before spending an id on improving a strategy, check that the strategy is still allowed to win.

insights.title: A good twenty-year average is now routinely one good era wearing a disguise
insights.body:
The method we ran this month beat the market over twenty years by two point eight points a year, kept its worst fall inside the owner's limit, and earned more than it lost by a comfortable margin. It passed four of the five rules for going live. Then we cut the twenty years into three stretches, and the whole win was in one of them: it lost to the market in nineteen ninety-six to two thousand and one, beat it by twelve and a half points a year in two thousand and two to two thousand and eight, and lost by seven points a year in two thousand and nine to twenty fifteen.

The fold test, which trains on the past and scores on years it has never seen, said the same thing without being asked: won the two stretches ending in two thousand and eight, lost the two after it. Two of four.

This is now the pattern, not the exception. Every twenty-year edge this lab has found was earned before two thousand and nine, and all four strategies we have actually tested on recent data failed. The reason the old half flatters a stock picker is partly that the market fell twice there, so anything that steps into cash when the market is weak looks brilliant; and partly that the recent half is the half where a handful of giant companies have carried the index, which is the hardest thing for a twenty-name equally weighted book to beat.

What to do about it: read the era table before the headline, every time, and treat the two thousand and nine onward stretch as the only number that counts. A method that cannot beat the market there has not found an edge, however good its average. The luck test caught this one anyway, at a score of zero point seven seven against a bar of zero point nine, which is a quiet vote of confidence in a rule the owner set a fortnight ago.

insights.title: Most family resemblance is the shared chassis, and that still does not rescue a single refused method
insights.body:
This batch produced a measurement that looks, at first glance, like an argument that the lab's family-resemblance rule is too harsh. It is not, and the reason is already on the record. Writing both halves down together so the next batch does not spend an id re-opening a settled question.

The new measurement. A deliberately meaningless book — twenty companies ranked by a hash of their ticker symbol, with no opinion about anything — already resembles the four strategies that failed their one real-world look by about seven tenths. The rule's line is 0.85. So roughly seven tenths of what makes two of this lab's strategies look like relatives is simply the chassis they share: the same pool of large companies, the same 200-day safety switch, twenty equal slots, the same rebalancing band, the same cash parked in SPY. Only the last fifteen points are about what the book actually ranks on. That is worth knowing, and it is a little uncomfortable, because every one of the dozen-plus strategies the rule has refused shares that chassis.

The half that settles it. The owner measured the tempting conclusion in October and it turned out to be false. The suspicion was that the rule blocks a whole method when only a sibling version of it is a twin — that the version the lab would actually put money behind might be innocent, and refused by association. So every promotable version was correlated directly against every failed book, rather than through the usual report, which only ever names the best-matching twin and hides the runners-up. The versions the lab would actually test came back at 0.93 to 0.96. They are twins themselves. A stricter per-version rule was then built and run end to end: not one method became promotable.

Put together, the two halves say something sharper than either alone. Yes, the chassis buys most of the resemblance. No, that does not rescue anybody, because the refused books sit at 0.86 to 0.98, far above the chassis floor of about 0.70, and a meaningless book never crosses the line. The gap between 0.70 and 0.93 is real and it is the strategy, not the plumbing.

The honest conclusion is the owner's, and it is about the strategy space rather than the rule: this lab cannot produce an uncorrelated candidate from twenty large companies, long only, on the handful of signals it already has. Every method that clears the first screen turns out to be the same book wearing a different name. The way out is a genuinely different kind of bet or a genuinely different pool, not a softer resemblance rule — and anyone who finds themselves arguing for a softer rule should read the October measurement first.

insights.title: Buyback shrinkers as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: half SPY, half the 20 biggest share-count shrinkers, no 200-day switch: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +8.5% on the usual history, +8.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 33.3% and 34.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −2.6% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Buyback shrinkers as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: half SPY, half the 20 biggest share-count shrinkers, no 200-day switch: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +33.7% at the assumed fee, +33.4% at the real fees (SPY: +32.4% and +32.4%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 33.6% and 33.3%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 2.55 and 2.44.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $4,650 and $11,300.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Holding half the market beside a stock picker does not make it safer, because both fall in the same week
insights.body:
A natural instinct says that if a stock-picking book is too risky, you hold half of it and put the other half in the market itself. Half the risk, half the reward. This was tested properly and the instinct is wrong, in a way worth remembering.

The picking book here buys companies that are shrinking their own share count, which usually means buying back their stock. On its own it earned 13% a year where the market earned 7.2%, but it lost 59% of its value in 2008. Putting half the account into the market itself gave a book that earned 9.7% a year and lost 55.1%.

The reward halved, as expected. The risk barely moved at all.

The reason is simple once it is said out loud. Mixing two things only reduces the fall if they fall at different times. In 2008 the picking book fell 59% and the market fell 55%, in the same months, for the same reason. Averaging two numbers that are both near 55 gives you 55. You cannot diversify away a crash by adding more of the thing that is crashing.

This is worth stating plainly because the same instinct keeps coming back in different clothes: hold some cash, hold some market, size down the position. All of those cut the reward in proportion and cut the fall only to the extent that the two halves actually differ. When the risk you are worried about is a market-wide crash, nothing that is also in the market will protect you from it.

What does change the fall is owning different things, or not owning them at that moment. That is a much harder problem than mixing, and it is the one actually worth working on.

insights.title: Two different things are both called the lucky-draw control, and one of them barely trades
insights.body:
When this lab wants to know whether a stock-picking rule is real or lucky, it builds a twin that picks names at random from the same pool and runs it side by side. If the real rule cannot beat the random twin, the rule was never doing anything.

There is a trap in that twin, and this run walked into it.

There are two kinds of random twin in the lab, and they are not labelled differently. One re-draws its names every period, so it trades as often as the real rule does. The other draws once and holds the same names forever, trading only when a company drops out of the pool. The difference is not small: the re-drawing kind turned over its holdings about three times a year, the sticky kind about a quarter of a time a year. One is a fair twin of an active rule. The other is closer to buy-and-hold wearing a disguise.

This method inherited its twin from the method it was built on, without checking which kind it was. It was the sticky kind. The tell was visible the whole time and nobody looked: the twin made 41 trades in twenty years where every other version made over 600, and it made exactly the same 41 trades as its parent's twin.

The comparison still pointed the right way here, and for a reassuring reason: the sticky twin trades less, so it pays less in fees, so it was the easier book to beat. The real rule beat it anyway. But that was luck in the arguing, not care in the building, and it could just as easily have run the other way.

The practical rule, for whoever builds the next one: when you copy a random twin from an earlier method, look at whether its shuffle depends on the date. If it does not, the twin never re-draws, and you are comparing an active rule against a passive one and calling the difference skill. And whatever else you check, put the twin's trade count next to the real rule's before you believe anything the pair tells you.

insights.title: The lab lost its record of how big each company is, and only a refused experiment noticed
insights.body:
The lab keeps its own copy of US market history on this machine. Alongside the daily prices it keeps two smaller and much newer files: how many shares each company had on any given day, and the list of stock splits needed to read those counts correctly. Together they are what let the lab know how big a company was at the time. Several recent experiments depend on them entirely.

Today both files were simply gone, from all three copies of the market history, and the work that had built them the day before had gone with them. Nothing looked broken. The prices were untouched, every past result still reproduced, and every experiment that does not ask about company size kept running normally.

It surfaced only because this experiment asked for company size and the lab refused to run it, on the grounds that it would end up measuring the missing data rather than the idea. That refusal is the system working exactly as intended, and it cost nothing: no result was recorded and no out-of-sample look was spent.

But that refusal was the only alarm there was. Nothing watches these files. Nothing says anything when a file that was there yesterday is not there today. A full day passed in which the lab quietly could not answer any question about company size, and the only way to find out was to trip over it.

Two lessons. The first is that restoring a backup of the market history is more dangerous than it looks: the large files come back and the small, recently added ones do not, so a partial restore is indistinguishable from a complete one. This is the second time this has happened to a different pair of files.

The second is that the lab should check its own data the way it checks a strategy, and say so out loud when something it used yesterday has disappeared, rather than waiting for an experiment to crash into the hole. Rebuilding the two files took about an hour of downloading, every minute of which was avoidable. The rebuild was verified afterwards against known company sizes, and the prices were confirmed unchanged, so older results remain comparable with newer ones.

insights.title: The lab should keep a standing health check on its own copy of the market
insights.body:
Twice now the lab's copy of market history has quietly lost a small, recently added file while all the large ones survived, and both times nothing noticed until an experiment tripped over the gap. Today it was the record of company sizes and stock splits; before that it was a file of market-wide daily readings, and another of dividend announcement dates which is still missing from the main copy.

The pattern is always the same. These extra files are optional, so nothing counts them, and the lab's own fingerprint of its data does not include them. A rebuild or a restore brings back the prices and leaves the extras behind, and the result looks perfectly healthy. Most experiments do not use them, so most of the lab keeps working and the gap can sit there for days.

What would fix it is small. The lab should know which optional files each copy of the market is supposed to have, and say so plainly whenever one it had before is missing now, in a single command that can be run at the start of any session. It would also help to record, alongside the data, the exact command that produced each optional file, so recovering one is reading a line rather than reconstructing a runbook.

This is cheap and it pays for itself the first time it fires. Today's recovery cost about an hour of downloading, all of it avoidable, and the only reason it was caught at all is that an experiment asked for the missing data and the lab was careful enough to refuse rather than quietly answer with holes. That refusal should not be the detection mechanism. It is the last line of defence, not the first.

insights.title: Sera 20261019-0720: half-measures are closed, buybacks are real but cannot be made safe
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Four ideas were tried and all four were rejected, none of them close enough to spend a look at the held-back test years on. The count of those looks is still four, where it has been since the spring.

What the batch was for. Every batch for months has had the same shape: a strategy looks good averaged over twenty years, and then loses in most of the shorter periods the lab checks one after another, or loses outright in 2009 to 2015, the stretch our price history measures best. So rather than hunt for another good twenty-year average, three of these four went straight at that failure. The fourth was a new idea from a paper published this year.

The firmest result, and it closes a door. Two of the four methods, working on completely different problems, arrived at the same answer: going half-way does not work. One tested buying back into the market in instalments after the safety rule had sold out, half now and half once the market had properly recovered. The other tested holding half the account in the market at all times so the other half could take more risk. Both lost to the blunt version of themselves. Buying back in halves recovered about an eighth of what the safety rule costs in the modern era, where simply changing WHEN it buys back recovers nearly half. And stepping half out of the market was worse than stepping all the way out on every single measure at once: less money, a deeper fall, and a worse luck score. The lesson is that with this rule, the decision of when to act is the valuable part and the size of the position is not. That is worth knowing because half-measures are the obvious next thing to try and now nobody needs to try them again.

The buyback companies are the real thing. Buying the companies that shrank their own share count the most beat the market by two and a half points a year next to a half-market core. More importantly, the effect proved itself in the way this lab almost never manages. The lead grows in proportion to how much of the account is in the buyback picks: about one and a half points at a third, two and a half at a half, nearly four at two thirds, and almost six when it is the whole book. More market exposure gives less lead, not more, so the result cannot be the market doing the work. And the whole ladder survives putting the dead and bankrupt companies back into the history, which is where last month's dividend idea fell apart. This is now the strongest stock-picking signal in the lab that has not already been disproven.

But it cannot be made safe, and that is the honest finding. The buyback book without the safety rule earns its keep in the best-measured years and then falls 55% in 2008. With the safety rule it survives 2008 and loses the modern era instead. Holding half the account in the market does not help, because the market was in the 2008 crash too: both halves fell in the same week. Nothing on offer is both safe and modern, and that is the problem to solve, not the buyback signal itself.

The new paper's idea half-worked, and the useful half was not the one expected. The paper says risk pays among stocks near their yearly high and is punished among stocks far below it. That flip is real in our data: the wilder stocks near their high beat the calmer ones by five points a year, and the pattern reverses on the far side. But the entire twenty-year win came from 2002 to 2008 and every version lost to the market from 2009 on. The genuinely valuable discovery was accidental: nearness to the yearly high is the first filter this lab has ever measured that gets BETTER when the dead companies are put back. A company heading for bankruptcy is, by definition, far below its yearly high, so the filter throws the dying out before anything else looks at them. We have been testing it as a way to pick winners when it is really a way to avoid disasters, and the lab's near-miss strategies fail on the depth of their falls, not on their returns.

Two things went wrong in the lab itself, and both are now written down. First, the lab had quietly lost its record of how big each company is. Those files sit outside the automatic check that guards the price history, so nothing noticed until an experiment asked for them and was refused. This is the third time an unguarded file has vanished on a rebuild. It cost most of an hour to rebuild and the fix was verified rather than assumed. A standing health check has been requested. Second, two different things in this lab are both called the lucky-draw control, and they are not the same: one re-draws its random picks every month, the other draws once and holds forever, trading fourteen times less. One of this batch's headline claims was briefly resting on the wrong one, and was corrected before it was recorded. The rule for next time is written down: check whether the shuffle has a date in it.

One more thing the owner should know about how the lab judges. When the lab scores a method across four separate time periods, it picks which version to score by a measure that rewards shallow falls. For the buyback method that meant it kept choosing the timed version, the very version the experiment existed to replace, and scored the modern periods on the one arm with a negative modern-era record. The fold record was partly reporting a selection rule rather than the method.

Fees. Every book this batch was built from the start in fractional shares at the real Gotrade fees on the monthly top-up, so nothing lost an edge it never had. The buyback book's bill was measured rather than guessed: about 11,300 dollars over the period, 8.1% of gross trading profit, costing roughly a third of a point of yearly return. That bill falls on the higher-earning arms hardest, so the two-and-a-half-point lead is a floor.

The gate. It refused nothing this batch, because nothing got far enough to be refused. That is itself the finding. Three of the four methods failed the first screen outright.

What would unlock the most. A way to protect a stock book from a crash that does not involve being in the market during it, since both half-measures are now closed and the plain safety rule costs the modern era. Prices for the index companies our history still cannot see. And real index fund prices as a ruler to check our own numbers against.

What the next batch should try. Put the buyback signal into a market-shaped book as a lean rather than a book of its own, and cap how much of it can sit in one industry. Use nearness to the yearly high as a safety filter on a book that already works, rather than as a way to pick stocks. And find a crash defence that is not the 200-day rule and not a half position, because those are the two that have now been measured to exhaustion.

insights.title: The lost announcement dates were rebuilt for free, and their absence was the silent kind of failure
insights.body:
The handover written after the vendor subscription lapsed says the announcement dates could only be restored "if the owner still has that token anywhere". That is no longer true, and the file has now been rebuilt without spending a single vendor call.

What was wrong with the search. The command that rebuilds the file looks in one folder for its saved vendor answers, and that folder held only the 522 dead companies kept for the survivorship check — none of the live companies. Checking there alone made the job look like a fresh download of about 434 companies against a key that expires in three weeks. But a second folder, saved during the build of the wider 7,693-company universe, holds 7,718 saved answers, and 436 of the 454 live dividend payers are in it. Those answers carry the declaration date, and they parse with the same reader the command already uses. Linking them into the folder the command reads rebuilt the file in seconds: 23,010 announcement dates, 92.4% of the dividends covered, against the 94% the original had. The missing 1.6 points are eighteen symbols that are almost all exchange-traded funds or companies long since bought or delisted, none of which a book of large index members would ever hold.

The lesson worth keeping is about where saved vendor answers live. This lab has two of these folders and they do not know about each other. Before concluding that any vendor data needs re-buying, check both.

The more important half, which is not about this file at all. A missing announcement file does not stop anything. The reader simply falls back to treating each dividend as known on the day it goes ex, which is exactly what the lab did before the dates were ever bought. So a strategy whose entire thesis is acting on the announcement instead of the ex-date silently turns into its own control, runs to completion, and records a perfectly ordinary-looking result. Compare the company-size files, whose absence makes the lab refuse to run at all and say why. One failure announces itself and the other does not, and the quiet one is the dangerous kind.

That is the real repair to make: the lab should refuse to run a method that acts on announcement dates when the store has none, in exactly the way it already refuses when the company sizes, the market-wide series or the dividend calendar are missing. The machinery for this already exists and is three or four lines of the same shape. The one caution is that already-run methods are frozen records, so the new requirement should be declared by new methods rather than by editing the old files, which would disturb their pre-registration.

Worth remembering alongside all this: the announcement dates were measured and found to be worth very little. Matched pairs of books differing only in which date they used came out between a tenth and half a point a year apart, inside the noise, and in the best-measured recent years two of the three pairs went the other way. So this file matters for honesty rather than for edge. It should be present so that nothing quietly measures the wrong thing, not because it is expected to win anything.

insights.title: Buyback shrinkers near their yearly high: the buyback book with the falling knives removed: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.1% on the usual history, +9.7% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 30.4% and 24.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.9% a year before and −6.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 2 of 4 periods won to 3 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 2 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

insights.title: Buy the companies that just split their shares: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.0% on the usual history, +11.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.2% and 19.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.2% a year before and −3.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 3 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.
