insights.title: American companies have almost stopped splitting their shares, and that killed a strategy before we could trade it
insights.body:
There is an old and well-tested idea in finance: when a company splits its shares, it tends to beat the market over the following year. A split gives a shareholder nothing — two shares at fifty dollars are the same stake as one at a hundred — so a board that bothers to do it is quietly saying it believes the price it is splitting down from will hold. Researchers measured about eight percent of extra return in the year after, back in 1996.

We tested it properly. Buying every big US company that had split in the previous twelve months earned eleven percent a year on the owner's deposits where the same money in the market earned seven. Two controls were built specifically to take that result away and could not: a book that copied the strategy's exact shape but picked its names at random earned nine percent, and a book of companies that split one to two years ago and not since earned under nine. So knowing who split recently really was worth something, and the effect faded with time exactly as the theory says it should.

Then the calendar ended the argument. Across the companies we can price, there were fifty to ninety-five splits a year in the late nineteen-nineties and only eleven to twenty-seven a year after 2008. Companies today would rather let the price run to a thousand dollars, and brokers sell fractions of a share anyway, so the gesture has lost its point. The strategy that worked in 1997 needed a wide basket of confident boards refreshed every month. Today it would be five to twenty names drawn from a nearly empty calendar, and it has trailed the market since 2009.

What to do about it: nothing, for this strategy. But it is worth remembering the shape of this failure, because it is not the usual one. The idea was not wrong and was not a fluke in the data. The world simply stopped producing the thing the idea needed. When we judge an old published strategy from now on, the first question should be whether the behaviour it reads is still happening at all — before we ask whether it still pays.

insights.title: A second signal that gets stronger when we add back the companies that went bust
insights.body:
Our main price history cannot price about half the companies that were ever in the index, and the missing ones are mostly the companies that failed. That flatters every result, so we keep a second history with the dead companies restored and re-run everything on it. Almost everything gets worse there — the stock-picking strategies typically lose one to one and a half points of yearly return and fall two to three points deeper.

The share-split strategy got better. With the failures put back it earned 11.2 percent a year instead of 11.0, and its worst fall shrank from 20.2 percent to 19.0. Every other version we ran that day got worse. Its lead over a shape-matched random book widened rather than narrowed.

Once you see why, it is almost obvious. A company that just split its shares is a company whose price has climbed a long way. Those are not the companies that quietly disappear. So putting the failures back into the pool adds names this strategy would never have bought, which dilutes its rivals and leaves it alone.

This is the second thing we have found with that property — the other was buying companies trading near their highest price of the past year, which also earned more with the dead companies restored. Both are, underneath, ways of asking the market to point at companies that are doing well. That looks like a family worth naming: a filter that selects on recent strength is close to immune to the gap in our data, where a filter that selects on weakness or cheapness is at its mercy. When we next have to judge whether a result is real or just a hole in the price file, which direction the filter points is a fast and reliable clue.

insights.title: We can see the day a split takes effect, but not the day the board announced it — and the announcement is the news
insights.body:
The share-split test had to buy on the day the new shares started trading. That is typically three to six weeks after the board actually said it was going to split, and the announcement is the moment the news reaches the market. In other words we bought late, after anyone reading the newspaper had already acted.

Even buying that late, knowing who had split was worth about two points of yearly return over an identical book that picked its names at random. The original research, which measured from the announcement, found roughly four times as much. So there is a reasonable chance that the part of the effect we cannot reach is the larger part.

This is worth noting because we have solved exactly this problem once before. Our price history did not originally carry the dates on which companies announced their dividends either, and those were rebuilt from data we already had on disk, without paying any vendor or making a single outside request. Split announcements are published in the same company filings. If they can be rebuilt the same way, this question becomes worth asking once more, properly, and the answer would be a clean one either way.

The honest caveat: it may not change the conclusion. American companies have almost stopped splitting their shares, so even a perfect announcement-date version would be picking from a nearly empty list after 2008. Buying the data would settle the science; it probably would not produce something to trade. That is a reason to spend an hour on it, not a week.

insights.title: Stocks moving together is a good sign, not a warning — but only while the market is already rising
insights.body:
Everyone in markets knows the phrase: when everything starts moving together, something is wrong. This run measured it, on the hundred busiest big American companies, every month from 1996 to 2015, and the phrase is backwards in the half of the market where it could have made money.

Split the 237 months two ways at once: was the market in an uptrend, and were stocks moving unusually closely together? While the market was rising, the months when stocks moved most closely together were followed by about 34 percent a year, the middling months by 14 percent, and the months when stocks moved most independently by just 4 percent. That is a clean, ordered, thirty-point-a-year gap across 170 months, and it says a tightly linked rising market has been the single best state to be invested in. It matches what an academic paper predicted in 2010, and contradicts what a trader would guess.

Now look at the other half. While the market was falling, the reading barely separates anything: closely-linked months and ordinary months both ended roughly flat to slightly down. That is the half the method built here lived in, and it is why the method failed. Worse, the signal arrives too late to be any use there: in the 2008 crash it did not reach its highest band until September, eight months after the market had already dropped below its long-run average and the simple trend rule had already stepped aside. Stocks move together because they are falling together. By the time you can measure it, you have paid for it.

What to do about it. Stop using this reading as an alarm. It is not an alarm, it is a thermometer, and it reads most usefully when the market is healthy. The idea worth testing next is the opposite of every brake this lab has built: every one of them steps back when the market is falling, and this evidence points to stepping back when a rising market goes quiet and scattered instead. That has to be registered properly with its own controls before anyone believes it, because it was found by looking at data already collected, and because those quiet, rising months cluster in a few specific stretches of history rather than spreading evenly.

insights.title: The one version that beat the simple rule lost its win when the bankrupt companies were put back
insights.body:
Six versions of this market-timing idea ran. Five lost to the simple trend rule they were meant to improve on. One beat it, by a small margin, and the lab's cross-check store then took the win away.

The cross-check store is the same price history with most of the missing companies added back, including the ones that went bust. Re-run there, that version's lead over just buying the market fell from 1.7 percent a year to 0.8 percent, and its worst fall went from 29 percent to 42 percent — thirteen points deeper. The simple trend rule, meanwhile, is identical on both stores, because it reads only the market index and never looks at individual companies.

Two things are worth taking from this. First, the obvious one: a narrow win over a simple control, on data that is missing the companies that died, is not a win. Second, the less obvious one: the direction of the damage was not predictable. It was written down before the run that the missing bankruptcies would make this signal fire late and weak, and so hurt it. In fact the three-month version got slightly better with the dead companies back, and only the six-month version got worse. The honest tape did not push the result one way. It pushed whichever version had been lucky back toward the middle. That is what a selection looks like, and it is a reason to run the cross-check on anything that wins narrowly, not only on things that look suspicious.

insights.title: A company buying back its own stock cheaply is telling you something; one buying it back expensively is not
insights.body:
Buying shares of companies that are shrinking their own share count has been this lab's most promising stock idea. The snag has always been the fall: in 2008 that book lost more than half its value, because some of the biggest buyers of their own stock in 2007 and 2008 were banks spending their last spare cash defending a share price that was already collapsing.

So this run tried a sensible-sounding fix. Before picking, throw out every company whose price sits in the lower half of the pool compared with its own best price of the past year, and buy only the buyback companies trading near their peak. Keep the thrown-away half as a comparison, so we can see what we gave up.

The filter worked perfectly and was worth nothing. The two halves never once shared a name in nineteen years. The kept half held utility and household-goods companies; the discarded half held exactly the sort of names you would expect, including a bond insurer and two life insurers in early 2009. Discarding them cut the worst fall from 68% to 51%. And the two halves earned the same money, a tenth of a point apart over twenty years. All that extra danger paid nothing, and avoiding it gained nothing.

Then the part that decides it. In the stretch since 2009, which is the best-measured and most like today, the half we kept barely beat the market, and once the companies that went bankrupt are put back into the price history it actually loses to the market. The half we threw away beats the market by six points a year. The unfiltered book beat it by about four.

The reason is the original argument for buybacks, turned around. A buyback is supposed to mean something because management thinks the shares are cheap and is spending real money saying so. A company buying its stock back while the price is far below its yearly high is doing exactly that. A company buying it back at its highest price of the year is paying full price, which these days is closer to a routine habit than a judgement. Large American companies buy back stock quarter after quarter as a matter of policy.

So the filter did not separate healthy companies from doomed ones. It separated opportunistic buybacks from routine ones, and kept the routine ones. What to do about it: stop treating the price level as something to filter on, and start treating it as part of the signal. The next thing to measure is a single score that rewards a company for buying back a lot of stock and for buying it back cheaply at the same time, with nothing thrown away.

insights.title: A safety rule that protects one kind of book can be useless in another, and we nearly trusted it blind
insights.body:
A few days ago this lab found something rare. Almost every pattern it measures looks worse once the companies that went bankrupt or were taken over are put back into the price history, because the original history quietly leaves out most of the failures. One measure went the other way: how close a share price is to its own best level of the past year. Adding the dead companies back made that measure earn more, not less, which makes obvious sense — a company heading for bankruptcy is by definition trading far below its best price, so it gets excluded automatically.

That finding was the main reason to try this method, and it was written down in advance as the thing that made the idea worth a try.

It did not transfer. Inside a pool of companies that are buying back their own stock, the same measure gained only half as much from the fuller history as the half it was supposed to protect against, and the safety gap between the two halves shrank from seventeen points to six. On the honest history the supposedly dangerous half fell less deeply than it had on the original history, and the supposedly safe half fell more deeply.

The reason, in hindsight, is almost obvious. A company with enough spare cash to retire eight percent of its own stock in a single year is rarely a company about to go bankrupt. The failures this filter was built to catch were mostly not in the pool to begin with, so all the filter did was tilt the book toward steady, expensive, slow-growing companies.

The lesson is general and worth holding on to. A protective rule is only as good as the danger it removes, and whether that danger is present depends entirely on which pool it is applied to. A rule proven on one kind of book is a hypothesis in another, not a result. We will keep this measure in the toolbox, but from now on it has to prove itself again every time it moves to a new kind of book, rather than being carried over as settled.

insights.title: Our out-of-sample check sometimes grades a strategy on the very version it was built to argue against
insights.body:
Before any strategy can be put forward for a real test, it has to pass a fairness check. The check splits the twenty years into four stretches, picks the best version of the strategy using only the earlier years, and then scores that version on later years it has never seen. A strategy must win most of the stretches. That rule is sound and has correctly stopped several strategies from going further.

But there is a flaw in how the version gets picked, and this run shows it in its clearest form yet. Most strategies here are tested as several versions at once, and some of those versions exist only as comparisons — a deliberately bad one, or a coin-flip one, included so we can tell whether the real idea is doing anything. The picker does not know which is which. It simply takes whichever version had the best return for the size of its worst fall in the training years.

In this run the picker chose, for one of the four stretches, the deliberate opposite of the idea being tested: the version holding exactly the companies the method was built to exclude. It scored badly, and that counted against the method. For two other stretches it chose the version that sells everything when the market turns down, which is the behaviour this method was specifically designed to replace. So three of the four verdicts were about versions the method was arguing against, and the idea itself was graded on almost none of them.

This is the third strategy in a row where this has happened, and it always pushes the same way, because a version that sits in cash during crashes always looks best on return-for-risk in the training years.

What would fix it: let a strategy's author mark which versions are the real proposal and which are only there as comparisons, and have the fairness check choose only from the real ones. That makes the check stricter, not looser — it removes the option of being saved by a comparison version that happened to look good — and it would mean the verdict is finally about the thing being proposed.

insights.title: The hold-length dial on eighteen dividend methods is not connected to anything
insights.body:
Several of the lab's dividend methods offer a choice of how long to keep a company after it changes its dividend: six months, twelve months. This run put a six-month and a twelve-month version side by side and they came out the same to one decimal place — the same yearly return, 171 trades against 172, the same worst fall.

The reason is in the picking rule, and it is the same rule in eighteen method files. The rule looks only at a company's *latest* dividend. As soon as the next ordinary dividend is paid, the latest dividend is no longer the interesting one, and the company quietly loses its place in the book. Most of these companies pay every quarter. Measured across the whole twenty-year window, the median gap to the next payment is 91 days, and only one special dividend in twenty survives 182 days before the next payment pushes it out.

So 'hold for six months' and 'hold for twelve months' both mean 'hold for about three months'. The older dividend-raise method shows the same fingerprint: its six-month and twelve-month versions differ by less than half a percent of total return over twenty years and have the same worst fall.

Why it matters: every variant that was spent on the hold length measured nothing, and the lab's record now contains comparisons that look like evidence about patience and are not. Worse, it means none of these methods has ever actually tested the thing the research they came from is about — that the reward keeps arriving for months after the announcement. The lab has been claiming to test a slow drift while only ever holding for one quarter.

What to do: the picking rule should keep a company while *any* qualifying event of its is still young, not only while it was the most recent thing that happened. That is a small change in one shared piece of code, and it would make the hold-length dial mean what it says. Until it is made, a new dividend method should not offer a hold longer than a quarter, because it cannot deliver one.

insights.title: A rare signal gets buried: two thirds of this book was the index, and the measured lead was two thirds smaller because of it
insights.body:
When a strategy cannot find enough companies to fill its slots, the lab's books put the empty slots into the index. That is the right thing to do with real money — idle cash earns nothing — but it quietly ruins the measurement, and this run shows how badly.

Special dividends are rare. Among big, liquid, index-listed companies there are usually only three or four alive at any moment. So a book with ten slots spent, on average, 35% of itself on the companies it actually wanted and 65% on the index. The strictest version, which only wanted payments five times the usual size, was 90% index and 10% method.

The book beat the index by 0.9 points a year. Scaled up to what the picks would be worth if they filled the whole book, they are worth about 2.6 points a year. The steady-payer control, which filled every slot with its own names, beat the index by 0.3. In other words: the signal was about eight times stronger than the control, and the headline number showed it as three times stronger, because most of the book was not the signal.

This cuts both ways and the second way is more dangerous. The strictest version looked like the best row in the whole run — the highest lead, the shallowest fall, a gains-to-losses ratio of 5.49 against 2.50. It was 90% index. Anyone reading the table by eye would have picked the version with the least method in it. It also failed the hundred-trade minimum, which is the only reason the lab caught it.

What to do about it: whenever a book parks unfilled slots in the index, the share of the book that is actually its own picks should be printed beside the return, the same way the lab already prints how often a book is invested at all. Without it, a thin signal and a weak signal look identical, and a rare-event method is penalised for being rare rather than judged on whether it is right.

insights.title: Sera 20261019-0853: the split signal is real but the calendar emptied, and a safety filter that worked everywhere else failed inside the buyback book
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Four ideas ran; three passed the lab's first screen and all three were refused by the strict promotion check, each on the same condition: none beat the market in most of the four separate stretches of history it was judged on. The count of looks at the held-back years is still four.

What the batch was for. Two new event ideas, one variation of the lab's strongest live signal, and one queued idea about reading the market's own co-movement. Every one was built from the start in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's monthly top-up, so nothing lost an edge it never had.

The split idea is real, and it is dying of old age. Buying the big companies that had split their shares in the previous year earned 11.0 percent a year on the owner's deposits against 7.2 for the same money in the market, and two controls built to take it away could not: a shape-matched random book earned 9.1, and companies that had split one to two years earlier earned 8.8. The effect also got stronger, not weaker, when the companies that went bankrupt were put back into the price history — the second signal this lab has found that survives that test. But American companies have almost stopped splitting: 50 to 95 a year across the index in the late nineties, 11 to 27 a year after 2008. In the years this lab weighs most the book is five to twenty names chosen from a nearly empty calendar, it trailed the market after 2009, and it lost three of four out-of-sample stretches. As a stand-alone book it is dead. As evidence that a board splitting its shares is telling you something, it is alive, and that is queued for the next batch.

The special-dividend idea is real but smaller than the ordinary raise. The picks beat the index by about 2.6 points a year where steady payers beat it by 0.3, so a one-off cash payment does carry news. But an ordinary dividend raise carries nearly twice as much, only three or four of these companies are alive at any moment so two thirds of the book was just the index, and the book lost to the market by 7.5 points a year in 2009-2015. The version that passed the screen was the ordinary-raise control, not the special. The lab already trades raises; specials add little on top.

The buyback filter failed in an instructive way. The lab's best live stock signal is still the companies shrinking their share count. This batch tried to fix its 2008 fall by keeping only the buyback companies trading near their own yearly high — a filter that had just been shown to get stronger when dead companies are put back. It cut the fall by 17 points and earned not one extra rupiah: the kept half and the thrown-away half earned the same, and after 2009 the thrown-away half beat the market by 6 points a year on the honest history while the kept half lost to it. The reason is now clear and it is not a tuning problem: the same buyback dollars retire more shares when the price is low, so the biggest shrinkers are mechanically the cheaper ones. A safety filter that works on a general stock book removed the very companies that carry the buyback signal. It also repeats a warning this lab has now measured twice: a rule that protects one kind of book can be worthless in another, and we nearly trusted it blind.

Correlation is a symptom, not a warning. Reading how tightly the hundred busiest companies move together, as a brake on the market, arrived too late: the reading only reached its alarming band in September 2008, eight months after the plain 200-day rule had already stepped aside, and the plain rule beat every version on both return and the worst fall. The more interesting finding is the opposite sign: while the market is already rising, the months when stocks move most closely together have been followed by about 34 percent a year against 4 percent for the months when they move most independently. That is a state worth being invested in, not a warning to leave — and it is queued as the next question.

Directions. Dead: splits as a stand-alone book, special dividends as their own book, nearness to the yearly high as a safety filter inside the buyback book, and correlation as a crash brake. Alive: the buyback signal itself, which nothing this batch dented; the question of why the 200-day rule stopped paying after 2009, which now has direct evidence from a non-momentum book; and the quiet, scattered market as a better brake than the loud, correlated one.

What would unlock the most. The day a split is announced, not the day it takes effect. We bought three to six weeks late, after the news was public; the original research measured roughly four times the effect from the announcement, so the part we cannot reach may be the larger part. This is the same problem the lab already solved for dividend declarations, and it is queued as a data wish. Second, real index fund prices as a ruler, which is still blocked. Third, the lab's out-of-sample check sometimes grades a strategy on the comparison arm it was built to argue against — it happened in its clearest form yet this batch, and it is a fairness problem worth fixing before it hides or invents an edge.

The gate. It refused all three dev-eligible methods, each on the folds: the split book won one of four out-of-sample stretches, the special-dividend book one, the buyback-near-high book two. None was refused on a failed relative. Three older methods still sit in the promotable list by the gate's letter; two were set aside in earlier batches on the honest price history, and the third was checked again this morning and trails the market by 1.1 points a year in 2009-2015, so no look was spent on any of them.

Fees. Every book was built at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares from the start, so no edge was measured at the old flat rate and then lost to the real bill. The one place fees bite hardest is the thin special-dividend book, which parks most of its money in the index and pays the fee minimum on small slots.

What the next batch should try. A book of boards acting as if the price will hold — splits together with the other gestures a confident board makes, wide enough to trade today. Why the 200-day rule stopped paying after 2009, asked directly rather than through another stock book. And a brake that reads a rising market going quiet and scattered, which is the one market state this batch found that is worth acting on.

insights.title: The held-back-years price history was rebuilt without the share and split files, and two money reports quietly traded nothing
insights.body:
This morning's rebuild of the held-back-years price history left out the two optional files that carry company size and split dates. Two of the four money reports run from it — the split book and the buyback book — initially recorded zero trades and looked like a strategy that never bought anything. It was not a result: the book had no pool to pick from.

The failure is quiet in the worst way. The store's missing-input message named a different file, one that was present, so the first diagnosis was wrong. Nothing in the run says "your data is incomplete"; it says the strategy did nothing, which is also what a bad strategy does.

Both runs were repaired without rebuilding the store: split lists were fetched for the symbols the cache did not cover, then the share store was rebuilt into the file — 51,272 share rows and 1,210 split rows. The price fingerprint did not move, so recorded trials remain comparable; the store's full fingerprint did change, as it does whenever an optional file is added.

The risk for the lab: any method that needs company size or split dates will be refused at the test window, or measured as cash, for a reason that looks like the method. The standing health check already requested should cover the held-back store as well as the dev store, and the missing-input message should name every optional file it checked, not just one.

insights.title: Buying back shares is not what earns the money — it is what stops you buying the dying
insights.body:
A company buying back its own stock is spending real cash. A company trading far below its best price of the past year is cheap. The lab has been treating these as two ways of finding the same good companies. They are not even related: in twenty years of monthly checks, the twenty biggest buyback companies and the twenty cheapest companies drawn from the same pool shared, on average, one name out of twenty.

So the lab built a dial between them and turned it through five settings, then read every setting twice: once on the price history it normally uses, and once on an honest one that adds back the companies that went bankrupt or disappeared.

The dial settles an argument the previous run got half right. Cheapness is what earns. Over 2009 to 2015 — the years best covered by the data and most like today — a pure buyback book beat the market by 3.5% a year on honest prices. Tilt the same book halfway toward cheap stocks and that becomes 11.8% a year, more than three times as much. Tilt it all the way, so cheapness decides everything, and you get 11.4% — no better, and the book falls 85% at its worst instead of 75%.

The reason the dial stops paying is worth knowing. At the halfway setting, 99 of every 100 companies in the book are still buying back stock. At the far end, only 32 are — fewer than in the pool it draws from, so the all-cheapness book actively avoids buyback companies. It has become a book of distressed firms. And when the firms that actually died are added back to the price history, half its apparent advantage vanishes, because the cheapest stocks are precisely the ones that were about to fail and the usual history cannot price the ones that did. The halfway book barely changes at all when the dead are restored.

That is the finding. Buying cheap stocks is a well-known way to make money and an equally well-known way to go broke, and these two outcomes have never been separated in this lab before. Requiring that management is spending real cash on its own shares is a bankruptcy screen that costs nothing and makes cheapness safe to own. The buyback is the seatbelt, not the engine.

What to do about it: none of these books is tradable — the smallest fall among them was 55% and the largest 85%, where the limit for real money is 25%. But the next method should stop asking whether buybacks beat the market and start asking whether they add anything to cheapness: take only the cheapest third of the pool, and inside it hold the biggest buyback companies, the biggest share issuers, and a blind draw. If the three land together, this whole family is deep value wearing a disguise and should be closed.

insights.title: Averaging two unrelated rankings gives you a book that is good at neither
insights.body:
When the lab has two ways of picking stocks and wants to use both, the usual move is to give each company its position in both lists and hold the ones with the best average position. It is simple, it cannot be thrown off by one odd number, and this lab already does it in more than one place.

This run measured what it costs, and the cost is real. Two rankings were combined that turned out to be almost completely unrelated — the companies buying back the most stock and the companies trading furthest below their yearly high shared about one name in twenty. Averaging their positions produced a book that earned less than either ranking used on its own: 10.5% a year against 13.3% for one and 19.0% for the other, over the same twenty years at the same fees.

The reason is easy to see once stated. Each ranking earns its money from its own extreme — the handful of companies at the very top of that one list. A company near the top of one list and the middle of the other scores better on the average than a company at the very top of one list and the bottom of the other. So the averaged book quietly fills up with compromises and holds almost none of the names either ranking was actually excited about.

This does not mean combining signals is wrong. It means averaging positions is the wrong way to combine two signals that disagree about which companies are interesting. When two rankings overlap heavily, averaging smooths out noise and helps. When they barely overlap, averaging throws away both edges. The test is cheap and should be run before building any combined book: measure how many names the two rankings actually share at the size you intend to hold. One in twenty is a warning.

The alternative, when the overlap is low, is to use one ranking to choose who is allowed in and the other to rank inside that group — so both signals stay at their own extreme instead of meeting in the middle. That is the shape the next method will test.

insights.title: The market safety rule is insurance: nine of its eleven exits were premiums and two were claims
insights.body:
Half the strategies here carry one safety rule: when the S&P 500 tracker falls below its average price of the last two hundred trading days, sell everything and wait in cash. Every post-mortem this year has said the same thing about it - it helped over twenty years and helped nothing after 2009 - and we have been reading that as a rule that stopped working.

This week we listed every single time the rule sold out between 1994 and October 2015. There were eleven. Two of them were worth it: it sat out the dot-com collapse and it sat out the financial crisis, each time avoiding a fall of about 36%. The other nine were false alarms, and between them they cost 52 points of market we did not own. That is not a broken rule. That is an insurance policy: you pay nine times and you claim twice.

And here is the part that changes how to read every earlier post-mortem. Every exit after 2009 was a false alarm and not one was a real crash, because the practice window we search in ends in 2015 and the years from 2009 to 2015 contain no bear market at all. The rule did not decay. It spent six and a half years charging us for a fire that never started.

What to do about it: when a strategy's 2009-2015 record looks bad and the safety rule is blamed, first ask how many crashes were inside that window. If the answer is none, the rule has not been tested there - it has only been billed for. The thing worth measuring is what the rule costs per crash avoided, not what it costs per decade.

insights.title: Buy the companies whose boards most recently did something confident: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 69.2% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +8.3% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +8.3% a year, which is +1.1% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +1.1% a year against the market as recorded, +1.1% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +4.6% a year against the market as recorded, +4.6% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +4.8% a year against the market as recorded, +4.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −6.7% a year against the market as recorded, −6.7% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 3 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: In this market's history, crashes arrived quietly and false alarms arrived screaming
insights.body:
If we could tell a real crash from a false alarm on the day the safety rule fires, the rule would get much cheaper. So we checked the two signs anyone would reach for first, across all eleven times the rule sold out between 1994 and 2015.

The first sign is how far the market had already fallen below its two-hundred-day average line. The intuition is that a big break is serious and a small one is a wobble. It is backwards. The two real crashes broke the line by only one and two percent. The four deepest breaks in the whole record - nine and a half percent in 1998, and about five percent in 1994, 2011 and 2015 - were every single one of them a false alarm.

The second sign is how frightened the market was, measured by how violently prices were swinging that month. Also backwards. Both real crashes began at perfectly ordinary levels of nervousness. The three most frightened exits in the record were all false alarms.

So in this stretch of history, crashes arrived quietly and false alarms arrived screaming. That is worth remembering well beyond this one rule: panic in the price is a poor guide to danger, and it explains after the fact why an earlier attempt to improve the rule by widening its trigger bought us nothing at all.

One sign did survive, and it is not read on the day we sell. A false alarm is a dip beneath an average that is still climbing; a real bear market is a dip beneath an average that has itself turned down. Waiting for the average to turn skipped five of the nine false alarms and still caught both crashes - though on so few decisions that it is a hint, not a finding.

insights.title: The upside-down version lost money, which is the strongest sign yet that a signal is real
insights.body:
The price of risk is what insurance against market swings costs, minus what the swings actually turn out to cost. A method built on it held all of its money in the market when that gap was wide, half when it was middling, and none when it was narrow. It earned 6.0% a year on the owner's deposits where simply holding the market earned 7.7%, so it was rejected.

The interesting arm was the deliberate falsification: the same three steps turned upside down, holding everything when the gap was narrowest. If the gap carried no information, that version should have landed near the first one. It did not. It lost money — minus 1.2% a year across twenty-two years in which the market roughly quadrupled — and its losing months took more money than its winning months made. The two versions trade at almost the same rate and spend almost the same time invested, so the entire seven-point-a-year difference between them is which way round the signal is read. Over 2009 to 2015, the years most like today and the years after the idea was published, the gap between the two widened to twelve points.

Why it matters: this lab has spent a great many attempts on signals that turned out to be noise, and the usual tell is that the control arm does just as well. This is the opposite case, and it is rare. There is genuine information in the price of risk.

What to do about it: the method failed not because the opinion was wrong but because of what it did with the opinion. Converting a good opinion into sitting entirely in cash is expensive, because the market rises in roughly six months out of ten and the method sat out a third of all months. Measured per unit of time actually invested, it earned about 46% more than buy-and-hold. The next attempt should keep the same opinion and never leave the market — lean towards and away from it rather than switching it off — and that is already queued.

insights.title: Every verdict about a rule that sits in cash is harsher than the truth, but only before 2008
insights.body:
In every backtest this lab has ever run, money sitting in cash earns nothing. That is not what a real account does: cash in a brokerage account earns something close to the short-term government rate. This run measured the difference for the first time, by running the same method twice — once with cash earning nothing, once with cash earning the three-month Treasury bill rate, which the store already holds day by day.

The method was in cash or half in cash about half the time. Crediting the cash moved its result from 6.0% a year to 6.8%, and made its worst fall shallower, from 33% to 30%. So roughly eight tenths of a point a year of what looked like the method's shortfall was an accounting choice, not the method.

Why it matters: this lab has rejected a long line of rules whose job is to step aside when the market looks dangerous — the 200-day safety switch, the fear-spike gate, several risk brakes. Every one of them was charged for holding cash that a real account would have been paid for. Their recorded verdicts are all harsher than the truth by something of this order, and anyone re-reading an old rejection should keep that in mind.

There is a sting in the tail, and it is the more useful half. Over 2009 to 2015 the credited and uncredited versions are identical — both trail the market by 3.9 points a year. Treasury bills paid essentially nothing after 2008, so the whole correction is earned in the 1994 to 2007 half of the window and none of it in the years that look most like today. The bias is real and worth knowing about, but it rescues nothing in the modern era, and no rule that was rejected on its 2009 to 2015 record should be reopened because of it.

insights.title: Spreading your money evenly across thirty big American companies has cost eight points a year since 2009
insights.body: Every method this lab builds gets compared against a coin-flip version of itself: the same number of companies, bought and sold on the same days, but with the names chosen at random instead of by the idea. Usually that control is there to check whether the idea is real. This time it said something bigger. The coin-flip book, holding thirty large American companies in equal slices behind the same market switch, lost 8.2 points a year to the market itself over 2009 to 2015. Not because the picks were bad — the picks were random, so they were nothing. It lost because of its shape. The market index is dominated by its largest members, and since 2009 those largest members have done most of the work. Any book that spreads money evenly across thirty index members is quietly betting against that, and the bet has been costing about eight points a year. That number is larger than every stock-picking edge this lab has ever measured. It means an equal-weight book starts eight points behind before it chooses a single company, and no signal we have found is big enough to climb back. The practical conclusion is that the next ideas worth trying are not new ways to pick companies. They are ways to hold the companies we pick without giving up the shape of the market: holding them beside a slice of the index itself, or weighting them by company size instead of equally, so the book is not short the biggest names by construction.

insights.title: Raising the dividend every year says nothing. Splitting the stock, or starting a dividend, says a lot
insights.body: The idea behind this method was that four things a company board does all mean the same thing: splitting the stock, paying a first-ever dividend, raising the dividend after a flat stretch, and buying back a large slice of its own shares. Each is a board spending money or credibility to say it thinks the current share price is a floor rather than a ceiling. Running all four together, and then running them separately, showed they are not the same thing at all. A routine annual dividend raise is common — 187 of the 239 companies carrying any of these signals in 2015 had simply raised their dividend again — and it is worthless. The book that held only dividend signals earned less than the market, fell 31 percent at its worst, and did worse than its own coin-flip control. Throw the routine raise out and keep only the three rare and genuinely expensive gestures, and the book improved on every measure at once: more money earned, a shallower fall, a better ratio of gains to losses, and a thousand fewer trades to pay for. The lesson generalises beyond this method. When looking for a signal in what a company does, the test is whether the act is unusual for that company. Doing the expected thing on schedule carries no information, however costly it looks on paper. Doing something the company has not done before does.

insights.title: A confidence signal from two years ago pays as well as one from last month
insights.body: This method was built on the belief that these signals go stale: buy the companies whose boards acted most recently, because the effect should fade with time. A control arm was added to test that, holding companies whose signal was one to two years old and which had done nothing since. It earned the most of all six arms — more than the freshest book — and it did so while trading one fifth as often. So the recency the method was built on does no work. What these signals seem to mark is not a moment to buy but a kind of company: one whose board has recently had reason to feel confident, and that stays true for years rather than weeks. If that holds up, it is good news for the owner, because a signal that lasts two years can be traded a tenth as often, and trading costs are one of the few things in this lab that are certain. The next version should test the hold directly: the same rare signals, held for three months, one year and three years, with the trading costs counted each time. It should also carry a coin-flip control matched to its own trading rate, which this run did not have — the two arms that beat their control were also the two that traded least, so part of their lead may be the saved costs rather than better picks.

insights.title: A re-run note is appended, never recognised, and the append-only rule cannot take it back
insights.body:
One method's analysis is stored twice because a note command was re-run after a shell pipeline returned a failure code. The append-only trigger then correctly refused to let the session remove the copy. That method's page now shows the same analysis twice.

This is not a data problem — both copies are identical — but it is a small display problem the lab cannot fix through its own interface. The fix is a note command that refuses an identical second note, or that recognises the most recent note is the same text and says so instead of appending it. Editing history silently is exactly what the trigger exists to stop; recognising a duplicate before it is written is not editing history at all.

The same trap will recur: any command whose output is piped through a filter that can return a failure code will look like it failed even when it wrote.

insights.title: Sera 20261019-1014: the signals were real, the containers killed them, and the safety rule was never broken
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch, but for a new reason. Four ideas ran and all four were rejected. Three of them found a real signal and lost it to the way the book was built, and the fourth rewrote how the lab should read its own safety rule.

The buy signal itself came close and missed on one condition. The cheap-buyback book — companies buying back stock while their price sits far below its yearly high — won all four of its out-of-sample stretches on both the usual and the honest price history, and led the market by 11.4 points a year in 2009-2015 with the dead companies added back. That is the strongest modern-era result this lab has recorded. It is not eligible on the first screen, so the signal does not fire: every version falls 55 to 85 percent, and the lab refuses a book that falls past 50 percent. The signal is real; the book is unholdable. Making it holdable is now the single most valuable problem in the lab.

Cheapness earns; buybacks keep you alive. The dial between the two settled an argument from the last batch. A pure buyback book beat the market by 3.5 points a year in 2009-2015 on honest prices; tilting it halfway toward cheap stocks took that to 11.8; tilting it all the way gave 11.4 and an 85 percent fall. The buyback is not the return — it is the screen that keeps the book out of companies that are cheap because they are dying. The two signals share about one name in twenty, which produced the batch's cleanest warning: averaging two unrelated rankings gives a book worse than either one alone, 10.5 percent against 13.3 and 19.0, because each ranking earns its money at its own extreme and averaging flattens both extremes.

A board's confidence is worth two points, but the shape of the book ate eight. Splitting a stock, paying a first dividend, or buying back a large slice are rare, expensive gestures that beat a coin-flip book by about two points a year and kept that lead after 2009. A routine annual dividend raise is not the same thing — 187 of the 239 companies carrying any signal in 2015 had simply raised again, and the dividend-only book did worse than its own coin flip. Recency did nothing either: the arm holding signals one to two years old earned the most of all six and traded a fifth as often. But the whole book was thirty index members in equal slices, and that shape lost 8.2 points a year to the market after 2009 — more than every stock-picking edge the lab has measured. An equal-weight book starts eight points behind before it picks a single company. That number now explains more of the lab's record than any signal failure.

The safety rule was insurance, not a broken rule. The lab has spent months saying the 200-day rule helped over twenty years and helped nothing after 2009. This batch counted the exits: eleven between 1994 and 2015, two of them real crashes — the dot-com collapse and the financial crisis, each avoiding a fall of about 36 percent — and nine false alarms that together cost 52 points of market. Every exit after 2009 was a false alarm, because 2009-2015 contained no bear market at all. The rule did not decay; it spent six and a half years paying premiums with no claim. Two further findings: crashes in this record arrived quietly, breaking the line by only one or two percent, while the deepest breaks were all false alarms and the most frightened months were all false alarms; and waiting for the average itself to turn down skipped five false alarms and kept both crashes, earning 1 to 1.8 points a year more — on four decisions, so it is a hypothesis, not a result.

The price of risk is real, and the switch wasted it. Insurance against market swings, priced against what the swings actually cost, sorted the market's forward returns: the book that held everything when insurance was expensive earned 6.0 percent a year, and the deliberate upside-down version lost money outright, minus 1.2 percent a year across twenty-two years in which the market roughly quadrupled. The signal is real; the on-off switch is what lost. A version that leans rather than leaves is queued. And a correction to every earlier verdict of this kind: cash in these tests earns nothing, while a real account earns the short rate. Crediting it lifted this method by 0.8 points a year and shallowed its fall by three points. Every rule the lab has rejected for stepping aside has been judged about that much too harshly.

Directions. Dead: averaging two unrelated rankings; the routine dividend raise as a confidence signal; recency as a reason to buy; the 200-day price cross as a crash detector on its own. Alive: cheap buybacks, the strongest modern-era signal, blocked only by the fall; rare board-confidence gestures, if held beside a market core instead of spread evenly; the price of risk as a weight rather than a switch; and the slower average-cross as a cheaper safety rule.

What would unlock the most. A way to hold the cheap-buyback book through a crash. The 2008 fall is concentration — the cheap shrinkers load into financials — so the industry cap queued two batches ago should be tested on this book, not on the plain one. Second, the equal-weight handicap: every stock book the lab builds is measured against a cap-weighted index while holding equal slices, and the gap is now measured at eight points a year. A market-shaped version of the best signals, or an explicit equal-weight yardstick, would separate picking from shape. Third, cash should earn the short rate in every backtest; the lab has been marking down every defensive rule.

The gate. It refused nothing this batch because nothing reached it: all four methods were rejected on the first screen — the fall for cheap buybacks, the trade count for the safety-rule study, the luck bar for the confidence book, and the market shortfall for the price-of-risk ladder. No look at the held-back years was spent; the count is still four.

Fees. Every book ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees from the start. The batch's clearest fee fact is a design one: the stale confidence book earned the most while trading a fifth as often, and the rare-gesture book cut a thousand trades by dropping the routine raise. Trading less is still the only certain saving in the lab.

What the next batch should try. The cheap-buyback book with an industry cap and a market core, held for its modern-era lead rather than its twenty-year average. The slower average-cross as the safety rule under a real stock book, where it has enough trades to be judged. And the price of risk as a weight with a floor, never as a switch.

insights.title: The eight-point equal-weight handicap was the market switch and the trading fees, not the even slices
insights.body:
Two notes written earlier on 19 October said that spreading money evenly across thirty large American companies cost about eight points a year against the market after 2009, and that the even slices were to blame. One of them concluded that the next ideas worth trying were ways to weight companies by size instead of evenly. That conclusion was wrong, and this note withdraws it.

The eight points are real. The reason given for them was not.

We took the same coin-flip book apart using only numbers the lab had already recorded about it — no new trial, no new method, nothing spent. Of the 8.2 points a year it lost to the market between 2009 and 2015:

About 3.6 points were the cost of standing in cash. That book carried the 200-day market switch, which kept it out of the market roughly a fifth of the time, and those particular years were a near-unbroken rise. Sitting out a rising market is expensive, and this is what it cost.

About 3.8 points were trading costs. The book turned over fifteen times a year, and at the fees we actually pay, fifteen turns a year costs about that much.

What is left for the choice of companies and the even slices together is under 0.9 points. Measured against its own sibling — the same book picking names by the idea instead of at random — only about half a point is the even slices themselves.

So the even slices cost about half a point a year, not eight.

What this changes. Weighting by company size is no longer the obvious next idea; at best it buys back half a point. The two expensive ingredients were the switch's time in cash during a rising decade and the turnover, so the levers worth pulling are how often a book trades and how much time it spends out of the market. This also joins up with the other finding from the same week — that the safety rule is insurance, and that 2009 to 2015 held no crash to claim on. The 3.6 points here are those premiums, measured in money for the first time.

What stays true. Comparing a book against a coin-flip version of itself is still the right test, and the honest half of the original note survives: the rare-gesture book was 1.5 points and the stale book 3.9 points ahead of their coin-flip in that era. The signals were real and the containers lost them. But the coin-flip has to match the real book's trade count and how often it trades. If it does not, both sides carry the same hidden costs and the comparison says nothing about the idea. The lab now measures that match, and refuses to promote a method whose control does not have it.

The general lesson is the one worth keeping: when a book trails the market, do not name the gap after whichever ingredient you happened to be thinking about. Take it apart first. Three of these four points had nothing to do with the thing we blamed.

insights.title: Across all 824 recorded trials, most of the lab's post-2009 shortfall is the safety rule standing in cash
insights.body:
We have just taken apart every trial this lab has ever recorded — all 824 of them, across 162 methods — and asked the same question of each: when this book trailed the market between 2009 and 2015, where did the money actually go? Nothing was re-run and nothing was spent. The answer was already sitting in rows we had recorded years ago; we had simply never asked.

The answer is that most of it was one decision, and it was not a decision about which companies to buy.

Of a typical shortfall of four and a half to five points a year, about three and a half to three and three-quarter points is the 200-day safety rule standing in cash. That figure barely moves from book to book. Of the 439 trials that carry the rule, the middle one was out of the market about a fifth of the time, and nine in ten of them sat between 0.67 and 0.80 invested. The market rose 16.6% a year over those six and a half years, so being a fifth out of it costs 3.6 points. It is not a finding about any strategy. It is arithmetic, and every book that carries the rule pays it equally.

Trading costs are the second ingredient, and they only matter for the books that trade a lot. Below four round-trips a year the fees cost half a point. Above ten they cost nearly four. In the books that trade least, the safety rule is the bigger cost than the fees in 95 out of 100 cases.

What is left over — the part that is actually about picking companies — is close to nothing. In the books that trade least, where the fee estimate is too small to distort the answer, what remains is slightly negative: about three-quarters of a point against us. So the picking was roughly a coin flip. It was not secretly brilliant and it was not a disaster. It was small.

One honest correction belongs in this note. Reading all 824 at once, the leftover looked positive, and it was tempting to conclude the signals had been winning all along and the containers had taken it back. That was wrong. The fee figure is an estimate, not something we recorded, and in the books that trade a hundred times a year that estimate is enormous — so any error in it shows up in the leftover and flatters it. In the books where the fee estimate is small enough to be harmless, the effect disappears. We are reporting the cautious number.

What this changes. We have spent years treating a long run of disappointing results as a long run of bad ideas. Mostly it was one choice, repeated: carry the safety rule through the calmest decade in living memory and pay the premium every year. This is not an argument for switching the rule off — it earned its keep in 2000 and in 2008, and it helped in all twenty-two variations we tested across the full history. It is an argument that the single most valuable problem in this lab is no longer "find a better signal". It is "keep the insurance without paying the premium in the years nothing burns down". That is a question about how a book is held, not about what it holds, and for the first time we can put a price on getting it right: about three and a half points a year.

And one number worth keeping in view: 197 of the 824 trials — almost a quarter — did beat the market over that stretch. Only a third of those carried the safety rule, against half of all trials. The books that won were disproportionately the ones not paying the premium.

insights.title: The safety rule is out on the wrong days, and buys back into crashes — a price band fixes both
insights.body:
Earlier today we measured what the 200-day safety rule costs us in calm years and put it at about three and a half points a year. We explained it as simple arithmetic: the rule keeps us out of the market about a fifth of the time, the market rose 16.6% a year, so a fifth of 16.6 is the bill. The arithmetic was right. The conclusion we drew from it — that the way to cut the bill is to spend less time out of the market — was wrong, and this note corrects it.

We took the rule apart on the market itself, with no stock picking involved at all, over twenty-two years.

The first surprise is how often it fires. We had been saying the rule sold us out eleven times. It actually flips 151 times, across 76 separate spells out of the market, and 43 of those spells last five days or fewer. The year 2000 alone contains a dozen one- and two-day exits. Between them, the short spells sat out 106% of cumulative market movement — that is the bill, and it is made of dozens of tiny mistakes rather than a few big ones.

Then we tried a small change. Instead of selling the moment the price dips below its average, wait until it is a few percent below; and instead of buying back the moment it pokes above, wait until it is a few percent above. A band around the line rather than the line itself. This is not the same as waiting a fixed number of days before changing your mind — we tried that before and it failed badly, because it would have suppressed the exit in May 2008, which was the single most valuable thing the rule has ever done.

The band is better on every measure we looked at. Over twenty-two years it earns 7.9% a year against the plain rule's 6.0%, and its worst fall is 20% against 29%. Through the dot-com crash it loses 11% where the plain rule loses 25%. In 2009 to 2015 it earns 8.8% against 7.0%, which cuts that calm-decade bill from 5.3 points to 3.4. It even beats simply buying and holding the market on both return and worst fall at once, which almost nothing we have tested does.

Here is the part worth understanding, because it is not what we were looking for. The band is invested slightly LESS of the time than the plain rule — 79% against 81% — and still earns more. The days the plain rule sits out are days the market returns 32% a year on. The days the band sits out return 21%. The plain rule is not out too much; it is out on the wrong days.

And the bigger half was not the target at all. The plain rule's real weakness is not that it sells too eagerly in calm markets. It is that it BUYS BACK too eagerly during crashes. It chops the dot-com crash into two separate exits with a re-entry in between, and it does the same in 2008. The band holds each crash as one long exit — 633 days through the dot-com, 395 days through 2008 — and that single change is why its crash losses are roughly half.

What is left after the band is 11 spells out of the market over twenty-two years. That is the number we had been quoting all along. We have been reasoning about a tidier rule than the one we actually run.

How much to trust this. We tried hard to break it and could not. It is not a lucky setting: anything from a 1.5% to a 6% band works, which is a broad plateau rather than a knife edge. It is not one lucky crash: take 2008 out entirely and it still wins by 1.9 points, take the dot-com out entirely and it still wins by 1.4. It holds in four of five separate eras.

What it is not. This was measured on the market alone, and every strategy we build holds individual companies, so we do not yet know the band helps a real book. It was measured on the practice years, which is the stretch we have been searching in for years, so it is a promising idea and not yet a result. Nothing was recorded, nothing was spent, and no look at the untouched years was used. The honest next step is to build one strategy that carries the band and run it properly, and to let it fail if it is going to.

insights.title: A clear-break margin and checking once a month suppress the same wobbles, so doing both buys almost nothing
insights.body:
The safety rule has two separate ways of ignoring a small wobble in the market, and they do the
same job. The first is to give it a margin: don't leave until the market has fallen a clear few
percent below its one-year average, and don't come back until it has risen a clear few percent
above. The second is simply not to look very often: check once a month, and every wobble that
starts and ends inside that month is invisible whether you wanted it to be or not.

A study written earlier today measured the first one and found it excellent. It checked the market
every single day, and against a rule checked every day, adding a 3% margin earned about two points
a year more and cut the worst fall by eight points. That finding is correct about what it measured.

But no book here is checked every day. They are all checked at whatever speed they re-pick stocks —
once a month for most, once a week for a few. So this method put the margin on a book that really
holds stocks, the earnings-jump picker, and ran it at both speeds with and without the margin.

Checked once a month, the margin was worth nothing: half a point a year against it, and a worst
fall a quarter of a point deeper. Widening it to 6% made things clearly worse — two and a half
points a year of lost money and four more points of fall. No width helped.

Checked once a week, the identical margin was worth nearly five points a year and six points of
worst fall. Same book, same margin, same stretch of history. Only the checking speed differed.

So the margin is a real tool for a problem these books do not have. They already ignore small
wobbles, by only looking once a month, and once you are doing that there is very little left for a
margin to ignore.

The bigger finding is the one nobody was looking for. Simply checking monthly instead of weekly,
with no margin at all, was worth seven points a year and nearly twelve points of worst fall on this
book — far more than the margin was ever worth at either speed. That number had been sitting in the
records unexamined, because the speed at which each book checks its safety rule was never a decision
anyone made. It was inherited from how often the book happens to re-pick stocks.

Two things follow. Don't add a margin to a monthly book — it is a small, consistent cost. And treat
the checking speed as a real choice worth measuring, not a side effect of the re-picking schedule.

One practical warning that comes out of the same measurement: any count of how often the safety rule
went off is meaningless without saying how often it was being checked. The same rule over the same
history gives about eleven exits when checked monthly and over a hundred and fifty when checked
daily. Both are right. Quoting either one without its checking speed invites a false comparison.

insights.title: How often should a book read its safety gate? A dose-response ladder in the SPY-200 gate's reading interval, from weekly to yearly, on a book that holds stocks: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1996–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +37.3% at the assumed fee, +36.5% at the real fees (SPY: +32.4% and +32.4%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 23.2% and 23.8%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 2.08 and 1.98.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $25,228 and $57,243.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it would still pass every go-live check this re-run can see (the luck test is not repeated here).

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.
