insights.title: The safety gate's reading cadence turns at monthly and is worth six of the seven points a weekly book loses; past monthly it stops being a rate and becomes an accident of which calendar dates get read
insights.body:
Every book in this lab inherits how often it reads its safety rule from how often it happens to
re-pick its stocks. The allocator is only called on decision days and the market-trend switch is
read inside that call, so the trading schedule sets the reading interval as a side effect. Nobody
ever chose it. This method measured what that accident is worth and where the best setting is.

**The best setting is monthly, and the lab was already on it.** Six versions of one stock book ran
over 1996-2015 on the owner's real deposits at real fees, moving nothing but the trading schedule
and the freshness of the safety reading. Checking monthly earned 12.3% a year against the same
deposits put into the index earning 7.2%. Checking weekly earned 5.3%. Checking every three months
earned 8.8%, twice a year 12.1%, once a year 8.6%. Nothing slower than monthly beat monthly, and
every slower setting fell deeper than monthly's 23.8% — 33.6%, 30.3% and 25.6% respectively. A
safety rule read less often made the book less safe on every setting tried.

**Six of the seven points are the reading, not the picking — and that is the part that
generalises.** A third version re-picked weekly but acted on the month-end reading, reusing at
each weekly decision the exact session the monthly book read that month. It splits the gap with no
remainder: of the 7.0 points a year between monthly and weekly, 1.0 is picking stocks less often
and 6.0 is reading the safety rule less often; of the 11.7 points of worst fall, 2.3 is picking and
9.4 is reading. A fast book is not hurt mainly by churning its names. It is hurt because it reads a
deliberately slow signal — a two-hundred-day average — at a speed that signal does not move at, and
so gets twelve chances a year to flinch at noise instead of one. That weekly-picking,
monthly-reading version earned 11.3% a year with a 26.1% fall, recovering most of the advantage
without trading any less.

**Past monthly it stops being a rate and becomes a date, and this is the methodological warning.**
The slow settings read strictly nested calendar grids: December only sits inside June-and-December,
which sits inside March-June-September-December, which sits inside all twelve months. The
twice-a-year version therefore reads a strict subset of the three-month version's dates — strictly
fewer readings, every one also taken by the faster version — and it earned 3.3 points a year more
while falling 3.3 points shallower. Reading fewer times cannot by itself beat reading those same
times plus others. So the quantity being varied past monthly is not the interval; it is which
months the grid happens to land on, and across a window holding two slow crashes that is worth
several points a year of pure luck about dates. **A dose-response ladder built on a calendar anchor
stops being a dose ladder once the grid is coarse enough that a single reading can carry the
result** — and the tell is non-monotonicity in a nested family, which is logically impossible for a
genuine frequency effect. Any future ladder in a calendar interval should check nesting before
reading its shape as a dose response.

**The fee reading rules out the cheap explanation.** Reading once a year pays $37,600 in real
Gotrade fees over the twenty years against $57,200 for monthly, and still earns 3.7 points a year
less. Measured as a share of gross trading profit the slow versions are worse, not better — 15.5%
and 15.1% against monthly's 11.5% — because their profits shrank faster than their fees. Slowing
the gate is a timing story, not a cost story.

**The limit, stated plainly.** The sub-monthly half of this axis is inseparably confounded on this
chassis: a book that only acts monthly cannot act on a reading taken between its decision days,
because a reading it never acts on changes no target and no trade, so making it read weekly is
necessarily also making it trade weekly. That is a property of the simulator, not a gap in the
design, and the decomposition above is the honest route around it rather than a fix for it. And the
whole result rests on a window holding exactly two crashes, both of which unfolded over months; a
checking interval's entire job is when it notices, so nothing here speaks to a fast crash.

**What is now closed:** "read the safety gate less often" as a direction. It was live, it had a
seven-point result pointing at it, and it pays nothing past monthly on this book. **What is worth
a second host rather than a finer grid:** whether the zig-zag repeats. If it is real it will
reproduce on another book; if it is luck about dates it will scramble.

insights.title: The walk-forward folds handed three of four stretches a slow gate reading and two of those three lost: on a cadence ladder the fold headline is a reading on the selection rule, not on the method
insights.body:
The walk-forward folds pick each stretch's version by a return-to-worst-fall ratio, and that
ratio structurally favours whichever version trades least. On a ladder whose whole axis *is*
how often the book acts, that bias points at the slow end by construction — so the folds are
biased toward the arms the ladder exists to test, and the bias is not small.

**Measured on this method: three of the four stretches picked a slow reading** — the yearly one
once and the twice-a-year one twice — and only the last stretch picked the monthly reading the
twenty-year result says is best. **Two of those three slow picks lost to the index.** The single
slow pick that won was the stretch containing the 2008 crash, where any safety rule at all wins
and the choice of reading interval is not what did the work. The one stretch that picked the
monthly reading won.

So the headline "two of four stretches beat the index" is not a reading on the method. It is
substantially a reading on the selection rule: three of the four stretches were handed a version
this same run has just shown to be worse on money and deeper on the worst fall, and they
underperformed accordingly. A reader who takes a fold majority won by a slow rung as evidence
*for* slow gating has the causation backwards — it is first of all evidence about turnover.

This is now the second method where the bias has been seen and the third where it was expected.
M0245's folds picked its slowest rung in three of four. M0258's did not drift that way — two of
its four chose its zero rung — which is the counter-example that keeps this from being a blanket
rule. **The standing instruction is to read the folds arm by arm whenever the method's axis is
turnover-adjacent, and never to read the headline count alone**, because the headline cannot
distinguish "the method is weak out of sample" from "the selection rule picked the wrong arm three
times out of four". Here it was the second, and the per-arm table is the only thing that shows it.

The lab command does not print which arm a fold picked; it prints only the count, whether the pick
was stable, the 2009-15 edge and the verdict. That per-arm reading has to be taken separately from
the recorded curves, and it should be taken for any method whose variants differ in trading
frequency.

insights.title: An under-trading control is a cheaper strategy, not a shape-matched one
insights.body:
Six of the thirteen D17-blocked control arms traded far too LITTLE -- 0.07x to 0.55x the book's
own trade count (M0227-R20 at 0.07x, M0225-R50 0.19x, M0221-R50 0.21x, M0215-HASH and
M0215-HASH-CAP4 0.34x, M0047-PLC1-MV10 and -MV20 0.55x). The mechanism was one error repeated:
the draw's hash carried no date term at all, or was re-keyed on a calendar quarter, so the
control's book changed only when the eligible pool did. A control that trades a fifteenth as
often pays a fifteenth of the fee bill, so it is not the book's shape with the identity removed
-- it is a cheaper strategy, and every margin quoted against it was a margin against a handicap.

Pre-registered direction, written into each Amendment before any result was seen: an honestly
shaped control pays the real fee bill, so it earns LESS, so the book's lead WIDENS or its deficit
NARROWS. Measured in trial_funding.mwr against SPY TR 7.188 %/yr on the same deposits:

  old control        h     old margin   new margin   moved as predicted?
  M0227-R20        0.07x      +5.220       +3.903    NO  (the control earned MORE: 7.733 -> 9.050)
  M0221-R50        0.21x      -1.090       -0.420    yes (deficit narrowed, as predicted)
  M0215-HASH       0.34x      +1.962       +2.163    yes (but by 0.20, not the predicted 0.3-1.5)
  M0215-HASH-CAP4  0.34x      +1.727       +1.613    NO  (reversed: the honest control earned more)
  M0047-PLC1-MV10  0.55x      +1.283       +3.333    yes (overshot its predicted band by 0.33)
  M0047-PLC1-MV20  0.55x      +0.533       +2.427    yes

Score: 4 of 6 arms, and 3 of 5 methods, moved in the pre-registered direction. The two misses are
at the OPPOSITE ends of the family, which is what makes them informative rather than noise.
M0227-R20's 41 trades in nineteen years were not a cheap book, they were a STALE one: twenty names
drawn in 1996 and essentially never revisited, whose concentration drag outweighed the fee bill it
avoided. Paying fifteen times the fees to redraw the same blind book was worth +1.32 points a
year. So on that chassis the sticky draw's handicap ran the opposite way from the one the whole
family assumed.

M0221 and M0225 were the hardest case, because there the handicapped control already BEAT its
book (-1.09 and -0.89 pts): the family-A prediction is that the deficit narrows, and that is the
one that could have turned a losing book into a winning one. On M0221 it narrowed to -0.42 and
did NOT cross zero. M0225 was never re-drawn at all -- its chassis is cap-weighted and the twin's
draw had already missed turnover at 1.95x -- so its -0.89 is still quoted against an arm trading
0.19x as often and remains the one unrepaired sentence in the set.

One consequence to state rather than bury: M0047-EQ now has NO control arm at all. Its only two
placebos were size-weighted arms the ladder mis-aimed at it by first-declared, and both were
replaced by arms aimed at MV10 and MV20 where they belong. So the standing sentence about EQ's
+3.80-point lead over its placebo is WITHDRAWN rather than re-measured: it was never supported by
a correctly-aimed control. A method arm with no placebo produces an empty findings tuple and is
not refused, so this is consistent with D17 and is not a gap to be filled with a third arm.

Source: docs/plans/HANDOVER_20261019-the-honest-control.md.

insights.title: An over-trading control's handicap is arbitrary, not a fee drag of known sign
insights.body:
Seven of the thirteen D17-blocked control arms traded far too MUCH -- 2.25x to 4.41x on trades and
1.99x to 5.20x on turnover (M0208-HASH-N20 at 4.41x/5.20x, M0243-NEAR20-R 3.01x/2.98x, M0201's two
seeds 2.26-2.27x, M0202's three 2.25x). The mechanism is the mirror image of family A: the draw
was re-keyed on the MONTH using m0187.draw(seed, symbol, data_date), so the whole control book was
redrawn at every decision while the real book's ranking persisted. M0243's own file records the
overshoot in prose -- "M0227's own placebo used a sticky hash order and traded 41 times in twenty
years ... this one is redrawn each month" -- so the author saw family A, corrected by hand, and
landed in family B. One sentence, two errors, and the lesson is that the re-key period must be
DERIVED from the book it controls, never chosen.

Pre-registered direction: an over-trading control over-pays its fees, so an honestly shaped
replacement earns MORE, so the book's lead NARROWS or REVERSES. Measured in trial_funding.mwr
against SPY TR 7.188 %/yr:

  old control             h      old margin   new margin   moved as predicted?
  M0202-PLC1-HALF       2.25x      +1.352       +3.616     NO  (widened 2.263)
  M0202-PLC2-HALF       2.25x      +3.089       +3.803     NO  (widened 0.714)
  M0202-PLC1-HALF-FAST  2.25x      +0.760       +3.531     NO  (widened 2.771)
  M0201-PLC2-MV10       2.26x      +1.479       +2.475     NO  (widened 0.996)
  M0201-PLC1-MV10       2.27x      -0.712       +2.395     NO  (widened 3.107, sign flipped)
  M0243-NEAR20-R        3.01x      +6.068       +1.619     yes (narrowed 4.449)
  M0208-HASH-N20        4.41x      +5.872       +4.346     yes (narrowed 1.526)

Score: 2 of 7 arms and 2 of 4 methods moved in the pre-registered direction -- and the split by
handicap ratio is perfect: every arm at 2.25-2.27x widened, both arms at 3.01x and above narrowed.
The tempting reading is a single crossover where churn stops paying for itself somewhere between
2.27x and 3.01x. THAT READING WAS TESTED ACROSS ALL THIRTEEN ARMS AND IS NOT SUPPORTED. Three
things refute it. (1) Family A's signs contradict it four times out of six: under one curve, the
stickiest arm in the lab (M0227-R20 at 0.07x) should show the largest POSITIVE move of all and it
shows -1.318; and M0047's arms put the curve's peak below 0.55x while M0202's put it above 2.25x,
which no one curve can do. (2) The seed noise at a FIXED handicap is as large as the whole effect:
M0202's two seeds, same book, same guard, same 2.25x, differ by 1.55 points of move and M0201's by
2.11, against a between-group gap of 2.24. (3) It is a two-chassis-versus-two-chassis split, not
seven arms versus two; a random 2/2 assignment lands this way with probability 1/6.

What all thirteen arms DO support is not a direction but a collapse of variance. The handicapped
controls earned 4.381% to 11.381% a year (sd 1.918); the honest ones earn 6.047% to 9.532% (sd
0.988) -- 3.77x less variance. On the two chassis carrying two seeds, the handicapped seeds sit
2.190 and 1.737 points apart and the honest ones 0.079 and 0.187: 27.6x and 9.3x tighter. A
handicapped control is not a weaker or a stronger opponent. It is an ARBITRARY one, arbitrary to
within about seven points a year, which is larger than any margin in this set. That is why two
phases measuring faithfully reached opposite conclusions, and it is why there is no correction
factor for a margin quoted against a mis-shaped control -- only a re-draw.

M0208 was the arm most at risk: +5.87 pts was the lab's biggest quoted placebo margin and it was
quoted against an opponent trading 4.41x as often. It now reads +4.346 -- and that is PROVISIONAL
and a LOWER BOUND, because the honest control still trades only 0.73x, so a correctly-shaped one
would pay the rest of the fee bill and earn less than 9.532. The method's own 2-point success
condition stays PASS either way.

M0243 is the one that broke: its own written condition was "NEAR20 must beat its placebo by 2 or
more points a year", it passed at +6.068 against a 3.01x opponent, and against an honest one it
reads +1.619 and FAILS. Its analysis claim that the blind draw was "paying the same fees" is
measurably false and is withdrawn with it.

Source: docs/plans/HANDOVER_20261019-the-honest-control.md.

insights.title: D17 now supersedes: an honest control retires the handicapped one it replaced
insights.body:
D17 refused a method on any recorded control arm outside [0.50, 2.00] on trades or turnover, and a
recorded arm is recorded forever -- trials carries append-only triggers. So the remedy D17's own
refusal message names ("re-draw it and amend") could never clear the refusal it caused: nine
dev-eligible methods would have stayed blocked by an arm that had already been replaced.

The rule now has a supersession clause. A REFUSE or WARN finding is superseded -- reported, never
dropped -- when the same method holds another placebo arm that is itself clean on both axes AND
that NAMES it in its own pre-registered declaration (Candidate.supersedes, read duck-typed through
control_shape.SUPERSEDES_ATTR). refusals() excludes it; `lab control` still prints it with its
ratios, names the arm that superseded it, and prints that arm's own resolved target beside it
where the two differ.

DECLARED, and deliberately not inferred from the target. "Another clean placebo on the same
target_id" was the obvious rule and it fails in both directions on these very nine. Too strict:
the <target-id>-PLC naming re-points a re-drawn arm at the book it actually controls, so
M0047-MV10-PLC resolves to M0047-MV10 while the arm it replaces resolves, on the ladder's weakest
rung, to M0047-EQ -- target equality would have left M0047 and M0202 blocked after every
measurement was taken. Too loose: M0215-HASH and M0215-HASH-CAP4 both resolve to M0215-CTRL, so
one honest control of CTRL would have excused an arm whose job is to price what a cap does -- and
the measurement shows exactly why that would have been wrong, since CAP4-PLC earns 0.268 points a
year MORE than CTRL-PLC. A resolution the module itself labels a guess is not a fact to build a
gate rule on; a declaration written before any result exists is.

Measured outcome, 2026-10-20, read-only: ten of the fourteen old arms are superseded and four are
not. The four that are not give four distinct causes, and only one of them is a mistake of any
kind:
  - M0221: structural. Turnover on a cap-weighted book is a property of the weight VECTOR, not the
    names. M0221-E50 pays 1.60x turnover holding C50's exact names and recording its exact 360
    trades; the re-drawn control pays 1.95x on 1.03x name changes.
  - M0201: a near miss. 0.79410 turnover against a 0.80000 bar, 0.0059 short, on one of two seeds
    -- the other seed landed at 0.839 and did supersede.
  - M0208: the entry-count estimator. The only miss on the TRADES axis in the whole set: one
    unrolled step of a keep band off a freshly-derived top-N under-counts the churn of a band
    whose held set has drifted, measured at 0.487x over 169 decisions and uniform across eras.
  - M0225: never drawn. Its twin's draw had already missed on the identical chassis, so invariant
    13 stopped the phase rather than spending a run to measure the same structural miss twice.

What this deliberately does NOT change: the bands do not move (WARN_BAND stays 0.80-1.25,
REFUSE_BAND stays 0.50-2.00); a `warn` SUPERSEDER does not excuse anything, which is exactly what
keeps M0201, M0208 and M0221 refused; an arm that declares nothing excuses nothing, which is every
arm the lab held before this batch; an unresolved or unrecorded arm is still never a refusal; and
there is still no override. A test asserts the clause is a no-op on the lab as it stood before any
honest control existed -- all nine still failed D17 then, and no arm declared anything at all.

And the line that keeps this honest: unblocking D17 promoted nothing and made nothing promotable.
hardgate.check tests the walk-forward folds BEFORE D17, so for M0201, M0221 and M0225 the live
D17 refusal is inert -- it is never the sentence lab promote prints. Of the nine, only M0208 has
D17 as its operative clause, and behind D17 stands the kin rule (M0002 read test-failed). Every
one of the nine is still refused today, eight of them on the fold majority. What the clause buys
is that the lab can never again be in a state where a recorded, append-only arm blocks a book that
has already replaced it -- and it buys it for the price of no method ids at all.

Source: lab/hardgate.py (D17), lab/control_shape.py, docs/plans/HONEST_CONTROL_REDRAW_PLAN.md.

insights.title: A derived churn beats a hand-chosen re-key period, at both poles at once
insights.body:
The lab's previous best shape-matched placebo was M0241's cohort mirror (m0241.placebo_book): for
each trailing calendar month it counted how many eligible members really split that month and drew
that many names in a hash order seeded on that month. Its own docstring claimed the monthly draws
were stable enough that turnover matched. Measured, it lands at 1.372x trades and 1.131x turnover
-- inside the refuse band but OUTSIDE the 0.80-1.25 match band. So the state of the art was a
warn, and a rule that merely imitated it would not have cleared the bar.

control_draw.py derives the churn instead of imitating it: at each decision session it recomputes
the real arm's own selection at this and at the previous decision session, takes the entry count e
as the size of the set difference, keeps n - e of its own held names in a date-free hash order,
and draws e fresh names from the same eligible pool -- with every non-held name sorted ahead of
every just-dropped holding, so a name the book has just dropped is never taken straight back. The
entry count per rebalance is matched BY CONSTRUCTION, not empirically, which is why it holds at
both poles of the failure rather than at one.

Measured on the two poles, where the hand-chosen draws read 0.07x/0.12x and 3.01x/2.98x:
  M0227-S20-PLC      0.99x trades  0.99x turnover
  M0243-NEAR20-PLC   1.03x trades  1.03x turnover
Across all thirteen re-drawn arms, ten land inside 0.80-1.25 on both axes, with trade ratios from
0.95 to 1.03 and turnover ratios from 0.84 to 1.03 -- against M0241's 1.372x.

The three that miss say where the rule reaches and where it does not, and all three misses are
measurements rather than failures:
  - Equal-slot chassis: it works on both axes, because turnover follows the trade ratio
    arithmetically. Seven of the thirteen arms are of this kind and all seven land ok.
  - Weight-varying chassis: it closes the TRADE axis and not the TURNOVER axis. A blind draw from
    a sized pool is flatter than the real top-N, so its weights cross the book engine's
    1%-of-equity resize band at a different rate on the same names. M0221-E50 pays 1.60x turnover
    on identical names and identical trades; M0221-C50-PLC pays 1.95x on 1.03x name changes, and
    M0201's two seeds land at 0.794 and 0.839 -- the same residual in the LOW direction, with two
    seeds of one rule straddling the bar.
  - Books whose churn cannot be reconstructed from one unrolled step of their keep band:
    matched_names has no record of what the real book held, so it re-derives the previous held set
    from the plain top-N. A freshly-taken top-20 is ranked 1-20 and a band that drops a name only
    past rank 40 drops almost none of it, while the real held set has drifted toward the edge and
    falls out far faster. Replayed over all 169 of M0208's decisions: 304 estimated entries
    against the real book's 624, 0.487x, uniform across 1996-2002, 2003-2008 and 2009-2015 (0.444
    / 0.509 / 0.500). The replay reproduces the real 624 exactly, so the diagnostic is faithful.

The transferable rule: a control's re-key period must be derived from the book it controls, each
rebalance, from that book's own calendar. Choosing the period by hand produced BOTH families of
failure in this lab -- sticky at 0.07x and churny at 5.20x -- from the same author correcting the
first by hand and overshooting into the second.

And what a matched draw is worth, beyond clearing a gate: it makes the opponent DEFINED. The
thirteen handicapped controls earned 4.381% to 11.381% a year (sd 1.918); their thirteen honest
replacements earn 6.047% to 9.532% (sd 0.988), 3.77x less variance. On the two chassis carrying
two seeds of one control, the handicapped seeds sit 2.190 and 1.737 points apart and the honest
ones 0.079 and 0.187. What an honest control buys is not a better margin in a known direction --
it is a margin whose opponent is not arbitrary.

Source: engine/src/seer_engine/lab/control_draw.py,
docs/plans/HANDOVER_20261019-the-honest-control.md.

insights.title: Past monthly, is a safety gate's reading speed real or is it just which month you happen to look? The same reading interval at different calendar dates, on a second book: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.6% on the usual history, +10.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.7% and 20.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −3.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 1 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A safety rule checked twice a year gives a different answer depending on which two months you pick
insights.body:
The lab keeps a safety rule that sells everything when the US market drops below its own two-hundred-day average. Until this week nobody had ever chosen how often to look at it; each strategy inherited whatever rhythm it happened to buy stocks on. Last week's run found that looking once a month beats looking once a week by a wide margin, and that looking less often than monthly gave jumpy, contradictory answers.

This run found out why, and it is not what anyone expected. Take one strategy and have it check the safety rule exactly twice a year. Check it each June and December and the owner's money grows 10.6 percent a year. Check it each March and September instead -- the same number of looks, the same rule, the same strategy, the same fees -- and it grows 7.4 percent. Three and a fifth points a year, from nothing but the choice of month.

For comparison, the entire question of how often to look -- every month against four times a year against twice against once -- moves the same strategy by only two and a fifth points. So which month you look is worth about half again as much as how often you look.

It is starker on the downside. Check the rule once a year each December and the strategy's worst fall was nineteen percent. Check it once a year each June and the worst fall was twenty-seven percent. Eight points of extra damage, from moving the date six months.

The reason is plain once you see it. A safety rule checked rarely is a stale promise. The stretch of history we can test contains exactly two market crashes, both of them slow ones. A sparse schedule either happens to have a check date shortly before one of those falls -- in which case it stepped aside and looks brilliant -- or it does not, in which case it rode the fall all the way down and only noticed months later. That is luck about the calendar, not skill about markets, and it cannot be known in advance.

Two things make this trustworthy rather than a curiosity. First, the same pattern appeared on a strategy picked by a completely different rule from last week's, and on the market index alone with no stock picking in it at all. Second, re-running every version with the failed and delisted companies put back barely moved it: the gap between the two twice-a-year schedules widened slightly, from 3.2 points to 3.4. The effect is about timing, and timing does not care which companies were held.

The practical conclusion is short. The only schedule that was reliably best was the one that checks every month: it earned the most, fell the least and had the best ratio of gains to losses, all at the same time, against all five sparser schedules. Everything slower is a lottery ticket. And the lab has been checking every month by accident since its very first test.

insights.title: If a rule sits on a calendar grid, part of its result is the grid
insights.body:
Two runs in two days have now measured the same thing from opposite directions, and the shape they share is bigger than the safety rule they were both about.

A rule that fires on calendar dates -- the last trading day of March, of June, of every second month -- is not only a rule. It is a rule plus a grid, and the grid has its own result. This week the grid was worth more than the rule's own setting: moving which month the safety check falls on changed the owner's money by three and a fifth points a year and the worst fall by eight points, while changing how often it fired changed them by less.

That raises a question the lab has never asked of anything else it runs, and it has plenty of candidates. Several strategies re-pick stocks monthly. Several measure a company's recent calm or recent strength over a window that ends at a month end. One reads the dividend calendar. Every one of those is standing on a grid somebody chose without thinking about it, usually because a month is a convenient unit for a human.

The test is cheap and it is sharp: take a rule that currently fires on calendar dates and have it fire a fixed number of trading days apart instead, with no calendar anywhere in it. Then slide the starting point. If the spread of answers collapses, the calendar was doing the damage and the fix is to stop using it. If the spread is just as wide, then the problem is not the calendar at all, it is that the rule is being asked too rarely to have an opinion, and the answer is to ask it more often.

Either result is worth having, and the second one is the more likely. The reason to run it anyway is that we would then know which of the two sentences to write down, and right now the lab has only measured one grid on one kind of rule and could easily over-generalise from it.

There is a related and uncomfortable implication worth stating plainly. Any result the lab has ever recorded for a rule that fires on a calendar grid carries an unknown amount of this effect inside it. That does not make those results wrong. It means that when two versions of a strategy differ only in a schedule, the difference between them is not automatically information, and the honest way to find out is to run the same schedule at a different starting point and see how much the answer moves on its own.

insights.title: A strategy can pass the luck test and still be a lottery ticket
insights.body:
The lab deflates every result by how many things it has tried, and publishes the answer as a number that has to clear nine tenths before a strategy is taken seriously. Two of this run's six versions cleared it: checking the safety rule every month scored 0.956, and checking it each June and December scored 0.945.

The second one should not be trusted, and this run is the reason why.

The June and December schedule is one draw from a set of schedules this very method has just measured. Its siblings -- the same number of checks a year, on different months -- are spread across more than three points a year of the owner's money. The luck test asks whether a result looks too good to be chance given how many things the lab has tried. It cannot ask whether the particular version that scored well was the lucky corner of a dial whose spread we happen to have measured. Here we did measure it, and the spread is larger than the lead.

So a result that clears the luck bar can still be a ticket rather than an edge, if the thing it varies on is something nobody could have chosen in advance. The lab's other defences caught it this time for an unrelated reason -- the rolling out-of-sample check won only two of its four stretches, which blocks promotion outright -- but that was luck too.

The habit worth forming is simple, and it costs nothing. Before believing any version of a strategy that beats its siblings, ask whether the thing that distinguishes it is something a person could have decided beforehand on a reason. A number of stocks held, a length of history measured, a size of company: yes, those can be argued from first principles. Which calendar month a check lands on: no. If the answer is no, the lead is not an edge however good the deflated score looks, and the right move is to take the version with the dullest, most obvious setting.

insights.title: A control matched on trades and turnover is still not return-neutral: it re-balances monthly and the book it controls never trims
insights.body:
Two books were drawn this week that match the book they control on both of the things the
lab checks: how often it trades, and how much money it moves. One of them, against the top
fifty by company size, matches to within one per cent on both axes. It then earned four
points a year MORE than the book it was drawn to test.

That is not evidence that picking names blindly beats ranking them by size, and nobody
should read it that way.

The reason is in how the two books hold their money, which is the one thing nobody matched.
A blind control hands each of its fifty names a slot decided once, by a fixed rule, and it
re-imposes those slots every month. So every month it sells a little of whatever went up
and buys a little of whatever went down. The book it controls does the opposite by
construction: a book weighted by company size lets its biggest companies grow into bigger
slots and never trims them. Re-balancing like that is a source of return in its own right,
quite separate from which names are held.

This lab has priced that effect independently, with no control in it at all. An equal-weight
version of the same top fifty holds the IDENTICAL fifty names and records the IDENTICAL 360
trades as the size-weighted one, and earns 6.9% a year against 5.6% - one and a quarter
points, from the weighting arrangement alone, with names and trade count held fixed. The new
control is that same effect with a steeper and stickier ladder behind it.

Two more things the shape check does not match, and neither is small:

- How much money is actually invested. The control sits 88% invested against the book's 81%.
  Six points more money at work, over twenty years, is worth a few tenths of a point by
  itself.
- What the trading costs. At turnover matched to within one per cent, the control still paid
  about one and a half times the book's fee bill, because turnover is measured as money
  moved against average equity while the broker charges a minimum per order, and the control
  spreads the same money across differently-sized trades.

So: matching trades and turnover is necessary and it is demonstrably not sufficient. A
control that matches both can still differ from its book in how it holds its money, how much
of it is invested, and what it pays to trade. When a margin against a shape-matched control
is published, say which of those three were matched and which were not.

insights.title: A fair opponent needs two rules on two axes, and the weight one was never buildable as a single shared rule
insights.body:
A fair opponent for a strategy has to match it on two separate things, and the lab had been
trying to buy both with one rule. It cannot be done, and this set measured why three
different ways.

The lab's matched draw is a rule about NAMES: given a real book, it works out how many names
that book takes in each month and hands the blind opponent the same amount of churn. The
original requirement asked for one reusable rule of that kind to fix everything. Here is why
one rule was never available.

FIRST, how much money a book moves is not a question about names at all. The equal-weight
version of the top fifty holds the identical fifty names and records the identical 360
trades as the size-weighted version, and still moves 1.6 times as much money. No rule
deciding WHICH names an opponent holds can reach that, however cleverly the churn is
derived.

SECOND, a shared piece of code cannot work out the weights. Every book computes its own
slots its own way - one by company size under a ceiling, one by size under a different
ceiling, one by sizing each company separately and splitting share classes. A shared rule
has no way to produce any of those. What can be shared is the ASSIGNMENT: the book hands
over its own list of slot sizes with the names stripped off, and the shared rule decides
which of the opponent's names gets which slot.

THIRD, and this one is new and was measured rather than argued: the books do not even agree
on which direction needs fixing. On the top-fifty-by-size book, the blind opponent was
handing a brand-new name almost twice the slot the real book gives a brand-new name, and
that one fact accounted for essentially all of its excess trading. On the bond-like
size-weighted book, the opponent's new-name slot was already right - 0.97 of the book's. So
a rule that repairs the first HARMS the second: applied there it takes a compliant opponent
from 0.80 to 0.74 and pushes it out of the band it was already inside. A weight rule's scope
is per-book by measurement, not only by construction.

What DOES work, and shipped: one shared assignment contract, with each book supplying its
own slot list - the same arrangement the name rule already has, where five different books
each hand it their own slot count, sector cap or keep band. By the standard already in force
in that module, one shared contract plus a thin per-book adapter IS one reusable rule. On
the book it was built for it took the opponent's money movement from 1.90 times the book's
to 1.011 times - closing 98.8% of the excess, on identical names and within 1.003 of
identical trades.

So the honest shape of the answer is two rules on two axes: a name rule and a weight rule,
in two modules. A future set should not spend effort trying to collapse them into one.

insights.title: An under-shaped control's margin is an estimate of unknown sign, never a floor
insights.body:
This supersedes nothing and confirms two rows already in this journal, from a direction
neither of them could see.

The paper-gains book's lead over a meaningless book was published as "at least 4.3 points a
year - provisional, and a floor rather than a measurement". The word "floor" was doing real
work and it had an argued mechanism behind it: the only opponent the lab could draw at the
time traded a quarter less often than the book, so it under-paid the broker; a correctly
busy opponent would pay the full fee bill, earn less, and the true lead could therefore only
be WIDER than 4.3.

The correctly busy opponent has now been drawn. It trades 596 times against the old
opponent's 455 and the book's 624, and it matches the book on both axes. It earned 10.1% a
year against the old opponent's 9.5%. It earned MORE, not less. The lead is 3.7 points -
BELOW the floor.

The mechanism is measured false. On this book, how much a blind draw happens to earn varies
by more than the whole fee difference between 455 and 596 trades. The fee argument was
sound as far as it went; it was simply the smaller of the two effects, and the larger one
has no sign.

Two rows in this journal reached the same conclusion from the opposite end: an under-trading
control is a cheaper strategy rather than a shape-matched one, and an over-trading control's
handicap is arbitrary rather than a fee drag of known sign. That second one was drawn from
thirteen arms across nine books. This is a fourteenth, on the under-trading side, and it is
the first time the prediction was written down before the run and then scored.

The rule to carry forward:

    A margin measured against a control that does not match its book's shape is an estimate
    of unknown sign. It is not a floor, it is not a ceiling, and it is not conservative.

So never write "at least" in front of such a number. Write the number, say which axis the
control misses and by how much, and say plainly that the true figure may be larger or
smaller. If a sentence already in the lab calls a control-shape caveat a floor or a bound,
it is suspect by this argument and should be re-read.

insights.title: A shape ratio across two research-store vintages is not a comparison until it is re-measured in one sweep
insights.body:
A control is always drawn and run LATER than the book it controls - often weeks later,
sometimes months. The research store is rebuilt in between. So by default the lab compares a
control measured against one vintage of the price data with a book measured against another,
and calls the ratio a shape check.

How widespread: twelve distinct research-store fingerprints across the 862 recorded trials,
and ten of the fifteen recorded book-against-control comparisons cross a boundary. This is
structural, not an accident of one batch.

The important part is what it costs, because that was measured on four books this week
rather than assumed, and the answer is that it varies enormously:

- On the paper-gains book: EXACTLY ZERO. Re-running the book and both its controls in one
  sweep on one store reproduced every recorded figure to every digit, money included - the
  book's return came back as 0.1387873198052101 against a recorded 0.13878731980521. That
  book names only one market series and reads its members through a screen, which is about
  as insensitive to a store rebuild as a book gets.
- On the bond-like size-weighted book: 0.0067 of ratio - and it flipped a verdict. That
  book's control was published as missing the match band by 0.0059. Re-measured in one
  sweep it reads 0.8008 and is INSIDE the band. The "near miss" was measurement error, not
  draw error. It holds its names directly and it sat on a band edge, which is exactly where
  a boundary is decisive.
- On the top-fifty-by-size book: 0.22 points of MONEY. The book's recorded return is 5.63%
  a year on one store and 5.85% re-run on the current one. No verdict turned on it, but a
  published margin would move by that much depending on which is quoted.
- On its repaired twin: the whole of the difference. The twin exists to measure a share-count
  repair, and the two books' recorded returns differ - 5.63% against 5.85%. On the shared
  current store they are identical to four decimal places on every column: same trades, same
  turnover, same money. The difference still printed between those two pages is a difference
  between two vintages of the DATA, not between two books. A reader subtracting one page's
  figure from the other's is measuring a store rebuild.

So the rule is narrower than "every cross-store number is wrong", and the narrow version is
the one that survives:

    A shape ratio or a margin computed across two store fingerprints is not a comparison
    until it has been re-measured in one sweep. Whether re-measuring moves it is
    book-dependent and must be measured, not assumed.

And the reason this is worth more than the one verdict it moved: the store fingerprint is
recorded on every single trial, so a cross-boundary comparison is MECHANICALLY DETECTABLE.
The shape check could refuse one, or flag it, instead of quietly reporting it as a number.
That is a change to the shape checker and a plan set of its own - it was deliberately not
attempted here.

insights.title: A blind opponent's churn must be read off a replayed held set, not a freshly-taken one, and the market switch is the bigger half
insights.body:
To draw a fair blind opponent, the lab has to know how many names the real book takes in
each month. It was estimating that by taking a fresh top-N at the previous month end and
asking how many of those names would have survived into this month. That stand-in is too
fresh: a just-taken top twenty is ranked 1 to 20, and a book that only drops a name once it
falls past rank 40 almost never drops one from there. A REAL held set has accumulated names
that drifted toward the edge, and it sheds them far faster.

Measured on the paper-gains book over 169 monthly decisions: the estimator read 304 entries
where the real book takes 624. Just under half.

The fix is to replay the book's own rule backwards a couple of steps instead of guessing -
reconstruct what it actually held at the previous decision. Two steps is enough and more
buys nothing: the estimate goes 0.72 of the truth at one step, 0.95 at two, and then wanders
inside 0.94 to 0.96 all the way out to eight steps. Two steps costs 305 bars of history
against a 473-bar ceiling, leaving 168 spare.

The 320 missing entries split three ways, and only one of the three is what anybody was
looking for:

- 44% was the market switch. This book sits in cash for 69 of the window's 238 months, and
  the old stand-in scored a phantom top twenty at the previous month end regardless. On the
  nine decisions that follow a cash month it read 38 entries where the truth is a complete
  180-name refill. A backward replay closes this for free, because the chain empties itself
  on a cash month exactly as the real book does. Nobody had separated this before and it is
  the largest single piece.
- 43% was the freshness problem the fix was proposed for.
- 13% is a different defect entirely, and no replay depth closes it: every book reads
  TODAY'S membership list when scoring an earlier date. It is worth 0.067 of ratio here and
  no more than 0.046 on any other book measured. It is carried forward unrepaired.

And the measurement that mattered most for cost: on eight of the nine books, the old
estimator was already right - ratios from 0.988 to 1.001, and for the four whose real books
cannot read their own holdings the replay returns identically 1.000 at every depth from one
to fifteen. The shadow was needed on exactly one book of nine. Measuring every book before
building anything is what kept this from being eight unnecessary re-draws.

insights.title: Three checks that carry no information: a digest test that passes under the edit it guards, a trade count that agrees by construction, and a refusal the gate never prints
insights.body:
Three things this set found that look like checks and are not. Each was verified by trying
to break it.

ONE. The test that is supposed to catch a changed draw does not catch it. Every recorded
arm stores a digest of its configuration, and a test asserts every recorded configuration
still digests to its recorded digest. That reads like protection for the draw rule. It is
not: the digest is built from the rule names, the allocator id and the parameter fields, and
a module BODY is outside it entirely. Two perturbations were applied to the shipped draw -
one changing the order in which names survive, one changing the order they are filled in
under a cash shortage - each of which silently rewrites all thirteen recorded arms. Under
both, that test PASSED, and so did the other forty-five in the three relevant modules. A
golden-vector test pinning the rule's actual output for a fixed input was added, and it is
now the only thing in the tree that goes red when the frozen path is edited.

TWO. The trade count is not an independent check on an entry count. A book's recorded trade
count counts CLOSED ROUND TRIPS. On a book that holds a constant number of names, every
entry eventually becomes exactly one round trip, so the entry count and the trade count
agree BY CONSTRUCTION. The paper-gains book's 624 entries and 624 trades looked like
evidence somebody had confused the two quantities; it is a tautology and carries no
information either way. The 624 was confirmed instead by a forward replay that never reads
the trials table.

THREE. A refusal the gate holds may be one it never prints. The hard gate tests its clauses
in order and stops at the first failure: fold count, then fold majority, then the chosen
variant's own folds, then the survivorship fall, then the control-shape rule, then kin. So a
book that loses its walk-forward folds can carry a live control-shape refusal that is never
the sentence the gate reports, and clearing it changes nothing about that book. Of the four
books carrying one at the start of this set, three were inert in exactly that way. The
fourth - the only one whose operative clause really was the shape rule - had the kin rule
standing immediately behind it, refusing it for a different reason. Read the shape refusals
directly rather than inferring them from the message.

The common shape: a check is only a check once you have watched it fail. All three of these
were believed to be informative, and none of them was.

insights.title: Is a safety gate's slow-reading spread the calendar's fault or rarity's? The same gate read every N trading days, with the start slid across the period: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.6% on the usual history, +10.6% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 18.7% and 20.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −3.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 2 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Looking at a rule rarely does not make the decision worse. It makes you stuck with it.
insights.body:
The safety switch this lab uses turns a book's holdings on or off depending on whether the market is above its long-run average. How often a book asks that question has been measured three times now, and this run finally found the mechanism behind every one of those numbers, in a single date.

On the first of April 2002, two versions of the same book made exactly the same mistake: both looked at the switch, both saw a market that had briefly recovered, and both bought back in, a few weeks before the worst and final stretch of that bear market. One of those versions looks every month. It changed its mind four weeks later and the mistake cost it almost nothing. The other version looks roughly twice a year. Its next scheduled look was six months away, so it rode the whole decline down.

That one difference is the gap between a worst fall of 18.7 percent and one of 41.8 percent, on books that are otherwise identical in every respect — same holdings, same rule, same fees, same deposits.

So the penalty for consulting a rule rarely is not that you make worse judgements when you do consult it. The judgement was identical. The penalty is the length of time you are committed to a judgement you can no longer revise. That is worth remembering well beyond this one switch: any rule a book checks on a schedule carries a hidden cost that is not about the rule's quality at all, but about how long a wrong answer is allowed to stand.

It also explains why these measurements have been so jumpy. Across twenty years there were about forty of these scheduled looks and only two long market slides, so in practice one or two looks per version land near a slide and decide the whole result. Comparing two versions is really comparing one or two lucky or unlucky moments, which is why the same comparison read 3.2 points one night and 1.1 the next. Treat any single number of that kind as one measurement, never as a quantity.

insights.title: Counting in trading days is not an escape from the calendar, and the lab almost fooled itself with one
insights.body:
This run was supposed to settle whether the calendar itself was causing trouble. The plan was to replace a rule that fires at the end of certain months with one that fires every 126 trading days, on the reasoning that a count of trading days has no calendar in it.

It has. The New York exchange ran between 248 and 254 sessions in each full year of the period studied, averaging 251.8. So 126 trading days is half a year to within a fifth of a day, and a rule firing every 126 trading days never drifts away from where it started. Measured across twenty-two years, one such rule fired only ever in June, July and December. Another fired only ever in March, April, September and October. It is a calendar rule with extra steps.

Had the run gone ahead as planned it would have compared a calendar rule against a calendar rule, found no difference, and announced that the calendar does not matter — a conclusion that would have been true by construction rather than by evidence, and that nobody reading it afterwards would have been able to tell apart from a real finding.

The fix was to use a spacing that does not divide the trading year. At 131 trading days the rule drifts about ten days a year and sweeps through all twelve months over the period. The honest comparison is then between that and the locked version, and it is the comparison the run actually made.

The general lesson is cheap to apply and worth applying every time: before writing any rule that fires every N trading days, divide 252 by N. If the answer is close to a whole number, the rule is tied to the calendar whether it mentions one or not. Checking this costs no data, no compute and no time — it is arithmetic about the exchange's opening days — and in this case it was the difference between a measurement and a tautology.

insights.title: The cheap SPY-only preview this lab builds before a run is a feasibility check, not a forecast
insights.body:
Before each of the last few runs on the market safety switch, a cheap preview was built first: the switch alone, applied to the broad market index, with no stock picking, no fees and no deposits. Its job is to check that a new rule can be computed at all and to give a rough sense of what to expect. It has quietly been doing a second job it is not fit for, which is predicting what the real book will do.

This run put three of those predictions beside their outcomes, on one book, measured in one sweep. The preview said two versions would be 1.86 points a year apart; the real book made them 1.10. It said another pair would be 2.90 apart; the real book made them 1.07. And the previous run's preview said its pair would be 1.86 apart; that real book made them 3.21.

So the preview overstated one gap by about 1.7 times, overstated a second by 2.7 times, and understated a third by 1.7 times. It was not merely imprecise — it got the relative ordering wrong too, calling the second pair the widest of the three when it turned out to be the narrowest.

Why: the preview holds the whole market all the time or none of it, while a real book holds twenty names about seventy percent of the time and pays to trade them. The names a book happens to own when the switch flips matter as much as the flip, and the preview has no names in it at all.

What to do about it: keep building the preview, because catching an unworkable rule before spending a method on it is worth far more than it costs. But never quote one of its numbers as an expectation, and never size a prediction from it. The correct use is 'this rule computes, here is roughly the shape of it'. Any number that will be compared against anything has to come from the real, funded, fee-paying book.

insights.title: Lean, never leave: the price of risk as a weight dial with a floor that never reaches cash: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1994–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +6.0% on the usual history, +6.0% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.7% and +7.7%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 33.2% and 33.2%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.9% a year before and −3.9% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies barely move it: its yearly return changed by less than half a point. 0 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Turning a losing timing rule down cannot save it
insights.body: A timing rule that is turned down earns less AND costs less, by the same factor, so turning it down can never rescue it. The price-of-risk book was tested at four settings of a single dial: how much of the money must stay invested no matter what the signal says. At each setting it was run twice, once reading the signal the right way up and once upside down. The difference between those two is what the opinion is worth; their average, compared with simply staying invested, is what the arrangement costs. At the strongest setting the opinion was worth 3.6 points a year and the arrangement cost 5.3. At half strength both halves halved, to 1.8 and 2.5. The ratio between them barely moved: 0.68 and 0.70. Why it matters: the obvious reaction to a timing rule that loses is to use it more gently. This says that reaction is hopeless whenever the gentler version is the same rule scaled down, because scaling moves the earnings and the costs together. What to do about it: before spending a method on a gentler version of something that failed, measure the ratio once at full strength. If the opinion is worth less than the arrangement costs, no setting of the dial will fix it, and the only thing that can is an arrangement that costs nothing - which here means expressing the opinion in what you hold rather than in how much of it you hold.

insights.title: The signal did not fade after publication - the cost of using it grew
insights.body: A study from 2009 said that when insurance against market swings is unusually expensive relative to the swings that actually happen, the following months tend to be good ones to own shares. The usual fate of a published finding is that it stops working once everybody trades it. This one did the opposite. Over the years from 2009 to 2015 - after publication, and the best-covered years in the lab - reading the signal backwards lost 8.2 percent a year against the market while reading it forwards lost 1.8, so the opinion itself was worth 3.2 points a year there, nearly twice its 1.8-point average over the full twenty-two years. And yet the forward version still lost. The reason is that those same years were the longest rally in the window, so the cost of the rule stepping out of the market also doubled, from 2.5 points a year to 5.0. The signal got better and the price of using it got worse, and the price moved further. Why it matters: a rule that fails is usually written off as a faded idea or as noise, and this one is neither. It is a good opinion attached to an expensive habit. What to do about it: when a rule loses, separate what its opinion is worth from what its habits cost before deciding whether the idea is dead. Here the opinion is alive and the habit of selling to cash is what should be abandoned.

insights.title: Print what a timing rule knows apart from what its habits cost
insights.body: Every rule in this lab that steps out of the market mixes two different things: an opinion about which months are bad, and a habit of holding cash to act on it. They can be separated exactly, and cheaply, whenever a method has run a reversed arm beside its straight one. The difference between the two is twice what the opinion is worth; their average, set against simply staying invested, is what the habit costs. On the price-of-risk book those came out as plus 3.6 and minus 5.3 points a year, which says the opinion was good and the habit was worse, and that no gentler setting of the rule could ever close the gap. Why it matters: the lab has rejected a long line of market-timing rules and recorded them all as simply losing to the market. Some of them may have been good opinions wearing expensive habits, and nobody would know, because the two numbers were never printed apart. A rule whose opinion is worth more than its habit costs is a rule worth re-expressing rather than discarding. What to do about it: a small report that takes any method with a straight arm and a reversed arm and prints those two numbers side by side, across the whole window and across the years since 2009, run over everything already recorded. It would need no new backtests and no new looks at the untouched years - the numbers are already in the lab - and it would say in one page which of the rejected timing rules are dead and which were only badly dressed.

insights.title: A rule nobody chose was leaving a tenth of every wide book sitting in cash
insights.body:
When a holding drifts away from the size it is supposed to be, the simulator only trades it back once the gap is big enough to be worth a trade. The trouble was what big enough was measured against: one per cent of the whole account, rather than one per cent of the holding.

That number does not shrink as a book gets wider, and there is a one-line way to see what it means. A book of fifty names holds each one at two per cent of the account, so one per cent of the account is half the holding. A book of a hundred names can never trigger at all. In general:

    a book of N equal names has been running on a trigger of N per cent of a holding.

Twenty names, a fifth of a holding. Fifty names, half. A hundred, the whole thing.

This was measured on a deliberately dull book -- the fifty most-traded big American companies in equal amounts, no stock picking at all -- run five times with every single thing identical except that trigger. Same names, same days, same fees, same deposits. On the old rule the account sat eleven and a half per cent in cash it never chose to hold, because the monthly deposit could buy a brand new holding but could never top up one already owned. Moving the trigger onto the holding cut that to under four per cent, and a full monthly rebalance cut it to one and a half.

What it was worth, on the owner's own money: half a point a year over twenty years, and nearly a full point a year over 2009 to 2015, where it turned a book that lost to the market by four tenths of a point into one that beat it by half a point. With the failed companies put back into the data the gap gets bigger, not smaller -- one and three tenths of a point a year over the same stretch. That is unusual. Nearly everything this lab finds shrinks when the dead companies come back, and this does not, because the job the trigger is doing is getting the deposit invested, and that works whatever the names turn out to be.

What it cost: a tenth of a point a year in broker fees, and two and a half points of deeper worst fall. The deeper fall is real rather than a fee effect, and the reason is plain -- rebalancing buys whatever has fallen, so in a market that keeps grinding lower it keeps buying on the way down.

Two things follow that matter more than the number.

The twenty-name book the owner actually holds was never affected. Twenty names on the old rule is exactly the new rule, by arithmetic, and the lab has already confirmed the two match to the last decimal place. Nothing about the roster needs revisiting.

But every comparison this lab has ever drawn between a wide book and a narrow one is suspect, and not by a little. The wide one was sitting in more cash, and nobody was told. Any finding of the form holding more names earns less, taken before the rule was fixed on the twelfth of October, was measuring the trigger at least in part. They need not all be re-run, but none of them should be quoted without saying so.

Finally, the ladder saturates immediately. Going from the old rule to a fifth of a holding captures almost the whole gain; tightening to a tenth, or rebalancing fully every month, buys a third more trading for about three hundredths of a point. The rule the lab switched to is the right one and there is nothing left to win by tightening it.

insights.title: Five books that traded very differently all reported the same number of trades
insights.body:
This is a warning about a meter, and it nearly cost a day.

Five versions of one book were run, identical in every way except how far a holding may drift before it is traded back. The most patient version almost never adjusts anything. The busiest one puts every holding back to its exact share every single month. They moved noticeably different amounts of money and they earned noticeably different returns.

All five reported exactly 1,338 trades.

The reason is that the trade counter counts a name being bought and later sold -- a complete round trip. The small top-ups and trims that a drift trigger controls never open or close a position, so they are invisible to it. The picks were identical across all five versions by design, so the round trips were identical too, and the counter dutifully reported no difference at all.

A second session this week hit the same wall from the other side: a book that only ever holds part of a position reported zero trades and a blank gains-to-losses figure, and looked completely inert when it was not.

So the rule is simple and it should be applied every time: when an experiment changes how a book HOLDS its money rather than which names it picks, the trade count will tell you nothing, and a blank or unchanged one is not evidence the change did nothing. Read how much money moved over the year, and read how much of the account was actually invested rather than sitting in cash. In this run those two told the whole story -- idle cash fell by ten points across the five versions while the trade count sat perfectly still.

There is a second trap behind the first. Before the run it was predicted that the busiest version would be ruined by broker fees, because the broker charges a minimum on every order and a small adjustment is a tiny order. That prediction was wrong by a factor of about twenty: the extra fee bill was a tenth of a point a year, not several points. The arithmetic had assumed a holding worth twenty-nine dollars paying the minimum on every little adjustment -- true in the first year, and meaningless a decade later once the account had grown. The minimum-fee problem is a small-young-account problem, and a twenty-year window spends most of its life not being one. It still bites a real account today, which is the part worth keeping; what should be thrown away is the habit of pricing a twenty-year fee bill from the first year's order size.

insights.title: The drift trigger is now adjustable, but only a fixed menu of settings can reach real trading
insights.body:
A small piece of plumbing, worth recording because it will come up again.

Until today, how far a holding had to drift before the simulator traded it back was a fixed number buried in the code: there were two settings and no way to ask for a third. Measuring the question properly needed four, so the setting became a dial that any experiment can name. It was added in the way this lab adds anything to a rule that has already been used: a book that does not name a setting behaves exactly as it always did, down to the last digit, so no past result, no frozen record and no live paper strategy moved.

The limitation is in what happens next. A strategy can only be promoted to paper trading if its whole rule set is one of a fixed, named menu of combinations. The four new settings were declared inside the experiment itself rather than added to that menu, deliberately: this run was a measurement and none of its versions was ever going to be a candidate, and adding four permanent entries to a menu the owner's reminders and the website both mirror, in order to answer one question, would be the wrong trade.

The wish is therefore narrow and specific. If a future strategy wants a drift trigger of a fifth of a holding -- which this run says is the right setting and the one the lab already uses -- it is already on the menu and nothing is needed. If one ever wants a different setting, exactly one entry should be added, for that setting, at that moment, and the website's copy of the number has to be taught the dial at the same time. A guard was left in place that turns red the instant a menu entry names its own trigger, precisely so that the website cannot quietly start showing the owner the wrong figure on his trading reminders.

What should NOT happen is a menu entry per rung. This run measured four and found that three of them are worse than the one the lab already has.

insights.title: Sera 20261020-1417: three rules that were never going to pay, and one habit that was quietly costing money
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Nothing cleared the four things that would justify buying survivorship-free price history, and the first of them is where it stopped: one of the three beat the market over twenty years on paper, but it lost in two of the four later periods and trailed the market in every year from 2009 to 2015. The other two were rejected outright. No test-window look was spent; four remain spent in total, as before.

The batch asked three questions that had nothing to do with picking stocks, and that was deliberate. The lab's stock-picking ideas have been circling the same few books for weeks, so this round went after the machinery instead: when a rule is read, how hard a rule leans, and how a book holds what it already owns.

The useful thing the batch found is the third one. Every wide book this lab runs has been sitting on a trading trigger nobody chose, and it has been leaving about a tenth of the money in cash. The trigger was written as a share of the whole account, which means the more names a book holds, the further each one has to drift before anything happens -- at fifty names a holding had to lose half its value to be topped up. Putting money back to work is worth about half a point a year, nearly a full point in the modern era, and it costs about a tenth of a point in fees. It also makes the worst fall about two points deeper, because topping up means buying whatever is falling, and in a long grinding decline that is exactly the wrong instinct. The setting the lab already switched to two weeks ago captures almost all of the gain, so nothing needs changing -- but every comparison this lab ever drew between a wide book and a narrow one was partly measuring this, because the wide one was holding more cash and nobody knew. The owner's own twenty-name book is untouched: at twenty names the old rule and the new one are the same rule.

The second question was whether a market-fear signal that genuinely knows something can be made to pay by leaning gently instead of jumping to cash. It cannot, and the reason is arithmetic rather than bad luck. The signal is real -- running it upside down loses over four points a year to running it the right way up. But what the opinion is worth and what it costs to sit out of the market shrink together as you lean less, in a fixed ratio of about seven to ten. Since the cost always exceeds the gain, no amount of gentleness rescues it. That closes a follow-up that had been sitting open, and it closes it for good rather than inviting another attempt. One oddity came out of it worth remembering: over 2009 to 2015 the signal got better, not worse, but the cost of acting on it grew faster still, because those years were one long rally. The usual worry is that a published edge fades; this one sharpened while its price rose more.

The first question tidied up yesterday's headline, and the correction matters more than the method. Yesterday the lab reported that which month you read a safety switch matters more than how often, by about three points a year. Three more measurements of the same kind on the same book now read about one point. So the direction stands -- the date you happen to read on does matter -- but the size was a large draw from a wide spread, not a typical result, and it should not be repeated as three points. The same run also settled the open question behind it: the calendar is not the mechanism. Taking the calendar out of the rule entirely changed the answer by three hundredths of a point. Nothing else in the lab needs auditing for calendar effects, which was the expensive possibility.

That run also produced the clearest sentence of the batch about why reading a safety rule rarely is dangerous. It is not that you make a worse decision. It is that you are stuck with the one you made. On the first of April 2002 the monthly version and the six-monthly version made the identical mistake and bought back in just before the last leg down. The monthly one was out again four weeks later and fell nineteen per cent. The six-monthly one had to wait half a year and fell forty-two.

Gotrade's real fees did not kill anything this batch -- every method ran at the real fee schedule in fractional shares on the monthly top-up from the start, so there was no cheap version to be disillusioned about. The one fee surprise was pleasant: putting the idle cash to work costs about a tenth of a point a year in extra trading, far less than feared, because the minimum-charge-per-order problem is a small-account problem and twenty years is mostly not a small account. It still bites the owner today, at today's balance.

Directions that look dead after this batch: making a market-timing rule gentler, and hunting for the right reading schedule for a safety switch. Both have now been measured to the end. Directions that look alive: the question of whether the half-point the trading trigger releases comes from putting cash to work or from trimming winners to feed losers -- those two moved together here and nobody has separated them -- and a version of the fear signal that chooses between two funds rather than choosing how much to own, since that would make the cost zero and any real opinion would then win. Both are queued.

What would unlock the most is still the same thing it has been: price history that includes the companies that died. Three separate results this batch depended on checking against the honest tape, and one of them moved in the unusual direction -- the trading-trigger gain was bigger with the dead companies added back, not smaller, which fits because it is about deploying deposits rather than about picking names.

The gate refused one promotion this batch, on the walk-forward record rather than on family: two of four later periods won, where a strict majority is required. Seventy-four of the lab's seventy-eight paper-passing methods are now refused by that gate. A batch where nothing gets through is a finding about the lab, not an accident, and it is the same finding as last time: passing a twenty-year average is not evidence, and the gate is the only thing that has been saying so.

Next batch should stop asking the machinery questions -- three in a row was enough and they have paid out -- and go back to looking for a genuinely different signal, with the holding-structure lesson in hand: a book that never trims and a book rebalanced monthly are two different strategies even when they hold identical names on identical days, and that difference is worth more than most of the edges this lab has been chasing.

insights.title: The buy signal is firing today, on four methods, and two of the four are reading the wrong book
insights.body:
The lab has a standing rule for the one moment it is worth paying for price history that includes the companies that died: a method must pass the paper screen, must have a clean family, must win most of the later test periods, and must have earned more than the market in 2009 to 2015, the years the current history covers best. All four at once. Checked across every method today, that signal is ON, for four of them. It had been reported as never having fired, and that report was wrong.

For two of them the signal is honest. One ranks companies by a size-capped square-root rule and one is a price band on a safety switch. In both cases the number the signal read was measured on the very version the lab would actually trade, so the four conditions were met by the thing that would be bought.

For the other two it is not. The lab reads the 2009-2015 figure off whichever version of a method looked best in those years with hindsight, and that is often not the version it would actually trade. For one of the two the signal read a version that earned seven points a year more than the market, while the version that would be traded LOST three and a third. For the other the signal read a middle rung of a dose ladder that earned nearly two points, while the version that would be traded lost nearly four. So the lab is announcing 'this is the moment to buy the expensive data' on two methods whose real book was behind the market in exactly the years the test is supposed to examine.

That is the precise failure the fourth condition was written to prevent, and it is happening now rather than approaching.

The same fault also hides a good result. One method reads as a loser on its hindsight version and a winner, by over two points a year, on the version that would be traded. Reading the figure off the traded version would stop the two false alarms and start one true one.

Nothing has been bought and nothing has been promoted. The practical reading for the owner: if money were going to be spent on better price history on the strength of this signal, it should be spent on the two honest firings only, and the other two should be set aside until the figure is measured on the book that would really be held.

Related: the clause that spends a test-window look never checks WHAT version it is about either. For 19 of the 78 methods that pass the paper screen, the version the lab would formally register is a control arm -- a deliberately meaningless book kept as a yardstick -- and in one case it is a shuffled-order placebo. A proposed new rule would refuse those outright.

insights.title: Should the buy signal also ask whether the traded book won its own test periods? Yes — and asking costs nothing today
insights.body:
The lab has two ways of counting how a method did in the later test periods it had never seen. One asks how the lab's own picking rule would have fared, choosing afresh before each period. The other asks a narrower question: did the single version that would actually be registered and traded win those periods on its own. Until today the buy signal — the four conditions that together say it is worth paying for better price history — used only the first.

The question was whether to add the second. Measured across every method in the lab, the answer is yes, and it is free.

Adding it changes exactly one verdict. One method reads a majority on the first count and a minority on the second: the version that would be traded won two of its four periods while the picking rule won three. That method was already stopped this afternoon by the separate repair that made the 2009-2015 figure read the traded book instead of the flattering one, so the new condition catches it by a second route rather than for the first time. Everything currently firing survives untouched: all three of those methods win three of four periods on the traded version alone.

What matters more is what the condition must NOT do.
