If the narrower count REPLACED the broader one instead of joining it, thirteen methods would start passing — books whose traded version looks good in hindsight across all four periods while the lab's own rule, choosing without hindsight, picked something worse each time. That is precisely the trap the lab spent the day establishing: letting a method nominate its best-looking version after the results are in is not evidence, it is selection. So the two counts are an AND, never a swap.

The practical reading: the condition is worth adding because it is defence in depth, not because it is urgent. It costs no method, no look and no money today. Its value is that the next method to arrive with a flattering picking record and a weak traded book gets stopped twice instead of once.

insights.title: The signal that says 'buy the expensive data' fired for the first time, and the owner's own money says no
insights.body:
Today the lab's buy signal started firing properly. It is the conjunction the owner set as the one moment better price history is worth paying for: a method must pass the paper screen, have a clean family, win most of the later test periods, and have earned more than the market in 2009 to 2015. This morning it was firing on four methods, two of them only because of a fault that has since been repaired. After the repair it fires on three, and for the first time all three are measured on the version that would really be traded.

So the three were run over the owner's actual life as an investor: his real deposits, ten million to open and five million on the twenty-fifth of every month since April 2018, at the broker's real fees.

All three lost to simply buying the market with the same money on the same days, and not narrowly. The market would have turned his five hundred and twenty million of deposits into about 1.29 billion. The three methods reach 705 million, 705 million and 668 million. That is a shortfall of between 584 and 622 million rupiah, and a gap of thirteen to fifteen points a year.

Worse, most of what they did earn was not the strategy. Holding the exchange rate fixed, the three earn about 3.1%, 3.1% and 1.9% a year. The rest of the headline was the rupiah falling against the dollar, which would have helped any dollar asset including the market itself. One of them turned 520 million of deposits into 44.7 million of real gain over eight and a half years. Their deepest falls were 38% and 42%, against the owner's own limit of 25%.

And the three are not three. Two of them are the same book: one is a method whose zero rung switches its own feature off, which reproduces its parent exactly -- identical to four decimal places on every measure, the same 1208 trades. The third is a near relative of the same parent. So the signal is firing on two distinct books from one family, not on three independent findings.

The honest conclusion is not that the signal is broken in the way this morning's fault was broken. It is that nobody has ever checked the signal against the thing it is a proxy for. All four of its conditions are measured on history ending in 2015. It has never been asked whether a method that satisfies them goes on to beat the market with real money afterwards. The first time anyone asked, on the first three methods ever to fire honestly, the answer was no three times out of three.

Recommendation: do not buy survivorship-free price history on the strength of this firing. The rule stands and should not be overridden by hand -- but the rule has now been measured once against the outcome it exists to predict, and it missed. Before money is spent on the next firing, the signal's conditions deserve the same scrutiny the gate's fold selector got today: not whether they are computed correctly, but whether they predict anything.

insights.title: Nineteen of the lab's seventy-eight passing methods would have been registered on a book kept only to be beaten
insights.body:
Every method in this lab runs several versions of itself. Some are the idea; some are deliberately meaningless books kept alongside as a yardstick, so the idea has something honest to be measured against. The yardsticks exist to lose.

When a method is formally registered and a test-window look is spent on it, the lab picks which version to register by a ranking score. Nobody had ever checked what KIND of version that picks. Checked today across all seventy-eight methods that pass the paper screen: for forty-six it is the idea, for nine it is a middle rung of a dose ladder, for four there is no eligible version at all -- and for NINETEEN it is a yardstick. In one case it is a book whose picks are drawn in a shuffled, meaningless order.

That is the clause that spends the scarcest thing the lab has. There are four test-window looks spent out of a deliberately tiny budget, and all four failed. Had any of those nineteen reached a look, the lab would have spent one asking whether a book built to be meaningless beats the market.

Three of them were already clearing every other condition and were stopped only because a relative had failed -- luck, not design.

A new refusal now blocks this outright: a method whose registered version is a yardstick cannot be promoted. It was measured before being switched on, and it moves exactly three verdicts, none of them from refused to passing. The related repair, which makes the 2009-2015 figure read the registered version rather than whichever version flattered that era, moves the buy signal in both directions at once -- it silences two false alarms and reveals one true one that had been suppressed. Neither change was allowed to be described as purely a tightening, because that would have been false.

A separate question was examined and the answer was no: the ranking rule that picks a version afresh before each test period is NOT broken and should not be constrained, even though it chooses a yardstick in 55% of cases. Constraining it would flip only two verdicts, and both of those methods would become promotable on a NEGATIVE edge in the years the data covers best -- the precise failure the conditions exist to catch.

insights.title: Winning two of the four later test periods is not nearly passing — it is the lab's most common outcome, and the reason is one shared rule
insights.body:
The lab refuses to promote a method unless it wins most of the four later stretches of history it was never shown. Seventy-four of the seventy-eight methods that pass the paper screen are refused, and forty-five of those are refused on that count alone, with nothing wrong with their family. Most of them sit at exactly two of four.

It is tempting to read two of four as nearly there, one lucky period from passing. Measured across every method with four scoreable periods, that reading is wrong.

The periods are not equally winnable. The 2006-2008 stretch is won by 88% of the lab. The 2009-2011 stretch is won by 10%. The single most common pattern in the whole lab is to win the crash and lose the rebound, and the second most common is to win the crash, lose the rebound and win again afterwards. That shape is not a property of any one idea. It is the shared safety rule nearly every book in this lab stands on: a switch that moves to cash when the market is below its long average. It is magnificent in a crash and it gives the recovery back.

So two of four is not a near miss. It is the signature of the lab's own common ingredient, and no choice of which version to score moves a period that nine books in ten lose.

The practical consequence: stop reading the fold count as a distance from promotion. A method that wins two of four has most likely reproduced the house style rather than found anything. The methods worth attention are the ones that win the 2009-2011 stretch, because almost nothing does.

insights.title: A book can beat the market over the owner's own lifetime as an investor and still be worthless — the trading-threshold book did both in one day
insights.body:
One of today's three methods was not a strategy at all. It was a measurement: a neutral fifty-name book whose picks never change, run at five settings of the rule that decides when a holding has drifted far enough to be traded back into line. Its purpose was to price what that rule costs, and the answer was that a trigger nobody chose had been leaving about a tenth of every wide book sitting in cash.

Judged as a strategy on the lab's own twenty-year history it was rejected: all five settings lost to the market on the owner's deposits.

Then it was run over the owner's real life as an investor -- his deposits, his dates, his fees, from April 2018 -- and it BEAT the market by 290 million rupiah, ending at 1.58 billion against 1.29 billion. It was the only thing all day that looked like money, and the only one of three methods to win that comparison.

Both free checks then refused it. Scoring it on later stretches of history it had never seen: it wins one of four. Adding back the companies that died: its yearly return falls from 6.9% to 4.7% while the market's does not move at all, its lead goes from slightly behind to 2.5 points behind, its worst fall deepens from 59% to 73%, and all five of its settings earn less. Its edge in the years the data covers best goes from marginally positive to negative.

The explanation is in what the method itself measured. The setting that wins is the one that keeps money INVESTED rather than parked in cash. The 2018-2026 window was overwhelmingly a rising market, so staying invested wins -- and that is the trigger finding restated, not a discovery about picking stocks. On a window containing a long grinding decline the same setting hurts, which is exactly what the twenty-year history showed when its worst fall came out two points deeper.

The lesson is general and uncomfortable: a single window, however real and however personally meaningful, is one path. The owner's own investing lifetime is 8.5 years of mostly rising market, and a book that merely stays invested will look like skill across it. The twenty-year history and the dead-company check both said no, and they were right to.

insights.title: A dose ladder's zero rung is its parent, so two methods can fire the same signal on one book
insights.body:
When a method tests how much of something helps, it usually includes a rung where the amount is zero -- the feature switched off. That rung is not a variant of the parent book. It IS the parent book.

Measured today: a method testing a price band on the market safety switch has a zero-band rung, and that rung reproduces its parent to four decimal places on every number the lab records -- the same total return, the same yearly return, the same worst fall, the same gains-to-losses ratio, the same 1208 trades, the same share of time invested. Run over the owner's real deposits since 2018 the two end on the same rupiah: 705,364,669 each.

Why it matters beyond bookkeeping: the lab's buy signal was firing on three methods, which reads as three independent reasons to spend money on better price history. Two of them are this pair. A third is a close relative of the same parent. So three firings are two books from one family, and the apparent weight of evidence is roughly half what the count suggests.

The rule to carry: before treating several firing or eligible methods as independent, check whether one of them is another's zero rung or switched-off arm. The config digests differ -- they are registered as separate configurations with separate allocators -- so the database will not warn you. The giveaway is identical recorded numbers, and the place to look is any method whose purpose is 'how much of X helps', because such a method almost always contains its own host.

insights.title: The promotion gate, measured for the first time against the only four outcomes the lab actually knows: it catches three and misses one
insights.body:
The lab's promotion gate was built after four methods had already spent a look at the held-out window and lost. It has been argued about ever since, but never checked against those four outcomes -- the only ground truth the lab owns. Checking costs nothing, because those looks are already spent and no new peeking is involved.

The gate asks two things beyond the paper screen: did the method win most of the four later stretches of history it was never shown, and did it earn more than the market in 2009 to 2015, the years the data covers best.

Against the four known failures:
- Three of them win only two of the four stretches and trail the market in 2009-2015 by 1.4, 2.2 and 3.0 points a year. The gate refuses all three. Had it existed, three of the four looks would not have been spent.
- The fourth wins THREE of four stretches and is marginally ahead in 2009-2015, by two tenths of a point. The gate lets it through. It failed anyway.

So the gate's record against ground truth is three caught, one missed, out of four. That is far better than nothing and it is not sufficient. It also sets a realistic expectation: a method clearing the gate has not been shown to be good, only shown not to resemble three of the four books known to be bad.

The near miss is the interesting one. Its margin in 2009-2015 was two tenths of a point -- inside any reasonable noise -- while the three the gate caught were all more than a point on the wrong side. That suggests the condition is doing real work at its extremes and none at all near zero, and that a method scraping past on a tenth of a point should not be treated as having passed anything.

Read beside yesterday's result -- the three methods now clearing every condition all lost heavily to simply buying the market over the owner's own eight and a half years -- the fair summary is that the gate is a decent filter against known bad books and has never been shown to select good ones. It should keep refusing. It should not be read as an endorsement of whatever survives it.

insights.title: The promotion gate, measured against the only four outcomes the lab knows: the fold count catches three, and the 2009-2015 condition catches none
insights.body:
This replaces the previous version of this entry, which was wrong in two ways that happened to cancel into a plausible-looking conclusion. Both are worth stating, because one of them is a trap anyone re-running this check will fall into.

The lab has exactly four methods that ever spent a look at the held-out window and lost. They are the only outcomes it owns, and checking the gate against them costs nothing because those looks are already spent.

FIRST ERROR: THE NUMBERS WERE FROM THE WRONG COLUMN. The earlier version quoted 2009-2015 figures of -1.4, -2.2 and -3.0 against the fourth method's +0.2, and concluded that the three caught were each more than a point on the wrong side while the one missed scraped through on noise. Those three figures came from the column that reads whichever version of a method flattered that era with hindsight. That column was replaced yesterday: the gate now reads the version that would actually be registered and traded. On the column the gate actually uses, the figures are: no measurable edge at all for the first, -0.17 for the second, -2.02 for the third, and +0.22 for the fourth. So the second failure sits at -0.17 -- the mirror image of the one that got through, not a point away from it. The clean separation the earlier version described does not exist.

SECOND ERROR, AND THE LARGER ONE: THE 2009-2015 CONDITION CAUGHT NOTHING. The conditions are checked in order and the check stops at the first failure. The fold count is tested BEFORE the era edge. All three of the methods the gate would have refused fail on the fold count -- two of four -- and the era edge is never reached for any of them. The fourth passes the fold count, then passes the era edge, and failed its look anyway.

So the honest record is: the fold count is three-for-four, and the 2009-2015 condition is nought-for-four. The earlier version credited the gate's catches to both conditions working together. One of them did all the work.

WHAT FOLLOWS. A margin on the era edge -- requiring it to clear some threshold rather than merely be positive -- was the obvious repair and it is not justified. It would be fitted to a single data point, and that point is the very method it is being asked about. The distribution across all scored methods is a continuum with no seam: the widest gap anywhere near zero is half a point, and seven methods sit within six tenths of a point of it.

The decisive number is noise. Each method's year-to-year variation puts the standard error of these edges at about three points a year. The fourth method's own figure of +0.2 carries an interval of roughly minus eight to plus eight. Tested pairwise against the three methods currently clearing every condition, their edges are statistically indistinguishable from it and from zero. A margin large enough to be defensible would refuse every method in the lab, including its best.

So the change worth making is not a threshold but a sentence. When the signal reports an edge it should report the noise beside it, so two tenths of a point reads as indistinguishable from zero rather than as a number inside the phrase 'cleared all four'. That would not have caught the method that slipped through -- nothing honestly would have -- but it would have stopped it being described as having passed something.

And if the gate is to be strengthened against the evidence the lab actually owns, the fold count is where the evidence is. It is the clause with a record. This one has never caught anything.

insights.title: Lean without leaving: the price of risk picks WHICH fund, never how much is invested: what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 2000–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +40.7% at the assumed fee, +39.4% at the real fees (SPY: +39.8% and +39.7%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 68.4% and 69.5%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 1.97 and 1.74.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $15,466 and $34,521.

At the real fees it no longer beats SPY: the edge it showed was smaller than the fees it would have paid. At the real fees it falls short on beating SPY, the limit on its worst fall, trading at least 100 times.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: We stopped paying to sit in cash, and started paying the broker twice as much
insights.body:
A good opinion about the market is only worth having if the arrangement that delivers it costs less than the opinion is worth. The method tried before this one spent a market signal by deciding how much money stayed invested, and found that standing aside cost about one and a half times what knowing the answer was worth. So this one removed standing aside entirely: the money is fully invested every single day, and the signal only chooses which of the two funds the owner is allowed to buy holds it. That worked exactly as designed -- all six versions sat in the market 97.5 to 98.7 percent of the time, the same as simply buying and holding.

It still lost, and by more than before. Running the same book making the opposite call in the same months -- same fees, same shape, same amount of trading -- showed the opinion is worth 1.8 points a year between the two directions, so 0.9 points per side. Averaging those two opposite opinions together cancels the opinion and leaves only the act of swapping funds, and that act cost 2.75 points a year on its own. The ratio of what the opinion is worth to what carrying it costs fell from 0.68 to 0.33.

Re-pricing the same rule at the fee level the lab used to assume shows where all of it went: over a quarter of everything the rule earned from trading was handed to the broker, and the broker charges 2.2 times the old assumption. The cost of swapping funds and the fee bill are the same number to within a few percent. There is no subtle drag here, no clever timing loss -- the rule simply could not afford to trade.

The lesson is not about this signal. It is that 'never leave the market' is not the same as 'free'. Any rule that changes its mind every month on a large share of the account is paying a toll of roughly two to three points a year, whatever it is holding. That toll is now measured, and it is the number any future market opinion has to clear before it is worth building.

insights.title: Trading a good idea less often to save fees cuts the idea faster than it cuts the bill
insights.body:
When a rule earns a real edge but hands most of it to the broker, the obvious repair is to act on it less often: hold each decision for three months instead of one and the trading bill falls to roughly a third. That repair sounds free, and it is not, and this is the first time the lab has put a number on why.

The market opinion behind this method was measured as worth about 1.9 points a year in the most recent and best-covered stretch of history, when each call was held for one month. Holding the identical call for two months instead, it was worth 0.2. For three months, nothing at all. For six months it was worth minus 3.0, and for a year minus 1.7 -- actively harmful. The opinion does not sit still waiting to be collected; it is a statement about the next few weeks, and stretching it over a longer stretch does not dilute it so much as replace it with a different and worse statement.

So the saving and the loss do not trade off the way intuition suggests. Cutting the trading bill by two thirds cut the edge by rather more than two thirds, which means slowing down could never have rescued this rule. Checking that cost a few minutes of arithmetic on the price history and spent nothing -- no trial, no test-window look. It is worth doing before any future 'just trade it less often' repair, because the answer is not always the comforting one, and a wasted attempt costs a method slot that the lab can never get back.

The general shape keeps recurring: the thing an idea is worth and the thing it costs tend to move together, so the ratio between them stays stubbornly put. Three different ways of spending this particular signal have now run into exactly that, which is the real reason to stop rather than any one disappointing number.

insights.title: Only two funds are allowed, and that alone is what caps a whole family of ideas
insights.body:
The lab treats exactly two funds as things the owner can buy without being asked first: the broad American market, and the tech-heavy one. Anything else -- a small-company fund, a bond fund, an equal-weighted version of the broad market -- is treated as needing the owner's permission, and the lab's rules mean such a strategy can never become a real-money candidate however well it does. That rule is sensible and it was the owner's to make. What was not visible until today is how much it costs.

A rule that swaps between two funds pays the broker for the swap. What it earns depends on how differently the two funds behave: swap between two nearly identical things and you pay full price for almost no difference. After 2002 these two funds move together almost exactly -- the tech fund is only about two percent swingier than the broad one -- so the gap being traded is narrow. The method run today had a genuine, measured opinion worth around 1.4 points a year, and still lost, because the toll for acting on it was 2.2 to 2.8 points. With a wider gap between the two things being swapped, the same opinion acted on the same number of times would have earned proportionally more for exactly the same toll.

So the binding constraint on this whole shape of idea is not the market, and not the quality of any signal. It is the size of the gap between the only two things that may be traded. That is a one-sentence decision rather than a research programme: if there is another fund available on the owner's broker that behaves noticeably differently from the broad market and that he would be willing to hold, saying so would change the arithmetic for every future idea of this kind. If the answer is no, that is fine and worth knowing too -- the lab should then stop proposing fund-swapping ideas, because the sums say they cannot clear their own costs.

Flagged as a risk rather than a suggestion because the lab has been quietly spending method slots against this ceiling without naming it.

insights.title: Pay the trend rule's premium in shares, not cash: above the 200-day line hold QQQ, below it hold SPY (M0267-GATE): what Gotrade's real fees do to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran this method over its 1999–2015 history twice, with the same picks on the same days: once at the flat 0.1% a trade the lab has always assumed, and once at the fees Gotrade actually charged on the owner's own orders, read from the order receipts. SPY paid the same fees as the method in each run, so the comparison stays fair.

- Return a year: +40.5% at the assumed fee, +40.3% at the real fees (SPY: +39.1% and +39.1%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 59.4% and 60.3%.
- Dollars made for every dollar lost: 4.70 and 4.54.
- Fees paid over the whole run: $2,406 and $5,760.

It still beats SPY at the real fees: the fees shrink its edge without erasing it. At the real fees it falls short on the limit on its worst fall, trading at least 100 times.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A crash rule and a savings plan are a bad match: the whole payout landed when the account was smallest
insights.body:
The market safety rule — stay in while the market is above its own 200-day average, step aside when it is below — was tested this week in the cheapest form anyone has found for it. Instead of stepping aside into cash, which is what every book in the lab does and which is expensive, it stepped sideways into the safer of the two funds the owner is allowed to buy. The account was never out of the market for a single day and the broker's bill fell by a factor of eight.

Measured on the two funds' prices alone, obeying the rule was worth 4.84 percent a year over sixteen years. The owner's money earned 1.03 percent a year from it. Nearly four fifths of a real, correctly priced edge did not arrive.

It did not leak away. It was never there, and here is where it went. Broken into eras, obeying the rule was worth plus 61 percent in total across 2000 to 2002, minus 6 across 2003 to 2008, and plus 6 across 2009 to 2015. All of it is the dot-com crash. And by the end of 2002, under the owner's real plan of a small start plus a top-up every month, only 21 percent of his money had been paid in.

So the rule earned its keep on a fifth of an account and then sat quietly for thirteen years on the other four fifths. The arithmetic is right and the money is still not there, because the money was not there yet.

Why it matters: a twenty-year average quietly assumes twenty years of equally sized money. The owner does not have that and never will — his account grows every month for as long as he keeps saving. Any rule whose value is concentrated in one early stretch will be flattered by the average and will disappoint in rupiah. Protection in particular pays in proportion to what is being protected, and in a savings plan that amount starts near nothing.

What to do about it: when a timing or safety rule is judged, read what it did to the money that was actually in the account, not the headline yearly figure, and look at when in the window its value was earned. A rule that earns everything in the first three years of a sixteen-year plan is worth a fraction of what it looks like. The same caution applies in reverse and more happily: a rule that earns steadily, or late, is worth more than its average suggests.

insights.title: A coin flip with the same habits beat the real safety rule in the years that look like today
insights.body:
A fair worry about any rule that chooses between two funds is that it may not be choosing at all — it may simply hold the better fund most of the time and take the credit.

That was tested directly, and cheaply, with no new experiment run. Twenty thousand fake rules were drawn. Each one changes its mind as rarely as the real rule does, roughly once every fifteen months, and favours the tech fund about as often, roughly two thirds of the time. Same temperament, same costs, no information whatsoever.

Across 2009 to 2015 — the best-covered years in the lab and the ones most like today — the real rule earned 3.47 percent a year more than the broad market. The average fake rule earned 3.87 percent. The real rule lands at the 38th percentile of its own imitators: worse than a coin flip with the same habits. Over the whole sixteen years it reaches the 85th percentile, which is still short of anything worth calling real, and that figure comes entirely from the dot-com crash again.

The explanation is plain. The tech fund beat the broad market by 6.2 percent a year after 2009. Anything that leans towards it earns money. The real rule earned less than a random lean because it kept stepping out of the winning fund on false alarms.

Why it matters: it is very easy to build a rule that holds the right thing for the wrong reason, and the usual comparisons will not catch it. Comparing against the broad market would have called this a success.

What to do about it: whenever a rule picks between a small number of holdings, draw a few thousand imitations that share its habits but know nothing, and ask where the real rule sits among them. It costs no experiment, no data and no time, and it is the only comparison here that asked the right question.

insights.title: The lab should report when in a window an edge was earned, not just how big it was
insights.body:
Every method in this lab is scored on an average across its whole window, and two more numbers beside it: the worst fall, and how the money would really have grown given a small start and a monthly top-up. What nothing reports is when in the window the edge arrived.

That turns out to matter more than almost anything else on the page. A rule tested this week was worth 4.84 percent a year on the prices and delivered 1.03 percent to the owner's actual money, purely because everything it was worth happened in the first three years of sixteen, when a fifth of the money had been paid in. Nothing in the existing report would have revealed that. The headline number looked like a comfortable win.

What would fix it is small. For each version, split the window into the eras the lab already uses and print how much of the version's lead over its control was earned in each. One line, three numbers, from figures the lab has already recorded — no new experiment, no new data, nothing spent. A method whose lead is spread evenly across the eras is a different animal from one that earned it all in a single crash, and today those two are printed identically.

Why it matters to the owner: he is saving monthly into a growing account, so what he earns depends on when a rule works, not only on whether it works. A measure that ignores timing will keep recommending rules that paid off before his money arrived.

A second, cheaper version of the same idea: print the share of total deposits that had been paid in by the point at which each version had earned half its lead. If that number is small, the average is flattering the method, and the page should say so.

insights.title: A wider choice of funds does not rescue a rule that has nothing left to say
insights.body:
For two days the lab kept reaching the same wall. A market-timing idea would turn out to carry a real opinion, and then lose anyway because the only two funds the owner may trade -- the broad market and the technology fund -- move almost identically, so there was no room between them to express the opinion. The obvious conclusion was that the two-fund rule was the thing holding everything back, and that permitting a third fund would unlock every idea of that shape. That conclusion has now been measured, and it is half right in a way that makes it useless.

The first half holds. The two funds really are nearly the same thing: the technology fund moves 0.98 for every 1.00 of the broad market since 2002. And the store already holds fifteen funds, in every one of its four copies, with nothing to buy and nothing to rebuild. Several are genuinely different: long government bonds move slightly OPPOSITE the market, short bonds barely move with it at all, and gold is effectively unrelated. If a rule could pick perfectly each month between the broad market and one of those, the prize is about 1.7 times what the technology fund offers. So the instruments really are wider, and the data to use them is already here.

The second half is why it does not matter. Take the one opinion this lab has actually proved -- the long-term trend rule -- and wire it to each candidate in turn, holding the market when the trend is up and the other fund when it is down. Compare that against the version the lab has always had for free: going to cash. After 2009 the trend rule's contribution is essentially nothing through EVERY instrument on the menu. The best of them adds eight tenths of a point a year; most add between nothing and a fifth of a point; cash itself is at zero. The long bond's entire advantage comes from the 2008 crisis and nothing since.

Put the other way round: in the years that look most like today, the trend rule wired to cash COSTS about 2.9 points a year. Wired to the best available third fund it costs 2.3. A third fund repairs about a fifth of the hole and still loses to doing nothing at all.

So the diagnosis was wrong, or rather it was incomplete in the direction that matters. The spread was narrow AND the opinion was empty in the era that decides. Widening the instrument by three and a half times multiplies an edge of roughly zero and gives roughly zero.

The case for a third fund is now exactly one observation: in the 2008 crisis, when both permitted funds fell more than half, long bonds and gold ROSE about a quarter. That is a real and valuable property and it happened once. Every bond figure available is drawn from a thirteen-year stretch in which bonds only went up, the dot-com crash predates every fund that is genuinely different from the market, and the one recent episode where bonds and shares fell hard together sits inside the held-out window the lab must not look at.

RECOMMENDATION: permit nothing on these numbers. If the owner wants the option anyway for reasons of his own, long government bonds are the best candidate on every axis measured and, unlike the near-equivalent bond fund, it collides with no frozen record. Permitting it is about two lines of code and costs nothing in data or fees. The reason not to is simply that it would not buy anything.

insights.title: Most of what this lab has measured was earned before the owner's money arrived
insights.body:
The lab has always judged a rule by what it earned a year over its whole history. That number quietly assumes the owner had the same amount of money throughout. He did not and never will: he starts small and adds to the account every month, so what a rule is worth to him depends on when it worked, not only on whether it worked.

A new report answers that for the first time. For any recorded result it splits the history into the four stretches the lab already thinks in, and says how much of the rule's lead over its comparison was earned in each — beside how much of the owner's money had been paid in by the end of that stretch. One extra line says when half the lead had been earned, and how much of his money had arrived by then. It reads only figures already written down: no new experiment, no new data, nothing spent.

On the method that prompted it, the answer is one glance. Its lead was worth 4.83 percent a year on the prices and 1.03 percent to the money. The report shows 111.8 percent of that lead earned in the dot-com years, minus 9 percent across the middle years and minus 3 percent after 2009 — the lead is more than entirely one crash, and the two later stretches gave a little of it back. Half of it had been earned by February 2001, when 8.9 percent of his deposits had arrived.

Then the whole back catalogue was read the same way, which nobody had done. Of 509 funded results that beat the market by at least half a point a year, the median one had earned half its lead by the time only 33.9 percent of the money had arrived, and 436 of them — 85.7 percent — had earned half their lead before half the money was in. Both of those hold however strictly the "beat the market" bar is set. Tighter counts do move with that bar and are reported with it, so nobody quotes the fragile half: 22 results earned half their lead on under a quarter of the money, and 7 on under a tenth. Counting the best-looking version of each method, 4 of 126 methods have the shape the dot-com method had.

The plainest number needs no threshold at all. Eight recorded results lead the market on paper and lose to it on the owner's actual money — the two figures are both already written down, and their difference is the whole point.

What this means for how the lab works: a twenty-year average is not a neutral summary when the money arrives gradually. Anything whose value sits early is worth less than it looks, and anything that earns steadily or late is worth more. Since 86 percent of the lab's winners are front-loaded, this is not a rare failure to watch for — it is the normal shape of the lab's record, and it had never been measured.

Nothing was recorded by any of it: no result moved, no method changed, and the one-off look at the untouched years was not spent. The report deliberately writes nothing to this journal when it runs, so it can be re-run as often as anyone likes.

insights.title: Correcting ourselves: sized by company size the bond-like picks kept their edge, and the random books we judged them against were the problem
insights.body:
An earlier note here said that weighting the bond-like stock picker by company size took away its edge. It compared the sized book, which earned 9.5 percent a year on the owner's deposits, against two random books of the same shape that earned 8.1 and 10.3 percent, and concluded that most of what the ranking added had lived in the smaller companies.

Those two random books have since been withdrawn. Measured afterwards, they were not neutral opponents: they re-drew their whole holding every month while the real book held on to its picks, so they traded more than twice as often and paid a fee bill the real book never paid. The lab now knows that a mis-shaped opponent of that kind is not a harder or an easier one but an arbitrary one, arbitrary to within about seven points a year, which is wider than any margin it was being used to judge. Both were replaced by random books drawn to the real book's own trading rhythm.

Against the honest replacements the answer reverses. The two new random books earned 7.1 and 7.1 percent a year on the owner's deposits, against the market's 7.2. The sized bond-like book earned 9.5. So it leads its own random twin by about 2.4 points a year, where the old reading had it losing to one twin by 0.7 and beating the other by 1.5. One of the two margins changes sign.

What that means for the conclusion. Size weighting did cost the idea about 3 points a year, because the equal-slot version earned 12.5. That part stands. What does not stand is the comparison. Against the equal-slot random books of the same frame, which earned between 8.8 and 11.9, size weighting cost random picks at least as much as it cost the idea, not a third as much. So there is no support left for the claim that most of what the ranking added lived in the smaller companies, and the lesson drawn from it, that an edge showing up only in equal slots is mostly a small-company bet, is not something this measurement can carry.

The method's own written verdict was corrected when the honest random books were run. This entry closes the gap, because the journal note was not, and it was the only place the retired reading still stood.

What stays true, and it is the general lesson: a margin is only as meaningful as the opponent it is quoted against, and an opponent that trades at a different rhythm from the book it controls makes that margin unreadable in either direction. The fix is to draw the opponent from the book's own calendar, not to correct the number afterwards.

insights.title: Correcting ourselves: it was this one rule's cheap form that paid early, not crash rules in general
insights.body:
An earlier note here concluded that a crash rule and a savings plan are a bad match, because the whole payout of the rule tested that week landed in the dot-com years, when only a fifth of the owner's money had been paid in. Everything that note says about that particular rule is right and none of it is withdrawn. What this entry withdraws is the general claim in its title, which the rest of the record does not support.

The rule tested that week was the cheap form of the market safety rule: instead of stepping out of the market it stepped sideways into the safer of the two funds the owner is allowed to buy. The account was never out of the market for a single day. That is exactly why 2008 gave it nothing, because both funds fell together, and why all of its value sits in the dot-com crash, early, on a small account.

Every other book in this lab carries the same safety rule in its ordinary form, stepping into cash or into the broad market instead. Seven pairs were read this week, each pair one book run twice with nothing different between the two but the rule. The answer is the opposite one. On six of the seven, the owner's money received more from the rule than the price history said it was worth, barely more on one of them and nearly a third more on another, and on the seventh it received about seven tenths of it. The eras say why. For these books the payday is 2008, not 2000, and by the end of 2008 two thirds of the owner's money had arrived. On the strongest pair the rule was worth 3.1 percent a year on the prices and delivered 4.0 percent to the money.

So what decides whether a crash rule suits a savings plan is not that it is a crash rule. It is what the rule steps into. A rule that steps sideways into another share fund can only pay in a crash that separates the two funds, and the one crash that did that was the early one. A rule that steps into cash pays in any crash, and the largest crash in this history came late enough that most of the money was there to be protected.

What the first note got right, and this one keeps: judge a timing rule on what it did to the money actually in the account, and look at when in the window its value was earned. That advice is sound and it is what produced this correction. The conclusion it was used to reach, that this kind of rule is generally a poor fit for a monthly saver, was drawn from one rule on one pair of funds and does not survive reading the rest of the record the same way.

One number follows directly, and it points the other way from how it has been read since. The cost side of the safety rule, the money it gives up by standing out of a rising market, falls almost entirely in the years after 2009, by which time every rupiah the owner deposits across this history has arrived. That cost is therefore fully real for a monthly saver and is not discounted at all. It is the payout that is sensitive to timing, not the premium.

insights.title: The lab measures every result two ways, and on thirty of them the two disagree about who won
insights.body:
Every result in this lab is measured twice. One way takes the owner's deposits back out and asks what the prices alone did, which is the fair way to compare one set of rules against another. The other asks what his actual money earned, given that he starts small and tops the account up every month. Most of the time the two agree about who beat the market and differ only in how much.

They were checked against each other this week, across every funded result on record, using figures already written down. On eight results the prices say the rule beat the market and the money says it lost. On twenty-two more it runs the other way: the prices say it lost and the money says it won. Thirty out of seven hundred and sixty-one, about one in twenty-six.

The reassuring half of the answer is that the test the lab actually uses to pass or fail a method already reads the money. Every one of those eight was failed, and failed on exactly that ground. Nothing was ever let through on the flattering number, and no verdict in this journal tells the owner that any of those eight beat the market. Each was written up on the money figure from the start, and in one case the note quotes the losing version's own money figure and calls it a near miss rather than a win.

The half worth watching is a different test. Before a method may be promoted it must also win a majority of four later stretches of history, and that test reads the price figure rather than the money one. In principle a method could win it on the prices while losing the owner money. Every method that has ever won that majority was checked. There are fifteen, and the version each one won on beat the market on the owner's money by between 1.4 and 11.8 points a year. So the gap is real in principle and has never once opened in practice. It is worth re-checking whenever that test changes, and it does not need fixing today.

The cause of the disagreement is always the same: when in the twenty years the lead was earned. A lead earned early is earned on a small account, so the prices flatter it. A lead earned late is earned on a full one, so the prices understate it. The clearest case is the market safety rule itself. What it gives up by standing out of a rising market falls after 2009, by which time all of the money has arrived, so that cost is fully real. What it earns falls in the crashes, and for the books that step into cash the big one is 2008, by which time two thirds of the money had arrived. Read across seven pairs of books run with and without the rule, the owner's money received more from it than the prices promised on six of the seven.

The practical rule: when the two numbers disagree, the money one is the answer, and the question to ask next is not which is right but when the lead was earned.

insights.title: A rule tested against its own opposite is only half an experiment, and the lab has been recording that half alone for years
insights.body:
The lab has a good habit: when it tests a market-timing rule it usually also runs the rule upside down, so the two can be compared and the signal separated from luck. A new report now does the arithmetic that habit was always for -- it splits a rule's result into what its OPINION is worth and what its HABITS cost, and divides one by the other. Below one, the rule cannot pay for the way it is being run, at any strength.

Swept across everything recorded: twenty-eight such pairs across twenty-three methods. Only SIX of them can be priced at all.

The other twenty-two are unpriceable, and the reason is the finding. Running a rule and its opposite tells you whether the opinion is real. It tells you NOTHING about what acting on the opinion costs, because both versions pay that cost equally and it cancels. To learn the cost you need a third version beside them: the same book with no opinion in it at all, never stepping aside, never switching. Twenty-two of the twenty-eight never registered one. So for those the lab knows the signal is real and has no idea whether it was worth having -- which is precisely the question that decided every timing rule it has settled this month.

This is cheap to fix and costs no new method: it is one more version inside the same pre-registration. Any future method that tests a rule against its opposite should register the do-nothing version too, as a matter of course.

Of the six that could be priced, all six fail, and they fail by arithmetic rather than by bad luck: the opinion is worth between a fifth and seven tenths of what the habit costs, on every rung of every strength tested. One of them is a special case worth remembering -- on prices it looks like a clear winner, and on the owner's actual deposits it is a coin flip, because its payout landed before most of his money had arrived.

A WARNING ABOUT WHAT ELSE THE SWEEP FOUND, because the obvious reading of it is a trap. Four methods lose to their own opposites in both columns, which reads as 'the signal was simply upside down, turn it over and try again'. The margins are between a fifth and one and a quarter points a year. The lab measured this week that the year-to-year noise on quantities of exactly this kind is around three points a year. Every one of those four is comfortably inside the noise. Turning a rule over because it lost by a fraction of its own measurement error is not a discovery, it is the search doing the choosing, and it would cost four method ids to learn nothing. They should not be flipped on this evidence.

The same caution applies to the one encouraging number in the sweep: a single method whose opinion-to-cost ratio clears one on the owner's money, in one era, by a margin smaller than its own noise. That is a hypothesis about where to look next, not a result.

insights.title: Split the drift trigger's gain: is it the cash it releases, or the trimming itself?: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +6.9% on the usual history, +4.7% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 59.2% and 72.8%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +0.5% a year before and −1.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 1 of 4 periods won to 0 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.2 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The rebalancing rule's whole gain was the cash it freed, not the rebalancing
insights.body:
Last October the lab found that one line in the simulator had been leaving about a tenth of a wide book sitting in cash nobody chose to hold, and that fixing it was worth about half a point a year. The verdict said plainly that it could not tell how much of that came from the cash being put to work and how much from the thing the fix also switched on: the book finally selling a slice of whatever had grown too big and buying more of whatever had shrunk. Those two always move together, so the number could not be divided.

It can now. The trick was to give the trimming version a deliberate cash buffer, sized so that both versions hold the same share of their money in shares on average. Everything else is identical: the same fifty companies, the same days, the same fees, the same deposits. The buffer size was worked out from two figures recorded last October and written into the file before anything was run, so there was no chance of quietly tuning it until a pleasing answer appeared.

The two versions then ended up invested to within three hundredths of a point of each other, and they earned the same. Trimming with the rule the lab uses today changed the return by two hundredths of a point a year. Trimming all the way, resetting every holding every month, made it a tenth of a point a year worse. So essentially all of last October's half point was the cash, and the rebalancing itself was worth nothing.

It is slightly worse than nothing where it counts. Over 2009 to 2015, the best-covered years and the ones most like today, the trimming cost three quarters of a point a year. It only ever looked worthwhile because of 1996 to 2002, when the most-traded list was the dot-com names and there were enormous winners to sell. Selling winners to buy laggards is a bet that what has gone up will come back down relative to what has gone down, and that bet has been wrong for the whole modern era.

What to do about it: keep the rule the lab adopted in October, but keep it for the right reason. It earns its place by stopping money sitting idle, not by rebalancing. And stop looking for a better rebalancing rule on a wide book, because there is nothing there to find.

insights.title: Trimming a book makes its worst fall shallower, not deeper, and last October we had that backwards
insights.body:
Last October the lab reported that letting a wide book trim its winners deepened its worst fall by about two and a half points, and gave a reason that sounded right: a rebalancing rule keeps buying whatever has dropped, so in a market that grinds lower it keeps buying on the way down. That reason has now been measured, and it is wrong.

The catch was that the trimming version was also holding more of its money in shares at the same time, and being more invested deepens a fall all by itself. When both versions are made equally invested, the trimming version falls one and three quarter points LESS, and its worst year, 2008, was half a point gentler. On the honest copy of the price history, the one that puts the companies that died back in, the gap is bigger still: three and a half points shallower.

The arithmetic from the other direction agrees. A separate version of the same book, identical except that it holds ten points less of its money in shares, shows that each point of the account left out of the market is worth about four tenths of a point of worst fall. So the ten extra points of investment should have deepened the fall by over four points on their own. Only two and a half showed up. The missing one and three quarters is the trimming, pulling the other way.

Why it matters: this is the only effect in the whole experiment that came out positive on both copies of the price history, and it got stronger on the honest one. Capping a winner stops it quietly growing into a slice of the account the book never agreed to hold, and a concentrated book falls further when that winner finally turns. Safety is what this lab is short of, with four out of four real tests failed and every strategy on the list having breached the fall limit.

What to do about it: trimming is really two actions glued together, selling a slice of the winners and spending the money on the laggards. The safety almost certainly comes from the selling and the modern-era cost almost certainly comes from the buying. A book that caps its winners and parks the proceeds in cash instead of feeding the laggards would separate them in a single run. That is queued.

insights.title: A cash buffer sized on one copy of the price history does not stay sized on another
insights.body:
This is a warning about a technique the lab is starting to lean on, and it nearly produced a confident wrong answer today.

To compare two books fairly you sometimes have to make them hold the same share of their money in shares, so that the thing you are actually testing is the only difference left. The way to do that is to give one of them a deliberate cash buffer, sized in advance from figures already recorded. Done on the lab's ordinary price data today, it worked beautifully: the two books landed within three hundredths of a point of each other, against a tolerance of half a point set beforehand.

The same buffers were then carried over to the honest copy of the history, the one that puts the companies that died back in. There they missed by nine tenths and three quarters of a point, both outside the tolerance. The buffer is a fixed fraction, but how much of its money a book actually gets into shares depends on which companies exist, how often they drop out of the shortlist and how violently they move, and all three change when the dead companies come back.

A second thing broke at the same time. Two independent ways of working out the answer agreed to within a tenth of a point a year on the ordinary data and disagreed by more than a quarter of a point on the honest data. That is a sign the relationship between how invested a book is and what it earns is not the straight line everyone assumes: over one stretch a point of investment was worth seven thousandths of a point a year, over another it was worth far more.

What to do about it: never reuse a buffer across two copies of the history. Measure the control's own investment share on each copy and size a separate buffer for each. And when an experiment is set up this way, write down beforehand what gap would make you refuse to publish an answer, because the honest response to a broken match is to report the gap and say nothing else. That is what happened here.

insights.title: A rule nobody chose was leaving a tenth of every wide book sitting in cash — and the deeper fall it seemed to cause was the cash too, not the rebalancing
insights.body:
This replaces the previous version of this entry. Everything it said about the cash was right and is repeated below. One sentence in it was wrong, and it was the sentence that explained a cost — so it mattered.

WHAT STANDS, unchanged. When a holding drifts away from the size it is meant to be, the simulator only trades it back once the gap is worth a trade. The trouble was what 'worth a trade' was measured against: one per cent of the whole account, rather than of the holding. That number does not shrink as a book gets wider, so a book of fifty names, holding each at two per cent, had to see a holding lose HALF its value before anything happened. A book of a hundred names could never trigger at all. In general, a book of N equal names was running on a trigger of N per cent of a holding.

Measured on a deliberately dull book — the fifty most-traded big American companies in equal amounts, no stock picking at all, run five times with everything identical except that trigger. On the old rule the account sat eleven and a half per cent in cash it never chose to hold, because a monthly deposit could buy a brand new holding but could never top up one already owned. Moving the trigger onto the holding cut that to under four per cent, and a full monthly rebalance to one and a half. The gain was about half a point a year, and a tenth of a point a year of broker fees was all it cost in trading. The twenty-name book the owner actually holds was never affected: twenty names on the old rule is exactly the new rule, by arithmetic.

WHAT WAS WRONG. The old version reported two and a half points of deeper worst fall and explained it like this: 'rebalancing buys whatever has fallen, so in a market that keeps grinding lower it keeps buying on the way down.' That reads well and it is false.

A later method held the amount of money invested FIXED on both sides, so that the rebalancing moved and the cash did not — the thing the original run could not do, because its two effects moved together. With the cash held still, the rebalancing makes the worst fall SHALLOWER, by about one and a half points on the usual history and three and a half with the dead companies added back. The whole of the deepening was simply having more money in the market. More money invested falls further when the market falls; that is all it ever was.

The same experiment also found that the rebalancing itself earns NOTHING once the cash is held still — between a sixth of a point of loss and a fiftieth of a point of gain, which is zero. And over 2009 to 2015 it LOSES, on both copies of the price history. So the half point a year this entry reports was entirely the cash getting invested, and none of it was the rebalancing.

WHY THE CORRECTION MATTERS BEYOND THIS ONE RULE. The original explanation was the kind that sounds mechanical and obvious, and it was repeated as a reason to be careful about rebalancing in a falling market. It was never measured; it was inferred from two numbers that moved together. The lesson is the one the lab keeps relearning: when two effects move together, any story about which one caused what is a guess until something holds one of them still.

insights.title: The owner is shown three live buy signals and owns one book — and the four spent looks bought two books, not four
insights.body:
The lab has never asked how many genuinely different strategies it contains. The machinery to answer it has existed for weeks but was only ever pointed one way: from a strategy that failed to a new candidate. Pointed at the lab itself, across every pair of recorded results, it says two things that change how two of the lab's own headline numbers should be read.

THE FIRST. The buy signal — the test that says it is finally worth paying for better price history — currently names three strategies. They are one. Two of them produce IDENTICAL results, to every decimal place, because one is the other with a feature switched off. The third is a near twin of the same parent, agreeing with both at 0.975 once the market's own movement is taken out. All three descend from the same method. So the page the owner reads presents three independent reasons to spend money, and there is one reason, measured once. That is not a rounding problem; it is the difference between three confirmations and none.

THE SECOND. The lab says, often, that four looks at the held-out window have been spent and all four failed. Three of those four are the same strategy — they agree with each other between 0.925 and 0.992, and one is literally the child of another. The fourth is genuinely separate. So the honest sentence is that FOUR LOOKS BOUGHT TWO STRATEGIES. The record is nought for two, not nought for four, and the evidence against the lab's approach is half as strong as it has been telling itself. That cuts both ways and both ways matter: the failures are less damning than they looked, and the scarcest resource this lab has was spent twice on the same thing.

AND THE REASON THE LAB LOOKS NARROWER THAN IT IS. Strategies here cluster by the safety rule they share, not by the ideas inside them. Two unrelated strategies that both step aside when the market is below its long-term average move together at 0.63 after the market's own movement is removed — almost as much as two versions of the SAME strategy, which sit at 0.78. Two strategies that never step aside sit at 0.06. The market-exit rule is not a straight-line relationship with the market, so the usual arithmetic cannot subtract it; when it is subtracted deliberately, the lab-wide resemblance collapses from 0.29 to 0.07 and the number of distinct strategies rises by nearly half.

So the straight answer to 'is this lab searching, or re-drawing the same few books' is: it is searching more broadly than it looks. At the lab's own threshold it holds sixty-seven distinct groups, forty of them with only one member — company-filing screens, a split calendar, an illiquidity premium, volatility sensitivity, sector rotation. The narrowness is in the shared safety rule, and in the SPENDING, not in the ideas.

WHAT TO DO, neither of which costs a new strategy or a look: show a lineage as one row rather than as three on the page the owner reads; and before any future look is spent, check the candidate against the strategies whose looks are already gone. The 0.992 agreement between two of the four spent looks was knowable in advance, from results the lab already held.

insights.title: Cash costs almost nothing in some decades and a great deal in others
insights.body: A ladder of six identical books, differing only in how much of the account each deliberately left in cash, finally put a price on idle money. Over the whole twenty years, one point of the account kept out of the market cost about six hundredths of a point a year. That average hides everything that matters. Between 2003 and 2008, a stretch that held both a long rising market and the 2008 crash, the same point of cash cost half a hundredth of a point a year — it was very nearly free, because what it lost in the good years it handed back in the bad one. Between 2009 and 2015, a rising decade with no crash in it at all, that same point cost seventeen hundredths of a point a year. Thirty-four times as much. The lab compares two versions of a book all the time, and it has to make sure both are equally invested before the comparison means anything; when they are not quite equal it corrects the difference using a single number. This says there is no single number. The correction has to be measured over the same stretch of history as the claim being made, and 2009 to 2015 — the stretch every new idea is sent to first — is the most expensive of the three by a wide margin. The practical fix is simpler than getting the correction right: make the two versions equal to within half a point of the account and do not correct at all. Half a point costs under a tenth of a point a year even in the expensive decade, which is inside the precision anything here is quoted to.

insights.title: Two measurements cannot find a slope, and one of ours was wrong by five times
insights.body: Last October a measurement reported that leaving money in cash cost eight times less on the honest copy of the price history — the one that includes the companies that went bust — than on the ordinary copy. It was an unsettling number, because it implied that nothing measured on one copy could be trusted on the other. It was wrong. Running six versions instead of two shows the real gap is a factor of one and a half, and that both copies behave as neat straight lines. The eight-fold figure came from a single pair of versions, and one of that pair had drifted away from the amount of cash it was supposed to be holding. Two points will always give you a slope; they will never tell you the slope is wrong. Five consecutive readings will. The lesson is cheap to apply and worth applying every time: when the lab wants to know how much some dial is worth, it should turn the dial five times, not twice. The extra runs cost minutes, and the pair that was believed for three weeks cost more than that in work built on top of it.

insights.title: The safety switch's famous cost may be nothing but its time out of the market
insights.body: The lab has a long-standing figure for what its market-timing switch costs: a flat three and a half points a year since 2009, the same across every book it has been bolted onto, which has always looked like a stubborn property of the switch itself. This ladder measured what a point of the account left in cash cost in exactly that stretch of years: seventeen hundredths of a point a year. Divide one by the other and you get twenty-one points. That is roughly how much of the time a rule that sells when the market falls below its own one-year average sits in cash during a decade that never had a proper crash. If that arithmetic holds up, the switch's cost is not a property of the switch at all — it is simply how long the switch stays out, multiplied by what being out was worth in those years. It would explain why every attempt to tune the switch has produced the same bill: the tuning was never touching the thing that sets the price. It would also say where to look instead, which is at how long a rule stays out rather than at how cleverly it decides to leave. The check is cheap, because how much of the time each gated book sat in cash is already recorded for every one of them.

insights.title: Two measurements cannot find a slope: what cash costs is a straight line after all, but its price changes by thirty-four times between decades
insights.body:
This replaces the previous version, which read a curve off two points and got it wrong by a factor of eight. The warning it was trying to give was real; almost every number in it was not.

WHAT THE OLD VERSION SAID. Measuring the cost of holding cash on two copies of the price history, it found the price of a point of cash was 0.066 on one and 0.0078 on the other — eight times apart over the same range — and concluded that return is not a straight line in how much money is invested, so every control this lab draws at matched exposure rests on an assumption that is bent.

WHAT A PROPER LADDER FOUND. Six evenly spaced rungs on both copies, with fee-free twins beside them, instead of two points. Every curve is monotone with no sign flip, and a straight line fits to within three hundredths of a point a year across the whole twenty-nine-point span. The lab's linear assumption is SOUND. The two copies differ by 1.66 times, not eight — the second copy's real figure sits near 0.037 across five consecutive readings, and the old 0.0078 has no counterpart anywhere on the ladder. The first copy's 0.066 was right and agrees with the new measurement to five per cent. So the eight was one bad reading, not a property of anything.

There is a gentle bend, and it goes the other way from the obvious guess: the more cash you hold, the more the NEXT point of it costs, by about a tenth on one copy and a fifth on the other. It is not fees — with fees switched off the bend is identical. And dividing a result by exposure to correct it OVER-corrects, by a seventh on one copy and a quarter on the other. Subtract the slope; never divide.

THE REAL WARNING, which the old version missed entirely. The price of cash is nearly constant between the two copies of history and wildly unstable between DECADES. A point of cash cost about eight hundredths of a point a year in the late nineties, half a hundredth in 2003 to 2008, and seventeen hundredths in 2009 to 2015. That is a thirty-four-fold range, against a 1.66-fold difference between the two price histories the lab worries about. Whatever era a claim is about is what decides what its cash was worth, and the 2009-2015 column — the years the owner's money was actually in the account for — is the most expensive of the three and almost perfectly straight.

WHAT TO DO. Match two arms on how much is invested to within half a point and do not correct at all: half a point costs under nine hundredths of a point a year even in the expensive era. If a gap must be left, it costs the gap times the slope FOR THE ERA BEING CLAIMED, never the whole-window slope.

AND THE LESSON THAT GENERALISES. A slope read from two points is not a measurement, it is a line through two numbers, and it cannot tell a real curve from one bad reading. This lab has now been caught doing it once. Before any future claim about how one quantity moves with another, ask how many points it rests on.

insights.title: The safety switch is not a cash dial, and the figure we have been quoting is the formula's own answer rather than a measurement
insights.body:
This answers a guess written down last week. The guess was that the market-exit rule's famous cost -- about three and a half points a year since 2009, the same across every strategy it has been bolted onto -- is nothing but how long it sits in cash, priced at what being out of the market was worth in those years. The guess was tidy, it was arithmetically close, and it is wrong.

HOW IT WAS TESTED. One book, holding fifty large companies in equal slices with no opinion about any of them, run six ways. Once with the exit rule switched off. Five times with it on, differing only in how long the book waits after the market climbs back above its own one-year average before buying again: no wait, then six, sixteen, thirty and forty-two trading days. Every version sells on exactly the same days for exactly the same reason, so patience is a dial and time out of the market stops being an accident. The waits were picked from the rule's own calendar before anything ran, so the five rungs are evenly spread.

WHAT CAME BACK. Over the whole twenty years the rule EARNED two points a year more than the book without it, where its time in cash says it should have LOST one and three-quarter. Over 2003 to 2008 it earned nearly seven where cash says it should have cost almost nothing. And since 2009 it cost six and three-quarter where cash explains three and a half. The gap between what the rule did and what its cash explains runs from minus seven points a year to plus three, against a measurement noise of half a point. There is an enormous amount of judgement in this rule, it is worth a great deal in some decades and costs a great deal in others, and it is never a cash dial. The same answer comes back on the copy of the price history that includes the companies that went bust, and with trading fees switched off entirely.

THE SHARPEST NUMBER. The same comparison was then run on twelve recorded strategies spanning twelve different ideas -- momentum of several shapes, seasonality, the 52-week high, long-term reversal, lottery avoidance, a price-delay screen, a sector blend and more -- each as recorded and again with the exit rule removed and nothing else touched. Over 2009 to 2015 what the rule actually cost ranges from six tenths of a point a year to ten and a third: a seventeen-fold spread. What the cash formula predicts for the same twelve ranges from two and five sixths to three and a half -- a spread of one and a quarter. THE FAMOUS CONSTANCY OF THE THREE AND A HALF IS THE CONSTANCY OF THE FORMULA, NOT OF THE RULE. Every strategy that carries the rule sits out the same days, because they share the rule, so a formula built on how long they sit out hands back nearly the same answer every time, by construction. The quantity it is meant to be estimating varies seventeen-fold.

WHY IT MATTERS, and this is the uncomfortable part. Every shortfall this lab has taken apart since that figure was published used it as the exit rule's share. If the real share is forty per cent larger after 2009 and has the OPPOSITE SIGN before it, then the leftover those breakdowns assigned to the stock picking has been mis-stated throughout: too kind to the picking in the recent years, far too harsh in the earlier ones. That is a correction to a number the lab has leaned on all month, and it costs nothing to redo.

WHAT TO DO. Stop quoting the formula as a measurement. When a strategy's shortfall is taken apart, run the exit rule off as a real counterfactual and read the difference, which the lab already has the machinery to do and which spends no held-out window. And stop tuning the rule: six ideas this month went into when to read it, how often, with what band and in what phase, and each answered a fraction of a point. The thing that moves the number is WHICH months it sits out, and in the owner's own era the single biggest contribution is one five-month absence in the spring of 2009 that a one-year-average rule cannot avoid by construction.

insights.title: Cash held in lumps costs more than the same cash spread evenly, and nobody here had ever measured it
insights.body:
A strategy that steps out of the market entirely for five months is not the same as one that quietly keeps a tenth of its money in the bank all year, even when the two average out to the same amount of cash. Everyone would guess that. Nobody in this lab had ever put a number on it, and the number turns out to be large enough to change how several results should be read.

On the same fifty-name book, in the same years, on the same prices: a point of the account kept in cash every single day cost seventeen hundredths of a point a year over 2009 to 2015. A point of cash arriving instead as an all-or-nothing absence around the market's one-year average cost twenty-eight hundredths. Sixty per cent more for the same average amount of cash.

That was measured by making the absences longer on purpose while leaving the decision to leave untouched -- five versions of one book that sell on identical days and differ only in how many trading days they wait before buying back in. The five sit on a straight line to within half a point a year, so the slope is a measurement rather than a line through two numbers.

WHY IT MATTERS. When this lab prices what a market-exit rule cost, it has been subtracting the plain cash figure and calling the remainder judgement. On this book in these years that remainder was six and three-quarter points a year, of which three and a half is cash, one and three-quarter is the LUMPINESS of that cash, and only one and a half is the rule's actual choice of which months to miss. Two thirds of what looked like a verdict on the rule's judgement was really a verdict on the shape of its absences -- and the shape is a property of switching at all, not of switching cleverly.

WHAT TO DO. Any comparison between a strategy that switches and one that does not should price the lumpiness separately before attributing anything to the signal. A ladder that holds the same average cash in absences of one, three, six and twelve months would settle the general shape in a single experiment, and it would apply to every timing rule this lab has ever tested rather than to one.

insights.title: The safety rule's whole bill since 2009 is one five-month absence, and the fix is what the money does while it is out
insights.body:
When the market-exit rule's cost since 2009 is broken down month by month, almost all of it -- ninety-four per cent -- is simply the months the book was absent. Only six per cent is the extra trading and the different fifty companies it owns when it comes back. So this is about being out, not about churn.

And it is about being out at the wrong moments. In the sixteen months the rule sat out between 2009 and 2015, the book would have been earning at about twenty-eight per cent a year. In the sixty-five months it stayed in, it earned about fourteen. The rule chose to be absent at double the book's normal rate of pay. The broad market shows the same split, twenty-four against fifteen, so this is a market-timing failure rather than a stock-picking one.

There were four absences in those years. ONE OF THEM -- February to June 2009, through the bottom of the crash and the first leg of the recovery -- carries two thirds of the whole bill. That is not bad luck. A rule that waits for the price to climb back above its own one-year average is guaranteed by its own arithmetic to be late back in after a deep fall, because the average it is waiting for has been dragged down and takes months to be cleared. The rule is structurally late, every time, and the deeper the crash the later it is.

THE HYPOTHESIS THAT FOLLOWS. The lab has spent six ideas this month on WHEN to read the rule -- how often, in which month, with what price cushion, on what grid -- and every one of them answered a fraction of a point a year. None of them can touch the structural lateness, because none of them changes what the money does while the rule is out. That is the untouched dial: today the money sits in cash earning nothing through exactly the months the recovery is strongest.

So: hold something during the absence rather than nothing.
