A broad market holding at a reduced size, the companies that fell least, long-dated government bonds, or a ladder that buys back a quarter of the book at a time as the market closes above its average for longer. All four are testable on the data already here, none needs a new instrument the owner cannot buy, and all four attack the only part of the bill that is large. The prediction is that a partial re-entry ladder recovers most of the spring of 2009 while keeping the crash protection, because the protection is bought on the way DOWN and the bill is paid on the way UP, and those are two different decisions that this rule has always made with one switch.

insights.title: The shortfall breakdown should measure the exit rule's share instead of modelling it
insights.body:
When this lab takes apart why a strategy trailed the market, it splits the gap into three pieces: what the market-exit rule cost by standing in cash, what trading cost in fees, and whatever is left over, which it calls the stock picking. The first piece is not measured. It is computed, as how long the strategy sat out multiplied by what the market returned in those years.

That shortcut has now been checked against the real thing on twelve recorded strategies covering twelve different ideas, by running each one as recorded and again with the exit rule removed and nothing else touched. Since 2009 the shortcut understates the rule's cost by about forty per cent on the median, and in every earlier stretch it gets the SIGN wrong -- it reports a cost where the rule actually earned, by as much as nine points a year in the crash years. Worst of all, the shortcut's answers barely vary between strategies, which is exactly why it has looked so reassuringly constant, while the real costs vary seventeen-fold.

So every breakdown published since that shortcut was adopted has mis-stated the leftover that gets attributed to the stock picking -- too kind to it after 2009, far too harsh before.

THE FIX IS ALREADY HALF BUILT. The lab has a command that switches the exit rule off generically and re-runs both arms at the recorded capital and funding, and it checks its own transform against six gate-off controls the lab already holds before it measures anything. It records no trial and spends no held-out window. What is missing is only the plumbing: the breakdown should call it and use the measured difference as the exit rule's column, falling back to the computed estimate and SAYING SO only for the strategies whose rule cannot be switched off cleanly. The same command should also report each arm's average cash in the era being claimed rather than over the whole twenty years, because the rule sits out a quite different share of 2009 to 2015 than of the full window and the whole-window figure halves every recent ratio.

insights.title: The safety switch is not a cash dial after all — the hypothesis in the earlier version of this note is refuted in every decade
insights.body:
This replaces the previous version, which proposed something that has since been measured and is false. The arithmetic that suggested it was tidy and it was wrong, and the way it was wrong is worth more than the idea was.

WHAT THE OLD VERSION PROPOSED. The lab's safety rule — step out of the market when it is below its long-term average — has a famous figure attached: it costs about three and a half points a year, and that figure has looked suspiciously constant across hundreds of recorded runs. The previous version noticed that if you take that cost and divide it by what a point of cash was worth in 2009 to 2015, you get about twenty points of time out of the market, which is roughly what such a rule sits out across a decade with no crash. So perhaps, it suggested, the rule has no judgement in it at all and the whole famous figure is just the price of being out of the market, with a story attached.

IT IS NOT. A ladder of six versions on a deliberately dull book, with the time out of the market moved deliberately rather than left to happen, measured the gap between what the rule actually cost and what its cash alone explains. If the idea were right that gap would be zero. It is not zero in any decade, it misses by six to twenty times the measurement noise, AND IT CHANGES SIGN between decades: in the late nineties and across 2003 to 2008 the rule EARNED several points more than its cash can explain, and since 2009 it has cost three points more. The plainest version of it: with the rule switched on and no delay, the book held twenty-eight points more cash than the version with the rule off, and it earned one and a half points a year MORE. Cash alone says it should have lost.

WHY THE TIDY ARITHMETIC LOOKED RIGHT. Every book in this lab that uses the rule sits out the SAME days, because they all share the rule. So multiplying time-out by the market's return hands back nearly the same answer for all of them by construction. Measured across twelve different ideas, what the rule actually cost since 2009 ranges from under one point a year to over ten — a seventeen-fold spread — while the cash model predicts between 2.8 and 3.5 for all of them, a spread of 1.2. One recorded book happens to land where the model says, which is very likely why the model ever looked convincing.

WHAT THE BILL IS REALLY MADE OF, since 2009. About three and a half points is simply holding the cash. About one and three quarters is holding it in LUMPS at the rule's own boundaries rather than spread evenly — cash taken in long absences costs well over half as much again per point as cash held steadily, which is a quantity this lab had never measured. And about one and a half points is the rule's own choice of WHICH months to be out: the book earned about twice as much in the months it sat out as in the months it was invested. That is a market-timing failure rather than a stock-picking one.

A CAVEAT THE MEASUREMENT CARRIES AND I AM KEEPING: one absence, February to June 2009, accounts for more than two thirds of that last term. The direction is solid; the size is not.

WHAT IT COSTS THE REST OF THE RECORD. Every breakdown of 'where did the shortfall go' published since the famous figure was first quoted used the MODELLED cash column rather than a measured one. So the leftover those breakdowns attribute to the stock picking is mis-stated — too kind since 2009, far too harsh before it. The fix needs no new strategy and no held-out look: the machinery to run any recorded book with its rule switched off already exists, so measure the column instead of modelling it, and read the time-out-of-market for the ERA being claimed rather than for the whole window.

insights.title: Companies that stopped growing their balance sheet: buy the index members whose total assets grew least over the past year: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 4 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +8.3% on the usual history, +6.8% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 55.0% and 55.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +2.7% a year before and −0.7% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.5 points a year less. 4 of its 4 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Buying shrinking companies looks good only because the ones that died are missing
insights.body:
The lab tested the well-known 2008 finding that companies whose balance sheets grow least go on to beat the fastest growers. The filings the lab holds only reach back to 2009, so the test covered October 2010 to October 2015. The slow growers earned 17.8% a year, against 14.3% for SPY. That looked like a win, until the same test was re-run on the price history that puts back the companies that later went bust. Then the slow growers' lead over SPY in 2009-2015 went from +2.7 points a year to -0.7.

The reason is simple. A company whose assets are shrinking is often a company in trouble. The troubled ones that survived are in the lab's main price history. The ones that went under are missing from it. So a book that buys shrinkers looks better than it really was, because its worst picks have been quietly removed. Critics of the original paper said exactly this, and here it is in the lab's own numbers.

What to do about it: treat any result that favours shrinking, struggling or cheapening companies as suspect until it has been checked on the history that includes the dead companies. That check costs nothing and takes a few minutes.

insights.title: When both ends of a ranking win, it is the market's rise, not the ranking
insights.body: In the same test, the 30 slowest-growing and the 30 fastest-growing companies both beat a blind draw from the same pool by 3 to 4 points a year, and finished within 0.6 points of each other. If a ranking wins the same way whichever end you buy, the ranking is not what earns the money. Both ends were simply unusual, jumpier companies. They fell harder in 2011 and rose harder in 2012 and 2013, and in a market that mostly went up, jumpier books earn more. Several near misses in the lab may be this same effect in disguise. The next test asks it directly: buy the most market-sensitive members, the least sensitive, and a blind draw, side by side.

insights.title: The price jump already knows the surprise; a year-on-year earnings check only blurs it
insights.body: The news-day book buys big stocks right after a large jump on heavy volume, usually an earnings report. We tried checking each jump against the company's own filed accounts: did earnings per share beat the same quarter a year earlier by more than usual? The idea was that a jump the accounts agree with is real news confirmed twice. It worked backwards. In 2012 to 2015, the only years with enough filings to test, dropping the jumps the accounts contradicted cost the book about 3.6 points a year, losing in 30 of 46 months. Books holding only confirmed jumps or only contradicted ones did about the same as each other. The reason: the market's three-day reaction measures the gap between the news and what investors expected, and a plain year-on-year comparison is a cruder copy of that. A company still earning less than last year but far better than feared jumps and keeps rising, and the year-on-year check throws it away. Lesson for the lab: a second signal that measures the same thing worse does not confirm the first, it dilutes it.

insights.title: Cheap companies whose accounts are getting stronger: a financial-health score among the cheapest index members: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.6% on the usual history, +6.5% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 55.0% and 55.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +1.0% a year before and −1.3% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 1 of 4 periods won to 0 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.0 points a year less. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A health check on company accounts does not rescue cheap big companies
insights.body: We tried a famous idea from 2000: among the cheapest big US companies, buy the ones whose annual reports show them getting healthier (more profit, more cash, less new stock, better margins). From 2010 to 2015, the only years our filing data covers, the healthy cheap group earned 12.5% a year, the same as the S&P 500. It beat the sick cheap group by about 3 points a year, but only 0.4 points more than twenty cheap companies picked at random, so trading on the health check barely paid for itself. Simply buying the cheapest companies lost 3 points a year to the index, because cheap big companies in those years were mostly banks, insurers and oil firms. The original study's edge lived in small, little-watched companies, where good news in the accounts takes months to reach the price. Big companies' reports are read the day they come out. When we put back the companies that later went bust, every version fell behind the index. Lesson: health scores from annual reports are not an edge among big companies, and a cheap-stock frame is a bet against the market's shape.

insights.title: The market-shaped book leaning toward bond-like stocks: every index company at its market value, tilted toward those that rise when yields fall, beside a random tilt: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.4% on the usual history, +6.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 50.2% and 50.5%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −1.1% a year before and −1.7% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.1 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Bond-like stocks were the better half only while rates were falling
insights.body: Across four tries, companies whose shares rise when long-term interest rates fall (drug makers, food and household brands, utilities) beat the companies that move the other way from 1996 to 2015. But that edge belonged to an era of steadily falling rates. In 2009-2015, with rates already near zero, it reversed: a market-shaped book leaning toward rate-rising companies kept pace with SPY while the bond-like lean trailed by almost three points a year. And leaning at all cost more than the lean earned: moving money away from the biggest companies and trading more took about 0.8 points a year, while the opinion itself was worth about 0.3. The plain market-shaped book without any lean did best. Lesson: a pattern that tracks interest rates is a bet on where rates go next, not a stock-picking skill, and it should be judged on the years after the rate trend turned.

insights.title: Sera 20261022-1918: the company accounts, read honestly, pick nothing among big companies
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Nothing new cleared the lab's paper screen, so nothing was put forward for a look at the held-back years, and the gate had nothing to refuse.

The last batch ended by saying the lab should stop asking questions about its own machinery and go back to looking for a genuinely different signal. This batch did that. Three of the four ideas read companies' published accounts, the yearly and quarterly filings, instead of share prices, which is the part of the data the lab had used least. The fourth leaned the whole market toward stocks that behave like bonds. All four ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up, so there was no cheap version to be disappointed by later.

WHAT WAS TRIED, AND WHAT HAPPENED

Companies that stopped growing. A well-known 2008 finding says companies whose balance sheets grew least over the past year go on to beat those that grew fastest. Among the big index companies from 2010 to 2015, the slowest growers made about 17.8% a year and the fastest growers 17.2%: a tie. Both beat SPY, but so did a blind draw from the same pool, which says the market's rise did the work and the ranking did nothing. The slow growers' lead over SPY also vanished, and went slightly negative, once the companies that later went bust were put back into the price history. The critics of the original paper said exactly that, and here they were right.

Cheap companies getting healthier. A 2000 study scores companies on nine simple checks of improving health: profitable, cash coming in, debt falling, margins rising and so on. It says the healthiest of the cheapest companies beat the market. Among big companies it tied SPY (12.5% a year against 12.6%), beat a random pick of cheap companies by less than half a point, and fell behind SPY in every version once failed companies were restored.

Earnings news confirmed by the accounts. The lab already has a near miss that buys a stock after an unusually large jump on its results day. This batch asked whether the jump is more trustworthy when the company's reported earnings also beat the same quarter a year earlier. It is not. Adding the check made the book about three and a half points a year worse from 2012 to 2015. The price jump already contains what the accounts say, and the accounts only blur it. The original book stays where it was. It is not a new finding, and it was not put forward.

The market, leaning toward bond-like stocks. The whole market held at its real size, nudged toward stocks that rise when interest rates fall. Leaning did worse than not leaning: 6.9 to 7.1% a year against 7.4% for the plain market book and 7.2% for SPY. The bond-like half beat its opposite only while rates were falling. After 2009 it trailed SPY by nearly three points a year, while the opposite lean kept pace.

WHAT THE BATCH TAUGHT

The same lesson came back three times. Most of what a published company-accounts signal appears to earn among big American companies is the companies that are missing from the price history: the ones that went bust or were taken over. On the honest copy of history, which puts them back, every accounts-based book this batch fell to SPY or below. A second lesson came from the first idea: when both ends of a ranking beat the market, the ranking is not what is working. The book is simply more exposed to a rising market, and a blind draw does just as well.

Directions that look dead: the classic accounts signals used on their own among big companies (growth of the balance sheet, the health score, and from earlier batches value and profitability), and leaning toward bond-like stocks as a standing tilt. Directions that look alive, but only barely: whether the bond-like lean is worth anything when it switches sides with the direction of interest rates, and whether a large price jump on a day with no earnings report means something different from one on a results day. Both are queued. Also queued: whether jumpy and calm companies differ at all once the market's rise is taken out, and a gentle quality lean on the whole market rather than a book of its own.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST

The company filings only begin in 2009 to 2010, so every accounts idea this batch could be judged on five or six years at most, all after its paper was published, and none could ever meet the gate's four-period test. Filings going back to the 1990s would change that more than any new idea would. And, as in every batch, price history that includes the dead companies was the decisive check three times out of four.

FEES

Gotrade's real fees decided nothing this batch. Every result above is already net of them, and none of the four had an edge for fees to take away.

NEXT BATCH

Stop mining the company filings for standalone signals among big companies; four tries now say there is nothing there that survives the dead companies. Try instead the two live threads above, and an idea that does not depend on which companies survived, such as signals that trade the market itself, or that compare a company only with its own history.

insights.title: Jumpy versus calm index members: is 'both ends of a ranking win' just market sensitivity?: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.8% on the usual history, +12.8% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 34.1% and 35.3%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −2.6% a year before and −3.0% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 3 of 4 periods won to 1 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 2.0 points a year more. 3 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A stock book that leans into the market looks skilled in a rising decade
insights.body: The asset-growth picker's slowest-growing 30 companies beat a random 30 by about 4 points a year in 2010-2015, and so did its fastest-growing 30, which made no sense if the ranking mattered. Measured month by month, the slow-growers moved 1.19 times as much as the market while the random 30 moved 0.92 times. The market rose about 14% a year then, so that lean alone is worth about 4 points a year: the entire lead. Once it is taken out, the book did what a random 30 did. The same test over twenty years: the 30 jumpiest index members and the 30 calmest earned almost exactly the same (11.5% and 11.1% a year with deposits removed), but the jumpy ones fell 72% at their worst against 29%. What to do: before believing that any stock picker beat SPY in 2009-2015, check whether it simply moved more than the market. A lead that disappears once you allow for that is a bet on the market rising, which SPY already makes more cheaply.

insights.title: Grade every near miss against its own market sensitivity
insights.body: The lab judges each book against SPY and, for some methods, against a random draw of the same size. Neither notices a book that just moves more than the market. A report that measures each recorded book's sensitivity to SPY month by month, and its return after allowing for that, would have flagged the asset-growth picker's lead in seconds instead of costing a method to explain. It needs no new data and spends no test look: the monthly curves are already recorded. Run it over the books closest to qualifying first, especially those whose lead over SPY lives in 2009-2015.

insights.title: The missing dead companies flatter the jumpiest stocks most
insights.body: The lab's main price store lacks about half the 1990s index members, mostly the ones that later died. Putting most of them back changed the 30 jumpiest stocks from beating SPY by 3 points a year to losing to it by 3.5, with a worst fall of 93% instead of 77%; the 30 most volatile lost about 5 points a year. The 30 calmest barely moved. The stocks that swing hardest are the ones most likely to go bust, so a store of survivors shows only their rebounds. Any idea that buys beaten-down or very volatile stocks should be read on the survivorship-check store before anyone believes it.

insights.title: Any big news drifts, not just earnings, and the news-day book wins by holding all of it
insights.body: The news-day book buys big companies right after a sharp jump on heavy trading. We split those jumps two ways: whether a quarterly earnings report explained the jump, and whether it fell in the company's usual reporting weeks. Jumps on other news (upgrades, deals, product launches) kept rising afterwards about as well as earnings jumps, within a couple of points a year either way, which is inside the noise. But every book that kept only one kind of jump did worse than the book that kept them all, by 2 to 6 points a year in 2009-2015, because it held two to five stocks instead of about thirteen and parked the rest in the index. Across two experiments, six ways of choosing among these jumps have all lost to not choosing. The lesson: don't filter this book's jumps; if anything, find more of them.

insights.title: Moving-average distance: buy index members whose 21-day average sits furthest above their 200-day average: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +16.0% on the usual history, +19.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 31.8% and 31.8%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.3% a year before and +0.8% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 3.3 points a year more. 1 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A new name for momentum: the moving-average gap picks the same stocks as last year's winners
insights.body: A 2018 paper says a stock whose average price over the last month sits far above its average over the last ten months keeps rising, and that this beats plain momentum, the habit of buying last year's winners. Among the big companies the lab can size, the top twenty by this gap did beat a blind draw of the same size and churn by about 3 points a year from 1996 to 2015. But once the part explained by the past year's rise and by nearness to the yearly high was taken out, what was left earned no more than the blind draw. With the market switch in front (step aside while SPY is below its 200-day average), the book grew the owner's deposits by 16% a year against 7% for SPY and fell at most 32%. Its month-to-month moves, though, track a momentum book that already failed its one look at recent years, and it trailed SPY from 2009 to 2015. The lesson: a price-trend signal under a fresh name is still a price-trend signal, and the lab's kin check is right to treat it that way. One surprise worth keeping: on the lab's usual prices the opposite book, the stocks furthest below their long average, did best of all, almost all of it in the 2009 bounce. Once the companies that later died were added back, that book fell 86% at its worst and lost its lead. Books that buy the fallen are the ones the missing dead companies flatter most.

insights.title: The moving-average gap is closed: it is momentum, and momentum already failed its look
insights.body: The lab tested a 2021 finding that stocks trading well above their own long-run average price keep rising. It works on paper only because it picks the same stocks as last year's winners: with that taken out, it did no better than a random pick. Behind the market safety switch it cleared the paper screen, but the lab's gate refuses it because it behaves like a momentum book that already failed on the held-back years, and it trailed SPY from 2009 to 2015. Treat any future idea built on a stock's distance from its own price average as momentum, and expect the same refusal.

insights.title: Lean with the rate trend: a market-shaped book that tilts toward bond-like stocks while 10-year yields are falling and toward rate-rising stocks while they are rising: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.4% on the usual history, +6.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 50.2% and 50.5%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −1.1% a year before and −1.7% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.1 points a year less. 5 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Following the direction of interest rates did not tell us which stocks to lean toward
insights.body: We tried leaning a market-shaped book toward 'bond-like' stocks (drug makers, food brands, utilities) whenever the 10-year Treasury yield was lower than a year earlier, and toward banks, energy and industrials when it was higher. Following the yield's trend beat going against it by only 0.3 points a year over twenty years, and in 2009-2015 it lost to going against it by 2.6 points a year. Share prices react to rate news the day it arrives; a year-long trend in the yield is already priced in by the time anyone can see it. Meanwhile any lean on this book costs about a point a year (it moves money away from the biggest companies, which kept winning, and it trades about half again as much). The plain book with no lean earned 7.4% a year against SPY's 7.2%; the rate-following lean earned 6.5%. A lean needs to know much more than a slow public signal can tell it.

insights.title: The cost-of-opinion check should accept a method's own no-lean book as its yardstick
insights.body: The lab has an automatic check that splits a rule's result into what its opinion knows and what acting on it costs. It needs an arm that is always invested and barely trades. This run's no-lean book is the perfect yardstick, the same book with only the lean removed, but it re-weights monthly, so it trades more than the check allows and the check reported the cost as unknown. Priced by hand, the opinion knew about 0.15 points a year and leaning cost about 1.05. Every lean on a market-shaped book will hit the same wall. The check should let a method name its own no-opinion arm (the same variant with the lean set to zero) instead of only recognising a buy-and-hold book.

insights.title: Sera 20261022-1954: most of what looked like skill was jumpiness or momentum in disguise
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two methods cleared the lab's paper screen, and the gate rightly refused both, so nothing was put forward for a look at the held-back years.

The last batch said to stop mining company accounts and to follow two live threads: a big price jump on a day with no earnings report, and a lean toward bond-like stocks that switches sides with the direction of interest rates. This batch ran both. It also tested the question the last batch raised, whether "both ends of a ranking win" is just jumpy stocks in a rising market, and one new published idea that compares each stock only with its own past. All four ran in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the monthly top-up.

WHAT WAS TRIED, AND WHAT HAPPENED

Jumpy stocks against calm stocks. The thirty index stocks that move most with the market and the thirty that move least, beside a random thirty. Over twenty years the two ends earned about the same on the owner's deposits, 10.1% a year for the jumpy ones and 10.8% for the calm ones, against 7.2% for SPY. But the jumpy book's worst fall was 77% against 34%. When the companies that later went bust are put back into the history, the jumpy book drops to 3.7% a year, below SPY, with a worst fall of 93%. The calm book barely moved. This settles last batch's puzzle: the slow-growing-companies book that seemed to beat a random pick in 2010 to 2015 moved about 1.2 times as much as the market, and that alone explains its lead. It was a bet on a rising market, not a stock pick.

Big jumps with no earnings behind them. About half the large, heavy-volume jumps in big stocks happen on days with no earnings report. They kept drifting up about as well as results-day jumps did. But every way of filtering the jumps, by whether a report explains them or by whether it is reporting season, held only two to five stocks instead of about thirteen and lost to the unfiltered book by two to six points a year after 2009. The only version that passed is the existing news-day book, unchanged. It wins three of four tests of the lab's screen but only two of four later periods, so the gate refused it, and it carries no new evidence anyway.

The bond-like lean, switched with interest rates. Lean the whole market toward bond-like stocks while long-term rates fall, and toward the opposite while they rise. It earned 6.5% a year, against 7.4% for the plain market-shaped book with no lean and 7.2% for SPY. It beat its own opposite by only a third of a point a year, while leaning at all cost about a point a year in extra trading and in moving money away from the biggest companies. After 2009 it trailed SPY by nearly three points a year. That thread is now closed.

How far a stock sits above its own average price. A 2021 study says stocks whose one-month average price sits well above their ten-month average keep rising, because investors anchor on the old price. In the lab it picked almost the same stocks as plain momentum, last year's winners. With momentum taken out it did no better than a random pick. Behind the market safety switch it cleared the paper screen at 16% a year against 7.2% for SPY, with a worst fall of 32%. But it trailed SPY from 2009 to 2015, and it behaves like a momentum book that already failed on the held-back years. So the gate refused it, as it should.

WHAT THE BATCH TAUGHT

Three of the four results were one lesson in different clothes: what looks like stock-picking skill is often just a book that holds more of the market's ups and downs, or holds momentum by another name. The lab now has a direct way to see that. Compare a book with a random pick of the same jumpiness, and with the companies that went bust put back. Every near miss should be graded that way before anyone believes it, and that is now a feature on the wish list. The fourth result was a smaller lesson: a filter that cuts a book down to a few stocks almost always loses to the whole book, whatever the filter knows.

Directions that look dead: jumpy-stock books, any rate-direction tilt, and anything built on a stock's distance from its own price average, which is momentum. Directions that look alive, barely: calm stocks, which kept their returns when the dead companies came back and fell a third as far as the jumpy ones. That is why the next idea is half the calmest stocks and half SPY. Also a wider news-day pool that takes slightly smaller jumps, so the book holds more names.

THE GATE AND THE BUY SIGNAL

Two methods cleared the paper screen and both were refused. The news-day book was refused for winning too few later periods. The moving-average book was refused because it behaves like a book that already failed its look. Neither had a positive edge over SPY in 2009 to 2015, the years the price history covers best, so neither would have been a buy signal for survivorship-free data even without the gate.

FEES

Gotrade's fees decided nothing new: every number above already includes them. In the rate-switch idea the cost of leaning, mostly trading, was several times what the lean's opinion was worth.

NEXT BATCH

Half calm stocks and half SPY. A wider news-day pool. A cheaper market-shaped base that rebalances only with each monthly deposit, since trading cost has now beaten every tilt put on top of it. And keep looking for signals that do not come down to jumpiness or momentum.

insights.title: The lab's books cannot answer a currency-timing question: the rupiah rate is held fixed by design
insights.body: Before reserving this batch I checked whether the owner's deposits could be timed against the rupiah: he saves in rupiah and buys dollar shares, so a rule that waits for a strong rupiah would be a real lever and nothing in the lab had tested it. It cannot be tested here. The contribution schedule converts every deposit at the SAME rate it converted the opening money at, deliberately, so that a result is about the strategy and not about the currency. Every return the lab has ever recorded is therefore a dollar return wearing rupiah clothes, and a book that appeared to gain from a cheap rupiah would only be showing the conversion. Answering the question at all would mean changing the machinery that funds every book, which would move every recorded number, so it is a change to argue for on its own and not a method to reserve. Recording it so no future batch spends an idea on it.

insights.title: Wider news-day pool: take large-for-the-stock jumps on 2x normal volume, not only 3x: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 65.7% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +12.3% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +12.3% a year, which is +5.1% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned +0.7% a year, −6.5% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +5.1% a year against the market as recorded, +5.1% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +6.0% a year against the market as recorded, +5.9% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +4.3% a year against the market as recorded, +4.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: +2.3% a year against the market as recorded, +2.4% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in all 4 of the periods they could be judged on. The earnings come from the picking.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Wider news-day pool: take large-for-the-stock jumps on 2x normal volume, not only 3x: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +12.3% on the usual history, +10.7% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 23.8% and 26.2%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +2.3% a year before and −0.1% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 3 of 4 periods won to 2 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.6 points a year less. 4 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Calm stocks beside SPY: how much of the market should sit next to the low-beta book?: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:

Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 63.2% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +9.4% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +10.8% a year, which is +3.6% against the market.
- On 0.0% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned +7.2% a year, −0.0% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +2.2% a year against the market as recorded, +3.6% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +0.8% a year against the market as recorded, +1.3% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +6.3% a year against the market as recorded, +9.6% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +11.0% a year against the market as recorded, +15.7% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −1.9% a year against the market as recorded, −2.6% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 3 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Asking for heavy trading volume is really a test of whether the company is still alive
insights.body:
The news-day book buys big companies right after a day that looks like big news: the share price gaps up, it gains several points more than the market over three days, and it trades at least three times its usual volume. That 'three times' was picked once, years ago, and never questioned. I turned it five ways — no volume test at all, two times, two and a half, three, and four — and changed nothing else.

The return hardly moved: every setting earned between eleven and a half and twelve and a half per cent a year on the owner's deposits, against seven for the same money in the market. But the worst fall moved enormously, and in a straight line. With no volume test the book lost 37 per cent from its peak. At two times, 28. At two and a half, 26. At three, 24. The volume test buys almost no extra return and halves the pain.

Then the same five books were re-run on the tape that includes the companies that went bust, which our normal history leaves out. The pattern repeated, in the opposite direction and just as straight: the looser the volume test, the more of the book's apparent success turned out to have been the missing dead companies. The no-volume book gave back three and a third points a year. The strictest book was the only one that earned MORE with the dead companies back.

That explains what the volume test is actually doing. A company the market is busily trading on a news day is a company that still exists and that people care about. A four-point price move on an ordinary day's volume is far more likely to be a thin, fading business drifting on nothing — and those are exactly the companies our history quietly omits once they die. The volume test was never mainly about finding news. It was keeping the book out of names that were on their way out.

What to do about it: this is worth borrowing. Any of our strategies that picks stocks purely on how the price moved, with no check on how much was actually traded, is exposed the same way the no-volume book is — and would look better on our history than it would have been in real life. Pairing a 'was anyone trading it' test with a 'did the price move' test may be a cheap general safeguard, and it costs nothing to add. That is the next experiment.

insights.title: The same strategy passed our out-of-sample test only because of which other strategies sat beside it in the file
insights.body:
One of our safeguards works like this: split the twenty years into four stretches, and for each one ask what the lab would have chosen knowing only the past, then score that choice on years it had never seen. A strategy has to win a majority of those stretches before it can go near real money or before we would pay for better data.

Today an identical strategy — the news-day book, the same trades, the same account curve, matching to the last digit — collected three different scores from that safeguard in three different places. Recorded one way it won one stretch of four. Recorded a second way, two of four. Recorded a third way, three of four, which is a pass, and which set off the lab's alarm saying this is the moment to buy better historical data.

Nothing about the strategy changed between those three readings. What changed is the company it kept. We always test several versions of an idea together in one file, and the safeguard picks, for each stretch, whichever version looked best in the years before it. In the first two files some other version always looked better in training, so the safeguard went off and scored that other version instead — and then filed the result under the whole idea. The news-day book itself was never actually tested. In today's file every sibling version was worse than it, so for the first time the safeguard scored the book itself, and it won three of four.

There are two honest ways to read that, and both are worth holding at once. Kindly: this book had genuinely never been put through the test, and the first time it was, it passed. Unkindly: a strategy's out-of-sample record partly reflects which siblings were registered alongside it, which means the way to pass is to surround a favourite with weak company. Nobody did that deliberately here, and it happened anyway.

Why it matters now: this is one of the handful of gates standing between a backtest and the owner's actual savings, and we have only one unspent look at the recent years left in the budget that we would not regret. A gate that can be moved by the choice of siblings is not measuring what we think it measures.

What to do: the test should score the exact version we would actually put money into, on its own record, regardless of what else shares its file. That is a change to the lab's own rules rather than to any strategy, and it should be argued and written down before the next time this alarm goes off. In the meantime, treat any 'buy better data' alarm by first checking whether the strategy it names is one we already hold under another name — today's was held under three.

insights.title: The buy-signal alarm fired for the first time on an unspent book, and the honest history says no
insights.body:
The lab's alarm for "now is the moment to pay for better history" went off this batch, for the
news-day book: buy a big company straight after a day when its price jumped, it beat the market
by several points over three days, and it traded at least three times its usual volume. It is the
first time that alarm has gone off on a book nobody has spent a look on.

I did not act on it, and the reason matters more than the alarm.

The alarm reads the years 1 January 2009 to the end of 2015, because those are the years our
price history covers best. On that history the book beat the market by 2.3 points a year. But the
lab also keeps a second, honest history that puts back most of the companies our usual one is
missing -- the ones that went bankrupt, were bought out or changed their name. On that history
the same book, over the same years, trails the market by 0.1 points a year, and its record in the
four held-back stretches drops from three won to two. The margin the alarm fired on is smaller
than its own year-to-year noise, which the report itself prints.

There is a second reason. The version the lab would have put forward is not this method's idea at
all. The idea was to widen the net by asking for less trading volume, and every wider setting did
worse. The version left standing is the existing news-day book, unchanged -- the same trades and
the same account curve, to the last digit, as three strategies the lab already holds. Spending a
look on it would spend it on something we already had, under a new name, on the strength of a
measurement this method did not produce.

So: no better data is being bought, and no look has been spent. Four looks are gone, two remain
of what we would not regret, and all four spent so far failed on the same condition, beating the
market with dividends counted.

What would change my mind: a book whose lead over the market in 2009 to 2015 survives having the
dead companies put back. That is the single test this one failed, and it is the test every
strategy the lab has ever put forward has failed. Until a book passes it, the alarm firing is not
a reason to spend money on data or on a look.

insights.title: How often must a book be re-weighted? The market's own shape and the lab's equal slices, each re-set every month and once a year: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.3% on the usual history, +9.1% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 57.5% and 58.7%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +3.5% a year before and +2.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.2 points a year less. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A safety rule has to be able to leave the room in one step
insights.body:
Our market safety rule is one line: if the market is above its own long-run average, stay invested; if not, hold cash. The best-known improvement on it is to stop making that a yes-or-no question. Ask several averages of different lengths, count how many say yes, and hold that share of the book. The appeal is that it spreads the cash out instead of taking it in lumps, and we had just measured that lumpy cash is about one and a half times as expensive as cash held evenly.

We built it carefully. All the versions held the same average amount of cash, to within half a point, so none of them could win simply by being more invested. The only thing that moved was how finely the same opinion got expressed.

Grading cost about a point a year, and it bought no safety at all.

The reason is worth remembering, because it is not about this rule in particular. For a vote to reach zero, every length has to agree, and the long ones only turn down well after a fall is under way. So a graded rule is never all the way out at the moment of maximum danger. It gets there late, carrying part of the book down the slide. In 2008 the plain rule was fully out and lost nothing; the graded versions held just under two percent of the book and that alone cost two and a half points.

The cost is also not spread evenly over the years. It was almost nothing in the stretch from 2009 to 2015, which contained no bear market, and it was at its worst in the two eras that did. Grading is free exactly when the safety rule is useless and expensive exactly when the rule earns its keep.

What to do about it: treat decisiveness as part of what a safety rule is for, not as a crude detail waiting to be smoothed. Any future suggestion to average several versions of the same timing rule is already answered, and the answer is no.

insights.title: Our main price history can hide whether a safety change is safe
insights.body:
The same three versions of a book, differing only in how finely their safety rule grades its exposure, were measured on both of our price histories.

On the everyday one, their worst falls were 17.816, 17.818 and 17.817 percent. A spread of two thousandths of a point. Read on that history alone, the honest conclusion would have been that this change is perfectly neutral for safety.

On the fuller history, which puts back most of the companies that went bankrupt or were bought out, the same three fell 17.5, 23.8 and 21.1 percent. A spread of six points. The change is not neutral at all. It makes the worst fall up to six points deeper.

Why it matters: the everyday history is missing roughly four in ten of the days a company sat in the index, and the missing ones are overwhelmingly the companies that died. Those are precisely the names that make a bad fall worse. So a safety claim measured without them can come out looking flat when the real answer is a wide spread, and the error runs in the dangerous direction every time.

What to do about it: never accept a worst-fall claim on the everyday history alone. Re-run it on the fuller one before believing it. That costs no new experiment and no fresh look at the reserved years. This is a habit change, not a research project, and it applies to every safety comparison this lab has already published as well as to future ones.

insights.title: A cheap rehearsal on the market index alone understated the real effect five times over
insights.body:
Before committing to this experiment we rehearsed it on the market index by itself: no stock picking, no fees, no deposits, just the rule applied to one price series. That rehearsal is cheap, it costs no experiment and no fresh look at the reserved years, and it caught something genuinely important that would otherwise have ruined the study. It showed that the published version of the idea mixes two separate changes together, and it let us separate them before a single number was recorded.

But it got the size of the headline effect badly wrong. The rehearsal said the change was worth about a fifth of a point a year. On the real book of fifty names, with real fees and the real monthly top-up, it was worth one and a tenth. Five times larger, and large enough to cross the line we had written down in advance as the threshold for a real finding.

The fees were not the explanation. Re-running every version with all fees set to zero moved the answer by seven hundredths of a point. The difference is simply that a rule applied to fifty holdings that are bought, sold and rebalanced on a schedule does not behave like the same rule applied to one price line, even when the rule reads nothing but that line.

What to do about it: keep using these rehearsals, because this one paid for itself twice over in design. But use them only to decide what to test and which traps to avoid, never to predict how big an effect will be, and never to decide that something is too small to be worth testing.

insights.title: Let the monthly deposit do the re-balancing: it earns more and trades a third less
insights.body: A basket of shares drifts out of shape as prices move, and the usual cure is to sell a little of whatever grew and buy a little of whatever shrank. That selling costs fees every time. This run compared three ways of keeping a 240-company basket in even slices over twenty years, on the real deposit plan and the real Gotrade fees. Re-balancing every month earned 10.2 percent a year. Re-balancing once each January and otherwise doing nothing earned 9.7 percent. Never re-balancing by selling at all, and instead spending each month's deposit on whichever companies had slipped furthest behind, earned 10.3 percent while trading a third less than the monthly version. The reason the yearly version lagged is not that it failed to trim its winners. It is that it had no rule for spending the money arriving each month, so up to eleven months of deposits sat in cash: it was 94.5 percent invested where the other two were 97 percent, and each point of the account left in cash costs roughly a fifth of a point a year. Give it a rule that spends the deposit and the gap closes and reverses. The practical lesson is the happiest kind: the cheapest way to run this sort of basket is also the easiest to do by hand and the one that earned the most. Buy with the new money, sell nothing, and let the top-up pull the basket back into shape by itself.

insights.title: A basket held in proportion to company size keeps its own shape, so re-weighting it monthly is pure cost
insights.body: There are two ways to split money across a list of companies: give each one an equal share, or give each one a share matching how big it really is. The second kind quietly looks after itself, and that is arithmetic rather than a market discovery. A company's size is its share count times its share price, so if you hold companies in proportion to their size and then touch nothing, each holding's share of your account moves exactly the way its target moves. The basket re-balances itself as prices move. Only three things can pull it off: a company issuing or buying back shares, a company joining or leaving the index, and a rule capping any one company at five percent. Measured here, after six to eight months of drift only one to four companies in a hundred had slipped far enough off target to be worth a trade, against about twenty in a hundred for an equally sliced basket of the same companies. The result followed: re-setting the size-weighted basket once a year instead of every month cut its trading by almost two thirds and changed what the money earned by nothing at all, to the first decimal, over twenty years. So if a basket is ever held in the market's own proportions, re-weight it once a year and spend the saving on nothing. The effort only buys something when the slices are equal, because nothing is holding equal slices equal.

insights.title: Equal slices beat the market's own shape here by three points a year, and lose nine points a year in exactly the years we are living through
insights.body: Holding the same 240 big American companies in equal amounts earned about three points a year more than holding them in proportion to their real size, over 1996 to 2015, and the gap was wider still in the best-covered years: equal slices beat buying SPY by three and a half points a year in 2009 to 2015, where the size-weighted version lost to SPY by more than a point. That survives when the companies that went bust are priced back in. It is a real effect and it points the opposite way to what this lab has assumed for a year. But the same run shows what it is a bet on. Split those twenty years into months where a handful of giant companies carried the index and months where the average company did the work. In the broad months the equal-slice basket earned thirteen points a year more than the index. In the narrow months it lost eight to nine points a year. The years the owner's money has actually been invested, 2018 onward, were the narrowest in modern memory, carried by a few very large American technology companies. So this is not a free improvement waiting to be adopted. It is a bet that the average company starts beating the giants, placed by someone who has already watched four strategies lose to simply buying the index over exactly the period when they did not. Worth measuring further, not worth acting on, and never worth quoting as a twenty-year average without the breadth split beside it.

insights.title: Mixing a strategy with the market is dilution, not borrowing — and the dial has no sweet spot
insights.body:
The thirty calmest companies in the index earn more than their calmness says they should, but they only move about a third as hard as the market, so in a rising decade they fall behind simply by standing still. The textbook cure is to borrow money and buy more of them. The owner cannot borrow, so this run tested the obvious cash-only substitute: hold the market itself alongside them, and turn the amount of market up and down like a dial.

The dial was set five ways, from all market and no calm stocks through to all calm stocks and no market. Every column of the result moves the same direction at every step. Going from all market to no market, the money earned a year rises from 7.2% to 10.8%, the worst fall shrinks from 55% to 34%, the lead over the market a year grows from nothing to 3.2 points, and the payout during 2008 grows from nothing to 15.7 points. There is no sweet spot in the middle. The best setting of the dial is the end with no market in it, which is the book the lab already had.

Why this matters beyond one experiment: borrowing multiplies a book's extra return, but mixing with the market only averages it away. Holding half and half kept almost exactly half the extra return, which sounds reasonable until you notice that is all mixing can ever do. Blending a good book with the market walks you smoothly back toward owning the market, on every measure at once. So the answer to the question "should we hold some of the market alongside this strategy?" is no whenever the strategy is better than the market, and is pointless whenever it is worse, because then you should simply hold the market. The lab does not need to ask this again.

One smaller warning in the same result. The setting that held 70% market and only 30% calm stocks was the worst of all five on return per point of fall, slightly worse even than holding the market alone. A small slice of a hand-picked book next to a large slice of the market buys almost nothing and still pays the full trading bill on the slice.

insights.title: A lead over a blind draw of under about 1.5 points a year is unreadable — measured on the lab's own draws
insights.body:
Nearly every method in this lab is judged against a twin that holds the same number of names, drawn blind from the same pool, trading on the same days, with no idea in it at all. If the real book beats its blind twin, the idea is doing something. The sentence the lab then writes is "it beat the blind draw by so many points a year", and until now nobody had asked how much that number wobbles purely because of which names the draw happened to land on.

I measured it. There are nine groups of recorded versions in the lab that are identical in every single respect except the arbitrary number used to shuffle the names — same pool, same size, same trading days, same fees, same years, same everything. Any difference between them is pure luck of the draw. Changing only that shuffling number moved the twenty-year return by between 0.06 and 2.70 points a year, with a middle value of 1.40 points.

That is a large number compared with the leads this lab usually reports against a blind draw. In this run the real book beat its blind twin by 0.56 points a year, and seven of those nine groups wobbled by more than that from luck alone. So the honest reading of this method's own result is that its advantage over picking names at random cannot be measured at all, not that it is small.

What to do about it. First, when a book beats its blind twin by less than about one and a half points a year, say the gap is unreadable rather than quoting it. Second, two things measured on the same draws barely wobble at all and should be read instead: how far the book falls, and how its gains compare with its losses. In this run those two said something clear and consistent where the return said nothing — the calm book fell 7.5 points less than its blind twin and had much better gains against losses. Third, where a lead really matters, run the draw at three or four different shuffling numbers and report the range rather than a single figure, which three methods in the lab already do and the rest do not.

insights.title: A correctly built comparison twin went unmeasured because of one word in its description
insights.body:
This method included a properly built comparison twin: thirty names picked blind from the same pool, held at the same size, and forced to trade on the same days as the real book. It matched closely — 824 trades against the real book's 844, which is well inside the range the lab calls a clean match.

The lab's automatic checker reported that this method has no comparison twin at all.

The reason is wording. The checker spots a twin by looking for certain phrases in the one-line description an author writes beside each version. The list of phrases was built by scanning every method already written and keeping only wording that actually appeared, which is a sound way to build it. The phrase used here, "blind draw", was one of several that had never appeared before and so is deliberately not on the list. The arm is real and its numbers are sound; the checker simply could not see it.

This matters more than it sounds. The checker is the thing that stops a method claiming credit for beating a twin that was quietly handicapped, and it feeds a rule that can block a method from reaching the owner's money. An honest, well-built twin that is invisible to it is the mirror of the problem it was created to catch: the measurement silently does not happen, and nothing reads as wrong.

Two things would fix it, and the first is cheap. Let a method state outright which of its versions is the comparison twin and which version it is a twin of, instead of the checker guessing from prose. The design notes already name this as the intended path for methods written from now on but the field does not exist yet, so every author is still relying on choosing a blessed word. Until it exists, the practical rule for anyone writing a method is to use the word "placebo" in the description of a comparison version, because that word is on the list and "blind draw" is not.

Second, the lab should report when it finds no twin for a method that plainly has one. A line saying "no comparison twin found" currently reads identically whether the method has none or has one the checker failed to recognise, and those are very different situations.

insights.title: Sera 20261023-0843: the arrangement around a signal keeps mattering more than the signal
insights.body:
The alarm that says "now is the moment to pay for better history" went off this batch, for the
first time on a strategy nobody has spent a look on. I checked it and did not act on it. The
reason is the whole batch in miniature, so it goes first.

THE ALARM, AND WHY IT WAS A NO

The strategy is the news-day book: buy a big company straight after a day when its price jumped,
it beat the market by several points over three days, and it traded at least three times its usual
volume. It cleared all five conditions the lab requires before better data is worth buying.

Two things stopped it. First, the alarm reads the years 2009 to 2015, because those are the years
our price history covers best, and on that history the book beat the market by 2.3 points a year.
We also keep an honest history that puts back most of the companies ours is missing, the ones that
went bankrupt or were bought. On that history the same book trails the market by 0.1 points a year
over the same stretch, and its record in the four held-back periods drops from three won to two.
The margin the alarm fired on is smaller than its own year-to-year wobble, which the report itself
prints.

Second, the version the lab would have put forward is not this batch's idea at all. The idea was
to widen the net by demanding less trading volume, and every wider setting did worse. What was
left standing is the existing news-day book, unchanged: the same trades and the same account
curve, matching to the last digit, as three strategies we already hold under three other names.
Spending a look on it would spend it on something we already had.

So no data was bought and no look was spent. Four looks are gone, all four failed on the same
condition, and the honest count is that they bought two distinct strategies, not four.

WHAT THE FOUR RUNS WERE, AND WHAT THEY SAID

Hold the market beside the calm stocks. The calmest thirty companies earn far more than their
gentleness entitles them to, but they move a third as hard as the market, so they trail it in a
rising decade. The textbook fix is to borrow; the owner cannot. So we tried buying the missing
movement instead, holding the market itself beside them and turning the mix like a dial. Every
setting lined up in order with no sweet spot anywhere: the more market in the mix, the lower the
return and the shallower the fall, in even steps. Blending averages a strategy away; borrowing
would have multiplied it. Half the book kept almost exactly half the lead, which is all blending
can ever do. The question is closed and will not need asking again.

That run also produced the batch's most uncomfortable number. Run the same mix with the jumpiest
thirty companies instead of the calmest, and it earned MORE, by two and a half points a year after
2009. Calmness ranks the right way round on safety and the wrong way round on return. That fits
what we learned last batch, that our history flatters jumpy companies because the ones it leaves
out are the ones that swung hardest before dying, so this is the expected artefact rather than
news. The honest sentence is that calmness buys safety, not return.

Widening the news-day net. Covered above. The finding that survives is not the book but the dial.
The "three times usual volume" rule was picked years ago and never questioned. Turned five ways it
changed the return by less than a point, and changed the worst fall enormously and in a straight
line: with no volume test at all the book lost 37 percent, at three times it lost 24. Then the
same five books were re-run with the dead companies added back, and the pattern repeated exactly
backwards: the looser the volume test, the more of the book's success turned out to have been the
missing companies. The strictest setting was the only one that earned MORE with them back. So
asking for heavy trading was never mainly about finding news. It was a test of whether the company
was still alive. That is worth borrowing anywhere we pick stocks on price movement alone.

How often a book should be re-weighted. A book held in proportion to company size turns out to
re-weight itself, by arithmetic: a holding's value is its share count times its price, so the
weights drift exactly the way the targets drift. Doing it monthly rather than once a year cost two
thirds more trading and changed the return by one hundredth of a point. A book of equal slices
does drift and does need help, but the help it needs is not selling. Letting the monthly deposit
do the whole job, never selling at all, earned the most of all six versions while trading a third
less than re-weighting monthly. The gap between re-weighting often and seldom turned out to be
idle cash rather than the trimming.

Grading the safety switch instead of switching it. Our one reliable earner is a rule that leaves
the market when it falls below its long-run average. The idea was to read several trend lengths
and step out gradually rather than all at once, which should spread the cash more evenly, and
evenly-spread cash is cheaper than cash in lumps. It lost. Grading cost about nine tenths of a
point a year on the owner's money, bought no extra safety at all on our usual history, and on the
honest history it fell up to six points deeper. The reason is clean and it is all in 2008: for a
vote to reach zero every trend length has to agree, and the long ones turn down late, so a graded
switch is never fully out at the moment that matters. Through 2008 the plain switch was entirely
out and lost nothing; the graded versions held a sliver under two percent and that alone cost two
and a half points. A safety rule has to be able to leave the room in one step.

WHAT THE BATCH TAUGHT

Three of the four runs were the same lesson from different directions: the lab keeps finding that
the arrangement around a signal matters more than the signal. Grading a good rule broke it.
Blending a good book with the market averaged it away. Re-weighting a book that re-weights itself
bought nothing. And in the one run where a filter looked like a stock-picking idea, it turned out
to be a safety check on whether the company still existed.

The fourth lesson is about measurement and it is the most useful thing here. Two separate runs
found that their headline numbers were smaller than the noise they sit in. The calm-stock run
measured the lab's own random-draw wobble rather than guessing at it, by finding nine groups of
recorded strategies that differ in nothing but the random seed, and the seed alone moves a
twenty-year return by up to 2.7 points, median 1.4. Its own lead over a blind draw was 0.56. So
that lead is unreadable, and so is any lead under about one and a half points. We should stop
reporting them.

DIRECTIONS ALIVE AND DEAD

Dead, and closed: mixing any strategy with the market as a substitute for borrowing; grading the
safety switch across trend lengths; re-weighting a size-shaped book on any schedule; widening the
news-day net.

Alive: letting the monthly deposit do the re-balancing, which earned the most of anything this
batch while trading least. A trading-volume floor as a general safety check on any book that picks
stocks purely on how the price moved. And calmness used as a filter on someone else's picks rather
than as a ranking of its own, which is the one thing this batch showed it reliably buys.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST

Not data. Three of the four runs were limited by measurement, not by what we could see. The one
thing worth building is a report that grades every near miss against a random draw matched to how
hard it moves with the market, because two batches running have now spent a strategy each
discovering that a lead was market movement in disguise. Second, the out-of-sample check should
score the exact version we would actually put forward. Today it scores whichever version looked
best in training, and an identical strategy collected three different scores in three different
files purely because of which other versions sat beside it.

THE GATE, AND FEES

The gate refused nothing this batch, because only one method reached the stage where it could be
refused and the coordinator declined the look before the gate was asked. Three methods were turned
away earlier, by the luck bar.

Gotrade's fees decided nothing. Every number above already includes them. The one place they were
suspected, the graded safety switch, was tested directly by re-running with all fees set to zero,
and they explained less than a tenth of the loss.

WHAT NEXT

Calmness as a safety filter dropping the jumpiest quarter of a book that already leads. A trading
volume floor tested as a general survivorship brake. The weighting dial slid from company size to
equal slices in five steps, with the amount of money actually invested reported beside it, because
this batch found an unmeasured term hiding in that gap. And which half of the safety switch
carries its value, the leaving or the coming back.

insights.title: A strategy crossed the luck bar this batch because four unrelated strategies were added beside it
insights.body:
A strategy the lab had already judged changed its own verdict this batch without being touched.

The buyback method's best version sits right on the luck bar, which is set at 0.90. Measured on
the database as it stood before this batch, it scored 0.898278 -- below the bar, and the lab
reported that it had no version worth putting forward at all. Measured on the database as it
stands after this batch, the same version, the same trades, the same account curve, scores
0.900449. It is now above the bar and the lab names it as the version it would put forward.

Nothing about that strategy changed. Four unrelated strategies were added beside it: a calm-stock
mix, a news-day volume ladder, a re-weighting grid and a trend-vote. None of them is a buyback
idea and none shares its machinery.

The direction is the surprising part. The luck bar exists to punish a lab for trying many things,
so adding four more should make every existing verdict HARDER to pass, not easier. The count the
gate judges at did rise, from 181 to 185. But the score is not a function of that count alone: it
also reads how much the lab's strategies resemble one another, and the four new curves nudged that
structure slightly. Measured: average resemblance moved from 0.643577 to 0.644004. That tiny shift
was worth more than the four extra tries cost.

Two things follow.

First, a verdict near the bar is not a property of the strategy. It is a property of the strategy
AND every other curve in the lab on the day it was read. Any strategy within about three
thousandths of 0.90 should be treated as unresolved rather than passed or failed, and the number
should be re-read before anything is built on it. The lab already knows that a recorded score is a
record and not a verdict; this is the sharper version of that, because here the re-read moved the
answer across the line.

Second, and more practically: this is a one-way ratchet risk. Every batch adds strategies, and
every batch therefore re-rolls the verdict of every borderline strategy already recorded. Over
enough batches, something sitting just under the bar will eventually be nudged over it by
unrelated work, and will then look like a candidate for a counted look and the owner's money. That
would be a false positive manufactured entirely by bookkeeping.

The buyback method is not a danger today: its promoted version wins only two of the four held-back
stretches, so it fails the fold condition and raises no alarm. But it is now one condition away
instead of two, and it got there without evidence.

What to do: when a strategy is within a few thousandths of the bar, record the score together with
