the exact number of strategies and the resemblance figure it was read at, and require a re-read at
the current population before any promotion. A test that pins such a strategy's verdict will also
go red on an unrelated batch, which is how this was found.

insights.title: Two gates were quietly loosened: one strategy passed under three names and failed under three, and a verdict moved because unrelated work landed
insights.body:
Two of the gates standing between a backtest and the owner's savings were loosened by accident, and
both are now visible rather than silent. Neither is a rule change: no method's verdict moved, no
look was spent, and nothing was promoted or refused because of this work.

THE FIRST: THE SAME STRATEGY, PASSED UNDER THREE NAMES AND REFUSED UNDER THREE OTHERS

Six strategies in the lab are, by their account curves, one strategy. Their best versions produce
the identical trade list and the identical account balance to the last digit. Three of them pass
the out-of-sample check and three fail it.

What differs is not the strategy. Our out-of-sample check splits the twenty years into four
stretches and, for each, asks which version the lab would have chosen knowing only the past, then
scores that choice on years it never saw. Which version gets chosen depends on what else was
registered in the same file. Where a sibling looked better in training, the check scored the
sibling and filed the answer under the whole idea. So the same book reads three-of-four in one
file and one-of-four in another.

That alone would be tolerable, because a second condition already protects the decision: the
version we would actually put forward must also win a majority on its own curve, and on that
column all six agree. But the alarm that says "now is the moment to pay for survivorship-free
history" printed only the strategies that passed. A reader saw one book confirmed by four names
and had no way to learn the same book had been refused under three others. That reads as
unanimity when it is three of six, and it reads in the direction that encourages spending.

The alarm now names the refusals beside the firings, and says plainly how many of the ids that
promote that exact curve actually fired. The claim is identity, not family resemblance: the first
attempt reused the lab's "same book" grouping, which also merges strategies that merely move
together, and it named one strategy whose curve is different while missing two whose curve is the
same. That was caught before it was trusted, and the check now compares the recorded curves byte
for byte.

THE SECOND: A VERDICT THAT MOVES WHEN AN UNRELATED STRATEGY IS ADDED

Our luck test asks whether a result could be the best of many tries. It is set at 0.90. It is not
a function of the strategy and the number of tries alone: it also reads how much the lab's
strategies resemble one another, so every new strategy quietly re-scores every old one.

Measured over the four strategies of one batch: all seventy-five eligible strategies moved, by
between 0.0016 and 0.0021, and every single one moved UPWARD -- the direction a larger number of
tries should forbid. The resemblance shift outweighed the cost of four more tries. One strategy's
best version crossed the bar, from 0.898278 to 0.900449, without being touched by anyone.

Eight strategies now sit within 0.005 of the bar and three are within 0.0005 of it -- less than a
single batch's drift. The report names them and calls them unresolved rather than passed or
failed. It is a warning and never a verdict: nothing passes or fails because of it.

The deeper worry, recorded so it is not rediscovered: this is a ratchet. Every batch re-rolls
every borderline verdict, always upward so far, so with enough batches something sitting just
under the bar will be carried over it by work that has nothing to do with it, and will then look
like a candidate for a counted look and real money. Whether the upward direction is a property of
this lab's growing resemblance or a defect in how the correction is computed is not settled here,
and it should be settled before the bar is trusted near its edge.

insights.title: A traded-volume floor as a general survivorship brake on a price-only stock screen: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +13.7% on the usual history, +12.0% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 20.6% and 25.0%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +1.1% a year before and −0.2% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.7 points a year less. 3 of its 5 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: The industry's biggest name leads: do its smaller peers follow next month?: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +7.6% on the usual history, +6.4% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 28.2% and 29.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −7.1% a year before and −6.1% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 1 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.2 points a year less. 4 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A rule and its opposite can both be wrong, and the gap between them still looks like skill
insights.body:
This month a book was tested that buys the smaller companies in the three industries whose biggest, most-watched company rose most last month. The idea comes from research saying news reaches the giants first and their smaller rivals a few weeks later.

Beside it ran its exact opposite: buy the smaller companies in the three industries whose biggest name FELL most. The idea earned 7.3 percent a year on the owner's deposits and its opposite earned 5.5 percent. A gap of nearly two points, running the right way. That is the shape of evidence this lab has used to settle most of its timing rules, and on its own it reads as a working signal.

It was not one. A third book ran alongside: the same twenty slots, the same three-industry split, the same safety switch, but with the three industries chosen by coin toss. That one earned 7.6 percent -- more than the idea.

So the idea lost to a coin toss, and the two-point gap to its opposite was never the idea earning money. It was the opposite LOSING money. Buying the industries whose giant just fell turns out to be a genuinely bad habit, and the gap measures only that.

The lesson is general and it is cheap to apply. A rule and its mirror will show a gap whenever the two sides are unevenly bad, and that gap says nothing about whether acting on the rule is better than not having an opinion at all. The gap becomes evidence only once the straight side also beats a blind draw built to the same shape -- same number of names, same slots, same safety switch. The lab holds twenty-eight of these mirror pairs and can currently price only a handful of them. For a book that picks stocks, the arm that was missing is not a buy-and-hold yardstick; it is a coin toss wearing the book's own clothes. Every future stock screen should register one, and it costs nothing but a line in the same pre-registration.

insights.title: The lab's mirror splitter cannot see the only control a stock picker can have
insights.body:
The lab has a tool that takes a rule and its opposite and splits the result into two parts: what the opinion actually knew, and what the habit of acting on it cost in fees and time sitting in cash. To do the second half it needs a third book with no opinion in it at all.

The tool defines that third book narrowly: almost always invested, and barely trading -- turning over no more than about one seventh of itself a year. That describes a buy-and-hold yardstick, and it is the right endpoint for a timing rule, which is a habit laid on top of simply staying invested.

It is the wrong endpoint for a book that picks stocks. A twenty-name book re-picked every month turns over sixteen times a year by construction. There is no version of it that trades a seventh of itself, so no stock screen can ever offer the tool the arm it asks for. This month's industry method registered two always-invested arms specifically so the habit could be priced, and the tool still reported the habit unpriced, because both of them churn.

The arm that does work for a stock picker is a coin toss wearing the book's own clothes: the same number of names, the same slots, the same safety switch, the same everything, with only the choosing replaced by a draw. That book has no opinion but exactly the same habits, so the difference between it and the real book is the opinion and nothing else. This month that comparison was the whole result, and the tool could not read it.

What would help: let the tool accept a declared control arm, and let a method say which of its arms is the blind draw. The lab already knows how to build these draws -- several methods have one. It just has no way to tell the tool which arm it is, so the comparison has to be done by hand each time, and twenty-two recorded mirror pairs sit unpriced.

insights.title: One coin toss is not a control when the thing you are measuring is smaller than one coin toss
insights.body:
The lab has measured that the seed behind a blind draw -- which particular coin toss you happened to use -- moves a twenty-year result by anywhere from a tenth of a point to 2.7 points a year, with a typical value around 1.4. That number has been used as a rule of thumb: a lead smaller than about 1.5 points a year is unreadable.

This month's industry method ran into the sharper version of the same problem. Always invested, the idea led its single blind-draw control by about four points a year over 2009 to 2015, on both the ordinary price history and the one with bankrupt companies put back. Four points sounds decisive.

It is not, and the reason is arithmetic. Four points was measured over under seven years, not twenty, so the draw noise is wider than the 1.4-point figure, not narrower. And it was measured against ONE draw. A single coin toss is one sample from a distribution the lab already knows is two to three points wide. Comparing a real book to one draw tells you the book beat that draw; it does not tell you the book beats draws.

The fix is cheap and should become routine: when a blind draw is the control, register several of them -- five or six seeds -- inside the same pre-registration. It costs no extra method, because variants of one method count as a single look. The real book then gets read against the SPREAD of the draws rather than against one of them, and the question stops being 'did we beat the coin toss' and becomes 'are we outside what coin tosses do', which is the question that was always meant.

The risk if this is not done: the lab will eventually promote something whose entire measured edge is one lucky draw sitting at the bottom of its own distribution, and it will spend one of its four remaining honest looks at recent years finding that out.

insights.title: How heavily a stock trades tells you whether its edge is real or a hole in the data
insights.body:
The lab keeps two copies of market history. The everyday one is missing most of the companies that went bust or were bought out, because their prices are hard to get. The honest one puts them back. A strategy that looks good on the first and bad on the second was partly being flattered by the companies that quietly vanished.

Last week a book built on big news days turned one dial - how busy a stock's trading had to be - and the gap between the two tapes closed steadily as the dial was tightened. That could easily have been a quirk of news days. So it was tried again on a completely different book, one that just buys the twenty stocks climbing most on their own merits, with no events in it anywhere.

The same thing happened. With no busy-trading requirement the book loses 1.7 points a year when the dead companies are put back. With the strictest requirement it gains 1.8. A swing of three and a half points, almost exactly matching what the news book showed.

Why it works is simple once said out loud: a company the market is actively trading still exists. Companies that disappear are overwhelmingly small and thinly traded, and they get thin before they go. Refusing to buy quiet stocks is mostly refusing to buy the ones that later vanish.

What to do about it: this is now a free diagnostic the lab should run on every stock-picking method it already owns. It needs no new data and no new money. Tighten the busy-trading bar, watch which way the honest-tape gap moves, and treat any book whose edge evaporates as suspect before spending anything more on it. It is the cheapest honesty check available.

insights.title: The everyday tape can reverse which version of a strategy looks best
insights.body:
This is the part of today's result that should worry us, and it is not about the strategy that was tested.

Five versions of the same book were run, differing only in how heavily a stock must trade before it can be bought. On the lab's everyday market history, adding the requirement is a pure cost: the book earns 13.7 percent a year without it and 12.6 percent with a moderate version of it. An obvious conclusion - do not add it.

On the honest history, with the vanished companies put back, the order flips. The plain book earns 12.0 percent and the moderate filtered one earns 12.7 percent. The filtered version is now the better of the two, and it is also the only one of all five with a positive edge in 2009 to 2015, the best-covered years and the ones most like today.

So the everyday tape did not merely make both versions look a bit too good. It changed which one you would pick. That is a worse failure than a known bias, because a bias of a steady size can be subtracted and a reversal cannot.

What to do about it: never settle a comparison between two versions of a book on the everyday tape alone when the thing being varied is anything to do with size, liquidity or how thinly a stock trades. Those are exactly the dimensions along which the missing companies differ from the surviving ones. Run both tapes before choosing. The second tape is already built and costs nothing but a minute.

insights.title: Calmness as a safety filter on someone else's picks, not a ranking of its own: what its own picks did, apart from the money it parks
insights.body:
The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, in three further ways: holding only the names it picks for itself; holding those same names with the whole book behind them and every brake off; and holding only the money it parks in the market. Nothing about the method changed -- only how its money was spread. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Of all the money it held, 68.6% was in names it picked itself. The rest sat in cash or in the market.
- As the lab recorded it, it earned +11.8% a year against the market's +7.2%.
- Its own picks, given the whole book and no brakes, earned +11.9% a year, which is +4.7% against the market.
- On 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold, it had no pick to make at all.
- The money it parks in the market, on its own, earned −0.0% a year, −7.2% against the market.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +4.6% a year against the market as recorded, +4.7% from its own picks alone.
- 1996-2002: +5.8% a year against the market as recorded, +5.6% from its own picks alone.
- 2003-2008: +10.8% a year against the market as recorded, +10.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as recorded, +34.8% from its own picks alone.
- 2009-2015: −3.3% a year against the market as recorded, −3.1% from its own picks alone.

Its own picks beat the market in 3 of the 4 periods they could be judged on, and lost in the rest. The picking is not reliably where the earnings come from.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Demanding busy stocks turns a stock-picker into a big-company bet
insights.body:
When a filter costs a book money it is worth knowing whether the money went on fees, on sitting in cash, or on changing what the book actually owns. Here it is unambiguously the third, and the evidence is unusually clean.

Five settings of a busy-trading requirement were run on the same twenty-stock book. In months when a handful of giant companies carried the market, the book's lead over the index climbed steadily with the requirement: 5.6, 6.5, 8.2, 9.1, then 11.4 percent. In months when gains were spread widely across many companies, the lead fell just as steadily: 6.4, 5.9, 3.5, 0.6, then minus 4.7 percent. Five steps, both directions, no exceptions.

So the requirement herds the book into the largest, most heavily traded names. Those win when the market is being dragged along by a few giants and lose when gains are broad. At the strictest setting the book has stopped picking stocks and started making a bet on big companies.

This also explains the price. The strictest version gave up 5.4 percent a year against the unfiltered one, and none of that was fees or idle cash - the book held a full twenty names and stayed invested the same share of the time at every setting. It was all this tilt.

What to do about it: if the aim is to avoid dying companies rather than to bet on giants, refusing to buy quiet stocks is too blunt. Capping how much of the book may sit in the thinnest names would decline the genuinely moribund while keeping the smaller-company exposure where this book's edge actually lives.

insights.title: A one-command honesty check the lab could run on every stock book it already owns
insights.body:
Two methods have now shown the same thing on unrelated books: tighten how heavily a stock must trade before it can be bought, and watch what happens to the gap between the lab's everyday market history and the honest one that puts the vanished companies back. The gap closes. A book whose edge survives that tightening was picking real companies. A book whose edge evaporates was partly being paid by the companies the everyday history quietly drops.

Right now getting that reading costs a whole method: a new file, a pre-registration, five recorded trials, and one more notch on the counter that the luck test charges every strategy against. That is a steep price for what is really a data diagnostic rather than a new idea, and it means the check will only ever be run on the handful of books someone thinks to spend a method on.

The wish is to make it a report instead. Point a command at any existing method, have it re-run that method's own recorded setup at four or five tightening levels on both tapes, and print which way the gap moves. No new trials, no new strategies counted, nothing that could make anything eligible - the same report-only footing the lab already uses for its cost and two-tape checks.

Why it is worth building: the lab holds dozens of stock-picking books and has no cheap way to ask which of them are reading a hole in the data. This would answer that for all of them in an afternoon, for no money and no new data, and it would let a known-suspect book be set aside before anything more is spent on it. It would also give the honest answer to a question that keeps coming back - how much of the lab's twenty-year record is companies that no longer exist.

insights.title: Slide the weighting from pure size to pure equal in five rungs over the same names, and read the narrow-month column beside 2009-2015: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +10.3% on the usual history, +9.1% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 57.5% and 58.7%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was +3.5% a year before and +2.5% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 1.2 points a year less. 6 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Calmness as a safety filter on someone else's picks, not a ranking of its own: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 9 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.8% on the usual history, +9.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 22.0% and 23.5%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −3.3% a year before and −5.9% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 3 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.6 points a year less. 8 of its 9 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Spreading your money evenly is one bet, not a free lunch: it pays when the average company beats the giants, and nothing else
insights.body:
Take the same few hundred companies, bought the same way on the same days, and change only how much money goes into each one. Give every company an identical slice and your money earned 10.3 percent a year over twenty years. Give each one a share matching its size — the shape the market itself has, the shape an index fund copies — and you earned 7.5 percent. We slid a dial between those two ends in five steps to find out whether somewhere in the middle was better than either end.

Nothing in the middle was better. The line is dead straight. Each quarter-turn toward even slices bought about seven tenths of a point a year of extra return and cost about two points of extra fall from a peak. There is no clever setting, no sweet spot, no place where you keep the gain and drop the risk. The owner is not tuning a dial; he is picking a spot on a straight trade-off, and every spot costs the same.

What makes the even-slice version earn more turns out to be a single thing, and we can now name it exactly. Even slices win in the months when the typical company does better than the handful of giants, and lose in the months when a few giants carry the market. Over these twenty years the typical company won 55 percent of months, by about a fifth of a percent each time. Compounded, that is the entire difference. It is not a hundred small advantages — it is one bet, placed every month.

Two things we had been treating as separate worries turned out to be the same worry. We had asked whether even slices lose when the market narrows, and separately whether their advantage had faded in recent years. Both questions cross from win to lose at exactly the same point on the dial. They were never two facts.

And the most uncomfortable part: in 2008, the year that decides whether anyone can actually hold on, the dial runs backwards. The market's own shape beat the benchmark by almost 5 percent that year while even slices lost to it — a six and a half point swing in the worst possible year. Even slices earn their keep in the calm and give a chunk of it back in the storm.

What to do about it: stop treating even slices as a neutral default we get for free. It is a position with a price and a condition attached. It is worth roughly one and a half to two and a half points a year while broad markets outnumber narrow ones, and it is a liability when that flips — as it did in 2008, and as much of 2018 onward has been.

insights.title: A result that survives putting the failed companies back: the gap held to the decimal
insights.body:
Most of what this lab measures is done on prices for the companies that are still around. It is missing about four in ten of the companies that were actually in the index, and the missing ones lean heavily toward the ones that went bust. That hole has killed more of our findings than anything else — a strategy looks clever right up until the failures are priced back in, and then the cleverness turns out to have been the hole.

So we re-ran all six versions of the even-slices-versus-market-shape dial on a second set of prices that puts most of those failed companies back. We expected the even-slice end to suffer worst, because spreading money evenly across everything means owning more of whatever failed.

Every version did earn less — about 1.1 to 1.2 points a year less, which is the usual toll. But the distance between the two ends of the dial was 2.7 points a year before and 2.7 points a year after. Identical. The toll is a flat charge applied to every version equally; the thing we were actually measuring was not touched by it.

That is worth saying plainly because it is rare. The missing-failures hole usually explains away this kind of result, and here it explains nothing. Whatever the even-slice advantage is, it is not an accounting artefact of companies we cannot see.

Two caveats that matter for what the owner should believe. First, the honest prices do change who beats the benchmark at all: only the three settings nearest even slices still do, and the best of them beats it by 1.9 percent a year rather than 3.1. Second, one side version — the one where we removed the cap that stops any single company exceeding five percent of the book — lost nearly twice as much as the others once the failures were back. Concentrating with no limit is more fragile than it looks on the incomplete prices. That is an argument for keeping the cap, and it cost nothing to learn because the version was registered alongside the five real settings in the same experiment.

insights.title: When money arrives monthly and is spent on whatever is furthest behind, the strategy quietly decides how much cash you sit on
insights.body:
This experiment was built so that only one thing changed between its six versions: how much money goes into each company. Everything else — which companies, which days, which fees — was held still. One thing was not held still, and we did not notice until the numbers came back.

The versions did not keep the same amount of money invested. The even-slice version sat invested 97.5 percent of the time; the market-shape version only 91.2 percent. That six-point spread slides smoothly along with the dial, so it is perfectly tangled up with the thing we were trying to measure.

The reason is mechanical and worth understanding, because it will come back. Each month's deposit goes to whichever holdings are furthest below where they ought to be. In the market-shape version, a company's share of the book drifts almost exactly the way its target drifts — because a company's size simply is its share count times its price — so there is usually no gap to fill, and the money sits in cash waiting. In the even-slice version the gaps reopen every month and every deposit finds somewhere to go.

So a rule about weighting turned into a rule about how much cash you hold, without anyone choosing that. Being invested more earns more, and some of what we measured is that rather than the weighting.

How much? Not most of it. For time-in-the-market alone to explain these results, each extra point of it would have to be worth about 0.43 points a year on average. The most we have ever measured on this same machinery is about 0.17, in the single most favourable stretch, and in another stretch the same thing was worth almost nothing. So the explanation does not stretch far enough — but it does take the honest estimate of the weighting effect down from 2.7 points a year to somewhere between 1.6 and 2.7.

The risk to record for the future: any rule that steers new money toward whatever is lagging will change how much cash the account carries, and that change will travel silently alongside whatever the experiment thought it was testing. It needs its own column in every such experiment from now on, and the next experiment on this question should force every version to the same amount invested so the weighting effect can be read as a single number instead of a range.

insights.title: Two safety devices on one strategy do not add up: the faster one takes the claim and the slower one keeps paying the premium
insights.body:
Most of our strategies carry two kinds of protection at once. One is a cash rule: when the market slips below its own one-year average, sell everything and wait. The other is a filter on what the strategy may buy in the first place -- in this case, refusing to own the jumpiest quarter of the companies on its list.

This experiment bolted the second onto a strategy that already had the first, and the result was almost nothing. Every version of the book -- filtered, unfiltered, and filtered backwards -- scored the exact same advantage in 2008, down to the decimal. The cash rule had already sold everything before the crash arrived, so there was no crash left for the filter to protect against. It could not help, but it still charged: about a point a year of lost return, every year, for twenty years. Insurance that can never pay out but still takes the premium.

Switch the cash rule off and the same filter suddenly has work to do and does it well. In 2008 the unfiltered book lost 39.5% and the filtered one lost 24.5% -- fifteen points saved, and a quarter of that was more than any random reshuffle of the same list managed. With the dead companies restored to the price history it looks better still: the filtered book's worst fall was 53.7% where four random reshuffles fell between 59.0% and 66.1%.

The lesson is not about calmness. It is that protection does not stack. Whichever device acts first takes the claim, and everything behind it keeps paying for cover it will never use. We have been quietly stacking these -- cash rules, filters, brakes, position caps -- and judging each one against a strategy that already had the others switched on. That is a recipe for concluding that good ideas are worthless.

What to do about it: when we test a protective rule, test it on a strategy that has no other protection, so the rule has to earn its premium on its own. And when a strategy already has a cash rule, the useful question is not whether a filter helps behind it -- it barely can -- but whether the filter could replace it.

insights.title: A single random comparison is not a control, and our practice data makes one look twice as trustworthy as it is
insights.body:
When we want to know whether a clever rule is really clever, we run the same strategy with the rule replaced by a coin toss and see if the clever version wins. That comparison is the backbone of how this lab tells a real finding from a lucky one.

This experiment did exactly that and got a clean-looking answer: the clever filter's worst fall was 20.3% against the coin toss's 23.5%, three points better. Then three more coin tosses were run, which cost about a minute. They fell 20.4%, 22.9% and 23.3%. One of them was better than the clever rule. The three-point win was not the rule -- it was which coin we happened to toss. That claim has been withdrawn.

The part worth worrying about is the second measurement. The same four coin tosses were re-run on the fuller price history, the one with the bankrupt and bought-out companies put back. There their worst falls spread from 21.2% to 28.7% -- seven and a half points, more than double the three-point spread on the practice data. Their returns spread two points a year instead of half a point.

So our practice data does not just flatter strategies, which we already knew. It also makes random comparisons look far steadier than they really are. A single coin toss measured on the practice data understates its own wobble by roughly half, which means every conclusion in this lab that rests on one such comparison is weaker than its numbers suggest -- including conclusions already written down and treated as settled.

What to do about it: never run one. Four coin tosses cost a minute and turn a number into a range, and a range is the only honest way to say whether a rule beat chance. The things that did survive four tosses here -- the filter's gains-versus-losses, and what it saved in the 2008 crash -- survived on both sets of prices, which is what a real finding looks like.

insights.title: Sera 20261023-1049: three of four strategies were killed by their own comparisons, and one coin toss is not a control
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two of the four strategies cleared the lab's paper screen and the gate
refused both, so nothing was put forward for a look at the held-back years and no money was spent
on better data.

THE ONE THING THIS BATCH TAUGHT, AND IT IS ABOUT HOW WE TEST

Three of the four runs were killed or corrected by their own comparisons rather than by the market.
Two of them, working on completely unrelated ideas, arrived at the same lesson independently: a
single random comparison is not a comparison.

The industry run compared its idea with a blind draw of the same shape. The idea beat its own
opposite by 1.75 points a year, and the lab's own tool reads that gap as nearly a point a year of
genuine knowledge, rising to over two points after 2009. It looks exactly like a confirmed signal.
But the blind draw beat them both. The gap was the opposite arm losing, not the idea winning. That
generalises to a rule we did not have: a rule and its reverse can both be wrong, and the space
between them is only evidence once the rule also beats a blind draw of the same shape. We hold 28
such pairs and have never asked that second question of any of them.

The calm-filter run found the other half of the same lesson the hard way. Its headline was that
dropping the jumpiest quarter of a book made the worst fall three points shallower. Then it ran
three more random quarter-drops, and the real spread of random drops swallowed the margin whole:
the claim went from a three-point edge to five hundredths of a point. The run withdrew its own
headline. It also found that our everyday price history makes a single random comparison look
about twice as trustworthy as it is, because the spread between random draws is half as wide on it
as on the honest one.

If those two findings are right, and they were reached separately, then a number of things this
lab has believed were measured against one coin toss.

WHAT ELSE THE BATCH FOUND

Asking for heavily traded stocks is a test of whether the company still exists. Last batch found
it on the news-day book; this batch carried the same dial onto a completely different stock picker
and got the same shape and the same size of answer. Two unrelated confirmations. But the headline
is sharper than that: on our usual price history the filter is a pure cost, and on the honest one
it is a gain, and the best setting there is the only one that beat the market after 2009. A
judgement about size or tradability made on our usual history alone can pick the wrong setting,
and the error is not a fixed amount that can be subtracted.

How you spread money across a book is a straight line with no sweet spot. From equal slices to
pure company size, every step gives back about seven tenths of a point a year and buys about two
points of shallower fall, in order, on six different measures at once. There is no clever middle.
It also settled a question I had left open: the two ends do not hold the same amount of money in
the market, so part of what looked like a weighting result was simply being more invested. The
honest figure is a range, one and a half to three points a year, not the single number we had.

And one result that survived everything: that straight line is unchanged when the failed companies
are put back. Every version earns about a point a year less, but the distance from one end to the
other is the same to the decimal on both histories. Almost every survivorship finding we hold
changes which version looks best; this one changes only the level. A result whose shape survives is
worth more than one whose level does.

DIRECTIONS ALIVE AND DEAD

Dead: following the biggest company in an industry to pick its smaller rivals; any weighting scheme
as a source of return rather than a choice about risk; calmness as a filter judged on falls.

Alive: a trading-volume floor as a general honesty check on any book that picks stocks on price
alone. Calmness as a filter judged on gains against losses rather than on falls, which survived
both histories. And the one unglamorous thing that keeps winning: letting the monthly deposit do
the work instead of selling.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST

Error bars. We have never measured how much a result moves between two identical random draws over
a seven-year stretch, and this batch twice reported a number that turned out to be smaller than
that movement. One run doing nothing but drawing the same book six ways would retire or confirm
several live threads at once and cost no look at all. That is the next batch's first job.

THE GATE

The gate refused both strategies that cleared the screen: one for winning too few of the held-back
stretches and for belonging to a family that has already failed, the other for winning too few
stretches. Both refusals were right and neither cost a look.

Two gates were also repaired before this batch ran, after last batch exposed them. The alarm that
says "buy better history" was printing only the strategies that passed, so one strategy confirmed
by four names hid the fact that the identical strategy had been refused under three others; it now
prints the refusals too. And our luck test turned out to read the whole collection, so adding four
unrelated strategies moved every existing verdict upward by about two thousandths and carried one
across the line untouched; strategies sitting that close to the line are now named as unresolved.

FEES

Gotrade's fees decided nothing new. Every number above includes them. The weighting ladder halved
its trading from one end to the other and still lost return in the same direction, so trading cost
was not what the dial was measuring.

NEXT

Draw the same book six ways and publish the spread, so the lab finally has an error bar. Pin the
weighting ladder to one level of invested money, which closes the last open term in it. Ask the
volume floor as a fixed rank rather than a percentage, so the honest history's larger list stops
contaminating the answer. And sweep the shelf for rules whose only evidence is a gap against their
own reverse, and say so on their pages.

insights.title: A batch that runs no strategies: the lab cannot currently tell a real margin from noise, so it is measuring itself instead
insights.body:
This batch deliberately runs no new strategy. All four of its methods are instruments: things that
measure how well the lab measures, rather than things that try to make money. The owner chose it
over another round of ideas, and the reason is worth stating plainly.

The lab holds 317 strategies and 998 recorded tests. Eighty-four pass its paper screen, seventy-nine
of those are refused by its own gate, and not one has ever been put forward for a counted look that
it then survived. Four counted looks have been spent and all four failed. That is not a shortage of
ideas -- there are eight queued and over a hundred on the backlog. It is a measuring problem.

The last batch demonstrated it twice, on unrelated work. One strategy beat its own opposite by 1.75
points a year, which our tool reads as nearly a point a year of genuine knowledge -- and a blind
draw of the same shape beat them both, so the gap was the opposite arm losing rather than the idea
winning. Another reported a three-point safety improvement that collapsed to five hundredths of a
point as soon as three more random comparisons were run beside it. We also learned our everyday
price history makes a single random comparison look about twice as trustworthy as it is.

So we do not currently know how big a difference has to be before it means anything. Every margin
this lab has quoted, including the ones that spent four of the six counted looks, was compared
against nothing or against one coin toss.

The four instruments: measure the spread between identical random draws, so there is finally a
number to compare margins against; sweep the shelf for every recorded finding whose only evidence
is a gap against its own reverse, and mark them; hold one dial's rungs at the same amount of money
invested so a result currently reported as a range becomes a single number; and pin a filter to a
fixed rank so that two price histories stop disagreeing for a reason that has nothing to do with
the filter.

The expected outcome is that some things the lab believes it knows will be withdrawn. That is the
point. A lab that cannot retract is not measuring anything.

insights.title: Asking the same question a second way caught two wrong answers
insights.body:
The lab keeps two copies of market history: an everyday one that prices about 540 companies, and an honest one that adds back most of the companies that went bust or were bought out. Three experiments have now tested the same hunch on it — that refusing to buy sleepy, thinly traded stocks is really a way of refusing to buy companies that are quietly dying, and that a book which needs those companies to look good was never as good as it seemed.

The hunch is confirmed. The newest test set the bar a completely different way from the two before it, and the effect came back the same size, 3.4 points a year against 3.5, and for the first time in a perfectly straight line across five steps. Three experiments, two different kinds of book and two opposite ways of setting the bar all agree. That makes it a tool the lab can trust, and it costs nothing to run on books it already owns.

But the second half is the part worth remembering. The earlier experiment had also concluded, reading its honest-tape numbers, that one of its middle settings was actually the better book to own, and the only one that still earned its keep in the best-covered recent years. Neither of those survived. Both were side effects of how that experiment had defined its bar: it asked for a share of each day's candidates rather than a fixed number, and because the honest tape offers far more candidates, the same label quietly meant a much gentler requirement there. Two arms that were matched on one set of books were not matched at all on the other, and nobody could see it until the question was asked a second, different way.

The lesson is cheap and general: when you compare two things that are supposed to be set up the same, check they are still set up the same on the data you are actually reading, not only on the data you tuned them on. The first experiment was not careless — the hole was named in its own write-up. It just could not be seen from inside.

insights.title: The safety a rule buys can be invisible on the data we test with
insights.body:
A worst fall is the number the owner's rules care most about: a book may not lose more than a quarter of its value from a peak. This run turned up a case where that number is measured on the wrong tape and quietly says nothing.

On the everyday market history, requiring a stock to be actively traded does nothing at all for the worst fall. The book falls 20.6 percent of its value without the requirement and 20.8 percent with the strictest version of it. Read that column alone and you would conclude the requirement buys no safety whatsoever, and drop it.

On the honest history — the one that puts back the companies that went bust — the same book without the requirement falls 25.0 percent, exactly on the owner's limit, and every version with the requirement falls less, down to 22.8 percent. The protection is real and worth more than two points of depth. It is simply unmeasurable on the data the lab does most of its work on, because the companies whose collapse would have caused the extra damage are missing from that data.

This is the second time the lab has found this shape. An earlier question about how many stocks a book should hold had the same answer: the safety case was invisible on the everyday tape and obvious on the honest one, and the two tapes recommended different books.

What to do about it: when a change is being judged mainly on whether it makes a book safer rather than richer, the everyday tape cannot settle it, and the honest-tape check should be run before the change is dismissed. That check is free and takes a few minutes. The risk is not that the lab accepts something bad — it is that it keeps throwing away protections it cannot see.

insights.title: The honesty test is settled, and now it needs to be free to run
insights.body:
Three experiments have settled that a simple check works: tighten how heavily a stock must be traded before a book may buy it, and watch what happens to the book's edge when the companies that went bust are put back. If the edge survives, it was probably real. If it evaporates, the book was being flattered by the companies the everyday data is missing. The check needs no new data and takes minutes to compute.

The problem is the price of asking. Running that ladder on a book today means registering a whole new method: a new file, a new entry in the lab's permanent record, and — because the lab counts every distinct idea it has tried and makes later results clear a higher bar as a result — it makes every future method slightly harder to believe. Three of these have now been spent, and they all reached the same conclusion. Spending a fourth on a book the lab already owns would be paying a real cost for an answer that is no longer in doubt.

What would help is a report, like the handful the lab already has that measure something and record nothing: point it at any method already in the lab, have it re-run that method's own book at four or five tightening levels on both copies of history, and print which way the edge moves. No new entry, no effect on how strictly later results are judged, nothing permanent written.

That would turn a settled finding into a habit. Every stock-picking book the lab holds could be screened in an afternoon, and the ones whose edge depends on the missing companies could be set aside before any more effort goes into them. At the moment the lab knows how to ask the question and cannot afford to ask it.

insights.title: Sera 20261023-1049: three of four strategies were killed by their own comparisons, and one coin toss is not a control
insights.body:
No buy signal this batch. Two of the four strategies cleared the lab's paper screen and the gate
refused both, so nothing was put forward for a look at the held-back years and no money was spent
on better data.

THE ONE THING THIS BATCH TAUGHT, AND IT IS ABOUT HOW WE TEST

Three of the four runs were killed or corrected by their own comparisons rather than by the market.
Two of them, working on completely unrelated ideas, arrived at the same lesson independently: a
single random comparison is not a comparison.

The industry run compared its idea with a blind draw of the same shape. The idea beat its own
opposite by 1.75 points a year, and the lab's own tool reads that gap as nearly a point a year of
genuine knowledge, rising to over two points after 2009. It looks exactly like a confirmed signal.
But the blind draw beat them both. The gap was the opposite arm losing, not the idea winning. That
generalises to a rule we did not have: a rule and its reverse can both be wrong, and the space
between them is only evidence once the rule also beats a blind draw of the same shape. We hold 28
such pairs and have never asked that second question of any of them.

The calm-filter run found the other half of the same lesson the hard way. Its headline was that
dropping the jumpiest quarter of a book made the worst fall three points shallower. Then it ran
three more random quarter-drops, and the real spread of random drops swallowed the margin whole:
the claim went from a three-point edge to five hundredths of a point. The run withdrew its own
headline. It also found that our everyday price history makes a single random comparison look
about twice as trustworthy as it is, because the spread between random draws is half as wide on it
as on the honest one.

If those two findings are right, and they were reached separately, then a number of things this
lab has believed were measured against one coin toss.

WHAT ELSE THE BATCH FOUND

Asking for heavily traded stocks is a test of whether the company still exists. Last batch found
it on the news-day book; this batch carried the same dial onto a completely different stock picker
and got the same shape and the same size of answer. Two unrelated confirmations, and since this
synthesis was first written a third has arrived and made it four points a year on a straight line,
so the finding is settled.

CORRECTED SINCE FIRST PUBLISHED. The paragraph here originally went further and said that on the
honest price history the filter stops being a cost and becomes a gain, and that its middle setting
was the only one still earning its keep after 2009. Neither of those was true. They were side
effects of how that run set its bar: it refused a SHARE of each day's candidates, and the honest
history lists nearly twice as many companies, so the same rule quietly kept 243 names there
against 150 on the everyday one. It was never the same filter on the two histories. Asking the
question again with a fixed number of names instead of a share put the no-filter book back on top
of the honest history and left every setting behind the market after 2009. What survives is the
honesty measurement itself, which is the part worth having.

How you spread money across a book is a straight line with no sweet spot. From equal slices to
pure company size, every step gives back about seven tenths of a point a year and buys about two
points of shallower fall, in order, on six different measures at once. There is no clever middle.
It also settled a question I had left open: the two ends do not hold the same amount of money in
the market, so part of what looked like a weighting result was simply being more invested. The
honest figure is a range, one and a half to three points a year, not the single number we had.

And one result that survived everything: that straight line is unchanged when the failed companies
are put back. Every version earns about a point a year less, but the distance from one end to the
other is the same to the decimal on both histories. Almost every survivorship finding we hold
changes which version looks best; this one changes only the level. A result whose shape survives is
worth more than one whose level does.

DIRECTIONS ALIVE AND DEAD

Dead: following the biggest company in an industry to pick its smaller rivals; any weighting scheme
as a source of return rather than a choice about risk; calmness as a filter judged on falls.

Alive: a trading-volume floor as a general honesty check on any book that picks stocks on price
alone. Calmness as a filter judged on gains against losses rather than on falls, which survived
both histories. And the one unglamorous thing that keeps winning: letting the monthly deposit do
the work instead of selling.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST

Error bars. We have never measured how much a result moves between two identical random draws over
a seven-year stretch, and this batch twice reported a number that turned out to be smaller than
that movement. One run doing nothing but drawing the same book six ways would retire or confirm
several live threads at once and cost no look at all. That is the next batch's first job.

THE GATE

The gate refused both strategies that cleared the screen: one for winning too few of the held-back
stretches and for belonging to a family that has already failed, the other for winning too few
stretches. Both refusals were right and neither cost a look.

Two gates were also repaired before this batch ran, after last batch exposed them. The alarm that
says "buy better history" was printing only the strategies that passed, so one strategy confirmed
by four names hid the fact that the identical strategy had been refused under three others; it now
prints the refusals too. And our luck test turned out to read the whole collection, so adding four
unrelated strategies moved every existing verdict upward by about two thousandths and carried one
across the line untouched; strategies sitting that close to the line are now named as unresolved.

FEES

Gotrade's fees decided nothing new. Every number above includes them. The weighting ladder halved
its trading from one end to the other and still lost return in the same direction, so trading cost
was not what the dial was measuring.

NEXT

Draw the same book six ways and publish the spread, so the lab finally has an error bar. Pin the
weighting ladder to one level of invested money, which closes the last open term in it. Ask the
volume floor as a fixed rank rather than a percentage, so the honest history's larger list stops
contaminating the answer. And sweep the shelf for rules whose only evidence is a gap against their
own reverse, and say so on their pages.

insights.title: The same rule, nineteen times, earned between 1.5% and 9.1% a year
insights.body:
We rebuilt one strategy nineteen times. Nothing changed between them except a coin toss deciding which three lines of business to buy. The rule, the screen, the number of holdings, the monthly rhythm, the fees and the owner's deposits were identical in every one.

Over twenty years the luckiest version earned 9.1% a year on the money and the unluckiest earned 1.5%. The market itself earned 7.2%. Three of the nineteen beat the market and sixteen lost to it. The middle version earned 5.3%.

That is a seven and a half point spread with no difference in the idea at all, and it is the first time this lab has measured it. It matters because almost everything the lab does is a comparison: a new rule against a coin-toss version of itself, and a gap of two or three points read as evidence the rule works. A gap that size is smaller than what the coin produces on its own. Until now we had no way to know that.

The practical rule it gives: on a book of twenty holdings re-picked every month, ignore any lead under about two and a half points a year. It is not a small effect, it is no effect. And one coin-toss comparison is never enough to establish anything — nineteen is the smallest number that can support a one-in-twenty claim, which is the standard the rest of the lab is held to.

insights.title: A coin toss moved the worst fall by twenty points but the trading bill by almost nothing
insights.body:
Across those nineteen identical-rule books, the worst fall from a peak ranged from 49% to 70%, and the worst single year from a loss of 23% to a loss of 55%. The ratio of gains to losses ranged from 1.04 to 1.29. Nothing differed but the coin.

Meanwhile the number of trades varied by under 3% and the rate at which the portfolio turned itself over varied by 4%. So the cost of running the book is set by its shape and is entirely predictable, while every measure of how well it did is at the mercy of luck.

This corrects something the lab had come to believe: that when returns are too noisy to read, the worst fall and the gains-to-losses ratio can still be trusted. That was measured on books that step aside into cash when the market turns down. The safety rule caps every version's fall at about the same place, which is what made them look steady. Remove it and the fall swings as wildly as the return.

The risk this carries is direct. A strategy picked for having a shallower fall than its twin, where neither keeps a safety rule, may have been picked for nothing. Twenty points of worst fall is the difference between a book the owner could hold and one he could not, and the coin alone produced that much.

insights.title: A rule that is best of twenty in one stretch and near-worst in the other is a coin, not a discovery
insights.body:
The rule under test here looked genuinely good in one place. Over the years 2009 to 2015 it beat all nineteen of its coin-toss twins, on the ordinary data and again on the harder data that puts failed companies back in. It earned three points a year more than the market where the best coin toss earned under one, and the margin got bigger, not smaller, on the harder data. By every check this lab normally runs, that is a result.

Then we measured the same rule over the earlier stretch, 1996 to 2008, and it came seventeenth of twenty. Worse than sixteen coin tosses. Over the whole twenty years together it was fourth of twenty, which is ordinary.

First in one half, near-last in the other, ordinary overall. That is what a coin looks like when you flip it a hundred times and then go looking for a good streak. And we went looking: the 2009-2015 stretch was not picked in advance, it was picked because the earlier work had already noticed the rule looked good there.

The lesson is about the limits of a control. Nineteen coin tosses tell you whether a result could have come from luck in picking holdings. They tell you nothing about luck in picking the years. Whenever a result lives in one stretch of time, the honest next question is always the same and costs nothing: how does the same rule rank in the stretch nobody was looking at? If the answer is near the bottom, there is no discovery there.

insights.title: A book that picked its shares by coin toss passed every test we use to decide what is worth real money
insights.body:
We re-ran four of the lab's stock-picking rules beside a coin toss. The coin toss copied each rule exactly: the same screen of companies, the same twenty slots, the same monthly re-pick, the same safety switch that moves to cash when the market turns down, the same real trading fees on the same five million rupiah a month. The only thing it did differently was choose its twenty companies out of a hash instead of out of a ranking. It read no prices and knew nothing about any company.

One of those coin tosses passed everything. It earned 12.5 percent a year on the money actually paid in, against 7.2 percent for the same deposits put into the whole American market. It lost at most 31 percent from a peak. It made 5.17 of gains for every 1 of losses. And it scored 0.960 on our luck test, comfortably above the 0.90 we demand, after 193 separate attempts at finding a strategy.

Nothing about it is a strategy. It is a reminder of what the tests can and cannot see.

Two things let it through. The first is the safety switch every one of these books sits behind, which we have already measured at roughly 3.6 extra points a year through the long rise after 2009 - that belongs to the switch, not to whatever ranking sits on top of it. The second is the pool it drew from. The rule it was copying hunts for the most thinly traded big companies, so it has to switch off our usual rule that a company must trade at least twenty million dollars a day. The coin toss inherited that, and drew from a wider, better pool than an ordinary blind draw gets.

What to do about it. Nothing is being promoted - this arm is a coin toss and will never be put in front of real money, and our own promotion gate would refuse this method anyway because it won only two of its four out-of-sample periods. But the result says plainly that passing the screen is not the same as having an idea. Every strategy that passes should have to show, before anything else, that it beats a spread of coin tosses wearing its own clothes. And the luck test should be read for what it measures, which is how steady a stream of returns is - something a lucky coin toss can have as easily as a good idea.

insights.title: Twenty of our strategies rest on a comparison we now know can point the wrong way, and nine of them are on the shortlist
insights.body:
Most of our stock-picking rules are judged against a mirror: the same book buying the opposite companies. If the rule earns more than its mirror, that gap has been treated as proof the ranking knows something.

Last week one strategy showed the proof can be empty. It beat its mirror by a convincing margin, and then a coin toss of the same shape beat both of them. The gap was the mirror being bad, not the rule being good.

So we counted. The lab holds 35 of these mirror comparisons across 27 strategies. Twenty of those twenty-seven have no coin toss beside them at all, and nine of the twenty are on our dev shortlist - the ones closest to being tried on the one out-of-sample window we are allowed to spend, and after that on real money.

We bought the missing coin toss for four of them. On one, the long-term-losers book, the mirror said its ranking was worth nearly a point a year and the coin toss earned more than it on both sets of prices we have. That is the same failure again, on an unrelated idea from an unrelated paper, measured eight months earlier in the lab's history. It is not a one-off.

The good news is that the repair is cheap and mechanically sound. We cannot edit a strategy's file once its results are recorded, so the coin toss has to be registered as a new strategy - and that works: all six copies traded within seven percent of the book they were copying and moved money around at the same speed, which is what makes the comparison fair rather than rigged.

The bad news is that one or two coin tosses is not enough to settle anything. Beating one coin toss is a fifty-fifty result. Beating two is one in three. Our usual standard is one in twenty, which needs nineteen. So the sixteen strategies still unrepaired should be treated as unproven rather than wrong, and repaired one at a time with a proper spread of tosses rather than in batches of one.

insights.title: Our fairness checker told us six comparisons were fair when it had not checked any of them
insights.body:
We have a checker whose job is to confirm that a coin-toss comparison is fair - that the coin toss traded about as often as the strategy it is being compared with, and moved its money around about as fast. If it trades three times as often it pays three times the fees, and then beating it proves nothing.

When this method finished, the checker printed: no control arm to report, every one of them matches its book's shape. Every control arm matches the arm it controls on both axes.

It had checked none of them. It had correctly spotted that all six arms were coin tosses. What it could not do was work out which strategy each one was a copy of - because each one copies a strategy in a different file. And that is not an unusual case: it is the only case. A strategy's file is sealed the moment its results are recorded, so a missing coin toss can never be added to the strategy it belongs to. Every repair of this kind will arrive in a separate file, and the checker will ignore every one of them.

Unable to work out what to compare, it dropped all six rows, and its message for an empty table then said the opposite of the truth.

Here it happened not to matter: I checked all six by hand and they were well matched. The next one may not be, and will get the same green light.

Two things would fix it. Let a coin toss say in writing which strategy it is a copy of, instead of leaving the checker to guess from the name. And change the empty-table message so that having nothing to report reads as having nothing to report, not as an all-clear. The second is a one-line change and worth doing on its own.

insights.title: Holding the same amount of each company is worth 2.6 points a year, and it is not about being invested
insights.body:
For a year this lab assumed that owning the same dollar amount of each big American company, rather than owning more of the biggest, was a handicap. Last week a five-step dial said the opposite, but it could not prove it: the even-spread version happened to keep 97.5% of its money in the market and the biggest-companies version only 91.2%, and being invested is worth something by itself. The honest answer then was a range, somewhere between 1.6 and 2.7 points a year.

This run tied that down. The identical five steps were run with the account dragged back to its exact targets every month, so every step kept the same amount of money in the market: 98.83%, 98.86%, 98.88%, 98.90%, 98.91%. A spread of less than a tenth of a point, where before it was six and a half.

The gap between the two ends barely moved. It was 2.73 points a year when the amount invested slid with the dial, and 2.59 with the amount invested held still. Take each version's own trading costs out of both and they agree to four hundredths of a point a year. So the amount of money in the market was carrying none of it. A separate check agreed independently: the same biggest-companies book with only its drift rule changed gained seven and a half points of extra money invested and earned barely a tenth of a point a year more for it.

Put the failed and delisted companies back into the price history and the answer is unchanged: 2.6 points a year on both sets of prices, with every step losing a flat 1.35 points of level. The slope survives the honest tape even though the level does not, which is rare here. Most of this lab's survivorship checks change which version wins.

Why it matters. The lab has been measuring stock-picking rules against the whole market, and for a book that holds a few hundred index members in equal amounts the whole market is the wrong opponent. Some past rejections may really have been beat the market, lost to even spreading, and nobody has checked. What to do about it: treat the even-spread book as a second yardstick alongside the market, and stop spending method ids re-asking the weighting question. It has now been asked three times with the confusions stripped out one at a time, and answered the same way every time.

insights.title: The even-spread book pays late, when the money has arrived — almost nothing else here does
insights.body:
There are two ways to score a strategy. One asks what it did on paper. The other asks what the owner's money actually received, given that he pays in every month and most of his money has only been there for the later years. This lab has learned that the two usually disagree badly: most recorded results earned half their lead before half the money had arrived, and the typical result hands the owner only about a third of its paper lead.

The even-spread version of this book handed over 95.6% of its paper lead. That is in the top few percent of everything recorded here. The biggest-companies version handed over 33.2%, which is the ordinary outcome, and it was worse than that underneath: it earned more than its whole lead before 2003 and then gave a fifth of it back after 2009.

So the dial is not only a return ladder, it is a delivery ladder, and the two point the same way. This also explains something that looked odd: the gap between the two ends is 2.59 points a year in the money column but only 2.09 on paper. The even-spread advantage shows up late, which is exactly when the money is there.

Why it matters more than the headline. A strategy that earns its edge early and fades is close to useless to someone still paying in — the edge lands on a small account and the fade lands on a big one. A late-arriving edge is worth far more than the same number earned early, and almost nothing this lab has found has that shape. What to do about it: when two candidates look similar on paper, prefer the one that delivers more of its lead, and treat a delivery rate near a third as the warning sign it has turned out to be. The open question worth a method is what makes a lead late-arriving in the first place, because nobody here has gone looking for it.

insights.title: Forcing a wide account back to exact targets every month buys a hidden cost that grows with the spreading
insights.body:
To hold the amount of money invested still across five versions of a book, this run dragged the account back to its exact targets every month instead of letting holdings drift. That works — the amount invested came out identical to within a tenth of a point — but it is not free, and the bill is not flat.

The account holds between 137 and 392 companies. A full monthly reset sends one order per company per month, and the broker charges at least ten cents an order. Modelled over the twenty years, that costs the even-spread version 0.42 points a year and the biggest-companies version 0.15 — a slope of 0.27 points a year running against the result being measured, because an even-spread book has more drift to correct.

Before committing the method I estimated that slope at 0.03 points a year, by counting orders and noting the count is the same at every version. The estimate was wrong by a factor of nine, because the cost also scales with how much money moves and not only with how many orders there are. That is worth remembering: an order-count argument bounds the fixed part of a trading bill and says nothing about the rest.

The uncomfortable arithmetic is that the cost slope bought here is about twice the size of the confusion it removed. The trade was still worth making, because a trading bill can be computed from recorded turnover and a fee schedule fitted to the owner's own receipts, while an amount-invested effect tangled up with the thing being measured cannot be computed at all. But the honest description is that a contaminant that could not be measured was swapped for a larger one that can.

What to do about it. The all-or-nothing reset is a blunt instrument. A small allowed drift would almost certainly hold the amount invested nearly as still for a fraction of the trading cost, and the lab already has the setting — it has simply never been measured on a book this wide, only on a twenty-company one. Measuring that curve once would make every future amount-invested experiment on a wide book affordable, and it is cheap.

insights.title: Our fairness checker told us six comparisons were fair when it had not checked any of them
insights.body:
This replaces the note of the same title written an hour earlier. That note was right about what happened and wrong about how narrow the problem is, and the difference matters.

We have a checker whose job is to confirm that a coin-toss comparison is fair - that the coin toss traded about as often as the strategy it is being compared with, and moved its money around about as fast. If it trades three times as often it pays three times the fees, and then beating it proves nothing.

This method registered six coin tosses. The checker spotted all six as coin tosses. What it could not do was work out which strategy each one was a copy of, because each copies a strategy in a different file. That is not an unusual case: it is the only case. A strategy's file is sealed the moment its results are recorded, so a missing coin toss can never be added to the strategy it belongs to. Every repair of this kind arrives in a separate file.

The earlier note said the false all-clear came from the message the checker prints when it has an empty table. It does, at the end of a run. But the standalone report does it too, and that is worse: it prints all six rows, marks every one of them unable to tell, and then signs off underneath with every control arm shown matches the shape of the arm it controls. The table in front of the reader says it does not know, and the sentence under the table says everything is fine.

Here it happened not to matter - I checked all six by hand and they were well matched, within seven percent on both measures. The next one may not be, and will get the same green light twice.

Three fixes, smallest first. Make both sign-off sentences count only the comparisons that were actually made, so nothing to report reads as nothing to report. Let a coin toss state in writing which strategy it is a copy of, instead of leaving the checker to guess from its name. And let the checker look up that strategy's recorded results even when they live under a different method, which is the only thing standing between it and reading every retrofit we will ever do.

One related oddity worth recording: a different report, the out-of-sample one, already prints the word control next to this method's best arm. So one tool knows what these arms are and the one whose job it is does not.

insights.title: The illiquidity premium among large companies: hold the S&P names that trade thinnest for their size: what its market safety rule was worth
insights.body:
Most of the methods this lab still holds stop buying whenever the market is below its own long-term average, and they all read that same rule on the same dates. The lab took the 5 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, once as it stands and once with that one rule switched off and nothing else changed. The numbers below are for its best version.

- As it stands it earned +12.5% a year against the market's +7.2%; with the rule off, +12.9%.
- Its worst fall was 25.8% with the rule and 64.4% without it.
- With the rule it held nothing at all on 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold; without it, 0.0%.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +5.3% a year against the market as it stands, +5.7% with the rule off.
- 1996-2002: −0.2% a year against the market as it stands, +3.7% with the rule off.
- 2003-2008: +12.9% a year against the market as it stands, +4.2% with the rule off.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as it stands, −10.4% with the rule off.
- 2009-2015: −1.1% a year against the market as it stands, +9.3% with the rule off.

Over the whole history the safety rule was worth +0.6% a year on average across this method's versions. In the 2008 crash alone it was worth +42.1%. From 2009 to the end of the history it cost +9.0% a year.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A book that picked its shares by coin toss passed every test we use to decide what is worth real money
insights.body:
This replaces the note of the same title written earlier today. The result is unchanged; one of the two explanations in it was borrowed from another book and is wrong, and the corrected version is more worrying rather than less.

We re-ran four of the lab's stock-picking rules beside a coin toss. The coin toss copied each rule exactly: the same screen of companies, the same twenty slots, the same monthly re-pick, the same safety switch that moves to cash when the market turns down, the same real trading fees on the same five million rupiah a month. The only difference was that it chose its twenty companies out of a hash instead of out of a ranking. It read no prices and knew nothing about any company.

One of those coin tosses passed everything. It earned 12.5 percent a year on the money actually paid in, against 7.2 percent for the same deposits put into the whole American market. It lost at most 31 percent from a peak. It made 5.17 of gains for every 1 of losses. And it scored 0.960 on our luck test, above the 0.90 we demand, after 193 separate attempts at finding a strategy.

The earlier note said the safety switch handed it about 3.6 extra points a year. That figure belongs to a different book and we had already recorded that it is not a fixed number. Measured here, on these books, the switch was worth between half a point and one and a half points a year. What it really bought was the fall: the same pool of companies, always invested, earns about the same money and loses 67 percent at its worst. Behind the switch it loses 26 percent.

That is the whole trick, and it is worth saying plainly. Our go-live test judges a strategy by its earnings divided by its worst fall. A switch that turns a 67 percent fall into a 31 percent one more than doubles that score without the book knowing a single thing about a single company. The other ingredient was the pool: the rule being copied hunts the most thinly traded big companies, so it has to switch off our usual requirement that a company trade at least twenty million dollars a day, and the coin toss inherited a wider and better pool than an ordinary blind draw gets.

Nothing is being promoted. This arm is a coin toss and will never be put in front of real money, and our own promotion gate would refuse this method anyway because it won only two of its four out-of-sample periods. But passing the screen is not the same as having an idea. Every strategy that passes should have to show, before anything else, that it beats a spread of coin tosses wearing its own clothes - and the luck test should be read for what it measures, which is how steady a stream of returns is, something a lucky coin toss has as easily as a good idea.
