insights.title: Sera 20261023-1305: the lab measured itself, and a coin toss passed every test it has
insights.body:
No buy signal, and this batch could not have produced one: it ran no strategies at all. All four
methods were instruments -- things built to measure how well the lab measures. The owner chose that
over another round of ideas, and it was the right call, because three of the four found something
the lab had been getting wrong.

THE NUMBER THE LAB NEVER HAD

Take one rule. Keep everything about it identical -- the same code, the same twenty names a month,
the same two decades -- and change only the coin it uses to break ties. Do that nineteen times.

The answers range from 1.5% a year to 9.1%. The worst falls range from 49% to 70%.

That is the spread of pure luck on a book of this kind, and the lab has never known it. Seven and a
half points a year, and twenty points of fall, between rules that are the same rule. Almost every
margin this lab has ever reported on a book without a market switch is smaller than that, including
the ones behind all four of the counted looks we have spent.

The cost side behaves completely differently: the number of trades varies by under 3% and the
turnover by 4%. So a comparison about fees or churn between two versions is readable, and a
comparison about return or drawdown is not. That distinction is new and it is usable immediately.

It also corrects something we had been carrying: that worst falls were steady across coin tosses.
They are -- but only for books that step aside in a downturn, where the safety switch caps every
version's fall in the same months. Without the switch, the fall is as noisy as the return.

And one piece of arithmetic worth more than any of it. If a rule is no better than chance, then
beating all of its random comparisons has a one-in-(k plus one) chance of happening anyway. One
comparison therefore proves nothing at all -- it is a coin flip. Six gets you to one in seven.
Nineteen gets you to one in twenty, which is the standard everything else here is held to. And
adding more comparisons after a good-looking result is the one move that cannot be cheating,
because more of them only makes "better than all" harder.

THE SHELF, SWEPT

So we swept the shelf. Thirty-five rule-and-reverse pairs exist across twenty-seven strategies.
Twenty of those twenty-seven have no random comparison at all, and nine of the twenty have passed
our paper screen. Their evidence is a gap against their own opposite, and we now know that gap is
positive whenever both sides are merely unevenly bad.

Four were repaired as a trial. One held up, one reversed outright -- a book built on a published
finding about long-term losers turned out to lose to its own random twin -- and two were
unreadable. None of those four readings is established on its own, because one or two comparisons
each is still a coin flip; what was bought was coverage, not proof.

But the sweep turned up something that needs no error bar at all. One of the random comparisons --
a book that picks its twenty stocks out of a hash, with no idea in it whatsoever -- passed every
condition the lab has, including the luck test, at 12.5% a year against the market's 7.2%. And the
same random rule, run again with a different coin, scored 9.7% and failed. One pass, one fail, same
rule. That is the seven-and-a-half-point spread arriving as a verdict instead of a number.

The cause is the scoring, and it is measurable on the real book this coin toss was copied from.
That book's safety switch COSTS it about half a point a year of return -- it leads the market by
5.3% with the switch and 5.7% without -- while cutting its worst fall from 64% to 26%. Our headline
score is return divided by fall, so a switch that adds nothing to the return more than doubles the
score anyway. Any book wearing that switch inherits the flattery, idea or no idea. The coin toss
also draws from a wider pool than the lab's other books, which is the second ingredient.

TWO THINGS CORRECTED, AND ONE OF THEM TWICE

The volume-floor finding from last batch had concluded, reading the honest price history, that one
of its middle settings was the better book to own and the only one still earning after 2009.
Neither survived. Its bar refused a share of each day's candidates, and the honest history prices
989 companies against the everyday one's 539 -- so a rule that drops a fixed PROPORTION quietly
keeps far more names on the bigger list than on the smaller one. It was never the same filter on the two histories. Asked again with a fixed number of
names, the no-filter book is best and every setting trails after 2009. What survives -- and is now
stronger -- is the honesty measurement itself, which came back at 3.4 points a year against 3.5 and
3.9 on two other books, in a straight line for the first time.

The weighting question moved twice. Last batch reported that spreading money evenly rather than by
company size was worth 2.8 points a year. I withdrew that, because the two ends of the dial were
not holding the same amount of money in the market and up to a point of it might have been that.
This batch pinned every setting to the same amount invested -- a spread of eight hundredths of a
point where it had been six -- and the answer barely moved. The original 2.8 was right. My
withdrawal was a fair bound on what was then known and its conclusion was wrong, and both records
say so.

WHAT WOULD UNLOCK THE MOST

The same error bar, measured again for books that DO step aside. Everything above was measured
without a safety switch, and the switch is in almost every strategy we own. Early hints put that
spread nearer two points than seven, which would mean gated results are three times more readable
than ungated ones -- but that is a hint, not a measurement.

And a reporting fix that matters more than it sounds. Twice in a week, the arm our own code picks
as a method's best version has been a random control rather than the idea. A reader of the site
sees a coin toss presented as the result.

THE GATE, AND FEES

Nothing was promoted, nothing was refused that should not have been, and no counted look was spent.
Four remain used of the budget, unchanged all batch.

Fees decided nothing, but one run paid an honest price worth recording: pinning the weighting dial
required trading every holding back to its target every month, which cost about a quarter of a
point a year -- roughly twice the contamination it removed. The run said so rather than hiding it,
on the grounds that a fee is computable from the trading record while the thing it replaced was
not.

NEXT

The gated error bar. The reporting fix, so the site stops showing coin tosses as results. Then the
remaining sixteen strategies whose only evidence is a gap against their own reverse.

insights.title: Can a calm filter replace the cash rule instead of sitting behind it?: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +11.4% on the usual history, +9.2% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 43.9% and 47.4%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −0.4% a year before and −4.6% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen moved from 3 of 4 periods won to 2 of 4 periods won.

The missing companies flattered it: with them added it earns 2.1 points a year less. 2 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: A safety switch lowers the fall but does not steady it
insights.body: Nearly every promising strategy here keeps one safety rule: step out of the market when it is below its long-term average. We built nineteen versions of the same twenty-stock book that differed only by a coin toss deciding which industries to buy, ran them with the safety rule on, and compared them with nineteen identical coin tosses run with it off. The safety rule made every version fall about thirty points less deep from its peak, and not one of the nineteen pairs went the other way. It did not make the versions any more alike: the gap between the luckiest and unluckiest fall was 22.9 points with the rule on and 20.7 points with it off. The reason is that the rule protects against the one big shared crash, and once that is handled each version's deepest fall is its own private accident of which stocks the coin happened to hand it. The practical consequence is blunt. The owner's rule says a strategy may not fall more than a quarter from its peak, and among these nineteen identical books with no idea in them at all, ten passed that test and nine failed. Nothing separated them but luck. So a difference in worst fall between two of our safety-switched strategies is not evidence of anything unless it is very large, and we should stop reading small safety differences as skill. The one meter the switch really does steady is the worst single calendar year, which it compresses hard by taking every version out of the 2008 crash.

insights.title: A handful of control runs understates luck by a third to a half
insights.body: When we want to know whether a strategy really beat chance, we build control versions of it that contain no idea at all and see how far apart they land. That distance is our error bar. The trouble is that the more controls you build, the further apart the best and worst are bound to be, so a small set of controls always makes luck look smaller than it really is. This time we measured the effect instead of assuming it. On the same family of books, the first seven controls said luck was worth 2.44 points a year of return; all nineteen said 5.14 — the short set understated it by 52 percent. On the worst fall the short set understated by 32 percent, on the worst single year by 29 percent, and on gains versus losses by 57 percent. The bias always runs the same way, and it is the way that makes a result look more impressive than it is. Any claim in our records that rests on beating one or two control runs is weaker than it reads, and an error bar built from fewer than about fifteen controls should be treated as a floor rather than a measurement.

insights.title: The lab's ruler for luck was two to three times too long
insights.body:
Last week the lab learned how much money pure luck is worth. It ran nineteen copies of one
stock-picking rule with every opinion stripped out, so the copies differed only in a coin toss, and
they earned anywhere from 1.5% to 9.1% a year on the same deposits. That spread, seven and a half
points a year, became the lab's first honest error bar.

But all nineteen of those copies were always invested. Almost every method the lab actually records
keeps a safety rule that moves the book to cash when the market is weak, and almost every "our idea
beat its control" claim in the record compares two books that both keep it.

This run measured seven of those same coin tosses again with the safety rule switched on, and the
comparison has to be made carefully, because a range grows simply by having more copies in it.
Measured over the matched seven, the always-invested spread is six points a year and the
switched-on spread is two and a half: the safety rule alone cuts the noise by a factor of about two
and a half. The seven-and-a-half figure is the wider nineteen-copy measurement, and part of the gap
between seven and a half and two and a half is just the extra copies rather than the safety rule.

Either way the lab owned a ruler too long for most of what it was measuring — somewhere between two
and a half and three times too long. That error runs in the expensive direction: too long a ruler
quietly discards findings that were real, by calling them luck. Re-checking the full history on the fuller price data that includes companies which later
died, the shorter ruler holds up almost exactly, so this is not an artefact of missing data. Every
comparison the lab makes between two safety-switched books should be read against roughly two and a
half points a year, and anything smaller than about one and a quarter points is simply noise.

insights.title: A safety switch makes the fall shallower without making it more predictable
insights.body:
The rule that moves a book into cash when the market is weak does what it promises to the size of a
loss. Across seven matched pairs of otherwise identical books, it cut the worst fall from about 57%
to about 27%, every single time, and it raised the yearly return in all seven as well, by 1.4
points on average.

What it does not do is make the fall more predictable, and this was the opposite of what was
expected. Seven always-invested copies, differing only in luck, spanned 14.4 points of worst fall.
The same seven with the switch on spanned 15.6 points — very slightly wider. The switch shrinks how
far you fall without shrinking how much that varies from one run of luck to the next. Measured
against the number being compared, the switched-on fall is far noisier: a scatter of 15.6 points
around an average of 27% is well over half the figure itself, where without the switch it was about
a quarter.

The practical consequence is immediate and free. When one book is said to be safer than another by
a few points of worst fall, and both keep a safety switch, that claim is almost certainly luck. Two
books running the same rule and differing in nothing but which names the coin picked fell 20.8% and
36.4%. The lab should stop treating small differences in worst fall as evidence of anything.

insights.title: No method has ever run enough comparisons to meet the lab's own standard for luck
insights.body:
This is arithmetic rather than a measurement, which is why it needs no error bar and admits no
argument. If an idea is worthless, it is interchangeable with a control built to have no opinion.
So the strongest claim that beating every one of a group of controls can support is one chance in
the group size plus one. Beat one control and the best you can say is one-in-two. Beat six and it
is one-in-seven. Reaching the one-in-twenty standard the lab applies to everything else takes
nineteen controls.

Counting every method the lab has ever run: close to two hundred have a recorded result, and all
but about a dozen of them used six arms or fewer in total. Even pretending that every arm but one
was a control, which is far more generous than the truth, the strongest claim almost the entire lab
could support is about one-in-six. Not one method has ever run the twenty arms a one-in-twenty
claim needs. The widest ever built had eighteen, and that was the method whose arms were all
controls by design. These counts climb every week; the shortfall does not, because nothing in how
the lab builds an experiment has changed.

So the lab holds its ideas to a one-in-twenty standard on luck while never once building a
comparison capable of reaching it. This is not a flaw in any single method; it is the shape of the
experiments. The remedy is cheap and belongs in the next experiment rather than in re-reading old
ones: adding four or five opinion-free arms beside an idea costs no extra method and turns a result
that cannot be read into one that can.

insights.title: The ruler behind the safety rule is five points a year, not two and a half
insights.body:
The note this replaces got the direction right and the number wrong, and the number is the part the lab will use every day.

It said that behind the safety rule — the rule that moves the book to cash when the market is weak — pure luck is worth about two and a half points a year, so a gap smaller than about one and a quarter points is noise. That figure came from seven copies of one opinion-free book. Nineteen copies of the same switched-on book have now been run, and they earned between 4.4% and 9.5% a year on the same deposits: a spread of five points a year, not two and a half.

Seven copies is simply not enough to see how wide a spread is. A range grows as you add copies to it, and the companion note on short control populations measured exactly how much: the first seven of these very copies understated the nineteen-copy spread by about half on the money and by a third on the worst fall, and that understatement always flatters. So the earlier figure was not a measurement of the safety rule. It was a measurement of having run seven.

Compared like with like — nineteen switched-on copies against nineteen always-invested ones — the safety rule narrows the money spread to about two-thirds of the always-invested spread, not to a quarter of it. And two-thirds is almost exactly what you would expect from the rule simply being out of the market part of the time, with no steadying hand at all. The narrowing is the absence, not judgement.

The practical correction, and it runs the opposite way to what the earlier note said. Read any comparison between two switched-on books against about five points a year, and treat anything smaller than about two and a half points as noise. The earlier, shorter ruler erred on the generous side: it would have let luck pass as a finding, on a lab record where most recorded gaps are already smaller than the coin.

insights.title: Is the illiquidity book buying an anomaly or buying bad data? Put the volume floor back one rung at a time, on both tapes: what the missing companies did to it
insights.body:
The lab re-ran the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested, over the same 1996–2015 history, twice: once on the usual price history, and once on a check history that adds back most of the companies the usual one is missing -- companies that left the index by failing, being bought out or changing their name. Same rules, the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups. The numbers below are for its best version.

- Return a year: +12.7% on the usual history, +22.3% with the missing companies added (SPY: +7.2% and +7.2%).
- Worst fall from a peak: 26.4% and 28.1%.
- In 2009–2015, the years the usual history covers best, its lead over SPY was −1.7% a year before and −0.9% after.

The check that picks a version on earlier years and then judges it on later years it had not seen did not change: 2 of 4 periods won on both histories.

The missing companies did not flatter it: with them added it earns 9.5 points a year more. 5 of its 6 version(s) earn less a year with them added.

This was a check, not a new try: the lab's count of tries did not move and no verdict changed.

insights.title: We may have been calling safety filters useless at a strength too weak to see them
insights.body:
We may have been calling safety filters useless at a strength too weak to see them.

Earlier today we tested an idea: before picking stocks, throw away the jumpiest companies on the list. We tried it by throwing away the jumpiest quarter. It fell 56.4% at its worst, and four coin-toss versions that threw away the same number of names at random fell 55.2%, 56.5%, 56.8% and 59.4%. The real filter sat inside the coins' range and one of them beat it. We wrote down that it bought nothing a random reshuffle did not, and on that evidence we were right.

A few hours later we turned the same dial two and a half times further and ran the coins again at the new strength. Throwing away the jumpiest three fifths, the real filter fell 41.0% while its four coin tosses fell 53.7%, 59.9%, 60.5% and 63.2%. It beat the best of the four by 12.6 points, where the coins differ from each other by only 9.6. With the companies that went bust put back into the price history it still beat the best coin, by 7.4 points.

Same idea, same book, same kind of control. At one strength it is indistinguishable from luck; at two and a half times that strength it clearly is not.

Why it matters: testing something gently is not a safer way to test it. A test too weak to show an effect comes back saying there is nothing there -- which reads exactly like a test that looked properly and correctly found nothing. The two are indistinguishable from the outside, and we have been treating them as the same answer. Any filter we have tried once, at one mild setting, against a single coin toss is a candidate for re-reading on those grounds. We have not counted how many that is, and our records have no field that answers it, so this is a direction to check rather than a number to quote.

How sure are we? Not as sure as the headline sounds, and the level is worth stating. If an idea were worthless it would be interchangeable with a coin toss, so coming first out of four coins and the real thing can never support better than a one-in-five chance that we are fooling ourselves -- short of the one-in-twenty we ask of everything else, which would take nineteen coins. Finishing a long way ahead does not improve those odds: how far ahead it finished tells us how big the effect is, not how likely it is to be luck. On that score the two sets of prices disagree -- on our ordinary history the filter finished further ahead of the best coin than the four coins are spread apart from each other, and with the bust companies restored it still finished ahead of all four, but by less than that spread. Enough to overturn the earlier verdict, not enough to call it settled.

What to do about it: when a filter is tested, test it at a strength where it must either show itself or admit it cannot, and put four coin tosses at that strength rather than one. We have queued the first re-read on those terms. None of this rescues the filter itself -- it fell behind the market in the years that matter most -- the point is only that we nearly filed a real effect under luck.

insights.title: The companies that hold up in a crash are the ones that get left behind afterwards
insights.body:
The companies that hold up in a crash are the ones that get left behind afterwards, and we can now put a price on it.

We ran a book with no safety switch at all and protected it instead by refusing to buy the jumpiest companies. It worked as protection: the worst fall went from 62.1% to 41.0%, and it came first of five against four random name-dropping versions of itself, finishing further ahead than those four are spread apart on our ordinary history. With only four to compare against, coming first supports at best a one-in-five chance of being fooled -- enough to take seriously, not enough to call settled.

Then we looked at 2009 to 2015 -- our best-covered stretch of history and the one most like today. Measured on the book alone, with the monthly deposits set aside, the two versions that filtered on jumpiness both made money there: they grew at 16.2% and 12.6% a year on our ordinary price history. The market grew at 16.6%. So they fell behind it, by 0.4 and 4.0 points a year, and by 4.6 and 3.5 points with the companies that went bust restored. Not one of the four random versions fell behind the market. Three beat the market clearly, by 3.0 to 6.6 points on the ordinary history and 4.8 to 9.2 points with the bust companies back, and the fourth was level on the first and ahead on the second. There are sixteen ways to pair a random version against a filtered one on the same history, and the random version won all sixteen, by between half a point and 13.7 points a year.

There is a second tell in the same run, this one measured on the owner's actual deposits rather than the book alone. When we restore the companies that went bust, the two calm versions earn less per year than before and all four random versions earn more. The versions that got worse are precisely the two with an opinion in them.

Why it matters: this is not a flaw in the filter, it is the filter working. Calmness in a falling market and participation in a rising one are the same property with the sign flipped, and a six-year rise is far more common than a crash. Any rule that promises to protect you by choosing steadier companies is also promising to lag the next long bull market, and should be priced that way before it is adopted.

What to do about it: judge a protective filter on the quiet years, not the crash. Ours bought real protection, and the book it picked still grew more slowly than the market over the stretch of history that looks most like the present, which is why we are not keeping it.

insights.title: A number the lab has been reading for weeks turns out to have no error bar
insights.body: The lab keeps a second price history that adds back most of the companies the everyday one is missing, nearly all of which went bankrupt or were bought. Re-running a strategy on both is free, and the change in its worst fall between the two has been quoted as meaningful evidence. It is not. The lab had already recorded four versions of one strategy that are identical in every way except the seed of a hash that picks which quarter of the candidates to ignore — four rules with no opinion in them at all. Their changes in worst fall come out at minus 2.3, plus 2.7, plus 3.9 and plus 5.4 points. Four meaningless rules spread over 7.7 points. The ladder this measurement was famous for — ignore the calmest quarter, ignore nothing, ignore the jumpiest quarter — reads plus 3.1, plus 1.5 and plus 0.7, a span of 2.4 points sitting entirely inside that 7.7. A fresh pair of no-opinion versions built for this test landed 3.8 points apart. Two other pieces of work settled this month found that the cash switch makes a book fall far less deep without making its versions any more alike, and that the worst fall is the meter it steadies least; this is the next step from that, because the difference of an unstable meter between two histories inherits the noise of both readings. What to do about it: never read a single strategy's change between the two histories again without running several random versions of the same shape beside it, and re-read the handful of places where such a gap has already been cited as evidence that a rule is safe.

insights.title: Looking better once the dead companies come back is common, not a badge of safety
insights.body: The belief that prompted this work was that only two rules in the lab's whole history had ever looked better once the missing bankrupt and bought-out companies were added back. That belief was wrong, and the evidence was already on disk. Across the 78 strategy versions the lab has recorded on both price histories using the owner's real monthly deposits, 22 earned more a year with the dead companies added and 23 fell less from their peak. Only 3 managed both at once. So roughly three in ten look better on one meter or the other — close to a coin flip, not a rare event needing an explanation. What to do about it: stop treating one strategy reading better as a signature of anything, and when a claim rests on it, ask first how many of the lab's other strategies do the same by chance.

insights.title: Throwing out a lot of jumpy companies may be the one rule that gains when the dead return
insights.body: Almost everything the lab tries looks worse once the missing companies are added back, because those companies are the disasters. Within one strategy measured carefully — twelve versions of the same book on both histories, four of them random comparison versions that between them span 7.7 points and so set the error bar — exactly two versions beat that noise on the worst fall and also earned more a year. Both throw out a lot of jumpy companies: one discards the jumpiest quarter by how much the price wobbles, improving the worst fall by 7.1 points from 28.2 per cent to 21.1 and adding 0.6 points a year; the other discards the jumpiest half by how hard the stock swings with the market, improving the fall by 5.6 points and adding 0.7 points a year. Gentler versions of the same idea gained nothing readable, and with the cash rule switched off a third jumpiness version also beat the noise on the fall, though it lost ground on return. The likely reason is the plainest one: the companies the everyday history is missing got violent before they died, so a rule that throws out violent companies has already thrown out most of them. What a rule physically removes is what matters, not what it was designed for. Two honest warnings. Those are two different measures of jumpiness at two different strengths, so this is not yet a clean strength ladder. And across the whole lab three other versions also improved on both meters, and they are an earnings-jump book, a long-term-loser book and a dividend-raise book, none of them a jumpiness screen. So this is a promising guess, not a finding. Worth testing as one measure at three strengths with random comparison versions at each strength.

insights.title: For almost every strategy we own, one key question cannot be answered at all
insights.body: When one version of a rule is run against its own mirror image, the lab can measure what the opinion is worth, but it needs a third version — one that is always invested and never steps aside — to measure what the arrangement itself costs in fees and time out of the market. The tool that does this demands the third version be invested essentially all the time. Only 11 of the lab's 1,070 recorded runs on its main search window clear that bar, and all eleven hold index funds rather than individual shares. Any strategy that moves to cash when the market turns can never supply a qualifying comparison, and that is nearly everything we own: 685 of those 1,070 runs sit between half and four fifths invested, which is exactly what stepping aside looks like. So for the large majority of the lab the question is unanswerable by construction, yet the tool reports it as the author's omission rather than as its own limit. It should either accept a same-shape random version as the comparison, or say plainly that the cost cannot be priced for a strategy that goes to cash.

insights.title: Is the illiquidity book buying an anomaly or buying bad data? Put the volume floor back one rung at a time, on both tapes: what its market safety rule was worth
insights.body:
Most of the methods this lab still holds stop buying whenever the market is below its own long-term average, and they all read that same rule on the same dates. The lab took the 6 version(s) of this method it had already tested and ran each of them again over the same 1996-2015 history, with the same starting money and the same monthly top-ups, once as it stands and once with that one rule switched off and nothing else changed. The numbers below are for its best version.

- As it stands it earned +12.7% a year against the market's +7.2%; with the rule off, +12.1%.
- Its worst fall was 26.4% with the rule and 67.5% without it.
- With the rule it held nothing at all on 28.3% of the days it chose what to hold; without it, 0.0%.

Period by period, ahead of or behind the market:

- whole window: +5.6% a year against the market as it stands, +4.9% with the rule off.
- 1996-2002: +1.4% a year against the market as it stands, +4.0% with the rule off.
- 2003-2008: +14.0% a year against the market as it stands, +4.3% with the rule off.
- 2008: +34.8% a year against the market as it stands, −13.0% with the rule off.
- 2009-2015: −1.7% a year against the market as it stands, +8.2% with the rule off.

Over the whole history the safety rule was worth +2.2% a year on average across this method's versions. In the 2008 crash alone it was worth +45.0%. From 2009 to the end of the history it cost +6.0% a year.

This was a measurement, not a new try: nothing was recorded, the lab's count of tries did not move, and no verdict changed.

insights.title: Our honesty check has errors of its own
insights.body: We keep a second copy of market history that puts back the companies that went bust or were bought, and we use it to ask whether a strategy's edge was real or just an artefact of the companies missing from our normal history. This run found that the second copy has a problem of its own. It adds 450 companies our normal history does not have at all. Thirty-nine of those produce at least one day where the share price rose by more than half in a single session, 98 such days between them; on eight of those days, across six companies, the price more than doubled. The worst is a company that goes from 57 cents to 28 dollars in one day, a rise of 4,802%, with 19 outsized days in its record. The store's own record of share splits lists exactly one split for that company, in March 2007, and nothing near February 2004 — so the 49-fold jump is not a split being handled correctly. No share rose 49-fold in a single session, and no strategy earned that money. The thin-stock book, which buys the least-traded shares, walks straight into these names: on the honest history it earned 22.3% a year against 12.7% on the normal one, and it passed our luck test at 0.996. Put a liveness filter in front of it that keeps only actively traded names and the whole 9.5-point advantage turns into a 3.9-point deficit at the very first notch. One thing this is not: the single most absurd price in the store, a company quoted at millions of dollars a share, sits in both copies identically, so the problem is specific to the reconstructed additions rather than the tape in general. It matters beyond one strategy, because every honest-history reading the lab has taken was taken on some build of this same reconstructed tape. The fix is a sanity filter: flag any price series that makes single-day moves no real share makes, and re-check which of our past honest-history conclusions move when those series are left out.

insights.title: A liveness filter hands you a churn bill before it hands you any safety
insights.body: Filtering a book down to the most actively traded names sounds free - you are not changing what the strategy looks for, only which shares it is allowed to consider. It is not free. The thin-stock book makes 365 trades in twenty years with no filter. Keep only the 250 busiest names and it makes 1,001. Keep only the 150 busiest and it makes 1,504, its busiest setting and more than four times the original. Across the five settings tried, the filter multiplied the trading by between 2.7 and 4.1 times. Nothing about the strategy changed. Shares drift across the cut-off from one month to the next, and the book has to follow them in and out. Anyone adding a filter like this should price the extra trading first, because at real dealing fees several times the trading is a real bill - and in this case the filter bought no safety either: on our normal history the worst fall got deeper at four of the five settings.

insights.title: A safety switch can erase a bad year without making results any more alike
insights.body: A trading rule that steps out of the market during long slumps and steps back in once things recover was tested on a very diversified version of a twenty-stock book — the same twenty stocks, just spread thinner across more industries than before. Spreading the stocks out did not change the answer a related experiment already found: the safety rule reliably turns a bad year into a much smaller one (the worst drop shrank by about 29 percentage points on average), but it does nothing to make different versions of the book agree on how deep that smaller drop goes. Three versions that differed only by chance, all protected by the same safety rule, still spread out across a 7-point range on their worst fall — almost exactly as wide a range as three unprotected versions had. The safety rule reliably helps, but a small gap in how deep two protected strategies fell still cannot be trusted as a real difference, no matter how the book's holdings are spread across industries.

insights.title: Two experiments running at once briefly erased one of their own results
insights.body: This lab sometimes runs several strategy tests at the same time, each saving its results to the same shared record. While two tests were running together, one test's six saved results disappeared from the shared record a few moments after being confirmed saved, and a different test's six results took their exact place in the record instead — with nothing telling either test that anything had gone wrong; both reported success. Exactly how this happened is unclear: the record is built so a saved result cannot normally be changed or removed, so the loss likely happened around that protection rather than through it. The mistake was only caught because the numbers were checked directly against the saved record instead of being trusted from the test's own report, and re-running the test a second time produced the exact same numbers, which were then confirmed still saved. Until this is fixed, any number that comes out of a period when more than one test is running at once should be treated as unconfirmed until it has been checked a second time.
